This was more of an inspirational novel than a mystery. And whatever mystery there was, I kind of figured out. Narrated by 13 year old Frank, it is set in 1961 and opens with a murder of a youg boy along the railroad tracks. This turns out to be a red herring. Frank's father is a minister, and the sprituality is found from Frank and his younger brother Jake's discoveries of "ordinary grace". It is a pleasant enough book to pass the time, but I expected something more.

I LOVED Jurassic Park. But it's not getting 5 stars for me because of REASONS. If you like science and if you like dinossaurs, this is your book! I think Crichton bring in to it the best of both to make an amazing tale of how humans can be stupid and yet you do not care because of how mesmerized you are by all this scientific greatness (yet, this not being real.) It is slower than the movie - regarding the action, but still manage to put you on the edge of your sit in some moments. It's very witty, very funny, very thrilling and I found it to be very smart (especially Malcolm, and not the math moments).
A satisfying sequel. I liked that the ending was left open for a third installment, one I'm seriously hoping for because the whole Hybrid attack and alien probe stuff was left unresolved.

This book had an interesting premises. In my honest opinion, this book had a lot of potential and I was incredibly excited to read it. I don't know how popular mermaids are right now when it comes to the YA readers out there but I've always had an interest in them. Imagine my disappointed when I got something not what I was expecting at all. There were a few good points in the story itself, which is probably what kept me hooked into this story and helped me finish it in the first place, but they were still far and few in between. The rest was just horrible. The story is about a merman (but don't call him, or anyone of his kind, that! That's considered rude to them. Call them Syrena instead...) who is in search of the person who can talk to fishes in the ocean. I mean, I'm not quite sure how they couldn't have figured that out sooner or when someone even noticed that something was up with the sea life but eh. With that being said, however, Syrena don't really like interacting with other humans so to tell Galen that he has to be sent off to find a human even though he doesn't like humans is a bit of an inconsistency. But hey, that's okay, it's just one out of many weird things going on that don't really get explained all that well. But he isn't convinced that she- being Emma- can talk to the sea animals anyways. As if getting the sensation of being 'shocked' didn't help him out since that's- according to the book- how Syrena know they found their mate. But it takes a little shark incident and the loss of Emma's friend, Chloe (which I despised because not only did I like that character a lot, it was a way to show Galen that she can INDEED talk to fish. SURELY there could have been a better way to show that she can talk to fish than a needless death, come on...), for him to realize that she is of Poseidon (see what that title did there? Immediate stalker time. Galen immediately moves over to where Emma lives. And talks to her. And convinces her that, after a short time, to tell Emma her mother that they are dating because it would be incredibly weird if they hung out a lot if they weren't dating. I'm sure just saying that you two are just friends who wanted to hang out a lot and get to know each other would've been just fine. They pretend to be in a relationship for a majority of the book until Galen actually kisses her in a 'I actually really like you' sort of way thinking 'We're actually dating even though we really shouldn't and you should be dating Grom  but what the hell- lets do this' and afterwards Emma is like, 'oh hey, that was a good kiss, you almost fooled me for a second. You fooled mom for sure.' But it slowly becomes clear that he falls in love with Emma. Emma, however, not so much. In fact, I'm surprised that she decides to date him after finding out that she didn't have to mate with Grom BUT that overturns when we find out his to-be mate ISN'T OF POSEIDON so wow, total waste of time???? YEAH . I'm also surprised when he tried to get her back DURING her date with her current boyfriend and gets irritated when Emma's boyfriend touches her leg and kisses her. EVEN THOUGH HE'S HER BOYFRIEND. He even drags her away from him. I wouldn't have left with him. No matter what message he was trying to send, I would've told him to tell me later. As in, next day, or... never. Not someone I would've wanted to date. This isn't one of the worst parts when it comes to who was dating who. Rayna spent most of her time irritated because she was actually married off to a Syrena- her childhood best friend, I should add... someone who knew she never wanted to marry him- without her even knowing. It happened and she was never even present for the ceremony at all. She should have annulled the marriage when she had the chance but, oh, the King finds Rayna too annoying so he was happy that there's someone else who can deal with her now so of course he's not going to turn the marriage now. Ha hah... hah... But, even better: after seeing him kiss a girl, she immediately flips and decides... HEY. I actually love this asshole. Let's go mate! It made everything Emma said about Rayna having her own mind and how she should choose who she should date... pointless. In fact, it never comes up again. Emma doesn't mentioned it again. In fact, when Emma talks about Grom and her probably needing to marry him, she doesn't complain about how it should be her choice on who she marries or mate... other than she just doesn't want to mate with him. She just accepts it. She should have fought a bit more for herself and who she wants to be with... . I only got used to Emma's mom til the end, to be quite honest. I do mean quite literally, I should add- I never understood why she was so clingy to her own daughter until the last page. Everything clicked into place then and, honestly, probably made me like her mother that much more. She's probably the only character that I liked in the end but... something tells me that'll change if I read the second book. IF. I most likely won't if it's going to be anything like this book. It switched between two point of views- Galen and Emma- but even though I knew which point of view was going to be which due to consistencies, I have to confess that I got a bit lost at points with how things are written. Maybe because both of the voices were beginning to blur in my head after a while. This is becoming more of a rant than a well thought-out review but it doesn't change how I feel about this book. It could've been handled so much better than it was. I wish for a better stories for mermaids- they deserve so much better.

Viet Than Nguyen's 2016 Pulitzer-winning debut novel is about a spy, a spook, a double agent, a sympathizer, which is meta because the book itself is a double agent, too. This dude works for a general for the South Vietnamese - that's the US side - but secretly he's a communist. He's able to live this double life because he can see both sides, he can sympathize. What we're talking about is code switching. That's a cool-sounding word for what Nguyen himself has done all his life. He arrived in the US at age 4, fleeing the Vietnam War's aftermath, and is now a professor at the University of Southern California. Like all immigrants and various minorities and other people, he learned to behave one way around, say, the kids at his predominantly white Catholic prep school, and another way while working at his parents' grocery store. He freely admits that that's what we're talking about: I knew that my autobiographical experience of wearing a mask, of having two faces, of always pretending, of doubting my own interiority, could be allegorised. And so the spy would be the vehicle for these emotional experiences and exaggerated to a great degree so it would be much more interesting. This is a good idea but it has this one drawback, which is that you get all excited to read about spies and find yourself - well, I mean, you are, there are spies, and double crosses and murders and all kinds of exciting things, but you have this weird suspicious feeling all along, like, "This doesn't really feel like a thriller. This feels...awfully literary." And that shouldn't be a problem, I've heard of literature, that sounds great, but - look, the obvious thing to do is compare it to Graham Greene's mighty The Quiet American, and I liked that one better. But listen, it's not just double agents, either. At one point - brace yourself here. So this guy, who everyone thinks is on the US side of the just-finished war, he flees to the US, where he gets hired as a sortof ethnic consultant on a Vietnamese movie and flown to the Philippines where they're shooting it, and he ends up mourning his mother at a fake cemetery built for the movie, and while he's mourning her the director tries to assassinate him by "accidentally" catching him in some special effects? So he's almost real murdered by a fake murder in a fake movie about a real war that he's faking his role in, and we are pretty far down the rabbit hole here. If you're starting to wonder how he keeps his sides straight, well, so is he. That's part of what we're talking about here, of course. The ending is going to throw another layer on the whole thing: it turns out that this entire book is the guy's confession after he's captured. That means it might all be made up; he's responsible for the death of another agent, and it's basically impossible to tell whether he's been turned or not. We end up in Pirandello territory: so deep in so many layers of characters playing parts that we can't touch the bottom anymore. It sounds like there's a lot going on, and we're not even done yet. There's, like, there's also waterboarding. And here's another weird thing: it's all a little bit funny. I mean, no, it isn't, but Nguyen is attempting a Slaughterhouse-Five /Catch-22 tightrope act: the tone here is satirical. Funny, or at least funny-ish, even as it talks about horrors. This is always tricky. He does okay with it. We're not short on ambition here, and Nguyen pretty much pulls it off. I'm not shocked he won the Pulitzer. Especially for a debut novel, this is pretty impressive stuff. And I did like it! But I didn't totally love it. It impressed me more than it engrossed me, and that's because it's a sleeper agent itself: a literary book masquerading as a spy thriller. I saw through it. I know what you're up to, Nguyen. You can't fool me. You wrote literature.

Originally posted to my blog: http://tamaraniac.com/2016/02/the-ban... I've heard a lot of people saying that Bands of Mourning has been their favorite Mistborn Era II book so far. I'm not sure if it was that for me, but it was certainly the most entertaining and definitely the most game changing. I felt like the main group of characters really hit their stride in this book, and there were so many HILARIOUS moments. I was cracking up while reading this quite a few times, up to and past the points where I was in total shock due to astonishing developments and / or pure amazingness. The plot was a tiny bit confusing to me in this one. It wasn't that I totally couldn't follow it or anything, but there were times where I was thinking, "This is great and all but where's the plot?" and times where the information was moving so fast that I could barely keep up. There were also tiny details I would miss, be briefly confused by, and then move on with. Never the less, I thoroughly enjoyed the whole thing and the story that all the parts coalesced to create was pretty mind blowing. That is pretty much all I can say without melting into a ridiculous mess of ALL CAPS and spoilers. Seriously, so many spoilers. If you've read all the Mistborn books to date, fell free to keep scrolling so we can scream together about all these new developments. If you haven't, well... You should really get on that. This book was WILD. The Wax & Wayne series has always been more fun for me than the original trilogy because Wax & Wayne is hilarity and fast fights and crazy banter while the original trilogy (which I love love LOVE too but in a different way) is all doom and destruction and "AHH THE WORLD IS ENDING." Shadows of Self started to bring in more of the world-being-at-stake stuff but Bands of Mourning really brought it all in and made things crazy, mashing all the best aspects together to make something that was great but also felt a lot different at times. While it still had my beloved Era II characters, this third book was an entirely new beast compared to the first two. Basically, Parts One and Two of this book were all "Could this be any more hilarious and adorable and clever?" and then Part Three was just "EVERYTHING I THOUGHT I KNEW WAS A LIE!" I'm pretty sure I started freaking out the moment Allik started talking and kept freaking out until the last sentence of that epilogue. But, hold up. Let's backtrack a little bit. The group dynamic of these characters came into itself in this book and it worked SO WELL. They all understood each other, and worked so well together, and really balanced each other out, with Wayne and Marasi outwitting each other, and Steris's backup plans, and Wax's leadership... It was perfect. Then again, as we saw in the (total hilarious) scene where they're all freaking out the hotel manager, put all five of them in a room together and they can be an absolute MENACE to anyone else nearby. After finding Steris ridiculous and kind of annoying in Alloy of Law, the events of Shadows of Self led me to start liking her. Bands of Mourning made me love her. Steris and Marasi both really shined in Bands. (More on Mara later) Near the end, when Steris was talking about how useless she was to the mission as a whole I was just like, "Psssssh no girl you saved their asses like twenty times." It was pretty amazing how she made her lists and was able to predict and prepare for pretty much everything. Steris was great. I also started shipping Wax and Steris a lot. There were so many fantastic moments between those two. Them searching through the finance records, (and Wax getting super competitive with it) Wax flying them up above the mists... Actually it was pretty adorable just how much Steris liked it when he flew them around. Speaking of ships: Wayne and MeLaan. I'd like to say I totally didn't expect it, but I actually kind of saw it coming. Though, near the beginning of the book I kind of thought it was setting up for Marasi/Wayne and I'm very glad that didn't happen. Wayne and MeLaan were already such bros (the whole accents thing yes) so I guess I kind of ship it. I don't really have strong feeling either way? They do make a really hilarious pair either way. Then we had the ball scene which was really great, with Steris pulling some totally surprising stunts and being in her element, (though I'm a little disappointed that Wax and Steris never got to dancing together) and the scene where Wayne and Marasi went to search the graveyard, which was equally fantastic. (Mara tricking Wayne into given back his stolen goods by putting out something he'd rather "trade" for was GENIUS) Super big turning point where Wax is framed for murder. Finally, we get to the warehouse and the ship. The ship was SO COOL. When they were talking about how it was odd I was thinking "could it be a flying ship...?" and it was and my life was made. FLYING SHIP. It was so cool how it worked on feruchemy and allomancy! Not to mention there are OTHER PEOPLE. That's... really, really big. I wonder sometimes if Sanderson will ever not manage to totally shock me with his plot twists but he always comes through. I kind of knew that Telsin wasn't going to be on their side. I didn't want to, because how much can Wax take? but the spunky, spirited, rebellious Telsin we met in the prologue... She wouldn't have just been waiting around for someone to rescue her. I was a little surprised that she was actually higher up in the Set than Suit though. That is... certainly interesting. MARASI WITH THE BANDS OF MOURNING. WAXILLIUM WITH THE BANDS OF MOURNING. Honestly, those scenes were some of the most amazing. I also was so happy about all the character development that happened around them. Marasi has really found her place (and her peace) now and that is so great. (also, she's totally right. purses are so useful) Plus the way they kind of shared a moment about the power in the Bands... I like how their friendship has moved so far beyond the whole "I used to be obsessed with you" awkwardness and has grown into something where they can share witty banter and things like that. Wax DIED. Wax DIED and CAME BACK TO LIFE. I was shocked by a lot of things in this book, but that was something I was entirely blindsided by. I was kind of expecting some major character death going into this book (which actually didn't end up happening in the end?) but I never expected it to be Wax. I love Wax. I loooove Waxillium. Currently he's one of my very, very favorite fictional characters. (and if I'm entirely honest with myself I have a huge crush on him too) He's so analytical and smart and has gone through so much. He's amazing but he also just really needs a hug. When he was paralyzed and I thought he was actually going to die (okay he did but also... you know) I was kind of losing it. Wax couldn't die, but... I wouldn't really put it past Sanderson. Thank goodness he survived is all I'm saying. Also, what Wayne did when he though Wax was dead. That just physically pains me... That whole scene around Wax's death, with all the characters in various states of hopelessness and them all finding ways to pull through and win. So much sadness and so much joy. That whole climax was so perfect. Right when I thought my world could be changed no more... That epilogue comes along and totally shakes everything up. Is it the Lord Ruler? Is it... Kelsier?!? (I do not dare to hope on that one) How would they have lived? That whole part is something I could theorize about for hours, and go a little bit out of my mind over, so I shall endeavor to leave it be. For now.

Patricia Briggs's books are excellent and this is no exception. I would recommend reading the novella that proceeds this book, in the anthology On The Prowl, before reading this book. In the strictest sense you don't need it to understand what is going on, the same way you don't need to see A New Hope to understand what's going on in The Empire Strikes Back. If you skip it you really miss out on a lot of the character development. Taking place in the same world as the Mercy books this book focuses in on the werewolves, making their aspect of the world deeper and more alive, revealing things we would never otherwise found out about. Anna is truly a different type of heroine then you usually see in urban fantasy - she's sensitive, vulnerable, and damaged. Even though she can take care of herself is isn't a though chick, but she doesn't sit back and let things happen to her either. Between the heroine and the plot this book's theme seems to be emotional strength - acquiring it, using it, lacking it, and needing it. The conflict starts out distant and becomes personal, and it ends in a way I didn't expect. This is definitely one of Briggs' strongest works so far. The book's biggest weakness is that it's in third person. Now and then it was frustrating to know what was going on because I could see the whole picture while the characters were still fitting the pieces together. Also the first chapter doesn't seem to fit in at first, but don't let it put you off because it is important and it does fit in. One great thing about this book is that even though it takes place in the same world as the Mercy books you don't have to read one series to make the other make sense - they stand by themselves at the same time that they support each other.

Enough with the angsty youths already! This is a smart book. But it's too long and the unnecessary drama tried my patience. Is it designed to attract this infamous YA audience? I don't think so. This is of course not the only weirdly juvenile contemporary fantasy out there. I guess I simply don't get the genre. The older characters are more interesting (Amat! ), except for the one around whom the plot revolves. His over-the-top whining, irresponsibility and bizarre pro-life fixation are strangely induldged by everyone else. Which bring me to A Shadow in Summer's serious versimilitude issues. The main plot makes little sense, and not only because of that character. The inscrutable reasoning of one of the implicated parties is never quite revealed which doesn't help. More generally, the setting's politics remain obscure. The lack of exposition and the focus on the subjectivity of a few characters (and then on their fancies and emotional reactions!) leaves too much unexplained. The author's approach would have worked in a historical setting but readers don't know enough about this setting for the author to have used so little background exposition. Some of the subplots seemed forced as well, featuring quasi-Freudian or simply reckless behavior on the part of many characters. And what's going on with the price of (low-quality) paper? I hope it's some kind of setup for the sequels because the ways paper was used were jarring. Now the good parts... The setting is the best part. It's on the whole unremarkable but it's nicely detailed as far as daily life is concerned and has a couple of great features. Most obviously, the non-verbal language inspired by Aristoi (but suprassing the source). It's not a mere gimmick. Even the abscence of non-verbal signifiers is meaningful. It helps the reader understand the characters without exposition or internal dialogue. It also makes the interactions between characters subtler, without some of the crutches used by other authors such as super-human body-language reading skills. The central psychomachic fantasy concept is intriguing and seems to have lots of potential but I think it was badly underused in this installment of the series. The plot isn't monomythical or aping a Hollywood blockbuster, nor is it overly manipulative or facile in the way it tries to hook the readers. It's a somewhat violent world but on-page violence is restrained. I like that but evidently some readers didn't (you've been warned!). There even is an explicit jab at wish-fulfillment epic fantasies in the book (don't worry: it's seamless). And the writing is enjoyable and picturesque while remaining mostly non-obstrustive, although a bit too flowery for my taste sometimes (considering the topics). Finally, I thought the ending was good (I'm picky about those).

Whew, what a ride! There were twists there were turns, my theories held no water and it was brilliant. I loved the rush this book gave me and the ending: perfect. Jasper really overcame a horrible childhood and it was truly a miracle that he didn't turn out just how his parents wanted him to. Well there is that saying about best laid plans. The depths of depravity was truly astounding and fits perfectly in the world of fiction. For all Jazz thought he knew, there was always something he really didn't and I'm grateful (acting like he is a real person for a moment) that he wasn't truly aware and that his child's mind was still fickle enough that the true horrors weren't weighing on him those four years his father was away. I'm glad Howie and Connie  survived their ordeals and that Aunt Sam wasn't really Ugly J so Howie wasn't even more traumatised. It was really a whammy to know that Connie had been played like a fine tuned violin by Ugly J. I wanted a bit more history on Ugly J as a killer though but we can't all have everything. It was definitely sad to read the moment Jazz's fantasy about his mom was killed but still his upbringing helped him triumph in the end and that is the perfect bit of irony.
I really love the New Species series.

I have had a strong dislike for the Queen of Heart ever since reading Alice in Wonderland. Marissa Meyer has given me a different perspective Heartless is set in Lewis Carrol's epic world of Wonderland with a big emphasis on the Queen of Heart. Everyone is a little mad here. Catherine is your "typical" teenage girl with dreams of becoming the kingdom's greatest baker along with her maid. During an evening at the ball, she encounters the King of Heart's new Court Jester, who with just one look stops her in her tracks. The Court Jester brought a new kind of joy into Cath's life. He showed her a different way of looking at the world. There was a whirlwind of adventure, of deception. A love so sweet, who wouldn't want it. We see the Hatter trying to run away from time and time slowly catching up to him. We see parents pushing their hopes and dreams upon their child with no consideration of what she might want and the consequences of those actions. Finally, we see what turned such a loving girl into a ruthless, cold-hearted Queen. I have made my decision as to how I feel about Cath. How do you feel about her after delving into the world of Wonderland?

I'm in Book 2 at the time of this writing: Dune is _really_ good. I'm actually surprised by how wrapped up I get in it and how full the control Herbert seems to have over the conflicting parties is. Sometimes the narrator allows the characters to get a little chatty, which in most authors I would consider amateur but Herbert gets away with for an as yet undefined reason. Once I figure it out, I'm going to try and put it to use myself. I think it might just be the reader thinking a little subconsciously "I'm having fun but also have no fucking idea what is going on, so someone better tell me soon," and then someone does, so you end up not minding it. I'm not settled on that explanation though. Update after having concluded the title: The book remained good all the way through the end but lost its touch of mastery somewhere in the middle of Book 2. To avoid spoilers I won't specify, but there is a point where the title stop being manipulated by the author and starts becoming a skeletal chain of plot points without connective tissue. Since I noticed this had happened, I've been trying to decide whether connectivity and social immersion were something that only started happening in later Sci-fi/Fantasy titles, but I don't think so; Dune had this quality at the beginning and lost it in the middle. Overall, the title remains much better than average, especially for a dated title. Highly recommended for Sci-Fi/Fantasy buffs looking to bolster their genre knowledge.

Addicted. Also, Why is everyone acting like 3 college aged dudes trying to get with a high school freshman is normal??? Like, if you ask me we saw that one (Lee being a HUGE EVIL CREEP) coming. PS. Not feelin' good about the nickname "Jailbait." V creepy.

Overall, I guess that I enjoyed the book. I thought the story of Tin Win and Mi Mi was sweet and sad and almost magical. BUT I was annoyed by the passivity of Tim Win. His feelings were profound and yet he was ok with living without her for fifty years? Really? Why? If he was truly content why suddenly go back to Burma? I'm too cynical for this book. The timeline for U Ba and Julia didn't make a great deal of sense to me either - their ages did not seem to reconcile. Perhaps I need to re read the early sections of the book to clear things up. I'm also not sure why they needed to add the "twist" at the end. To make the overall story arc more sad?
It was enjoyable but I expected to like it more considering the hype which I really don't get

4.5 STARS The Bronze Horseman was beautiful and intense and at the same time incredibly emotionally draining. First off, I think the book was advertised wrong. I read somewhere that there was a love quadrangle or something? And there really isn't. It's obvious from the start it's only Alexander and Tatiana and the people that get in their way. There were some problems I had with the book (which is why it didn't get 5 stars), most of which had to do with the main characters and their relationship. The Characters: Tatiana Metanov was sometimes frustrating. Although she had a nice character arc, she frequently did stupid things in the name of love and rarely stood up for herself. She let other people control her life, as Alexander pointed out. I suppose since Tatiana was a young woman in the Soviet Union in the 1940s, I can't hold her to the same standard as an American woman in the 21st century but it still would have been nice to see her stand up for herself, for herself and not for Alexander or anyone else. She also, as mentioned, did many risky things that easily could not have paid off (and it was very lucky that it did) for her family and Alexander. I guess my point is that she barely did anything for her own personal gain. There was always an underlying motive for her, whether it was for Alexander, Dasha, Pasha, the old ladies in Lazarevo, etc. Don't get me wrong, despite my criticisms, I still liked her and thought she was brave and strong for her family. In the same way, although I loved Alexander, I had some problems with him too. For one, especially in the second half of the book, he got to be really controlling and overprotective, which personally, annoys me in a character. I actually thought he changed radically from the first to the second half and not in the best way. I also thought he could have handled the whole Dasha situation better. Like for example NOT sleeping with her twenty times and breaking up with her from the beginning (instead of just waiting for her to die), despite Tatiana's protests. And finally, the relationship angst at the beginning was irritating at times and the sex, later on, was ok at first but then got annoyingly repetitive and is it even possible to orgasm that many times? The Other Characters: Dimitri - WHAT A FUCKING ASSHOLE Dasha - You were kind of bitchy although it still sucks that you died The Plot: I don't know much about the specifics of Russia during World War II except the main ideas that I learned from class. However, The Bronze Horseman seemed so incredibly realistic in its portrayal of life in Leningrad during 1941. I literally felt as though I was in Leningrad with the family as they were running out of food and other provisions. It was so realistic that at one point when I stopped reading because I had to get ready to go to a party, I realized that I had run out of eyeliner and, I shit you not, I thought to myself, oh no that's another thing we don't have anymore. And multiple times when I stopped reading for a minute, I was unsure whether I actually had food in the fridge. I also felt cold, as they did in the book, even though it was like 100 degrees outside. I'm probably just weird in having those thoughts but it made reading The Bronze Horseman that much more interesting for me. I think that their struggles in Leningrad were my favorite parts of the story. The parts in Lazarevo was less realistic  Probably because of their wedding, their happiness, and constant sex , but then again, what do I know? Maybe Lazarevo was like that during the war. The only other problem I had was that the book was very long. It probably could have been like 25%-30% less. Also, side note, I really liked the writing style and seeing things from both Tatiana's and Alexander's perspective. I also thought that the jumping around and withholding information from the readers enhanced the story. Even though the ending was devastating, I thought that it was an accurate portrayal of real life in that there is not always a happy ending. That was, of course, before I realized that there were two more books in the series, which are bound to make their love story as unbelievable as possible. All in all, I flew through The Bronze Horseman and I loved it, although all my griping probably made it seem like I didn't. I'm definitely going to continue on with the series but I probably need to take an emotional break before I read the second book.

After all of the contemporary stories I've been reading lately, a change was needed to get myself away from the same story on repeat. Throne of Glass met this requirement, and completely blew me away in the process of fulfilling my needs. Celaena Sardothien is the top assassin of Adarlan. When we meet her, she's been in what is essentially a death camp for a year. She's weakened, and missing pieces of her old self. However, we get hints of the old Celaena - enough that we realize just how dangerous and compelling she can be. She'd been betrayed, which is what led to her capture, and she was meant to die in Endovier (the prison/death camp where she was held). She is offered a chance at freedom by the Crown Prince, Dorian, if she competes in a tournament and wins. Winning would make her the King's Champion, and she'd be forced to kill his enemies. But, things go awry when competitors start dying. Celaena begins to investigate the mysterious murders --- and that's when things really get interesting. First of all, I'd like to point out that it took Maas TEN YEARS to create this story. The world building (along with the character building) is utterly fantastic and was obviously methodically plotted piece by piece. So many twists and turns, shocks and surprises that you'll be left wondering who can be trusted. And, these characters --- The Captain of the Guard Chaol Westfall is probably the most intriguing character in the story. He's in charge of Celaena - both her training and making sure she doesn't attempt escape - and is hard to read in the beginning. His actions towards her are understandable considering the roles they play at the castle, but it doesn't take away from the ability to fall in love with him a bit. I was shocked to find there was a love triangle in this story. It's subtle, but I assure you, you will have a hard time choosing sides until the very end of the book. And, I am still not 100% either team. Yet. Prince Dorian was actually a pleasant surprise. I expected the typical royal - spoiled, arrogant, and used to getting his way. He was some of these things, but not in a way that made him unlikable. He's charming and I also feel there's more to him than we have seen. Dorian's struggles stem from what he wants versus who he is and what he can have. Celaena herself is just a strong female, but one who has been semi-broken by what happened to her over a year ago. She wants revenge and freedom, but first must fulfill her obligations. While I've seen her called selfish and arrogant, I'd have to disagree to some extent. She was, by far, the most dangerous assassin in the kingdom. That itself carries a lot of stress and expectations. I think she had an image to uphold, and that was a lot of her act. Yes, she was spoiled by her lifestyle, but I think part of that is from her real identity as well. The supporting "cast" is just as magnificent as the main ones I've mentioned. Somehow, Maas has fleshed out even the few minor characters we interact with, showing her superior writing skills. The king, the duke, Kaltain, and Nehemia all had roles that weren't as obvious, but we could feel their intentions all the same. I was going to say that if you enjoy the fantasy genre, you'll love this book, but that's a lie. If you enjoy epic tales with a mysterious plot filled with secrets, READ THIS BOOK. If you like getting lost in books, READ THIS BOOK. If you enjoy stories that feel so real, you believe it's happening before your eyes, READ THIS BOOK. If you want to fall in love with a story, its characters, and be changed by a book, READ THRONE OF GLASS.

Asking For It is such an important book. Eighteen year old Emma O'Donovan lives in a small town in Ireland and like a lot of teenage girls she likes to go out with her friends and party. One night she goes to a party, gets drunk, takes some drugs and flirts with a few guys. The next morning, she wakes up on her front porch with absolutely no memory of what happened the night before. But not to worry: there are hundreds of photos posted to Facebook which show exactly what happened to her. Emma O'Donovan is beautiful and she knows it. She's confident, she's selfish and not a very good friend. Emma is not a likeable character and the decision to make her so makes this story all the harder to read. Generally it is difficult to sympathise with unlikeable characters and that is the point here: we don't have to like Emma. Being unlikeable doesn't mean that you weren't raped. You can be the bitch of the century and no still means no. Emma being so unlikable opens the reader's eyes to the way we (society as a whole) tend to think about rape victims: their personal life is always dragged up. How promiscuous are they, how often do they get drunk, how often do they have sex, what kind of clothes do they wear, are they a nice person? Emma deals with all of this in the aftermath of her rape. The people of her town completely turn against her in favour of her rapists and the media are constantly discussing her. Is it any wonder that so few rape victims report their assault? The reactions and behaviour of her friends and family (particularly her parents) were one of the hardest aspects to read for me. I really just could not believe the attitude of her parents and their utter unwillingness to just believe their daughter. They were more interested in their image and losing their "friends" and that was just utterly heartbreaking. Emma's brother is probably the only decent character in the entire book. As for the ending: I think it ended in the right way. I was majorly pissed off at her parents for being relieved and happy at her decision but it is realistic. I'm glad that O'Neill didn't give us a happy ending or wrap things up nicely because it is never going to be over for Emma. She has been completely ostracised from the community she lives in, she's given up her dreams and she is forever going to be haunted by what happened to her. It reflects the society we live in where many victims don't get the justice they deserve. I can't stress enough how important I think this book is, especially in today's society. There are countless cases in the media concerning rape, and what is defined as consent, as well as rapists who get off incredibly lightly whilst victims are left to suffer. Asking For It deals with the issue of not explicitly saying no but not saying yes either, a lack of memory of the rape, slut-shaming, victim-blaming and the increasing use of social media. This is a must-read for everyone.

I think the rating is currently low because killing Quinn seemed like a bit of a cop out way to get the family back together. She was also so perfect and sweet like Beth March. . It seemed like it was going somewhere with Quinn wanting to learn more about her Bengali grandmother, but then of course didn't. All in all, it was ok.

I just keep wanting more and more while reading this series. If I could be anybody, any character from a book, movie, TV show,... anything, I would want to be Kate Daniels. She's tough and always knows what to say (usually something snarky), but she also has a very big heart and cares deeply for the people she loves, even while she keeps telling herself she doesn't want any kind of relationship with the people around her. She really is one of the best female characters I've ever read about.

This series is shaping out to be raw, dark, dirty and gritty. Filthy is a fitting title. "I could never be normal and pretend like I wasn't a f*cked up human being. Because I was. I was broken, a destroyed hunk of flesh with a heart that kept beating." I think this sums up Faye in a nutshell. She's so broken and hasn't got a clue, or a care, to try to put herself together again or try to heal. I kept hoping she'd reach out to Rhett to help her, but no. And that scene with her step-dad Taylor was unreal. I was completely grossed out and that's part of what made this such a fantastic read!

** spoiler alert ** (These comments are based on KU ebook, not an ARC.) I definitely agree with other GRs reviewers who felt this book had a Kristen Ashley feel. I LOVED the witty, back and forth banter between Mia, the heroine, and Lexie, the spitting image of herself, teenage daughter. I actually found myself giggling aloud at times. Honestly, they were freaking fantastic together. Not saying I agreed with all her parenting choices, but I loved how close they were. The brooding hero, Bull, well, I've got quite a bit of beef still bugging me in regards to how he treated Mia well into the first half of the story. Yeah, he definitely reminded me of Tack from KA's Motorcycle Man, minus not being the Pres of the club, and Tack's lady love, Tyra, whipped that misbehaving bad boy right into shape straight from the start. Mia could have definitely benefitted from mimicking Tyra's behavior in dealing with her biker man. I felt Bull got away with way too much bull in regards to how he treated Mia. Sure, I get he was emotionally damaged from losing his previous woman in such a tragic, horrific way, but I expected the heroine here to have more self-respect and, frankly, hit him upside the head from their first hello to make him snap out of it. Instead, she felt more like a doormat he wiped his feet on. It took some blood and bullets to remove his blinders and finally see life wasn't worth living without her and Lexie. The excuse we are basically given is Mia has a broken past, as well, so doesn't expect much in the way of relationships. Well, I certainly expected more...from both of them. Fortunately, I got it, but not until nearly the end. Overall, I did really enjoy this and plan to read the other books in this series. I'm keeping my fingers crossed the author's writing style will remain the same throughout all of them, because I absolutely loved the witty banter. **spoilers possible** Romance Safety Gang: Bull mentally refers to having sex with a club ho on two separate occasions after meeting the heroine to try to stop thinking of her. When he is intimate with the heroine at 20%, he yells at her and tells her to leave, which, of course, makes her feel used. He's afraid of getting close to someone/losing them like he did Laurie. Mia at one point tries to make a stand about how wrong it was for him to treat her that way, but her self-respect quickly flies out the window and they are intimate again, where he immediately informs her that's all he can give her...meaning no relationship, not even friendship. Meaning, he is so broken he has nothing else to give. She agrees to that deal. Yeah, I wasn't happy about that. At 33% after another quick romp, they seem to have a tender moment then he obviously started thinking of Laurie's demise and reminds her, "You know what this is, right?...Just sex," and tells her to leave. Next sexcapade involved him holding her down and spanking her, like he threatened to do earlier (eyeroll)...and she was mad he did it but loved it at the same time (double eyeroll). Repeating pattern of him out of the blue having sex with her then just walking away, without so much as a word. His treatment of her dramatically changes after a shooting incident. That's when I actually started to like the guy...finally. Yeah, I was really worried for awhile that wasn't going to happen. Mia does at one point predictably push him way. Even goes on a date with another man. Then her past catches up with her in a very big way. Title: Out of the Ashes, stand-alone but part of a series, HEA, no love triangle, no cheating, no OW/OM drama (except what I mentioned in spoiler), some violence, domestic abuse, heroine had brief abusive marriage that caused her to go on the run, Bull's OW had been tortured/raped and died from those injuries.

This book gave me a run for my money...literally. I held on to this book long after I met my library renewal limit and it's due date. It's that good. Having read French's previous novels and experienced with the signature French roller coaster, I wasn't sure what to expect this round. In the end, it was an amazing read. There were very little unanswered questions left in the end, unlike in In the Woods and The Likeness , leaving me with a solid and agreeable ending. However, that doesn't mean that all loose threads were tied up -  I still don't understand how Frank's Da knew the truth before it came out (the little warning he gave Frank before everything unraveled). And then there's also the matter of Frank picking the scent up right away after finding out who Imelda spilled to without solid evidence. As with Imelda, just because Shay knew about their plans to run away doesn't directly lead to him being the killer; that part of the plot rolled too quick for my taste. I've also always loved French's ability to humanize and sympathize with the protagonist and that ability has only grown stronger with her work and is clearly at it's peak in Faithful Place Although French makes it clear through Frank's POV that he wasn't buying Shay's self-righteous martyrdom, she gave the readers enough information to form their own opinions - and I felt like I understood the building pressure Shay must've felt throughout his life to balance between creating a new life for himself, independent and separate from his detrimental family while trying to keep one foot in to protect his mother and siblings and the consequential desperation that moved him to confront Rosie. I just love protagonists with back-stories - it doesn't justify what they've done (obviously) but at least the audience has a better understanding of why they did it. Absolutely can't wait to pick up Broken Harbor

DNF at 73%. "I wasn't even sure whose wall it had been to begin with - hers or mine. But I would have spent my entire life tearing it down if I could have only predicted what was on the other side." THE REVIEW You know those books that you're so engrossed in that you think about them when you're away from them? The ones you dream about returning to when you're busy attending to "real life" stuff? Well, that's how Aly Martinez' The Fall Up started for me. Not only did it have a beautiful cover and an interesting synopsis - as soon as I started reading, I was instantly drawn in by these two very intriguing characters. From the very first pages, Levee and Sam had some really great banter going on. They were both quick-witted and funny, and I was really looking forward to learning more about them as characters, and more about their reasons for being on the bridge night after night. So yeah - promising start. BUT... Then they had sex. A few days after meeting each other. Which is all well and good - if you want to have sex with someone two days or even two minutes after you meet them, then that's no one's business but your own... HOWEVER, what I don't want to see is you getting crazy intense about someone just because you had sex with them once, and had a couple of very short conversations and therefore all of a sudden have this incredible and somewhat magical (*coughimaginarycough*) connection... Which is exactly what happened with Sam and Levee. No thank you. I really thought these two characters could have had a wonderful relationship - especially considering a lot of the sensitive subject matter brought in fairly early on - but, instead, it was like some sort of switch was flicked as soon as they did The Deed. All of a sudden, all they could think about was the next time they would be able to bump uglies, and it really took away from how strong the story started. Which is a shame, really, because The Fall Up had the potential to be a really touching and emotional love story. (Sorry, there's more ranting still to come...) AND, just when I thought that the author choosing lust over love was quite bad enough on its own, in walks my most dreaded enemy: INSTA-LOVE. Why, why, why? Look, I'm going to be straight here: I read a lot of romance. I know it's fiction. I don't expect it to be incredibly realistic, okay? I get that you have to move your plot forward. I get that you're writing a romance novel. But seriously, you don't have to have your characters fall in love after two weeks - most of, which I might add, have been spent apart/arguing/having sex, and not much more. There's a big difference between love and infatuation, and romance authors need to stop acting like they're both the same thing, because I'm starting to get pretty bored of reading about it. Ahem. (Rant over.) The last note I had written down on The Fall Up was "actually rolling my eyes right now," which I think pretty much sums up my feelings about the rest of this novel... Martinez could have done so much more with this novel if she'd executed it better and spent more time making the heavy issues it dealt with more realistic, and less time on fluffing up the romance to an extent where it became cheesy and ridiculous. I'm actually really sad to be giving another low rating, but here we are. Onwards and upwards, I hope... "I was falling fast for that man, and I could only hope I was taking him with me."

A magnificently eerie book. I picked this up because so many people on Goodreads labeled it "weird fiction" --- a genre dominated by one of my favorite writers, China Mieville. But the work has much more in common with Mark Z. Danielewski or the graphic novels by Charles Burns --- there's a strong lyrical quality with a heavy dose of otherness. The book starts off at a distance. We are following a team of of four researchers into Area X, an area which has been set off for reasons that are never fully explained. Our team members intentionally do not use names, so we view the world through the eyes of "the biologist". The biologist herself is reserved. There are hints of a shadowy, unknown entrance into the area, but no real details. In short, the opening is an odd mix of the mysterious and the impersonal, and I found it tough going at the start. However, VanderMeer does an excellent job of throwing in emotional context and hints of the strangeness of Area X, with the result that I was hooked about halfway in. Moreover, the alienness in the book (when it appears) is done amazingly well; VanderMeer is able to convey a great deal of detail and texture while images still appear muddled, confusing, and wholly different. If you are interested in the different, I give this a strong recommendation.

MY OPINION: ***** THE BEST BOOK EVER Okay, so this was one of those one day reads. Actually, almost-two-hour reads. I needed some summer reads. Those quick romantic ones that are thrilling, easy to read, and short. And amazing. I haven't found a good contemporary novel lately and I was starting to think about giving up. So I went to the library and picked up about three. No, four. I started reading a lot of them but none of them were good enough for me after the first couple of chapters. I wanted a one day read... just for fun and also to get caught up on my Goodreads reading challenge, which I am pitifully behind on and keep lowering gradually so I can feel better about myself... Yeah. Then I picked up this one and the font was that type of typeface that is really easy to read. I know that sounds weird, but I honestly judge books by the font. Not the covers, not the first chapter, not the blurb. I judge them by the font AND DO NOT JUDGE ME :D Okay, so this book was amazing. Wonderful. Beautiful. Sad. Happy. Romantic. Gorgeous. Yeah. I have a whole list of adjectives about this book. This book is about a girl named Annie whose boyfriend passed away in a fatal accident. She kind of blamed herself because she broke up with him? But they got back together before the accident! I really don't understand that part but maybe because it was about 11 at night and my brain was sleepy and unfunctional. So she starts training for this marathon that her boyfriend, Kyle, always wanted to run in but never got to... The thing is, she was/is a horrible runner. So she finds this trainer named Matt who has an expensive fee but is a really good coach (I LEGIT WROTE COUCH). She soons starts to run really well, though she has stomach and muscle problems, as well as a runner's knee. But she meets Matt's brother, Jeremiah (SWOON), who she soon feels drawn to. Yeah, so that's the climax. Basically, Annie feels like she can't date anymore after what happened with Kyle, but she really likes Jeremiah (AND SO DO I). Jeremiah is an adrenaline junkie who constantly hurt himself doing really dangerous things. The one thing that I didn't like about this book was... Jeremiah and Annie went REALLY fast in the beginning. I mean, they were legit almost doing IT when they didn't even know each other's LAST NAMES. Jeremiah was so sweet, amazing, gorgeous, and brave. He was really nice and I REALLY NEED HIM TO BE REAL. How come all of the best guys only exist in books and then we get to REAL LIFE and almost all of them are like BLARGH. Annie was so determined and brave and I actually liked her! I know, that sounds mean or weird, but I almost NEVER like the main character. I really loved this book and I really need to read more books by this author or I will spontaneously combust. I was expecting it to be all magical and action filled but while there was a bit of magic and some action there was sooooo much romance. Celaena was so defined by her relationships with men, she cared desperately about whether or not they fancied her and really seemed to hang a fair portion of her self worth on that, and I really didn't like the love triangle thing I can see building up, her relationship with Chaol is weird and a bit stockholmy and the relationship with Dorian seems better but it's also unbalanced- he has a lot more power than her there. I was expecting it to be more fantasy as well- there are elements of magic, other than one plot line  the murders   they don't play a massive part, the world Celaena lives in just seems like a generic medieval fantasy world with some exotic names. There's so much mystery in this books- but it mostly seems to be obtained by leaving vast chunks of information out- I still don't really understand how/when/why magic happens. Celaena seems determined to ignore her tragic past- we get enough hints to let us know it was sad but nothing is really explained, it's just annoying. We get the competition explained to us, but there's no explanation of why the competition is happening and what the king hopes to get from it. All the mystery means that the romance is pretty much the only area of Celaena's life that is vaguely straightforward which throws even more emphasis on it. There were bits I enjoyed reading but as it went on and on it just got more frustrating how much was being hinted at but not explained and I didn't feel a sense of completion when I got to the end of the book- it felt like a lot of loose ends are hanging about, I know it's part of a series, but I'd still like to feel that I've finished a book with that satisfied sense of "it makes sense now" when I get to the end of it. I might read the next in the series but probably not.
