I adored this tale. I don't often read books that follow the beauty and the beast theme but I am certainly glad that I found this one. I read and rated Beast a while ago so my memory's a bit fuzzy but I'm going to do my best to review it because I do remember thinking that this book deserved to be written about. The main characters were precious. I'm not sure how that will sound to some people but for me that is the best word to describe my feelings for both Christopher and Ashleigh. They became characters that I truly cared about and talked about with my friends and family; anyone who would listen. Their story was beautiful and there were times during the story when my heart beat faster, a smile crossed my face, or tears came to my eyes. However, in reality I would give this story 3.5 stars. The reason being that at times, I felt as if the story was dragging. I just didn't enjoy it as much towards the end. That's not to say that I wasn't still happy (this book made me very happy) but there were points that I was bored. CAUTION: BIG SPOILER I also wasn't expecting Christopher's facial reconstruction surgery. I would have loved the story equally had his faced remained tragically beautiful. Still, when he explained to Ashleigh his reasons I got all warm and fuzzy inside. I always enjoy reading Pepper Pace's stories and I look forward to reading many more.

2 1/2 stars. My immediate thought after finishing: what was the point? Of course not all books have to have "a point," but with this type of story and these types of characters, there needs to be something more to draw all of these sloppy strings together in the end. I never warmed to Miranda/Melissa. I don't want to say that I hated her, but there was never anything that made me feel sympathetic toward her. It shouldn't be said that she deserved to be raped  but I found myself constantly questioning her state of mind and the validity of her feelings. I never doubted that Andrew was not murdered by her, and that Charlene wasn't being silenced by her fall due to what she remembered. Beyond that I loved all of the other characters I wish the book had been narrated by Mick or Forrest or Charlene. I was fascinated by Lucy and Andrew's public relationship, and Mick and Forrest's extremely private one. I wish more had been explored about Andrew - to rape someone in such close quarters feels very strange to me. He would have had no way of guaranteeing that Miranda wouldn't have said something. I also wished the book had spent more time on the biology and environmental science of the island. The latter writing and the "ghost" - another thing that made me question Miranda's state of mind, felt unnecessary. Too much time was spent away from the claustrophobic nature of the novel, which lessened the tension. And killing Mick, plus the side plot about him pretending to be the father felt weird. They both did nothing for the story.

Oh wow... I'm a bit at loss for words here. This book kept me completely enthralled from the very first page. Ms Ward writes in such a way it makes you feel as if you're right there in the book, with the characters. The book is ugly, and gory and bloody - but it's also beautiful, heart warming, and reading it feels like having come home. Dark Lover is brick of a book, and so much happens. All the time. Yet, it's never hard to keep the players straight, or their various story-lines, or the over all plot. Ms Ward doesn't play around with fancy words (other than series specific vamp words, but you quickly learn what they mean), and she doesn't try to talk over the readers' heads. I almost want to dive right into the next book in the series, but at the same time I want to wait for a bit to let Dark Lover absorb completely first. If you like vamps and love stories and blood and scary (sexy) dudes - this book is so for you. Me, I'm just sad I'm so late to the game. Feels like the whole worlds has read these books already.

Such a good book and so important for getting a trans character into YA literature. It is well written and a quick read. I liked the depth of the story and the characters. I am hoping to see more books about trans characters following this one, I feel like though this was only one example of an experience that a trans person may encounter there are many other experiences that can be portrayed in literature. I read LGBTQIA+ books for different perspectives and to help me learn, even though fiction is hardly for education. I am optimistic that we will continue to get more own voices stories like this that continue to give a deeper perspective to situations that some readers don't experience.

Empire of Storms is a very surprising book for me. I honestly wasn't as eager to read it after Queen of Shadows because of the events that happend previous to EoS. I had a hard time getting used to the changes and different turns the series took through out Crown of Midnight and the following books. Lots of things changed in this series since I read Throne of Glass. #1 Point of Views Throne of Glass started of as a fantastic but very small world where you had Celaena as a protagonist and point of view during the story and Chaol and Dorian and a few more as supporting characters. But in EoS I can't shake the feeling that we entered a total different story. We have several point of views because nearly every character who is involved with the story gets his own voice. I love that. I love multiple PoVs so much but I still feel weird that this story changed so much. Not necessarily in a bad way but it needs some time getting used to through Queen of Shadow were it started and now in Eos. #2 Aelin doesn't feel like the protagonist Actually that point is a big positive change for me. I couldn't stand Aelin in Queen of Shadows and she is still my least favourite character. I loved Celaena and even though she was only a fracture of the character that Aelin is now I still liked her way more as the badass assassin she was in the beginning. But anyway, I think in Eos Aelin gets pushed back a lot into the background because there a lots of amazing characters that shine through the story. One of them is definitely Elide. Her character stood out for me in this story. But all of the others as well. I still don't enjoy the Rowan and Aelin scences because for me there are just over the top. But other than this I loved the character and storytelling changes. #3 Sex scenes / Love scenes - lots of Acomaf vibes We get three very explicit scenes in Eos and it reminded me a lot of A Court of Mist and Fury. Feels like SJM really enjoyed writing sex scenes and thought to bring more into her other series as well. I don't mind at all. SJM knows how to write sex scenes. This is the thing that was irritating for me though. The similarities to Acomaf really stood out. If you don't read both of her series you won't see it but Rowan and Aelin and Feyre and Rhysand relationship are very similar (up until the secret marriage . #4 Chaol I'm very conflicted when it comes to Chaol. I'm not happy that he is not in this book. I'm not happy how she decided to make him into this irrelavant side character. But I also think Chaol doesn't belong to them anymore. He wouldn't fit in with this group with all their magic and crazy things that go on. Chaol belonged in a non-magic world with Celaena and he doesn't fit beside Aelin or in this world. I'm upset and I miss him as a character but I'm happy that he isn't dragged through the dirt even more by SJM. But all in all, I think Eos was 10 times better than QoS and HoF and even though the series has changed a lot since ToG I don't mind. I love the changes and I think they've been for the better. We get a bigger world, we get lots of amazing characters and twists and turns we couldn't have seen coming. I'm excited for the next book and hope to see a familiar face again because I missed him a lot throughout Eos.

I have no idea how to rate this book. It was certainly enlightening in a horrifying way. I am now even more terrified of Queen Levana. She is a zealot to her cause, willing to do anything to accomplish it. Not because she believes she's cruel, but because she believes in the rightness of her rule and her mission. Even more frightening, she has no real understanding of human emotions, even while she has the power to manipulate others' thoughts. Although there were brief moments I felt pity for Levana, they were overshadowed by the skin crawling creepiness of everything she has done. Author Marissa Meyer has done an excellent job at building Levana's character throughout this book by degrees of horror: from lonely, disfigured child to a Queen so focused on overtaking the galaxy that she will let nothing or no one get in her way. We do get glimpses of a lot of characters that come to play in the future of the series, and after reading this, all my hope and fears are centered on them. I am even more anxious for the final book to release. I'm not going to rate the triangle factor as the 'romance' in this book is disturbing at best, and Levana is incapable of knowing what a true relationship is - even friendship. But I do think this is a valuable addition to the series, and a fascinating look at the mind of a villain (who would never see herself as such).

Even though 'The Score' is a short novel - my copy runs to a distinctly svelte 158 pages - this is clearly Richard Stark going for epic. The idea of robbing not just a bank, or a factory pay-roll, but an entire city is just genius. It's a big idea, but one Stark puts across with a beautiful economy. Of course a raid like this needs a sizeable crew and each of the gang of rogues who are pulled together for this heist is beautifully and efficiently sketched in just a few sentences. (What's more for fans of the series this is the very first appearance of Alan Grofield, Shakespearean actor, thief and the other character the Richard Stark name would write books about. Although am I the only one who thinks it out of character for Parker to change his opinion and be so accepting of the woman Grofield runs away from the robbery with? Surely after that Parker would never have worked with him again. ) It's a fantastic concept and the actual heist is terrifically executed, so it's just a shame that it all falls flat towards the end, with the final quarter being a lacklustre tying together of loose ends. Yes, it fits Stark/Westlake's view that these are books about professionals as that last section is about the downtime and bickering for a gang of professionals after such a crime, but - as other Parker novels expertly prove - you can marry that professionalism to drama and suspense. Here Stark fails to do that, so ends with a damp squib rather than more explosions. I read a remark the other day about the existential nature of the Parker books, and there is a definite lack of a God, be it either the religious kind or the omnipotent god of crime fiction who generally makes sure that the rules of basic morality are upheld and bad people get their comeuppance. Instead these books are about men who make their own rules and carve out their own kind of chaotic order from the void. But for all their shaping of their own world, since they only really come alive when they're working and committing these crimes, they are essentially like Sisyphus just pushing a rock up a hill again and again and again. The money always runs out and a fresh scheme - or is it always just variations on the same scheme? - always starts up. It's a theory I'll think over more as I re-read the rest of these books, but what certainly struck me about this one is that it has a kind of gleeful nihilism. The city that's raided - Copper Canyon - is small town Americana at its finest: a sleepy police department; teenagers who are a bit rebellious but respectful; a place where everybody knows everybody else. It's a town that should have its own Jessica Fletcher, the kind of city David Lynch would love. And here it's blown apart. It's peace and serenity destroyed, and there's no authority figure who can make it right, no Jessica Fletcher who can solve the crime. From being a sleepy berg its suddenly dragged to the edge of the abyss for seemingly no reason whatsoever. The book revels in this destruction, but then forgets about it - the men who cause this chaos walk away with a shrug of their shoulders and scarcely a glance back. There is no authority, no rules, no moral God - this is Parker's world and you better get used to it.

The Snow Maiden (Snegurochka) is my favorite fairy tale. (I prefer the version in which the snow maiden is the child of Father Ice and the Goddess of Spring/one of her handmaidens, but I don't have a favorite ending: either she melts when she and the other children are playing by leaping over a small fire and she gets too close to the flames or because she loved the shepherd boy so much that she willing walked out into the sunlight when he begged her to.) So, I was intrigued when I heard that this book was based upon the story of the Snowmaiden. It is very very loosely based on the fairy tale. There is a middle-aged childless couple -- Jack and Mabel -- and a mysterious little girl -- Faina -- who seems to be their little snow girl brought to life. That's where the similarities end. The Snow Child spoke very deeply to some people I know, but it didn't affect me the same way. The first three-fourths of the book are very slow. I didn't really connect with any of the characters. Out of all of them, I was most drawn to Mabel. I pitied her greatly. She was like a bit like Charlie Brown. Mabel's raw grief over her stillbirth (and other implied pregnancy losses) was palpable and gut-wrenching for me. I wanted to slap her husband for running away and hiding every time that he thought Mabel would cry. He would even say things like 'I thought Mabel was going to cry, so I pretended not to notice and hid in the barn.' She was filled with sadness and longing and had to keep watching others get the things that she wanted. Jack is proud and stoic. Ester is eccentric, unladylike, and a true frontierswoman. George is her good-natured husband. Garrett is their youngest son suffocating behind the shadow of his brothers. Faina is mysterious, aloof, and possibly magical. I would have liked to see much more of Faina, but that would have ruined the air of mystery about her that the author wanted to create. At first, she seems like a supernatural being, but then the story goes to great length to dispel this notion and paint her as a person raised like an Inuit by her Slavic trapper father utterly in tune with the wilderness. I wanted to see how she could survive alone outside during winter in a place that "killed grown men." I wanted to see more of her feral ways. I was also curious how, despite being so in sync she with the natural world and her own sexuality, she didn't know she was or could become pregnant . That seemed out of character for someone who had spent a lifetime observing the life cycles of the animals around her. Reading this book reminded me that I don't like Alaska or even the mystique of it. The author does a fantastic job creating the atmosphere. I felt cold just reading it, and it conjured memories of all the terrible stories set during the Yukon Gold Rush that I was forced to read in Middle School like White Fang, The Call of the Wild, and The Cremation of Sam McGee. I don't understand why anyone would want to homestead in Alaska. It must be a man versus nature instinct that I lack. I don't think the cold, dark, near starvation, swarms of mosquitos, and constant threat of death sound the slightest bit exciting. The Oregon Trail sounded bad enough even without the Donner Party. And that ending, what happened? Most of the book is spent disproving the idea that Faina is magical, and then she vanishes, and it turns out she is a supernatural creature after all? Or wasn't she? Did her fever cause her to melt? Did she just strip naked and crawl off to die alone in the wilderness that was the only place she was ever at peace? If so, why couldn't they find her body or her tracks or her remains? Was she the ghost of the child of the dead trapper? Jack found a photo of her as a baby with her mother in the trapper's cabin, so she existed at some point in human form. Did she die with her mother and continue on with her father in spirit form? It was too open-ended for me. I wanted a clearer resolution.

The description of this book (even the paragraph here at Goodreads) is misleading... Yes, Grace is a rocket scientist. Yes, she meets Grey, transported from 12th century Scotland 4 years earlier, on a plane. Yes, the tiny prop job plane does crash. BUT... Grace has a baby with her, and the crash happens only a few miles away from home and help. The entire book isn't really about Grey and Grace trying to survive the crash and a wintry storm... it's about whether Grey and Grace are true matches, whether they can recognize it, whether they can bridge the gap in centuries and male-female relationships, and whether Grace can give her sister's baby to his true father, a blood-feud sworn enemy of Grey. This book can be a good read, if you're in the mood to allow quite a bit of suspension of belief and just want a fun romance with a sexy 12th century Highlander. But if you try to analyze it at all, the book either gets confusing or just plain falls apart. I'm giving it 3 stars because: 1. Grey is a sexy, alpha-male Highlander who's learned to mostly become a modern male. It was a fun read. It was very late when I finished the book. Will I read on in the series? Not sure. The problem is that my local library doesn't carry this series, and I'm not sure that I want to purchase another book, Kindle or otherwise, to see if the series is worth reading. Here are my thoughts about this book: SPOILERS AHEAD 1. Pendaar: He's the magician/wizard behind the whole time travel thing. He's the one who knows that Grey's match is in the 21st century, while Grey is in the 12th century. In fact, if Grey and his match don't find one another, Pendaar's replacement wizard/magician will never be born. But no one - past or present - seems to know or trust Pendaar. Grey has no idea of any of this... he has no idea why he and 9 others (including 6 blood-feud enemies from another clan) were transported to the 21st century. He has no idea why Daar (Pendaar), the priest they find upon "arriving", helps them and trains them in the modern world, including how to drive. And why would they believe that simply because Daar said it, that Grey and his clansmen belonged in Maine? And should open a ski resort-spa in Maine?? Grace: She's a rocket scientist, literally. So she's all about the science. But there's a lot about life and love that Grace has no idea. She learns that when her sister, Mary, dies and leaves Baby in her care. So Grace is in transition and has just come through some heavy-duty emotional stuff and is grieving when she meets Grey and this adventure begins. But Grace seems almost completely unable to cope with every-day life. She either relies on or gets used to Grey and his clan of big, strong Highland men to rescue her and take care of her, even as she attempts to assert her own independence. Grace insists that Grey help his neighbors, especially his sworn enemy, MacBain. And she threatens to not see him anymore unless he does. Grace even seems to bargain sex for Grey to bend to her will. Grace is confused. And confusing. She's been thrown into the midst of circumstances and emotions she's never dealt with before. So I try to give her credit for at least attempting to be strong... doing her best to be a mother to Baby... trying to have a life. But I can't help but be a little disturbed that Grey is constantly almost mauling Grace -- grabbing her and kissing her thoroughly, and Grace doesn't seem to have a problem with that. For all that Grey might be sexy and all, it seems difficult to believe that a modern woman could trust and want a relationship with a man who seems to be all about the physical and demands physical in return. Yes, Grey is also seen as a caring man who does his best to protect and care for Grace and Baby. But always on HIS terms... and as modern as he is, he's still got 12th century thinking about men and women. Oh, he believes that women are equals (but does he treat Grace that way, especially when he wants a kiss? ), and he doesn't want to stand in the way of her career. But his actions, especially the intimate ones, are almost always because he grabs her. To be fair, Grace welcomes his attentions - she doesn't tell him no; in fact, she tells him yes, a lot. But how can Grace know or feel anything that is real in the midst of all of this? The threat: Yes, there must be a threat. And this time, it's because Grace is THE ONLY ONE who can decode the transmissions from a newly launched space pod to test her ion propulsion theories. Of course her boss is her current (or is it former) boyfriend... although neither of them are in love, and it turns out, they've never had sex (because Grace is a virgin). And of course this boss has sold out to the enemy, who's coming to take Grace and her precious technology away. And of course, only the combined forces of Grey, his sworn enemy MacBain (Baby's father), and Daar/Pendaar can stop that from happening. The "magic": There are a lot of blue lights, white lights, and black lights floating around. I think the blue light is supposed to be Mary, watching over Grace until she and Grey get together and Baby gets to his father. The white light has something to do with every time Grace and Grey kiss or have sex. And the black lights are obviously the evil coming for Grace. But... it's just weird. The resolution: Yes, this is a romance, so there is a happily-ever-after (HEA) in store. * Grace finally turns Baby over to his father with Grey's support. * Baby finally gets a name, Robbie. * Grace and Grey do get married... at the Summer Solstice celebration. Grace insists, rather belatedly, that Grey date her. And being modern and all, that "dating" means that they can have sex at will. Grace just refuses to live with Grey until they're married. * Michael MacBain and Grey's clan make up, realizing that their common past and grappling with the present and future mean they need one another. In fact, when Grace's six hulking step-brothers make a to-do about Grace being 4 months pregnant at her wedding, Michael takes sides with Grey's clan. * The bad guys, conveniently including Grace's boss and ex, are hurled through time by Pendaar/Daar... I think we're to assume that they land in the past -- the exact time is unknown. Cynical? Yes, I'm afraid by the light of day, I am. But if you read the book as I originally did, being willing to go with the flow and suspend a lot of questions and disbelief, it's a fun read.

More reviews on my blog  Inside My Library Mind Rating: 3.5-4 I have seen this book pop up from time to time in the bookish community in the past year. As always, what drew me to it is not the story itself, but the title. I tend to verge towards books with interesting titles. And that title! I love it. Matched with the gorgeous cover, the book was instantly on my radar. This is a multiple POV story and we follow four different teenagers' perspectives as they deal with their lives in the rural part of Alaska in the 1970s. That's what really makes this book stand out. The setting is so unique and different than what you're used to. I know nothing about Alaska and it was really interesting to see a story that is set against that backdrop, and we even got to explore a bit of politics, with some mention of the statehood and how it affected the citizens of Alaska. Also, the Alaskan imagery was really pretty, and made this almost magical atmosphere. Which leads me to my next point, and that's the writing. Hitchcock's writing is really beautiful. It's sort of hazy and poetic and matches the backdrop she created perfectly. It's really atmospheric and it really pulls you into the story. This is obviously a character driven story, and the characters are wonderful. I really enjoyed all of them. We follow Dora who comes from a difficult family background, Ruth who finds herself dealing with a very serious secret, Alyce who struggles between her dreams of being a dancer and the fear of disappointing her father and finally, Hank who is struggling to protect his brothers the only way he knows how. I enjoyed every single one of them in a different way. I found them all interesting, and I wasn't eager to spend more time with a specific character - I loved every single perspective. And there's also a myriad of side characters that are spectacular and their relationships to our main four were wonderfully portrayed. However, I was really detached from the characters and the story for the first half of the book. I loved the characters, the writing, the plot, but I just wasn't connecting with it. I am not entirely sure why. But, when the POVs started to converge and mix, that's when I started to become more invested in the story, and by the end it really got to me. This is a quiet, and unassuming novel, but also a very heartwarming one. It's a story about family and friendship, dark at times, but very rewarding by the end. I would highly recommend it.

2.8 Stars Unfortunately, the book felt generic... Romantic Heat: I'm just a girl, standing in front of a dragon, asking him to love me Pacing:  pass the popcorn, the movie is starting Promising POV: Pretty sure I've read this before Will I read your next book:   Depends on what else comes out that month So, the cover is terrible. And the tagline, "X-book-you-loved meets y-book-you-loved in this new book that we also want you to love," is, unsurprisingly, misleading. BUT, but, it wasn't actually terrible. ...It had dragons that aren't really dragons and mostly look like really, really ridiculously good-looking (insert Zoolander voice) humans, and a race of bird people that don't really look like birds and actually just look like really, really ridiculously good-looking (insert Zoolander voice) humans with feathers instead of hair. There was a magical object. And an epic Romeo and Juliet "love for the ages" thing happening. A sassy outcast. A loyal, underdeveloped best-friend. A pseudo love triangle. And much, much more. But let me tell you what I actually thought  the book got right. I loved the country hopping. It was awesome. Though, like most things in the book, I wish it could have been explored a little bit more. Apart from the Black Forest, the NYC library and a random apartment in Strasbourg, none of the places were allowed to come to life very vividly. This was in part because the author also had two entirely separate fantasy worlds to build in the frame of one story. The locations never became characters, which is a shame when you are bouncing around from Kyoto to Paris to Scotland to NYC to etc...  But  I liked that the world hopping existed. It gave the story more scope. I loved the magical logic of the natural arches and places of travel as gates. And I felt like there was a very clear sense of both Grey, the author, and the main character's affection for travel. (Though some cultural representation would have been nice.) Echo was actually a relatively effective main character. After Grey let go of her obsession with food a little bit and allowed the character to gain some depth, I actually enjoyed Echo's sassiness. Sure there was some Mary-Sue stuff happening. But I liked that Echo wasn't an expert fighter, and instead she ran from trouble. I also liked that traveling with and using magic took a toll on her because she is human. She wasn't invincible, even if  she ended up being the key to ending a centuries long magical war, which, let's be honest, is super Mary-Sue. I'm not sure I understand why the Firebird would choose a human vessel, given that a) it is magical and b) its last vessel was Avicen. I also loved both Echo's and Grey's obvious adoration of books and mythology. I like a main-character that quotes Shakespeare and I believe her. A lot of people were frustrated by the purple prose, particularly in relation to physical descriptions. First, props to Grey for never once giving us a physical description of Echo. We had a clear sense of who the character was without being told that she was beautiful or she had hair like sunshine or chocolate and eyes like blah or blah. I appreciate that the author wasn't hung up on our lead character's physical appearance. On the other hand, Grey deserves a slap on the wrist for having exclusively beautiful male characters and spending excessive amounts of time describing their beauty. Even the dude with one eye is apparently super hot. It was definitely a bit much, and pretty objectifying. Which brings me to Casius. I am going to to go on a rant here in a minute,  but first...   I think working the idea of some kind of cosmic predestination into the romance helps to mitigate some of my complaints about it. The notion that Casius is drawn to the vessel of the firebird and Rose (the last vessel) is taking over Echo's body a bit, explains away some of the insta-love. It could be really interesting if Grey actually decides to explore the complications of the two brains/memories - one body thing Echo has going on at the end in the next installment of the series. Echo feels like she can't trust her own body and Casius thinks he loves Echo but maybe he just loves the echo of Rose... moving on...   rant commencing now... Why is it, that in YA novels there is always some hundred year old, thousand year old, immortal dude who falls in love with a teenage human? I know the teenage humans in these books are always super, duper special teenage humans, but even so, teenage humans are the literal worst. Teenagers are going through all kinds of hormonal and emotional upheaval. They over-react. They have very little framework for making logical choices and judgements. They are horny as f**k but are only just learning about their own sexuality--they very rarely have ownership over it. A lot of times, they aren't even physically done growing yet. They usually have some kind of acne. They are only just starting to shape their political views. I'm not trying to rag on teenagers or being a teen. It is an amazing time. Falling in love for the first time is nuts and awesome and awful. Feeling everything so strongly is fantastic. And coming into your own confidence is great. BUT,   but, why, oh why, would a man who has lived, in the case of this book, 250 years and ruled over a bloodthirsty, magical war fall in love with a seventeen year-old girl? Even if, as we are told, she is really charming. I get why a thousand year old vampire might have the hots for a ripe, young teenager. He's literally a dead guy being brought back to life by his lover's youthfulness. But this is such a weird trope to me. I am not especially old. But in my mid twenties, I cannot imagine having to date a teenager. As I said, teenagers are the worst. So you think about all the teenagers a 250 year old dragon man must have met--dragon teenagers must be as ridiculous as human teenagers, right?-- and you have to ask yourself why he is setting the bar for romance so low. Does this trope bother other people as much as it annoys me? I just feel like it transforms even creative YA heroines into the worst Mary-Sues. rant fini Anyway, like I said, I actually liked many aspects of the book. It was exceptionally read-able. But it didn't feel fresh. It was actually pretty derivative, and it is hard not to compare a book about a quest for the firebird with the Grisha series (which I loved), hence the just short of 3 stars rating. I don't know that I care to read the next installment. But I saw creative potential from the author and I thought the pacing of the story was pretty solid. Grey got some things right, and the book was a fun, but pretty shallow read.

Actual Rating: 3.5/5. This book was a really good read. It was quirky and fun to read and I had a great time reading it. Throughout the entire book, Jasmine overcomes the hatred (strong dislike would be more accurate) and become friends with him. The exchanges they have are fun to read and had me smiling. Read more reviews at What Danielle Did Next WHEN THE WORLD WAS FLAT (AND WE WERE IN LOVE) is one of those books where I'm tempted to just push it into your hands and shoo you away to read it because I am terrified of giving away any spoilers! The story of Lillie, a young girl from Nebraska who has a nagging feeling she's met new boy Tom before is both highly original and captivating. I read this book in a matter of hours, compelled to turn the pages until the stirring conclusion. Ingrid Jonach has created characters whom are realistic and endearing and a story filled with mystery and intrigue and (most importantly for the girlish side of me) love. Six months ago Lillie was a well put together, organised young woman who's biggest worry was what crazy new-age scheme her mother would thrust on her next and what plans she and her friends Sylvie and Jo had for the weekend. Then...the nightmares started. Hazy, yet terrifying, Lillie slowly begins to dread going to sleep as a sinister figure stalks her dreams. As time progresses the dreams become more vivid and Lillie finds it hard to distinguish between reality and nightmare when darkness falls. When Tom enters the picture, playing hot and cold with her emotions, Lillie finds herself even more confused. As she and Tom dance around each other, taking one step forward and one step back simultaneously, she wonders if she'll ever get the answers she seeks. Who is Tom? Why does she recognise him? Who is the shadowy figure in her dreams and why is her best friend acting like she's in "Invasion of the Body Snatchers"? One thing I found incredibly interesting about this book is how the relationship between Tom and Lillie developed as the book progresses. At first as Lillie meets Tom, drawn to his mysterious nature I feared the dreaded insta-love, even more so when Tom acts like he's repelled by her one minute and swooping in as saviour the next. However while their relationship is indeed central to the plot, Lillie doesn't lose herself in this boy and I was happy to note that Jonach places a great emphasis on the female friendships Lillie has with Jo and Sylvie. Their presence is felt throughout the book and they are never relegated to the shadows as Lillie and Tom's story takes shape. Indeed the same can be said for Lillie's relationship with her mother. While Deb might not be a fan of conventional parenting she is always there for her daughter which in YA is rare particularly when the boy enters the picture. Lillie and Tom's connection is mind bending and captivating as is the reason for Lillie's nightmarish dreams and loathe to give away any spoilers let me just say it made the whole story wildly romantic for me and while I'm not the sharpest tool in the box when it comes to Einstein and physics, Jonach's use of science to weave a story that is equal parts dream-like and realistic is no small feat and is both exceptional and captivating. Highly recommend!

Stephen L. Carter had researched Lincoln's era before writing this novel, and was aware of how unpopular Lincoln had been. That's why he imagined that if Lincoln had survived being shot by John Wilkes Booth, he might very well have been impeached. When I saw this title for the first time, I also recognized it as a realistic possibility. The central character of this speculative fiction actually wasn't Lincoln. It was the fictional free African American clerk at the law firm in charge of Lincoln's defense. Her name was Abigail Canner, and Lincoln was her hero. She considered him the Great Emancipator. As far as Abigail was concerned, Lincoln was the one who had brought about a new world for the members of her race. And in that new world, Abigail could dream of becoming a lawyer. Abigail is a courageous and determined idealist. This is shown when early in the novel one of the lawyers at the firm is murdered along with an African American woman named Rebecca. Both the police and the remaining partner at the firm tell Abigail not to investigate these killings, but Abigail refuses to leave this case alone. She wants justice for the victims, and she wants to discover the truth behind the murders. She learned that truth and justice aren't very high priorities in the pragmatic realm of politicians. Someone else might have become cynical and disillusioned, but Abigail maintained her values. So this has good characterization, a suspenseful mystery sub-plot and politics that will remind readers of current events on Capitol Hill. The Impeachment of Abraham Lincoln is truly a thought provoking alternate history that I recommend. For my complete review see http://wwwbookbabe.blogspot.com/2014/...

Two years ago, after the The Dark Knight Rises screening massacre in Colorado, I read Columbine by Dave Cullen, an incredible account of the Columbine High School massacre in April 1999, to try to understand the way of thinking of mass shooters-- what drove them? Why kill the innocent? Usually, personality and/or mental disorders are the underlying reasons. In Columbine's case, Eric Harris was a "classic psychopath," while Dylan Klebold was a depressed and angry teenager who made friends with the wrong guy. These are quotes by Dave Cullen after his research and analysis on Harris: He already knew where it would end. Every page pointed in the same direction. His purpose was not self-discovery but self-lionisation. Psychopaths appear charming and likable, but it's an act. They are cold-hearted manipulators who will do anything for their own gain. See, Oliver Reznick reminded me a lot of Eric Harris. It started when they killed the doe, a deer, a female deer, and Oliver mentioned the natural selection-- they were both obsessed with it. After that, the similarities kept on appearing. They were so alike that it was like I was reading more glimpses of Harris's life before the incident. Chloe was his Dylan, but there were hints throughout that she might also be an Eric. After the months of hardship that she's been through, she was jealous, angry, wanted out and needed someone to help her break free. Oliver was glad to. With that knowledge, we'd believe that Chloe would learn from him, be responsible for the "accident" and get away with it. Also, if you read Dangerous Girls, that was a given. I wasn't even surprised that she was the one who stabbed Ethan and killed Oliver. But still, the author won't let you breathe comfortably yet, because the most twisted and shocking part of the story, same with Dangerous Girls, came in the penultimate chapter-- we got a glimpse of Chloe's true and newly-developed messed-up mentality. Which begs the question: Will she be worse than Oliver? Although this book didn't have as much mystery as Dangerous Girls, it's still as thrilling and haunting. This story is more about the development of a person from being normal to the eyes of other people into a dangerous one, and like what was said in the opening paragraph, the circumstances and choices which drove them to be that way. You can never really know someone. You can never know anyone at all. Abigail Haas writes beautifully. She knows how much mystery to put to grasp a reader's attention and curiosity throughout the entire book. She keeps you second-guessing, directs you to her complex characters' dark and dangerous minds, and you follow anyway. I will purchase and read any Young Adult Mystery-Thrillers that she writes from now on.

When Cleo's entire family was murdered by Mannix, the king's adviser, Clio has inherited the powers of her mother, the Oracle of Sheehan. Now hunted by Mannix, Clio seeks refuge in Sheehan's sister city, Morek, by dressing up as a slave. If anyone discovers her identity, she will have her heart cut out as a sacrifice to the Deities on top of the pyramid. Clio has no choice but to win the trust of Riece, the prison's guard that won't hesitate to kill her if he discovers who she truly is. But the visions she sees are of Mannix bringing up a barbarian army into Sheehan and she's the only one that has the power and foresight to stop him. Can she embrace her destiny and sacrifice everything for her city? Wow. I don't recall ever reading a book in the POV of an Oracle before, but now that I have, the only thing I can say is that was so enthralling. I really loved how Cleo used her powers for a greater good and even though she wasn't able to save everybody, I'm glad that she stood up for the innocent slaves.The writing was fluid and very easy to read. Yes, there is a love triangle and yes the ending was so surprising that it left me rocking back and forth in my corner in absolute denial. HA! LIES. Riece can now be mine. Muahahah. The thing is I don't understand where did the Oracles come from? How did it happen? Why does Cleo suddenly have fighting skills that come with the power? Why can't she predict her own death? Also, I don't really get it. If the Oracle can't have any lover, how the fuck are they to have kids? I don't know how it works in your world there but I'm pretty sure that it goes like this: Girl+Guy+Sex= Child. (I don't know there. I might be wrong.) So many questions are left unanswered. The world building needs a bit more work. Although I thought that Cleo was a little naive at times, I had to constantly remind myself that I'm dealing with a fifteen year old here. Hopefully, she'll have time to wisen-up in the sequels and be even more of a bad-ass. I liked it a lot. Definitely recommend it.

I love middle grade books. Find them to be amazing and well written. This is the second middle grade book by Lauren Oliver that I have read. I adored her first MG book; Liesl and Po. It was perfect. And I knew I needed to own The Spindlers when it released. The cover is gorgeous. And I liked the summary a lot. And now that I have finished it, I can say that it is amazing. Not perfect, but extremely good and very well written. With amazing lead character girl, and other great characters. While The Spindlers is not as perfect at Liesl and Po, it is still perfect. It is written really well, and the characters are likeable. I did like the world Lauren has created for this book. But some things did confuse me, and was a bit too much Fantasy. But I still enjoyed it all, for the most part :D And even though I found a few things a bit silly, I still loved reading about it all. Even the big female rat wearing clothes and make-up. Even enjoyed the Spindlers. The creepy creatures. I will be sharing a few details about it all :) It really was a great book. So sweet, as well. The main character in this book is Liza, and the whole book is from her point of view. I liked that. Liza is a young girl living with her younger brother and mother and father. Then one day she wakes up and her brother is different. Not himself. Still looks like him, and remember everything about him, he just doesn't act like himself. Liza knows right away that his soul has been taken by the Spindlers. Taken Below. She knows this because her old babysitter Anna told them all about them. About the creatures living below them. And I actually liked that :) I do enjoy fantasy books. Liza decides to go get her brother, Patrick's, soul back. This is where the journey begins. I won't say all the things that happen. Will mention a few things, though :) A few characters ;p While going Below, Liza meets someone. She meets a rat. A female rat almost as tall as she is. This rat is named Mirabella. She's not like other rats; cause she wears clothes and make-up. And she stands on two legs instead of four. She is a weird creature. But also pretty awesome. I did like her. Even though she was annoying most of the time, and I disliked her for a bit near the end. But she was pretty awesome :) We get to see so many creatures in this book. I did like the Spindlers. Even though they were awful and creepy and a bit scary. They were really interesting :) Then there were the Scawgs. Wish we had seen more of those. Even though they did seem a bit worse than the Spindlers. In my opinion, at least ;p I did like what we did get to see about them, though. Cause they were pretty creepy and awful. But also so fascinating and interesting to read about. One of the highlights of this book ;) Also liked reading about the nocturna. They were a bit weird, but I also liked them. Because they were special. The plot in this book is special. And unique, in a way. Even though it does remind me of many books. But I really didn't mind that. Because for one, this is a middle grade book. No romance. And a non-complicated main character. Sort of. And the creatures in this book were special and unique, and I did love them all. Pretty much, at least ;p Anyway. I liked the story in this book. I'm not really sure what else to say. I don't want to spoil this book. Just know that I liked the characters a lot, and the writing, and the story. And I did love the ending. The book is a bit short, and I wished it had been longer. But I was also happy with what there were. I think you should read this book. But you should be liking middle grade books :) Haven't read MG yet? Then you must start with Liesl and Po by Lauren. <3 It is so good. Best middle grade book I have read so far :)

Superb conclusion to this 2 part series. What a rollercoaster of a ride and emotions. It's sick, twisted and perverse, but oh so good! This book is actually written from 3 PoV's and we get the thoughts and feelings of Benny, Jade and Dillon. I liked Benny's chapters, it was good to get inside his mind, but also get the flashbacks from his childhood that are featured. This book continues from where Pretty Stolen Dolls ended. So we jump straight back into the crazy world of Benjamin and his Dolls. So Jade is back in Benny's 'care', back as his prisoner and his dolly. But things have changed for Jade - she's not the child she once was. She's now a lot tougher and a lot more determined to play with Benny's mind. Dillon is brilliant in this book! I love his character and his fight for Jade is brilliant to read. But nothing about this book is easy. There is plenty of action in this book and some major plot twists that you won't see coming at all. My heart was racing the whole time whilst reading this and I simply could not put it down. I needed to get to the end, I needed to see what was going to happen and I needed to know how it was going to end.... OMG THAT ENDING!!!!! This book is full of darkness and suspense. You don't know what's coming and what the authors are going to hit you with next. The writing flows brilliantly, and the way these 2 authors have created such a fantastic story together is simply brilliant! At no point does it feel rushed. A perfect duet of darkness, full of twisted, creepy, crazy, happenings! You won't know what has hit you, yet I got so much feeling out of this book it's making me question my own mind! 5 'sick, sick, sick' stars!! Lou 4TLoReading Blog

I liked this book. Really, I did. I was going to give it 4 stars, but then the last few pages just ... *sigh* The book is a sort of book-within-a-book: we find out (not so early on), that we're reading a "biographical" story that Adam Walker, our main character, is writing. Each section takes place in a different season: Spring, Summer, Fall. And each section  is written from a different point of view. No problemo there. I'm with Auster on this, I'm digging it, I'm digging the ploys he uses, the literary tricks, all that jazz. I didn't mind the three seasonal sections to Walker's book, or the shifting narrator. I also didn't mind the total brake-screeching flip to Cecile's point of view. However, that last section did lose some points with me. I was fine with the shift in narrator, even shifting away from the 1967 book (although that kind of made me... sad? No, not sad. I was just sorry to see us stray from Walker's book, but I saw what Auster was doing with it as plot, finishing the Born story with the only person who knew the end of the Born story). But it just felt like it draaaaaged on longer than it needed to. And yet, I don't know what I would cut out. Maybe it was that I felt like we'd invested so much in reading Walker's book for the first 3/4 of the book, that now that we were reading someone else's work (Cecile's diary) , we spent too much time away from Walker's book. That might be it. Whatever it was, it felt like the Cecile/Born  story could have been snipped a little, and thus it was sort of a let-down ending to what had been a decent book. So then, this book brings into question a lot about certainty/ambiguity/What do we know?/What do we not know?/What can we believe?/unreliable narrators (And I wouldn't have made most of these connections without the  21st Century Literature group). It makes for a really baffling read, but baffling in a good way. The kind of baffling read that gives your brain a workout. Plus, it's a crazy-ass, mixed-up story, so you can get sucked into all of the "What?!?!" and "Say wha?!?!" moments.

What Happens Now is so much different than what I expected it to be. I thought that it was going to be a dark tale about depression and cutting, but turns out that it's not. It's much lighter than that, although that's not to say that it doesn't mention those things. But actually, I think that I prefer it this way. What Happens Now is different from most YA contemporary romance because it delves into the serious stuff about relationships, where they fight about things that matter in relationships. Most other books have couples who often fight just because of some misunderstanding or something similarly unimportant. In this book, Camden and Ari talked about the fact that there should be a give and take in their relationship. I really admired how they actually talked about things to each other, instead of making the other just guess. Well, Camden sometimes did, but Ari always talked to him whenever that happens. What Happens Now features a lot of relationships, such as an old friendship, new friendships, mother-daughter, sister-half sister, and daughter-stepfather. It was actually quite surprising to see how Ari was closer to her stepfather rather than her mom, and it's a welcome one because most YA would feature characters who hate their stepfathers. However, Ari has a rocky relationship with her mom, mostly I think because they just don't have the same "language" of things, so they get what the other is trying to convey. The only thing that I didn't really like with this book is the fact that it has a not-so-solid beginning and ending. The beginning weirded me out a little, and I was completely thrown of by it. Because of the beginning, I thought this was going to be another book just focused on the main character's relationship with a boy. The ending, on the other hand, felt inadequate to me. I didn't feel a sense of closure, and as I said, they always talked things through in their relationship, so I felt disappointed that they didn't do so in the end. I just felt like there was something lacking. But actually, with this book - and this is the first time ever that I am going to say this - I think I would have preferred it if they didn't get back together. Ari had a lot of progress and realizations after they broke up, and I thought this might be a book about how you could love someone, but know when they might be wrong for you, so you just have to let go of that, even if they helped you become a better person. But in a way, I'm also glad that they ended up together, because in the end Camden was also able to realize his mistake. Overall, What Happens Now is a great and quick read. I wouldn't really classify it as a light read - although I did mention that it's lighter than what I expected it to be - because it tackles a lot of things, which you have to read this book to find out. So yes, I do encourage you to read this book. I know that it might not be for everyone, but I really liked reading it.

I received this book from NetGalley. Overall, I liked this book. It definitely has some issues, but the story is really entertaining so I was able to look past most of the flaws. First, the introduction is not very good, but it the story does get better so don't let the intro stop you. The authors do more telling than showing or allowing the reader to see the world through the characters eyes in the first few chapters. At one point Dani stops in her lobby to admire the building that she lives in and to describe it to herself. At another point Zoe decides to describe exactly what she is wearing as she is changing. None of these details added to the story and they really should have been left out. Fortunately, the premise of the story was enough for me to keep reading. I was intrigued by what was going on in the world and kept going to see what would happen. I am glad that I continued on with this story. The overall concept was really neat and I thought that it was well done. I liked the idea that the virus changed most people that survived and though the addition of people having special powers was a neat twist. I also liked the survival aspect of the book. There were still a few things that I didn't like  mainly Dani getting over the death of her fiance so quickly. The guy just died and while she felt some remorse it just didn't feel like enough. I wish the authors would have left the Cam portion out entirely and had just made Dani single as this would have made her actions a little more likable. I found as the book progressed I ended up liking Dani (despite her actions in the beginning) more than Zoe. Another part that I felt should have been left out were the emails, they got better as the story progressed but felt unnecessary and most of the time just recapped what we had already read. The book would have been a lot better without these exchanges included or if they had contained material that we did not just read about. Even with these complaints,the story is still really entertaiing and kept me reading from page to page. I also grew to like the characters as the story progressed and wanted to find out what happened to them. I found this entertaining enough to read the second book. I think this definitely could have been edited a bit more to include some of the unnecessary parts but overall I really enjoyed.

4/5 stars Heartless by Marissa Meyer is a book I heard mixed reviews from. I wasn't sure if I would enjoy it,but I actually really like it. Heartless is a retelling of Alice in Wonderland and is a prequel to the story about how the Queen of hearts became the queen of hearts. This story follow a girl named Catherine and all she wants in life is to be a baker and open a bakery. Unfortunately she happens to be one of the kings favourite people. She goes to a ball and meets the court joker and starts to like him a bit more than she expected too. I really liked this book though a few things kept me from giving it a 5 star rating. The first thing is world building. I think that the world building could of been better. Even though most people are familiar with the world of Hearts/Wonderland, I feel like the story could of been even better with more world building. The second thing was the romance. Hear me out please. My complaint is that it felt too rushed and very much like our good old friend insta love. I feel like is Meyer made the romance longer as well it could of made the ending have a bit more sense, but again not drag it out too much or the story would of been too long. However I liked the book enough to push the insta love aside while reading but I feel as if i have to address it here. Remember this is the story of how the Queen of Hearts became the Queen of Hearts. This is a prequel to Alice in Wonderland. The ending to me  was so sad. I could not believe how a sweet girl can be so greedy and ruthless.
Not as good as 1, but more world building and twisty at the end.

Let the Great World Spin is a novel that takes time. Time to read, time to absorb, and time to make decisions about. McCann's work is filled with poignant lines that you want to scribble down on a piece of paper and thrust in some drawer so that one day you might come upon them again and say "Yes, that's it. He got that exactly right." In 1974, a tightrope walker made an insane yet impressive journey along a wire stretched between the towers of the WTC. This remarkable event serves as McCann's jumping point--a moment that links a host of people across the city, not just those who stood on the streets below, ignoring their responsibilities to watch in awe. The characters we meet come from various backgrounds and lifestyles. On the surface, they seem to have little in common. Along the way, however, it becomes clear that each of them struggles with life, they all try their best, they all suffer for their failures. God is mentioned several times throughout, both as a guiding force and as someone in dire need of an ass-kicking. The most common feeling they share is one of sliding. Sliding through life, letting things go, shrugging things off, trying to fit into the lives they've created for themselves. The Irish immigrants, the It girl, the hookers on the stroll, the woman from Park Avenue and many more--they all share a desperation to deal with the facts of their present. They've all suffered loss and it's caused them to live in a world that slides on by while they linger on thoughts of how they got to this point and how they can muster up the oomph to carry on. The tightrope walker serves as a stark contrast. He is free. He lives for this moment where he feels the air above and below, where he can dare to do the impossible and make it his own. He recreates himself through his walks. He isn't, as one character thinks, making a mockery of death. Instead he is celebrating life and all that's made possible through sheer perseverance. It took me ages to get through this book. It's dense. There are connections to be made and layers to peel away. There are moments that resonate and others I can't relate to at all. But it was thought-provoking and often felt like a puzzle to be unraveled: Connect the dots, who knows whom, compare and contrast and find the commonality that links all these disparate creatures, ponder their lives and contemplate what would have made them whole. I'm sure there's a lesson or three to be gleaned from these lives, from McCann's lovely prose and the naked discussion of failure. At the end though, it all comes down to this: "The world spins. We stumble on. It is enough."

2 stars. Love is friendship that has caught fire. It is quiet understanding, mutual confidence, sharing and forgiving. It is loyalty through good and bad times. It settles for less than perfection and makes allowances for human weaknesses. If you're a fan of the NA genre you'e probably going to love Built. It was fast paced and sexy, with a great tattooed H and just the right amount of angst. But to me? Built was just an okay read. I didn't connect to the characters or their stories, meaning I didn't care about what was happening. I was caught off guard by the Hyde reveal, but it didn't really make me feel much. I kind of liked Zeb, and I definitely liked Hyde, but aside from that? Meh. Sayer didn't seem all that interesting to me, and as I kept reading my opinion of her didn't change. And this book had a huuuuuuge case of instalust. It started right from the prologue and didn't let up. Zeb fell in lust with Sayer at first sight and decided he wanted to have her. He was pretty upfront about wanting to date her, though, which I appreciated. Sayer, for her turn, couldn't make up her mind and kept trying to convince herself that Zeb didn't want anything serious with her. Another problem I had, but this is more of a personal pet peeve than anything: really long paragraphs. Just blocks of text that covered most of the page. That made it really hard for me to focus on what I was reading. Maybe I'm outgrowing these kind of books? I don't know. There wasn't anything in Built that kept me glued to my Kindle, turning pages to see what was going to happen next. I was not invested in Sayer and Zeb's relationship at all. I was actually more interested in a few of the side-characters than in them as a couple, to be honest. The one high point was Hyde and all moments with Hyde. Overall, this was not a bad book. If I read it a few years ago I probably would have loved it. But as it is, I couldn't connect to it. I'm sure Jay Crownover and NA fans will have a great time reading it if they give it a chance, though. Series: #1 in the spin-off Saints of Denver series. POV: Told from Sayer and Zeb's POVs. Content Warnings: Abuse. Instalove: Insta-instalust. Yeah, it was that quick. Steam: So steamy it was the entire focus of a few chapters. Love Triangle: No. Cheating: No. Cliffhanger: No. HEA: Yes. Up Next: Charged

Fairy tales are either usually really good or really terrible, IMHO. This one might be in a class of its own because the realism is so stark, and the fairy tale aspects are more mysterious. And that combination makes for one of the best reads I've had in a long time. Plus these characters and their relationships, as well as the setting of Alaska homesteaders, all make for a riveting reading experience.

The romance was the best part, the two main characters' relationship developed in a believable way, the difficulty of Denna's betrothal to Mare's brother and the two of them not knowing whether the other felt the same came across beautifully. The politics didn't work so well. The court intrigue and the murders and assassinations felt remote, it didn't really feel like Denna and Mare had a lot of personal stake in it. Even the prohibition against magic thing didn't work too well, at no point in the book did I really feel like Denna was at risk of being discovered until the climax when she suddenly was. No one was looking in her direction until then. I picked this book up because of the romance (and lesbihonest, isn't that why most of us picked up this book?) and I got what I wanted, which is a sweet story about two princesses falling in love. I didn't really set my expectations too high for the politics and other stuff but I would be interested in delving more into the magic system of this world, the author gives you enough to work with there but it's not too detailed (but it's also not too info-dump-y either). This book met my expectations but didn't exceed them, which is why I gave it four stars.

I picked up this book after seeing Ginger from Greads! rave about it. I saw her amazing review and immediately requested the book from my library. Once it came it was a 4-week loan and I had lots of other books to read so I kind of forgot about it. Last weekend I had a good friend visiting and she saw the book sitting on my shelf and said she couldn't believe we'd never talked about it before, that she and her friends had passed it around to each other in college, and that she really liked it. When I picked it up this weekend to start reading it I was kind of appalled at the condition of the library book. I debated not reading it, but my curiosity and belief that if I returned it I'd never read it got the better of me and I decided I'd take the chance of getting bedbugs or god-knows what else was that was undoubtably lurking between the pages. I loved this book, I really did. I loved Beatrice and I loved the overall tone of the book. Even though Beatrice and Jacob's relationship was so insta-love, something I'm normally not a fan of, I still believed it and wanted them to be together even though it's not a relationship I would ever want to be in myself. And Jacob is not a guy I would ever want to date, he's way too artsy/broody/out there for me, but I absolutely loved the way he was with Beatrice. My love of Beatrice goes deep. I saw a lot of myself in Beatrice, both good and bad and big and small. We both have lingering distrust and fear of abandonment from crappy relationships with our parents and we both tend to push people away because of it. And we also both have a highly developed sense of smell that sometimes causes us to do strange things. I loved her commitment to her work and how she was proud of her business and never apologized her for success. I also really loved her attitude towards sex. She wanted sex, she liked sex, she had sex. Overall I really loved the way that the sex in Beatrice and Jacob's relationship was depicted. It just felt so real to me. Going into the book I knew it was going to destroy me. I knew Beatrice and Jacob's relationship wasn't going to have a happy ending. In one way I'm glad I knew this because I don't think I could have dealt with that coming out of no where but in another way I spent so much of the book dreading what I knew was coming and guessing how it was going to happen (I never guessed correctly until right before it happened). One of my favorite things about this book was the quotability. I'm not one who normally pulls quotes out of books, but this one had some real winners, both because they were profound or because I related to them so well. Some of my favorites: "I usually prefer my own company to any old idiot, unless I'm really horny." "He winked at me when he walked by and, for kicks, I almost tripped him, but I held back. I didn't want Jacob to think I was mean." "I had visions of becoming the twenty first century's answer to Anais Nin. When I'm dead, I want strangers to read about all the awesome sex I had and wish they could be so lucky." "That's why I always thought if I ever had to go to jail, I'd rather get thrown in for life as opposed to say, thirty years. With life, you just sit back and chill and get on with whatever it is you do inside a prison for the remainder of your days. Thirty years, and you're counting the years by the minutes." "All I could think of was, why can't I be as stupid as Lucille? Why can't I blame all my successes and all my failures in The Lord Jesus Christ Almighty? I would be so fucking happy if I lived like that." "...You can't put life on pause and then catch up when you have more energy to give. You have to play it all the way through to the end." "But I believe in the possibility of everything." So when Jacob died it was terrible, obviously. I shed many, many tears and lost a considerable amount of snot. I feel like most of the time when someone dies I'm upset for the person/people who are left. And I was sad for Beatrice, absolutely, but I was more sad for Jacob. I just can't stop picturing him under the water, aware that he was drowning and that this was the end. What was he thinking? Earlier in the book he said how death didn't scare him and I hope he wasn't scared at that moment. But part of me also wanted him to be scared and sad and upset that he's never going to see his Trixie again. I don't know why I felt like that. I didn't have particularly strong feelings about Jacob while I was reading, I don't know where they came from at the end.

1.5 stars It's been weeks since I picked this up from the library and I still question myself: Why did I even borrow it in the first place? While the name did attract me, reminding me of the Humpty Dumpty rhyme and the font giving it a thrilling feel, the cover should have been a huge turn-off. I just can't find a single appealing thing about the cover. "Don't judge a book by its cover." Okay, so I read the summary. But it didn't exactly make me really wanna read it, just the passing thought of "oh that sounds cool". But then, I guess I was bored and tired from walking up and down the rows of shelves and just so overwhelmed by the book choices that I was not able to make a rational decision then. So I made an irrational decision, and I borrowed it. They All Fall Down wasn't exactly a pain to read (I did finish it in five days after all). It was an easy read and I managed to get to the end quickly but it was a bore fest throughout. Where's the mystery? Where's the thrill? The girls on the list (except Kenzie) were so chill that you wouldn't think that people were dying. It's just "keep your secrets to yourself and no one gets hurt". Once again: Where is the mystery? Oh, but wait, what is this list you mention? Let me tell you: it's called The Hottie List. It's a list of apparently the hottest girls in the school and is decided by the boys' votes. And this year, being on the list might get you killed. So guess who's on the list this year? That's right, our dear female protagonist who could care less about her looks but somehow manages to land herself on the list, claiming the fifth spot, no less. And that drives a wedge between her friendship with her best friend (who I have forgotten the name of and cannot be bothered to look up). Our dear female protagonist then proceeds to catch the attention of two guys, one of which thinks that now that she's on the list, she's worthy of his attention, and the other just thinks that she's in danger. One is the golden boy, the other is the bad boy. And who does our dear female protagonist choose? Why the bad boy of course, despite having had a crush on the golden boy. The bad boy, also, doesn't care about the list. I guess they were made for each other after all. I have a huge HUGE problem with the ending. It bothers me even now. Assassins?? The FBI??? Are Kenzie and friends working for the FBI now???? They're a bunch of high school students. What can they do against a secret organization of trained assassins?? Also, Kenzie indirectly kills someone (aka the evil grandfather by pushing him off a cliff) and she feels little to zero remorse over it?? Did she think it was in the name of revenge or something???????? Do you see the NUMBER OF QUESTION MARKS I HAVE?????????? I am a logical person and I just do not understand the logic in this ending. But well, 1.5 stars for decent writing and plot. At least it wasn't a total mess. Instagram // Blog // Tumblr // Twitter

It is rare that I like a book about or by men/boys. I loved this book. It took a bit for me to get into, as it usually does with boy narrators, but I was invested in the story and each character. Even the supporting characters, like Jill, Berry, Spoony, Rashad's parents, Will, and English, were full of depth and brought out the best in Quinn and Rashad. What I appreciate most about books is their characters' development. One of the more common reasons I dislike books is because I feel that the character is the same person at the end of the book as they were in the beginning. I felt like every character changed, or their true nature was revealed (such as Guzzo). Jill's storyline could easily have been obnoxious--just a love interest or flat. Instead, she pushed Quinn to keep going when he felt himself weaken. They didn't kiss in the entire book, or indicate at all that there could be a relationship between them. They were friends before anything, and Jill inspired Quinn to be a better person. That was enough for him. And that was refreshing as a woman reading this book! In general, there wasn't the casual misogyny that so often comes from books with boy narrators, and that made a huge difference for me as a woman reader.

I was a little nervous about reading this since I was disappointed by the last book. But I heard that this was a lot better. Although in the beginning I was less interested in reading Adrian's POV. I was much more interested in Sydney and the re education center. I was really interested in Duncan. I was also glad that Adrian didn't stay but a few weeks at Court. I wanted to yell at him the whole time. I've heard that some was pissed at Nina for kissing Adrian. I'm not. I don't blame Nina. It was exactly like Sonya had told Adrian. Nina was falling for Adrian and he was sending her mixed signals. Not saying that Adrian did it on purpose or knew what he was doing. Honestly if I was Nina I would of came to the same conclusion she had. My favorite part was the after the escape. Marcus should of known Sydney would divert from the plan. Honestly, Sydney's reasons made sense. And I loved the outcome. And the fallout because of it! And the ending! I'm ready for the next/last book. One thing I had noticed and not sure how I feel about it. Going in the first book in the series, I was under the impression that this series was supposed to be more about Jill. Wasn't that the connection to the title Bloodlines and the series name? Although with knowing Sydney was the narrative, I guess I always knew the series would be more about Sydney. I loved the whole wedding part! I love that even though the main reason to get marry so soon was it should protect her from the Alchemists, Adrian was able to give her a wedding to remember, and not just a trip to the courthouse for some quickie wedding. Even though before he thought about a marriage would provide her with protection, I kept on mentally yelling at them to call Abe. I have no doubt in my mind that the Alchemists took Jill.

Ruby Dixon definitely writes engaging stories featuring strong, protective alpha males. I love IPB, so I knew I had to try this dragon story out too. I will definitely be reading the next book in the series. I had flashes of King Kong as the book starts. Beautiful woman used as bait to lure the savage beast to his own death. But that was where the similarities ended. The story took off in a direction readers of IPB will be familiar with. Yes, Kael is very similar to a group of blue, horned aliens we all know and love. But hey that formula works. If it ain't broke don't fix it! My only peeve was that our heroine,  Claudia, kept going back and forth, not telling Kael why she was upset. She thought that she had to choose between Kael and her sister and friend. Those aren't the only choices, hun. You can have both. And mind-reading Kael, who knew when she was thinking she might fall or other things, never picked up on the fact that she missed her sister? But I still loved the story and can't wait to read what happened to Claudia's friend.
