Or will humans start having empathy for androids? It is easier to answer that second question. One only has to look at popularity of stuff like sex dolls. One may argue that if they aren't even more popular than it is because their resemblance is only limited to physical featured and at that features that are constant. If they had facial features and could talk ... the resemblance would be stronger. Now this is about sex drive and, as we know, it is for almost all of us, only humans that attract our sex instinct. And even that can be so easily fooled by robotics. What chance then our empathy and compassion has, with which we are so liberal as to extend it to animals ? How easy it could be to feel sorry for machine? Remember 'it's a small wonder'? The reasons why people - those sensitive fools, find cats and dogs so cute, adorable and so on, is because of similarity their faces have with us - you know the eyes and stuff. Cartoonists and toy makers make animal faces a lot more vertical (especially when it comes to teddy bears) because that makes them *coughs* 'cute'. So how long can it be before robotics get to the level of getting that sympathy? Of course, it will change the very roles robots might play. They might slowly change from being our servants or slaves for whom we feel nothing to a child for parents who can't have one for themselves. (there is an amazing Twilight zone episode about one such subject). People always fool themselves - how far we can pretend to be from a kid who make play with plastic toys and make sands in castles? Supposing an epidemic disease affecting new borns spreads out - won't the new wanna be parents want to have robotic children instead? They can be exactly like normal children - assuming they can made to err, to cry for no reason, smell like children and stuff; while still shielding their parents from fear of that loss. - Hey those sounds like ideas of a great novel, somebody should totally write one like that. (it might also be a good reason to have genetically engineered children - think  Gattaca. The walk to humanoids might not be that simple though. if we were to deny humanity to a thing that looks so human, so like us - it is possible that we might question our own humanity. That might explain the eeriness and discomfort (called  Uncanny Valley ) these humanoids generate as their resemble people more and more. In fact, such fears and doubts might be there in creators themselves - what Asimov called  Frankenstein complex. Some of these themes show up in this book (see! I was always talking about the book). In this case, the change is beginning to be visible. Some of the androids have come to revolt against slavery imposed on them. Some of the human have developed feeling towards them - sexual as well as platonic. But the government and general laws are still against the mix and match relation (like racial laws some western countries and caste laws of India). Since animals are becoming a rarity (the nulcear war thing), electronic animals are cheaper replacements (an actual animal pet is a luxury) - and as far as artificial animals go, humans are more liberal with emotions. The artificial animals must be fed like humans, they fall sick and all. (I can never understand people wanting to have pets and animals) It might sound stupid until you realize how much you love an artificial Mickey mouse while actual mouse will probably scare you. People are becoming more and more like machines - there are moods organs that people use to change their moods by dialing numbers. Trigger warning for feminists kind of folks - they might not like number 594: 'pleased acknowledgment of husband's superior wisdom in all matters'. (the only woman that is not a machine is a house wife) Even the religion is technological - using a device called empathy box to replace the traditional churches. This religion has its outcasts too - people who can't pass tests of empathy are treated like mentally retarded are in our present society. The founder of religion turns out to be a fraud - but like several aspects where real life religion has been discovered to lie (creationism, the source of diseases and like); the uncomfortable truth doesn't disturb the faith of the people. What about humanoids? There are two things worth discussing. One is the sort of existential crisis they get - because they are created in a way to observe, learn and be more and more like humans - of course, at some point, they figure out they will never be humans. It must like a dusky complexioned girl who was told only fairly complexioned girls are pretty and they try rubbing whitening creams over and over and over to their disappointment. The other thing is while humanoids seem to be developing feelings we have for ourselves - self identity, ambition and such like self- worthies thingies (and thus so many humanoid runaways); that doesn't seem to be the case with the feelings we have towards others - love, sexual attraction and compassion (let us just call it LSC), whether it is LSC towards human beings or other machines (though in last we have a couple of exceptions. And thus while the humanoids easily generate such feelings in humans for themselves - LSC,; they themselves do not seem to have those feelings in return. Humanoids can look at people and know that the latter are having those feelings - and can pretend to have them too. But they don't feel anything themselves, thus an obvious advantage over humans vulnerable to sentiments. And they don't even understand animals' feelings, maybe because they never were supposed to learn to resemble them. This makes them perfect psychopaths. Studies show that psychopaths can read facial emotions of sorrow and like but they do not react to those feelings the way we do - by feeling the sorrow too. In some cases, they might actually turn curious and or get pleasure from causing pain, that is - be sadists. Moreover, psychopathic criminals too tend show cruelty towards animals in their childhood. They too might generate feelings in you - and use those feelings to emotionally kidnap and blackmail you. Andys in the book do all these things.

Fairy tales are wondrous. They offer us a look into a world that we aspire to. They show us possibilities and tell us that dreams can come true. Well, they also perpetuate gender assimilation in children and are one of the very first ways children learn culture (and the English Lit student in my is obliged to point out at this juncture that fairy tales really aren't as harmless as they are portrayed). What does this all have to do with The False Princess, you ask me? Well, The False Princess is a Cinderella story in reverse and one of the most empowering novels I have read to date. Stick with me and I shall count the ways (and whys) I love this book. Imagine having the floor swept away from you. Imagine being told that the person you thought you were is not not who you are. If that's not confusing to you, well, you don't have much in common with our heroine. She does not just lose her home, her parents, her friends but also her very identity: her name. She's no longer Nalia. She is now Sinda. Not the crown princess but an orphan - a dyer's niece. And now that her purpose in life has been taken away (to be Queen) Sinda fast realizes that not only does she not have an identity, she also does not have a set of skills that she can use to survive in a world which has very quickly turned hostile. And then she discovers her magic... I like Sinda. She could have been so easily been an annoying character, immersed in her melodramatic life and at the cruel turns of fate but she wasn't. Ms. Neal writes a heroine who is cognizant of her unfolding fate and instead of remaining static throughout the novel, she evolves and is changed by the things she experiences during the course of her journey. The way her sense of betrayal and subsequent lashing out at Keirnan is realistically portrayed. I also appreciated the careful removal of any sentimentality that might have coloured her relationship with her aunt. I feel like I must also mention the relationships between the girls. So often in novels I read, the girls are either somehow inferior to the protagonist (in which case, they are given the title of "the best friend") or superior (in terms of beauty in which case they will be The Enemy). In The False Princess, Ms. Neal imbues each girl with their own set of qualities that do not clash with the protagonists in such a way that the readers need to prove who the better woman is. They also manage to forge a relationship between themselves that is refreshing. The love interest is really sweet and let's face it, I'm a sucker for guys who know when to back off. The plot is fast paced at times and honeyed at others - the story knows when to move fast and when to stroll and there was never a moment that I felt I needed to skip ahead or read slower. The supporting cast of characters are all carefully developed and feel like real people instead of cardboard cutouts from the Store of Side Characters. The False Princess is a story about a girl who realizes that it is not necessary to be a princess to be happy. A girl who loses everything and then regains everything she lost. A girl who learns that family is something one can make for herself. That fairy godmothers and pumpkins can only take you so far. That the real magic resides inside of you. This is an explosive debut and I am looking forward to reading whatever Ms. Neal comes up with next.

Be with me By J. Lynn We first meet Jase, in Wait for You/Trust in Me. Jase was invaluable in helping Cam, his best friend, survive a devastating life-altering crisis. With Jase's unwavering support, advice, and "tough love", Cam successfully overcomes his personal demons and returns to college, whereby, he meets Avery, the reclusive, reticent redhead. Be with me, the next installment of the Wait for You series, is Jase and Tess's story... Jase, brooding, intense, enigmatic, and secretive is one gorgeous "hott" guy. He attracts all the ladies on campus. He's ELF, funny, flirty, seductive, with no strings attached. A BMOC, a respected member of his frat, Jase enjoys a good time. Just don't expect anything long-term or serious. He's complicated and...a mess! He's attracted to Tess...but, oh, wait! She's Cam's, his best friend, little sister and definitely, off limits! Besides, Jase has more pressing concerns and responsibilities that deter him from developing any long-term romantic relationship or emotional commitments. Therefore, Jase tries to avoid Tess, tries to ignore this attraction, albeit unsuccessfully. And Tess... She "crushed on" Jase the first time he crossed her threshold to visit her brother, Cam. Obsessed over a stolen kiss, Tess's infatuation with Jase grows; she definitely wants him! However, she does not know if Jase has similar feelings. Does he regard her only as Cam's little sister, or did the kiss have a special meaning for him as well, a precursor for something deeper and more substantial. Healing from an injury, Tess places her dance career on hold and attends the same college as Cam and Jase. Her initial encounters with Jase are awkward and painful. How can he ignore their special moment? He's indifferent and distant. On the other hand, he can't seem to stay away from her. He flirts, teases, and then apologizes for his "inappropriate" attraction. Sooo frustrating! Life becomes more complicated as Tess and Jase, each face an uncertain future; Tess has a debilitating injury, a torn ACL that may affect her dance career, and Jase, faces the responsibility of being a father. "You are planning on leaving, Tess. You aren't thinking about sticking around. And I'll be damned if that boy gets hurt...(Jase)" In addition, Tess needs to contend with her past; a sordid relationship with her abusive, violent boyfriend, Jeremy. The "Jeremy" situation caused immense anguish for her family and Cam, in particular. Once revealed, Cam explodes, confronts Jeremy, and let's just say, the situation ends badly! Cam's violent actions negatively affect his future; specifically, sentenced to house arrest and mandatory counseling. Tess feels guilty for "being stupid" and for being the cause of distress for her brother and family. However, circumstances (as they may) lead Tess to become roommates with Debbie, another girl who suffers from an abusive relationship. Can she help Debbie by sharing her personal experience, and by offering advice and support? More importantly, can Tess overcome her own guilt? Jase helps. With each other's support, comfort, and encouragement, Tess and Jase's relationship deepens. Do I like Jase? Sometimes. He's baffling, frustrating, but I gotta love him! "I'm sorry--- (Jase)" This seems to be his mantra. Throughout the book, he continually apologizes to Tess. Yes, Jase suffers emotional turmoil and angst. Similar to many tortured heroes, he's considerate, perceptive, and protective; and yet, he can be distant, caustic, and abrasive. Jase wants to follow his heart, but he feels he must listen to his mind. Jase harbors a deep-seated fear of becoming emotionally intimate, of losing another loved one. His scars have not healed. He wants Tess, but " he cannot have her". Jase is frustrating with his indecisive, on/again/off /again attitude. He constantly apologizes for his actions, his attraction, and sexual innuendos. He flirts, teases, comforts; then, pulls away... "I'm not attracted to you, not like that...(Jase) What...what are you doing here, Jase... (Tess) I shouldn't have said the sh** that I said to you earlier. It wasn't right and I was lying. (Jase)" Overall, Be with me  is a good read as Jase and Tess are worth meeting!

NOTE I'm sorry for any grammar mistakes you read. Public school has failed me miserably, but some of those mistakes are just me typing too fast. Also, I know it might not be right. But, I can't help comparing books to other books I have read. So, if I compare this book to the Dresden Series, it 's not my fault, I'm just spoiled by Jim Butcher. Sorry to Mr. Aaronovitch and all his hardcore fans. Plot: 4 out of 5 Police Constable Peter Grant just finish with his probationary period all British constables suffer, being a street cop. He now wants to be assigned to the Murder Investigation Team (A Homicide Detective). His commanding officer believes Grant is unfit to become a Homicide Detective because he's too easily distracted, so he assigns him to Case Progression Unit (The paper pushers of the British's Police force. They make sure the real cops are doing real police work instead of writing papers).Grant trying to find a way out of being a paper pushers, goes on a stakeout looking for a ghost he met at a earlier crime scene. During this stakeout he meets Detective Chief Inspector Thomas Nightingale who eventually has him assigned to Economic and Specialist Crime. Thus starting Peter Grant's journey as a apprentice wizard and solving supernatural crime. Which is just as well because magic is on the raise and there is an supernatural serial killer on the loose. Cover: 3 out of 5 I never really thought about the cover of this book, it's not bad but it isn't anything special. I did however, find it interesting that the original American cover of this book had a black guy on it, but the publishers had the black guy turned into a silhouette. (I'm guessing) A black guy on the cover of a book wouldn't sell as well. Doesn't really matter though, it's not like the author tried to hide that the protagonist is black. Characters: 3 out 5 Peter Grant is the main protagonist. He's suppose to come off as corky, nerdy, funny, and lovable guy but he's not. He's just a really nice guy, too nice in fact. He isn't corky, he's just easily distracted and has a slightly above average IQ (He would be great at Trivia Pursuit but he won't be solving cancer or anything like that.) If nerdy is just another way to say your awkward around pretty women and will forever be stuck in the friend zone, then yeah he's very nerdy. He also isn't funny. AT ALL!! He's just a nice guy, bland really. Thomas Nightingale is Grant's Master (His wizard teacher). He's a really posh upper-crust British man, who drives a sweet car. He was born in the 1900's but now because magic is on the raise again, he's starting age backwards. I don't know how Grant isn't funny, Nightingale is his straight man. He practically hands Grant material to make witty one liners Lesley May is just a typical stereotype of a female police officer in this genre. She kick's ass and take's names, and is an all around better cop than Grant. Think Karen Murphy (Dresden Series) but with no daddy issues and a lot more trust in her wizard. She's also his love interest, which is not saying much. They knew each other since the academy, been partners for 2 years, he's met her family and been shopping at the mall with them, But for some reason he just doesn't make a move. Beverley Brook is a Water Nymph and is Grant's other love interest. Lady Ty serves as a minor antagonist and is also a water nymph. She really politically connected and wants to turn Grant's division into some sort of ministry of magic. (I'm guessing)She's trying to do this because it will be easier for her to control. Molly is the Folly's (Wizard Headquarters) maid. She likes the appear out nowhere like she's lurch, and overfeed the Folly's occupants. Her jaw opens wider than it should be able and she has really sharp teeth. It's weird but I find Molly to be the most interesting character in this book, even though she doesn't say one word . Final Thoughts: 3.3 out of 5 On a whole, I can't say that I didn't enjoy this book. But, I can't say it will be enjoyable for everyone who likes the whole magically powered detective genre. My main problem with this series is the protagonist, Peter Grant. I like the fact that the protagonist is black(like me), I find it so cool that a black guy is the main hero in a urban fantasy novel. They're usually stoic or the muscle side characters. But, that might also be the reason why I find the protagonist boring. He lacks a certain jen nes a qua, a certain oomph that will make him go from being a nerd to a super nerd. He's a lot like me, but I don't want to read about me, I want to read about super me. That's why I read fantasy's and Peter Grant just doesn't cut it. I will most likely read the other books in the series but I'm not rushing to read them.

Leveling the Field by Megan Erickson is book four in her Gamers series and it doesn't disappoint. Filled with romance, heat, drama, and emotion, Ms. Erickson gives us her own modern spin on the classic tale of Beauty and the Beast, with two characters who have both experienced loss and find strength in each other. The story is about Lissa Kingsman, a photographer, who is hired to take a photo of a reclusive magazine executive, Ethan Talley, for an upcoming article. However, he proves to be more than just camera shy. With scars as a reminder of a tragic past, Ethan has been holding himself from getting close to anyone. That is until the lovely, sassy, and absolutely likable Lissa comes into his world. Leveling the Field is a great story that had strong characters, humor, lots of heat and also just pulls at your heartstrings at times. I also loved the family relationships between Lissa and her family, and Ethan with his sister. Plus, my favorite scenes involved glitter. You'll have to read to find out more. Overall, I happily recommend and can't wait to read more by Ms. Erickson. (I voluntarily reviewed an ARC of this book I received from the publisher via NetGalley in exchange for my honest review.)

I liked this book more than some of the others because of the intensity of the action and the development of the characters. Percy is really growing up and I can't wait to read the conclusion. It's not a perfectly written story, and there are a lot of magical fixes that take away problems, but it works for the story and I enjoyed it. The mythology is done well, also, and it adds a great depth/history to the story.

Okay, so. First off, I have to say there were some things that really bothered me in this book and were unnecessary. The first part, Lady Of Shadows, was the most problematic to me. I didn't recognize the characters I had come to care about and even love in the previous installments. It's definitely a "it's you, not me" situation, because as much as I could see the flaws in Heir Of Fire and its general slowness, I still greatly enjoyed most of it and especially the message that it conveyed: that even if you are brought down a thousand times, you can still find the force to stand up and reclaim your life. Some of the internal monologues Celaena gave really got me and even made me tear up at times. So, the first part of this book, which I was hoping would be a triumph and a great setup for the rest of the series, ended up being really meh for me, and left me quite disappointed. The second part, Queen Of Light, was definitely much, much better. I gaped at the intensity of some scenes, and things happened that I never saw coming. The characters started behaving more in-character, so I enjoyed it and thought it was amazing, really. I don't have any complaint about Queen Of Light. I just don't understand why Sarah J. Maas, who is a talented author and a clever one at that, made these rookie mistakes; she could have set up Rowan and Aelin much more smoothly, as a couple. I like them a lot more than I liked Chaol and Celaena together, but it didn't make much sense that they were lusting after each other after three seconds, when they just said in Heir Of Fire there was no attraction whatsoever. She could have taken her time to develop the relationship and not make Chaol look like a spoiled selfish brat in the first part of this novel. . Overall, the bits I really loved where every scene in which Lysandra was in; Elide, Asterin and please, Manon, wake up! I wanted to slap her sometimes. Her and her Blackbeak obedience. And, I'll say it again, I loved the second part of the book. I am looking forward to the sequels, even though I hope Sarah doesn't pull another Lady Of Shadows because I've had enough. 4 stars.

Boy, I do love Rainbow Rowell. Once again, I am struck by how she either has an amazing memory, or kept A LOT of journals, because practically nothing about this book feels like it was written NOW looking back on THEN (in this case, 1999). We've got two stories folding into one -- two young women working for a small market newspaper carry on conversations over email, and these are in email form and read delightfully like what the best kind of snappy email exchanges between friends can be -- that mix of completely topical remarks and longer, more thoughtful ideas all jumbled together. The other story is about Lincoln, the IT guy, whose job involves reading employees' emails so that people sending personal correspondence can be reprimanded. Lincoln can't really bring himself to send mindless reprimands to the two women, because he finds himself fascinated by their conversations (and you see where this is going), especially fascinated by one of the email writers. As great as this writing is, as cute and funny and just ON the conversations are, from almost the beginning it was getting a little uncomfortably close to the creepy "Say Anything" model of obsessive attraction. It's that thing where in the world of the story, where the reader has the Big Picture and can see how well-intentioned everyone is, you can buy it, but if you start thinking about it in real life, it's highly questionable. The author seems aware of this, the characters are aware of it, but it's still in Book World where it's all going to get wrapped up. I still enjoyed it so, so much, but this issue was always on the back burner.
Stunning. Brilliant. Heartbreakingly beautiful. The perfect final book for Jake and Tru. I miss it already. Full review to come!

The Good: It's heartbreaking, the idea that a dying woman would hope against all evidence that her soon to be orphaned baby would be ok, and die not knowing. This is a cheesy, soppy story but very sweet. I love 19th century London as a setting, and there are some great characters in the story, particularly the gang of villains. It was sometimes quite funny too. The Bad: It's a strange story, in that all this dramatic stuff happens around the main character, being a small child who does little more than suffer, endure, and cry. It feels like a cheap plot device. The book is also very preachy, and I say this as someone who agrees with most of the sentiments expressed here by Dickens. I don't need a fucking lecture, Charles. It also has one of those convoluted inheritance  plots. 'Friends' character the protagonist is most like: Oliver is not much of a protagonist. He is like a cross between Ross and Joey. The real heroes of the tale are Mr Brownlow (also like Joey) and the awesome Nancy, who is good-hearted but nuts, like Phoebe.

Changeling, Philippa Gregory's first YA novel in her new Order of Darkness series, takes two teenagers - Luca and Isolde - on an intersecting journey into danger. Too bad they have both sworn to remain celibate - the chemistry is there and is bound to cause them increasing problems as the series rolls on. As star characters, they tick the most-needed boxes. Luca, the changeling of the title, has a brilliant mind and a talent for problem solving, linked with a mysterious past. He's also tall, dark and handsome. Isolde - tall, blond and beautiful - is born into a noble and wealthy family. Her status should guarantee her a life of comfort, independence and no little power but she is speedily deprived of her rightful inheritance by a scheming and unscrupulous brother. The story proceeds swiftly as Isolde's world disintegrates. Gregory uses the mindset of the late Middle Ages with skill to paint a picture of a society very different from our own. Western Europe is only dimly aware of zero as a factor in mathematics; witchcraft is a standard diagnosis for women who don't fit with society's expectations; women have few rights, except through their husbands; burning at the stake is a normal way of dealing with dubious opinions; werewolves and other monsters lurk round every corner. One thing hasn't changed: people, then as now, were quick to jump to conclusions, and to judge unfairly through prejudice and ignorance. A key element in the plot, this tendency is countered by the few characters who actively resist this temptation. Gregory makes the point strongly, without being too overt and preachy. The story is told mostly through the eyes of Luca and to a lesser extent, Isolde, though the point of view does shift around to other characters as well - at times a little abruptly. Even when we see events through Luca and Isolde, we don't engage well enough with their inner thoughts and troubles. This is most noticeable during one of the central and most dramatic episodes in the book. Isolde and her Muslim servant Ishraq are surprised in the middle of dissecting a dead nun. Dissection was not only illegal in Italy in 1453AD, it was considered a terrible sin. And their captors are none other than agents of The Inquisition. Yet Isolde's reactions immediately afterwards focus neither on the compulsion that drove her and Ishraq to this deed - frightful to anyone in such a setting - nor on the horror of the experience or the enormity of their actions, but simply on the need for escape. Gregory, I'm sure, wants to preserve Isolde's motives and reactions for a dramatic denouement near the end of the book, but by doing so she strips Isolde of depth and authenticity as a character. Luca is a more rounded and grounded character, but without any real flaws or serious introspection, he also becomes a little two-dimensional. Frieze, Luca's servant, saves the book. His personality, voice, humour and ingenuity provide great colour and interest. Ishraq has a wealth of unexpected talent and skill, and between them, these two threaten to highjack both stage centre and the ongoing plot. Gregory's style is less burdened with "foresoothery" than her adult fiction writing, and she builds the book to a fast-moving, intriguing and emotional end. Some non-sequiturs may be the result either of haste or over-light editing - on page one, Luca doesn't know why he has been imprisoned; on page three, he knows exactly what he has done and why he must be in such trouble. As the first book in a series, the plot arc is rather episodical. Effectively, the book contains two separate stories, the first set in a nunnery, the second in a village. Both have dramatic and exciting climaxes; their only real connection is the presence of the same group of characters and the somewhat undeveloped notion that Luca is on a quest. It is this motif - a journey studded by problems and a wide variety of adventures which will undoubtedly fuel the Order of Darkness series.

Still brilliantly addictive, but didn't get to me as much as In the Woods and The Likeness. I thought the mystery was easier to solve (not necessarily a bad thing) and not so many things were at stake (definitely a good thing for my nerves, but). I'm kind of sad that I read The Secret Place before this one, I'd like to read more about Holly and Frank from Stephen's POV now...

Ever since discovering Across The Wide And Lonesome Prairie: The Oregon Trail Diary Of Hattie Campbell in third grade (and consequently the Dear America series) I've been a fan of historical fiction written in diary form. This book is right up there with These Is My Words: The Diary of Sarah Agnes Prine, 1881-1901 in quality. (Though I think I enjoyed the latter slightly more.) In any case, I thought this book was well written and the voice seemed appropriate for the time. I found myself engaged in Mattie's story, rejoicing in her triumphs and sorrow in with her in tragedies. I highly recommend this to fans of historical fiction.

It's hard to pinpoint my thoughts on this book though I can say that I quite liked it. It was believable and drew me in Susie's world slowly. I would probably recommend this to older readers since there are some mature themes present.

Brilliant, beautiful novel. Very well-developed characters, a lot of subtlety, a galaxy-spanning story told as a love story, almost a coming-of-age story despite the maturity of the main characters. I've seen it compared with LeGuin and it has several similarly anthropological influences for sure, handled deftly. Lots of beautiful surges of emotion and clever lines and plot twists, though some of the plot twists go a bit over the top. Also a lot of the metaphor of "you can never cross the same river twice", stories coming full circle to end where they began, only not. Definitely a must-read.

I have mixed feelings about this book. Let me start with the good ones. I love the thrill that it gave me. I like how the story revolved around bikes and racing. It was a breath of fresh air to me. I like how the author was able to make me feel like I'm really in the race with them. I was exhilarated whenever Kenzie was driving. I also like it that Kenzie and Hayden's romance didn't spout all of a sudden. It took time and it took setting aside some of their prejudices against one another. The push and pull was a good factor, at least to me. One thing that didn't work for me was the Romeo and Juliet vibe going around in the book. I found some scenes unnecessary. Kenzie's strong opposition about going to the "other team's" territory was very ironic, given the fact that it ended the way it did. Kenzie's attitude was also off-putting. Once again, I would reiterate that I liked the push an pull in this book, however, Kenzie could have curbed her bitchiness a little. There's no other way to say it. She was sometimes downright bitchy to Hayden that she annoyed me a lot. Frankly speaking, I really liked the premise of the book. The way they were in the races were amazing to read about. Kenzie is a badass out there, and of course, Hayden is too. I just can't discount the over-the-top conflict between two groups and the way Kenzie acted in some scenes. Anyway, this was still an entertaining read. I was provided with an ARC by the publisher in exchange for an honest review.

As a vampire novella, I Am Legend is a pillar of its genre. It introduced science to what had previously been a genre of superstition and myth. In that way, I loved it. The science and pursuit of science was interesting. However, all the genre-breaking in the world could not make up for the sexist asshat that was Robert Neville. If this is a representation of Richard Matheson's ownmental workings, I put any female who had to come in contact with him. I have never been more appalled with a character's behavior and consciousness in my literary life. Neville was a disgusting excuse for a human being, who thought little  of singling female vampires out for experimentation; regularly fantasized about raping unconcious female vampires; and ran down, hit, captured, imprisoned, and considered raping and killing the first human (of course, an attractive woman) he comes in contact with in over three years. He got a far more noble end than he deserved, and I wish he had been impaled and flayed by the vampire goon squad who captured him. If this is how the average male thinks, I am not impressed. I enjoyed a few of the other short stories-- the killer doll one was particularly good-- but most were bland. I don't think I will be seeking out his other works.

This is a weird book. At first I wasn't sure what was going on and in many places I was about to stop reading but something kept me going. I'm glad I kept reading. The characters are all clearly messed up and a reflection of what's messed up about the world. Without preaching, this books is a harsh look at our society while being funny unapologetic.

CSM - you are now officially one of my favourite authors! This is a stellar offering from Mr. Sheehan truly. The Last Hour was a book of a lots - a lot of great writing, great characters, beautiful touching moments, incredible strength in Carrie & Ray, and it's obvious it had a lot of thought behind it. What a read this was, I loved how the story was so much more than just the love story of Carrie & Ray. His time in Afghanistan is fleshed out on the pages and it was just as every bit riveting, wrenching. I have to say though I didn't know whether to be angry or appreciative of the ending. I couldn't believe it was happening as I cried my freakin' eyes out at 3am in the morning. Very rare do you read a book where not only does it not have the HEA against all odds, but one that rips your heart out and is the worst scenario possible. That's a hard thing for an author to pull off without turning the reader against the story. But CSM found a way for it to feel complete and organic in the story arc. It kept the integrity of the plot intact and made Ray's plight all the more powerful, impactful. I appreciated it but damn did it ever hurt. So brutal! In short, truly amazing! This book - get it, read it, devour it, love it. 10 stars.

A lot of my friends say this book is amazing. I shelved it as TBR, then got the book. But oh my, it left me so disappointed. I expected it to be five-star amazing. I wanted to love this book, but I just could not. I do not like the idea of Hannah sending out those tapes. Who would blame their suicide on someone else? The only reason I can think of is to make them feel guilty. Also, this Hannah's tape/Clay's thoughts format made the book boring - it lacked plot twist. All along in my mind, I was silently pleading, Please let the thirteenth person be Clay. I wanted to know if Hannah had feelings for him. I simply couldn't put the book down before knowing about that. But Clay turned out to be the ninth receiver of the tapes, and after that my excitement completely died. This is a good book. I just didn't love it that much.

The best Star Wars book I've read since the New Jedi Order. Annileen is a GREAT character - one of the first female SW characters I've liked in a long time. This book finally had the right balance of action, introspection, and relationships - a balance that Star Wars has struggled with lately. I listened to the audio, and the audio is terrific. Miller does an excellent Kenobi.

4.5 Stars I LOVED this book. Absolutely beautiful. I loved the characters, the story and the writing... the icing on the cake was its from Jake's POV. Let me just say the kids are awesome. And I mean seriously awesome. I adored them. You just can't help but love them and Reagan is special. Her HI won me over. This book must be experienced. I couldn't put it down. I've always loved both that has kids in them and they it revolves on them. They matter in the story. They are the root of the story and the love Chelsea had for these kids warmed me to tip of my toes. I loved EVERYTHING about this story. YOU NEED TO READ IT. GO ON. You can thank me later.

THERE ARE SPOILERS I honestly can't believe that I haven't written a review for this one yet. I read it a while back and have read it a couple times since. My love and adoration for this book has not faltered once. It's beautifully written, just like My Life Next Door was. As a second book, this one did not disappoint as they sometimes do. Now, a lot of people have mentioned in their reviews that the flashbacks that Gwen had were confusing and somewhat annoying. I found them to be the opposite - more than a little insightful into what Gwen felt and how the events between her and Cass transpired. Though it was a little confusing on the first read-through as to what was thinking back and what was real time, it was fairly clear and even easier to follow on the second and third readings. Starting on characters, I think everyone in this story was well-rounded and well thought-out. I love how I can really connect with all the characters in this book, though I may not approve of their choices. In the book, Vivien (Gwen's best friend) is with Nic (Gwen's brother). This, I thought, would have been awkward at times, and it was. However, the romance between them was absolutely adorable and I loved it to pieces. Throughout the course of the book, however, Nic grows more and more focused on bagging swim captain and keeping it out of Cass Somers' hands. Viv, we find out at the end, was cheating on Nic with Spencer for a little bit, and hadn't told him yet. The whole thing came out when Nic finds that he isn't swim captain - Cass and Spence are. Sucks, I agree. I felt so bad for Nic and so mad at Viv for doing something like that - I didn't think she would. Honestly, though, I totally get it. I don't like cheating, but in books, we see people go through these situations where it happens, and it's not to hurt someone (necessarily), but it's because these people have fallen for each other, or things have changed, and I just can't fault the characters for it. Now that I have that view, in my own life, I can't fault people either. I mean, honestly, adults: think back to when you were a teenager with hormones and a messed-up brain, all those things that accompany growing up. Were there never times when you went just a little bad, considered or did things you really shouldn't have (especially in romantic situations?) I'm sure everyone did at one point or another. No one is perfect, after all. So before you condemn Viv and Spence, take a look at their situation. Take a look and how Nic was acting. He's no longer the happy, carefree team-player that he was. He's not the same guy. And Spence  is  a good guy. So don't be so mad at Viv. Take a look at the situation. I sympathize, and personally, I get it. It made sense. Sometimes it happens. Gwen Castle: She is really, really cool. She's more grown up than a lot of people I know and a lot of the other people in the story that are her age. She takes care of her little brother, Emory (who's adorable), deals with her dad and his rather annoying behavior (I did like him better by the end), all the while supporting Nic and her best friend, Viv. She's got a lot on her plate, relationship issues aside. *Another thing I noticed in a lot of review is that readers did not like that the main conflict in the plot involved sex and that Gwen was a "player". That made me a little mad because she is not someone who has a lot of one-night stands, as is made perfectly clear in the book. If you actually read it, you'd know that she and Cass were rash and went a little too fast, and she thought what was beautiful between them was because of a "reputation" that she had, and one that he'd heard about and taken advantage of. The thing with Alex happened because she was bummed and hurting over Cass. Gentle (sort of) reminder: SHE'S SEVENTEEN!!! What occupied your mind when you were that age? Probably boys and stolen kisses, right? Have some sympathy, people. She just found out that the guy she liked was supposedly only interested in her for sex. How would you feel? I'm guessing you might exact revenge just like Gwen did, or do something else (perhaps less drastic, but still. You wouldn't be happy). There's a lot of bad blood between them because of that and it's like a shock to her system when she finds out that she'll be seeing the guy who ripped her heart out every day on an island where she can't escape him. Cass Somers: Everyone lift your hands and give an "AMEN" 'cause chivalry is not dead. Cass is a hero that will melt your heart. Besides the physical, he's so great with kids (just look at him with Em) and actually had good intentions toward Gwen, despite the miscommunication between them. This book was so beautifully written, and it holds a place right in my heart. The setting, the ending, the figuring out of what to do, finding yourself and what you'll do for the rest of your life... Huntley Fitzpatrick is an author not to be missed. And this book is on the list of ones to read before you turn twenty.
Another great installment in the Georgina Kincaid series! The mystery component was a little predictable, but I love all the characters and relationships. I was crying by the end!

This one was better than the first. Now I'm sad to learn that the next books will not focus on Cyn and Raphael. The book held my interest from start to finish. There is no real twist in the story, but I enjoyed watching it all unfold. It's fast pace and lingering questions are answered. Jabil is a bastard and one you hate and never love. He's not a villain to be admired. I want to know who will get the territory and if the girls got their estate back including the house and money.

CUTESY!! Thank God Ms. Lane can write light too! If this was like Chase in Shadow I might die. XD The only thing I didn't like was it ended abruptly and Donnie & Yandro didn't have sex in the story. But it was nice to read about Donnie & Yandro's backstory. :D

I'm a little torn about this book. There's plenty in it I love. The world of Mercy Thompson never gets boring. I never feel like I overstayed my welcome. There are some Urban Fantasy series that get old or lose track of what they're about... but not Mercy's world. Still, I still asked myself 'where is this going?' for most of the book. The villain: When I found out what he was I started wondering if Patricia Briggs were going to add  gods   into the mix now. Maybe that will be the next big thing she'll add to the world? If that's the case, Mercy has to level up (to use a gaming slang), like, right now! I think Gary and Coyote might serve that purpose in Mercy's life. Briggs does seem to be leading to that - with Gary and Coyote sort of guiding Mercy now. Besides, there's one short story in Shifting Shadows that had a Neil Gaiman vibe to it and totally opens up the possibility for bigger, nastier things that could come out and play. The short story sort of implies that there are things that came into the New World with the immigrant population that even fae, vampires and werewolves don't really get. No one really knows what is out there. There's an echo of that in this book, too. If she's going that way, damn!, I can't wait to read what comes next. OK... on to the things I didn't like: The ending left me wanting a little. It felt so sudden. I actually checked my kindle to make sure I hadn't jumped ahead or something. Besides, I hated Christy with a passion. I was right there with Mercy when  she said 'why not let him have Christy?' That bitch deserves to go down and she had it easy, if you ask me. Lastly, even though I like that the pack is ambivalent about Mercy, I think it was about time they started warming up to her. Not all of them. I get it. But some of them. I felt like screaming at Mary Jo and Honey and Aurielle in this book. Over all, a good book that left me wanting more. I hope Patricia Briggs wants to keep writing these novels because I sure want to keep reading them!

It's a really sweet story. What bothered me a bit was that it lacks depth but since it's a children's book I shouldn't complain about that. I did, however, have tears in my eyes when Tuck stood by Winnie's grave. In my opinion she made a wise choice not drinking from that water. I probably would have done the same.

So this was the book I was looking for when I read Bad Mommy. The Secrets She Keeps had a way darker tone and felt like a new level of crazy. I realllllly enjoyed this book and the dynamics between Agatha and Meg. Agatha is not your typical main character and even though she has her flaws and crazy side, I loved being inside her head. She is different, entertaining, dark and it was so nice to be reading something that was so out of the ordinary. I find that my reviews are shorter when I really enjoy a book. There wasn't much to nitpick over this one, except the ending. SOMEONE EXPLAIN THE ENDING TO ME!! Did Agatha kill herself? Did she live? Was she in a dream? What about her daughter coming to get her. SO MANY QUESTIONS! But all in all, I really liked this book.

this book brought me a RIDICULOUS amount of nostalgia and then, it didn't. i cried so many times because LET ME TELL YOU: i picked up cinder when i first started blogging, read scarlet and for whatever reason, was able to go to the marissa meyer signing [my first signing ever!] so i have memories with this series. Stars Above was magical in every way possible. There was so much new material on the events that took place and events that were only briefly mentioned. By far, the wedding was my favorite story and I'm just so glad it wasn't predictable at all! Go read this and be prepared to cry a little bit [or a lot, if you're like me.]

I stopped on page 230. There was no way I could finish this book. Too many characters to keep track of, and the only real reason I had gotten this far was because of the fact that I wanted to know what would happen to Krystal and her mom and Robbie. I mean, I might just skip to the back and have a look myself, but I'm not sure yet. I love J.K. Rowling, I really do, but I did not love this book. Keep writing things like Harry Potter!

This book dealt with heavier issues than I was expecting, but that just made me like it even more. Elise definitely has some issues, but I also found her really easy to relate to. She was a realistic character, as were all of the other characters in this book, which I appreciated. A lot of the time you get a fully developed main character but rather flat side characters. That was not the case here. I had to go back and look up this quote, but it's one of my favorites. As is the whole scene where she destroys her sister's project. . "Don't be special." That's what I would say to my younger self if I could pinpoint the moment when I went astray. That's absolutely true. If you want to fit in, you can't be special. You just have to decide if fitting in is worth giving up what makes you special. I wish I had been able to read this book when I was in high school.

This wasn't a bad book, but after reading so much brilliant Young Adult work lately, this felt a little too juvenile. The ending was also still a bit confusing to me -- while it's not necessary to spell everything out for the reader, I thought it could use a bit more fleshing out.

The Color Purple by Alice Walker did not grab me until I noticed I was falling in love with some of the characters. Celie for her open honesty and ability to rise above the terrible things the men in her life put her through, Nettie for being an intellectual and for never giving up, Shug for being herself and not giving any f***s about it, and Sofia for being a strong female not only in spirit but physically as well. It's obvious the female characters make The Color Purple what it is and I enjoyed getting to know each of these ladies. I felt the character development was very believable especially for Albert and Celie who went through the biggest transformations. The ending was perfect and touching. 4/5 stars

The moment I heard about this book, I had to have it. I needed it. So today, once I finally got it, I spent the day reading it instead of studying. Totally blaming my grades on this. See, I used to be a bandom fangirl. I am in the period of time the bartender was talking about. For me, it was never one direction or even real boy bands. It started with the click five and evolved into the pop punk scene ( all time low were my main thing, but also pierce the veil, Sleeping With Sirens, My Chemical Romance, Bring Me The Horizon, panic!, basically the whole emo package). The thing is, when I look back at that period, I don't feel embarrassed at all. There's a gorgeous sense of community. I loved the support, I loved knowing what Alex would answer in interviews before he'd answer, I loved recognizing exactly from where each gif was, I loved the people, the instant friendships just because we love the same music. I used to stay up until 3 on school days to listen to their radio show live so I could live-blog and it was just  fun . Also, yes, I wrote fan fiction. Of that I am ashamed. But I'm also thankful. There's no way I could have ever evolved into writing original work without the support I received from the fanfiction community. People will tell you its amazing, that they cried for hours or laughed in the middle of a class because of my words. It boosts your confidence like nothing else I've ever experienced. I wanted to feel that in this book. I wanted to see how happy you can get when omg I wrote a cute make out scene between Alex and Jack (I realize nowadays that's inappropriate but in my defense, Alex wasn't married to Lisa in those days and come on, they were making out on stage all the time) and it made someone happy and they liked. That feeling of fangirling together was amazing. So yeah. Nowadays, I'm not quite that lost 9th grader. I love music (All Time Low aren't that great of a band tho. Their new stuff is repetitive. Also weightless isn't the literary masterpiece I used to think it was) but I care less about the band. I'm not active in fandoms anymore. I still remember my fandom days warmly. They were fun and I think All Time Low will always have some place in my heart. I have never met or stalked them (I will admit that when Mark Hoppus came to Israel, I went out of my way in case I'd see him but I didn't so oh well) but I do feel like I know a publicized part of them. That's okay too. Fangirls get a bad name. I hoped this book would help. It has insights but inevitably, it mocks them. I used to feel similar things (OMG JACK'S SKUNK HAIR, SHUT UP ZACK IS AWESOME HES JUST QUIET). I didn't sympathize with them. They were crazy. I'd hoped this book would be more real, showing how a fandom can be both a toxic and loving environment. I also felt this unrealistic vibe. This book had the opportunity to discuss serious issues. There is a problem with how boy bands are forced to do things they don't want to. There is a problem with the celebrity lifestyle and the problems it causes to the celebrity. The bandom community definitely has a problem with bullying (shoutout to all the death threats I've received through the years). Instead of attaching these issues, it mocks everything, ignoring the beauty of fandoms. Yeah, the MC has some nice monologues but as a whole, I felt that the fangirls were a gross parody. They were wild in an unrealistic way. I also felt like the unreliable narrator didn't work. It really didn't. It was unnecessary. I think it didn't work with this book's ideas. The gay thing wasn't dealt with well either. Come on, it's 2016, band members are out all the time. I'm tired of hearing about that blackmail. Make it funny, like he still sleeps with a teddy bear or he can't walk into a house with his left foot first. Gay doesn't work for me anymore. All in all, it was a fun read. I have a billion things to do so I won't say everything I want. Do I recommend it? Maybe. It wasn't what I'd hoped but it was entertaining. Also Cait Grace's review is on point. what I'm taking with me * Rupert is a suckish name. * if the mood strikes, I could totally kill Rian (Any atl fans wanna get angry at me for saying he's the least attractive and talented? * Fat shaming is always a good way to make instant humor! Or not.

I went into this book pretty dubious. I haven't been that crazy about the series, I didn't really like the heroine from previous books, the hero sounded improbable, and I tend to get put off by the "abused heroine must be gently coaxed into liking sex" plot. To my surprise, I liked almost everything about it. I just loved the characters. Charlie (she eschews her birth name, Chantel) is a tall, strong woman who's always felt oversized and unfeminine, especially next to her tiny ballerina mom. The one time she tried to be "feminine" it backfired in the worst possible way, so now she's just given up on the whole idea. Here's a typical thought: "He was taller than her. Stronger. Masculine enough to make her feel feminine. Sort of." But Charlie wants to be a mom, and she knows that her hangups aren't a good thing to put onto a child. So she asks Clay to help her get over her fear of sex, hoping she'll then be able to find some nice normal shlub to be with. Clay, a famous former underwear model, is far from ordinary and he gives new meaning to "not just a pretty face." He's worked hard to stay grounded and down to earth, helped by his late wife; her death has left him sad, without being all emo about it. At 31, he's ready to begin a new career -- and when he meet Charlie, he thinks he might also be ready to feel something special for a woman again. Here's how he sees her: "They were at eye level with each other. He liked that. He liked how she was strong and very much his equal." The two pair up surprisingly well, with Clay's self-confidence a good match for Charlie's awkward standoffishness. The love scenes between them are not just tender -- Clay, thorough as always, has read up on how best to help women in this situation -- but sweet and funny: "Don't do that." "Don't do what?" "Face me. I'm not ready." "It's just a penis. You've seen them before." "The last one attacked me." "Mine is more well mannered." His voice sounded as if he were amused. She glared at his back. "Are you laughing? This isn't funny." "It's a little funny." The story succeeds so wonderfully because these two seemingly disparate people are alike in many ways. Both have trouble being taken seriously: everyone assumes Clay is too pretty to be smart or reliable, and no one believed that a girl like Charlie could have been raped, not even her own mother. And they have so much to offer each other. Clay appreciates Charlie for being strong and real, and for seeing more in him than a great butt; unlike virtually everyone else in his life, she takes his plans and ambitions seriously. And Charlie desperately needs someone who recognizes her beauty and likes her just the way she is. There's a bit of sequel baiting -- how many books does this series need? On the other hand, it hit one out of the park on the 9th book so never mind -- and near the end they both get stupid, Clay more forgivebly than Charlie. Even the most insecure woman in the world should have understood what was going on with him. Even so, I loved this pair so much, and it was such a delightful surprise, I have to give it 5 stars.

George R.R. Martin, I forgive you for the horrors of the fourth book. A Dance with Dragons lived up to all the expectations for the fantasy genre set up by the first book. Although it took me a long time to read this novel (12 days), I loved every single word that was shared. Whereas I though almost every viewpoint was wasted in the fourth, the viewpoints in this book were thoughtful and added to the story. George R.R. Martin sets up a story that is engaging, and with the same quality content of the first three books. With each page turn, the reader got on her feet. He ties up some loose ends from the forth book and does so in a way that leaves the reader feeling satisfied. All the character arcs fit together so complexly and so perfectly. It's like a puzzle, where all the pieces fit together. This is truly a global book, where something that happens in one part of the world affects another. I especially enjoyed seeing Daenerys Targaryen, Jon Snow, and Tyrion Lannister. They were greatly missed in the fourth book. Their perspectives were especially enticing, with conflicts so great, the reader has no idea what will happen next. I also was glad to see Arya again, my favorite character. I don't know what I would do if I had to wait until the sixth book to see her again! Overall, it's a 5 star book and will remain a fantasy classic for ages to come. The next book cannot come fast enough! I wish there were a release date so I can wait for a set date.

I struggle to understand what anyone got out of this. I found the writing pretentious and saccharine and I was also irritated that I wasn't really supposed to be feeling this because I was supposed to be all weepy or some shit, and I wasn't allowed to feel it because it's rude to feel that about the prose of the deceased, a principle of etiquette I invented when reading this, applied to myself and then I judged myself for deviating from it. My mum was terminally ill for I think 9/18 months she was given. Other sad shit happened to me--though I would hardly put it in a book and pretend you had to read it! (Fuck, I'm SO Rude. Better luck next year)--and I tend to think other people's experience of sad stuff is equal or greater to mine and it's actually a nice way to live: you err on the side of compassion and get pleasantly surprised if people are like 'Nope: got both parents! #Sux2BU'--so what I mean is, reading this, I assumed everyone either had or will have someone close to them who will wrestle through this situation, and it teaches you way more than this book ever could. So I suppose it's a supplement for those people who haven't had that experience. This sounds like I'm gloating but how the hell could I gloat about a thing like this? If I am, Jesus! Let me have it. Also, why bother to put yourself through this now? Every single one of us gets out of bed in the morning because we've planned to deal with death when we come to it. Death: the ultimate deadline to procrastinate! The mechanics of enjoying this book I think also must be prurient to some degree--they always must be in cases of books like these. The first half is that whole, 'Be thankful you have legs because this 12 year-old got some wild disease you've never heard of--isn't life terrifying?!' You know, that whole weird phase we exercised when the TV serieses House et al were popular. There's really nothing to learn from that. One of the most important lessons about the author's situation is that no one ultimately gets a free pass in life. That being the case, why should I pay particular attention to this dying man's document over anyone else's? Is this a unique, interesting account of someone struggling with his circumstances? I guess it's rarer than most. When Still Alice the film came out, people got mad that it seemed to suggest it was sadder to get Alzheimer's if you were younger. I don't know about that but the same applies here, sorta. (I'm not using my whole brain on this because I didn't like it.) Then people must like it because the guy was well-read and kept making literary references (which, by the way, I will not even forgive a dying man for, because I FUCKING HATE that)? That he was trained as a neurosurgeon, so... so? The only insight that appeared original was that statistics don't offer relief from the inevitability of death, which is the opposite of what I posted in a blog last week or something. Of course they do: knowing I'm more likely to die at 80 than tomorrow allows me to indulge in petty arguments for decades. And I'm gonna! Sorry, mate. You had a tough run, and as you say, life doesn't afford you concessions. I sure don't. I hold out for better luck but don't demand or expect it. What can you do, really? Read better books.

Review found here. After reading Just One Year, I feel completely satisfied. It's like the feeling I get after the first serving on Thanksgiving: I feel full but not stuffed. Usually I proceed to continue to stuff my face with deliciousness, but in this case, I'm good. Trilogies are taking over the publishing world, but as they say, there are two sides to every story, and Gayle Forman has mastered the ability to tell both sides in full in only two books. It's miraculous! Just One Year jumps back to That Day. Well, the day after That Day. Willem is in the hospital, and because he has a bit of a head injury, he doesn't remember Allison. When you've only known someone for one day, no matter how life-shattering that day is, no matter how inmportant that person is, if you take a spill that temporarily wipes out your short term memory, you won't remember that person. Of course, Willem does eventually remember Allyson but by the time he escapes the hospital, he's SOL because 1. she's long gone, and 2. he only knows her as Lulu. Now, I know some of you may be incredulous as to the fact that Allison never got around to telling Willem her real name. Let's flash back to High School Mary. She once met a handsome boy from a rival high school's marching band. They met on a Saturday night after a competition and spent hours talking. They never exchanged names. HSM (High School Mary, not High School Musical) was sad. However, fortuitously, their football teams played very next Friday, and they met once more. This time, they exchanged names and then, through a mutual friend, numbers. They then proceeded to date for about two and a half months until it was no longer new and exciting, and the 40-minute distance overcame their mutual feelings of admiration and like-like. *sigh* L'amore. So easily broken by distances between Holland and New York or even just two suburbs. So as you can see, I believe this premise whole-heartedly. What I really like about this duology is that it really explores Allyson and Willem as people, not just their relationship. Most romances describe how the couple gets together. Very few detail the staying-together part. I think that's why books like JOD and JOY and Katie Cotugno's debut How to Love are so exciting. These stories do showcase the getting-together part, but they also show how hard life can make it to stay together. These stories show the ugly side, which is the leaving part, and then the bulk describes how the characters grow, how they morph, and how they attempt to find one another once more. It's lovely. Willem at the beginning of Just One Day is not the same as the Willem at the beginning of Just One Year. He is not the same in the middle either, nor at the end. This novel is so heartbreaking because the boy we met in Allyson's story was a goofy, cocky, charming young man who seems extraordinarily carefree. The boy in Just One Year, in contrast, is broken both body and soul. He's actually got very deep emotional scars in addition to the physical ones he acquired in Paris. Willem is lost in place and in time. He doesn't seem to really fit anywhere, which is why he travels so much. However, he even loses that, and it's like his entire being pales. He becomes someone less. Then, slowly, through the novel, he evolves as he tries to get himself back. He travels through Paris, the Netherlands, Mexico, and India looking for pieces of himself almost more than he's looking for Allyson. When reading Just One Day, I identified with Allyson's story as a girl who was trying to grow into a woman, but I actually went through that part of my life years ago. Now, while reading Just One Year, I found myself identifying more with Willem. A few years ago, I had some traumatic family turbulence, like Willem, and it truly crushed me. It's something I still haven't dealt with entirely, even though I've had time, just as Willem has. I often feel like I don't have a place in this world, that I am unwanted, and those are demons Willem has to face. Every part of me ached in solidarity with each blow Willem is dealt. Gayle is brilliant because she brings these ugly truths to light, but she does it in a kind way. Thus, they don't feel quite so ugly. Just One Day explores the notion that people love differently, and even the people close to us can feel like strangers if we don't accept the way that they love us and they don't accept the way we love them. If you have not read Just One Day or Just One Year, I recommend them highly. Can two people with so little in common find their way back to one another? Or should they just accept one perfect day with a near-stranger and move on? You'll have to find out for yourself. No, seriously. Go read it. Now.

The message I came away with from this book is one that I've been slowly chipping away at my whole life, I think. I think it all ties in with a tattoo that I have yet to get but have been thinking about forever, and that is "While there is life, there is hope." I have struggled with depression my whole life and one thing I've learned is that there is always more to life, to everything, than what you can see in that moment. When you're depressed, it's impossible to see anything beyond your own misery. But I've learned to cling to that logic, however impossible it seems in that moment, that what I'm experiencing isn't everything. No matter what, there is still something to live for. That is what Seth learns in this book. I really loved the way the author mirrored this theme by constantly having Seth in situations where he literally couldn't see more than a few feet ahead of him (or sometimes at all) but he had to keep moving forward anyway. There was always darkness before a big discovery. I love the message. I love the way this book kept me guessing, constantly. I couldn't put it down. I loved the writing - I have been so burned by self-indulgent authors lately, it was so refreshing to read a sparsely written book that didn't get bogged down by its own wordiness. The story and the message got to shine because the words didn't get in the way. Very much appreciated. I didn't love everything, though. I found a couple of the characters  especially Regine, and to a lesser extent Tomasz  very irritating, and a lot of the dialogue involving those characters had me rolling my eyes. I think they were supposed to be funny but those were the moments that reminded me I was reading YA. And I hated the Driver. What the F was up with the Driver? Every time they heard that stupid engine, I was like "Oh great, this again." Every time, it was just a pointless action scene that was getting between me and all the good stuff. I don't even know what the point of him was. But then again, neither did Seth and maybe that is is the point. Mind blown. Ultimately a really good read, but one that will most likely  leave you with more questions than answers . Maybe there will be a sequel! Rainbow Rowell could write a story about office supplies, and I would probably love it. Not because she wrote it, but because she would write it so well. I am a huge fan of character driven books - give me all the characterization! - and that is exactly what Rowell writes. Real, flawed, characters that come to life in my head. Who cares what they're even doing? (Except that I happen to like her plots, too, so.) Carry On was Rowell's take on a Chosen One story, and she chose to write about "the worst Chosen One who was ever chosen." Simon was brave, and honest, and loyal, and had more power than he knew what to do with, but he was also lost, and clueless, and damaged, and missing the innate chosenness, for lack of a better word. He did what he did because it was expected of him, because people told him to, because he had to. I think a defining moment was when Simon is told that he is not The Chosen One, and all he feels is relief because he's known that all along. In most Chosen One stories, when the hero finds out that s/he was not actually special and chosen, s/he decides that that doesn't matter. S/he has to save the world anyway. Simon was perfectly willing to give his power to the Mage and just let him handle it. I loved the idea that language and words were powerful. That we make them that way. I love Baz. Completely. And I feel like I'm in the minority here, but I also really liked Agatha. I liked that someone that came from magic, what everyone wanted and was fighting for, just didn't want it. She turned around and got as far away as she could from it. I loved that. There were a few things that I did not like about this book, though. First, a lot of the times it read like an American trying to write "British," like a lot of Harry Potter fanfiction. Which, I mean, is exactly what was going on here, but still. Second, there were way too many loose ends left loose. Nicodemus becomes important enough to warrant his own POV, and yet, he just basically disappears after that? What happens with him? Does he find out about Ebb? How? We kept hearing from Lucy, but none of that actually went anywhere. We know that she died after having Simon, or lost too much of herself while pregnant with him to stay alive, but what actually happened? If she didn't get trapped back behind the Veil, then couldn't she still try to talk to Simon? Does she ever get her story told? Third, Simon deserved more at the end. I know that this probably falls under "loose ends," but he deserves his own point. He lost his magic. He lost his Mage. He lost his school. He's stuck with wings and a tail. He deserved to learn the truth about his parents. He deserved to know that he was not the son of Normals. He deserved to know that the Humdrum was not his fault. That he was made that way. And whenever he would go on about not being The Chosen One and actually being The Greatest Threat, I kept waiting for someone to point out to him that the Mage was the Threat. That Simon really did cause his fall. That he was good, after all. But I guess no one ever found out what the Mage did. Ugh. Fourth, I get that writing the eighth book in a fantasy series as a standalone novel is hard, and I think that she did a great job with it, but i want more. I want to see how the characters got to this point. I want the story-building and characterization that you can only get in a series. I think that the deaths would have hit me harder had I had eight books to really care about the secondary characters. Instead, they were just more of a plot point. Fifth, this could very well only be an issue because I read Fangirl, but the plot was pretty predictable. No less enjoyable to read, but I still saw all the big moments coming. Despite all of that, though, Simon and Baz came to life for me, and I do not want to say goodbye to them, and that is what makes a good book in my opinion.

The cat knocked over a pile of books I have yet to find a home for (which is why I read ebooks for the most part now) and this was one. I have not read it in a few years but I remembered how much I did plus I have his 'Zombie Survival Guide' in my backpack for when the horde shows up I am ready to go. So many books focus on the terror during, but Max is focusing on what happens after. What is the world like? What have peoples psyches become? How does this effect the children? Government? Economics? Even more addressed in his personal compilation using the information he collected for an official report addresses. This book is really interesting. But fair warning, if you are looking for the blood, the guts and the infection of a traditional zombiesque novel Z style you maybe disappointed because this is after the war. But I beseech you to give it a chance. I just acquired the audio version of this book and it is worth every penny. It has a cast, each tale being told in their own voice. I found myself crying, horrified, terrified at times and shocked. The story structure is in a type of retelling of the oral accounts from the survivors, so hearing the story is so powerful. The audio format is the maple syrup on the bacon that is the book! I can go to sleep listening to this (yes I am a glutton for punishment and obviously a masochist when it comes to my dream cycles). The sociological implications being addressed with each story from each survivor our 'Author' interviews. I realize this probably has been an issue with some readers, especially those that want their zombies fed to them on a plateful of "BRAAAAAAAAAINS". But the tale could not be any different without it being just another book about zombies. Being a medievalist I adore the oral format, I truly enjoyed how he presents each of them, how he let the stories flow from each person to the next, a global bonfire. A futuristic book of post apocalyptic lays with the tragic nature of the stories. At the same time more complex due to the subject nature. Each tale like a mini-short of horror and survival with each persons experience. It is an elegant and dark mockumentary compiled together in a simple and powerful presentation. The cover is under spoken in a color of rusty orange, the Z standing out. The font is jagged and the flames in the background psychologically presented us with the end and the beginning. I recommend this to someone who wants a step up from the fictional tales and that want to take this belief to the next level...who knows these tales may actually help you when patient zero emerges, so take notes!
