Within the brotherhood, Rhage is the vampire with the strongest appetites. He's the best fighter, the quickest to act on his impulses, and the most voracious lover--for inside him burns a ferocious curse cast by the Scribe Virgin. Owned by this dark side, Rhage fears the times when his inner dragon is unleashed, making him a danger to everyone around him. Mary Luce, a survivor of many hardships, is unwittingly thrown into the vampire world and reliant on Rhage's protection. With a life-threatening curse of her own, Mary is not looking for love. She lost her faith in miracles years ago. But when Rhage's intense animal attraction turns into something more emotional, he knows that he must make Mary his alone. And while their enemies close in, Mary fights desperately to gain life eternal with the one she loves... This was a decent entry into the series, although I just wasn't that happy with Rhage and Mary. Don't get me wrong, their story is great and everything and I'm really glad that they both get a happy ending-ish. But they also kind of ticked me off. Mary yo-yoed too much between "I don't want anything and this moment is fine, feel free to move on" and "Back off lady. She also ticked me off when she'd be on a "move on, please" moment and get pissed when it would look like Rhage was doing just that. Rhage was way too caveman-esque for me. Too much "This is what I want so it's going to happen" I did think Rhage's curse was interesting. What a way to make you seriously think about you actions and the consequences thereof. It was also interesting to see him go from a man who did things just this side of crazy to essentially keep his monster at bay to someone who found a way to manage the beast and who didn't have to ride the edge of adrenaline to keep himself together. John Matthew was a surprise. I'm glad he wasn't a stalker, he just couldn't communicate so that made things a little difficult. It was cool to see the way Tohrment and Wellsie took him in once he accepted the invitation to train. I am wondering if there's more to his character though...something just feels...well, not necessarily off but different. A good different, but different nonetheless. I can't wait to see how his training goes. Like with Dark Lover , I loved the relationship between all of the brothers. They all looked after each other and worked well together. They all know how each other works and know the good and bad signs. They also understand that as a member of the Brotherhood, sometimes you have to do things that you don't enjoy to your brother in order to keep him alive Like the rythe. It shined some interesting light on Zsadist (the whole book did to be honest, but that's a different story); There was also when Zsadist forced Phury to beat him; I do want to know more about that... . And I loved the way that they have just pulled Butch into the fold (granted it's because V has seen that he stays around, but still). And that they did the same to Mary after a fashion. Then there's Zsadist and Bella. Those two had some delicious sexual tension and I want more! With the little cliffhanger there, something tells me their book is going to be full of more heat and some awesome asskicking.

UPDATE: I decided to take down another star. Actual Rating: 2.5 Let me first get things straight. I liked this book, but there were parts of this book that made me think "What the fuck?" I finished reading this in two hours and had about an entire night to think through this review and I'm still quite unsure on how to rate it. I thoroughly enjoyed the first 50% of the book. The whole idea of this forbidden love affair at the law firm was interesting enough. And unlike most erotic romance novels, this book wasn't all sex, sex, sex, heart break, sex, sex, sex. No. I actually enjoyed the gradual romance plot that developed in this book. There was no insta-love or even insta-lust. There is a difference between love at first sight and being attracted to someone from the first time you meet them, and this book brought that out really well. What Brad and Julia had was purely sexual attraction. Neither of them confused it for being anything more than that. Furthermore, I really liked the characters. Yes, there were parts where both of them annoyed me but I liked them, over all. Julia Campbell is an intern at a law firm. She is really good looking. So good looking that every guy wants to bone her. Now, if her character was not well done, I would have labeled her as a Mary Sue. In fact, in the beginning I thought Julia was a Mary Sue by the amount of time she talks about her own good looks, but she isn't. She has only slept with a total of two men, confused both her relationships to being in love. She is one of those girls who believes that sex means intimacy and that there is no point in having sex with someone if you aren't in love with them. But that has not stopped her from being a cock tease. She goes out, finds attractive men, leads them on and sends them back home. What a bitch, right? Everyone warns Julia to stay away from the notorious divorced, divorce lawyer, Brad De Luca, because she is exactly his type. What type that is, I still don't know. "There is a reason that you were not assigned to Brad. Stay away from him." Is it that she is young? (*cough* pedophile). Is it that she is so beautiful? Or is it the very simple fact that she is a girl? I really don't know. Everyone at the law firm has a very bad opinion about Brad. Apparently he bangs anything that has a hole in between it's legs. Everyone in this book make Brad out to be such a bad guy, one of those typical conceited bastards with a bloated ego, you can imagine yourself rolling your eyes before the said character is even introduced. "What Mr. Broward was probably too proper to say, is that Brad is incorrigible! He stopped getting female interns three years ago because he couldn't keep his hands off of them. He is divorced, due to another one of his...relationships, and is never without some young thing on his arm. He's Italian, you know how those men are." She pronounced the word "Italian" like it was some kind of diseased animal, and waved her hand like that should explain everything. "Bottom line," she fixed her steely gaze on me, "you are exactly his type. You need to stay as far away from Brad De Luca as you can get." From the way he was described I was pretty sure I was going to hate this man. But boy, I couldn't have been more wrong. I actually ended up liking Brad De Luca. To be quite honest, he is probably the only reason I enjoyed this book as much as I did. He is as incorrigible as everyone makes him out to be, but he is so honest about the way he lives his life. "Julia, I don't need you to attack me just because you don't believe in my lifestyle choices. I have absolute confidence in my sexual relationships and don't need to explain them to anyone. I am choosing to explain them to you because I hope to fuck you in the future and I don't want to do it with any misplaced expectations on your part." He isn't even one of those men who like to dominate and control women! "Why didn't you just say you didn't like it? I would have been more than happy to eat it all myself Julia." "I did say I didn't like it. You were so pushy about me eating it, and so enthusiastic about it. I didn't want to disappoint you." I sounded like a freakin' child, but it had come out of my mouth, no point in trying to put it back in. "I'm not your father, Julia." His grin faded slightly but he kept his tone light. "You don't have to do as I tell you." Like I said, this book was very gradual, very subtle, there was more dialogues and talk about sex than the real action. Julia and Brad had sex only after 70% of the book was done. They had sex a total of two times in the entire book. But there was plenty of dirty sex talk that I felt was sufficient. The reason I had to reduce 2.5 stars from this book is how this book turned out when it was nearing the end. After the whole Brad De Luca debacle, Julia starts to refer herself as "Old Julia" and "New Julia." Did she really need a man to bring out a change in her? Then there was the part in the very end where he gets all possessive. And then Julia agrees to do some freaky shit like have threesome just because Brad is into it. Me no Gusta.

The Deal conveyed important messages but it was also fun and steamy in all the right places ;) Hannah is beautiful and smart. What I love most about her is how upfront she was about her past. A Book Riot article I ran across recently asked the question: what is it about magical boarding schools? Why are they such appealing settings for books? This is exactly I wanted to read on a rainy Saturday home sick, and it was also exactly what I want to read all the time.

I read this book knowing nothing of what it was about. I didn't even read the synopsis. And I vehemently encourage everyone to do the same. Because it seriously cannot be explained in a synopsis, and it might just give you a wrong idea of what it is really about. The only thing you need to know, if you haven't read it yet, is that it is AWESOME. <<Once upon a time, an angel and a devil fell in love. It did not end well.>> With this beginning, who wouldn't want to read it? Disclaimer: The following contains a very spoiled review. Beware. This book was such a huge surprise. I was not expecting to fall in love with it, especially when I realised it was about angels. I'm kind of a sceptic when it comes to the whole angels and devils lore. It's not like I've read a lot about it and have not enjoyed it, on the contrary actually. I tend to stay away from it on instinct. But this one surpassed my expectations on the genre. My infatuation with this started out with the writing. Sadly, I have come to expect mostly poor or mediocre writing when it comes to young adult novels, but the writing here was almost flawless. It was melodic, pure and it made sense, which lately I've found to be rare. The characters were loveable and real and raw and OMG I love them so very much. Karou, the main character was so relatable. She was a strong and kick-ass protagonist, and she was, (yes, thank god) NOT stupid or vapid. Zuzana might easily be my favourite character. At least she was the one I could see more of myself in. She was a tiny and full of energy little thing. <<She thought Zuzana's tininess was perfect, like a fairy you found in the woods and wanted to put in your pocket. Though in Zuzana's case, the fairy was likely to be rabid, and bite.>> Brimstone, the most enigmatic and fear-inspiring character was incredibly well constructed. I had no idea what he really was up to during the book, up until the very end. I just knew I loved him. He had an unique way of seeing things. <<"I don't know many rules to live by," he'd said. "But here's one. It's simple. Don't put anything unnecessary into yourself. No poisons or chemicals, no fumes or smoke or alcohol, no sharp objects, no inessential needles - drug or tattoo - and... no inessential penises, either. And that's the thing about Laini Taylor. She makes these statements, which make you laugh, but they have so much truth to them too. <<"It's a condition of monsters that they do not perceive themselves as such. The dragon, you know, hunkered in the village devouring maidens, heard the townsfolk cry 'Monster!' and looked behind him. <<"Have you ever asked yourself, do monsters make war, or does war make monsters? And then Akiva. He's such a mystery in the beginning, but my heart melted for him throughout the story. <<"Once upon a time, a little girl was raised by monsters. But angels burned the doorway to their world, and she was all alone. It's here that the plot thickens. We begin to see both sides of a war we don't understand. And the relationship between Akiva and Karou deepens. And this is the reason why this book does not have 5 stars. The romance was so quick. Karou knows he's her enemy, and yet she lets herself fall for him, faster than a shooting star. It is beautiful, and I loved reading it, but it still seemed too sudden. I would have expected her to take a little longer to come to terms with the situation, and not jump straight into his arms. <<"Once upon a time, an angel lay dying in the mist. And a devil knelt over him and smiled. We then learn about Madrigal and her story with Akiva. And this was beautiful in a Romeo and Juliet way. A love destined to end badly before it even begun. Madrigal is the one who teaches Akiva to hope. To hope for love, for a future, for peace. For a new way of living. One where war and death are not the main elements. <<"Hope can be a powerful force. Maybe there's no actual magic in it, but when you know what you can hope for most and hold it like a light within you, you can make things happen, almost like magic. The breaking of the wishbone was very emotional, and though I had mostly guessed who Karou was, there were still some elements of surprise. <<"Such a little thing, and brittle, and the sound it made: a sharp, clean snap." I actually cried in this book. If you know me, you know I seldom do. The part where Madrigal is in prison and Brimstone visits her is what got me. Not the actual being-in-prison thing, but that this was where the relationship of something akin to father and daughter was most prominent. <<"They know, child. They already know. And they aren't ashamed of you, either." Either It was as close as he would come, and it was good enough.>> <<"Do you remember the wishbone, when I was younger?" "I remember." "I finally made a wish on it. Or... a hope, I suppose, as there was no real magic in it." "Hope is the real magic, child." In sum, this reads like a fairytale, and deep down, it might as well be one. But it is not the kind of fairytale I would expect to read. There is ugliness here, and war and reality. And that is why I loved it. It was not sunshine and rainbows. It was real. That ending though, it broke my heart. I really need to know what happened. And there are so many unanswered questions in this volume. I cannot wait to dive into the next.

You can also find this review on my blog: Wings of Nephilim I'm beginning to wonder if the Grisha Trilogy has ruined me for the liking the darker character more than the main love interest. Then ultimately being crushed because things don't work out the way I want them too. We had a few main characters. Our heroine, Kyra. I liked her for about 70% of the book. I mean you have to be an idiot to think you can join an assassin's guild and not kill anyone. Seriously. . The romance was more on the side burner. There were elements of romance and brushes of it but the brunt of the story was action and thievery/assassinry. I don't really know if I can constitute this as a love triangle. I mean there are two guys (I didn't really count Flick, he doesn't have a chance in hell) James and Tristam. Tristam...is just boring. He's a typical knight, chivalrous, brave, etc., blah, blah, blah. She had zero romantic chemistry with him. Then of course we have our darker character. James, the leader of the assassin guild. He's mysterious, kinda evil, has big plans to change the world through whatever means he deems necessary, manipulative...can you tell which one I liked better yet? I don't know what YA authors have against going against the grain. I mean I tried not to like him too much because I knew it was all Tristam (for whatever reason) but I can't help which characters pull me in. He said it a few times, she could have been the best. I think that would have made for a much more interesting story. One of my biggest issue with this book is the lack of description. I genuinely don't have a good image of what those three characters even look like. She never legitimately describes them! There was a general lack of description in the whole novel. Scenery didn't have much of a description either. I enjoyed myself within the book up until the last "arc" with the Makvani. I just...didn't like the direction the book went. Is it so hard/terrible to have a character skilled at what they do? Why do they have to coincidentally be half-blooded with some mystical race that explains their better than average abilities? Why? It took all of her skill out and just made it a cop out to explain why she was more agile than most people. How terrible it would be if she was just GOOD at something. This was where we got a bit of a plot twist. Did I see it coming? Not necessarily. Did I like it? Not really. I like the Makvani themselves, just not Kyra's incorporation with them. The pacing was well done, I was never bored and it was an easy read. I am interested in what else will happen as this looks like Goodreads said this is a series. I hope to see more of James. I want him to escape and for him to be right. Hahaha. I want Kyra to go dark and rescue him actually. That would be amazing to read. Well if this IS a series, I do plan to read the next one. It was an interesting novel to read, a fun world and a great debut novel for this author.

OH WAIT SHE WANTED TO BE POPULAR *smacks head* that was the reason why she treated her friends like they were not good enough. This book was freaking amazing, like wow. But still, couldn't give it a 5/5 stars even if I wanted to, because there were certain things that really bothered me, so now this is only a 4 stars for me. And I'm going to get it out first why I took down half a star so I can rave about the book afterwards. Here's the thing. I'm going to be the first person to defend this book that this isn't a Harry Potter fanfic. After reading the whole book, anyone can see that. There's such a unique world building and some of the elements of the magickal world just blew my mind away. I especially liked the canon about the spells. But I have to admit that it took time for me to see it, which was like the first 20% of the book. I could barely push myself through it, it reminded me of HP so much and I was so fucking annoyed, seriously. It took time for the world building to show the differences and show the actual originality of Rainbow Rowell, but like I said, it was a drag to get there. The other thing that bothered me was how predictible it was. I felt like I always knew what was going to happen like at least 100 pages before it happened. Which I felt was a bit too much for me. I was expecting a huge twist at the end to blow my mind and it didn't come and it was a bit disappointing for me. After writing these two negativities I realise it might seem like a pretty "meh" book to some of you. Well, lemme tell you something. It's not. With those two negativities with any other book I wouldn't have given more than 3 stars, but GOSH THIS BOOK. THIS BOOK IS FUCKING AMAZING, OK? Ok. I'm so glad we agree on that one. So, let's talk about the positivities, because there are so many. (Like half of it is Baz, seriously.) I looooooooooooved the story, even though it was predictable. It was a well thought out, well written story which knew exactly when to drop little hints here and there and when to release more information with making the reader wanna know and read more. Which is one of the most important element of any story in my opinion. But what really made it amazing was the characters. The amazing, diverse, well written, fucking badass and awesome characters! Ok, maybe I wouldn't exactly call Agatha badass in that sense of the way, but it took a certain kind of courage to turn your back to the magickal world and live among Normals when you could have lived your life in such easier ways. I'm pretty sure I loved all the characters. (Except for Agatha. She annoyed the shit out of me from the first moment she showed up. But I even learned to appreciate her in the end, especially because of the choice that I mentioned above.) Simon really was the world Chosen One like EVER, I really don't know how he managed to survive this long while he was constantly under attack. Probably only because of Penny, who was like the most awesome and badass character and I loved how cool and strong and badass female character she was and how she managed to be all of those things while she was "suposed to be" only the friend of the Chosen One, and how she had none of that. She was right in the middle and most of the time (or all the time, really) she even enjoyed it. It was driving her. I loved the character of Baz's mom and I wish we could have gotten more about her and what the magickal world looked like while she was sort of in charge and I wondered a couple of times how it would have changed the world the book took place in if she didn't die. Would have been war between her and the Mage? Would have it taken this long? Or would have a simple duel solved it all? Would she have came out of it on top or bottom? It would have definitely been a completely different story then. Speaking of the Mage, I so fucking saw that coming. I knew it from like the very first chapter that was from his point of view and I was sort of doing fist bumps in the air when it all was confirmed. Not even kidding. I don't wanna say too much about Ebb and Nicodemus, because I don't wanna spoil anything, but lemme just say that I enjoyed a hell of a lot their parts. Is there any chance Rainbow Rowell plans on giving us another "fanfiction" that shows their story? When they were kids and went to Watford. It could also show more of Baz's mom. It would literally make my heart go wild. Not even kidding here. Pls, Rainbow Rowell. PLS. And no, I did not forget about Baz, in case you're wondering. I was simply saving the best for last. Just. BAZ. I don't even know where to begin to explain how much I love this not-human-blood-sucking, sarcastic shithead. Because that's what he is. But he's also intelligent and kind and thoughtful and just so fucking in love with Simon Snow it hurts. Everything about Baz is either really painful or really happy, but absolutely and totally full of feels. Like all the feels, everywhere. I just love the bastard so fucking much it's not even funny anymore. Ok, now, other things I really enjoyed in the book: Did I rave about the spells yet? Because GOSH, the system and the work behind the spells is just so so so amazing, seriously. I also like the whole magickal world the writer built up, including the fact that these people actually live in the 21th century, meaning they know how to use a fucking laptop or a phone, which was such a delight to read (Really, who fucking believes muggles don't bring their muggle shit into Hogwarts? Like, seriously? How can students still write on parchment and with ink and quill?!?!?!?!?!?!) Also, the creatures featured in the book were really interesting, had nice twists on the already known ones and totally original ones appeared too, which I was really enjoying. I also loved how there were different point of views for the chapters and I liked how the writer wasn't afraid to use different lengths for each chapter, which varied from 2 lines to idk how many 20-30 pages long chapters too, which was pretty fun tbh. Ok, I guess that's it. Jesus, this turned into a fucking ramble. I'm really sorry about that. I need to figure out how to not to do that in the future tbh.

The opening lines of A Spear of Summer Grass are enough to entice most readers; they were enough to entice me. "Don't believe the stories you have heard about me. I have never killed anyone, and I have never stolen another woman's husband. Oh, if I find one lying around unattended, I might climb on, but I never took one that didn't want taking." Based purely on those opening words the story of Delilah Drummond was begging to be read. Her story is predictable and even a bit cliche in parts but she is a pleasurable character with a very complex past. The problem with this book lies with the supporting characters and the some of the content which other readers may find offensive. There are extreme highs and lows within the story leaving this overall a very average read. The highlight of the novel was Delilah herself. Her mother, referred to as "Mossy" was a scandalous woman who was frequently married and divorced leaving Delilah with no true father figure; they moved regularly as the novel refers to their lives in various countries and continents leaving Delilah with no true stability; she suffers loss and see tragedy at a very young age so is it really any wonder that her character is selfish and cold seeking pleasure without any true emotional attachment? It is natural that Delilah would protect herself by closing off to any emotional connection and instead rely on affairs with married men and marrying for money instead of love. She can't be hurt if she doesn't feel. This life works for the young Delilah until she finds herself too deep in scandal after the death of her most recent husband and is exiled to Africa and hidden away on the plantation of one of her previous step-fathers, Nigel. It is only here, in this untamed wilderness, away from the parties and the high society of Paris, that Delilah is able to find a new perspective and open herself up to true feelings of love. The story itself is a bit cliche in parts. Delilah, one of the few white settlers in a savage Africa finds herself almost immediately inundated by African villagers who look to her as a medical savior. They expect to her to have "white medicine" and be able to heal all of their ailments. Since she worked for four years as a nurse during the war she is able to help them. It is a story arc that was included primarily to show Delilah's growth and transformation as she grew from a selfish promiscuous tart to a compassionate woman. It is reminiscent of many other African fiction novels and does not offer anything unique to A Spear of Summer Grass. It is a underlying storyline, a mild arc really, that is included to teach Delilah love and compassion. I enjoyed it despite it being a bit formula and predictable. There are moments in the story that I suspect may offend other readers. During a scene with Delilah and Ryder (another central character - a long-haired and gritty white man prominent in Africa) he threatens her and states that he could have his way with her and then throw her body to the hyenas. Out of context it's an offensive threat of rape but within the context of the novel it's an idle threat (considering what the reader has learned of Ryder's character) that calls attention to Delilah's promiscuity and her habit of sexually teasing men in order to have them at her beck and call. That may have worked in Paris but she's now living in Africa and there is a different culture and new threats. The same applies to mentions of domestic violence. The reader must consider the setting, the characters and the intent or it may be offensive. It's historic (set in the mid 1920's), it's cultural (with a setting in the wilds of Africa) and it tells the story of a young woman who finds her purpose in the most unlikely of situations. It's worth a read. Review by Ashley LaMar Closed the Cover

Four years ago, Harry Bosch shot and killed the serial killer known as the Dollmaker. He had not set out to do so. He was following a lead, and he found himself, late one night, alone and with no time calling for back-up, suddenly confronting the killer in the man's bedroom. Surprised, the man reached for something under his pillow, after Bosch had told him several times to show him his hands. Bosch fired a kill-shot. To Bosch's horror, he realized the man was going for his toupee. After an extensive investigation, Bosch's shot was determined to be a "clean" one, meaning that he had followed police protocol. The evidence found at the man's house also confirmed that he was the serial killer. Four years later, the man's widow is suing Bosch and the LAPD in a civil case, claiming that her husband had not been the killer, that Bosch had planted evidence on the scene, that the LAPD was covering up Bosch's crime because they wanted to close the case. Bosch knows he did the right thing by killing Norman Church, but he also wishes the incident had gone differently. This is the set-up for Michael Connelly's third book in his long-running Harry Bosch series, "The Concrete Blonde". The title refers to the recent discovery of another body that may have been done by the Dollmaker. Police discover it based on a note sent to the police department, alluding to the fact that Bosch did, indeed, kill the wrong guy. Bad timing, considering the most-hyped court case since the Rodney King trial has just begun. Alternating deftly between riveting court-room drama and a race to investigate whether the Dollmaker is still at large or whether a copycat is on the loose, "The Concrete Blonde" is brilliant suspense writing and police procedural at its best.

This review is going to be one of my more mature and well-thought-over reviews. Don't get me wrong, it wasn't a terrible book. If it is any consolation, I want to read the next one. One thing that hit me was the swearing. I mean, this thing should have come with a warning! Being a teenager, I am no stranger to these swear words. However, I found the constant use of such profanities quite excessive. It made the writing seem lazy, as if Holly Black could not think of other words for the characters to say. That being said, this may just be her perception of the language teenagers use. I believe that swear words can be used for effect at some specific events in a story, but the fact that they were scattered around rather frequently did not appeal to my taste. The next thing I would like to point out is that the story took a while to get to the main plot point. At many points of the story, I found that something was happening, then two sentences later it was resolved. This lack of expanding on events confused me, and I found myself having to re-read parts. I also noticed that there were some parts that could have gone unwritten and not have an effect on the story. Personally, i thought it was over halfway through the book until the actual plot point came to being. I also found that I lacked any bond with certain characters. One of these characters was Janet. We meet her, she pops up here and there in the story,  then she dies. Full stop. Was I supposed to care? I'm not entirely sure. Another of these characters was Corny. He seemed kinda sketchy to me. He was way to interested in Kaye's whole Faery issues, then he becomes enchanted by Nephamael before coming to and stabbing him repeatedly. If that doesn't scream psycho, I don't know what does. I mean, he got himself into the mess, crawled into a  Faery  Court, yet Kaye and himself seemed surprised when he was put under a spell. I did not form much of a bond to Kaye or Roiben (which I can't be sure I am pronouncing correctly) either, though I was more interested in them and probably would worry slightly if they were in danger, but not greatly. I just feel like more effort could have been put in to giving readers something more to go on to form an emotional attachment to the characters. On a lighter note, when I did eventually get into the story, I found myself quite enjoying it. In fact, I thought it ended too quickly. I would have wanted the action and similar parts to have been described in more detail and to have lasted longer. Now that I know you don't have to read Valiant to read Ironside, since Valiant (2nd book in Black's series) is a seperate story, but Ironside continues with this one, I am going to read Ironside ASAP. I apologize to those who took the time to read my long review on a rather old book, and please make sure if you have not read the book that you don't read the spoilers!

Maddie has lost everything twice over. After experiencing almost unimaginable tragedy, she was betrayed by those she trusted most. With nothing left, she leaves, driving aimlessly south as she tries to outrun her past. What's supposed to be a quick stop in a sleepy beach town becomes a longer stay when she accepts a job at a homey cafe, befriends the locals, and meets a little girl with whom she has an amazing connection. Gabe's life hasn't been easy, especially when it comes to love, but he's since built his entire world around his daughter Noie. Terrified of strangers for some unexplained reason, Noie surprises everyone when she immediately attaches herself to Maddie, telling everyone they're friends. While their connection brings Gabe and Maddie closer to each other, it also opens an otherworldly door to finally healing and moving on. The ending to the story was so abrupt that I thought I'd somehow skipped a chapter. It didn't make for a bad read, but even though it implied a happily ever after, it seemed to leave some loose ends and had me wondering what would happen next. While this move was obviously intentional, it was rather disappointing after becoming so wrapped up in the characters. Were it not for the quick drop-off of an ending, I probably would have said this book was perfect. I loved that Noie wasn't just a replacement for what Maddie had lost, but rather a link to it. I also loved the slow build of her relationship with Gabe. But in the end, I'm not sure I'd classify it as romance first. It was more the tale of one woman beginning to heal and move on, and while the romance certainly played a part, it wasn't the main focus of the story. In any case, it's a lovely story about friendship, healing, and finding a new start, and I recommend it to anyone who enjoys something more meaningful than just another romance novel. I received this book through IFB Tours in exchange for an honest review, but I'm far too opinionated to let a freebie influence my opinions or reviews.

I'll just come right out and say that overrall I was disappointed with this book. I gave it 3 stars out of respect for the author and the previous books; and this is still my favorite series out there. But 3 stars says 'liked it' and 2 stars says 'it was ok', and my initial reaction after finishing it last night was 'it was ok.' I didn't wait quite as long as others for this book, but I did wait 4 years for it come out. It seems to me that Martin's editor really needs to rein him in and make him tighten up the story. It's like he doesn't know how to write where he needs the story to go so he stalls by writing way too much fluff. I feel nothing was really accomplished by this book, and if there had been some much needed editing I don't think the split of Feast and Dance would have been needed. There is 1 great book combined in those 2 books. And after finishing this one I don't like the way they were split; by storyline instead of by timeline. This book had some really amazing moments. When I started reading it was 'meh' to me for awhile, but then things would pick up and there would be a couple chapters of pure awesomeness. Then there would be some more blah chapters. I didn't really care that much about Dany's storyline. I'm in the same frame of mind as Ser Jorah, she really just needs to make her way to Westeros. This book got her no closer to that goal, and its starting to get old. And neither Tyrion nor Victarion makes it to her. Really? We left Feast with them on their way, and for their entire storylines in Dance they are still...on...their...way. I did however enjoy Jon's chapters, he is definately one of my favorites in the series. He has to make some tough decisions, and we will see if they are wise ones or not. However, I was devastated when reading Jon's final chapter. There are so few good characters left that killing Jon leaves hardly anybody to cheer for anymore. Of course, after reading some GRRM message boards no one thinks he's actually dead. I need to go and reread that chapter, but we shall see. Tyrion's chapters, usually my favorites, were a bit dull this time around. Way too much time spent on boats and getting nowhere in the process. I guess I will stop there since I'm being kind of a downer. I feel a little bit bad about that because I absolutely LOVE this series. I am hoping that on a reread I will enjoy this book more. That is what happened when reading Feast for the second time, so perhaps it could happen again. But my first reaction is a bit of disappointment. I would still recommend people pick up this series, and this book if they have read through Feast. I haven't given up on George or ASOIAF, and I don't recommend others do either.

I read this for my Buddy Reading Club on Instagram (actually that is still on going, but I got a bit excited with it). Ain't I a bad dude? Making Faces was the kind of palette cleanser needed from time to time. It is a nice, cute, simple story, full of memorable characters, and plagued by some of the cliches you would expect from a book like this. It is the story of Fern, the self proclaimed "ugly girl" that falls for the beautiful, perfect, wrestler boy who happens to also be an old soul with a love for Shakespeare. Now I made it sound horrible. Damn it, that really wasn't my intention. Making Faces is actually a really good book! Well, the first half of it anyway. Basically, without spoiling much, Ambrose, the love interest, goes to war and a bomb goes off, kills his comrades and leaves him horribly disfigured. The book is made up from two parts for me, part two starting when Ambrose starts falling for Fern, after he returns from the war. Part one is great! Thee are so many sweet little moments that made me smile. Ambrose is not your typical mean jock. And that is what makes this book different from others of it's kind. Side characters, like Bailey, are also great and overall make you care about the whole universe. The war and the PTSD subjects are treated well,  which is a huge plus for me personally. But then we have the second part. The falling in love part. It is not that it is bad. It is also not the fact that I am a guy. After finishing, I talked with a friend of mine who also read the book and she shared my opinion. The love part of the story is pretty much where the cliches come in. We also have the bad guy here. Well not exactly a bad guy, but he is one dimensional enough to call him that. The story moves quite fast in this part and the conclusion is not only predictable, but also a bit boring. All in all, I enjoyed Making Faces and I think a lot of you would too.

I loved the premise and tightly written setup, but the bulk of the investigation felt a bit draggy. I also got tired of watching Ginger tackle the constant chorus of "You can't do that, it's not safe!" that followed her from scene to scene. Yes, it's realistic. It's still tedious, though. My biggest issue was that during another perfect opportunity to raise the stakes, the characters made a plan, seemed to have heaps of time to implement it, tweaked it slightly during the process, and then carried it off without a hitch. Personally, I'd have liked to see a bit more complexity. That part of the ending also felt off because Ginger's biggest worry during the battle was that killing the German spies could let them carry secrets back to their commanders. But the spies were there to learn how to set up that kind of after-death report, so they wouldn't have had an existing binding that let them get home and check in. Maybe there was another way for the ghosts to get that info across? I guess it worked as an excuse to get Ginger closer to the action, but a little more justification might have been nice. Ghost Talkers is a good book; I just wish it had been a little more even.

The story is about Sam, one of the mean girls at her high school. She died, but then wakes up the next morning on the exact same day of her death. And this cycle goes on for seven days (seven friggin days! crazy). During these 'repeats', Sam learns to try and change other people, and also change herself. I disliked the first few chapters because Sam and her friends (especially Lindsay) were VERY VERY MEAN. It feels like whenever I read their endless rants/schemes/bad-assery (if such word exists), I despise them and I would not want to read any further, but then I'll get curious and read again,haha. But as the story progresses, when Sam was starting to do some changes, the story was having more sense. The second half was deeper and we can see how Sam grows. There were mini stories that will reveal why this character was like this to the other character (I just don't want to give spoilers). Sam actually have gotten used to the cycle and have this mentality of "Oh, screw it, next day these things did not happen" So she'll do basically whatever she wants. My favorite part is Kent and Sam's relationship. Kent was one of my favorite characters because he's so nice even of Sam was such a bitch to her  (but he still likes her,boo) . I can't imagine someone who's like that in real life. I kinda wish there's a real Kent out there,heehee. One last thing, I think Sam focused more on her friends rather than on her family. But hey, it's the author's vision so who am I to criticize,haha. I just wished there was one day on her cycles that she focused on her family  (sure she spent time with her little sister but I think I was looking for more drama on her relationship with her parents because hellooo, you'll gonna die and you won't want to be with you family?) I'm just thinking aloud here. Overall, I have learned from this book that we, normal human beings with no (or rather unsure) fate on what comes after death, should be a bit more considerate on our life decisions. Sam had to learn life's lessons for 7 days. I don't think all of us would have the same privilege.

This book was alright. I liked both of the main characters, and Simon in particular, but the transition between being friends (I loved their friendship) and lovers was kind of abrupt for me. The first half of the novel went along at a proper pace, and then it seemed to speed up for the sake of fitting in all of the plot, and that's where it lost me somewhat. It wasn't bad, but I didn't feel like it had the same draw as the earlier parts. And the scene where Daphne takes advantage of Simon when he's drunk and too slow to keep from possibly getting her pregnant  left a bad taste in my mouth. Even though I think she was right in the things that she said to Simon about not letting his father rule his life , I didn't like how she essentially bullied and guilted him into her way of thinking . It wasn't enough to make me completely dislike the story, but it did taint it. So 4 stars for the first half and 2 stars for the second half, averaging out to a 3-star rating for the book as a whole.

I'll admit it, I have a soft spot for quasi-historical/fantasy lady assassins, especially lady assassins who have to play up the ladying to do the assassining. And this book is a great example of that. It's a little fluffy in its delivery, which mightn't have even been noticeable if its opening sequence hadn't been so very grim - I don't even mean what happens, but when our first-person narrator's response to (mild spoiler for the first chapter?) being beaten by her new husband and thrown into a locked cellar to await burny religious justice  is to smile because this means she wins over her father's intentions... I expect the rest of the book to be darker than it was. To have a complexity between her trauma and her morals and her training and her humanity. Alas, not quite. But still good quasi-historical lady-assassin fun, with bonus!we-have-to-pretend-to-be-lovers (another trope for which I have fondness).

This book (and series) is a bit perplexing to me. First of all, I struggle a lot with the main character, Chess. The book is completely about her, we as readers are privy to her thoughts and emotions... and she is a ragingly self-destructive junkie. So I am not sure there is a way to really be comfortable with Chess. She just kind of... sucks. I mean, don't get me wrong - there are more and more tidbits about her past which really helped me understand why she is the way she is. She she has some strongly good impulses. But she just does not value herself at all, she has no agency in her own life, except to escape from it and all the terrible things that have happened to her, and occasionally to help people. It frustrated the hell out of me while reading this book. Nevertheless, Chess and her (slow) growth as a person, is definitely the most interesting part of the series for me. The world building continues to be just OK. The plot was just OK. I found myself skimming a good bit. Chess as a narrator is kind of all over the place. And it's hard to focus on plot and setting when the main character is such a damn train wreck. But it's the kind of thing you can't look away from... The way Chess handles her relationships just pissed me off for so long within the book - I had no trouble getting inside her head, and understanding why she was doing what she was doing, but I was uncomfortable being sympathetic with her. She was just not acting in a way that you can act in a relationship! Running around and screwing people... for drugs... she is just not right. I feel for her, and I think feeling for her pissed me off more than a little. I was very glad when the other foot fell  thank god for Terrible and the hell he puts her through for all of her lies! I was feeling indignant with her so when he lashed out at her, I found myself cheering him on... and alas, pitying her for the even greater, inevitable spiral of self-hate that is forthcoming. As much as I bitch, I am definitely going to keep reading this series. I have to know what happens to Chess, and Terrible, and I can't possibly see how she has anywhere to go but in the right direction at this point - if only she finds the courage to show up for her own life, I will be behind her all the way...

Practically thrown away by her husband because she cannot bear an heir, Charlotte tries to reinvent herself in the Edge. She was unprepared for the people of the Edge and quickly finds herself shot for helping a child, penniless and without her horse. Only by the kindness of Rose, George and Jack's grandmother was Charlotte able to survive. Richard Mar is on the run from Slavers. He is the famous slaver Hunter and they have wounded him grievously. Landing on Charlotte's door step, her healing Richard starts an avalanche of disaster on Charlotte and her friends in the Edge. Bound together by the slaver's destruction, Charlotte and Richard must take on a nearly impossible task... bring an end to the slavers lawlessness and heartache. This book turned out to be more A than I thought. I've seen it stuck with the YA label so often I didn't realize it was more Older Young Adult than Young Adult. It's got some explicit situations. I didn't find them to be too terribly explicit compared to the pile of shitty bodice rippers I found in a box in the garage when I was 14 and snickered my way through but it depends on the audience, really. I liked this one, I think I may have mentioned. The characters had depth and their actions felt more real than a lot of the stuff I've seen cranked out recently. Paranormal events without vampires or werewolves or the new, in thing: fairies. Yay! Not that I don't like them every now and then but I am drowning in creature of the night angst left and right. Jenny doesn't really do angst. She does tired, she does lonely, she does accepting that sometimes her world is going to just be plain shitty, but not really angst. She gets up off her butt and does the things she likes and builds a world around her that comforts her and helps her family out best she can. Seth is just Seth. I'm not sure how much I was into him. He was a bit more vague but I think a jock football star is just kind of going to be that way in most books. He gains some depth the more majour of a character he becomes but he doesn't turn into some sort of super awesome misunderstood genius or anything ridiculous and/or gag inducing like that. Ashleigh... Oh Ashleigh. She is a shitty bitch. She's got her life of assholery planned out seemingly since birth and it's not even like she knows why, which I think is kind of true of most people who are bent on assholery on a wider scale. But she makes her slithery way pretty far up the ladder, and never mind the little people. The one thing I never did figure out  is Seth's Never Around Parents - he's remarkably well adjusted for someone who's parents show up ONCE. She's not allowed over there because he's not supposed to be seeing her but they're conveniently never around so she can practically live over there every weekend. Her dad doesn't mind - he's progressive like that, or something? Uhh.. I didn't see the point in the cemetery scenes or the third floor subplot, which turned out to be just sentences on the side of the story's road, either. So, I actually did like a book as much as people said I would, for once.

This is why Lanyon is one of my favorite authors ever. Fair Game has everything I look for in a novel: good standalone plot, good mystery that I didn't solve until just before the MC did, good sexual tension, good sex, good suspense, several viable suspects, a reasonable reason for the MC to get involved in a case, good suspense and action, individual characters, strong women characters, and lots of danger and near-death and oh-my-God-I-was-so-scared-I'd-lose yous to make me ecstatic. It was so good that I forgive the main character for saying he didn't like Seattle. He at least loved the Pacific Northwest; he just didn't love the big city. (Yes, I'm making excuses...) I just wish one of his main characters were a racial minority. Lanyon's not very good about that. Nitpicks: 1.I have been to five different universities in my unsuccessful quest to not enter the real world, and I have never been to one that would notice, let alone care, if an undergraduate disappeared. A specific teacher might, but not the president of the university. (mild spoiler) And two kids disappearing who had nothing in common at all, would not be a huge coincidence. College kids run off on benders and fall in bed with someone and blow off their classes and do some drugs and lose track of time and take off for something really fun at the last minute, etc., etc., all the time. The story takes place at "Puget Sound University" in Tacoma. It's obvious that it's supposed to be the University of Puget Sound which is also in Tacoma. That is a big enough school that no one would notice or care. Seattle University is nowhere near any wharf or harbor, and any sit down restaurants on the piers are extremely pricey. No wharf-side restaurant would be a popular meeting place for SU students who would have to drive there and pay enormous fees for parking, in addition to the food costs. Creative license, sure, but huge geographical inconsistencies bug me. Favorite quotes: "Christ. Only in academia did people talk such bullshit and expect to be taken seriously." (By someone who was a professor.) "Mrachek, Leslie hovered in his office doorway." (He remembers students by how they appear on the roll sheet which is what made me laugh.) "All cynics are disappointed idealists. The more stars in the eyes, the harder the fall." "'I'll see you at five.' 'Wear something sexy.' 'Asshole.' 'That will certainly work.'" Because of the lack of positive minorities and the terrible inaccuracies, 4.5 stars, rounded up because everything else was so great. Happy ending? Yes, strong HFN. Note to Lanyon: I am happy to fact-check your Pacific Northwest stories for you for free. Seriously. There are so many readers and writers of M/M fiction (we have a whole conference for it now) that it's important to get it right.

4.5 stars. It's a mix of a casebook "created by John Watson" and brief sections on various aspects of the show, Holmes' mythology, and how each episode relates to the Doyle version. The sections written by John have post-it notes from John, Sherlock and occasionally Mycroft. The font used for John and Mycroft's writing was fine, but the font used for Sherlock doesn't look right to me at all. I'm not sure what font it is but it just doesn't fit. It seems too neat and print like. Part of me thinks he'd use elegant cursive and not care if other people could read it or not, but he's so fastidious about grammar that I think he'd want his writing to be legible so he could communicate clearly. I want to see that sign from Scandal in Belgravia to compare the writing. The casebook also contains a few pages on 221B, though it's mostly the living room and kitchen. Some of the post-it note conversations are pretty amusing. Sherlock makes fun of John having a casebook at all (of course). He has apparently arranged John's ties by dominant color theme and is quite annoyed with the suggestion that John might arrange his own ties. Where John describes his date in The Blind Banker Sherlock has a post-it note calling it the Best. Date. Ever. and when he talks about the subsequent kidnapping Sherlock's note is 2nd. Best. Date. Ever. When talking about the apartment we get a few titles that Sherlock's reading as well as a tall stack of My Weekly which Sherlock apparently reads, but of course that doesn't track with not knowing who Connie Prince was. I enjoyed it, and if you like the show you should check it out.

It started off really mysterious, cool, and intriguing. Midway when they found out what the Unbroken Spine was, I was a little confused & off put. I did like how the Dragon Song Chronicles played a part in unraveling the mystery, but uncovering the secrets and the plan was way more exciting than the actual message. The story was pretty heart-felt at the end. I was expecting more though. Spoiler: That lady from Google disappointed me as well.

First of all, I'm pretty sure this is my favorite book in the Mistborn series, including the original trilogy. The characters are fantastic, the plot is great, and you learn so much more about the world Brandon Sanderson has created. It all combines for an excellent read. I think my favorite part of this book (and the new era of Mistborn in general) has to be the characters. I'm pretty sure there isn't a boring character throughout the whole book. Wax, who is a character I had some troubles with in the previous books, is actually relatable in this book. Then there's Steris, who is just a breath of fresh air. (My favorite part relating to her is that conversation with Marasi when she's trying to figure out how to be less worthless. I love how she seems to be self-deprecating but she just wants to figure out how to better contribute to the group. )(Also, her relationship with Wax is great in this book.) Marasi definitely got better in this book for me, as she used to be my least favorite character. Now she fits right in and I actually enjoyed her perspective. MeLaan was great, as usual, and I love the fact that she was more of a main character in this book. Then, of course, there's Wayne, who is the greatest character to ever grace this earth. I love absolutely everything about him. His humor is fantastic, his relationship with the other characters is great to read, (the banter with Wax about being old was hilarious. But it's obvious that he deeply cares about Wax, as displayed toward the end when Wax was dying.) and his personality is just interesting to think about. Most of the time I wish he was the main character, probably just because I want to read about everything from his perspective. In all honesty, I could probably write this entire review about Wayne, but I won't. (I can't forget about Allik, the newest character, who was instantly unique and interesting to read about. Plus his character introduces a whole different civilization to explore, which is great for future books.) If I had to choose, I would say that the plot is the weakest part of this book. The beginning was a bit slow, but I was all for it by the end of the book. It's hard to talk about anything specific without risking spoilers, but I would say the plot of this book is definitely better than the plot of Shadows of Self, in my opinion. (Plus, what is up with the epilogue?? And I have to wait almost 3 years to read about that? I hope they invent time machines soon.) Overall, if you have not read these books, you are missing out on a huge experience. Even if you don't normally read fantasy, you should read these. I love everything about them.

There were aspects of this that I really enjoyed but it was too long, too repetitive, and too ridiculous for me. I've admittedly never been to the opera, so maybe for opera fans this book is right on target. It's certainly very theatrical, very high drama. Plenty of jewels and lavish gowns. Lots of plotting, schemes within schemes within schemes, back stabbing, love, and betrayal. My main problem was the repetition, each go 'round getting increasingly absurd but not really progressing the plot or bringing us any place new. If this were 200 pages shorter I would've liked it quite a bit.

Sooooo, the similarities between this and the Hunger Games continues with the unnecessary death of a sibling right at the end and the distrust of the supposedly better side . Although I'd still recommend this series to Hunger Games/dystopian fans because it does stay pretty steady in quality and there is a lot of action, the writing just kind of threw me off. "I did this. Then I did this. I felt like this." I didn't believe anything she said because it just sounded so matter-of-fact. And sometimes she chose to explain things that I think even younger readers could have figured out on their own, so that kind of takes you out of the story and feels a little patronizing. Also, her relationship with Thomas seemed... weird. It wasn't a big part of the story, which is something I liked actually, so I kind of wish it just wasn't there at all. It was just like every once in a while... "oh yeah, and I love Thomas." I guess for the teens that need romance? I think they should have just been friends. Anyway, if you like the first two books, I think you'd like this one. The twists and explanations for things aren't super surprising or even that interesting, but the action is still there. But one more thing... if she killed the other professors wouldn't THAT be enough to say she'll do whatever's necessary without having to kill Dr. Barnes???? I never could understand that bit.

Okay, I see what the fuss is about now. I think it crossed the line between classic and thriller a few times, but that's okay. As someone who is an 80s baby, a gamer, and nerd all rolled into one (though you could argue those are all generational characteristics) -- this book is a future Last Starfighter, which the book does reference a few times of course... mixed with this movie: Still the trailer park setting, but it's a dystopian future, where the environment is wrecked, there's no more oil, and everyone eagerly signs up to be indentured servants (aka slaves to corporations). In such crappy times, everyone turns to Virtual Reality, where they can live on Discworld, or Azeroth, or any number of magical worlds. Really, in a way this makes sense--why go to a horrible school, making your way through crime ridden streets, or stay safely in your house in a school limited only by imagination, where everyone is muted, and has to pay attention while the teacher shows you Saturn's moons on one of their virtual moons? Of course the inverse to that is if everyone is escaping real world problems by plugging into machines, then there's no one present to fix all the current actual ones. (Which frankly to me seemed rather unfixable in the book, no matter how much money is offered as the grand game quest.) The only thing I disliked is that one of the heroes--Art3mis--they make a big deal about how shy she is about her looks and doesn't want to meet in person, etc., etc., and then it turns out she just has a birthmark--of course that looks just like some cool German dueling scar on one cheek, that she artfully covers with long hair. So cliched, I rolled my eyes, and I think Cline could have done something more interesting there. But this book is very much teen aged boy wish fulfillment, so standard.

3.5 stars. Of course, I love the TV series and I also love this book series. Many people said this book was good, and that was true. I did have some problems with it though, even though I was used to them by now. Basically, the premise of this book was that everyone kept thinking that the liars were lying about everything that came out of her mouth. Although they do lie a lot, I felt bad for how much they get looked down upon by others. The first problem I had with this book was Emily. She is the most paranoid out of them all, and maybe that is because of how close her and Alison actually got, but by the seventh book, it gets quite annoying. She goes to this Amish town because A tells her too. Okay, first off, why would you listen to A after everything that has happened with A? Wtf are you thinking?! Then, she assumes that Wilden killed her Amish friend's sister automatically. She jumps to conclusions way too quickly, and I was quite frankly done with her by the end of this. The next problem was how much these girls actually believed A. Spencer listened to A when they told her that her mom had something to do with 'that night.' Why would you trust A? Are you stupid?! Aria listened to A and completely thought that Ali killed herself because of some woman. Finally, Hanna thinks this Iris girl killed Alison because of her dream or whatever it was. Needless to say, I was annoyed with their dumb decisions during this book. I still love them all though. The last thing I was annoyed with was the abrupt ending. I did enjoy the ending because of the huge plot twist, but I felt it was a bit rushed. They rush to get the girls out of jail, and it was rushed learning the 'true killer.' I personally do not think this old guy killed Ali. I was completely shocked that Jenna died though. I didn't see it coming. I figured she would get attacked soon because of all of the hints, but I guess her time came in this book. Even though I had problems with this book, I still love both series. I'm still going to continue on to the eighth book, which I hear is a good one.

Although, I simply refuse to accept Jon is dead. Others have come back from worse than this, and as it wasn't actually confirmed in a follow-up chapter that he's dead, I've decided he's not. But Ramsay Snow/Bolton/Whatshisname comes pretty close. - I still don't care very much about Theon. Or any of the ironborn, really. - If what they have now is autumn, I'd hate to see what winter will actually be like. This is the sequel to "The Witch Hunter," so if you haven't read that one, I suggest not reading this review. SPOILERS WILL BE ABOUND!! Like seriously. Go and read the first book. In fact, I had the pleasure of meeting this lovely woman FOUR DAYS BEFORE THE RELEASE OF THE FIRST BOOK at the wonderful Books of Wonder (18 West 18th Street in NYC for those who want to know... like go and support them. They are absolutely fabulous) and you know what she did? She released it FOUR DAYS EARLY TO SIGN IT FOR US. It was magical. And I devoured the first book. The second book...? Well. Although I did devour it, I feel like it wasn't as good as the first. I feel that way about a lot of things actually. But this is a bit different. Because it had nothing to do with story line and EVERYTHING to do with character. (Honestly this will be a short review, considering that it is a sequel and everything I had to say about this series is in my review of the first book, which I'm sure is up on Goodreads somewhere. Actually it is not. I guess I didn't have much to say about it.) This book is a low 4 Stars. There. That's all you get. The reason why? There's not much I can say without spoiling ANYTHING. So read the blurb above and know my rating and then, after reading it and thinking about it yourself, you can come back and read the rest of this review. Okay. The reason this review is short is because, like I stated above, there isn't much for me to gripe about except for character development. Yup. That's about it. So what was it about the characters that I didn't like? 1 - Elizabeth was just SO WHINY. That's right, I said it. The strong witch hunter of the first book just goes bleh. Like one minute she's beating people up, she loses her stigma and then BAM. All of her badass qualities go along with it. Even the final battle at the end is kind of flat because I had expected her to act that way since the beginning. Like come on already! Ugh. 2 - John REALLY pissed me off. Like SUPER pissed me off. Like jump-off-a-bridge-and-kill-yourself pissed me off. (Don't do that though, because we need you.) I was so annoyed with him by the end that even HE didn't redeem himself. 3 - Fifer and Schulyer were so much more assertive in the first book and they kind of fell flat in this one. They ended up being wall characters, where they are there but not important. Schulyer had ONE MAJOR SCENE. THAT WAS IT. Like WTH?! And Fifer I felt like wasn't important at all! That's my only problem, honestly. I enjoyed the plot, because, well, Blackwell NEEDED to just go away already. I hated that dude. And I guess I felt bad for Malcolm. A little. The writing was gorgeous like it was in the first book, with a world that was definitely unique. Although I still don't understand how magic works in this book and who's got it, it's okay because I accepted it. It worked for the people who actually had it. I also thought that the way it progressed made sense, although I REALLY wanted to slap Elizabeth across the face to wake her up from her pining and self-pity. Throughout the entire book. But whatever. I enjoyed this ending to this series, a duology. I want another book, just to see what happens next, but it's okay. I enjoyed where it ended. BUT WHAT HAPPENED TO CHIME??? That little witch. Maybe she fell into the river and went away. Hopefully. Anyway, that's about it. Told you it would be short. I just can't think of anything else to say. Like I said, a low four stars for this book. I can't exactly rate it like I would other books properly, because if this was a stand-alone it would've gotten three and a half stars, but since the first book was worth the five stars I gave it, I have to bring this down a star.

This book had so much potential. I love time travel, and the first few chapters were awesome. Then, at some point after Nate gets shot  things grow stagnant. Their motivations are muddled, their actions have little or nor consequences, they make wild assumptions from limited info that lead them on more useless running around. It was around this point that my wife asked me to stop reading it to her. I finished it on my own so I could review it for my blog. The "masterful" plotting that is advertised on the cover consists of: Them going back to kill a boy before he becomes a villain but the boy realizing they're right and killing himself. Everything else is filler. They talk about time travel once or twice (and I guess most of the book takes place in the past, but it seems like such a small part of the story that at points I forgot I was reading sci-fi.) Sometimes this can be a good thing. But in this case, I felt like I was reading a really poorly plotted YA contemporary with some chases and torture thrown in for excitement. Did we ever even find out what all the torture was about? Why does he need those stupid notebook pages anyway? Hasn't he already made his machine? And what's that with the gun suddenly jamming when Em finally gets the courage to pull the trigger. Of course it works fine later. The whole book would've been over fifty pages earlier if the stupid gun hadn't jammed. I'd recommend this to people who like contemporary romances that don't make a lot of sense but have a lot of character-building memories to treasure. (To clarify, the only character building is done in the book. With the language and the casual sex/underage drinking it's not going to do anything for your teen's character.)

I have a lot of thoughts about this book, so forgive the slightly ranty review. I will also have some hidden spoilers, so peruse at your own peril. Overall, I enjoyed it. The story is about a land where each queen gives birth to triplets. Each girl has a 'special' power. In this generation, Katherine is a poisoner, Arsinoe is a naturalist and Mirabella is an elemental. They are separated as children and at their coming of age, whoever kills the other two within the year, gets to be the next queen. The narrative follows each of the sisters' stories in turn, chapter by chapter. It was fun getting to know the sisters, the guardian families that raised them, and generally how the 'queen-making' worked. There were references and characters from the main land, so I assumed they are on an isolated island that does things quite differently from the rest of the world (I would have definitely benefitted from a map, but maybe this is an issue in the ARC only). Kudos also to how Blake incorporates the elements of a matriarchal society, Beltane, religion and other historical rituals. However, it felt like I was reading three distinctly different stories for the majority of the book. That said, when the sisters met occasionally and when all three worlds collided towards the end, it was generally better. I liked Katherine's story the best. I think it's because her power was the clearest to me. Poisoners have been the ruling class for generations. They are immune to poisons and Katherine also has a gift for creating them. I also really liked Jules and her mountain cat familiar Camden, who are Arsinoe's best friends. Basically, everyone was more interesting than Mirabella, the 'strongest' of the sisters. I couldn't tell you most other characters that I actually liked, because there were too many characters just generally. None of the names and personalities really stood out and the third person narration did little to endear any of them. Then something happened midway through the book that really just jarred me. I read on and eventually figured out why the author thought it was necessary, but it was really sudden and I was angry that it happened and it soured my mood for the rest of the book. If you want to know, it was when Joseph (? ), Jules' love, got caught in a storm and saved by Mirabella. Then they sleep together, and it's made out to be like he wasn't aware of any of this happening, because he thinks he's delirious or dead or in a dream. It was so sudden and poorly done, and my heart went out to Jules a LOT. The other main issue I had with the book was that I could see the twist ending coming a mile away. I had an inkling that Arsinoe and Katherine were 'switched', and they really had each other's powers. Mainly because of Arsinoe's not-so-subtle name; there was even a mention of why she was named probably to throw readers off the scent, but only made me more suspicious. There were also just one too many mentions about their lack of powers. I don't really delight in guessing twists too quickly - in fact, I really enjoy being oblivious for much of the book I'm reading. I was disappointed when I guessed it, and the fact that it wasn't revealed until the very last page irked me even more. I do think the next book will be interesting, and I'll probably read on to see where the story goes. If you're looking for a light fantasy read, then this is for you.

Absolutely brilliant and terrifying! And the most petrifying plot twist I've ever read!!! TOM! FREAKING TOM! The Lockwood series are not for the faint of heart. People will ask: "What, the bloody hell, is she talking about? This book is targeting middle-school children! Does she get scared by her own bloody shadow?" and I'll just send my army of rabid bunnies after them, because reasons. This series will leave you with eyes wide open during the night and feet shivering under your covers. Nothing will be able to get the chill out of you. Ok, enough with the threats, for now, and WELCOME once again to the scariest London in fictional existence. Ghosts are all over the place and it's up to children to defend the British isle from this nasty infestation (cause adults can't see them, you see). Sounds cute and jolly doesn't it? WRONG!! We join our favorite agents, Lockwood, Lucy and George, as they learn to deal with the new found popularity of their agency. After exorcising a particularly nasty ghost (and a couple of crazy adults brandishing kitchen utensils), the trio is once again overwhelmed with the number of cases arriving each day and the lack of order and hygiene in their home. A secretary is required, someone who can deal with the clients, organize their schedule and clean the mess in their kitchen. And, oh joy, it doesn't take long for Lockwood to find Holy - the perfect assistant and Lucy's worst nightmare. Oh, and there's also - a massive outbreak of ghosts in Chelsea - where different agencies are working together to resolve the ever increasing attacks and panic. - a pushy client with a murderous ghost in her home - and if things weren't hard enough for Lucy, battling ghosts (and Holy for Lockwood's attention), she also has to deal with her talent getting more and more powerful, both helping her colleagues, but also endangering their lives at the same time. AND THAT ENDING!!!!!! GRRRR!!! Sometimes I think writers are intentionally evil. Ending the book with a twist and leaving us alone in our misery for months, until we get the sequel. There are books that just click with you, and this one clicked with me. I was sucked into the world, I interacted with the characters, I was emotionally involved with everything that was happening and I completely forgot that this is just a work of fiction. An absolutely great experience for me. I can't guarantee that this will be one of THE BOOKS for you, but it was a wonderful ride nevertheless. If you decide to give the series a go, I hope you enjoy them.

I remain utterly torn on what star rating to give this book. On one hand, I love the heroine and her unreliable viewpoint and her no-nonsense attitude and her utter courage and quite understandable fear and her acceptance of her own sexuality. I love the style of the narration, the way it managed to work in dry wit and sarcasm without the ridiculous asides that so many books nowadays favor. I love the variety of characters we got and the largely nonjudgemental way they are presented to us. I love the odd things that our heroine fixates on. I love that, in a genre stuffed with 'othernaturals' we here get not only a couple kinds I'm not used to seeing, but we actually get one that makes me feel uneasy in the way I think vampires and werewolves used to for people. On the other hand, our heroine's clinging to the idea that she's undesirable are so pronounced that they go past realistic or even empathizeable to irritating. There are times the story gets very slow, and while it's astoundingly fun when it's on, there's very little of substance to it. I had a lot of fun, but even having just finished it this morning, the things I remember about it, the scenes and details so memorable that I'll take them with me, are very few and far between. It's like a popcorn flick in dead tree form. And most of all, when I rate something 4 or 5 stars, that means it's pretty much something I'd recommend anyone at least give a shot. But in this book's case, I know quite a few people I think would probably not be able to get past the writing style. Overall, I thought the pacing worked pretty well, better than I expected given the writing style. I really did like the character. I was pretty okay with the romance as well, where usually the romance is the thing in a book I try to rush past to get to stuff I actually care about. It was fun and quick and I'm going to definitely be picking up the sequel. But I can only give it a 3 stars.

Sweet heaven, this was tedious. Just how many trap doors and escapes and recaptures and escapes and more trap doors and escapes and recaptures do we have to go through? I started to suspect something when the action started far from when the novel ended. When they were, for about the jillionth time, captured again, I finally gave up and checked Wiki. Wiki has saved me countless hours of plowing through tedious books such as this just to at least know what eventually happened. Thank you, Wiki. Remind me to gladly donate the next time you ask. The short version is: lots of stuff happens, the author only bothers to give personalities to approximately 1/3 of the cast, none of which are actually interesting (Campion seemed to have promise for a moment, but a man who acts like an idiot without a gun  who transforms into a man who acts like an idiot with a gun  is, in my opinion, not in any way more likeable). And as for that ending... good god! Again, thank you Wiki, a thousand times, thank you for giving me the ultimate, and irritatingly stupid ending, which is Abbershaw, after some thought and research, pays a visit to the killer - Petrie himself. Having fallen in love with a young girl, he found she was the puppet of evil criminals, and enraged by their treatment of her, he resolved to track them down. When he found his own uncle was one of them, he felt he had no choice but to slay him, inventing the dagger ritual to give him the chance. Abbershaw lets him go, on condition he enters a monastery. First my review for TECKLA, then the omnibus. I felt bad throughout most of this book, because Vlad felt bad, because he had troubles in his personal life. Felt in the mood for something superhero themed, and this came up as a recommendation. Very solid writing. Plot and characterization is done pretty darn well. I'm still of the opinion that it doesn't bring that much newness to the superhero genre, but I still really enjoyed it. In fact, this story is pretty much a parody on the superhero theme. You can see the parallels of "real" superheroes with Superman, Batman (Hawk), and other little details. It's quite fun to pick out references. The family dynamics fantastically written. I can imagine Suzanne trying to be the mediator and the two stubborn ones just feeling angry and defensive over nothing. I absolutely love how Daddy Olympus goes berserk over her boyfriends. It's really adorable. And the little details of Suzanne cooking with her hands or descriptions of the house really makes this book go beyond the cliche. I do wonder, though, what would happen if there were a superhero for technology. Celia would probably lose her niche as an accountant. I am a little ambivalent on the romance. I don't mind Celia and Arthur getting together, but it's a little odd the way the author switches back and forth from Dr Mentis to Arthur and back again when Celia refers to him. It makes me either think of him as a lot older or her age, depending on the name. And honestly, he feels wayyy older than her. Plot was fairly predictable. Bad guy tries to take over the city, he fails, etc. There is one moment in the book that I was actually shocked for a few moments. I could not believe that the author would let Captain Olympus die  . But I am glad it happened because it changed a lot of things, especially perspective. I thought the ending was too rushed, the snipbits of epilogue. But what can you do? Overall, a very solid read if you want to read about superheroes. 3 stars.
