dnf @ 53% I tried with this book. I honestly did. While I wasn't enjoying the beginning, I was really hoping that if I got farther enough that the novel would get better. I mean, this book is so popular and so hyped I really wanted to enjoy it. For me, personally, I didn't though. (Warning: spoiler part may be ranty & if you like this book I am in no means trying to offend you. If you don't wanna hear it, then don't read it.) I have not read a lot of books which talk about important issues like suicide, so this book is definitely valuable in that case. But while reading it, it almost felt like Jay Asher was glamorizing suicide. I mean, seriously? Hannah Baker definitely went through a lot of problems with her life, and I am definitely not disregarding that or trying to belittle that. She felt like she had reason to commit suicide and I am NOT going against that fact. But what I found as a problem in this book that Hannah, literally BLAMES these people for her suicide. "I committed suicide because YOU spread a rumor about me and YOU pretended to be my friend". No. No. Stop. I understand that these people hurt you, and in the end, you felt helpless against them. But it's one thing to to tell them to change their behaviors and another thing to commit suicide to prove a point that THEY made you do this. While reading the novel, I kinda despised Hannah. All Hannah did was repeat the same things over and over again, continuously emphasizing that her suicide was this person's fault. Honestly. Read this quote, directly from the book: "And yet the whole time Courtney was using me, she thought she was polishing up her image in my eyes. Can you say... backfire?" What? What does this line mean? "Backfire"? Are you seriously saying that you killing yourself is revenge at her for using you? "I'm gonna kill myself. That'll show her." That is LITERALLY what the line translates to. To me, Hannah was just such an annoying character. Every single time she kept repeating 'you're to blame for MY death' she was being too dramatic. I know I am supposed to feel depressed for her, as this is a SUICIDE novel, but I just couldn't. Hannah was petty, overly emotional, and literally committed suicide to make a point to others and I just don't condone that. Maybe Jay Asher wanted to make this book relatable for suicidal people, but after reading reviews from ACTUAL people who had thoughts of suicide, they confirmed my suspicion that this book was just written based on the overall generalization of suicide. It's kind of like The Fault in Our Stars-- that book is based on the overgeneralization of cancer and a lot of ACTUAL people with cancer can't relate to it. Like I said before. This book glamorizes suicide and I really don't think it's okay. Another thing I disliked about this book was the writing. Besides the fact that I found the entire book to be problematic, the book just seemed to drag on forever. The book is written in a fashion thought to be of how teenagers talk, and I found it SO annoying. Lines were literally repeated over and over. All the characters kept repeating questions instead of any actual answers being provided. Clay: "Why did you do this Hannah..... Why didn't you do this" LITERALLY THE ENTIRE NOVEL (well at least up to the point I read to). Anyways, reading further would just kinda be like torturing myself, because I could not connect to Hannah in any way at all and I just could not read it. I found it boring. Simple as that. Anyways, despite finding this book to be extremely problematic, the only reason I decided to read it was so I could watch the Netflix series. I'm still gonna give the show a try, because maybe the problems that were emphasized in the book are not as prominent in the show. Again, I never EVER want anyone to misunderstand my dislike for this book as belittlement for anyone who actually has suicidal thoughts. Everyone SHOULD think before they act/speak. Although it seems as Jay Asher TRIED to send out that message, it came out completely malformed to me. It seemed more like a girl blaming a bunch of people for her choice, rather than teaching them to think before acting.

An interesting, if tragic story of one man's search for meaning. Unfortunately, as fascinated as I was by McCandless's story (as a fan of Thoreau and minimalism, I could identify with his adventure), I didn't end up enjoying this book all that much. I'm not sure why this is. Maybe it was because of the side stories diverting from McCandless, but I found myself skimming through many sections, asking myself what the point in them was... Or maybe it was because Krakauer spent so much time explaining and trying to understand McCandless's motivations (and defending him) rather than just telling his story. In all, I'm happy I read the book, even if a little bit confused about what it was about.

** spoiler alert ** This was a deeply lyrical book. I enjoyed reading it more for the wording than anything else. But I felt a connection to the characters that evaporated as soon as I put the book down. There was no real strength or development in any of them, that I could track; just people who continued down the paths of their lives in whatever way they expected them to unfold. In a way I suppose that follows, given that there are some fairy tale-like vines weaving through this story thematically and allegorically, but it wasn't enough to make me care about what happened to them; I was never in fear that any character would experience something they couldn't handle (this may also be partly due to to the fact that Boy & Snow didn't really seem to react to anything with any passion). I also found the ending (SPOILER ALERT) to be problematic and sort of anti-climactic. The revelation that Frank was in fact Frances would have been more impactful if that was the real grist of the book -- Boy having run away from her abusive parent only to find that maybe the abuse was motivated by a suppression of identity. What upset me was the transphobic way that was handled -- that Frances must be the "real" Frank and somehow also not a physically and mentally abusive psychopath -- which also implied that Frank's abusiveness was somehow directly related to his being trans. I understand that it was set in the 50's (I was actually caught on Mia's "termination" for a while, thinking she was being unduly formal in describing being fired, before I realized what she meant) but that sort of ambiguous treatment of the character's identity and mental health left me feeling uneasy. Again, it seemed like the action in this book only really developed in the last 10 pages or so, leaving me to wonder if there was ever an intended sequel in the works...

Double Play is more, how do I put this, serious-ish than Kate Angell's Richmond Rogues books. Angell's books have a more light-hearted tone than Shalvis's books. Double Play focuses on two of the more potentially negative aspects of baseball: the relationship between the players and the media, and the usage of performance-enhancing drugs. The heroine, Holly, is a reporter/blogger doing a feature on the hero's team. The hero, Pace, basically wants nothing to do with her. *gasp* Conflict! Angell does a better job of incorporating baseball scenes, but Shalvis demonstrates that the media can be a double-edged sword for the media. I liked the fact that Holly made friends with the players, but she wasn't about to compromise her ideals. I would've liked a bit more emphasis on her isolation so that when she finally decides to set down roots, it had more impact. Pace doesn't want to talk to Holly and feels the need to hide pieces of himself from her, but, by extension, he is also hiding them from the reader. As a result, we don't get to know him as well. Shalvis touches on his relationship with Tucker and Redd, but Pace's strongest and clearest relationship in the book is with Wade. I wanted to see how Tucker and Redd were woven into the fabric of Pace's life to heighten the tension of the eventual revelation that Tucker and Redd were supplying the players with the drugs. Tucker was indirectly responsible for the black mark on Pace's record and I wanted the sense of betrayal to be dripping off the page. I'd classify Double Play as a bit better than Angell's books, just because it focuses on one couple and has more of a linear story. However, it's worth nothing that despite their common baseball theme, Angell and Shalvis are very different authors.

2.5 stars. "All magic comes with a price." Frozen Tides follows on with the tradition of being a installment filed with action, schemes and intrigue, and copious amount of teenage romance. It picks up where Gathering Darkness left off and it is an absolute rollercoaster. New POV characters are introduced, old ones return, and the stakes are higher than ever. Morgan Rhodes' writing continues to be simple and entertaining. The novel is fast-paced and each POV character has an unique voice, and it is easy to fall headlong into the story. Sadly, this installment is a step back for me. The focus on romance and recycling of relationships takes from the development of characters and very important plot points, making so impacting twists fall completely flat. Where Gathering Darkness won me over, this book lost me. One of the staples of this series is the romance aspect, but this time around I found the focus on it was detrimental to other parts of the plot. Again, a few twists which I am positive were supposed to leave me shocked did not affect me at all. Some of them even felt out of character. As a book that is told in mutual POV, I do have to give Rhodes props for writing unique characters and shifting from one POV to the other. All chapters flow in a way that is smooth and engaging, which makes this for a very fast read (if you have the time to sit down and read the book, haha). I actually loved the introduction of new POV characters, they are interesting and add depth to the story, while also helping flesh out the world-building a little bit more. Unfortunately, most of the returning characters did not keep my interest. Where the previous installment is great for its character development, in this one they seem like caricatures of themselves. This also impacts the shocking twists, as they end up not transmitting any kind of emotion to the reader. In the end, Frozen Tides is a disappointment., at least for me. The novel lets most of its plot and character development get sidelined in favor of instalove and romance, the twists have no effect, which makes the story all kinds of unbelievable. Hopefully this won't hold true for the next installment, as I know Rhodes is capable of writing a great story. Series: #4 in the Falling Kingdom series. POV: Told from Jonas, Magnus, Cleo, Lucia, Felix, POVs. Content Warnings: A little bit of incest. Instalove: Yes, as always. Love Triangle: Yes, as always. Cheating: A little bit, I guess? Cliffhanger: Yes. HEA: Not yet. Up Next: Crystal Storm

Okay, I honestly wasn't expecting much from this book. Its a fairly common premise, at least these days post Percy Jackson. Twist off of Greek mythology, add romance, a bit of end of the world doomsday threats and of course, high school. I actually ended up avoiding this title when I say it pop up on the recommendations list. Until, I was bored, found it at the local library and tried it out just see see if this would be another series I could find myself lost in. The first third, was okay, a bit off. After, I found myself really enjoying the novel. I cannot say its an amazing book, but I would gift it a solid 3 out of 5 stars, with a exception that after its sequel is released and if its decet, bump it out a half star. As the conclusion leaves me wanting more but feeling a bit disappointed that it wasn't more powerful. The Story So, there is a fallen from grace Prince of the Underworld, named Haden. Hint, Hades... Haden. Sorry, obvious parallel. Anyway, the Underworld is seeking out a champion to go out into the world above for a mission. The King seeks out an Oracle, who has proclaimed that the only one to save the Underworld would be Haden by seeking out a Boon (or human wife) to bring back home. Her name is Daphne Raines. Am I the only one who thinks, Daphne a flower, Raines... Rains? Another parallel. All to provide symbolism to the retelling of the story of Hades and Persephone. Unfortunately, makes the conclusion rather predictable, which makes the plot unable to stand on its own (without the strength of its characters) very well. The story truly begins once both characters reach Olympus Hills High School, a prestigious school in California. Here they meet a handful of new characters and the interactions between them all can be quite funny, sweet and/or cute. The story itself plays out like a half novel. The end, has a bit of a conclusion, but sorts of cuts off. You think there would another chapter, but it just ends. I am bothered by that. It loses something without a proper emotional conclusion. However, once the sequel is out, that will not likely play as large as a role in the flaws of the novel. The rest is an interesting take on classic Greek mythology and a typical high school YA novel theme. The Characters So the story is a bit stereotypical, with a few nice twists. The characters are what sets this story above. Not every character is great. But our two leads are quite interesting. Daphne has an interesting perspective, mostly from her connection to music. She is strong willed, determined and tends to have an open mind, which is needed for her to adapt to the world she will be presented with. Haden, as many have already said in these reviews, has the character type os Zuko from Avatar. The fallen Prince who seeks the regain honor and acceptance from his father and the kingdom. Add that with his out of world attitude, from never being a part of the world above. Plus, his emotionally linked sense of morality, and he is by far my favorite character of the lot. Every scene with him, not just from his POV is fun. The rest are a bit predictable. Its hard to explain why without giving out spoilers, but most "surprises" weren't that shocking. However, they are still fun to read about overall. Special attention to the Hell cat for simply being adorable, but maybe that's because I have a soft spot for Cats. The Writing There were a few parts of the writing that really urked me, especially in the beginning. The POV's in the first third of the novel were repeats of the same scenes over and over again. It made the flow a bit off. As I was often forced to relive the same scene in my mind without too much new information to justify it. Later on, that remedies itself, however there were still quite a few lines that just didn't seem quite right. Maybe it was done on purpose, for later foreshadowing in future books, but as it is now, the writing could use a bit of polish. Overall This was a fun book to read and get sucked into when the flow was stable. The beginning was hard to get into because of the POV's and later on there wasn't enough of a conclusion to feel satisfied. Does it do its job to want to read the next, yes, but it also doesn't leave me feeling that good either. SPOILERS! One, Rowen is obviously the guy Daphne sensed in the beginning, I know this will likely be the next antagonist in the sequel, but still. It was a bit too obvious when they explained the invisibility helm thing. I can already predict that Book two will cover the winter season, deal with Rowen, then go into the Underworld, where Book 3 shall begin. It would surprise me if it doesn't follow this path. Next, Haden and Daphne's relationship. I liked them together. I liked how their relationship developed for the most part. Until the end. Halfway through the book, we get a kiss, have a fall out between them, and they sort of make up. Haden admits, to himself and his father he loves her. And they hold hands in the end. That's it. There was more action in the middle then their is in the end, after they both start to really acknowledge their feelings. That doesn't feel quite natural. It adds to the disappointing cut scene at the end. Sorry, I needed a kiss or something more than holding hands after everything that came prior. Finally, Tobin's sister. You know, I think its rather obvious she didn't die, that Dax was in love with her, and frankly, I think she is the "man" on the motorcycle. She will be the added trump card to break the war between her people and those of the man she loves. I could be wrong, but come on. It does seem to very obviously point to it, using misconceptions to the authors advantage. But thats just me complaining.

** spoiler alert ** I bought this book for my sister's 16th birthday, which mean, naturally, I got to read it too. She said, "Make sure you are by yourself when you get close to the end. You're gonna cry." She was wrong. I mean, I did cry, but I was nearly forcing myself too. Now let me explain. This book was incredible! I mean, this book! Ahhhhh! I loved it. Now, here's why. It ended perfectly. In the beginning, I didn't like the switching from Tris to Tobias, Tris to Tobias, but now I see why. The book ties up all its ends nicely, perfectly, neatly. Not to say everyone ends up happy in the end. I don't what the fuss was about that too many people died. Only two people die. Two main, central characters, but still. This book just blew my mind. There was a part in the middle that was boring, but it was over soon enough and the action was back on. Now, on to serious stuff. Ms. Roth writes very child-like. I don't mean this in a bad way, at all. Her words are simple, easy to read and easy to relate to. She keeps stuff simple, short, will not extra frills, all while making you feel exactly what she wants you to feel. I don't think Ms. Roth wanted us to cry in the end. I felt exactly like Tobias did...Stuck, my hearing and feelings muffled, left standing still, no emotion, lifeless. But I was okay with the ending. I'm not mad. Ms. Roth did something no one ever attempts to do. She is a groundbreaker. How can I hate her for that. You've done well, Ms. Roth. You're simply amazing. I can't wait to see if she has more in store for us about a different world, different characters, a different time. I'll read every single book she comes out with, no doubt! I would recommend this series to EVERYONE!

3.5 stars. This book was a slow starter for me, but I did end up enjoying it. This is the story of Ainsley and Lambo. Lambo is Ainsley's brother Ryan's best friend. He and Ainsley first meet at Ryan's college graduation party and sparks fly. But they come crashing back to earth when Lambo learns Ainsley is only 16. Over the years, they avoid each other, but they can no longer deny their attraction when they go to Vegas with Ryan 8 years later. But Ainsley has a problem,  She has a traumatic past. Her father sexually abused her and physically abused her brother and mother before killing her mother and himself. Ainsley has a kind of mental block towards sex because of this abuse and, though she has tried, her body clams up when she has tried to have sex. Now, at age 24, she is desperate to lose her virginity. So desperate that she opens up to Lambo and he agrees to help her work through her problem. Up until this point, Lambo really rubbed me the wrong way. He came off as a hornball manwhore. And though, I liked Ainsley well enough, I didn't feel their connection. It seemed like their attempts to help Ainsley work through her sexual problem were very clinical and impersonal. I didn't feel the heat. But as Ainsley and Lambo spent more time together and got to really know each other and like each other, I did start to feel their chemistry. Lambo, once he decided he wanted Ainsley, did a total 180 and became really sweet and loving. Ainsley took some convincing and Lambo was able to sooth her fears of being in a relationship with him. By the end of the book, I really liked them as a couple and I enjoyed watching their relationship develop. Despite the fact that the book deals with some serious issues  like sexual abuse and Ainsley having depression and being bipolar  , the book is refreshingly angst free. Once Ainsley and Lambo committed to each other and admitted they loved each other, there was no big betrayal to tear them apart. They did have to work through sharing their relationship with Ryan, but once they overcame that hurdle, it was smooth sailing. I also really liked the epilogue and glimpse into their future together. Overall, I did enjoy this book a lot. The story was original and well layered. This was my first book I have read by Elizabeth Brown, although it is the second in the series, but I do plan on going back and reading The Lessons (book 1 in the series, which is Ryan and Natalie's story). *I received this book in exchange for an honest review.

This was amazing! I'm quickly revising my growing list of books that should be nominated for next year's Hugo, and this one certainly fits the bill. The ideas are really awesome. Two big ones, slamming against each other in a truly horrific and out-there way, and all the while, our MC, Faller, falls through the skies on his quest. The book has a parallel structure to it. The present mess and the past slowing catching up to where the present mess began. Revealing the events that made a world that has been broken into city-sized chunks that are repelled from each other as if we were all a part of quantum physics was nearly as fun as jumping and falling from each one of these lands. And what's the other big idea? A virus that wipes everyone's memories. That reveal was pretty amazing, too, as was the epic battle between two old friends, one of whom blames the other for his wife's death and the Faller, who has lost all his memories. Each world-island is just a dystopian present-day world that we know, with no one remembering how to use technology, no power to run things, and not even the ability to read. It feels pretty hopeless, but Faller has the picture of his wife and a map directing him far, far below, through the clouds and islands, to where he might find the answers. Any answers. It's a pretty sweet setup, and the adventure is downright awesome. But how could something like this, the inclusion of a duplication machine, a singularity, and an Earth turned into a macroscopic version of quantum fields actually resolve into a glorious story, rather than a cool premise? Ah, don't worry about that. It does. Rely on the author to walk you through the cool reveals and set us up for one hell of an awesome resolution. :) He pulls it off. I'm really excited for this year's best SF, and this one certainly fits that bill. :) This was really gloriously cool SF. Great concepts, fearless execution and a very solid story with characters that I can't help but love. Woo Hoo!!! Thanks to Netgalley for this ARC!

Eeeek! Too much information for my squeamish stomach. I know Mary Roach has thousands of fans, but I found her relishing of gruesome details a bit unpleasant. I also found the chapters dealing with the historical treatment of cadavers more interesting than the chapters on how they are used now. I thought some of the chapters on contemporary usage were a bit boring, and could have been edited down. The titles of the chapters of the book give a good indication of the contents. A HEAD IS A TERRIBLE THING TO WASTE Practising surgery on the dead. CRIMES OF ANATOMY Body snatching and other sordid tales from the dawn of human dissection. LIFE AFTER DEATH. On human decay and what can be done about it. DEAD MAN DRIVING Human crash test dummies and the ghastly, necessary science of impact tolerance. BEYOND THE BLACK BOX When the bodies of the passengers must tell the story of a crash. THE CADAVER WHO JOINED THE ARMY The sticky ethics of bullets and bombs. HOLY CADAVER The crucifixion experiments HOW TO KNOW IF YOU'RE DEAD Beating-heart cadavers, live burial, and the scientific search for the soul. JUST A HEAD Decapitation, reanimation, and the human head transplant 10 EAT ME Medicinal cannibalism and the case of the human dumplings. OUT OF THE FIRE, INTO THE COMPOST BINS And other ways to end up. REMAINS OF THE AUTHOR Will she or won't she? And as usual, herewith a few notes of things that I found of personal interest, mostly in the author's own words. (The links are mine...) SURGEON APPRENTICES The author was surprised to learn that even when surgeons are in residencies, they aren't typically given an opportunity to practice operations on donated cadavers. Students learn surgery the way they have always learned: by watching experienced surgeons at work. HISTORY: A DESPERATE NEED FOR CADAVERS FOR DISSECTION The tradition of using executed criminals for dissections persisted and hit its stride in 18th and 19th century Britain. While the number of medical schools grew, the number of cadavers stayed roughly the same, and the anatomists faced a chronic shortage of material. Back then no one donated his body to science. The churchgoing masses believed in a literal, corporal rising from the grave, and dissection was thought of as pretty much spoiling your chances of resurrection. It was not unheard of for an anatomist to tote freshly deceased family members over to the dissecting chamber for a morning before dropping them off at the churchyard. Seventeenth-century surgeon-anatomist William Harvey, famous for discovering the human circulatory system, also deserves fame for being one of few medical men in history so dedicated to his calling that he could dissect his own father and sister. Harvey did what he did because the alternatives - stealing the corpses of someone else's loved ones or giving up his research - were unacceptable to him. By 1828, the demands of London's anatomy schools were such that ten full-time body snatchers and two hundred or so part-timers were kept busy through the dissecting "season". (Anatomy course were held only between October and May, to avoid the stench and swiftness of summer-time decomposition.) DENTURES When bodies were too decomposed to dissect, often the teeth were pulled and sold to dentists, for making dentures. PROTECTION - KEEPING BODIES SAFE FROM BODY-SNATCHERS Entrepreneurs came up with an arsenal of anti-resurrectionist products and service, affordable only to the rich. Iron cages called mortsafes could be set in concrete above the grave or underground, around the coffin. Churches in Scotland built graveyard "dead houses", locked buildings where a body could be left to decompose until its structures and organs had disintegrated to the point where they were of no use to anatomists. You could buy patented spring-closure coffins, coffins outfitted with cast-iron corpse straps, double and even triple coffins. MURDER In the first quarter of the 19th century, William Burke and William Hare, realising there was money in cadavers, murdered 15 people before they were caught. FORENSICS RESEARCH At the University of Tennessee Medical Centre there is a forested grove dedicated to the study of human decay. Cadavers are left out in the open, and studied to help further research in the field of criminal forensics. HOW TO CHECK THAT PEOPLE ARE REALLY DEAD The problem, for centuries, was that doctors couldn't tell for sure whether the heart had ceased to beat, or whether they were merely having trouble hearing it. The stethoscope wasn't invented until the mid-1800s. To allay patients' considerable fears of live burial, as well as their own insecurities, 18th and 19th physicians devised a diverting roster of methods for verifying death. (These often involved loud noises, or hurting the cadaver so that the pain might return them to consciousness.) None of these techniques gained wide acceptance, and most doctors felt that putrefaction was the only reliable way to verify that someone was dead. And so it was that special buildings, called waiting mortuaries, were built for the purpose of warehousing the mouldering dead. These were huge, ornate halls, common in Germany in the 1800s. Some had separate halls for male and female cadavers. Others were segregated by class. Attendants were employed to keep watch for signs of life, which they did via a system of strings linking the fingers of corpses to a bell...so that any motion on the part of the deceased would alert the attendant, who was posted, owing to the considerable stench, in a separate room. As years passed and not a single resident was saved, the establishments began to close.173 THE HUMAN COMPOST MOVEMENT. This centres on a tiny island called Lyron, in Sweden, and was initiated by biologist-entrepreneur Susanne Wiigh-Masak. She founded a company called Promessa, which seeks to replace cremation with a technologically enhanced form of organic compositng. Promessa http://www.promessa.se/ HOW CADAVERS ARE USED Upward of 80 percent of the bodies left to science are used for anatomy lab dissections. New Mexico's Maxwell Museum of Anthropology accepts bodies specifically to harvest the bones. They are not assimilated into skeletons, but used individually. They are added to the university's osteological collection, and used to study everything from forensics to the skeletal manifestations of diseases. FAQ: Re donating one's body for bone harvesting. The Maxwell Museum of Anthropology, New Mexico. http://www.unm.edu/~osteolab/faq.html No one in this country is making skeletons for medical schools. The vast majority of the world's medical school skeletons have, over the years, been imported from Calcutta, but no longer, as several stories emerged about abuses in obtaining the bodies. If you want to donate your brain, Harvard's McClean Hospital has 'The Brain Bank'. The Harvard Brain Bank & how to donate a brain... https://hbtrc.mclean.harvard.edu/ PLASTINATION This is the process of taking organic tissue and replacing the water in it with a liquid silicone polymer, turning the organism into a permanently preserved version of itself. it was developed by German anatomist Gunther von Hagens. He makes educational models for anatomy programes. he is best known, however, for his controversial platinated whole-body art exhibit, "Korperwelten" or in England, "Bodyworlds" - which has toured Europe for the past 5 years, raising eyebrows and tidy sums of cash. The skinless bodies are posed as living people in action: swimming, riding (plastinated horse included), playing chess. The bodies in the show were donated by their owners specifically for this purpose. (von Hagens leaves a stack of donor forms at the exit of the exhibit. According to a 2001 London Observer article, the doner list is up to 3,700.) Flickr pix of Bodyworlds/plastination exhibition https://www.flickr.com/search/?text=b... HOW DO YOU WANT TO DISPOSE OF YOUR BODY? The author makes an interesting point that the kindest thing to do is to leave it up to your nearest and dearest. All in all I thought this was a so-so read. Loved the chapter dealing with the history of how cadavers were obtained for autopsies. Plus loved reading about plastination (although I was one of those who found the famous/notorious plastination exhibition quite offensive at the time.) The rest of the book I rather skimmed though. Finally - whinge, whinge, whinge - another non-fiction book without an index. Not good. The Guardian review of Stiff... https://www.theguardian.com/books/200...

4 Not in Hollywood anymore stars! Source: eARC for Honest Review Courtesy of Author and The Next Step PR Usually with Alessandra Torre her books are very erotic or dark, however Hollywood Dirt was more sweet and fun, which was a very pleasant surprise. Sure there some steamy parts and some asshole parts but when you have a rooster named Cocky in it,  how can it be anything but awesome. This was not a rebound, this was not infatuation, this was the end of his life as he knew it, . Cole Masten is the Hollywood 'it' man but after being screwed over by his wife, he hops on a plane to nowhere Georgia to lick his wounds. Summer Jenkins has been wronged once, and may have a chip on her shoulder, but she also has a plan. As soon as Cole lands in Quincy he meets Summer and their love/hate relationship begins. Summer has always liked Cole from afar, but is not impressed when she finally meets him in person. As Cole's licking his wounds, the last thing he wants is a new relationship, but there's something about Summer that sets him off. Plus she's the perfect person for his movie. Now he just has to convince her. Summer needs money to help with her plan, so she eventually agrees to be part of Cole's film. She will just continue to hate him up close instead of from the sidelines. However, hating him ended up not being as easy as she originally thought, because Cole's not as much of an asshole as she first thought him to be. As we said in these parts, that egg had been laid. It couldn't be put back in the chicken now. Cole's so intrigued by Summer that he can't stay away, but he doesn't know what category to place her in, as she's so not Hollywood. But what she is, is real. he was beginning to remember what it felt like to be an actual man, not just Hollywood's version of one. Cole and Summer love / hate relationship is in full swing for most of the book with moments of steam and sweet. "Well," he said to the bird, " I guess it's just me and you." Damn Summer. Damn her to hell. Summer has a past and throughout the majority of the book we are waiting to find out what it is. But as she plots along with this movie, she starts to lose a bit of herself. "No Country. In Hollywood, off camera, you can't be yourself. You can't be weak, you can't be honest, and you can't be genuine. Not if you want to survive." Once the past comes out, it's finally a bridge for these two, where the love portion outweighs the hate portion of their relationship. Thankfully for Cocky or these two would have had a lot harder time finding their way to each other. One of my favorite parts is that I loved having Brad Deluca from Innocence series in this story. I didn't realize how much I missed him till he appeared. I quite liked this story. It was cute, funny and sexy. These two may have been polar opposites but they so worked once they both got their chips off their shoulders.

Wow. This series really appeals to my feminist side. Not only does it make boys of high standing look like idiots, it makes girls way smarter and skilled than them. Although Sophronia is a rather enjoyable character with a charming sense of humor, I must admit- she is a Mary-Sue. I think she is about fifteen years old in this novel, and she is already flirting off a storm and attracting boys. Not only that, but she is miraculously skilled in every subject while beating the teachers at their own game. I find this hard to believe, but I have come to accept this flaw in her character. My feminist side wins. One thing I loved most was the wit and the language Gail Carriger put into the novel. There is use of elevated vocabulary, and she almost makes it sound as if I am reading a novel from a few centuries ago. Most of all, her humor had me laughing out loud like a mad person. Another thing about this book was it's combination of feminine wiles and strength. The girls, and sometimes Sophronia towards Felix, act like simpering, empty-headed  things . They flirt, they faint, the squeal. But at the end of the day, the one who can whip out a knife from under their skirts or poison someone's drink is the girls. Especially Sophronia. Lastly, the romance. I spy with my little eye a love triangle. Another  one. I've pretty much had it with indecisive girls in novels,  especially  after reading The Selection. I could care less about who they choose, and frankly, they might as well date a turtle while they're at it. However, despite the annoying and unbelievable naivety of Sophronia, I am enjoying the fact that Soap has an actual chance with her. I'm not saying that Felix is a scumbag or an annoying flirt (which he is at times), he's pretty tolerable once you get past his patheticness. Soap is amazing. I've actually never read a book where a white female gets together with a black male. I'm not trying to be racist or anything; in fact, I adore Sophronia and Soap as a couple. I've been rooting for them since they first met. I think Sophronia has actual affection towards him, and I am looking forward to the day they get together. ESPECIALLY after that kiss, that made me dreams come true. So overall, besides a slightly overpowered female protagonist, a bit of inconsistency in the plot, and some annoying characters, Curtsies & Conspiracies is a great sequel. I will be highly anticipating the next one.

Synopsis: The past few years held more surprises than part-angel Clara Gardner ever could have anticipated. Yet through the dizzying high of first love to the agonizing low of losing someone close to her, the one thing she could no longer deny was that she was never meant to have a normal life. Since discovering the special role she plays among the other angel-bloods, Clara has been determined to protect Tucker Avery from the evil that follows her . even if it means breaking both their hearts. Leaving town seemed like the best option, so she's headed back to California--and so is Christian Prescott, the irresistible boy from the vision that started her on this journey in the first place. As Clara makes her way in a world that is frighteningly new, she discovers that the fallen angel who attacked her is watching her every move. And he's not the only one. With the battle against the Black Wings looming, Clara knows she must finally fulfill her destiny. But it won't come without sacrifices and betrayal. In the riveting finale of the Unearthly series, Clara must choose her fate once and for all. My Thoughts: This final installment in the Unearthly series starts off with Clara, Angela and Christian starting their freshman year at Stanford. Clara has left Tucker back in Wyoming because she believes it's better and safer for him if she isn't with him. Too bad that she can't help but be around him. So many times during the book, she ends up right where Tucker is. Jeffrey is also still missing. At least, he is until he shows up on campus to see Clara. There's some back and forth throughout the book of them getting along and arguing, but in the end, they do right by one another. In the end, Clara does right by everyone. Of course, the biggest thing in this series has been Clara's purpose. What is it? Well, she seems to have figured it out and she really came through. There were a few times where she wallowed and felt bad for herself, but she rallied. I felt proud of her. She did a couple of impossible things, but Clara is far from one of those annoyingly perfect heroines. She can be selfish. She wasn't always brave, but she did so much. I really like Clara as a heroine. Even with all of her imperfections. I was so happy that she did what she did for Angela. That she saved her brother and that he saved her. Of course, I knew which of the boys she would end up with. I feel slightly bad for Christian since Tucker ends up with an extended life span and what not. Though, he stayed true to himself. Even when he was so, so frustrated by the fact that Clara couldn't get over Tucker. I was proud of him for what he said in the end. He really is an awesome guy. It was an interesting way of working things out. In a way, I wish she would have gone the other way. Done something breakthrough in the genre. It wasn't bad, though. I was a little shocked that she did what she did. I didn't expect that. We got a lot of revelations in this book. Some parentage revelations. How Clara's mom knew the things that she knew. Apparently, she finds them out from Clara herself when Clara travels to the past and meets a younger version of her mother. No wonder her mother kept so many secrets. Some new skills. A trip to hell. A baby. Betrayal. And lots of times where I cried. I cried quite a few times, but that wasn't surprising. Cynthia Hand seems to be good and making me weep. I really liked the book. I think things were wrapped up pretty well. There's a sense of closure, but also the possibility of more. We get to see our characters find their happiness and I was so happy for all of them. All in all, a good ending.

In short: Though Defiance by C.J. Redwine was missing certain aspects that kept it from being truly amazing, it was still an exciting and enjoyable read. As I've already mentioned, I've been loving this recent influx of books in the historical high fantasy genre - all seemingly with kick ass heroines who know how to wield a weapon - and so I was very excited to pick up Defiance. Except Defiance wasn't quite what I had been expecting: it's actually a fantasy-dystopian set in a world where fossil fuels are becoming depleted and while looking for more, humans accidentally stumble upon a dragon-serpent-monster-thing from the depths of the Earth. A totalitarian leader controls the people who live inside his city's walls in exchange for protection from the monster. Though I really wish the world building in Defiance would have been more fleshed out as I was left with a ton of questions, I do think the premise was interesting and exciting. The strength of Defiance comes from C.J. Redwine's beautiful and gripping writing, especially with respect to scenes of grief. Emotions aren't just glossed over, but fully realized and explored in her characters in these scenes, and I really appreciated that the time was taken to do so. Defiance is written effectively as a dual narrative, with love interests Rachel and Logan getting equal page time. Rachel and Logan were both likeable characters in their own way - Rachel with her stubborn fierceness and Logan with his logical and steadfast demeanour - and I thought they were perfectly compatible and their romance was nice and sweet. Still, likeable characters and a nice romance doesn't exactly translate to amazing and memorable, and therein lies my biggest fault with Defiance. I was missing that "Wow Factor" that would have really elevated Defiance from being a good read to an absolutely fantastic one. The characters were strong and enjoyable, but were lacking a certain specialness that would have set them apart and made them truly memorable in my mind. The romance was awfully sweet and nice, which I love, but because it developed quite early on and was pretty predictable, it was lacking that romantic tension that makes the chemistry sizzle off the page. The premise was intriguing for sure, but the world building needed to be more developed to be truly impressive. Overall, I really did like Defiance and I think this first book sets up great potential for the series at large. C.J. Redwine is a talented writer and I look forward to reading more from her. Though parts of Defiance were missing that je ne sais quoi, it was still an exciting story and one that I look forward to continuing in the sequels still to come.

What a great prequel! I love The Maze Runner books! Now, before someone comments "but your ratings are so low", I know, I know, I know. I loved The Maze Runner; the action; the characters; the mystery. The Scorch Trials I enjoyed a little less, since the pace dropped so much and well... no real answers were given near the end of the second book. As for The Death Cure... that 'HAE' sort of ending really ruined the rest of the book for me ( I mean Thomas just went like "fuck it, I'm gonna let everyone die and live my life with the other munies in this place we claim for ourselves. It just felt so... cheap idk. I understood his actions, seeing what he's all gone through but... Thomas never seemed like a guy whom would stop caring and only look out for himself, you know? ). But despite all this, I enjoyed this series so much, and I consider it a favorite anyway. The Fever Code Review:  BIG AND SMALL SPOILERS THROUGHOUT THE REVIEW! I enjoyed this prequel so much! Did I get all the answers I wanted? No, it's a James Dashner book after all and that man likes his secrets. Which is cool with me, because our MC's didn't get all the answers either. But I did find out so much stuff that was still great to finally know about. In TFC we get a big look into the lives of the Gladers before they enter the maze. We see them life and grow in the WICKED headquarters, get tested (as much consiously as subconsiously), make friendships etc. I got to see Thomas and Teresa grow together and also saw them grow apart, which was rather sad. They start out as friends, grow into something you thing might grow into love, only for Teresa to betray Thomas in the end. Because, sad as it may be, Teresa believed in WICKED and stays loyal to them, while Thomas grows more and more tired of the lies, the hurt WICKED feeds him. The story starts with Thomas being taken to WICKED and ends with him deciding he wants to enter the maze. BUT not because of the cure, or because WICKED asked him too... no. Thomas decides to go into the maze to save his friends. Thomas watches the Gladers when they're in the maze, sees their despair, their pain, and at some point he decides that it's enough. 'WICKED was never going to stop. They were never, never going to stop.' He won't put his friends through this any longer. And in order to save them, he plans to enter the Maze, convincing dr. Paige that he and Teresa need to go in with their memories intact. But Teresa and Paige betray him, by actually taking his memories from him anyway. And the story ends with Thomas waking up in the Box. So... what does all this mean? Well: 1) Thomas became aware that WICKED was in fact not all 'good'. And he planned to get his friends out of the maze! Despite that Thomas firsts believes helping WICKED was the right thing, he did realize that it wasn't. He wasn't a 'bad guy' in the end, which Thomas feared for in TMR books. 2) It is shown in the end that Teresa (and Aris) didn't get their memories wiped, and therefor were fully aware of what WICKED was and what horrible things were planned for Thomas and the Gladers throughout TMR books. 3) You find out in TFC what the Purge is. (meh) 4) Ava Paige is a horrible, lying, mischevious person: '"It was me, Thomas. I know you won't remember this, but I want to say the words to you anyway. Explain myself. It was me who infected Chencellor Anderson and his senior staff. They wanted to end things after the Maze Trials. They wanted to give up. And I could never allow that, could I? What we're trying to achieve is much too important."' NOW on a side note: Newt. My baby. My favorite character... with his 'bloody this and bloody that', his longish hair, his everything... I cried so much for you in this book. The epilogue is from Newts past, revealing he has a sister named Lizzy-renamed Sonya(!!? I freaked out a little at this). I loved that little reveal, and seeing Newt and his sister say goodbye before he is sent into the maze.. it's so sweet and sad. But the part in this book that broke my heart was seeing Newt attempt his suicide. We read how Thomas sees it in an observation room and guys... It's so sad! :( My poor baby. 'Those groans turned into sobs. A deep, painful cry that made Thomas's chest hurt. Newt suddenly let out an anguished howl, then screamed into the air. "I hate you. I hate you!"' For me, some unresolved stuff was explained... and some wasn't. But I enjoyed learning some secrets and revelations and for me, this book was a great addition in TMRseries. And a great conclusion of some sorts too! I recommend reading this series in publication order; because the suspense is great in that order!

A gladiatrix in Caesar's Rome! I wanted to like this book -- and I did like about 1/3 of it. Our heroine, Fallon, the only surviving warrior daughter of a British chieftain, is kidnapped and sold as a slave, ends up, along with her new friend the Germanic captive Elke, in a ludus of female gladiators run by the mysterious Lady Achillea and under the patronage of Julius Caesar himself. All of this was excellent! Yes, so the mysteries of Lady Achillea were fairly obvious, and the other girls in the ludus weren't sketched particularly fully or interestingly, and the rivalries and friendships played out in a pretty clicheed way-- but it was gripping, good fun, with periodic fights and dangers. But around this, there was a series of tedious romance plots. The book gets off to an incredibly slow start as Fallon angsts about her love for Mael and fends off the advances of Mael's brother Aeddan (yawn). Once in Rome, she meets and falls for a young Roman aristocrat with the teeth-clenchingly wrong name of 'Caius Antonius Varro'; he's also tedious, with the exception of one pretty good sparring scene. I could have done without any of these completely formulaic romances and a strict focus on Fallon negotiating her friendships and loyalties. Finally, I have to note a few oddities, because I'm a pedant like that. (But I forbear to mention the Latin, or the misunderstanding of some key legal/cultural concepts. I'm not that much of a pedant!) All in all, I liked what this book did with the heroine's perspective: the year is 46 bce but we get almost nothing by way of Roman politics-- because they aren't relevant to Fallon or her life. Which is good, I think, but the way even the Roman characters talked about politics was about a decade off. No mention of the fact that Caesar had just been named dictator for an unprecedented 10 year term. No mention of the recent civil war. It was a bit disappointing to find that Pontius Aquila -- the tribune known to history pretty much exclusively because he needled Caesar by neglecting to rise in his presence (he was also one of the Caesaricides and died at Munda) -- is repurposed as a totally bland villain  who is holding nefarious cannibalistic rituals to the god Dis in his house for... the lolz? All that said, I will probably read the sequel, because it was fairly enjoyable-- and a nice change from the endless parade of YA novels about Cleopatra Selene.

This is a Quickie Review. For the full review, please visit The Romanceaholic. Expected Release Date: February 22, 2011 (Available Now!) Publisher: HarperCollins Imprint: Avon Author's Website: http://www.julieannelong.com/ My Source for This Book: Amazon.com Part of a Series: Yes, Book 5, Pennyroyal Green Series Best Read In Order: Worked well as a standalone Steam Level: Hot When Ian Eversea is caught with his pants down -- literally -- by the Duke of Falconbridge, in the bedroom of Falconbridge's fiance, he is right to fear for his life. However, some of the vicious rumors circling the Duke are true, especially the one that intimates that he savors his revenge as a dish best served cold. Being forced to escape out a window without his clothes, Ian knows that he has gotten off lightly. A short time later, Ian's family, knowing nothing of this incident, is thrilled to discover that they are to have an incredibly distinguished guest for a few weeks -- Alex Moncrieffe, the Duke of Falconbridge. Unfortunately for them, Moncrieffe has decided to partake of his revenge, by taking something valuable and beloved from Ian -- his sister. Intending to seduce and then discard Genevieve, he's astonished to discover that while she's a bit on the plain side, there is so much more to her than first appears, and he cannot help but to find himself intrigued by her. Recovering from the heartbreak of discovering that the man she loves is not only oblivious to her feelings but actually intends to wed her best friend, Genevieve is not exactly sparkling company for the Duke. Far from discouraging him, however, he's intrigued by her quick thinking and obvious personal depths, as well as the mystery of her heartbreak, and soon an unlikely friendship blossoms. Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed it. Between Moncrieffe's dark past, Genevieve's heartbreak, the revenge plot, and the delightful ongoing torment of Ian, I simply couldn't put it down. While I was incredibly frustrate with Genevieve towards the end, I couldn't put it down. Recommended for fans of brutally painful unrequited love, of dark and brooding older heroes entranced by a younger and surprisingly mature heroine, and of grand gestures by heroes gambling for the heroine's heart. 4/5 Stars

Another good yarn. Good action and drama. No long and tedious infodumps that I noticed. Very few breakdowns in realism compared to the first book. However, I have two major complaints: 1) It seems like Weber is developing a specific pattern of storytelling in order to create suspense: Honor is pitted against unbeatable odds, but some random lucky accidents start tipping the scale, making the bad guys screw up due to incompetence, until The Final Battle where Honor manage to carry the day through dogged heorism, tactical skills and sheer dumb luck. And manage to get most of her crew killed in the process, seriously, she lost something like 75% of her crew TWICE within three? With some rough calculations, this leaves around 12,5% of her original crew alive after the second book, each of which would have lost something like 7 out of 8 of their friends just because she NEVER backs down in order to live and fight another day? If that is not something that will cause resentment, I don't know what is. Furthermore, considering the poor results from the fleet excercises in the first book, it ought to be considered EXTREMELY bad luck to end up serving under her at this point. If something isn't changed in some of the very next books, I seriously consider abandoning the series and adding the books to my "psychology and motivation messed up"-bookshelf. 2) The diplomatic development is VERY strange: Going ahead and defending the system without signing a (defence) treaty first would mean that a) They were putting their fleet detachment at risk without any benefit to themselves b) IF the Masadans had managed to conquer the planet (which was a real risk after they managed to wipe out their navy plus Manticorian support), they would have no excuse to go back and liberate the planet. c) IF the Havenites had swooped in with a superior force to take over the planet, the battered remains of the Manticorian fleet detachment would be forced to either sit on the fence and watching the Havenites take over the planet, or, despite being told to mind their own business, starting the war themselves by attacking the Havenite expiditionary force. Furthermore, it is a bit strange that the Manticorians only aim at establishing a strategic foothold in one of two neighboring star systems... kinda like if the Japanese had accepted an American occupation of the other end of Iwo Jima island before Pearl Harbor Considering how much effort the author has put into making the political games interesting and realistic, I'm really surprised that the author didn't consider these aspects.

3.5 stars I wasn't in love with this urban fantasy novel, but it read fairly well. The heroine Makenna Fraser works for the SPI agency, aka Supernatural Protection & Investigation. She is a seer - she sees supernatural beings no matter how many layers of glamour they put on to blend with the humans of New York. The story is a supernatural thriller with a tint of humor, and all the details mesh well in the fascinating world the author constructed. There are dragons and goblins there, gorgons and werewolves, vampires and wizards. Anyone from any race could be a baddy or a good guy, just like in real life, and I like this aspect of supernatural America. The protagonist is a charming young woman. She doesn't have any special powers except the power of seeing things as they are, so she doesn't aspire to the superhero status. She lets other, more muscled guys, to shield her puny self, while she always tries to do the right thing, which is protecting the innocent, be it a benevolent 1000-year-old gorgon or an enigmatic goblin with the not-so-honest intentions towards her. In this case, protecting the innocent means stopping a terrible conspiracy scheduled for Halloween. Only one day is left, and the clock is ticking, while Makenna and her fellow SPI agents scramble frantically in their search for the villain who wants all the supernaturals eliminated from the city and surrounding areas. I like Makenna. She is a living woman, a bit cynical and a lot humane, colorful and controversial. Unfortunately, aside from her, all the other characters are only half-cooked, shadowy silhouettes rather than flesh and blood persons, which weakens this novel. The other problematic aspect of the book is its beginning. The book is the second in a series, and the entire first chapter is a huge and boring info dump, where the author crams most of the background from the first book. As far as I could tell, none of it is necessary for the story. As soon as the plot starts rolling in chapter two, the action is swift and original, reflecting Shearin's boundless imagination, and all the facts and descriptions the reader needs unfold naturally throughout the story. Overall, the book is a nice addition to the series and a crazy romp through New York's supernatural community. If you like sexy goblins and dragons with a sense of humor, this book is for you.

Talulla Rising is the sequel to The Last Werewolf, one of my favorite books of 2011. Like TLW, Talulla Rising is a bloody book about monsters and the meaning of life, with a tremendous amount of no-holds-barred, very gruesome violence perpetrated to different degrees and with different amounts of enjoyment by just about everyone we encounter. TLW ended quite shockingly, with the titular last werewolf, Jake Marlowe, ending up not being the last after all. Jake met Talulla, and their shared love and bloodlust was both powerful and scary. TLW ends with Jake's death, and Talulla is left to carry on by herself, heartbreaken, hunted, and pregnant with Jake's baby, a situation thought impossible until now. Talulla Rising picks up just a few months after the end of the previous book, with Talulla sequestered in remote Alaska, suffering through her Curse's response to the pregnancy and fearful about birth, motherhood, and the looming question of how to stay alive and how to keep her baby safe. Needless to say, it doesn't go well, violence pops in at the most inopportune time, and Talulla is forced into a non-stop, desperate course of action that continues the bloodshed (and occasional dismemberment) that we've come to expect in these blood-soaked werewolf books. I won't give away any other plot details, but will say that I was surprised to hear that Glen Duncan had written a sequel to TLW, as I thought it wrapped up as a stand-alone novel. Likewise, after finishing Talulla Rising, I thought the story was done (despite a few loose plot threads), but just read that a third and final book is planned. Of course I'll read the next one. Glen Duncan is a powerful and magnificent writer, who twists and turns the English language in all sorts of unexpected and beautiful ways. While the writing itself was more remarkable in the first book, perhaps because TLW seemed a much more contemplative narrative than Tallula Rising, Duncan's skill with words is evident in TR as well. A final note: With a female protagonist, the emphasis on the werewolf's monthly Curse takes on new meaning, as Talulla suffers through the rage and physical changes imposed on her body, a slave to her biology, yet also undeniably delighting in her power and fearlessness. Talulla's thoughts and fears regarding motherhood are also quite interesting, and her self-doubt about her maternal instincts -- while taken to the the extreme, as most new mothers don't literally fear eating their young -- is not unusual for someone experiencing a first pregnancy and the crushing changes, both physical and emotional, that ensue. My recommendation: Read The Last Werewolf, and then read Talulla Rising, but be warned. These books are not for the faint of heart. No hearts and flowers in this story about new motherhood. Well, maybe a few hearts, but they tend to get eaten.

My favorite types of books are the ones that I'm initially suspicious of and then they proceed to slap me in the face with their awesomeness. You know what I mean? I've had this experience with Delirium and Vampire Academy and this one did the same thing. The Program is set in an alternate reality where suicide is an all out epidemic not just with teenagers but with adults. Everyone is depressed and suicidal and no one really knows why. We follow Sloane and James as they struggle to stay together. My favorite parts of this novel is that nothing is handed over to the characters. Sloane and James get thrown in the program and they do lose their memories,  but the great thing is that they're real, flawed characters. James and Sloane aren't perfect, but they do have a deep love and genuinely care about each other. I loved all the characters in The Program. Their friendship with one another was really nice to read and reminded me of my own friends. The world is believable and while the mention of 'rebels' took me out of it somewhat, I'm glad to read the conclusion of this series, The Treatment, which I will be reading for June. I really cannot formulate eough of a thought to give this book an in-depth review, so let's do this one bullet-point style. WARNING: SPOILERY RANTY THINGS AHEAD Things I enjoyed: Batshit!Insane!Cersei: This was, by far, the highlight of the book. I have always wanted to know how the inside of her head worked, and watching this woman who seems to be the epitome of conniving ice queen grace slowly fall apart at the seams was an absolute delight. And her final chapter was just beyond perfect. Love them or hate them, this series needs more House Lannister. Jaime: Because everyone loves a smartass and it's nice to see he's not as dumb as everyone thinks he is. I am enjoying watching him evolve without losing s much of what made him likable in the first place. Everyone in House Greyjoy Whose Name Isn't Theon: Who knew they'd end up being the most badass house in Westeros? Asha, Euron, Victarion and Aeron are now some of my favorite people in the series. Too bad Theon gives his entire family a bad name. I did not give House Greyjoy a fair shake before going into this book. I love them now. They are my house. And, like the Lannisters, the series needs more of them. I can't wait to see how this whole "abduct Dany and make her your bride" thing blows up in their faces. Almost no Jon Snow: You heard me. I don't get what the big deal about Jon is. His chapters are completely tedious and he gets stuck with the most annoying companions (Sam, Ygritte, etc). I have to struggle through most of his chapters. The only ones of his I have really enjoyed was when he was with Mance Rayder, and that was more to do with Mance than Jon. Littlefinger, You Scheming Prick: Specifically, his last words in Alayne's last chapter. By the Seven, I want you to pull this off. Things I Did Not Enjoy: Lady Stoneheart: Does no one in this series get to rest in peace? C'mon, Martin, that's just cruel. What Pretty Much Amounts to the Complete and Utter Obliteration of House Stark: Yes, technically that happened last volume. But having both Arya and Sansa lose their names is just the last straw. Brienne: What. The. Fuck. Was. The. Point. Of. Her. Arc. And. Why. Was. So. Damn. Much. Time. Spent. Going. Absolutely. Fucking. Nowhere. These chapters could've been spent on almost anything else and they would've been way more relevant. To elaborate: if the reader already knows where Sansa is and that Brienne is not and will never head in that direction, THIS ENTIRE SECTION IS ABSOLUTELY FREAKING POINTLESS. THIS IS NOT HOW YOU BUILD SUSPENSE, MARTIN. BAD WRITER. BAD! Everything Happening in Dorne: Because there is already enough going on in this series without dragging them into the thick of things. Samwell: I get it, you're a coward. And fat. And Gilly cries a lot. Can we skip all this and move on? That's it!?!?!? : Where the hell were the cliffhangers that inevitably leave the readers raging that Martin kills everything they have ever loved? Or loved to hate? After the Bran thing, then the Ned thing and the Dany thing, in the first book; the Renly thing and the second Dany thing in the second book, and the Red Wedding, the other wedding and that one guy getting nailed with a crossbow while taking a shit in the third book; I was kind of expecting something awesome to happen here. And it never did. Overall Summation: While Martin has given us some cliffhangers in each character's closing chapter, there's nothing that makes me HAVE to pick up ADwD. I am seriously considering skipping books 5-whatever (cause it's going to take more than 7 to wrap this mess up), reading the cliff notes' version of each, then *maybe* coming back for the last installment, provided Martin lives long enough to finish the series (my money is on "he won't"). The narrative has sprawled into too many routes I'm just not interested in taking, and Martin seems to enjoy taking the scenic, meandering path more and more often. If I'm going to invest in a 800+ page book, I need a little more to work with.

This was an amazing book. I couldn't put it down coming close to the end. The book is well written with the characters well developed. It was a little too descriptive is some cases, sometimes taking away from the readability, but fortunately, it didn't take away from the excitement. The plot twists got you dizzy at some times, but made the book even more enjoyable. I figured out what the crux behind the murder of Teys was about early in the game, or I should say, I had a feeling. However, I didn't think that Roberta was responsible, other than being present. All the other plot lines, and back stories, seemed to me a sleight of hand by the author, to lead us away from the killer, and questioning the truth. But that is the basis of the story, isn't it. It's not just about finding the killer, it's about finding the truth. And shouldn't that be what we all should be aiming for in life? I still don't understand how the priest got away scot free. Shouldn't he have been charged with perverting the course of justice or something, for interfering with evidence? Moreso, I just wanted to see him pay for his transgressions. This book also needed an epilogue. Something to say what happens next to Roberta, Gillian, Tessa and Havers. Did Havers get back into CID? Or patch things up with her parents? Did Tessa come back into her girls' lives? Did they catch the ripper? But I just realised that this is the first in a series, so it's possible that the author planned it this way. I'll have to hunt down the others in the series. I got this book in my local library, and I sure hope they have the others.

The title is certainly accurate. The Lee family sucks all the fun out of dysfunctional, by never ever communicating their needs or wants, and then being sad and resentful when their needs aren't met. The writing is very lovely, and the character development is well done, but I'm just so aggravated with these people. So much anguish can be avoided by just opening your mouth and speaking to one another. I didn't really enjoy the book. How does a wife never tell her husband that she'd like to go back to school? How does a teenaged son not lash out verbally at his parents' double standard of academic expectations and acknowledgments? How does Lydia think she can pass a driver test without studying, and think she can swim without having learned? And on and on. I do get why Lydia never balked at her parents' expectations, but it doesn't explain the rest of the family's passivity and resentment. 2.5 stars

Meanwhile, the acolytes are still gunning for her, the court she has unexpectedly acquired needs tending to, the mages want her under their thumb and Mircea, as usual, also has a plan up his sleeve that he wants to use Cassie for. The lovely Rainbow Rowell has done another very finely written book. The pacing was pretty on point, the characters were enjoyable (except Agatha), the plot was intriguing, and the British grammar and spelling was so much fun to read; the whole book was very well done. " But why did I give it 4 out of 5 stars? " you ask. I'm a sucker (haha :) ) for a good ole fantasy. Sometimes, I'm looking for a fast-paced contemporary with battles and action scenes every page. Other times, I'm looking for a more relaxed fantasy. This book has just the right amount of both. While the novel was not all blood, guts, and gore, it had higher-intensity scenes that made me want to make sure everything went down the way I wanted it to. I have never read Harry Potter (yes, I know, unfriend me if you like; I'm sorry), but I really enjoyed reading this, which I have heard is not unlike Harry Potter. I liked reading about the magic and Watford and the way everything worked. I was kind of confused on some (maybe a lot) of the parts, but maybe that was my doing by not reading Harry Potter. Despite my state of confusion, I thoroughly enjoyed reading about this magickal world. I always thought of casting spells as simple as saying a specific phrase or word and have your wand out and voila! Your spell has activated, for lack of a better word. However, I learned that this magic system is like some modern languages in the 21st century (I'm thinking Mandarin Chinese? If I'm wrong please tell me). To cast a spell, the caster (?) has to say the phrase a specific way and emphasize the right part to get the desired outcome. I think that's super cool, but I'd probably get super confused and "accidentally" have someone spontaneously combust or something. I really enjoyed the multiple pov thing going on here. I like reading about everything that was going on, not just Simon and Baz, but I did like reading about them. Simon was a good character. He wasn't a  weak  protagonist, but I don't think that he is the greatest. Mediumish. Now, let us talk about Tyrannus Basilton Grimm-Pitch. Wouldn't that look good monogrammed? That's such a cool name, and it comes with pretty cool powers, too. He kind of reminds me of the insecure bully who has a boat-load of bravado but in reality is kind of insecure and not as brave on the inside. Baz is brave, no doubt about that, but he is more than he let people see of him. He has depth, and I like that. And can we talk about the dynamic between  Baz and Penelope? I love it! I think they have a great budding frenemy relationship coming along. Penelope is a really strong female character, and I like her persistence and loyalty to Simon. Then we have Agatha Wellbelove. Ick. Carry{ing} on... A few of the things that caught my sweater were Agatha, my confusion, and the romance. None of the romance really clicked with me the way other Rainbow Rowell's romances have. Agatha was such a dead weight that I really just felt that she was put in the story to add to the drama and cast of characters, but I suppose in a way I admire her for  trying to move on from the magic, that most people would love to have, by leaving Watford and living in California with her normal friends. Another negative was the "plot twists". While I didn't predict the actual outcome, I could sort of think that maybe what was going to happen. And I didn't really feel anything for the  big, unfortunate  twist. Overall, I really liked this and I am glad I read this. It was quite appropriate for the month of October, with magic and vampires and all, and I am happy to have picked it up shortly after the release date. Most everything was good, and I think you deserve an "Aero (which is a chocolate thing in England)" reading all of this :)

Edit 2 June 2017: I'm adding Tasha's review as a link here because she discusses the ableism in this book, which I don't really touch on. (Note: all page numbers are from my hardcover edition) I wanted to like this book. I'd been excited to read it for months. On a basic writing level, there's nothing wrong with it. The writing style is easy to read and the protagonist's voice is fairly strong. I also really liked the peach motif that cropped up here and there, usually tied to sumptuous descriptions that made me kinda hungry. However, I find I had a lot of issues with the book in terms of structure and prejudice. I'm not an expert on racism, being a white person, but the more I think about it, the more it seems so obvious that I don't understand how so many people have missed it. My first issue circulates around the one and only black character in the entire book, Gemma. As far as I can tell, the author is white, and Gemma's manner of speech was very stereotypical. I almost wanted to keep a tally of how many times she prefaced a sentence with "girl" or threw in some other awkwardly-executed AAVE grammatical mannerisms. Page 70: "Because, girl." Gemma growls. "Our dance parties are epic." Page 140: Her eyes narrow and it's like I can hear the "Oh no he didn't" loud as a bullhorn. Page 150: "Girl, don't you lie." Gemma is straight to the point. Page 187: "Girl." Gemma is attacking a slice of veggie pizza. There are undoubtedly more examples. These are just the ones I noted in my Goodreads statuses. I know it's not just a quirk of being southern since, with the exception of some really uncomfortable AAVE appropriation coming from Jo and her friend, Dana, she was the only character who consistently spoke like this. If the representation had been more varied (as in, Gemma wasn't the only black character in the whole book), it wouldn't have been as much of an issue. EDIT: Another reader also pointed out that this perpetuates the "sassy black girl" stereotype, which I should have noted originally. Sidenote: we as white people need to stop saying "yaaaas" (which Dana says on page 22). Can we stop appropriating from AAVE already? Please. My crops are dying. Unrelated to the racism of the dialogue, I also hated that Gemma's attempts to invade Jo's privacy by getting into her phone were treated as a silly little quirk rather than a horrible thing to do. Biphobia also rears its ugly head in this book. The most blatant occasion is on PAGE THREE where Jo, the lesbian narrator, says: I nod toward the late twentyish, early thirtyish bi-curious cougar Dana had been flirting with before she deigned to check up on me. There's no good reason the word needs to be there as it does not impact the plot in any way. As a bisexual, this is a word I never want to see again because it is used to invalidate bi women's queerness as just a phase she'll grow out of once her so-called curiosity has been sated. I also had issues with the plot, especially after the mid-point of the book. Honestly, most of the drama could've been solved with one basic conversation. Jo's internal freakout over thinking Mary Carlson would be angry to find she was lying would have been nothing compared to what ultimately transpired because she just would not communicate. Seriously. One little conversation explaining to Mary Carlson why she couldn't come out and so much of the drama would've been resolved before it began. And don't get me started on Mary Carlson trying to force Jo out of the closet . That was not okay, even if Jo wasn't being entirely honest at that point. And yet Mary Carlson isn't criticised for this. Jo is the one who is forced to apologise for lying  and Mary Carlson gets away with everything, even though it was horrible of her to try and force Jo to out herself before she was in a position to do so . They're living in a judgemental small town in the South, for God's sake. You'd think she'd know better. Also, the rival love interest was such a flat, cardboard villain. At least give her some complexity. Come on. Just because she's an antagonist doesn't mean she has to be a horrible human being with absolutely no depth or redeeming qualities. When things weren't being ridiculous between the main couple, they were pretty cute together. I also liked the development of the relationship between Jo and her stepmother, even if I didn't think the stepmother should've gotten away with as much of her low-level homophobia as she did. But all that cuteness was often punctuated by these issues so ultimately I couldn't like the book as much as I wanted to.

Lily Doyle was an army brat who followed her father from one battlefield to the next all her life. When her father died he made his commanding officer, Neville Wyatt, promise to keep her safe. With the French army about to overtake them, Neville hastily married Lily so that, as an officer's wife, she would be treated well. But in the battle, Lily was killed and Neville was terribly wounded. Eventually he returned to England to take up his title as Earl of Killbourne, and even resolved to marry again, this time to his childhood friend. But just as they are about to wed--Lily bursts into the church. Because, it turns out, Lily was taken prisoner instead of killed, and has endured a year of captivity and months of hardship to be at Neville's side once more. Neville is an honorable man, and truly cares for Lily. He immediately sets her up as his Countess, and defends her from his shocked family. But Lily has had no experience in high society, and she continually embarasses and shocks his family and villagers with her ignorance and rough manners. She feels trapped and bored, talking to people about subjects she has no interest or experience with, bound by rules she doesn't know. And so when Neville finds out that their marriage was never legally finalized, Lily refuses to legally marry him, thus freeing each of them from their unequal match. Instead, she becomes his cousin Elizabeth's paid companion; Elizabeth, a strong-minded woman with a love plot of her own, hires tutors so she may learn English and music. Lily revels in leaving behind her illiteracy and ignorance. In a passage I particularly enjoyed, Neville gets angry that Elizabeth is changing his free-spirited love by making her like all the rest of Society, but Elizabeth points out to him that Lily's fundamental character isn't changing, but rather her horizons are expanding as she learns more. Learning gives her more options, more choices, than she had before. A murder plot is foiled, Neville and Lily confess their love, and finally they marry again, this time publicly acknowledged as equals. I loved that this wasn't an easy Cinderella tale, nor (despite her introduction) was Lily a Manic Pixie Dream Girl. This felt like a particularly rich, dense book, with lots of relationships, side characters, and plots. The lovers weren't seperated by a misunderstanding, let alone a silly one that could have been easily cleared up. There were serious issues* that Lily and Neville had to work out, and schemes by other characters that had to be dealt with. *Trigger warningLily was raped while a prisoner, and she, Neville, and Elizabeth all talk and think about it a great deal over the course of the novel. I don't think there's any victim-blaming (although Lily does struggle with survivor guilt) or detailed flash backs.
