What in the hell. My brain hurts. I should have loved this book. It had all the ingredients necessary to take me to reading bliss. Alas, it wasn't meant to be. This book took gfy to a whole different level. That level is called irritating. So, every man in this book is straight, and feels the need to talk about how straight they are, until they aren't anymore because they fall face first onto a dick. Standard gfy formula, right? Wrong. Because the characters are apparently still completely heterosexual even after being dickmatized. In one case, the guy talks about how straight he is although he has a long term boyfriend. 3 out of 4 couples, including the MC's, have some version of this storyline. Nothing about bisexuality, or sexual fluidity. Not a thing. Nope, just straight men fucking other straight men when they aren't talking about how straight they are. I was so confused. Behold, the plot of Frat House Troopers as summarized by a completely fictitious conversation between the MC's: Brandt: Broseph, my anus goes into hiding at the sight of two guys getting it on. It's such a hardship, watching porn vids for this completely plausible undercover job. Donnelly: Ew, you said anus...those are gross Bro. Gross. Brandt: Is it weird that when my heterosexuality feels threatened I sometimes need to reconfirm it with the occasional homophobic comment? Donnelly: Completely normal, I do the same. But I'm a little more tolerant because my brother was gay. Still, I'm totally straight because the sight of two guys smexin makes me cover my eyes like a child during a horror movie. Brandt: Yea, me too. Totally straight. Loooooove me some mammaries. But, lately the sight of naked men gives me a semi. I'm still like 99% sure I'm straight since I'm so manly. Um, excuse me while I punch you in the shoulder to assert my Machismo. Bro. Donnelly: ...Wanna jerk off together? It came off like the characters were feeding into the idea that manly men aren't gay, or gay men aren't manly. So all the really macho men who fall in love with their one special guy are still completely straight. Because, manly. Ugh. When the MC's got together my mind kept wandering off. It was just so out of the blue. I was SO bored. I didn't have much of a clue they were even attracted to each other. Brandt spends most of the book worrying over his attraction to other men. Apparently, I skimmed the blurb because I totally thought Brandt would end up with Nick . Then, Brandt and Donnelly both get personality transplants. I almost gave up, but I made it to the end. I persevered. And you know what? I regret that decision. At times this book was funny and I laughed obnoxiously. At times it was pretty damn hot. At times it was a little offensive. At times it was so unrealistic and confusing that it made me ask myself "what the fuck am I reading?!" In conclusion: Brandt's adventures in porn = fun. The actual romance = bored to tears. 2 Stars

3.5 stars I'm not entirely sure how to rate Fun Home by Alison Bechdel because I have nothing to compare it to. This was my very first exposure to a graphic novel. A well constructed story very well written and demonstrating an adept insight into human psychology with respect to intelligence as IQ against the basic (and complex) emotional needs to love and to be loved. Keyes comes to the conclusion that (Charlie's driving determination) to have high intelligence and not love is pointless. What Keyes is moving towards here is the recognition of what we now know to be a truism in psychology: EQ, emotional intelligence, is just as valid a form of measurement of intelligence as IQ is - although the modern capitalist male-oriented logical-rational-practical economic structure may not be fit to accommodate this validity. Yet in all forms of people-problem-oriented social spheres, having the medical degree may not be as practical in helping people with emotional problems that are just as debilitating as long-term disease or disability as providing physiological diagnoses. EQ is now recognised in the common realm as a measurably practical ability, but you don't need it to be an IT manager, for example. (Actually, you do - it's just that they don't know this, and might even deny it). But Algernon and Charlie face worse irritations. Algernon articulates his by bashing himself against the walls of his cage; Charlie demonstrates his by excluding everyone he loves (Alice) or likes (Burt, Dr. Strauss) from giving him any comfort or help during the final phase of his demise. What psychologists might refer to as 'paradoxical denial', perhaps. He becomes a hikikomori - a recluse, unable to leave the house, as he slides into his unloved isolation and depression. (Sounds like being unemployed, to me). In the end, though, no matter how well written or constructed this story is, as science fiction it's very limited. As psychological drama, it's reasonably limited, but as personal drama, its intense. (The word 'I' appears 13 times in one short paragraph). Branded as an early landmark of sf, this is not in the class of some of our recent mind-expanding space opera, and thus, while I thought it an excellent personal drama, I was frustrated by its narrow confines within the given genre. Like the much-vaunted Stranger in a Strange Land (Heinlein, 1961), it is a very human tale of needs and displacement, of being essentially alien in 'human' society, but its scope is very limited, and in the end, not gripping. Give me good old space opera any day.

This book opens with a large and perfect suburban house burning to the ground. In a peaceful planned community outside of Cleveland in the late nineties, the Richardsons are a popular, well-respected, and prosperous family. Well, except for the youngest daughter, the black sheep whose rebellious actions make her mother perennially annoyed. The Richardsons also have a rental duplex, and Mrs. Richardson always tries to find deserving people to live in it - poor people who deserve a leg up. When she rents to a single mother and daughter named Mia and Pearl, she feels proud of herself, and even asks Mia to do housekeeping and cooking for her. Mia is an artist and her daughter Pearl is a sophomore in high school, and they soon become involved in the lives of the Richardsons, since the kids are all similar ages. Mrs. Richardson strongly believes in living with careful planning, in following the rules and a path that leads to a nice house with smart attractive children in a good neighborhood. Mia, her housekeeper/tenant, lives a totally different life - choosing poverty and moving often so she can devote herself to art photography. This conflict in beliefs leads to a plot that left me feeling like I had to keep reading. Transracial adoption, abortion, and what it means to be a good mother are all explored with sensitivity and perfect descriptions of why all the different characters feel as they do. I had such a negative reaction to one of the characters that I had to constantly remind myself it wasn't real. Carla Hayden, the Librarian of Congress, was interviewed by the New York Times for their By the Book column, and she answered one question by talking about a book that made her extremely mad at the main character, and how that is a sign of a good book, if it makes you forget it's fiction and hooks you in to feeling strong emotions. This is an excellent book for people who like to delve deep into the perspectives of characters, and for those who enjoy seeing the underbelly of perfect suburban life. I received a free electronic copy of this title from Edelweiss and the publisher.

After how much I hated Kitty in the previous book, I didn't think there would be any way to redeem her character. I was pleasantly surprised though. She was still annoying a lot of the time, but she was much more tolerable in this. The main problems I had with Kitty surrounded the romance with Benjy and the crappy way she treated Knox. For most of the book, Kitty was separated from the two guys and it seemed like she was more focused on the things that mattered, like the revolution. However, Kitty's improvement aside, as the final book in a trilogy, it wasn't as great as I was hoping. The plot kind of lacked the punch and excitement that I found in 'Captive'. My favorite part of the entire series has been Knox and I was really sad that he was basically non-existent in this. As for the romance, I don't even know where to start. The relationship between Kitty and Benjy was super weird in this book. It felt like the author was bringing up problems between them just so Kitty and Knox could get together. Their break-up came off as very forced. The actual conversation was well done, but it seemed like it was written for some different couple that I didn't know. I've always thought that Benjy was extremely bland and boring. However, if the author had ever given him some type of personality, I might have actually been hit hard by that scene. The first two books were all about how madly in love Kitty and Benjy were. I didn't buy that they were happy and willing to die for each other and randomly in the beginning of this book they had all these deep seated issues. I wish that there had been some hints of them growing apart in previous books because with the way it was executed, it came out of nowhere. I had a similar problem with Knox and Kitty's relationship. There was so much hate towards Knox on Kitty's behalf in the last book that it completely ruined any chances of me wanting them together as a couple. It was difficult to even attempt to repair their relationship when Knox was missing for the majority of the time. There was just no transition between Kitty hating Knox and then her saying she loved him. You can't just have the protagonist head over heels for one guy and then decide to have her fall for some other guy with practically zero development. As much as I love Knox, I didn't feel the chemistry between them like that. I thought he deserved someone better than Kitty . The ending left me feeling a bit disappointed. I get that Daxton couldn't be defeated within the first few pages because that would be extremely boring and anti-climactic, but it seemed pretty drawn out. It wouldn't have bothered me if there hadn't been a certain dumb assassination plan. I couldn't believe that Kitty had one clear shot to kill Daxton and instead of shooting him in the head, she shot him in the torso. The shock of her and the co-conspirators after Daxton survived was the most laughable thing ever. I'm sorry, but wouldn't you expect a guy who has had many attempts on his life to wear a bullet proof vest? It shouldn't be that surprising that he took precautions . Also, I didn't understand how Kitty was able to convince everyone she was Lila after the real Lila was killed . And speaking of resolution, it tends rather abruptly, without feeling like a story that has any containment in itself - and I realise it's part of a series, but it just seems to end a bit out of nowhere.

The adventures, mysteries and despair of the erudite and precocious 13-year-old Lemony Snicket continues! The adults are still condescending and foolishly arrogant (not to mention the sinister and evil ones), and Hangfire's evil plot continues. What does he want with the children? How will Lemony Snicket ever save his sister? How does this series end? These are the wrong questions. The real questions are how great was that ending, how is Lemony Snicket (cough cough Daniel Handler cough) so funny, and what books will he mention or suggest next book? Snappy dialogue, equal parts obvious and subverted mysteries, and villains and heroes similar to the Series of Unfortunate Events. Basically every child and most adults should read this series. Except now I have to wait for the next one to come out...

4.5 stars -Another heartpounding entry. A great spy action/adventure series, The Crystal Whisperer starts off with a tease (we'll get to that later) and then dives straight into some crazy action that never lets up even as we get to that ending. Oh that ending *stares off in the distance* This is a series that is best to experience firsthand, so I will keep this as free of spoilers as absolutely necessary. OK, let's start this. -So funny and smart. March (my favoritest OCD former/kind of current assassin) and Island, (awkward woman/my spirit twin), have some precious down time from their last mission and come oh so close to finally doing the deed. Instead, the past comes rushing back when a plane literally disintegrates, killing all aboard. The world believes it's Dries, Island's long lost father, and trying to unravel the mystery of the Crystal Whisperer takes them all over the globe in a race to stop another disaster. And along, the way, we get some more romance. -Not quite a standalone. While there's plenty of recapping of the adventures of the two earlier books (Spotless and Beating Ruby), I think the story won't have the same impact if you haven't read those. Since they're great, I have no hesitation in recommending them. -The epitome of dangling the carrot. Ok, *deep sigh* I know Ms. Monk delights in the frustrated tears of her readers, so this is not just a lovely postscript where they bang like bunnies in a secluded area while discussing their feelings. *grumbles* I mean, I would love that, but I think it's all part and parcel of the torture...I mean, joy of March and Island's romance that keeps me coming back for more. March and Island's road to romance (ok, road to banging like bunnies anyway) has been fraught with tension and has driven me crazy in the best possible way. -That ending. Speaking of cliffhangers, this ending had my heart in my throat and I kept trying to flip to the next page, even after I realized that THIS is where Ms. Monk left us. It's freaking torture. I loathe cliffhangers with the heat of a thousand suns (so I had to shave a little off the rating because of it) and yet, this series is definitely the exception to my rule. I'm truly hoping it all comes to a satisfying conclusion, but in all honesty the journey has been phenomenal. 4.5 stars I truly enjoyed this so much, and it's a testament to Ms. Monk's writing that I adore it so much because I LOATHE cliffhangers. A smart, funny, emotional and tumultuous adventure that kept my heart in its grip throughout, even as the ending decided to do a tapdance on it. So, *distractedly* yes, I definitely recommend this, though I suggest starting from the beginning so you can get the full March and Island effect. I need it to be May right now. **ARC provided by author for review** For more reviews, visit

i'm not going to rate this book. I am, however, going to talk about it. If you're looking for a teacher-student  romance , I personally don't think this fits the bill. I wouldn't call the disturbing relationship that this 38 year old married man with children started with his 14 year old clueless English student romantic. In fact, romantic would be the last word I would use to describe this book. When I got to the second page and the story went right into their first sexual encounter I thought, "Well, that's one way to start an affair." It simply came out of left field. You see, I was still thinking that I was going to read a romance story. I had absolutely no idea that this was a story about abuse (both physical and emotional) and the consequences that this 38 year old man left for this poor girl to deal with when he left her. At one point as I was reading one of the million sexscapades this girl has (if you don't think highly of your neighborhood slut, good luck reading this one). I haven't felt so conflicted in my feelings about a heroine in a very long time. Sarah was a classless (I had no issues with this) selfish (huge issue with this) whore (no issue with this). The selfish bit was what had me shaking me head and thinking, "Why am I still reading?...oh, that's right, my morbid curiosity strikes again." She sleeps with anything that can get their dick up, and that's fine. I think by the end of it I understood why she did this, but at that point I didn't care. When I got to 70% I thought, "Okay, the plot thickens, maybe something will happen now?..." I'm about to go into full blown spoiler mode now, so if you do not like spoilers do not read. What bothered me the most is that her old teacher comes back 8 years later. Eight years later he comes into her life waving divorce papers, showing her photos of how happy his family used to be so that she can see what "he left for her". Give me a mother fucking break, you sick twisted bastard with wrinkly balls. He does this AFTER he physically abuses her the second day of seeing her, giving her such deep bite marks that her thighs are left bleeding, and throws her on the side of the road. Completely discards her like yesterday's trash. He constantly, CONSTANTLY belittles her. Constantly tells her how ugly she is, how worthless she is. I had a huge issue with this. HUGE FUCKING ISSUE with this. To me, that's worse than the physical abuse. I don't do well with emotional abuse but I thought it was there for a reason so I kept reading. Needless to say, I was, at that point, reading a fucking trainwreck. I was just waiting for somebody to get ran over and left for dead. Well, when it happens, it happens to the person I least thought should be dead. As it usually does. And Sarah made a comment that made me think the same. She had been fucking her best friend Jamie for a while, had fallen in love with him but was too afraid to admit that to him. She was afraid that he would leave his wife and baby to be with her because she was so emotionally closed off that she couldn't fathom having someone truly 100% putting her first (even though she knew Jamie always put her first). Well, very very late into the book, a couple of pages before it ends, Jamie commits suicide after Sarah goes to see him. She had been living with her old teacher for a year then and looked like a skeleton, with bones comes out everywhere. The teacher admits that he did take advantage of her by seducing her when she was 14. That he knew she would let him because he had met her mother at a school open house and her mother was cold and heartless and he knew that any slight touch would make Sarah crumble at his feet. He was obsessed with her, but not because he was in love with her. He was obsessed with controlling her. So her best friend Jamie kills himself and Sarah goes back home to her ex-teacher/live in boyfriend who makes her quit her job so that he can have full access to her and beat her and rapes her after he drugs her (though it's not rape bc she willingly gives herself to him anyway, even after she comes off of her high and sees she's full of gashes and bloodied). And when she goes back to him, she finds him in a state that makes her think he's dead. He's not, but she thinks he is (this is just after she attended Jamie's funeral) and that's when she "realizes that she could live without him, despite previously thinking she couldn't." So in the end she has hope for herself. She's practically dying, only holding on by a string because she's that underfed and beat up. Yet, 100% into the book she finally has hope. After the man who was in love with her his entire life committed suicide because of her. I don't even know how to feel about that, to be honest. . It's not a story for the weak hearted, that's for sure. I can't say I didn't like it because after having hours to process it, I guess in a sense I'm glad it wasn't your typical story. I wouldn't consider this a romance, though. I would say this is a story about a 14 year old girl who is abused by her English teacher that grows up slutting around because he left her and she doesn't know how to sort out the feelings she's left with. She doesn't know how to deal with the only person (ever) in her life that has told her he loved her, leaving her so she decides to shut out love from her life. She decides to turn a blind eye to the person who does love her, who would do anything for her, who would die for her, because she's too worried about having just a physical connection with someone. It's a story about a girl who reunites with the bastard who shaped her to be this heartless cow and starts an abusive relationship with him again. So that's it: physical and emotionally abused girl falls into the same trap twice because she wants to be manipulated and tossed around. Because she is so self-destructive and thinks so little of herself that it makes this all right.
Opposition read like fanfiction. So yay? Nay? Hard to say. (But I still quite enjoyed it nonetheless.)

READ IN ENGLISH I was really looking forward to Allegiant, as I liked the first two novel (Divergent & Insurgent). It was completely NOT what I expected. *SPOILERS AHEAD!!! The first few chapters I had some trouble reading, as it felt nagging and actually boring. After they escape the city, this is fortunately no longer a problem, but questions are raised. I had the most problems with a) They had people genetically engineered to be selfless, brave, smart, honest, (good? ), but after that backfired, they could no longer use this technology to return a certain set of genes? b) I still don't see how a faction based society could be of any help, or how this would increase the rate of Divergent people... c) As soon as Tris/Four and the rest of them are in the compound, they never discuss sending a message to the city about what is actually happening to them. It is as if they've already settled with the idea that they are just guinea pigs in an experiment. Nevertheless, I just couldn't stop reading (after the first few chapters) even though it was Christmas. Ans last, but not least, the ending! I was already raging about the easy way of solving things, Caleb didn't even have to die, cause Tris *magically* is resistant to all serum, but especially when she wants to be. I even raged about the HP-like Limbo I thought Veronica Roth had put into the story. But it then turned out that she was just dead. :shock: I didn't see that coming! After reading this I might even get afraid again the main character won't make it to the end and live happily ever after...

This is a terrific read. Imagine if there had been a couple of real-life magicians in the 1800s. Susanna Clarke lets her imagination run wild and gives us some terrific set pieces, starting with stone statues coming alive. Another thing I love about this novel is the mass of side-stories in the footnotes. Nabokov used this to great effect in Pale Fire, although what he was doing was quite different. (Shameless plug: I also used a lot of footnotes in Apocalypse Later.) I think I'm right in saying this was Clarke's first novel, it took her eight years (it's a massive novel), and that she was a literary agent. It was a deserving winner of a Hugo. Tremendous creation of an alternative history.

This book was, too put it simply, amazing. I absolutely loved it. I think I like it too much to write an actual review, so I'm just going to write down some bullet points on what I loved. - Hatta is one of my new favorite characters ever!!! I loved him to bits. The ending killed me. When he went crazy and admitted he was in love with Jest I just... - The world building in Heartless was phenomenal. I read Alice in Wonderland in preparation of this, and I think that Marissa Meyer did a great job in portraying Wonderland in the same way that Lewis Carroll did. Everything was so weird and illogical, and yet it seemed so normal. There are talking animals and food that can make you shrink, but it seems commonplace and completely normal. - The ending was definitely the best part of the book. That's not to say that the rest of the book wasn't enjoyable, but for the first half of the book, it's more like a 4-star book than a 5-star book. Still really good, but it's not as compelling as the ending. - I really loved Chess. He was so much fun to read about, and I wish he had more lines, because I adored every scene with him. - Cath's decent into madness/evil was really well done! When you first meet Cath she's super sweet! Well, she's not always the nicest, but she mostly is. She went crazy pretty quickly, but as I was reading the book, there were little hints that she already had a semi-violent nature. (For example, she imagines a party guest choking to death.) - I liked Jest, but I didn't love him. I think I was so focused on the world building while reading this (I love Wonderland!) that I didn't focus as much on him, so maybe I'll find him more swoon-worthy then. He was really nice though, so that was great. I'm not a huge fan of "bad boys". Basically, I loved this book and thought it was near-perfect. I definitely recommend it!

How to describe this excellent book? It encompasses romance, mystery, melodrama and horror. But at the heart I think it's a ghost story, albeit one without a literal ghost. The book is aptly named, as even though she is dead when she begins, Rebecca drives all the action forward. "Last night I dreamt I went to Manderlay" again is the famous first line, and the first few chapters do feel like a dream. It's when the narrator and her new husband Maxim actually reach the house that the book takes on a solidity, and you can feel the cold breeze blow through the pages. By her own admission our protagonist is diffident, shy and carries a hopeless sense of inferiority, that can make her at times a frustratingly nervous and over-wrought narrator. Certainly for the early stages of the book I thought that all her problems could be resolved if she just worked up the courage to speak to her husband, and then that conversation happens and the bigger mystery emerges. Just one final comment on Mrs Danvers, who is truly one of the great literary villians. One question though: which poor sod was Mr Danvers?

Okay, confession time. I've actually never read any Philip K. Dick before this... I know. Bad nerd. They've always been on my list, but the book club seems to the be only thing that gets me to bump the classics up to the top. Another confession, I've never watched Blade Runner start to finish (I always walked in when my dad was in the middle, so I feel like I've seen it a dozen times, but never in the correct order). I'm glad about this, because it let me appreciate the book without trying to predict the movie. So onto the book: Naturally, I enjoyed it. I've never heard anything but good things about it, and it was everything I expected while still managing to surprise. The whole idea of empathy as the idea that makes us human while the story tugs at our own empathy throughout the story is incredibly well-constructed. I love the idea that animals are the way we demonstrate humanity, and that the most disturbing scene in the entire book operated on my empathy for a spider. Brilliant. The android vs. human theme has obviously drawn a great deal from this book since the time of its publishing, and that alone makes it worth a read. The way our empathy shifts between them, Decker's preference of knowing the artificiality of his toad at the end of the day, but that not stopping his wife from declaring his attachment to it , it resonates through the science fiction of the seventies and onward. While the book wasn't an emotional revelation for me, I still feel I am a better person for having read it, and I hope many other people who have put off reading the classics as newer and shinier books arrive (I still need Ancillary Sword and I need it badly!) will take the time to explore where these new and shinier books came from. Also, it's only 123 pages. I wish more modern authors could capture that amount of depth in that few words. Just brilliant. It's becoming a lost art.

**3 Stars** Ok, so I liked the concept of the book.... Grey is a witch along with her mother and identical twin sister Charlene. Grey dies in her sleep and wakes up 2 months later in her sister's body. Her mom had someone do a resurrection spell that went wrong, and now Grey and Charlene share the same body. They each have control for 24 hours every other day. There were a few things I didn't like about the book. Nolan: Nolan was introduced as the sweet innocent good guy you want Grey to end up with. Then all of a sudden, after spying Grey and Raj kissing, he does a complete about face and is ready to help Charlene kill her (purge her soul from her body). This is absolutely crazy especially as Nolan knows Raj's reputation. Charlene: Where do I start? I think the biggest thing was that Charlene killed Grey and had absolutely no remorse for doing so. Then 2 days after killing Grey, she tries to kill another girl who slept with her boyfriend and succeeds in putting her in a coma. Once she finds out that Grey can't go back to her own body, Charlene wants to kill her again... because she messed up the relationship with Charlene and her boyfriend. I mean... come on... The first kill was accidental, but no remorse... really? You just killed your twin sister!!! Who never did anything to you. Oh, and you had been blocking her powers for years because you were jealous she was more talented. I did like Raj, I just wish we had seen more about him. You do find out he isn't who he is thought to be, but I would have liked to know a little more about who he is.

A great read; fast paced and with Chance's trademark style whereby you read 20 pages and 'Think what the hell just happened there? ', but all in all very satisfying. I normally prefer the Cassie Palmer books to those featuring Dory, which to date have been high on action and lower on humour, but this one gets the balance just right. There is a hilarious shopping scene in the first half of the book with Dory and a minor character; and Dory/Dorina seem to be able to pull out humour from a range of lucky escapes. As the novel progresses there is a lot more break-neck paced action leaving me convinced I need to re-read the book several times to feel I've got all the twists and turns of the plotline. Mircea is revealead as much more vulnerable than in any book so far and if you are a Marlowe fan then you will be delighted. My favourite character in this one has to be Ray-a surprise as he seemed little more than a 'tool'in the previous book - and not just in the narrative function. the first meeting of Dory and Cassie was a nice touch, and left me wanting more. In fact I found it hard to fault this one: the novel managed to reveal more of the Dory/Louis Cesar/Mircea narrative whilst at the same time develop the vampire/fey politics and interweave Chance's bizzare Cassie Palmer 'gods' narrative and clarify some of the issues. If you're a fan of the Dory or Cassie books then you'll love it. If you've never read Dory 1 + 2-don't start with this one - you will have no idea what is going on. You can get away without reading the Cassie books but some of this won't make sense and the subtleties will be lost.

Vicky is a young aristocrat that has earned her family's wrath for posing nude for her illicit art class, something that well-brought-up girls would never consider doing. She is given two choices, marry a man of her parent's choosing or go live in the country with her great aunt. But Vicky has bigger plans, like going to college, unfortunately without her parents' support she won't be able to afford it. Though this book includes many tropes that have been seen time and again (romance from wrong side of the tracks, love triangle, parents trying to keep their daughter down), but it is such a fresh and fun book that I did not even mind. I also like that the author didn't make things easy for Vicky at all which made the book seem more realistic. Though there is a bit of reconciling at the end with her parents, they don't "see the light" and pay for her art school. I would recommend this book to fans of Downton Abbey, people who like feminist fiction, and those interested in the suffrage movement. It is a really great read.

John Taylor is hired to find the unholy grail. The cup used by Judas at the last supper. His employer is the vatican but there are other people searching for the grail, and other denziens of the nightside including angels from both above and below. John recruits Shotgun Suzie to help him. In this one you find out more about John and he learns more about the world that is the nightside and his place in it.

** spoiler alert ** This book was awesome. Every aspect of it kept the pages turning and kept me completely fascinated by the story the author created. It was great. In Ink Exchange I was a bit preoccupied with Ash and Seth's story, but here I nearly forgot about them. Ani and Devlin took center stage and belonged there. Plot: Brilliant. I loved how it started out with Ani and Devlin's stories being separate and how they slowly came together. I also liked how every minor character had a running story, and it all crashed together in the climax. Characters: Great. Melissa Marr clearly has a talent with creating characters that the reader cares about. Ani was great, and she was a strong character. After seeing too many weak female characters in YA lately, Ani was excellent. And her faery ability to feed off of emotions and physical contact was interesting. I also loved Devlin. He had a complicated past, and battling instincts inside him, but he was still a good guy whether he wanted to admit it or not. Ani and Devlin's relationship was also great. Of the other characters, I probably liked Rae and Irial best. I liked Irial better in Radiant Shadows than I did in Ink Exchange, and I thought Rae was an excellent part of this story. Ending: Also great. The Shadow Court was an interesting addition to the series, and I liked how it relates to the title of this book. I also now really, really want to see how that plays out in the mortal realm, because the Dark Court no longer has an opposite. Will they have to add another court? Will something happen to either to Shadow Court or the Dark Court? I don't know, but I'm certainly going to read any books Melissa Marr writes in hopes of finding out. Writing: As if I haven't complemented it enough. It was brilliant as well. Dark and mysterious would be two words I'd use to describe it, and both of those fit perfectly with the story. Overall: A Must-Read for anyone who's read the rest of the series. But, it can also stand alone. Everything is explained enough that although I read Wicked Lovely and Ink Exchange almost a year ago it all still made sense, and I'm sure it would make sense even if I hadn't. But, having general knowledge of the series and the recurring characters is helpful, so I'd suggest starting with Wicked Lovely and Ink Exchange before reading this one.
I don't know why, but I just couldn't get into this one.

A quick, easy read about a young girl who "inherits" a box with buttons that, if pushed, can cause serious destruction. As she grows, she discovers the gifts and sorrows of the box. I would definitely mark this as a young adult read, even though my library had it in adult fiction. The story does fall a bit flat though, in that it never goes into real detail about what the box actually does . And while the question you initially go into this story with is "What would you do if you had the ability to destroy...? ", that question is never really addressed in the actual story. It's more about the weight of having that ability handed to you, instead of what someone might do with it. Of course, perhaps that is why the box was given to her in the first place, rather than someone who would use it?
I loved this, but I wish it had been a reimagining of Carroll's book instead of a prequel for it, that way I could've enjoyed a happy ending rather than a tragic one.

To be honest, I am very disappointed in this one. Most of the story was boring, there was too little romantic action between Merit and Ethan en the end was just ridiculous. First, Neill spent four entire books on telling us how E & M feel about each other and is writing about all this sexual tension. Then, after all these problems, all the waiting they end up together, only to ignore their feelings after a day or so. At this point I was already quite annoyed since, although a little tension is always good, their problems were just a little too over the top. It isn't realistic. And then, boy, oh boy. Then they're about to make up and Ethan dies. DIES. Unbe-fucking-lievable. These series won't be the same without the arrogant House Master. - There will be less drama - There will be a lot of grieving and sadness - There will be no romance for Merit, and even if there is, no one can compete with Ethan. There's been too much stuff going on between them. I predict that, from now on, these series will suck -- no pun intended-- and won't get much praise anymore.

Gosh! Why did I wait so long to read this... This book rocks, it's so much better than the first book. It's action packed and less sadistic, but overall a much better story. The release of the fourth book of this series made me pick this up, it was a wise decision, it has been a long time since I read book like this.

Loved the humorous takes on workout culture. Wanted to know more about the main character and some of her relationships. I would have liked to spend more time with the characters and less time bouncing around between fitness crazes for the funny operations. But I would still recommend if you're interested.

I've had this book on my to-read list for literally years, even though I was unsure of whether it would actually be any good, before it became the first in a series of seven books. I love the different take on the mythical creature side of things. Having read a lot of YA fantasy books that focus around the currently popular vampires and werewolves, and the ever popular fairies and angels, it was very refreshing to have one focused around Banshees! Banshees are not a creature I have seen much of in books before let alone as the main character. There was also the appearance of Grim Reapers, which reminded me of the Shinigami in Black Butler. The story itself was interesting, I was eager to discover why Kaylee has these premonitions and why girls were being killed off one a day. The twist at the end when it is revealed that it was Kaylee's Aunt who sent the reaper after the girls was a real surprise. However it backfired when the reaper went after Sophie, which I also didn't see coming as Emma had already died and I had guessed that it would be one or the other of them, not both. Overall I enjoyed this book and learnt lots about Bean Sidhe. I am intrigued to see where Vincent takes this story in the rest of the series.

I'm putting this review as a spoiler, not because I'm actually giving away spoilers (it's a nonfiction how-to book), but because most of those who follow me on Goodreads are probably not interested in a book on this subject. This is an excellent book on potty training. It's the sort of approach that I swore I would never try. And then, potty training my first child took a year, with four several week intensive stints that ended in a constantly-screaming child who was afraid of going near the bathroom. I was not going to re-use any of the methods I used for my first child. And I was willing to take drastic measures to have potty training happen better and faster. A friend recommended this book, and even leant it to me. I admit, the first few days of using this book I cried. Not when I was around my child--Glowacki spends a lot of time talking about how your attitude about potty training impacts whether or not it is successful, and that you're child picks up on your underlying emotion. But it was challenging because I let my child run around the house without wearing anything, which meant I had to clean up accidents. And no one likes to clean up accidents. Here's the thing though. I had a highly intensive two or three days. But in the weeks since then, my daughter has used the toilet almost perfectly. She asks to use it, she uses it by herself. And it's awesome. And she's almost night-trained. Was it worth a few hard days just to be done with potty training? YES. Would I have been able to do this with my first child? I wish that I had been. My life would've been much happier. The author recommends potty training your child between 18 and 33 months or something. But my child was 35 months and it worked fine. The initial chapters are about really adjusting your attitudes towards potty training as a parent. But it works. Well-worth the read. And I would definitely recommend this method to others.

So, first of all, I am in love with John Green. The way he writes, the characters, even the ones I don't like, style, everything. Genius. And it takes one to spot one :D After I finished TFiOS I wasn't sure if I liked the book or I didn't. In the end I decided I did. Same with LfA. Nice characters, amazingly written, good plot and so on. But then again, there is something, something that was missing. Probably the way they discovered the truth and stuff. It wasn't as magnificent or as surprising as I would've liked it to be. It was good, of course it was good, but still. Something was missing. There is one thing, one simple rule about writing and it is- you need to have either great writing skills and imagination or great experience. Or in other words, you must have felt it in order to write it. And that's the thing about suicides, about young people wishing to die, it's not that easy to catch that and it certainly it's not that easy to make it believable. I suppose that was my problem with the book. I am still not sure if I like Alaska, or I don't. I like smart characters, ones who read, ones who search for meaning and find amazing quotes in their books that just stay forever in their minds. And I am glad she was flawed, no one likes perfect characters. But then again, she was moody, okay. Probably bi-polar. She has been through a lot. Okay. But give her some more credit, even the craziest person, the drunkest, wouldn't do that. You don't just decide to kill yourself. Even if your disorder is at max and you are at your worst. I've been there. I know. This is my only problem with this kind of fiction. How believable it is, how does the writer show that his characters really really feel. But I am not going to twist my soul and say I didn't like it, because I really did. So 4 stars it is. Well done, John Green. Even if I am not sure I like your stories, I still love them.

I remember getting introduced to the works of Lackey...in college, a friend with a larger shelf of sff than I had suggested I might like her series, Arrows of the Queen. And I did. And then the Diana Tregarde series and the Herald Vanyel series were great. But then came the Bardic Voices series, and I started noticing the weakness of her writing (bringing in a second POV character in the last fourth of a book? really?) and she's been sliding down since then. I stopped buying the Valdemar books with the Gryphon series. But I still keep hoping that I'll get back to the feeling I had with the first books, that people can make themselves and the world a better place by banding together. So Changes is part of the history of Valdemar. The third book where the quiet (but powerful) orphan Mags is training as a spy and dealing with his friends' family problems. This might be a good book for someone with a low emotional quotient, as Mags' empathy allows him to explain, in great detail, how/why a person is feeling/acting in a way, and to discuss or think about ways to change the basic situation. Things that other authors suggest, Lackey instead tells. She does have a fair amount of repetition, and plot points that seem bluntly foreshadowed. The ending leaves loose ends, so I know there is another book in the series. My prediction is that  after Amily's leg is fixed, she ends up the next King's Own Herald. Or else Mags does, and Amily gets Dallen. And there are at least two marriages. Weaknesses that others haven't mentioned (I agree about the tiresomeness of the dialect) include the we-just-happen-to-have-that-gift in this book. And the role of the Heartstone in explaining what's happening. And the looseness of the class schedules. And how little sleep Nikolas seems to get. And convenient Companion abilities. Strengths--there isn't a single pairbond happening. It's a quick read.

I'm going to be totally honest with everyone reading this right now. I had seen the previews for the movie adaption of this book and as a big fan of Daniel Radcliffe I thought, "Hey! It's based on a book! I should read the book before I see it or else that'll bug me through the whole movie!" So I went into this book only knowing that a guy has horns and people seem to do terrible things around them. It is pretty much that. For the first part of the book. Suddenly there are childhood flashbacks and you get to learn more about Ig, his family and his one and only love, Merren Williams. After all of that it then becomes a revenge tale. I really liked it. It started aout really good, kind of slowed down in the middle but then picked up momentum. I really wish the book would have gone more into detail about a few things, like was Ig always going to get the horns? Were they only meant to seek revenge or were they always meant to be there? And what about that friggin' tree house? Good book. I still recommend to those looking for an unconventional revenge story.

Mostly it's like many reviewers are saying: If you are expecting a secret or a stunning mystery, you will not find one, because reading this with your eyes open and your inner Sherlock awake, you solve the essence of the riddle more or less at the end of part 1 (of 5). It would probably be different, if the "Liars" would have been marketed as a beachy coming-of-age-tale spanning several luxurious summers in High Society than as a mystery with a twist that makes you reel (paraphrased. I've forgotten the wording already. One last thought: I guess the alcohol was to blame. Without its consumption the 'rebellion' might have ended differently. Or not?
So many plot twists in this one. Definitely more interesting than the first even though the characters are still meh.

Hannah and Garrett have Ethics together. Hannah has aced the class, while Garrett? Not so much. So he plans to hound Hannah until she agrees to tutor him. Hannah wants nothing to do with the captain of the hockey team, aka a dumb jock. But Hannah wants Justin, a football player to notice her, so she finally makes a deal with Garrett - help her win Justin, and she'll tutor him through Ethics. But then so much more happens, and along the way, so does romance. The Good, The Bad and Everything In Between (and honestly, it's all good) -Excellent writing: I've been a fan of Elle Kennedy's Out of Uniform series, and when I heard about this book, there was no doubt I was going to 1-click it. It's got three of my favorite things - hockey, music and the "boy helps girl get other boy until he realizes he wants her for himself" trope. Nothing's as satisfying as seeing the player fall in love and this completely lived up to my expectations. I would have devoured this book in one sitting except for that pesky need to sleep and actually go to work, which believe me, ticked me off when all I wanted to do was keep reading. I couldn't seem to stop myself from highlighting the witty banter (as you can tell from my fave quotes), and there is so much more to be found. Ms. Kennedy's writing style flows so well, and she can create characters that you absolutely adore, but aren't cookie-cutter perfection. Such as... -Incredibly likeable leads: Hannah and Garrett are fantastic, fully realized characters who have lives outside of this romance. You see them live those lives with friends, and their school lives are explored in detail without weighing down the narrative. Hannah stands up for herself, but not shrewish or unsympathetic. Garrett can be crude and completely full of himself, but he's also loving, loyal and determined. The 'verse builds slowly and in a believable way and allows you to get to know them, and see them run the gamut of emotions. They aren't friends at first, but they come together out of necessity, but you truly get to the chance to see them become friends then lovers. -There's some angst, but not by the bucketful: As fully realized characters, neither have had the ideal pasts. Garrett's was heartbreaking and Hannah's in particular, is a difficult but an all too common tale. It's not fair, and it isn't wrapped up in a bow, but like life, they move on and they live theirs. Even when things go wrong, and it's a romance, so it's bound to happen, they eventually talk it out and act like the young adults they are. They're determined to live, not wallow and I adored that about them. "Well, that's the best revenge right there, Garrett. Living well and being happy is how we get over the shit in our past." MILD SPOILER ALERT -They're friends at first, so there are other people involved: Fair warning, Garrett does have a random or two but it never detracts from the overall romance. Hannah has a huge crush on Justin and it doesn't just miraculously disappear but once Hannah and Garrett really connect in a romantic way, there is no one else. -I even loved the secondary characters: All of Garrett's teammates intrigued me. From Tucker and his cooking, Logan and his need to acronym the hell out of everything, Dean and his man-hoish ways, I want to get to know these guys better, and I really hope that they get a chance to hook up with Hannah's friends or meet new girls and let me see their stories play out as well. The Bottom Line I loved it. It's an enjoyable story that I can see myself reading again and again, so I highly recommend it. There's a full 'verse just waiting to be explored at Briar and I'm really eager to visit it again.

And they all lived happily ever after ... ish. The concluding volume of the Phedre trilogy irons out some problems that were egregious in the second, and in general is a much more solid read. There are still vast stretches of travel descriptions that can be skimmed without missing any of the plot, and Carey's writing, though good, is not beautiful enough to make the passages enjoyable simply as prose. (The long pointless stretches seemed to get longer and more pointless as the book reached the ending; maybe I was just impatient to GET TO THE POINT ALREADY.) Speaking of points, it was nice that there was finally a greater purpose to Phedre's Super Special Masochism Powers, and the way the two plots interlocked was generally well done, despite killing off the Final Boss halfway through the book. Some cool new characters were introduced, and the familiar characters from the first two book behaved consistently with what we'd seen before, while also actually displaying growth and maturity. All in all, a solid conclusion to a solid fantasy series.

It is not very often that I find myself in the position I'm currently in: rabidly, insanely delighted to levels that would terrify any sane person. I want nothing more than to shriek and squeal and jump around in delight. I want to pull a Lottie La Bouff from Disney's The Princess and the Frog when she is at her most pleased. Those who have known me since college have likely seen me do something similar (though significantly restrained for the sake of propriety in public) often enough when I was younger, but I've had very little reason to do so in the last few years. Until now. Books rarely turn me into a squealing fangirl. Well, they used to, with some frequency at that, but it appeared I had sobered up significantly since I turned a quarter of a century. This might partly be maturity, though I mostly attribute it to the fact that I am taking up my masters', and am trying to set up a book review website, as well. Since my undergraduate years the need for distance and objectivity have been drilled into me, and it is something I try to maintain even in the book reviews I write, even though they are personal expressions of opinion and so need not be entirely academic. Scott Lynch's The Lies of Locke Lamora, the first book in a series titled The Gentlemen Bastards, shattered all of that. Most books that I enjoy press a small set of buttons but miss others: I like the characters, but feel so-so about the setting. I like the world, but the plotline is a bit wobbly for my tastes. I like the plot, but the characters do not necessarily fit a particular trope that I enjoy. This does not mean, of course, that do not like the book in question; it simply doesn't make me want to jump around like I've eaten too much sugar, or write a review with a lot of italics for emphasis. The Lies of Locke Lamora however, has done something only a very small handful of books have done in the past few years: it pressed all my buttons, at the same time. First: the setting. I adore the Renaissance, as I have mentioned several times before in previous reviews, and enjoy it thoroughly in historical novels. However, when the Renaissance is used as an analogue for a fantasy world, as opposed to the usual Medieval period, then my enthusiasm goes right through the roof. Fantasy novels set in Renaissance-analogues are so rare that it almost hurts; the last one I read was Tigana by Guy Gavriel Kay, and that, while I enjoyed it enough, I did not particularly care for. As a matter of fact, I thought The Lions of Al-Rassan was a better read, and that one is set in an analogue of Medieval Spain during the Reconquista. Camorr, the main setting of the novel, is an analogue of 16th-century Venice. While I have a deep, abiding bias towards Florence, I will admit that Renaissance Venice is an equally appealing prospect as a setting. Although the surface similarities between Venice and Camorr are obvious, it is the feel of Camorrian culture that really brings the similarity to life. The Renaissance, as a period in history, had its own particular vibrancy, an energy of creativity and mischief that does not seem prevalent in the Medieval period, and so seems absent in fantasies that are set in worlds that are Medieval-analogues. Camorr, however, cannot be considered a carbon-copy of Venice itself. The culture of Camorr, while similar in some respects, is entirely its own. The way corruption is treated in Camorr, for instance, is interesting, and very Camorrian, but not necessarily Venetian. The culture of thieves and whores and gangs, the "Right People of Camorr," as they're called in the novel, is again very Camorrian and not Venetian. While something like the Shifting Revel of Camorr could conceivably have existed in historical Venice, the type of entertainments in the Camorrian version would probably shock even the most debauched Venetian. Thus, in reading the novel, the reader will recognize much, but discover much, much more. Once, when I was younger, I liked my heroes to be appropriately heroic: noble, self-sacrificing, and just out-and-out good. Nowadays, however, I find myself inexorably drawn, and favoring, rogues: characters who are not necessarily noble or self-sacrificing, and whose morals might be more than a little skewed. Wit and cleverness are always appreciated - the sharper, the better. Ingenuity is vital, because that is what rogues are known for: the ability to use their brains and their wits more than their physical strength to get what they want. In Locke Lamora, not only is the titular character an excellent example of the above, but he is also surrounded by people who are just like that, to varying degrees. Take Father Chains, the Gentlemen Bastards' mentor. He educates his wards, including Locke, in the art of the con, and in the art of "false-facing:" pretending to be something one is not in order to better carry out a scheme. He is extremely intelligent, cautious, and a meticulous planner - nothing is ever for nothing when it comes to anything Chains does. He teaches the Gentlemen Bastards to become the best con-men, the best deceivers in Camorr. Locke is his star pupil, though even said star pupil is not without problems of his own - in the interlude chapter titled "Minor Prophecy," Chains predicts that Locke's cleverness will one day get him into such deep trouble that he will be unable to get himself out of it. Locke, only fourteen in that interlude, scoffs and says that will never happen. Unfortunately, at this point the reader is already aware that Chains's prophecy has become all too true. And now that I speak of Locke, I think it is only right that I talk about him, as well. Locke Lamora is everything I enjoy about rogues: witty, too clever for his own good, and (in the first book, at least) really rather shallow. Some readers have actually found fault in this, but I think that Locke is just right the way he is: a shallow, self-serving bastard, his only redeeming quality being his extreme loyalty to his fellow Gentlemen Bastards. This comes as no surprise: Locke really has not experienced true, genuine tragedy up until the events of Locke Lamora, and so can afford to be the shallow rogue that he is. Of course, later events will change things for him in a very big way. It helps to keep in mind that Lynch plans to write a seven-book sequence of novels, and that Locke Lamora is only Book One in that seven-book series. It is quite obvious that Lynch is taking his time with character development for Locke, who will, in all likelihood, grow more complex even as he commits mistakes and loses people along the way. By Book Seven, I expect he'll be quite an interesting, well-rounded character. While it helps that Locke is an enjoyable character on his own, the other supporting characters are equally great fun as well. Jean Tannen, Locke's best friend and the muscle to his brains, has a special place in my heart. When he first comes into Chains' care it is obvious that he doesn't quite have the same aptitude for crime as Locke, nor does he have the same easy confidence and good looks as the Sanza Brothers. He does, however, have a great deal of physical strength, the math skills of a merchant, and - maybe most importantly - a great deal of common sense. Jean's role is not only to act as muscle for the Gentlemen Bastards, but as the Voice of Reason: a role that is in itself both difficult and necessary, given the way Locke is at the start of the novel. And then there are the women. Though the central characters of Locke Lamora are men, there are quite a few females who play significant roles. Chief of them definitely has to be the mysterious Sabetha, one of Chains's original proteges even before Locke came into his care - and who, it is stated very clearly early on in the novel, is Locke's one true love. She is never seen in the novel, not even in the flashbacks, and is only ever mentioned in passing. This makes her even more intriguing, especially as the reader gets to know Locke and the rest of the Gentlemen Bastards better. Aside from Sabetha, there are other, more visible female characters, all of whom are just as intriguing and fascinating and strong as the male characters. Nazca Barsavi, for instance, is initially introduced as the spoiled daughter of Capa Barsavi, and famous for her iron-shod shoes. As a grown-up, however, she is not just a spoiled daughter, but a capable and intelligent young woman with a good head on her shoulders. It is made known that, although she has a pair of older brothers, her father wants her to be his heir. It is implied that she is more sensible than her brothers, and thus is the best choice to take Capa Barsavi's place as leader of the Right People of Camorr. There are also Dona Sofia Salvara and Dona Vorchenza - the former a minor noble notable for her skills in alchemy, and the latter being something much, much more, than just Camorr's resident gossip-monger to the rich and noble. Though they are a wife and a widow (or spinster, I'm not entirely sure), respectively, they both wield significant power in their own right: Dona Salvara's reputation as an alchemist is entirely separate from her status as a wife (in fact it is implied it was her husband who was lucky to have married her, not the other way around), and Dona Vorchenza's true role in Camorran politics might be considered one of the most important. One other thing - perhaps the thing - that I loved most about this novel was the dialogue and narration. Everyone seems to have their own ready supply of wit, and even the narrative comes off as very witty, and quite funny as well. There is never a dull moment in this book, whether it is the Gentlemen Bastards ragging on each other, or the narrator describing some district or custom of Camorr. Locke and his closest friend and accomplice Jean Tannen have their own unique voices, though Father Chains is especially delightful. Be warned, however, that there is a great deal of swearing in this novel - not even made-up swearing, but actual, honest-to-goodness real-world four-letter-words, and they are used with remarkable frequency. Some readers have found this to be jarring, since the swear-words used tend to clash with the somewhat "higher" language used elsewhere, but I do not find the swear-words jarring at all. In fact, they have been used well, if rather copiously, and there are times when the swearing can get rather, dare I say it, poetic. It takes reading the book to understand what I mean, but the quote below should illustrate my point well enough: "Someday, Locke Lamora," he [Father Chains] said, "someday you're going to fuck up so magnificently, so ambitiously, so overwhelmingly that the sky will light up and the moons will spin and the gods themselves will shit comets with glee. And I just hope I'm still around to see it." Needless to say, readers adverse to swearing might want to skip this book entirely, but I do hope said readers will at least attempt to cringe their way through the book, because despite all the swearing, it really is a very well-told story. Overall, The Lies of Locke Lamora is a fantastic read - though I suppose this is already expected, given what I said at the beginning of this review. There is honestly very little that I found negative in this book, except maybe that it ends on a right and proper cliffhanger and I cannot get my hands on the second book soon enough. Of course, that flaw needs to be taken as a recommendation, because for readers who love rogues, and who love their rogues witty and far too intelligent and maybe potty-mouthed, then this is absolute perfection, and they shall be squirming in their seats to read the next book.
I'm never going to be able to look at life the same way again. What is parallel universe me doing? Is she going to stab me in the back? That bitch.

The more I read, the more bored I get with typical novel structures. Things get predictable after a while - you have such solid expectations from the onset that the structure of novels begins to run together, and unless they do a lot to stand out, they just feel like they're going through the motions. My general theme this year is that I'm just bored of what I'm reading. More than half of my ratings so far in 2016 have been either 3-stars or 2-stars - nothing is surprising me, and nothing is standing out. Reading is becoming more and more of a chore, and I'm getting increasingly desperate for something new. Even novels that I thought would offer something new, like  Up from the Sea or  Baad have turned out to be predictable, despite unusual premises. So I should be happy to have read this book. The storytelling is non-chronological! It's about a former-model who lost her voice and severely burnt her face in an accident! It has a trans woman in it, and it was (originally) published in 1999! The book literally asks me to skip around from chapter to chapter! This is definitely one of the most unusual, unconventional books I've ever read. I should've been grateful for this. But if  John Dies at the End taught me anything, it's that while unusual books may be bad for different reasons than cliched ones, they can be just as bad, if not worse. This isn't nearly as bad as John Dies at the End, but it was still not nearly as good as I expected it to be, and even if it was bad in an interesting way that I've never seen before, that doesn't prevent it from being bad. I'll admit that for the first 50 pages or so, I was kind of into it. There was a certain intrigue that came with the structure. The story is told completely non-chronologically, and while asking the reader to jump around the book to find the next chapter was kind of gimmicky, it actually does contribute to the hazy, unpredictable mood rather well. Not to mention that the story was just so weird - Palahniuk finds original and unusual ways to be vulgar, and the main cast consists entirely of counterculture weirdos, written so that you never quite have a grip on who they really are and why they act the way they do. To borrow a description from Brows Held High, the effect is kind of like you're hungover and someone's asking you to describe the book you read last night. I really have never read anything like it, and the disorienting feel of the book really did put me in a mindset that I've never been put in before while reading a book. But as the book went on, some problems began to arise. After a while of this disorienting stuff, I began to ask myself why exactly Palahniuk was doing this. What was the point? What was he trying to say with it? And having read the book, from start to finish, I can definitively say: nothing. There is no point to any of this, and he says nothing. Palahniuk is trolling the reader - you go into this experimental book, thinking that it's going to be experimental because Palahniuk has something to say that can only be said in this format. And instead, you find that there's just nothing behind it. You would think that things would make more sense as the book goes on, but they actually start to make less and less sense as you continue. There are a lot of plot twists to this novel, a lot of them related to Daisy, our protagonist, being an unreliable narrator. The twists start out fairly clever, but as the book goes on, they get more and more contrived, less and less realistic, to the point where I realized that this book was never meant to have any connection to reality. Likewise, the characters start out as archetypal caricatures, and only get more exaggerated as the book goes on. They might switch archetypes, but they remain caricatures nonetheless, and by the end of the novel, they're less like people and more like embodiments of jealousy, hedonism, or senselessness. Palahniuk has said that by making the reader jump around the book to find the next chapter and telling the story non-chronologically, he wanted to imitate the feel of gossip magazines he read, when he didn't read in order and only vaguely understood the point of each article. That feeling turns out to be more all-pervading in this book than I expected. Rather than taking place in the real world, this book feels like it takes place in one of those gossip magazines, where there's constant drama, constant betrayals and falling in and out of love and cheating and sex and drugs and an unbelievable lack of connection to a logical or emotional reality. If you look at National Enquirer headlines and say, "Yup, this seems legit," I can imagine you connecting to the reality of this novel. Beyond that, there's no way you could believe any of this. "But that's the point!" you might be saying. And yes, that is the point. And I'll say this: Palahniuk succeeds on the terms he lays out for himself. His goal was to write the most weird, vulgar, unrealistic, and alienating novel he possibly could, and he succeeds. Everything that works about this book works on those grounds. But I just have no interest in reading that. I want to read experimental books because authors often write these books when they think of a new way to say something. Some of the best experimental books I've ever read find new ways of communicating things, so that they're more profound than they could possibly be otherwise. I know I've mentioned this book in my reviews a million times by now, but I want to point you once again to  Liar by Justine Larbalestier. The older I get, the more I appreciate just what this book accomplished, just because I've seen so many other books fail to reach the same heights. Liar is honestly unusual in a lot of the same ways Invisible Monsters is - both feature non-chronological storytelling, and both have unreliable narrators. But Larbalestier has something to say with Liar. She's not just being weird because weird books get attention, she uses the unusual format to portray grief and confusion about one's identity in ways that traditional storytelling could never have accomplished. Each plot twist (and there are a lot of very good plot twists in Liar) is beyond unexpected, but all of them fit perfectly into the tapestry that Liar weaves. It's books like Liar that make me want to read experimental books. I have no use for something like this, that's weird just for the sake of it. If I'm being honest, I find this book unbearably pretentious. (This was not helped, by the way, by the sections that don't actually involve the story or characters at all, but instead chronicle events in Palahniuk's life, for no discernible reason. It's a terrible, pointless addition to the remix.) This asks you to entertain its idiosyncrasies, not because it has anything to offer, but because it's associated with particular ideas. Even if those ideas happen to be weirdness and inventive vulgarness, as they are here, it's just not a sustainable foundation for a novel.This book doesn't use its tabloid-like world as a metaphor for any aspect of the real world, or to reveal anything about the human condition. It has no real connection to reality, and therefore cannot comment on it. It completely lacks value outside of itself. It's worth noting, also, that this book is pretty transmisogynistic. It might seem kind of silly to complain about the real-world ramifications of a novel that so clearly doesn't purport to represent the real world. But problematic ideas in books have consequences, even when they try not to. Palahniuk treats trans women the same way he does parents who are paranoid about being victims of violence because they're allies of gay people, or people who tour houses that are for sale just so that they can steal drugs, or any of the other bizarre archetypes he writes about in this novel. To him, the idea of a trans woman is something he can use to bolster the bizarre mood of his novel, rather than real people who suffer real oppression. So Brandy, the trans woman in this novel, is never seen dealing with the stigma and violence associated with being a trans woman. Instead, she spends most of her time being obsessed with femininity and vaginas. And there's nothing tongue-in-cheek about this. Most people today have very few expectations of what a trans woman is, and few ideas about stereotypes about trans women. That means there's nothing in here that could make them take this portrayal as anything but complete earnest. And yes, it turns out at the end of the book that Brandy probably wasn't actually trans, she's just a cis guy who took estrogen and got a bunch of surgery for reasons I'm not entirely clear on . But nevertheless, harmful stereotypes of trans women are built up and reinforced by this novel. As it turns out, when a novel has nothing that it wants to say, it ends up saying things by accident. And what this novel says by accident is not just inaccurate, but dangerous and harmful. There are things I begrudgingly admire about this novel. I admire how much Palahniuk builds up a mood for this novel. I admire that even though the story is non-chronological, there is a coherent and focused dramatic structure based on what information Palahniuk chooses to withhold and when he chooses to give it to us. I admire that Palahniuk had a clear vision, and for the most part, he executed it precisely. But I don't have the patience for something this pretentious and transmisogynistic. There are plenty of people who like this novel, but I have trouble imagining what use it could possibly have to anybody. If you're deeply, deeply bored of what you've been reading and just want any change, even a bad one, go ahead and give this a try. Otherwise, I can almost guarantee that this book has nothing to offer to you.
