This book was painful to get through. To much poetry, not enough movement in the plot. The beginning started out okay, but the last half was like trying to swim through tar. There were far too many descriptions of situations, past and present, which made the storyline feel very disjointed. Add to that that we suddenly had dual POV in this second book, whereas we only had a single POV in the first book, so that added to the incredibly disjointed feeling. I tend to hate dual POV stories anyway, but considering that the series didn't start out that way made this technique even more disconcerting when used here. Also... it was as if the author started writing and then was like, "Well shoot, I hated how much stuff I took away from the MC in the first book. Let me just give it all back to her," and indeed she did. Cassia got her society back (somehow magically reinstated with full citizenship, no questions asked), she got her grandfather's DNA, and even the microcard with Xander's information on it (that she'd just spent two books whining about losing). This book was like some great cosmic reset that made me come away from it feeling like I hadn't progressed anywhere at all. I'm already two thirds of the way invested in this trilogy, so you can bet I'll go ahead and finish it, but wow was this book disappointing. It deserves a few stars because I still (kind of sort of) care about what happens to the characters, but this sequel definitely did not live up to it's predecessor.

I hate writing the introduction on my reviews. I feel like I say the same things over and over again but here we go anyway. That Thing Between Eli & Gwen somehow was a 3.5 star read for me but made it into my favorites. Let me try and explain. First I'll say what I hated... I took off one entire star solely on the wording/sentence structure that drove me a bit insane. The writing was perfect. There were no errors in spelling or grammar that I noticed but my problem was in how everyone talked. Yeah, I don't use contraction words every time I speak but when I was reading and felt like the flow of the conversation called for a, for instance, "We're, They're, It'll, It's, Don't etc., It was we are, they are, it will, it is and do not. Honestly it would trip me up almost every time it happened because it messed up the flow. It felt like when you're listening to a really great CD and the thing skips and it just ticks you off because you were just starting to feel the magic. The second thing I hated is a spoiler. I'm warning you now to not read this if you don't want a spoiler because... IT IS A SPOILER. IT'S SOMETHING THAT HAPPENS AT THE END OF THE BOOK SO DON'T HIT "VIEW SPOLER". Okay? Can I just say that running away from a guy you just realized you were in love with due to the fact he became a father is totally understandable? I totally get that, but I was really annoyed that after she decided that she loved him enough to stay she left anyway. If she had finished her "dream" and went back to him after, that would have been a little better but she came home early. She didn't even finish what she left Eli to do! That irritated me a bit. Right, so now if I haven't scared you off with the bad, let me tell you about the good. Because there was SO MUCH GOOD. Gwen and Eli had amazing chemistry from the very first confrontation to the end of the book. J.J. McAvoy remained consistent in everything she did. I loved how much she focused on their careers and she proved their love for what they did. Eli, the doctor, was hot. I mean... HAWT. He was the perfect mixture of romantic, sweet, possessive, trusting and scorching hot. Gwen was so quirky! She was a goofy gal that loved her art and made a killing being a "con artist". (No people, she isn't really a con artist. The good doctor just thinks she is.) Gwen, the artist, was free spirited and remained that way. They didn't try to change each other and not only was that refreshing, it was fun to witness. They complimented each other in their differences. The moment Eli's bride-to-be ran off with Gwens finance, I was sold on the story. Their banter, friendship and eventual romance was absolutely believable. They didn't jump into each others arms and they actually had hostility between them in the beginning. (Honestly, who wouldn't after that epic disaster?) When Eli went to the wedding Gwen was in, I think I fell in love with him. He was her rock and he didn't even realize what was happening. This is easily one of my favorite stories. It's been on my to-read list for freaking forever and I finally had an opportunity to read it. So glad I did! This is definitely special.

First sentence: Everyone has heard the rumors about the Olympic village-not the details of the world-class amenities and supercharged meal plans, but the whispers about the trouble athletes get into once they're off the track and in the sack. Okay, so I absolutely adored SCORING WILDER and once I found out there was going to be another sports romance coming from R.S. Grey I instantly became excited and knew I had to read it. What's even better? THE SUMMER GAMES: SETTLING THE SCORE has cameos from the characters from SCORING WILDER. How freaking awesome is that? It is set five-years after the end of SCORING WILDER and is focused on a different couple, so if you haven't read SCORING WILDER then you can totally read this book first. SIZZLING CHEMISTRY Andie and Freddie meet at a party and sparks fly between them. There is a bit of insta-lust going on here, but I enjoyed the hell out of it. They each feel a connection and pull to be around the other. They can't stay away. It doesn't take long for those sparks to turn into a blazing fire of passion. I couldn't help falling in love with Freddie right along with Andie. And I was rooting for them from the start. AMAZING CHARACTERS My favorite thing about this book was the character development. Each character had their own distinctive personality and shined on the pages. We have Andie who is a badass who kicks ass at soccer and is ready to take on whatever life throws her way. Then we have Freddie who is terrific, he's sexy and a little on the brooding side, and he's absolutely irresistible. And we have Kinsley and Becca who were awesome. But my favorite character in the book was Georgie, Freddie's sister. She's hilarious and will have you laughing out loud. Can we please get a Georgie book? Conclusion: THE SUMMER GAMES: SETTLING THE SCORE has a mix of humor, witty dialogue, sexy characters, and girl friendships along with a touch of tension and passion. The writing flowed flawlessly and this was a fast paced read. Andie and Freddie had me on the edge of my seat. I grinned throughout the book. I couldn't get enough of it. I devoured it. The characters shined on the pages and I absolutely loved every one of them, well, except for one but that may be spoiler-ish although I think everyone who reads this will hate her so. THE SUMMER GAMES: SETTLING THE SCORE was so much fun to read. It's refreshing, light, and delightful. I can't wait to read more in this series. Recommended To: Sports romance fans. Also, fans of SCORING WILDER.

I can't help liking Paulo Coelho. This is the one and only full-length novel I've read in Portuguese; I originally read it about a year after leaving Brazil (probably in 2005). In Portuguese the language and the words are just stunning--reading it makes you feel like you're wandering through a grove of words, spontaneously grown into being. In English I pay less attention to the language and the sound of the words, though it's easier to pay attention to the meaning and the message. And this is a book that admits to having a message: we all have Personal Legends, and it's worth the costs to seek after them. There's awesome insights here on seeking after your dreams, and it really is inspiring. This is a book that I can't read if I'm in a skeptical or cynical mood--if I'm looking to critique, I don't enjoy the book and get as much out of it. I also had to stop myself from going into overly-feminist mode and wondering why it is that only men get to follow their personal legends and why all the women always have to stay at home and wait while this do so. Fortunately I've read other books by Coelho with awesome female protagonists, so I know it's not an intentional slight. I reread this novel for book group, and it provided a good basis for discussion.

Meh. This is probably meant to draw a new generation in to the [Sisterhood of the Travelling Pants], but it didn't really work that well for me. It felt a bit formulaic. Three girls, friends since primary school, have begun to go their separate ways. They face challenges and ups and downs and in the end, realize their friendships mean more than popularity or grades or anything else. I had a few problems with it. First, the setting was poorly done. There was no real sense of place. If I hadn't read The Sisterhood, I'd have had no idea where I was. There were also sort of random references to The Sisterhood, but in a way that led me to believe they would have something to do with the story. Nope. The worst was when one of the three girls stops eating, loses lots of weight and is definitely flirting with anorexia, finds her mother drunk and can't wake her up, calls 911. Mum goes to hospital, diagnosed alcoholic, admits self to rehab, while daughter goes to stay with her friends. No discussion of getting help for the girl with anorexia. In fact, more of a sense that she can just decide to start eating again and can solve this all herself. Very disturbing. Some mature themes, boys, making out, sexual references. It has its moments, but overall, not really that impressive. I had this listed as read - 4 years ago. If that's true, it was totally Un-memorable.

This is the seventh book in the Sebastian St. Cyr Regency era mystery series. The series should be read in order as there are constant references to what has gone before and the ongoing mystery surrounding Sebastian's life even if the murder itself is begun and resolved with in the book as are all of them in the series. This is a great series for the mystery buff who loves authentic historical setting, strong plots and stronger characters. This one has Sebastian and Hero teaming to solve the murder of Hero's friend, Gabrielle Tennyson, an unusual young lady who is a female scholar searching for the site of the true Camelot. Gabrielle's murder leaves many suspects and many motives. It is the task of Sebastian and Hero, married just days now, to wade through all the secrets and facts to discover the right one as they also must race against the clock to save Gabrielle's two missing nephews who disappeared near the time of her murder. As layer upon layer are peeled back we meet the ruthless former businessman owner of the land and his cold, narrow-minded wife, the hot tempered foreman on the dig, the grieving brother of the deceased, a paroled French officer, an arrogant cousin, a pompous scholar and most disturbing of all a dangerous tavern owner who bears striking resemblance to Sebastian. Hero, in her part of the investigation, discovers that her father has fingers in the pie and her loyalty between a new husband who is her father's enemy and her father are tested. And they are supremely tested because her father has motive to harm Gabrielle too and she has become aware that she has feelings for Sebastian that challenge her to realize that he is more to her than just the father of her unborn child. Sebastian, too, is surprised at his desire to have more with Hero than a marriage in name only because he is still trying to sort through his feelings about Kat. He must also accept the truth of what he finds out about himself as he investigates Gabrielle's murder. As usual, Ms. Harris, has written a well written plot that twists and turns its way to the awful truth. There are many truths revealed and a few hints of things that will carry into the next book. The pace of the book never stalled out in my opinion as answers were sought and danger threatened. This is a wonderful series and I love how it has a murder to solve, but Sebastian's past is an ongoing mystery to be solved. I also like the way relationships are handled in the series between Sebastian and Hero and with their respective families. There is not an easy or instant solution. Looking forward to the next installment!

This book was fantastic. It was everything a good thriller should be: fast pacing, suspenseful, with a clever plot and brilliant main characters. The style may be a little dry, but I think thrillers do not need to be written beautifully, and anyway the introspective parts were quite powerful. However, the pace was never slow and there were some truly terrific parts which made me jump on my seat. I had high hopes for this book but at the same time I was a little worried about the characters - Hannibal Lecter, precisely. Of course I watched the movies (but not the one about this book - I will do it as soon as possible! ), and I was worried that I would constantly think about Anthony Hopkins's perfect interpretation and not appreciate the book character that much. But after all, when a character works so well on screen, it is not just thanks to the actor but also because the original character has a strong appeal: and indeed Dr. Lecter in the book is brilliantly drawn, his words are fascinating and terrifying at the same time, and he ends up being completely realistic. The only bad thing about the book is the fact that he appears so little, which surprised me: but he surely leaves a strong impression. His conversation with Will is chilling and probably my favourite part in the book, and his letters are highly disturbing. Will Graham is an equally good hero: skilled and smart, but also tormented and marked after his not-so-nice encounter with Lecter. He is a very good guy, who cares and suffers for the victims, but there is also a disturbing darkness inside him, mostly because he has a particular empathy which allows him to enter into the killers' minds. As Lecter says, he and Will are the same: Graham could potentially become a killer (and a very good one, lol), but he works for the good and constantly battles against his darkest side. This is way it is always exciting to follow him through his investigation. Even though Lecter is amazing, the main villain of the book is Francis Dolarhyde, the Red Dragon. I must admit at first I was not very impressed, but well, I changed my mind after he set fire to Lounds . Good Lord! I am very sorry for thinking you weren't as creepy as Lecter, Francis, I really am. The flashbacks about his childhood are equally well done, so much that after reading them you discover you feel a little sorry for him after all - yes, I know, creepy. And his relationship with Reba is also very interesting to read. 5 stars well deserved, and now I cannot wait to read the next one!

"The body artist" is Lauren Hartke. Third wife of a failed filmmaker. The Body Artist opens with a brief interaction between Lauren and her husband, followed, in quick succession, by the suicide of the husband/failed filmmaker and the arrival of a stranger who barely communicates. Like Kaspar Hauser, the stranger enters the narrative without explanation. Unlike Kaspar Hauser, he doesn't carry a note. Nothing in the form of an explanation. Lauren is startled by his arrival, and considers alerting the landlord. But something prevents her... Loneliness? Curiosity? Her reasons for the initial acceptance is unclear. But her reason for continued acceptance is derived entirely from the stranger's uncanny ability to mimic her husband's voice. He repeats things her husband has said, and in a voice that captures all of her husband's mannerisms. And yet the stranger is unable to communicate in the most basic way. There's a code in the simplest conversation that tells the speaker what's going on outside the bare acoustics. This was missing when they talked. There was a missing beat. It was hard for her to find the tempo. All they had were unadjusted words.... - pg. Lauren devises numerous theories to explain the stranger's abilities and disabilities. Variously, he is compared to a tape recorder, a synthesized voice from an answering machine... She called Mariella and got the answering machine. A synthesized voice said, Please / leave / a mess/age af/ter / the / tone. The words were not spoken but generated and they were separated by brief but deep dimensions. She hung up and called back, just to hear the voice again.... - pg. But nothing brings her closer to understanding his existence. She is undeterred. She may have been trying to reach her husband through a stranger who is seemingly a simulacrum of her husband, but the stranger becomes more interesting unto himself. This is best demonstrated when Lauren calls a friend to hear the answering machine, and hangs up when the friend answers. When she called again and Mariella answered, she put down the phone, softly, and stood completely still. - pg. At the same time, the stranger becomes less interesting to the reader. It is Lauren's investigation that captivates us. Admittedly, DeLillo's women leave something to be desired. Lauren spends much of the novel haunted by her husband (directly or vicariously through the stranger)... Sometimes he didn't appear and sometimes he appeared but didn't eat and once he was missing for six or seven hours and she went through the house and then down the driveway in the dark, shining a flashlight in the trees and calmly saying "Where are you?" - pg. She spends a portion of the novel obsessing over her appearance (which may be attributed to her profession, but is encumbered by the author's decision to sexualize activities that should be personal to the female character and therefore devoid of the male gaze) She began to work naked in a cold room. She did her crossovers on the bare floor, and her pelvic stretches, which were mockingly erotic and erotic both.... - pg. In the end, it is suggested that the so-called "haunting" may not have been a literal haunting, but part the artist's creative process. Consider the episode with the answering machine... Lauren is silent when her friend answers. Is it because she wanted to hear the answering machine instead of her friend, or is she rehearsing the part of the silent stranger? "How simple it would be if I could say this is a piece that comes directly out of what happened to Rey. But I can't. Be nice if I could say this is the drama of men and women versus death. I want to say that but I can't. It's too small and secluded and complicated and I can't and I can't and I can't." - pg.

I was not anticipating falling in love with this book series. I was on Goodreads a couple of months ago, and I was looking for a good book series with a strong female protagonist when I stumbled upon Jacqueline Carey's Kushiel series. What struck me as most interesting about the books at the time was the consistently high ratings for each book of the trilogy: each book had a 4-star or higher review, which I found unusual. And, as I soon found out, these ratings were almost accurate - only, I would have given the books 5 stars, not 4. But we'll get to that. Taking place in a sprawling, lush reimagining of early modern Europe, Kushiel's Chosen picks up right after the events of Kushiel's Dart. The main character, Phedre no Delaunay, has now become part of the noble society that she catered to in the last book as, essentially, a body slave. Terre D'Ange, where the story takes place, treats prostitution as a religious, honorable calling. Phedre is a beautiful young anguisette, so called because she is "pricked by Kushiel's Dart" - she has a red mote on her eye which indicates that she is the deity Kushiel's chosen, born to endure and enjoy pain as pleasure. Rather than treat this as some sort of twisted BDSM erotica tale, Jacqueline Carey manages to handle the subject with grace and surprisingly little mention. The real draws of this story, she makes very clear within the first few chapters: the stunning and detailed backdrop of Terre D'Ange, the wonderful and intriguing character development, the compelling conflict, and, of course, the love story between Phedre and her chevalier Joscelin Verreuil. Carey's language is descriptive and poetic, and takes on a formal-sounding style which firmly places the reader in the renaissance-esque Terre D'Ange. The plot, as with the first installment, is a twisting, intricately woven set of political ties, covert relations, and international intrigue. This is not some courtly drama set in the queen's palace, where everyone is in love with everyone and the plot point revolves around some waifish damsel. If you're looking for bodice-rippers, I suggest Philippa Gregory's retellings of Tudor England. No, Kushiel's Chosen is the big leagues of epic fantasy, up there with A Song of Ice and Fire as a tale that will leave you questioning and breathless to the close. Finally, let's talk characters, possibly my favorite aspect of this series aside from the marvelous setting Carey has created for these books. Careful and dynamic character development is one of Kushiel's Chosen's many strengths. Ms. Carey is not afraid to put her characters through the wringer, something I exceedingly admire as I become more familiar with her work. The protagonist of the series is a woman, which is slightly unusual for an epic fantasy series, as far as my experiences have been. On top of that, Phedre is a strong, clever woman who at every occasion proves herself to be able to take care of herself and her country. Being a courtesan does not make her any less a capable and daring leading lady, something I greatly appreciate as a female reader. Furthermore, her love interest Joscelin is not present merely to save Phedre's life or play the knight in shining armor, which makes for a more interesting relationship between the two. Overall, I cannot recommend this series highly enough. It really blindsided me with how amazing the setting, characters, and plot turned out to be. It's a long read, but once you're immersed into the world of Terre D'Ange, you'll be hard-pressed to leave it.

My review can also be found here: teenreadfiend "If there's one thing Mare Barrow knows, it's that she's different." Glass Sword, the sequel to Victoria Aveyard's Red Queen, started right where the story left off, with Mare and company fleeing from Maven and the rest of the Silvers. The same elements that made Red Queen so likeable continued in this sequel and we continued to learn more about the characters that we loved in the first book. What I Liked About It: We learned even more about the characters we were introduced to in the first novel, allowing readers to better understand their motives and choices. We were also introduced to a large amount of new and lovable characters. The plot was just as unpredictable as the original. There were so many things that happened that had me at the edge of my seat as I was reading it. The fight scene at the prison was amazing, as was the cliffhanger at the end. I can't wait to find out what happened with Cal, Kilorn, and the rest of the group after they were (hopefully) let go. The death of the queen. She was by far my least favourite character and I was incredibly happy to see her go. Especially since she was so evil. What I Didn't Like About It: Shade's death. He was my favourite character and it hurts to see him gone. That being said though, I like seeing what it has done to Mare and look forward to seeing how it continues to change her in the next book. Once again, I loved this novel. Aveyard did an amazing job making Glass Sword just as good as Red Queen. I continued to love these characters, this story, and this world overall. Can't wait for the next one!

***Stephen King Fan speaking, you might need to add a grain of salt*** This is King's first attempt at a 100% noir detective. Where he clearly toyed with the idea in 11/22/63, this work truly fits the genre, with no supernatural frills, just pure old-fashioned detective work and rather disturbing humans. Is this a masterly-written piece of literature? No. It is a summer read, a thrill-seeking ride in a style seen use by many writers, from James Patterson, to John Grisham, to Dan Brown, but with some redeeming qualities that show King has a natural knack for the genre: Evilness. Something King is, in my opinion, better at then almost any writer out there is coming up with characters who are so eerily believably evil. It is the kind of mentally deranged that somehow houses in all of us, and which might lead to many awful news bulletins. In Mr Mercedes King manages to put such a character to paper, with a bone-chilling crispness that leaves me awestruck. 4 Stars, if you need a fantastic poolside thriller/detective this summer, grab this one!

Actual Rating: 3.75 Bout of Books 11.0 Book #1 Its been two years since I read the first part of this book and I still love the characters, the world and the whole concept of this series. Lady Thief picked up where Scarlet left off. We're back with the gang, Robin, John, Much, and Scarlet. But this wouldn't be a sequel if the same things that happened in the first book happened in this book. Scarlet had to sacrifice her marital freedom in the first book in order to save Robin and that decision has staggering effects on everything that she does going forward. They live in a world where a wife has a duty to her husband, and adultery is one of the greatest sins. So when the man who has hunted her for her entire life, the man who has tried to torture and kill her, the man who is her husband, Gisborne, comes to her with a deal that will result in the annulment of her marriage, of course Scarlet accepts. From there on everything just gets crazy and if I'm being completely honest...a little bit annoying. Don't let the rating fool you, I enjoyed this book very much. Scarlet is still a character I very much enjoy and I love her tenacity, fire and passion. I love watching her interact with her friends and the people who think themselves above her. I love the secondary characters, and how they play a part in who Scarlet is. There were just too many things that annoyed me. The first and main thing being the beatings Scarlet took throughout this book. I mean she was bruised up and in pain through the entire thing. And I understand the need to make a character go through hard times and adversity, but at some point you have to draw a line. The first person to beat on her was her own love, Robin Hood. And we can get into a whole conversation about domestic violence, however, Robin hitting Scarlet isn't my issue. He was sleeping both times, reacting to nightmares of a war he fought long ago, and would have attacked a puppy if it were close to him when the nightmares hit. My problem with this was the guilt Scarlet felt afterwards. She hid her bruises and the hand she broke on his face from him because she didn't want him to feel bad. -- Why shouldn't he feel bad. Maybe if he sees what he's done, he'll suck up his fear and talk about his nightmares and, I don't know, STOP HAVING THEM!?! I really just didn't like the guilt Scarlet was made to feel after her boyfriend was the one who did wrong. After this initial abuse, Scarlet was just taking hit after hit after hit and it got to the point where I was desensitized to it. It got old for me. You're using this extreme method to get sympathy for a character that I already love, so all of the punishments, and torture was unnecessary and really started to annoy me after the fifth time it happened. There was a big twist in this book that I really didn't care for because I felt like it was just a recycled version of the twist used in the first book, only this time it was on a larger scale. I just wish this book had a little bit more depth to it than it did. The first one had adventure, and friendship, fighting, hardships, loyalty and honor, mystery and mischief. Where this one fell flat on all accounts except for the fighting and friendship. It seems like there is going to be another book in this series, I'll most likely be reading it to see what happens next but I hope its a better read than Lady Thief was.

From the way everyone raved about the book, I thought I would be hungry for Oreos, but I'm left a little homesick for Waffle House. They're just not up here on this side of Canada, and I have yet to find another place that can make a satisfying pile of greasy hashbrowns all the way. I read this book in three freaking hours - sorry, not sorry. It's hard to pick a spot to start from in raving about this. Simon, the funniest teenager with the funniest family full of in-jokes and made up worlds about Oreos? The diverse characters who existed because they were there with their own lives outside of Simon's personal world, not because the author went through a check list of diverse characters to include? The humorous but touching and courageous e-mails between Simon and Blue? I won't delve into Blue so much because I don't want to give away any hints about the mystery, but I have to say that from the very beginning, I knew I would not be disappointed in who Blue ended up being. Simon crushes on him so hard, and it's adorable and sweet. Anyone who could make Simon that twitterpated without revealing their name or face was not going to disappoint me when the reveal happened. Simon himself is a fantastic character. He's awkward sometimes. He's funny. He's introspective. He's a teenager. An honest-to-goodness teenager who doesn't want to make a big deal about his sexuality. His family really had me in stitches, and much of Simon's humor is developed because of them. Their reality show obsession. Their dog named Bieber. The Halloween costumes. The thing they did on Christmas Eve day was the only time I put the book down since I started reading because I had to go to a different room and laugh so I wouldn't wake up my spouse. It was kind of terrible but it was so funny. The story is a little on the simple side, but it's addicting like Oreos because all the characters are so well-crafted. Especially Taylor.

She fills her sketchbooks with monsters that may or may not be real: she speaks many languages--not all of them human; and her bright blue hair actually grows out of her head that color. Who is she? That is the question that haunts her, and she's about to find out. Taylor is an all star writer. She creates amazing worlds, tight plots, and characters you can't help but sympathize with. In this case, both the "good" and the "bad." And then there's her writing itself- simply beautiful. I love seeing the world through her eyes- such a treat. You just can't help but savor it. The story is compelling, fascinating, fun/funny, and horrifying. Very, very hard to put down. I can't wait to read the next one. (And- the movie rights were purchased, so here's hoping. This will also make a fabulous movie!)

This was a wonderful time traveling adventure! This is the first book I have read by Eoin Colfer and I am sure it will not be the last. He does a good job bringing two different worlds together in a frantic game of cat and mouse. In current time we have young Chevron, a 16 year old FBI agent who is hustled away from being further known by the public. She is sent to London, to 'baby-sit' a pot with the instructions to notify her new superior if anything comes out. For 6 months she is bored when suddenly a boy materializes holding a knife over a mutated man. The boy, Riley,is from the past 110 year ago and warns her that Garrick is Death and is coming for him! This book is creative and fast paced! At first I was baffles about a 16 year old being in the FBI but that does get explained. At least enough to make the story flow along. Chevron and Riley are constantly trying to run away from Garrick, who is one deadly opponent! I loved Riley's character the best. He seemed very down to earth, practical, caring, smart and fun to be around. While the plot jumped around between the three main characters' points of view, Riley's is one I would have liked to see more. Chevron seemed to have a neat personality, with a sassy edge but I just couldn't get quite as into her. Garrick annoyed me. Also, he is merged with another man after he travels through time which muddles his character too much for my taste. Again, the pace was great for most of this book. Constantly moving forward, while unfolding lots of back-story on the characters. While parts of the book were predictable it was still an enjoyable read and the ending does leave you wondering what is ahead in the next book! *I received a copy of this book from Disney Book Group in return for a fair and honest review. No money or gifts were exchanged/involved. The opinions stated in this review are my own!

I'm not sure why he didn't assume that the guy who acted like a dog wasn't just developmentally delayed or mentally ill. Roma didn't come across this dense in the previous book. I love that Matt asked if he was straight not if he was gay. This is sometimes laugh out loud funny. There was a scene where Lance is having to explain mates and a sex life to Roman but was really uncomfortable about it. I thought the subtlety of this part was hilarious: "You're mates. Yes, sir. I know that." "Which means we... you know... have sex." Lance looked panicked. "Only in human form, though! Me. Not him. I mean, he only has a human form. But--" He cleared his throat. " --to be clear, it's proper etiquette... if you want to.... I mean, most humans would not have sex with dogs. In dog form." Roman was disciplined enough not to roll his eyes. "Yes, sir. I believe dogs feel pretty much the same way. "Lance is so cute in this scene. There's a later scene, too, and it's so adorable and funny how hard he's finding it to explain sex stuff to Roman. Roman was also funny in his confusion. How did people ever figure it out without smells... heat smells... to make it clear who was and wasn't receptive and when? What if you were wrong? How did you ever find out? Did you just say 'Hey, would you like to be mounted?' Or was that considered insulting? "The author also avoided cliched metaphors by turning them into something different that still worked, for example, "Her mind was a sharp as glass." Nice. It's really cool to have a shifter who loves being human. In most shifter books, it's almost as if the shifter resents the human half and just wants to be free to run, not cooped up in this human body. I love how much Roman loves being human. Some of this feels a little out of character for him. A little too joyous when he's been so solemn, but I love it. As I said, five stars.

Audiobook version. And I don't know if it's just the audio version, because I've skimmed a couple other reviews and didn't see it mentioned, but there was a glitch/typo in the first chapter, when we still only know the MC as "he" - the narration refers to him by name. Twenty minutes of pure pronouns, one use of a proper noun. I thought maybe I'd misheard, but then in the second chapter, sure enough, the character's name IS Ethan - and I already knew that because of this glitch in the first chapter. It's not a big deal to know his name, but it IS a big deal to go into a book like this, where the reader is gathering clues and trying to figure out what's going on, with an awareness that there is at least one sloppy mistake in the book and may be more. If I pick up a weird clue, can I count on it being a deliberate part of the narrative, or will I put a lot of thought into it and then find out it was just a glitch? So one little mistake kind of lowered my commitment to the book overall. Beyond that...  I didn't buy the explanation. Even if I gloss over the incredibly fast evolution (probably best understood as a series of mutations, but... still), there are other problems. Pilcher and co. have the mind-control technology to turn people into Stepford-esque drones who will believe all their lies without question, but they don't have the mind-control to keep people from committing suicide if they know the truth? Bullshit, and if Ethan is the independent-thinking stud we're told he is, he should have known that. (Maybe he does, and the ending of this story is just a fake-out - maybe he's just going deep undercover. But for a satisfying ending, the author should have let us in on that!). And Pilcher has the foresight and resources to stockpile endless rows of futuristic cars (and, I assume, the fuel to run them? ), but he can't buy a few long-distance drones or other surveillance devices that would tell him more about the world he woke up in? He has enough stored energy to power the freezers and then run an entire town, but he can't set up a system to record what happened in the world and how human civilization destroyed itself? Other niggles, too. Overall, it just wasn't a satisfying solution. So, not a great book for me. I didn't know it was a TV series until I started reading... maybe it'd be better on TV, where I'd have less time to think about stuff?

EDIT 9/12/17: I remembered something incredible Maas included that I originally forgot to put in my review. During the sex scene between Chaol and Yrene, there was spoken consent. Chaol outright asked if she was okay having sex, and Yrene explicitly said "yes" before anything happened. That is SO important. And even better, Maas didn't have that question ruin the moment, or seem awkward, because it ISN'T and SHOULDN'T BE. So important. This is absolutely, without a doubt, Maas' best work, and the best book in the Throne of Glass series by far. I truly want to go back and lower my ratings from the other books because none of them compare to this. The emotional journey, the intricacy, the information we learn, and the character arcs are absolutely incredible. I have never in my life seen a fantasy author give so much attention and care to a disabled character. I was so sure going into this that Sarah wouldn't write this respectfully, but I was so wonderfully shocked at how much time we spent watching Chaol recover, whether it was through exercises, Yrene's healing, or his own emotional journey, and how incredible the ending message with his disability was. Ending on saying that he was no less of a man, in or out of a chair was so beautifully positive I had tears in my eyes (keep in mind, this is coming from an able-bodied person, so I'm still not the voice you should be listening to). In addition, Yrene's own personal journey, and all the tie-ins to The Assassin's Blade could not have been more enjoyable. And our new group of bratty royals... god I loved the new culture Sarah brought us into with Antica. Sartaq and Nesryn's relationship, though I wasn't at first into, was a slow-burn, respectful growth, and I'm really glad she ultimately included it. Plus, the information they learned about Maeve being a Valg Queen literally blew my mind. I should have guessed that in Heir of Fire, for it has all been staring us in the face since them, but I still didn't put it together. Plus, their scene with the spiders was INCREDIBLY crafted in my opinion. Even further, Sarah finally included the diversity in appearance, skin color and culture that readers have been asking for, and I was pleasantly surprised in that it wasn't forced at all. I never felt like there was a moment when she was forcing a description of skin color, or trying to prove that she could write a diverse book. It just... flowed. Everything about this book was incredible, and I cannot wait for the seventh book (I'm literally ten times more excited than I was going into this book) and how Yrene and the healers will use their powers against Erawan and the Valg. Overall, I think Maas rediscovered her love of writing, the world she created, and these characters she's worked with for so many years. She was writing with vigor I haven't felt from her in so long, and I felt like she was truly invested in the story more than ever before. This book is imperative to the series, and, while slow, undoubtedly the best book Maas has written to date. Don't hesitate to read it. You won't be disappointed.

Overall i enjoyed the book. It took a little while for me to get into, but that's probably because I was reading the majority of this at work and couldn't really relax into the story like I usually do. I did enjoy the character of Lady Darby otherwise known as Kiera. I feel as though she managed to keep the delicate balance of being a highly intelligent woman capable of being helpful in the investigation as well as a lady living in Scotland 1830. When i read a mystery book set back in the day featuring heroine the women often shunt off all everything that makes them a lady of the times. This isn't modern day we're talking about here I don't need a raging feminist in the 1800s. Unless she is done well and is believable for her time period. I'm glad she had a partner, seriously a lot of the detective females wouldn't get into as much trouble if they actually confided in someone for a change. Kiera is of course the stereotypical oddball of society, shunned by the social elite because of her eccentricities. However in this case it doesn't diminish her character in any way. She's knows people are talking about her behind her back and in her face but she still manages to hold on to her dignity. And i love how important family was to her, and she truly cares about the children her nieces and nephews. Sometimes i think an author is afraid to make the strong female lead have a feminine side that doesn't have anything to do with sex. I want a kick butt character who's not afraid to admit she knits and enjoys it! but i digress. I liked Kiera I enjoyed listening to her voice. and she's a bit like me. You can talk about me all you want but don't you dare go after my sister. Blood will be spilled. She's not a complete wallflower, she puts down a lady who keeps slandering her reputation and  she totally knifes the dude whodunnit  . I also enjoyed her relationship with Gage, and the grudging respect developing to genuine admiration for each other that develops. Plus these two did try to work together from the get go. Sure they had secrets but compared to other partnerships I can believe these two can actually work together and it's not something shoehorned in for the plot. I do want to find out more about Gage and where he's coming from, what it's like to live with his inspector father. I don't know maybe it's just me but i feel like the guy was probably overbearing with his son. I could be wrong though. Anyway I'm looking forward to reading the next book in the series. Oh and i should mention the cover... It's pretty and I like it. I totally want a cloak like that. In answer to the recommendation question. Yes. I do recommend reading this book. You may or may not like it. I was ambivalent throughout the first half of the book, but you might get into it quicker than I did. Or not. Either way give it a try. Now on to my next book.

I felt like this had a nice mix of thought provoking themes and pointless action. I mean, it's a guy killing androids, so that's pretty cool and it holds up the first half quite nicely. Still, it ended on an interesting note. I liked the commentary on empathy and humanity. The way people love to help others because they value empathy but a lot of them don't actually empathize with anyone on a real level. I think it worked well to end with the robotic toad. That really tied everything together for me. He went from the "extravagant" electric sheep to a real goat to an electric toad. Sort of like how you think you have empathy, but when you feel real empathy, you realize it's exhausting and it's sometimes easier to be alone. Or maybe that's not the point at all. One flaw with the book was that the metaphors did feel rushed at the end. They weren't really discussed at length until the last fifty pages. Still, that's better with slapping you in the face with symbolism before you even know what's going on. Overall, it was just enjoyable. I didn't have any problems with it. Every time I thought I was entering a boring part, someone exciting would happen. It wasn't pointless. This is just a solid book. I highly recommend it.

Hale? HALE! This is a HALE book, much to my excitement. There is plenty of Hale, and not just the one you're thinking (have I mentioned Hale's name enough? My only issue with this book (because as usually, I love the delightful characters and smooth writing) is that I felt the plot lost the "it" factor towards the end. I ended up questioning the author's decision to "trick" the reader for a page or two, and the shift (BEING VERY VERY VAGUE, HOPEFULLY NO SPOILERS) between the 'bridge' and the 'train' was really.. confusing? Like after reading the part on the train, the transition felt very clunky. Okay, these are spoilers: Like the part when "Reginald" died, that whole part I was on board, but then when Carter was writing Kat and Hale's reactions, I didn't like the forced emotion (considering Kat must have known the plan). It felt tacky and manipulative. Also, to expand on the bridge and train thing, how did Garrett like, leave prison? I thought he 'killed' a guy. Don't they lock you up for that? What? Anyway, there were also parts of the plot that I wasn't a huge fan of (we know the antagonist's plan too early on), or that the heist was underwhelming (it was sneaky, but not... heist-y enough for me, or imaginative enough). HOWEVER, it's still getting 4/5 from me because although there were some parts I wasn't the most pleased with, I still had and wonderful time reading it and escaping into Kat's world. I thought Ally Carter dealt with so many great themes in an impacting way (I really adored the way Carter wrote about Kat stealing Hale), the themes of family and friendship really stood out and I greatly enjoyed it.

Bear with me: when I watched the Clint Eastwood movie Unforgiven I felt like Eastwood was ending an entire genre. This is tired, said Clint, its beats are tired, its cliches are tired, there's nothing more for it to say, I'm gonna give you one last great Western and that's enough, okay? And the movie had such overwhelming eulogic power that it almost succeeded. (It didn't, of course, but it was years before anyone dared to make another one.) And I got the same feeling from The Awakening. I felt that it was hammering the nails into the coffin of a genre - the genre of novels that end the way Awakening ends, which is sortof a startling lot of books. With this mixture of irritation and love - "I'm sick to death of this stupid story" but also, "And here's one more great story." That to me is its brilliance: it tells a familiar story, but it's simultaneously furious at the very story it's telling, at the world it's telling it in, and when it ends it intends not to end this specific story but this entire story, the telling of this story, the existence of it. It didn't work either. But A for effort! We all got it coming, kid.

I downloaded the free version onto my Kindle. It didn't have an introduction or any commentary. All I knew before I started reading was that it was a creepy short-story about a woman's descent into madness. I didn't even know when it was written or where or when the story was supposed to have taken place. I thought that telling the story solely through the narrator's diary entries was really interesting and unique...the slow slide into insanity was so plainly evident in her writing. It made me think of the frog put into a pot of cool water...the frog doesn't jump out as the heat is gradually turned up and before the frog knows it, he's being boiled. The narrator is brought to this nice vacation house and doesn't fight or even protest as she is driven crazy in that room! I wanted to yell at her to run, to get out of there before it was too late! That "nursery" that she stayed in...I really thought that maybe that room was never actually a nursery. The bars on the windows, the splintered bed that's nailed to the floor, the rings in the walls and, of course, the ripped up yellow wallpaper...it all led me to think that this was a room where other people had been held prisoner and left alone until they were out of their minds. I also wasn't sure if the husband and sister-in-law were totally innocent or was this their evil plan all along. The end was chilling! After I finished reading it, I read some of the reviews and I discovered that the story is full of feminist symbolism about the oppression of women. Yes, all of that is pretty clear, but I still just enjoyed it as a creepy short-story.

And if that is sinful, let me be damned for it!" pg. Edited 12/9/2011 Here's a bit from a paper I wrote (I did end up having to read it for AP English so I spoke too soon!) Blanche is riding the streetcar named Desire but she also paid fare for a streetcar named Madness. A Streetcar Named Desire is set in the late 1940s. This was a time when mental illness was finally beginning to receive acknowledgement. In 1946 President Truman signed the National Mental Health Act of 1946 which gave a "significant amount of funding for research into causes, prevention and treatment of mental illness" (Harlow, The 1940s). Thus Tennessee Williams was not breaking a taboo by creating a character with a mental illness that does end up being committed to a hospital. Rather he helped people adjust to the idea that people had mental illnesses and it was something that could be helped; he also used his play to show how people can be driven to madness. Blanche arrives in New Orleans and it soon becomes clear that something is not quite right about her; she is flighty and takes long baths to calm her "nerves." Before she is reunited with her sister she reminds herself that she must "keep hold of myself!" (I.i). She pours herself a drink as she waits for Stella and has another when Stella enters the apartment, the drinks subdue her. Stella notices right away that Blanche is different, she tells her "you seem a little bit nervous or overwrought or something" (I.i.). Blanche has managed to remain calm throughout the beginning of Scene One, nitpicking at Stella's clothes and appearance, Stanley, and their apartment. But then she proceeds to have the first of many hysterical outbursts and the reader catches a glimpse of the turmoil Blanche is in as she berates Stella for leaving her to care for Belle Reve alone. Blanche is more shaken by the concept of death itself than she is by her loved ones she was left to bury, "Funerals are quiet, but deaths-not always. Sometimes their breathing is hoarse, and sometimes it rattles, and sometimes they even cry out to you, 'don't let me go!' As if you were able to stop them! But funerals are quiet, with pretty flowers. And, oh, what gorgeous boxes they pack them away in!" (I. i.). This scene presents the first signs of Blanche's nervous breakdown. Her breakdown was driven by being left alone to care for Belle Reve, she was delicate, used to being taken care of and she had no idea how to take responsibility and mange Belle Reve when her relatives began to die off. Like all humans her survival instinct kicked in but she was unable to grow accustomed to work. She makes devastating mistakes as a teacher. Eventaully Blanche is put in a mental institution. The Doctor realizes that Blanche is not a threat to anyone, she lives in her own world and he enters her world to gain her trust. He removes his hat and treats her kindly, something she is not used to from the Kowalski home where Stanley had nothing but harsh words for her. The Doctor then acts like a gentleman by offering Blanche his arm, Blanche is then reminded of her many beaus at home who treated her nicely and offered her their arms. This one seemingly simple act convinces Blanche to go with the doctor, he offers her the opportunity to re-enter her magical world. This is a world where she was used to "depending on the kindness of the strangers" (I. xi), a world that began to crumble when Allan died and was snatched away completely when she lost Belle Reve. Blanche's breakdown began when she was overcome by guilt at the cruel words she said to Allan that resulted in his death. Upon losing Belle Reve she finds herself alone and utterly dependent on herself. She is unable to handle the magnitude of independence and so she attempts to rediscover love and gain protection with many different men but this does not satisfy her. Her dissatisfaction is dulled by her reliance on alcohol, with the help of alcohol she is able to ignore the guilt she feels over her actions with various strangers. The alcohol only serves to hold off her descent into madness because she believes she is in control. Her breakdown is exacerbated by the cruelty of Stanley who completely when he rapes her because he has done a horrific act by taking control, exactly what she wanted. The realization that Stanley took all control away from her drives Blanche to complete madness. Stella refuses to believe that Stanley raped Blanche but she does recognize that Blanche needs help and that living in the violent world of Stanley is not healthy for Blanche. Blanche's downward spiral into madness is caused by her own actions and refusal to face reality but the suffocating environment of Stanley leads to her ruination.

Proof Of Forever, on first glance, is Disney material. From the cover to the theme to the entire idea of being thrown back into time courtesy of a Photo Booth. Very idyllic. And that is the frame of mind I went with into this book. And I'm pleased to report, that this book was nothing like the cheese fest or the fluffy cotton candy I expected. It was honest and real and even though it wasn't perfect, it's going to be a book I'm going to remember for a long while. This book is about time travel but it's not your typical Sci-Fi. This book is also technically about four girls and their (mis)adventures, but it's about so many more characters. Basically, Proof Of Forever is not your typical Contemporary so DO NOT judge it that way. The book follows four girls, Tali, Luce, Zoe and Joy. They used to be best friends and they'd sworn to remain best friends after their last summer at Camp Okahatchee. But as these things usually go, life got in the way, and they drifted apart, almost becoming strangers to each other. But two years later, when Joy suggests they all meet up at the reunion night of Camp OK, they grudgingly agree, only to be thrown back into time to two years ago, when they were fifteen; their last summer at the camp. There they realise that they have to do everything the way they'd done it before, so as not to alter their futures. But while their bodies might be fifteen years old, each of them have changed and grown. The book is all about how they deal with their growth and reconcile themselves with the people that they've grown into (or will grow into) and their attempts to go back to their time again. The book was rather predictable where it came to plot--I was sure right away about certain things that would happen and I turned to to be right. This is the precise reason I found myself having a so-so opinion where it came to the story itself. Talking about each character is a little easier, because the end result was predictable (to me, at least), the way they went about their days at the camp weren't. They were not all perfect human beings, and they did a lot of things that I didn't quite agree with, but I suppose it did enhance the whole learning curve that the girls experienced. I'll also admit--the book is rather slow. It's written as third person POV, in four different POVs, and while I'd like to say that each girl had a different, unique voice, that isn't completely true. After a certain point, the characters started to blend into one for me, which sucks, and I had to physically make notes trying to remember who is who. It might be just me, but yeah. That happened. Again, if you do choose to read the book, don't do it for the story itself, meaning the time-travelling part. I found myself enjoying the symbolism behind each character and what they learnt and how they learnt it, and I think you might too. The writing too was not quite my type, but it was perfect for the mood of the book,and that was amazing. It doesn't grab you, but it definitely lures you into continuing to read the book. All in all, as far as "coming-of-age" YA goes, Proof of Forever may be something you might want to try if you're looking for a bitter sweet ending and a couple of cute summer romances! I waffled on this rating a few times. On the one hand, I liked the background we get on Nightingale, on the Folly, Molly, and Peter's father. I liked the new villain and his sinister powers - very intimidating. I'm looking forward to seeing more of him. I liked the follow-up on Lindsey after what happened to her at the end of Midnight Riot - Peter's trepidation about how to relate to her and not lose her trust, despite his horror at the condition of her face. And the revelation that  Lindsey can do magic  opens up some great possibilities for future stories. My problem with this volume can be summed up in one word - Simone. Her story was superfluous, her relationship with Peter went nowhere, and the sex scenes distracted from the actual plot. When there are so many characters that Peter had great chemistry with - Nightingale, Lindsey, his father - why spend so much time on a character whose relationship with Peter is almost entirely physical? Still, I will be reading Whispers Under Ground, abd I hope it follows up on the interesting parts of this volume, and not the boring ones.

I read the Vampire Academy series a while ago, but am doing a re-read with Belle, Bree and Mands. Here are my responses to the questions (they're spoilers! What was your experience reading Vampire Academy for the first time? How did you get into it, and what did you think about it? I read Twilight for the first time right around the time Breaking Dawn came out - I read a book a day and finished them all in the first 4 days of my uni holidays. So I hit the bookstores looking for similar reads, and I found Vampire Academy. I think I also bought the first four books together, binge read them, and then had to wait for books 5 and 6 to come out. What did you think of it upon rereading it? I still liked it!! It was good to get back to where it all started, but it's really weird to read the book knowing how everything changes, especially by the time you get through the Bloodlines books as well. What was your reaction to the characters and did it change from the first time you read it? I loved Lissa and Christian! Seeing them again was awesome. Before I began, I was convinced that I love Rose. I remember that my review of the first two Bloodlines books are heavily focussed on how much I don't like Sydney. So it surprised me to find that I kind of disliked Rose upon re-reading VA. I remember Rose as the Rose from Last Sacrifice, but Rose in VA is extremely selfish and impetuous. She's brash, she doesn't really care about anyone else, and she treats Lissa like she's really dumb or something. What did you think of the relationships in the novel - Rose and Dimitri, Rose and Lissa etc? I really liked Dimitri, but this time around I was disappointed at how obvious he makes his feelings for Rose. Not that I blame him, but he's her TEACHER. I think I'm getting older and seeing things in a new light! Also, Rose treats Lissa like a child. There's a lot of love there, but very little respect (I feel). Rose basically makes decisions for Lissa and is completely over-protective. I felt uncomfortable with how Rose kept important details about her powers and her past from Lissa to "protect" her. It makes me realise that a lot of the hate surrounding Lissa (to do with how she's "weak" or "useless" or a "bitch") probably has to do with how Rose thinks of her. Do you think you'd feel differently about the book if you read it for the first time now? I think I'd like it less. When I read the first time I was caught up in Rose's story, but there's actually a lot in this book that's just plain wrong. Rose taking Lissa away from the school is the STUPIDEST decision she could have made, the furor over the blood-drinking seems juvenile now, as do her interactions with Mia. It's also not obvious from reading this book that things are going to get as awesome, and as dark, as they eventually do. Finally, I read this book with the movie's tone in mind - many folk defend the movie by saying the first book is lighter than the others. And yes, it is, but I think the book still carries a lot of gravitas despite some juvenile seeming scenes.

Okay, I know some people didn't like this book, but I say otherwise. I LOVED IT. The plot-- it was cool. I liked it. The characters-- yes. YES. The writing style-- amazing! And LOGAN. LOGAN. He's so freaking sexy just-- just stop dude. Rachel? She's badass. She's badass and has emotions. Thank you, C.J. Redwine! Thank you for not making Rachel an emotionless bitch. Thank you. I have a few tiny problems, though: 1) There were so many deaths. I mean, sure, I guess they were necessary for the plot, but it made my heart hurt too much. I mean, it's not really a problem, but ;-; 2) The beginning was a little rushed. So many things were happening it was a little bit difficult to keep track. 3) The world building. Okay, I know this is Dystopia, and I know Dystopian Worlds can be annoyingly annoying. Defiance's world wasn't really ANNOYING, it was just, well, confusing. If they had this new fangled technology, why do they not have proper plumbing where hot water comes immediately? Why do they need to fill up their bathtubs with BUCKETS of boiled water? Why is there a "Cursed One" anyways? How was humanity able to create a giant wall without the Cursed One coming in and stuff? If the Cursed One can sense people and sound a stuff, then why didn't they just go smash into the wall? See, I think the major problem in this book is the Cursed One. It's really hard to understand. I'm going to talk a little bit more about the characters. Specifically Logan. Okay, I understand why some people hate Logan. He DID say and think some mean stuff about Rachel, but that was the beginning! One thing about Logan and Rachel, though, is that the romance felt rushed. WHEN DID HE EVEN START LIKING HER? I enjoyed the romance though. Logan can be sexy when he wants to be. That kiss scene was super dramatic, though. I was mad at Logan for hating Willow and what was his name again her brother. They did NOTHING wrong and Logan pretty much dissed them. But his protectiveness for Rachel was really sweet and stuff. And he was absolutely HILARIOUS. Who the heck even repeats the Periodic Table to cope with pain? And when the times he was speechless about Rachel's beauty-- absolutely HILARIOUS. And when Willow said that he should just say that he wanted to "kiss her senseless" and he just almost immediately said "give us a couple of hours" and immediately started kissing Rachel, I almost died laughing. And blushing. I'm like spontaneously going back and forth. Okay, I make no sense. This book actually WAS nice. It was extremely detailed, and it gave me an adrenaline rush. It's extremely easy to hate the Commander, and it's extremely easy to just fall in love with the Rachel x Logan ship. THIS REVIEW IS ALL OVER THE PLACE I'M SORRY.

4 Stars for Fern and Ambrose An ARC was provided for me through NetGalley in exchange for an honest review. This book is so beautiful but also so sad. If you think that the title of this book is not making much sense, don't worry it will after reading this book, tho I have to admit that it is a unique and slightly strange title. When I started that book I haven't read the blurb and that's why I thought it's a typical sweet and fluffy book about first love, but I was so wrong. It was about love yes, but it also was about growing up, learning to live with terrible circumstances, thriving after bad accidents and learning to love yourself. The writing was beautiful, but there were so many sad and terrible scenes, that I wanted to scream at Amy why she is doing this to be. Luckily there were enough sweet scenes that compensated the bad scenes. Fern, one of our lovely protagonists, is the typical shy and sweet nerd girl, who doesn't think she is pretty. But she is a wonderful and lovely character with a incredibly good heart. Ambrose is the typical good looking popular guy, who is sporty and actually a pretty soft guy, but that doesn't mean he can't be a douchebag. Bailey has Duchenne muscular dystrophy, but his deadly illness doesn't stop him from being a funny optimistic guy, who enjoys his life. The story is predictive at times, our ugly duckling turns into a beautiful swan and Ambrose totally falls for Fern. The blurb alone also tells us pretty much what will happen in the book and makes it even more predictable. But that doesn't mean that the book gets boring or that I didn't enjoy it. Ambrose and Fern together were pretty cute. But they also anooyed me a little bit. They were constantly unsure about their feelings for each other and it was a long time a mix between kissing and flirting but still not being together because they were both guarded. While it's realistic that way and better than insta love, I was still frustated. One scene in the book was so sad and unfair and I'm really sad that something like this probably happens every day in real life. I mean the scene in which Becker hits Rita, leaves her in the car, leaves Bailey drown and then runs away. I knew that Bailey would die in this book, but I never thought that his life would end because some asshole left him to die. I was so so glad that Rita is ok, and that she and her son could get away from her abusive husband. I couldn't believe it when he came back and hurt Fern badly, because apparently he didn't get that he has already done enough damage. It's really upsetting that bastards like him are not just a product of fantasy. The end of this book was beautiful, but a bit rushed. And I like the bonus material at the end of the book. They named their son 'Bailey'. *sobs*

Love transcended all of this, apparently. Love transcended breath, eczema, fear of sex, and an imbalance in physical appearance. If love was real, then these bodily, human details could seem insignificant. I really enjoyed this book. This book is perfect I did not want it to end. ... she sat in a corner on the unswept floor and attempted to position herself so she would appear unobtrusive yet not pathetic, which was a difficult balance My favourite character is Jules because in some ways, I identify with her. I can relate with her. In the beginning, she is jealous, petty, self-absorbed, and obsessed with comparing her life to that of her friends. Nobody tells you how long you should keep doing something before you give up forever. The Interestings is a book that follows a group of six children who meet at a camp for kids to explore their creativity. Four of them remain close friends even after camp. The camp has mostly rich kids, but there are some "scholarship kids". Jules and Ethan are scholarship kids. The other four are Ash, Jonah, Goodman and Cindy. A first kiss, Jules had thought, was supposed to magnetize you to the other person; the magnet and the metal were meant to fuse and melt on contact into a sizzling brew of silver and red The story doesn't just end with the kids as teenagers, but we follow their lives through adulthood, marriage and having kids. Wolitzer does a good job of writing a story that is truthful and mostly accurate to what life is like for teenagers. There might have been a little exaggeration with the ease of access to drugs etc. The story is told mostly from Jules' perspective but sometimes we see things from Ethan and Jonah's perspectives. ... by designating something new, you are already hastening its oldness I love how she describes the relationships - friendships, romances, family. The awkwardness of teenage years; trying desperately to blend in with people; feeling inadequate or incapable in "their" midst. The book made me laugh, think, question, wonder, and sometimes, it even shocked me. Sex at twenty-two wasn't college sex at eighteen, which carried with it a freight of insecurities, nerve endings, and shame. Sex at twenty-two also wasn't self-sex at twelve, which was just about being quiet and discreet in your narrow bed and thinking how strange it was that you could feel this way just by doing this. She writes things that people like to not talk about in a simple, yet humorous way. The story flows well and you're never left confused about what's going on. You can't actually dislike any of the characters. They all have redeemable qualities in all of the bad. Part of the beauty of love was that you didn't need to explain it to anyone else. You could refuse to explain. With love apparently, you didn't necessarily feel the need to explain anything at all. As a teenager, I understand the points in this book. Because, some of the questions the book raises are the things I ask myself from time to time: "Who will I be when I grow older?" "What's in the world for me?" "Will my dreams and hopes come true?" "How much would my life be different/easier if I had wealthier parents?" I really wasn't expecting a very thought provoking book but this book surprised me and I'd definitely recommend it to anyone. But she knew that you didn't always have to marry your soulmate, and you didn't even have to marry an Interesting. You didn't always need to be the dazzler, the firecracker, the one who cracked evryone up, or made everyone want to sleep with you, or be the one who wrote and starred in the play that got the standing ovation. You could cease to be obsessed with the idea of being interesting

2015 Reading Challenge: a book a friend recommended This was wonderful. I could say it was great or fun or addictive, but somehow none of those words would be sufficient. I like the word wonderful. It's soft and sweet, it makes me smile. Which is exactly like this book. I get why people here and there are comparing it to a Sarah Dessen novel; it does feel really similar. Except, when I usually don't rate Sarah Dessen books over 3 stars (there's just always something holding me back from higher ratings despite my enjoyment of them, I don't know what it is) this one is an easy 4. It's one of those books of which the writing style and the imagery make me wax nostalgic about a dozen different things. About my own childhood and adolescence, about the nature of friendships, about little beach towns along the Pacific coast, etc. Which will probably not make sense to anyone who isn't me, as it's a very personal thing and different for everyone, but I LOVE when a book manages to bring that very specific feeling to the surface. These teenagers all feel like people I would've been friends with in high school, or would've wanted to be friends with, in any case. They had to grow up faster than most kids their age, because of what happened to their friend when they were 8, and maybe that's why they never felt like the 'typical teenager' to me. And Drew. Man, I love Drew. On a different note, this book is also really female-friendly. To give but one example of many: "Oliver, seriously," I [Emmy] said. "Ignore them. Please don't do something stupid like avenge my honor or whatever." He finally looked away. "I'm not," he said. "You can probably avenge yourself much better than I could, anyway." There's a couple of references like this, and it just caught my eye every time. Which, come to think of it, it's kind of sad that this is a thing that's rare enough to be so noticeable to me, but it is. I liked that Oliver was conflicted about his dad. That seems like a very natural response to me. He was always going to be torn up about it, naturally, but the way it was revealed that Oliver was the one who'd put the wheels in motion for the police to find him, while at the same time making sure his dad wouldn't be there to get arrested, was well-done and well-handled. The only thing I wish had gone differently, is the conversation between Emmy and her parents. I wanted that to come about naturally, instead of them having to find out through the guidance counselor. Obviously I get why she kept putting it off, but not telling them before having an open house at her high school wasn't the smartest idea. Aside from that, I really had no complaints whatsoever. I was also pleasantly surprised by the ending. I knew Emmy would end up going off to college, but I thought the goodbye scene between her and Oliver was extremely well done. It wasn't too tearful or overly melodramatic - or full of promises between two 18-year-olds that leave you wondering how long it's going to take them to start breaking those promises. No. It's simple and sweet, emotional in a believable way. You're left thinking that they're going to be okay, that despite the distance they'll figure things out and always end up with each other. Because they're Emmy and Oliver. And I love that. Had I started this book on the weekend, I'm pretty sure I would've read it in one sitting. It put me in a good mood and had me smiling for most of the day. Wonderful.
It was an OK book, but I don't think I'll be continuing with the series.

I found myself quite pulled into the book and rather enjoyed the couple hours it took me to read it. The only thing I wasn't a big fan of was the fact that Mattie was so guy obsessed. She thought pretty much every male character in the book was cute and found herself falling for all of them. At least that's what it seemed like to me.
