The Healer's Apprentice is one of those rare and special books that promises to be amazing the moment you set eyes on them and then follows through in spades! I enjoy historicals and romantic adventures so, needless to say, this book was right up my alley. It's a realistic retelling, loosely based on (or should I say inspired by), a popular fairy tale but I wasn't aware of that when I started reading and, even after I knew, it took me a good chunk of the book to figure out which story. I really liked that aspect - that it was such a unique take on the tale that I had no idea where it was going to go. Almost all of the characters are likeable - even one who ends up being a cad was rather likeable on the surface. He reminded me of Willoughby from Sense & Sensibility - someone you pity because they had such potential. The romance was well-developed and it hit my absolute favorite trope when it comes to romance with simmering attraction that is always held back due to various obstacles. While not a magical fantasy, it touched upon those spots by containing unique spiritual warfare. It's a tricky subject and I appreciated the effort though I did have some frustrations with the way a few things went. Namely, I do not believe Christians can be demon possessed and I believe the Holy Spirit protects us from such attacks. While Rose was never possessed or attacked outright (as it was more of a fear attack? ), I had niggles over that whole situation. As for the big bad guy - whatever he sprinkled on Rose didn't bother me too much. But I didn't like that her prayers & the prayers of Frau Geruscha didn't drive the demons from her room in the first place and then that she was so terrified that she couldn't even pray later and Hamlin had to save the day. And why was Frau Geruscha telling him what to pray? Didn't he already know? And why didn't she just pray herself? The man's gotta do it? All in all, a highly recommended read

*sigh* This was a tough one for me. Objectively, I know it was good. Really, really good. But I wasn't in the mood for this book and as a result, I slogged through it and got irrationally annoyed way more than I should have. My heart wants to give it 3 stars but logic prevails and I'll give it the 4 stars I know deep down that it deserves. But I'm still going to bitch about the things that annoyed me! Too many POVs. If your story is told from one POV, great. Two POVs is awesome. Three POVs...okay, I'll allow it. But 4+ POVs and you're just being annoying. Especially when some of those POVs are from characters so minor that they barely have a personality let alone a reason to have a POV (Lenos, I'm looking at you). Too many times, the chapter changes/POV changes were unnecessary because it just regurgitated the action at the end of the previous chapter with not enough new perspective added to warrant repeating what another character just experienced. AND SPEAKING OF LENOS. I really thought the author was going to go somewhere with him, what with all the mentions of how he was wary of Lila and her powers and such. I was sure it was going to come out that he was Lila's father (or even Kell's) but nope. He was just cannon fodder. AND SPEAKING OF THE MYSTERY BEHIND KELL'S AND LILA'S ORIGINS. Those storylines went no where. (PLEASE OH PLEASE DON'T TELL ME THERE'S ANOTHER BOOK IN THE SERIES.) Why were there so many mentions of the knife with Kell's real initials on them? And Maris telling him she'd been the one to put the memory spell on him so that he couldn't remember where he came from and giving him the paper with (supposedly) the secret of his early life. Just to drive home the fact that all he wanted was to belong to the Maresh family and didn't care where he came from? WE ALREADY KNEW THAT. And Lila and her mysterious glass eye, which was obviously removed to hide the fact that she was Antari. But why? And by whom? There was no resolution. (I half-suspected it to be revealed that OOOPS Lila & Kell were brother & sister which....ewwwww....but nope, nada, their mysterious backgrounds were dropped.) There was also no resolution to all the talk about how the Veskans and Faroans viewed Kell's powers and how he was quite possibly in danger because of them. But it came to nothing. Assassination attempt by the Sea Serpents notwithstanding. I also felt everything was a little bit anti-climatic. Holland's death was no surprise. He had a lot to atone for and a death wish. I knew poor, precious Hastra was a Dead Man Walking in book 2 when he showed himself to be TOO PURE FOR THIS WORLD. It was pretty obvious that King Maxim was going to die as soon as he started concocting his (flop) spell. You knew either the Veskans or the Faroans were going to turn traitor and while the author made Lord Sol-An-Ar seem the more likely candidate, I wasn't shocked when it turned out to be Prince Col and Princess Cora. The Queen's death was a mild surprise but I barely blinked when it happened because she didn't have much of a personality until this book. You knew Osaron would be defeated and all the mains would end up with a happy ending. And then there's Lila. I absolutely DESPISE the trope in which someone finds out they have magical powers and are almost immediately adept (if not THE BESTEST) at wielding those powers almost immediately. Her success in the tournament after only a crash course in magic from Alucard annoyed me in book 2 but her being almost on level with Kell and Holland (both of whom had been trained for years) in this book was eyeroll-inducing. And OF COURSE she was the only Antari to come out of the final battle virtually unscathed. Holland ended up powerless and Kell ended up with less powers which caused him pain to even use. Also, this book was too long by about 100 pages. All the plot threads that came to nothing could've been dropped, along with some of the POVs and the constant repeating of what just happened in the previous chapter. The first 75% of the book dragged. So you're probably wondering what I did about the book. Well, the writing and world building is really great. And the final battle was ASTOUNDING and written in vivid, dynamic prose. (I would LOVE to see what a really great director could do visually with that battle on screen.)

I received this book to review for the ReadIt&Reap program in the ShutUp&Read  group. Thanks to the mods and the author for providing this book for us to read. Every time I start a new book/series that involves vampires I worry that I'm about to waste time reading the same story I've read so many times before. I love vampire stories, but they need to bring something fresh to the table, and be somewhat original for me to actually enjoy them. This book did that. The first few pages of this book I struggled with. It quickly seemed like a story that I felt disinterested in, because it was the typical boy meets girl story. In a matter of two days the main characters become obsessed in love with each other, and I almost stopped right there. I kept reading because Camille was a genuinely interesting character, in my opinion. She has been abused, betrayed, abandoned, and more by people she loved and trusted. She was a broken woman, fleeing her problems, and just trying to get away from it all to live a normal life. Quite a relatable scenario in the sense that most woman don't actually flee the country to get away from our problems, but sometimes we would like to! This author definitely has skills in character development. At first, we are introduced to this fragile, damaged woman, and after she finds out about the vampires she transforms into a sarcastic, more confident person. That's also right after her ex just tried to kill her in her sleep! She's still drawn and attracted to Gavin, but this time she's not just jumping into things so quickly. She demands answers. Gavin was okay as a character. I didn't love him or hate him. He was just nothing special in comparison to all of the men I read about each day. Audrey and Gabe were great. I really liked them. The plot itself did go beyond expectations, and I was happy for that. Introducing real issues such as physical and emotional abuse to readers who may or may not know how that feels can be tough. I feel the author did a superb job with this. The adventure of going through Samira to enter Amaranth was exciting. I'm glad that loser, Andrew, got what he deserved! It a nutshell this is a pretty short, fast paced paranormal story that does keep you interested until the very end. It starts off rocky, but finds it's footing rather quickly. By the end of this book you will really want to know what's going to happen next. Very entertaining, enjoyable read, that I would recommend to all paranormal fans of any age. The quality of writing is high A wonderful start to an exciting series I look forward to continuing. 3.5 stars. This is just a side note, but I love that Breaking Benjamin was mentioned. Loveeee them! One more sidenote: the cover is gorgeous!

October "Toby" Daye, is half human/half Daoine Fae, mother of Gillian, P.I. Unfortunately, her better half and daughter don't know about the Fae and when she goes missing for 14 yrs and is presumed dead, then suddenly reappears without a believable story, her private life goes to hell. (This isn't a spoiler as it all happens in the first couple of pages). This is a great adventure tale about the Fae living uneasily beside us humans and the changelings that try to straddle both sides of the fence. There is no pretty, pretty fairy stuff happening here, it is basically all hard core magic, violence, a bit of politics and murder, with the odd sprinkling of nuances and friends that Toby didn't realize she had. So, this 1st book is about the murder of Evening Winterose, an old friend of Tobys' and the Binding she placed on Toby to find the killers. Looking forward to the next book.

I'm usually quite late in reading books with a lot of hype surrounding them, but this one stuck out to me when I was looking for a small book to carry around in my bag. It did not stay in my bag for long. I read the majority of this in one sitting - there just never seemed to be a right place to put it down. It was a beautiful story and immensely sad. I found myself connecting with Mia on so many levels. She has so much to live for but has also lost so much, questioning whether to live or die at times seemed like an impossible to choice to make. This book made me consider what my choice would be. Would I stay or go if faced with this situation. I honestly don't know. Would I want to choose? I wonder if there are some people who this does happen to - people that hover between this world and the next and get to decide whether to live or die. Are they the lucky ones? I don't know the answers to any of the questions this story raised for me, but it gave me a lot to think about when I went to bed after I'd finished it.
Fascinating world with interesting characters.

I don't really know what to say about this book. One the one hand, I always enjoyed myself while reading it, but on the other I recognize that it is flawed. The main flaw, imo, isn't in Rothfuss's ideas, but in the need to spend 100 pages on any one of them. Faelurian wasn't a terrible idea, but 65 pages of Faelurian was. Tracking the bandits wasn't a bad idea, but 100 pages of slowing trudging through the woods before the climax of that story line was. The whole Adem story line wasn't bad, but again, it was too long. In short, all the stories were too long. GRRM can get away with going into excruciating detail because he has an immense world with 500 different characters, so if you ever get bogged down in a single story line, at least you'll know there are 6-10 chapters before you have to return to Davos (fml, Davos...). Rothfuss tries to go into the same amount of detail with only one character, and at the end of the day, it doesn't work out. I wonder how on earth this story could have a satisfying ending while keeping the same pace, especially given the established 3-day retelling structure, and what we know about Kvothe and other events in the present We know that all of the bad guys are still around in the present, and we know that the world is going to shit, and we know that Kvothe is like a wounded little puppy with all his super powers locked up in the trunk at the end of his bed. Given the three day structure, this is either where we are going to leave him at the end of the story, or Rothfuss will have to break the 3-day structure and advance into the presnt . I agree with a lot of the flaws pointed out in some of the other popular reviews, but at the end of the day, I was and am caught up in the story, and flaws aside, that is really all I can ask for from a book.

This was an excellent second installment to the Finishing School Series! I thoroughly enjoyed Etiquette & Espionage and, were it written by anyone other than the brilliant Miss Carriger, I would worry that Curtsies & Conspiracies wouldn't live up to expectations. However it excelled, going above and beyond anything I could dream up! Sophronia was just as I remembered her and the adventures that she and her friends undertake are as just gripping and amusing as those they encountered in E&E. On top of old friends (and enemies, if that's not too strong a word) this novel also introduces some new faces. Watching how and where they fit, as you try to untangle the mysteries surrounding a certain young lady of quali-tay, is pure entertainment. More than anything, it was a treat to be reacquainted my beloved Bumbersnoot! And with dear Lord Akeldama! This was a pure joy to read and I cannot wait to get started on Waistcoats and Weaponry! P.S. Are these not just the best book titles you ever had the pleasure of reading?

I expected to like this book, and, you know, I did like it. I liked the premise, liked the plot, liked becoming immersed in the lives of these characters and following them for decades. I appreciated the gentle humor and the mild intrigue related to the Goodman storyline. I thought the cover was fabulous. But as far as I'm concerned, this book had two problems, one minor and one more serious. The minor problem for me was Julie (excuse me, Jules) Jacobson. If you've read the book, surely you remember Jules. How could you forget her? She's just sooo great, totally worthy of the undying devotion of her cooler, more successful friends. And so incredibly funny! Didn't she just have you in stitches the entire time you were reading? No? Me neither. The many wonderful qualities ascribed to Jules by her friends were not even slightly evident to me. My Goodreads friend Glenn astutely pointed out that Jules, in contrast to her wealthy, privileged friends, is probably ordinary on purpose, to give the reader someone to identify with. I agree with this point, but I still think Jules could have been just a wee bit more interesting, and the fact that she isn't--the fact that the way she's described doesn't match the way she comes across--is a pretty big flaw in this novel, at least to me. Things got even more ridiculous when Jules decided to go back and run Spirit-in-the-Woods . I mean, come on. What's more pathetic than a fiftysomething still pining for her teenage years? I was immediately put in mind of Tommy Sherman, former jock who came back to Lawndale High to relive his glory days, hitting on the cheerleaders and accusing Daria of being a Misery Chick. And once you get that image in your head, just try to get rid of it. But my dislike of Jules wasn't a dealbreaker. Honestly, disliking a character while reading can be kind of fun (particularly if she makes you think of Daria). No, my main problem with this book was that I just didn't feel emotionally invested. When misfortunes and tragedies befell these characters, I didn't really feel anything. In spite of all the time I spent with these people, I just didn't really care about them--until the end, when Ethan is diagnosed with cancer , but by then I was so used to not caring that I actually got angry that the book was finally making me care. And, in fact, I now realize I didn't really care about the characters in The Uncoupling, either--although interestingly, I did care about the characters in Sleepwalking, Wolitzer's very first novel. Maybe early Wolitzer is more for me? I'll investigate this further, but as for The Interestings, while it was (wait for it) interesting, it just didn't rock my world.

SQUEEEEEEEEEEEE!!!! So, um... wow! I'm a bit lost for words, because... Can you imagine? I nearly missed this wonderful story. *shakes head at self* From the very beginning Curtis and da Silva had me smile. Let's just say, insta-love this is not ;-) I won't give much away, but it was just so lovely how annoyance turned into desire, turned into feelings. I felt that their scenes had a lot of depths. I highly recommend this book, but since I was so late to the party, I'm guessing everyone has already read it ;-) 4.5 stars What finally pushed me over the edge to give this book a real chance was Alexis Hall's post here. So, if you need any more convincing, have a look, but beware of some spoilers. My friend EE also just wrote their review, which would have convinced me to read the book, too, had they been a bit earlier. It's really damn good.

Overall, this book was just amazing. I mean it. As you're reading, you get to glimpse into many people's lives and you get to know these people in only a few pages (trust me, they're enough!) And it's very hard to believe that this is a work of fiction, because it's so wonderfully written and so realistic that you would think it's referring to real facts. Every story, however short, managed to struck me, to surprise me and to move me. Each story could give me something I would never expect and meet all my expectations at the same time. I particularly loved A Perfect Day for Bananafish, where we get to know about Seymour Glass' death (I read all of Salinger's other works before reading this one, so I actually knew a lot about the Glass family upfront) ; For Esme -- With Love and Squalor; Pretty Mouth and Green My Eyes, which had me very puzzled at the end. In fact, it was never made clear if Lee was actually sleeping with Arthur's wife or not, since Arthur, who was supposedly being cheated on, stated his wife had just come back home at the end of the book, when the reader perfectly knows that the woman who one would assume is Arthur's wife is lying right beside Lee. The doubt here is if the woman lying next to Lee isn't Arthur's wife and--provided she is--, if Arthur is lying to Lee so he doesn't worry too much or if he is because he's understood Lee is his wife's lover. We'll never know and deciding which option is the most likely one is totally up to you. Along with telling you something about the characters, this choice is going to tell you something about yourself! I also loved Teddy. The ending of this one tale is as open to interpretation as the one in Pretty Mouth and Green My Eyes. But there's more to it. Because it's the last tale of the book, it makes the whole book a ring composition, to me. It was really engrossing to compare the different religious doctrines in Salinger's works and the one in Teddy was probably referring to Buddhism--unlike the one Franny is so bonded to. What they all have in common, though, is a vision of a reality detached from all concrete connotations and related to a more abstract, spiritual world. And it doesn't take religion to share this vision! There are so many points throughout the book that can inspire you in a number of different ways, along with offering some wonderful leisure. One of the best books I've read. This is sadly the only book I still had to read by Salinger and I'm kind of sad that I can't enjoy any more of his works. I'm actually more than "kind of sad". But I'm sure that re-reading books such as Salinger's can be everlastingly revealing and fascinating. I only wish that I could thank Salinger himself for giving me so much through his books.

I finished this a couple of weeks ago and haven't gotten around to writing the review, so now I have to remember all of my feelings. And there were a lot of them! This book is Kate Daniels cranked to 100. There was almost an air of the ridiculous in the juxtaposition between HILARIOUS moments )Kate naked except for her underwear and a tutu, doing ballet on a tiny stage; Ascanio trying to counsel the deputy not to quit; everything with Roman ever)  and truly terrible things happening (Kate nearly losing her own personality, either due to the magic or as a result of her stroke in the last book; the whole thing with the woman she stole from her father; the fight with Jim) . It was a crazy roller coaster. I kept having to stop the audiobook when hilarious things were happening, because I knew that if I stopped when awful shit was going on I'd have trouble picking it up again. I felt like there was some stuff that maybe got cut from the book that I would love to read. Like, we never got an explanation as to why Barabbas was dressed like a rogue in the battle, and where he ran off to when Kate said "go". TBH I just want an entire other book just about that battle so I could see all the things. I wanted to see Desandra kill a mammoth! Also,  BARABBAS AND CHRISTOPHER, OMG MY LITTLE SHIPPER'S HEART GAAAAAAAH . I am sad that there are relationships that are never going to be the same. That kind of thing is hitting me kind of hard right now because of IRL stuff. I always have trouble watching people I love fight with each other, it's worse than fighting with someone myself, and I just got so invested in these relationships that it nearly broke me when they started to fall apart. I cried a lot. At work. It was a problem. But now I have to wait, like, ten months for the next one. I'll never make it...

Initial Impressions 2/11/17: WHEW, I made it! I listened to the audiobook and it was quite the long journey, but I am all about Michael Kramer so it's totally worth it! It took me over a month (really!?) but I did it! I think my one... "let down" so to speak (I'm not really let down but I can't come up with a better word right now) of the book is that ALL of the reveals were in the end. So much happened in the last few chapters that it was excitement overload and I would have loved a bit more of that throughout the whole book to keep excitement levels high, but that seems to be an evolution that happens in Sanderson's later works rather than his earlier ones. My Sanderson theory that the theme of pretty much everyone of his books seems to be something along the lines of (possible spoiler for pretty much any Sanderson book) "the gods are among us"  seems to hold true! I figured it was coming, especially considering (more Sanderson series spoilers) everything that I learned (and what all you other people learned who read the Mistborn series before anything else) in the Mistborn series started to really delve into creation theories and history and how all of the Cosmere is connected. I really like it though! I'm catching on to it so it's not as much of a shock or twist to see that coming in the ending of THE WAY OF KINGS (well, I guess it kiiiiind of started that way too) but I'm so, so, so anxious to learn more about it! The characters in this book were fantastic! I LOVED Kaladin and for some reason I was surprised to see what his role was throughout this whole book. I was expecting a Kelsier sort of situation where his history involved a hardship and he ended up with that as a shadow of his past but really his present ends up being one of his greatest hardships and he's not on anyone's favorable side throughout the book (until he takes matters into his own hands and starts to work on those leadership skills). I basically fell a little bit in love with him and I can't wait to see what his future holds because it looks... bright *snicker* I also love noble and wise and apparently super important Dalinar. Obviously he's important as a main character but I loved what his fate ended up being and naturally, I can't wait to see what happens to him in the second book and where things go from here. Readers are able to guess at what is happening to him throughout the book but I'm not quite sure what it REALLY means yet and why it's happening to Dalinar. I wasn't the BIGGEST fan of Shallan but that's also because I didn't really care for her narrator in the audio (not that I have issues with Kate Reading (also how is THAT for an audiobook narrator's last name!?) but meh. Female narrator. And I love Michael Kramer. A lot.) so I didn't get into her character as much. I actually find myself not really liking a lot of Sanderson's female characters except for Vin. I don't dislike them but I just find the male characters much more interesting and apparently prefer their story lines much better. I think part of it is because the women are figuring things out (you go, gals!) and the men are in the action so there's just a bit more draw to some of those action-based scenes. I'm also enjoying the new world of Roshar and exploring everything that is has to offer! The cultures/races/people are interesting (especially with some recent reveals) and I love learning about all of the different people and places in Brandon Sanderson's worlds. Book two looks like it'll explore that history and creation even more which is totally my fantasy addiction and the reason I can't put Sanderson books down! I haven't felt as connected to a world since Scadrial but they're all quite interesting and I have a feeling I'll be learning much more about Roshar soon! I don't know why I thought this series was only three books so there goes my plan to binge read them all this year....... Well, I guess I can still binge read them (as long as Oathbringer is still on track for later 2017) but I just won't be finishing the series when I do. Why do I do this to myself??? I'm in the middle of too many Sanderson series. Or rather, he seems to trap us in his series (okay, I'm not really that upset about being in the middle of all of his books) and won't let us go! Just the waaaaait though. I'm so glad I was able to binge Mistborn because this is going to be a long journey with The Stormlight Archive!

An unabashed five stars for my old friend Celaena Sardothien, whose story is a little different but whose soul remains the same. I was a great fan of the original "Queen of Glass" on Fictionpress, so yes, I know what's changed and what happened next in the original. Finding out where these changes will take us and how that affects the outcome excites me. "Every little movement has a meaning of its own," as the song goes. This was solid fantasy YA before fantasy YA got swallowed by the Paranormal/SF/F YA monster movement. It's the long-lost second cousin of the genre (three times removed) and well worth the read. The elements are there -- magic, a love triangle, a strong heroine -- but they're not tropes; they're legitimate pieces of what Maas wrote. She takes what we think we're going to see and twists. Celaena herself isn't the average plain-Jane who scorns fashion and angsts all over the bleeding place. She eats a pound and a half of candy because it's there! She gets a puppy! She's friends with men AND women! And her background is hinted at, but she doesn't make a huge deal out of it. She's here, she's now, and she's on a specific hero's journey. Dorian and Chaol treat her well, which I must say is refreshing given the proliferation of asshole love interests. I even feel sorry for the villain when she gets hers, and wonder if one change is to her fate . Throne of Glass takes me back to what fantasy was when I was in high school a decade ago (oh, how time flies). This is what I aspired to be as a writer. This is what I hoped was going to hit shelves. This made it, finally, onto my bookshelf and I am so proud that it has.

The Book is extremely descriptive of its plot, setting, whether important or unimportant. It'll describle it in a way that recreates a vivid movie of its own in your mind. I think OASIS, part of the book, even if it's not an original creation, is a pretty relatable one too. Basically a virtual reality interface (via retina goggles) to a gaming/reality system , we have mages, monsters, robots, space opera, all sorts of chaotic destruction that every loyal science fiction or fantasy fan would ache for, which makes me wonder: Why is the rating 4/5 instead of 5/5? Well, let's start with the small irritable things like frequent references "by name" and "by explanation", to each and every writer, book, movie, anime, audio etc - especially in the 80s, simply to serve plot purpose (while the book is in the 2040s) . Sometimes, I feel like I'm reading a lot of names, can I skip to the next paragraph and get done with the riddle? Which brings me to the riddle  - this is a minor issue, but an issue nevertheless. There was nothing wrong with it. But, initially during the hunt , I felt like solving the riddle , but knowing that the riddles were just for the character no matter what , was a huge bummer. Bringing me to the final part - because of the whole descriptive nature of the story, did anyone think this was a bit DRAGGING? A really important thought IMO is, never write a line/scene in a book/TV Show/film UNLESS it is relevant to the storyline. (eg: the sword exchange after Shoto meets Wade informing him of Daito's death was never used in the story) Which also brings me to the ending - I was kinda "hoping" for a Titanic ending , or someone destroying OASIS after saving it - bla bla bla , instead of the war  - but then, it wouldn't be apt for a movie... In the end, I think this would make an amazing movie. But only if in the hands of a good director, talented cast and with a hopefully high budget - let's see in 2017.

I finished this book a few nights ago. Had I reviewed it then my negativity would have been much more emphatic. PLEASE NOTICE: THERE WILL BE SPOILERS FOR THE FIRST TWO VOLUMES IN THIS REVIEW. I WILL BE ASSUMING THAT YOU HAVE READ The Maze Runner AND The Scorch Trials. PLEASE BE AWARE OF THIS BEFORE YOU GO ON. So why as high as a 2 if I'm very disappointed in the book? It/they does/do tie their plot line up...mostly. There are times in each book (the first two more than the third) where they are interesting and draw you in. Sadly on the whole the simple logical inconsistencies and plot holes outweigh anything good...for me. Repeat that's for me. I know some will and do like these more than me. I will relate my thoughts here and leave it to them to do the same in their reviews. This series in some ways could be said to harken back to Lemony Snicket as the entire trilogy could be called a "series of unfortunate events" (or maybe more accurately "A Series of Evil, Planned yet Pointless Events") . It's more accurate however to harken back to Roger Ebert (see Roger Ebert's Glossary of Movie Terms: http://academic.sun.ac.za/forlang/ber...). He came up with the term, "A Dead Teenager Movie". Well these are "Dead Teenager Books". The plots of the first two can pretty much be summed up with, you start with a large number of teenagers and slowly kill them off." Added to this the plot device of dropping obscure pointless clues that eventually lead you to the idea that all this death by slow torturous means is somehow tied in with the world being in "catastrophe" and that what's being done to the teenagers is somehow tied in with finding a cure for a world spanning plague. By the time you get to the third entry to this mess you're simply hoping that the writer will fill in the blanks and explain how putting two large groups of young people through hell err this idiocy will in some way bring about a cure... well he tries. He gives us the story of the group (WICKED) behind this "genius" plan (that's sarcasm just in case you're not sure), the idea behind it, the purpose... I'll give a little on that in a spoiler below. Bottom line? Well I think you probably already know my take on it from the use of the word "idiocy". My thoughts are...what kind of maniacs came up with this idea?? Then of course there's a main character Thomas (we were lead to believe early on that we might have 2 main characters)... The decisions Thomas makes in this book are flatly incomprehensible. He also develops the disease that I've seen so often in YA books. He becomes dense as a locust fence post, as thick as frozen pea soup. In short he suddenly (in spite of being supposedly on of the smartest in the land) can't see what the reader will have spotted two chapters ago. In short (if it's not too late to say "in short") while the writer ties the story up and gives an acceptable ending...sort of, this is a disappointing ending to a series I held out/struggled through to see where it was going. A strained and questionable 2 stars. The whole idea behind all this manufactured misery is that the "plague" ( of course released by the government after the huge solar flares to "control population") attacks the brain. Some people are immune to the effects. Somehow neither do they pass the sickness along. They have the disease, they just don't pass it along, yeah go figure. The "big wigs" of all the governments of the world decide they need to know why the immunes don't lose their minds...how to do this? Why put implants in their brains (one of which allows WICKED to take control of said brain) put them through horrific trials, kill them off one, a few, or several at a time, destroy their ability to trust one another...or anyone. Then study the patterns in their brain. Yeah, real logical. (And who came up with a population control plague that they didn't know everything about BEFORE THEY RELEASED IT INTO THE WORLD'S POPULATION????????? AND without a cure or even a vaccine. Bright huh?) Then there's Thomas who decides to rebel against WICKED but also consistently refuses to have the memories of his life back. When information is important, when they need to know all they can know Thomas is afraid he'll change his mind if he remembers everything...so he insists on staying in the dark. Then there's Teresa who looks to be a sort of co-protagonist...but isn't. I'm sure that in some cases from the first book young men began to identify with Thomas and young women with Teresa, except we sort of dump her here. She turns out to be expendable...and is expended to make room for a different "love interest". I could go on but the bottom line is the book(s)/book fails to live up to it's (their) potential, including the ending which has a rabbit out the hat feeling to it. Don't really care for it, don't really hate it...barely 2 stars.

Best way to boil down this story would be to say it's a romance (YA-ish... it gets pretty R rated sometomes) meets Schrodinger's cat meets that 90's TV show "Sliders." It was an interesting concept to have the character moving between dimensions and inhabiting new worlds and lives. However, it does bring up the moral/ethical issue of "inhabiting" another person. Essentially they are hijacking the consciousness of their other selves in different dimensions. The version of them there just fades into the background. However, the current versions are somewhat aware of the the other version is doing in their body, like twilight sleep. O and RUSSIA. The rest of this will be blocked for spoilers. There is a lot of controversy of the sex scene between Marguerite and Paul. I understand that she fell in love with the Paul in that dimension and when she had sex with him, she was acting on that love. The scene would have been a beautiful moment between the two IF SHE WAS IN HER OWN BODY AT THE TIME! It's kinda like she raped herself by proxy and deceived Paul because he thought he was with his Marguerite. So basically I'm really rather conflicted about the scene. The science was a little hokey. Basically a magic necklace allows you to go to other dimensions and also does a bunch of other stuff. Its able to work because reasons... Yes, I do see the irony in pointing out that the science was unbelievable in a "science-fiction" novel. I bought into the mythos and went along with it. Just wanted there to be some more concreate reasoning besides "It works cause I say so." I really didn't see all the twists coming at the end. Overall, it was a pretty good book. Not amazing, but pretty good.

Monster Stepbrother was a good book. I think that my expectations were a little too big and so it kind of felt lacking. But you should give it a try, because the reviews are really all over the place, book tastes tend to vary among readers. So all of the needed elements for this to be an unforgettable book were there but it felt short. I think that the main reason was that both of the main characters couldn't make up their minds. I understood both of their stories but I couldn't achieve that final click with them so the normal empathy that I feel for the characters was lacking during most of it. One thing that I hated was that Oliver was such a hot and cold guy. I really hated his on-off relationship with Bianca. Seriously his answer to everything was hooking up ith her. And his stupid reasoning to almost marry her ... duhhhh Stupid guy really. At some point my eyes almost rolled out of my head, I like my heroes devoted to the heroines (I like that once they star hooking up with the heroine they stop hooking with others) and this guy was not that.... So the steam level was good (a little less "slut" name-calling would have been appreciated but what the hell ) but like I said I missed that something that hooks and grabs my undivided attention.

So my main problems with this book were regarding the concept and the writing. While the overall plot of the novel intrigued me, I realized fairly quickly that I'd seen it done before, and that this book in particular added nothing new to the conversation. At some points this reminded me a lot of Black Mirror's season 3, episode 1: everyone's constant need to be seen through social media, and to be liked, and talked about, and their complete and utter desperation when someone didn't respond to their posts the way they thought they would, which verged on childish most of the time. The writing was the bigger problem. I simply hated it. I think this will make a strong movie, because it easily reads like one; but as a book, it was pretty bad. There were pages full of dialogue, with no description of anything else that might've been happening at the time; the author seemed unable to use commas and broke down his paragraphs into annoying short sentences that messed with the flow of my reading; and the characters were ridiculous. They all followed the same flat, one-dimensional mold, and they were all childish and self-absorbed. I do understand that this was most likely done on purpose, to show how the Circle ate their brains or whatever, but it doesn't mean I have to like it. Reading a book filled to the brim with unlikeable, stupid characters is usually not a pleasant reading experience. Mae, in particular, was the most stupid out of all of them. I was tired of her by the 20% mark and having to watch her walk around being selfish through the rest of the novel was my own private hell. Also I figured out the whole Kalden/Ty thing literally the first time he showed up and Mae couldn't come up with it??? Seriously. So dumb. Also this book committed my #1 book sin: it referrenced things that had happened in the plot but hadn't actually been shown to us in the book. JUST WRITE THE GODDAMN SCENE. I hate when authors do this because to me it sounds like they were too lazy to actually sit down and write a few more paragraphs and decided to have events happen off-screen. I'm giving this a second star because the ending was pretty satisfying aside from the fact that it was cut short because the author didn't actually write out what happened, just Mae recollecting about it. I only picked this up because I've had it on Kindle for two years, and now that the movie is coming up, I wanted to see what I thought of the story before actually watching it -- I have a feeling this will be one of those rare cases where the movie is, in fact, better than the book.

It just seems like what two fifth graders would do when they like each other I may be reading the other books in the series, but not so sure
BR with the amazing MacHalo girls I'll get back to this someday because I just can't get into it right now. On to mercenary fairies.

If you read Wet by Stacy Kestwick, this is the 2nd book that ties up the story of West and Sadie. In book one we were left on a cliff hanger seeing West with another women in his arms. Book two picks up right were we left off. The prologue is from West's point of view; and By-George I am glad for that. The rest of the book is from Sadie's POV. After seeing West have Aubrey in his arms coming off of his boat, she knew that it was over. Her heart broke and that was the end of it. Book one there was so must angst between West and Sadie because of Aubrey (a.k.a. Home Wrecker!). In this book Sadie is trying with all her might to forget about West and move on. Problem is, he won't letter her. I really enjoyed the first book and I couldn't wait for the 2nd. I even preorder it, which I only will do with some books. This was one of them. YOU MUST READ THE FIRST BOOK! This is a series. There is no stand alone with it. If you ever read and enjoyed, Off the Record by K.A Linde then you will enjoy this book. It is sweet but spicy; Hot but with a good amount of Steam. Sadie begins to be stronger and more determined to not allow people to walk over her. She even learns new things about herself and some of her friends. If you recall from book one, the douche-bag ex-boyfriend of Sadie's. Well that guy makes an appearance, and let me tell you, it is not the kind we would want to see. But her BF is always to the rescue.

** spoiler alert ** Gosh. I liked this book more than I have the past several. The main female character was my favorite of the series. So why am I giving it a 3? First: I just don't get the logic of "he's got a crush on his best male friend, but if he hooks up with a woman that's built like a boy, he'll get over it!" This isn't to say that I mind that Jane is described differently than the standard stunningly-gorgeous HEA romance chick. I'm glad of it. But one of her attractions for Vishous seems to be that she's built like a boy, and that doesn't make sense. Second: man, I just *hate* that ending. If the Scribe Virgin's sacrifice had brought Jane back to life (heck, say it's because she drank Vishous' blood and it kept her in a state of barely-life - it's not like half the rules in this universe haven't gone out the window anyway), I would have been able to buy into it more. But Jane can go around...as a ghost...and basically live the same life she's always lived, so long as she focuses hard enough on being material? She's just sitting down eating dinner with them like nothing happened? WHAT? WHAT??? THE HELL??? That makes no sense. NONE. Third: I am so, SO very tired of one of Ward's tropes: the person with the unhappy family life. Vishous was horribly abused as a child. Zsadist was kidnapped and sexually tortured. Phury was basically ignored by his parents after Z was kidnapped. Bella was shunned because of bad relationship choices and has no relationship with her parents to speak of. Beth grew up in foster homes. And on and on and ON. And now Jane with the distant family relationship and the dead sister. The only template for a happy family we had were Tohr and Wellsie, and then Wellsie got killed. I'm so very tired of it. For once, can't Ward have a character that has good family relationships, a character that can't easily abandon her current life to go off with her vamp man? I see that Manny Manello is going to be the next buddy of Vishous and Butch. Wonder if he will have the same transformation that Butch did?

Real rating: 3.5 Anyway, I rated the first "Omnibus" with 4, so you can imagine that I am not really satisfied with the second book. This book described the beginning of the silo world, although until at the end of the book, I still not really grasped what's going on, why, how the nano treatment fitted in the story, were there any other worlds like the silos, what happened to all those silos that went dark for centuries, why did Donald survive the outside world, etc etc. Well, maybe the author wants to leave it open for discussion, or all these things will be explained in the third book. In summary, the book followed the life of people in Silo 1 (Donald's story), Silo 18 (Mission's story), and Silo 17 (Jimmy's story, or, Solo's story; yes, this part was about the background of how Jimmy became Solo, and at the end of the book, Jules arrived). Donald's story is quite long-winding, though. And I don't think the Mission's story is needed. Maybe the author intended to show how a resistance upheaval was started, and how those people involved in the resistance were dealt with, but these issues have been described in Book 1. However, I am looking forward for Book 3, curious to see the end of the story. Especially after Donald and his sister saw the green landscape outside the silos' boundaries.

This was a well done thriller, and also an interesting exploration of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder. I took particular note of that because we have an author visit this Wednesday night at the Burbank Public Library by David J. Morris, author of The Evil Hours, which is a sort of hybrid autobiography and medical dissertation on PTSD. I run hot and cold on Tami Hoag's books: I absolutely loved Kill the Messenger, one of her stand-alones, but almost every time I try to read one that is part of a series, I am disappointed. This one apparently bears some relation to previous books, but the connection was slight enough that I was able to read it without backtracking. I liked that she dealt with the issue of PTSD from two perspectives--one a veteran, the other not--because it highlights that it's not just something suffered by those who have been traumatized by war. She also did a great job of showing the issues that those surrounding the victim--family, friends, people with whom they come in contact as part of a daily routine (waitresses, traffic cops)--experience. Finally, it was just a great whodunnit that pulled in a case and people from the past and tied them to the present-day events of the story.

I received a copy of this book via Edelweiss for free in exchange for a honest and unbiased reviews. Big thanks to the publisher, HarperTeen! Missing for a decade, Oliver is suddenly back home. Emmy and Oliver were best friends growing up and she wants to reconnect with him, but she doesn't know how. This book was pure adorableness (yes, I said adorableness) from beginning to end. I loved how Emmy went out of her way to be kind to Oliver. I also loved her awkwardness and rambling. What's the first thing she does when she makes eye contact with Oliver? Sticks out tongue and crosses her eyes. See? Adorable. Emmy and Oliver's relationship was wonderful. I loved how Emmy and Oliver started of as friends and THEN evolved into something more. I just love when instalove isn't involved! Emmy's other friends, Caro and Drew, make for even more fantastic relationships throughout this book! Since Oliver's disappearance a decade ago, Emmy's parents have become very protective over Emmy, which in turn causes a riff between Emmy and her parents. One of her favorite things to do, surfing, has been kept a secret from her parents. Emmy fears that if her parents knew about her surfing, they would make her quit and classify it as "too dangerous." The issues and drama within this book are very real and relatable. The growth in each character is well paced and not rushed. The relationship between Emmy and her parents, her friends, and Oliver grew in such a way, that it makes it easy for readers to believe in the story. Same goes for Oliver's relationship with his mom. This book is a quiet and non-explosive read, but I think that is what makes this story so real. Many young adult novels today are so fabricated that it makes it hard to believe their stories. This book's realness and believably are what make Emmy & Oliver stand out from the rest.

I lucked out on this one as my local library system obtained copies of this latest volume incredibly fast. The book was published on the October 13th and I had a copy in my hands by the 20th! Sounds great, but with a lot of people putting it on hold I only had 3 weeks to work through the 785 pages. But with two reading intensive weekends I managed it. Overall I did not like this as much as most of the previous volumes. Less than one year of time is covered in this book and almost all of that was spent on the logistics and minor battles of the war against the Army of God. True there's some great detail in these sections and I wouldn't call them boring, just they went on for far to long. Like most of the others, the highlights of the book were the actions of the Navy. The sheer number of names in these books makes it impossible to remember who's who. Luckily there is a comprehensive reference at the end of the book (over 100 pages actually). I found I had to refer to this at the start of many chapters to figure out which side of the war the mentioned characters were on. The reference is great, than maps less so. They show a few places but a lot of the towns and rivers mentioned in the text are absent. Most of the major Charisian characters from other novels only play background roles in this book. Merlin does make for a few exciting scenes and it's interesting to note how his/her attitudes towards the Inquisitors has changed as their tactics become ever more brutal. In the early books he was hesitant to take direct action, but by this book he is willing to act as the angel of death when provoked enough. The ending was a bit predictable, but ended on the sort of scene that makes me want the next book right now, not in a year. This book has it's faults, but David Weber really knows how tell a good story.

On the one hand, Tretch is one of my favorite male characters in all of YA. He's charming and polite to everyone, he loves to read (even if I roll my eyes at most of his taste in Pretentious Male literature) and frequents a used bookstore, he likes all the same music I like, he doesn't swear and is only gross in one scene, and he is definitely a hopeless romantic. His emotions run close to the surface and he cries quite a bit, mostly without shame. The choice in cover models is perfect, too. He's also the master of that in-love-with-my-straight-friend trope, which is helped considerably by the fact that his best friend is equally nice, very tactile in his affection, and has no sense of boundaries or personal space. ("I'm gonna hop in the shower, but why get undressed in private when I could just strip while we're talking? Also, since you're staying over, let me loan you a pair of PJs before we get in bed. The same bed.") On the other, the story kind of ran out of steam around Christmas. I kept expecting it to build to a big, major event, but instead it was like a previously-opened and shaken bottle of pop that's been left so long, the carbonation has vanished without even being opened a second time. I was already mildly let down when he got over his crush, unsustainable though it may have been, but I really felt all the wind go out of my sails when Matt announced he was moving away. Suddenly it felt like the message was "nothing will bother you as long as you accept and are comfortable with yourself." Nah dude, I vote codependency 4 lyfe. And more to the point, that was such a great friendship, I just don't know why any author would want him to have to finish high school without a buddy like that at his side. I was also disappointed that I didn't connect with Tretch's family quite as much as I should have, but I got quite a kick out of Matt's dads, so there was that.
Fabulous as always. Love that little plot twist in the middle. Always makes me smile.

3.5 stars for me, though I'd recommend it to YA readers. Liked: * Big ideas about pain and addiction. * Engaging story. Didn't like: * YA. Nobody's fault, I'm just not a YA. * Moments of blinding stupidity from the main characters.

Wow, is this book some serious Gen X masturbatory theater. If you can deal with the serious 80s nostalgia porn you'll probably love this. And you'll love it because it's fun  and  because its nostalgic. I mean, you have to be a massive gamer/pop culture geek to love it, but I'm just going to go ahead and assume you are since you're either a friend of mine or reading the reviews for this book. If, however, you stumbled across this and pop culture and gaming are NOT your thing, run away now. This book is about 7000% gaming, movie and music references. Oh, and TV and anime, too. If you aren't big into at least one of those, this is going to be like driving spikes into your eyes. Also, it is SUPER obvious that the issue of  NET NEUTRALITY  was weighing heavy on Ernest Cline 's mind when he was writing this. IOI is obviously a stand in for our current ISP evils (Comcast, Verizon et. al) as they want to charge people to access the OASIS (ie the internet) where it is currently free and anyone can use it. Ultimately, pretty much everyone  bands together and brings IOI down to keep OASIS access free . The actual issue wasn't settled in the US until a couple of years after this book was published but I'd bet my paycheck Cline was celebrating the result.

"Have you read Wonder?" the girl asked excitedly. "No, I haven't." I was taken aback. Shouldn't I be giving her recommendations? "You HAVE to read it." It was one of the first enthusiastic recommendations I've gotten at my job as a bookseller, so I took it to heart. I bought it almost immediately after this interaction, and then sat on it for a while. I needed a palate cleanser after Kangaroo Notebook, and this was the perfect prescription. I was expecting this book to be maudlin and cheesy and make me uncomfortable. But really, it does a brilliant job showing that August Pullman is just a kid, and keeps the other characters grounded. One of my favorite parts was the very end. August gets an award during his fifth grade graduation. He's happy, but admits that he knows that he's getting that award because of his face, and the fact that no one wants to be him. It was so raw and honest and was such a unique example of how a well-loved kid would handle being looked at that way. Let's talk about his parents, though, because weren't they a bit too perfect? They were a bit too idealized for me. I get why we couldn't get their perspective in a kids' book, but they could have seemed a tiny bit less saintly.

"What thief does not fight to hold what he has?" "One that has something better," said Locke." How can I put all the feelings I felt into words ? Tell me !! It was so enjoyable reading The Lies of Locke Lamora. This book is ..... genius !! Lots of things was happening and lots and lots of them punched me on the face. It was really built well and it was smooth. I like Locke, he is so smart and sly>>>> I am not sure if it is okay to like him. The idea of him being able to do the things he does an to built a name for himself that big, I mean , so freaking Genius !!!! It never occurred to me that I'll ever like an adventure, or this type of novels , but I was proven wrong. There were lots of strong characters in this story. The author managed to make e , as a reader, like them even if they were the bad guys. In addition to the actions and battles, there were humor which was a good point in the story itself. Now I want to form my group of Gentlemen Bastards and rule our neighborhood. I'm going to look for a rich , strong , intelligent and well- known friends to help e in my goal ... *dreaming* I am exited to reading the second book and I hope it would be as nice as this one.

I think this is the first time I have ever thought seriously about returning a book for a refund. No character growth - if anything, all of the characters regressed. I cannot remember ever being so disappointed in a book. To steal a quote from another reviewer, if you were disappointed in Mockingjay, "this makes Mockingjay look like Dr. Seuss." Spoilers.... Not only was there zero character growth for anyone, there was actually regression for most characters. There were pointless character deaths to create angst for others, but it didn't really add up. Tory, in particular. Uriah is another. Some of the plot points were ridiculous. And frankly, the entire book, from beginning to end made me feel like reading this trilogy was a complete waste of my time. There is no happy ending. Everything is a lie. Tris steals her brother's chance at redemption and in doing so completely destroyed her own future.

I liked her previous books much better, but that's probably because the problems are more serious. The problem in this one is kind of skimmed over.

"Do you have to make a lot of decisions like that? I suppose you must do." "All the time," I said. "And each one is truly bad. All that can be said for them is that the alternatives are even worse." K.J. Parker is at his best in the novella, and, as always, I was captivated by the sharp wit and darkly ironic humor as well as the satirical worldbuilding and characters and finished the novella in a single reading session. Parker reminds me a bit of Wodehouse in the way he builds sympathy with the narrator through a chattering first-person narration. In this case, our narrator is an officer in a Rome-like empire whose ruling faction is beset by murderous intrigue-- think the Julio-Claudian era -- while also squabbling with and/or conquering its neighbors. In recent years, the empire has fallen prey to attacks by a mysterious unknown enemy with unknown goals and desires, and this enemy's ships have been seen again. Capitulating to the orders of the emperor's wife--who also happens to be his aunt--our narrator sets off to help the various abbeys and monasteries to help shore up their defenses against the mysterious invaders. While I think Parker is very gifted in characterization, he's not big on character development, which is one reason I so prefer his short fiction. In this case, we get plenty of time to get to know the narrator and his compatriots, including his romantic interest, without feeling stifled by the characers' staticness. The most rounded character, partially because the story is told in his voice, is the narrator himself. I found him highly sympathetic, a realist yet an optimist who is fond of books and sees himself as a coward despite his insistence on leading from the front. The only thing that really bothered me about him was how he seems to hold his wife's inability to have children against her, as if she should have provided a disclaimer before accepting his desperate proposal. As always, the story is a satire, and chock-full of quotable quotes. For example: "Does it say something about the nature of the beast called Empire? The idea is that Empire protects the towns and villages and little farms from the enemy, and in order to do so recruits soldiers, so that the towns and villages and little farms won't be laid waste, and grass won't grow in abandoned streets and good productive land won't be smothered in weeds and briars. But if the act of protection brings about the destruction it was designed to prevent-- well. I'm not a trained philosopher, so I'm not qualified to comment." If you're looking for a short, enjoyable novella with more than a tang of satire, then Mightier than the Sword is well worth a look. ~~I received this ebook through Netgalley from the publisher, Subterranean Press, in exchange for my honest review. Quotes were taken from an advanced reader copy and while they may not reflect the final phrasing, I believe they speak to the spirit of the novella as a whole.~~ Cross-posted on BookLikes

As seen on The Quiet Concert Oh my god, this sequel was amazing! Just days ago I posted my review of The Immortal Rules and was sad to say that I wasn't as impressed as I'd hoped to be. I enjoyed it, but I didn't love it. But this book. THIS BOOK. This book impressed me. This book I loved. The Eternity Cure was so much more than The Immortal Rules in so many ways. Most noticeably, the plot moved at a much faster pace and the stakes were MUCH higher. There was never a dull moment in this book. In fact, I was almost in a constant state of nervous excitement. And although that ending left me sobbing and speechless, I have to say that the events in this book were perfectly orchestrated for maximum feels. So so good. And I feel like the characters really grew into themselves. Allie was challenged a hell of a lot more, both physically and emotionally. She had to make a lot of really difficult decisions and I think that made her strong and compassionate personality come through even more so. And Zeke. *sigh*. I was not swooning Zeke in The Immortal Rules but I am swooning Zeke now. Hard. He was so much more badass this time around but still managed to keep that sweet way of his. And I never thought I'd say this, but Jackal grew on me. I might even care about him a little which makes me feel weird. His commentary was much appreciated. As for Sarren, he might just be the creepiest villain I have ever had the non-pleasure of reading about EVER. My god this guy gave me the chills and will in all likelihood give me nightmares as well. And Kanin was Kanin. He turned into this fatherly figure in my eyes. Rock solid. Let's just say I now understand what all the fuss is about. This book pulled me in, made my care for these characters, and left me dying to pick up The Forever Song (although to be honest I am a little scared to). It was expertly written and feel-inducing. I am still in awe.

I love this more each time I read it. All except that deadly scene in the pub where they carry on about which local cow the butcher might have bought and whether ghosts are real. Next time I read Silas Marner, I am going to Remember that that scene adds absolutely Nothing to the story and skip it. Otherwise, perfect!

Actual rating: 3.5 Well, it had a very promising start, but it squandered any remaining interest around the two-thirds mark. Stephen King knows how to write. He is a master of the written word, and he has a way of creating such dynamic and unique characters. But for all that, he failed on behalf of the women in this novel -- Any and all interesting women in this story were gone before 66% of this book was completed. I'm not saying there necessarily HAS to be female characters of worth in literature ALL the time... but, I mean, all the remaining vampire-hunting survivors were men. Give me a strong woman to root for after the halfway mark. . I've only read a handful of King novels and short stories, but I'm glad to have reacquainted myself.

Definitely my favorite standalone Guild Hunter in a while. It was cute and interesting. I really liked Holly, especially since we've been watching her journey since book one. It felt authentic to her. Speaking of authentic, I thought that Viper and his personality and romantic transformation felt right. He is definitely not one of my favorite characters from the series, but he was an awesome hero in this book. What's interesting is that Singh didn't change him. He was still the same person, I was just able to sympathize more with him when his actions were presented through his own eyes. The only negative was that some of the love story felt a little stale. You know, ancient powerful warrior meets strong young woman coming into her own and they commit to live or die together. It's still a great story, there was just a few times when I could have picked some of the dialogue up and put it in four other books in the series with no one being the wiser.

This book was interesting as a twist on a fairy tale. I guess it was supposed to be more of a twist on the Russian version of Sleeping Beauty, which I never really have heard of before so it was a bit different. The characters weren't extremely interesting to me- I just didn't really fall in love with any of them. The parts of the story involving magic were interesting, and I did enjoy the fact that the story alternated from the hero and heroines point of view to the bad witch Baba Yaga's point of view. It was interesting to see the story and plot from both sides. I also enjoyed the fact that right in the middle of a modern forest there was basically a portal back to the 9th century and that very little time would pass there when a lot of time had passed in today's time...the way that works really still has me stumped...does time just move slower there? Or is time suspended in that place indefinitely? I'm still not sure. I am glad there was a HEA for Ivan and his Sleeping Beauty, and that the ordinary boy found his princess.

This series has won my heart completely. I am so in love with Sarah J. Maas's writing. She is truly a queen of fantasy. My first Maas book was A Court of Thorns and Roses which quickly became an all time favorite of mine, along with its (aguably superior) sequel A Court of Mist and Fury. I went into this series expecting something good, and oh boy did it deliver. I'll admit, it took me a little while before I started warming up to Celaena in the first book. By this second installment she is one of my absolute favorite fictional characters. She's badass, mysterious, clever, and brave. I know that as this series continues I'll continue to learn more about her and her motivations. I'm so looking forward to it. I have to say I'm not surprised that she turned out to be the lost princess . I'm not sure if I inadvertently read that spoiler a long time ago, or if it was just a fairly obvious plot device. I also think I read somewhere that she was fae, but wasn't sure how or when that was going to fit into this series. Despite me expecting the reveal, I was still on the edge of my seat with that ending. How emotional for Chaol! (Still don't know if I particularly like him or not though, haha). On that note, the love triangle still leaves a lot to be desired in my opinion. I'm still pretty "meh" about both Dorian and Chaol. They're fine, I guess. I just don't feel that ~fire~ between Celaena and them. I'm still holding out for the kind of passion I saw in A Court of Mist and Fury. If you've read it, you know what I'm talking about ;) Another spoilery thing, I was devastated when  Nehemia was murdered. I was livid. I was so upset! I know why it was done for character development, or whatever, but I'm still pretty bitter about it >:( So the plot blew my socks off, the characters blew my socks off, the world building blew my socks off, in short, I have no more socks; they're all gone after this book! Haha. Super excited to start reading the next installment!

And Phury's too.... well.. alot with his back story- I don't get the whole celibacy thing... or maybe I missed it. The ending's a killer lol in a bad and good way- the story just kinda ends... I feel like I was plopped right back into reality going "WAIT?!?! what happens next?!!!" so... next book it is ! Final Notes: The hero - Rhage. pretty enough. bad enough. sweet enough. BUT.. when all the other brothers around I find interests being stolen away by Zhadist (I'm a masochist for his type) lol The heroine - dying of cancer but surprisingly strong :) I felt it was alot easier to connect with Mary than Beth in the previous book. lol plus you gotta love a woman that will put in work, chained "mate" or no lol The Plot - ROFL just realized it's not even CLOSE to being resolved- the Rhage and Mary thing is, but the rest not so much! I probably need to give this one another listen, because I feel like I'm not fully getting all the stuff with the Lessers.... The sex - does not disappoint ;) The end - as stated above- I feel like i was abruptly transported back to reality lol wondering what the h*** was going on! I just finished listening to the audio CD narrated by Jesse Bernstein and I really enjoyed the recording. The book is an interesting one involving an ordinary young man, Jacob, who finds himself thrown into some extremely extraordinary situations both in his native Florida and half a world away on a tiny island off the coast of Wales. The plot was well thought out for the most part; I only really had trouble with the age difference between Jacob and Emma not to mention Emma's previous romantic entanglement with Jacob's grandfather! . The narration, by Jessie Bernstein, is well done in a variety of voices and accents which helps to keep the listener's attention. It was very obviously set up for a sequel and I would like to know where it goes from here but I haven't heard good things about Hollow City so I will have to think about it for awhile.

you like trying different people's skin on for size. you're fascinated by the way the mind works, the way it breaks, the way people survive things no one should be able to survive. T H O U G H T S: cold cases are a thing of the past. the naturals, a misfit team of young profilers, are faced with a chain of brutal murders and their dangerous code. the stakes are high. the tension is building. the characters are outside their comfort zone. all in pushes boundaries, constructing a mystery more complex and convoluted than ever before. it is both intellectual and clever, emotional and intimate. granted, it was long. bordering on tediously dragging. elements of the series are repeated predictably {how many times can someone try to kill the main character?} and are disappointingly unrealistic {how can so many cases connect so personally to the characters?}. the final twist is shocking, but ridiculous in its impossibility. and so much of this series is too over-the-top, too unbelievable. in the first book, the killer was the agent training the main character and also her {long lost!} aunt. book two conveniently featured a serial killer who emulated dean's father. and book three? oh, boy. the owner of the casino the naturals lodge at in LA happens to be sloane's {long lost!} father. one of the victims happens to be her {long lost!} brother. one of the killer's targets happens to be michael. the case involves a cult and - guess what? - lia apparently grew up in a cult! and the case is linked to judd's daughter and cassie's mother. what is the chance of all this happening? ha ha haaaa. jennifer lynn barnes knows how to push her characters. but while she explores the relationships and individual arcs of the game's key players with depth and detail, they still remain two-dimensional and stereotypical, stagnant in character development. the naturals series is entertaining and engaging, but too ridiculous in its premises and developments to feel real. R A T I N G: plot // 4 pacing // 3 language // 4 story world // 4 protagonist // 3 antagonist // 4 3.5 stars everything but true infinity has its end. all mortal men must die. but you were never meant to be mortal. you were born for things such as these.

Another solid entry in the Mercyverse. This book gets straight to the action and there's a good deal of interesting fae things going on. There are some new characters, some old returning characters, and plenty of spunk, as always (although a strange absence of coyote-shifting). I enjoyed it for what it was, but I find myself wishing this series were a bit less popcorn and a bit more grit. I never feel that stakes are particularly high. I never feel that any of the main characters are ever really in danger of dying or being irreparably harmed. *previous book spoiler* Even when Mercy was raped, her damage seemed much shorter lived than was realistic, and during a scene at the beginning of this book where Adam is chasing Mercy through the house as a precursor to sex, all I could think was, "Really???" Don't get me wrong. I love a lot of the characters, and I don't want them to die or be destroyed, but if there's no threat, it becomes too sitcom. I always know that every Mercy book is going to wrap up into a neat little bow, with all the main characters safe or recovering, Adam being obnoxiously perfect, and everyone realizing that Mercy was right/brave/worthy or whatever aspect of her was in question this book. There's no real over-arching plot other than the basic "what happened in a previous book may show up again later." It's just another episode. I can see why this series works so well as a graphic novel, but as a fantasy novel. I'm beginning to wonder what the point is.
"I see", she said. Do you ? Do you see ? Do you realise how much I want to grad your face and kiss you until you can't breathe ?

This was everything I wanted it to be! I honestly couldn't put this down. I loved its fast and always moving pace; it constantly kept me on the edge of my seat. And I liked that it wasn't afraid to go places; to take those necessary plot risks to keep the plot developing. I really liked Em and Cas as characters. Em shows great character growth throughout and Cas is just a sweetheart. And their romance was exactly what I wanted to read and see. While this story does borrow characteristics and tropes common to the genre, (I think many readers will draw parallels to other novels) I still had a lot of fun with this story. It still felt fresh to me and it definitely has its own unique quirks to make it stand out on its own.
