Caitlin Doughty helped me. At first, I don't mind saying, she repulsed me with her (what I thought initially) childish and macabre sense of humor. What happened over the course of reading this book is that I became informed--reminded and informed--about the "responsible exposure to decomposition" which we as a culture are so good at hiding, denying, refusing. If I never completely relaxed, I think that is quite normal. But she really earned her $24.95 for the price of the book. That's a lot of teaching going on. I don't want to be responsible for the shock readers might feel who stumbled onto this review by accident. This book is about the crematory industry and death. It is useful, but if that is not what you came for, don't read this book nor this review. Caitlin Doughty reminds me of the little minx Lauren Ambrose that played in the TV serial Six Feet Under. They look nothing alike. It is a personality thing...and the subject matter, of course. I thought I would just skim this because I was having difficulty entering into the humor of this book, but I found myself learning things...slowing down...nodding my head...reading aloud to family...and laughing, against my will, at some of the scenes Doughty conjured in my head. Doughty makes an awful lot of sense. She is a licensed mortician, youngish. She worked in a crematory at the beginning of her career, after obtaining a degree in Medieval Studies. She'd done her thesis on medieval witches accused of roasting dead infants and grinding their bones. "A year later I found myself literally roasting dead infants and grinding their bones....[those witches] were burned alive at the stake. I, on the other hand, ...was thanked by the poor parents for my care and concern. Things change." See what I mean about her sense of humor? Anyway, what I learned was extremely useful. She relates the story of a woman who said that her mother died "unexpectedly" after hospice care for six months. Doughty didn't buy it:"When a young person dies unexpectedly, the family will likely face what [Jessica] Mitford called the 'necessity of buying a product of which they are totally ignorant.' The sudden death of a young person is a horrible tragedy. In their sorrow the family should not have to worry that a funeral home would take advantage and upsell them to a more expensive casket or funeral-service package. But anyone who works in the death industry can readily tell you that a slim minority of cases involves the sudden death of a young person. Most deaths come after long, significant diseases or very lengthy lives...why [someone would] not look up the best funeral homes in the area, compare prices, ask friends and family, figure out what's legal, or most important, talk to her mother about what she herself wanted when she died? ...Refusing to talk about it and then calling it 'unexpected' is not an acceptable excuse." Doughty does the work of sharing the history of the business of funeral homes with us: How it developed into a huge industry in the United States as opposed to cremation, and how Jessica Mitford--yes, that Jessica Mitford--almost single-handedly turned public opinion around with her book, The American Way of Death, published in 1963, the same year Pope Pius VI overturned the ban on cremation for Catholics. Cremation is still the lesser-used option, but there is a movement afoot now to take back the business of dying with home wakes and 'natural burials' in bucolic settings. Doughty does address the latter option, saying that she's decided on a natural burial for herself. "Not only is a natural burial by far the most ecologically sound way to perish, it doubles down on the fear of fragmentation and loss of control. Making the choice to be naturally buried says, 'Not only am I aware that I'm a helpless, fragmented mass of organic matter, I celebrate it. Vive la decay!'" A website she doesn't mention gives the range of options for those who want a modicum of control, from home wakes to natural burial: WBUR Radio piece with links. After hearing Doughty's stories and watching some of her YouTube video series, and knowing that she hints at times to prefer being torn apart by buzzards on a hilltop in Tibet rather than be cremated, one just has to think...about death: what it is and how it affects us. Doughty may be irreverent, but she's earned it. She earns our forgiveness with her admission: "Everything I was learning at Westwind I wanted to shout from the rooftops. The daily reminders of death cast each day in more vivid tones...my work at Westwind had given me access to emotions I didn't know I was capable of. I would start laughing or crying at the drop of a damn hat...[my] emotional range was blasted apart, allowing for ecstasy and despair like I had never experienced...I went from thinking it was strange that we don't see any dead bodies anymore to believe their absence was the root cause of major problems in the modern world. Corpses keep the living tethered to reality." Doughty quotes the social critic Camille Paglia: "Human beings are not nature's favorites. We are merely one of a multitude of species upon which nature indiscriminately exerts its force." Irresistibly, Doughty shares the original Hans Christian Anderson story of "The Little Mermaid," to go with her vignette about growing up in Hawai'i. Kids' story "The Little Mermaid" is not, despite Disney's re-creation of the fable in film, and adults reading it in 1836 when it was published would learn not to complain about their lot in life because things could be a whole lot worse. She tells us about the wide menacing smile of a skull. "It was unnerving to think this same deranged grin lurks just beneath the flesh of everyone's face, the frowning, the crying, even the dying." And she tells us that "Buddhist monks hoping to detach themselves from lust and curb their desire for permanence would meditate on the form of a rotting corpse." Yes, she can be gruesome, but what she managed to do is keep my skittering mind focused on the issue of death for a couple hours, for a day. Who wants to think about this? Nobody. But it is a truth, and frankly, like Doughty, I would always have preferred to have been initiated into the secrets of reality than told as a child that there really is "a happy ending." It keeps things real, and it keeps us focused, and it keeps us striving. Because, darn it, the scythe is at the door.

Note: This book not working on Kindle and forcing me to use Cloud Reader was annoying! GRR Thoughtless might be the perfect title for this book. Or maybe Careless. Or Insensitive. I have mixed feelings about this book. I liked it at first - I thought Denny and Kiera were so cute. When Denny accepts the Tuscon job and they break up, I could even understand Kiera sleeping with Kellan that first time. But everything after that just pissed me off. I felt so awful for both Denny and Kellan as Kiera flip flopped between both of their beds, repeatedly. She would have sex with Kellan, then the next night have sex with Denny. I understood her being torn between two guys - it makes sense that she would be afraid to give up the guy she loves who is her rock for the guy she is passionate for who has a bad reputation with girls and who might leave her. I get that. But I hated her when she kept it up for so long. When Kellan would finally have enough and try to leave, she would beg him to stay and once even used sex to get him to stay. When he started dating other women, she purposely made out with Denny in front of him to make him jealous. The fight scene... just wow. I was shocked Denny would go there, it just didn't fit his personality at all. I was so glad that both Denny and Kellan dumped her. It was exactly what she deserved and it kind of made me mad that so much blame was put on Kellan when she was a willing participant and in fact begged for it multiple times. The reunion between Kellan and Kiera was cute, but to be totally honest I don't think she deserved it. She didn't deserve the tattoo or the songs or the incredibly sweet makeup session. I am not one of those people who hates all female heroines, but I really hated this one. I don't think she deserved the happy ending. That said, this author has talent and even though I hated Kiera, I was swept up in the story and couldn't put it down. I just read the entire book in one sitting and I'm sitting here contemplating starting the sequel even though it's 2am.

So much better than the first book. Vic becomes more of a real person here, and more sympathetic, too, as we see how terrifying it can be to be constantly surrounded by the dead. I really enjoyed this one. However, in light of the fact that the topic of "women can't write gay men" that has been on my mind lately, Vic does strike me, at times, as a little bit of a chick with a dick--not always, but there are a few times that, especially since that was at the forefront of my consciousness, I was kinda like, "hmm, this sounds more like a woman trying to hard to write a man than an actual man." For example, there are a few times when Vic outright comments about certain behaviors like "must be a man thing" - and that really stuck out to me. I get the idea of his maybe not knowing how a straight man would think, but he IS a man. It seemed odd. I don't really see myself as thinking (when something happens) "Oh, it must be a woman thing." I could see my self SAYING that, potentially, to someone else, like, "Oh, it's a woman thing," but not inwardly... Nevertheless, I really like Vic, and I really only noticed these things because I was super cognizant of the idea at the moment. I'm looking forward to reading the next book.

I was so intrigued by the characterization in the first few pages that I just had to read this book. It's short and I read it very quickly, but in the end it was something of a disappointment. Like many first-person narratives, this story is told by an old woman, Helen, looking back on her childhood: specifically, the summer of 1945, when she was ten and left for the summer in the care of her 22-year-old cousin, Flora. Readers are alerted from the first page that the summer will end in tragedy, and in the meanwhile we read about the often troubled relationship between the two main characters, as well as their interactions with others in the community. While the characterization is the best thing about this book, the plot is the crux of my problem with it. At various points in the story the older Helen interjects discussions of her remorse, such that the ultimate tragedy is quite predictable; but it's easy to see why Godwin made this choice, because without the promise of something dramatic eventually happening, readers might give up on the mundane account of Helen's life that precedes it. Personally, I don't require dramatic events to keep my interest in a story, but I do like more tension and momentum than this book provides: something needs to be at stake, be it a relationship, someone's position in the community, or a character's choice of direction in life. Unfortunately, here there just isn't much; Helen and Flora go about their daily routines, and the bulk of the book leads up to the tragedy only indirectly. Since what happens is an accident, there's only so much building up to it that can be done. Then it ends. This is frustrating because there are two potentially great stories lurking just beneath the surface: one about how Helen's remorse affects her and her attempts to atone, and the other about Helen and Flora's family, with its colorful characters and many secrets. We hear almost nothing about Helen's life after that summer. We do learn something about several of the relatives and their secrets, but I wanted more. Because there are some excellent characters here: the eponymous Flora is one; Helen's grandmother, father and mother are all fascinating and deserve more page time than they get; Flora's relatives are intriguing as well, and I was disappointed not to meet them. Helen is a serviceable narrator with a decent amount of complexity, but this was not one of those books that renders a child protagonist so believably as to take me back to how it felt to be her age. Outside of the family, the secondary characters are a mixed bag: Finn, the war veteran who captures both Helen's and Flora's affections, was not as interesting to me as he was to them; Mrs. Jones, on the other hand, was vivid and believable. The characters' relationships are believable, and their interactions often fun to read. Other than that, the writing and dialogue are solid, although the characters have a tendency to sound writerly when they talk for more than a few sentences at a time. I liked the use of the grandmother's letters to show another side of her character, but for someone meant to be so discreet and reserved, her circumlocutions are awfully transparent; it tends to be immediately obvious to the reader what she's talking about even when she's evidently trying to obscure it. Overall, an okay book, but one that had the potential to be better with some smarter editing. If you're a big fan of character studies and less concerned about plot, this book may be right for you; on the other hand, I tend to be more interested in character than plot myself, and still found it lacking in momentum. It's short and decently written, just not as good as I expected.
2.5 stars Not one of her best works.

I don't think I would have been able to get through this entire book if not for the fact I was listening to the audio book instead of reading it myself. I am not a fan of novels that have little to no dialogue or have long stretches where noting happens. I get bored easily. Mr. Koontz is a talented writer but this book just wasn't for me. I found most of it very dull. I did enjoy the last 10% or so but that is because it was the big finish so a lot was happening all at once and that kept me entertained. I'll try another book of his in the future but I'll be more selective with my choice.

During the height of the Cold War, an asteroid appears above Earth. It's not just a regular asteroid though! It kinda just hangs out, like the Moon, and when researchers land upon it, they discover that it's terraformed inside, and that it is bigger on the inside than the outside. (Whoa!) Some kind of weird space-time thing, the researchers suppose, so they bring to 'the Stone' one Patricia Vasquez, a grad student in her early 20s who does a lot of math stuff that no one really understands but seems sufficiently space-timey to potentially be of use. When Patricia arrives she discovers that there are very complicated and yet haphazard firewalls in place to control the flow of information about the Stone, but because of her unique space-time knowledge, she's going to get the Super-High Clearance, the kind where you are burdened with all sorts of heavy facts but can't talk about it to anyone, because maybe then it will leak to the Reds, who are only sort of invited to research on the Stone, and all hell will break lose! Even with the advanced security procedures of "just please don't mention any of the batshit insane and extremely terrifying things you learn to anyone!" all hell, in fact, does break lose. Then follows some Cold War-y stuff that is really dated, and the adventures with space-time REALLY begin. I was fairly entertained while reading, and was pleased that after a few hundred pages, Bear finally let a Soviet person have an emotion. It ends with some interesting loose ends, but fear not, potential reader, you will not be denied the several paragraph of description of Patricia Vasquez's boobs that you long for! I mean, how I am supposed to envision the young mathematician from LA who touches the square root of space-time without knowing what her rack looks like?! But also, props to Bear for making his main science brain a young Chicana woman, and a fully-developed (heh) character at that. The fact there were a number of interesting and able female characters did help counter-balance all the Red Scare propaganda nonsense. Will probably not seek out the sequels, but if I stumble across one somewhere, I'll take it as a message from space-time to give it a whirl.

I would like to start off by saying that the author does a wonderful job with descriptives and doesn't bore by overusing them. E.M. Tippets manages to transport the reader into the scene fabulously. The story went at a slow pace which allowed me to really immerse myself in this world and get to know each and every character really well. All of her characters had depth to them which I thought was absolutely fantastic. Madison is a sixteen year old girl who is quite naive and sadly, a bit of a pushover. She lets people walk all over her and that was frustrating to read. She is such a sweet girl and she can't seem to grasp the reality that she is an all-around amazing person who deserves better. Her best friend Kailie is one of the main problems that I hoped she would kick to the curb. I kind of really hated her. She uses and abuses Madison. I sort of felt bad for Kailie when I saw how she was treated by her parents. Even though it's not an excuse, I understand why she then treated Madison badly. I was glad to see that Madison had support. From her brother to random schoolmates, others loved and cared enough to stick up for her and basically fight her battles for her. Madison catches three different boys' eyes. It was easy for me to choose my favorite right from the get-go. I liked that there wasn't really insta-love with any of them. In fact there was barely any like. She struggles with her feeling with one of the boys. I loved this section because it felt really believable for me. The one that she ends up with was of course the one I wanted for her. There's an interesting dynamic between the two characters. I enjoyed seeing their relationship develop. Their relationship was written the way I wish more couples were written in YA/NA novels. Mormonism and religion in general is a huge part of this book. Maybe it's just because I'm open-minded or what not but it didn't really bother me. I didn't feel overwhelmed by the information. If anything, I enjoyed the knowledge. This next bit is a quote that I found really cute and made me smile because Maddison finally realizes that she is amazing and beautiful. I'm calling it a spoiler just in case readers want to be surprised by the guy she chooses in the end. JP made me feel desirable as a supermodel. Alex makes me feel like he'd walk past a line of supermodels without a second look, just for the chance to hold me, and now he's given me his jacket so the whole world will know that he wants me to be with him and no one else. I've had this book on my TBR list for a while and am so happy I finally had the chance to read it. I am now officially a fan of E.M. Tippetts. Her writing is beautifully done and she sets herself apart from other authors with her style. I look forward to reading her work in the future. *An eCopy of this book was provided by the author for an honest review

I had really been looking forward to this, figuring it for a great summer read. I have the barest of connections with some of the major elements of the story-distant relations of an Irish Catholic family, growing up in Massachusetts(although the wrong side of the state from this family), and vacationing in Maine, though not having a summer house there. I liked all of those elements of the story, but the execution was poorly done. There was a lot of telling about what happens, and you get a great image of what the lives of the women in this story are like, but you don't actually see them living those lives. You are just hearing someone tell you about it. The character I connected most to was Maggie, only because she is close to my age, but I still didn't feel like I really knew her. The women all seemed to be realistic and acted in honest ways in their situations. However, the book description indicated these women would be spending the summer together in the family house in Maine, but what happens, and how they get there, is very different. The first of them doesn't even arrive there until halfway through the book. I found Alice the most frustrating character. I could see similarities to my own relatives in her, and I understand in some sense why she acted the way she did, but her refusal to budge on giving the house to the church without her family's consent infuriated me, and wasn't resolved in a way I was happy with. I really thought that with the story's purported focus on family that she would come around and decide to let the family have the house. I can see that she felt she needed to do it to atone for what she felt she did wrong, but it still seemed to clearly be the wrong choice. There were many parts of the book that I liked, but overall I found it a letdown.
4.5 stars Man, this was good

I'll be honest; I didn't like Nikki Heat very much in this one. I guess some of the stuff, like she could speak French, but went on a semester abroad her freshman year. That just seemed stupid to me. On the TV Show Castle, he's always talking about how deep, intelligent, and what a subtly complicated character Nikki Heat is when anybody comes in and tries to make their own description of her (like with the movie, reviews, etc). I think the ghost writer was trying so hard to live up to all the specifications, they fell show there. I especially scoffed when the omniscient narrator said that she had played Ophelia in Hamlet and a few other leads when she was a drama major at Northwester her freshman year when she was a drama major. I actually was a theatre major when I was in college, and freshman never got the leads in the plays the University's Theatre department put on. Maybe in some universities, but that actress would have to be the shiz-nit, like somebody on full scholarship that doesn't need it they're so awesome and had all this professional credit behind them. It wouldn't be somebody who'd walk out of the theatre department for anything, even a relative's death. I did like Nikki's response at the ending, though, when it was just her. I got irritated with Rook's attempts at being Nathan Fillion in the prior books, but this book was so very superior when it came to Rook's handling. At the same time, let's remember nobody can replace Nathan Fillion's comic chops and his impeccable timing (don't you dare argue with me!!!!!!). I just wish we got to see a darker, deeper side to Rook asides from being Nikki's 'partner.' I like the way that greater story arc was handled. It seems that the ghost writer was given an excellent path to follow in the run of the series and I really like picking up the subtle nods to story lines and plot points in the show. It's a lot of fun to watch the show and catch little things that come up that I enjoy. The F. Scott Fitzgerald quote was an "a-ha!" moment because I literally just watched the episode in which Detective Beckett says that. They didn't actually catch Tyler or find out what was in the pouch that Nicole Bernadine was trying to get, which sort of sucked, but it set up the next novel. I hope it gets solved! Overall, I enjoy Richard Castle's books because, let's be honest people, there's only 22 episodes a year and that'll never be enough for this fangirl!

To be quite honest, I'm having a hard time figuring out how I feel about this book. On one hand, Heartless is a fantastic retelling. It has the whimsical, nonsensical feel of the Wonderland we've all come to know with the same lovable, crazy characters that take you right back to the original story but Meyer puts enough of her own creative spin on it to leave you questioning everything you think you know and feel about the Queen of Hearts. You feel for her. You get attached to her and her impossible dreams and you want her to have her happy ending. But that's just the thing... Everyone knows the story of the Queen of Hearts. Everyone knows what she becomes. And I find myself wishing that I didn't. Here's the thing. I knew from the first page of this book what would happen to our future Queen of Hearts. I've seen Alice and Wonderland. I knew just how crazy and ruthless and heartless she was. I knew she had to marry that ridiculous King to even get the title of Queen. I knew Cath was never going to have her bakery, that Hatta was obviously going to go mad. And I knew she was never going to end up with Jest and he was going to die. I knew all these things but that didn't stop me from hoping that maybe, just maybe they weren't going to happen. And maybe that makes me more of a fool than Jest. The first half, possibly three fourths of this book, I spent irritated. Not with the writing or the plot. Mostly just the characters. Cath's parents I wanted to choke with the laces of her corset for their disregard to their daughters feelings and the pressure they kept putting on her to marry the King - I'm convinced they are literally half the reason everything went to shit. If they'd just listened to their damn daughter Jest wouldn't have died and she wouldn't have gone stark raving mad but whatever. The King I wanted Jest to knock over the head with his scepter every time he came around a corner or called Cath "his sweet" because he was literally the most in the way, irritating character and I couldn't stand her having to marry him. Mary Anne kept flighting back and forth between actually wanting the bakery and telling Cath to be happy with what she had. While the rest of Hearts was just full of spineless airheads who'd rather gossip about a engagement than actually worry about the thing that was threatening them. The only characters I actually really wanted around for most of this book were the Raven, Hatta and obviously Jest. They were the only ones who seemed to have their heads on straight and most of the time I just wanted Jest to whisk her away to Chess and goodriddens to them all. Wouldn't that have been a lovely ending? But once I got into the last hundred pages or so, things really started to pick up for me. I loved when Jest kissed her in that meadow and admitted everything to her, when he sacrificed himself so her reputation wouldn't get tarnished and showed up at the ball to take her to Chess. I had hope for maybe fifty pages that this was going to turn out okay. They were going to go through the maze, get to Chess, she'd become Queen and help defeat the Red Queen and she would actually get to be with Jest and have her bakery. But I knew how this story ended. I knew Meyer wasn't going to change the original story line and all my hope crumbled as soon as those creepy sisters showed that drawing and Cath was dumb enough to go through that door to save Mary Anne. I literally wanted to shout at her to leave them to fend for themselves. She might be your best friend but she told your parents something you confessed to her in confidence because she thought it was for the best. Leave them to deal with the Jabberwacky. Because if you don't step through that mirror you're condemning Jest to death and you're to loose everything you care about. But, of course, she walked through that fucking door. Because how else does she have a reason to become the ruthless Queen of Hearts? I think I felt as empty as Cath did at the end of this book when Jest was dead. Like what's the point anymore? But don't mistake my irritation with the characters and disappointment with the ending for not liking this book. Because overall, I really did enjoy it. I love Meyer's way of storytelling and making fairytales her own and it really gave me a whole new perspective on the Queen of Hearts. I got to see what made her into the Queen that she becomes and by the end of it, I actually sympathized and agreed with her. Like yeah, I'd want my heart ripped out to if the one person I loved was taken away from me because of my own stupid mistake and the decisions of everyone around me. Who would want to feel anything after that? What makes it so hard for me to judge is the ending. Because I wanted a different one. I wanted Cath and Jest to be happy but I knew that wasn't going to happen, that it wasn't supposed to happen, so I can't feel justified in faulting Meyer for it when it wasn't really her ending to change. For now, I'll stick with the four stars. It's not up to par with the Lunar Chronicles for me but I was still captivated by the story she gave to the misunderstood Queen of Hearts.

I think this book, for me, was more of a three star read, but I bumped it up to 4 because I loved AJ so much from book #1. I dunno, I just can't give AJ less than four stars, haha! He was hot stuff in this one, don't get me wrong, but I didn't get a rockstar vibe from him, he just felt kind of average. Sweet and still adorable, but kind of like a friend's boyfriend that you'd hear about, not as crazy sexy as I expected. But that is probably just me, poor AJ, my expectations must have been too high. I think a lot of it had to do with Mia, I like to love the main female characters in a book, but I didn't connect with her as much as I wish I could and I think my enjoyment of AJ was reduced a bit because of that. He was forced to prove himself over and over again, and I have to admire his patience because it was wearing on mine. Downsides to this one: overuse of the word twat- with anything on the end of it, and also douche used in the same way. I don't have anything against either word, but I noticed they appeared a lot. Upsides: Abby, loved her! I seriously can't wait for more of her + Jake. I also really like Lily, I hope we can somehow get a book with her and Bray, they seem really cute together. (notes for Mock Newbery) I really liked this, especially the narrator's voice, and the supporting cast that was unified but diverse. I can't understand why people make a big deal out of the narrator never being named. I really didn't find it distracting, and it made the book feel very personal (which I think is probably what the author intended). I would have liked parts of the book to be deepened, though. The length was good, but a couple of scenes felt too long and didactic (like the scene in the prison), while I didn't think there was enough development and detail about the girls' friendship. What we got was great--but I never felt as attached to D as I was to the narrator and Neeka. When the secrets come out at the end, I didn't feel the sense of shock that I think should have been there, because I never had the feeling that I thought I knew D well. Probably this book will really, really resonate with some kids, but for kids who don't know anything about Tupac, I don't think there's enough detail/development for them to really "get" it. I'm sure, if this book wins any Newbery honors, it will shock some parents and teachers to their cores. Newbery: probably not, because of the uneven development.

I have very mixed feelings about this short story. There were things I hated and there were things I loved. Unfortunately, there was more of the first ones. I was looking forward to meeting Quentin's parents and I expected them to be either awesome or terrible. They were neither. At times, they were nice, at times, I wanted them to go away, but they didn't leave lasting impression on me. Although it was interesting to see other characters from Quentin's POV, I mostly disliked how everyone acted. The only ones who were acting according to their characters were May and Tybalt and they were amazing. Toby was mostly quiet and Raj was acting all weird. Which brings me to the thing I disliked the most - romance in this short story was SO forced. It came out of nowhere and I think it would be better if it didn't happen at all. Now it feels like there's potential love triangle (Quentin, Raj, Dean)  and that's the one thing I don't like. Can't anyone stay just friends?

First Sentence: "They came from Memphis, Thebes, and Heliopolis to see the Savior born." Cleopatra Selene has just lost her mother, the more famous Cleopatra and is now on her way to Rome with the man she believes drove both of her parents to their deaths, Octavian (known to history as Augustus Caesar). She is marched in chains through Rome with her two brothers, Helios Alexander and Ptolemy Philadelphus. In Rome, she is thrown into a world of politics, intrigue, and magic. It all adds up to a fascinating and readable story. I've read quite a bit about Cleopatra, but never about her children so I was very interested to read this book. It was quite a fun read. I didn't care for the magic element to begin with but it grew on me after awhile. I admired Selene's determination to not only survive but thrive as a prisoner of Rome. She was a very strong young woman and I especially enjoyed the conversations between Selene and Octavian. All of the characters were well-drawn. I learned quite a bit about Rome and a lot about ancient religions during the time. I have a few issues with the book though. The book dragged a bit in the middle. It's also the first of a series which means the ending isn't nearly as much of an ending as I would have liked. That being said I will probably read the next book in the series just to see what happens. I would recommend this book to anyone wanting a fictional look at what happened after Cleopatra's death to her 3 children. Its a worthwhile read. Feed is a zombie thriller with some extra meat to chew on. In fact, the zombies are more of a setting and backdrop than a foreground part of the story. We wouldn't have a story without zombies, but the characters don't spend their entire time evading their diseased clutches. The meat of the story isn't blood-splattering zombie action, it's about journalistic ethics and what some people will do to pursue (or cover up) the truth. The characters spend most of their time at a computer writing about the presidential campaign in a society that has to deal with zombies on a regular basis... and constantly saying the same things over and over again, such as "I have a headache" or "We have to put our hands in a box and get scanned to see if we're infected." I understand this is the way society works in the book, but I don't need to be reminded of it every time. I would have given the book four stars if it weren't so flipping repetitive. Seriously, it could have been 200 pages shorter and a much tighter narrative. I'm looking forward to reading the next volume in this trilogy, but I hope it shambles along at a swifter pace.

Some chapters were less a story than a (very expensive) shopping list, and the ending just sort of petered out -- maybe waiting for a sequel? But it's a lot of fun for a beach read, and to be honest I did stay up all night reading it.

I am having mixed feelings after reading this book. The author no doubt has done a great job in curating the story and I was effectively wound up with the ongoings in this strange dystopian world of human beings and androids. It was a well written plot with convincing characters. In the end it all comes up to a moral standpoint or what we call 'empathy' which is one of the many things that separate androids from humans. Was Rick doing a morally correct thing by 'retiring' those androids? Was it so bad for the androids to wish to emulate human beings or to be left alone? Reading the story had me thinking whether we are doing any good by moving forward with all sorts of technological development if this is the future that we are heading towards.It is still debatable. I definitely need to read this book again to get some more understanding. However all in all this was a very well written book and I look forward to reading more books by Philip K. Dick.

I did this on audiobook and if you ever decide to try this out, audiobook is the way to go. I am really picky about audiobooks. If the voice sounds even slightly different than the way I think it should, it can ruin the entire book for me. Really. So, now I am adding this beauty to my long list of THREE audiobooks that I felt actually enhanced the book experience (the others? On the Jellicoe Road and Graffiti Moon). I couldn't say for sure that I would have rated this five stars if I had read it, but having it read to me? Five stars for sure. Although, truthfully, it's a mystery/thriller but deep down it's about a truly romantic man and that really surprised me, so maybe I would have given it five stars, after all. Anyway, this guys voice is just...wow. Honestly? It's enough to make you want to rip your clothes off (no worries, not only did I restrain myself, but there isn't anything like that in this book anyway - WHAT?!? He's IRISH). This narrator was SO good that at one point I was folding laundry and he starts in on the part where Frank kisses Nora and asks, "Where have you been? Where have you been all these years?" and a few minutes later I realized that I had stopped folding clothes and was standing there like an idiot with my mouth wide open.
the dialogue was a little much, and Sabine's and Ken's love didn't seem too real. this is a light, easy read. not reading again though.

Title: Before I Fall Series: Standalone Author: Lauren Oliver Rating: 4.75 Stars "I'm dead, but I can't stop living." A similar thing happened to me with this book, like with The 5th Wave. I started watching the movie that was based on Before I Fall and halfway through it I decided that I wanted to read the book, so I paused it and the next thing I know - I'm lost in the book. Before I Fall turned out to be more than just a young adult novel about the what-ifs and being stuck in a time loop. It had depth and made me really think about certain things, which was refreshing as it's been a while since I've read a book like that. The heroine, Sam, was the mean girl, the popular one in school, so the first instinct was to dislike her but as we experience everything from her point of view, we don't just see a cold exterior but also the whys. "Try not to judge. Remember that we're the same, you and me. I thought I would live forever too." One of my favorite things about the book was character development. It was so real and well written. It didn't happen in an instant, but rather over time and I loved it. The author really did a great job. The ending took me by surprise, in a way. I both: subconsciously expected it but didn't see it coming until much later. I think that, even though I found it sad that Sam died in the end as she came so far and did everything right, the book wouldn't have been as memorable and her character - heroic (can't think of any other word) if she would have lived. I would really like to see what happened afterwards to the characters. "That's the thing about best friends. That's what they do. They keep you from spinning off the edge." Before I Fall was a remarkable and an unforgettable read and I personally found it inspiring. Since this was the author's first book, I can't wait to read some of her other works (which are already on my tbr shelf) and see how she has grown.

I absolutely love this series -- it's so charming and funny! Yes, the feminist Girl Power message is fairly simplistic, and while I would normally find this pandering, this title has such a great energy that this hasn't bothered me in the least. Also, points for diversity and awesome female friendships. Volume 3 starts right where volume 2 left us: Adrienne and Bedelia are still on their quest to save the former's sisters, but they decide to make a quick pit stop to save another princess who looks in need of rescuing. Their new companion is in fact not a "real" princess, but Raven Xingtao, daughter of the Pirate King. Jealous that she's the heir to her father's pirate empire, her younger brothers convinced good ol' Dad to lock her up and Raven is none too happy about this. As I said, this title has a wonderful energy to it with lots of quippy dialogue alongside the action and adventure. There's been an artist switch since volume 2 and I have to say that I preferred the art in this volume quite a bit. The action scenes are drawn really well, with lots of movement and fluidity, and everything is really colourful which suits the tone of the story. The only quibble I had was I was annoyed that Adrienne and Raven decided to become "honorary sisters" when there was obviously so much chemistry between the two. Ah well. I'm really excited that Raven is getting her own series! I'll definitely have to check out this spin-off at some point and I look forward to volume 4 of this main title.
For a paranormal romance, it wasn't truly awful. I liked the idea of a djinn instead of a vampire or what have you. Kind of weird energy sex.

It was good book. I've mixed feelings about it though. On one hand, the plot was intriguing and fun, but on the other hand, it seemed to drag on. This book is all about online gaming, contains references and entire plot parts based on real life games and movies many of us know growing up. So that way, the book feels like a forgotten childhood friend showing up suddenly and remembering all the memories. I also felt the book could have been a lot shorter. I felt bored at times and frustrated too, as the protagonist seemed to rant and obsess over games too much that was not relevant to the plot. But I would admit this was a goof book which brought back childhood memories of playing video games and how emotional I used to be about winning and losing in them.

I loved the Native elements. Things got a bit confusing when the supportive character, Grandmother, hit us with walls of text towards the end. The whole idea in and of itself was beautiful, I liked the idea of what the author was trying to do. Though it was done in a rather complicated and messy way. The love story in and of itself was fabulous. Between the main character and her father (page 205-206 made me tear up), the love story between Mom and Dad, between the twins. The love story between Main Character Natalie and Matt was pretty awful, as well as with Beau. It felt sort of overly dramatized and forced. Don't get me wrong, I'm all for insta-attraction. It happens. But... there was nothing there. No glue to hold the two together to make them want one another so much. He's just handsome and she's "so pretty". Vapid reasons to want to suddenly marry and have babies less than three months later. And Matt, poor, poor Matt. He started out so nice, though clingy and unable to move on. I blame Natalie for this because she didn't draw a clear line in the sand. She pretty much forced the guy into awkward situations that would absolutely be interpreted by a hurting heart wrong. I don't like how the author excused Natalie for being a clingy ex and all but refusing to let Matt heal and move on by blaming it on feminism. When one side of the relationship didn't see the break-up coming (something Natalie was well aware of) it's usually best to give them distance to heal. Who wants to be in their ex's lives 24/7 after breaking up? Natalie, apparently. Actually, thinking about it, Natalie was extremely selfish most of the book; her actions towards her mother, her behavior about her own identity, her unwillingness to let people in and give them access to her because she's such a special snow-flake. My own personal issue was how much drinking was going on. I don't know if it's a small town Kentucky thing, or if people's parents just don't really care, or if teenagers don't really care- but all that drinking was just too much. Everything they did centered around or involved alcohol somehow. That bothered me on a personal level. Good book, worth the read. Didn't really blow my mind or change my world.
Still giving it a 3star because the author managed increase my interest about halfway in.

My frustration with Stephen King lies in how uneven he is--he alternates from genius to mediocre, and sometimes downright awful. Mediocre is okay if that's the best you can do, but when I know you're capable of genius, I expect better. While Bag of Bones might not rise to the level of genius, it is certainly the most enjoyable of his books that I've read in awhile. It's probably going to go on the shelf next to my other favorites of his, 'Salem's Lot and Needful Things. It will never be The Stand or any of the Dark Tower books, but it is a truly enjoyable read. King shows more care in world and plot building in this book than he has in some time, and develops some characters that seem real (even likable! ), rather than just moving cutouts around the flannel board. It was better plotted and better anchored, and it wasn't as overly self-referential as many of his works have been since his accident. (Did you hear? He was in an accident while jogging! He was hit by a van! He almost died! I bet you didn't know! Because he's never talked about it since!) I also didn't get that "I am Stephen Goddam King and I don't need no stinkin' editor" vibe.He actually thought this one through and wrote like the talented storyteller he really is...when he can bother to expend the effort. As a side note, I really liked how he handled the relationship between Jo and Mike. It felt like a relationship between two adults, like a real marriage. He handled it without the "tee-hee, I get to talk about sex! How far can I push the envelope?" juvenile side trips, where he rights about intercourse like a 13 year old who just saw a Playboy for the first time. Thank God.

I read this all in one sitting which helped me to not compare the book and the show and just appreciate the story for what it was. The psychic was a nice touch and the relationship between Aria and Noel is developing nicely. I was very surprised about Hanna being in a rehab facility and how shady her roomie ended up being. I was so pleased that Spencer FINALLY got some answers about her parentage and that it helped fix her relationship with her family. Slightly leaning to 3.5 Stars Not every story is pretty, not every story is perfect, but this is their story; one that the characters dictated and I just sat back and typed. - Christine Zolendz, Author's Note What I Liked: The book started off with a bloody, intriguing bang so it was easy to get into it because of that. The author stepped away from New Adult for her second series. Although I liked Fall From Grace, Saving Grace was a DNF for me which led me to returning Scars and Songs because I was afraid of getting even more disappointed. Kudos to Ms. Zolendz for not playing it safe by sticking to the same genre and reaching out to a more mature audience. I didn't think I would read her works again after Saving Grace but this book intrigued me. The characters are not angsty, broken college students. They are angsty, broken thirty-something adults. Somehow angsty, broken adults is not as annoying for me as angsty, broken college students. Go figure. When the two main characters meet, I thought it was going to be another one of those  super insta-lust, then uncontrollable smexing and from there they will fall into insta-love kind of relationship which irritates the hell out of me nowadays. But surprisingly, although it started of as your typical insta-lust stories, their issues pulled through which resulted to antagonism and far, far away from insta-love. Thank goodness. Kade's POV was of a mentally twisted recluse who hates people and doesn't have a problem showing it. With Samantha he's like some sort of weird stalker but it was hilarious to read how he always ends up insulting her because he doesn't understand why he's feeling the way he does and totally go about it the wrong way. He didn't instantly changed for the better after meeting Samantha, there was a process and that made it more believable. Kade's past is very tragic and I totally understand why he is the way he is. There is a book two but their relationship does not end in a cliffhanger! It is more of a HFN than a HEA ending but readers can stop here if they are satisfied with the book's ending. I really appreciate that. It gives the readers a choice. If you want more then you can have more, but you can also end here if you are satisfied with how this book ends. What I Didn't Like: I've read this book two days ago and I'm trying to remember what I like most about Samantha but I'm coming up blank. I honestly don't remember much about her. I know she also has a tragic past but it is still very much shrouded in mystery so I didn't really connect with her that much. This book was too wordy for my taste, when it came to the part where they finally talked about their past and their feelings, I was really interested. And then they just went on and on with the talking and frankly, I got a little bored with all the sappiness. There was definitely chemistry between Kade and Samantha but it was too drawn out that when they finally come together, it was more of a "good riddance" for me than a "FINALLY!" Although their relationship ends in a HFN, there is still a lot of questions regarding Samantha and what she's running away from exactly. I know she's been an abused, battered wife but I wish we were given more of a backstory regarding her father and his connections with her husband and how big her issues against them really are. I know that was purposely left out for the next book but it was harder for me to understand Samantha's issues because I know so little of it, throwing me a little bone would've helped me out in connecting to her more. Overall, I did enjoy Brutally Beautiful even if I got a little bored with its wordiness. I really like how the author did not play it safe and stuck with the same genre. Both character's voice were witty and sarcastic with a dark sense of humor that I enjoyed. This is not as dark and twisted as I thought it would be so some readers who like reading very dark romances might be disappointed but it was just the right amount of dark and twisted for me. Would I read the second book? I might wait for other readers' input first but that's more because I don't want the whole Saving Grace disappointment to happen again but I definitely want to find out more on what happens to Kade and Sam and to finally unravel the mystery of her past.

Oh, book, I wanted to like you more. Time magic, mysterious magic rulers and an angsty love story - sure, I'm in. However, you suffered from a lot of problems. First - the pacing - you were fairly slow paced, with bursts of plot happening here and there. Second, I think you were a little bogged down in its own mythology - it happens a lot in fantasy, so it's not surprising, just disappointing when I see it yet again. It felt like it was too many things smushed into the same story -  dystopian city, immortals that represent Time, Death, etc, forbidden magic, plus magic vs technology. I'm sure all these elements can come together in a story - but it didn't mesh well in your story. It always felt choppy. Third - I didn't like the whole "tournament" part of the storyline - it really felt shoe-horned into the story to give you a Hunger Games vibe. All that being said - I still read you to the end for some reason. I liked Kai as a main character for the most part. I liked her determination and I even liked her crushing on Avan, which surprised me, because I usually get a little tired of the angsty love in a lot of teen fantasy. I wished I had had more Irra - he was a strange and interesting character. I don't think I'll be reading your sequel - I just didn't care enough about the characters or the strange mythology to give up the time I could use to read another book. Sorry, book, but I'm not a fan.

I have recently been more and more interested in the dystopian genre. I think it is the thought of reading about different worlds that fascinates me. Either way, I am so glad that I had read this book, it kept me on my toes and wanting to see what would happen next. I enjoyed the storyline to this book. I mean, being segregated due to mental illnesses? The fact that the "pures" live behind gated communities and the "crazies" or impures, live out on the streets just grabbed my attention. This is very unique and different and I congratulate Ms. Merle for being the creative genius behind it. I loved Ana as a character and found her to be very brave. She did not think of the consequences that she, herself, would have to face, she just trudged on and tried to do the best thing for everyone else. I thought she was well-developed and the reader was actually able to identify with her. Jasper on the other hand was kind of a mystery to me. The short amount that we actually got to see the "real" him, I did see a very sweet young man and was able to understand why Ana would fall for him. But, when Ana meets Cole, I knew right away that she would be falling hard for him. Cole is a bad boy with a tender side. He stands up for what he believes in and stands up for everyone he cares about. Now, for Ana's father. I cannot express how aggravated I got while reading this book. The ending had my blood boiling and was sooo hoping that it all would work out somehow. We are kind of left on a cliff hanger and I am sure hoping there will be another book!

I mostly went into it hoping for an answer to the question Mal asks in the episode where he's shot, "What's a Shepherd doing with credentials like that." That question isn't really answered in this story? It's almost more confusing, since he's all but thrown out of the military?? so... eh. The art is kind of mediocre, too. I'm not really a big reader of western comics but you could hardly tell some of these people were people. like. idk. it was kind of ugly.
