Update May 2017: Well, I enjoyed this book a little more the 2nd time around. I understand the way relationships develop slightly better as I tried reading for more details, such as timeframe. I do think it was still too quick of a change of heart, and there is definitely a lack of "try". Feyre doesn't try to understand how Tamlin feels. It's only about what she wants. Tamlin obviously goes good guy in 1st book to bad guy (see my comments below in "Extreme Portrayal Change of Character. "), but she doesn't see how she could help him, or how he could get help to deal with his problems. I'm still not a huge fan of the love interest which makes it un-fun to read when a good portion of the plot is romance. I care a lot for most of the side characters, but I'm not too interested with Feyre or Rhys. In any case, I'm leaving my rating at 3 stars, because I can't say more than just liking it. It's certainly a guilty pleasure read. Original Review To be honest, I think I need to re-read this book to give it a better review. A lot of this comes from what actually occurs in the book and me probably needing to digest it. I flew through it pretty quickly as well, but part of that was me skimming due to lack of interest. I did not like this book as much as I thought I would, and I do not like it as much as everyone else appears to. It was not a bad book at all, don't get me wrong, but I can't help but feel disappointed as a reader and let me tell you why. Unoriginal. I felt like I was reading another book of The Throne of Glass series by this same author. Yes, I realize that it is the same author and so the writing will be similar, however, I felt that Feyre really started to act just like Celaena (heroine of other series). Feyre does and did grow between this book and the first, but she seemed to literally grow into Celaena. She responds to situations just as Celaena would, I pretty much thought I was reading from Celaena's point of view. I know they are both supposed to be strong heroines, but there should be more diversity to portray this. It shouldn't be about lashing out to the extreme to stand up for yourself. Celaena is an assassin and that makes sense for her to do this, but Feyre still has the backstory of growing up as a human whose family lost all their money and she had to hunt to care for them. That is a strong backstory to build a strong heroine from and I feel that was all lost. Too Long. As I said before I was skimming some parts due to lack of interest. To be honest, I can't really tell you what those parts were even for. Did they actually accomplish anything meaningful to the plot? It felt like it was pretty much Feyre learning to better control her powers, to get to know The Night Court, looking for the book, and learning to love Rhysand/getting over Tamlin. Was it anything else? Why is this book 640 pages? It doesn't need to be. It probably could've been a lot closer to the first book's length (which I also felt was probably a little too long at some parts, that too could've been shorter). This series needs better editing, just because she is a best selling author doesn't mean the editor can let everything pass. Extreme Portrayal Change of Character. This goes along with Feyre becoming Celaena, but this happens to Tamlin as well. He goes from protective lover to overprotective prison guard. All of a sudden Feyre is locked away and she isn't allowed to leave. Yes, no one would like being locked away, but Tamlin doesn't explain anything to Feyre. He is just a sudden bad guy so when the romance flips to Rhysand it is way better for Feyre and you, the reader, as a fan and a person, should see that Rhys is 100% better for Feyre, no questions asked. This is not a love triangle, don't you see that reader? I, the author, never intended for Tamlin to be a possibility. He is a really bad person for locking Feyre up. Feyre hates him for this and can never forgive him. Feyre is also the mate of Rhys, so now Tamlin will never happen. I'll stop talking as if I am the author, but again, this makes Feyre feel very Celaena like, and Tamlin is bad so no more Team Tamlin guys. I will have a hard time justifying this since again, extreme portrayal change of Tamlin, but he was just trying to protect Feyre. He loves her and didn't want harm to come to her. He kept looking for her in the end because he cares for her. I have to say that I think I am probably team Rhys now (I liked Tamlin before) but a lot of this is from the sheer force of the writing of Tamlin being bad and not so much that Rhys is better. This is also where I think my re-read of the book will be helpful to write a better review. I think I still really like the first book as a standalone, and then this book could've been the first book to a new series about new characters in the same world as the first book. The plot shift from "loose Beauty and the Beast re-telling" to "high fantasy to stop evil king" was too huge, and I don't think it made sense to continue on with Feyre's story just to have all this drama with romance. The new plot is a good plot-- all typical fantasy readers will enjoy it, but it was a huge shift.

3.5 stars (very close to a 4, though, which is what I had it rated as before and still tempts me to put it up). I listened to this as an audiobook read by Nadia May. Overall I enjoyed this more than I was expecting - it works particularly well as an audiobook because the characters are so pronounced in their dialogues and it picks up the pace a little (which can be a problem with Dickens, although this is one of his shorter and more plot-driven works). Dickens can be long-winded and a bit miserable, yet I still feel the hate towards him is (somewhat) unwarranted. I should say that this is technically a re-read for me, although it was so long ago that it's like reading it for the first time - I read it when I was 10, and am now 21. I find it interesting that when I was a kid I felt sorry for Oliver and somewhat identified with him (by age), whereas now as an adult I feel more of a protective instinct towards him. He doesn't actually occupy the entire novel, however, especially for an eponymous character, and is pretty passive and gets pushed around a lot. I found myself calling it 'Oliver the Obscure' at times because his suffering is so consistent and painful to read/hear about, but that's obviously part of why it was written. Anti-Semitism with regards to Fagin (or 'the Jew', as Dickens constantly calls him) is a serious turn off for this novel: not only is it more explicit than in your average classic, but it contrasts so sharply with all the work Dickens does to make you feel sorry for the poor (which features to the point of hitting you over the head with it). The female characters, although not misogynistic in framing, tend to be a bit wet and fall flat, once again this is a problem with Dickens in general, but less of an issue here since Nancy is a compelling character and has a little more 'to' her than other Dickens women. Usually I am against any censorship or editing of old texts for their prejudiced elements, especially when they are part of what makes a period piece what it is, but here I think it would actually help the enjoyment of a modern reader if the anti-Semitism was at least toned down - I know some editions do this, so an edited version might recommend itself here (and on a lighter note, calling your characters 'Master Bates' and 'little Dick' might not be well advised either!). I haven't read much Dickens, so I hope they're not all like this. Again, there are other more colourful and interesting characters in the book, but it's a shame he doesn't execute that across the board. You can definitely tell that Dickens relies on archetypes and stereotypes. Usually I find that I enjoy the second half of a book more than the first because I need a little time to get 'settled' into what I'm reading, but here I preferred the first half, probably because it seemed more focused, featuring Oliver more in a central role while the second half focuses on minor characters, and because there are a few boring and less important parts in the third quarter (though the audiobook helped me to avoid getting bogged down). Dickens also makes it a bit obvious what will happen at times, so you end up waiting around for the inevitable, especially when the old gentleman just can't quite place Oliver, making it pretty obvious that Oliver is his long lost grandson . Dickens is also a bit reliant on coincidence (his characters run into each other by chance a lot), but I notice this in other 19th-century novelists as well, so he may just be a product of his time. However, the novel does manage to find all its plot threads and tie them all up together at the end. Overall I certainly enjoyed the experience - it's dark, but lighter and more story-oriented than most Dickens, and a good place to start if you are new to him - but I find myself a little lost as to what the message is supposed to be. It cannot be that the poor are brought down by calamity and not their own nature, since we have some characters who are unfortunate but ultimately good (Oliver, Nancy) but other characters who are simply wicked (Sikes), so it cannot be that those swept up in crime are purely in that position because of circumstance. In the end it is still somewhat classist and prejudiced, not just because of the anti-Semitism but because the nature vs. nurture argument amounts to Oliver turning out to be middle-class all along - his 'reward' for being good . Maybe the message is that the poor aren't *all* bad? (The parts where Dickens demonstrates the inescabability of poverty make a good point.) I like that, despite the odds, there is at least a smidgeon of sympathy for Fagin as an undercurrent of the text, and more than a little bit for Dodger and Charlie Bates, so although Oliver seems to embody the little angel (in a way no 10-year-old boy actually does) and Sikes is very much the Victorian villain, Dickens still finds room for some shades of grey. In any case, if you can get past some pacing issues and questionable caricatures, the overall experience this book offers can be very memorable.

Light, sweet read! I won a copy of this book in a giveaway and as a lover of stories about musicians I was very excited to read it. It was a quick light read perfect for a day at the beach. It is a story about Kylie, a young girl dreaming to make it big on the country music scene meeting Trace, country music star on a downward spiral of drinking to escape his problems. It is a rather cliche love story about an innocent girl taming/saving bad boy musicians. What made this book work for me was the cute way it was written. It is told from Kylie's POV and she is a fun upbeat character, full of determination and cute humour. She was both innocent and naive and at the same time strong enough to make it on her own. I liked Trace as well. He had his bad moments but ultimately he was just a good guy struggling with his past and his present under the spotlight. There was some going back and forth in the relationship between Kylie and Trace. Some of the things they did were plain stupid and completely illogical Trace brings Mia to Kylie's birthday party, behaving like she is his date, yet later tell Kylie he just wanted to introduce Mia to her. Earlier the same morning he wanted to get back together with Kylie but she kind of rejected him for no reason at all. I like the way the book was written, the inclusion of song lyrics was nice. It is a good debut novel for Caisey Quinn.

I randomly picked this out of the books I had sitting on my kindle while looking for something to keep my busy between appointments last week. It was a quick, low-key read that is very YA-flavored. It's not an adult romance masquerading as YA (what do you call that these days, New Adult? ): the characters are written as the teenagers they actually are: shallow, angsty, flighty, inconsistent, and young. (Most of the time. The author does give Ariel the super-bizarre occasional x-rated thought, which would be fine for a teenager, except the Boyd also points out on a few occasions how completely innocent Ariel is, to the point where she can't even envision what a man's naked chest looks like.) The perspective was perfectly suitable, though it wore on me toward the end of the book, the same way being in a room full of teenagers would wear on me in reality. The mystery in the story intrigued me - Ariel's friend turned weird one night and then disappeared, remaining missing at the opening of the story - but the ways in which that personal tragedy could have been explored and really brought to life got a little bit lost in the teenage drama and the vague supernatural elements. Said elements were fine, but by the end of the story, part of the explanation for them seemed to still be missing. Boyd's prose is decent, though she occasionally uses a very bizarre turn of phrase. During a tender smoochy moment between our protagonists: "I could see the darkening evening sky, lousy with stars." Lousy. Mmm, romantic! Boyd's other fault is the occasional misunderstanding of how time functions. A dinner is cleaned up, a pizza ordered and then delivered in the time it takes Ariel to go downstairs, open a drawer, pull out a necklace, and go back upstairs. A text message is sent to a friend asking him to call the police, the friend does that, the police drive across town, wander lost through a confusing basement for 20 minutes, all in the time it takes the protagonists and villain to have a two-page conversation. There are a few other examples. Nothing heinous, but it did pull me out of the flow of the story every time. I'd like to know more about this story - what's with the family secret? What is the town's secret? What is the principal's secret? What happened to Jenna? But three more books seems like a lot of work to get there. That's a lot of teen angst. Maybe after another break for something sturdy and classic.

Off base was a compelling and enjoyable book. Both Pike and Zack were interesting, likable although occasionally frustrating characters. It took me awhile to warm up to Pike but I really enjoyed his growth throughout this book and seeing him through Zack's eyes. Zack is a Navy Seal who hasn't come out do to both is family's very religious background and his job as a Seal. Yes DADT has been repealed but he's still working in the most Alpha Male Military Bastion and while things are changing in the military there are always a few who don't like/accept the changes. I understood Zack's resistance to coming out but what I had a harder time with was his acceptance/giving in of the bullying/blackmail. Both Pike and Zack came across as younger than the early twenties they were written as and although I'm not usually a fan of younger characters I enjoyed this one. The romance was sweet and yet the chemistry was hot and there were plenty of sex scenes between the two. I loved the secondary characters and can't wait to read the next book since Apollo stole the show for me.

Meh! That's what this left me with. Halfway through the book I wanted to smack Joshua [oh sorry! Do you not care about me enough so I have to call you Josh?] for being so damn perfect. I mean, really? It seemed like everything Amelia did (or didn't do) he was perfectly fine with. She tells him that she's a ghost and that he literally died, yet he goes about it like it's a normal day. Really, dude? You're not the least bit creeped out that you can see and speak to a dead girl while no one else can? Okay. That makes sense. And then there was Amelia who I thought was going to be one of those kickass MC's, but no. I was tragically wrong. Ever since she "saves" Josh[ua] from drowning, she becomes completely obsessed with him. I can kind of understand that since she just knows that he saw her, but come on! She runs away from him when he comes back to see her! You're supposed to be strongly attracted to him, yet you're running away because you're an idiot! Jeez! Oh, and she repeatedly calls Josh her "sweetheart"! Do you know how frustrating that is? Do you? I don't care if you died in 1899 or 1999, you are not to ever call your boyfriend your "sweetheart"! Ever! There wasn't really anything to this story. It was incredibly long for no reason. Everything really could've been solved when Amelia first met Eli, but of course that wasn't going to happen. Not enough romance, not enough swooning...NO. I didn't swoon over anyone and the romance between Josh and Amelia was quite possibly the most annoying thing I ever witnessed. "I think I kind of love you." No! No, no, no! You either say, "I love you" or you don't at all! Gosh! Anyway, I'll admit that I liked Eli...somewhat. He made this story more bearable than it really should have been. The only thing about him was his big REASON to make Amelia his. His death wasn't that tragic either. I expected something that would make me go "Aww, Eli! ", but that didn't happen. Other than that, I liked Ruth because she hated Amelia as much as I did and even went so far as to bar her from their house. I wish she went through with the whole exorcism thing because who doesn't like a good exorcism? Especially when it has to do with Amelia? In conclusion, I'm glad I won it in a contest. If I bought it, then I'd try and return it. It wasn't a truly horrible book *cough cough Shiver cough cough*, but I'd only recommend it if you like predictable books where you can pretty much guess what happens next on every page. That's what I did, and I'd say that 9 out of 10 times I was right. So there's going to be a sequel, which I can understand why, but I don't know if I'll read it. This wasn't a quick read by any means, and since Amelia didn't really grow a pair in this book, then I'm pretty sure I won't be getting the sequel. Sigh.

Drama, drama, drama... it's all about the wonderful drama. Best Soap Opera, ever. Betrayals and instant forgivenesses, reseeding the world with magic and epic old-ones battles, and syrupy phone-homes to literally transparent characters. What's not to love?

For some reason it took me a while to start this one. I don't think I was quite ready for it mentally. Gin and her friends are great characters to read - but when it came out - I was in a dark place mentally anyway that I knew I couldn't handle visiting them. I'm glad I did wait because I really enjoyed this one.
My least favourite Steinbeck.

I love this world but to be honest, I was preparing for a lag in the story. It didn't happened! This was everything I love about Mercy and more. I think what really made the story for me was that we learned more about Mercy's parentage and we meet a brother. Coyote (Mercy's dad)is a trickster god and enjoys when his children's lives are "interesting." Mercy is ALWAYS in trouble so I think he must have a soft spot for her. I also like the dot connecting that Mercy too is a trickster but she does it to protect and sometime for vengeance. I couldn't love her more. I spent a lot of this book being really pissed at Adam because he let his ex move back home but I admit that this did provide extra tension in the story so it worked. Patricia Briggs did it again and if you haven't read this series, you should start with book 1 and enjoy the ride!

"You know, Ellie, Nightbird is just another name for 'moth'. Maybe that's where your dreams come from." I would like to thank Netgalley and Tor books for providing me this review copy for an honest review. Where do I even start with this? Until now my head is just overflowing with possibilities on what will happen on the next book. That's a bit of a spoiler isn't it? Yes, there will be sequel! And this baby, ended in a way that you will surely ask for more. This is how I looked like as I was reading this. This is chronologically arranged, starting from when I started reading it up to when it ended. STARTED READING: AT ABOUT 30%: AT ABOUT 60%: AT ABOUT 80%: AFTER FINISHING: THIS BOOK WAS A SUCKER PUNCH TO THE GUT OR FACE... WHATEVER! It will keep you guessing up until the last minute, even after they're already revealing the secret behind the mystery, you are still guessing if it's true or not. For the GIST Ellis doesn't know how she got on that train going to Gamin, Maine. All she remembered was waking up from a nightmare, and in front of her was a nurse who knows her, but she had no memory of ever knowing her. Upon her arrival to the town, she was greeted warmly by people she had never met, but knew her. Doctor Carmichael (who prefers to be called Uncle) picks her up from the train station and takes her to her cousin, Jenny, to recover from an illness she also does not have any memory of. She still gets dreams, and the dreams are getting more and more vivid. She doesn't distinguish which is real and which is a dream anymore. She wants to trust in someone, but she doesn't know who she can trust, especially now that everyone can't seem to tell her what happened to her. No one tells her anything. She wants answers, and she will find them no matter what it takes. MY RATING WRITING: 17 PLOT: 20 CHARACTERS: 17 UNPREDICTABILITY: 20 PACING: 5 ENJOYABILITY: 8 87 points WRITING I just have one thing to say about the writing, it was damn eerie. It has that mysterious vibe oozing through its pages. It will make you flip through its pages faster than you should. I usually don't like third person narration, except for maybe the Harry Potter series and Cassie Clare's books, but this one worked for me. Waking up without a memory will cause you to be confused, puzzled, and lost. I've never lost my memory, so I couldn't really confirm if this was an accurate thinking of a person who had amnesia. But I kind of think it was as close as it could get to it. PLOT UNIQUE. The plot of this book is nothing I've ever read before. I wasn't exactly sure at first, if it was going to be a paranormal book, or just an otherworldly contemporary book. The story doesn't really giveaway too much of wha was going to happen until the last few pages of the book. This book was like a puzzle with missing pieces, that we were trying to complete. As the story progress, we get one piece of the puzzle at a time until the whole picture is revealed. It was amazing. CHARACTERS Ellis was an admirable character. She may have lost her memory, but she doesn't give up in finding out the truth about who she was, and what was going on around her, because there was a lot going on in the background. There was a lot of thing we weren't able to see at first. She thinks before she speaks. Although everyone tells her she was sick or something, it didn't break her spirit. I liked that about her. She knew she'd be a fool to trust anyone, which was the right decision. Although, there was a point she misjudged someone, which I kind of thought she would. I don't want to get too much on the details about the other characters because I'd probably give away too much if I did. There were a lot of secondary characters, but not all of them had a role, most of them are just pawns on the game that one of them was playing... So no, I wouldn't tell you guys anymore about the characters. PREDICTABILITY I still gave this a perfect score on my book, because majority of the time I was just shaking my head in disbelief that what I was thinking about is so far from the truth. I did guess one thing right though, I guessed who the evil villan was! PACING It was too slow for my taste, but towards the last quarter of the book, all the truth came out in the open and hit you all at once. ENJOYABILITY I love my mystery so I definitely enjoyed this book! FINAL RAMBLINGS I am totally impressed with this book! I would have finished this earlier had I not been irritated with the Bluefire reader. *NOTE TO SELF: never send a galley through Bluefire!! Romance was not a big thing in this book so if you're looking for paranormal romance in this novel, better look for it some place else. There is pseudoromance I guess, but I'm not really sure until I get the next book which I want right now!! Oh and the cover's gorgeous! I should have given plus points for that. Publisher's should always remember that the cover gives the book additional pull to its audience. What else am I missing? I think that's all for my review of this book! Would I recommend it? Abso-fucking-lutely! I'm not really sure if this was supposed to be YA or adult or something, but younger readers could read this. No mature themes that I have read, just a little bit of gory stuff towards the end. VERY FINAL NOTE I don't get the title. Why was it Unwept? Maybe I missed it somehow. I'll probably skim through it at some point to figure it out!

I liked that you actually get to see Aaron's thought processes as he prepares to take back Quill. It makes him a more rounded villan. I was pleasantly surprised that the author actually killed off Mr. Today. It adds a lot to the story. However, the first half of the book is really slow and while I understand why Mr. Today's magic  disappears, why does all the magic disappear? It doesn't make any sense. Also, the island of silence isn't important at all in this book.

These books get more and more ridiculous  I mean, Lucifer is inhabiting Bliss' body? Of courrrrrse he is   but I can't help but love them. So bad, but so good. Although  Jack and Schuyler really bother me as a couple. Team Oliver. I am enjoying the transition Mimi is making from spoiled brat to someone worth liking... maybe she + Oliver can smooch it up later. Yes please.

I was a little on the fence about this book the whole way through. I ultimately ended up liking it enough to want to continue with the series, but it was really slow going I had a lot of problems with it.

Well, this is one of those books where I liked it enough to finish it but I'm kinda waffling on whether I'd continue the series. It was decent and parts of it were entertaining. It just didn't really grab me and the most interesting character to me was barely in the book. I was just sort of... okay. Oh well.

Borrowed this from the library and renewed it three times because I kept putting it off. I was about to return it, unread, until I read the back cover a 4th time and decided why not. I am so glad I read this. I love the MCs so much that I am saddened that their story is over and there's no need for a part deux.

I loved this read! The female protagonist is smart, athletic, and finally takes her life into her own hands which creates the conflict of this story. Rowan is a second child and is hidden away because her existence is forbidden. Imagine being forced into hidden panels in the walls of your home whenever there is a knock at the door. Crazy, I know! I have had this book on my TBR for probably over a year now. I watched a few of Joey's YouTube Videos and was interesting in his autobiography seeing as he is a very popular and successful gay YouTuber. Also, his pretty awesome book trailer may have had a little sway in my need to read this. But why did I take so long to pick it up? Not too sure but I am kicking myself in the butt now. There is a lot of world building in this first book which, to me, makes a hell lot of sense seeing as it is dystopian and *duh* a first book. Some people have a problem with this but I didn't see those issues in this one. There are also a lot of social commentary that can be applied to our current world events and I love that dystopian novels do this so well. I mean one child rule, environmental destruction, political corruption and possible more with a closer read. I will also mention that there is a love triangle but it's one that has not been done or at the very least definitely not overdone. Now trust me I do get sick of the overly done love triangles that seem to plague young adult fiction but I do love them when they are done well or bring in a new element. I was cheering for this love triangle after I figured it out and I still don't know what team I am rooting for because it is so well done. I recommend this book to those who like a lighter dystopia and an interesting read.

So there's been a lot of talk about Richelle Mead's new series. Some good, some bad, a lot of it just mostly disappointed it isn't like Vampire Academy. And it's not, like Vampire Academy I mean, but for me that was pretty much ok. I haven't yet finished her uber popular VA series (don't throw things at me, I swear I'll get to the last 3 books soon!) and though I am a fan, I knew from the summary that this would be something else. And I like that. I mean, why would an author pretty much write the same book over and over again? I admit that it took me a while to really get into the story, mostly because there's just so much to this world you don't know and while I thought her writing style is as engaging as ever, it did take a little bit longer for me to connect to the MCs here than it did with Rose, I really liked both Justin and Mae! They are both very strong, very well fleshed out main characters, flaws and all, and I love that! They're complicated and human and just full of character and though I didn't necessarily always agree with their choices, I could root for them and for me that's really important. I loved that Mae is actually the strongest physically of the two. This world that Richelle Mead has created in Gameboard of the Gods is fascinating! There's a whole set of rules and intrigue and I loved all the religions that were mentioned! It's fascinating that with religion pretty much being banned, all these little cults pop up and Christianity isn't really all that big anymore. And seriously, I LOVED the paranormal twist on all this! The book definitely got more excited once that part started creeping into the storyline and I was amazed by how much I was enjoying reading it then! It was a bit slow to start, but in the end it was so worth sticking with this book! It probably helped that I had a lot of time on my hands and could just read a huge part of it at a time. If you're expecting VA, you'll be disappointed (just like so many people were that The Casual Vacancy wasn't Harry Potter), but if you go into Gameboard of the Gods with an open mind and heart, I think you can definitely come to love this new series that Richelle Mead has crafted! It's a bit dark and mature and I really enjoyed it! My rating: 4 stars

Great title, right? Though a bit misleading, it's suitably wacky for the premise: a young guy falls for a chick who may be from outer space on a mission to find her soul mate (or who may very well just be crazy). I liked the story at first, enjoyed its oddness. I could even accept that Zelda with the mean green eyes liked to run around in bikinis (this is a book targeted at young guys, after all). But I became disenchanted with it as it began to dawn on me that all the men in the story were passive idiots while all the women were aggressive, obnoxious tramps and vixens. It also didn't feel appropriate to me for a young adult audience. There's sex and violence happening, albeit off-screen and hinted at rather than in-your-face, but the book didn't have to go there at all. Also, there's the message that "sometimes you need to do something very wrong to accomplish something very good." BZZZT. Nope. Don't believe that one, kids. Could have been a fun romp of a story, soured instead by some issues. I would not recommend it.

This is actually my second read of Y: The Last Man, so really this is a review of the entire series, rather than just this one volume. It is one of my favorite stories of all time, by one of my favorite writers of all time. The Last Man is awesome. In a genre that is dominated by male characters, Vaughan decided to make a series where almost the entire cast is female. The main character, Yorick Brown, is a man, but he is not the dominating force, by any means. Agent 355 and Dr. Mann are just as crucial to the story as he is. While it is almost entirely a female cast, it is not at all a "girly" story. It's pretty neutral, really. It does, however, do an awesome job making diverse and strong female characters. Many writers when given a cast of a lot of female characters would have sexualized the living daylights out of them, but Vaughan doesn't. While being a story about gender, Vaughan treats every character like a human. You won't find any weak, poorly-written female characters in here. On top of that, Vaughan is not at all shy about diversity. Agent 355 and Dr. Mann are both women of color. There are plenty LGBT members to be found. Many women are filling in roles that are previously assumed to be "male roles" such as scientists, government agents, generals, and leaders, with no difficulty at all. The story is very well written. Every character feels real, all the dialogue is gorgeous. Many things brought up in the series made me stop and think, including a conversation Yorick had with a girl about all the rock stars who died. I really cannot say enough to give this series justice. It really is incredible. I would recommend this series to pretty much anyone.

Critically Plot - 5 out of 5 stars Loved this so much! Super fast paced with so many twists and turns. We finally get some revelations on something that is prominent in the entire series. There's a wonderful introduction into this specific kingdom and the people that reside there. And my favorite part is the closure, so satisfying! Writing Style - 4 out of 5 stars Simple but engaging. Definitely got better when immersed into the mystery and intrigue. Also, they're so many beautiful, detailed descriptions that really capture the setting. Characters - 5 out of 5 stars I love all the characters in this series, so many of my favorites come back in this book and it's glorious! As for the main characters in this one in particular, I adore Bitterblue. She is overwhelmed and bewildered as a teen queen but also intuitive, strong, compassionate and determined to do her best in her charge and to move her country forward. Saf, or Sapphire is a new character introduced and we first meet him as he is stealing but he's definitely not what he seems. He's mischievous and strong but honest and working toward the betterment of the kingdom. Teddy, who is also new and best friends with Saf, is my boo. He's enthusiastic, open, quirky, brave and trusting and a great relief to the sometimes heavy plot. Emotionally This is definitely my favorite book in the trilogy! I love how we got new characters and got to reconnect with all the ones from the previous books. The tension and mystery are so great in this book. Bitteblue knows someone is deceiving her but who it is. So she kind of goes undercover into her kingdom to see how things are really like and everything is much different than she's told. To me, that would be so true for any teenage queen when handed a place coming back from being manipulated for 30 years. She ends up finding these story bars full of people who listen to the stories and histories of her kingdom and that's where she meets Saf and Teddy. I love their interactions together because they're always full of laughter, challengers, mystery and tension. The mystery of the kingdom was super interesting and intriguing. There are so many facets to it (what Leck did, what he made others do, what people around him carried out in his name) and they all reveal themselves bit by bit, so it keeps you interested as well as guessing and wanting more. I never saw any of them coming and everything showed itself at the right time to move the plot forward. The past characters! I was so excited to see my beloved from Graceling and so happy that the characters from Fire also showed up, even if it was a little weird to think of Fire as an old woman. They all had mini plots that integrated themselves into the mayor plot and those pieces flowed very well. It was very interesting to see them after a few years and notice their changes. I was a little disappointed that the ending was left so open, even the romance between Saf and Bitterblue since it was the end of the series. I would've liked a more solid finish with a harder closure but I still enjoyed the one that I got.

I LOVE Victoria Schwab and all her books but I was disappointed with this one. I don't really like action that much and this book had A LOT of action. Too much action for me. I would have loved much more character moments than I got. In the end some of the questions I really wanted answers to weren't answered - and I appreciate why Schwab chose not to answer them but it still left me a bit disappointed. So it's a good book - writing as always is amazing - characters were great. But for me personally there was just something lacking that made me not enjoy this book as much as I enjoyed the other two.

This was a fun book with a clever premises. The guy responsible for web security reads flagged emails. He falls in love with a repeat offender. She is unaware that he is reading her email and he has no idea what she looks like. Unfortunately, it falls apart in the end into rom-com schmaltz.

No. This was not good. The protagonist was unlikable and therefore I was unsympathetic for how she became the nasty red queen of hearts who liked to say "Off with their head". It had a lot of potential but the motivations behind what happened felt forced and I'm just annoyed because I still don't really understand why Cath couldn't have just done what the he'll she wanted in the first place. If she was that good at baking surely she would have been able to start a business. Nope. Didn't like this.

17-year-old Seth drowns off the north-west Pacific coast, and wakes to find himself in a post-apocalyptic version of a town in England where he lived until the age of 8, when a tragedy caused the family to emigrate to the USA. Is it his own personal hell, or is something else going on? This might be described as a teen version of The Matrix, although there are major differences. Seth's character and history are nothing like Neo's, and the ending is very different. I felt for Seth and what he was going through, both before and after the drowning incident. I loved the beginning of this, and the way it draws the reader slowly into what is going on (and what happened to Seth before, too). It ends with a cliffhanger - or is it? I'm not sure. If that's the end and there's no sequel planned, I suppose it's not a cliffhanger at all, but the actual end of Seth's story. Having thought of that, I'm bumping it up to 5 stars.

This book was the worst in a series of books that are pretty cool. This book itself is boring and constantly lectures you about global warming. It has almost nothing to do with the story that has been building in the other books and is in my opinion a waste of time. If I wanted to be lectured about going green I would research it myself, and even then I wouldn't feel like it was being shoved down my throat. I got a copy for review in exchange for an honest review. I really enjoyed this book, it has a nice story, a good lead character and that I-want-to-keep-reading feeling. The story is about Alexa, just a normal teenager, altough we immediately notice she is not really normal. There are some strange things that don't add up and we get the feeling there's something more. The beginning is a bit confusing, but in a good sense, I know something's up but not yet what exactly and that makes the events seem a bit confusing. Until the vampires attack. I think this is one of the best parts of the book, there is action and Alexa wants to protect Nelly, her sister, and she makes some difficult descisions. After that we get some insight in who and what some people are and we are introduced to some new people. The story flows really nicely and it kept me curious enough to keep reading. I has that feeling of wanting to continue the book. One of the few minpoints is that we still get so less knowlegde about the world, there are three types of vampires and there are werewolves. But what do these vampires do? do they need blood? how much? What do they learn and the werewolves, do they change in real wolves? what do they learn? We do get some answheres, but it is clear that only Alexa and her race are the main focus of this book. Which brings me to another minpoint  Alexa's race. She is a warrior, the only one. I just think this makes her way to special. Everyone treath her like she is their savior, but really she is just one teenage girl. I just think I would like the book better if she wasn't the last warrior  . Then the characters, well I immediately liked Alexa, she is strong, help others and will put even her live in line to protect those she loves. She also has a bit of a temper, which she has difficulties to control. Only thing I didn't like about Alexa is that she smokes, I think smoking is a disgusting habbit and it made it a bit more difficult to identify myself with Alexa. Two other characters I really liked where Akira and Soraja. Both are cute little girls who I immediately liked. Akira sadly has only a small part in this story. Then we have some other characters and a love triangle, or square. We have three boys who are in love with Alexa. I do not like love traingles. And in this book it is obvious who Alexa will end up with and I think it is a bit unconvincing due to that. And then we have ther fact that  she get's a relationship with Jackson, who we know almost nothing about and really all the evidence points to Kayden, he is the one Alexa should be with. It is so obvious who Alexa should be with that I feel like the other two are more of a distraction. Also I think we don't get to know enough of them. I could't get a good idea who they where and two of them just irritated me. Jackson only made those comments all the time to emphasize how beautifull Alexa is, but those comments just felt empty. I don't know why he couldn't just be a good nice friend who Alexa trust. And Tommy, well we really don't know him, we don't get to know him. But he still is Alexa's friend and then make some semi-fights with Jackson. To conclude: a really nice story with some good characters. There where some minor parts I didn't like, but overall it was just a good enjoyable story. The ending leaves us with many questions left and I really want to know what happens next.

Kila wakes up one day with no idea who she is. She must relearn how to walk, how to talk, how to eat, how to learn. She has been slated. Because she is a criminal. Kila knows she's not a normal happy-go-lucky-normal slated. She has vivid nightmares that almost seem like...memories. With the help of Sam, another slated, Kila must try to figure out what has happened to her. And if she deserved it. I love the premise of this book. A government that erases memories of rebels. I can so see that happening if we found that sort of technology. And the synopsis made it seem like Kila played a huge part in the rebels' cause making her a dangerous person had she not been slated. Add the fact of Kila being able to remember some things made this book a must read. But I was...disappointed. It just didn't deliver to the point of the expectations I had set. I think the main problem with this book was (this may be the first time I've ever said this) the inclusion of romance. I feel like without Ben distracting Kila, she could have made some many more discoveries about what happened to her, rather than focusing on his perfect hair. I also feel like without him she would have been braver and taken more risks in discovering where the disappearing people are going, and why she has a family who hasn't seen her for ten years. Instead, we're left with little discovered in those areas, and more discovered in what it feels like to kiss a guy. Now, had I actually felt like the romance was one like Clary and Jace's or Peeta and Katniss's I would have been totally fine with the amount of romance. But I really didn't care for Sam and felt like Kila was too new to being slated to be in a relationship. I also feel like Kila could be amazingly thick headed sometimes. I do not get how she could miss that her "father" is not to be trusted when it is showed so blatantly. Or how she was so trusting of Mrs. Ali. (Which hasn't been proven to be a mistake yet, but I find it hard to believe she can be trusted.) I found this book weirdly written. This could very well be because the author isn't American, but to me this book felt...unedited. And I really didn't end up caring about any other characters' welfare but Kila's. Like with Ben being (what we all know is not dead) dead. I didn't care all that much. I do wish that we could have seen some of what Kila's involvement in the resistance had been. I feel like had I, I may be more enticed to read the next book. (Which ,at the moment, I don't think I will.) All in all, this book wasn't terrible. I do, however, wish Kila had been more focused on self discovery rather than Ben.

(Review originally published at Red Adept Reviews.) Overall: 4 1/2 stars Plot/Storyline: 4 1/4 stars This is simply a very rich retelling of Cinderella, with many of the well-known details intact, and a few changes and additions. If you are a fan of the Celtic style of fairy tale/folklore - with fairies as a magical race that humans stumbled across at their own peril - I believe this will be extra pleasing. Ash interacts with the fairy race throughout the story and this adds a level of suspense and danger since it's not all bibbity bobbity boo, and there are stories throughout to remind us of how dangerous these interactions can be. The love story - Ash and the huntress - is not treated as controversial. In this world, people don't seem to give a thought to it as a forbidden thing, and the treatment is matter of fact. People fall in love and this one girl, Ash, almost without realizing it falls in love with the Royal Huntress. There is more controversy in the class difference between someone who looks and acts like a scullery maid and a person who is part of the royal court. Their relationship is only overtly romantic well into the book, and this aspect is quite G-rated. (It's worth noting that the author comments on her blog that "in Ash's world, there is no homosexuality or heterosexuality; there is only love. The story is about her falling in love. It's not about her being gay.") The novel length is of benefit to the story, allowing Lo to give more time to Ash's profound grief over the loss of her parents, particularly her mother, as well as to show our heroine as a tough character, and to wed this tale, with the most popular tellings of French or German derivation, with the storytelling traditions of the British Isles. One of my complaints is that the author downplays Ash's dilemma between a life with the fairies and love in the real world. I think it could make her feelings seem shallower than had been intended, and her transition perhaps seemed less than completely explained. The other complaint is the ending. It ends happily, as it should! However, the resolution was simply too easy, as if the writer couldn't think of a more complex way to get the same result. To say more would be to spoil, but there was definitely some missing conflict. Characters: 4 1/4 stars Ash is a likable character, with courage and spirit. Whether or not you'll consider her intelligent is a matter of how you perceive her interactions with the fairy world since pretty much every story she'd read and her mother and everyone who believed in fairies told you they don't play! However, in the beginning she was longing to be with her dead mother and felt she had nothing left for her, and so it makes some sense to me. I would have liked at least one more scene where we get to see what's in the love interest's heart, but - as is often the case with romantic stories - it's enough that a sympathetic character found love. Lo made one of the stepsisters awful, but still with a hint of girlish hopes for herself, and one on the brink of likable. The stepmother seemed to have a justification for her actions, or at least she was able to justify it in her own mind. For the most part, I cannot say the secondary characters were fully fleshed out, but fairytales do tend to be told in broad strokes. Writing style: 4 1/2 stars Lo does a nice job of making the story feel both traditional and new - honoring folktales and traditions while seamlessly including a message of acceptance. By having it not matter to these people, in Once Upon A Time Land, that a girl's heart is given to another girl, it points out pretty sharply that it's odd that it bothers so many people in this world. As someone who enjoys fairytales, and folktales, and the reimagining of them, I found the author's choices and treatment of this story to be quite satisfactory.

This review was originally posted on Fifty Shades of Books 4 out of 5 Stars Easy Virtue has been on my Kindle for ages now, and I finally got around to reading it. In short, I really liked it, but I am a bit frustrated at the heroine, and at the huge, massive, gaping cliffhanger at the end of the book. So... Easy Virtue is my first book by Mia Asher and tells the story of Blaire White, an "ugly little duckling" who used to be the outsider at school and grow up as an only child to two messed-up parents who never made her feel loved. The moment Blaire grew up and turned into a beautiful and sexy woman, she moved to New York, started to pursue her own personal path to vengeance and became a self proclaimed gold-digger. "I am allowed to be that selfish girl who likes to put herself first, the girl who would rather have an expensive bag that a love letter." In other words, Blaire is not ashamed to admit that she sleeps with rich and famous of New York in exchange for money, clothes, trendy purses, and fancy places to stay. She never gives or expects anything more than sex. However, after her latest prey dumped her, she accidentally meets Ronan who is a wonderful and handsome man, but who's rather the "nice guy next door" rather then the type of guy she usually goes for. And as she ;efts herself grow more and more close to him, she starts to become afraid of what Ronan would think of her if he know the truth, and braces herself for the sting of the rejection... "Once upon a time, there was an unloved Blaire (...) She promised that she would never let herself grow close to anyone; that she would never let love cut her wings and make a prisoner of her once again. That way she would remain safe and unharmed." It is difficult for me to cast a vote on that book just yet. There was this huge cliffhanger, and there feeling that there is much more to the story the reader needs to know. But I am definitely intrigued and despite the fact that I do not agree with Blaire's behaviour (and that it is frankly difficult to relate to her), my interested is piqued, and I can't wait for the next part to be released, as I really, really want to know if Blaire will take the risk of choosing love over money. This book managed to change the plot focus entirely while simultaneously rehashing the problems from Insurgent. I quite liked the themes in Allegiant, especially as those of family from Divergent were revisited, but the execution was mediocre and the plot is still nonsensical. In light of this third book, the first two could have been condensed into one book because who gives a bird doo about what happened there now. The way bioethics was handled in this book troubles me deeply. We have enough people in this world who think scientists don't care about the scientific method, and so while I'm all in support of evil scientists and the big bad of book 1, I am not okay with an entire, otherwise upright human civilization participating in massively unethical experiments that the legislation since the 1960s Stanford experiments have essentially quashed forever in the US. If there is one thing everyone should learn from this review, it is that THIS IS NOT HOW WE SCIENCE! So back on topic: Allegiant switches between Tris's and Tobias's POV. It's a little interesting, I certainly find Tobias more interesting as a character now, but their voices are indistinguishable and in at least a dozen times, I found myself halfway through a chapter before realizing that I was in one's head and not the other's. I think if the phrase 'but I don't really care' pops up, it's 70% likely to be Tobias. Anyway, supporting characters were useless, blah blah, still like most of them more than the leads though. One thing Divergent did well was representation, there was definitely an attempt to make it diverse...but including minorities speaks well of the author, not necessarily the book itself. The denouement/epilogue read like it was the end of the book at nearly every page. That's what happens when you've got a million fragments of themes that you want to tie up with pithy statements, I guess. The Divergent trilogy just reads like it didn't know what it wanted to be and was not read with a fresh set of eyes before it was shipped off. If I had to sum this book up in one sentence, it would be "Tris is always right." Not much improvement from its predecessors in terms of style, but it certainly exceeded my expectations and had some lines I liked. The less you think about this series, the better it'll go down. To be fair, I'm likely harsh against the style because I was reading two exquisitely written books before two in this series, but I'm pretty sure it's rough. 2.5/5 stars for this book, and 2/5 for the trilogy. ***** Major series spoilers ahead ***** Alright, let me outright say that unrealistic plots are common of pop action fantasy/sci-fi. Take The Matrix, for instance--humans as batteries, really? Ever heard of trophic pyramids? So I won't dock Roth for the experiment setup, but taking that as a given, the premise still doesn't make sense. Quick summary, apparently the faction-world of Chicago was a giant experiment to cultivate genetically pure people, the Divergent, from genetically damaged people, who are believed to be emotionally and morally deficient. (They were damaged from historical movements to gene-clean.) Anyway, if researchers could already identify what are 'pure' genes, and had the methods to change genes, and also--here's the kicker--individually gene-cleaned participants before throwing memory-wiped versions of them into Chicago, then why didn't they just...gene-clean people? Why wait for genetically damaged people to procreate until they produced mutant babies? And why do you think genetically damaged people are going to create genetically pure offspring? Plus, apparently the Bureau of Genetic Welfare (who runs this particular experiment) has been messing around inside the city. They want to protect their Divergent population, yes? So they extract a few individual Divergent over the years, then hand Jeanine the attack serum so she can kill the high Divergent population of Abnegation, but then intervene before people start killing too many of the factionless, who have a high Divergent population. Um...one of those things is not like the others. And no, the reasoning given also didn't make any sense because of the existence of a certain memory serum and how giving it to a few Abnegation leaders would have solved everything. I could write a book about these sorts of elements, but I will refrain. It suffices to say that nearly none of the characters ever choose a course of action that would suit their goals because, I dunno, they're too dumb to figure it out. Tobias picks up many flaws that need to be resolved in this book. I honestly like them, I think his insecurity and obsessiveness are interesting and give him a lot more depth, and actually make sense given his past. What doesn't make sense is why these qualities didn't manifest before this book (given that Tris is oh so perceptive). The potential was wasted. Also, I find Caleb's betrayal still impossible to believe. Since you clearly love your sister, why did you let Jeanine torture and try to kill her, as implied? oh, because Jeanine is *very persuasive*. We're told this again and again, and that's it. Every time the question comes up, 'yo Caleb why'd you do that', all we get is that Jeanine is very persuasive. Discounting the hostage taking, Jeanine's most persuasive line is basically wailing 'but I'm trying to save this city!!' like the most generic and puerile villain ever even though you could tell that she wasn't meant to be so eyerollingly dumb. Deaths were overall pointless, and I don't even care. Tris should have died by death serum because our world has already perfected poison gas. The future did not need a fancy pants serum to kill people....actually I'm not even going to talk about the serums because they didn't make any sense. I'm done with this series, and good riddance.

Rating: I really liked it (4 stars) This is the fourth book I've read by Karen Witemeyer and she has definitely cemented her place on my list of favourite authors. To Win Her Heart is not my favourite book of hers (that would be A Tailor-Made Bride, followed closely by Short-Straw Bride) but it was a light, cute and enjoyable read nonetheless. Solid 4 star material. Yes, a lot of the themes and elements were similar to those in her other books, but part of the charm of her stories is that even though there are similarities all the heroes and heroines she creates are distinctly different people with their own personalities and endearing quirks. And the unique details of each of their occupations, the small day-to-day details casually woven throughout and the unique figures of speech ("a hill of beans") are all insightful and help make the settings come alive. Levi's speech impediment was the perfect detail to make him memorable in the sea of oh-too-perfect heroes in Christian fiction (that and his enormous towering hulk). It gave him a vulnerable side and also provided opportunities to inject some humour into the story (I loved his creative vocabulary choices in order to cover up his difficulty with certain words). I was glad the author chose not to go down the path of having the heroine diligently work with the hero to overcome his 'disability' and magically cure him; it would've felt contrived and it was refreshing that the heroine was able to accept - and love - him for the whole person that he was. The line that packed the most emotional punch for me was on the second last page when Levi says "I'm thorry, Mama." For a character so self-conscious about his lisp it showed how much he loved his mother that he didn't care what anyone would think, he just wanted so badly to say those words to her . I wasn't such a huge fan of Eden (excellent name choice though, Levi too) as she was a little too hung-up on the past and a bit holier-than-thou, but she was readable and I didn't dislike her. Is there a Happy Ending? Yes! Not the too-perfect and therefore unbelievable kind, but the genuine kind where every tiny little detail isn't perfect but the characters are happy and you know they'll stay happy together and cope with whatever life throws at them, be it either good or bad, or both. But hopefully mostly good! Content Rating: PG I've rated this PG mostly because there is some violence (a fairly brutal punch-up scene) and also because one of the characters comes onto the heroine fairly strongly, trying by turn to cajole or intimidate her into marrying him. There are also some references to prostitutes (or 'harlots' as the uppity ladies of the town call them) but they're very light and not central to the story. In general the content is light enough for teen readers but I don't think the story and themes would really interest them anyway so the caution is probably unnecessary. The romance is 100% clean; no lewd remarks, no mauling each other or deep impassioned kisses and best of all, no bedroom scenes! A coup for the clean romance category which manages to capture and convey the attraction and real regard between the couple without the need to resort to being physically explicit. Both the hero and the heroine have the usual pint of god-fearing Christian spirit flowing through their veins and struggle a little in their own ways to 'give their life into God's keeping', but overall it wasn't too prevalent and was easy enough to read without coming across as preachy. If a little more overt Christianity than I prefer is the downside to reading a Witemeyer book in exchange for such a light, endearing and clean romance, then it's one I'm perfectly willing to accept. Romance Rating: From the very first it was conveyed beautifully how utterly captivated Levi was by Eden (both her personality and her physical person) and how very precious he thought she was as a complete and whole person, not just a pretty face. Eden was slower to reciprocate his regard but once she did her feelings for him felt genuine. A lot of it was in the small details of each that become dear to the other, both in personality and appearance. (And I've now got me a bit of a hankering for a mighty fine giant of a blacksmith of my own with some nice curly dark hair!)

*This review will also appear on A Leisure Moment* "I'll love you forever. Even when I can't." I confess, this is my first Colleen Hoover book. Deitre told me one day that I had to start reading her stuff and gave me two titles to start with: the first was Confess, the second Maybe Someday. So after finishing my current read, I decided that I was going to pick up Confess and read it before classes started back and it devoured all of my time. Boy, was that the right decision to make! Once I picked this book up I could barely put it down--I didn't want to put it down. The prologue starts the book off with a bang. If you're faint at heart, you might even be in tears by the time you reach page ten. My tears came later, but still there were tears. Auburn Mason Reed was likeable and relatable, and I instantly loved her character. She had drive and ambition, and she had a brain inside her head to help her get the job done. She just needed a job that would pay better than her first so that things might start to look up. I enjoyed learning more about her as the story progressed. I would start to think I knew everything about her character, and then she threw me for a major loop. Auburn had dimension, drive, and heart, all good things for a main character. Also telling half of the story was Owen. I love when stories are told through two sets of eyes. Auburn and Owen saw each other in amazing ways, building their characters as if I was talking to them instead of constantly in their head. While Owen's art said something about him--and the art in this novel is beautiful--how he described Auburn spoke volumes of his character, too. I easily fell in love with him and wanted him to get the girl and what he would define as happiness. Some of what I loved most about this book I can't talk about because I don't want to ruin anything. However, one of my favorite parts was how Auburn loved Adam and Owen. She loved Adam as much as she loved him when he was still alive. Even though her love for Adam never wavered, she opened her heart to Owen. Both boys meant something to her. First love and last love blended together to make a beautiful and heartfelt love story. If you're wondering whether or not you should read a Colleen Hoover novel, you should! Stop standing in that aisle at the bookstore with the book in your hand and run to the register. I can't believe I waited this long to read her work. Confess gave me goosebumps. Halfway through the last chapter, I just started crying--crying about the raw pain, endless hope, and selfless love story condensed into one book. "I'll love you forever. Even when I shouldn't." Rating: 4.2 Stars "Whatever you want," he says, "and you will want it, the owner of the box always does. It's normal. Wanting to know things is what the human race is all about. Exploration, Gwendy! Both the disease and the cure!" Yet another absorbing story by Stephen King. Gwendy's Button Box brings to life King's trademark style, a style that gives a strong sense of place and an unsettling sense of something other. When Gwendy is handed a mysterious button box, she finds herself capable of fulfilling most of her wishes and without her say so. As the years pass the box is a constant in Gwendy's life. A secret that she both wants to be rid off, and keep to herself. As always with King, things start taking a dark turn when Gwendy's curiosity makes her push one of the buttons of her box. A quick and vivid novel that perfectly combines humor and drama. King has done it again.

** I received a copy of this book from Netgalley and Crown Publishing in exchange for an honest review** Warnings about this book: It takes place during WWII and the Holocaust, main character accidentally outs her trans friend  though it's handled very well, small amounts (though explicit) sexual content, slavery discussion (in reference to golem , misogyny (in relation to how Esther is treated on a textual level), classism (Esther is of the upper class, and realizes this) Overall Feelings: When I went into this book, I definitely realized that I was not its intended audience. In a sea of overtly blonde and Christian heroines, the book was written for a Jewish audience, and was a Jewish book, through and through. While it was slow initially, it picked up (and didn't stop) once I got past around fifty pages, and I figured out that all of that was exposition so that the story would make sense. It's very heavy on history, but with the mixture of fantasy elements, it's blended seamlessly. If you wanted supplementary material, you could just look up the regions and cultures in the book. Beautiful writing and an engaging Jeanne d'Arc story, The Book of Esther: A Novel didn't let me go in a story that left me constantly wondering how it would advance. Full Review: I have issues sorting out the entirety of my feelings for this book. To begin with, it was incredibly refreshing to read a book thoroughly about Jewish life, without any hand-holding or comparison to Christianity. The book was a celebration of what it meant to be Jewish and, even as a Muslim, I found myself tearing up on multiple occasions at the strong sense of identity and community Esther shared with the Khazar people and fellow Jews. Another thing that was so good was that, even though Esther is Jewish and the book is about them being Jewish and trying to continue their Jewish livelihood, she struggles with her religion (particularly because she's so young and confused as to how she wants to live and how she wants to lead her army). Something I've noticed in novels that are written about non-Christian characters is that they're never allowed to struggle with their faith- otherwise they'll be called a "fake" Jew or Muslim or Hindu. But Barton breathed life into Esther, and made her real. A little Jewish girl will not live her whole life without doubting if she's doing right by her religion at least once. Seeing her struggle with temptation (be it with Shimon or with Amit ) gave the story one extra kick that I loved immediately. Just from the summary, I had assumed that Esther would transition. Yet, when she doesn't (which is not a spoiler, considering the summary again), she makes it very explicit that the only thing she wants to break is the gender role, not her actual gender. I'm glad that that wasn't seen as the whole solution- that her becoming a man would've solved all of her problems, even though she didn't truly want to become a man. Another thing that was well-handled was the transgender character in this. I won't name names solely so that I can keep this paragraph spoiler free and everyone can read this.One of the best parts of the book is the fact that he transitioned by the faith in Hashem- trans characters are so rarely allowed to be religious that, when this was shown, I got emotional. He is, in fact, one of the most religious characters in this book, and one that goes strictly by the laws of the Torah and the state. Esther and him share a romance, and I've never seen chemistry written that well- they're allowed to have spats and, when she accidentally outs him, he is rightfully angry and has to work to forgive her. On top of that, Esther comes to her own terms that he is a man (and the narrative never once misgenders him), and the fact that she is attracted to him is never impeded by the fact that he was once a woman. I want a book about him alone- that's how well-written his character was. Another one of my favorite parts is when Esther reunites with Rukhl . To be honest, at the beginning, their relationship made me uncomfortable because it seemed more like Esther was using her for charity instead of actual friendship (with Rukhl being a refugee). The best part is that Esther realizes this . In what is honestly some of the best character development, Esther drops this internal monologue: "As Esther sat her horse, [...] the realization dawned that she had never known Rukhl. She'd admired her strength in the face of hardship, felt proud to be one of the few people of her class to have a connection to someone in the camp. Giving her food had let her feel useful and virtuous. But it was a misnomer to call this a friendship." Coming into this book, I hadn't expected deep commentary on classism and the social divide, as well as how the rich use the poor and disadvantaged to make themselves feel better. Duke Leto Atreides knows Arrakis is a trap, but he must enter it regardless. Onto this dangerous planet which is the only place one can find the much-treasured spice, he brings his beloved concubine, Jessica, and his son and heir Paul as well as his many trusted advisors - one of whom is a traitor planted by his enemy Baron Vladimir Harkkonen. While the story is set on a non-Earth planet, with laser weapons, invisible personal shields, spaceships and other typically science fiction fare, it also features typically fantasy devices like prophecies, hand to hand combat, and nomadic people. The two genres mesh together wonderfully, mixing it up spiritually, politically, even environmentally. There's so many layers to the world building you can't help but feel impressed. I was a bit disappointed by the way Herbert told the reader virtually from the start who was the traitor, it did create more sympathy for certain characters (sorry for the vagueness, trying not to make spoilers), but i feel it would have been more fun/suspenseful if we hadn't known immediately, before any treachery was even wrought. I did love the fact that most of the women portrayed in the story were strong and fleshed-out. The political plays were interesting, complex but not to the point where you couldn't make sense of it all. Also I was a bit weirded out by the normal sounding names of Paul and Jessica thrown in amongst all the more unusual names. Not a big issue, just a random 'huh?' moment. Ending related spoiler here: I did feel a touch jipped at the end after all the wind-up of Thufir thinking Jessica was the traitor and they were going to meet at the end and I was expecting some ka-blewy action, but then that sub-plot fizzled at the end. Apart from that the ending was intriguing and satisfying. I can definitely see how this is a bestselling book and recommend it for science fiction fans, fantasy lovers and people who dig political intrigue.

Meh. Why is LKH still writing this series? It's like she's forgotten what it's about. Between random 30 page monologues about Anita's sex life, more monologues about how she "speaks guy", and even more about how she's a monster....I don't even know what it's about anymore. 3 confused stars Never thought I'd say this, but I can't with this book and the reason I can't is because I kinda, sorta don't like the main character Toby. Not liking the MC has never stopped me from reading a book, continuing a series, or enjoying the writing. But I can't with this book. There are too many things wrong with it--pacing's too slow, tone too depressing, main character too apathetic--and generally I don't find the fae that interesting. However, despite all of that, Seanan McGuire's got a good thing going here like a world with loads of potential and a long-term story arc. I especially like the setting(s), magic, courtly politics, depths and complexity of the world building, and I would like to be optimistic and say I'll pick up the second book some time in the near future, but realistically that's probably not gonna happen because Toby makes it too difficult to care about her and her story. Also, the first half of this book was too much of an uphill slog and the second half was repetitive, especially the action sequences. Toby kept getting almost killed too many times. By the Nth time, I was like, maybe you're better off dead...? Another thing I couldn't get into was the mystery. Didn't care about the victim; didn't care about Toby's connection to her either. Finally, this book feels like it's the middle book of an ongoing series, not the first. Too many things crucial to plot and character development are summed up rather than shown. I can't imagine how the next book is any different, and that's why I'm quitting this series, but if it happens to be a book of the month, then maybe I'll read it.

Hmm.... This is a 2.5 generously rounded up to 3. This really wasn't what I was expecting... not that I can clearly articulate what exactly I WAS expecting, but it certainly wasn't this. Everything HAPPENED TO HIM, instead of him actually doing anything the entire story. And so I quickly found myself not caring all these things that kept happening to him. The other characters, on the other hand, were much more interesting. I really like the Marquis, Door, Hunter, Old Bailey, and I particularly liked Mr. Croup and Mr. Vandemar and their dynamics, even if some of their dialogue and descriptions were repetitive and circular (as was much of the rest of the book as well). I did however like the idea and premise of a London Below, and most of the world he built, but everything as a whole felt a bit flat (even the . And the plot felt like it meandered around (much like Richard himself) until close to the end where we finally find out what the hell it is we're doing and why we're tagging along with Door and Company. That too, that some Angel with a God complex was responsible for the whole journey and just wanted her to open the door to Heaven so It can take over, as well as Door's answer to being betrayed by It and the main conflict resolution of sending It to another dimension, was so completely anti-climactic. I'm not sure how to rate this as a story loosely based off of a fairy tale (I'm not familiar with Donkey Skin other than the basics, and I don't WANT to be, thanks), but as a story, this was actually one of the better Mercedes Lackey books I've read. I recall Gates of Sleep being a bit dull, and Phoenix and Ashes being good, but that it took a long time to get to that point. This book is in the same vein to me as Phoenix and Ashes--it takes awhile for the action to happen, but it doesn't disappoint. However, I do have to take away points because it took even LONGER for the action to happen. Much of the book is spent with Suzanne's home life, and then Suzanne's job as a milk maid. These aren't necessarily bad chapters, if the book were longer. But since it isn't, I feel these chapters could have been shorter so that more of the main story could be added. I was far more interested about Suzanne becoming a nurse, and the men going off to war  than I was about Suzanne's former domestic life. She also could have used those pages to go into Peter and Suzanne's relationship more. Most of it is spent with Suzanne pining after Charles and Peter pining after Suzanne (at least his feelings for her aren't like a five second thing), and Suzanne only realizes she likes Peter in the absolute LAST page of the book. I would have liked to see her realize it sooner, and for them to spend time as an actual couple. Them spending time as friends was great too, but I would have at least liked to see them spend time as a couple too. A last page declaration wasn't enough for me. This kind of frustrated me. I did actually like Peter, though--which is unusual for me for Lackey's male leads, as I just kind of think to myself 'well, he's OK'. Lately, anyway. Another gripe I had was Suzanne only becoming... I guess interesting is the word I'm looking for.. during the middle of the book. Suzanne's domestic life and as a domestic person wasn't that interesting, and she wasn't that that interesting during that time, either. And her being a passive Earth Mage wasn't that exciting, either. She only gets a personality when she runs away because her dad is seriously crazy , and that is about half way through the book. But it takes past that for her to really shine as a character. Like I said, I wasn't that interested in her as a character until way later. I had spent nearly half the book wondering when Suzanne would become the strong willed heroine Mercedes Lackey writes so well, and she doesn't disappoint in the end (Suzanne actually shows growth as a character, which I haven't seen in awhile for Mercedes Lackey). But it DOES take awhile. In the mean time, read the book for Peter, as he's great all the way through. I'm half joking there, though--it's not that boring as to make you hate it and feel you have to endure until Peter shows up. But it's not super exciting, either. I'm just saying it wasn't super exciting. The final gripe is with Suzanne's father, Richard. I get there needs to be some bad guy. I get he's supposed to be grief stricken and whatnot. But to seriously consider killing his daughter, who even if he did get what he wanted, he'd be inbreeding and with a CORPSE? It's a bit extreme of a contrast of character. I don't know why, but I was somewhat hoping for some kind of realization at some point that he was being crazy (by Richard himself) or even for an actual form of redemption. But the bad guys in Lackey's work are always bad, and never can change. It'd be interesting to read that someone else was really the super bad guy or something, I dunno why. Like he'd still have to pay for what he did, but he finally snaps the hell out of his nasty plan. Or something. I just don't like stock villains, I guess. And where was Rebecca ACTUALLY appearing as a ghost and reaming him out? I was waiting for it, and it never happened. THAT was super disappointing. I guess it happened through fae, but it wasn't her. Also, worth noting for fans of the series, Maya and Peter Scott make another appearance. It's about time, I think. I don't remember them being in any books other than brief mentions for awhile. But I haven't read Reserved For The Cat or The Wizard of London, so I don't know if I missed them there. Anyway, complaints aside, it's a good book, and one of the better ones Lackey has written for this series that I've read. It's definitely worth your time.

I have a theory regarding what it might be that kept me from going - and I'm going to put that behind a spoiler tag because it might be considered a bit spoiler-y. So what I think threw me off with this novel - and doesn't make me too excited for the next one - is that the love triangle that was hinted at in the first book but also seemed to be finished because Calla chose Seth over Ren is back.
