I never thought I'd say this about any character in any book, but I am sooo... This is the first I've reviewed of the series, and I have to admit that The Iron Queen is actually my favorite and the best of the four. But...I love finally getting the story from Ice-Boy's point of view. A human lost in Faery, Meghan's fish out of water POV was fun to follow, but I often wondered went on behind the ever cold glares of the Winter Prince. Note: Spoilers ahead if you haven't read the first three books! In The Iron Queen, Meghan released Ash from the duty of being her sworn knight, ultimately untethering their bond and sparing his life. And before she transfered the power of the Iron King into the land itself, she ordered Ash to leave the Iron Realm and to never come back, knowing he would otherwise, even though the iron would kill him in a heartbeat now that his protective charm was spent. Who knew once Meghan gave the power to the Iron Realm itself that the land would turn around and return the favor, healing her injuries and making her the official Iron Queen. But what's done is done. Meghan now an Iron faery, and Ash a Winter faery, the two realms would not be allowed to marry...not that Ash could survive in Meghan's kingdom anyway. Having sworn that he would do whatever it takes to be by her side to love and protect her, Ash journeys beyond the end of the faery world in search of a soul. Along with Puck, the Cat Sith, and two more unexpected allies, five members of the faery world travel beyond the end of the world and through the gauntlet so Ash can go through the trials to earn a soul. Becoming human is the only way in which Ash can stand beside Meghan, but does he really know what it means to have a soul? Subjected to physical weakness, lack of magic, a conscience and mortality, Ash is forced to endure everything that is beautiful - and deadly - about being human. When he realizes he'll never be able to physically protect Meghan again, will he really go through with accepting a soul, or remain the ever strong Winter Prince to protect her from afar...even if it means being apart forever? Friendships will be tested. Actions will have consequences. Lives will be lost. And the deathly duel hanging over the heads of Ash and Puck will finally come to an end. What can I say about The Iron Knight? Well, most likely you've already beaten me to this novel. I can only say I'm sorry it took me this long to read the last two books. What I really enjoyed about following Ash was getting a glimpse of the decades he spent as the Winter Prince. Temporarily given a soul, he's forced to endure all the cruel, souless things that he did to others through the course of his life...and boy did he do some nasty things. It's like he stood before the pearly gates and was forced to account for every bad thing he ever did. Besides an overwhelmingly guilty conscience plaguing his soul, his lack of magic and strength make him realize just how weak he'll be if he earns a soul and accepts. He'll never be able to protect Meghan, who will undoubtably be under constant attack by members of the other realms. So what's an Ice-Boy to do? Meghan proved to be an exceptionally strong-willed human forced to survive in a magically-influenced land that constantly tried to kill her off. Could Ash atone for his sins and prove himself worthy as well? Guess you'll have to read to find out for yourself! Yeah...I'm cruel that way. But I promise, you'll be rewarded with an ending you won't see coming. ARC provided by publisher via NetGalley.
Not sure what I was really expecting, but this was quite juvenile. Potentially good story line, but too much talking about boobs, the mall, and cool cars.

While the weather in Holland hasn't gotten the message that it's almost Summer, or even Spring, I was in the mood for some cute Summery contemporary romance. And granted, there's not much to this summary, but it sounded like it would be just the thing! Seeing Magan from Rather Be Reading go WTF??? made me a bit cautious though, cause she doesn't do this often and I trust her opinion. But all this aside, Flirting In Italian started off ok, sure I was a bit annoyed at the description of Violet's mother, seemingly being nothing more than an overprotective, fragile woman. And only one of the four girls, Kelly, was immediately endearing to me, but I was willing to look past all that. Because it held the promise of some cute summer romance and family secrets and I'm SO into that! And I was enjoying myself reading the first part of the book, with the girls going ga-ga over the hot Italian boys and learning more about the culture and just generally trying to form a friendship with each other. Only one of the boys, Andrea, seemed like a winner to me, though I can imagine the attraction of the others just as easily, they just didn't do it for me. But we were doing ok, I wasn't expecting this to be an amazing read for me, but enjoyable looked doable. Right up until we got a little bit closer to the end and the 'family mystery' started getting more storytime. And it was then that I just found myself staring at the pages in disbelief and thinking 'These people are ALL CRAZY!'. Because really, they were. And Violet's right away believing someone's out to get her and suspecting everyone, even the girls she's there with and it was just weird. Also, this whole thing started with Violet being curious about a portrait she'd seen that had a girl in it that looked exactly like she did and wanting to find out more about her. She's always questioned whether she was adopted because she looks nothing like her parents. But of course it's a more logical solution to just lie to your mother about your reason for wanting to spend the Summer in Italy than just asking her if she'd been adopted or if her father wasn't her father after all. Obviously. *rolls eyes* The romance wasn't working for me, Luca was just a bit too messed up and I didn't know if he even really liked Violet or not and it was just confusing as hell. And while I get the attraction of just such a guy, it felt off and I didn't swoon right along with Violet, like I'd wanted to. Now it's time for a little rant that will contain spoilers: ***SPOILER, LIGHT UP TO READ*** Seriously, if there'd been ANY chance of me being some guy's cousin, not to mention half-SISTER later on, I'd NOT be thinking of pursuing a relationship with him! Can you say incest? Also, WTF WAS UP WITH THAT ENDING??? I mean, GAH! These people are beyond crazy and it didn't seem believable and it was just WEIRD! The family servant is trying to poison Violet... Yes, cause that's completely logical. And why the hell didn't Violet text Kelly like she'd promised to when she found out something wasn't adding up? YOU STUPID GIRL! ***END OF SPOILER*** I just had to get that out, sorry! I did like the exploring of the Italian culture and the girls forming a grudging friendship over a mean Italian girl. I liked that Paige spoke her mind and owned up to her shortcomings, it was refreshing. I also liked that dancing was such a stress-reliever for Violet, I'm the same way. Music is the thing I turn to when I'm stressed/sad/happy, basically no matter what mood I'm in, music makes it better. I also liked that she discovered a new side of herself that wanted to be an artist. I started to get worried towards the end because I didn't know how everything would get wrapped up in those last 30 pages, because I was fully believing this to be a standalone. And the end made me SO angry because NOTHING is resolved and all the big plot points are still wide open! Turns out there's going to be a companion novel. I don't really mind a cliffhanger ending, but this wasn't one, it was just me being left completely unfulfilled with all my questions unanswered and let's just say that's not a good place to be after finishing a book. I'm so mad at that ending that I don't think I'll even pick up the companion novel. Basically, this novel had the promise of being a cute summer read with some mystery included in it, but I didn't much care for the execution. And the ending left me raging, looking for my torch and pitchfork. It wasn't for me, I don't like being left with a sense of having wasted my time because nothing got resolved AT ALL. My rating: 1,5 stars

Wow! Eve & Adam was definitely not what I expected. This is a book that was so easy to read and get lost into it. It starts off immediately with Eve getting hurt and her mom fighting to bring her back to her medical facility. There's where she was given the best project of all. Create boy. Adam. Now that's a project that I would love to do. I would love to create my own boy/guy if given a chance. He'd have green eyes, perfect white straight teeth and a killer smile. LOL. In Eve & Adam you get a few characters that bring so much to this story. You have a best friend in this story who has to be the most reckless person I've encountered in a book. Next you have Solo, he's smart and witty. He's up to something but you have to read to figure it out. And last but definitely not least, Eve. She's a smart girl who is bored out of her mind and wants nothing more than to have her best friend by her side. Together all three go through a journey where you should expect the unexpected. As revelations come into play, you'll see the reasons behind certain people's actions. It's bizarre. Ms. Applegate and her husband Michael Grant delivers a book that will draw you in from page one. You have a bit of mystery and some romance. I definitely enjoyed this book and can't wait for book two is will be called "Adam & Eve". I give this book a 4 stars and a definite Good Choice for Reading. http://www.goodchoicereading.com/2012...

I have mixed feelings about 'Eidolon'. When I read the first book 'Radiance' I thought it was an amazingly new and fresh concept. I just loved it! Then we get to this book and I am left feeling a little bewildered and bummed. The reason for my bewilderment is that I just cannot understand why at the end of the last book Secmis killed herself to raise the galla. I don't think such an abhorrent creature would kill herself all willy-nilly like that when she loves terrorizing people so much. You can't do that if you're dead so I have a hard time understanding her reasoning for doing so. The viper queen was an exceptionally old Kai who clearly wanted to live for what seems like forever. If that so is the case and she went to great lengths to insure her survival, why then would she kill herself? Makes no sense to me. I thought perhaps that she was now queen of the galla as she summoned them and there would be some big blowout bash at the end of the book but that didn't happen. What a shame because that would have been awesome! Now I understand the author ended 'Radiance' the way she did to segue into 'Eidolon' to make it seem intense and dramatic but I just think it's inconsistent with a character such as Secmis. Now as to why I am bummed is simply the fact that it seems to me that often times when you are reading another installment into a series the initial impression of said series can wane. The first books create a new world, new characters, new relations, new everything! It's exciting and full of mystery. Not to mention the romantical tension between two people is always fantastic because when they finally get together is makes me go 'Aww! So my beef is that after the first book in any series, the second and so on and so forth usually lose their luster. In Eidolon for the most part a lot of the story was told at Saggara which is a little boring, not to mention all the drama. Sooo much drama in this one. Granted some drama between Ildiko and Brishen is understandable due to the circumstances but at the same time I find that there is another inconstancy Ildiko said that she would wait for Brishen to return from being the Wraith King so that he would have a kingdom and beloved wife to return to. Brishen was very happy about that because he loves Ildiko and refuses to give her up as queen even though she can't give him any children. So with that mindset, how is it at the end of the book one of them proclaims that the baby 'saved' their marriage. If neither of them were giving up on said marriage that seems off to say unless Brishen would have taken on a concubine but that seems to go against his character. Besides all that the story was okay. Brishen, Serovek, and company risk war to save the world and go on an adventure to defeat the galla. That mixed in with Ildiko bits and the occasional snippets of Kirgipa and you have 'Eidolon'. It was a passable read I just wasn't is as into it or is as excited to read it as I was with 'Radiance' which is a shame. I don't know if there will be another entry in the 'Wraith Kings' series but I will keep my eyes peeled for it. Even though this book didn't tickle my fancy too much I know that Draven can write so I shall maintain hope that if she does make another that it will be fantastic and that I'll have to snatch it up!

I kind of struggled giving this a 1 star. It deserves something like a 1.5--I most likely will read the second one because I haven't quite given up on this story, but where to start? 1) The characters. Absolutely hated them all with the fire of a thousand suns. So this could fall under it's a "me" not the book, but there was far too much telling and not enough showing. Let's take Buffy for example A. We're told over and over how funny she is, and how tragic the death and betrayal and all that because of hilarious and vibrant she was. Not once throughout the entire book does she say anything remotely funny. Not once, and there's tons of opportunties for levity. Now all the characters seem like driven, moody, antisocial automatons, so veer back between annoying and repulsive. So the deaths at the first speech (7 people I think? not going to get the book out) and then the many deaths at the farm, she still says nothing? Still keeps taking money to fulfill some apocalyptic Christian death wish? (well she does say grace at the table which I guess is the tip off). And people are still really sad and crushed, like Dumbledore just died. Throughout the book though when we do see Buffy, she's either off with her boyfriend, or planting thousands of barely detectable listening devices but no scene where you actually see any personality. The parents! That could have been an interesting plot line, but again we're just told that they're "cold" and attention seeking (while the entire book, every few pages the character is pulling out their phone to check website's popularity). The noble senator! You get told by a very reliable reporter who has basically handed you the nomination for presidency that your sinister-as-fuck vice president who hates your guts and is salivating at replacing you MURDERED your daughter and in-laws and what is your reaction? Call the secret service! Police! Demand evidence! Nope, you yank her press priviliges and toss her out, saying you'll come around for the evidence later. And this is never really mentioned again, although it cost the sulky Georgia and a not insignificant amount of people their lives. Ugh. 2) The pacing. The book is relatively huge and there is sooooooooooooooo much repetition. I like big books too! Bring it! But every time they go in and out of a door is described in great detail that the effect is greatly diminished. I get it, the future is a terrible terrible place and genuine kudos to the author for the futuristic world she's created. She's actually fantastic at big ideas, surroundings (though some pruning required) and she has a good story here. The pacing, ridiculous amounts of superflous detail, bad dialogue and flat Mary Sue characters drag down what is an origial thriller. 3) Where it goes from here? I will read the next one though my hopes not super high. Still it's a very original book even with the flaws--40 years after the zombie outbreak, US is basically taken back but ruled by CONSTANT bloodtesting, rules, isolation and fear. A kind of depressing book to be reading now with the soda can bomb, people actually advocating for us to just be anesthetized, packed into tubes, and flown like characters from Aliens universe for travel.

I came across this book while weeding. It had me at the blurb, "Finally, a novel that puts the "pissed" back into "epistolary."" The novel is told in a series of Letters of Recommendation written by a Creative Writing professor at a small Midwestern university. The LORs alternate between job recommendations for Prof. Fitger's students and various award/promotion/transfer nominations for colleagues, friends, and an ex-wife. Also included are details of the renovation to the building that houses both the lowly English department as well as those charlatans in Economics. The writing reminds me a bit of Alexander McCall Smith, and it is a fun little read, though the very end gets a bit dark. Recommended for anyone who has had a relationship with academia and/or has written a letter of recommendation.
Beautiful and scary.

Much like many of my favorite series (Harry Potter, Percy Jackson), the Mediator series really grew up in its third installment, which was definitely the best one yet. If the Mediator series is meant as a riff on / rip-off / loving homage to Buffy the Vampire Slayer, this installment hearkens back to the series landmark episode "Lie to Me" - where it turns out good and evil are not black and white, and sometimes humans really suck. No longer are the antagonists some hostile ghost or a shady businessman. Instead, Suze finds herself in the middle of some wronged parties who keep perpetuating a vicious cycle against each other. You have some popular kids who bullied the nerds, and through their negligence left one in a coma. You have the bullied nerd and avenging brother killing those popular kids. You then have their ghosts trying to kill him. It's all messy, and a real moral quandary for Suze. Cabot does a wonderful job of fleshing them all out, and showing the reader (and Suze) how valid yet misguided all their POVs are. She also begins to add depth to Suze's stepbrothers, who are slowly evolving from punchlines into characters... though this does seem to come at the expense of Suze's friends, who barely get a line all book. This book made me immediately reach for the next one as soon as I finished.

I feel I've been waiting for my entire life for this book. As an introvert, reading this book felt like validation for what others have labeled antisocial or uncooperative behavior. Well-researched with great anecdotes and stories.

Mine is the seventh story in the Club Sin series, and this might be one of the reasons why I didn't enjoy it all that much - not having read the other books in the series. However, I also found Presley to be very insecure and quite naive, and Dmitri didn't really seem all that dominant to me. My Mine review: I do kind of wish I had read the other Club Sin novels before I got to Mine, but at the same time, I really wanted to read this! A short, sexy romp was what I was looking for, and I didn't really get that, though. There is a lot going on in Mine, and very little of it has to do with what is happening at Club Sin, or even in Dmitri and Presley's bedroom. After two years living the BDSM lifestyle, I found some of Presley's reactions to be quite strange, especially because she didn't really trust Dmitri 100%. Dmitri was very upset over a security leak at the club, with photos of several members having been taken without any of them realizing it. Wanting to take every necessary step in order to take care of that problem, as well as his job as the president of Ace casino, he wasn't really present for Presley. Which to me seemed quite natural, really. Even a married couple know that sometimes, the job has to be done, and in order to do so efficiently there might be less coddling and taking care of personal feelings for a little while. Presley only managed for two days before she decided it was too much, that she needed more respect and love, and so she left while Dmitri was away on business. So on the one hand, she wanted him to take care of her, to be the submissive who needed her dominant at every turn, on the other, she wanted to be treated as a partner, but she didn't really do much to show that she could be that for him. The writing in Mine is well done, and I am sure that fans of the series will find this more enjoyable than I did. The past tense in third person perspective worked well, as it showed both Presley's and Dmitri's inner thoughts. And I know I will be reading more of Kennedy's stories in the future, as I think this one was a case of it's not the book; it's me. Some of my favorite Mine quotes: What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas. People who visited Las Vegas were typically on the hunt for a wild weekend getaway. Others wanted to spend their nights in a casino. For Dmitri Pratt, Vegas was his home. He enjoyed what Vegas could offer those who visited the city, but he preferred saying, What happens in Club Sin stays in Club Sin. He knew this situation couldn't wait, and he hastily reminded himself that his members counted on him to make this right. Shoving away his selfish needs to feel better than he did now, he fastened the other cufflink to his shirt, taking in Ace's Presidential Suite.This review was originally posted on (un)Conventional Bookviews

Hillary Monahan's Mary: The Summoning was a book that I have mixed feelings about because although I liked some aspects of it, other parts could have been improved upon. Here is my list of pros and cons about Mary: The Summoning: Pros: - I liked that Monahan created a background for Mary. She wasn't just some ghost, but a girl with a history, which made me want to know why she became so full of fury that she eventually became Bloody Mary. - Although Mary: The Summoning was full of horror scenes, they weren't too frightening. While some people might be disappointed by that, I was actually content about not having to worry about whether Mary was coming for me. If you're a scaredy-cat but want to read a horror novel, I would suggest giving Mary: The Summoning a try. - I loved what happened to Jess  at the end. She totally deserved it! Cons: - I thought there was a lot of telling rather than showing in Mary: The Summoning. For example, before we even really get to know Shauna and her friends, we're told about their personalities and group dynamics. - Shauna and her friends weren't very memorable. - I would have liked to know more about Mary's background. Three letters addressed from Mary to her sister just weren't enough since they only painted a brief picture of her life. - I wasn't too pleased that by the time story ended, Jess' motives for wanting to summon Mary remained unclear. I had thought that Mary: The Summoning was a standalone, but Goodreads confirms otherwise. Honestly, I'm extremely surprised that one book wasn't sufficient for the overall story arc.

It's been a while since I read an "East of the Sun, West of the Moon" retelling. Based on the synopsis and other reviews, I was cautiously optimistic. I also picked this up because I loved the cover art. Characters: Cassie is a generally likable protagonist. She's grown up at a research station on the ice and, thus, enjoyed a less than standard upbringing. Her mother is dead, her father is emotionally distant, and she dreams of one day heading her own station, tracking and studying polar bears. She is resourceful, capable and prides herself on her rational, logical mind. Which makes it fun to see Bear toss logic out the window. Bear is different, to say the least; he comes across as, if not centuries old, otherworldly, steeped in magic. The other munaqsri vary from down to earth to vaguely paying attention to downright selfish. The Trolls, the little I saw of them, were appropriately unsettling, but I think the author could have upped the horror factor with better results. I also wish I'd seen more of Cassie's "family" at the research station. They seemed like fun and interesting folk, but their snapshot appearances were too short to know much. Romance: Cassie and her husband, Bear. It's a special relationship, to say the least (and could also be kind of creepy if you stop and think about it too hard). Despite being technically married (to a polar bear), after setting some boundaries (cue ax scene), Cassie and Bear become friends, partners, and eventually more. For the most part, the romance is slow and sweet, nothing graphic or too rushed. Plot: Really intriguing reasoning and world building for why Bear is the way he is, why he made the deal involving the marriage in the first place, why he continues to pursue it, etc. The idea of the munaqsri was pretty cool, and its effect on the journey made sense. However, in general, the portions of the story featuring Cassie and Bear together had better speed and transitions and were more enjoyable than those wherein Cassie was alone trying to survive/escape. Though I understand its purpose in the course of the plot, I could have done without the pregnancy, and Cassie's being trapped (for nearly a year) in Father Forest's cottage was a particular low point for me, pace- and plot-wise. She does all these smart survival things, makes it to the mainland, and walks into a prison full of drugs. The lead-up to and the distraction allowing her escape also didn't work well for me. My only other complaint might be that, at times, several characters exhibited what I found to be odd reasoning and/or a strange moodiness. Writing: Overall, I was pleased with the writing style -- limited third person Point of view, past tense, and good descriptions. Conclusion: Here, I was a little disappointed. There turned out to be one solution to everyone's problems, and it was, not so simple, but simple enough that I wondered no one had figured it out before. More importantly, though, was the sheer drop of an ending. It ran something along the lines of, "Oh, solution! Happiness! Everything's going to be okay now. End scene/book." I understand that everything will be fine again, but I still would have liked some winding down after that climax followed by an immediate end. Final Thoughts: Despite my displeasure with certain portions of the plot and the abrupt ending, I did enjoy this story. It was an interesting and well done take on an old fairy tale. I would probably read further fairy tale retellings from this author, though preferably without the pregnancy.

I liked this book because it was super quirky and eccentric. I love these books with these characters that you see in society so rarely; the hippies and the roundabout strange people. Bee is a somewhat grounded descendant of a strange person and I really connected with her because my mother is an exaggerated version of Bernadette and I know that the feat of appearing to be true to yourself when all anyone sees is the product of your mother is difficult, but Bee did it well. Characterized novels are my thing, and the characters drove this book. It's a premise that takes books by SAA and Jennifer Crusie to a whole new level on an entirely different plane, and it worked for me; I search these books out like I do good coffee. The only thing that kept me loving this novel was that it was hard to get through at times. I found myself soldiering on through the style that didn't seem to flow naturally as its characters did. It tended to be a bit more choppy than stylistic. If you can get past that, it really is a delightful read.

4 Stars Overall Opinion:  This was an enjoyable read for sure. I was worried that it would be another one that I had built up too much in my head, and it was a little, but it was still a success! I really enjoy Aly Martinez and her storytelling skills. I am excited to get to the next book! Even though I was expecting that shocker on the last page, I really want to see how it all plays out... Brief Summary of the Storyline:  I really do think it is best for one to go in kinda blind, so I'll try to keep this pretty vague. This is Elisabeth, Roman and Clare's story. Elisabeth and Roman went through grueling infertility issues, and after the loss of their child ended up divorced. 2 years later, they are reunited and now oddly connected with Clare. Clare is married to a powerful and bad man who consistently abuses her. She has a young daughter, and she can't find any hope that she'll ever be able to successfully leave him. Roman is determined to correct his pasts mistakes with Elisabeth and use this opportunity to win her back for good. There are some sexy times, a few sad and sweet moments, and some suspenseful events...will all 3 get a HEA? POV: This alternated between Elisabeth, Roman, and Clare's and POV. Overall Pace of Story:  Good. I never skimmed, and I thought it flowed well. Instalove: Yes. They get married the day after their first date. Normally instalove really bothers me, but for some reason I didn't get bothered at all by this. We experience that first date, and I felt their connection enough for it to be believable. H rating: 4 stars. Roman. I liked him. He was alpha and pushy, but not too OTT to where it is an issue. He knew that he messed up and he was ready to fix it! h rating: 4 stars. Elisabeth. I liked her. She had gone through a horrible situation, and I understood her reluctance to trust the H again. Other h (h2) rating: 4 stars. Clare. **Ok, so just to put this out there -- she is not romantically involved with either of the other 2 mcs (Roman and Elisabeth), so in NO WAY is this a triangle type situation. ** I felt like she was truly a 3rd mc though and she deserved a rating as well, so that's what I'm doing here. I really liked her strength. She was in a horrible situation, but she remained strong for her daughter. She wasn't the stereotypical battered wife too! Psychologically, she seeemed sound and it wasn't a situation where she made excuses for the abuse -- no, she knew it was a jacked situation but she just didn't see a way out. Sadness level:  Low/moderate. I teared up a few times, but I never needed any tissues. Push/Pull: Yes  The h is hesitant to trust the H again, so she pushes him away for a little bit. The H is the main pursuer. Heat level: Moderate. They have some good chemistry and scenes, but I did feel like they were more about the emotional connection rather than the physical. Descriptive sex: Yes Safe sex: Yes and no. Both the h and H had issues with infertility, so no condoms or birth control was really necessary. They did discuss that they hadn't been with anyone since they had last been together intimately ~3 years prior. No mention of past partners or practices before marriage. OW/OM drama: Extremely mild  The h is friends with a man and at the very beginning (before h and H are reunited) he asks her out and she reluctantly agrees. He comes around after the h and H are reunited, and she tells him that they aren't going to go out. The H is jealous because of his presence, but it really doesn't cause that much drama. Sex scene with OW or OM: No Cheating: No Separation: Yes The h and H are separated/divorced for ~2 years. Neither of them had other partners during this separation. Possible Triggers: Yes  Infertility, divorce, drug trafficking/violence, and domestic violence. Closure:  This ends on a cliffhanger -- BUT the next book, Transfer, is already out :) How I got it: It was part of my scribed subscription. Safety: I'd call this one either Safe or Safe with exception depending on personal preferences. - Does Not have cheating - Does Not have a descriptive sex scene with OW/OM -  Does have the h pushing the H away -  Does have a ~2 year separation between the h and H -  Does  have abuse -  Does Not have OTT sad parts - Does Not have a HEA ending.

2.5-2.75 stars Lord Fenton has a perfectly maintained reputation as a London dandy. Though his style is close to being foppish, he's still considered god ton everywhere. Only his mother knows that his foppish demeanor is a careful facade designed to annoy his cold father and hide his true sensitive soul. When Lord Chariton threatens to disinherit his only son in favor of a cousin, Lord Fenton agrees to do anything to save his inheritance. He must agree to agree to a certain set of conditions, including marrying a suitable future Countess in 6 months time! Charles is reluctant to agree but he can not give up his inheritance. Society's belles have never interested him much; they're all as empty-headed as he pretends to be. Only Alice Stanbridge seems to have enough spunk to interest him, plus he knew her when she was a child and his mother adores her - problem solved! Alice is the youngest daughter and middle child of her family. Her mother died when Alice was born. She feels unloved. She's happiest when working in her garden- a garden Lord Fenton helped secure for her when she was 10 years old. She has adored him ever since and is thrilled at his marriage proposal. When she discovers Lord Fenton's true reason for marrying her, she resolves to harden her heart unless he can show her his true self. The two engage in a battle of wills determined to win at any cost but then there comes a time when Lord Fenton truly needs Alice. Does he have the courage to go through a great trial and open his heart to his bride? This is not my favorite of the Proper Romance series so far. It was slow to begin with. The Foxcroft section improves the plot but it's full of predictable plot lines and the message is not heavy handed but almost a bit too strong. Though I did almost get teary eyed at the end. The ending is a bit rushed. I would like to know what happens with Alice and Charles after that. I really did not like Lord Fenton for the majority of the book. He hides behind a foppish facade and alcohol to avoid his problems and emotions. He was kind to Amber and extended himself to try to help his old school friend Thomas in A Heart Revealed. I found him charming then but not in his own story. He is an alcoholic - not in danger of becoming a drunkard as he thinks. He is mean to Alice. In the last few chapters, as secrets are revealed and he goes through a great trial, his character improves. He learns why his parents are the way they are. He has to learn to trust Alice and trust himself to reveal his true self to her. He's a very sensitive man for all he plays the carefree fop. He feels very deeply and he fears feeling and facing his emotions. He's so determined NOT to be his father, he drives Alice away the same way Lord Chariton drove Lady Chariton away. I really liked Alice. Her character growth is excellent. She is still a young girl in the beginning of the novel - 10 years old- and in danger of becoming a hoyden. All she wants is a place to belong. Later, when she's grown and "out", she's still a naive, young girl. She just wants to be loved. I liked how she could hold her own when Charles taunted her. Then as the story progresses, she learns the meaning of love and how to give it. She learns how to be a friend, a wife and an adult. The one thing I didn't like was her initial reaction to Adam and even Mrs. Gage. It's accurate but it's distasteful. My favorite character is Lady Chariton. My heart broke for her as her secrets were revealed. She was always a loving mother no matter what. Her husband is, of course, my least favorite character. He's a bully and a cruel man. He chose to harden his heart so I really don't have sympathy for him. The big fault with this story is Adam. If he is supposed to have Down's Syndrome, he wouldn't have survived to adulthood. I was hoping for an author's note explaining people's attitudes towards people with cognitive differences, including Jane Austen's brother. It's too bad Lord Chariton chose that path. I think Adam could have been taught what he needed to know about estate management with Charles to help him. Because of the attitudes at the time, the characters wouldn't understand and didn't give him a chance. It's sad but at the same time, Adam has had a great life- even better than Charles because Adam knows his adoptive mother only as his mother and knows she loves him unconditionally whereas Charles feels his father doesn't love him at all and only tolerates him conditionally. Charles, in some ways, is more handicapped than Adam because of his overly sensitive nature and because of the way his father has treated him. I think Christian romance lovers will enjoy this story but you don't have to be Christian to like it. The moral is only mildly Christian. There isn't any overt preaching and only an occassional mention of God and the grace of God.

Ships don't love other ships. The beginning: the first 75-100 pages have a good number of reminders of what happened in Justice and Sword, and while those who are good at remembering large-scale plot from year to year might be bored with it, it was helpful for me. Who was this person? What was going on with the Ghost Gate, again? Ah, right. The middle: Breq's been kind of getting to me over the last book and a half, and not always in a good way. I love her determination, but she's also a meddling know-it-all who never hesitates to let someone who's had a meltdown know just how they could have performed better. There's nothing like being mortally injured in the dark vacuum of space  for giving you some perspective! The end: some things are left open, as they necessarily must be. It reminded me a lot of the ending of Downbelow Station , but wasn't identical by any means. Leckie's been open about her SF influences, the powers involved are quite different, and my overall impression is that those powers, in the end, aren't what matters most. People, living from day to day, moving forward, politicking, eating and drinking together, protecting those they love, bickering, making mistakes and getting hurt and recovering. And singing. And laughing. Well, I laughed. And I'm kind of glad I don't know what the egg song sounds like. Great series. Highly recommended.

3 of 5 stars: It was OK. I really wanted to give this book a higher rating, but it fell flat :-( The first three books in the series were quite amusing. The first book had some entertainment value, even though the writing was technically horrible. And even though I really don't believe Dan had, when researching serial killers, never read the Dexter books. But anyways, the Dexter angle disappeared in the second book, and the writing improved. It gave us something fresh and nice, a complicated and conflicted YA character, without going into love triangles (however, he slightly strayed there in the third book). The third book was actually quite nice. It seemed he started following his own Writing Excuses advice, and the quality went up several notches. But now....the fourth book... The writing is OK. But John is no longer John. I understand that a character should grow and you can't keep hanging in the angsty teenager spiel. But once a sociopath, always a sociopath. You don't suddenly grow empathy or something. Which he kinda does. The tension from the first books (will he go over the edge or will he hang on to his humanity  This question even quite literally near the end of this book  ) disappears from the story, and with it most of the fun, the edge the previous books had. He's just a mouthy kid, who thinks he's brilliant. Dan tells us John's brilliant, but he never really shows it. John doesn't do well in an ensemble setting, both in-story as as a book. I hope the quality improves in the next two books, but based on the reviews I've read, I rather doubt it. Too bad.

"You said yourself that the people of Luna need a revolutionary." She lifted her chin, holding his gaze. "So I'm going to Luna, and I'm going to start a revolution." I've just learned that Winter is the last book in this series. And I'm really, really sad about it. No joke. This is the first YA series in a very long time where I was so excited to get to the next book in the series. So excited that I broke one of my rules, which is that I write the review of a book before moving on to the next one in the series, to keep my thoughts fresh. When I saw that Overdrive had Fairest in audiobook form, I downloaded it immediately after finishing this, because I didn't want to leave this world yet. Not even to switch to the damn Hamilton soundtrack for the 800th time. This world is just so incredible. Meyer has such a way with fairytale mythology. She set up this story so subtly in Scarlet. I'm not be overly familiar with the Rapunzel storyline, so it didn't register until far into this book that Thorne's surname was picked specifically because he's Cress's "Prince Charming" . That's some excellent set up/pay out. Well played. I have to admit, Cress is my least favorite of the women so far. It's not really her fault, and she gets some truly fantastic moments. But she's too innocent, too naive. It's heart wrenching at times, wonderfully innocent and childlike at others. But it's also really frustrating and annoying. I know she'll be better in Winter, because she had so much character growth throughout this one. Scarlet was fairly absent throughout this story, though her interrogation by the Lunars was really hard to listen to. Our very small introduction to Princess Winter was fucking fantastic, though. It had me overly pumped for that book. Which, incidentally, is not on Overdrive. Which means I have to get the ebook copy. Which means a slower read. Which is ANNOYING. Cinder, however, shone bright like a...cyborg... just pretend I didn't say that. Something that annoys the hell out of me in stories with missing/rightful queens/kings is the assumption by the missing heir and/or their handlers that the world is just DYING for them to come back to power. That they're going to raise the banners, and write drinking songs about the returned monarch. WOO HOO, TIME TO RETAKE MY THRONE LIKE EVERYONE WANTS. See: Game of Thrones, Throne of Glass. See: The poor folk give no fucks who has the throne, so long as they get to eat, and get to survive the war that will obviously occur when they try to take their seat back. They're not interested in backing someone just because they're "supposed to be" the ruler. Cinder worries throughout this volume if the people want her as their ruler. She acknowledges she hasn't ever been a monarch before, she knows nothing about her home and her kingdom. She's terrified. LONG LIVE THE QUEEN, BITCHES. All the support she got in this book filled my heart with such joy. Especially the woman in Africa who stood up to the military. GAH LOVE GAH. Seriously, I'm really sad to finish this series.

Every book I've ever read by Colleen Hoover has left me feeling conflicted, but that doesn't stop me from reading them. I got a BookBub alert that this one was free on Kindle, so I snapped it up and actually ended up starting it that same day. It's a quick read with an immersive plot, just like I've come to expect from Hoover. I was surprised at how little drama this book had compared to books of hers that I'd previously read... until I got about 80% in, because that's where it all is. The basics, to start: Sky meets Holder at the grocery store one day. He's the first boy she's ever been attracted to in her entire life, but he acts really strange around her and she figures that, of course, he'd be the one boy on the planet not banging her door down to get with her. But then they run into each other a few more times, and she realizes that he's sweet and he does like her, he's just weird about showing it. It's not long before Sky and Holder become close, but Holder's erratic moods make their relationship (if you could even call it that) rocky. When you add in a traumatic past, huge hidden secrets, and teenage hormones, you've got a recipe for some over-the-top drama. Now, things I liked: Sky's new friend at school, Breckin, is honestly the best character in the book. He's present for all of probably thirty or so pages, but he's the most likeable character in the entire book. He's funny, he and Sky have a great connection, and even though it feels like he's just there so the book doesn't solely focus on Sky and Holder, he was a great addition. (I probably would have preferred a book about Breckin over what I got in this book.) There might have been some serious instalove here (even if the characters don't refer to it that way), but I could definitely feel the connection between Sky and Holder. Hoover's writing, as always, drew me in. In any of her books that I've ever read, I want to keep going even when I hate what's going on. Things I disliked (spoilers ahead): 1. All the slut shaming. It's in every Hoover book I've read so far, and it's so frustrating. Our MC is ~super edgy~ because she sneaks boys into her room to make out. Just make out, nothing more, she wants us to know. Because she'd be a slut if she did anything more, and what kind of MC would she be then? Her and her BFF also lovingly refer to each other as "slut" or "whore" and I have never understood why that's a thing. Holder's mood swings. Sky starts off on the right foot with this. She's creeped out. She's disturbed. She thinks he's super hot, but she wants nothing to do with him. But then he smiles and she throws caution to the wind, putting up with a guy who constantly throws temper tantrums, goes weeks at a time without talking to her, punches the hoods of random cars when he gets upset, and practically stalks her until she falls in love with him. The entire last quarter was completely over the top. Let's wrap up everything that happens to the MC's in this book, because this is what took my rating down to two stars: **serious spoilers ahead** * Sky's mother dies when Sky is very young. * Her father repeatedly rapes her as a small child. * She's kidnapped and told that her father gave her up. * Holder witnessed the kidnapping and still blames himself for it, even though he too was a small child at the time and DID tell an adult, and it's not his fault that the adult didn't listen. * Holder's twin sister (Lesslie) commits suicide, and he feels guilty over this too. * Surprise! Holder and Lesslie were best friends with Sky when she was little. Also, Sky's father raped Lesslie, too. * Sky's "adoptive" mother is actually her biological aunt, who was ALSO repeatedly raped by Sky's father as a teenager. * When Sky confronts her father, he shoots himself in the head in front of her. I mean, this is just too much. At some point, I just started rolling my eyes as another and another and ANOTHER dramatic twist came one right after the other. The sexual abuse is not handled well at all. Sky has repressed it. I get that. It was really traumatic for her, and as a young child, she didn't really understand what was happening, only that she didn't like it and it made her sad. That's all fine. But the idea that Sky can go from completely shutting herself down emotionally when she's in any sort of physical relationship with a boy -- I'm talking not even kissing someone without zoning out -- to falling all over Holder, having orgasms out of nowhere, begging him to have sex with her just after she's uncovered her repressed memories... I just can't buy it. Why does nobody in this book suggest therapy? Sky has had an incredibly traumatic life. I mean, see the list above. It's crazy. But Sky just talks to Holder, takes a shower, has some sex, and she's magically ok? No, she needs professional help. This is insane. Overall: I wanted to like this book. And while I was reading it, at some points, I actually did. But in general, I can't put up with all of this. There's too much going on to actually do any of it well. When you have me literally rolling my eyes at the plot twists, you've gone too far. And that's what this book did. It went too far.

I watched this movie about a year ago, without having read the book. At the time, I wasn't too impressed and I wasn't intrigued enough to go pick up the books right away. I had always meant to read this trilogy eventually, since it's been compared a great deal to The Hunger Games (both young-adult dystopian trilogies with female leads). While Divergent wasn't as good as The Hunger Games, I still found it very compelling and suspenseful, even after seeing the movie and knowing what was going to happen. That Roth was able to captivate me, despite knowing the plot is a testament to her writing. It's pretty simplistic, yet immersive. I would be listening while driving and not want to get out of the car when I arrived at my destination. The narrator for the audiobook, Emma Galvin, took some getting used to, but once I got into the meat of the book, her voice became less distracting. I was so engrossed with Tris' story and the action while listening that it wasn't until after I had finished the book and had some time to think about it that I realized how little of the book is devoted to world-building. I don't know if this is a result of Roth creating an overly simplistic society or if her plan all along was to keep the audience in the dark and provide very little detail, only divulging information when absolutely necessary. Or maybe it has everything to do with the first person point of view of the story. We see what Tris sees. We know what Tris knows. We question what Tris questions. We feel what Tris feels. It's also difficult when setting a story in an imagined world not to information dump and bog down the narrative with facts, so maybe that's what Roth was trying to avoid. If you're able to ignore the nagging questions in the back of your head and immerse yourself into the character's experiences then this is an enjoyable read. But I can see how some people would be annoyed by the shaky and somewhat illogical construction of the 5-faction system. I plan to read the rest of the trilogy, despite the less than favorable reviews for both Insurgent and Allegiant. I already have the Insurgent audiobook downloaded on my phone to listen to on my commute home. Narrator: Emma Galvin Length: 11 hrs 11 mins

I did not expect this book to be what it was. It was beautiful, and it was painful, and it was so emotional and just... oh, I have all the feels! It was actually a pleasant surprise. I expected it to be deep and thoughtful, but I didn't expect how emotionally connected I would get to the story. There was no rush to it, the pace of the story was very slow but not boring at all. It was important that we see how Nastya and Josh build on their relationship, which is so great in this time where insta-love seems to be the norm. I love that it wasn't insta-love for Nastya and Josh. I love that they took their time. I also really love the story of friendship. Drew has become one of my favorite people in the world. He is a wonderful friend and I fell a little in love with him too. There is so much to love about this book. I love that it tackled some really difficult emotions and issues. It was painful at parts, and the feelings are so real coming through the pages. This book has so much, it isn't one-dimensional at all, there is so much happening in the book and when you put everything together, it is just gorgeous. This book is everything.

Read more of my reviews at Cornerfolds.com! If you know me then you know that A Court of Thorns and Roses is easily in my top 5 favorite series of all time. I mean, my dog's middle name (yes, he has a middle name) is Rhysand. So it should come as no surprise that A Court of Wings and Ruin was my most anticipated read of 2017! I set aside time specifically for this book and was at the bookstore before I'm usually even awake getting the exclusive edition. I'm telling you all of this so that you'll understand how devastated I am that this book was actually pretty disappointing. A Court of Wings and Ruin picks up right after the end of A Court of Mist and Fury, with Feyre back in the Spring Court. Tamlin believes that she has not been acting of her own free will during her time with Rhys and is actually still in love with him. He doesn't realize that she's only with him to get vengeance for what happened to her, her sisters, and her friends when Tamlin and Ianthe sold her out to Hybern. Thus begins a 700 page journey to war and back for Feyre and company. Feyre killing the siblings from Hybern and destroying Ianthe was one of the most epic things I've ever read ever. I needed more of this in this book! There were certainly things I enjoyed about ACOWAR, so let's start there. I thought that Feyre was a total badass whenever she was facing down her enemies. I love how far she's come since book one and I always look forward to getting to see her fight, especially now that she's mastered her (many) powers! Feyre's flying lessons with Azriel were also fantastic! Although I do think she caught on just a tiny bit too soon (especially based on the information we're given about the difficulty Azriel had learning to fly) it was a lot of fun seeing them go back and forth with each other. One of my favorite parts of this book were the side characters! Obviously Lucien was my favorite of these. The beginning of his story arc was immensely satisfying, although it would have been nice if he'd been present a bit more throughout. As always, Cassian was spectacular and I his relationship with Nesta is one I am forever interested to know more about! I was glad to get to know the other High Lords better (or at all in some cases) and I loved the Bone Carver and the Suriel! These two have spent the rest of the series being utterly terrifying and I really liked seeing a different side to them. I'd love backstories for either! It's awesome when minor characters such as these are fleshed out. I am so sad that Lucien was basically sent off on a side quest for most of the book that we never got to see! I wanted so much more of him! I am really interested to see what happens with him and Elain since there seems to be absolutely zero interest on her part. I'm guessing we'll definitely get a book about Lucien in the future. The war with Hybern is what the entire series has been leading up to and it was done (mostly) right! It was tense in the right places and kept me on the edge of my seat. It did seem a little weird that it was over so quickly, but I still enjoyed it - especially the parts certain unique characters played and the havoc they wreaked. The different armies from each court was a lot of fun to read about, especially the Winter Court with its armored bears! And now on to the things I didn't like... There wasn't a "dislikes" section in my reviews for the previous two books, so this is a first for me. To start, I didn't love what became of Feyre and Rhysand's relationship. I rooted for them and fangirled so hard in ACOMAF! But in this one they've become disgustingly co-dependent, so much so that they're basically the same person. Gone is the strong, fiercely independent Feyre from books past and devilishly charming, cunning Rhys is also missing. Instead, they've become a single unit of wing- and mind-stroking High Fae who have sex at the most awkward times and constantly refer to each other as "my mate" instead of by name. Who has sex in the middle of a war?? Who makes licking dirt and blood off of someone sexy? I just. I can't believe what's happened to Feyre and Rhys. They were my absolute favorite in ACOMAF and I'm so sad that they've morphed into literal Feysand. Another issue I have is that a lot of characters in ACOWAR seemed quite out of character. Mor is a notable example who seemed to do a total 180 from her character in the last book, spending most of this one being rude and irritable. Even Rhysand was totally out of character for a major plot point. There were characters who went from good to bad to good again so often that I lost track. Characters who would normally trust each other suddenly choose not to for no apparent reason and others randomly reveal facts about themselves that are seemingly from left field. Luckily, Nesta remains her amazing self, but Elain as High Fae is like watching paint dry. A couple huge issues. First, Rhys forcing Mor into a situation with her abuser without at least warning her first and asking her consent. This is so unlike anything he's done until now that it totally threw me off. I felt the same way about Amren not telling anyone her plan for the final battle. What was the point of lying and tricking Feyre to the Cauldron? Why not just tell her what she planned to do? Next, Mor coming out as bisexual. Like, when? Where? There has been absolutely zero hint of this in the previous two books. Every single thing until now has pointed towards her being in love with Azriel but fighting it for some reason. I really think that SJM threw this in at the last minute because of the backlash she's received for having so few diverse characters. And, you know, good for her for listening! But this was not the way to do it, in my opinion. Finally, why does every single character need to be redeemed? I can sort of understand Jurian. He was dealt a bad hand and I can buy him going over to the good guys, but Tamlin? Is he good? Is he bad? CHOOSE ONE PLEASE! Then there's the ending. I can't say too much without spoilers, but it was not what I was expecting at all. AT ALL. Before I reached the end of the book I saw so many people who were in literal tears over what happens at the end and I cannot understand why. There was no real emotional impact, which I've become accustomed to with Maas books. It almost seems as if this book was written in a hurry to try to meet a deadline while packing in as much information as possible and leaving endless options for future novels. I was surprised at the number of new characters introduced in ACOWAR, even in the last few chapters. My main issue with the ending is two fold. First, that not one single main character died in the war. Cassian almost died (or should have died) multiple times, but somehow never did. Rhys dying would have accounted for the people saying this book broke them, but I wasn't even concerned when he "died" because I had a feeling he wasn't truly dead. The fact that Maas brought him back in the exact same way as Feyre in ACOTAR just added insult to injury. Amren would have been a perfect choice to let go, but even she couldn't stay gone! It was utterly ridiculous to me that Rhysand brought her back. I saw someone else compare this battle to Minas Tirith and I couldn't agree more. The multiple armies just happening to show up in the nick of time was laughable. Second, the end was so much cheese I almost choked. I could not believe the way this book wrapped up like a Disney movie with everyone getting their happily ever after and children literally laughing in the streets! After the emotional destruction of the first two books, I expected a book hangover of massive proportions, but this didn't leave me emotional at all. Except I'm a little disappointed. I was under the impression that this was the finale of this trilogy, but there were so many loose ends and unanswered questions that it's obvious the series will be dragged out for awhile. I knew there would be more books written in this universe, but I didn't expect so many storylines to be left open-ended. It made this book feel like just another book in a series rather than a true ending. I know my review might make it seem like I didn't like this book but I did enjoy it overall. There were far more issues that I'm used to in an ACOTAR novel and it didn't live up to my expectations. I'll still be reading future books set in this world, but I definitely won't be going in with expectations this high again. Actual rating: 3.5 stars

** spoiler alert ** This is the first Rachel Vincent book I've ever read, and I definitely plan on picking up some of her other series later on. Blood Bound takes place in a world where some people have special powers, those are are special each have a particular talent. Some can track down a person with just a name or a drop of blood, some can jam the signals and prevent people from being tracked, some can travel through shadows, some are human lie detectors, some can create contracts that will literally kill you if you fail to live up to whatever it is you have agreed to, etc. I love urban fantasy, so I am always excited to read about a different world, and with the genre being so crowded now, it is interesting to see a take on a different world without vampires, weres, etc. While the new ideas were interesting, I am going to have to say that I found some of it to be a bit too much. For example  in this world, a father, who has never met his child, can mentally decide to assign them a middle name which can then be used to track them - it doesn't matter if the child or the mother or anyone else knows the name, it can just be mentally given. I am willing to believe that a tracker can find someone just through their name (in this world a person's name has a lot of power) but that other part just seemed to be a bit much. Anyway, the title comes from the more important parts of the mythology that the author presents; in this world it is possible to bind a person to the word through oaths. A person can even be bound without their consent so long as someone has access to their blood. Needless to say this creates a very complicated world in which each character is bound to certain contracts/oaths/promises. One interesting aspect to the writing is that the author uses multiple POVs; half the story is told from Liv's POV and the other half from Cam's. Normally I have no problems whatsoever with this technique, I actually really enjoy getting to see action from different perspectives. The nice thing about this book is that despite switching POVs the author did not backtrack and make us reread scenes from a different perspective, the story was always moving forward which was nice. The only problem I had with the switching was that it was not consistent, a change could happen in the middle of a chapter, or we could go a couple of chapters in Liv's POV before switching back to Cam's. I can understand not having an even amount of time for each character, the author would want to put whoever was more involved in the scene on the front line, but it would have been nice if there was some indication when the shifts happened, the way it read to me was a bit disorienting because of the unexpected switches. Overall the book was a lot of fun to read, it was a pretty quick, I was drawn into the characters and the world they inhabited, I was able to guess the surprise about Hadley from a mile away but at least I could also see why the characters in the book couldn't see it, and by the end it left me desperately curious to find out what happens in the next book (too bad for me that the second in the trilogy won't come out until 2012). The book is meant to be part of a series, so of course there is a significant cliffhanger but the main mystery/action plot was wrapped up nicely which makes up for a cliffhanger (I can't stand it when books that are parts of series come out and it takes three books to wrap up one mystery, each book should have its own beginning, middle, and end - whether it is part of a series or not).

Kel is the only girl training to be a page in her year. Sexism is rampant, of course, so Kel must work twice as hard as her adversaries to prove her worth and strength. This was a straightforward but enjoyable read. It's the first book I've read by Tamora Pierce after giving up on Trickster's Choice back in middle school. Pierce is clearly a talented writer, especially when it comes to action scenes. Despite this sounding more like a children's book, she's not afraid to get a bit dark or violent. First Test was published in 2000, but it has a distinct 1980s fantasy vibe; authors from that time period just have a style that feels different from modern fantasy. The structure of the narrative itself is similar to that of any boarding school story, with Harry Potter inevitably coming to mind. Kel makes friends and enemies, contends with a teacher who hates her, receives fancy gifts from a mysterious benefactor, and works hard to improve herself, with all that training culminating in a final battle against monsters. Kel is only ten years old in this book, which somewhat scrapes the line of believability. Perhaps if she had been thirteen or so, I would have felt less skeptical about her physical strength and emotional maturity (but perhaps I am underestimating children!). I suspect Pierce wanted to have puberty be the focus of Kel's character growth in the next book. For me, the main flaws of First Test were its focus on the mundane aspects of daily life and its predictability. The arc of the story could be easily guessed by the book blurb, and magic is only occasionally present. However, the friendship between Neal and Kel is wonderfully developed and the writing style is so readable that I have no doubt I will pick up the second in the series, especially since I've heard later books feature a shift in tone. Many characters and events mentioned in this book, such as Alanna and the Immortal Wars, seem to be the focal point in Pierce's other series. It's impressive that the author has created such an expansive world with many stories to tell. Side Note: The spidren made me have Inuyasha flashbacks.

For Beatrice - I cherished, you perished, The world's been nightmarished. For Beatrice - We are like boats passing in the night - particularly you. Well, I was expecting to be disappointed and I'm sad to say that I wasn't disappointed. Almost nothing is explained. We have no idea why the damn sugar bowl is so important, what was in it, why it caused a schism, etc. We don't know the purpose of VFD. We never learn what the schism was about. We have very little idea of what became of the Quagmires, Hector, Fiona, Fernald, Phil, or anybody who was at the hotel when it burned down. What was the question mark? What was so terrible about the man with a beard but no hair and the woman with hair but no beard? What happened to the Baudelaire fortune? Hell, what happened to anybody and anything? We do get closure on two characters, Kit Snicket and Count Olaf (they die),  and the Baudelaire kids ride off into the sunset, so to speak. And we find out who Beatrice is, as well as who Lemony Snicket is, but it's still quite incomplete. This lack of resolution would be infuriating if I weren't expecting it from about halfway through the series. As it is, I was prepped and could take it in stride, but if you need your stories neatly wrapped up at the end, then please heed Lemony Snicket's own advice which he suggests approximately 157 times, and don't read any of these books. This book could almost be a standalone as so little of what happens in it has any bearing on what went on before. We learn more mysteries from the Baudelaire children's past, and there are references to previous events galore, but the plot in here is almost wholly separate from the rest of the larger tale. I enjoyed the story. It was just as ridiculous as all the others, and had its charms. I also enjoyed the journey, or at least I'm so accustomed to the style that I was able to gloss over the annoying characteristics. I'm glad I read this series, yet I'm also quite glad to be done with it. I don't foresee a reread happening. You probably noticed two dedications to Beatrice above. That's because this book includes an extra chapter which serves as book 14 in its entirety. It includes an extra dedication and extra bios which you can see below. One of the many things that make one go "Hey, neato" is how all the books are set up. There are 13 books, each with 13 chapters. Introducing a 14th book with one chapter is a departure from his formula, but it still fits because he likes taking something with the potential to be in put in apple pie order and then adding a wart to it. (Please excuse me for indulging in a mixed metaphor; it's late). By this point you know whether or not you want to read this, so use your own judgement. 3.5 stars rounded up to four here. Bios LEMONY SNICKET is the author of all 170 chapters of A Series of Unfortunate Events. He is almost finished. LEMONY SNICKET is still at large. BRETT HELQUIST (regular bio stuff). He is hopeful that with the publication of the last book in A Series of Unfortunate Events, he'll be able to step outside more often in the daytime, and sleep better at night. A love letter to nerds, video games, and the 80s, this book will make you want to go back in time to your childhood, when a quarter could entertain you for hours. It's not often a book can take you so convincingly into both the beloved past and the frightening future, but this one does it. This was such an entertaining book, I honestly couldn't put it down once I'd started it. The blurb on the cover says, "Willy Wonka meets The Matrix," and that's such a perfect description. The Willy Wonka: There once was a very rich man who had no heirs. He wanted to find a fitting person to carry on his company and legacy, so he created a contest to find that person. In comparison to Halliday's contest, Willy Wonka's seems much simpler: the boy with the genuine heart wins the prize. The world in 2044 is much more complicated place. There are too many people, and not enough resources, leading to worldwide starvation and a culture where someone like Parzival has to scramble to survive. When Halliday dies and his contest is announced, it seems like the perfect route to freedom for the videogame-crazed orphan. Of course, it's also the route to freedom for billions world-wide, including an evil corporation that wants to take over the world. The Matrix: The virtual reality that Parzival and the rest of the world have come to live in the majority of the time is called the OASIS. Unlike the Matrix, people are fully aware when they are plugged into the OASIS, but that doesn't mean it isn't their main reality. When Halliday and his partner Ogden Morrow created the OASIS, it started out as the gold standard of video games but quickly morphed into a way of life, a way to escape reality, and the biggest industry on the planet. Anything you can imagine, you can achieve. Of course, that sort of freedom always comes with a price, and if you're a poor kid like Parzival, you can't afford it. The OASIS is a way of life, but it's also a video game, where you can go on quests, level up, collect items and weapons, and play games within the game. And Halliday sets up the greatest game of all, all wrapped around an intricate knowledge of his favorite things: classic video games, movies, music, and tv shows, especially in the 80s, the time of his youth. In order to solve these intricate puzzles, those searching for the ultimate prize (known to all as gunters) dedicate years of their lives to studying and mastering Halliday's favorite things. The game itself was fascinating. The clues were one of those things where, if you knew what you were looking at, it was totally obvious, but if you didn't know, they it was mind-wrenchingly difficult. The integration of different types of games was entertaining and fascinating, jumping from D&D style games to classic arcade to a new kind of movie-immersion game, which, BTW, I would LOOOOOOVE to play. Who doesn't want to play their favorite role in their favorite movie? Parzival, Aech, and Art3mis are all clever people, and it was fun watching them figure out the clues, even if they did get distracted sometimes, by each other and by life in general. This wasn't just a fun "let's see who wins first! yay everyone!" sort of contest, though. The stakes were high right from the beginning. The Evil Corporation (IOI) made their intentions clear right from the beginning, making sure everyone knew that they weren't going to let anything stand in their way. Lives were at stake, and lives were lost, in the real world, where you couldn't just regenerate and start again at Level 1. It definitely made the action more fast-paced and real, because there was no way of guessing who was going to make it through to the end. And just a note on the end. I LOVE that Parzival ended up with Halladay's infinity powers at the end, and just deleted all the sixers in one fell swoop. And then restored his friends and all their stuff. :) Made me smile so big! I love the friendships in this book because they developed in a way that is becoming more prevalent as time passes: online. Gone is the time when if you said you met someone on the internet, people looked at you strange. The same is true in 2044: Parzival and his best friend of 5+ years, Aech, had never even met in person. Parzival and Art3mis could date and maybe even fall in love, without ever seeing each other's face. It's more about the inside than the outside. I loved when Parzival and Aech finally meet in person, and even though Aech is not what Parzival expected, he was still his best friend, the person he spent hours upon hours with in the OASIS, hanging out and sharing everything from video game obsessions to their "mutual admiration of the female form." Yes, race, gender, and sexual orientation still matter to some, but to the most important people, the ones you love you the most, they shouldn't. All in all, I enjoyed this book so much that I want to reread it again immediately, make notes of all the popculture/nerd references, and look everything up. I keep thinking of more sections I liked and want to talk about (note: giant robots that you can fly. yes! ), and if I write about every one of them, you might as well just read the book instead of this review. I want to read every book that's mentioned, watch every movie and tvshow, listen to all the music, and play every game. It's not often that this happens, but this book makes me want to go out and buy copies for all my friends, because I know they'll love it, too. Maybe we're just a giant bunch of nerds, but I'm ok with that. I happen to have met most of them online, so it's fitting. Notes on a second reading: I pretty much wanted to read this book again right away, but held back until I could get the audio book from the library, so I could listen to it this time. And it's just as good the second time around. Wil Wheaton read this one, and he did a great job.

The first book was good, but I liked this one more. We see Rue really having to grow up more once she actually has to face long term consequences both for her parents, her love interest, her friends, and herself. Yep. Carriger touched on all of those relationships instead of just focusing on one (which is why I wouldn't categorize this as a romance even though it's an important part of the book). I have reconciled myself to her involvement with Quesnel. I still think he keeps too many secrets, but he does feel strongly about her. I am really unsure why Prudence continues to put up with Aggie as her engineer because all the woman does is pick fights with everyone but Quesnel. I would have fired her. Wanting to protect her friend is one thing; being a judgmental bitch to everyone is another. I'm sure there are lots of people who would have loved to work on Rue's ship instead of her. Carriger actually introduced a gypsy-like culture that I really loved. I enjoyed the glimpse of a culture where gender roles seemed to be more assigned to the things one did, while not liking that it seemed to leave the woman's role pretty powerless. The werecats also have a different culture more centered around many women to one man . So while not much attention is paid to Egyptian culture, I feel like this one had more depth as far as world building went. Still like all the characters (except Aggie), but no one really stands out as someone I would want to know myself. I'd actually prefer to stay far away from them since most of them are very actively interested in manipulating those around them. Amusing to read about though.
