It's better than Throne Of Glass. There is more action, twists, some character development (Dorian, of course, and Celaena in the second half of the book), some character degradation (Celaena when it's so obvious the author has no idea what she wants Celaena to be), new minor characters who spiced up plot a bit and less love triangle. Overall, a solid sequel, though not what I was expecting. Celaena is still strong heroine, but she's likeable only because she's so different from other YA female protagonists. Supposedly, this is a story about assassins. Celaena kills only when she has to save her own life and to be fair it isn't often. Presumably, this is a story about violence and there isn't much of it. Maybe I expect too much from Young Adult book but I don't like to be lead on. Her emotions are inconsistent, she's so selfish it sometimes blinds her. She's fearless, but only when it suits her. But, something happens in the middle of the book, which makes Celaena go dark and I adore it. Author finally went from telling us how Celaena is a vicious assassin to actually showing it. Dorian is the biggest suprise in the series so far. He was my favorite from the start and it hasn't changed. One of the biggest twists include him so I hope it'll give him a bigger role in the series. He surely deserves it. I just wish he'll stop following Celaena around like a lost puppy. It's time for him to become a ruler and stop being a pawn in his father's game, whatever it is. And he's so funny, I can't stop chuckling. He really brings light into the series and pretty much is the biggest reason I'm still interested in the series. He also goes a little dark, but I'm scared he'll need something drastic to shaken him up. Chaol still has no personality and bores me to death. He's the same person he was in TOG with only difference he's loyalties lie upon Celaena's feet and not someone he spent most of his life learning how to defend. I can't stop rolling my eyes at his every POV. He serves only as Celaena's love interest and we know nothing about his traits besides that he loves Celaena and that he'll do anything for her. Just give me a break. Nehemia is a hero. I can't say nothing less. If only Celaena had her back. She was so selfless and fearless - a true leader. She was and still is one of my favorites. She had many secrets, but at least her priorities had the right order. Thankfully, the whole love triangle situation is cleared up. I can't say I'm satisfied with the outcome, but I wouldn't be even if Celaena chose differently. Both her relationships are platonic, fragile and destructive for everyone but her. Chaol and Dorian keep on making concessions but she does nothing in return, unless she's in the mood. Celaena made up her mind in the first third of the book and repeated her decision in the final chapter so there is no misunderstandings. But I hope she'll also let the other one go. It simply doesn't work with either of them. How can Maas not see the potential that Chaol and Dorian's friendship has? Their conversation and banter were witty and hilarious. Also, it's touching how much Dorian appreciates Chaol. It's such a waste they let some girl ruin it. The plot has more action but it's still weak. Basically, it involves Celaena wandering around playing with Wyrdmarks and her conversations with Mort. I couldn't care less. The plot twists which include Dorian, Nehemia and Archer pretty much saved the book for me. Maas made some brave moves, but story is still predictible. There were some funny moments: " The prince then glanced at Chaol and chuckled. "And here I was, thinking that all the ladies were out so early for me and Roland. When all of them catch a vicious cold, I'll let their fathers know that you're to blame." Chaol's cheeks colored ever-so-slightly. So he wasn't as ignorant of their morning audience as he'd led her to believe. Then Fleetfoot came sprinting down the row, a scroll of paper in her jaws... Fleetfoot just zoomed on by, a blur of gold.A moment later, when the little librarian came waddling into view and asked if they'd seen a dog, Celaena only shook her head and said that she had heard something--in the opposite direction. And then she told him to keep his voicedown because this was a library. So, are you going to ask me whatever it is you dragged me out here to ask, or am I just going to enjoy freezing my ass off for the rest of the night?" Dorian said. If you were impressed by TOG you'll definitely love COM even more. But for me, it's nothing special. It has potential but unfortunately keeps on being a typical YA novel. I want more. I want to have my jaw dropped, to feel actual fear for my favorite characters, to not be bored by some plotlines. I was so frustrated when it was revealed that Celaena doesn't kill her targets. Yeah, I know it's the right thing to do, but I signed up for reckless, strong-tempered and angry assassin, not for this cheezy girl who can't control her hormones and looks for every oportunity not to obey. And don't get me started on her argument with Nehemia. CELAENA IS A FREAKING FAE QUEEN OF TERRASEN, BUT HEY, WHY WOULD SHE PARTICIPATE IN A REVOLUTON THAT WOULD FREE SEVERAL NATIONS FROM TYRANNY, IT SO APSURD, HOW CAN NEHEMIA BE SO STUPID, WHY WOULD ONE PRINCESS OF EYLLWE WANT HER PEOPLE TO BE FREE. I wanted to beat her up with a bat. I can't take any of Celaena's emotions siriously and she makes me so furious. She decides she doesn't like Dorian anymore, then she hooks up with Chaol because he's the one, then he makes her angry, so she tries to KILL HIM and then Dorian is again her prince and she'll come back for him, but she'll always choose Chaol. JUST LEAVE DORIAN ALONE ALREADY. How am I supposed to root for any couple when it so obvious Celaena isn't really capable of real feelings? It seems she only really loved Nehemia and even that friendship ended up being one-sided. Yes, I'm still team Dorian and it ain't gonna change. But it doesn't mean I want him to end up with Celaena. He deserves better than her. They're still my guilty pleasure, but she's to messed up to be with anyone, and it's obvious he isn't enough for her. I think their friendship could be strong and powerful. I hope they don't go into romantic stuff again, I hope he'll get over her already, I'm so tired of him moping over her. Biggest twist of all - DORIAN HAS FREAKIN MAGIC. It's so awesome. I can't wait to read about him fighting his inner demons and learning to cotrol his magic. This can't be bad. Celaena said he has raw magic, the purest and strongest of all. I'm so excited. I really don't understand how can anyone still ship Chaol and Celaena after everything. She tried to kill him. Let me repeat that - SHE.TRIED.TO.KILL.HIM. Chaol is a fucking invertebrate. After Celaena tried TO TAKE HIS LIFE AWAY he tells her her loves he does everything to protect her and he pretty much whines about how his life doesn't make sense without her. I'm siriously gonna vomit. Truth be told, they had some memorable moments even after fatal event, but it's to weird for me. Nehemia's death was painful and drastic, but unanticipated and necessary. Celaena needed some trigger to lose her mind. Bravo Maas, bravo. I'll miss her and probably whine how I want her back, but this was such a brave move. Honestly, Archer as a villain was a big suprise for me. I definitely wasn't expecting that. He responsible for Nehemia's death? Bold move. But I think it could've been done better. Like, Celaena actually confiding in him begore finding out who he really is? I guess, it would make Celaena less perfect and we surely wouldn't want that, ugh. The thing that made me full of rage was how petty Chaol and Celaena were towards Dorian. Like, he had NO SECRETS, but hey, why would they trust him, when they can hide some crucial information from him. FUCK YOU BOTH.

First things first, this series is a definite must read for all of those readers who love reading vampire stories. I would have to say though, this book ended with a definite hook. Makes sense, there is a fifth book that will be released in June. That is just not soon enough for my liking, especially considering the huge hook at the end of this book. In this book, I already felt like I knew the characters pretty well. In the beginning, however, they introduced Lucy's cousin Christabel who has no knowledge of the existence of vampires. Boy does that change. It is interesting to watch the struggle the other characters go through in order to keep Christabel in the dark. In the end, it was just bad luck that opened her eyes to a whole other world. I was shocked when Connor wasn't the one to save Christabels life from a mortal wound by turning her. Leaving it to Aiden, a vampire of the breed of Hel-blar. In the end it all works out for Christabel though. And it may be one of the best things to happen to the different tribes of vampires. I was not expecting the book to end the way it did. Lucy receiving a text from Solange to meet. It never occurred to me that she would find Solange at their special Oak Tree covered in blood. Kierans at that. The hook did its job quite nicely though, making me sit on the edge of my seat waiting patiently for the next book in the series to be released. June. I can wait till June, right? All in all, these books were well written, with enough suspense and action to keep the pages turning quickly. Keep me up late at night because I just couldn't seem to get enough of them. I fell in love with all of the characters. They all have their own personalities. The characters portray their own uniqueness. I was laughing, crying, and in shock throughout the series. Really, need I say more? I highly recommend these books to all YA vampire novel lovers. Check them out!

This is another book that seems to have a lot of high ratings, and yet it left me underwhelmed. It's a suspense novel about two girls in their late teens, who are starting to wonder if their childhood testimony against a man convicted of multiple murders, a man who is now on death row, was inaccurate. At the time they were sure they saw him--or at least the prosecutors convinced them to be sure--but now there is another murder, and they are starting to wonder. One of the girls, Tessa, is also looking for her mother and sister, whom she hasn't seen in a decade. They start digging around discover some unpleasant and dangerous stuff. The plot sounded exciting, but the execution was kind of plodding. It was 250 pages of not much happening, and then just too much happening at the end. I love a good surprise as much as anyone, but all the big 'reveals' seemed just thrown in at random. The actual killer was someone who wasn't even featured in the story, except for one extremely brief mention. And the whole twist about Tessa's mom just came out of the blue. A few hints at the beginning of the story can go a long way towards a satisfying ending. I also found the writing to be pedestrian and overly slangy, and the characters didn't grab me, so I just don't understand the hype on this one.

I learned some new things with Unscrupulous - hello 'vajazzled'. Taddy Brill is a strong, independent female that had to take charge of her own life at 16 when her parents abandoned her. I marvel at her strength and determination. She has surrounded herself with a new family - Lex, Vive & Blake - her friends from school that have formed a bond so that each other knows the others will always be there. A chance encounter at an exclusive club brings Taddy into Warner Truman's universe only she thinks he is Garner and that he is cheating on his fiance/wife. Several months later at a police station in Cannes, Taddy and Warner cross paths again only this time Warner isn't going to let Taddy go. Can Taddy push through her abandonment/unloved issues from childhood to truly let Warner in? It is so much fun being in Taddy's world - Avery Aster keeps the dialogue clicking on all cylinders as well as giving you panty melting sex scenes. A great escape that will leave you smiling! *ARC received from publisher

I went to go see Batman V Superman recently with a friend in the cinema. I'd kind of been looking forward to it, I had an acceptable level of Batman/Superman knowledge under my belt and I thought I'd be the target audience, and yet as I watched it I realised I wasn't, in fact, the target audience. The movie really was aimed towards hardcore Batman/Superman fans who already had an excellent knowledge of the source material, so I found myself kind of enjoying it, but never really able to pick up on all the insider winks and nudges the movie was trying to throw my way. This book make me feel like I was watching Batman V Superman all over again. Don't get me wrong, there were things that I liked. I really liked the interesting set-up and how it was kind-of-but-not-too-similar to Sword Art Online, which I freaking love. I liked the idea of an immersive game, and how the OASIS was kind of a mix between Second Life and WoW, and how such a world might be used in the future. And then there were a whole bunch of things I didn't like. I half-liked, half-loathed Wade Watts AKA Parzival. He was at best the stereotypical cute nerdy guy that sits two desks behind you at school, the one who wows you with his niche area of expertise and total lack of body hair - wait, that's not the stereotypical cute nerdy guy for you? Weird. At worst, he was the really, really annoying guy at the comic book store who's berating you for not knowing enough about obscure 80's trivia. I can see why some people would enjoy reading about him. He's kind of set up as the ultimate nerd, one whose obsession with a particular area actually pays off for once. Personally he wasn't for me. The other thing I didn't enjoy was the narration style. The author is incredibly fond of "tell, don't show". In fact, I found Ready Player One to be laden down with a lot of exposition which generally served no purpose. Lots and lots of ideas or concepts or inside information on obscure 80's pop culture were introduced and then never raised again. Large chunks of time were skipped over, only for Wade to turn around at a certain point and say things like, "conveniently, seven months ago I did this". Real convenient, Mr. Watts, real convenient. And that's really weird, because the author demonstrated he was absolutely capable of setting up important plot lines in advance. The best example I can think of is the quarter won after the perfect game of Pac-Man. You see Wade go through the game, win the quarter, and then it becomes a valuable asset about 100 pages later. This is the perfect avenue to set up a realistic way for Wade to gain something important but not necessarily need it immediately - unlike *coughcough* those conveniently aquired IOI passwords, which resulted in the aforementioned "Well, seven months ago I did something super smart, and I'm only telling you about this now!" Not cool, Wade. Wade himself was a little problematic. He's set up as this character that doesn't recognise the outside world as one he wants to live in, but then later in the same paragraph he'll realise that the OASIS is a fictional reality. He says he only eats junk food and never does physical activity if he can help it, and then on the same page he says he's lost a significant amount of weight over the past two months as a result of a strict gym/controlled eating routine. I feel like he could have been set up better if most of the narrative didn't feel like an inside joke or an afterthought. The other characters were... so so. Aech is set up as Wade's best friend... and then we don't hear from him for the majority of the book. Daito and Shoto really only come into play right at the end of the novel, and their defining characteristics seem to be that they're Japanese and have honour and bow a lot. And Art3mis! She's at least 95% Manic Pixie Dreamgirl material, and 5% let's-get-down-to-business. Overall this book was hit-and-miss for me. There were some bits that were great and I really enjoyed, mainly most of the latter portions of the book, and there were some bits that didn't make sense or left me feeling extremely 'meh'. If you like 80's trivia, you'll get a kick out of this, because the author seems determined to jam in as many references as possible. If, like me, your childhood and teenaged years were post-80's, a lot of these references will go over your head, and you'll be sitting there hoping the strength of the narrative can make up for the lack of insider knowledge.

BEWARE! At the very beginning of this story, first few pages, the character's dog dies. I don't deal with that well so I felt I needed to put that out to like minded people. It came up to play a few times, too, so beware. Still, I loved this story and it was just another from Maxfield who I've begun to expect the best from. It was fast-paced and suspenseful. The plot was good if not unique, although I figured out the bad guy as soon as he appeared . I liked the way this was about a psychic who hated it and the story wasn't fanciful. It was gritty and harsh like most good thrillers which made the psychic thing work for me. Vilifying the FBI, though, is so old and annoying that detracted from the plot for me. The characters were wonderful and the MCs and most of the others distinct. There were strong, intelligent, and respectable women even. One woman was obsessive about her vintage Mustang--not her husband, her. The emotions and reactions of the characters felt real as well. They weren't cookie cutter or stereotypical yet not improbable. It was refreshing. I particularly liked the different reactions to a kid coming out. I liked that people had a problem with it but came around. I loved the Star Trek references, especially how they noticed how annoying it was that an attorney spoke like Shatner. Kevin actually nicknamed Connor "Trekkie" for a while which grew into a term of endearment which was adorable. These guys were a little young for detectives (twenty five and twenty eight who'd been off the force for a couple of years). One of the characters was a total idiot because he biked without a helmet and said he also rode a horse without one. You know how high that fall is? Not using a helmet when on a bicycle is stupid. On an unpredictable animal with a mind of it's own it's asinine. The editing errors were the worst I've ever seen, though. It wasn't just missing lettrs like a spell-checker would miss, and it wasn't just a wrong name or a missing word here are there. It was constant and there were some sentences that were hard to figure out. There were at least two I never was able to figure out what they were supposed to be. A couple of times POV was changed mid-scene, and a couple of scenes went for many paragraphs before I even knew whose head we were supposed to be in. That's too impersonal for me. One great thing I really appreciated was the discussion about domestic violence in the gay community. I did feel it was slightly over preachy but it was so great that a easy punch to the jaw was not acceptable to anyone. The final obligatory separation was unnecessary and too formulaic. The one guy left when the other really needed him. I understand the thoughts but they weren't spelled out well enough nor reasonable as they were explained and therefore it felt false . But yet I loved the book. You know it has to be good if I am only docking half a star for all these problems and rounding back up again.

Firstly, let me make it clear that there is actually more than one J M Barrie 'Peter Pan' story (something that I did not initially realise). There is 'Peter Pan and Wendy,' which is the story we are all familiar with (immortalised - inaccurately - by Disney); there is 'Peter Pan in Kensington Gardens,' which tells the story of him as a baby with the lost boys when he was originally abandoned, (which I have not yet read) and then 'The Little White Bird' (which I have not read either), but is a set of stories in which Peter also appears. However, this is the most famous of the narratives and I read it mainly because I was looking for famous pirate descriptions for a scheme of work I wanted to teach to my Year 7s. I know, I am very dull! So...the story is pretty much what one would expect if you have encountered Peter in his many big screen incarnations: Peter encourages Wendy, John and Michael to fly off to Neverland to the Lost Boys. Wendy becomes their surrogate mother and they undertake a whole series of adventures together until they begin to miss home. Of course, there are the famous faces: Captain Hook who captures them all and is always looking to gain revenge on Peter; Tinkerbell who adores Peter and is reliant on the clapping of children to survive; Tiger Lily and her deadly crew and of course the Darling family waiting patiently and desperately at home while their children undertake the adventure of a lifetime. Oh how lovely? What a smashing tale for children? What a sweet little narrative about childhood and innocence? NO! NO! NO! NO! This was a highly disturbing and even distasteful children's tale in my opinion and I can only assume that the glowing reviews it seems to receive are based on the fact that too often we read this book wearing Disney blinkers, seeing what we want to and not recognising its dark underbelly. So what were my problems? (I'm afraid that there will have to be a list as there are simply too many): The obvious violence delivered callously and without remorse throughout (I have no issue with violence, but not in a young children's narrative) Peter's characterisation - there is nothing appealing about this arrogant, deceitful, manipulative imp, who cares for little but himself and this never changes! SPOILER: Tinkerbell nearly dies and is devoted to Peter, but a year later she has vanished and he can't even be bothered to remember her name. This is a sadistic bully who becomes infuriated when his domination of the lost boys fails and is quite content to undertake violence simply for the pleasure of doing so. He is quite content to take Wendy, John and Michael from their families knowing how much the others yearn for a mother and that in the process, they will lose theirs. He even refuses to allow the Lost Boys to talk about their lost mothers in order to maintain his hold over them and his lie that all mothers are silly and horrid creatures. The novel begins with Mrs Darling rummaging around in her children's BRAINS...yes BRAINS...to tidy up their minds! Barrie describes: 'Mrs. Darling first heard of Peter when she was tidying up her children's minds. It is the nightly custom of every good mother after her children are asleep to rummage in their minds and put things straight for next morning, repacking into their proper places the many articles that have wandered during the day. If you could keep awake (but of course you can't) you would see your own mother doing this, and you would find it very interesting to watch her. It is quite like tidying up drawers' The implication being she is sorting out their thoughts and removing anything unsuitable like some form of Edwardian brainwashing! The portrayal of Mr Darling who can only be described as an absolute buffoon. He is an aggressive and cruel man who abuses the lovely dog Nana feeding her his medicine because he is too cowardly to take it himself and it is this that results in his children being abducted. The implication is that he is a clock watcher who wants an easy life and that his wife has had to manipulate him and her menstrual cycle in order to conceive the second two children that he never wanted! However, when the children vanish, his behaviour can only be classified as bizarre: he sleeps in a kennel even going to work with it as penance. Ludicrous! At one point, Barry describes how the fairies return through the forest 'FROM AN ORGY!' And I quote: 'After a time he fell asleep, and some unsteady fairies had to climb over him on their way home from an orgy'. Surely inappropriate and peculiar in a children's novel. SPOILER: At the end of the novel, we are told that Wendy's ancestor's return to Peter (when he bothers to remember them, such is his egotism) to do his spring cleaning on a yearly basis! Well, what a mother you have become Wendy! What mother would allow their child to return to place of danger and death with some a mendacious creature as Peter knowing there was no way to access them again. Moreover, the implication seems to be that, this is all such women are good for: cleaning! In fact, the novel is obviously misogynistic throughout. The message is that all mothers fail and are essentially useless creatures. Peter hates mothers (although his reason is that she abanadoned him, but Barrie seems to blame her for giving up hope and barring the window and having another child after years of his absence, implying that she should have lived eternally with the guilt and blame of his loss and never moved on). At one point we are told, 'mothers alone are always willing to be the buffer' implying it is perfectly acceptable to blame them for everything. Likewise, Mrs Darling, who seems a fairly caring, attentive if vacuous woman, is blamed for the loss of her children. Barrie tells us 'so long as mothers are like this, their children will take advantage of them' so clearly generosity of spirit and loving your children, is a terrible flaw in woman kind. Moreover, the sole function of Wendy's descendants is to become Peter's mother in turn! In short, this is a novel that presents women as useless creatures whose only use is for cleaning, breeding and raising little brats. The only other female figures presented are in the mode of the femme fatale - they seem deceptive, cruel and use their physical attraction to manipulate men such as Tiger Lily who uses her physical charms to rule the Indians and Tinkerbell, who out of female jealousy, gets the Lost Boys to shoot Wendy. So what Barrie presents us with is the disturbing Victorian dichotomy that women are either the angel in the house of the whore in the street. Having said this, Barrie actually appears misanthropic as well. He has little good to say about anyone (least of all children). Ironically, the one redeeming feature of this novel is that all the proceeds went to Great Ormond Street Hospital to help fund cures for children's genetic diseases. And for that one admirable action, I give this book a lonely star. Because, in short, this is a terribly disturbing book, written by a terribly disturbing mind - if only his mother had 'tidied it up'!

I had mixed feelings about this one. On one hand, it had many of the things that I liked about the first two Dune books: a complex interdependence between politics, personal relationships, and ecology, an appreciation for the capacity and limitations of the human mind, and some thoroughly haunting imagery. These aspects come together and (finally) gain momentum towards the story's conclusion. But along the way, it seemed that the depth and believability of the characters became lost. The central characters are the Atreides royal twins, Leto II and Ghanima, who carry several millennia's worth of memories from their predecessors. It seemed an opportunity for some fascinating storytelling, yet the outcome is that these two are frequently incomprehensible, arrogant, and creepy, and it became a disappointment any time the point of view would shift to either of them. In the earlier Dune books, Paul Atreides (and others) earned the reader's interest through his actions and well-articulated ideas. In this book, it seems as though the reader's interest is simply expected because of who the twins are. With the entire story hinging on them and their plans, it became difficult to care about where the whole thing would end up, even if some of the other characters (e.g., Farad'n) were more interesting. Ultimately, I think this book showed the (inner) decline of the Atreides family and allies. The group once functioned as a formidable unit whose strength came from their mutual loyalty. This book sees those people, and their descendants, abandon one another in many different ways. Even if the book ends with one of them beginning a reign that would last thousands of years , it seems like a hollow, sour course for the Atreides to take. I'm not sure if I'll continue reading the series, since apparently the next book is even more Leto-centric.

I hurried up about reading We Are All Completely Beside Ourselves because my aunt talked about reading it, and since she doesn't seem to be a big reader, I thought it'd be interesting (and maybe add to dinner table conversation the next time she visits). She told me about the twist in a somewhat oblique way that had me wondering how the facts fit together. When I hit the apparently infamous page 77, though, it does all make sense; if I hadn't needed to return this to the library for the next patron who reserved it, I'd have reread the first 77 pages and figured out where there's subtler foreshadowing and so on. I wasn't looking for it in the right places, so if it was there, it passed me by. All in all, it's an interesting story, based on the idea of raising a chimp among humans and seeing how much we can humanise them, which has been done in various experiments. It's hard to say more about the themes of the book without spoilering people for page 77, because the whole way the plot comes together relies on that reveal, and whether it works for you. For me, it did. I got the book out of the library at 5.30pm and finished it by 11pm; I feel that the voice is engaging, the unchronological way of telling the story works well, and the mystery/twist combined with that narrative voice worked for me, because Rosemary (the narrator) speaks to the reader. It's like an oral story in some ways -- you're being told a story by someone who finds it difficult, who is feeling their way into telling it. There are things I didn't like very much about this book, even so; some of the plotlines/characters didn't seem to add much. Some of it was all part of the red herrings, of course, to lead the reader astray. But I was unsure about the whole character of Harlow -- her later appearances seemed unnecessary, and that first performative scene with her the best and most revealing thing about her character (revealing both herself and Rosemary, I mean). The lost suitcase plot... shrug? The puppet... what? So needless to say, given how fast I devoured it, I did quite enjoy it. I haven't a clue what I'll have to say about it when my aunt visits again, though; I'm still thinking about it all. (Mum, this book is very anti-animal experimentation, it'd drive you nuts. Squirt, don't read it, it'll upset you.)

NO SPOILERS. NO TE PREOCUPES. Bodies could be beacons, too, Saul knew. A lighthouse was a fixed beacon for a fixed purpose; a person was a moving one. But people still emanated light in their way, still shone across the miles as a warning, an invitation, or even just a static signal. People opened up so they became a brightness, or they went dark. They turned their light inward sometimes, so you couldn't see it, because they had no other choice. The final exploration of Area X. After the catastrophic and horrifying events that took place in Authority, this ragtag group of individuals is not really an expedition, but a patchwork mash-up of survivors trying to make sense of the feral, mysterious, blossoming explosion of nature called Area X. To recap: Area X is a large area of coast and swampland in Florida that is completely cut-off from humanity. Vines grow over everything, the ocean teams with fish, and the land is overflowing with an abundance of animals - some familiar, and some never seen before by human eyes. When the border went up, 30 years ago - 1,500 people died (or were never seen again and assumed dead) as they were consumed by this sudden apparition of wilderness. Now, the government has been sending in expeditions composed of teams of scientists in a desperate attempt to understand what's going on. Those expeditions have been massive failures. The teams either kill themselves, kill each other, disappear, or come back - as personality-less, hollow shells of their former selves. One notable expedition came back riddled with cancer - all of them died within 6 months of coming back. No one knows how anyone returns - they just appear, disoriented and confused. This book is, I believe, the weakest of the trilogy. Annihilation is the strongest. You can read Annihilation and enjoy it, love it, and never read the other two books. It can stand on its own two feet. But if you want answers (like I did) you will continue reading - because Annihilation sure leaves you with a lot of questions. That being said, I still think Acceptance deserves five stars. The writing is gorgeous. She had panicked for a second as the water pressed in on her, evoked her own drowning. But then something had turned on, or had come back, and raging against her own death, she had exulted in the sensation of the sea, welcomed having to fight her way to the surface - bursting through such a joyful hysteria of biomass - as a sort of proof that she was not ---, that she was some new thing that could, wanting to survive, cast out her fear of drowning belonging to another. --- = character's name x-ed out so no spoilers Look at this. bursting through such a joyful hysteria of biomass. I mean, that is just exquisite. And the book is brimming with wonderful amazing sentences and paragraphs that you can get lost in. I read the book twice: I read it, and then turned to page 1 immediately to read it again. Half of this was because it was so beautiful, half of it was because there are a lot of complex things going on in this book that need a second reading to really coalesce in your mind. This book is a horror story. Not 'horror' as in Stephen King, buckets of blood and possessed cars and stuff. (Not dissing him, I'm a King fan - but it's a different kind of scary). Horror as in slow, creeping insanity, doppelgangers, hearing strange noises in the kitchen at night, etc. etc. etc. There's no villain, there's no tangible enemy of any kind. That's what makes it so frightening. Some of the stupider characters in the book just can't seem to grasp that you can't fight Area X with guns and bullets - in fact, you can't fight it at all. It's as pointless as raging against the ocean or the sky. Z had walked into the light to find Y staring at her with fear, with suspicion, and she had smiled at Y, had told her not to be afraid. Not to be afraid. Why be afraid of what you could not prevent? Did not want to prevent. Were they not evidence of survival? Were they not evidence of some kind? Both of them. There was nothing to warn anyone about. The world went on, even as it fell apart, changed irrevocably, became something strange and different. *Z and Y used in place of actual character names. It's also science-fiction. I've heard it described as "cli-fi," as in science fiction with a slant on "we're destroying our planet," a la Paolo Bacigalupi, but I hate this term. It makes a reader think that this is going to be preachy or self-righteous and that is not at all what this trilogy is like. It is fun, exciting, and edge-of-your-seat reading. I didn't find it the least bit sanctimonious. So read on with no fear! Except, perhaps, the fear that comes with reading any horror novel. Some of the reasons I think this is the weakest entry in the trilogy: We are in a lot of people's heads. Four different 'main characters' in this one, and we get all their points of view. Three in third-person and one in second-person (which is fun. I like second-person when it's done well). However, being involved in so many different POVs is adding a bit of complexity to an already very complex book. This is one reason I suggest reading it twice. Another thing is that the first half of the book is not that exciting, not that 'scary.' VanderMeer doesn't really start delivering the blows until page 193. From then on it's a faster-paced freefall into awesomeness, but you do have to get through that first half to reach this. IT'S WORTH IT. And the first half is not a slog - far from it. VanderMeer's writing is beautiful and you are also, by this point, familiar with - and curious about - the characters so that you are interested in seeing them and getting to know them better. But still, fair warning. Don't get fed up with the lack of 'action' and quit early. There's some great twists in here, and I was happy with the way everything turned up. Even though VanderMeer is not super-explicit, I feel like I have a pretty firm understanding of Area X and what it does after closing this book. People who need a very direct, pat explanation and everything spelled out for them ARE NOT going to be happy or satisfied with this trilogy. However, if you want an amazing trilogy with beautiful writing, fascinating and mysterious concepts, OMG-OMG-OMG horror that will have you riveted - this is the trilogy for you. You are still there for a moment, looking out over the sea toward the lighthouse and the beautiful awful brightness of the world. Before you are nowhere. Before you are everywhere. P.S. VanderMeer also - throughout the whole trilogy does a GREAT and AMAZING job of making characters of all different types: black, white, Latino, Asian, gay, hetero, bisexual - without making it seem glaring. He does this so seamlessly, so effortlessly, that the reader just falls into this. So many authors try to make "diverse characters" but end up drawing so much attention to their "diverseness" that it's distracting and annoying. "Look at this character. He's Indian. He's eating chapati. Did I mention he's Indian? He says, "Namaste" in this one scene. BECAUSE HE'S INDIAN." I hate this. Authors who do this are missing the whole entire point of making a 'diverse' cast of characters. The idea is not to hammer home how wonderful you are and how progressive you are for having non-white, or non-heterosexual characters - it's to make having non-white and non-heterosexual characters just a normal part of life. Not questioned, not commented upon to excess, not overanalyzed - just existing. VanderMeer pulls this off perfectly. So does Michael J. Martinez, whose The Daedalus Incident I also highly recommend. P.P.S. People closest to nature already tend to survive and even thrive in Area X, unlike people who are wrapped up in cities and humanity and bureaucracy and taking showers and stuff. LOL But seriously, this is why the biologist gets along so splendidly (comparatively) in Area X than the others. P.P.P.S. Strong women. If you enjoy strong women and female characters who are strong but NOT Mary-Sues, this is the trilogy for you. Multi-faceted, a mixture of goodness and malice, playing both the heroes of the piece and the villains, VanderMeer is wonderful in this regard.

I'm skeptical that Stephen King wrote this book. It reminds me SO much of N0S4R2, by his son Joe Hill, going for shock value rather than King's haunting insane imagination. So much of it was over-explaining a stereotypical villain, with mom issues and a love of computers. Uninteresting, but gruesome and gory in a way that was totally unnecessary to make a great book. So many crucial points in the investigation pivoted on the silliest concepts--they sat and puzzled over why there wasn't a business card for the tech guy for so long. Who keeps business cards anymore? Seemed bizarre and outdated. It doesn't make any sense for that to be a plot point. The cops really wouldn't have come across the fact that the dealership gives a second key, and it might have been in the glovebox, or about the key hacking, the first time around? Come on. And then at the end, they're all rushing to prevent this bomb exploding, going crazy because they can't get through to the security over the phone, but at that point wouldn't it have made more sense to call 911? All of it seemed hinged on such weak premises. I never had any sympathy/empathy/understanding for Bill Hodges as a main character. He seemed to me like an out-of-touch older man who probably needs to be arrested for withholding evidence from the police and drawing a teenager and a mentally ill woman into his drama. Yuck.

Woah. That moment when you are completely sideswiped by the beauty and terror of something. When you can't stop reading. When you must know what happens, but you're terrified. That moment. For 300+ pages. I had zero expectations when I picked up this book. I had heard very little about it (not surprising, it was written in 1985, and not the sort of thing my friends typically read for fun), and came in expecting nothing. In all honesty, I only learned about this book and picked it up thanks to NPR. I was looking for my next audiobook, and they recommended Claire Danes' reading. This book is the book on my TBR list which has been read by the most people I know. Not just read, but also most rated and most reviewed. And the overall ratings are incredibly high among my friends, as well. Woah. The Handmaid's Tale is a very terrifying, very possible dystopia. We follow the story of Offred through her experiences as a Handmaid. In a world of declining fertility and increasing sexual activity, there is a coup in America. The world changes, seemingly overnight. The Sons of Jacob rule and the age of Gilead begins. Offred remembers "the before times", but those memories are fragmented. Partially she is choosing to forget as a coping mechanism. Partially she is unable to remember since there is nothing but her mind to hold these memories. The most fascinating part of this is book is how the story is told. Time and place are often unclear. Offred frequently slips between "the before times" and now. She jumps from describing what she's doing to living in her mind. It can be a challenge to keep up with sometimes, but it was also a fascinating way to experience Offred's mental positions. Throughout the entire book, I was looking for an explanation of what happened and how this happened. How did the world turn against women in this way? Very logically, Offred did not provide this insight. I think if my world turned around like this, I wouldn't be able to place my finger on it either. The fall of America and rise of Gilead was not Offred's story to tell. Instead, at the end of the book, there is a transcript from a keynote speaker at a convention. This keynote speaker talks about the validity of The Handmaid's Tale, as well as loosely addresses the events leading up to and following this moment. It offered a view of Gilead I had been longing for while still keeping Offred's story true to herself. A stroke of genius in my opinion. All in all, a surprising novel. I greatly enjoyed it, even thought I felt horrified most of the time. I recommend this book for lovers of dystopia, feminists, and those fascinated by the embroiling of religion and politics.

4 Brilliant Stars! Source: eARC for Honest Review Courtesy of Atria Books via NetGalley Wow! This was my first K.A. Tucker book I know I know, I have heard so many good things about K.A. Tucker and finally I got to read her brilliance. This book was a multiple POV with one POV being in the present while the other POV was in the past tying the whole story together. It's also about two souls being meant to be intertwined even though reality made it difficult, fate still kicked ass for these two. I always have a hard time reading when cheating is the theme but with this even though it wasn't the morally correct decision you were able to understand why they made the decisions they did. Jesse meets a stranger on the side of the road who changes his path in life with one random kiss. He later re-meets this stranger only to get caught in a morally changed tangled web leading to a case of amnesia and a chance of starting over. The whole time I was biting my fingernails to find out how it all played out. I don't want to say too much about what happens in the book because I think it would would ruin the whole experience. I think it was brilliantly written yet a bit long. There were elements that I felt were drawn out too long and could have been shorter but all in all I did love it and I can NOT wait to read more from K.A. Tucker. FIRST OF ALL THAT COVER IS BEAUTIFUL! I was happy with how this book turned out! It took me a tiny bit of time to get into the story, but I got drawn in soon enough, and couldn't put it down! One thing that made it so appealing for me was this whole idea of time AND space travel. The constant scene change made the story progress constantly and evenly, and kept me anticipating the next area. Passenger is a book that has an incredible rhythm. There is a constant beat and a beautiful melody, like a music piece. It was pretty to read, which doesn't make much sense unless you read it! So Etta is a violin prodigy and somewhat surprisingly finds out that she can travel through time. She meets Nicholas and together they go through a kind of time-space scavenger hunt where they need to find an Astrolabe, a device that can create these sorts of portals to go through time. The villain, Cyrus Ironwood, is easily hatable, even though he isn't always looming. He has one scene and that's it, but that one scene is enough to make me hate him. Etta, the 'pirate', is so great! She is fiery and stubborn, but also sweet and confident. Nicholas is also great, and one thing I appreciated with this book is that it did something that YA books don't usually do - it covered racism. Nicholas is of color, and they go through times where that is shunned upon. But besides that, he is incredibly brave and caring. Their relationship is a tiny bit insta-lovey, but it evolved nicely anyway! This book was funny at times! Just simple situations had humorous twists to them that I really appreciated! Spoilers! The ending messed me up! I thought they pulled a Tris! ;-; I'm glad they didn't though! Now I'm hoping Nicholas's character may develop more! When Etta's mom throws a knife at her... wow I was not seeing their reunion be like that! Even though Sophia practically dies, I still don't like her. I feel like some things were a bit too easy for Etta to figure out. End One thing I really would have enjoyed is if the author would have given an explanation as to why these select families can time travel. Do they protect something? Or do they just have these powers? Did I miss this part in the book? Something that was pretty cool: the Astrolabe is something like a sexton, that measures time and location and position in space. We talked about astrolabes with my dad before it even came up in the book! You should look them up, they look so cool! Also, Etta's family name is "Linden". We were in an area of Germany where Linden was written everywhere! I gave this book a 4/5 starts :)

I loved the beginning of the story, Mike is really interesting, and I like his comparison of his brain to ants. The other scientists are intriguing, and it's all mysteriousy and stuff. But then, I mean, I figured out the first "twist" basically immediately (were we supposed to maybe?) And then the bugmen... I just couldn't quite connect with that whole idea. There's a dragon or something? Huh? And they just eat.... everything... and if they're just travelling between dimensions, does that mean there's only one group of them or something? It didn't make sense to me. I'm not sure how else the story could have gone, but I just didn't like the bugmen. I thought they were dumb and nonsensical and pointless. But yeah, I'd probably read more of Mike if his character's story were to continue on in some way.

This book surprised me. I really enjoyed it. It started out as a very typical read, NA; then it changed over the course of the book. It almost felt like the author changed her mind about 20% through and decided to give the characters flaws and depth. The writing was sharp and clever. The two mains felt real and not at all cardboard. My issue with the book was the  first breakup scene, at the college campus, after class. I really felt like the misunderstanding/miscommunication was forced and contrived and   it pulled me out of the story in a big way. After fighting for her for so long, being so patient, he was suddenly over her/done/pushing her away because of one conversation after class? No... it felt really out of character and like a plot point. It irritated me so much I had to remove a star... :-\ BUT overall, this is a great NA!!! If you enjoy NA (and even if you don't usually) I highly recommend this book.

Just amazing! If you do know me personally, you would know that this story of August Pullman is very close to my heart. Reading this felt like having a conversation with someone like myself although by no means I would say that our case is similar. August Pullman is much stronger and optimistic than myself, he easily puts me to shame although he is just a fictional character. Saying that, I consider he is real which is somewhat true because I am aware of just how many Augusts in this world, battling society's cruel treatment and perception everyday and I would like to borrow that strength. It's interesting how I started reading with a mindset that this book will be a heart-breaking, depressive tear-jerker. Instead, I smiled, I laughed, I shed happy tears, I shed sad tears (unexpectedly because the dog dies :'( The only drawback was when the book was narrated from Justin POV. I just couldn't stand the lack of proper punctuation. Other than that, I'd say that 'Wonder' is a gift to humanity.

"Depression is like a heaviness that you can't escape. It crushes down on you, making even the smallest things like tying your shoes or chewing on toast seem like a twenty-mile hike uphill. Depression is a part of you; it's in your bones and your blood. If I know anything about it, this is what I know: It's impossible to escape." Rating: 5 stars My Heart and Other Black Holes has been a favourite of mine for a long time. The first time I read this book must be around two years ago, and I still loved rereading this book for the second time. I realised I had never written a proper review of this, even though I have a lot to say, which is why I'm finally forcing myself to make my thoughts coherent so I can write them down in a review everyone will be able to understand. Well, I'm gonna try doing that.. So first off, this book is about Aysel (pronounced as Uh-zell) and she is pretty much done with everything. She wants to die. The thing is, she's afraid her survival-instincts will prevent her from commiting suicide and nothing scares her more than a failed attempt. Then she discovers a website where people can find their Suicide Partner and Aysel is convinced she's found the solution to her problem and so she meets up with Roman, a boy her age who is haunted by guilt. Everything seems to be going well; Roman and Aysel meet up more frequently, and start planning their deaths. As the date they've chosen to die on nears, something weird seems to be happening to Aysel. She's suddenly starting to see things... Differently. And as this is happening, doubt settles in. Is dying with Roman really what she wants to do? I cried several times, reading this book. We follow Aysel's sadness, her way of thinking about herself and the world and it's achingly real and messed up. "I can hear their whispered insults, but it all sounds like a mumble of hisses to me. And no matter what it is that they're saying, it can't be worse then what I imagine at night when I lie in bed wondering if it's physically possible to claw away your own genetics." What was really inriguing, is that Aysel thinks about her depression and desire to die in a most peculiar way: a scienctific way, and it's beautifully haunting. "Sometimes I wonder if gravity is te problem. It keeps us all grounded, gives us a false sense of stability when really we're all just bodies in motion. Gravity keeps us from floating up into space, it keeps us from involuntarily crashing into one another. It saves the human race from being a big hot mess. I wish gravity would go away and just let us all be a big mess. But we also get to see the changes in Aysel's way of thinking. "Maybe it's all relative, not just light and time like Einstein theorized, but everything. Like life can seem awful and unfixable until the universe shifts a little and the observation point is altered, and then suddenly, everything seems more bearable." *This is going to be contain minor spoilers (mainly about the romance in this book). They're kinda predictable but if you're sensitive to that stuff: I hereby warn you :P* My Heart and other Black Holes is a road full of changes in Aysel's mind and heart and although I would have liked those to happen more slowly, I disagree with the people who say that those changes are initiated by her feelings for Roman. Yes, the thoughts about the possibility that Aysel might want to live occur only after meeting and developing feelings for Roman, but Roman was the catalyst, rather than the cause I think. The cause of the not wanting to die anymore was (I think) the process of actually planning her death. She finally gets the sense of finalty, that soon she won't have to be living like this anymore. She starts feeling more reckless and along with that, excited. And with that excitement, I think, she starts realising that contrary to what she used to think, there are still things to be excited about and so she starts dreaming. So even though I would have liked this process to have gone more slowly, I still loved it regardless. My favourite quotes of MHaOB: * "Sometimes I wonder if my heart is like a black hole - it's so dense that there's no room for light, but that doesn't mean it can't still suck me in." * "I bet if you cut open my stomach, the black slug of depression would slide out. Guidance counsellors always love to say, "Just think positvely," but that's impossible when you have this thing inside of you, strangling every ouce of happiness you can muster. My body is an efficient happy-thought-killing machine." * "I gaze out at the concession stands and game booths that are becoming tinier and tinier. I wonder if dying is like that. Everything in your mind becomes tinier and tinier until it all disappears." * "And maybe the black slug will always live inside of me. Maybe I'll always have bad days where the heaviness weems unbearable. But as cheesy as it sounds, maybe the good days will make it worth getting through the bad ones." * "Maybe it's time for me to fight back against the sadness inside of me."

I was a little surprised that I enjoyed When the Marquess Falls because the whole Hellions of Havisham series wasn't up to par with the other series that Lorraine Heath has written. In fact, I hated The Earl Takes All because the heroine COULD NOT tell the difference between her husband and his twin who was masquerading as HIM! HONESTLY! When the Marquess Falls is George, the Mad Marques' HEA or rather, sad HEA. If you read The Viscount and the Vixen, you would know what I mean. WtMF is about the hellions' guardian the Marquess of Marsden who lost his wife Linnie to childbirth. This is NOT a spoiler by the way because it is stated in all 3 books of the series. So yes, WtMF is a prequel and really shows us how the Marquess of Marsden fell, married, and lost the love of his life. Surprisingly, I enjoyed it. I think because I read The Viscount and the Vixen and was very intrigued by the old Marquess? He does have an interesting life and I think he just drowned himself in his sorrow and basically had alcohol-induced hallucinations. Also, I am such a fan of the friends to lovers and romance between classes tropes, so I am really biased! As much as I enjoyed the plot, I wasn't a fan of the writing. Heath's writing feels off somehow than her usual and felt too...I don't know, child like? I don't know how to describe it precisely, only that it was different than her usual writing. The end was a little too dramatic though and the animated movie Anastasia dancing sequence when she sang Once Upon a December flashed through my mind when I read the last scene. And also the last scene in Somewhere in Time, where Elise McKenna finally reunited with Richard in the clouds. Like I said, too dramatic for me. I enjoyed When the Marquess Falls despite the faults. However, if you haven't read the other books in the series, or at least read The Viscount and the Vixen, you wouldn't enjoy it as much as I did. pooled ink Reviews: 3 Stars? 3.5 Stars? ...I'm undecided...The writing is superb but it's not my favorite book The Casual Vacancy is a gritty unforgiving slice of humanity in the form of a small English town. Everyone's truths, dark secrets, and honest nature are revealed to the reader in one steady, tragic tale. The characters are all quite well developed and what really makes this book work is that it constantly switches between each character's mind. This tactic reveals how they make wrong assumptions, shrewd guesses, and what they all really think about their neighbors and the fight to fill the casual vacancy left by Barry. Truly Rowling's writing skills gleam on every page, the calibre of writing cannot be argued with, and it will suck you into the story effortlessly, but whether you like the story is a different matter. Some people will not like this book because they wish to ignore or refuse to accept the realities exposed within it. Some people will not like this book because it's simply not their cup of tea. Some people will not like this book because it strikes too close to home. But there is an audience for it. Of that I am sure. I surprised myself by discovering how much I did like this book. It's not a pleasant story at all but it's honest and somehow despite it all I appreciate the honesty in it. Will I read it again? Book number 25 in my 2012 Reading Challenge of 50 Books is The Lovely Bones by Alice Sebold. The Lovely Bones tells the tale of a 14 year old girl who is brutally raped and murdered by one of the neighbours. The young girl, Susie Salmon, is not able to rest peacefully and from heaven, she watches as her murderer gets away, her family falls apart and innocent people are held trial for an act of violence which they did not commit. There are no secrets in The Lovely Bones as the narrative is being told through the eyes of Susie Salmon. Susie is able to witness all of the feelings, suspicions and mishaps of those she has left behind on earth, including her killer George Harvey. The narrative is introduced quite abruptly as the first event to occur in the novel is the rape and murder of Susie Salmon. Although it is a violent act, the events were laid out gently with much care, leaving the reader feeling almost as violated as Susie since it is such an odd juxtaposition. Throughout the beginning and chunk of the narrative, author Sebold takes sufficient times to explore the events following Susie's abduction. The Police are still unable to locate her body or find any leads while Susie's father has high (and correct) suspicions of Susie's murderer. However, the police are unable to find enough striking evidence against him and after a few days of awkward altercations, the one who is known as George Harvey flees the town. After several years of investigation with nothing more than a found tuque and a novel, the police announce the the case of Susie Salmon is closed. Unable to rest peacefully, Susie is left with feelings of despair in heaven. She still watches the earth below as her family falls apart and her mother commits adultery and leaves her family. The situation is grave. Admittedly, this book is again, what I like to call an "exploration book". This year, I have been reading several books which do not typically fall into the genre in which I usually read. I had a difficult time reading this book this time around as I was unaccustomed to reading such acts of violence towards children or the innocent, especially ones that are so well described. It is true that it is not within my comfort zone but I especially found it so since currently, they are wrapping up trials for the Tori Stafford case --a young girl, younger than Susie Salmon, who was abducted, raped and murdered by two people residing in her own community. I cannot necessarily say that I enjoyed the narrative of the book, as much of the time I felt violated or offended for Susie's behalf, even as I read about her sister's "teenage triumphs". However, I did feel compelled to continue reading it. For a deed that is so treacherous, I felt that Sebold, as a first-time author when this book was released, did a fine job in juxtaposing something so taboo with writing that is organic, peaceful and compelling. Consequently, like the Greek Sirens leading me to my doom, I felt that Sebold continued to utilize and manipulate most of the narrative in that continuous graceful and delicate pattern. Permissibly, I must confess that I did not like how the book concluded. With all the attention and detail that was given throughout, the ending of the novel was quite rash. It ended abruptly with no delicate ties, no ribbons, no HAEs, no reflecting thoughts, no cliffhangers, just the end. Susie explains that her retelling of 10 years was her life and sometimes, it unfortunately ends that way. Then, Susie wishes us long and happy lives. After all of that reading investment, I could not help but shake my head as it was comparable to the end of the Harry Potter series. I don't know if some authors understand that the conclusions to their novels must also be massaged and molded with the same precision as the rest of their novel. I just feel like I got the middle finger at the end of the book; that's all. Overall, I am rating The Lovely Bones 2.5 out of 5 stars. I found it compelling and difficult to put down or stop thinking about; however, the narrative was a little vicious and the idea of Heaven a little altruistic. I feel that if the ending was given more attention, I would have rated this about a 3.5 or 4. But that is just my opinion. But there you have it! 2.5/5, which coincidentally is where I am at in my reading challenge. The Lovely Bones is Book 25 out of 50. Half way there!

I can see where the "nothing happens" that other people have mentioned comes from but for me that was one of the best things about it. It doesn't have one specific plot, it's more of a one summer journal. I guess that's why it's called This One Summer. And things do happen. Creepy apocalyptic scenario and some good characters. I was hooked from the first page, too scared to go to the toilet in the middle of the night after reading for a few hours straight and the ending was about as conclusive as i was expecing. Not quite 5 stars for me - after we start adventuring beyond the rig i felt the creepiness factor slowed a bit and Nikki was a little convenient by the end, i also felt our shambolic baddies changed and it would have been much creepier to have them a bit more malevolent and with less obvious purpose or control. Tedious book with altogether too much about fashion. It is understood not all heroines can be Eliza Bennets or Margaret Hales, however in comparison, I find Arabella's character bland and boring. The only respite in the book comes in the form of Beaumaris' humour and conversations with his dog. Though I am sure it was the point of the book, it is beyond me why someone so suave, assured, rich and sensible would take preference to someone impulsive, immature and lacking any spunk, with little more than her looks to recommend her.

Not bad, not brilliant either. I had a few problems with the novel. There are a couple of elements that are left unexplained, which didn't make sense even with a sequel coming up. Also, I don't like the relationship between Emma and Bennet being based on the attraction of the original Emma and the Rake. Meh, I always dislike romances like that, because really, it feels so forced and impersonal right? Being in love with someone just because you're experiencing someone elses feelings. I liked the mythology beind the ghostkeepers, little of it as we get, and behind the ghost and ghasts. I also liked Emma so and so. She's quirky and sweet and definitely loveable. On the other hand, that boy crazy side of hers is irksome. All the other characters were perfectly likeable. This read like young Young Adult lit, but that's fine; it was still enjoyable and I'll probably read the second installment too.

I was iffy at first, but this book quickly grew on me. Strangely, even though this book was all about angels, demons, war, heaven and hell, and so on, it wasn't as heavy as I thought it would be. This kind of felt like a paranormal novel, lite-version. Sure, there was the threat of dire circumstances, but it sort of came off as more of a light read to me. I did like the whole idea of the grays. They were pretty much like a succubus, but with kisses instead of sexing someone up. By the end of the story, most of the conflict was wrapped up, but there are still a lot of things left unanswered. I'm interested to see where things go with the rest of the series. Sam was the type of protagonist I liked to read about. I was so glad that she was different from most heroines in YA books these days. Her personality in general just seemed very real to me. I liked how she level-headed she was. There were two groups of people telling her two different things, but she knew not to trust either group completely. Sam wasn't one of those annoying leads that took things at face value and ran with whoever last spoke to her. I can't stand when a character trusts the bad guys and gets all upset when she finds out she betrayed the good guys and etc. Sam wasn't the best heroine of all time, but in comparison to other books, I was happy reading from her POV. The other characters were fun as well. I liked the group of angels and demons the most. Besides them, the other secondary characters were a bit flat or I just didn't care much about them. I don't know why, but I didn't like Carly even before she became a gray. I felt like a jerk, but I couldn't muster up any sadness when she got pulled into the Hollow . Bishop was a cool character, but I honestly have no clue what his deal is. Especially with what Sam finds out about him in the last chapter or so. His relationship with Kraven has me confused and I can't wait for light to be shone on that. I think Bishop and Sam are sort of cute together, but there was something missing to me. I did like how they met though. The whole randomly stabbing a kid eating out of a dumpster had me WTF-ing. To be honest, I'm more interested in Kraven. There's just something more interesting about the douche bag guy in a story and Kraven fits that bill perfectly. His sarcastic and inappropriate comments had me laughing. I liked how there seemed to be more behind the exterior. Based on the description of the next book, I'm hoping that there'll be some Kraven/Sam action.

1.5 stars. I really thought I would like this a lot more. It might have been a 2 or even a 3 without all of the casual misogyny and slut shaming. But damn, did that ever ruin the book for me. Don't get me wrong. That it is not all, by far, what is wrong here, but it's a good portion. Some choice excerpts of said misogyny: "I need Aislin, I say to my mother". "Aislin is a drunken slut," she replies, without looking up from her laptop Cute slut shaming! And it also serves to set up Eve's mother as the "villain" which, as it turns out, is not at all necessary. Even without the blatant misogyny and slut shaming I think I would still be unhappy with this professional businesswoman cast as a villain. I am/have been a professional businesswoman. I know all too well the dangers of life as a woman in the business world. When you're "too soft" you're regarded as "a woman" and something along the lines of "too soft to handle this business world." Then, when you catch on to this, and realize that you should start acting more "like a man", i.e. assertive, like a boss, etc...you're still punished! When you act like a man you are a "bitch", you're "cold" and "frigid". "Bossy". Words that are never ascribed to a man for having the same exact characteristics. And it is really infuriating and I have suffered for it already in my professional life. I don't need it in my fiction, you know? Let's move on: I also don't understand why I should let some guy fondle me when I know the relationship has no future. I don't need to be groped that badly. Yeah, so, you should *never* "let" a guy fondle you. It should be purely consensual. It really, really worries me when these sort of rape culture run rampant memes permeate in YA literature. We need to let younger readers know, unequivocally, that this behavior is unacceptable. Sexual activity should be exciting and consensual! Accept no substitutes! Other than the misogyny and slut shaming, this book still just wasn't that awesome. For someone who didn't enjoy it, the plus side is that it was a really quick read. The downside is that it was a quick read because it was *ridiculously* fast paced. Honestly, it felt like a whirlwind. Everything of the actual plot sequential happens because the story demands it. I feel like if the book were longer and the chance was there to develop the characters more and know them better it would have been a vastly different book. But, that's not the case. And alllll of that demonizing of Eve's mother just for her to  not be the big bad we thought she was . Wow, the bad guys were actually Solo's parents. "What a shock", I say to myself, dryly. The only upside here for me is that I've heard such good things of Grant's Gone series. I really hope the casual misogyny problem is not there for those novels.

For all that hype around this book, it certainly didn't live up to it. The initial premise seemed interesting at first glance, but proved to be a real disappointment. I seriously wonder whether to continue because the whole "ride" was just "meh" and I am not sure I would decide to venture on another "adventure". Actual rating of 1.5 stars. For sure it wasn't unbearable to read but I wasn't exactly thrilled. The plot was extremely predictable. Practically the only thing I wasn't quite expecting was that Ryan would end up a Mage. Predictability combined with annoying main character is certainly among my most favourite combinations of all time. True, Harper wasn't a Katniss-level annoying but this doesn't change the fact that she was. All the more that she was hard to connect to. I know, I know. I guess people like the girly-girl type but not me. Her behavior was outrageously stupid and incomprehensible most of the time. For someone who is apparently "smart, beautiful and altogether perfect", she sure is at the bottom of that category - especially the smart part. But still I could see how much the author tried to make her really clever. It was so forced that Harper seemed more pretentious that anything else. Now I remember that scene about the map of Middle Earth in David's room. Seriously? Why should "nerds" always be associated with the Lord of the Rings? And David having that "hipster" feel, must only mean he liked LOTR "before it was cool", right? Ridiculous. I heard many people found this book hilarious. I didn't find even a single funny line in this whole thing. It was plain boring. Even the so-called touching moments were "meh" for me. As I am the type to bawl my eyes out at the slightest thing, this should serve as concrete proof of how poorly written this book is. Generally, everything about this book was too forced to seem even remotely believable. I am vastly disappointed at how no one pays attention to obvious things like these. And the whole "save the world" thing is getting quite old, considering how an Oracle doesn't exactly have so much power as to put the whole world in danger when practically no one knows about him. But anyways...
