"You will never be my friend. You will always be my enemy" This book was the second installment for Throne of Glass by: Sarah J. Maas, it was a great continuation off of the first novel, but didn't lose the original plot line. I enjoyed this book as much as I enjoyed the  Throne of Glass and  The Assassin's Blade. I have this theory where the second book in the series is almost always the worst. This book is one of the few that wasn't a let-down! I was just an enamored with the world of mystery and assassins as I was with the first one! We are thrown, hastily, back into Rifthold. Where the King gives the name of a person that has double-crossed him and wants them taken care of. She soon discovers who the next target is: Archer Finn, former love interest and teacher. What the King doesn't know is that Celaena is faking the deaths. Which could put her head on the chopping block. Things get more tense when she discovers that Archer could be a potential ally in a small rebel group that is forming. To add even more to her plate, she has to try to unlock the secrets and the source of the Kings Power. "She was a whirlwind of steel and blood. As he watched her cut through the men like they were stalks of wheat in a field, he understood how she had gotten so close to touching Endovier's wall that day. And at last--after all these months--he saw the lethal predator he'd expected to find in the mines. There was nothing human in her eyes, nothing remotely merciful." Celaena is still completely badass and witty. My love for her character never faltered, I feel it only growing stronger. In this book, we finally unlock the side of her that is death, personified. And, oh, how delicious that part was. We got to see the side of her that was completely ruthless and unstoppable especially when the ones she loves are involved. Chaol in this book is a little more carefree with his emotions toward Celaena. He still does his job with seriousness, but we are also let into a side that was locked away before, his family. We also watch as his relationship with Celaena rides the roller-coaster of the century. Dorian Havilliard.... He is still passionate, and kind-hearted. But now he's become more of recluse and awkward as he takes the steps in finding himself and how he's gonna run the kingdom someday with knowing what he knows. "Do not let the light go out." With the way things left off at the end, I'm left scrambling to decide what is going to happen! We're left wondering what will happen to Celaena as she makes the journey of a lifetime. I can't help, but wonder what she'll discover when she arrives at her new destination. We are left wondering what will happen to Chaol when he rejoins his family and if Dorian will win this battle that is about to begin against a ruling king. This book also took so many bends and turns. I hated that it ended. I can't wait for the next one!

Endymion continues the story begun in Hyperion and The Fall of Hyperion...however, it isn't a direct sequel. The "Fall" has occurred some two centuries ago and the Hegemony (a far-future conglomerate of multiple planets) is now run by the Pax, enforced by the "miraculous" resurrection symbiotes discovered by Father Lenar Hoyt in Hyperion. Farcasting (traveling instantaneously through portals) is now impossible. Raul Endymion lives on the planet of Hyperion and is hand selected by Martin Silenus to go on a quest. He is to protect and escort the child, Aenea (the future "messiah") to her final destination somewhere in a far-flung solar system. Joining them is the enigmatic and loyal android, A. Bettik. They are pursued by Pax forces, led by the anti-hero, Father Captain De Soya. I never thought that science fiction could be beautiful. It sounds cheesy, but it's true. DS so deftly and luminously portrays far-future life, that it actually becomes believable. The desert planets of Hebron and Qom-Riyadh, the dessicated elegance of God's Grove, the icy tundra of Sol Draconi Septem...all so alien, yet so oddly familiar at the same time. The relationship between Raul, Aenea and A. Bettik was what really cemented this book for me. The three of them formed a tangible connection, one that could not be broken despite fear, devastation, loss, agony. I know that the next book in the series, The Rise of Endymion discusses moral and ethical issues related to the future of humanity but in this book, there is the one overarching theme of love. Love at its nascent stages, love blooming, love between adult and child, love between friends. Such a simple concept, but love really does conquer all.
I first read this years ago and didn't like it very much. This second reading was much more enjoyable! I've upped my rating from two to four stars.

This is one weird book. For about the first 60% it was feeling like the best I'd read this year, but having finished, my feelings are mixed. The narrator, Rose, works a typist in a New York City police precinct in the 1920s. When the precinct starts cracking down on speakeasies, a new typist is hired: the glamorous Odalie, who seems to be Rose's opposite in every way. Rose is an orphan who rents half a bedroom at a cheap boardinghouse and lives a solitary life, and she quickly falls under Odalie's spell, though she realizes Odalie's behavior deviates from her own strict sense of morality. To say more would be to spoil it; though between the extensive foreshadowing and reading reviews beforehand, I found the story to develop as I'd predicted it, the plot still kept me enthralled. So, the good stuff. The book is very well-written, with a strong voice, and the obvious unreliability of Rose's narration is engaging and keeps the reader guessing. The author keeps the tension simmering even through fairly mundane events, and while the pacing is on the slow side, it fits the story well. Rose and Odalie's relationship rings true, though it's evident from the beginning that it's not as healthy as Rose would like to believe. It's quite an atmospheric book, bringing Prohibition-era New York to life: the speakeasies of course are fun, as is seeing how the police station operates. The characters and settings are vivid; I'm inclined to call the book cinematic, although not in an entirely complimentary way: with the exception of Rose--who has enough complexity to share--it never felt like there was much to the characters beneath the surface. Even Odalie seems more glamor than substance, although perhaps that's intentional: she's likely sociopathic, incapable of affection, remorse, or change, and therefore inherently hollow. Unfortunately, some of my interest was lost when Rose and Odalie spend several chapters vacationing at a socialite couple's seaside mansion; I find rich people throwing parties to be one of the most boring subjects ever, although I realize that's idiosyncratic and if you're interested in this book for the Great Gatsby-like setting, it won't bother you in the least. And then there's the ending. It's a puzzle, and if you like endings that throw the entire book into question, you'll eat it up. As for me, I prefer the sort of unreliable narrators who allow readers to figure out what's going on by reading between the lines, and the possibility that Rose was delusional or lying the entire time just left me baffled. Neither of the most obvious explanations for the book really make sense. One is that Rose and Odalie were either the same person all along or that Rose made Odalie up. Which I don't much like because it throws out the entire story, most of which is about Rose and Odalie's relationship, and much of it featuring the two of them in the company of others, who do in fact behave as if there are two different women there. The other is that the story did mostly take place as Rose narrated it, and Odalie set Rose up. But then, how to explain those weird scenes where Rose seemed to be turning into Odalie? And if Rose's face was splashed all over the newspapers as "Ginevra"/Odalie, surely someone who knew one or the other would've come forward to point out the mistake. In the end, I'm glad I read this, because it's well-written and I found the story and its narrator captivating. And I would read another book by this author--I just hope it makes a little more sense!

This was a well-written story about Matt, who begins the book in a self-sacrificing relationship with a user of a boyfriend, and then is caught up in an abduction overseas. Among his SEAL rescuers is Mope/Travis, a SEAL who is gay and closeted in this pre-repeal story. The growth and confidence that Matt gains in his interactions with Mope and all the other SEALs empower him to move forward in his life. The guys were well-portrayed. Petey in particular was an inspired character as the cheerfully asshole teammate who becomes a good friend to Matt. The plot was believable, the progression of relationships worked very well. A few minor points made this book less than 5 stars for me. I did think that Matt's easy return to his life after the abduction was too simple and smooth. Maybe the author was trying to avoid clicheed PTSD, but I think a few more mood swings and other symptoms would have been more realistic after that ordeal. The ex-boyfriend was a bit predictably unpleasant, although not too OTT, and Matt's willful blindness about him went on longer than seemed plausible. The ease with which the team took Matt to heart was a bit surprising - especially in its unanimity. Lovely, fun, and a great plot driver, but a bit surprising. The end also bugged me - if someone has nearly drowned, to the point of unconsciousness, low heart rate and needing CPR, you should damned well get them to a hospital to be checked out ASAP, have chest Xrays, maybe start antibiotics against inhalation pneumonia etc. I loved the scene at the beach, but I'd have liked to see Travis spend a night worrying while Matt was hospitalized for tests and observation, before having the scene happen the next day. But despite minor quibbles, this was a solid read with some memorable and imaginative characters, and nice relationships, not just between the MC's. I really wouldn't mind seeing the sequel of these two guys working to become a couple more out in the open but still under the umbrella of DADT as it then stood, with the issues of Travis's father and military constraints, separations and missions.

It's so satisfying to finally find a book that lives up to its hype. I think my favorite part is the sense of mystery surrounding the entire "world", much like Lost, without the supernatural aspects. 4.5 stars, rounded up to 5 because of how hooked I was in some parts.

...I just finished this, and I'm speechless. I don't know what it was I expected when I picked this book up, but it definitely wasn't to be blown away the way I was. This is the best YA novel I have read in a very, very long time. The concept of this was so different from what I'm used to seeing. It was a completely unique concept and the author crafted it beautifully. That's the other thing about this book. The writing was superb. The worldbuilding was great, for one thing, but the language in itself just seemed to blow the rest of this genre in its entirety out of the water. I underlined countless words and passages in this book to use for inspiration for my own writing. This novel managed to be eloquent without seeming slow paced or pretentious, and that in itself is an accomplishment. At first I thought that a story set in Prague would at least account for any issues with the writing (I have low standards for YA these days). But I needn't have worried at all! I was actually caught off guard by the combined beauty and aesthetic of the setting with the wonderful writing. It all pieced together into the most wonderful, picturesque story I could have dreamed of from a YA book. And Karou and Akiva... I SHIP IT SOOOOO HARD OH MY GOD OH MY GOD OH MY GODDDDDD NEVER, and I mean NEVER in my entire life have I shipped a YA couple as much as I ship these two. Especially a canon one. But the author crafted their relationship, the beautiful tragedy, the pain, so wonderfully that I couldn't resist! Not to mention, I live for forbidden love stories. They're my kryptonite, and it seems like I've finally found one done right. And can we just talk about how wonderful it is to read from Karou's point of view? She accomplishes what every other YA author tries to do and fails. She's witty and sarcastic without trying so hard to be witty and sarcastic. I genuinely laughed at some of her nice little one liners. Plus, she actually questions the things Akiva tells her once she's kind of thrown into the paranormal world. She argues with him, she puts her family first. FINALLY, a believable protagonist! Not to mention the fact that we get to see things from Akiva's point of view, too? That he's treated like a person with conflicts and demons and emotions? Once again, finally we have a YA author treating the male characters other than the patriarchy's favorite version of a stoic, hunky male protector. The best thing about Akiva isn't that he isn't that...it's that he is, and he knows it's making him miserable. He doesn't want to be a fierce warrior, he wants to stop fighting and get to live life and be silly with his love. I just I knew they were in love before they kissed. And that right there is how you write a romance. Take me, rest of this series. I'm yours.

Haha I waited so long to talk about it until I could do it justice, but now I've waited so long I don't have much to say besides IT'S AMAZING. My favorite thing about Veronica Roth's series is how hard she pushes her characters. She doesn't back down and she has created such fantastic characters that they can handle what she throws at them. I love it. They make big mistakes, they make hard choices. It's amazing. This book is full of complicated situations and she deals with every single one in a way that I feel like she thoroughly covered them. Four's family situation, Tris' brother, the memory serum. I ESPECIALLY loved how she found a [mostly] non-violent solution to the entire problem of the story, like Four solved the problem by just asking his mom to stop and their relationship was what resolved everything. I really appreciated that.

"Break my heart," he said. "Break it in pieces. I give you permission." Definitely do not remember giving my permission though. So here is you head start, this book will break your heart, permission or not. This book is a little too much of everything and that is exactly its charm. It made me feel so much while reading it. As soon as I opened the book and read the first couple pages the agony and sadness took over because my heart just can't deal with Jules who carries the weight of the world and can't even have his Emma. And how fierce Emma has to deal with more shit than she needs, or Kit who is suddenly thrown into all this, or how cruel the world can be to lil Ty, or Dianna or Kieran, etc, etc. I care more about the characters than I do about the story and that's not necessarily a bad thing in my opinion because there is just so much going on with them. I understand that might not be for everyone, looots of povs, but I enjoyed it thoroughly. It felt so lively reading about the Blackthorn's and their companions. Although it was cool to see more of the shadow hunter world, especially the Fearie Courts. The ending killed me. I was so routing for everything to be finally 'good', and I knew it wouldn't be sugersweet but I didn't see this coming at all. HOW COULD LIVVY BE KILLED, WHAT ABOUT TY? THEY WERE A TEAM! JULLIAN DEFINITELY CANT DEAL WITH THIS AND OH LORD WHAT ABOUT THEIR CURSE?!!? Things were gonna be good :( ? I have become to really despise the Clave, Jullian and Kieran might have some competition in that. How can they be such bigots man, how?

Jorg Ancrath, you cocky, smartass, magnificent bastard... why can't I quit you? Anyway, I'm beginning to really like anthologies, especially when they are from series I like. This one had 2 stories I had already read (though I read Unfettered before the Broken Empire, so I think Select Mode was more understandable this go around since I had some reference to what was happening). The Secret, which was one of my favorite stories in Blackguards, was just as good the second time around, even knowing the end. Everything else was new to me. Sleeping Beauty was my favorite of the bunch. It includes Jorg being a smartass (which I love), and strange Builder shit that I need to know the origin and use of (which I also love, because I'm a dork). And it ends with the antagonist more or less actually dying in a fire, because basically 'fuck you, I'm Jorg Ancrath, bitch' *walks off nonchalantly while shit explodes behind him* - which is just... awesome. A Red Kent origin story, a Nuban origin story featuring Snorri's dad, and several instances of Makin being a fucking badass were also high points for me. So, can we have one of these anthologies for Jalan and Snorri..... please?

Re-read: 04/10/2017 This book was equal parts heartbreaking and amazing. I'm sure a lot of people were upset with Adrian in this book. Yes, he screwed up. He gave up. So what? Are you telling me that if you were in his place, you wouldn't give up for sure? Let's sum it up: the love of his life was violently taken away from him, he had no way of finding her, for weeks, he kept trying to reach her and failing, he felt useless and what's more, he kept using spirit which kept driving him over the edge. All the while he kept hearing his dead aunt talking to him. So all in all, things were not looking great for Adrian and even though I would have loved it if he kept being the best boyfriend ever and just kept trying over and over again, I understand why he gave up. He is not perfect. None of us are, we are just people, we give up and we make mistakes. And that's exactly the reason why I love Mead's characters - they are flawed and realistic. Unlike Adrian, Sydney was stronger than ever. I was really worried about Sydney getting brainwashed, but don't worry, guys. Sydney is smarter than all of the sadistic Alchemists combined and small little thing like being tortured for months can't break her. For real now - I'm so, so mad at Alchemists. When I imagine that Sydney spent MONTHS there, I want to go there and set them all on fire. However, as painful it was to see Sydney suffer, it was amazing to see what lengths her friends are willing to go to to save her. (Sydney and Eddie's reunion was ALMOST as sweet as her reunion with Adrian. And Hopper.) The ending was really surprising and a little bit over the top in my opinion (I'm talking about the wedding ), but nevertheless, I liked it. It seemed like a thing Adrian would definitely do. It didn't seem like a thing Sydney would do, but I guess that months of imprisonment make a person realize and re-evaluate some things. So even though Adrian made some mistakes in this one, he is still the perfect book boyfriend, especially because he is not perfect at all. He and Sydney will forever be my guilty pleasure. Original review: 30/07/2014 "I've made it a rule in my life not to pick fights with children, cute animals, or ignorant old men. I will, however make an exception for you if you ever touch or insult  my wife   again." I have liked Sydney from the page one of The Bloodlines and as the story progressed, I have come to love her. It was this book, however, that made me truly admire her. Usually when something bad happens to someone, it makes them stronger but also more violent or revengeful. But that's not Sydney's case. Suffering makes her stronger, but she stays just as caring, loving and moral as before. I have actually expected this would happen sooner or later as soon as I realized what twisted creatures (I'm not going to call them people) alchemists are. And they stood up (in a negative sense of word) to all my expectations. What I didn't expect was the second half of the book (although I have to say the twist in the end wasn't really surprising and I even have a theory on who might have done it). Who I felt the worst for in this book, however, wasn't  Sydney   who suffered the most or  Jill   who will probably suffer in the next book. The one I felt and still feel the most sorry for is  Eddie. Really, I don't know if Richelle hates him, but throughout the whole Vampire Academy and Bloodlines series, he is the one who has suffered the most. Let's have a quick recap: Eddie becomes a source of blood for Strigoi and later watches (even though he is high on endorphins) his best friend die. (Frostbite) Later he is taken by Strigoi and almost dies AGAIN. (Shadow Kiss) After that he is given second chance with the gang in Palm Springs, BUT everything goes down a few times resulting in Sydney being taken away while Eddie is protecting her. (Fiery Heart) And all that apparently isn't enough so Jill, which is not only Eddie's assignment but also his "loved one", goes missing. (Silver Shadows) Richelle Mead seriously needs to give Eddie a break! You can hate me and argue with me, but in my opinion Eddie is the most selfless and caring character that has been introduced in VA/Bloodlines. He is an amazing fighter and even greater friend. He wouldn't mind doing anything for the ones he loves and I don't only mean Jill (let me remind you of Micah and Lee and everyone else Eddie wouldn't mind setting her up with because he is not "good enough"), I also mean everyone else, Rose, Sydney.... When he found out about the taboo Sydney and Adrian were commiting by being together, he was surprised, of course, but he was also supportive and didn't doubt them for a second. Because he is a f...ing good person! So, dear Richelle, just leave Eddie alone (and by alone I mean with Jill), please! I have to say I'm really looking forward to the next book but I also don't want it to come out since it will be the last Bloodlines novel. And I don't want to say goodbye to my friends from Palm Srpings just yet. Or ever.
A surprisingly cheerful book given its subject matter.

I should've finished this 4 days ago. But I've had like 0 reading time this week. Anyway, I actually enjoyed this book a lot more than I thought I would. It's totally cliche and kind of cheesy but I really enjoyed the overall story.

Well, I have now fallen in love with another author and series!! This book hooked me from the get go and there wasn't a part in the book where I was bored or thinking about anything else. The characters are people whom I fell in love with; and I absolutely adored Stephen ( Bianca's best friend). The story begins on an airplane flight where Bianca and Stephen are steward and stewardess working. Bianca notices a man sitting in first class who is intently watching her and she becomes nervous as he is super hot, and she is immediately attracted to him. The millionaires's name happens to be James Cavendish, and he begins to pursue Bianca relentlessly and is desperate to have a chance at meeting up with her after work. When these two come together and start their affair, they make fireworks together! They end up in a scorching hot BDSM relationship that becomes extremely intense very quickly. Both James and Bianca have some trauma in their pasts and not everything is smooth sailing for this couple. The story has many bumps along the way and there are a few major situations that arise towards the end of the book. Of course,it ends at a point where I am itching to read Book #2! This was a thoroughly entertaining read with some sizzling hot sex on the side. The bond between Stephen and Bianca was so endearing, and I loved how loyal they were to one another. They share a very difficult past together and have been there for one another since they were teenagers. I would love to see Stephen get his own story and HEA as I think he is such a kind soul with some very heavy baggage. I loved this read and am glad that I can jump right into the next book. This one is going on my keeper shelf and I will be rereading it in the future!

It's really weird for me to give My Life Next Door 5/5 stars and for me to give What I thought was True a 2/5 because the jump is so drastic. I was really looking forward to reading this book because MLND blew me away-it was funny, romantic, and memorable. This book? Not so much. For starters, I could barely stand Gwen, who is as judgmental as she is dull. She has a past, and she lets boys have their way with her and she doesn't understand why they make fun of her and do not respect her? She doesn't have any interest outside of Cass. Like what did she like to do on her free time? Read? Listen to music? Go shopping? Anything?? She was also so timid and I felt like I could barely relate to her, which is sad because she is the narrator, she is suppose to be my anchor to the story. I liked Cass, he was sweet and all but he didn't woo me in any way. I also didn't understand why they liked each other so much, most of their conversations were pretty boring to be honest. Also, family-the aspect I thought the author did so well in her first book fell flat for me. There was so much groundwork there, so much to be done but I didn't feel close to anyone in Gwen's family at all. We barely got to know them, so to me they were just there in the background which I know a lot of authors do, but I felt disappointed because Gwen's family did seem interesting. One character that did stand out for me, was Nico. I like his story, and it's really relatable. What I didn't like was  Vivian. UGH. I can't stand cheaters. Said she's been in love with him all her life, and goes behind his back and starts dating some guy (SPENCER! Of all people) and doesn't tell him. That's a real winner right there. I can understand her falling out of love with him because their end goals are so different, but to do it in that way, is beyond wrong. I also hated how Gwen just forgave her. Really girl? I felt as if that was handled really unrealistically. Another aspect that bothered me was the pacing of the story, and how basically nothing happens. Really. There are little moments here and there, but I felt as if I was on a ride that only went one speed and one direction. I'm hoping Huntley Fitzpatrick's next book won't disappoint because this one...I can't even.

Anya's Ghost - Vera Brosgol Rating: Skipping class one day, Anya Borzakovskaya falls into a well and meets Emily, a girl who died almost a century ago. After the initial shock of being haunted by a ghost, Anya realizes that her new friend can help her get better grades and maybe a hot boyfriend, but Emily - whose claim to have been murdered hides a more horrible truth - however has her own idea of what Anya's life should be and starts to threaten Anya's family to get her to do what she wants, until Anya confronts her and helps her move on. This coming-of-age story with its paranormal touch was highly enjoyable and Anya, with her struggles to fit in (disassociating herself from her Russian heritage, wanting to be friends with the "right" people, worrying about body image), was remarkably relatable. I liked how Emily seemed to gain power and changed her appearance as she overtook Anya's life, making me wonder what would have happened if the situation had continued. I also enjoyed the art style, which uses only shades of purple. My only wish would have been to see more of Anya's new self confidence at the end. "I don't think murder is an appropriate reaction to disappointment."

Another dystopian society story. A large earthquake has diminished the population and almost everyone is homeless. Mia finds herself in a struggle between two cultish societies who both see her potential and want to use her for their cause. But which one is right?

Fun to read and to know that the villain would be getting her comeuppance somehow. When a mid-40s women's magazine editor returns from a long medical leave, she finds a former assistant has usurped her and that the magazine has become an app. Things that bothered me about this (so I didn't think about them): Where is HR when all the workplace abuse is going on? And the main quandary, that there's NO WAY a successful woman in her 40s would be that ignorant of technology. Maybe if she'd been depicted as more of a Grace Coddington? But as it was, it wholly strained credulity.

If you aren't reading Saga, stop what you are doing, get up, and buy all of these comics. They're definitely for mature audiences, so if this is the first grown-up comic you've picked up, you might be surprised, but it has brilliant art, a fantastic story, and is pretty much the best thing ever.

4 Stars Overall Opinion:  This was not what I was expecting, but in a good way! I was expecting a story about nasty dirty affair and revenge, and this really wasn't it. I didn't read any spoiler reviews and went in blind, and I think that was the best thing I could've done -- so I'm going to try my hardest to not give too much away! It was a pleasant surprise, and even though the author had me guessing up until the end -- I was extremely happy with the ending and that I got a HEA! If you feel like you really need spoilers -- pm me ;) Brief Summary of the Storyline:  Again, I'll keep this brief in hopes of not ruining it. This is Maverick's story. Maverick grew up being best friends with Kael, and in love with his older brother Killian. She loves both brothers, but in different ways. She is heartbroken when Killian ends up marrying her older sister, and Kael is there to help her pick up the pieces. They end up getting married as well. She struggles with her conflicted feelings, and after some big ups and downs she does eventually get a HEA ending. POV: This alternated between Maverick and Kael's POV. Overall Pace of Story:  Good. I never skimmed, and I thought it flowed well. It does jump between the present, the past year, and farther into the past. Instalove: No, they've known each other their whole lives. H rating: 4.5 stars. (Won't say name to prevent giving things away). I really liked him! He really loved the h and always had her in mind in everything he did. He was hot! He also was really sweet. h rating: 4 stars. Maverick. I liked her a lot more than I expected. She was really struggling with her love life, and I actually sympathized with her instead of getting frustrated with her (which I often do in love triangle type stories). Sadness level: Low/moderate. There was definitely some angst, but I wouldn't say it was OTT and I never cried. I remember reading reviews that said others did though... Push/Pull: Yes  The h is conflicted in her feelings at first, but she comes around not that long after. The H is the main pursuer (but he also lets her figure things out on her own and doesn't push). Heat level: Moderate. They have some hot scenes (some in public places) and chemistry, but not so much it takes away from the story. Descriptive sex: Yes Safe sex: Yes and no. Mentions of birth control. I don't remember any mention of previous practices or STD status. OW/OM drama: Yes  The h is struggling with her still strong feelings for one brother when she is married to another. Sex scene with OW or OM: Yes  Most of the scenes are with one man, and then there is one scene with another man that is a descriptive memory. Cheating: Yes IMO, but not what I expected. There is only one instance where the h kisses OM that I would call it cheating, but it doesn't go further than that and she tells the H about it. Possible Triggers: Yes Unrequited love, loss of a parent, and act of violence in the workplace. Closure:  This had good closure with a HEA ending. It ended just how I wanted it to :) How I got it: I paid the $3.99 on Amazon. Safety: This one is probably Not Safe for most of the safety gals. - Does  have cheating (see above spoiler) -  Does have a separation between the h and H -  Does Not have abuse -  Does Not have OTT sad parts - Does  have a HEA ending

Oh this was painful... The author did not do a very good job villianizing Grace's parents. I felt more sorry for her folks than I did for her. "Oh lord, she's 17, how dare they leave her alone to go to a dinner party?"... "Oh how cruel, they caught her in bed with her boyfriend at 3 in the morning and they grounded her"... The entire book complains about how immature her parents are, when she's the most immature character in the book. Uuggghhh. I understand that the authors trying to make the parents out to be the bad guys. Sam's parents were definately bad guys, that was believeable. Why didn't she just make her parents as horrible as his? I think it would have been more realistic to make the parents so horrible with money that Grace had to work a part time job to pay bills. Then I could believe that she had horrible parents. But no, they're actually financially well off and buy her whatever she wants so I don't quite understand the problem. Maybe I just can't relate to teenage angst anymore or maybe it's because I'm a parent myself, but this book made me want to smack Grace. When I was her age, if I had been caught in bed with a boy at 3 in the morning I would have been crucified. Not only would they have taken away my car keys, they would have SOLD THE CAR. My bedroom door would have been removed to make sure I could never hide anything like that again. I had to walk bare foot in 3 feet of snow to get to school! Uphill! Both WAYS!! For once, can I read a YA novel who's main female character does NOT have major issues with their mothers. I have 2 daughter and this is scaring the crap out of me. They want to spend time with their kids, then they're over-bearing. They want to finally go back to work and have a career (cause you know after 17 years of raising these brats, heaven forbid they have their own lives), then they're neglecting their children. You just can't win with these YA novels, why is the mother always the bad guy??? "My mother drinks too much" Well she raised you and took care of you for 17 years and puts up with your snotty attitude, I don't blame her. I want to buy the woman a drink after this novel!

Rating: 2.5 I'm a bit ambivalent about this one. I liked the world that this book created, and found the City and the Brother absolutely creepy (as was no doubt intended), but I can't say that I was all that interested in the characters of what happened to them. In fact, the only character I was really interested in at all was Lucas - probably because he was the only one who showed any real depth (though can we please find a reason for loving someone other than 'you're beautiful'???). I really didn't like Raffy at all - pretty much the entire time he was petulant, angry and/or whiny, as well as being completely unforgiving. And Evie... most of the time I found her boring, some of the time I didn't understand her at all, and the rest of the time I was completely frustrated by how easily lead she was! Does she have any real personality of her own? In the beginning I could see why she was with Raffy - he was the only person she could be herself with, but there definitely wasn't any spark. Then they tried to show spark between her and Lucas, but I had no idea why she was suddenly kissing him! But absolutely worst of all was when she was about to tell Raffy about Lucas and then had sex with him, only to tell him she'd kissed his brother! WHO DOES THAT?!?!? All told, I'm still not really sure what to make of this book. It didn't grab me, but it was readable enough and still interesting in parts. I didn't particularly like the characters, but found the world intriguing enough that I'm probably going to give book 2 a try. I'll wait and see how I feel then. But for now, I'm still kinda 'meh' on this one.
Book One: Couldn't put it down. Book Two: Still good, but not as good as Book 1 Book Three: Could barely get through it, what did I just waste my time reading? What started great ended with a "meh."

Beautiful Creatures Review Full formatting of this review at link above. (WITH GIFS, who doesn't love gifs?!) Hello, all. Welcome to my dissertation on the young adult novel titled Beautiful Creatures. (Not really, but it felt like I was writing one because of how long this is) I don't think I've ever had so many mixed feelings about a book before. What better rating to give a book that you are confused about than the in-between, non-committal three stars? Since everyone pretty much knows what BEAUTIFUL CREATURES is all about by now, I'll save you the long explanation and back-story and get straight to my opinion. I made my thoughts into three basic lists, so you don't have to read the whole thing. I'm just so thoughtful like that. You're welcome. Pros: Male Lead Magic Family Concept of Witchcraft Macon Ravenwood and Boo Radley Ridley Cons: Male Lead (Yes, I know what I did there) Romance Ethan's dad Gatlin the town cult Death of favorite characters Two authors, different goals Simple ways this could have been better: One author (whoever was less focused on the romance aspect) Getting rid of Ethan Getting rid of the romance altogether Not killing off my favorite character The Male Lead A.K.A Ethan Wate I can really appreciate it when an author, in this case-two female authors-go out of the norm and decide to write a YA novel through the male's point of view. This can change the story so drastically, and in many cases, Ethan's POV was a strong Pro in BEAUTIFUL CREATURES. I was imagining how the story might have changed if it was in Lena's POV instead, and realized it would not have been as enjoyable. The negative side of this is that I didn't care for Ethan much at all. He has some crap-butt friends in the beginning, which only makes me wonder what kind of a person he really is. Sure, as soon as he meets Lena he "changes," but is that really realistic? I don't really know of a guy like that who would dump all of his friends, turn against them, and become a social pariah for a girl he met two days ago. Also, Ethan takes everything in stride, rarely questioning anything or thinking something was a little off. Communicating through thought? No problem. Lena's house changing every time he does in? Psh. Becoming a dragon? Well that doesn't happen, but if it did, I guarantee Ethan wouldn't even blink an eye. Magic and the whole concept of Casters Fantastic. Loved these parts. You're surprised, right? I really enjoyed learning about Caster history and Lena's family. There are so many different kinds of magic and creatures and I found them all so amazing and really wish a bigger part of the story had focused more on the magic aspects rather than the romance. Almost everyone in Lena's family has a different power, and I liked how the authors took time to really come up with each individual's abilities and names. Family I love reading about relationships. Something that actually ties with romance in my book is familial relationships. So while I disliked the romance in BEAUTIFUL CREATURES, I loved experiencing the connections between Ethan and Amma, and Lena and her family. Especially Lena and Macon, they were my favorite duo. These relationships seemed deeper and more genuine than Ethan and Lena's teenage insta-love. I hated their interactions with each other. A negative to the family aspect is Ethan's dad, who I really wish wasn't in the story at all. He doesn't add anything, and if the authors were trying to keep at least one parent in Ethan's life they should have just killed off his dad and left him with Amma. I would much rather prefer Ethan being an orphan than someone with a father attached solely by word instead of actuality. Gatlin the Cult Seriously? Seriously? You are telling me that the entire town conspires against a fifteen year old girl simply because she isn't from around here? You are telling me everyone blames her for all the strange things that happen around the town? A fifteen year old girl no one really knows that everyone just has insta-hate for? A town meeting is called where Lena is displayed in front of the entire town and the whole thing is symbolic of the Salem Witch Trials? Just to expel her from school? In what case is this even remotely plausible or realistic? These people are crazy, and the authors are even more so if they thought this could happen and readers would think it was conceivable. Sheer ridiculousness. Two authors, different goals I can not think of a better way to word this than Karen did on Goodreads: " one lady said "i want to write a paranormal romance!" the other lady said "i want to write a civil war-era southern love story. well, let's smooosh them together! it is a great idea!!" Pick one and focus on it, strengthen just that one side of the plot rather than have two weak ones. Honestly, if you were to taken Ethan or the romance out of this book, I really think this could have been around four stars instead of the 2.5 I am rating it. I will be reading the sequel, because I own it. Finally, if you disagree with me, that's cool. I respect your opinion, so let me have mine.

I wasn't really sure about this from the beginning pages, because S. is a much more involved reading experience than I'm used to. There's the novel of The Ship of Theseus, then there's the marginalia, the miscellaneous notes between the pages, and so many names to remember! Yet slowly but surely, I was hooked. I haven't read a book so slowly in years; there was just so much per page that it took significantly longer to read than a typical novel. However this forced me to go slowly and really savor the unique reading experience, and I think that made me enjoy it more than I might have otherwise. There's a lot to take in, and I used book-tabs to keep track of Jen & Eric's clues about Straka's identity, any lists of "Who's who?" between the S members and the characters in SoT, and to mark chapters (since flipping through the book is made difficult by the stuff; you don't want those postcards and letters falling out!). I usually only read for 40-50 pages (or less) in a single sitting, but for those pages, I was completely immersed. S. is a really unique reading experience, and it's a book lover's dream. It looks, feels, and even smells like an old library book. All the details were carefully crafted, and it's a beautiful book -- both physically and plotwise. A few things that I wished had been clearer by the end of the book, as some things were a bit vague because we're reading notes, not a true prose-form story: What was the significance of Signe and what was the role of S in her life? Also who exactly were her parents? What was with the "new S"? What about Serin? Did these people finally leave Jen alone? What was the deal with all that? Was Moody behind it? This definitely never gets resolved by the end of the book/notes. 5/5 stars because the plot of the marginalia & the novel itself were fantastic, the presentation was really unique and very well done, and the book itself is just so darn cool.

I nabbed this one at the Scholastic sale, and I initially just put it directly onto my shelf, but I was in need of a distraction last week, and it caught my eye. I really enjoyed Ripper; the original story is just endlessly fascinating. I also hear people raving all the time about Maureen Johnson, and although I wasn't a huge fan of 13 Little Blue Envelopes, I was willing to give her another shot. I'm glad I did -- this book is solidly enjoyable. It's not the greatest YA I've read all year (or even all month), but as a series-starter, it's a decent read. I'm not entirely sure I feel the need to rush out and pick up the second entry, but I suppose if I run across it sometime (maybe at next year's half-price sale! ), I'll pick it up. Anyway. Plot. Aurora, or Rory as she prefers, is a New Orleans native whose parents are transferred to Bristol, England. Since Rory has always wanted to go to boarding school, her parents give her the option to attend school anywhere she would like, and she chooses a school in London. Although the story takes place in modern times, boarding school is one of those settings (kind of like the circus...) that always feels more like historical fiction. It doesn't help that this book deals with Jack the Ripper -- all of the phones and computers sound out of place! Anyway, Rory begins attending Wexford, located in London's East End...which just happens to be the site of the infamous Jack the Ripper murders. And wouldn't you know it, some crazy copycat is committing murders in the same locations, modeled after the originals! The police have no suspects, no witnesses, and the one murder caught on camera seems to have been tampered with. After all, there's no way a knife could hover in thin air all on its own, right? Rory's start to her school year is fairly typical. She and her roommate "Jazza" get along great (they're both lovely, bookish, nerds), and she even meets cutie pie Prefect Jerome and develops an immediate crush. Of course there's the mandatory daily "sports" sessions of field hockey, which sounds exactly as torturous as Rory describes, and mean-girl Prefect Charlotte is quite a pill. But I liked that Rory was able to find a place for herself at Wexford in a way that felt realistic. She doesn't immediately become the most popular girl on campus (as an American transplant, she's something of a curiosity, especially given that she's Southern), but she also isn't immediately ostracized by a clique of "mean girls." It's lucky that she and her roommate happen to get along and be so much alike, but that's not totally outside the realm of possibility -- I've seen it happen firsthand! Not long after arriving at Wexford, Rory nearly chokes to death on her dinner -- it seems to be a minor complication in an otherwise decent start to a new school year, but Rory's life begins to change from the moment she chokes. First of all, there's this weird dude in the library named Alistair, who's always lounging in the same spot. Then, there's her weird new roommate Boo, who doesn't appear to have any interest in school or studying, but does love following Rory around. Strangest of all, is the bald man lurking outside of her dorm that only Rory was able to see... Long story short -- Rory can see ghosts. Her near-death experience combined with genetic something-or-other resulted in her newfound ability. And crazy roommate Boo (who, although described as Indian reminded me of no one so much as Rebel Wilson) is a fellow "Shade" assigned to watch Rory. It seems that the bald man might be connected to the Ripper case...he may even be the Ripper, and Rory needs protection so she can develop her abilities unharmed. Boo brings a few other Shades into the mix -- Stephen and Callum, two equally surly English lads (though for different reasons). They've caught on to the fact that the Ripper might not be entirely human, and are conducting their own investigation. Apparently, they were at one time connected to the London police. It's unclear whether or not they still are, or if they're some sort of rogue operation, or if they're super-duper secret (so secret the police don't even know about them...). Based on how the resolution is handled, I'm guessing that's information we'll find out in the next book. Like I said in an update, this reminded me a LOT of The Diviners (although I think it may have actually come out first). I liked that Johnson, like Bray, didn't spend a lot of time waffling about whether or not the ghosts were real. We find out fairly early on that yes, there are ghosts, and some people can see them. I also liked Johnson's explanation for how people come by this ability -- it reminded me a bit of the "werewolf gene" on Vampire Diaries (for the life of me, I can't remember if this is how it worked in the books or not). Certain people have the gene, dormant. If people with the "werewolf" gene kill someone (or are responsible for a death, I guess), the gene "wakes up" and they become a werewolf. But I suppose there are, potentially, people in that universe with the gene who never become werewolves because they never activate it. It's basically the reverse principle here -- if you have the gene and you have a near-death experience...before the age of 19...you get the ability. Again, there are likely lots of people with a dormant gene who never had a near-death experience to activate it. I also liked that it's not just the experience that gives you ghost-seeing powers. It seems like others in Rory's family might be carriers of the gene as well -- another topic I think will be explored in the next book. Although it wasn't nearly as creepy as The Diviners (which did actually give me nightmares), I really liked the overall tone, and the subject matter is sort of perfect for creating that -- as one of the characters says: Jack the Ripper is one of the most terrifying murder cases, because he legitimately got away with it. Even though he "only" killed a few people, no one ever caught him, and no one even knows who he might be -- the theories are practically endless. I was actually hoping that  the ghost would be the ghost of actual Jack, not just some random guy who went nuts because he could see ghosts...and then became one. There's also this interesting ghost discrimination thing happening among the Shades -- they have the ability to destroy ghosts, basically send them into the light, or whatever, but they disagree on whether or not they should do so. There's this whole idea of "being one of them" *pearl clutch* that raises all sorts of interesting questions. Also, this has to be a universe in which Ghostbusters does not exist, because the whole "destroying ghosts with phones" thing was just ripe for a "who ya gonna call?" joke. Also-also, calling it right now  Rory is totally a human terminus...or a ghost grim reaper . Overall, I really liked this. I loved Rory as a narrator, and I liked that Johnson didn't forget she was from New Orleans -- she makes reference to her home quite a bit. I also loved the setting -- it made me want to visit London...and maybe read up on some Jack the Ripper theories.

Unfortunately, I'm marking this book as a DNF. Don't get me wrong, I loved the concept. A LGBTQ relationship in a fantasy world is always something I'm interested in and fully support, but I just wasn't a fan of the execution. The characters felt two-dimensional; there was a lot of introductions of new characters without much time to get to know them--I was unbelievably confused and had basically no idea what was going on for the first quarter of this book. It goes without saying that I couldn't get through this book, though it had lots of potential. Perhaps other people will enjoy this novel more than I did.

WHY WOULD YOU DO THIS TO ME GREG? HUH!? a CLIFFHANGER?? Really!! I suppose it's a tribute to the writing that it can start out as wacky (think Star Trek TOS) as this one did (and let me tell you, it doesn't exactly get  less wacky as the story goes on), that I even friggin' care what happens next. *Possible spoilers below * The whole plot is a bit confusing at first. The best way I can explain it is if you're familiar with The Elder Scrolls, then think of the titular 'Infernal City' as a soul stone...but, like, bajillion times bigger. It involves a city with thousands upon thousands of people who treat life, and the energy that creates it, as a commodity: something that can be bought, sold, and (yes) consumed. If you're not familiar with The Elder Scrolls, the book does a pretty good job of explaining things along the way, so you would probably still be able to pick up on what's going on without any familiarity with this world. Just be aware that it may seem a bit wacky at first. The four POV characters are Annig (an alchemist) and Mere-Glim (her BFF), Attrebus (Prince) , and Colin (Investigator). The writer did a great job of writing these guys in their own perspective without making it first person, which I appreciate immensely  because I think first person narratives are overused and cheap At the start these people seem to have nothing to do with each other. They seem to be all on their own trajectories storytelling-wise, and their stories are told concurrently. For a while I was kinda scratching my head, wondering what these people had to do with each other and when/if they're ever gonna meet up. But it was actually interesting aspect of the story; something that added to the mystery involving the Infernal City and watching it all start to come together. My favorite of the characters was Colin. I think it's nice that they've finally written a necro-mage type who is not an evil guy. They could have easily passed him off as a very calloused individual (especially after that first 'initiation' scene) but instead it's more like he can't help but care about people, even if they're beyond help. It's very interesting, I hope they have more of him in the next book.

Hmm okay. I'm going to give this book 4 stars for now because I really did like it. The story was intriguing and captivating, the world and character building was really great, but the romance was really not. Dimension travel is something I've never read about before and I will admit it had me hooked from the beginning. Seeing Marguerite wake up in new lives where she lived as someone completely different but still fundamentally her was really interesting. I loved her family and the story of the firebird and the company that wants the power and all of that. Super intriguing and interesting. Love story though? Doesn't fit. I'm extremely over love triangles. Like completely done. And while this book SEEMS to finish with the end of the love triangle, it does not really make up for the book. Not only was the love triangle completely weird, it was random. So much chemistry with Theo to start and that goes no where. It's almost like she stops liking him instantly. It's almost... unbelievable in the sense that you don't really understand how this decision was made. And then you have Paul. Now with Paul it's weird because the Paul she loves is not the one who is in her dimension, it's the Paul from another dimension and because of that she doesn't want to really be with Paul from her dimension. That's really ridiculous and confusing to me but oh well. I mean I really liked the book but there were problems with the weird romance. But I'm going to continue on in the series and I do recommend the book if you can get past a love triangle. The only thing I will say about this triangle is that she doesn't love both of them together. Like it's kind of starts with one and then moves on to the other so it's more bearable.

However, I already love the book before those happened so that didn't really bothered me. Recommended read!

As book 3 of the Partials Sequence, Ruins doesn't disappoint. The series' thus far has established itself as smart and unique with a large dose of strong characters, and Ruins brings it all home with a flourish. As is the case with a lot of trilogies, Book 3 feels more like the second half of book 2, but that isn't a bad thing. Kira Walker and her supporting quest continue in their quest to better the end of the world while unraveling the numerous mysteries surrounding who actually caused it. The character complexity and development continue to be excellent, and the plot does a good job of moving foward at a nice pace. While this series leaned more to the sci-fi side of things (less feels and magic, more science and actions), Dan does a good job of bringing in an emotional ending that you can't help but appreciate. The trilogy is tied up well, but not too neatly, and you walk away happy because the ending made sense. I feel like trilogy endings are often shots in the dark, and often feel rushed or incomplete, but the author pulled it off very well. I recommend this book, and the whole series to anyone who likes dystopian, paranormal or scifi. 4.5/5 stars.

In Heartless Ms. Meyer had the daunting task of taking us on a journey in which we already know the destination. Even though I have never read Alice in Wonderland I knew the Queen of Hearts to be a heartless b*tch. I have read Cinder and most of Scarlet and was underwhelmed by the writing in both. However, in her new book Ms. Meyer shows abundant improvement in her writing and storytelling. She exhibits much more muchiness in general. In this whimsical and charming tale we embark on an adventure to Wonderland but it is not Alice's adventure, it is Lady Catherine Pinkerton's. We get to see how Catherine, a sweet and caring young girl who loves to bake evolves into the merciless, cruel, and cold Queen of Hearts. The Wonderland setting is revamped a bit and resembles Victorian London. Imagine Victorian London in stark black and white, drop in bits of red and other vivid colors, add talking animals and every day objects which are alive and animated and you have Lady Catherine's Wonderland. There are some rather straightforward foreshadowing and clues to the ending of the story (or to the beginning, depending on how one wishes to view it). However, don't the majority of us already know the Queen of Hearts? I didn't feel spoiled or jilted by obvious clues presented in the story, as a matter of fact there was more than one twist I didn't see coming and one twist I made up in my own mind that never came to fruition. Perhaps my favorite parts of the book were the witty one liners that were funny and clever and made me feel both childlike and smart at the same time for understanding them. Ms. Meyer has woven all the elements of darkness and light, fate and free will, and love and hatred into an unforgettable story of the evolution of the Red Queen from a young girl who dreamed of true love and freedom to a madwoman best remembered for the phrase Off with his head.

This was a unique book that merges an old fairy tale with the realities of an Alaskan winter in the 1920s. This isn't an action-packed book. Nor is it a fairy tale. This is a book about survival in the wilderness, about the limits of love and the strains life can put on it. This is a book about the definition of family. I would have preferred for the connections between the fairy tale and the characters' lives to be a little more subtle rather than constantly spelled out for the reader. Still, all the characters were interesting and well fleshed out. Most of all Mabel and Faina. The landscape is described in such a way that you can feel how lonely they are in the middle of nowhere even as you are in awe of the beauty. Faina did lose a bit of her charm as she started to be a bigger part of the Mabel and Jack's lives. But this loss of magic was balanced by the detailed changes in Jack and Mabel. I would have given this book 5 stars. Except that I was disappointed by the ending.

I enjoyed this installment in the downside series much more than the first book. Maybe that was because I had a firm grip on the universe. I understood what the hell actually happened to their world by this point, and definitely had a better understanding of the magic incorporated. Chess though in the book drove me to sheer insanity. When I wanted her to be rational and think she charged in guns blazing and when I wanted her to act and make a stand she stood completely still allowing everything to go to hell in a hand basket. Lex continued to annoy me and Terrible continued to captivate me in this book as well. I definitely had Terrible Fever reading this book! The plot to the cases Chess was working were both a bit odd. On one hand she is investigating an haunting for the church at the home of a famous Hollywood actor. She is also investigating a string of murders in Downside which focuses on prostitutes. The first case seemed overly dramatic and silly, the second case was super intense and scary but in the end really confusing and pretty sick. The ending left me freaked, pissed, and scared for the characters. And I was pretty convinced what I expected to happen for all the characters in the 3rd book had just been destroyed by the end of this book. So crazy. All in all a great read and one that made me start reading the 3rd book as soon as I finished this one!

Review first appeared on my blog: Book Addict 24-7 Let me just state that it's really not fair that I read Wanderlove by Kirsten Hubbard just before Gayle Forman's Just One Day. I'm going to be blunt and say that Forman's novel is more about self-discovery after a perfect day comes crashing down, rather than travelling, though it was oddly reminiscent of the themes found in Wanderlove (I'm just going to go out on a limb and state that Wanderlove has most likely ruined every other travelling book that I will ever come across). But even if it lacked the aspects of travelling I so yearned for, I still found it to be a fairly entertaining novel. It has the lesson of finding yourself amidst the chaos and confusion of abrupt change, how hiding your true self from the most important people in your life, especially yourself, may be disastrous, and how sometimes taking a chance is worth the risk of losing it all. The first part of the novel pulled me in immediately. Here you meet the less than perfect, but still sexy, Willem, a dutch actor. Allyson, the protagonist, is intrigued enough to break from her perfectionism and strict lifestyle to spend one day in Paris with this stranger. While I am a sucker for a storyline like this, I will note that it is rather cliche. "Carefree boy meets straight-laced girl. Carefree boy helps release straight-laced girl from the confines of her boring, controlled life." Ignoring the cliche, I will admit that they are cute together, making me want to read more about their adventures. It is when they are apart, however, that Allyson's behavior grates on my nerves. For all you know, someone has stripped her bare of who she once was because of one perfect day. But it makes sense, because in a way, that one perfect day stole the controlled and well-behaved Allyson, leaving someone unsure of what she wants out of life. That one perfect day is about more than just romance--but about who Allyson was pretending to be before Willem stepped in. So, the novel spends a good chunk of the story trying to put the broken Allyson back together again into a new and more free-spirited Allyson. Though this is enlightening and powerful, the delivery is dramatic and boring. I kept expecting more and wanting more of the storyline. I wanted Allyson to stand up to those around her, I wanted her to do something regarding her misery, but she was just as quiet and controlled as always, even if she was slowly dying inside (emotionally, of course). The conclusion though. Wow. THAT is a reason to keep reading this series. After all those months of suffering, Allyson finally returns to Europe and I loved it. The moment she decides to return, the story gains more life. Though the writing is indeed beautiful and descriptive, the editing is horrendous. I know it is inevitable for a few editing errors to slip through the cracks (no one is perfect), but wow. On one page alone there must have been about five mistakes. I can't even begin to explain how irritating this was. Even with my pickiness over the editing, I did love Allyson's character growth, the places she visited, and the many people she met. Would I read it all again? Probably, simply because of the travelling bits and Willem. Always for Willem. I recommend this one for readers who enjoy a good contemporary young adult read about self-discovery, romance, and a slight touch of travelling and exploration.

Well, as the sole human being who didn't read Harry Potter, I can say, without the shadow of the doubt cast by the unavoidable comparison with the children epic saga, that I loved this. Not only the whodunit part, which was beautifully drawn (though I guessed the killer, and guess being the operative word here, because as another reviewer (and author) so cleverly pointed out in her review the reveal of the killer was obvious in its un-obviousness ), and the delicious multi-layered characters, but also the glamorous sultry depiction of the high fashion world. Paparazzi, skinny beautiful supermodels, stoned out of their asses singers, fancy gay designers, ritzy areas, betrayals, scandals, all of these together. It was like reading and savoring a juicy trashy magazine from cover to cover on a rainy Sunday afternoon. Still, that wasn't what I loved most about it, but the classic undertones and the eighties Columbo aura. I could almost see Cormoran Strike wearing the specific trench coat and hat, in the middle of the 21st century modern London, and Robin blabbering Scooby-Doo style, with the big hair and large shoulder-padded suit jacket. It was good reading something that, though it looks so unoriginal at a first glance, proves to lack almost everything that the actual trend demands of the genre, the shocking twists and turns, the M. Night Shyamalan worthy andtheywerealreadydead finale, the mighty ,,showing" and the specific mystery thriller writing, short, dry and to the point. Personally, I found this return to the origins of the detective novel very original and refreshing, in a world of mystery thrillers bursting with breathtaking action and modern characters. Upon seeing that a lot of long term Harry Potter fans didn't love this and I so strongly did, I should definitely wonder if I would like Harry Potter. Probably not (twenty years too late for me), though it was mighty fun reading some other reviews, both raving and ranting, because all of them made this comparison, as expected. Still, I'm waiting for my baby to grow up, so we could read it together and maybe praise in one voice J. K. Rowling for the wonderful writer she seems to be.

I thought this was a fun contemporary to kick off my summer reads. However, I would have liked a bit more from it. The novel was set in New York, and since I've never been there I was really hoping to be absorbed into the setting and get a feel for what it feels like to be in the Big Apple. However, the setting descriptions fell to the wayside compared to the drama occurring between the characters. I never felt like I was walking the streets of New York in my new black stilettos, and I had hoped to experience that. I also wasn't a big fan of Harper. I understand that this book was a chance for her to grow and develop into a more confident young woman, but I was frustrated that she had to do so much lying and scheming in order to achieve that. And, by the end, everything is okay - her best friend forgives her, she gets the 'good boy' that was interested in her the whole time, AND she gets a job offer. It was just too perfect. I would have liked to see Harper crash and burn. Oh well. Overall, a fun read, and I would recommend it if you're interested in journalism, New York, or some summer romance.

Barrel Proof is the emotional, high impact, AMAZING finale to the Agents Irish and Whiskey series, and it does need to be read in order to understand what is going on. Aidan decides that he needs some space from Jamie following his betrayal, not because he wants to end things with Jamie but the complete opposite reason. He wants Jamie, he loves him, but he knows that his anger will overshadow that. So he requests what should be a simple solo job, undercover at a financial company. What he doesn't know is that things are coming to a head and he is in deeper than he realised. Oh my! This book, this series! I have loved every single book (even when Aidan was acting like a jerk). Nothing is said or done without reason, and they all become clear in this edition. Any loose ends are tied up, some in ways that I never envisaged. The story is fast-paced but very smooth. With both Jamie and Aidan at odds, plus Mel and Danny, there is lot angst in this book, so the sexy times are not as numerous. However, this didn't negatively impact the story in any way. In fact, it would have been odd to do it any other way. Heart-breaking and heart-fulfilling, this book is the perfect finale to the series, and Layla Reyne now has a brand new reader completely addicted to her work. Without a doubt, absolutely recommended by me. * A copy of this book was provided to me with no requirements for a review. I voluntarily read this book, and my comments here are my honest opinion. Merissa Archaeolibrarian - I Dig Good Books!

Holy crap that was great!! Justine is a hypochondriac who only wants freedom from her fear of dying from vein star syndrome so she can have a normal life. She quickly learns that she'll do just about anything to achieve that freedom and she soon finds out that becoming free from one fear enslaves you to another. Packard is a high-cap (a person with a psychic ability)who's searching for freedom and vengeance. He's a master manipulator who goes to extremes to achieve his end game. Mind Games is like no other Urban Fantasy I've read. I wasn't sure in the beginning if I was going to like it, but I think that had to do with me being a bit confused over what exactly a "high-cap" is and Justine's manic hypochondria. But soon the confusion was cleared and Justine's manic behavior levels out and I became immersed in the story. At times I felt very uncomfortable and a bit disturbed by what was going on. (but of course there was no way I could stop reading!) "When is good not good?" is one of my favorite quotes from the book. At times I felt bad for some of these characters and what was happening to them because I wasn't given their crimes in real-time, I have to take Packard's word that they did what he says they did. Both Justine and Packard, like most characters, are flawed and desperate. And with Justine in particular, you can see what she is going to do wrong, before she does, and all you can do is shake your heard and ride the wave with her. This story kept me on my toes and had me wanting to know what would happen next even though what could happen next would probably make me feel uncomfortable! Many times I found myself reacting with a "*gasp* NO!" or a "ohma damn!" The book does not end with a cliffhanger, thank goodness, but I am left not really trusting anyone and wondering in what direction book 2 heads and what will happen. But I do trust some more than others and am currently Team Packard  ;) Book two will be read in the very near future!
