The funny thing about writing reviews is that sometimes it's excruciatingly difficult to write a review about a book that you didn't enjoy, but sometimes even harder to write a review about a book that you loved with all your heart. Wonder is one of the latter types of books. I finished this one in a day last weekend, and have struggled to find the words to review it ever since. I first read a review of this book on GoodReads, written by the wonderful Wendy Darling, whose opinion on books I hold in high esteem. At the time, my library didn't yet have this book on order, since it was so new, but I immediately added the book to my TBR list. Once my copy arrived in the library, and I devoured it in a single day, I will definitely be purchasing a copy of this book, since I think it's a must-have for any library. Wonder is a middle-grade novel that would appeal to any age group. I recommended it at work to a woman with an eight-year old son and to some of my much older coworkers. As Wendy so eloquently put in her review, this book can be recommended to anyone with a beating heart. It'll warm your heart, break it a little and then leave you with a feeling of absolute satisfaction and euphoria. After finishing this book, I immediately told my husband that all elementary schools should have this book as a novel study. If more kids read Wonder, I sincerely believe that there would be no more bullying. It's the kind of book that touches your heart and makes a difference. The kind of book that sticks with you long after the final words have been read. The kind of book that makes your soul sing and makes you happy to be a reader. The kind of book that comes around once in a while and reminds how profoundly we have an impact on the lives of one another. I won't write anymore, since the slightest thoughts about the plot of this book have me tearing up all over again. But let me leave you with this: YOU MUST READ THIS BOOK. If you read nothing else this year, read this one. It's, hands down, the best book that I've read this year. Review also posted at: http://writergrrlreads.blogspot.ca/20...

*2.5 stars* I think this book was creative and interesting but overall the writing was substandard in my opinion. I think this is the very first sci-fi book I've ever read so I have nothing to compare it to and therefore don't have much to comment about in that aspect of the book. I was satisfied with the explanations given about how Adam was created and the gene program, etc. but someone who is an avid sci-fi fan might not be. The idea of creating a perfect person and discovering how different gene patterns create different people is a very intriguing idea to me and kept me interested. This book definitely didn't go the way I thought it would. I thought it would mostly focus on Eve creating a new human being--Adam. But that's actually a very small part of the book which really disappointed me. We don't even get to see Adam come to fruition first-hand, just bits and pieces of him being formed. I think the subplots brought some interesting parts to the storyline but I do wish that there had been more of an emphasis on what I thought was the actual point of the book. After Adam is created, we barely get to see him before the book is over. I think the story would've been much more interesting if we had been able to get to know Adam and been able to see how Eve's choices affected who he was and how a lab-created person would interact with various situations/people, etc. We get some instances where these things happen near the ending of the book but if the plot had focused more on the actual creation of Adam, we would've been able to see more of it. I also found it difficult to understand what exactly had happened to Eve in the beginning of the book. It took quite a bit of piecing together to figure out (as I understand it) that she was walking on the street when a car ran over her. There's lots of implications but it's never said what actually happened. Although I did like the characters and found them to be entertaining, they pretty much all had the same voice. The book flip-flops between different POVs, yet all of the characters have the same sense of humor and way of talking. Even Adam sounds the same apart from a few dry comments that you would expect from a lab-created person. I found Adam to be very entertaining in his naive, child-like view of the world in some ways. I wish that there had been more character development of him and also of all the rest of the characters. We know that Solo is angry with Terra but we never know really what happened to make him hate her so much. Eve hates her mother but we don't really know why either besides her seeming to be neglected a bit. There were a lot of unanswered questions in this book. It seems like it should have a second book to it but I don't believe there is one nor do the authors plan to write one. I was surprised when I got to the end of the book and saw that both of the authors were writers of the children's series of Animorphs. I read a few of them when I was in elementary school (mostly just the horse ones, I was obsessed with horses) and I remember liking them. Maybe the authors just got stuck in writing in the style of children's book and weren't able to amp up the writing for a young adult book. I'm not sure. But the book definitely could've been better written just purely grammatically let alone all of the loose ends left with the characters' backgrounds. Likes: Easy, quick read. The idea was very interesting. The characters were all enjoyable. Dislikes: All of the characters were basically the same. No character development. Actual pretense of the book (the creation of Adam) plays a very small part in the story. I also found the fact that every single person felt the need to gawk at Adam unrealistic. Everybody has different tastes and a seemingly "perfect" person will never seem attractive to everybody like how Adam is portrayed. Sure, lots of people might find him attractive but everybody he sees? Not so much methinks. The romance was too quick without enough interaction between the characters to support such a deep attachment in my opinion. Overall: Recommend? Yes. Because it was still enjoyable regardless of its lacking.

Up until the ending, I really did not understand why this book is widely considered to be the best (or at least the top five) of Christie's books. Then it happened, and I was like WHAT! Actually it was more like a double what, because not only was it a really daring ending, especially for being published in 1926, but I actually guessed the murderer! That has never happened to me before. I am THE WORST at guessing mystery endings. I am gullible and trusting and passive as a reader. Authors: take advantage of me shamelessly, and I will enjoy it. Make no mistake, it was entirely a guess. No deductions involved whatsoever. I merely thought of the thing I thought least likely and picked it. That it turned out to be true, and worked beautifully, is entirely accidental (on my part, not Agatha Christie's-her part was brilliant). I'm going to split the rest of this review up into spoiler and non-spoiler sections, because I just have to talk about the ending. Spoiler Free Zone: Knowing the ending for me is coloring everything I have to say about the rest of the book, but there are some things I am free to say without spoiling you. Firstly, the premise. The titular Roger Ackroyd, fresh off the suicide of his fiance, is murdered mysteriously in a country estate. Hercule Poirot is living next door in retirement, and is brought in on the case by Mr. Ackroyd's niece. The narrator, and Poirot's assistant for the case, is Dr. James Sheppard. He lives with his spinster sister Caroline, whom I adore. She plays daft but is actually very sharp. And of course, there are an assortment of relatives and friends who all behave mysteriously enough to warrant suspicion, and Poirot does his Poirot thing of being small and cute and condescending all at the same time. As a sidenote, I would highly recommend the audiobook for this one. Hugh Fraser does a wonderful job. His voice is like butter. Spoilers Ahoy: Seriously don't keep reading if you don't want to know. At the end of the book, Poirot warns all the major suspects that he is going to tell them everything, and that it would be in their best interest to give up all their secrets before he does it for them. This includes our narrator, Dr. Sheppard, who turns out to have been helping conceal the main suspect in the investigation, and having given no evidence of it in his account even to us the readers. And there's a reason for this, which is that the book we are reading is actually a document Sheppard constructed for the sole purpose of being read after the fact. He was convinced Poirot would be unable to solve the case, and like Poirot's past assistants, he could publish the document to acclaim. Only Poirot does solve the case and Dr. Sheppard is found out. Dr. Sheppard is the murderer. There were subtle clues all throughout the book, more in what he as narrator doesn't say than what he does. It was one of these instances that caused me to wonder, Hey, what if he was the murderer? And then I giggled a bunch, I'm sure. The book then becomes an artifact of the mystery itself. To get even more spoilery, Poirot allows Sheppard to finish up the book as a sort of confession, before Sheppard kills himself to save face. It was all very British. The ending retroactively made the rest of the book rise up several levels in my eyes, and I'd love an eventual re-read to see if I can pick up on all the clues. [4.5 stars]

I'm afraid I was ultimately quite disappointed in this book. It's a fantastic premise, which should be my crack: teenager from the rez, Fred Oday, becomes the only girl (and the only Indian (the terminology used in the book)) on the high school golf team. Surrounded by racist country club bullies, she has to try to make her way in the team, the school, and the world. Unfortunately, to me both Fred and Ryan, her romantic foil, came across as fairly flat characters. The alternating-point-of-view format seems to be rather a trend in YA fiction recently, and it really takes differentiated voices and a deft hand to pull it off; in my opinion, Fichera doesn't. I didn't feel the chemistry between these characters, and there really didn't seem enough to keep the romance going in the fact of Ryan's immense jerkitude. His apologies and reformation fall rather flat, and his very belated stance against his friend Seth, the villain of the piece, seems far too little too late. He just isn't a sympathetic character. Continuing to make apologies for a bloke who keeps calling Fred "Pocahontas" and chases her around the desert in a monster truck? Really? The cardboard-cutout Mean Girls were straight out of an 80s movie. There were no fleshed-out female characters apart from the lead - just the Mean Girls and Fred's (again, stereotypical) drunk mother. Fred's heritage could have been a fascinating storyline, but it was thoroughly under-explored, and, I suspect, under-researched. Most of what we get of the rez is poverty, booze, and a Magical Indian called "George Trueblood", who brings Pueblo and Cherokee (why Cherokee and Pueblo? We're not told) blessings to Fred's golf tournaments and walks around offering mysterious remarks. By the time we reached the rather convenient and tidy climax and resolution, I was just about on stereotype overload, and well and truly ready for the story to end. To make matters worse, my pet peeve "lame" was peppered throughout the text, regularly throwing me out of the story. This book barely made a two-star "meh" rating for me. Would I pick up another of Fichera's books? I might, if it was well-reviewed by reviewers I trust. Out of the blue, though, not at this point.

HOT DAMN. WOW. That ending was FLAWLESS. I am absolutely blown away by how well this came together. The pacing, perfect. The character development, magnifique. The structure and world building? Just right, and with room for improvement and further development! The story itself was a masterpiece of clever and wicked thinking, a masterful writing style, thought-provoking diary passages, and point-of-views that only added to the overall depth of the book as a whole. I'm floored. Who knew my first book for 2017 would be one of the toughest contenders for best book of the year I've ever seen? A total must-read for fans of science fiction who are looking for a new classic to pick up.

When Valerie reports her rape, things in her life start to go a bit haywire. People she doesn't know are hugging her in the halls. People she does know are ignoring her and calling her a liar. What will happen now? Can Valerie get past this and move on? This story was so raw, so real, I was so afraid to read it. Yes, rape is not uncommon (unfortunately) - but to read about it in a YA book so openly was scary. It really makes you think, makes you wonder. I felt so sorry for poor Valerie throughout the book. We know she has done the right thing, by coming forward, but to watch her lose everything she has ever known is heartbreaking. Valerie is the victim of the story, yet she doesn't feel that way. She gets taken out of her math class that she has with Adam - why her? She did nothing wrong and now she gets punished for it. Things like this throughout the book really hit hard, at how nasty and ignorant some people are. But there are the good parts too. Valerie learns to be strong, she makes a new friend, meets a new guy. She uses her experience to push forward. The only thing I didn't really like about the book was the ending. I don't usually post spoilers, but in this case, I have to get this off my chest. I know that not all rape cases win, but I felt they left too much open. What happened to all the blood (etc) samples they took? Why couldn't they prove it? Plus in the end when Valerie and Adam are talking in the office, he openly admits it, with the Councillor standing outside, yet she happens not to hear anything or do anything? Seriously, not cool. I recommend this book to all lovers of real, raw and heartbreaking fiction!

Instantly goes to my top-5 m/m romances. The plot is fast-paced and kept me on the edge of my seat, even if it was little more than the backdrop for the romance subplot, the gothic trappings were lovely (A+ usage of creepy-ass children's counting songs), and the protagonists are vivid. Also, I'm such a sucker for scenarios when a character has to do something that he finds morally abhorrent in order to save the day. Plus, a nice reversal of a stereotypical late-Victorian mental geography: when the protagonist speaks longingly of "returning to civilization," he means the home he made for himself in Shanghai, not his native England, where he finds the mores too hypocritical and stifling.

I'm a fan of Bear's New Amsterdam, but was less impressed with Blood and Iron, and based on the blurb of this book I was a bit iffy about picking it up, but then it was picked for a group read this month, so I decided to give it a whirl. First thing's first, I will say that the patois which turned me off the blurb a bit wasn't really much of an issue for me reading. Yes, it's colloquial and not entirely proper, but I'm not a total grammar snob, which is probably clear form my own reviews, and aside from a few words here and there which made me twitch, I was mostly able to just go with it. I am glad I read it in paper form, though, because I think it would've bothered me more in an electronic format. (Don't ask me to explain the mysteries of my brain... ) Anyway - I liked what we saw of the world, though it also leaves you feeling there's a lot more that we're not seeing. I also liked the characters. This story definitely had one of the more diverse cast of characters that I've seen, and they were all developed enough that it didn't feel like tokenism. (The one possible exception being Tomoatooah. It bothered me that they kept referring to him as "the Comanche", especially after they covered that Comanche is not their own term for themselves and means "the enemy". ) The first half of the story is small and personal - a town squabble between rival businesses, you could say, though the antagonist is a great bit giant git. I enjoyed the story, or found it interesting enough, but kept waiting for something more to happen. So it was a bit ironic when that something more happened and I found myself incredulous and sort of wishing to go back to the way things were. The second half of the story just felt like a different thing altogether. Things - which admittedly are hinted at in the beginning of the story, but which always feel "out there" - suddenly come to the fore, but in such a sort of weird way that it just didn't sit well with me. (I'm speaking primarily of the octopus sub, but the whole plot with the cholera was weird. It suffered fro villain monologuing. I mean, if the girls had gone back to town without knowing they were infected, that would be one thing. But if their told they're being infected with this super cholera, what would stop them from just going off to die somewhere secluded? ) Oh, also the bit with the sewing machine turned mecha-armour  was just weird, and I had a really hard time visualizing how that would work. Anyway - I did like the first half of the story, and I liked the overall ending well enough, though I felt Bantle got off a bit too easy. I might be on board with another in the series, assuming it gets continued - but I think I'll let others vet it first before I go rushing into anything. 2.5-ish. There's one question I really need answered. The character's name is Karen Memery. The blurb even has the bit where it's "like memory, but with an e." So why is the book called Memory? I thought it might have some plot relevance, but, if it did, it went over my head. (My reflexes are not as fast as Drax's, apparently... )

This is the first book I have read trying to follow the suggestions of "The Well-Educated Mind." I'll update this review when I finish doing the recommended analysis. But here are some of my initial impressions. This book is funny. Since it's a translation, it's hard to know how much of the word-play is original, but Sancho's way with words is hilarious. Pretty much all of the characters are completely hilarious, especially all of the various foiled lovers that Don Quixote is always meeting with (I can think of at least six different couples off the top of my head.) The way that so many people are completely willing to play along with Don Quixote is also amazing. I've actually read this book before, when I was in high school, but I didn't remember a whole lot. One thing I had forgotten was the ending. I think I had it confused in my mind with the musical Man of La Mancha, which is a lovely story but completely different from Don Quixote. In the original, Quixote regains his sanity and dies as Alonzo Quixano, renouncing knight-errantry as a silly enterprise. This is somehow a disappointment to his friends, even the ones who had been trying to get him to renounce the madness the whole time. It has different feel than the musical's triumphant return to madness at the end, but feels less contrived. I had also forgotten how "meta" the book is. Cervantes addresses the reader directly, but that's not the half of it. A book of the first part of Don Quixote's adventures in published in the middle of the story, and affects the outcome of the rest of the book as Quixote begins to meet people who have read about him. Then a fallacious sequel is released, prompting Quixote to make decisions to prove the second book wrong. It has a fun story-within-a-story vibe that I wasn't expecting to see in what some critics say is the first novel ever. So overall, I would say that is you think you know the story of Don Quixote because you know the part about the windmills, and you don't feel like reading the book because you heard it was long and dense, I would advise you to reconsider. I'm sure it depends on the translation, but I didn't find it hard going at all, and I enjoyed myself more than I expected.

** spoiler alert ** Originally published on my blog here in May 2000. Great Expectations is one of Dickens' shortest and best known novels, nine-tenths of it is also one of his best. The elements that made Dickens famous are all here with the exception (to a great extent) of social commentary. A young boy grows up in an atmospheric environment (the bleaker parts of the Kent countryside); he becomes involved with strange grotesque characters. It is perhaps rather more aimless than most of Dickens' novels; rather than achieving happiness through his own exertions, Pip has little to do except to be idle and expensive once adopted by an unknown benefactor. The important character in the book is not its nominal hero, but one of the grotesques, who are not usually allowed more than a cameo role by Dickens. Miss Havisham dominates most of the book, by her patronage of Pip (real and imagined) and Pip's love for her protege Estella. It is from the point of her death that Dickens seems to lose interest in the novel, wrapping the whole thing up in a few unsatisfying chapters. She is such a wonderful character that Dickens' fascination with her is easy to understand. Twisted by having been left at the altar, she has kept her house exactly as it was on the day of the wedding, with years of decay turning Satis House into a Gothic mausoleum, even the wedding breakfast being allowed to rot where it sits. She has brought up Estella to be the means of her revenge on the male sex - fascinating but heartless.

I don't know whether I'm setting myself up for a fall by suspecting some kind of paranormal activity I don't know what to peg this book as..suspense? Thriller? Messed up? I just dont see myself pulling people's hair out, jumping over tables and running across aisles in the bookstore to get the sequel.... P.S I love the cover of this book...so much. 3 stars because it suspended the hell out of me and because I like it ( If I loved it, would've been 4 stars. This volume offers a good if, again, somewhat standard resolution to the first major arc. And I have to say, I enjoy that this one takes an incredulous view of the "die for your friends" mentality many shonen shows do. I've always found it ridiculous how fast people dive straight for that, and I'm glad Fairy Tail addresses how much more important living for your friends is. but as fun as the resolution of the "demons" plight is and as cool as the fights are, it's the second half of the book that really stood out for me, as the team returns to find their guild house has been attacked by another guild, Phantom Lord. They're livid, as are many in the guild, but because of political reasons cannot go right out and kick butt. But then Phantom ups the ante, beating up three Fairy Tail members and leaving them hanging from a tree out in the open. Normally the art in this series is cute but nothing special. However, the image of the guild master looking at what's been done to his "children" is a pretty powerful few frames - I really liked it. The scene is set, and Fairy Tail attacks Phantom Lord's home base in retribution. Unfortunately, as they do this, other members of the Phantom Lord guild are kidnapping Lucy, for a reason yet unexplained. this was probably the most dramatic and gripping volume so far, launching full-bore into the next arc.

2.5 stars Girls. When you think of girls, you think of one word: Complicated. Just when you think you finally understand them, they surprise you. You never know what goes through their minds. What they think, why they do what they do. Mind you, not all girls are like that, but some are. And those are the ones that can be full of surprises. "Girls had to believe in anything but their own power, because if girls knew what they could do, imagine what they might." I really wanted to like Girls on Fire. I really did. And for most part, I did. But seeing that it had mixed reviews, I went in with no expectations. Thank God I did. Because while interesting, there wasn't much to see other than characters complaining and moaning about their 'pathetic' life. Let's start with the good parts I liked. The writing style is so beautiful at times. Like you could quote some of them and put them on Hallmark cards. "I took up space. I was a collection of cells and memories, awkward limbs and clumsy fashion crimes; I was the repository of my parents' expectations and evidence of their disappointments." Now let's start with the reasons why I didn't really like this book. First off, the characters were too black and white. When I was first introduced to Dex and Lacey, I was expecting them to have certain characteristics that would make them understandable. But that wasn't the case. Dex and Lacey are very manic. One minute they're fine, the next they're messed up. They were happy then they were depressed. They were calm then they were crazy. Their emotions were all over the place that it was hard to sympathize for them, let alone relate to them. By the end, I didn't really care for them as much. Second, too much grunge. The setting of the book is in the early 90's. I was born in 1995 so I don't have that many memories of the 90's. But from what I could gather, the early 90's were grunge, Kurt Cobain and for a while, satanism. But mainly grunge. Dear God the grunge. I hated it. Hated it! Literally every person in the book was acting like a grunge version of Holden Caulfield and it got annoying. Lacey bitching about her life and Dex complaining about her boring life. Ugh. And don't get me started on Lacey and her obsession with Kurt. I get it, he was deep and made people think. I don't need to be reminded about him thirty times throughout the book. Third, things felt way too forced. I get what Wasserman was trying to do with female relationships. But it came off as forced and didn't present itself in a cohesive way. I for the most part couldn't understand the main focus of the book. Verdict: While I like some parts, Girls on Fire just didn't do it for me, plot wise and story development. The characters did nothing but complain which made them unlikable. And the theme was lost among the story. Thanks for reading my review! -Cesar

A different sort of fantasy: the memoirs of a famed dragon naturalist, Lady Trent, from a Victorian-like era when scientific study was a scandalous interest for a society woman. The period voice means slow pacing and wordy prose, but also creates a strong sense of time and place. If you enjoy historical fiction, this is an enjoyable story of an upper class expedition to primitive parts seeking dragons. But it has all the problematic symptoms of imperialism you might expect of that setup. Gender, class, and cultural restraints are abundant. Lady Trent is clever enough to overcome gender restraints and find a way to follow her passion: dragons. But her success is less sympathetic for her use of class and cultural privelege to pursue them, particularly as she rarely recognizes that she's doing so. It would have been stronger as a single book, detailing Lady Trent's whole career, but as the start of a series, it fails. Lady Trent herself tells you throughout that these events are insignificant compared to the things she will later accomplish, yet for some reason, documents every detail anyway. Overall, enjoyable, because it's different from everything else on the market. But problematic and frustrating too.
1 1/2 - 2 stars. What the HELL did I just read?! I have no clue what even happened at the end. my brain hurts.

** spoiler alert ** This is it! The end of the Trylle trilogy! But I WASN'T disappointed! Queen Elora became weak and died, so Wendy had to step up as Queen. And had to marry Tove. Then she kissed Finn! Then she kissed Loki! and it all just got MORE EXCITING! There was so much suspense in this book, especially with the battle against Trylle and Vittra, and the love triangle between Finn, Wendy and Loki! I agree with Wendy, on how he didn't fight for her. Wendy was willing to do anything she could to be with Finn, but he just stood and waited for her, then kissing her at the randomest of times! But you know, I had this feeling in the pit of my stomach that they would end up together anyway. But then, when Wendy and Loki were kind of together, in the attack on the Vittra, I was still with Finn. I was rooting for Finn up until the moment I read this sentence: "Still staring at me, Oren lifted up his sword, and with one quick move, he stabbed Loki straight through the heart." That was what did it for me. My jaw DROPPED. I lost my breath. I was actually shocked. Then I LOVED LOKI! I saw the vunerable side of him, and how he came back for her. The epilogue was great, it contained all the information that I wanted to know (Unlike some other books *cough*Suzanne Collins*cough cough*). And the baby! That was just the cutest touch for me. The chapter just made my support of Wendy and Loki's reltionship grow stronger and they couldn't be more perfect. I must say, they are one of my favourite fictional couples! So yeah,

Robie is an experienced traveler. She's taken the flight from Honolulu to the Midway Atoll, a group of Pacific islands where her parents live, many times. When she has to get to Midway in a hurry after a visit with her aunt in Hawaii, she gets on the next cargo flight at the last minute. She knows the pilot, but on this flight, there's a new co-pilot named Max. All systems are go until a storm hits during the flight. The only passenger, Robie doesn't panic until the engine suddenly cuts out and Max shouts at her to put on a life jacket. They are over miles of Pacific Ocean. She sees Max struggle with a raft. And then . she's in the water. Fighting for her life. Max pulls her onto the raft, and that's when the real terror begins. They have no water. Their only food is a bag of Skittles. There are sharks. There is an island. But there's no sign of help on the way. Survival stories are some of my favorite kinds of stories. Maybe that's why I'm a munchie for the shows I Survived and shows like that. The Raft could've been a great book. It was, in a way. But then in another, it wasn't. I have really mixed feelings about it One of my biggest annoyances in this book was Robie. I found her incredibly annoying. She's visiting her aunt, but she's also getting a piecing on her nose. Of course Robie doesn't want to take the blame for her piercing, so her aunt tells her that she'd take the blame instead. Yep, that sounds pretty nice for Robie. I'm annoyed at how Robie is okay with that. I mean, really? When it came to the part where she was on the raft, I was frustrated with her selfishness. Whenever she found food and when it rained, she kept saying that she's wake up Max(who was probably having a concussion) for it later. What Robie did was fend for herself. I stopped being annoyed with that when it turned out that Robie had imagined Max being alive. He was actually dead when he was in the raft and she was hallucinating his actions after day two of being in the raft. Plot twist much. The only thing that I didn't like about this book was Robie. I had no problem with the book besides her. But since she's the narrator and protagonist of this book, I think that it should be a greater factor than a minor character should be. I was entertained with it, and the author did a pretty good job on the writing. I enjoyed how she kept throwing obstacles at Robie. It's not like I wanted Robie dead, it's just that I wanted to see how Robie would overpass them. I'll be looking forward to reading the author's other book, The Compound. Hopefully, it'll have a main character that won't be like Robie was.

I've heard good things about this book so I was quite happy to buy a copy. It's a quick and light read - there are some things I liked about it and there were some things I had problems with. On with the good things first: I liked how contemporary this is and that it made cultural references that I quickly recognised and became delighted by ('Archy' the Swedish Youtuber who makes funny gaming commentary videos rings a very familiar bell...) . Audrey was likeable as a character and I certainly can relate to some of her episodes of social anxiety (particularly when someone brings up a topic she doesn't want to talk about - oh how I can relate to that so much). She's likeable enough that I was definitely rooting for her to get better. Another thing I like about this is that, although there is romance, it doesn't take a central role in the story or take up most of the plot. The book is more about Audrey and her attempts to recover from her illness, her family members and their relationships with one another and her friendship-blossoming-into-romance bond with her brother's friend, Linus. Despite all the good things I liked about this book, there were certain bits I find myself cringing or rolling my eyes over. One of these was Audrey's family. Although they were interesting and funny at times (Mum obsessed with the Daily Mail, Dad always distracted by his mobile phone, older brother addicted to video games, younger brother just amusing and hilarious being a four-year-old), I can't help but think they're so over-exaggerated and were written like so just for laughs. I also couldn't help but compare them to the way I felt about the Whiteley siblings in Tabitha Suzuma's book Forbidden. Although the subject matters of the two books were vastly different (since Forbidden is pretty heavy compared to the more light-hearted Audrey), there was just something about Audrey's family that didn't click for me the way the Whiteley siblings did. I don't know. On to the next thing. And that is Audrey's relationship with Linus. Although I feel that Audrey deserves someone like Linus - and I can understand why she might like him since I found their initial interaction via notes very cute and also that he's such an understanding guy - I couldn't help but think that their relationship escalated quite fast and that it wasn't explored deeper. All throughout their developing relationship, I keep asking myself (and the book) what it was about Audrey that Linus seems to find so interesting, why did he develop feelings for her or how did it happen? Gradually, I began asking more questions - like who is this Linus anyway? Where does he live? What are the things he likes apart from LOC? What's his history? How did he get into video games in the first place? Why does his crazy granny live with him? Why does he like Audrey anyway? Who is Linus? Yes, I was aware that the book is written mostly in Audrey's perspective so we don't get much of an insight into Linus's thoughts. But still, I don't know Linus very well. And I feel like I don't know him well enough to like him the way Audrey feels about him. I don't know. I just didn't feel quite convinced but perhaps because this book was intended to be a light read that this might possibly be the reason why the romance was written like so. I think what disappointed me most about this book - and made me give it a three star rating - was the ending or at least the last one or two chapters that lead to the end. I felt the ending was too rushed and everything was tied up too neatly and quickly. I was just completely unconvinced by Mum suddenly embracing Frank's gaming lifestyle and letting him and his gaming team, including Audrey, to practice for their gaming tournament and then having Dad become addicted to LOC too. I just. UGH. At this point of the book, I was shaking my head and making frowny faces at the last few pages. Once I finished, I was disappointed still to never find out what was incident that made Audrey ill in the first place. I can understand why it was never revealed - since this was still in Audrey's POV and she didn't want to talk about it. But I was still curious and I still wanted to know. Also, the issue with Audrey's dark glasses. Audrey loses them when she went 'missing' and rarely noticed their absence once she was found and this revelation - that Audrey was able to go out and about without her glasses - was glossed over so quickly that it felt like it was insignificant. All throughout the book, we are constantly reminded that Audrey is defined by her dark glasses. She wears them whether she's outside and inside the house, even when she is among family members. To me, the glasses were such a big thing and to have them disposed so easily like that in that one scene was a bit disappointing. All in all, Finding Audrey was a mostly enjoyable book. It's good if you want a quick and light read. It is very funny at times, a bit heartbreaking too (Audrey and the descriptions of her anxiety can sometimes become quite relatable) and very cute and romantic (Audrey and Linus attempting to communicate). Will I recommend this book to you? Absolutely. Go and pick up a copy.

This book... was so predictable. This is the fourth John Green book I've read and maybe that makes me a bit more unfairly critical, but his formulaic writing is becoming unenjoyable. A nerdy loser, a popular girl who hates/resents popularity, a wisecracking sidekick, and a 'life-changing' road trip seem to make up all of John Green's books. It was an alright book, a fun, light read, but I like my books to have some sort of suspense. I mean, from basically the moment they met, it was clear that Lindsey and Colin were going to get together, and break his 'Katherine' spell . There... there just wasn't anything surprising or particularly amazing about this book. It was clear that Colin's theorem would end up being a dud (you don't need to be a prodigy to know that you can't make love an equation). I just finished the book feeling meh. It's not like it's his first book, Looking for Alaska was miles better, I just... eh. I was left disenchanted.

Started: January 28, 2015 Put on hold: January 29, 2015 Picked up again: February 20, 2015 Finished: February 28, 2015 Re-read: January 2017 "Throne of Glass" by Sarah J. Maas is a fantastic book. It evoked many emotions from me and kept me flipping pages through the night and into the morning. I legitimately cannot decide which male member of the love triangle I would prefer Celaena to end up with. I ship Celaena and Chaol just as much as I ship her with Dorian. That duel scene was really excruciating to read for me. I was kicking my bed and I threw my bookmark on the floor. There were also many cries of anguish. All in all, I give this book a 5/5 star rating. I highly recommend it to fans of Young Adult fantasy, strong female heroines, or general awesomeness.

I'll admit that for the first half of this book, I was bored. Watching Lindsay and Valentine trying to cope after a breakup annoyed the hell out of me. In fact, I only really liked the ending even though I wasn't really rooting for these two even in the first book. They were a toxic clash of two very terrible but unbelievably funny and likable characters. What I liked the most was the Valentine's reconciliation with his family and honestly understanding how he really felt about Olly. He matured really well as a character at 26 instead of remaining that ridiculously impulsive and easily angered snivel-ling 19 year old. Lindsay didn't feel like he changed much to me but he did become a bit humbled after getting fucked over a little during his travels. But damn, dude seriously did a lot of drugs though. In the end, it felt like they really deserves each other since they were much more matured.
The biggest success of this book is the one that I read it to the end.

A good dystopian novel, which would enrage any feminist. It took me about half the novel to really wrap my head around this new world, this society. I found it confusing at first with these titles like "Marthas" and "Angels". Also, I had to really focus or else I'd get confused as to if something is happening in the past or present. But it did make me think. Lot of good quotes in here that I've saved. I'd recommend it to mature readers because there is talk of intercourse and suicide. Though I do think it is an important novel that everyone should read. Not a very satisfying ending, in my opinion. For those who like spoilers: Moira does not die and Ofglen is good and Rita actually really cares about her and the Commander is a hypocrite and there's actually a "club" full of prostitutes, if you can even call them that because they don't get paid they just live there!!!! (Sorry, had to get that off my chest)

OMG I don't know if I should cry or laugh or what!! I honestly don't even have the words to describe the brilliance of this book and plot and author and everything. This is such a controversial storyline I don't even know my whole opinion on it as of yet. I really love this series, and I really wish this doesn't ever happen in real life. I mean, something that starts as a good thing like regeneration and stuff and it becomes the hell all these teenagers live in? No thank you. And that when they fight to get their basic human rights back, they only make things worse? I like all the characters I really didn't want any of them to die, even if I didn't know the name of the 500+ kids . Even Nelson and Cam and Starkey, who are annoying as H.E.L.L. That is, until he basically screwed everyone else just cause he wanted to be special. Idiot. Though, I do remember that once I literally hit the book multiple times thanks to Starkey. I'm not kidding. I really can't wait to read the rest of the series!

This book started out really promising for me - I liked the characters and I liked the hotel and town it's in. Then things went a little wrong for me. First,  the idea that somewhere, someone is hiding a bunch of original manuscripts (THREE unpublished Shakespeare plays??? Why are we hiding them? What are we protecting them from? What's the point of protecting them if no one ever gets to read them? If the point is to prevent people from ever reading this stuff, set a match to it and save everyone the effort. If that isn't the point, then publish them and move on. Also, how is archery a skill that is going to help protect this collected pile of apparently useless paper? Seriously? Archery? Like Jane is going to wander the halls with a bow and quiver. Second, this just gets bogged down in the details later in the book and i ended up skimming a lot because our intrepid sleuth doesn't really do much. At all. Aside from a thoroughly in-depth description of learning archery - which she's unbelievably good at right from the start. Funny that. Yet, we can't take the time to meet mysterious Sam, the owner of two horses we meet early on, one involved in a death. We don't find out how the rider of said horse came to be riding the horse alone when Sam doesn't just let people ride around on his horses without a guide. It's too bad, I'd added the next two books to my to-read list early on, but now I think I'm not going to continue with the series. Just too many problems for me.

Okay, all the emotions I felt in the first book? Triple that and that's what I felt about this book. I looooooooved how her identity was revealed! Definitely a goosebump-worthy moment. AND. I KNEW IT. hahaha

I will be honest with you. I would probably quit this series if it just focused on Lois. I know that sounds terrible, but hear me out. The two things I like most about this series are Lois herself (great in any incarnation, that character is), and the burgeoning relationship between Lois and her internet friend slash boyfriend (? )"SmallvilleGuy", who yes, is Clark Kent aka the future Superman. Everything else surrounding it? I do not care about. Really, at all. I do not care about any of Lois's paper or school friends. Both mysteries have been less than engaging for me. Unfortunately, the stuff I like the least about this series is the stuff that's front and center. I don't know, maybe it was just this one installment. I had similar complaints in the last book, but they were overshadowed maybe by the newness, and by Lois getting acclimated to her new city. But really, I just want more SmallvilleGuy and Lois interactions. It would be nice if they could actually meet and save the day together physically, not just digitally. That's always been my favorite part in Superman stories. I would have probably liked all of this had I read it as an actual teenager, to be fair. Current teenagers, girls especially, will probably relate a lot more than I can now. (Although I know it is possible for stories about teenagers to engage me emotionally because it happens all the time. I guess this just isn't one of them.) I will probably read the next one. Because I need Lois and SmallvilleGuy to meet. And other stuff.

I don't know, it just wasn't as good as the first one for me. There just seemed to be less of a plot for some reason. Which shouldn't really be the case because of the whole cancer  thing. I did finish it in one day so either I had a lot of time on my hands or it wasn't as bad as I think it is. Can't decide.

Words can't describe how happy I am that this ride is finally finished. This series hit rock bottom and I'm not sad to watch it go. Lorien Legacies had potential, but the writer's lack of skill and imagination ruined it all. The final book is usually the one with most action and excitement, but we got neither. This book was dragged in the first half, nothing happens besides the usual stuff - Setrakus Ra goes into hiding and John learn to master his new power. Garde plan their counter strike and to try to steal the ships. Basically, it's the plot of the last few books. John should've died. Five should've stayed dead. There are too many inconsistencies. How can Lorien teenagers tear through Mogs like it's piece of cake when adult warriors failed miserably which caused a whole PLANET to be forever unsurvivable? The author finally decided that he can't stretch this any longer. This is the last book, and instead of preparing for the final battle, they keep bulshitting each other, because obviously they had nothing better to do with their time. The plot is the identical like in the previous volumes - long and predictable. There is an attempt at the bittersweet ending, but all I had was a feeling like I'm gonna get diabetes. The ending is unexciting ,the writing style is plain and boring. The final battle was too easily won and anticlimactic when we consider having a build up of six books to reach the goal. From the book 4 this series only went downwards. But in book 5 I lost my patience, even though the book had some bright moments. The book 6 was the lowest point and I realised I only feel anger and deep boredom for this series. This book was not much better than the book 6. The pace was off. The apocalypse that was expected from the book 1 never came. Just a long and depressing wrap up of the series. This has been a hard series to get through simply because it's seven books that realistically could've been three or four. All characters are annoying. The new characters didn't play any role and were a complete waste of paper.I had no idea why the human Garde were introduced if they literally had no purpose. By the end, some characters are happy and living their potential, while others' future are foggy. All of the important characters survived which is completely unrealistic. I guess I semi-liked Nine, Six and Adam, because they were the only rational people who had the guts to do what has to be done, but they were still stereotypical and didn't evolve one bit from the first time they appeared. The last book didn't connect the reader to the characters and there was nothing to deepen the story or relationships. It was basically a marathon to finally see whether or not they will defeat the Mogs and if anyone will die. Half of the characters simply follows John as he saves the day. Moreover, author learned nothing from the previous volumes since he repeats his old mistakes over and over again. I still didn't know for a few pages who's POV it has been told from, and I'm so done with it, that I don't even bother to be upset. Numerous times I began reading a chapter with Four visualised in my head, only to realise a few pages later that I should've been picturing Six all along. By the way, why is Sam still there? I much preferred this harsher version of John than the whiny brat he's been in the previous books. He almost reminded me of the good lad I really liked in the book 1. It seems that finally he found a maturing path, but it's still quite obvious he doesn't have what it takes to be an effective leader. Until the day I die, I will be persistent in my belief that John is the one of the worst protagonist and heroes ever. Six and Nine went from being two most interesting characters in the earlier books to being Four's cheering squad. I don't know if it was author's intention to completely ruin Six's personality in order for her to become boring like the others, but I'm completely amazed how female voice sounds identical as male.

OFY at its finest, Strong Enough had plenty of elements I liked, even loved. From the first page, I felt drawn to Maxim. He is just the kind of character impossible to dislike: funny, charming, positive and hard working. I couldn't relate that much to him, but I loved him. The clash of personalities between Maxim and Derek was extremely well done and brought out an intensity level that made the pages sizzle with tension, without losing the needed touch of realism. I enjoyed seeing Derek deal with his fears and how he found in Maxim the strength he needed to fully embrace his true self. The sex scenes weren't stellar, but they were good enough to keep things interesting. The little scenes with Derek and Maxim in the kitchen were what made me give this a four star rating, instead of a three star rating. I love food and I love how food can connect people. It has absolutely everything to do with romance and I always like when authors use food to bring their characters together. Plus, it was cool to learn some Russian recipes! heh That said, I feel after all the struggle and angst I had to endure until Derek finally decided to be a man and take charge of his own life, I deserved a better epilogue. It wasn't enough at all.

Basically: Scandal meets Gallagher Girls. In Depth: After reading Jennifer Lynn Barnes 'The Naturals' series I knew that I wanted read more books by her so I ordered 'The Fixer' (it sounded very me) and you know that feeling when you're reading a book and you sit there at the end and just think, "this could have been written for me." That's how I felt at the end of this book. It was everything that I love in a book. This isn't so much a review as it is a bunch of words praising it and declaring my undying love. The Plot: This book effectively explores the idea of the person behind the scenes, the puppet masters of American politics. What makes this book stand out is the way the characters interact, the relationships between the characters. The plot and the writing, the way the story unfolds, was good, I enjoyed it. The plot twists kept me guessing and the writing style was easy and fun (and what I needed on a Sunday afternoon.) The story itself follows Tess who is a new arrival to DC and the sister to Ivy Kendrick who turns out to be a Fixer. On her first morning there Adam (Ivy's friend) tells Ivy that Justice Marquette has had a heart attack which triggers a series of events. It's these events that make the book as fast paced and entertaining as it is as well as completely gripping. The Characters: I loved the characters in this book and like the previous books I've read of Jennifer Lynn Barnes, like Ally Carters books, I felt like this book was an introduction to some awesome character development. The foundations have been laid and I cannot wait to see where they are going. I loved Tess, our protagonist. I felt like her anger at being taken from her home, conflicting with the fact she loved her sister (but was still angry) was reflected well throughout the book. I loved Ivy, the calm and collected older sister who only lost her cool when Tess acted out. I loved Brodie and Adam, Ivy's family of choice who love her. I loved Vivie, Asher, Emilia, Henry who were Tess's friends at Hardwicke. There were just a lot of characters that I really loved and for a variety of reasons, but they were all so great and individual and I cannot wait to see where they go in the next book. My Thoughts: Part of what I loved about this book is that political vibe mixed with the action and adventure that I love reading about. I also loved the writing style, and the characters. But for me it was the relationships and the potential with where they could go.

The Fallen Star is a testament to how imaginative the human mind can be, well, Jessica Sorensen's mind. The story is very original, gripping and a true page turner. There are cliffhangers but she is fast at putting the next book out so you don't have to wait in suspenseful anticipation for long. Great book!

I was nervous at first because this started a little slow but it wasn't long before I was pausing to make happy sighs and grinning my face off and chuckling out loud. The trifecta of good book signs, really. The main characters start things out with a meet-hate (the opposite of a meet-cute). He's a smooth operator. She's a sarcastic termagant (his words!). They do not hit it off. Except it turns out their siblings are marrying each other and they're going to have to suck it up and learn to get along because they're both good people who love their siblings and don't want to cause any scenes. And holy crap is the journey entertaining from there. Julie James always delivers good book for me but this was particularly stellar. Best romantic comedy I've read this year.

There's nothing not to like about the next volume in this series. The girls continue to discover who they are, though I think Daisy might be the one going through a true identity crisis (the girls blame her homeschooling, LOL), and I can seriously relate to that. I definitely believe that once we graduate high school and go off to college, we really question who we are as individuals because we're "in between" a teenager and a semi-adult, lol. My favorite parts were the ball scenes (the dresses!) and Susan trying to hide dating McGraw from Esther and Daisy . I respect Esther for wanting to be herself but scared too but she eventually broke and mold and it was awesome. People will like you for who you are, not who you try to be. I also love the girls' friendship! We always need positive female friendships in our lives and it's fun to see them in literature too! Seriously though, everything about this comic series is relatable. I hope Daisy is able to discover who she is and that she might just need some help from her friends.

Interesting concept but I was able to guess the killer early in the story. I found it irritating that dallas once again was emotional during the case and tried to pin the murder on the wrong person Jess was a prick but the way she tried to pin murder in him due to her emotional feelings on the subject was very wrong  . This is a 2nd book if this series in which this has happened.

I don't think Sarah J Maas will ever let us down. Sarah is a queen. Empire of Storms smashed me and broke me and it was everything I wanted in a book. Every book in this series just gets better and better and now there's only one left and I know its going to break me as well. Let's just say I was a sobbing mess at the end...

I got a copy of this free from NetGalley and was excited to start it. Despite the disturbing contemporary YA elements at the beginning (seventeen & fifteen-year-olds having a quicky in the bathroom) I was still invested in the characters and story. Then the fantasy element happened, which I was completely stoked about. The system of magic and conservation of energy was clever and original. But the plot itself devolved quickly into the standard fantasy romance cliche (that I'd actually just complained about in my review of Eve ) of a female protag going on an extended camping trip with a hot native who is abnoxious and savage, but protects her and suddenly becomes boyfriend worthy. Uggg. I really tried to continue. I thought it MUST get better if everyone's talking about it at BEA*. (*unconfirmed, that's just what they're advertising.) I read and read, trying to get un-bored, but only grew more annoyed with the characters and lack of a cohesive plot. (Not to mention, I HATE when authors resort to child sex abuse/violence in order to make a villain "really bad." It's lazy and flawed. It only shocks us because it's so above and beyond regular badguyness. But as soon as the public gets jaded, (I'm already fed up) child rape will be as ho hum as threatening to blow up the statue of liberty. Then how will these uninspired authors deign to make their bad guys really bad? They'll have to get increasingly deviant. Maybe they'll rape clowns next?!!! The horror! I kept finding excuses to read Healing Stone which I was also in the middle of. And incidentally, the latter made me cry today (in a good way), so if you're thinking about starting Angelini's latest genre mash-up, try Booher's fantasy instead. I think you'll find it more down to earth and coherent.

A haunting tale vividly painted against the harsh wintry blankets of Alaska, seamlessly threaded with elements of old romance, bitter survival and childhood pristineness. Not my typical cup of tea. I understand the attraction of this book for more read readers. This book has a certain depth absent in most YA books, which adds on to its literary quality. And like most "literal masterpieces", The Snow Child too has to have a semi-happy aka sad ending. Heck I can't think of any book hailed as a timeless classic having a perfect ending - Romeo and Juliet, Hamlet. It's all doom and gloom and tragedy. Well, maybe all save Anne of Green Gables and Pride and Prejudice. Hence it's no wonder why these two books hold so much appeal to me. Honestly speaking, I don't really like the book. But my reasons have almost nothing to do with the book per se, but more with my tastes, which are aligned so unfavourably against the book. Nevertheless, I would still highly recommend the book to anyone who needs a breath of fresh air away from the stifling pathetic archetypes of Twilight and whining airhead damsels in unfanthomable depression. But for the time being, I would like to stick to my simple world of adventures, comedy and uncomplicated happily-ever-afters.

<<Overview>> Newlywed star-crossed alien lovers have a baby that everybody wants. The fantasy, science fiction, and paranormal genres basically had an orgy and spit out the world of Saga. Stunning artwork with a vibrant color palette and totally unique character and race creation. It puts the 'graphic' in graphic novel. It's rated M for a reason. One of the best graphic novels I've ever read. Flawless art, compelling story, fantastic world. <<Plot>> When the opening scene of a graphic novel is your main female character screaming about shitting herself while giving birth in a dirty garage with her husband, you just know good things are in store. Alana and Marko are from different sides of a long and ongoing battle. We don't yet know how they met and fell in love, but we do know they ran away together, got married, and now have a beautiful baby girl. However, their hybrid offspring is mysteriously desired by all factions, and Marko and Alana have to find a way off of the planet. Their quest to make it into space is the core plot line of volume one. There are a lot of other little plots swirling around, however. We take a peek every now and then into the life of Prince Robot IV. I immediately took a dislike to IV, and he'll definitely be an entertaining villain. There is also The Will and his Lying Cat companion. I have mixed feelings about him, but for now I have him firmly in the anti-hero camp. I'm really, really intrigued by him. Overall, the plot was fantastic and entertaining. It didn't feel rushed in any way, but was definitely exciting. Having Marko and Alana already together and as parents creates an interesting and fresh dynamic to the graphic novel scene. <<Dialogue>> I haven't read anything else by Brian K. Vaughan, but I think I might have to now. His writing is perfection in this. Every bit of a dialogue feels genuine to the characters, and it moves the plot along beautifully. I also love how it feels that Saga is being narrated by baby Hazel from some indiscriminate time in her future. It adds a sense of mystery to the whole story, and really makes you want to find out how Hazel got to that point in her life. <<Cast>> Alana and Marko are definitely the two central characters in volume one. I loved their bantering, yet affectionate dynamic. We never see the build up to their relationship, we only get to see them at their worst. Alana has just delivered baby Hazel when they have to flee, suffering through very little sleep, a hostile planet, and a lot of pitfalls along the way. It's no surprise they're at each others' throats with all the hormones and stress flying around, but we do see a few moments of them that just makes me love them as a couple. I can't wait until they catch a few calm moments together, and we can maybe learn about their past. They're very relatable, despite them being fantasy characters from a fantasy world. They love their daughter beyond reason, they loved each other, but they're also dealing with emotions and petty jealousy just like any other non-alien couple. I'm really, really intrigued by The Will. I feel like he's being set up as an anti-hero, and there's nothing I love more than a good, conflicted character. I can't wait to see what happens to him, especially after the end. I'm so freakin' bummed that The Stalk died. I don't care if she was evil, she was kind of amazeballs. Izabel, the half-exploded teenage ghost that Alana and Marko pick up as a semi-permanent babysitter along the way, is definitely one of the best, and most endearing characters. She's so sweet, but very matter-of-fact. I think she's going to be a killer companion for Hazel. And as I mentioned above, the royal robot race. I just...ugh. They leave a sour taste in my mouth, which is a good thing. I love to hate villains. ;D <<Art>> The art. Just. I can't even. It is stunning. From the cover, with Alana boldly breastfeeding (take that, comic stereotypes), I just knew I was going to love this. Fiona Staples is now firmly in my favorite-artists-ever roster. The colors she uses are so vibrant and beautiful, I could easilyjust sit around and flip through Saga for hours. All the different aliens races that have been created are wonderful and unique. Not to mention, rocketship trees. Yeah. While there are a few wide shots, Saga really seems to be all about the characters. I'd also like to focus on them as well. * Alana: I love the decisions for Alana's character. She's beautiful, bold, and sexy. From her beautiful dragonfly-esque wings to her punky hair, Alana is hands down one of the most beautiful graphic novel heroines I've ever encountered. * Marko (and the Wreath inhabitants in general): I am a sucker for horns. Ram horns, deer horns, whatever. I freaking love horns. It's such a fantasy thing, but Vaughn and Staples have made it totally believable for a sci-fi setting. I want to be reborn on Wreath. D: * Royal Robots: Weird, but brilliant. Humanoid robots with classic television screens for faces. While typically blank, I absolutely loved when their emotions flare and images are projected on screen. * Vez: We only meet her briefly, but she makes an impact. A wizened old woman with a unicorn horn who walks around barefoot and is pretty much a bitch. I hope we see more of her. * The Stalk: Are there even words to accurately describe The Stalk? She's deadly, bizarre, but still weirdly sexy at the same time. The Stalk is basically half human, half spider. She has the head and torso of a human woman, and the eyes and lower body of a massive spider. She's definitely evil, but delightfully so, and she can multitask like a mother. The one scene where she's sprinting away from mad boars, holding her dress up, shooting multiple guns, and talking on her phone just had be rolling. I am still so sad she's dead. :( * Izabel: It takes balls to have a character be a preteen or teenage ghost missing the whole lower half of her body. A lot of artists would "neaten" up the wound. Nope. Izabel's innards are on display for everyone to see. But it just kind of adds to her...charm? Also, as a fair warning, this is rated M for a reason. The violence and sexual content are on a very graphic (hurhur) level. There's a lot of blood, organs are spilling of bodies, heads are getting chopped in half. And there's sex. Not just a tasteful scene of passion with a glimpse of breasts. Ladybits, manbits, all doing things and going places. This is not for the faint of heart. Also, I will forever have nightmares from the Sextillion greeters. Dear God. When all is said and done, I don't think I've genuinely enjoyed a graphic novel quite as much as I did Saga, and I think it's because it shouldn't work, but it does. It's a unique take on fantasy/sci-fi mash-up, and I'm so very excited to see where it's going next. Beautiful art, original characters, enchanting world, and engaging plot. I couldn't be happier.

Ehhhhhhh. Eh. I read the first 50 pages or so then started skimming then just gave up. I couldn't get into it so rather than waste my time on a chick-flick teen fairy love story I decided to just put it down and donate it to my local thrift store. Someone else can enjoy it, but I don't think I'm able to. Maybe if I was an 8th grader I would, when I bought this book, but time has passed and so has my interest for this book.

2.5 Stars I had actually heard of Maya Banks before I picked up Letting Go, but I had never read any of her previous work. This review is going to be a little tough for me to write because while I liked the writing style and the characters ok, it was the overall theme of the book that didn't sit well with me. Letting Go is the story of Josslyn who lost her husband, Carson, in an accident. Three years after his death, she decides it's time to stop mourning and get on with her life, more importantly, to explore her own sexuality and outlets that her husband couldn't give her. She decides to go to an exclusive club which caters to the dominant lifestyle, but while there she runs into her late husbands best friend and business partner, Dash. It seems Dash has been keeping secrets from Joss and not just his lifestyle, but also the fact that he's been in love with her since he met her. I'm sure you can already tell where this is going. Dash convinces Joss to let him dominant her and introduce her to the world she craves, but in return, she will belong to him and only him. After thinking it over, Joss agrees and their whirlwind affair takes flight. On one hand, this book is a good starting point for people who have never read any type of BDSM, D/s type books. Banks explains the lifestyle and the rules that go with it in an easy way, since Dash is explaining it to Joss it doesn't feel like information overload but more like you're learning with her. Also, the chemistry between Dash and Joss is obvious from the start. I liked them together and ultimately rooted for them, which is what I was supposed to do so that was well done. But, on the other hand, there were things that bugged me. Joss' sister-in-law, Kylie, drove me absolutely up the wall. When Joss tells her that she wants to start moving on, Kylie freaks out like it's the worst idea in the world. Then when Dash states that he's bringing in a new partner to the firm to help him out, she throws a fit and starts screaming. Everyone coddled her and I found her to be extremely childish and selfish. Other things that rubbed me the wrong way were things like this book taking place three years after Carson's death and Joss states over and over that she's ready to move on, yet at every turn she's bringing up Carson and comparing Dash to him which I felt wasn't fair. Then there was Dash's pet name for Joss - honey. Everything was 'honey this' and 'honey that'. How many times can you possibly say honey in the same conversation? At some point, it becomes condescending and not sweet at all. Banks also felt the need to repeat the same information over and over and over and over again...sometimes only half a page apart. Please trust that your audience can remember important information. Unfortunately, after reading this (and a few other) erotica type book, I've realized that this genre is not my cup of tea. While I understand that some people are enticed and interested in this type of lifestyle, I'm not and that hindered my enjoyment of the material. So just because I didn't like it, doesn't mean that someone else won't. Basically, it just wasn't for me. I received a copy of this novel from the publisher for my honest opinion and review. Big thanks to Berkeley Trade for allowing me partake in this tour.

This is the first Picoult book I've rated less than five stars. Maybe it was the plot. But I don't think so. Usually Picoult's vivid characters are what make her books stand out from the rest. Here though, everyone seemed pretty two-dimensional. It wasn't that I DISLIKED anyone; I just didn't connect to them. They were simply boring. This was made blatantly obvious by the switching perspectives. Everybody's voice was exactly the same. If not for the font changes, I never could have kept the narrators straight. And sometimes I still got confused. There was also a lot more about the Hopi than I would have preferred. It was pretty interesting at first. I liked the character more than most, and the culture fit into Delia's story smoothly. But it was sort of the same thing over and over again. I get it. Hopi. Cool. Move on. I was just plain bored from pages 100-300. I mean, it was a good story. I wanted to know what happened and I never considered abandoning the book. It just wasn't much fun to read. The ending  was pretty unsatisfying for me. Usually, I love it when the author leaves something hanging. I can keep thinking. It adds meaning. Here, though, I was just annoyed. I want to know if Delia's memories are real or not. I don't care if it adds a level of realism to leave it unknown. In this case, it didn't leave me pondering the science of memory. That wasn't the real point of the story, up until this point. The thought-provoking only works if it's completely related. Yet... I just like Picoult's books. This was emotional. It was exciting. The writing is just good. It somehow makes up for all these things. In my opinion. To be honest, my rating of this book might simply be because I've come to enjoy Picoult's writing from her other books. My favorite perspective was probably Andrew's. He's just the perfect character to show us the horrors of modern prison life. Did it have much to do with the book? I would argue that it did. No matter what Andrew goes through, he thinks of Delia. He does it for her. I think if we hadn't seen exactly what Andrew was willing to put up with for his daughter, we might not have sympathized with him. Maybe even wanted him to lose. The whole novel is expertly crafted. The characters, while not larger than life, were perfect for the story. You could understand everybody's conflicts and accept their faults. Everyone had made mistakes. This wasn't your classic  kidnapping   story. It was deep. I would have trouble accurately summarizing it without leaving out important moments. The court scenes were well-done. I didn't guess the verdict until the end. I would hate to be on that jury. So would I recommend this book? Yes. But only after you read My Sister's Keeper, Nineteen Minutes, and House Rules.

"Ryan and I are two people who used to be in love. What a beautiful thing to have been. What a sad thing to be." After I Do shows the delicious high of being in love. The kind of love that sparkly young eyes think will last forever as long as you just believe. Sigh. But when your partner's adorable oddities start grating on your nerves and you're feeling unappreciated and invisible and that beautiful love slowly turns to indifference, then resentment, and eventually plummets to full-out hate... what then? Taylor Jenkins Reid shows the disintegration of a marriage, which is hard, but watching her characters make a plan that does not immediately jump to divorce offered a lot of hope to me as a reader. Yes, there are relationships that need to be ended permanently but both of these characters acknowledge that not all is lost...it's just been painfully neglected over the years. I really enjoyed how Ms. Reid explored marriage in general and didn't shame any of her characters' choices. Personally, I didn't like that her characters were sexually active outside of their marriage during the separation but they both did it, eventually found out about it, and didn't seem bothered so I don't know why I am . I would recommend this book to anyone who is in or ever has been in a long-term relationship. Actually, even those who haven't could benefit. Being married for a number of years myself, I could relate to so much and found this book to be surprisingly optimistic. If you don't read this one, read something by Taylor Jenkins Reid. She's amazing! My favorite quote: "I know it will be OK because everything is OK in the end. And if it's not OK, it's not the end."

"You only get one life. It's actually your duty to live it as fully as possible." This book......... Oh God. This book.... How do you even describe it? A romance between an ordinary girl living in an ordinary world and a man who lived an extraordinary, risky life and is now stuck in a wheelchair? They met, fell in love, overcame some obstacles, and tada! Happily ever after! Nope. Nopity. Nope Honestly, romance didn't play as much for me in here. To me, Me Before You isn't just about the romance. It's being so much more than there already is in the life you live in now. As Will had been saying a lot in the book. Despite that, I would be lying if I said that this book didn't hurt me as much. But it did. It freaking did. I wanted to cry, then roll over and cry some more. Goddamn, did it hurt so much The characters felt real to me and the whole story realistic. Will's condition made it more heartbreaking and it made me understand why it's so hard living the way he is for a man like him. A man who took great risk and have a big life and adventure only to have his world tore down and shrink right before his eyes. And a girl whose world grew because this man helped her in many ways. He helped her expand her world and do more things for herself while she helped him see the bright side. The whole book was all full of joy and it gave me hope only for me to get crushed right at the end. I should've known. Me Before You is one of those books that was really hitting me straight in the heart. It's not because of the characters or anything like that, I mean I love the characters but it's also hitting me in another way because it's like the words I feel are written in the book and some were encouraging too. Like with Lou, I related to her a lot. Although I don't dress the way as she does and I'm not as cheery as her. I wear black a lot and I'm bad at talking to people. Hence the reason why I stay in my room. No, I connect with her in the way she lived her life. She had a very small world and stayed in her comfort zone, she also doesn't know what to with her life. And the fact that Will was showing her the way and keep pushing her and all that. It made me feel as if I was Lou herself. It made me want to go out there and see the world and do something with my life. This is what made this book so precious for me. "All I can say is that you make me... you make me into someone I couldn't even imagine. You make me happy, even when you're awful. I would rather be with you - even the you that you seem to think is diminished - than with anyone else in the world." My heart absolutely broke when Lou bared her heart to him only to be told she wasn't enough. That's a harsh thing to say to a person who just told you that she loved you. The whole trip was happy and all and suddenly, it plummeted so fast that it hurts. I'm happy however that her parents are finally able to provide for themselves and not rely on Lou because I'm pretty sure that one of the components of Lou afraid of going anywhere is because she's worried about her family. Also, I just wanna say that Treena was kinda annoying to me. I mean, I know that's how siblings are but I couldn't help the flare of anger that rose up whenever Treena was being selfish and her parents picking on her. Like seriously though? Lou is the one providing for all of them and this is what she gets? And nothing hurts me more than Lou thinking she couldn't do things because she's overshadowed by her brilliant sister. She keeps thinking she's not smart enough and she couldn't do things and all that when in reality, she can. And Will saw that and he helped her get out of that shell and that was so beautiful. Their effects on each other throughout the book just made me want to cry by how beautiful it is. I didn't cry when he died. Not really. The painful thing was that the anticipation, the wait, the ticking time of what was to come and knowing that there's nothing you can do to stop it. Knowing that any minute, he would go and kill himself. It hurts. Goodbyes are the hardest things. And I hate them. Now, I wanna talk about Will's decision. I knew it was going to happen. I knew before I read the book that he was going to die one way or another but I didn't expect Dignitas. I didn't know such thing existed until I read this book. It does exist. All throughout the book, I hoped even though I knew it. I had hopes that by some miracle he would change his mind and be with Lou because they deserve happy ever after even though I don't believe in them. But still, I understood Will. It was his choice and I wouldn't want to live the way he lived his life. No one would ever dream of such thing. He was suffering whether Louisa is there or not. And to go out the way he wanted was fitting for a man like Will or any person anyway. It was his choice as he had been saying. Sure, there's more things in stored for him but how can you expect someone to live a life who had no will to do so? You can't force someone to live a life where they truly can't stand it, where there is nothing but suffering for them. They're done and exhausted with that life. There's no reason to force them and make them suffer even more. "You can only actually help someone who wants to be helped." The later in the end made me cry too. My God, Will. He made sure that she would continue the path that he had set her on and that she wouldn't go back to the shell she was before she met him. And it's such a beautiful ending it hurts. I'm happy for her, though. For both of them. They didn't get to be together but in the end, he was free from suffering and content. She's still grieving but there's no doubt that she would be happy at some point. "Push yourself. Don't Settle. Just live well. Just LIVE."
