And if teen patrons are looking for a science-y book, I'm recommending "Evolution Me Other Freaks of Nature" Overall, I'm not mad at you Kristen Chandler. I see what you did there, and I can appreciate why others like this book. It's just not for me.

UPDATE 2016: I'm about half way through the show's first season and it is with slight (but only a little!) embarrassment that I admit that I actually really like it. So far it has managed to make Claire an actual character and actually find a balance of historical fiction with an indulgent side of romance that the book missed. I recommend it for anyone who, like me, really wanted to like the book but found it problematic. Warning: this review is long and unkind. What I liked: - Diana Gabaldon is not a bad writer. There are some descriptions and passages that are truly well done. With the exception of a tendency to be a little too micro-managey with descriptions (more below), my gripe with the book has more to do with plot, and characterization, not Ms. Galbadon's technical abilities. - There are some times, mostly early on, when the story makes an attempt to keep one foot in historical fiction territory. I actually enjoyed these parts, and would have gladly given the book as a whole a solid 3 stars if these narrative threads had been carried throughout the text and developed fully. Clan tensions, alliances, sanctioned yet secret affairs to provide heirs,  the rumblings of rebellion against the crown--ANY of which would have been a rich source of interesting plot material--are developed briefly and only so far as necessary to ensure drama between Claire and Jamie and, ultimately, position them for the HUNDREDS OF PAGES of sex and sentimentality that turn out to be the REAL driving force behind Outlander. What I didn't like: - Claire. Claire is mishandled, Claire is not well written, Claire is often petulant and annoying. Make no mistake about it, the focus of this book is Jamie Frasier. He is the most well-developed character in the entire story. Our main character however, our narrator, whom others have praised as being spunky and modern and admirable in her adaptability, is little more than a stand-in for the (arguably female) reader with holes Jamie can fill, a butt he can spank, and a face he can look at adoringly and say all the things the reader wishes a big gorgeous barbarian man would tenderly say to them. Save for a few sentences on her childhood in the beginning of the book and the fact that she was a combat nurse for the Allies in WWII and therefore is conveniently equipped to be useful and have something to physically do in the 18th century, Claire's background is flimsy at best. For me, she never felt like a whole person. Sure, she talks, but even acting as our narrator and primary window to the events of the story, she barely has a thought or emotion of her own. Honestly. I imagine the initial disorientation and then hard realization of her time-travel predicament would be slightly traumatizing. She gets teary-eyed once and becomes dizzy when she's finally able to confirm the year, but those moments are fleeting, over just as quickly as they come about, and then everything that follows taken easily in stride. We're in her head and STILL we have very little idea how she feels about things. No comparing of her new surroundings to her old, no reflection on the lack of modern conveniences, technology, or transportation. She has a thought that she'll need to find natural antiseptic plants and hope for the best in lieu of antibiotics for the injured, but that's about as far as that worry goes. A handful of times she recognizes landmarks from touring Scotland in the 20th century...but again, that's about all the connection we get: observations devoid of emotion. Didn't she just leave her husband of 8 years 200 years in the future? Barely a thought is given to Frank at all until Claire is being escorted back to the magic stones that transported her to 1743  when she says that he has been a constant, aching source of guilt since she arrived. Wait. Really? It took her 6 months and a LOT of graphic, guiltless sex to mention that oh no, this is how she's felt the ENTIRE TIME? And it's not isolated to her feelings about Frank. Emotions, the trauma of adjusting, even the thought to escape are either completely missing, pop up suddenly out of the blue with no organic build-up, or are mentioned in RETROSPECT like, oh yeah, pretend like all that subtlety and characterization and stuff was a part of the story until this point, okay? Also: Claire does have outbursts when she's frustrated or angry, and these outbursts involve stamping her feet, pouting, biting, and basically acting like a child. She also says "smart" and "quippy" things every now and again like telling Randall his wig is crooked as she slumps to the floor in pain, having just received his fist delivered squarely to her womb, asked if she had anything else to say. ZING! Could you really not have helped yourself on that one, Ms. Galbadon? Claire, as a character, as our heroine and main POV, was in a prime position to be very interesting: figuring out what's happened, adjusting to the 18th century, biding her time, planning escape, and navigating the politics and intrigue of the Highland life she's swept up into. But all of that is secondary to maneuvering her into Jamie Frasier's bed because THAT, dear readers, is what this story is actually about. - Jamie Frasier, you big, sensitive, virgin beefcake with BDSM tendencies. YOU, sir, are the reason we're all here. After the superfluous annoyances of establishing a plot are out of the way, the main event is this hunk of meat. Literally hundreds of pages are dedicated to Church-sanctioned sex between Jamie and Claire (she HAD to marry him to keep safe, guys! And, like, it was a way for Dougal to ensure the line of inheritance and stuff and, well...just know that Claire was FORCED to marry Jamie and it's cool with God) and warm, fuzzy scenes of their quaint 18th century domestic life. Jamie is the most well developed character in the entire book because dozens of pages are dedicated to Claire interviewing him about his childhood and feelings. We, the readers, are therefore privy to all the formative relationships and events in his past. Outlander wants you to be so thoroughly, completely in love with Jamie Frasier that you swoon hard, on cue, at all the right moments. It may not have worked for me personally, but if I had to objectively make a judgment call on how well the story hits the marks for people that WOULD be effective for, I'd say Diana Galbadon nailed it. But because I thought I'd signed on for a genre-bending historical fiction novel with a sci-fi/fantasy overtones and a romance subplot, being smacked in the face with 100% unabashed ROMANCE was irritating. - Jonathan Randall. Our villain. Jamie's nemesis. The ancestor of Claire's first husband, Frank. His sole motivation and defining characteristic is that he is an impotent sadist who really, REALLY wants to stick it in Jamie Frasier's bum . - Deus ex bovine. Claire's quick thinking and COWS save the day. - The weird pseudo-ritual Claire performs at the end of the book that involves opium, violent roleplay, and sex to snap Jamie out of his PTSD and give him the will, overnight, to somehow overcome severe infection and blood poisoning. What the HELL did I just read? -Sexual violence is, in turns: fetishized (instances of forced, bruising, rough sex between Jamie and Claire that is by every definition rape is somehow RATIONALIZED as the body being willing even if the mind isn't), overused as a plot point when there's little else going on (seriously, just have Claire get almost-raped another 4 times; it's been a brilliant, mature, dramatic narrative device every time! ), and bundled together with homosexuality (because wanting to "bugger" other men is vile and disgusting and is by no means ever a consensual act of love between two adults). - There's an interview in the back of my copy of Outlander where Diana Gabaldon admits she set out to write a practice novel of historical fiction and this character, Claire Beauchamp, popped up feisty and modern and took over. So Ms. Gabaldon said sure, be modern! We'll make you a time traveler! And that is EXACTLY the way it feels in the story. It gets Claire there and she gets to finally admit it to a couple people and she decides to stay. Then, in the last pages, FINALLY faces a dilemma about whether or not to use her knowledge of what's to come to help these people she's grown to care about in 1743. She also runs into a fellow time-traveler but the reveal is a hurried afterthought and kind of peters out immediately. This could have been brilliant and interesting aspect to the story. Instead, it's mishandled and weak. - I have a feeling the historical fiction aspects of the story, albeit all but abandoned in Outlander, are meant to be expanded upon in the rest of the series. This book as a stand-alone, however, sacrifices them ALL to make room for Jamie and Claire to fall in love and have lots of sex. - Finally, the micro-managing of details I mentioned before. This is the smallest of my gripes by far. As I said, I actually often enjoyed Diana Galbadon's writing ability. However, Claire's first-person narration sometimes knows more than it should about what others are thinking or feeling. For instance: "Murtagh, undisturbed by the less than cordial greeting, was eyeing the bear-clad figure closely, as though mentally stripping hair and years away." Which is promptly followed by dialogue that very clearly reveals the purpose of Murtagh closely eyeing the other man. Isolated, this isn't a big deal. But to repeatedly have ALL small interactions or exchanges interpreted so thoroughly got tiring. Let your writing BREATHE, woman. 2 stars. Despite everything above, I can't deny that I won't possibly read further in this series. I don't understand that inclination at all, but I suppose I'm a little interested to see if the historical fiction aspects ever get enough screen time to develop and become interesting.

I enjoyed this a lot more than I expected to. I became a fan of Regency romance quite a long time ago, and frankly, I've gotten sick of the genre. Everything became scripted, plots have become rote, or in some cases, just nonexistent, and too many h/h I've read lately have had the personality of lukewarm dishwater. This book is a lighthearted romp through Lady Alexandra's first Season, and it is thoroughly YA. There is romance, duh, since it is about catching a husband after all, but there's not much of it and it's more playful and sweet than anything. This book's steam level barely reaches PG-13. There is a mystery plot, but it does not get bogged down, and I loved Alex's entire family and her set of closest friends. Some qualms: - ALL of Alex's brothers have titles. Unless I'm severely mistaken on peerages, only the eldest son gets the entailed titles, but not only brother Will gets the pre-ducal marquesate, but middle brother is an Earl, and youngest brother also gets a title? Unless it's entailed in some really weird way, or they each got a title bestowed upon them (unlikely at their very young age) this isn't terribly realistic. - Way too many dukes and duchesses. I swear every other character is a duke/duchess/dowager - Everyone is too perfect. Alexandra's life is largely filled with open-minded, kindhearted people. Her friends are delightful and breathtakingly lovely. It makes for some pleasant reading, but does not altogether ring true.

I cried last night. I cried in the arms of a man that doesn't love me. I cried because there was no air to breath. I cried because I missed people I know, because I missed people I knew, because I missed people I never could've known. I cried because I am the healthiest member of my family, and because they are not. I cried because life goes on even when you are not allowed to move. I cried because I am tired. I cried because I am scared. I cried because everything will be something. Mostly because I didn't know what that something is. What does that say about this book? Absolutely nothing. Why did I write it then? Because it says something about me. And I want you to know me when I ask you to trust me that this BOOK is BEAUTIFUL.

This is a story of unconditional love and one woman's goal to attain it. All Jane wanted in life was to be loved. She was denied this love by the death of her parents and thus being orphaned. While the person who was entrusted to her care, her uncle, had plenty of love for her it was not long before he too passed from this world. Mrs Reed, his wife, was a cruel woman who raised her for nine years. She enjoyed no love from her children or from her. One housekeeper showed her polite attention at least. It was not until Mrs Reed shipped Jane off to an austere boarding school that Jane found love. The love she attained was from a kind superintendent, Miss Temple. She also found the love of a friend Helen Burns. But this love was snatched away from Jane yet again when Helen died while they both were attending the school. Jane became a teacher at the school, and soon after that Miss Temple married and she was lost to Jane too. Jane advertised in the paper as a woman seeking a position as a governess and she attained it at a place called Thornton. It is there she found her one and only romantic love, the master of the house, Edward Rochester. But love was not hers to attain just yet as on the day they were to be married it was revealed that he already had a wife. A mad wife, albeit still a wife. Jane had to make the painful decision to leave this hall quickly and impoverished. She then suffered poverty, luckily for only a short period. She was taken care of by the Rivers. After they have helped her they find out they are actually cousins. Jane receives a fortune by her, and their, uncle. Jane divides it equally having no concern for herself for the greatest gift they can give her is their love and she finally gets love and a family. While her male cousin St. John, a devout religious man keen to embark on a voyage to India, he wants to bring her as his wife. They have no love for each other and Jane refuses his proposal. She learns that terrible events have happened at Thornton. The mad wife had lit a fire, nearly killing everyone inside. She herself stands on top of the roof of the burning building and while Mr Rochester tries to save her she commits suicide. While escaping from the burning building Mr Rochester is blinded and his hand is cut off. Upon hearing this news Jane returns to him. They have loved each other from the moment they met and they wed. They live a happy existence for the rest of their days. In this end she receives the romantic love, immediate family love and the love from an extended family. Not such a tragic ending as I had expected! There are some gothic elements in this work (though not nearly as gothic as Charlotte Bronte's sister's work - Wuthering Heights). The moor provides an eerie place for strange dreams. Jane's painting too are of a dark nature. There are also elements of the supernatural in this book, one such occurrence is when the two lovers call out to each other in the night (though many miles apart) and still hear each other.

Okay. Welcome to one of the most confusing books I've read. Too many things happened, too many turncoats, too many deaths. There was only one thing that was clear, Patch and Nora were going to get together. This book, no, this SERIES could have been probably written in half the space it did. Nora must now lead all the nephilim, and Patch is kind of there to prevent her from dying. She becomes addicted to devilcraft and has to train to prove herself worthy of being the leader. The rest of the story is like fodder for ants. I have no idea why half of the things happened. Relationships felt short and forced when new characters were introduced, and old ones, particularly Marcie and Vee were nonexistent. Dante somehow becomes incredibly important in this book although no mention of him existed prior. I think part of the reason this book fails is that it tried to do too many things. There are a lot of good moments, Nora dealing with her addiction for one, and I guess Patch is always fun to read. But there are also a lot of loose ends and plot holes. Nora learning sword fighting in two days. The death of at least three characters. Vee being a  nephilim . I've noticed a pattern in Ms. Fitzpatrick's books, that most of the action doesn't start till 75% of the book has passed. The last 25% is always incredibly fast, and I devour the books. But the middle seems to drag on forever. At least this series is done forever. whoo! In short. The book had a lot of action, great chemistry between Nora and Patch, and vaguely entertaining. However, the lack of a cohesive plot, haphazard characters, and confusing writing sadly puts this series at a pretty low for me.

I have mixed feelings about this book. I liked the general storyline and Nico was a great hero, but Elizabeth was driving me nuts. I'm glad she finally went to therapy  because that girl was batshit crazy. She constantly insisted that she didn't want to play games with Nico and that's why she couldn't be with him, but all she did for the entire book was play games with his feelings. I'm still giving it 4 stars for Nico, and because it was funny and engaging, but Elizabeth gets zero stars from me. One other interesting thing is that the author gives you a choice on the heat level of the book. She wrote two versions of the chapter where they have sex for the first time: a fade to black version, and an "open door" version. I've never seen an author do that before. Of course, I went with the open door love scenes ;) but for those who do not like a lot of steam in their books, it's nice that she gives the reader a choice.
* My review of this book can be found on my YouTube channel: Suicide Notes from Beautiful Girls by Lynn Weingarten
5/10: Finished the book and it was above average. Not quite as good as past instalments. I did skim a few pages towards the end. But still, all in all, an OK/good read.

WOW this book is a mess. Which, to be fair, was exactly what I was expecting after part I, but still. It's all over the place and just like in book 1 there's not much world-building (people are calling this a dystopia, but it's not really), there's not much backstory or even explanations and descriptions about the Feelers, Seers and Readers. You kind of just get pulled along; and that's perfectly fine, but it also means this is never going to be a very good book. I didn't hate it, though. It reads like a train and it's very short and I mostly liked it because of Annie. I was super into Annie and Cole. As soon as she had her first vision in which she grabs a boy's hand and realises the feeling she's experiencing is her in love, in the future, I had a feeling it would be Cole. So I was very happy to be proven right later on. COLE. But yeah, I would've loved this had it been done better. Because the idea/concept is pretty great. The execution of said idea, however, is mostly disappointing.

This was a mixed bag, with some horribly terrible stories and some that are absolute MUST READS. The GOOD- These stories all deserve 5 stars and two thumbs WAY up! Secret Identity- If you only read one story it should be this one! Kelly Link is brilliant. Her narration has style and the story is incredibly interesting, different, and strange. She doesn't beat the 'geek' theme to death showing once again that she is the master of subtlety. Genius! The King of Pelinesse- This story is seemingly simple, but contains incredibly complex characters. Quiz Bowl Antichrist- Perhaps the best LGBT fiction I have ever read. It was funny and sincere with a main character that was human rather than a one-dimensional conduit for sexual politics. It's Just a Jump to the Left- Powerful. I think it speaks volumes that I read this story and wished it were a novel. I wanted more! The characters were interesting and, unlike most of the other stories in this book, it was set in the past. It was refreshing to have a geek story that took place pre-computer age. The Bad- The Quiet Knight- Just skip this one. The characters are one dimension and the story is pretty much non-existent. Seriously it is an absolute waste of time. You've been warned. The Ugly- One of Us- No. Just no. This story was filled to the brim with cliches. It tries to cram as many pop culture references in as possible which is no substitution for a well written story with fully developed characters. Nice try! (Well not really...did you even try?) This is like the BIG BANG THEORY without the canned laughter... The Wrath of Dawn- if there's one thing I hate it's nerds trying to prove their nerdiness. Please stop casting the blonde beautiful girl as evil, stupid, and less evolved than the mousey girl who is really into sci-fi. Freak the Geek- John Green you have to stop. Please. You are terrible and so is this laughably ridiculous story that is really about how everyone who isn't you is subhuman. GET OVER YOURSELF! **BONUS ROUND** The WTF Award goes to...The Truth About Dino Girl This started out great and then burst into flames during the last few pages. The main character did something so incredibly despicable which in and of itself does not a bad story make. However, the way this act of revenge is handled it is clear that the reader is supposed to see Dino girl's actions as appropriate which absolutely boggled my mind. To me this said more about the author than the characters, you can bet I won't be reading Barry Lyga anytime soon.

"I thought you didn't believe in fairy tales." His gaze held hers unwavering. "I believe in us." 4.5 stars. A tale of two beautifully broken people who find and fight for love. I struggled with my rating because Gabe was...a struggle. I struggled to like him at times. But Lordy, does he redeem himself in the most moving and memorable way. It was then I stopped struggling and fully believed that he was worthy of Kat, one of my favorite heroines in Romancelandia. I fully believed in their happily-ever-after. This is the fourth in a series about a team of investigative reporters at a Denver newspaper, but it works as a standalone. I read the other books years ago, and I'll admit that I felt some disappointment that three of the heroines left their jobs explicitly because they got married. To be crystal clear, I'm NOT judging them for this; I'm firmly in the "feminism means giving women more choices" camp. But it didn't seem very sensical, seeing as they had been portrayed as dedicated and driven professionals. And it didn't seem very fair that the women had to make the career sacrifices. Again, this is a "huh?" issue with the plot as opposed to personal disapproval of their choices. . Anyway, this book stood out in my memory as absofreakinglutely fantastic. When I recently came saw it at the library, I wanted to know whether it still stood out. And it absofreakinglutely did. For me, Kat was the star of the book. To the (unfortunately) many writers who struggle to craft a female character who is both strong AND vulnerable? Take note. Clare has created a wonderful example in Kat, who is intelligent, brave, and honest but never unlikeable, never veering into Mary Sue territory. Rejected by her parents and her siblings, Kat, like Gabe, knew betrayal. Unlike Gabe, she didn't shut down. She remained steadfast even as she struggled to come to terms with herself and her identity. You feel the doubts and discovery as she adjusts from life on a very traditional reservation to life in a very modern city. Clare's undoubtedly diligent research into Navajo culture is reflected in Kat. She felt real. The insights and observation of culture and ritual were stirring. Gabe. Oh, Gabe. Grandpa Red Crow recognized that Gabe did indeed have a good heart but lost his way. His dedication to his park ranger job and his desire to respect and protect nature is juxtaposed against his minimal regard and respect for women. Some readers love the he's-a-mean-manwhore-because-he-was-brutally-betrayed thing, but I usually don't. Many of Gabe's actions and thoughts weren't pretty. What I did love? Kat helped change him but never in a way that felt derivative of a tired old formula. Gabe lost his way, and Kat became his moral compass. She took him to task, albeit gently. She allowed him to connect with his former self, to confront and reconcile his pain. She made him want to be a better person. But only Kat was capable of doing this, and her uniqueness to Gabe is apparent. When he said that she was "the best thing that ever happened" to him, I wanted to fist pump even though I was a half-sobbing mess (you'll know why when you read it). While some of the sex scene language was a bit purple-y, I found them sweet and hot. Especially the hat game ;) The suspense kept me on the edge of the couch. There are eerie and unexpected twists. Please know that this takes some DARK turns not typically taken in romance novels. Alas, you need not fear too much! I'm not normally a fan of fast forwards to weddings and babies , but it couldn't have been more perfect or precious here. I was glad to see how much they risked and grew for each other and how much they got in return. It was a delightful ride, and I enjoyed their well-fought ending.

Great story. A world without books would be the most depressing place! I loved the book people, and the metamorphosis of Guy. I would probably give this more like 3.5 stars, because I felt that the ending was a little abrupt. I wish there had been just a little more to the ending, but overall a great read, one I'm sure I will return to in the future.

This was such a carefully crafted story that I cannot do anything but awe at the huge effort and dedication that went into it! Thank you Victoria, A Conjuring of Light was truly amazing! In myths, the hero survives. The evil is vanquished. The world is set right. Sometimes there are celebrations, and sometimes there are funerals. The dead are buried. The living move on. Nothing changes. Everything changes. This is a myth. This is not a myth. Each and every character we've met up until now is explored in depth, villains and good guys alike. The side characters are not cheap cardboards, when they go through rough times you'll suffer just as much as you'll do when one of the main ones does. New and charismatic personalities are introduced, old storylines investigated. The romance is not cumbersome, the characters don't need to cry over one another all the time to make us sure they're in love. They don't need angst to make their relationship grow. They have each other's back, they care, they fight, they communicate, they kiss, they part. God, oh god, how I loved the romance in this series! "Her [Lila's] heart was beating hard against her ribs, some primal part of her saying run, and she was running, just not away. She was tired of running away. So she was running into Kell. And he caught her." "I [Alucard] never wanted to leave. And if I'd known Rhy loved me then as much as I love him, I would never have stayed away." "He [Alucard] had spent the better part of an hour assembling the outfit. He couldn't decide between Alucard, the captain, and Emery, the noble. In the end, he had chosen neither. Today he was Alucard Emery, the man courting the king." This would have been such a perfect moment for a marriage proposal, you guys, I had already booked the venue myself! The plot is rich and intricate, so much happens but nothing happens out of the blue. Every instance is needed, be for a personal growth of one of the main characters, be for the perfect clousure for one of the side ones. I too was scared and kinda put off by the lenght of ACoL but, in hindsight, I wouldn't have wanted for any of it to be spared. The world-building of the Red London's world is astonishing. You feel like you've lived in this place all your life. You know how we wish we could have attended Hogwarts, roaming the castle, taking a field trip to Hogsmade, reading by the Great Lake? Well, what about making a great deal at the Sasenroche market, speaking fluent Arnisian, cheering your favourite mage at the Essen Tasch, buying a gorgeous dress from Calla's stand and repaying her with a beautiful trinket won at a game of Sanct, smelling of roses all the time, seeing the sun setting over Arnes' river while sitting on a bench, head resting of Kell's shoulder and... wh-what aRE YOU DOING IN MY DAYDREAM? GO AWAY! *cries in her pillow* "Love and loss are like a ship and the sea. They rise together. The more we love, the more we have to lose. But the only way to avoid loss is to avoid love. And what a sad world that would be." In no time this has become one of my favourite series of all time, I'll be re-reading it as soon as I'll have been able to buy myself the entire set! Anoche Kell and Lila and Rhy and Alucard, I hope I'll get to read more about you in the future! REVIEWS for A Darker shade of Magic here and A Gathering of Shadows here.

So, where have I been since about November 10th, 2014??? Trying to decide what to say about this book-- that's where. And I have finally decided to simply say this: I really enjoyed prequel to this book, 'The Fifth Wave' However, this book threw me for a bit of a loop... Rick Yancy takes this book to a dark spot with what happens to the youngest children--and I'm not exactly how I feel about it in a YA book. Also, and I realize that the world has ended and all, but compared to a lot of other books in this genre, there is quite a bit of language-- I am an adult and have no problem with it, but, if I handed this to my child who is almost within the intended target age range, and didn't know in advance that it is a bit 'mature', I'm not sure how I'd feel.

While this book was a step in the right direction, I still felt like something was always missing. The fighting scenes were vague and easily described. I guess you can say it was overly simplified. Surface sentences like, "they fought hard and dirty and only one man was left standing." really messed up the intensity of the scene. Who bit who? Who was on top? How did he die? Things like that really got on my nerves and I was unable to stay immersed in the story. This read had more fat than meat and well, I was left feeling unsatisfied. I don't know if I'll read anymore Brooks titles right now.

I loved Jurassic Park and The Lost World. Crichton's casual discussion of evolution is actually a great introduction to the topic disguised as science fiction. I found myself wondering how much of it was accurate, though, compared to some authors who may lightly research a topic so they have some vocabulary on the subject. I read Your Inner Fish: A Journey into the 3.5-Billion-Year History of the Human Body and Undeniable: Evolution and the Science of Creation immediately after because Crichton had inspired such an interest in the topic! And he really did prep me for the deeper discussion with his introduction on the subject. Crichton's characters are also deeper and more unique than the movies gave them credit. Especially the female characters. I LOVE a good female character, and Crichton wrote amazing women. I love their no nonsense attitude and strength. I love that they are actually kind of heroes. I love their depth and complexity. And not just the women on that last point. Crichton's characters are all 3D and believable, palpable even. Last, having seen the movies a hundred times already, there's actually additional suspense knowing when shit is about to hit the fan. Oh, the fences are down? YALL BOUT TO GET EATEN BY VELOCIRAPTORS!! But it's even better than in the movie. So much better!

M/M historical romance (turn of the last century); isn't listed as part of a series but seems to be set up for sequels. Captain Archie Curtis is not accustomed to subterfuge, and he is acutely uncomfortable at having accepted a country house party invitation under false pretences. But he also can't bring himself to ignore the rumour that his host bears responsibility for the devastating military accident that cost him the fingers of his right hand and the lives of most of his men. His attempts at investigation, however, are made more difficult by fellow houseguest Daniel da Silva: effeminate, witty, foreign, obviously queer, and altogether the most dislikable man Curtis has ever met. This is pretty great: engaging and well-characterised and romantic. There's a very modern and unsavoury mystery and resolution in there, but most of the plot is drawing room chatter, late-night sneaking about, action and danger, with a really lovely extended hurt/comfort section occupying most of the climax. Also a couple of great female characters in plot-important roles - both rather familiar stock figures of the country house mystery genre but with, of course, a twist. I liked the use of recognisable country house mystery characters in general, actually, and da Silva in particular: when he's introduced he's such a familiar figure of the genre, the too-urbane, effete foreigner who will almost certainly turn out to be either the villain or secretly a deadly young blade playing a foppish part. But will never, of course, become someone you're supposed to like, never become vulnerable or warm or sympathetic. Every time I read a K. J. Charles book (2 Magpie Lord books and this one, so far) I get unrealistically hopeful about the genre in general and spend an afternoon re-learning that most of what's out there is terrible. I understand that part of the fantasy for a lot of romance readers is that both partners be objectively and enviably desirable to everybody they've ever met, but god it's boring. All I want to know is that they want each other, in all their prickliness and individuality and fully equipped with emotional hangups, and Charles does that beautifully. (I'm not sure the King Solomon's Mines crossover fic element added anything in particular, but it didn't especially detract anything either, so.) Content warnings: some dubious consent that may also trip a particularly sensitive embarrassment squick (didn't for me, but hey), mentions of child sexual abuse (not of the protagonists), mentions of suicide. Specifics of the dubcon: kind of a fuck-or-die: characters have to perform sexual acts for a hidden audience to divert suspicion about their spying. Lol this was going to be a super-brief review. I'm so bad at brevity.

Me reading this entire book: What? Wait, what? I am not even sure what the concluding message was  - to be happy with what you have? To do whatever you feel is right? To trust in the cosmos, even though it dicks you around a bit? I am glad I read it, but am not sure if my lack of understanding is due to culture, time period, life station, or even just a bad translation - we read it as a group and there were some word changes that gave majorly different meanings.

So this one. After feeling rather luke-warm about books one and three, and absolutely loathing book two of this series, I picked up Radiant Shadows. Because I already had it. And its description intrigued me more than the others. Which is odd, really. I'm no fan of the Dark Court and this book is set right in their midst. But Ani's story got me. She's a very sympathetic character - she's half Dark Fey, half-human, and doesn't really feel like she belongs anywhere. She has a strange ability, even among half-fey, that makes her too dangerous to stay in the mortal world, but she doesn't feel truly accepted in the Dark Court - especially by her father, leader of the Hounds. Bannanach, who believes the Dark Court is rightfully hers, tries to use Ani to further her agenda, but Ani escapes with the help of Devlin. Devlin is "brother" to both Sorcha and Bannanch (meaning they, as the first faeries, created him), and so has dual natures warring within him, just like Ani. Devlin serves Sorcha as her assassin, since his Dark influence can be of use to her in that way, and Sorcha is all about order and practicality. Or she used to be. When she made Seth fey, she gave just a bit too much of herself away, and his return to the land of mortals has made her unstable, and the rest of Faerie along with her. Devlin is concerned about her, but is more concerned when he realizes Bannanch wants to use Ani. Ani - who he was supposed to kill as a child, on Sorcha's command. He did not, because of the intervention of one of the best characters in the series, Rae, who is basically a ghost, but cooler. She befriended Devlin a century or so before, and for reasons that are mysterious, asked him to spare Ani's life. Which he did. And so Ani and Devlin go on the run and grow closer. They are very well-matched and this makes for a nice love story. Ani's more disturbing Dark Court traits, such as the need to feed on negative emotions - and, as a hound, on "skin contact", are rather annoying but they are not her fault, and as I mentioned, she is a sympathetic character. Devlin comes into his own and realizes that he does not always need to be torn between his two natures, but can perhaps fuse them into one. Then things turn violent when Bannanach attacks, and in the ensuing chaos, a miraculous thing happens. I actually care about Irial! He's evil. Yes, yes he is. But he's cared for Ani and protected her since she was a child and she loves him. And he does valiant things for her, and for others in the Dark Court whom he loves. The Dark Court does kill, and harm, and enjoy it, but they also love. I still think this series errs on the disturbing and annoying side of this complexity, but at least this book showed a bit more of the...erm...human side of the Dark Court. Things with Sorcha escalate and Ani and Devlin must try to save the faerie who tried to kill Ani. I actually really loved how that part of the plot was resolved. I probably would have rated this book higher if it weren't for the addition of yet ANOTHER three-way relationship! Ani and Devlin fall in love and support each other to be better but then ALL OF A SUDDEN Rae inserts herself into their midst like "Oh, well, I've always loved Devlin and I saved you Ani and you guys have bodies and I don't so let's like have kinky three-ways where I possess one of you". Damn. So, so close. Hopefully I read too much into it and it was JUST a kiss but that suggestion was just too much for me. Like with Irial-Leslie-Niall, too gimmicky. At least Rae had the excuse of being a ghost and all three characters were likable, but still. URGH.

I waited to long to review this!! I can't remember everything I wanted to say.... :( Many people said this made them not hate Levana.... I think I hate her even more. More sympathy? A bit, but she is definitely twisted. Yeah, Levana will never be my favorite, but I hate Selena's mother more lol. Levana doesn't know what love means, yet says in Cinder that she married once for love and now she'll do it for power? *groans loudly* I did like how we got to see toddler Selena and Winter ^_^ they were so cute~~ Also, we learned more about Luna and it's Royalty which was interesting.

Guys, I don't even know? I picked this up because I was intrigued by the title, as a comics fan, but... okay. So I liked the start of the story. It's set in Iowa City/Coralville, which I liked, because I like Iowa City. The protagonists are a 17-year-old girl named Sheila, who works at a gas station, and a 20-something dude named Peter Parker, who frequents the gas station to buy cigarettes. Sheila suspects Peter Parker's ID is fake, because who would name their child after Spider-Man, right? Anyway, at first I liked Sheila a lot. High school misfit, saving up her money to go to France after high school with no set plan because she doesn't want to go straight to college and she wants to get out of Iowa. So she listens to French CDs and practices while she works at the gas station. Get it, Sheila. But then she lets herself be voluntarily kidnapped by Peter Parker and goes with him to Chicago? And he gives her a fake ID with the name Gwen Stacy, aka Peter Parker's first girlfriend who dies?? Again... I'm still interested, here. Is Peter going to kill her, or what. Then... okay, I described the plot of this to a co-worker and she said it sounded like it was written as an exquisite corpse story. (You know, where you fold over the page and pass it to the next person and they write something without having seen your part.) I agree, or maybe like it were part of an improv scene where the author just kept saying "Yes, and." Yes, and... Peter has accurate visions of death. Yes, and... Peter's long-thought-dead brother is actually alive and well in Chicago. Yes, and... Gwen decides to kidnap Peter's brother. Yes, and... coyotes are taking to the streets of Chicago. Yes, and... Gwen has visions of talking coyotes. Also it seemed like the Spider-Man thing was kind of used as a hook and then dropped? I'd be way into reading a book that used comic book characters/archetypes as a way to explore relationships but I just found this very confusing and weird. I'm seeing a lot of great reviews for it so it's totes possible that it just all went over my head. If anyone else I know has read it, I'd LOVE to talk about it.

Great story, and although I was less trusting than Sydney -  I thought Duncan was a plant  - there was twists and turns and action and drama and I couldn't put it down! Now to wait until the final one gets published! - Although I think the author finished this and then kind of set up for the final really quick, so it could almost stop with this one, it wasn't that much of a cliffhanger ending as they have been in the past. Lucky for my lack of patience!

I've been watching the Longmire series on television and it's good. The series and the book are not identical but neither detracts from the other. In the book, Walt is even more self-deprecating. He and Henry Standing Bear are thoroughly charming and funny. The author has caught their friendship and familiarity with each other and all the intimacy that that entails really really well. The last section turned much darker than I was anticipating but I could understand why the author went that way. I'm definitely reading more in this series. What a happy find.

I have thoughts, but I need to iron them out, so review to come. Horrible confession: I had this (library) book sitting next to my bathroom sink, which had a bit of water in it. I also have a cat who jumps up on the sink to drink the water. I am now paying for this book, whether I want to or not. I'm not really disappointed with this book. I think I would be, if I had loved Insurgent. To make the inevitable comparison, Insurgent was no Catching Fire. So, having already had my Divergent love deflated, I didn't go into this with high expectations. And to be fair, this book met my expectations, and even went above. So, thinking that way, I changed my rating from three stars to four. The pacing feels off with the story, like she wanted to cram so much action into one novel. I don't know if it should've been four novels or not. Trilogies seem to be the new it thing. But everything just flew by. HEY, we're in the Bureau. HEY, they're evil. HEY, we're going to rebel. HEY, they're rebelling over there. HEY, serums. HEY, death. HEY HEY HEY and done. I couldn't really get excited about any of the battling. With Insurgent, even in my disappointment, I found moments to get excited about, especially scenes involving Tris and Jeanine battling. Despite the fact that there are, arguably, Big Damn Moments happening all over this story, I never really clung to the book, lost in the moment, feeling adrenaline surging. And that's really disappointing, considering how everything started. From the start, when I saw that the novel was going to be told both from the perspective of Tris and Four, I knew one of them was going to die. That was a little frustrating, but maybe it's just me. Maybe others didn't see it coming. I was actually hoping for a very different outcome. I wanted one (or both) of them to have their memories wiped. I'd read in Entertainment Weekly that there was a big twist ending. It seemed too easy that the twist would be death of a main character. My coworker and I tossed out ideas of who the Big death would be, and she said Four. I could see it, especially at the end. But then with all the discussion of memory wipes, and all of the extreme rebel work to save Chicago, I got a little excited that at the end, the memory wipe would work, and we would start over. Maybe Tris would be paired with Peter, and Four would end up as one of the Factionless. Whole worlds of possibilities, the final scene being Tris and Four walking past each other on the street and not registering each other at all. I wonder if there's fanfiction to this affect out there. Maybe it's time to get back into that world. After I finished the book, I was looking at the cover, and thinking about the taglines for each book, all involving the word "choice". And thinking about how everything that happens in each book is based on choices. And setting aside all political metaphors, that's a really powerful message to walk away with. Factions aren't houses. No faction is Slytherin, all evil and dark ways. You choose, and what you do with what you gain makes you who you are. The reveal of what the factions mean was unexpected. I didn't see it coming, and it's really fascinating, in an Erudite way. Altering people's genetics, screwing everyone up, then figuring out what parts are "wrong", and grouping them likewise. It's kind of a mind fuck, and makes me want to re-read Divergent with this knowledge. GD versus GP. I would've liked a lot more information around this. Around the Purity War, the battle of the purebloods versus the mudbloods. Though...considering that the story is told from the perspective of two people who are thrown elbow-deep into this world, and have to try to grasp it all in a short period of time, it makes sense that we don't get a documentary. But it's frustrating to be given this depth of knowledge, and only get to skim the surface. I think my main problem is I wanted more exposition from this book. What we got feels very smushed. I feel like I know Tris's mother better than I know Tris herself. I would actually read a book about Tris's mother. She was amazing. Also, while I'm very happy that Tris got over her goddamn PTSD over guns, I would've liked for her to find a different way to fight. I realize that in the scenarios where she used the gun, hand-to-hand combat wasn't the ideal, but anyone can wield a quarter staff with a bit of practice. Sigh. I've recommended Divergent to so many people. A former coworker just finished it yesterday, and LOVED it, and I told her, I am not recommending the sequels, so if you want to follow up, you do so without my assistance. She said something that makes sense, which is she's not going to ruin the warm fuzzies she has about the book by reading something that will bring her opinion down. Sad. I still don't know what faction I would belong in. I don't really fit into any of them, though after finishing this review, I guess I should be an Erudite, knowledge-seeker.

Well. I hated this. So cliche, so many stereotypes. Suffocating mother, nagging older sister, listless mid-twenties man living with his mother, flighty and shallow ex-girlfriend, woman obsessed with Marriage supporting the long-term emotionally distant musician boyfriend who just won't propose. The gentle Midwestern "farm boy" who's gigantic so all the women can swoon over his manliness--like, constantly--but shy, so he's not threatening. Their actual meeting, when it finally happened, was too cheesy and unreal even for the early-2000s romantic comedies the book both mimicked and constantly referenced. But the worst part, the part that really made me feel kind of sick, was Jennifer's storyline with the pregnancy. I felt the same way when Miranda got pregnant on Sex and the City. Guys it is fucking creepy to romanticize an adult woman who really, really does not want to be pregnant, accidentally gets pregnant, freaks out because she really does not want to be pregnant, and then is eventually won over. Forcibly. By not having a choice anymore. Honestly, I was irritated by page three, and wouldn't have gone past page 50 if I hadn't been doing it for a reading challenge in the first place. My feeling probably would have stuck with irritation if not for the business with Jennifer, but I can't emphasize enough how creeped out I am by that plot.

The plot was predictable.And the mystery wasn't really much of a mystery. The character voices blended in together.The only one I could recognize was Agatha and that was just because of her annoyingly shallow and insipid comments. I also feel like all the characters fit into a formulaic structure. I didn't know that this would have multiple POVs. So, reading the first chapter (the first POV chapter of Auggie), where everything is what you would expect from a story centered around a boy who has deformed face because of some blahblah genetics, I said to myself, Well, nothing new here., and yawned. I didn't like the POV of Auggie. It just seems unreal to me. It even bored me a couple of times. Like I said, it's the kind of story you'd expect. And then Via's POV came. And I was like, "Oh God yes yes let's hear it!" It satisfied me. Really. The multiple POVs worked for me. We get to understand why the characters do what they do and how they try to let us know their points and situations and reasons they do such weird and unexpected things. And you will really feel their regrets. You will feel the jealousy of Via how great she is trying to understand the situation of her family. How great she is for a sister. You will understand how really nice Summer is. You will understand how Jack doesn't really mean the bad things he says about Auggie. You will understand why Merinda and Via's friendship starts to fade away. I liked the multiple POVs. In short, I liked the book if it isn't told by Auggie. I do not fancy the sun, I fancy how the planets and asteroids and everything revolve around it. I cannot have interests to a thing that moves and acts the way we expect. I didn't like the too much feel-good vibe of the book. And if I raise the ratings of the books with philosophies I agreed to, I will lower the ratings of the books with philosophies I don't agree to. Is this kind of thinking bad? I just don't believe what the book says about how every one of us is special as long as we'll surpass our limits with kindness blahblahblah... just no. Some of us are special, some of us are not. I guess we need to deal with it. And addition to that, I cannot accept that everybody but the real main villain get so super nice to Auggie. They get so kind and everything... So to sum it up, I liked the book. I liked the POVs other than Auggie. I don't like the overly unreal euphoric vibe of the book.

I am very conflicted. While Glass Sword did hold my attention, have good pacing, and go down a very different path than I thought it would, I just don't love it. I liked it. Problems arose in Mare's character, and as I kept reading I didn't like the direction she was headed. In the beginning, I understood and liked the changes to her personality. She's gone through unbelievable things, and it has obviously made her harder and colder. However, as the book progressed I started to like her less and less. Certain things she does, how she treats those around her, etc. Her character in this book is similar to that of Adelina from The Young Elites, but she doesn't have the excuse of her powers warping her mind. She kinda redeems herself at the end, like a tiny bit, but still. She's selfish and ruthless, preaching that Red lives are worth saving while also killing Silvers that pose no threat to her. She holds everything in and pushes everyone away. I got the feeling that Mare was unsure of who she was anymore, and took out her uncertainty on everyone around her. It's only until the very end that she realizes what's most important to her. Cal was actually my favorite character. He's not the same ignorant prince from book one. He has his own demons to deal with, but that doesn't stop him from retaining his compassion. He doesn't push people away like Mare does, and he knows better than to needlessly kill people. His relationship with Mare is odd, but I enjoyed how they found comfort in each other. Other than Mare and Cal, I didn't get a sense for any of the other characters. Kilorn is less annoying than before and he's a little more mature, but that's it. Shade, despite being a character that makes things happen, isn't developed much. Same with Farley and the newbloods they find. You only see glimpses of them, and after awhile it's hard to care about so many new characters you barely know. There isn't much world building. Lots of trees, lots of islands, the occasional building is described. I am still wishing for a map in these books. So many different countries are name dropped, different towns and villages that they go to. I kept wishing I had a map so I could see how far away they were from each other, where they are, etc. I really hope the publisher will put some funding into maps in the books. I did enjoy the plot. The recruiting missions were interesting, and shit does happen. Discovering newbloods and their unique powers. The prison break, etc. Mare was doing her best to accomplish her goal, to save Red lives. You don't see much of Maven. Asides from one physical encounter with Mare, you just hear about him. Like his flames, he's a shadow in Mare's life and the Guard's work. He haunts them, but Mare especially. Like book one, this ends in a cliffhanger. However, this was a cliffhanger I predicted. Given this is a four book series, what happens at the end was inevitable. I liked how it was handled and why Mare did it, her decision restored some compassion into her heart. I am interested in seeing how Mare will handle her new situation and how she'll interact with Maven. She's going to need to be a different kind of strong here. Ultimately, Glass Sword was a little disappointing, but Cal will keep me coming back. Worldbuilding and characterization need work still, but I digress. Honestly, I think this book, the entire series really, suffers with Mare as the sole narrator. She provides a very limited and unlikable narrator, and it detracted from my enjoyment of the book. As unlikely this probably is, I really hope I'll get Cal's POV in book three. I feel like it would add so much after the ending. You'd get to see what's happening on the Guard's end, and he'll probably work to free her. He's a more sympathetic character, and we'd be able to see the events of the book through the eyes of a Silver, someone who had privilege and will have very different feelings about their world compared to Mare. EDIT: The more I think about Glass Sword and Red Queen, the more I realize Aveyard's biggest writing struggles stem from her background as a screenwriter. Her writing is dialogue heavy and has Mare giving a lot of inner monologues. While there are descriptions, worldbuilding is lacking. It is incredibly difficult to picture the world Mare lives in. This all lines up with how a screenplay is typically written. Lots of dialogue, descriptions of the action, short character descriptions and the emotions they are portraying, and brief location descriptions. Don't get me wrong, her writing is good, but it's not great. A book isn't a movie, tv show, play, or musical. There are no visuals, the reader needs to be able to envision and imagine as much as possible without getting bogged down. I have a hard time picturing Mare's surroundings because there aren't enough descriptions. Her secondary characters also suffer from this because Mare doesn't say much about them. They easily become forgettable. Next book, I need less inner monologues and more worldbuilding, and a little more focus on secondary characters.

Shift is the sequel to Wool Omnibus; however, the book predominately takes place in the years prior to Wool. I would recommend reading Wool prior to reading Shift. Shift tells the story of how the silos came to be and what life was like in the silos prior to the events in Wool. If you are looking for what happens immediately after the events in Wool, you will be disappointed with Shift; however, I feel that Shift definitely adds to the story and universe. Shift provides important information for plot. Overall, I really enjoyed Shift. I thought it was really interesting to learn how the silos came to be. I think I may have enjoyed Shift more than I enjoyed Wool. The story was fairly tight, and I feel that the story flowed a bit better than Wool. I think Howey had a better idea of where he was going with this book and what story he wanted to tell. Audio: My only issue with this book was the audio. The reader's pacing, tone, and inflection were great. My problem was that sometimes that story jumped to a different time, and it wasn't readily noticeable. I would zone out for a few minutes and when I returned to the story I would have a hard time figuring out where in time I was for a little bit. I would have appreciated more noticeable chapter breaks. My problem with the audio is purely a personal preference and should not dissuade you from picking up Shift.

I highly advise for a third installment of this books. Please. With a twisty, complicated plot, with some For Darkness Shows the Stars people, the return of the Wild Poppy, technology like never before seen & lots of Justen & Persis. Plus Persis & Justen. PLEASE? I kid you not, this book heart attacked the shit out of me. I read it up to pieces & loved the fuck out of it! For starters, it has everything I like about a book; from the complicated not-love relationships to confusing friendships all the way to kickassery & action. So, here's the thing. This will be a non-review, where I will point out real, fair, not-made-up reasons of why there. Must. Be. A sequel. Okay? Okay. First things first. Oh my god, you, Persis! There is no doubt that she's my hero. I loved Persis determination to hide her real identity & be the most acclaimed air head on Albion's court so she could become the most acclaimed spy & savior of New Pacifica. Yes, yes, this was amazing! By day she's Persis Flake, court's shallow, stupid & uninterested girl, while by night *evil smile* she becomes the Wild Poppy, mastermind & responsible of saving aristos & enemies of the galatean revolution. Beautiful, brilliant, resourceful, she got it. Then again, if someone will cross the sea to risk her life like that, you can only expect it to worth something. Sure, she's saving lots of lives, but hey, the extreme amounts of action she gets in every scene is the real deal breaker. & for me too! The missions Persis carried away as the Wild Poppy in Galatea were total nail biters. & here's where I present to you, Reason #1 of why a sequel is needed I need MORE. More action! More badass spy scenes! More intrigue & conspiracy theories & fights with the bitch! Right. It's a fact that I'm all over Persis political mind, cleverness & sarcastic comments. She's great, the kind of character you wish were real, & that's perhaps why her disguise as the sweetest stupid bothered me at times. Is the best cover the Wild Poppy could yet, yes. You need wit to play dumb, fine. Still... Persis is the the Princess Regent closest friend. Isla doesn't have it easy, trying to rule over such macho society, what kind of help is Persis Flake? NONE, I tell you! On the other hand, Persis fucking Blake could have been a great social influence that could have helped her friend in her first months as regent of Albion. Ow, Isla... Ah, Isla was wonderful as ruler! (I shall whoosh about her later). The act also affected Persis' life too much. Clearly she was set to make some sacrifices in order to save people in Galatea, so hurt her reputation is not much in exchange. But what about her parents? Her relationship with her father was very damaged. & why must this happen when her mom was... sick. Anyway. Regardless of my feeling about Persis act, she was amazing at it. Now, lets see. Schemes & blindsides, consorting with the enemy in order to benefit your interests (as a spy! ), help the princess legitimate her rule through deception; a lie of a romance that ends in unexpected something (love)...? OMG, WHAT ARE YOU WAITING FOR! That is exactly the kind of love development I like! & man, does this book deliver. Beyond the fact that Persis & Justen are perfect for each other (& that Isla mentions it several times to nag Persis) is the fact that they deny it AND/or are to busy regarding the plot to realize. The major peeve I had with For Darkness Shows the Stars is that I wanted TENSION, but I got tension instead. & Elliot's passive-hysteric manners,too, but I just realized about that... Hell, Across a Star Swept Sea is made up of great, pointy, hurtful splinters of TENSION! Never mind my craziness, I loved that. Persis is neck deep with the Wild Poppy, & she can't trust Justen by any means because he's the enemy. That she has to fake a romance with him is bad enough; that he'd be her dream boy (smart, handsome & all that) makes it all kinds of worse. But she wouldn't let all those confusing feelings distract her. Instead she sails south to Galatea to save some galateans. Because she's badass like that. Justen, well, as a good revolutionary, he has too many prejudices against aristos. He brushed Persis as shallow & stupid all too quickly... the better for Persis & her act. Yet, when he was beginning to trust her & reach out of his revolutionary guilt & loneliness, BUM! You are dealing with an SPY, Justen! Not that he realizes. Then he kisses her to prove something, but that's not the point. Persis played some interesting psychological games with his head, driving his revolutionary guilt to the point that he feared his actions would hurt his sister, the person he loved the most. *happy sigh* Isn't it romantic? Oh, the confusion! Oh, the doubt! Oh my heart, this was so good. Is not just the circumstances of how they met or that there were lies upon lies. Persis' little heart & personal issues beyond the Wild Poppy affected her take on liking Justen when she shouldn't. Couldn't. Love was magma, shooting from the Earth. It had the potential to form pillars of rock that would last for a thousand years or plumes of ash that choked the sky. She would never love like her father, never let herself be loved like her mother.Our girl has kind of closed herself about the idea of love. She thinks that there's no boy alive who can love her because what she is & not in spite of it; because of her brilliance & not just her pretty face. Considering she's a little crazy, she might have been right. But then HE COMES AROUND & AAAH... Reason #2 of why a sequel is needed This is how I like my romances to happen. & just that. It was perfect. I want more of this (the contradictions) & more of them (the unexplored passion). The end was so very sweet, after that roller coaster of stuff they did & thought about each other, it was amazing. But I also need... more. Something more. I need to see, er, read them go beyond "this kiss I will give you is real". To finally see each other as they are, without the masks & with the secrets on the table. The sequel's plot should unite them AND challenge them as a couple. OH, YES! PLEASE, somebody hear this, I am begging you!! Talking about Justen, he was my great dilemma. One moment I was reaching for the darts to knock him out, the next I was loving him. What. I know, I didn't get it. & he bought Persis act too easily, he SHOULD have known better, so I kind of wanted to slap him, too. Anyway, I think that in this regard, one of the best parts of the book is when it hits him that he may have been more interested in her than he pretended to be. That he cared! Vania's visit had proved that. After all, she'd as good as threatened Persis yesterday. And Justen had almost bitten her head of for it. Dude, the realization made him want to slam his head on a wall. Now. Reason #3 of why a sequel is needed The women in this book are pure kickass material! They are so badass, & the boys... well, they used their brain, which is good, too! So Justen is a genius & Persis is badass as shit, okay. But Isla, OMG! Princess Regent Isla (along with Andrine, who is a total lady) was a master of regal shut-the-fuck-up faces. I LOVED how she managed her precarious situation on the power, given that the neighboring country had killed its queen & that the Councilman in her nation didn't respect her or acknowledge her as ruler because she is a woman. & she kicked some ass, too! In her very royal, queenly way, of course. "You think they like you because you're soft on them. But all you're teaching them is that you're soft." Now Isla did turn, and fixed Councilman Shift with her most royal glare. "And if I let your insult pass unpunished, sir? What am I teaching  you?" Shift's mouth snapped shut. In her defense, Councilman Shift was a total asshole. Also, it was her idea that Persis & Justen faked a relationship, so he could stay in Albion & do his anti-revolutionary investigation, while Persis could collect information from the enemy. Considering all the above, that can never be a bad idea. I see what you did there, Diana Peterfreund. In one hand we have Galatea, currently under a revolutionary rule of terror, previously ruled by a queen for hundreds of years. Where the problem is class inequality. On the other we have Albion, an almost paradise, ruled by kings since recently. Where the problem is gender inequality, & where the diseased King's daughter can't do more than wait for her baby brother to grow up & take the throne. *slow clapping* That. Reason #4 of why a sequel is needed Just imagine all the social, political & ideological things a sequel could deal with! That's be wonderful (specially if the darlings are involved). Plus some Andromeda's guilt, *muajajaja* Please! *sigh* It was everything I love in a romantic development & action, just bring another book & my year will be complete. No joke. I'll be waiting.

I loved this. Which I was not at all expecting, because I basically had no idea what this would be about, beyond what the summary told me. And I think it's better that way. It's better not knowing about the time-travel angle until it's first mentioned in the book itself, because it means I figured it out less quickly than I otherwise might have. I loved how this is such a simple story, yet with a few complex elements thrown in. I loved Miranda and all her classmates, and her mom and Richard and pretty much just every character in this book. Speaking of Richard, I was very pleased that there was absolutely no drama surrounding his character (as is often the case with a stepdad-figure) and no animosity or resentment of any kind on Miranda's part. That was really rather refreshing. This is one of those rare books that made me want to read it again right away after finishing. I could go on and on and start listing everything that made it work for me (including how much I loved the setting, also), but let's just say that I thought this was great, and leave it at that.

I am giving this book 1 start because I didn't connect with the story or the characters. My most hated quote: "I just want to forget it ever happened, in some ways. But in other ways? It was all that kept me sane" - Caden Yep, I don't think Caden feels regret... This book narrates the events after Ever wakes up from her coma, to find her sister abandoning her and her husband falling apart because of his guilt. Cheating always has consequences, and we realize that Caden knew that since the beginning, he always knew there was a possibility of Ever waking up, and that she was going to suffer because of his selfish actions. I guess that's why I don't like this story - the people who Ever loves the most, Eden and Caden, betrayed her, they both knew what they were doing was wrong, and that there was the possibility of Ever waking up and suffering, and THEY DIDN'T CARE! And I got the impression that Caden would do it all over again if presented with the circumstances, he even admit it to it. At the end of the book, Ever forgives them both and they all live uncomfortably but "HEA". Ever and Caden end up renewing their vows and raising Eden's and Caden's child. If I was Ever, I would always be wondering - is Caden thinking about me or is he thinking about my sister while having sex - kind of hard to let that one go. Sorry! This unjustified, selfish form of cheating is not my cup of tea!

I avoided this book for some time, under the vague impression that it was all about how special books are, how special people who read books are, how Great Literature can change your life. I hate stuff like that. The Uncommon Reader does have that theme, but in a completely unpretentious, charming way. The Queen is a wonderful character and the book is very funny. I love how disturbed the palace staff is by the Queen's new hobby - they can't quite figure out why reading books is a problem, but are sure that it is. And, of course, as the Queen grows bored with her duties and expands her mental horizons, they are proven perfectly correct.

Well that was different. Not my usual kind of comparison, but there are moments when you watch a show like Defiance or Life on Mars where suddenly everything clicks. You believe that the universe that's being shown to you could exist somewhere, and you see how everything fits together. The House of Shattered Wings is strongest when it has moments like this -- where you suddenly see how a disgraced Immortal from the Jade Empire could find himself in post-Fall Paris, struggling to survive . It's weakest when it focuses on plot. By the end of the book, I found myself completely indifferent to the actual story being told -- it's the world that drew me in. I'm looking forward to the sequel.

"I think you should learn, of course, and some days you must learn a great deal. But you should also have days when you allow what is already in you to swell up inside of you until it touches everything. And you can feel it inside you. If you never take time out to let that happen, then you just accumulate facts, and they begin to rattle around inside of you. You can make noise with them, but never really feel anything with them. It's hollow. "Here's a book that's lost none of its charm. Siblings Claudia and Jamie run away together and live in the Metropolitan Museum of Art for a week, uncovering a Michelangelo-related mystery and, along the way, learning a few things about family, grammar, and the joy of knowing secrets. "New York is a great city to hide out. No one notices no one. "Like all the best children's books, its example is disgraceful. The two children have only the dimmest sense of the panic they've thrown their parents into, they break into a museum repeatedly, and they cheerfully throw backpacks into sarcophagi and sleep in historically valuable beds. They also steal. Children who follow their advice will be very bad children. In addition, it's logistically improbable that any of this would work. "Everything gets over, and nothing is ever enough. Except the part you carry with you. It's the same as going on a vacation. Some people spend all their time on a vacation taking pictures so that when they get home they can show their friends evidence that they had a good time. They don't pause to let the vacation enter inside of them and take that home. "But for engendering a sense of the mystery and magic of art, and a sense of adventure, it is exemplary. And it's a wonderful New York book, no less today than it was in 1967. "If you think of doing something in New York City, you can be certain that at east two thousand other people have that same thought. Before this I'd never read a book about a closeted guy before and the angst that surrounded this was pretty intense. I enjoyed the first book- it was a little formulaic but it was a good read- but this book is so much better. I felt so much more involved with the characters and invested in their happiness. Basically this book is about Mac and his coming to terms with, accepting and being proud of who he is. Tony takes a bit of a back seat which is a shame, but Mac's journey was really a lovely one to read. Obviously he was pushed by tension/events/angst which I won't go into- so it kept me on my toes. Did not want to stop reading. In fact I think I read the whole thing in two sittings. Ben and Anna were ridiculously adorable and put a big grin on my face even during the worst moments. What gorgeous children. When Mac started to man up and come through for Tony it was just excellent, he was perfect and I was so proud of him and his journey. That's what I liked about this book. The murder sub plot was quite interesting for a while but was then it sort of lost momentum and I stopped caring except from how it directly impacted their little family. A bit more development with that would have been welcome though I suppose it would have detracted from the main focus - Mac. Only issues: I get the whole overcoming adversity thing but are police stations really like that?! I've read far too many books recently with massively stereotypical homophobic policemen - I'm sorry, which century are we in? I find it so difficult to believe that people like this still exist, let alone are allowed to carry a gun and call themselves a policeman... This may be hopelessly naive of me but sometimes I just scoffed at the screen- who has such ridiculous and hateful opinions? But yeah I enjoyed it but I don't feel the need to carry on the rest of the series. I enjoyed the whole Mac accepting who he was aspect of this book and now it's been resolved, I don't need any more. In my mind they have their HEA and, at least for now, I'm happy to leave it there.

When I picked Fairest up, I honestly thought by the time I finished reading it, I would have at least a small ounce of sympathy for Levana. I'd read Winter. I knew the truth behind her glamour and what had happened to her. Maybe it wasn't her fault she'd turned out so power hungry and terrible. Maybe the point of Fairest was to show that not all evil starts out as evil, even the evil Queen has tragedies in her past that are worth mourning over. Well, I was very clearly wrong. All Fairest did was just solidified my opinion that Levana is a delusional power hungry, selfish scared little girl who has let herself be ruled by her own jealously. And I think that might have been the point. There were very few instantaneous in this book that I felt any sympathy at all for young Levana. The only time I felt any at all for her, where in regards to her sister, Channery. Channery makes Levana look like a sweet cupcake in comparison. Channery literally manipulated her sister into burning herself in a fire because she was angry and made herself out to be the hero who tried to save her when the guards came in. She left Levana with a terrible scar on her body and not to mention herself esteem, which she never failed to take advantage of whenever she got the chance. It was a mercy that Cinder/Selene never had to meet or be raised by her mother because I cannot imagine what she would have turned out like if she had. Even her step mother was better than Channery would have been as parent. But as fair as my sympathy for Levana, that's where it stops. Everything else that happened to her, is her own fault, breed her own greed, jealously and unquenchable desire for power. I thought from reading Winter that her previous marriage to Winter's father, Evert, was a bit of love story. She fell in love with a palace guard who her sister didn't approve of but she married him anyway because it was true love but then something tragic happened and he was taken away from her, so then she become an evil Queen. But no. Levana didn't need any tragic accident to become a evil queen. She was literally just made that way. I was so shocked and disgusted when she started to manipulate Evert to fall in love with her after his wife died. She had this delusion so built up in her mind that he secretly loved her that she glamoured herself to look like Sol and tortured him with it until he was forced to give in and marry her for the good of himself and his child, Winter. The whole wedding scene was almost as revolting to me to read as Levana's wedding to Kai - though I don't think much can top that. I was literally in tears trying to get through that ceremony - and it just convinced me that Levana deserved absolutely everything that she got at the end of Winter. She was terrifying to read about when she was scheming about taking over Earth and changing the labor laws on Luna because he genuinely felt that what she was doing was for the good for Luna. She honestly thought the people loved her. She felt she deserved to be Queen and that Cinder/Selene would ruin everything for her and the Lunar people, so she had her set on fire and felt little to no remorse about it. That was probably one of the most disturbing sections to read from this story, how Levana came up with her fantasy of killing off Cinder/Selene and then how it unfolded. Dragging Winter away for a doctor's appointment, Selene waving at her from underneath the fork they'd built, and knowing the whole time that those were the last moments Cinder would ever get to be whole again. It was so heartbreaking and it just made me hate Levana more for what she did. And the icing on the cake was when, to further her own power, she staged an assassination of her own "husband", her own love, so she could make a marriage alliance with Earth, leaving poor Winter fatherless and left to the disposal of that terrible court. This book is just proof that she is just as terrible and vile, if not more so, than we originally believed her to be. But while I did gain no sympathy for her, I did come to understand her better. I can see why she hides behind her vial and why she's so paranoid about her own reflection. Her sister did irreversible damage to her that she's carried around her entire life. But that doesn't excuse what she's done or her intentions. She made her own choices and in the end she paid for them.
