Katie Porter is the pen name for authors Carrie Lofty and Lorelei Brown. Because of that, and because the series name is Vegas Top Guns, featuring some hottie air force pilots, I wanted to read this one. Unfortunately, I was kind of disappointed. Major Ryan Haverty is a pilot and instructor at a base in Las Vegas. One night out with some fellow pilots, he sets his eyes on a waitress named Cassandra. He sees her with her skirt and pantyhose with the seams up the back, and can barely drag his eyes away. Ryan grew up in a trailer park surrounded by people who openly talked about sex. Because of that (maybe?) he has convinced himself that he likes really dirty things in the bedroom (role play especially) and his previous fiance left him because of this. He would never let this desire be known to the public because he is too shamed. As a reader, this annoyed me because I feel like we truly never dive into this issue/insecurity he has. So he likes his sex partners to dress up as a french maid. I don't think this is too out of line kinky. But for whatever reason, this shames him. Cassandra works part-time in an art gallery, and is just waitressing until she has enough money, or a position available to move to the gallery full-time. She notices Ryan watching her in the restaurant, and after some big-time flirting, they head out on the town together. As Cass says: After half a year of polite and frankly inadequate lovemaking, Cass wanted to go for it. She wanted to have sex with the man who'd hit on an eighteen (blackjack). Something hot and daring. A memory in the making. "Tonight I like fast," she whispered. They plan to have a weekend full of fun, adventurous, carefree sex, which turns into much more. There is a lot of sex in this book, and it is dirty. I don't have a problem with the actual sex scenes. And I didn't necessarily mind how fast they start having a physical relationship. As I mentioned, there is a lot of role playing - french maid, high class hooker, that type of stuff. Ryan gets off on Cassandra wearing pigtails and telling him what a naughty man he is. Cassandra gets off on it too, although they don't really communicate that well with each other. Ryan is very screwed up over his big confession to his previous fiance that he likes things a little more spicy in the bedroom. Very shamed, always thinking Cassandra is going to come to her senses and treat him the same way once she realizes 'who' he really is. He brings this up to himself several times: "Yes, sir," she breathed. Oh shit, did he like that or what? He was turning out to be more of a sicko than he'd though. Or Regular people shut the doors and turned down the lights. Good, regular men didn't ask women to dress up and play stupid sex games. He wanted to at least make the attempt, no matter what turned him on. After this one risky night, he'd go back to being sane. Normal. Or He was rapidly starting to suspect Cassandra was a woman worth knowing. That meant treating her with the respect she deserved. No more weird stuff. Besides, sex had been fantastic no matter what they did. He didn't need seamed stockings and French accents. Wouldn't let himself need them. Dude - get a grip. First of all, from night one, they start with role play and never once does Cassandra object to it. It is actually her idea to go to an adult sex store and go into the dressing room to try things on. So why Ryan would think she isn't into this type of sexual play, I have no idea. Plus, the extent of their role play is dressing up and maybe talking in an accent. Nothing kinky. Or maybe I've read too many erotic books lately, but this is all pretty vanilla stuff. I didn't understand Ryan's mind frame at all and got so tired of his constant worrying over it because he never stopped doing it. And Cassandra never complained once. Outside of the sex scenes, I got bored and annoyed with the storyline. Nothing to keep me interested in reading. While Ryan obsessed over being such a dirty, sicko of a man, Cassandra fell kind of flat (although I did like her forwardness in the bedroom) and the story kind of fell apart for me. Rating: C-

I was hesitant picking this book. It was sold as a complete Nerdgasm for 80s kids. A complete nostalgia run. However, I'm a kid of the mid 90s. My nostalgia stems from Lord the Rings, Doctor Who, Battlestar Galatica and corny British children's TV. I'm not by any means a massive know it all of 80s stuff, although I love the Princess Bride, Time Bandits and the Breakfast Club. However, I'm less enamoured by certain aspects of 80s Pop Culture (Blade Runner, for anyone interested). Despite this, the constant 80s references weren't jarring and it made for quite an enjoyable read. The reason they weren't jarring? Because they were minutely explained by our narrator, Wade. And, here, begins our multitude of problems. This book is well loved and has risen to fame because it makes mid thirty year olds remember their youth, yet each bit of 80s culture is minutely explained and I was confused at who the audience was. 30 year olds with peter pan syndrome? Young adults born in the 1990s? It was helpful for me, as I knew exactly what Wade was on about, but what kind of vibe are you going for? This wasn't just a problem with the 80s references. The entire writing was an utter shambles. Firstly, Cline info dumps all. the. time. 99% of the time, it's not even interesting stuff that's crucial to the story. Nope, it's just incredibly dull window dressing. Nothing's described, it's just flat out told in the most awkward way. Secondly, the writing is first person. I don't like first person as much as third. Doubtless, first person can be done well, but this was no such case. Wade tells you stuff all the time, you can't infer or determine for yourself how he feels or what his relationship with said person is. It encourages lazy reading, and I was, for at least the first 70 pages bored. I don't want to be told that I-r0k is an 'obnoxious poseur' I want to be able to infer that for myself. Not only the writing, but the characters were all such charming special snowflakes. I have a feeling that the shitty writing over emphasised the special-ness of Wade. He was, especially in the first half, an obnoxious little know it all, and we had no perspective from this because it was all in damn first person. He was Hermione Granger prior to the troll in Harry Potter. The amazing lack of grief/ feeling towards characters was intense. Was I meant to weep for that old lady? You can't make me believe someone is your friend just because you say they are. This of course brings me onto something I was very annoyed with through the novel. He becomes obsessed with Art3mis, who is a sassy, strong female. You know what I mean. He saves her photos onto his hard drive, stalks her, obsessively reads her blog. Art3mis stood up to this obsession by saying 'you don't know me in real life', but Ready Player One was obviously a male nerd fantasy. Which is fine, if that's what you're into, but I'm not. Each woman you meet is either :  dead, dying, love interest, posing as male etc. The ultimate annoyance was Kira. Og's wife. She was booutiful, smart and the object of desire of two men, best friends who don't speak to each other because, get this: James didn't get the girl. Kira and Og creates their house to look like Riverrun, and creates games for kids to play, and woops oh no she gets killed before the story even starts! Don't worry readers, this woman whose only impact on the story is that she was lowved by James, is his obsession and the final puzzle is unlocked by her name! Ugh. This book just alienated me, after seeing lists of male creators and then all the female characters just treated as objects of desire... Can we not? Never the less this was not a complete crapfest, the world was unique and mesmerising and I very much enjoyed the quest and being in OASIS. Ultimately though, this book would have been far more successful as a film, something I would pay to see. Anyway instead of picking this up again, I'm just going to rewatch BSG

SPOILERS BELOW! This is a difficult book to review which is why I'm leaving it right on the halfway point with 3 stars. Everything about this book seems to echo the old media statement "Give the people what they want." On the one hand it's a good thing. RM clearly loves her fans and wants to please them. And the fans love her. On the other, it makes for a predictable book that treats everything with kid gloves. It's almost as if she found a check lists of all the things fans wanted to see happen and just went through adding them to the book. Adrian and Dimitri being related was never even mentioned as a possibility in the other books but I'd seen the theory on dozens of forums, especially here on goodreads. Rose and Dimitri able to have a baby...that one was everywhere. Marriage proposals, Alchemist changes, etc. etc. Just about everything fans asked for is in here. Which unfortunately means the book didn't take any risks whatsoever. All the challenges that the characters faced were pretty easily overcome. Human magic was quite interesting when it was first introduced to the series, now it seems that there is a spell for everything you can think of. Even the Harry Potter-verse had limits to what magic can and can't do but there doesn't seem to be any in this one. It got to the point where I was waiting for someone to say: "we need to teleport to Jupiter, breath in a zero oxygen environment and create a particle accelerator in two hours!" "No problem, I have just the spell for that!" Err...okay. And while I get Neil's decision, I don't get Olive's at all. A bunch of crazed monsters are attacking the camp, I'm pregnant, in labour and don't even have a weapon. This is the perfect time for me to run away by my self! WHAT?! ARE YOU FUCKING HIGH? For that utterly stupid decision alone she deserved to die. Nina ends up with a pretty crappy deal in all this too but all the main characters get a HEA so I guess it doesn't matter...*sigh* After reading this I would love to see RM go the complete opposite way with another spin-off. She could do a SUICIDE SQUAD version of VA. Get Tasha Ozera, Nina, Alicia, Avery and Neil into a group and have them doing so seriously crazy shit! That would get me excited because as soon as I saw the pattern of everyone getting what they wanted emerging, I got a bit bored with this book. Still it was nice to see everything wrapped up and although it came way too easy, (Love will conquer all? Hell, a monkey with bells palsy could conquer all when it's this easy) I'm glad everyone (minus Nina, Olive and Neil) ended up in a good place.

It was okay. That's it. Just okay. I don't think it was terribly written, but I don't think it was well-written either. I will start off with some positive notes. I enjoyed the main character, Dennaleia. I love her feminity, her sincerity, her gentleness, her wits, and how brave she eventually become. I love Nils, I think he's a great character and I truly cherish his friendship with Mare. I also like Casmiel. Now...on to the not so positive thoughts about the book. First off, the title bothers me. "Of Fire" makes perfect sense, but "and Stars" does not as it did not have any significant in the book. Maybe until like the very very end, but hardly any I did not have a lot of expectation diving into Of Fire and Stars. My only expectation for it was just some decent romance between the two princesses. Sadly, it didn't even reach that expectation of mine, and it wasn't even a lot that I was asking for. Was there romance? Yes, but it was seriously lacking. I feel like it was aimed to create this slow-burning romance between Denna and Mare, but it was not executed well at all. There were bits of hints from Denna's side about her growing romantic interest in Mare, but we didn't get any of that from Mare's side. Though suddenly, she was in love with Denna? The book was uninteresting for the most part. For more than half of the book, I simply continued to read just see if anything interesting was going to happened. It did get better in the last 150 pages, but it should have been interesting sooner because up until then there was nothing that was exciting to me. And the lack of world-building bothers me a lot. After finishing the book, I still have no clue of its settings and surroundings. When does it take place? What does the kingdom look like? What do the people look like? What do they wear? More explanation regarding The Six and how the magic works would have been nice. The Six were mentioned at least once per page, yet we hardly know anything about them except that it was significant and people worship them. Magic plays a heavy part in this book, but the explanation of it was very vague. So vague, that you don't exactly know how magic truly works in this world. The book was heavy on politics that makes very little sense. All we know is that Mynaria hates magic.....BUT WHY??! Why do they hate magic so much? What has happened that caused them to hate magic? There was hardly any character development. We were barely given any backstory for the characters to explain why they turned out the way they are or why they treated each other they way they do. For example, Mare's relationship with Thandi as it seemed like they were once civil when they were younger, so what changed? Or Mare's relationship with Nils, as it seemed that they might have once been lovers, but what have changed to have them be just friends now? Also...why did Nils have to die?? I see no reason why he must die. He was one of the very few intelligent characters, and it was really sad that he was easily killed off. This, I truly cannot accept. Of Fire and Stars had such a great potential to become an iconic YA with LGBTQIA+ representation, but very sadly those opportunities were missed. I have read fan-fictions that were better written and executed.

Well this was the first Laurann Dohner book where my brain wasn't screaming 'Raaaaaaaaaaape' for most of the book. (Or at least very ambiguous consent). However, this was probably the weakest of all her stuff I've read. Wait, that might not be fair. I didn't dislike it. It didn't bug me. It just seemed... weak. Her cyborg series I have issues with, but that's mostly the personality issues and coldness/raaaaaaape. The New Species I had issues with at first as the dialogue felt forced and raaaaaaaape. But then I grew to absolutely love the series, which both the rape and dialogue issues for the most part have been dealt with. The Zorn Warriors were my first delve into her works, and again dialogue and raaaaaaaape issues (well, the first book. the latter ones not so much). But those series, even with the dialogue issues, had much more overall development, and a stronger base. This just felt a little weak. The series had promise with Scarred and Kilt in Something Wicked This Way Comes, but it just so far doesn't seem to be living up. Plot was pretty basic. Alpha finds the gal he wants/rescues her. Another female wants the Alpha. He says no. She goes away. Alpha and gal mate. New random female whom we never met before attacks them because she wanted to be his mate. (It would have been better if it had been the first female and less out of left field.) The dialogue... meh. The female Jasmine (to which she gets referred to as Mine. And he is Chase. Mine To Chase. Hmm... trying to be clever there with the title tie in. Found it just awkward instead. ), I can see she was trying to make Jasmine witty and different, so when Chase first finds her locked away near death you get a weak "hi. did you buy that property I showed you?" Really? Again, I realize she was trying to be witty and different but it came across as blase considering the situation she was in. Then boom, she's turning and must be mated etc etc. Rush rush rush. Oh, and super secret den isn't so super secret since another wolf found them, not only found them but walked right in. Walked right in through the super secret chambers into their bedroom. He's supposedly living / sleeping in the equivalent of the batcave's panic room, but yet a wolf he doesn't like just strolls right in unexplained other than "i followed you." Then, the big dramatic action at the end? Our main character Justine literally passed out and everything happened off book. Really? Not a strong female character at all. I wouldn't be surprised if she pissed herself when she passed out. TSTL. Chase was a bit of an ass. I don't remember him from the first story in Scarred and Kilt. But he was definitely an ass in this one. He was meant to be an ass. So that Jasmine could yell at him that he's being an ass and thus show that 'she is the only one who can temper him and he could immediately be a better man.' Meh. I'll read the next, but I don't hold much hope for it. Much rather have her New Species series.

"People lie. They use you and they lie, all the while feeding you bullshit about being loyal and never leaving you. No one can make that promise, because life is all about seasons, and season change." Where do I start with this book? I'm struggling to finish this book actually. When I see the blurb and the cover, I'm expecting something fast-paced, intense and intriguing, but in the end it leaves me with.. Confusion. One thing that drawn me in is because it's written by Tarryn Fisher. No doubt, she's an incredible writer, deeply talented and this book is so beautifully written--with a bit prose here and there--but it's getting fizzled out more and more towards the end. This book revolves around the story of Senna and her ex, Isaac. Senna is a piece of work, absolutely. She's emotionally detached from everything except herself. She has a quite dark past which leads her to be cold, miserable, mistrustful, selfish, self-absorbed and broken one. I don't know, maybe because there's no any spesific backgrounds for her I feel like I can't get into her character. I keep waiting for what Fisher's trying to do with her, or is there any significant character development for her but in the end I can say I don't give any F for her. She's simply an annoying bland character and I don't know why some people loved her. Like, c'mon?! Constrastingly with Isaac, he's a very likable character. He's easy on the eyes, smart, anything you'll look for a man actually. "You've been silent your whole life. You were silent when we met, silent when you suffered. Silent when life kept hitting you. I was like that too, a little. But not like you. You are a stillness. And I tried to move you. It didn't work. But that doesn't mean you didn't move me. I heard everything you didn't say. I heard it so loudly that I couldn't shut it off. Your silence, Senna, I hear it so loudly." See? He's dreamy! What makes me baffled is, as a man who has those potentials, he again and again chasing a girl like Senna. I just don't get it. You're just too precious, Isaac. The story itself is quite good. It has potential but sometimes--even with Fisher's flawless writing--I feel like it's so far-fetched, too fictional and too wordy at some part. This book is packed with twists and turns, but they failed to surprised me. I keep reading because I'm so eager to know who done this to Senna and Isaac, but when the zookeeper (according to Senna) revealed, I'm like "Oh okay, we got 'em, so? What's next?". When I said I left with confusion, I mean it. I don't get the reason why the kidnapper do that to them, is it that simple? And when Senna's another ex coming out, I'm puzzled, what's so special that you see in her? To be real guys, she doesn't deserve you all. And all the things happened to Senna, it's like rubbing salt to the wound, she's been kidnapped for 14 months, got raped, got double mastectomy, got broken bones that'll never healed properly, has emotional breakdown and breakthrough, and then she got another cancer and then she's killed in the end?! , like what the F did I just read? This is obviously a heavy read. It's a psychological thriller and it plays with your mind. The idea of this book is interesting but fails in execution. In my case, it draines me emotionally and leaves me with big WTF feeling. But despite of the disappointing ending, I'd still recommend this to you, especially Gillian Flynn's fans, but don't put too high expectations for this.

trigger warnings for: transphobia, lesbophobia/homophobia, rape mentions, multiple secondary character deaths, amputation, physical violence, emotional abuse An #ownvoices novel with a teen trans lesbian superhero protagonist!! Sign me up. Honestly it was the protagonist that completely drew me to this book, and I have come out the other side adoring Danny. Dreadnought follows Danny Tozer, a 15 year old transgirl who witnesses the death of Dreadnought, the strongest superhero in her city, and inherits his powers as a result. The story then follows her immediate transition (being given Dreadnought's powers gives her her ideal body), her navigating what it means to be a superhero, and subsequent investigation and battle with the novel's Big Bad. Dreadnought definitely felt like a decent premise for a comic (and I got the feeling that April Daniels might have a little bit of a preference for Marvel), but it also totally works as a book. I LOVE that trans superheroes are coming to the forefront as central characters, with Alters (again those comic leanings) last September, and now with Dreadnought. Another one of the strong points of Dreadnought, that I wish we saw more of, was the relationship between Danny/Dreadnought and Sarah/Calamity. I loved that they learned things from each other and that Danny finally had someone in her life who she could trust and be safe with, even if she usually seemed to be in the most danger she'd ever faced with Calamity. Their friendship (though I really wouldn't mind if it developed into more) was definitely one of the most enjoyable parts of the story for me. I think the world building was good, as were the two ending battles. The idea of Danny being able to see a lattice as part of her powers was interesting to me because I haven't read anything like that before, and I'd love to see Danny exploring her powers a bit more in the future. One of the reasons why I didn't give this book five stars, is the sheer amount of transphobia and homophobia that Danny experiences. It really really made me uncomfortable, but I know that this is probably realistic. Danny receives it from almost everyone she encounters in the book. After coming out to her friend and rejecting him, he says he hopes she gets raped, which is frankly disgusting. Honestly most of the men in this book are absolute garbage, and the ones who aren't as bad as the rest end up dying , which ended up making me feel tired and distressed on Danny's behalf. I also think some parts of the story weren't given enough time, like Danny's interactions with the Legion (I thought they'd play a bigger part), Danny discovering and developing her powers, Utopia's motivations, and some of the secondary characters. Some of these may be addressed later but I'm not entirely sure. The difference between the majority of the female (I'm including Doc Impossible in this) characters and the majority of the male characters really highlighted how strong the female characters were, and I loved it, but I would've liked it better if Danny had some support from some male characters too, or just more support from the ones who did support her. Whilst Dreadnought isn't perfect, it is mostly a fun read and I am really looking forward to the sequel which is out this July. Read this book for Danny (and Sarah). Read this book for on page trans and lesbian rep, with those words being used multiple times. Read this book for the ending.

Claire Takata has very few memories of her father who died ten years ago when she was still a child. When she finds a mysterious letter from father to her stepfather - who she believed had never met each other - she enlists the help of her brothers and several other boys in the neighborhood to help her figure out who her father really was. Claire discovers that her father had been part of the yakuza - a Japanese organized crime syndicate, and she soon realizes that her investigation may have revealed her family's location to enemies of her father who are still out for revenge. The novel begins with the main character tied to a chair getting shouted at and slapped around by an unknown assailant. It gives the impression that the reader is in for an action-packed thriller. Unfortunately, this is not the case. On the positive side, Ink and Ashes has a diverse cast of characters and incorporates interesting elements of Japanese culture. For those who prefer to avoid books with teens behaving badly - drinking, drugs, sex, swearing - this would fit the bill. There is some violence, but that's about it. On the negative side, this book was way too long. There were so many details that didn't serve a purpose and could have easily been cut out to keep the plot moving along at a steadier clip. The character of Claire did not ring true for me nor did her relationships with the boys of the "Axis Powers," who were at times hard to distinguish from one another. The romance that develops between Claire and Forrest was so obviously going to happen and then sort of sickening when it finally did. It was a distraction from the central mystery of the book that only served to bog down the plot more. The adults in this book, though not the central focus, had some issues that were hard to ignore. Claire's mother exists quietly in the background preparing meals while her stepfather is constantly taking off on mysterious business trips. He makes up for this by being insanely overprotective in a borderline sexist manner when he is home. SPOILER: Neither is worse than her deceased father who it turns out was a criminal who murdered a teenage girl because her father owed money to his boss. It's fine to have characters who are terrible people but it doesn't seem like any of the shortcomings of the parents in this book are ever addressed, and everyone just seems ok with the knowledge that dear old dad murdered a teenage girl! Though this novel had potential, it ultimately fell flat for me. Optional purchase.

"You looked at me without an ounce of pity. You saw me. Not the chair or the injury. You saw me. It was the first time I'd felt ... seen. Felt awake, in a long time." Sarah J. Maas delivers all the feels with TOWER OF DAWN. Loyal readers of the series have long awaited to see how Chaol's narrative would unwind, what path he would take following all that's transpired. This story certainly gave us that and more. We saw deeper story lines for other characters like Nesryn and Yrene too (more on Yrene below). Front and center, however, was Chaol's journey of healing. Chaol--who has always been loyal, strong--shattered right along with the glass castle. He's been ripped apart emotionally, roiling in guilt over the blame he feels for letting his men, those he cares for, down. Now, his broken body sits in a chair, a vessel for his deeply broken spirit. So he and Nesryn travel to Antica, in hopes the legendary healers of the Torre Cesme will heal his body. They also hope to make allies of the southern empire in the looming war. Nesryn and Chaol meet the current khagan (Urus) and his children (one of which will be chosen to rule): Arghun, Sartaq, Hasar, Kashin and Duva. The youngest of them all, Tumelun, is at the center of a mysterious circumstance which has upset the entire family. All these new characters, along with the healers we meet, are crucial to Nesryn and Chaol's futures, as fates twine together in ways unforeseen. We meet Yrene Towers, a profoundly gifted healer who is sent to work on Chaol. Their relationship begins antagonistically and Yrene challenges Chaol every step of the way. Chaol must face his emotional demons if he is to heal physically--a task that Yrene discovers is much more difficult than expected. Echoes of the dark power that struck him remain, along with the many memories Chaol wishes to forget. "You may look at me with resentment Yrene Towers, and I will not blame you for it. But believe me when I say there is no one in Erilea who loathes me more than I do myself." Their fates tangle together in so many ways, and they both heal essential parts of the other. What's really beautiful about Chaol's journey is how intimate it felt, how he was able to dissociate physical vitality from core, emotional self-worth... meaning he learned to accept who he is now, that his disability didn't define him. There were so many times, especially nearing the end, when I couldn't stop crying from how certain scenes affected me, how devastated I felt as other scenes unfolded. Nesryn's story is a different one. She finally embarks on an adventure that takes her to some seriously scary places, confronting bone-chilling adversaries. Nesryn learns shocking truths that affect the bigger ToG story line too. There were so many evocative moments, details, threads in this book. I truly loved it--it was so much more than I expected. I loved Yrene and so many of the new characters. Their stories added a richness and depth I didn't know I needed and as usual, Maas took the time to explore their pasts and presents, their motivations and place in the higher story arc. And the end... gahhh CHILLS. I can't wait to continue on with the series and see what happens next. There is one more thing to say, but if you'd like to avoid spoilers, please stop here (and go read the book!) I also recommend you read THE ASSASSIN'S BLADE--which is the compilation of novellas, ideally before you read this book, although it's not necessary. I knew from very early on that Maas was switching love interests (from the moment Yrene walked in the room). While I don't mind that happening in books, I feel like it's probably happened one too many times. I worry that I'll begin holding back on investing myself in the relationships she builds in her stories. I think she runs the danger of diluting her ethos, making readers gun-shy to really believe and fall for the connections she's trying to build. So while this didn't really affect my overall rating--because honestly, I do love Chaol and Yrene together, and Nesryn and Sartaq--I think this is something to watch in novels to come. I love her books so much that I would just hate for that to weaken the emotional impact of any story she delivers.

"I smelled jasmine first - then saw stars. A sea of stars flickering beyond glowing pillars of moonstone that framed the sweeping view of endless snowcapped mountains. Welcome to the Night Court.." Setting: 4.5 out of 5 The world building in this book improved incredibly! We get to see the infamous Night Court in all its glory, and I couldn't have been more fascinated by Velaris and the Summer Court. Writing: 4.8 out of 5 This book kept me on edge the entire second half of the book! Sarah truly impressed me in this story so much, from the different back stories to the fighting scenes. The romance is full throttle and ohmysweetbabyjesus! By the end of the book, I WAS OBSESSED. The end of ACOTAR left me feeling curious, but the end of this one had me gearing up for my ships in battle! Character development: 4 out of 5 The single reason that I absolutely loved this book was because of Sarah's exceptional ability to make her readers love these characters! Feyre has always been this badass huntress but in the beginning of this book, she's broken. No one with a good heart would hurt innocent people and leave unscathed, and Feyre is no exception. Before starting this book, I was aware that there was another love interest. So when Rhysand posed as the bad boy in ACOTAR and then switched to this brooding guy, it threw me off at first - until I remembered that he bet on her in one of Amarantha's tasks. I still remember that part of ACOTAR making me think twice about who he really is. Feyre's character ARC is remarkable, and I couldn't be more proud of her for really modeling a strong female protagonist. Similarly, Rhysand's story and motives are fully revealed in this book, which makes him more charming than ever. The backstories also introduce several new characters that make the story beautifully well-rounded. Morrigan, Cassian, Azriel, Amren, and even Tarquin have a little piece of my heart. They emulate love and loyalty and prove themselves to be of the best. However, this is also my only issue with the book: the lack of diversity. The only character I could slightly see myself in is Amren, and I don't even know what kind of creature she is! On top of that, the characters were basically paired off with each other, which seemed too perfect and unrealistic. It's not that I loved them any less but I wanted more for them. Plot twist / storyline: 5 out of 5 The cliffhanger is BRILLIANT! It's ironic how Tamlin really turned out to be the Beast, which was problematic in the first few pages, but the King of Hybern? I will personally send him to hell myself for what he did to Nesta and Elain. "Until then," I said, staring toward the door as if I might see her walk through it, laughing and vibrant and beautiful, "we go to war." 4.60 stars

Mostly I think I loved this book. I can't stop thinking about it so that definitely says something. I finished it last night. I thought about it all this morning while getting ready for work, re-read the beginning and the end (twice) and now am sitting here gathering my thoughts to write a review for it. Let me say that this is not at all what I expected. I have read my fair share of Rock N' Roll books. I think I expected gritty, dirty, drama and lots of sex. I honestly should probably read through spoiler free reviews sometimes before I read a book because that was not what this book was at all. This was a journey and a story and I really got carried away with it. It just flowed so well for me. There was never too much of any one specific think to weigh the story down. Friends, the band, a record deal and touring all just happened. No lengthy craziness just fact. I loved that. So, I guess this was not the story of the band and was more the story of Jake and Parker. Well, hmmm...Ok, I loved them. Their friendship was beautiful. I mean, from the minute they met you could just feel it. They were just going to be best friends. This was going to be a friends to lovers story like no other and I was excited! I couldn't wait for them to realize what was between them and how much more it could be. But I did wait and wait and wait. But, no worries, the story was good so the wait was ok and the buildup was exciting and then, it happened and I just got confused, irritated and kind of angry. I swear I just kept saying WHAT? over and over in my head. My flowing journey kind of hit a road bump, you know like a record scratching? For as easy as this story was the entire time up until now this bit of "drama" and anger was not easy and changed the dynamic of the story. Don't read this part if you haven't read the book because I got some shit to say and it will spoil everything for you. Be warned. Ok, in order for Jake and Parker to be together there were some obstacles. Out of nowhere confusing obstacles. So, I guess the first thing I had to come to terms with was the fact that my beloved Jake was considered a whore? Really? Not just a whore but I guess a bad one, love em' and leave em' and do this often kind of guy. Um, I don't get it. I mean, there were only two guys mentioned, I guess the rest I just had to create in my head. I guess I was supposed to know he was out every night getting laid. I don't know when he was doing that though since it wasn't really explained. Next up, second obstacle, we find out Parker is gay. Well, I think we all kind of figured he was or was going to be or something but no, he gets outed in a very public way and it made me confused. I get that he never came out because of his parents but now, he has been disowned by his parents, is 25 years old, has been on his own and still doesn't come out. Ok, that is cool but now he has a roommate who is gay and is his best friend and I guess he still couldn't tell anyone. I don't think he was in denial, I think he knew he was gay I guess from what I can gather I think it was so ingrained in his brain that it was wrong that he just didn't do anything about it either way. So fine, I didn't like how this happened but yeah! It happened and now my boys are going to get somewhere and be together. Jake has realized he is in love with Parker and needs to tell him so they can ride off into the sunset...No. Of course this isn't what happens. What does happen is so out of character and so not the same as the rest of the story. Third obstacle...Parker now wants almost nothing to do with Jake. You know, Jake is a whore and only wants in Parker's pants. WHATTTTT??? Parker, Jake is your best friend and he loves you, he is your roommate and your band mate, YOU KNOW HIM and now you don't trust him, at all? I mean, you don't even seem to want to be friends with him anymore! WHAT??? Why is Parker doing this? He is out and he obviously wants to be with Jake but this is the road he takes? This is when we needed his POV. Maybe Jake came home every night after whoring and ran his mouth about it? Maybe Parker has been fighting his feelings for Jake because of who he thinks Jake is? I don't know. I guess that is what I am supposed to believe at this point but it was HARD to believe. Parker was angry about the blog entries too. He said all Jake was doing was talking about getting in his pants. I never saw them like that. I mean he spoke of Parker as his best friend and that he loved him. Yes, he called him his very hot best friend and did mention wanting him in his bed but he never once thought that would ever happen so why did this bother Parker so much? So, now I think they just lived in the same house for two weeks but really didn't interact or something. Ughhh...But now, FINALLY this is going to happen. Jake has had it and is going to get Parker, tell him how he feels and man, I can feel that sunset on my face...or maybe not. Fourth and final obstacle...Jake's move to win Parker, the let's be together, let me prove to you this is for real and a relationship and in order to prove that to you...WE WON'T HAVE SEX. Huh? This was just nuts and stupid. I guess I just don't understand why he has so much to prove to Parker to begin with. He doesn't just have to prove this is more than sex there are other fucking stupid frustrating rules as well. HE CAN'T SAY I LOVE YOU! He is actually not allowed to say it until Parker says he can. Seriously, I loved Parker the entire book until now. Here, this one is even better, Parker wants to keep it a secret. WHY???? Seriously, all of this would make sense if Jake just met Parker, pursued him and is trying to win him over but this is not what we are dealing with in this story. They did not just meet and Parker knows Jake and knows he wouldn't hurt him. But ok, the obstacles are out of the way. Parker agrees to give Jake a chance and now, finally they are together, secretly but together. Together like teenagers, abstaining from sex to prove some crazy makes no sense point but beautifully together. By this point though, I just lost the wind in my sails...Yes, I was kind of happy but not gushing like I thought I would be. I wasn't happy with what Parker was putting Jake through and I wasn't happy that Jake was ok with it. It's one thing to do anything for the other person because you love them so fucking much but seriously, it was like Parker wanted Jake to be someone different or something and that wasn't cool. Getting over the bump in the road wasn't easy and it didn't make me happy and then, well, the book kind of just wraps up fast. After what I went through to get the HEA I deserved more. Some "we are really together "time, something. I wanted to see them in love and happy. Honestly, I didn't even get to HEAR HIM SAY I LOVE YOU BECAUSE PARKER STOPPED HIM AGAIN!! Not to mention there was like one real sex scene. Come on! Anyway, all that in the spoilers and everything else I said does not mean I didn't like this book because seriously, even after that huge rant I am still thinking about it and I did truly like it. Not 5's obviously but no doubt a solid 4's. It was a great journey that I was really happy to go on. It was their journey and I didn't have to like their choices to like them as a couple and still thoroughly enjoy the story. Jake is one of the best characters and I would have never tired of hearing his voice. So, with this one, the great outweighed the bad and the frustrating (for the moment, right now, with more thought I could possible change my mind) and I am really glad I read it. Oh, one more thing. What was up with the footnotes? Now, I enjoyed them but I did not enjoy the interruption in my reading flow. I ended up keeping them open on one Kindle and reading on my other one. I don't know why they weren't just part of the book. Read.

I can't believe this series is over! While a lot of mysteries were explained and I feel I know a little bit more about the Baudelaires' lives and VFD, I still think a lot of things were left unsaid  why was the sugar bow so important? and where did it end up?? and if Count Olaf didn't set the fire in the Baudelaire mansion, who did?? and not everything was wrapped up in the way I wanted it to be. I still enjoyed the process of reading this series, however. Lemony Snicket's writing style is very metafictional (which I supposed it would have to be since  the author is also a character in the book  ) which is fun, though it can get a bit tiring sometimes, but that is middle grade. I had fun reading those books though, particularly the second half of the series, when the themes and the story gets a little more complex than just the Baudelaires running from guardian to guardian and from Count Olaf (whose story arc ends also with him in a more complex light than just that one dimensional villainous villain from book one). I think this series was definitely worth reading and I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys stories and mysteries. 2.5 stars. Hollowland was my favourite Amanda Hocking book, so my hopes may have been too high for this, it's sequel, and disappointment was inevitable. The first book left off with Remy doing a very brave thing that could have led to all sorts of interesting story lines...but unfortunately didn't. I don't know whether Hocking was maybe trying to create a real sense of 'hollowness' with this plot but that's how it felt. I like dystopia and don't expect Disney endings but there has to be some kind of point or lesson behind that bleakness and that didn't really come through for me other than the very unsubtle dialogues about appreciating small moments of happiness when you get them etc, etc. One of the reasons I usually find myself wanting to read a sequel is because I liked the characters and want to see what will happen to them next, so I was sad that Harlow and Lazlo occupied so little time in the text. Even Ripley was sidelined and didn't really feel there - which sums up a lot of the style of this book. Although there is plenty of action nothing really new happens and it all feels a bit rushed. There are quite a few character decisions and behaviour which didn't seem to make much sense  Why would they treat Remy so badly? How likely is it she could have survived multiple invasive surgeries without pain medication - surely she would have gone into shock and died? Why would they evacuate and just leave her tied up on the table if she was the last hope for mankind to find a cure? Why would Tatum - a soldier - wander off so stupidly to pee on some bushes when he had showed himself to be so resourceful and, come to that - what exactly was the point of killing him off, only to replace him with a virtual carbon copy in the shape of Boden? and virtually no detail devoted to describing the new characters, settings or even the dystopian vision/science. In many ways I know it could all be argued as being more 'realistic' but I couldn't help feeling that this sequel was largely pointless. It's not an awful book or even a maddeningly frustrating one but it just seems like a massively wasted opportunity, which is a real shame.
Love, Regret, String Theory... What if you could do it all over? Choose a pivotal point in your life and make a different decision. Would you do it? TWISTS ON TWISTS WITH A TWIST ON TOP.

"I have a story that will make you believe in God." The first part of the book contains Pi's exploration of three different faiths and ends with Pi's unanswered question of why he can't belong to all three. As someone who identifies as atheist I think it raises a good point, to me they are fundamentally so similar that they can't be mutually exclusive. The subject is dealt with the wit and humour it deserves as it does the experience of growing up with an older brother and somewhat distant parents. The second (and by far the largest) part of the book barely mentions God, religion or faith, and that if those words had been erased I wouldn't have noticed. It is also the part of the book which I found incredibly difficult to stop reading; the low battery warning on my phone being the reason I noticed I had lost a many hours in the book to Pi's tests of courage and perseverance. A Pan's Labyrinth-inspired retelling of Peter Pan - a retelling that follows closer to the original story, where Peter is an awful little shit, instead of the scrappy Disney hero - should have been My Shit. Alas, Unhooked is not My Shit. Somehow, despite all the easy potential for greatness, it manages to be uninspired, and generic, and, most insultingly, forgettable. Gwen is your typical YA heroine: bland and inoffensive. She's a reactionary character instead of one that instigates, and the extent of her characterization is her "specialness" and her relationship with the love interest. Though there is some genuine importance given to her relationship with her best friend, which I appreciate - even if I feel the relationship's importance is given too little build up by the time Maxwell tries to cash in on the supposed emotional investment. Olivia herself has too little characterization to compel me to care one way or another about her fate or Gwen's attachment to her. And I'm not sure how I'm supposed to care about Olivia when I could barely bring myself to care about Gwen. The Neverland characters are the only ones with marginal sparks of inventiveness. We have, here, the beginnings of a creepily deceptive Pan, a broken and morally bankrupt Hook, and a cunning, wild, vicious Tinker Bell. But the novel never lets them shine as they should because, well... they aren't the main characters. Their stories are restricted by Gwen's story and everything about Gwen is so very tame. Maxwell had some very good ideas. Taking Pan back to his original, disturbing likeness is appreciated. But somehow, despite going that route, the novel still remains safe. This is joining the ever growing list of YA novels that promise me darkness and danger and gray haze, only to shell out the same old harmless, vanilla narrative. Once again, disappointed yo.

So this is supposed to be a retelling of the polar bear fairy-tale, which I'm sure everyone who's browsing this book is familiar with, so I'm not even going to go into it. I also read the East of the Moon, West of the Sun and the book East, so you might say I've now entered into the elite club that specializes in the polar fairy tale collection. This book was not as bad as a lot of the reviews make it out to be. I thought it was a humorous and very contemporary take on the story, and I really don't think that the "birth control problem" that a lot of the other reviewers disliked was that big of a deal. Basically, she was taking birth control and Bear "fixed" her problem without telling her. But he didn't know that she was purposefully taking it and had no idea that it was intentional, so he thought he was helping to fix her health. That's how I took it from what was written. And don't get me wrong, I am very against guys trying to force their children on women, rapists, etc. But I really don't think that was what happened here. Seriously. I think my bigger question is why on earth would she have been taking birth control? I mean, the girl is only 17 or 19 (I forget which) and she's been in the Artic her whole life, living with her father and his (much older) research assistants and other postdoctoral candidates. Why the heck would she have needed the birth control?? There was no talk of her getting on birth control at all, and how would she have gotten it? She wouldn't have been doing hanky-panky with the other research assistants as some were her dad's age, or the other guys -- that would have been gross. So, that is my problem with the script. Also, Bear said it pretty loud and clear that he expected children, so the author really should have put in somewhere something about her actively NOT wanting to have kids (understandable; she's a kid) and secretly getting on birth control to stop his impregnating scheme. So that was kind of out of the blue. Other than that, I thought it was well done, especially the getting to the troll part -- very creative, and I like how that was done. And frankly, she had to be pregnant in order to give birth on troll land -- for the story and its ending to play out. So I can see why she had to be pregnant. And the going to Sedna and Father Forest and the North Wind, I liked all that. Some of the other reviewers were against all that and thought the beginning dragged out. I thought that was weird -- I mean, we were hardly into the first two chapters before the Bear shows up and by the fourth or fifth, they're already having a good time. So I don't know where the dragging out is. Unless they wanted MORE romance, but frankly the fairy isn't totally a "romance" fairy tale as it is a girl kicking butt in order to find her man -- not terribly heroic, but better than a girl waiting around for a man to come kicking butt to save her. And for once, this is a retelling that spends some time talking about trials she has to go through in order to reach him. Seriously, in the original fairy tale, that's where most of the action and narrative is. So, if you're looking for pure romance, this is probably not the way to go. But the main character is pretty feisty and kick-butt, and the retelling is pretty creative and I for one enjoyed the description as she travelled from one climate to the next...and she travels through a lot.

After falling in love with Peter Kenny's performance in The Player of Games I knew I was going to read the entire Culture series in Audiobook form. This has been a great decision up until "Excession". Banks is a great writer and Kenny is a great narrator so the failing is mostly on me but I really struggled to stay focused on this story for a variety of reasons. This is the first Culture book that does not have a main point of view character, it is more of an ensemble piece. Granted we spent more time with Gaynar Half-Owen (I'm sure that is not the correct spelling but that is what I'm going with!) but compared to our other viewpoint characters he is a little underwritten. There are huge cast of names to keep track of and most of these are "minds" sentient AI ships with quirky names. The problem with every ship having a quirky name is it is impossible to remember which ship did or said what. Well, except "Meatfucker" who could forget good ol Meatfucker. All of the communication between ships start with a long sequence of coordinates before each sentence which Kenny delivers in a kind of sing-song voice which became like an automatic cue for my brain to wonder what I am going to watch on Netflix next and whether Ada Palmer might marry me if I composed my fan letter oh-so-perfectly. Which is to say that my mind wandered a hell of a lot during this audiobook. A Culture story about the Minds and a Big Dumb Object is something I am very interested in but the format and subtleties of the plot kept me from really enjoying this. Too often it felt like homework. After I had finished I had to go and read up online to make sure I got everything I was supposed to. (I hadn't) It makes me feel better that a lot of people who read the paper book also struggled to follow everything going one. I'm not sure whether it was good or bad writing that frequently in the story a bunch of incomprehensible text would go by and then one of the human characters would just outright ask "what is going on" and we would get a sort of cliff notes version of what had just transpired. Banks is great at writing aliens and alien diplomacy and I thought the Affront were a fine addition to his pantheon. As much as I wanted to get inside the mind of the Minds I found myself enjoying the story most when it honed in on the Affront rather than another side plot with nondescript humans and Minds. (contains a spoiler for Use of Weapons as well) Use of Weapons was the last full Culture story I read with "State of the art" short stories in between. In Use of Weapons we find that the guy we were reading about is really the other guy we were reading about. It's a little bloody weird that in the very next novel we find that the character "Buyer" is really Gaynar Half-Owen" right? Like he JUST pulled that trick and now he does it again throwing in a sex change to really keep us off the scent? "Excession" is an interesting story about an "Outside context problem" where the Culture mighty as they are, are like ants to the next class of beings. It was just a real brain strain to pull out all of the details.

I really liked this story. It's always fun to find a fantasy tale with a m/m spin. This was wonderful because it focused on the plot and the characters and it wasn't graphic at all, like many m/m stories feel the need to be, even when it doesn't suit the plot. I liked the characters and the universe building and I wouldn't mind getting to read more of this world.

Note: I originally gave this series a three star review, but looking back on it I felt that it deserved less. 2'nd review (written on the 1'st of January 2014) First of all, I must admit that I didn't hate this book, at all. I found that it was a light and easy read, which I overall enjoyed and even liked quite a bit. But the thing that counted the most for me when reviewing and rating this book (I gave it two out of five stars), was that it was average. I've read it before, just with different names. I mean, the premise is basically the same as in The House of Night series by P.C and Kirsten Cast, with the badass heroine and the best friend who isn't like everybody else. What I found was very evident with this book, was that it was a first in a series. Nothing wrong about that, I assure you, I've read Marked and Dead Until Dark, but Vampire Academy was just a build-up. I felt that everything that was said and done were just to set the premise of the world and overall quite boring. I've heard that once you get through the first and the second book, this series gets oodles better, but I'm not interested in reading a series that gets better when it's not all that good to begin with. I've done that before, but life is too short to wait for a book series to get better. Of course, if I were to get the books for free, that would be a whole different matter. But it definitively wasn't bad. I just felt that it could have been shortened down, and maybe the writer could have put the first and the second book into one. Removed some of the cattiness and drama, and gone over to actually having a plot. Because when I read it, I was looking for a plot and some personality in the book, but it felt just like every other teenage read ever. A huge issue I had with this particular read though is the self-harm. I don't have anything against the self-harm in itself, because it is an issue that definitively needs to be addressed in young-adult fiction, it's just that it wasn't addressed. It existed for one or two pages, Rose told her to stop, she stopped. They didn't resolve the issue; it was just quit cold turkey. If you're going to address these kinds of issues in your books, then do it properly you moron. That was my thoughts after reading that part of the book. This had a lot to do with the rather low rating, because it probably lost a whole star for it. Just a question at the end: Why does every female vampy character have to be so damned sarcastic? Is it some kind of unwritten rule? Rose is good at it, Zoey Redbird is probably the queen of sarcasm (and whoring around, but that's for another time), Bella from Twilight isn't lost behind a wagon on it, and Sookie Stackhouse as well. I'm just wondering. Overall, as I've pointed out earlier, I enjoyed it, but it just didn't do enough for me. I liked the general plot a lot better than the House of Night series though, even though I missed the funny writing style and easy comedy from the latter, but Rose is a much more likeable character than Zoey. Even though both of them are very easily distracted by the opposite sex. I'm not going to go into the writing style, except for the fact that there were a few phrases and sentences I cringed at. But that's the case with a lot of newer writing, so I'm not going to bitch and moan too much about them. The writing in this was much better than that of the Switched book I reviewed earlier though, so I guess there is no complaining. Two out of five stars, would have three if there was a bit more character depth and issues were actually addressed. 1'st review (written when I first read it So. Yes. Vampire Academy. Let's just for a second take into account that I've read fanfiction better than this. But then again, I mostly read very good fanfiction. But some sentences I thought. WTF. Because I've read bad fanfiction better than that, you know? Overall. I liked it. It was light and easy and a great way for me to avoid writing my examns. If I obtain the other books cheap/free, I will read the rest. If not, I won't. It's clear that this is the start of a series, because it was kind of... I dunno, catty and not-important. I hope that when I read the second book, I will be more impressed with that. But and taking the new review policy into mind it wasn't bad per se. I just feel that it could have been shortened down a little bit. No. The plot could have been tighter. That's it. I didn't spot any plot holes though, but that could just be me not looking to closely. I'm just rambling. Never take my reviews into account for reading a book, because it's only what I mean. And this one, I can't really make up my mind about. I liked it, but I didn't like it. A question: Why does every female vampy character have to be so damned sarcastic? (read: the female vampy characters I've read about). It's Rose, and Zoey Redbird (from Marked) and Bella from (Twilight). I liked this a whole lot better than House of Night though. I missed the funny-writing and easy comedy from the HoN series, but I felt the character sort of had more depth? Even though both Rose and Zoey are boy-crazed and easily distracted. I'm not going to compare it to Twilight, because I have so many contradicting feelings about Twilight it's not even funny. I can compare one thing though. Bella and Rose. We don't really find out what they look like. Just that they have long, brown hair and (in Roses case) big boobs. I dunno. I'm gonna stop now.

Embedded in various levels of the Corhonase court, three spies from the enemy nation of Laurent, known to each other only by numbers, spend their days ferreting out valuable intelligence to pass on to their guardian. Just when they are given an even more vital mission - retrieving a secret code book that will allow the Laurentine military to decipher Corhonase communications - the Corhonase call in a spycatcher with a particular knack for compelling people to tell him the truth. With their lives in ever more imminent jeopardy and their cover identities (unbeknownst to each other) about to be locked in an arranged marriage that both parties dread, spies Saliel and Athan must step ever more carefully to complete their mission and get back home alive. I was hoping for a complex and compelling plot filled with intrigue and unexpected twists, but the whole espionage part of the story suffered from vague worldbuilding and plot holes (how inept are these spies that they can't even recognize each others' voices and almost accidentally betray themselves in conversation?!) and I didn't overly care for either of the main characters - Athan with his prejudices and hypocrisy ("I love you, Saliel, marry me! - Wait, you were born where? Ewww, that's disgusting, get away from me, how could I ever have allowed myself to touch you?! - No, I've reconsidered, I still love you despite your awful background, marry me!! - Wait, you're a witch?! Eww, how disgusting, I should turn you in and have you burned, how could I ever have allowed myself to touch you?!? - No, wait, I love you and want to spend my life with you after all, what's a little witchy stuff when you're sooo hot? How dare anyone be prejudiced against you, they should be ashamed of themselves!!" REALLY??) and whiny and frequently useless Saliel - so all their yes-no-maybe-agonizing over their feelings mostly just anoyed me.
>i>And the Mountains Echoed is a great book, but what really makes it interesting is that it isn't just one story, but rather a collection of stories intertwined with each other.
