Orginally posted at A Bookalicious Story. *3.5 stars* I've always loved tales of the sea, and have yet to find the perfect mermaid novel. The first time I laid eyes on OF POSEIDON was at Rachel's blog, My Reading Pile, and naturally, I went a little crazy after seeing that it will only be released a few months later. But then I chanced upon it on Netgalley, and needless to say, I requested it immediately. I started this book with very high expectations, as is the case with all mermaid novels (I have no idea why), and....I was quite disappointed actually. Not that it wasn't good, it's just not as good as what I was anticipating it to be, what with that stellar cover, intriguing title and storyline. My Brief Summary Emma is truly a klutz when on land - all two left feet and all - and when on a vacation with her best friend, Chloe, she tripped on her own foot and sprawled on top of one Galen Forza. One of the most handsome and sexy guys she's ever seen and she practically fell on him. But what Galen sees isn't a clumsy girl, he sees her impossibly purple eyes - a trait that can only mean she's one of them. A part of Syrena. But why doesn't she transform when she went into the water? How is it that she's living on land when one of the laws that govern their people is that all Syrenas are forbidden to go on land, much less stay there? And the fact that she doesn't recognise him as royalty? He's determined to find out as his mission on land is to be the ambassador of Syrena in the human world and to solve any Syrena-related issues on land. Emma's in for a shock as she finds herself face-to-face again with that handsome stranger in front of her locker back at school, and practically in every of her classes. He finds out that she has absolutely no knowledge of the world beneath the sea, and she finds out that the one person she's falling for is the Prince of Syrena. But then, if his mission is to teach her of her ancestry and such, then doesn't that mean what he feels for her isn't what she's always thought it to be? That she's just another person he has to get close to to complete his mission? Apart from emotional problems, she still has to worry about the underwater stalker behind her house. Is it friend or foe? Is Emma in danger underwater? My Thoughts Let me start with what I did like about OF POSEIDON: THE COVER!! It's absolutely stunning! The girl in a white dress underwater? The mysterious, dark blue sea around her? The title, the font...Everything's so surreal! Then comes the plot. Though the pace was relatively slow throughout the book, the plot did thicken and the pace did this crazy crescendo at the end, finally ending with a...cliffhanger!! One thing I dislike the most is cliffhangers, but the final revelation at the end was enough to shock me for awhile that I overlooked it quite entirely. Galen was trying to figure out who was stalking Emma the past couple of days whenever they enter the water, Syrenas being able to sense another of their kind when both are within range of each other under the shoreline. He was finally putting together the pieces and, BOOM - he revealed the person in his own cool style! You won't even be able to see it coming! I loved any stories related to the ocean, and incorporating powers and adventures underwater was enough to make me more than a little engrossed. For a surprise gift, Galen even brought Emma to see the infamous Titanic, docked at the bottom of the Atlantis. Emma was a kindred, compassionate heroine who cried for those who lost their lives aboard the Titanic when Galen brought her to see the ship. She's loyal to her friends even in the face of danger. However, one thing that I did not like about her was that she kept fainting. She came across as weak initially. Every time Galen tells her something big, she goes all woozy and...faints. It's supposed to be because of some biological change in her that's making her unstable for awhile, but still, it was rather annoying as it was only explained at a later time. Banks' writing style was cool, especially when she incorporated mindblowing facts about things which I know already, but haven't thought about it in depth. For example, she said that everyone had a finite number of heartbeats, that if your heart beat faster, you'd have a shorter life. Thus turtles, whose heartbeats per minute are incredibly low, live to about a century or more. I haven't confirmed the fact yet, but it does coincide with the evidence. Fallacy or not, it is some fodder for the mind, is it not? :P However, there is this one phrase that caught my attention: "whisper yell". That's a contradiction all by itself. I've seen this a couple of times already, is this a proper phrase? As in, approved by Cambridge? Or just some common authors' mistake? Now on to the things that I did not like. As I've mentioned earlier, the pace could be maddeningly slow at times. I took some time to finish reading this book, and I attribute it to the fact that I got bored a number of times. I'm not a fan of Contemporary Romance, and OF POSEIDON did tend towards that genre as Galen went to school with Emma, and them hanging out together at Galen's. I do like paranormal high school romances - as in, the supernatural hero and heroine goes to a regular, human high school kind of thing (cliched, yes I know) - but not when it becomes the typical teen romance where everything's so....adolescent and monotone. But I must concede the point that it did get very romantic at times. :X Haha. Swoon~ Not only with Galen and Emma, but with some other side characters who were just as...sexy as Galen. If not more. Galen's a cool hero, as far as I'm concerned, but not what I expected. He's brooding, he's a prince, he's a protective, possessive guy, he's handsome, everything's good. It's just...he's too perfect and typical a love interest in this genre. I've seen male protagonists of his ilk one too many times in the Paranormal Romance, Urban Fantasy, YA Lit section, don't you think? I wanted something more, something that will make a deep enough impression to let me remember him long after I've reached the The End. Someone like Christian Grey...hubba hubba... Haha, but that aside, my expectations were higher too because mermaids have always been one of my favourite mythical creatures, and for him to fall short... Hmm.. There was this loophole that I've spotted. *Please do not read it if you haven't read the book. MAJOR spoilers! If Emma's mom is Nalia, then Galen has surely met her before because she was Grom's intended, and therefore recognise her both in terms of appearance and when he sense her in water. Then how is it that he didn't when he saw her at Emma's house? Or when he sensed that underwater stalker, how did he not recognise that pulse he sensed? Other than that, I thought that OF POSEIDON was a pretty average, light, mermaid read. If you're in need of some YA Romance, part Contemporary, part Urban Fantasy, then maybe you'd like to try this out. P.S. Though there isn't a sequel announced for OF POSEIDON yet, the odds look good for one. That cliffhanger needs a resolution!! And there is still much that can happen, so yes, I'm hopeful. *eARC courtesy of Feiwel & Friends via Netgalley.

This book was recommended to me as part of a Goodreads Recommendation Swap in one of my Goodreads groups. I had a feeling this was not going to be my new favorite when I picked it up, but I enjoyed it more than I thought I would. I thought the book started off slow, but I wouldn't go so far as to say it was boring. At first, I didn't understand why there were so many characters and I started confusing people (especially because some of them had similar names.) Once things started picking up, I enjoyed the book much better. I liked the way the characters' stories were woven and how they all came together. My big set-back, however, was in the fantasy aspect. I am a bit of an avid fantasy/paranormal reader, and even with the main characters being fantasy creatures, I found the fantasy aspects lacking. The magic just wasn't there for me like I wanted it to. Considering the novel focuses on two creatures of fantasy, I wish that their potential had been explored further and really showcased in a stronger light. I think this would be good for someone possibly wanting to bridge in to fantasy and test the waters, because it was definitely more of a historical fiction with some fantasy elements.

I am so disappointed with this book, and the way it ended. The first part of the book felt long and dragged out, while the last 20 pages or so felt rushed...like the author was trying to tie up loose ends just to finish the book Penelope is still a bitch who has her sights set on the Prince of Bavaria, even though she is still married to Henry. Her social standing is in jeopardy as she flaunts her affair with the Prince all over NYC. She actually agrees to divorce Henry because she believes that the Prince is going to marry her. But in the end, she gets exactly what she deserves...a Prince that was just using her and a loveless marriage where both her and Henry will continue to have affairs . Henry is still spineless, although he doesn't seem to be much of a drinker anymore. It's the same thing with Henry that has been going on in the last two books...he can't stand up to his father and tell him that he is in love with Diana. Unfortunately, when he finally does tell his father that he wants to divorce Penelope, the father drops dead of a heart attack. Of course, Henry blames himself. When he finally gets the courage to tell Penelope that he wants a divorce, she agrees, and he proposes marriage to Diana. Of course, nothing is simple, and Diana chooses to go to Paris instead of marrying Henry . Oh Diana! How I hated you by the end of this book. All you did for two whole books was fantasize about you being married to Henry and then when he finally proposed to you, you tell him that you can't marry him and run off to live in Paris. I just don't get it. I mean Henry was even willing to come with you, but you refused that too. Why did you have such a sudden change of heart? Elizabeth finally finds out the truth about Snowden. Although I had suspected that Snowden was the one who had killed Will for a while now, I never dreamed that he would basically hold Elizabeth prisoner, and had plans to kill her after the baby was born. When Elizabeth shoved Snowden down the stairs, and he died, I was so happy for her that she had the strength to do it. But then she gives credit to he dead husband Will, who she believes was there in her and with her, and it was him who really killed Snowden. Come on! The man was drugging you and holding you prisoner. He was planning to kill you once the baby was born. Elizabeth should have been happy she was able to escape him and kill him in the process. Of course, Teddy comes swooping in to save the day, and marries Elizabeth. They have a bunch of kids and live happily ever after. Amazingly Carolina was the only character that I really liked. I did feel sorry for her marriage falling apart, but she came out on top again, and managed to create a beautiful life for her and her sister. I have had this series on my to-read shelf for so long. I had such high hopes for it. I was so disappointed. Oh well.
I'm calling it quits at page 39, although I don't like having unfinished books on my shelf. I'm disappointed, but I just can't get into this book.

The chase is on as Diana levels up her seduction game to win her husband back! Diana Steinbeck fully indulges herself in the BDSM realm the way she wanted to. Being a sub to her husband, Adam Steinbeck. However, Adam doesn't want her to be a submissive and as an experienced Dom, loving a sub was never in his league. He thought of her more than a consensual relationship and he wants her safe. With Diana's persuasion, is it possible Adam reconsiders t? Will she be able to save their marriage or part ways for good? The other book I'm reading was slow and I'm on the verge of having a reading slump, I decided to pick this one up. The conclusion in this duet was good and I like it but most parts were dragged out and I expected more. The story was less intense in comparison to the first book. Diana was stubborn and Adam becomes tamer Dom. I'm more invested with Adam's POV because he's complex and we get to hear his reasons on why he protects Diana from engaging in BDSM. It's well explained in my opinion. Final rating: 3 / 5

IMO it's more enjoyable & better written than most YA fantasy stuff these days, & the main characters (except Akiva ) are generally likable & interesting if you don't mind a little wish fulfillment. I personally like Karou's life & art in Prague more than the war stories in secondary world & the Romeo & Juliet style love story. The ending is promising though. OTHO, if you have issue w/ Edward/Bella relationship you might have issue w/ the romance in this book also.

I really liked this book. It was mostly slow during the middle, but it turned out to be an interesting read. Braith has some anger issues to work out, though. The ending left me with so many emotions, but I think that had to do with the overreactions to the situation. I mean, really? If Braith stopped for like 3 seconds he would have realized what happened and would have calmed down to assess the situation. But no. He had to go all incredible Hulk on us and break his room. Goodness! Pull. Yourself. Together. And lets not even get started on Aria. She was just like, "He betrayed me? Okay, I'll leave." Knowing full well that Jack was trying everything in his power to get her to leave as soon as he could. Now she thinks Braith never really wanted her for anything more than as a blood slave. Even though he clearly has feelings for her and there's a lot more to the situation then she cared to look at. They both just so easily dismiss each others attraction to the other at the first sign of rejection. Ugh! It made me want to slap them and let them know they are not betraying each other, if they would just open their eyes and notice! Even Braith can't use his blindness as an excuse for not seeing the truth in the situation. No excuses guys! Geez.. You know what this means? Aria is going to fall onto Max as her rebound guy! Woo! The next book will be fun! *rolls eye* Anyways! Great story, I'll be getting the second one asap.

Yesterday, a love was born. No, joke. I love this book so much that I finished it in one day, and I'm already on the second one(I don't read very fast). So, I'm going to try to write a review people can understand. Ok, so this book had litterally changed the way I look at books and how I review. It has set the bar really high. After being stuck in the Vampire Kisses(overalll series ratng: 2) and the Vampire Diaries(overall series rating: 3.5), I was in need of a good series for once. I made the mistake of constructing my to-read list by genre at first, which meant a lot of vampire series in a row. This one was a breath of fresh air, and I knew it would be. Everyone on Goodreads who reads youg adult books raved about this series, so I had high expectations. And boy were they met. The only reason I gave this book 4 instead of 5 stars is because of the high school drama, which hoestly wasn't that bad, and because there wasn't much of a plot. But I know somewhere in the next few books there will be a five. I know it. The world was very interesting and dynamic, although at the beginning it was hard to understand. There are the Moroi, good vampires, who can control the elements and have other powers. Some of the Moroi are royal, and they have an entire vampire royal class. Then there ae the Dhampir's. They are half vampires, half human, and their job is to protect the Moroi from the Strigoi(I forgot how it's spelled). The Strigoi are immortal vampires, and are evil. They are in a war with the Moroi. That's the gist of the world, there is so much more, but you learn about it as you go. The books are about Rose and Lissa. Lissa is a Moroi princess, and has powers beyond the elements, which is very rare among the Moroi(you find out more about this later). Rose is a Dhampir, and she is Lissa's guardian, as well as her best friend. First of all I loved Rose and Lissa's friendship, it was very real, and they are both very good characters. As a mater of fact, they are some of my favorite book characters to-date(that are female anyway). I don't want to give away the plot, but I HAVE to talk about the love interests. There is Dimitri(oh, hot Dimitri), who is Rose's mentor and trainer. I loved him so much(then again, I loved all the guys in this book(well most)). There is a spark between him and Rose, but they are forbidden to love each other. Then there is Christian. I love him and Lissa together, and I hope they stay together(and I love him too, of course). I also liked Mason, a good friend of Rose who has a crush on her. I really hope he finds somebody, since ROSE WILL BE FOREVER TAKEN BY DIMITRI. Just saying. Now, i have to end this review so I can go read Frostbite. Toodaloo.

This is a very quick, fun read, so much so that I feel a little mean giving such a low rating, but there were too many things that bugged me about it to go any higher. First of all, the CONSTANT '80s references were sort of cute at first, but they occur at such a ridiculously high volume that it rapidly becomes annoying. I was on board when it came to anything to do with the Hunt, when they were actually important, but when Wade is just sitting there going, "I saw a thing. It reminded me of that super-specific eighties reference. Also I turned on this iconic eighties song because I only like things from the eighties and nothing else," things got a little tedious. Next up, the dialogue. For the most part, it's okay, but there are so many instances of people saying things that no one would ever say, particularly to someone who is as familiar with the subject as you are. For example, at one point Aech goes, "It looks like Rivendell." And Wade says, "It looks exactly like Rivendell from the Lord of the Rings movies." What the hell, Wade? Aech clearly knows what Rivendell is, and we know that because Aech JUST referenced Rivendell! Why are you then elaborating to explain what it is? Having it as a narrative line such as, "Aech was right, it looked exactly like Rivendell from the Lord of the Rings movies" would have been fine, but as a line of dialogue it was absurd. That's definitely the worst example, but it's certainly not the only time something is over-explained to a room full of '80s gurus. The relationship with Art3mis. SO DINKY. Especially when they're at that dance club for Og's birthday. If you've ever read any dinky teen romance, you knew where this was going. Dance clubs as a plot device are just an excuse for "suddenly, the music changed and a slow song came on" (although in this case, they have to explicitly state which 80's song that slow song is) so that the characters can have a heartfelt bit of dialogue while they are in super close proximity. I don't want to spoil anything, but suffice it to say, the whole exchange was difficult to get through because the level of teen angst was through the roof. Anyway, I know it seems like I hated this, but I really didn't. Those things I just mentioned were annoying, and certainly took away from this getting a better review, but it's got a good pace, a fun story, and the Hunt is really cool. It should just probably be re-categorized as a teen novel so you know what you're getting yourself into.

5 stars!! Woahh I loved this book! I don't even know where to start, because I don't want to ruin the story for you, and trust me, it's worth the read. As a fan of love triangles, I must say this is pretty unique. There's no cheating, wich is a plus for me, and I liked both men, wich made everything even more interesting. This was my first book by Lisa Desrochers and it won't be the last one, because the writing was amazing. The story was realistic and original, since most of the story takes place in Rome, with a lot of distance between the two guys the heroine is interested in, and that's something you don't see so often in NA books. The characters were very likeable, even though sometimes you'd like to get some sense into Lexie, because some of her actions were questionable, but after all she was an enjoyable heroine, and really funny. The humor in the story makes the "taboo" thing lighter, it takes away some of the seriousness of the religion topic, wich could be difficult to understand depending on the people who is reading it, so in my opinion the author did a fantastic job with that. Also I found great how passionate Lisa made Lexie about art. She expressed her love for it perfectly, and you could picture yourself walking around the streets of Rome and looking at the Sistine Chapel. Things like those make a storyline even more complete and with a deeper meaning, so it was kind of educational too. Now about the characters. About the men. Oh, the men. I liked Trent right away. Maybe I was expecting a more complicated taboo situation, but overall it was good the way things happened. Trent was sweet, caring, and I loved his relationship with Lexie. He was there when she needed him, and viceversa, and he was going through some issues that only Lexie knew about. So yeah, I fell in love with him from the very first page. And then we have Alessandro. One of my favorite things about this story was how unconventional those guys were. I'm used to read about bad boys and womanizers, so I was impressed and amazed by Trent and especially Alessandro. This author made it clear how you can create something amazing without the typical troubled bad boy. Alessandro had his past, but he was trying to fix his mistakes by following his faith in God. We have a guy with morals and values, a sofisticated young man who gives you a sense of safety and confidence just by the way he talks and behaves. I absolutely loved his moments with Lexi, how little by little they become friends and everything develops from there. I don't thing the pace was slow or anything, I think all of that was necessary to comprehend how things could change and how that could affect someone's life or path. Lisa did an amazing work with that too, I felt everything and it made me think a lot. Another important thing that caught my attention was the fact that, for once, we don't see a very possesive or jealous guy over the girl. Both Trent and Alessandro wanted Lexie's happiness, and I loved how open she was about talking with them about her feelings, and they listened and gave her advice but they never acted possesive over her. While I loved both guys, I also had a favorite. I'm a hardcore and proud member of team Alessandro. I've read a lot of reviews and I saw most of you were team Trent, I could understand and respect that, but the good reverend has my heart. Maybe if Trent had more presence during the book my choice could be different, but we get to meet, know and love Alessandro from the start, and his personality (and yeah, also his looks and maybe the almost-priest thing) made me swoon over him. I felt a connection with his character that I didn't feel with Trent's. Alessandro gave me calm and I felt true admiration for him, after finding out about his past, and the way he cares about his family, and how easygoing and composed he is all the time. Also he is a great listener, and he always understands Lexie. He is a really unique character and I fell in love with him. I loved the relationship between Lexie and Alessandro, with her curiosity about his position of almost-priest and the funny situations between them (the erotic art scene was hilarious). And of course, he is sexy as hell. When he first kissed her my feelings were all over the place, and the moment when he asks her to take him as her lover, even though he knows she is in love with her stepbrother... oh God, no words. Nothing felt rushed with him, everything was perfect. So yeah, my heart was broken from 80% to the end, but I'm glad we're getting his book! The sad thing about love triangles is how dissapointed you feel when you have a favorite guy and he's not the choosen one. That was my case. But I don't think it would be fair if I judge the book by that, and this is a really good book that I highly recommend, and I'm not giving it 2 stars only because the end wasn't what I wanted (even though I'd suggest the author to write an alternative one, just because :P). Maybe said ending felt kinda rushed to me, but again, it could be the fact that my heart and mind were with the other guy, so I'm going to let it be. I think it's important to say, the sex and hot scenes were brilliant, charged of sexual chemistry and passion, and feelings. Well described and detailed, and also realistic, they left me breathless. And if I had to choose something this story shows and teaches you, is that everything happens for a reason, and everyone can find their path in life and where their heart is. Very well done, Lisa Desrochers. Now I can't wait for book #2!

I read books 3-7 in this series in two days (so I can't really separate out the plots well). Cute stories. I wish the characters were more likable and the fictional world of the book didn't have so many logical holes in it, but the creative plots kept me going to find out what the next adventure brought!

2 1/2 stars. I have a strange relationship with Victoria Aveyard, which mostly revolves around me picking up her books on a whim, reading them in a day and then rant about them. Because to be honest, I don't understand why so many people love this series so much. It's bland, it's dull, it borrows so many things from other popular YA series, becoming some kind of weird mash-up. The key for loving a fantasy book is in the world-building and the characters, right? Too bad, because this series lacked both. The world-building was pretty much non-existent, while being at the same time confusing. It's a dystopian novel (because if you don't write dystopia nowadays you're uncool), but it was vaguely mentioned that a long time ago there was a war and Silvers conquered the power. That's the only explanation we get. We have no idea why advanced technology exists, but everyone is wearing gowns and living in palaces. I still haven't understood why Norta is at war with other countries. And we're at book 2. The "characters". *coughs* Is Mare supposed to be a strong, likable heroine that makes a mistake once in a while? Because all I found here was an arrogant, annoying, self-entitled, selfish brat who somehow thinks she's above everyone else and elected herself the leader while there are other newbloods - Reds with Silver abilities - that have much more useful and cool powers than her. Mare thinks she is so important, that somehow every other character's actions revolve around her pretty much always. The other "characters" pale in comparison to her, but not because she is too good. Because literally none of them was fleshed out enough for the reader to care. They're just there for shock value, for useful powers, as tools to advance the plot. Cal's character was still as dull as ever, Maven was simply the madman sitting on the throne - and he could have been a gray character, he could have been so much more - every other Scarlet Guard member or newblood faded in the background. Something else the author will have to explain me is why on earth is Mare hated by all the female characters ever since this series started. I can't think of one female character who is friends with Mare. All the girls hate her on sight, even the newbloods who have no reason to (see Cameron Cole, who put up a fuss for nothing just to stir the plot a bit). She literally only surrounds herself with boys that pine over her, because she is oh so powerful, oh so tormented, such a leader. Despite my continuous dislike for this book, it was entertaining, more so than Red Queen. If you liked the first novel, you will probably enjoy this. I, however, think my journey with this series ends here.
Nice and exciting, but not my favourite of the series. Can't wait for more though clearly :D

I really loved Prized I wasn't sure if I would considering I had read some mediocre reviews about this novel and I had only given Birthmarked 3 stars. I was really surprised at just how much I loved this novel. On my second night of reading I read until 2 a.m. 2 a.m. I very rarely stay up late at night to read but I just could not put this book down. While reading the first novel I found myself somewhat bored and often would skip a paragraph or two if something had become drawn out. The only time I skipped a paragraph this time, which was hardly ever, was because I was so excited to see what was going to happen next and I couldn't handle the suspense. Their isn't must of an adventure in the novel,which I liked but Gaia is still her stubborn, rebellious self. (I'll talk more about that later though) Gaia enters a completely different world were the rules are far from the norm. In Sylum the women are in charge and make the rules. There is a shortage of women in this town which can only mean one thing for Gaia, that ever man in this city has a crush on her. In a way this part reminded me of Twilight. How Bella insists that she isn't beautiful and how all the men flock to her and that upsets her because she doesn't know what to do, especially when she befriends Jacob Black. This is exactly what happens to Gaia. She thinks she isn't beautiful because of her scar and that she could never be loved. You know how this story is going to turn out don't you? There are two men, who Gaia befriended, in particular who would chop off their right arm for Gaia if she asked them to. Of course she becomes confused on who she should pick and then Leon reappears (Oh how I love him) and things get even more confusing; not just for Gaia but for the city of Sylum. (That's the only thing that I wasn't crazy about in this novel, how at times Gaia reminded me of Bella Swan.) When Leon returns there is all this drama. If anyone who has read Hunger Games would notice the similarity of the situation with Gaia and Leon resembles Katniss and Peeta's situation when Peeta was captured and brain washed, but it's not as bad as that. Overall I really enjoyed this novel and I honestly wish Feb was here already just so I could start reading the next installment. I hate waiting. I can't to see how things go down when Leon and Gaia return to the enclave with the rest of Sylum. S**t is gonna go down! I can't wait to see how this plays out! Defiantly go pick up this book. Right now. Get in your car and drive to the nearest book store and get it, or download it to your e-reader. Note: I recommend reading Tortured (Book 1.5) before reading Prized. You can download it for free from Barnes and Nobles. It's very short, but it makes a big difference on how we see Leon in Prized.

And even though once again it was raaaaaaape. the drama towards the end of the book  At least it wasn't practically rape between the two main characters in their first meeting like it was in the first book. Also... less female hate in this book. Glenda or whatever her name is has grown on me. I never liked the mother though, and frankly I wish that they executed her for what she did. I found this book for free via Bookbub, and I loved the synopsis. I know that Bookbub books are often hit-or-miss, but I often have good luck with the first book in a trilogy. That is how the publisher wants to get you hooked into the rest of the series. Alas. You can tell I struggled by the fact that it took me almost two months to finish it. This book frustrated me on so many levels. First of all, it was incredibly predictable. I saw everything coming a mile away : Lost heir to a kingdom. Pendant which kept her magic hidden. Prince-Robin-Hood type-who-has-a-womanizing-reputation. Magic. MEGA mega magic from both her parents. Evil schoolboy. Evil magics. . The cliches and tropes filling the pages ruined all the possible surprises for me. The predictability made it hard to turn the pages. Not nearly as hard as the poor writing. God. The writing. It was like dragging myself over shards of splintered glass just to hear the main character reiterate a point a villain had expounded upon for 4 paragraphs. Everything was overly explained and too much detail was provided to answer questions just when the characters needed to know it. No sooner. Sentences often had multiple adjectives to the point of distraction. The writing was repetitive, pedantic, and had no real rhythm or flow. Sometimes, I even needed to reread a sentence to ensure that it was really written that way. Yuck. Then there is the main character. Yes, Aurora had a terrible childhood. And yes, she was pulled into a world where she was both hunted and revered and that's a lot for a 16-year-old. However. She often had little in her brain but Rafe, was constantly making poor decisions and going against everyone else's advice (they've lived in this world forever, you just 10 minutes. Listen to them for goodness sake), and revealed all sorts of things to people she never should have. I just... what? And the writing didn't help. She gasped and sighed and said "oh my" far too many times compared to normal girls. She was intolerable, intentionally ignorant, and unlikable. Props are given for the magic system, however. While it wasn't totally fleshed out, I can see it will go good places in the future. I also thought the cities had beautiful, easy-to-pronounce names. That rarely happens with such consistency.

But then why does he not want the Unseelie in the human world? Or does he? He has to be Fae because that would explain so much. Ryodan mentioned something about his middle name being Z as in the Omega. This makes me think it does have something to do with a type of hierarchy. I just don't have a fecking clue. wow...i don't know exactly why i decided to read this. i'm not really into the whole mafia thing...and the whole idea of a slave having a romantic relationship with someone who she belonged to kinda turned my stomach. that being said, i was taken completely by surprise. i really enjoyed the whole thing - not saying that there weren't parts that made me flinch or cringe, but as a novel, it was thought provoking and captured me as a reader. haven was broken yet strong...but carmine was broken too - he just expressed it by turning into a self-proclaimed ass. it is through their relationship that they both start to heal. the ending is not entirely neat and tidy. there are many things that i would have liked to see - i would have liked to see sal die. i would have liked to see haven and carmine escape "the life". i would have liked to see where the whole principessa storyline played out. it seemed to just end up hanging there with the only people left aware being members of the demarco family. and ivan hinting that sal had orchestrated the whole thing from before haven was born...  so yes, i still have questions... i hope to see a sequel to this and hopefully get answers to some of these questions. but regardless, sempre is an excellent read in its own right whether or not there is any follow up.

It's gonna be hard to write a review for this one, as I really think it's best to go into it not knowing much at all, but I'll do my best. Plot- I thought this plot was just fascinating. I think a basic premise would be : A boy wakes in a mysterious place & all he remembers is dying. The book follows him trying to unravel the mystery of where he's at, among other things. I think it was done brilliantly. There are flashbacks to his life before he dies, & sometimes I think when they're in a book, there's too many of them, & they detract from the main plot. In this book however, I think they were used very well, & I think each flashback was necessary, & they added a lot more to the main story. The plot was also almost...scary at times. I'm not sure if that's the right word, but for a lot of the book I had a great feeling of suspense, & I felt like there was something around every corner. I also think even though this plot is very deep, & emotionally heavy, there were brief moments of levity that I appreciated. I also really liked the ending, & how it left me thinking. I think this is a book where the plot really isn't just one layer deep, there's more to the plot than what it seems. There really is more than this. I'm sorry, but I couldn't help it, I had to use the title in here somewhere. Writing- I fell in love with Patrick Ness's writing in this. It just had some quality to it that I love. Great description, realistic dialogue, & it really helped set the tone for current situations. Ness really knows the English language, you could tell how his style would change depending on what he wanted you to feel during a certain scene. For example, his style shifted to short, choppy, unfinished sentences when emotions were running high, which made you feel on your toes, & it made you feel like the plot was moving a lot faster. While I appreciate beautiful writing such as that in Warm Bodies, where it's obviously beautiful with it's metaphors & it being so poetic, it's not my favorite. The writing in this book however, is now among my favorites. Characters- This is where I want to say more, but I can't because I don't want to spoil anything. So speaking in vague terms, I thought the characters were written very well, they each had depth to them, & the two main supporting characters were very unique. I liked Seth a lot as a main character, & I really did connect with him. I think his character development was done phenomenally, & I was really surprised by it. I wasn't expecting this book to have such a big emotional journey. There really is two parts to it, the actual mystery of figuring out where the hell he is, & the other mystery of his own emotions & who he is. Oh also, it was great to have Seth be gay, but not have it be only about him being gay, it really only mattered in the flashbacks, so yay for diversity! Overall- Wow I say I won't be able to write much & then I still do a long review. All I can say is that this book will mess with your mind, but in the best way possible, & I think everybody should at least give it a try. As an added bonus, the hardback of this book is really cool, so if that's not an extra push to get this book, I don't know what is.

This is the second book I've read by the Bronte sisters (the first being Wuthering Heights), and what I'm most struck by is how similar their tone and subject matter are. This, like Wuthering Heights, is a romance, and an intensely dark and angsty one at that - Charlotte, however, took more pity on her audience and gave us a slightly happier ending than Emily managed to. There's not much to say about Jane Eyre otherwise: it's a classic, and an accessible one with a superbly absorbing atmosphere and richly detailed characters. There was a lot of religion/spirituality mentioned here, especially in the ideals espoused by Jane herself speaking of which, am I the only one who thought her reasons for leaving Rochester the first time were a little contrived? . At some point, around 3/4 of the way through, I remember feeling like things were meandering a bit but it eventually comes together for a cathartic ending. 4 stars, mostly because it got a little too melodramatic at points. Also, note to self: remember to revisit the Bronte sisters the next time I want a soap opera in book form.

I thoroughly enjoyed this book! Even though I am not now, nor have I ever been from circus folk, I have a soft spot for stories about carnies. And when I saw this at the Scholastic sale a couple of weeks ago, I snapped it up instantly. Lexi (or Xandra, or X) Ryan has grown up in New York. She's a little snarky, a bit of a music snob, and a definite loner. Ever since her two best friends started dating each other, Lexi's been on her own. Her father spends most of his time working (he's a DJ, does some other nondescript music-y stuff), and her mother left when Lexi was 8. Lexi's not UNhappy with life in NYC, but she's not exactly thrilled about the prospect of senior year. Then her father dies and suddenly everything is taken away from her: with no money for private school tuition or her rent, Lexi has only one choice remaining: go find her mother. Her mother is something of a nomad, so the best her father's lawyer can track down is that Callie was, at some point, in the circus. Lexi hops a bus to Florida in search of the mother she's pretty sure she doesn't want to see. However, when she arrives at Circus Europa, her mother is gone -- she was with the show for a very short time, and it's been at least 6 months since anyone has seen her. But with nowhere else to go and now money to her name, Lexi decides to stay on at the circus. It doesn't take her long to fit in, make friends, and even find a couple of love interests. Lexi ultimately takes over fortune-teller duties, which is how she meets Nick, who is a pretty big jerk to her when they first meet (she's replacing his mother). But they're quickly develop a friendship and it doesn't take Nick long to start helping Lexi with her act (nor does it take Lexi long to develop a massive crush on Nick!). Lexi seems to have found a home at the circus, and with no other real plans, it seems like it could be permanent. Until an unexpected guest arrives one night. Interspersed with the circus narrative are chapters detailing Lexi's life in New York during the last few months before her father's accident. It's an interesting contrast to the circus, where Lexi fits in well and seems nearly fearless (perhaps because she has nothing left to lose by that point). You can see true growth in the character, and see her become comfortable with herself, and figure out what she wants to do with her life. I also liked that the "snotty trapeze sisters" turned out to be secretly awesome. I was totally prepared for this to turn into a story of circus mean girls. I was pleasantly surprised that it didn't. I know teenage girls can be terrible, but they can also be really amazing and supportive of each other. Lexi clearly needed some support, and it was great to see her find it. Although I preferred the circus chapters, the New York chapters served a definite narrative purpose, and I don't think telling the story in straightforward chronological order would have worked as well. It would actually have taken some of the focus off the circus and what it meant for Lexi, if the first 100ish pages had taken place entirely in New York. My only qualm is that I just wish the whole thing had been longer. The last few chapters felt rushed. This is apparently JJ Howard's debut novel, and I'm already looking forward to reading what she comes up with next. I loved Lexi's narration and she felt like a completely real character. The writing is very matter of fact, and although I could have done with a bit more emphasis on the setting (it's the freaking circus! ), the character development makes up for that. I also really love the title. It sounds exactly like something Lexi herself would say, years down the road, telling this story to her grandkids (or something). I can't wait to put this on my shelf and share it with my students. It's not officially released until April, so maybe they'll be as nerdily excited as me that they can read it early.

Full review also can be find here: https://fantasyraiders.wordpress.com/ Change of heart is the second book in Nicole Jacquelyn Fostering love series. Me being a fan of the author and loving the first book there was no question of reading this one also. This story is about Kat's adopted brother, Bram, and her foster sister Anita. If you read the first book, which is not required but strongly advised, you can guess that their relationship doesn't start with a right note. They constantly fight and bicker. It doesn't seem as if they like each other much. However one night changes everything. Anita wasn't my favorite character to date. She is really surly and honestly mean. She keeps herself behind a mile high wall and only shows her thorny, sarcastic side. Especially toward Bram, she is always starting a fight with him. In some way I could understand her self-protective actions thanks to her past, but after spending 14 years with a loving family, you would expect her to behave a bit kinder at least toward them. So yeah, her sarcasm and criticism was a bit too much for me. I think everything has a limit and she went too far at times, hurting her family without even realizing it. Oh and she is so unreasonable at time. [Springing the adoption on Bram out of the blue without talking about it beforehand and then expecting him to be ok with it in two seconds. Yeah that's not happening.] Bram on the other hand, I liked really much. Yeah, he is not an easy personality but an extremely good person underneath his facade. He is honest, kind, caring and handsome. He has his secrets and a hard past. From this sprang his view of marriage and children of his own, but other than that he works around it. However when facing a difficult choice he quickly realizes what he really wants and starts to fight for it with every fiber of his being. He is also quite patient and reliable, which he needs when dealing with Anita. I absolutely adored him. In some of its aspects this storyline has a lot of similarities to the first book, but still completely different. This book describes a stunningly beautiful love story, again. With heartbreak, humor, love and trust. The story is flows fluidly and I love how the characters interact. The family dynamics, their actions are simply amazing. There are also a lot of surprising twists in the plot regarding not just the main characters but also the whole family, this makes it unpredictable and exiting. I'm curious about the possible continuation because the author wrote this story in way the next book could go in a lot of different ways.

Aaron kicks this miniseries off with a...lot of talking between Cyclops and Wolverine. Knowing where this is headed (thanks, Marvel press corps), and given Aaron's ham-fisted dialogue (he doesn't seem to get either voice right) and foreshadowing, this doesn't start well. However artificial the premise kicks off the Sentinel re-launch, the initial wave of terror they create is at least believably illustrated. And the antagonists of this story are suitably menacing, but not for reasons I would've expected. they're downright sociopathic and slightly clever, which is a helluva contribution to the X-Men universe for Aaron to make. After reading the core story, I feel like this: like most of the non-Bendis-led events of Marvel's recent history (e.g. Shadowlands, Fear Itself), the main event comic is probably weaker than some of the supporting stories written alongside as tie-ins to the event. I can't prove that yet with this book, but even though there was some decent plotting and the dialogue improved slightly, this still felt entirely artificial and implausible. As in: with all the fights between Cyclops and Wolverine over the years, when Logan stuck around every time, is this *really* supposed to be the most convincing reason for a split to naturally and finally occur? I hope that Marvel follows through on this one, if they really intend for us to believe it. For now though, this feels like a squabble between teenagers on a schoolyard, and one that should blow over just as inconsequentially. I think one thing that frustrates me most about Marvel (and which might be colouring my attitude to what Aaron did here) is that they don't commit to change. Utopia is a great new concept and it's been executed masterfully by Fraction and others, but they do easily backslide into Xavier's school in Westchester - out of nostalgia, not because it hasn't been wrung dry of every fresh story that could be told. Best issue was Gillen's Regenesis. Good storytelling device, interesting snippets of what generally felt like believable and appropriate dialog (save a few begging moments). 3.5 stars - not great, but some moments of better-than-good. Marvel, don't squander this opportunity. Here are my plot notes because I can never remember who when and what, when I'm reading later books: Carlton Kilgore killed by his son Kade. Kade creates events to kick off sales of new Sentinel model. Hellfire club, which went mutant-free, gets taken over and killed off by Kade and his band of child billionaire weaponeers. Quentin Quire initiates the Sentinel launch by attacking the UN, then requests sanctuary in Utopia. Idie kills Helllfire club goons, thinks she's acting like the monster she believes she is.

Unlike most other novels, the main character dies in the first chapter. This automatically makes for an interesting book because it is not often that you can enjoy a story while knowing what happens at the end. There are many things I enjoyed about this novel, in particular: 3) I found Before I Fall to be extremely realistic. Lauren Oliver really understands teenagers, perhaps a lot more than they understand themselves. This, I think, is what makes Before I Fall stand out from other teenage novels. 2) I loved how the storyline was set out. When reading each chapter, we realise that the events in the story are linked together somehow but just like Samantha, we can't quite figure out how they are linked. We learn more and more each day (literally - the chapters are set out as Day 1, Day 2 etc) and slowly come to understand how every move Samantha makes has an effect on someone else's life. When we do find out at last it seems almost obvious but like real life we failed to notice the clues. Samantha's death also becomes more and more emotional as she struggles to change her fate. 3) I think that this book is important for young adults as it highlights the impact that school bullying has on individuals as well as an insight into bullies themselves - their reasons behind their actions. It comes with the important message that we need to notice those around us more because ignoring can have just as an effect as being involved. 4) The relationship between Samantha and her sister Izzy. I am an only child and so it is generally hard for me to grasp how siblings feel about each other but while reading this book I felt like I really could understand. It was one of the main things that made the book so terribly sad. Before I Fall has many beautiful and important things about it but I won't lie and say that I enjoyed it more than Delirium, but then again, it is a completely different storyline. P.S. More reviews at Rondo of a Possible World: YA Book Reviews There has been much anticipation over this novel for not just myself but throughout the blogger community. And I can say that Throne of Glass lived up to those expectations and qualified as one of my favorite novels of the year. The back story around Sarah J. Maas and the original production of her story titled Queen of Glass up on Fictionpress.net and gaining a huge fan base. With the idea of an assassin Cinderella, I mean, it wouldn't take long for me to reach out and pick something like that up. And after repealing her chapters from the website and setting out for traditional publishing, Throne of Glass was born. Now I can tell you that I did not feel like I was reading The Hunger Games, it didn't even come to mind while reading. I just had Assassins' Creed flickering around upstairs, but never The Hunger Games. So anyone fretting about that little tagline and comparison to this novel, there is no need! As characters go, Celaena Sardothien was tough as nails, witty beyond words, and pretty badass. An infamous assassin at seventeen and didn't give a shit to anything that threatened her. She knew that she was better than the King's men, and she showed it, and I liked her spunk. She survives a year in the brutal mines and outwits the guards, almost touching the very wall to freedom that they guard like they would the King. But when you throw the guys into the picture she became just a giddy girl falling in love. And that was where Celaena and I started having some issues together. And with the possible love triangle running beneath the words and pages, it just started to bug me more that I wished. And another thing that got to me was that she falls for the handsome Crown Prince Dorian, but she loathes his father, the King. Wouldn't you despise the son of the king, too? But because he's handsome, she starts making remarks about his beauty and I just ended up facepalming and rolling my eyes. I didn't want Celaena becoming like every other YA girl out there, but sometimes what I want is not what I get. The supporting characters hit the nail on the head. I did enjoy Crown Prince Dorian even though I didn't enjoy Celaena and his relationship. He was a different entity from his father and there was a sweet and down-to-earth nature about him, but there were times that I found him stiff and awkward and too drawn out. Chaol Westfall, the Captain of the Guard, I found to be a much lucid and developed character. His realistic qualities and protective nature really caught my heart on a string and took a giant tug. But in regards to the "love triangle" I don't really know where Maas is going to go in the series but I just hope this doesn't turn into a House of Night novel and we have more guys fawning over the protagonist than there are fingers on my hand. Even Nehemia was a strong character with an air of mystery, she kept me on my seat in-case my over assuming mind took me down dark corners. I enjoyed her company and friendly attitude with Celaena as well. One thing that really got me while reading was the intake of the fey in this book. I don't know if I'm the only one, but when I started reading and before I even started reading, I did not know there were going to be anything regarding faeries and feylike beings or anything magical and such. It wasn't a drawback as much as it was strange. Final Summation: World-building, anticipation and action that leaves you wanting more, Sarah J. Maas' Throne of Glass took me by storm. One of my favorite novels of the summer and the year. I'm hoping that there won't be overpowering love triangles or there will be some deaths by Celaena's hands because I would love to see her assassin killing skills in action in the next installment.

2.5 stars. This book was okay, but I couldn't really see why it's gotten so much praise. It started off fairly promising, and I loved the mysterious writing and urban fantasy setting in Prague. I really liked reading about Karou's storyline, her friends and art in Prague, and her visits and trips for Brimstone and the other monsters. Unfortunately, I started to lose interest after the...revelation that shifted the book in a different direction. I just couldn't get into Madrigal's storyline, she was the Mary Sue of magical animal-human hybrid creature land. All those chapters about the war and her going back and forth about whether she wanted to marry Thiago...and then there was Akiva. His relationship with both Karou and Madrigal was VERY insta-love-y, and I was so bored I found myself skimming most of their interactions. One other point that really bothered me: There was a sentence in which Akiva's eyes were being described as very determined and devoid of emotion, and I can't recall the precise wording but he was described as having a "jihadist" look. It really annoyed me that this was the word the author chose to use, and although it is a very small point in the context of this book, it's a really important discussion that needs to be had in a broader discourse about how we talk about violence. The go-to synonym for "sadistic" shouldn't be "jihadist". It's little details like this that reinforce stereotypes and cognitive biases that present a small group of violent extremists as the face of a peaceful major world religion.

4.5 Stars! "One is enough. It's unique. It's a chance, an opportunity, an experience. One is never greedy. One is independent. One can change everything." Jewel E. Ann has become my new favorite author!! I DEVOURED the Jack & Jill Series, and One features two characters from that series. Although this book can technically be read as a standalone, PLEASE PLEASE read the unforgettable books in the Jack & Jill Series first because there are some major spoilers. The author calls this genre Romantic Comedy but it so much more! Swoony romance, funny dialogue, dramatic moments and SEXY scenes...Cage and Lake are two very memorable characters. Lake became an amputee after a tragic car accident that took the life of her fiancee. She has moved away from her family in California to Minneapolis, where she once again runs into the football star Cage, with whom she once shared an unforgettable kiss. She cat get Cage out of her head and cant believe he remembers her, too. Cage really sees Lake, not her disability, and she can't get him out of head. "Mind if I lose the leg?" I asked. He shook his head. There really were no words to describe how his lack of any sort of reaction made me feel. Not one flinch. Not one nervous glance at my leg. Not one second of hesitation. Cage is sexy, warm and loving. He falls fast for Lake, who is impulsive, funny, a little insecure and very, very honest. She makes a living by testing artificial limbs, and her work takes her all over the world. A trip to China provides one of the BEST scenes in the whole book!! It is so hard to categorize any of Jewel E. Ann's books, they really cover all the bases and I ended up highlighting half this book. "My mouth said thank you, but my heart said I love you." Lake is quickly thrust into the world of NFL pro football and things aren't always easy. Her family makes an appearance in this book and they are always there to support her. There are some very dramatic moments in this book which provided some very unexpected and very surprising twists, as only this author can do. The supporting characters are, as always, absolutely fantastic (Flint! Hello!! Would love to read your story!!) Warm, sexy and laugh-out-loud funny, ONE is another home run from this amazing author. "Give me you. Give me every tear. Give me every breath. Give me every fear. Give me every touch. Give me every smile. Give me every day." (ARC provided by the author in return for an honest review.)

i feel like throughout the whole book, tension was building to something that never came. it was a rather flat story after Book 1. Mae was blindly taken over by The Circle to the detriment eventually to her best friend. the fact that Annie ends up in a coma, and that seems to have all but a paragraph dedicated to it, is weird I do get that it is supposed to be a desensitization to human interaction and more on the pursuit of knowledge but I feel like either side was conveyed hard enough. there was slight hope when Ty showed up - you would think The creator of The Circle could shut it down if he really wanted to. 3 stars is a generous rating

Once upon a time a young princess is born to a loving king and queen. Their kingdom of Kharuf is a bit poorer than their neighbor, but they have a wonderful spinning tradition and create the finest cloth. When the young princess is five they have a great party to celebrate her birthday. They invite all the magical creatures of the mountains even though they do not expect them to come. The creatures do come and they bestow wonderful gifts on the young princess. A demon queen also comes to the party. She bestows a curse on the young princess; a curse that affects the entire kingdom. A piskie is gives the final gift in an attempt to counter some of the demon's curse. The curse affects all the spinners in the kingdom. They all will become sick and die. The king and queen outlaw spinning in the hope that it will save their kingdom and their princess. All the spinners are forced to either flee across the desert or cross the mountains to the neighboring kingdom. Yashaa's mother was the head spinner in the kingdom. She and a few others stayed with the king and queen as long as possible. They had young children and could not make the desert journey. In the neighboring country of Qamih, they are not treated well and forced to live in a tent city at a crossroads. All the adults who were spinners are sick or dead. All the children have learned the spinner's craft, but because they have never set foot in Kharuf they are not sick with the curse. Yashaa's mother is dying and decides to send the children out to look for help. She believes they will go to the Maker King of Qamih and beg for help. Yashaa, young Arwa, dedicated Tariq and fierce Saoud decide to head to Kharuf instead and see if they can break the curse. They find Kharuf as destitute as they feared it would be. The Maker King has spent years driving it to ruin in order to claim it as his own when his son Maram marries the young princess Zahreh. Instead of breaking the curse, the group finds Princess Zahreh trapped in a tower and decides to rescue her. They escape through the countryside heading towards the desert in the hopes that they will outrun both Prince Maram and the demon queen who drives him. Of course you can not outrun fate and it is Zahreh's destiny to become the vessel for the demon queen. But you can twist your fate to suit your needs and with the help of the magical creatures Zahreh fights as hard as she can to recapture the demon queen and stop her from ruling them all. I adored A Thousand Nights and was very excited to learn there was going to be a companion novel. Spindle takes place thousands of years after the Storyteller Queen freed her king from the demons and created their mountain prison. The kingdoms of Kharuf and Qamih were created on either side of the mountains that hold the demons and their magical captors. Like A Thousand Nights, this to is a retelling of a fairy tale. The story of Sleeping Beauty has been remade into this beautiful story of Zahreh and her hero Yashaa. I loved the romance that blossomed between the two. Yashaa starts out resentful of the princess who has driven him from his home and made his mother ill. Then he becomes enamored with her and dedicated to her service. It is only after she gives him permission to hope does he realize the depth of his love. I loved how strong Zahreh was and how willing she was to do whatever needed to be done in order to save her family and kingdom, even if that meant sacrificing herself. I received this book from Netgalley.

While yes, this book was mostly filler, I really enjoyed it. More than I thought I would. I think, because I wasn't as obsessed with Red Queen like so many other readers were, I didn't have a lot riding on this sequel. I got to enjoy it without high expectations of excellence. The only part I didn't like was Kilorn expressing his feelings to Mare. I hate stories where every dude is in love with the main character. I wish they could have just had a wonderful friendship with zero romance. But that is a very small part of the book, so it didn't ruin the whole thing for me or anything. I can't wait to see what happens in King's Cage. Only two more days! Full Review to Come.
4.5 stars, LOVED this book!

4.25 stars I think James is treating Mike like crap. I've run into my tormentors since high school and I've never had the desire to be mean and certainly not humiliate them. Possibly boring personal story (includes a University of Washington football star): One even came up to me about 5 years later and apologized for how she'd treated me in school. I couldn't even remember her ever doing anything and now I can't even remember her name. My biggest bully was John McCallum who later went on to be the star quarterback for the University of Washington Huskies at that time. I didn't know this when I ran into him. He recognized me first and was perfectly nice and I was perfectly nice back. We made small talk including where we were going to school. He told me the UW but didn't brag about anything. When I told some friends about it a few days later, they laughed, told me who he was, and said that not knowing his almost celebrity status was probably my best revenge. I tell people the story because it's funny but at the same time, I feel bad that I didn't know and didn't acknowledge his achievement. The fact he didn't say anything about it or try to rub my face in his success tells me that he had changed and is actually a pretty decent guy. (Cool fact: his sister sued the school district in high school for sexism since girls couldn't play football. She won and tried out and made the team and became the first female high school football player in some large area. It might only have been Washington State but it might have been a bigger region. I don't remember. I was told she was actually really good and the school had a really good AAA team already. It's impressive she beat out other boys that were good too.) Anyway, he doesn't just humiliate Mike but insults him on several very personal levels and calls him a loser basically. He keeps it up even after he heard how hard it was for Mike. Not everyone is smart enough or talented enough to invent a machine that makes them rich. o glad the author keeps referring to white tank tops instead of calling them "wife beaters" which such an offensive term like it's okay to joke about it. Wow. I almost cried at the end. Weird. It was pretty formulaic. They never said "I love you," but I suppose that would have been instalove. I'm just not as fond of HFN as HEAs. But I still really liked it.

3.5 out of 5 stars. I enjoyed the banter between Eli and Gwen, and I loved how they started out as friends who understood each other before becoming lovers.That made the story much more worthwhile, however I did not really like that "twist" near the end. That plot line has been repeated in sooo many books I've read lately. Nothing wrong with him having a child or anything, it's just that I have been reading many books with that kind of plot twist that I'm a bit over and done with that. I can name at least 4 at the top of my head right now. Other than that, the story was sweet and sexy. Although, the ending could have been extended a bit more, I feel like it was bit too quick and swift for my liking.

When I first started this book I was worried it was going to finally be the one book that I wouldn't finish. I hated Samantha Kingston. She was a bitch, brat, spoiled and selfish. She was the girl who made my life in grade/middle school miserable. Not quite brave enough to be the first person to make fun of me, but certainly brave enough to keep it going once it started. Then she dies. From the beginning of the book Sam commentates that she doesn't believe that when you die, your whole life flashes before your eyes. She claims, it's only your "greatest hits." For her, it's portions of her life where she was the meanest. Where she succeeded in breaking a person's spirit, made them feel lower than dirt. After living through the day before the accident with Sam, I couldn't help but feel a karmic sense of justice. After all, she chose to join in tormenting Juliet Sykes at the party. She chose to say hateful words to Kent McFuller. She chose to get into her BFF's (Lindsay) car knowing that they had all been drinking and BFF can't even drive sober. The accident happens, she dies, then she wakes up. Sam finds herself stuck reliving her last day on earth over and over again, like some cosmic groundhog day joke. As she walks in her own footsteps she realizes that she doesn't like who she is, who she had become. She begins making small changes throughout her day to see if she could change the outcome. Soon, Sam realizes that the only way to redeem herself is to help Juliet Sykes. The girl her BFF had tormented since 5th grade. Sam eventually learns that she had replaced Juliet as Lindsay's best friend. Lindsay is the queen of mean girls. She has the bold tenacity that only a girl whose parent's way of apologizing is giving her everything she wants. I love how the author handed me this terrible character and slowly molded her into someone that I actually began to like. As Sam began standing up to Lindsay and trying to set things right, I began to hope. Although it was clear from the personalities of the other girls that they weren't going to change, I couldn't help but hope that Sam would get through to them. The more I read the more I needed to know if Sam was going to find her way into grace. Would she be able to save herself, Juliet, her friends? Would she manage to yank herself from her narcissistic self and become a decent human being? Sam was granted seven days. Seven days in which she relived her final day to try to fix years of poison laced words directed those less popular than her. Upon conclusion, she rested.

I just did not like this that much on either a regular or a Newbery level. I didn't think the dynamics of the school were very believable (most of the kids read too old to me, and the way it all worked out in the end was just TOO warm-n-fuzzy)--I think that was my main problem--and while this is way, way better than most guidance-counselor fiction, the writing did creep that way too often for my tastes. The big action scene near the end didn't work for me. I'm assuming there really are environmental education schools in New York where one of the evening activities is getting together to watch a movie in a park, so while I thought that was really strange and it didn't make sense to me, I give that a pass. But... logistically... there were a bunch of things in there that puzzled me. Perhaps most of all, the ending was both too feel-good and a little creepy. I was really uncomfortable with how we're supposed to think a school full of kids calling Auggie "Hey, little dude"--including kids his own age--was a great thing. Better than before? For sure. But so icky and condescending. All the kids thinking it's so great that Auggie won this school award? I mean, I don't think kids care about awards like that all that much, and even if they did, I would have expected more grumbling ("they only gave it to him because") than admiration. I liked that Julian never came around. That felt real to me. But I didn't like that he just won't be in school next year, problem solved. My favorite narrator, and the one that felt most real and natural to me, was Via's boyfriend Justin. I love that guy. I would like to say that I wish we'd gotten more of him, but I think it was probably a wise choice to give us just a taste and leave me wanting to know more. Likewise with Miranda. The scene at school that felt the MOST real to me was the one where Auggie is in his Halloween costume and hears his so-called friend talking about him. The kids' voices in that seemed spot-on, and I took what Jack said quite seriously and alarmedly. But then it was never really dealt with. The scene was, sure. But it seemed to me like it was kind of passed off as "I didn't really mean it" when at the time Auggie notes that he sounds very serious. I mean, Jack says he thought a lot about what he would do if he was in Auggie's situation, and I think that IS the kind of thing a kid would think about. I don't think he made that up on the spur of the moment. Perhaps further talk about suicide would have made the book too dark for its audience, but I felt like it left me hanging with something very serious. Overall: I think this has too many holes to make it a Newbery. And "Mom, thanks for making me go to school" (not an exact quote) sums up my philosophical problems.

Just a fantastic world Hugh Howey is created. And shockingly, unlike many stories of this nature, the backstory is just as compelling, as we get to hear how the Silos came to be created, and why everyone is down there. Can't wait to read Dust!

I don't care how old you are. Everyone should read this, whether they hate it or love it. People with conditions like Melody deserve to be heard and understood, instead of judged so overwhelmingly harshly as they often are today. It is necessary that everyone is respected as well as understood, this book is just a step closer to that ideal. But it's a necessary step that I dare each and every one of you to take.

This book was ok. I purchased it on a recommendation but now it's finished I've decided it's not a keeper so off to the rounds of the family it goes (maybe one of them will like it better). It seemed to me that there were some great ideas in this but I just couldn't connect with the characters. Especially Jacob's wife her paranoia seemed very much imposed on her rather than integrated into her personality. Perhaps we should have seen a chapter from her POV just prior to 'the bank statements'. And then it seems all is happy again and she doesn't hold any grudges about what her husband put her through. The idea of being able to communicate with people in a coma via MRI intrigued me (and sent me diving down google rabbit holes) so that was a pro for this book. It did seem strange though that the prior attempt of this with Amy got 'stuck' on the activity of tennis and that when she didn't respond as expected it was abandoned, maybe it was part of the testing protocol but it seemed a bit peculiar. Simon was a definite enigma considering the role it turned out he played and I can see the utility in having him only revealed as he appeared to others. I do wonder though that when the trial comes at the end that there was difficulty in extraditing him due to his crimes in other constituencies. So we're to believe that either through synchronicity he is identified as being the perpetrator for all of these crimes at the same time, or that after Alex identities him as a viable suspect that all of these police forces say "Oooh that's our man" for x. Hmmm I won't be recommending this to anyone but I have started it on the rounds rather than sending it straight to the donation pile so there is that. (Although if I hadn't happened to see my mother 30mins after I finished it the outcome may have been different.

Grace Stutter, having the responsibility of delivering her sisters baby to the father, since her sister died, waits six weeks before heading to Maine, having a feeling that she would be making a new start....but then her plane crashes on the mountain and she, the baby, and a sexy highland warrior -Greyland-are the survivors. Now they are pushed together out of survival, but a deep passion is awakened between them...a passion that burns slowly to a deep love that will change their lives forever..... I have never read this author, but I was in the mood for some good highlander romance, and I decided that after hearing some great things from this author, I knew that I needed to try her out, and I definitely wasn't disappointed. I just got this book a few hours ago, and just finished, I was that drawn into Charming The Highlander. I think I loved everything about this book. I just love it when you have time travel books when dealing with sexy highlanders from the past....so yummy with the accent, attitude and their fiery passion for a woman they love. There were definitely many witty moments throughout the story that would make you bow over and laugh your heart out. The writing was charming and tended to draw the reader in from the first to the very last page of the book. I felt like I was actually there in the story...the scenes were so vivid in detail....definitely a keeper for me!

A woman reflects on a significant friendship she had at age 15 while dealing with a troubled marriage. This reflection is likely precipitated by memories of her best friend's unplanned pregnancy and subsequent abortion in adolescence, contrasted with her own inability to conceive a child with her husband. The book does a good job of describing how significant events in female relationships change both the women and the relationships. Music is also a predominant theme throughout the story. Lorrie Moore skillfully constructs lovely and insightful prose.

The second installement in the Air Awakens series mantains the promises of its first book (Air Awakens). Between magic that grows, a bond ever so strong, painful deaths and enemies that spring up from everywhere, even between those who should be at her side, Vhalla has not a single second of peace in Fire Falling. The only issue I have is that she is a bit too whiny and relies strongly on others. She needs to grow up fast if she has to win the war and take her place at the side of her dark prince...maybe.

True rating on this would probably be 3.5 stars. This story is about Delaney Maxwell. Turns out she was crossing a frozen lake with her friend Decker and ended up falling in. Delaney ends up being underwater for 11 minutes and is dead when she is brought up and taken to the hospital. She is brought back and in a coma for 6 days and miraculously wakes up. I found Delaney as a character somewhat frustrating. I wanted to like her - I didn't not like her but there were times in the story where I was seriously questioning her ability to make decisions. I could feel her struggling with the fact that she was alive and what she was supposed to do with this new ability she had. I had a love/hate relationship with both Decker and Troy. There were times where I wanted to just shake them but they were both great characters in my opinion. The group of friends were another story (Janna, Tara, Justin, Kevin). The way they treated Delaney at the end was something else and while I understand the idea that someone would question how things ended, I can't believe that Decker would be ok with the way things went down between them all based on his feelings for Delaney. Overall, I really liked the premise of this book and am curious to see where the next one goes. It was a quick read and had a good story.

The overall plot of this book was a good read and I liked how it worked out in the end. The special celebrity assignment is used to further develop relationships and the characters. One scene in particular really gives you insight into Chess' feelings - she needed help they could both offer and called one and it didn't even occur to her to call the other. These characters really get to me - the way their emotions is portrayed raelly makes you empathize with them. When Terrible found Chess and Lex and the graves going at it, that scene was really awful. I couldn't get it out of my head and frantically kept reading hoping it would get turned around and be okay. It still wasn't by the end of the book, so I had to start the third last night and will probably finish it tonight - I HAVE to know what happens. I understand that Chess is an addict and she's self destructive because it's been pounded into her head that she's not worth anything, but her actions really frustrated me. I'm just glad that toward the end she started to realize some things and hope she keeps trying.

While this is a solid entry in the series, it didn't quite have the magic of the previous couple of books. I am hoping against hope that that's not because Kate and Curran have finally gotten their relationship together. I found myself thinking of Jeaniene Frost's Night Huntress series when I was reading this one. And not in a good way. I loved the first few books of that series, but, now that Cat and Bones are together (as are Kate and Curran), the series has become a little episodic (as was this book). The writing is still good in both series, but I don't want to feel like I'm watching a TV series where each episode resolves a crime (or some such) with very little overarching plot. It's early days for this series, so my fingers are crossed.
