Rating: BLOODY BRILLIANT!! ONE OF THE BEST PLOT TWISTS I'VE EVER READ! WOW. I had some problems with this book at the beginning, but soon I realised that this book was different, somehow special. It's startsin the typical way: An arranged marriage, our protagonist, the princess, doesn't want to marry a stranger whom she doesn't love. Then she flees at her wedding day and BOOM the adventure begins! It's not very adventurous at the beginning, but it was nice to see Lia enjoy a simple life as a tavern maid. It was light and fun, but then slowly things get darker and twisted. And I liked that a lot. I never felt as if nothing happened, I was never bored to read (though admittedly it took me a while to read this book). There was always something to happen. I usually hate love triangles, but in this case (due to the plot twist) it was okay. And it is clear from the start, whom Lia favours. And we (the readers) know who Rafe's and Kaden's identities are and Lia doesn't, what makes it much more interesting. So we know she's in love with  an Assassin who was sent to kill her, until the plot twist comes and we know that Rafe is the prince she was to marry and Kaden was the assassin. AMAZING! Mary E. Pearson plays with our feelings, I kind of felt "betrayed". I went back to some of the first chapters to make sure, it was real, to find the hints hidden .... ah it was super cool. It turned the whole story and made it better. Because if the story continued the way it was headed to, it would not have been this great. Still I had some issues with the book, for example Lia's escape at the beginning. It may seem well thought through, but in real life (middle ages) it would not have worked this way and this easy. They would've found her eventually. But okay. The other thing is with the invented language. I bet Mary E. Pearson has given a lot of thought into it, but for the story it was not necessary. Even without it, we would know it plays in a different world and that the nations there speak different languages. Every line or passage with this invented language (I couldn't pronounce) I simply skipped. Apart from this, I loved every other aspect of the book: the three main characters, the side characters (especially her loyal best friend Pauline), the world and its politics and the writing (three different first-person perspectives...never seen this before). And the "book in the book"-structure. (If you read it you'll understand. ) I can't wait to read the next book!! [And btw: I went into the book without reading the synopsis. After finishing the book I read it (I usually do this with the most of the books I read) and I noticed that it gives the reader the wrong perception of the story and it gives away too much. That's why I don't like reading the synopsis of a book.]
An author who can make me absolutely adore a set of characters in such a short time is an author that I'll continue to love. She can never really disappoint me. Also, Star Wars!

So, would Skitter be as good as The Hatching? That was what I hoped for when I started to read the book and after finishing it the same day as I started it can I only say that oh yes! It's just as creepy as the previous book and just as hard to put down. The story takes place after the first book ended (with an annoying cliffhanger gah!) and the world thinks the worst is over, the spiders are dead. The world is in ruin, but at least the danger is over, or is it? Now it seems that what happened in the first book was just the start, and now the fight for the survival of the whole human race starts all over again. And in North America the president faces a dilemma, to enact The Spanish Protocol or not... I love the structure of the book with several POV's and short chapters. It really makes the book nearly impossible to put down. Around 85% did I realize that the book would not be able to finish without some things unresolved and that I was looking forward to another cliffhanger. I suspected in the beginning of the book that this was the case and I was right. Skitter is a great horror book, perhaps not as gruesome as the first book. However, it has some really nasty parts and I recommend this book and the previous. However, you should really read The Hatching before you read Skitter. I want to thank the publisher for providing me with a free copy through NetGalley for an honest review!

This book has been out a long time and I just couldn't seem to pull it together to review it. Not that I'm conflicted, it's a solid 3, but that it's annoying. Basically this is the story of Tell and Georgia. They knew each other in high school when she was a cheerleader and he was a bit of a loser. Not a lot of money or sports participation and too smart for the redneck set so Tell tended to be less popular than the typical McKay. Georgia appeared popular but actually stood in the shadow of her domineering boyfriend whom she later married and divorced. She and Tell meet again and sparks that never caught in high school finally start to fly. Great, right? Except that a lot of this is rehash of Brandt and Jessie's story. The essential problems are very similar as is the trope. Guy who's harbored feelings for a woman he thought was unreachable (but who actually has major insecurity issues) finally gets the prize after years and years of pining. And the biggest distraction from both romances (Brandt/Jessie and Tell/Georgia) is the most compelling part of the story while being the most frustrating at the same time. I'm talking about Caspar. Tell, Brandt and Dalton's father. He was a verbally abusive drunk until a few years before this story takes place and now he's a verbally abusive recovering alcoholic/bible thumper. No arc there. The relationship's basically the same. But the really frustrating part to me is that Tell will say things about his dad usually being okay to be around, but then the only thing we see is Caspar being absolutely, no-holds-barred horrible. The only person worse than Caspar, IMO is Joan. Tell's mother. Yes, the poor, sainted Joan. In Brandt's book we found out that (background and rant follows) Joan had tricked Caspar into marriage by lying about being pregnant when she found out he was in love with someone else and wouldn't be coming to her for quickies anymore. Then, after he found out the truth but didn't leave her, she proceeded to stand by while he destroyed their kids' childhood in a bizarre, mean punishment on her. She enabled his abuse and continues even now with the "oh, woe is me!" when she never did anything to stop it. She finally leaves him, but not really for her sons who she threw to the dragon all those years, but for her grandchild out of town. So the sons have to take care of their drunken, abusive dad because their selfish, bitch mother thinks she's "earned" her freedom. Fuck. That. Shit. So, to me, the only thing that interests me here is what's going to eventually happen with Caspar. Is he going to just die? *cough*copout*cough* Or is he going to change in a positive way? Will Joan's secrets ever be revealed to her sons? Another shitty thing she did was telling Jessie the truth of what she did to Caspar and making her promise not to tell Brandt. Selfish bitch. Terrible mother, terrible grandmother, horrible person. There's the potential for a major blow-up there, but I don't get the sense it's going to happen because these two don't seem to be considered main characters even as they take over the story line. Don't get me wrong, I do NOT want them getting back together, I just think there's a story there to be developed and it's languishing as a go-to device for male lead angst instead. I guess I'm thinking about this story because Dalton's book is going to come out soon and I wonder if it's going to be another retread where Caspar is the hero's major issue and the only thing that changes by the end is that Dalton has a female he can obsess over rather than his wrecked childhood. Back to this book, though. Do I love Tell? Definitely. I want to hug him and squeeze him. Georgia gave me more trouble, but I felt some real sympathy for her and when she gave in to her feelings for Tell I thought they were a very good match. Shoehorning cameos from far too many McKay's was a bit much, but a few of the encounters worked. So ... kind of a read that just laid there. I'm both anticipating and dreading Dalton's book. With only two books left in the series and the last few (with the exception of the most recent, Gone Country, which I liked) ranging from "meh" to seriously frustrating, I'm keeping my expectations pretty low.
Kiersten White is hilarious! I'm looking forward to the rest of this series.

I liked this book, despite some misgivings. I agree with everyone else that the cover is misleading, and odd - its like, a cover from a completely different book, about chucks-wearing kids in love, which is not what this book is about. I liked Felicity's voice - she did make a lot of the differences between British English and American English, but I just spent the weekend with a British friend, and that's pretty much all we talked about, and we are full grown adults who have known each other for years. So yeah, it would probably be jarring for a kid. I also really liked Uncle Gideon. I always wanted a goofy uncle, but I never got one. There were, however, things that have really stuck in my craw in a bad way, such as Danny and Winnie did a terrible thing, right?? I know they are doing a good thing in the book, but holy catfish Batman, what sort of person runs off with their brother's wife/their husband's brother? Gideon is right to be mad, that is just way low. And yeah, its weird that Felicity just kind of rolls with it...Maybe its "stiff upper lip" and all that, but it didn't seem realistic for an 11 year old who is in other ways a bit immature to just kind of roll with that kind of news.

3.5 Stars On the bad days, I suspected that I would always be broken, that parts of me would never be quite right--and that those were the parts that made me good at the job. This book and its psychology is far from flawless but I'm glad that the author at least tries to come up with something quasi-clever. The book is filled with these sort of philosophical but really meaningless phrases. Knowing what people wanted and knowing what they feared were two sides of the same coin. I still appreciate the effort. I felt like there was a lot of wind up but not a lot of punch. There are moments that the author could've struck a home run but she just missed it. Darn. I was especially annoyed with the training wheels the FBI put on the kids especially considering the kids are far more advanced than the FBI's experts. Love Triangle I have never read a book in which romance felt more inappropriate than in this one, I mean their timing is extraordinarily sucky. Also, I think this is the first time in my reading history that I have ever ever ever ever ever ever thought, can't Cassie just date Michael and Dean? I know, it's an outrageous thought. I just don't want either of them to be sad and rejected. "If it had been me in the woods, if I'd been the one to go with Briggs, if I'd been the one you saw at the exact second..."...I mean, doesn't the fact that Cassie can't answer this say a lot about her immaturity and inability to make decisions? Michael Michael is kind of funny. "I take it you're Michael," she said. "The emotion reader with the attitude problem who's continually doing stupid things for girls." "That's hardly a fair assessment," Michael replied. "I do plenty of stupid things that aren't for girls, too." The author explores his character a bit more. But I'd never thought about the effect that being around a person like Dean would have on someone like Michael. I find it peculiar and intriguing the way Michael fills Cassie in on how Dean feels about her. It's bizarre that Michael would share so openly regarding his rival. Lia It's weird that because Lia is an expert liar her sarcasm is a little off because to the outside viewer she seems genuine. I felt sorry for her even as she takes her pain out on Cassie. Dean is Lia's only family and she doesn't like to share or see his loyalties shifting to someone else. "Dean is the only person I've ever known who's never lied to me." Sloane I think I love Sloane even more in this sequel. She is so adorably hilarious. She is definitely my favourite character. "Hypothetically speaking," she said, as if it were perfectly normal to bend over a bed and stare at someone until they woke up, "would constructing a model of the crime scene we saw on the video yesterday qualify as intruding on Dean's space?" I opened my mouth to tell Sloane that she was intruding on my space, but then processed her question. "Hypothetically speaking," I said, stifling a yawn and sitting up in bed, "have you already reconstructed the crime scene in question?" I love how Sloane's the odd one out. She's surrounded by all these people who are experts at psychology, manipulation, and mind games. And sometimes she just feels like the socially inept nerd in this world of subtle communication and high-class human readers. I tried to catch Sloane's eye, telegraphing that she should not, under any circumstances, tell her what Dean had told us about his father. Sloane met my eyes and nodded. "Dean told us this case looks a lot like his father's," Oh, Sloane. "You and Michael," Sloane said slowly. "There's nothing going on with Michael and me. Sloane tilted her head to one side. "You and Dean?" "There's nothing going on with Dean and me." Sloane stared at me for another three seconds, and then: "I give up." Clearly, she'd expended her capacity for girl talk. Dean This kid has had a horrible life. Just when I start to think he should just get over his past the author slams down another card that I didn't see coming. No one knows how to deal with him and yet everyone thinks they're the expert on What Dean Needs. On the romance side, it was nice to see Dean finally laying claim to Cassie instead of always wallowing in his unworthiness. I got frustrated with the FBI's stubborness when it's so obvious that just monitoring how the kids help them would solve a lot of problems. You can't let these kids sit around all day when they know the game's afoot. I seem to be finding a lot of inconsistencies in books nowadays. I find it hard to believe that the FBI would ask Dean to meet with his father on a such an unlikely lead especially when they won't even let them view evidence of the crime scenes. I find it even more difficult to believe that they would bring Cassie along especially when she would be no help whatsoever. Why didn't they freakin' take the lie detector? It's also really annoying when in a scuffle, Cassie is admiring Dean's skin tone. It's freakin' weird is what it is.

I'm not entirely sure, but I think I enjoyed this second one even better than the first. I normally don't like changes in perspective, or multiple narrating voices, and it had me slightly bewildered at first. But, I adjusted to it and finished the story with a sense of satisfaction. In this sequel, the story is told from several different points of view and from different timelines. The history of the silos is revealed, but the mystery over their true purpose is given more depth and paves the way for book 3.

I didn't think this one was much until all the secrets started coming out. I get that Zane had a crush on Keelie, it was sort of cute. But Keelie was so hot and cold about him, very wishy washy. Once they felt safe enough with each other to spill their secrets you can see how well matched they were. Zane's secrets were startling, but I loved that even as a kid he stood up for what was right. It was too bad that he couldn't share with his family because I know his family would have supported him and been proud of him. With Keelie's secret it seemed to be her downfall, one more thing that really changed her, caused her to become the Keelie we knew. "Shouldn't there be more distaste in our mouths for the abusers than for those who continue to love the abusers?" trigger warning: abusive relationship, domestic violence, sexual assault It Ends With Us isn't a book that changed me, nor is it a book that taught me things that I didn't already know. But it is a special book, nonetheless, not just because it is incredibly well-written, has complex characters who are painfully imperfect, and a plot that is--to quote Hoover herself--brave and bold. This book is special, because this book is important Abusive relationships is a subject that needs to be discussed more often, especially considering that even now, though we do hate and condemn abusers, almost all of us have asked this question at least once: "why didn't she leave him the first time he hit her? Why did she give him a second chance? Why didn't she walk away?" The answers to these questions are actually really simple, but to understand them is the hard part, and this is what Colleen Hoover tried to do with It Ends With Us. She did not simply answer the above questions with her eloquent writing and endearing characters--who despite all their good qualities--make profound terrible mistakes. She helped us understand why it is so hard to walk away from a toxic relationship--because sometimes, the abuser is not a misogynistic, sadistic monster but instead a charismatic, loving, compassionate, driven man with an unforgivable flaw. This is not a romance about true, unconditional love but rather about the inconceivable dangers of unconditional love . Unconditional love is a beautiful thing in the sense that it teaches you to love someone regardless of their flaws, but Lily's story--a story that is unfortunately a reality for many many women and men out there--is proof that there are some flaws that can never make up for all the goodness a person may hold in their heart. It Ends With Us may fall into the NA Romance category, and it maybe fictional (with a several elements from the writer's own life), but it's also a book that raises awareness. It is definitely a book that every adult should read regardless of whether or not they enjoy the genre, and I highly recommend it to everyone.

I've been chipping away at this book for quite a while. I have finally finished it. I thought that it was interesting but I don't live in the correct time to appreciate what others are saying about it. The book was still good, although some of the language and the world building were... eh I guess. Again, this is the polar opposite of what everyone else says about the book. The technology is, obviously, dated and so that is very distracting. However the Sumerian portions of the book were interesting and I'd never heard of them before. The characters in the book were OK I suppose, but they weren't anything to call Home about. I will say that that doesn't really go for the antagonist of the book whose name I don't remember at this point. I just thought he was a jackass but I guess that's the point. I'm actually just beating around the bush here. I didn't really like the book. At all at all. I guess it's just not my cup of tea. And I really like futuristic novels...

The last part of this novel was so jarring and hit me in a very emotional place. I will say mental health and the way these patients were treated during that time are well portrayed. I understand Grace - her darkness, terrors, reasons for detachment- truly she had suffered some terrible heartbreaking things. I enjoyed the platonic relationship between Grace and Thornhollow which reminded me somewhat of a tamer version of Watson and Sherlock. I felt like the plot could have been more interesting and Mindy could have been a little stronger in some parts. She has strong writing skills, the ability to really affect me but that wasn't used completely through out. It was okay. the last third I had to force myself to accept the normalcy of everything and how consequences were all brushed over on the fact that these characters were all 'insane' but it bothered me that there was no repercussions for Grace murdering a man except a light tongue lashing from the very doctor watching her go mad. It enraged me. It enraged me how Grace thought everyone was 'obligated' to help her frame her father. It just...no one helped her out of the pit she fell in. They just let her keep falling. Her mental issues were never 'addressed' just accepted

Honestly, I feel generous giving this book 3 stars. I loved the first book in the series. The second was okay. This one just felt like it would never end. It was too long and drawn out and very confusing at times. I also really felt like the romance completely overshadowed everything. When the bad guys are literally heading straight for you, and it's imperative that one go fight while the other help others escape to safety, DO NOT spend precious minutes telling each other ONCE AGAIN that they are the love of your life, you cannot live without them, and they must return to you. 4.5 Stars! I would so recommend this book to everyone! It was such a brave and heartbreaking journey from start to finish. Lately I've been finding it hard to read books that don't hook me in immediately but this book definitely reeled me in on the first page. The book is told from four perspectives; Emilia, a young Polish girl, a Lithuanian nurse called Joana, a mysterious Prussian called Florian & a German soldier named Alfred. Because the characters are all from different countries, they're all in different situations when it comes to the war and each of them has a secret. We don't find out these secrets until later in the book (which kind of annoyed me a little bit as everything was so mysterious and ambiguous but it didn't take a lot away from my reading experience). I liked 3 out of the 4 characters so reading the 4th persons monologue was kind of irritating as they were irritating BUT regardless, that perspective was needed to complete the puzzle so I put up with it. That 4th monologue was partially why this book wasn't a 5 Star book for me. The other reason why this just missed out on being a WHOPPING 5 stars is because I felt quite distant from the characters. I just wasn't really emotionally invested in any of them. I mean yes I liked them but I was just missing that kind of emotional attachment to the characters and the book. The only character I felt slightly attached to was the old shoemaker, he was a sweetheart. The writing was really good. It kept my attention throughout and instead of really swamping me with loads and loads of history and war talk, the story and history was very eloquently told. I get so overwhelmed with history because I'm so bad at remembering lots of names and numbers and places simultaneously and that's mainly why I don't read a lot of books about historical events. Ruta Sepetys did such a good job with the fictitious and the non-fictitious parts. I still can't believe that happened. That ship sinking killed so many innocent people, it's so hard for me to fathom something like that happening and hardly anybody knows about it!!! Everyone knows about titanic and the loss of life there was WAY less! It was absolutely heartbreaking. I love stories where the author shines light on something hardly anyone knows about. This book really reminded me of Sarah's Key by Tatiana de Rosnay and All The Light We Cannot See by Anthony Doerr (two MUST-READ books). I really liked the short alternating chapters too, they were always the perfect length. Sometimes short chapters can make the story kind of choppy and confusing but that didn't happen here. Bottom line is READ THIS BOOK. It's technically a YA book but it definitely would suit readers who don't read YA. I can't wait to read more by Ruta Sepetys!

I didn't love this book, but I did like it. The humor and witty dialogue really carried the story a long way. The book kicked off really well with two entertaining personalities from Aubrey and Chance. Right off the bat, you can see a truly sizzling chemistry that never fizzles out during their road trip. There are moments that show hesitancy from Chance, but the issue as to why is never acknowledge or made known. That is until the second half of the book which takes place after two years. Honestly, this time jump is where it all went downhill for me. Chance's predicament came out of left field a bit. Looking back, I could definitely piece together from the one clue given early on, but I think that aspect wasn't developed enough to give a nice flow to the story. The passion that the two once had or at least what they were building up to got lost on me at this section as well. I never again felt the same intensity and love worth fighting for. The determination from Chance to win her back brought a smile to face. At one point though, I think he needed to dial it back a little considering his actions began to stray over into the stalking category. The biggest problem I had with this story was Aubrey in the second half of the book. Aubrey's actions made me lose all respect for her. As much as Aubrey told Chance that she was with her boyfriend and she'd never cheat, she essentially did cheat. A bit of it was physical, but more emotional and mental than anything else. She would express interest in Chance one minute and then push him away the next. Her indecision was extremely grating the entire time. I was getting mixed signals so I could only imagine how difficult it was for Chance. She seemed to want her cake and eat it too and it just wasn't fair to those involved. That started to make me severely dislike Aubrey. This book will surely be loved by many, but unfortunately I can't get fully on board with that opinion. There were a few factors that I didn't enjoy, yet I have no doubt others wouldn't be bothered by them. That being said, if you really want to give this book a shot, go for it. Otherwise, I'd say pass.

I honestly have no words. The very fact that I'm even writing a review is indicative enough about how I feel about the novel. It wasn't a fairy tale, it was real. And I think that's what got to me the most. Nothing in the novel felt out of place, too rushed, or anything short of right. Honestly, I was hesitant about reading the novel at first, but I couldn't be happier I did. Man, this novel made me feel. At the end of it, I wanted to curse the author for making me feel this way, and thank him at the same time. I don't know. I was a wreck, truthfully. Without revealing anything, I think I understand the author now. To say the very least, each character had their personality, and to do anything different would've made the character something they weren't. Then it would kill the reason why we love the character in the first place  . But damn, it hurts. That being said, I encourage you to read this novel. Read it, live it, feel it. Become the invisible third person in Carrie and Ray's life. Let yourself feel the love. Because in the end, that was the premise, the motivation, and the outcome.

I think my true rating is 3.5 stars. It took me a while to get through this book - fair enough it's pretty big (350K), but also for most of the first half, while I enjoyed it, it didn't enthrall me enough to want to read it all the time, so I just read it every now and then when I had some time. Fortunately, it picked up more in the second half. :) If anyone's thinking of reading it, I will mention that you often have to sit through many pages of farming methods, government elections, and such. It doesn't interest me directly, but it's not necessarily a slog to get through, or I didn't find it such. :P I will say: I don't understand why the book is called "Anna Karenina" - of course she's a main character, but so much happened that did not surround nor concern her, so I didn't really like that. It didn't help that actually to me Anna was nearly insufferable! I'll put the rest under a spoiler tag, although the main plot is known to many people already, I think. I have limited sympathy for cheaters anyway, so I think already I was set to judge Anna quite harshly, but actually, at first I liked her and felt sorry for her. Her marriage to Alexey Alexandrovich was one of convenience, and I feel sorry for both of them for having to live in a loveless marriage and unable to do anything about it. But as we got to see Alexey Alexandrovich from others' viewpoints, I felt more sorry for him than Anna. He too was not happy in his marriage, and gave Anna the chance to keep seeing Vronsky and keep her position in society and see her son, with the stipulation that she do not see her lover in the house. So of course she brings Vronsky to the house... I couldn't stand the fact that she went swiftly from loving her son Seryozha dearly to indifference and back again to love, and the same with her and Vronsky's baby, whom she loved at first because it was Vronsky's and didn't care about Seryozha all of a sudden because he wasn't Vronsky's. I got tired of her wavering constantly back and forward in her irrational jealousy, and the self-pity she wallowed in all of the time, while she was the one driving Vronsky away from her emotionally by shutting him out. The fact that she deliberately entices men, including happily married men like Levin, to get them to fall in love with her, but whom she cares nothing about, just to make Vronsky jealous, pissed me off. Is she an adult or a fourteen year old girl? Now, I resented Vronsky too for his part in the cheating, and simultaneously felt sorry for him because he and Anna did deserve to have love, but I felt terrible for him for the drama that she pulled all the time for no other reason than to make the man jealous and convince herself that she did not love him, while she pushed him away from her, and the fact that he had shot himself in the chest for her! The fact that she killed herself to "make him love her" and force him to feel agony over her for the rest of his life enraged me. Objectively I sympathized with her for her situation, but I could not feel sorry for her, although obviously her mind was fragile if she was driven enough to suicide, but such a thing does not remove all faults and personal responsibility from someone. I think Tolstoy wrote Levin as a similar case, but then the antithesis to Anna. He too worried that Kitty did not love him, and had suicidal thoughts. I sympathized with him in the sense that he often wanted to be alone, and his struggle with faith. However, I feel that Levin actually made an effort to sort his life out when he was unhappy with it, whereas Anna seemed to expect someone else to do it for her, without knowing her thoughts and the extent of her unhappiness. When she did talk to Vronsky, it was to guilt him and wound him. I enjoyed the fact that Tolstoy wrote about many different characters, and it wasn't too difficult to keep on top of who everyone was. The book has been praised for its realism, and it was nice to read something that was carried on quite an ordinary plot in the end. I'm vaguely curious as to how the movie this year will tell the story, but I don't know if I'll be bothered much to see it. I love Keira Knightley, but I'm a bit tired of her in these same roles. :P Also, I'm annoyed that Domhnall Gleeson is playing Levin, because it's not how I pictured him at all, but I'm sure he'll do a good job. I was wary at first of Jude Law playing Alexey Alexandrovich - both he and Levin ended up quite dear to me - but I've seen pictures, and again, while very different from in my mind's eye, he suits the part well! So, perhaps I'll get round to seeing it one day, but it's a coincidence that it was announced - or I heard of it at least - while I was in the middle of reading the book!

This book is so incredibly hard to rate. I'm torn between giving it a rating anywhere from 3.75 to 5 stars. I really did enjoy this book, but it just took me so long to read! I could only handle a couple of chapters at a time, and I think that is mainly due to Mare's insane character development. In Red Queen, Mare was much more likable. Her character was certainly not perfect, but she was easier to understand. She went from being someone just trying to figure out the world she fell into, literally, into a character who is borderline ruthless and cold-hearted, and maybe a bit careless with others lives. Now I do think her character development was necessary for the future books, but I wish it had happened slowly instead of almost as soon as Glass Sword started. Just like in Red Queen, Victoria Aveyard's writing is beautiful and full of amazing quotes that just make you want to tab the hell out of the book. I just absolutely love her writing style, and she really does know how to catch her readers completely by surprise. Although, I'm not sure I will ever forgive her for Shade's death, he was the one character that I wasn't mad at half of the book! And Maven is still the worst ever, but can we take a minute to appreciate the Queen's death? That made me so incredibly happy, but still not worth Shade dying. And I absolutely loved the new additions to Mare's newblood army! I do feel like it was hard to keep them all straight because we were introduced to so many of these characters in such a short amount of time, but I did think they were such a great addition! And I absolutely love that this book doesn't focus on romance. There are elements there for a future romance, but it's not the main plot, and I totally appreciate that! I can't say I loved this book as much as Red Queen, but it was a great follow up, and I will be re-reading it in the future to see if my feelings change. Now I can't wait for the third installment in this series!

Mark Lawrence is one of those authors whose books I have to read within a week of publication. He has built a solid reputation due to two prior series which have given some of the most memorable characters in the SFF world. Hence I was eagerly awaiting the release of Red Sister. Needless to say the book was all that I had expected and more! Unlike the prior series, this one has a female protagonist and many good female supporting characters. As Brandon Sanderson writes in the post-script for 'Shadows of Silence in Forests of Hell' 'I did not want to write a story about a woman who was a femme fatale or a woman soldier who was a man with breasts' many female protagonists are just that - men with breasts. Not in this case. Novices at the Convent of Sweet Mercy and their teachers are distinct from the traditional cast. The closest comparison that I can make is the society of Aes Sedai from the Wheel of Time series by Robert Jordan. You have strict teachers, intense punishments, interesting syllabus, dangerous side-games, student politics, minor arch enemy, major arch enemy etc. So basically the White Tower (of Aes Sedai) meets Hogwarts, in a very innovative and exciting way. Characters and their relationships are very strong and the coming-of-age characters develop well. It also helps that you have a quick tongued protagonist who does not know when to shut her mouth ;). What appealed to me more than the characters is the scenes that define or develop them. There is a very haunting scene where the High Priest Jacob  beats a mule to death with disgusting cruelty  . Another scene that I can't shake off is the one with the Abbess and the candle. Generally fight scenes or meeting/parting scenes are memorable as they are pivotal moments in the story. However, the scenes listed above are described with such detail that you will remember them even after reading 100 books after this. The story is set on the planet Abeth which has a dying sun. The world setting seems pretty simple to start with - there are four basic 'tribes' from which the people of Abeth have descended and each tribe has a distinct ability. Many other series have such basic 'blood based' or genetic distinction. However, this book is interesting because though the differences are important they are not the main focus of the story. The abilities are woven well into the narrative so that they provide the right context without becoming a crutch for the story. World building is therefore interesting as it happens along with the story development instead of seeming as a break in the story. The prior two series by the author mixed elements of Science Fiction and Fantasy. In this also the same theme can be seen. There are space ships and magic working side by side without hitting a jarring note. Mark Lawerence has superficially covered the journey from advanced technology society to a Medieval setting in the previous series although it was not properly explored. Red Sister also has a similar setting - a space faring society that regresses to animal powered transport and scientific knowledge replaced by mystic religious practices. I hope the back story of the deterioration is brought out more in the subsequent books. Now if all this does not make you want to immediately put all plans aside and start reading, I don't know what will! I just have three questions for Mark - What's the obsession with Thorn(s)? - Can we make High Priest Jacob suffer more in the coming books? - Why oh why did you have to end the book with that line?!

I freely admit that I picked this series up because I was looking for a "book series like the Dresden Files". I'd tried several Urban Fantasy books and series. Some I liked more than others. Some I intensely disliked. This series has become my favorite (after Dresden). It seems to me to have gotten better with each installment. There are for my money some good Urban Fantasy reads out there, but few better than these. Starting with the first volume Mr. Jacka begins establishing his world and his characters. We get to know these people as they act and as they interact. Alex is a mage, a diviner. He can in short look "down the possible futures", the possible pathways things might take if certain things happen are done or said...you get the idea. The farther down the time stream things get the more "iffy" the futures get. This is not exactly combat magic. So far as the mages who have versions of magic that can suck your life away, burn you to ash, freeze you to ice shards...blow you to dust, this would seem to be a rather well, modest form of magic. Still, somehow Alex has managed to survive several (read A LOT) of attempts on his life. Also...and possibly more impressive the ones who have set out to kill Alex, most mages more powerful that he is or adepts with some serious "deadliness" have ended up dead. Alex is getting....known. This book picks up where we left off in the last volume. A friend of Alex who has walked away from him because of events in our last outing is in danger(you know, because of the stuff that happened in that last book I mentioned). "And" (one might say "of course") she doesn't seem to realize how much danger she's actually in. We will touch on new details of the world we're learning about, fill in some more details about the past we've been "considering" and tell an excellent story in the time of it. Are there any disappointments? Sure the same one I have with Jim Butcher's Dresden books. These writers can't turn out a novel a week...not even a month. So here I am again with another series of books where I have to wait for the next book next year. I keep telling you guys, I'm past sixty...how many more books can I wait for?? Sheesh. Five stars and highly recommended. There are a couple of things here that will I think remind my fellow readers of the Dresden books. I don't for a second think they were copied. As I've said after several thousand years of fiction how many "totally new" plot points can there be? Alex is mistrusted by the overall council of light mages...because he started out as the apprentice of a dark mage. In this book he gets made an offer that will bring him great power and advantage, but change him for the worse. Those are sort of common threads. Don't let it put you off. These are excellent reads I really can give them my highest recommendation. As noted, my highest recommendation. Enjoy.

I missed reading Wuthering Heights in high school, which is where it seems most people first encounter it. Frankly, I'm glad. I find I didn't appreciate most of the classics I was asked to read as a teenager. Charles Dickens is the best example; A Tale of Two Cities was incomprehensible to me in 10th grade, but full of intrigue, bravery and even humor when I tried it again as an adult. I already knew most of the key points in Wuthering Heights before opening the book: the moors, the tragic love story, the famous scene when Heathcliff dug of Catherine's grave. But my muddled comprehension of the plot didn't prepare me for the layers of darkness, torture and revenge. I also can't imagine why anyone would consider Heathcliff a romantic figure. I've rarely encountered a bigger villain in literature. He's an utter asshole; even his love for Catherine was twisted and wrong. One of the greatest points of the book is how all his plans are thwarted in the end, with Cathy and Hareton's budding attachment to one another. So one of the biggest lessons learned, and one that I continue learning every time I tackle a Classic I've missed, is experiencing a book firsthand will always exceed its reputation.

I honestly thought that this novel was going to be better since I enjoyed the first novel as well as the last novel. (Yeah, I read this series out of order.) I really liked Marcus' portrayals in the first and third novel, so I thought falling in love with this novel would be a no-brainer. I was wrong. This novel was is about Marcus and Regina, and the beginning of their relationship. Marcus is brash, upfront and uninhibited. He is short-tempered and he has a quick tongue. He's also very sensitive and hard-headed. Honestly, the list could go on. Regina, on the other hand, is at the top of society and hides a secret that could tear apart the fragile world that she thrives in. The ride was enjoyable but it was not one of her best. It felt a bit rushed. I loved the writing situations that she tried in this novel and the character traits that she created. Yet, personally, I didn't feel completely immersed in this novel. Now as other reviewers have said, this could possibly be a Beauty & the Beast adaptation, but I am not a fan of that tale. Normally I don't read fairytale retellings. There were moments during this novel where I felt the relationship did walk the line between verbally abusive and normal. Luckily the heroine wasn't didn't ever play the victim role. I also liked the symbolism in the novel although there were some symbols that didn't really mix well. For example, she mentions Odysseus and the Odyessy at the beginning. Then we don't really hear much about it until the first intimate scene when Marcus refers to her as a siren. Yet at the same time, she also tries to work the dragons-fairytale angle. IMO, it never felt like those two literary motifs worked together. This is a historical fiction novel, and I normally like the literary themes that she uses. But this time it felt as though the motifs/themes fell flat and didn't work well together. This novel fluctuated between a 3-3.5 star book for me. Overall, it was okay. It was enjoyable at times, but not one of Jeffries' best. The only reason it received three stars because of the effort it took to write and the writing situations that she used. It felt rushed and and like a lost opportunity. Despite that, i will continue to read her novels. If I ever return to this series, I will probably skip this novel.

Probably the only way I would've appreciated this novel more would be if I were a white collar, mid-life-crisis-having family man in the 70's. That should say at least something, considering I'm not by any stretch what you would call an adventure novel reader, and haven't even remotely settled myself into a stable enough existence to warrant feelings of stagnation and suburban humdrum. My kids and my mortgage are not dragging me down enough to compel me to thrill-seek in nature or join an underground boxing club or buy a red sports car, mostly because I don't have kids or a mortgage, I do not (fine, can't) fight, and cars are stupid and boring and purely a necessity for those of us who live in Oklahoma City, which is approximately 99.9% concrete. So this was not so much an escapist thing for me. It is just a jagged-edged, meditative, scary, gripping, awesomeawesome story. For anyone. Pretty much everyone knows about The Scene, whether or not they've actually watched the film, as certain quotes from it (you know the ones) have been disturbingly resistant to time. I am happy to report, though, that some license was taken with The Scene in the movie version as far as hillbilly lines are concerned, the lack of which made it just slightly more tolerable to read. And it is a blessedly brief moment, which is strange considering it is like the only thing people seem to remember about the story. It is not the only thing! It is not even the main thing, if you had reservations in that regard. But yeah, dude totally gets raped. That definitely happens. There was basically no reason for me to put that in spoiler tags, but some people around here just loooove to nag about how reviewers are always ruining their fun by telling them Romeo and Juliet both die and Rosemary gives birth to the antichrist and god kills everybody in a great flood, so I thought I'd cover my ass. SERIOUSLY no pun intended. This is not just some Chainsaw Massacre style horror story about scary redneck survivalist types, though, but rather a redemptive (for some) tale of struggle and resilience and friendship and the indomitable human spirit and how some of the least likely people harbor vast reserves of untapped strength which would crash open if they would only push themselves a little and blah blah blah. That sounds mocking, but I really mean it. Honestly, I was quite surprised by how taken I was with it. And I kiiiiiinda want to be Lewis now. The version of Lewis that can barely manage one pull-up, and still enjoys canoeing.

** spoiler alert ** The interwoven stories of Molly and Vivian are fully fleshed out and believable. Though I normally don't like kitschy narrative intertwining, it worked in this story. I found teenager Molly, caught up in the foster system, believable in speech and emotion (though I honestly don't have anything to base this on other than being a teenage girl a few years ago...). (ha) Vivian's story of being orphaned and then sent on a train to the Midwest seemed more fleshed out to me, for some reason. I wanted to know more about this time in our history and especially more about her experience once she found Dutchy. The one part that I did not find believable was her sudden wish to give away her daughter for adoption. I think that anyone with good family support would not be able to make that choice, but presumably there are people out there with that experience; it just didn't ring true for me in the novel.

3.5 stars. The story of a young orphaned girl who is sent off to find a wholesome new family in the Midwest, but is instead greeted with loveless (un)caregivers and hardship, though she eventually makes a peaceful life for herself. Much of the writing was exceptionally wonderful. The way Kline sets up the atmosphere and living situations Niamh faced was completely engrossing. My main objections are that a) the story felt a little cursory with Niamh going from place to place without enough development in each of them and b) as a personal plea to Ms. Kline- please don't kill off wonderful characters for the sake of being grown-up and literary, it ruins the reading experience for those of us that don't care about pretention.

I won't be able to stop myself, especially since I just finished the book and everything is still so fresh in my mind. When I start a book, they automatically get 3 stars. Then I add or subtract as I go along. This info will be important. To be honest, I ran across this book when I saw a GR list about beautiful YA covers. This really caught my eye. They say don't judge the book by its cover, but I'm glad I did this time. The cover made me look at the blurb, and that was all it took. Lieutenant Markov and the Grand Duchess Marguerite. 4.5 stars. Marguerite's questionable ethics concerning the Marguerite and Paul in Russia. 4 stars. Unresolved sexual tension and making me cry in real life because of non-cheesy, non-melodramatic but insanely beautiful dialogue. Not an easy feat. 5 stars. I was going to dock 2 stars for making me go through a rollercoaster of emotions when I found out there is a sequel, but that it won't be out til November 3, 2015. I WANT IT NOW!

** spoiler alert ** I loved the first half of this book. A middle aged childless couple in 1920's Alaska build a snow girl one stormy night and soon after, Faina comes into their lives wearing the snow girl's mittens and hat. The scenes of the snowball fight, the chicken plucking, the evolving friendship with the Benson's and the setting of building a life in the harsh wilderness were all wonderful. The is-she-or-isn't-she-real-ness of Faina was intriguing and I found myself as happy as Mabel with the little life they built. Then several years go by and I found myself really struggling with the path the story takes. Mabel and Jack are getting old and so is Faina. Then Faina and the Benson's son fall in love and the story no longer seems magical. The fact that Faina gets really feverish when she is inside isn't enough to keep me believing in her. And frankly, if she isn't magic, then the story loses much of its appeal for me. Now of course, in the end, I can't say she wasn't magical. Ivey brings us back to the magic in the end but in a way that didn't seem especially climactic. In fact, I found myself asking, "That's it??" I wonder if she just didn't know how to bring this lovely world to closure.

Do you ever feel like you're an alien? Or like other people are reading completely different books than you are? Am I somehow genetically incapable of liking anything? WHAT DOES IT ALL MEAN. What I thought I thought I was getting with this book: a psychologically twisty, emotionally intense version of those dull "Generic Billionaire Meets Human Female" books, where the characters were going to be real and the chemistry raging. What I actually got: exactly the same book as those dull "Generic Billionaire Meets Human Female" books, except this one is geek-flavored: instead of the hero being built like an MMA fighter, he is a young David Bowie with an unusually long neck. I quit so early I almost wanted to return it, even though it was the nearly-free price of 99 cents. I just find this type of book really frustrating, and I felt kinda betrayed by the enthusiastic "this is so much better than most books like this!" reviews. Here's some prose: I turned the menu over to the list of desserts. "Today's sorbet is passion fruit." "Passion fruit?" he asked, one eyebrow raised like he was skeptical of it. "Nah," I joked. "That's the name of my Lord Lightning cover band." That made him laugh. Did it? DID IT REALLY? IS THAT EVEN A JOKE? "Lord Lightning" is the name of some super famous but mysterious rock star who is performing near the venue where the heroine is filling in as a server when the long-necked billionaire enters. I think you are supposed to not instantly guess that the mystery billionaire is presumably Lord Lightning, which by the way is a really terrible, uncool name for a rock star. Right? Right??????? The light from outside was stark and bluish compared to the soft amber lights in the bar, making his cheekbones look impossibly sharp. His hair was dangerously blond, almost white, and cropped close to his head. His age was impossible to gauge; he could've been a young forty or a haunted twenty. He was gorgeous and striking and his voice had a slight British twinge to it as he said, "Oh, just try to work it into every conversation, do you?" Then he orders the passion fruit sorbet and then makes her eat some of it. It isn't sexy, it's awkward. They have an exchange where she is supposed to be nervously blathering and he is supposed to be cool and in charge. It doesn't feel that way. After a while, she notices his body again: His neck was long and graceful, and he had not the slightest bit of slouch in his posture, like a male figure skater. Erm. Ashley, tell me something," he said, angling his head as if to see me better. "Would you like to try something else new?" "Something else?" I echoed. "What do you mean?" "Are you bored? Tired of the rat race? Looking for a little adventure?" "Well, sure, who isn't?" I said. He nodded at my automatic response. "Indeed. Ashley, I'm bored. I would like to play a game. And I would like someone to play it with me." "I bet you say that to all the girls," I joked. His expression darkened, surprising me. "Actually, it takes a very special person to pique my interesting." He thinks I'm special, I thought? Oh good lord! Man. I hate that sort of thing. Like anvils dropping from the sky rather than something an actual human would do/say/feel/think. The hero has been in this restaurant for long enough to have a total of maybe 1 minute of interaction with the heroine. We as the audience have yet to see anything, even separate from her interaction with the hero, that makes us find her "special" or interesting or charismatic, or to see anything in her interaction with him that makes what happens next seem reasonable. It's all so rushed, so paint-by-numbers, so devoid of charm, chemistry, HUMANITY. DO PEOPLE LIKE THIS SORT OF THING? What do you like about it? What are you seeing that I'm unable to see? Then he makes his actual proposal to his waitress who he has known for 3-4 minutes now. Here it is, in all its sexy glory: "The game is very simple. I ask you to do something, and you do it." "Something like what?" "Something like this: I have a marble in my jacket pocket. I'd like you to reach into the pocket, take out the marble, and put it in your mouth. I'll also have another bourbon and a glass of water, and when you bring me back the drinks, put the marble into the glass of bourbon. That's how you'll return it to me." His voice deepened and it felt like silk sliding over my skin. "Would you do that, Ashley?" This is the type of thing I mean. I understand what the book is telling us is happening. But it feels like I, as the reader, am being asked to do all of the work in imagining this scene as sexy, compelling, so compelling that the heroine (whose name is actually not Ashley, for reasons) does what is actually a pretty weird thing for a complete stranger. I don't actually feel that the heroine is hot for the hero - it's just words on a page informing me that she is. Signposts letting me know what is allegedly going on. But I don't feel that the book is actually SHOWING me, it's just telling me. Eventually Karina (the heroine's real name) returns with fresh drinks and his weird, unsexy sex marble in her mouth. At last I stopped in front of his table, drew in a deep breath, and set down the glass of water. I then held up the shot glass of bourbon as if I were smelling it, brought the marble out until I held it with just my lips in an O shape, and let it go, almost like I was blowing him a kiss. The marble fell with a plop and I set the bourbon on the table, resisting the urge to wipe my lips. I settled for licking them. (I find this kind of gross, not sexy. YMMV, I get that.) I just don't understand. Why would a woman who is a harried graduate student we have little other information about do this or find this sexy? I feel like if you're a writer setting up a story where your heroine is going to do something transgressive and sexually fancy with a complete stranger, you need to spend some time setting up for us her character in a way that makes this plausible - almost inevitable. Like show us how she is stifled in her life, how her sexual selfhood feels boxed in and trapped. Show us her life and character in such a way that when Mr. Long Neck shows up, we understand that he is the inevitable release valve. But that's not what happens here. It's just more of the exact same "Generic Billionaire/Human Female" nonsense, except instead of being mainstream/vapid/dull, it's kinda geeky/vapid/dull.

This is really a story about incredibly bad parenting. James and Marilyn spend 16 years trying to mould their oldest daughter into everything they never were while simultaneously ignoring their other two kids. It's almost shocking that all three didn't end up dead instead of just the eldest. Now you might think the eldest died by suicide because of everything she's been through, but you'd be wrong. I was quite surprised myself to find that  she actually died because she was stupid. She thought she could change everything bad by reenacting a near-death experience forgetting there was someone there to save her the first time I would have rated it higher if I liked any of the main characters. The only one I really did like was the youngest daughter who barely had a part to play in this story until the end. If you like fictional but realistic stories, this is one to try.

I really really enjoyed this book. It was my first Holly Black book and I was not disappointed. I've seen people give this book bad reviews for the shittiest reasons and I get it. I mean, nothing is perfect! But this certainly deserves more fans. Reasons being : All the characters have a very beautiful relation with one another and their lives interweave perfectly. Badass female protagonist. Do I need to say more? Faeries. Folklore. Sleeping prince in a glass coffin. Magic. Monsters. King. Court. Romance LGBT characters who are perfectly normal and not overly filled with the rainbow shit what people assume gay people like supposedly. I was not bored even for a single minute. This was fast paced, filled with action and mystery and sometimes creepy. Even though I'm not a huge fan of faeries, this book certainly did not take me down the same road. However there were some aspects which were cringe worthy, I fell in love with the writing style Holly has. I liked the characters and felt what they felt. I liked how the thing wrapped up in the end. A perfect end to a stand alone novel, not like some which leave you hanging with tons of questions. Since everything was justified one way or the other throughout the book without us knowing it happening. I absolutely loved night Hazel even though I did like the day one pretty much equally. I loved John and Ben. Carter was okay and the parents made absolutely no sense to me. They were all cracked up. I was indifferent to the horned boy. Recommend it to fans of Holly Black and people who like fae. Quotes I liked "There's a monster in our wood. She'll get you if you're not good. Drag you under leaves and sticks. Punish you for all your tricks. A nest of hair and gnawed bone. You are never, ever coming... home." "Down a path worn into the woods, past a stream and a hollowed-out log full of pill bugs and termites, was a glass coffin. It rested right on the ground, and in it slept a boy with horns on his head and ears as pointed as knives." "Once, there was a girl who vowed she would save everyone in the world, but forgot herself." "We love until we do not. For us, love doesn't fade gradually. It snaps like a branch bent too far." "I love like in the storybooks. I love you like in the ballads. I love you like a lightning bolt. I've loved you since the third month you came and spoke with me. I loved that you made me want to laugh. I loved the way you were kind and the way you would pause when you spoke, as though you were waiting for me to answer you. I love you and I am mocking no one when I kiss you, no one at all." "I wanted to be in love like in the storybooks and songs and ballads. Love that hits you like a lightning bolt. And I'm sorry, because yeah, I get that you think I'm ridiculous. I get that you think I'm hilarious. I know, I get that you're mocking me. I get how stupid I am, but at least I know." I read this book for Week 4 of the #ReadProud challenge. This is a novel in verse, about three people: a trans Latina woman who works in a GLBTQ youth center, a white teenage wrestler who was AMAB trying to come to terms with his gender identity (to say closer would be a spoiler - one of my issues with the book was this, see below. And yes, he uses he pronouns in the book), and a white cis girl who is also a wrestler. I was not sure why the poetic form was chosen for the book. Poetic minimalism needs to have striking imagery, something that worked very well e.g., in Brown Girl Dreaming by Jacqueline Woodson; or grabbing rhythm, e.g., as in The Crossover by Kwame Alexander. This book did not particularly succeed at either. It was also one of those books with one of my most disliked twists: minority identity as plot twist. The protagonist spends most of the book thinking he is a trans woman, in quite gender-essentialist terms (one cannot be a trans woman because one's not interested in wearing high heels? exCUSE me? ), and then almost to the end, the trans Latina character, aka Token Character of Color Introduced By White Author To Help the Protagonist, cluebats him that he is genderqueer. He is completely surprised by this despite having spent a lot of time earlier googling trans-related things, and it is not made clear to the reader either how this is different from queer. The gender essentialism is also not addressed at all. There could have been some discussion about how a very femme presentation is required for trans women from many cis gatekeepers, especially doctors, but there was nothing. Also, fully one third of the book was taken up by the cis straight girl feeling miserable that her love interest was distracted by the whole gender feels thing, and in the end they ended up separating. My first reaction was "Good riddance", because she came across as genuinely aggravating, but my second was, how is this kind of narrative supposed to help gender-nonconforming teens? In addition to the author making 100% sure we understood that the trans woman character was physically abused, ended up in the hospital etc. due to trans-related hate crimes. And that is before we get to the whole "people who commit hate crimes are suppressing their own feelings about their minority background" theme. Sure, it does happen sometimes, my former synagogue had an ex-Neo-Nazi, but still. With so few nonbinary narratives, especially in mainstream contemporary YA, does this have to be one of them? I also think that mental health professionals and other people working with marginalized teens writing YA about their clients is potentially quite problematic and I am troubled that this is apparently a trend; I just talked about this phenomenon in my review to Simon vs the Homo Sapiens Agenda, so you can see more of my thoughts there. My usual disclaimer about the source of the book: I got it from the Iowa City Public Library

My only criticism of this book would be that it may be too clever, and too aware of its own cleverness. The narrative style alone, with stories nestled inside stories, makes it worth the read, but it can also get a little preachy in parts. Also, I find David Mitchell, in general, seems to have a hard time writing about the future; as in The Bone Clocks he goes a little overboard on the whole terrifying futuristic dystopia thing-- it seems that he just gets too fixated on world building and working in as many terrifying thoughts as possible, and this seems to come at the expense of more meaningful character development which is much more evident in his stories set in the past or the present. Also, he seems to have a weird obsession with torturing literary critics, whether it's locking them in prisons (as in The Bone Clocks) or throwing them off roofs as in Cloud Atlas. It's a little strange; and his recurring theme of cannibalism is kind of odd too-- but it all works with the story, just a bit of a weird motif.

The Capture strays away from the usual pattern the previous books have taken. The story focuses on Jake's character, his brother Tom and the Yeerk which has been controlling his brother. The Animorphs discover the Yeerks are trying to take over a hospital so they can have access to humans and easily create human controllers. The Animorphs destroy a Yeerk pool within the hospital but unfortunately Jake get hit, passes out and falls into the pool, where a Yeerk (the same one who controlled Tom) proceeded to take over his body. The Animorphs feel something wrong with Jake and monitor him for three days until the Yeerk in him dies. The internal struggle with the Yeerk was really interesting. There were definitely more discoveries about the Yeerks' schemes and a look into how Tom became a controller. This book was a bit more emotional and less action-packed. It was good because the characters were further developed (though I seem to dislike Cassie more as the series goes on because she's too goody two shoes...). Once again, Ax does not fail to entertain and I'm really looking forward his POV in book #8! Animorphs is so easy to read even when I don't feel like reading. I'm easily taken away and immersed in their world.

I'm not saying that all books with high ratings on Goodreads are necessarily bad, but I am saying that often I am suspicious of books with ratings over 4--especially if they're 4.1+ and "classics" in any genre--because it seems like people who might have read a book and enjoyed it as a child just think, "oh yeah, warm fuzzies for that one--5 stars." Luckily there are some great reviews of this book out there. Heinlein" at The Book Smugglers "The Moon Is a Harsh Mansplainer (1966) by Robert A. Heinlein" at From Couch to Moon

Plus, it was my first time reading a LGBTQ+ novel which doesn't belong to the YA genre. That was a breath of fresh air. I love myself some mystery. And needless to say, this book delivered. I originally assumed that the author was gonna focus on the LGBTQ+ part and just make a half-assed attempt at plotting the mystery but boy, was I wrong. It was well thought out and it kept me guessing throughout the story. I was also drawn to the chemistry between the main characters. Did I mention the sex scenes? Ho-ly crap. It's my first time reading detailed gay sex scenes, and honestly? I can't say I didn't enjoy it ;) One more thing I loved about the book was the real world problems the main characters face. (PTSD and achromatopsia)  It's always interesting to read about actual problems people face in the world and expand my knowledge on them as well as try to understand what they have to go through in their daily lives. With that said, I'm looking forward to reading the next book in this series! (It's also probably time I check out some of Edgar Allen Poe's works.) Is falling in love with someone's story the same thing as falling in love with the person himself? This is the only decent thing in this book. Entertainment weekly described this book to be "the hottest YA title to hit the bookstores since The Hunger Games" is it though?! IS IT? I think you need to go and rethink your life choices if you think this was anything close to being as good as THG. This book was a complete snooze fest and I haven't been this bored with a book in about a year now; so you can guess my big disappointment! This book is readable yes but I would rather stick hot needles through my eyes than sit through another 360 odd pages of this story. I'm not going to lie. The idea behind it is fantastic. But the book. Ew no. Cassia lives in a world where the society controls everything. Where you work, who you get married to, how many children you have, ect. Therefore on their 17th birthday's (why 17? What's so special about that) all the teenagers go to the Match Banquet dressed in their pretty clothes and await their perfect match to be shown on a screen. The couple later on then get aquatinted, get married and have kids. But when Cassia is matched with her childhood bestfriend Xander her life couldn't be any better. She already knows her match and they can speed along their getting to know each other and she won't have to move away from her family. But once Cassia returns home and watches her Banquet a different face flashes before her eyes; Ky, another guy she already knows. Isn't Cassia just the luckiest! This is where the boring and predictable and very annoying part of the story begins. A love triangle. Obviously. I don't understand the hype for this book at all! Yes I'm late with reading this book and I'm glad I am. Actually no I wish I never read this tragedy. Ally's writing is decent enough for me not to throw the book out of my window but the rest? Dull. There's no passion in her writing, no urgency, no real desire to make this world come into life. It's as if Ally was bored of her own dull work and couldn't be bothered to make this book at all interesting. The relationships between the characters were dull, the society that she created was dull, the conflict if there ever was any was dull and not to mention the dull conversations between the characters. Actually no. The conversations were ugly. They were hard to read. "Once you want something, everything changes." Erm no. Let me just burn the page this quote was on. "Now that I've found the way to fly, which direction should I go into the night?" How about anywhere but near me. "Do not go gentle." I can't remember where this is from but is this a sexual innuendo I smell here? Nope. There was nothing in this book that was remotely fun or funny or at all interesting! I looked up some of these quotes just to show the kind of nonsense that's in this book and it made me hate it even more. I forgot some of the stupid stuff that's in here. And the stupid, stupid love triangle! This made me so mad!!! Cassia is matched with Xander and that pretty much means she will eventually marry him and she knows this. She agrees with the society but then goes off and has a relationship with Ky while poor cute little Xander has no idea. THAT'S CALLED CHEATING YOU SLUT. "I came up on the screen, too, Cassia. But he was the one you chose to see." And look at him. He's heartbroken because not only did Cassia chose to run away with Ky she also ruined Xander's life. Bitch.

Her eyes narrowed, the gold like living ember. He'd never seen anyone so beautiful. This witch had been crafted from the darkness between the stars. How does one go from having Aelin and Rowan being their favorite characters in Heir of Fire, to having them be their LEAST favorite characters in Queen of Shadows. I mean how did Maas manage to reverse my opinion that quickly with just one book? This has got to be a really disappointing sequel. I LIVED for Rowan in Heir of Fire. He was such a great addition to the large cast of characters in the series. But that snarky hard core bad ass completely disappeared in this book. Nope. Now, this dude is nothing but a pussy whipped puppy. If you're one of those people that was hard core shipping Rowaelin, then you'll love this book. I, however, do not fall for Sarah J Maas's writing. I'm not going to completely hate a character (Chaol), just so I can love another one (Rowan) because you indirectly told me to. It was blatantly obvious that is exactly what was going on in this book. Does she not know how to create a new love interest without ruining an old one? Gtfoh. She's slowly writing him out of the book because she changed her mind. But she did not do it the right way. She used the same technique a lot of New Adult authors use. Make one of the love interest an asshole so people like the other dude more. I know Chaol always had those opinions against magic. But the way he felt about Aelin in this book is no different than the way Aelin felt about Manon. I mean, both Chaol and Aelin had a lot of negative opinions and prejudice again those who were not like them. Chaol might have said a few mean things that cut deep. But Aelin literally got physical with Manon. Even after Manon gave Aelin the information she wanted, even after Manon told her she could save Dorian, she still abused her and refused to give her water. Yet this fandom loves to give double standards when it comes to Chaol and Aelin. If you're going to reprimand Chaol for the shit he did in this book, then reprimand Aelin as well, because she's really not that innocent. This was the best part (not really): Aelin: If there was any way to save Dorian, I would try to find it. Also Aelin: *skips and prances in different dresses and does a sexy fashion show for Rowan instead of trying to find a way to get Dorian the fuck out of there. Okay Aelin...sounds fake but okay... My other favorite part (not really): Chaol was basically the only person in the book that was so invested in saving Dorian (THANK YOU CHAOL). Aelin, however, was ready to let him die. She didn't even try to find a way to save him. She didn't even TRY. But when Dorian does come back to reality, she had the nerve to say "I came back for you." NO YOU DIDN'T GET THE FUCK OUTTA HERE. YOU WAS ABOUT TO LET HIM DIE BUT YOU'RE NOT GOING TO LET HIM KNOW THAT ARE YOU? No Dorian, Chaol and Manon were the real ones that came back for you. But yes, let Aelin take all the credit. Smh....the nerve. The problem with Maas is that she does a lot of telling and no showing. She constantly tells us that Aelin is brave, and she is fire, and she is amazeballs. Literally the amount of Aelin praise in this book has got to be a joke. No, it was not woman empowerment, it was unnecessary praise. She had to make sure that EVERY. SINGLE. CHARACTER. praised about the powerful Aelin Ashryver Galathynius. No really, every single character fell at her feet and started kissing them. Chaol, the only person who didn't fall to her feet, was literally destroyed as a character. Thanks Maas. I also don't think Maas understands the idea of warfare. Like why is everyone making allies with Aelin? The reasons Maas gives are totally not realistic. I know this book has wyvers, shapeshifters, Valg princes, etc. But the idea of warfare should be realistic. This is WAR. This is where PEOPLE DIE. So her making allies so easily just makes no sense. There'd have to be way more convincing done on her part than what this book provided. It shouldn't be that easy to create an army. But it seems everyone is willing to join forces with her so easily. BUT WHY?!? The only reason this book got a three stars was for Manon and Dorian. They're the only ones that saved the book from getting a lowly one start. I may not have been that invested in Manon's story line in Heir of Fire, but this book completely changed my feelings about her. Literally, both Aelin and Rowan could die and I won't even think twice about shedding a tear. But I swear if Maas even touches Manon or Dorian, I will flip a shit. R.I.P Chaol. I'm sorry you been done wrong bebe. I will always love your ass.

I liked Scythe. It was a good book and it was what I have come to expect from Neal Shusterman. Shusterman is an author that comes up with new and creative ways to challenge the way we think about things. All of his books are unique and are a breath of fresh air when everything in the YA spectrum seems to be full of the same thing (my own writings included). But unfortunately 'liked' is all I can say for it right now. It took me a long time to get into the book but by the end I was reading it as I walked to and from my breaks at work as well as spending my break time reading it. It really picked up after the death of Scythe Faraday. I did, however, find myself falling in love with the main characters. Rowan in particular. He definitely gave the book a little more spine. He had so much character growth through out the book as well as being able to hold on the Rowan we were first introduced to. The twist and turns in this book were enough to keep you on the edge of your seat without feeling like you were being violently ripped into another book entirely. Altogether, Scythe was a good book enough book to reignite my craving for reading books of this sort, but not amazing enough to satisfy it.

3.5/5 stars Violet Fairdale is the top guardian trainee of her class. She does everything as quickly and efficiently as possible. And one mission is going to jeopardize it all. After taking care of a serpent that was about to attack a human boy, Violet unknowingly brings him into the Fae realm with her. That breaks the two biggest rules out there. Nate is a human who is suddenly bombarded with the fact that there are Fae creatures out there that hunt dangerous creatures to protect humanity. Things suddenly got a lot more complicated for Violet. To be completely honest, I have some mixed feelings about this book. I enjoyed it, but I didn't love it. Violet was a pretty kickass character and I really liked reading all the fighting scenes where she whips her amazing moves and defeats all the bad guys. But at the same time, her entire world is essentially shaken but one human boy. With the addition of Nate, Violet finds her life thrown in a cycle of betrayal, mysteries, and unknown danger. Violet's world becomes completely surrounded by Nate and I just didn't feel like they had a connection that strong to begin with. Building off of that, I didn't really like Nate. Sorry Nate-lovers, but he just didn't appeal to me. He did have a sweet side to him at times, but I felt like he was so easily swayed by others and so willing to betray family and people he cared about so easily for a chance at finding who he was. He was just too willing in my opinion to hand over Violet to the Unseelie Prince that I just can't get myself to like him. Plus, he did that after Violet risked so much for him  . I understand that finding out that Fae exist and that your mom is connected is kind of mind blowing, but I didn't support his actions and yeah...I didn't like him. Other than my problems with the romance and Nate, I did enjoy the story. It was really action packed and you learn a lot about the Fae world in just the first book. Obviously there are a ton of Fae related books out there like the Iron Fey series, but I did think that Rachel Morgan put a very unique twist on the whole world. The writing was definitely really entertaining and fun to read and I thoroughly enjoyed the world. Oh, one more thing. There is a sort of resolution between Violet and an old friend turned enemy which I thought was probably the best part of the story. Her bickering with Ryn was really entertaining to read at her expense and at the beginning I did really hate him. As the story continued, there was a lot that was revealed about Violet and Ryn's past and you do start to feel for him. He turns from a completely jerk and bully to someone who actually has a heart, and I do mean that. So I definitely liked the turnout in their relationship and while they're still frenemies, I'm holding out hope! With that said, I would probably pick up the next two books if I can just because I really want to see what happens next. The ending does kind of leave you hanging with a lot of questions. I do recommend this book mainly for the world and less so for the characters. So if you're a big character person, you might get slightly frustrated.
