Strong 3.5 (Rounded to 4 stars) Maddie is a girl that you will be able to relate to if you ever found yourself falling for someone that you think is totally wrong for you. Hey, maybe that guy's dad wasn't a dirty cop that murdered your parents (I would hope) but I think a few of us can understand the essence of the conflict, myself included. This is pretty much the premise of the story. And it makes for a really intense plot line. In that regard, it totally delivered. It is most definitely an emotional rollercoaster. That being said, she had no indication that Kyle even knew of his father's involvement, so I did have some conflicts with her placing her childhood friend and first love in the 'apple doesn't fall far from the tree' category. I struggled with the lack of believable reaction when she finally tells Kyle what she had seen that night and why she keeps trying to pull away from him. But I will not deny that I was hooked into this story. I followed along with its fast pace and suspense from the beginning, and enjoyed every minute of it to the very end. If this unusual romantic plot line doesn't intrigue you, I don't know what will. This is definitely a novel worth checking out. *I received a eBook copy of this book for free to review from the author/publisher; this in no way influenced my review, all opinions are 100% honest and my own.

** spoiler alert ** So, this review really has spoilers. So, if you're not into that, you'd better read a different review. Imma start out by spoiling everything: I was not upset that Tris died. Au contraire: I was thrilled. Not that I have anything against her, she just needed to die. In fact, my biggest problem with the book was that her death wasn't enough. The world had to end in chaos. There just wasn't room for anything else. Too many things could have gone wrong that didn't. Too many. And what's with all the serums? If you find out that a memory serum exists and that memories can be replaced, I say: don't do anything. Chances are you don't have enough information to make an informed decision. It seemed like anytime something went wrong in this book, there'd be another serum that magically appeared. It made me think that there's definitely no debate between creation/evolution... The world was appeared a week and a half ago. We began to exist with previous memories stored in us. Why? I don't know. Probably some alien experiment. And Tris makes it out of Chicago and finds out there's SOOOOooooo much more than Chicago. But when she gets to the Bureau of Genetic Whatever, and offs David and replaces the memories of everybody living there, nobody in the rest of the United States has a problem with that. And, I felt like a GD fool when I'd read "GD." Because to me, those initials already stand for something, so I had to work to make my mind read them as "Genetically Damaged." Whatever. Take this review with grain of salt. I'm a GD tired guy, and I think I may have finally reached the end of my dystopian rope. I didn't think it'd ever arrive - and now here it is all at once, bursting like the One-Hoss Shay

This is one of those books that, like Out of My Mind, allows kids a glimpse into the inner life of someone who seems very different from themselves - a window into a different experience based on physical appearances. The perspective shifts between several characters, which felt very effective and allowed the story to be about both August's own experiences and the way other kids and teens interact with him. The writing is straightforward but the style still feels lovely, somehow. There was one plot element that spoiled the potential emotional resonance of the story. At the graduation ceremony, when the principal is about to give out the special Beecher award, I knew what was coming and began cringing. As I read the story, there were many things I felt that other kids learned from being around Auggie, but he never struck me as a lesson in kindness. Perhaps his presence encouraged the other kids to learn to be kinder? But Auggie himself never exemplified the spirit of kindness. He was just being a normal kid. And giving him an award for kindness completely detracts from that aspect of the book and undermines what I thought was the primary theme of the story. That issue aside, I thought the story and characters were well-constructed and I enjoyed reading it. Source: my public library

Reviews show this is actually fan's LEAST favorite of Sarah Waters. If that's the case, than I'm going to absolutely love everything she writes. The writing, tone, feel, and ambiance of the book was great- moody, brooding, with a hint of drama, romance, and crime- all without feeling forced. The beginning is very slow-moving, and the focus being more on characters feelings, explorations, and psychological reactions. Once the reveal happened the book really picked up the pace, got moving, and kept actively interesting plot-wise. It's hard to describes this book without spoilers. It's post WWI London, and Frances has lost her male family to the war. Her and her mother are forced to taken in boarders (the title Paying Guests), Lillian and Len Barber. There is tension, build up, and backstory of Lillian and Len, culminating in romance. About halfway though the "reveal" happens, and the rest is dealing with a crime, and the consequences of it. I loved showing the LGBT aspect in a world that didn't talk about this. I love the unfolding of the crime scene, the different characters being brought in, wondering if Lillian will be caught, and watching her and Frances stress out about the situation. I actually "guessed wrong" and thought that Charley was going to be Len's lover! lol The ending was left a little short for me though. It wasn't a cliffhanger, but I was left with a "what's next" thought. Not in a good, think it over way- but in a "did I miss the last chapter?" way. However, if you are an audiobook person- the narrator was FABULOUS. I'm hoping she narrates others of Water's books, because I'm on board. I'm really excited to read Fingersmith, whenever that may be.

This book was referred to me by a professional who I knew was quite capable and intelligent, but was not the loud fast-talking go-getter type that I was used to dealing with at work. Having gotten tired of the aggressive types at work who talk so fast that you cannot keep up with them, and are wrong too much of the time in what they say, I was starting to think in terms of myself and Asperger's, or being in the spectrum--as though this might be considered a negative attribute by society. The book Quiet labels thoughtfulness as introversion--not a pathology--and describes it as being a feature and not a bug. The book puts our overly-aggressive society in historical perspective and gives instructions on how to use our soft power. It legitimizes introverts and establishes that we have a rightful place in society.

I FEEL SO BETRAYED RIGHT NOW!!! dY~!dY~!dY~! For starters, I pushed myself through the first half of this book based on the merits of the first two in the series, which I LOVED. Right now, I'm wishing I'd just stopped reading after The Glass Sword and imagined my own ending. First of all, Mare makes zero attempt to escape from Maven's prison, or even make life difficult for her captor's co-conspirators. SHE EVEN PUBLICLY THROWS HER PEOPLE IN THE SCARLET GUARD UNDER THE BUS, and I'm supposed to believe it wasn't an act of self-preservation but selflessness to prevent more deaths?! She can justify this by telling us she had no other choice?! YES, YOU DID MARE!! You could have made Maven look like a fool by telling the truth!! You could have prevented further division in the Reds and newbloods by urging them to join the Scarlet Guard!!! And Maven?? He wasn't frightening. He wasn't psychotic. He wasn't notable in their world or from a reader's perspective. He was weak and lazy!! He let his fiancA(c)e publicly defy him. He let his lords talk back to him. He left Mare totally alone; he didn't torture her, didn't play mind games with her. He did nothing!!!! But we keep being told how fear-provoking and unstable he is. HE WAS NOTHING!!! He was just...there, and we as readers were supposed to fear him because Mare told us to. Umm, no thank you. AND DON'T EVEN GET ME STARTED ON THE ENDING!! What did I just read?!! Are these even the same characters?!! Was this even the same author of the first two books?!!!!!? Perhaps I could have respected Cal's choice if we'd seen throughout the series or even THIS BOOK how he still felt torn over the crown. Instead, I got whiplash from how "deeply in real love" they were, to Cal casually considering taking back the crown, and Mare storming away, hurt. HE DIDN'T WALK AWAY, MARE. YOU DID. YOU. DID. And I can't believe how "shocked" everyone was (including Mare and Cal *insert eye roll*) that anyone expected the crown of Norta to return to Cal. And to say that the absolute zero closure on Maven left me highly unsatisfied would be a massive, gargantuan understatement. He and Mare never fought with their powers. Cal never fought Maven with his powers. I kept waiting on that epic moment where fire met fire and Cal and Maven got locked in a fierce battle, over Mare and the crown. I kept waiting for Mare to track Maven and fry him inside out. I imagined if under any circumstance Cal could be convinced to retake the crown, it would ONLY be with Mare by his side. Instead...there's nothing. There were no surprises in this book comparable to the jaw-dropping, caught-in-a-dead-stare plot twists of the first two. I kept waiting for something to happen, but either I saw it coming, or nothing ever did (OR the scene would ebb before reaching a climax). The few genuine surprises in this book are so small that I would think "Cool" and continue reading, waiting for what I thought was the inevitably, awe-inspiring, shocking developments I was accustomed to in the first two books. But it just never happened. I'm sorry this is such an angry review, but I'm genuinely angry and so disappointed right now. Even if a fourth book was written to make it all better, I'm not sure I'd read it unless I was SURE I wouldn't be left feeling betrayed as a reader. *facepalm* **edit: I've had a little time to calm down, now. I'm not happy about this, and not just because it didn't end the way I'd hoped. I did see that there is a fourth book coming next year. I might read it. Might. If I've had time to lick my wounds clean by then. I'm an optimistic idealist, so I will hope for the best. A fourth book can't redeem this one, but it can redeem the series (in my opinion...I realize not everyone feels this way, and that's okay.)

I will start off by saying that I am an adult reading this YA book, so my rating and review may be better if I was younger. I will also say that I knew what this book was about before reading it because last year I read the second book before this one without realizing it. My review for the second book is probably pretty similar to this one. I wouldn't have felt the need to read this one but I already had it and I knew it would be a quick read. This could have been a really good book. The topic is so serious, important and personal to so many people out there that it really could have been a good book. The main character in the story is Oakley, a 16 year old girl who hasn't spoken a word in many years. The reason why she hasn't spoken isn't revealed until almost the end of the story but it is pretty easy to infer that she has been molested and that her dad is somehow involved. The only time I was able to connect or feel anything towards the book is when Oakley's boyfriend and family find out what happened, but even then there was internal commentary/thoughts that characters had that almost ruined the moment for me. The characters to me were very flat and undeveloped. I didn't care about any of them. Because the main character didn't speak throughout the book, there was so much internal dialogue from Oakley and Cole that was unnecessary and even cheesy. I know a lot of the internal dialogue are things that most teens probably have "I'm not good enough for him" or "did I just say that, I am such a loser", but to me, it took away from the story and made it immature. I also really don't like it when authors feel the need to talk "teen" "Are you gonna go to the party" Not all teens say words like "gonna". I find that it really dumbs down the characters. So again, maybe if I was still a teen reading this, I would have enjoyed it more, so take my review with a grain of salt.

Rating 2.5-3 I received a copy of Are You Still There in exchange for an honest review. When I was approved for this book I was so excited! The synopsis sounded so good! But it was actually a bit of a disappointment. I still loved the idea of a bomb threat in a school, and the setting up of the school helpline. I thought that was a really good idea since shootings and violence are things that are happening more and more often. And I did enjoy this part of the book at first...however after a while it started to drag a lot. It seemed like not much was happening for over half of the book. It did pick back up again towards the end for the last 15% or so but not enough to make me enjoy the book more. I didn't like Gabi at all. She was so annoying. At first I didn't mind her but as it went along she just got worse. especially when she was speaking to the bomber over the helpline and refused to get the phone call traced? I just couldn't understand her at all! She was really big headed and snobby at times too   . I also didn't like the romance between Gabi and Miguel...it was just so cheesy and rushed! I didn't connect to it at all. The only characters I did like were Chloe and Janae!

Under the copyright info, there's a quote that says "this book will ruin you." True words. HOW TO BREAK A BOY was thrilling, vicious, and still sweet, all at once. The story of Olivia and her friends making their way through a claustrophobic Southern town is unputdownable, even through questionable actions that make it a tough read sometimes. It rips you apart and makes you think about how people become who they are, and how we have the power to change. Best of all, this book makes you think. About toxic friendships, about the power of groupthink and manipulation, and how it plays into our own lives. Content warnings: Death/grief, alcoholism, incredibly cruel bullying

I'm torn on this book. The first third of the book I didn't like at all. It was jumbled, confusing, annoying and I did not care for the characters at all. By the 2nd third I was starting to care a little bit, and it was less annoying, though still jumbled and confused. The last third however, was awesome. It was great, fast paced, it made sense, I feel in love with the people and the cause. I felt like I was part of the world. And then it kicked me in the gut with one of the most heart wrenching scenes I've ever read. It hit me so hard I didn't even cry, and I usually do. I actually got sick to my stomach and was almost sick. Then, hours later, the next morning, I'm in the shower and I burst into sobbing tears. That's impressive. I mean, that a book could effect me so. You know tragedy is coming in this book, I mean, look at the subject. But it just wasn't what I expected. Not the way I expected So the fact that by the end I cared so much makes me want to give it a great rating. However, if it wasn't for part of a book club sort of thing, with so others pushing me to finish, I'd have never gotten through it. Which put me at 3 stars.

I'm not sure what I was expecting with Threats of Sea and Sky, I was hoping for action/adventure, with romance. It was definitely met all the criteria, and it turned out to be a pretty decent read altogether. I liked Breena, and I loved that she was feisty and smart. I felt like Jennifer Ellision did a great job of creating a believable world and characters. That being said, there was just something about this book that didn't work for me. I can't exactly put my finger on it, but it left me feeling like this book was just okay. The side characters were a definite plus in this book. I liked that Aleta was a kind of flip side to Breena. Showing how Breena might be if her father hadn't left. Caden was interesting, although I didn't love the romance there. Also, there was a definite twist at the end that has potential, and so I'm hopeful that the next book will bring more to the table. I'm not really sure why I didn't absolutely love this book, it was made up of all the right stuff. I didn't have high expectations, but I think I was still expecting something a little more. I give it 3 out of 5 stars.

2.75 stars The Things I Didn't Say is not the first book I have read by Kylie Fornasier. In fact, the first book I read by her, Masquerade was very good. I adored it. I had unintentionally high expectations going into this book and I'm sad to say I was a little disappointed. Before I get to the nit picky things that annoyed me about this book I will tell you the things I liked: - Fornasier's take on selective mutism. I have only read one other book on mutism; Until Friday Night, and I found that I preferred the way that it was written in this one. It felt more genuine and real. I can't say for sure how accurate it is- I don't have selective mutism- but it felt real to me. - The Family Dynamics. I loved the first third of the book where we were hanging out with Piper's family. The dialogue felt incredibly genuine and reminded me of my own family- which I loved. I was a little disappointed that the family got shoved into the background in the last two thirds of the book, I would have loved to read more about them all. (They were still there, just not as much as I would have liked) Things that annoyed me: (spoilers will be hidden so don't click on them!) - The not-so-subtle drops of "smelling Eucalyptus" to give the book an obvious Australian setting. I found it was a little awkward at times. - Pacing/ How much time has passed. I was a little confused toward the end of the book when it was suddenly the end of the school year and time for graduation. I think that there needed to be something more to show me how much time had passed because for a second I felt like I had been thrown a complete left wheel. I remember thinking "Woah! Wait a minute. Did I miss some pages!?" I thought perhaps breaking the book into terms/ semesters might have helped with that. - Pretty much the entire ending. I'm sorry, but the ending ruined the book for me. I was really having a great time until the end when we've somehow skipped to graduation, haven't had a formal and her recently ex-boyfriend is suddenly in a coma from a soccer accident. LIKE WHAT? It felt disjointed and like a tele-movie. Was it really necessary? Did you have to "fridge" her man to make her have some character growth? I started to take everything less seriously from that point on. - The title. The title obviously makes sense when you get to the end and the whole reason she's saying this is because she's freaking out that she never spoke to her boyfriend, but I didn't feel like that was what the whole theme of the book was. I thought that it was more about her growing and recovering from her selective mutism. Not that the guy she liked was in a coma. I really felt like it took away from a story with a wonderful message. The title kind of makes you think, "wait a minute, was the whole point of this book that she should have just spoken to her boyfriend?" Overall, I enjoyed this book; particularly the first two thirds of it. It was a fast, easy read that I managed to read in one sitting. While this book wasn't my favourite, you might still love it. So I say, if the synopsis intrigues you, give it a go. It will be out in Australia 02/05/16.

I really loved this book. Ms. Thomas creates characters that are not prefect but lovable and rich. Usually I pick sides and hate the other person, but this book I was unable to that. They both have their reasons of acting cruelly and why they misunderstand one another. They both act foolishly, but I felt like I could see myself doing the same thing. If Camden is angry about her methods, I would hope he will let her know, they can fight, then kiss, and move on. I think Camden realizes that if he wants this marrage to work that is what he is going to have to deal with, but I wish he would say: I know you are going to angry me in the future, but I am going to stay and have it out with you, and I will love you anyways.

I deactivated my Facebook account and in the meantime have gone to three movies and read an entire book, the latter over three days--something I haven't done since I was a teen without the time-consuming demands of being an adult. The book was All the Birds, Singing, one I've been eyeing in audiobook format from one of my local library branches for about a year. I found it super cheap in a used book shop on a recent overnight getaway, and devoured it. After completing it, I read a smattering of other reviews to help me articulate what I wanted to say about it. None of the reviews I read address some of the more challenging parts for me like the menacing, supernatural presence on Jake's BC island home, or the lack of transition or closure to her time as sheep shearer on an Australian farm . Mechanically, it's a really good book. Wyld builds a structure that is tricky without showing off. She creates a tone that is compelling, and peoples it with vividly drawn characters and a lushly imagined landscape. She explores the theme of self-identity in characters who are inversions of our expectations of male/female and rural/urban. She deftly combines a sense of tragedy and menace with hope and strength and redemption. What I didn't like about the book was the deflated resolution of the magical realism presence of the supernatural animal threatening Jake . What was that? There wasn't enough textual evidence to support it as a real or imagined experience. But it seems to serve as a bonding element between Jake, a neighbor's son (who enters the story about halfway through and becomes a minor transitioning device), and Lloyd. The best I can come up with is that it serves as a reminder of her past that Jake has to live with in her settled, emotionally comfortable life now--a sort of albatross, I suspect. Nonetheless, this book deserves the accolades it has received. Wyld is quite skilled and has some really interesting ideas about how we construct ourselves, about happenstance tragedy and grace, and about how we reconcile the varying episodes in our lives. And she does it in an unusual and compelling way.

I guess I expected more after all those year of waiting for the Shadow saga's resolution. The beginning was great, introducing us to Bean and Petra's special babies, now full blown geniuses at the age of six. The middle sags, and then sags some more. I just could not get excited about the Formics again. The big payoff is very ambitious in bringing both series together and providing us with a very satisfying conclusion. That's a good thing because after the infuriatingly terrible Empire books I was really ready for something good from Card, and he delivered, if barely. As an aside, I always found Bean a better character than Ender. I suspect that Card himself liked Bean more as well because, all in all, Bean ended up having a much better life. He certainly got a much better death.<\spoiler> Considering Ender is the nominal hero of the over-reaching story, I find it interesting.

Couple of things: -Thank god for the lack of swearing and pop culture references. -Making the reader reach for a dictionary doesn't win points. -Character-building is stilted, like the rest of the books. If I had to describe Kahlil's behavior in three adjectives it would be paying back debts, curiosity, and one last thing that I can't quite remember but the point is, each of these attributes is blatantly stated and waved around for a chapter before it goes back to being hidden. They aren't integrated into the character at all. There's no mention of why Kahlil stays to look after the children, why he has a particular affinity to these children when there are so many of them in the world, or anything else. Grace is mentioned to be almost done with her degree and then it's never mentioned again. I don't even think I can come up with attributes for her, other than hot-tempered and hard-working. -World-building is odd too. If the normal and the paranormal are so well integrated, you would think that Grace would have neighbors that would want to help her out. Family friends. Not to mention the lack of knowledge we ever end up learning about Djinns. There's no sense of age, of Kahlil being vastly older than Grace even though he is. He's seen things that she will never see, he knows things that will take her a lifetime to learn... there's just no sense of him being different from her other than personality-wise. -conflict. You can't just throw two people in a room and make them mad and angry. There has to be a reason they are angry. And dumb things like being touched really don't count. But this is the best book I've read from Thea Harrison yet, and I suspect a lot of it has to do with the first point. Unfortunately, from the preview of the next book, it looks like we're going back to the swearing and pop-culture references and "I'm a super cool bad-ass." Count me out.

First of all- would it kill the author/editor/whoever to insert some section breaks?!?!?! That was really the most annoying part of the novel, because scenes were not separated on the page whatsoever. Also, it was frequently hard to tell who was speaking because the narration around the dialogue was disorganized and somewhat chaotic. However, other than those two frustrating issues, this book was a pleasurable read. I most enjoyed how realistic the plot and characters were; the "drama" of the issues at hand seemed to play out exactly as they would in real life. And there were enough little plot twists to keep me interested, and humor to fill in wonderfully where anything else may be lacking. So it was mostly an enjoyable read, with some layout issues providing minor annoyance.

I really liked this one. I thought it was a little bit predictable but I was also okay with that. I liked the set up and how things came to pass. But I definitely liked the writing style in the first section better than in the next two. However, this novel really stands out in my mind of YA post-apocalpytic narrative and I would recommend it if you are looking for another dystopian novel. I thought the flashback/present writing style of section two and three was a little off putting. It didn't really help me connect to the story more -- it actually made me feel more disconnected from it because of the constant switching. As well, I wasn't a huge fan of the fact that the Ward was shown with such negative connotations. I wrote a post about positive therapy depictions in YA Fiction on Aphonic Sarah which is run by the lovely Sarah so if you are looking for books that feature positive therapy depictions, this book is not for you. However, I was enamoured with this book. I liked how everything played out and I was really curious as to what the "big reveal" would be (I was correct). I thought that the idea behind it was really solid and I think it was something that has been done but also added something new to the narrative. I was a big fan of how this could be plausible in the future. This *could* happen if we aren't careful with biological warfare . And I loved that Amy was really involved in what it meant morally and how far humans were willing to go to save humanity. I thought the moral conflicts in this one re: killing and the women getting pregnant were super interesting but definitely not developed enough. I would have liked just a bit more time spent on them so that we could really get a feel for the end times in this. But I also think part of that is due to how those last two sections were written. We weren't given enough time in either narrative to really get centred in a specific storyline before being shifted to something else. Therefore, there wasn't enough time to really have these discussions. I liked the bond that Amy formed with Baby and that she was so willing to protect her. I also liked that this didn't mean she wasn't able to bond with Adam -- even though we only got limited screentime with him. I think it was really great that she was able to still connect with people even though she was so isolated from the world. I thought that there were a lot of kickass females in this one but it still felt like no one really got the screentime they deserved. I would have liked more scenes with Amy and Kay. I thought Kay was a great mentor for Amy and it was really great to have them interact in a way that we didn't really get to see with Amy and her Mother. I think there were a lot of dynamics that could have been explored in this one that didn't really get their time to shine because of the writing style. Overall, I really recommend this one. I enjoyed my reading of it and think that this adds to the narrative of post-apocalyptic YA novels. If you are looking for something a little different that has a lot of action but also has you questioning everything you learn along the way, this one is for you. I am sitting here, trying to figure out why this book was such a chore for me to get through. There were many aspects of Limitless that I enjoyed. The premise was unique- a 'magic' drug that could make you smarter, more efficient, more outgoing, more successful than you could ever be without it. It's like 'You' only better! Who wouldn't want this? SOunds too good to be true. Which, of course, it is. <> While suffering from writer's block and a general life slump, Eddie Spinola accidentally runs into his ex brouther in law who he hasn't seen in ten years and also was his drug dealer, stops to have a drink and leaves with a 'magic' pill that he knows absolutely nothing about other than it will change his life and solve all his problems. He, of course, blindly pops the pill which turns him into a much smarter, more efficient version of himself. Needing to have more he meets his BIL who ends up being murdered during his visit. After calling the police Eddie searches the apartment and steals the rest of the pills, still having no idea what they are, side effects, etc. He also steals a black book of names and numbers in hopes of finding more of the Smart Drug. He does turn into a Super Eddie and finds great female and financial success while on the mind altering meds but gets involved with a Russian mobster (?) to front him cash to invest in the market faster who then torments him throughout the book. The murder investigation goes stale quickly which is strange to him but he's too busy turning into Donald Trump. He then begins to have bizarre neurological side effects, black outs, lost time where he 'may' have murdered an important Mexican citizen, but is making so much money and is so brilliant he thinks he may run for the Presidency on day- delusions of grandeure a side effect I suppose. <> For me, the story was quite interesting but went off on too many tangents, with too many loose ends and unbelievable decisions I couldn't really enjoy myself. And then.... it just ended with no real conclusion. Not a favorite for me..

The cover of this book is gorgeous and the blurb promises a lot of tension. I was so excited to read it that I pre-ordered it - only to get stuck working on other things so I didn't have time to pick it up for nearly a month! It was exactly what I hoped for, though - a sweet romance with plenty of sexual tension leading up to the couple getting together. The romance is between a man in his mid-thirties and his son's best friend - age gap 16 years, though as they mostly bonded over carpentry there didn't seem to be a noticeable gap in maturity. Both men treated each other as equals and the age gap didn't affect their relationship dynamic, mainly just the plot. So if you're 'icked out' by age differences you don't need to be worried - but, conversely, if you're looking for a daddy/boy scenario this book probably isn't for you. Wood, Screws & Nails is written in third person alternating its focus between the two men. Most of the plot tension comes from Aaron, the older man, worrying about his son and about his feelings for his son's best friend. Aaron is a total sweetie. We get plenty of chances to see what a nice guy he is, both as a father and as a friend. But 21-year-old Malachi is definitely my favorite character. He's hard-working and dedicated and an all-around nice guy. He's also sexually forward and hot as hell - maybe I'm just a sucker for Brazilian boys, but then again, who isn't? Mal's flirting is equal parts bold and adorable, and it's his flirting around the pool table in a couple of scenes which sells their relationship for me. The book centered around a house being renovated and I thought the writers did a perfect job of describing the carpentry involved, to make it believable and a rich environment without slowing down the story. Overall, this is a sweet sexy story about two people who are obviously perfect for each other despite differences in age and situation.
I've picked this book up twice, and cannot get into the story, so I am leaving it. It simply does not "grab" my attention.

Ultimately this was 2 1/2 stars. I received this book in exchange for an honest review. The formatting of the book was tedious but I pushed through. The paragraphs are horrid. There was no indent or a space between paragraphs so it all just blurred together. I also found the book a little tedious. There was a lot of rape in this book so you definitely should not read this book if that is a trigger for you. I struggled with rape being a main plot point. It seems that many authors now a days want to pull rape into their book to show what a good man is vs. a bad man. There are other plot lines that you can do and not have rape or the threat of being raped be the main plot in the story. The concept of the book with the gods and goddesses was interesting. I haven't read a romance with Gods and goddesses before so I was excited. Unfortunately the characters were not that amazing to me. You really didn't get to know them which was frustrating for me. The main character Alex felt more like a Bella Swan in the "how can anyone love me" sort of way. She was more bad ass than Bella but the insecurities started to truly annoy me. I do give the author props in keeping me (for the most part) entertained. I was able to over look the formatting and focus on the fast paced plot line. I'm curious about the rest of the series but honestly, I'm not compelled to read the other books.

So much potential, so little of it realized. It's an interesting premise, but Darnielle has nothing interesting to say about it. I don't need to be told what to think about a thing, and I don't really need to know what the author thinks about a thing, but I would at least like to know what his characters think about a thing. So many sentences in this book were like "and then I saw something that reminded me of a memory," without any further explanation as to what those things were. At the end, we can only speculate about why Sean did what he did, and why the criminally underdeveloped Lance and Carrie and Chris Haynes did what they did. So what, then, is the point? Given that Sean has a pretty decent life (sure he's a nerd but so were many of us, and he has parents in a marriage that is at least semi-functional, and he's even getting a little action which is more than a lot of high school nerds can say), is this just a story about a guy who shoots himself in the face just so he has a reason to feel the isolation that he's already been inexplicably feeling ? And then lives to regret his stupid, stupid decision? The mail-order text-based adventure game stuff was cool and a thing I haven't read about before, but it was largely shunted aside in favor of....nothing, essentially, it seems like. Hence the two stars. People seem to like this but I think they're giving Darnielle more credit than he deserves for using his status as "one of the best lyricists of our time" to push out a piece of half-baked crap.

Let me start of by saying, I expected more out of this book. I was really excited about this book and couldn't wait to get my hands on it. But once I picked it up, I had a hard time staying into the story. I found myself putting down and having a hard time to pick it back up. I just didn't buy into the plot at all. I never expected Ember to receive the news of her new residence without taking immediate action to remove herself and her sister from there. I also liked Olivia who is Ember's little sister. She's a sweet little girl who doesn't really understand what's going on around her. And it's best it stays that way. I'll definitely continue the series and pick up other book of hers.Which I read raving reviews about and I am looking forward to reading her other work. As for Cursed, I recommend this book to fans of X-Men and fans of Shatter Me. Check it out and tell me what you think of it. http://www.goodchoicereading.com/2012...

Knightquest is a fun read. The description of Jean-Paul Valley's inner-life paints him in a much more sympathetic light than we saw in the first book. Although he continues to be overly brash in his reactions to criminals and deviate from the moral structure that Bruce Wayne put in place for Batman, we also finally get to see what inner demons (or angels) drive him to act as he does. One of my favorite aspects of the storyline is that Valley seems to develop an affinity for Wayne's style of vigilantism. Although he weaponizes the batsuit more than Wayne ever had(which makes for some really great art) he also realizes the importance of doing the detective work that he despises and chooses to save the lives of bystanders before capturing criminals with increasing regularity. Of course, much of this character development is eradicated in the moment that he faces off with Abattoir and allows him to die. This in itself was a fascinating moment because in a lot of ways not making a decision was the only way that he could be sure that he wasn't following his programming. He was not true to the mantle of the bat, but he avoided making a pre-ordained decision, which is an extraodinary moment of strength of Valley even as it is an awful moment of immorality for the Batman. Criticizing storytelling is always a little difficult with comic books turned into a larger tome. Robin was the most common manifestation of this. He would pop up every third comic book or so and remind us that he's not around because Valley would strangle him if he was. One kind of cool element was that there were villains who Avery hadn't encountered and were, therefore, just as fresh to him as they would be to the novice reader. He underestimated the Joker, misinterpreted Cat Woman's motives, and was unnecessarily violent with Mr. Freeze. The novelty of a novice Batman interacting with classic villains made for great moments. I would also argue that there was a definite lack of punch in the storytelling surrounding Abattoir. The fact that Valley let him die was deplorable, but understandable. It did not make sense that Abattoir's cousin was still left to die. Neither Valley nor Robin (who happened to be on site as well and had researched Abattoir and his hide-out more thoroughly) found or saved Abbatoir's victim. It made for an interesting plot point since Valley also reacted with an eerie nonchalance upon hearing that the man he had been trying to save had died, but the fact that no one looked for him in what I believe was the exact same building made very little sense. It was a poor storytelling moment. It was also interesting to see Bruce Wayne musing about retirement and Tim Drake realizing that a better home life for him might damage his life as a super hero. How far down the rabbit hole of superherohood does Drake have to be for a better home life to seem like a curse instead of a blessing?

I'm wavering between three and four stars for Feed. I'll start with the things that annoyed me -- and it's really one big one: the narration. There is no reason given for why the narrator is saying all these things: if she were narrating in her head, there'd be no need for the massive infodumps, because she knows what's going on and how the zombie apocalypse started. Also, for plot reasons, it shouldn't be in past tense, it doesn't make logical sense for it to be in past tense, unless she's narrating from beyond the grave : if that's the case, there's no explanation of that. She also mentions details that don't turn out to be relevant, in a way that makes me expect them to be -- e.g. mentioning backup batteries and how Buffy didn't check them, and then it just doesn't mention them again. Also, I have to say, I didn't get emotionally connected with the story until the end of the second part, and I wasn't really emotionally connected until the end of the third. Mind you, I fought tears through the fourth and fifth parts, so it's not as though I never connected with it. I enjoyed the characters, particularly the minor ones: Mahir, Senator Ryman, Emily Ryman. I did think the villain was a bit of a cardboard cut-out: you knew he'd be evil all along, just because the narrator doesn't like him. If zombies freak you out, I don't recommend it. If disease freaks you out, I don't recommend it. If you want a zombie book with politics and an emotional kick, I recommend it. Just don't blame me if the narrator bugs you and the first part is kinda slow.

I've seen so many good reviews of this series and now I've finally started reading it myself. This book was great and I really liked it. The most engrossing thing about it is the world. Sarah J.Maas created an unusual universe which somewhat resembles Middle Ages. After tons of books about our modern world I was pleased to read something new like this one. This world is well thought out and there was even a map of it in the book! The names confused me at first. They were unfamiliar and difficult to pronounce but eventually I got used to them. Actually they make this series more unusual and outstanding. Also the main concept is interesting and catching. For instance, the extraordinary idea of making the main character an assassin. This already sounds intriguing. The plot with competition to find the King's Champion was exciting and, intertwined with cruel murders, even absorbing. Moreover, I couldn't not appreciate the fact that the main characters are bookworms. When Celaena said she didn't need any company if she had books, I wanted to shake her hand. This and her night reading are evidence that she is one of us. However, there are some things about this book I didn't like. The first is the relationships between main characters. They seemed weird to me and throughout the majority of the book I was like "What the hell is going on?". Thank God it wasn't a love triangle to the full extent. In the first half of the book Celaena and Chaol were reminding me of Romitri from Vampire Academy. They quarreled a lot and sneered at each other but in the second half their relations became better as the captain began to trust Celaena more. What really confused me is the relationship between Celaena and Dorian. Why the hell was it needed to draw them together and to set them apart at the end of the book? What's the point? To my mind this love story was irrelevant if they wouldn't be together anyway. Generally, I don't ship Celaena neither with Chaol nor with Dorian but if I had to choose, I'd give my preference to Chaol. Also the first half of the book seemed a bit boring to me: there wasn't too much action and a lot of characters. But the second one was way better as the plot began to develop and more characters appeared. Nevertheless, I don't regret reading this book at all and I'm looking forward to reading the next ones. I'm really curious to know what will happen next!

This book had so much promise that never came to tuition. At first, I thought each of the characters was going to develop into something special, but Marin ended up being the only one that really intrigued me. I should have been engaged with Petronella, but Nella's character wasn't written with consistency. In a blink of the eye, she went from being a naive, 17th century, young girl to talking and behaving like an astute, modern woman. The plot started slowly. It was a hundred pages before anything happened. Thank goodness, the plot did pick up, because the unexpected twists ended up being the best part of the book. Once the action got going, I believed in the plot until the last sentence, but unfortunately, the end was a letdown. I couldn't believe that there was no real explanation for the miniaturist. How did she know the things that she knew? Was the red spot ever really on the dog? Was she a sorcerer? Why was the miniaturist named Petronella? To have a book named The Miniaturist and not answer any questions about the miniaturist is just baffling. I am tempted to give this book three stars, because the writing is good, and there were times when I couldn't put it down, but, when it was all said and done, I was disappointed. There was no real point, and there was no resolution to the central question.

I tend to enjoy story of more experienced men saving younger guys in trouble so this book was perfect for me. Noah was the typical older guy that hasn't been in a relationship or gotten laid in a long time but is always helping others out. Jeremy the bright kid with a lot going for him but is in a bad situation. The one thing that is a little different is Jeremy is a hustler and although he has been living on the streets and is being chased by the "bad guys" he isn't jaded nor is he a naive kid either. He has a mixure of enthusiams tempered with a more serious outlook on his future. He is determined to make it through school and go to college avoiding drugs and being a hustler. Noah makes an interesting counterpoint to Jeremy since in a lot of ways he was Jeremy except he ended up being pulled into the life with the same trick that was used on Jeremy. His relationship with Billy set up in various flashbacks was sad especially when he ended up having to deal with Willie. I enjoyed this book a lot and look forward to others in the series.

Wow. I guess I'm not a comic book person. I was surprised this encompassed a lot of the stereotypes I imagined comics would have. A ton of dialogue and action with little else. Aside from the older heroes like Jessica Jones, Captain America and Iron Man (whom I believe the author assumes the reader will already know about), the younger heroes are not really developed at all; which is odd considering that this series is about the Young Avengers. I guess one will learn more about them in later volumes, but you'd think there'd be more character development in the first volume, right? The character development, the world building and any kind of description was immensely diminutive. So I didn't feel anything for any of the characters. I think what they spent the most time "describing" (if you can even call it that) was the time travel element and even then there were so many holes in the logic. Also, the romance literally came out of no where. It had no base. I'm not exaggerating, in one comic book box thingyy, one hero (wow I don't even remember their names), I think he's the iron lad, saves another hero named Cassie and in the next little box thingy they're making out.... They literally met 15 MINUTES AGO!!! And that baseless kiss begins a serious relationship. I thought this would be like the Ms. Marvel comics, where the protagonist is developed really well. You know the protagonist's best female friend, best male friend, her religious official, and her parents by the end of the first volume. And you actually see her parents quite frequently. They're not "always absent" like adults tend to be on tv and in the Young Avenger Vol. You KNOW Kamila Khan (the female protagonist in the Ms. Marvel series). The Ms. Marvel comics also do not ONLY encompass action and dialogue. There's substance. It touches on topics like the importance of culture, the way Muslims are viewed/portrayed by society, the malignant terms attributed to generation "me", and so much more that I won't get into now because I'm supposed to be reviewing the Young Avengers. I guess I thought all comics would be like Ms. Marvel and have substantial, non-superficial content in addition to action and dialogue. It was kind of fun...like watching those Saturday morning cartoons as a kid but, I don't think I'll continue with this series.

This second book in the newsflesh series takes the world created in the first volume and spins it on its ear, causing the reader (and the characters) to question the most fundamental assumptions about how Mira Grant's zombies work. Political intrigue, decaying corpses munching on their neighbors, and vast global conspiracy all take their appropriate places and all contribute to the interesting take on the zombie apocalypse. Some of the science of the virology escapes me. I find myself sometimes skimming the first dialogue between some of the scientists as it is too technical, and waiting for one of the other characters to explain it to some of the "less science-y" people in the book. Scientist explains something. Everyone goes "hunh?" Smart-guy explains science stuff in small words to the main character. is a pattern repeated often enough in the book to take notice of, and to generate a little irritation as the book rolls through some fairly new (to me) bio-hazard / immunology / virology concepts. Word of warning. This book ends on a MASSIVE CLIFFHANGER, if you're not ready to wait for the third book, you'll be better off getting yourself a copy of this book and then squirreling it away until the third installment comes out - Because you WILL want to read this book, but you may want to read three immediately after. I love George's appearance in the second book. I am confused as all hell as to how rick goes from "junior blogger" to "vice president of the USA" in the space of like 5 pages. I was a little disappointed that there wasn't more interaction between Ryman and the bloggers. after he was so much a part of the first book he kind of feels like a loose end in the second installment.

First Line: "England was a wicked bitch who wished him ill." I have read so many stories lately which involve a man who has loved a woman from afar for many years because he does not perceive himself to be good enough for her. It is romantic in a way, but I also find myself a little insulted as it also implies that the woman is not smart enough to decide what is good enough for herself. Also, it always seems in stories where the good girl gets tired of being so boringly good and begins to act naughty, her behavior is never really that shocking. I suppose when they have never stepped a toe out of line in their life, their little shenanigans must seem exciting, but I usually find it less that thrilling. For the most part, this is true of Gwen's actions in the story. However, I did very much enjoy her excersion into the seediest part of Paris and her adventures in the infamous Moulin Rouge (I wonder if she met Iwan McGregor there?). Even though this book contains these over-used premises I still found myself enjoying it. Duran made it work well. I thought the relationship between Gwen and Alex was sweet and developed nicely through the story. I'll look forward to more books by this author as her skill grows. Tone: Mischevious, Romantic Setting: England, London, France, Paris, Italy, Venice Characters: Jilted bride-to-be, Merchant Language: Intense Pace: Steady Other Elements: Moulin Rouge, Challenging Societal Expectations, Orphan

I was very pleasantly surprised with Thief with no Shadow when I read it some time ago. It had just the right amount of plot, romance, character development and world building. Unfortunately, the same can't really be said about The Laurentine Spy. Although I enjoyed it somewhat, the overall story doesn't really have a plotline built on an understandable background. It has no detail, no exploration, no foundation. This because the book is basically just a romance story, with shades of a plot that is never defined. The espionage subplot just plays second fiddle to the romance, and you have no understanding of why something is happening and have no resolution for it. It's just tacked to the romance as a way for the main characters, Saliel and Athan, to meet, interact, and fall for each other. And that's a pity because the set-up seemed interesting. I would have loved to know more about the Laurentine-Corhonase wars/rivalry and what the purpose of the espionage was. Not having particular interest in romance as a genre (I like my books with consistent plotlines with shades of romance, not half assed plots thrown in to try and give some substance to a novel), the story didn't really grab me. It didn't help that the character development wasn't entirely successful. For example, it appears both Saliel and Athan care for each other's safety when the novel starts, even though you have no idea how they first met and why they have developed this fondness for one another that makes them protective of each other. The last third of the book was... anti-climatic, I guess is the best word. It was the culmination of the romance, yes, and it was great to see beliefs and prejudices shattered because of love, but it didn't really satisfy. Possibly because the espionage plotline got finished just as carelessly as it was used as a plot device. It's a nice quick read, though, if you're basically looking for a romance story in a low fantasy setting with some suspense elements, but not nearly as satisfying if you're looking for consistent plotline and world building.

Finally made the review after 3 days and halfway through the second book. I first decided to read this book just because a lot of people recommended it and not knowing anything about the story except how the writer was famous for being a good one, but I didn't really have that many expectations about it, especially because I wasn't really in the mood for yet "another" dystopian novel with a boy main character living amongst boys. Boy was I wrong. (Hehe see what I did there.) At first yes, I do admit that I was annoyed by the writing style. it reminded me a little bit of Room, and I wasn't very bothered with its style and for this one I gradually started to enjoy it except for a lot of the grammar and spelling mistakes because I hate misspellings. But the story itself was amazing! The premise of the whole world itself was very interesting. At first my thought was that everyone had the ability to read other people's minds, which is the common "skill" seen in other movies or books and I was quite interested when it turns out that in this world, the problem was that you project your thoughts to other people. And other than the world, the story itself was excellent for me. I both loved and hated how fast-paced it was and how everything seems to never stop happening, because sometimes I keep thinking omg this is improbable in the real world for a person to experience so many things in a time span like that. But everything seems to fall into place appropriately and I love the action in the story as well. As for the characters, I really didn't know what to feel about Todd in the first one third of the book. Even though we were reading his thoughts and all, I actually didn't really like him or felt attached to him in any way, mostly because in the beginning he was mostly just grumbling all the time and hating everything that happens to him. But then when things actually start to happen and the pace starts to quicken I began to really like him. Especially when Manchee died. Now that moment really did some damage to me. I sort of almost kind of knew it was coming because, what loyal animal in any book ever survives in this kind of situation anyway? But seriously, that scene broke me up and I both hated it and loved it. I hated the fact that it happened, but I loved it in how it shaped and changed Todd and made him grow up and shows part of his weakness or something like that. And other than that particular scene there were a lot of parts that really shaped the characters (meaning Todd and Viola) and I really liked how you can really see their development about themselves and towards each other. And yes I do like their relationship, especially towards the end and along the second book (whoops sorry for mentioning the second book). I liked how no romance was actually implied (THANK YOU SO MUCH), and how in this first book it's mostly just them only having each other and taking care of each other and getting to know each other. I loved the part where Todd just looks at Viola and realises he could actually "read" her even though she doesn't have any Noise. And I think it's really cute and I wouldn't mind them getting together romantically. But for me the other characters, other than the three I mentioned were kind of meh. The antagonists weren't very interesting for me. I hated Aaron and I just keep thinking why isn't he dead yet. But I sort of don't really see his motive and I don't really understand him, even though the kinds of antagonists I really like in a book is ones who have a real goal/motive that is actually understandable, and I didn't see that in Aaron or the Mayor. I also saw that most of the book, the antagonist or the main plot conflict was just Todd and Viola trying to outrun an army and so it's not really clear as in how villainous the antagonist is. So other than that I really loved this book. It was a roller-coaster ride and it was an amazing page-turner. I also cannot help but compare it to other dystopian books I've read, and the most familiar one is of course the Maze Runner. And compared to the first two books of that series that I have read, this one is WAY WAY WAY better and I regret reading that and not this one. I also hate that this didn't have as much hype as the other one, but I also cannot see this series being turned into a movie because it'll be technically really difficult. So yeah definitely recommend this to anyone interested in the genre and anyone who likes action, fast-paced books that are emotionally draining.

The Falconer was picked as this month's book club choice & overall I can honestly say I really liked it, and was left wanting  more . I loved the steampunk aspects of the world May built, and I can honestly say that it was the most convincing steampunk that I've read in a while. Usually I find steampunk novels to be lacking in the actual amount of technology, or the novel is so oversaturated with references that the story takes a hit. I gave this book 3 stars instead of 4, because I struggled with the pacing near the middle of the book. I became more than a little annoyed with Aileana & how self-centered she is. The Falconer was redeemed (for me) thanks to the love I have for Kiaran & Derrick. I especially loved their interactions. Derrick adds humor and "humanity" to Aileana's world, and without him I feel that the story would have been flat. I also enjoyed the minor characters. I was also VERY pleased that there was not a love triangle. I appreciated the role Gavin played in Aileana's life, and the opportunities a relationship with him could afford her. I was just so thankful that she didn't spend the whole book mooning over Gavin and Kiaran & trying to make a choice between the two. That ending though. That conclusion was intense and kept me on my toes. And I really enjoyed that there wasn't a happy ending where Aileana somehow manages to do the impossible. She's not fully trained, and failure was more likely than success. It adds a depth and believability to the characters and their situation that a win could never do.

2.5 stars. You don't know the effect your words have on me, Lady Firebrand. It took years to build up this ice. You will melt it and then I will be broken. I feel like I say this more often than not nowadays, but: recently, I have been in a reading rut. Back in the day (before I was in my late twenties, and therefore essentially a fossil) I could easily finish an entire book in a matter of hours. Now? I'm lucky if I can finish a book in a week. And oh boy, does this frustrate the life out of me -- especially when I am crumbling under the weight of an ever-growing to be read list. (Ever-growing because I have this problem where my bank card keeps falling into card machines and paying for new books. An unfortunate problem to have. Also a story for another day.) Why are you telling us this, Shaunna? you may ask. What in the world is the point of this introductory ramble? Well, for one, it's been a long time since I've spent any time writing an entire book review. I am rusty. It's definitely going to take a while for me to get into The Zone again. For... two? For... second? Whatever. In the last twenty-four hours, I, Shaunna, read an entire book. A full one. And I cannot express how happy I am to be able to say that! The name of this book? Well, I'm sure you guessed that already based on the title of this review. However, if you did not (fair), or if you didn't bother to read the title (also fair), then this book is Elly Blake's young adult fantasy, Frostblood -- and I'm going to do my best to concisely ramble about everything I thought about this little book that so avidly held my attention. Frostblood tells the story of Ruby Otrera, a seventeen year old girl born with fire running through her veins. She must hide her gift from the world, however, as she lives in a land ruled by Frostbloods -- and the Frostbloods want her kind dead. When soldiers come to raid Ruby's village on a winter's day, she is captured and, after a few different twists and turns, finds herself fighting not only for her own life in the Frostblood King's arena, but for the future of her world. Elly Blake's debut novel has left me with a lot of mixed feelings. Now, I'm sure you've assumed already that, since this was the first book that I've devoured so quickly in such a long time that I was absolutely hooked and am so madly in love with this book that I want to sing its praises from the rooftops. Well, you'd be right about the former -- but certainly not the latter. Although Elly Blake's Frostblood kept me eagerly turning pages, and although the plot was fairly addictive, overall, this novel fell quite flat. Usually, I'm not one to be particularly bothered by cliches in the books I read -- especially when it comes to YA literature, as stories aimed toward this demographic are usually rife with cliches -- if not, at least, playing host to a few. However, Blake's Frostblood is made of so many cliches that I found myself rolling my eyes on several occasions, and it all became pretty unbearable by the novel's concluding chapter. I won't list all of these cliches or this review will likely end up the length of Blake's entire novel, but here's a few of the things that elicited sighs and eye rolls during my experience of Frostblood: - Ruby is the Chosen One. She is, like many YA protagonists, a special snowflake, different from anyone else in her world. Therefore, everyone gravitates towards her (including our Generic Fantasy Love Interest), and she magically gets good at everything just at the perfect moment (can't use your gift? Well, now you're fighting a giant beast, you most definitely can!) - Generic Fantasy Love Interest (AKA, Arcus) smells of "soap and pine". (Have you ever met a boy who smells like pine? Most of the boys I meet smell of smoke/excessive cologne/occasionally unbrushed teeth. Maybe I'm looking in the wrong places...) Anyway, he is Dark and Brooding and Mysterious, and is always mean to Ruby -- so obviously she falls in love with him, because we all love boys who are mean to us when we are the protagonist of a YA novel. Of course, his being mean to her just means that he is harbouring Very Secret Feelings for her (even though there is approximately zero chemistry between the two of them) and he will therefore do anything to win the heart of Ruby the Chosen One, even if it means risking his life. I did not root for this romance one bit. Can you tell? - Ruby just loves books, even though they are barely mentioned until several chapters in, where she just has to save the books from the library because they are too darn precious to let burn. Hello, hi. Just because you are the protagonist of a YA novel, it does not mean that you have to love books. It won't make you any less relatable. I promise. Anyway, I'm sure you get the idea. Cliches, cliches, cliches galore. With all that said, Frostblood wasn't completely terrible. The writing, although nothing special, was easy and addictive reading, and there was some funny and witty dialogue in places. I found some of the lore in regards to the magic in the novel to be interesting -- even if it did need fleshing out in a lot of places. There was a plot twist that, for all of the novel's predictability, genuinely caught me off guard, and I very much enjoy being caught off guard when reading. Overall, this was a light and relatively fun read, and people who don't mind fantasy novels that aren't overly detailed, or those who are only just delving into the young adult fantasy genre, will probably find more enjoyment in Frostblood than I did. All in all, a decent debut novel, but nothing to be writing home about. Face them all like a warrior, whether you are one or not.

It has been a long time since I've reviewed any books due to my practicum (despite reading so many of books during the course of my practicum). This book though, made me feel so much for Lane - her pain, joy and love for Kale. I would've given the book a 4-star if it I didn't hate Lane's family or Kale so much. Based on the title, you would have thought Harry is the hero of the story. Well....he's not. He's the heroine's uncle. The story started with Lane rushing back to UK from US to attend her uncle's funeral. Lane dreaded the moment when she had to meet Kale, her best friend and first and only love, but she also regretted for not being there for her uncle when he passed away and not keeping in touch with the rest of her family. So, after Lane's uncle's funeral, Lane starts to contemplate if she wants to return to UK and mend her relationship with her family. The story alternates between past and present. It started out pretty well, and the need to know what happened in the past that caused the rift between Lane and her family as well as Kale, kept me reading on and on till the end. So, I guess the story is pretty well-written. Only, I didn't like how the way Lane's family reacted to Lane's confession of loving Kale. Her whole family (except her uncle) believed it was just a childish crush. I mean, seriously? Even strangers can see that Lane love Kale (*roll eyes*) - by strangers, I mean me. There is also the fact that her family (except her uncle) weren't supportive of Lane's decision to leave UK at all, which goes on for the whole of six years she was gone. Here I thought her family really love her but it seems like her uncle act more like the father than her own father. Then, there's Kale. Well.....based on all the flashbacks, he is kind of sweet. I sort loved him in the beginning, but after he "forgotten" about THAT night, my heart broke just like Lane's did. What he did was unforgivable and when he revealed that he didn't actually forgot about THAT night at the end of the story, I just gave up on the story. At the end, when Lane and Kale finally got over THE talk, they jump straight into having sex. I get that both have them have pent up sexual tensions, but you just reconciled, shouldn't you at least go out on a few actual dates before jumping into having sex....? Ugh..... It was okay as a whole, it was well-written to the point where I cried for Lane whenever her heart broke but whenever I think about the ending or Kale....let's just say I won't reread the story anytime soon.

Excellent, but not quite perfect. First let's appreciate the satisfying alliteration and pleasing arrangement of vowels in that title. This book is like a crazy melting pot of Ocean's 11, the Godfather, Renaissance Venice with some fantasy magic, and a little bit of Arya Stark's shitty internship at the House of Black and White added in. It sounds bananas, but it really did work. The characters are where this book really shines. It doesn't take much to pull you in and make you like them, even when they are morally dubious at best. Locke is an irresistible protagonist, and the rest of the gang are jolly accomplices. Even the villains and marks were well written. The plot was well paced, with only two real slow downs during the prologue and at the start of the third act. The end of the second act was almost up there with the Red Wedding as far as shock and awe. This book was very well written and edited for the most part. I was afraid it might veer off into too much fantasy mumbo jumbo, but it always pulled back to the main characters just in time. But, the one thing that marred the book for me was the absolutely shitty murder of Nazca. At that point in the book, she is really the only interesting female character and she is brutally murdered purely to upset her father. I fucking hate it when female characters are killed for the express purpose of making male characters emote. Once we find out later what the Grey King's revenge was for, it makes more sense, but it still sucks. At least a short chapter could have been included showing her going out in a blaze of glory, rather than dying off-page and then presented to her father in a literal barrel of piss. I am cautiously hopeful that the rest of the series both lives up to, and improves upon the mistake of, this book.

3.5 Stars Overall Opinion:  This was my first experience with a shifter romance, and it was enjoyable. I desperately needed to get out of a book slump, and I think changing up genres helped a little. I don't think, however, that I'm going to jump right into reading a lot of shifter romances. It did open up my options for these times that I need something different though. I struggled a little with learning the lingo at times, but I was able to connect the dots after a while and follow along. The reason for my not so high rating is that I did have some issues with it feeling like it was lagging at times, the repetitive dialogue (like about how unknowingly sensual she was, how she was mistreated because she was 'latent', "la la land" references, etc. ), and the ending. Brief Summary of the Storyline:  This is Taryn and Trey's story. Taryn wakes up in an unusual place, and finds out that Trey had his enforcers drug and kidnap her. He needs her help in forming alliances to go against his uncle who is another alpha that wants to take over his pack. In order to get away from a forced mating to an alpha she has no interest in that was arranged by her father, she agrees to playing along with the act that they are true mates until the conflict with his uncle is over in 3 months. They spend more and more time together and the act turns into more and they fall in love. There is some family and pack drama, some hot sexy times, and some more family and pack drama...but they get a HFN ending. POV: This alternated between focusing on Taryn and Trey in 3rd person narrative (often from paragraph to paragraph which took me a while to get used to). Overall Pace of Story:  Ok. Long. I did feel like it dragged at times, but I never skimmed. I wanted something like a jump ahead epilogue at the end that I didn't get, so I felt unfulfilled with the ending. Instalove: Kind of. They are instantly feeling strong feelings due to their wolfs' reaction to the other. I didn't find it annoying. I just figured it's part of the 'shifter' type romance. H rating: 3.5 stars. Trey. I like him better than the h, but I had issues with how he pushed her away at times. h rating: 3 stars. Taryn. I liked her in the beginning, but her "sarcastic wit" felt a little old after a while. I wanted her to be serious for once! I am a naturally sarcastic person, and I was raised in a sarcastic home -- so don't get me wrong, I like sarcasm! But it was just a little OTT for me. Sadness level: Low. No tissues needed. Push/Pull: Yes There is some pushing away done by both the h and H at first, and then just the H. He hurts the h by his pushing away after they have mated, but he does go after her to make up for his mistake (after a little while). Heat level: Moderate. They have some hot chemistry and scenes, but not too much to take away from the story. Descriptive sex: Yes Safe sex: Not really -- they're shifters, so I'm not sure if these books usually fall under the same line of safe sex practices. OW/OM drama: Yes  There is a OW in the pack that the H had been with sexually once a long time before the h was in the picture, and she had it in her mind that they were going to mate. Mindfucked! Immediately after reading the first book, I went and purchased this one. If I was mesmerized by the first book, it didn't hold a candle to this one. One minute I can't breathe because I'm so much shock at the disturbing nature of some of the thing Caleb makes Olivia do, and the next I'm head over heel in love with his ability to display his loving nature despite his tormented soul. Weird, I know. C. J. Roberts blew it out of the park with the easy transitioning between past and present. It always kept me guessing about if what I thought was going to take place actually did. It almost made me feel that Olivia could have been telling Agent Matthew the story from book 1. The way Roberts never shied away from the graphic nature of the underground world of human trafficking gave it realism. Five stars without a doubt.
