I'm not sure how to deal with this book. It ruined my heart. And my mind. Yet it was all kinds of perfect. Sigh. I loved this book so much. I'm pretty sure I love it more than Wolf By Wolf, but I love them both so much. This second and final book was all I wanted it to be. Despite that heartbreak. Gah. It was so exciting and real. I love reading about Yael so much. Getting to know how her story ends was the very best thing. Though I do wish there had been a third book. Sad face. But the ending is perfect. There doesn't need to be more. I really enjoyed reading this. Once I started, I could not stop until I finished it. So exciting and evil all the time. Blood For Blood is so long and so heartbreaking. There is so much happening at all times and I'm not sure how to describe it all. Because I loved this book so much and I need you all to read this series too. Because these books are so important. They are heartbreaking and so real, despite being an alternative version of our world. most of the Hitler stuff did happen, just years ago. And reading about it again in this book was so heartbreaking. Sniffs. I just don't get how it could have happened. People suck. Anyway. This book. This book tells an incredible story. I loved reading about Yael. I loved that this book starts right after Wolf By Wolf ended. I loved that Yael and Luka are in the same space for almost the whole book, because they are so awesome together. The plot in this book is so amazing. I loved reading about how Yael had escaped the death camp all those years ago, loved reading about how they changed her, though it was the most heartbreaking thing. Yet written so good. I loved reading about what Yael could do. Ack. She's just so awesome. I liked reading about how awful the war with Hitler was, despite how evil and sad it was. So many people got killed. So many people were hurt. There is even a bit torture in this book. Shudders. Even so, I loved it. This book is pretty tragic, though. Because, yeah, so many people die. People close to Yael. Sniffs. Some deaths broke my heart so much. I'm still not over it. But they were also written so well and I did feel like they had to happen. Maybe. Okay, I might not forgive it, but it was written good. Just so sad. Gah. This book is full of betrayals. And I did not approve at all. Hmph. There are a few amazing moments too, though, and those were the very best. Not as many kisses as I wanted, lol, but still so much awesome. Blood For Blood is told from the point of view of Yael. But also Luka. And also Felix. Most it Yael, though. But gosh, I loved reading the other point of views too. Okay, fine, I only loved reading from Luka. Whom is the most awesome boy and I fell more and more in love with him on every page. Sigh. But then there were Felix. And I don't know. I loved him in book one, how he protected his sister. But uuugh. He was awful in this one. I shall never forgive him. I did not like the things he did at all. It makes me a bit sad. We also get to see a bit about Adele, the real version of her. And, hah, I can't help it. I hated her. I hated her so much. And I'm so glad that Luka didn't feel anything for her anymore. Just, ugh. This girl was not a girl I would have enjoyed reading about, lol. Though I did read about her and Luka in the awesome short story, Iron To Iron. But yeah. I didn't like her then either. But I did like reading about her, sort of, I just did not like her at all, lol. And I didn't see why Felix wanted to protect her so badly. Sigh. She was not nice. Reading about Luka and Yael was so much fun. Because Luka thought she was Adele for all of the first book. But in the very beginning of this one, he gets to know that she is not Adele. And I loved it so much. So glad it was out in the open right away. So happy to read about how he felt about it too, because he did notice that she was different from the Adele he knew the year before, and I loved how he cared for Yael, once he realized she wasn't Adele. How he was confused about it, yet never mean or anything like that. I can't deal with how amazing this book was. And I'm sure I'm not describing it all that well. Ack. But yeah. I loved it oh so much. I loved getting to know Yael more, see more about her past. I loved reading about the few people who loved her too. Her found-family was the best. It broke my heart how much Yael has lost, and is still losing. She deserved the whole world. Sad face. I also sort of liked reading about Felix's past, though it didn't make me love him, sadly. I'm still mad at him. Hmph. I didn't like his ending. Sigh. But we also got to see more of Luka's past. And gah. I can't love this book anymore than I do after this book. He's just the best. I loved reading about how he grew up, though it broke my heart, because his dad was so mean. Hmph. I loved how Luka changes a bit in this book. I love how he just always gets better. And I loved that he quit smoking, lol. I shipped Yael and Luka so much. And I loved reading about them together. I loved reading about how they got closer, became better friends too. Just so amazing. There is just so much happening in this book. I can't share all of it. It is so exciting and heartbreaking and evil. I loved every moment of it. Thank you for writing this perfect book Ryan. <3 You are the best. I loved reading about the war, how they tried to stop Hitler, and getting to know so many secrets. So awesome. Blood For Blood was perfection. Everything I wanted in a final book. It broke my heart into a million pieces, but I still love it the most. You must all read this gorgeous book. You will love it too. I promise. This review was first posted on my blog, Carina's Books, here: http://carinabooks.blogspot.no/2016/0...

I first read Swordspoint almost twenty years ago and fell for it hard. It was a revelation, with its high drama and intense romance (between two men!). I'm happy to say that the intervening time has been mostly kind to it. The novel's subtitle is "A Melodrama of Manners" and aside from the more overtly melodramatic events like kidnapping and revenge, and duels to the death, there are battles of words with dramatic, high stakes; the moving of political chess pieces on the board; and a trial with a surprise witness. I was completely drawn in to the small-scale, interpersonal duels of words and wits and, while I can't say I liked anyone on stage, coming to understand them again, and remembering my past experience of the novel while reading, was both enlightening and fun. I'd forgotten all of the political wrangling, and the reasons Richard St. Vier got so deeply embroiled with the poisonous people on the Hill, despite his sincere desire to not have his job as a hired sword follow him, or his lover, back home to Riverside. And I'd forgotten about poor Lord Horn, too. While there's no doubt he's kind of creepy, I don't see him as being evil. He also basically gets killed as a by-blow of plots by people much more politically savvy than himself  so I felt a little sorry for him. And I'd also forgotten about Michael, though the novel itself shuffles him offstage about three-fourths of the way through, so I guess that's forgivable. How about that central romance, though? Twenty years ago I was all over it and its resolution had me crying. Today? Richard and Alec feel young. These two men's love affair, with each of them in his own way drawn like a moth to the other's desire for destruction, has a terrible beauty--it's destined to burn brightly, and burn out fast. And then there's Diana. She's an awesome villain, cool as a cucumber while she effortlessly wrecks people. I really, really wanted her to lose, or even to show a chink in her armor at some point, and in the end she does, at least on the small scale, but she will no doubt be back in that battle with a new and better strategy soon . Maybe because Diana is so magnetic, aside from her, there isn't a female character that particularly stands out. Katherine is a tool in the hands of the powerful, brought onstage so we can see her helpless tears, and the rest of the women are walk-ons, or part of a herd of Riversiders who push Richard or Alec toward the next plot point, or exemplars of this or that stratum of society. Strangely, considering just how many of the men are gay or bisexual, we see no hint of lesbianism. That said, although this story was written in the late '80s, homosexuality in Swordspoint is only remarked on insofar as it might affect a noble family's ability to propagate itself, so that's pretty cool. Speaking of burning brightly and burning out fast, I tore through Swordspoint and didn't much feel like reading the short stories that come after it in this edition. I'll move on to them, the other two full Riverside novels, and the Tremontaine serial in the near future, because I want to see more of these characters and this world, and how it changes with the times. Swordspoint itself is elegant, elaborate, just twisty enough, and was a joy to re-read.

This is the third Megan Abbott book I've read, and all I can say is...keep 'em coming. Her period noir novels have a hard-boiled narration by a woman in a world usually populated by men. Women are usually the peripheral characters, but not in these books. Here the women are the stars of this down and dirty show, and the men are peripheral. The dialogue is snappy and the "broads" are tough. The young woman who is narrating this story is taken under the wing of Gloria Denton, a former showgirl (with apparently great "gams") who is her icy cold, cunning mob-connected mentor, introducing her to a world of casinos, racetracks, and lots of money. I loved the use of colors Abbott uses throughout the book describing the outfits these two women wear. Describing Gloria's closet of clothes "...rows of satiny luscious fabrics, from gauzy to thick brocade, eggshell to midnight blue. And next to this finery, she had a long row of stiff, tailored suits in pastels. These she wore to the races."
Lots of flying, thinking, and looking at sick people. Incredibly "ho-hum" ending to this series.

Vivian Gandillon is a werewolf. That is, she's a sixteen-year-old human girl. And she's a wolf. And not just any wolf, but the daughter of the pack's alpha pair. She, too, is destined to become a leader. Yet she is so tired of the fighting among the wolves--and it is pretty vicious stuff. She wonders if it would be better to explore her human nature with Aiden, a boy who is enchanted with the idea of wolves. With the reality, though? While Vivian is deciding whether she should reveal her true nature to Aiden, a werewolf is killing locals. Vivian can't remember doing the killing, but she keeps finding evidence that she is the culprit. High school housekeeping: There are several reasons that Blood and Chocolate has held up as a good YA read. Throughout the novel, Vivian is unsure about her place in the wolf pack. But there are times when she must enter the extremes of her wolf nature to defend herself and her mother. The scenes, both among the wolves and between Aiden and Vivian were very edgy when the book was published--this is a sensuous book, the sort of thing we see more often now. But best of all is that the ending is a surprise. Not your usual 'I'm in love with an alien species' denouement. Try it. NOTE: This review is also posted on my blog School Library Lady.

"The Young Elites" is an excellent book. It is way darker than Legend and it is not a dystopian story - it's more of a dark fantasy story. The writing was on point (but I really love Marie Lu's writing so that's not a surprise). The big surprise for me is how my feelings shifted through the book. I had a hard time liking Adelina as a protagonist but in the end she is the character who I understand the most and therefore really like. The opposite is true regarding all of the other characters. Except Violetta - I also had a hard time liking her but in the end I feel like she only wanted to protect Adelina. But the best part of the book is the story itself. There is a bigger meaning behind all of it and I really enjoyed reading something so dark for once. I'm really excited to read the next installment and to see the story evolve.

It took me some time to finish this book, and that is because it was a little bit confusing at first. The main character Sam is a very popular girl who cares so much about what people think of her. I was very irritated when after she died, she didn't do anything different even though she had the chance and she knew about her mistakes. In the end though she makes some better choices and also I was very happy to see her with Kent. "I vowed after that day that I would be your hero too, no matter how long it took" Kent was sooo nice. Such an interesting character. The boy who at first looked totally out of place, soon came to be the only one who could understand Sam, the only one who still had hope for her, the one who did not give up on her no matter what. "I guess that's what saying good-bye is always like--like jumping off an edge. The worst part is making the choice to do it. Once you're in the air, there's nothing you can do but let go." I liked the writing, though in my opinion the book's best features were the unique concept and characters. "So many things become beautiful when you really look."

Best of the series. I wasn't convinced a relationship between Sean (Captain of the station) and Eve (a paramedic) was going to work, but this actually ended up being the most realistic relationship in the series. First of all they've known each other for several years - since before Sean's wife and children died. I was disappointed that turns out his marriage was on the rocks before she died - but it made sense in the course of the suspense plot. I loved the flashbacks to when he was a young man in the Marines and his friendship gone bad. As in the first book, the villain has a relationship with the hero which makes it so much creepier. Since Sean was complaining that Blair didn't like sex and was all prissy, it's unrealistic to expect that she was having a hot affair with the creepy guy who is not described as handsome or even very clean. I dislike the typical plot point where the dead wife/husband turns out to be awful anyway. But with cute, kinky, lusty Sean at home why is the supposedly frigid wife having an affair with anyone? The obligatory-for-JD anal sex scene was at least indoors this time, and a bit toned back from previous books thankfully. Ranking the entire series, I liked the first and last the best. The middle books were all kinda the same and the couples didn't really work for me. It is best to read at least #4 before this one, because you get much of the start up to Sean's alcoholism in book #4.

...Meh. I'm generally a fan of the series but this is the weakest book so far. I reeeally liked books #4 and #5 (my favourites along with #1) but Hoarfrost was just... meh. It's not bad in the sense that I was aggravated by the characters (I love them all) or the plot (yay Jack London-ish setting)... it was just... meh. What I did not like was the switching POVs. They felt weird and just served to highlight the fact that ~something~ was going on with Griffin's mind . Also the plot took forever to finally move along -- I feel like I had a similar complaint about book #3, also not a favourite. But yeah, much as I like the Jack London-esque atmosphere, the first half of the book was very lacking in eldritch abominations. I was reading two books at the same time, this and a fluffy romcom, and I managed to have a nightmare about the romcom. This offends me personally. Weren't you supposed to be creepy, book? Pros: Christine and Iskander. Whenever Whyborne got sappy (which is, like, 99% of his chapters) I imagined Christine being like, "Good gad, man, stop touching your husband's face and get a move on!" Everything improves instantly with the addition of Christine, and that's a fact. Also at the end I was hoping that the reverend would marry Christine and Iskander during the final battle, like in Pirates of the Caribbean 3. Much disappointment when he didn't. But I guess we have to have the wedding in the next book? Possibly with eldritch abominations as bridesmaids?

This book has a bunch of really nice ideas and whimsical, satirical settings that make you think you're just about to read something brilliant. Unfortunately that moment never really came for me. Honestly this book has been hyped beyond belief. The whole time I was reading it I was thinking of other authors who had done it better. Midwestern gal in a strange land? Abarat was there and far more disturbing. Adult commentary in a middle school book with creepy undertones? Anything written by Paul Stewart or Terry Pratchett for that matter. Remember the Garth Nix middle-school books about the days of the week? More creative than this. I could go on. It's not that I dislike the book particularly, it's well written and there is some lovely scenery. The best scene for me was September in Autumn, talking down her death and turning into a tree, even if again the reasons behind this felt pretty weak. What was it? Something like: nothing changes in the land of transition... but she does ...because she ate weird food... but it's still meant to be a metaphor about the transient nature of nature in a static world..? I guess? But it's all a bit ... hollow. Characters have very flimsy motivations for anything - even the protagonist! We're repeatedly told of how heartless September is but she spends the entire story literally sacrificing pieces of her self for the wellbeing of strangers. The whole Wyverary concept felt very forced, his 'encyclopedic' knowledge gimmick disappears about halfway through the book. And the SAT words randomly sprinkled all over the place to make September look well read is just so cheesy and put-upon. Don't even get me started on the Marquess. I think I'm mostly annoyed because this is yet another book I'm reading that feels like it was promoted and 'raved' about beyond reason, I mean jesus, I've barely seen a bad critical review about it. It's getting 3 stars because I didn't hate it. It was easy enough to read, the plot came together in the end, and the scenery was pleasant. It's an okay novel but just that.

"I remember my dad saying that sometimes you can be inserted into another person's life just by witnessing something you were never really supposed to be a part of." This is so beautiful. I didn't even take notes while reading this because I was so hooked into it. All four of these characters whose perspectives we read from were so human and sad and I just wanted to protect them from all the bad things in their worlds. And, the way their stories are interconnected in such unpredictable ways. I was *squealing*. The ending may be to neatly wrapped up for some people, but for me it worked. I was so desperate to see those happy endings. The writing in this was so beautiful, and the only complaint I have was that this was such a short book. I wanted it to go on and on forever.

I would rate the writing as B+. If it was brought up to an A/A+ I think this book would be excellent :) Can't wait to read the next book. -I would have written a more thorough review, but since this series is very popular and one of my favourite series, I'm pretty sure someone else has made all of the necessary points. I recieved an ARC from Edelweiss in exchange for an honest review. Oh MAN, people are gonna be split on this book. I really enjoyed it-- Kelsea has come into her own as a queen, even if it's a queen in a cage. The book opens with her captured by Morte soldiers, headed to the enemy. She and the Red Queen should be mortal enemies... but in some ways, they're too similar. Finally seeing Kelsea and the Red Queen interact was fantastic, the RQ was fleshed out into a character that, while not good, was at least somewhat sympathetic. Kelsea's flashbacks (narrative flashbacks?) have gotten incredibly vivid, and for someone who read Invasion of the Tearling as soon as it came out, it took me a while to remember everything that had led to this point. But once I could piece it together, it flowed pretty easily. (Side note: my husband is reading the trilogy now and I'm envious that he can do it in a few months instead of a couple years.) The ending... oh man, people are going to FLIP THEIR SHIT over the ending. It's a hard twist, and I think it ended well, but I know that a LOT of YA readers are going to be angry that it doesn't end with romance and a happily ever after on the throne. I liked it, I thought it was a brave narrative choice, even if I was somewhat skeptical of the mechanics of it. That ending is what brought this down to a four for me. I've already recommended the series a few times after reading this, so it was clearly still worth the time and I enjoyed it.

This book was...I'm flabbergasted. I keep thinking of words like incredible and phenomenal but mostly I guess I'd call it unique. It's unlike anything else I've ever read! (Warning, this is gonna be a longggg review!!) I'm stunned (and a little embarrassed) that I put off reading this for so long! I've seen this book numerous times and every time I'd read the description I'd think, This just doesn't sound like my kind of book. By some miracle, I won the whole trilogy in a giveaway. As soon as I saw the GORGEOUS covers and reread the description, I knew I needed to read this book. There is so much I love about this book, where do I begin? The character's names! I love how unique they all were without being too hard to pronounce or way too out there and ridiculous. Also, all th traveling Karou did. Laini Taylor brought all of those exotic places and languages to life and made me want to travel! And the whole idea of this book is incredible! The Angel/Chimaera world is so complex, it took me awhile to even begin comprehending it. (Still not sure I completely do yet, actually)  As far as I can tell, the angels and chimaera live in this alternate world, together? I'm still stuck on the mentality of angels living in the clouds, over everything. It's hard to imagine both races sharing a world. Karou is such a fascinating character. If I'm being honest, I liked her better in the beginning. She's funny, enigmatic, and bizarre. She's pretty and she knows it (which I actually like about her and Akiva. There's none of that "insert angst filled teen name here who thinks they are just average looking and nothing special but they really are gorgeous" garbage) She gets out of a relationship and wants to be a cat that doesn't need to be petted and loved and purrs for no one (something along those lines) and I'm like Yeah you go girl! But she wants to be that cherished cat. She craves love, not just the romantic kind, but from her surrogate family. She doesn't want to be alone, and desperately feels lonely and like she's missing something. Although, I'm throwing it out there, she sometimes comes off as spoiled and bratty to Brimstone. Oh, Brimstone! We learn so much about him but I want to know MORE. His dedication to his work, and in turn, his race. His compassion for Karou and Madrigal (will I shall spill my guts about soon) The torture of his past. I would love to read a few chapters from his POV. Now, Akiva. In the beginning, he was a stereotype for angels. I was immediately driven nuts by the fact that he was so careless about being seen! No discretion whatsoever! I was also puzzled with his rebellious actions and creative mind. He falls for the enemy, twice, sort of and teaches himself basic magic skills that no one else knows because of their lost teachings. But then, underneath his dead, soulless, anguish filled eyes, we learn the truth. Oh. My. Goodness. Quite a web here. Personally, I don't really believe or want to believe in reincarnation, so when it seemed Karou was a reincarnation of someone I was like, lame, but the way it was done with the chimaera is so unique! I had a feeling Karou and Madrigal were connected, but still, when the pieces of this puzzle fell together, it was breathtaking. Karou recalling her/Madrigal's past was riveting! I was on again, off again, and then right back on again with this romance. Madrigal   saved Akiva and it set off a chain of events. He yearns for her, and, subconsciously, she yearns for him. He risks his life just to see her again and in the brief moments they are together, it's love. When it...abruptly ends, he looses himself. Re meeting her in the form of  Karou   the chemistry is instantly back. Again, another belief I don't possess is love at first sight, so I didn't really like it, but how can I deny them! The most heart wrenching moments for me were  The very vivid descriptions of Madrigal hearing Akiva's screams. And Akiva telling Karou "they're dead". What does that mean!?? Brimstone and gang? All chimaera? Probably the former. So know my question is, why is she still trying to get to that other world? And what happened with her and Akiva? I am SO ecstatic that I can jump right into the next book!

I was sort of surprised by how much I liked this. The blurb sounds a bit ordinary, successful NYC attorney has to go back home to take care of his younger brothers when his parents die. Redneck neighbor is straight but... It's very well written and the characters were presented with real world challenges. It's also not super angsty which I liked, since the setup could make it seem very emotional. There is a second book about one of the minor characters in this book and I will definitely read it because I like the author's work.

I keep thinking I know would to expect from this series, but so far every book has been a game changer. Not that I'm complaining, it definitely keeps things interesting. I did not see the whole thing with Ben coming. I always thought it would be Cormac/Kitty. To be honest, I was less than thrilled when Ben and Kitty got together at first. Not because I don't like Ben, he's been one of my favorite characters from the start, but I just like Cormac a little bit more. That's just my luck though. I always root for the wrong couple. Cormac aside, the dynamic between Kitty and Ben was surprising good though. There is opportunity for lots of character development for both of them in the future. That seems to be the biggest strength of this series: taking characters in impossible situation and showing how they can grow to overcome their obstacles. Kitty's development so far has been a joy to read about and it looks like Ben will be headed in the same direction. I'm a bit miffed though that Cormac ended up in jail... although I admit that this was the only possible outcome that wasn't a complete cliche. I hope though that there will be some sort of time jump in the next book so that he will get to be a part of it. This is definitely shaping up to be one hell of an interesting series. I can't wait to see where the next book will lead us.
Wonderful...If you read nothing else this year., read this one!

Hm. I'm seeing all of these positive reviews and I feel like I didn't read the same book as most of these people. I'm not really even sure how to review this book! I did appreciate Rowell's author's note at the end -- the novel is simply a tribute to characters she couldn't get out of her head, after sort of half-creating the story in Fangirl. But at the same time...excited as I was for this before it came out, I'm not quite sure this needed to exist. I disagree that you need to have read Fangirl to understand or appreciate the story here. As Rowell says, this isn't meant to be Cath's version of the story, or even the "real" story, but Rowell's version. Which is almost meta enough to make my head hurt. So in theory it stands on its own...except it kind of doesn't. Clearly the story owes a great deal to the legacy of Harry Potter, so much so that it reads a LOT like Harry Potter fan fiction. I've read a sickening amount of fan fiction in my day (mostly of the HP variety) and there are definitely great stories out there. And in the context of fan fiction, this is probably one of them. But as a story that simply stands on its own (like, say, Fangirl! ), it doesn't work. It's been argued before (I think in reference to the abomination that is 50 Shades) that the issue with fan fiction lies in character development. Fan fiction writers have an easier job in that regard, because JK Rowling or whoever has already done most of the work developing the characters, and even creating the settings. You're moving preexisting characters around a preexisting world, and it takes an incredibly talented writer to make you forget that fact. Those writers do exist, but they're rare. And again, you're still relying on the work the original author has already done -- you kind of have to! I was trying to imagine reading this book in a world where I haven't read Harry Potter...or even in a world where Harry Potter didn't exist. But the whole time I felt like I was filling in blanks in the plot or the characters with details from Rowling's series. Simon is Harry, Baz is Draco, Penelope is Hermione, Agatha is an amalgamation of the less important side characters always sidelined by The Trio, and the Mage is Evil Dumbledore...in fact, I would argue that this is actually an alternate reality story wherein Dumbledore was the actual villain. Rowling definitely hints at the possibility in the 7th book, that Dumbledore's aggressive concern for "the greater good" bordered on Nazi-like . The other problem is that this reads very much like the last book of a series. Imagine you just randomly picked up Deathly Hallows without having read the six books preceding it. You'd be confused, but you'd eventually pick up enough backstory to make sense of the narrative. That's what's happening here. The problem is, I don't think Rowell had any interest in actually writing an 8-book fantasy series. The characters introduced in Fangirl were already in the 7th of 8 books, and those are the characters Rowell created and grew attached to. Obviously she crafted a bit of a backstory for them, but I don't think she had dreams of a franchise, nor was she interested in going back to the beginning. All well and good except...it's basically like she just wrote the last book of a series, and the last book of a series is really missing something if you haven't read the...however many books that come before it. You can't just say "oh, nothing interesting happened in Simon's first seven years at school," because of course it did. We hear about it, minimally. It just doesn't feel enough like a stand alone novel. Even though it's over 500 pages long, it still feels like too much has to happen in too little time. It's both too slow and too fast. We have flashbacks to the Mage and Lucy...Simon's parents, and all of their generation. And although the Marauders in Harry Potter left me cold ("greatest story Rowling never wrote" my ass), I found myself far more interested in the Mage and Lucy and Fiona and Ebb and Nicodemus than any of these other fools. Perhaps because those characters were truly original creations, rather than simple imitations. And in the end, so much of this just feels like an excuse to get Simon and Baz making out. Here's the positive -- Rowell is a great writer. Her dialogue is great and I love her sense of humor. Agatha's anti-magic asides were some of my favorites ("Why is there a spell to stick things to the wall? Seriously, Tape. Exists." Love it!). Fangirl is still one of my absolute favorite books, and I had such high hopes for this. I figured if anyone could make a pseudo-HP story work, Rowell had the chops. But my primary reaction to this is just disappointment. I wanted to like it so badly. It's not aggressively terrible...which is almost worse! It took me over two months to finally sit down and finish, and I think that's only because ABC Family has been playing the movies back to back all weekend and I kind of wanted an HP fix. Also I'm on a total book binge over Christmas break. I didn't hate this, I just wish it had been more...something. Interesting? Exciting? Original? I can't even completely put my finger on what would make it better. Sad face.

I admit it - I love these books!!! What books am I talking about? Books like the Fifty Shades of Grey trilogy or Sylvia Day's Crossfire novels. You know you like them, too; you just won't admit it in public. That's why you read them on your Kindle, your Nook, or your iPad - so no one knows your dirty little secret. I'm familiar with this strategy because it's what I do, duh. Although, I did buy the actual Fifty Shades of Grey books because Target had them on sale and I had to have them one right after the other. Target is closer than the library; I was that desperate. So, enough about you... why did I wait so long to read this? Because I'm completely tri-polar when it comes to my reading (bi-polar with everything else). One minute I want all the pretty-covered young adult books, the next minute I need a good urban fantasy to get my action on. When those thrills are exhausted, I need some lovin' with a good romance in the form of either a new adult or one of these "erotica lite" books. I call this new crop of hot and heavy books for hard-up moms (like me) "erotica lite" because I personally don't feel they are true erotica in the same form as all the other erotica that's been around forever. You compare Release Me to some of the stuff that Ann Rice has written and this pales to some of the hard core images that Ms. Rice can conjure up with her words. Even compared to Fifty Shades, Release Me is a bit on the tamer side. I'm not a scholar on erotica, this is all just my humble, Ohio State-educated opinion. Release Me was another example of the right book at the right time. I was behind in reading my ARCs and everything was looking like a chore. So I picked up Release Me and bang! Done in 2 evenings. That's quick for me! Story / Tempo I read this story so quickly because it's a fast, quick, easy read. It's told from Nikki's POV and we meet her as she attends an art event for her boss. Her boss has given her the assignment of capturing the attention of multimillionaire Damien Stark to procure a meeting to pitch their company's newest product. Nikki is actually a very smart, intelligent woman and she knows how to play the game. She won't let her boss use her for her looks alone but she also has no problem with getting cozy with Damien Stark. She's had her eyes on him for quite some time. The story spends quite a bit of plot-time establishing the relationship between Damien and Nikki so the story is light on drama. There is a plot/drama behind the relationship and that's where I liked this book a bit better than other books I've read of this "genre". This drama appears to continue into the next book, if the ending is any indication. At least I hope it does. Who doesn't love drama mixed in with hot lovin'? Characters Yes, we do have a mysterious, hot, tortured multimillionaire in this book. But our lady interest, Nikki, is smart, educated, strong, and is able to say "no" and mean it. And Damien likes it. Nikki has her own past issues that Damien wants to help Nikki with as well. I really can't help but fall for Damien. I hope we get just a bit more personality out of him in the next books because while he was hiding his past from Nikki and the public, he was keeping himself hidden from the reader, too. Someone please get the song "Darling Nikki" by Prince out of my head!!!! Every time I saw Nikki's name in print I kept hearing Prince scream. And no, kiddies, Prince's version is NOT a remake of the Foo Fighter's version. I should come over and smack you if you think that. But back to my review... I was torn between rating this book a 3.5 star and 4 star review. Four stars won out in the end because I need to read Claim Me (Stark Trilogy #2) as soon as I can get my hands on it and because Release Me was exactly what it should have been, an utterly enjoyable, fun read that can distract you from life for hours. I'm someone who enjoys deep connections to books and their characters who live in them. I have many favorites and almost favorites. That being said, I don't think there is any series that has provoked more of an emotional response in me than Fitz's journeys with the Fool. This last adventure of theirs was an (almost) perfect way to end those journeys. First the negative. (Some SPOILERS ahead). There were a number of inconsistencies with prior books, details overlooked by the editors. Bee's maid was named Careful in book #1, not Caution. Fitz said he was taking Verity's sword with him and not an axe, but apparently he did the opposite. The familial connections between Malta and Althea and Wintrow and Ronica kept getting garbled (understandably so, but still). These (and others) are minor things, but they distracted me and took me out of the story just a tiny bit. More taxing for me was Fitz's path through the first half of the book. It meandered; it indulged in the Liveship and Dragon characters just a bit too much, in ways that didn't serve the story; above all, it was repetitive. Fitz and the Fool kept having the same arguments in the same way, with no seeming self awareness of that. I admit I was disappointed around the halfway point. However, Bee's path remained strong and intriguing and well constructed throughout. Once I did hit that halfway point, I couldn't decide who I wanted to read more. The second half of the book is everything I wanted it to be. It was full of change, uncertainty, consequences, emotion, love, anger... all facets of life, really. The big finale at Clerres was just right and simply heartbreaking. The closing chapters of the book were exactly as I would've wished had I allowed myself to think that far ahead. A strong ending is really everything. I would've given 4 stars (out of pre-existing love) to the first half, but the second is Robin Hobb at her finest. She not only had to wrap up this trilogy, but also the previous two (or four, really), and she really did it. I cannot fully convey how amazing Hobb is and how much her work has touched me (and I can't even estimate how many tissues I've gone through). Her dedication at the end speaks to me. I think the best book she's ever done is book #2 of this series, Fool's Quest, because it was as perfect as the second half of this one the whole way through. However, this final chapter will always hold a special place in my heart.

I initially passed this book up on NetGalley when I saw it. The cover with the girl standing in front of the clock just didn't appeal to me. (I mean, yes, that scene does happen in the book, so I can't complain - but it didn't call out to me.) However, after reading several glowing reviews of the book, and seeing THIS cover (with the bird skull) - which is a work of beauty on its own - I had to go back and grab it. And boy am I glad that I did! This book is GREAT! It's an original fairytale, in the best tradition. It has elements of 'Mr. Fox' (http://www.authorama.com/english-fair...), 'The Robber Bridegroom' and 'Bluebeard' - as well as other old tales - but it's very much its own thing. Our heroine, Rhea, is a wonderful mix of wise and wisecracking. She's tough and capable, but as a miller's daughter, she knows that she has no recourse when a Lord informs her family that he intends on marrying her. Lord Crevan, though somewhat enigmatic, is known to be a friend of her town's leader, and things could go very poorly indeed for both her and her family if she doesn't acquiesce. So when Crevan summons her to come alone to his manor, at night, although she knows it's 'not right' - she goes. When she arrives, Lord Crevan is not in residence - but there are other women there. She learns that she is not the first woman to be selected by Crevan - indeed, she is to be his seventh bride. Even this polygamy might be something Rhea would accept, for the sake of her family - but Crevan is also a sorcerer, and his schemes involving dark magic may involve worse fates than servitude - indeed, worse fates than death. Beautiful, eerie, humorous and entertaining - I was wholly won over by the story. Many thanks to Amazon and NetGalley for the opportunity to read. As always, my opinion is solely my own.

This is a very long book and for a highly impatient person such as myself, this book is surprisingly interesting, in fact, so much so that I manage to finish it without feeling bored midway. I guess what's great about this book is the characters. From Vito (I prefer to call him Cic), Sophie, Nick, Catherine, Uncle Harry, and all the way to the killer, I think they all have unique personalities that breathe life into the story. The romance is typical of the genre (boy meets girl, then some misunderstanding, followed by reconciliation, boy becomes knight and girl his princess, and then they live happily ever after, the end), there is nothing mind-blowing but overall, it's sweet and warms the heart. I give this 4/5 instead of 5/5 because of the imperfection in the plot: For a killer so dumb, I am surprised it takes the police so long to sniff him out. I mean  he has been killing real people and inserting their voices and faces to his games! He's lucky none of the loved ones of his victims are hard-core players or he would have been sent to jail a long time ago. What surprises me more is the fact that Rose (the author) also thinks the killer is pretty dumb and pretty much says it through one of her characters (VC). If he intends to kill real people to put into games, shouldn't he be using models from other countries or at least select models across statelines to make the process of detecting the crime more difficult. No, the killer is way to arrogant and confident that his crimes will never be exposed and he pays with his life for his mistakes (a good thing as I hate to see murderers go unpunished). This book seems to be the first of 3 in the Daniel Vartanian series though I have a problem with the labeling of this series in Goodreads. I think it's more appropriate if it's just named Vartanian, #1

She has a special power that creates chaos because she's had no training behind it and doesn't understand what she is truly capable of. I was pretty lukewarm to this book at first, but once the action picked up, OH MY GOD! I seriously sat down and read it straight through. Next thing I knew, it was 3 am and my brain was complete mush from powering through. There was just something very easy about this book. I've seen some reviews that pick apart the story, but I was too sucked into the plot to think too deep into the world building. The tone of the book was so depressing. I wasn't outright sobbing, but there was just something so unfair about the things these teens were subjected to in the Program. It was one of those times where you're desperately hoping that the characters will find a way out of their predicament. Most books will have the protagonist pull off some risky plan at the last moment, but there was none of that here. I felt terrible for Sloane and how helpless she was in the situation. It was such a downer to read this story and realize that 'this or that' was going to happen and they had no control over it. While I wasn't sure in the beginning, I actually really liked the writing style. I thought that the way the memory loss was handled was done very well. There were wisps here and there where you could see that something was slowly going wrong. There was this scene that took place after Realm wiped Sloane's memory of the day  and there was just something very eerie about it. Speaking of less depressing parts, I thought the deja vu moments between Sloane, James, and Lacy were so cute. None of them remembered each other, but I liked how little tidbits from their lives pre-Program popped up in their conversations, such as Lacey talking about Evan . The best part of the book had to be Sloane and James relationship. I don't normally read books where the characters are already boyfriend and girlfriend, but I loved these two so much. I didn't feel any of the disconnect that I normally get when I'm thrown into the middle of a book relationship. They seemed a bit codependent in the first section of the story, but, with the world they were living, I didn't blame them. There was something so tragic about them, like they were drowning and all they had was each other to keep them afloat. The flashbacks were a huge part in making me feel invested in their relationship. They felt real and I spent the entire book wishing that they'd get their happy ending. Overall, I loved this book. You just know a book is good when you go to stop reading and you keep deciding to pick it back up and read a little more. The one thing I have to ding it for is how the set up for the sequel was executed. The story had been moving at a nice pace and then, all of a sudden, this whole rebel thing was squished into the last few pages. Other than that, it was amazing.

The journey and transformation that Cassie goes through is astounding. She starts out as a stubborn teenage girl and develops into a strong young woman. She endures unbelievable trials and manages to stay strong through it all. That's something I'm completely astounded by. ***The rest of this review will contain content that could be considered as spoilers, but are a critical part of why I didn't enjoy certain aspects of this book! (Oh, and I knew all this going into the book, and it all happens in the first 100 pages or so, so I don't think of them as huge spoilers, but they kinda are at the same time) So if you're brave enough to read on, the biggest reason I didn't like this book was Bear. He was controlling and brainwashing. Cassie wants desperately to leave the castle, but he convinces her to stay at the castle for a week. At the start of the following chapter, it's been many weeks, and now they're best friends. The reader missed out on any character/relationship development. And then she finally gets a chance to visit her family for a few days, but she can't wait to get back to bear and ditches them, only bringing back some statistically stuff and birth control... And then 3 magical months later, guess what? Bear manipulated her birth control not to work without even letting her know. So out of anger and curiosity, she wants to see what kind of weirdo would do that to her, and then poof, he abandons her (as these tales tend to go), and she goes east of the sun, west of the moon to save him, putting this lunatic, brainwashing polar bear above herself and unborn child. She doesn't care about the fact that she's thousands of miles from humanity and he didn't even leave her an enchanted blanket or something. And finally when they reunited at the end with their pretty little baby (who, I might add, is actually a troll princess ), he doesn't make it up to her in any way, and she even goes so far as to forgive him for looking at his face, while he doesn't apologize for impregnating her and making her walk thousands of miles. ***End of spoilery portion*** Here's a spoiler-free summary of what I just took up 3 giant paragraphs of complaining: There's no relationship development. Bear is a controlling jerk. Cassie is so brainwashed that she makes irrational and dangerous decisions. Things aren't properly resolved by the end. I'm kind of sad I didn't like it more, because it seems like the rest of the world loved it!

** spoiler alert ** If I could, I think I would give this novel a 3.5. Though there are many things that I would change, I admit that the plot was interesting enough to keep me reading. Colleen Hoover's way of teasing the reader to find out more background was intriguing, and though not always worth the wait, ultimately paid off in the end. First of all, I found the relationship between Owen and Auburn to be forced at times and a little too "teenage fan fiction" for my taste. In fact, the entire Target scene makes me cringe, but because I'm so familiar with the Target layout, I will probably never be able to walk past aisle 13 without thinking of that stupid scene and cursing Colleen Hoover. However, there were some times that their intimate moments seemed electric and well-written which is why I was still able to give this novel a 4/5. Same thing with the entire character and conflict with Trey. I found him too one-dimensional and merely there to stir up drama, but I also enjoyed the feeling of dread and hopelessness when Auburn and Mason realize when he abuses his power. I could also look past the teenage faction fiction vibe because I appreciated the plot. Hoover did a good job of dropping plot points just when the reader needs them. The only gripe I have with this is that since the novel is told from both Owen and Auburn's perspective, the reader feels a little cheated when major points are delivered. For example, the reveal of AJ was so frustrating to me because, yes, Auburn mentioned "he" multiple times (and we assumed it was her inability to get over Adam), but after the AJ reveal, AJ is ALL she talks about. I understand it was withheld for plot reasons, but in a first person narrative, this particular concept didn't seem realistic to me. I did however find the connection between Auburn and Owen to be worth it in the end. I knew they were connected somehow through the hospital, but the true narrative wasn't revealed until the very last "chapter." I felt the final connection that Adam and Owen had truly made some of the more annoying aspects of the novel forgivable. Admittedly, I feel dumb for not realizing that Owen's "confession business" had something to do with it, but I'm glad I didn't because it made the pay off worth it.

"I don't want to be telling this story." Yes, I'm shelving it under Horror. I'm also going to be swearing a lot in the review. It's the kind of book that elicits sheer red and blinding rage. The Handmaid's Tale is one of those books I was really torn about wanting to read. On one hand, it's a female-focused dystopian story, and I do love my worldbuilding. On the other hand, it's a story about a society which reduces the worth of women down to their reproductive capabilities. The latter is so viscerally horrific to me (particularly as a person who realizes that she has been lucky enough to be born into the threshold of the time period where it's almost-not the accepted norm) that I would have avoided the story for the rest of my life on the grounds that it hits far too close to home. However, I had a couple of challenges on goodreads groups that let me tick this book off, so I shrugged off the dread and read it. While I was exactly as pissed off about the book and what happened in it as anticipated, I was also relieved because it was primarily a story about rebellion in the face of such bullshit nonsense fuckery. This rebellion is robust, organized and frankly awe-inspiring, but we only catch glimpses of it (Designated-Ofglen the First MY GLORIOUS CHILD I WANT YOUR BOOK), as our Narrator only encounters this rebellion, and is not really a part of it. Our unnamed narrator (whose designation, I suppose you could call it, is Offred- and no that is not her name and I am willing to fight anyone who disagrees with me on this) is cast in the role of the emotionally traumatized everywoman who's just trying to survive. She is a passive character to whom the plot happens, and she does little to nothing to influence the story. That's okay, because given the kind of life she has been living and the kind of indoctrination she has been going through, it's frankly a miracle that she still has the ability to think otherwise. The Narrator's story is about survival in the face of overwhelming emotional torture. This book is not about rape as much as it is about indoctrination- about building a culture of passivity on the basis of skewed "logic", and rigorously enforcing it till even thinking otherwise is abnormal. Thoughtcrime is a terrifying concept- but the "Republic"of Gilead has not progressed quite so far into Orwellian mechanisms- the method of control used is mostly the fear of punishment, death and mutilation. (There was this horrifying scene my brain cooked up when I was evaluating the possible methods of rebellion. Towards the end, the Narrator's words have despair itched into every syllable, and I was thinking of ways where a Handmaid could well- commit murder-suicide. And then my brain said- "look, if your value is equal to the value of your womb, then all they would have to do to a transgressor is cut off their limbs" and yeah. My brain was not a happy place when I was reading this book.) The story is bleak and intensely character-focused, but the ultimate aim is to tell the story of the world she's living in and how it works, not the story of her. I suppose that's one of the ways you can use a passive protagonist. As the world is as important as the character, I'd like to make a few notes on specific parts of the book. Be warned of heightened emotions. Marked for possible spoilers. The First Person Framing Device used here is significant- the last chapter of the book is probably my favourite, mostly because it's set in the future at a time where Gilead is gone and oh god that is such a RELIEF. The Narrative has been reconstructed from old cassette tapes sometime in the future, and the last chapter is set at a conference where an overview of the reassembling process has been given, along with theories on who exactly the narrator was. The speech fills in a few of the holes in the Narrative, future historians analyzing yet another period in history from the safety of their armchairs. Which I realize is a mean thing to say as trivializing the events of the past is one of the ways we use to deal with the magnitude of the events of the past- but that's a different topic altogether. While I don't have much in the way of a liveblog, most scenes with the Commander in it (with the exception of the scrabble scene), particularly when he explains the philosophy of this new world and why it works and why it's better, had me staring at the wall vibrating with the need to punch something. "die, you sonovabitch", "he's either an idiot or a liar", "hypocrite, hypocrite, hypocrite", "DIE." and "fucker" are a few of the phrases I used to comment on his justification of Gilead- please note that I was reading this book as fast as I possibly could but that I simply could not look at the revolting nonsense spouting out of his mouth without commenting on it- I may have exploded otherwise. The casual misuse of power, the disregard for human lives and human worth, all justified with the ever-present goal of the greater good. It made me want to scream. One point of the flashback that resonated with me was Luke comforting the Narrator after her accounts were frozen. It's painful and hideous, but her emotions at that time were terrifyingly spot-on. It's the same kind of emotions I have, the way I see the women in the last generation of my family, see the way they have such little agency merely because they do only the housework and do not work to bring in money and think "not me please god never me." However well-intentioned the person doing the comforting is, it's hard for their words to have any meaning if they have not experienced the same thing. And "it's just a job" is not accurate. It's freedom and economic independence and /options/. It's power because that's what power is- your ability to have more options. And loss of power never not painful. On a sidenote, one of the Commanders' complaints (and his complaints, his rationalizations, are all so unapolegetically centered on the men) is how there was nothing left for men to do. And I just- look, the loss of power is staggering. But there is loss of power because one's options are taken away from you, and loss of power because others are now getting the same options. I'd just like to point out the two are not identical- they are not even comparable. Another point of interest is the female compliance in the new regime, and the justifications offered for the same. The Aunts want power or have a corrupted form of faith, the wives and possibly the marthas and the handmaids think oh dear god it could be worse. So they build to themselves a palace of one-sided beliefs and rationalizations, saying how we don't get raped anymore (which is just... no. that's not how rape works.) and how the men now respect us more. One of the most interesting points was the ritual where the handmaids, the most oppressed, the most beaten down, were allowed to tear a man to death with their bare hands. A very useful method of releasing pressure valves, as the Archivist-Professor notes in the last chapter. What else is there? The moment of anger when I realized the "names" of the handmaids were "Of-ASSHOLE COMMANDER NAME", followed by me refusing to think of her as "Offred" because that would be painful. The sadness I felt when the Narrator tried to speak to god, to ask them what was happening, and why it was happening and to please have mercy. The anger and irritation with logic I felt when the professor at the end point out that you should judge a society by the time and the circumstances because there are always reasons, because I was torn between being a reasonable person who could try to analyze and understand more, and between being a person who just wanted to scream till everyone stopped. talking. such. nonsense. Dehumanization. It's a tough topic to deal with. Good job, Margaret Atwood. //salutes

This review was originally posted on Bedtime Bookworm ** This is the second book in 5th Wave series. There may be mild spoilers in this review for The 5th Wave. The Audiobook I listened to this on audio, just like I did for the first book in the series. I really love the female narrator, Phoebe Strole. The male narrator is different in this book compared to the first one, but I enjoyed his narration as well. I hardly touched the physical book during this read because I enjoyed the audiobook so much. However, there were a few scenes I found confusing and had to refer to the text to completely understand what was going on. That scene where Ringer and Razor are using the baseball analogy to speak in code?? So confusing on audio haha. I'm not sure I completely understood even after reading the text though. The World I find this apocalyptic world so fascinating! It's so cut throat and dangerous to live in. This sounds sadistic, but I think it's so interesting to create a world where you can't trust anybody else - it's just such an interesting concept to explore. The summary isn't kidding when it talks about taking away our humanity. The aliens in this series have taken our humanity away by making it so you can't trust that another person is really human and won't hurt you - even children. What a terrible feeling to not be able to trust ANYBODY. It would be so lonely living in a world like that. The Characters We get many more POVs in this book. While we do see some aspects from Cassie and Evan's POVs, we also get other POVs. A large portion of the book is told from Ringer's POV. As much as I enjoyed Cassie and Evan from the first book, I found Ringer to be a very interesting perspective. She is such a strong character! Her personality is very different from Cassie's and I found her perspective to be refreshing. There is a different couple in this book as the central romance story line and I really enjoyed that as well - totally shipped it! The Plot Just like the first book, I found the plot of this book to be fast paced and action packed. It was such a page turner! The chapters are typically short as well (and most ending with a cliffhanger! ), which always helps me to keep reading. There were so many exciting moments and plots twist, especially at the end of the story, that I could hardly believe it. OMG those scenes at the end when Ringer escapes - my heart was in my throat and I was in disbelief in how it went. Not at all what I was expecting. I know a lot of other readers felt this book suffered from second book syndrome or that not much happened in it. I honestly don't feel that way at all! I feel like so much happened in this book, and I was so excited to continue the series after I finished it. In Summary Overall, I really loved this book! I loved the different character perspectives we are introduced to and I found the plot to be exciting and full of unexpected twists and turns. I really enjoyed the narrators and definitely recommend this book on audio if you like audiobooks. I recommend this book (and series) to sci-fi lovers, especially if you enjoy alien invasions and post apocalyptic settings. What is your favorite alien invasion book or series? Let me know in the comments!

I love Kristen Ashley. I love her writing style and the characters she creates and this book did not let her down. I LOVED this book!! If I could give it more than 5 stars I would. Right from the very fist page this story grabs your attention and drags you straight in. After suffering and surviving an abusive marriage for 7 years Kia Clemintine finally finds herself free from hell. She goes on a trip to Europe which is where she meets the gorgeous sports star Sam Cooper. Now if there is one thing that Kristen Ashley excells at, it is creating a hot alpha male and Sam is certainly this. with nearly half the book set in beautiful locations in Europe, the scene is set for Sam to get Kia to start trusting him. After 7 years with a man who abused her, Kia has some trust issues, but Sam is determined to prove to her he is not like him. Kia starts to trust Sam and opens herself wide open to him. She shares her life and her demons with him and she stars to really start living her life again. But Sam has his own demons and even though he gives Kia the life she has always deserved, he has trouble coming to tems with his own hell and Kia is worried why he won't share his demons with her The sub characters in this book play a vital role to the main story and you can't help but fall in love with them all. The scenery throughout the whole book is just beautiful and the story will have you laughing and crying throughout. This is a full on typical Kristen Ashley book, a beautiful story with laughter and tears, romance and some seriously hot men. Lee Nightingale even makes a cameo appearance! If Kristen Ashley is not you type of thing then you won't enjoy this book, but think you need to ask yourself, "why the hell is she not your thing?!". This book is brilliant, emotional and heart warming and it will leave you thinking about it way after you have finished the last page. My favourite quote from the whole book really sums up the whole feel of the book....  you got one life, never use it to just breathe.

He puts up a facade that we are beginning to see though and I totally hope that he ends up with Vi. I was confused by the end when a few scenes were retold from Ryns point of view. It just didn;t add much and I wasn;t sure if it was a novella or what. I did like the Part with Nate as it was a scene that we weren;t previously present for. Thought, for sure, he was a lock to show up in this story. And "Hell- the fuck - lo" may have unseated my long time literary gem "fidiot" as my favorite. But the last quarter of this book was a slog. I didn't like Sam. I just didn't. Most of the time, I just thought he was an ass. And when he finally explained himself...I still just thought he was an ass. Did not love him. I liked Kia. She made some bad choices, but watching her sort of grow out of her ex-husband's shadow was a bit of fun. Though at times, I wondered if she could see that she was still really being BULLIED by Sam...sure he didn't hit her, but really his attitude was still abusive. And the epilogue went on and on and on. I did like the final detail of the maitre d', that was cool. And then I also have to admit, that though this book was not my favorite KA ever and I will not be revisiting this story...the story and the characters had depth. I love the characters and how well developed they were. The love story was so very real, so very passionate, and has unfortunately the potential to be so very tragic .Two people who aren't supposed to be together, yet find a way, tragedy pulled them apart, circumstances bring them back together, and then again tragedy happens. Where will this go? I don't know, but I will definitely find out, because I can't wait to read the next book in the series.

While I loved the narration of the audiobook, I just couldn't stay glued to this story as much as I originally thought I would, and found myself constantly backing up to re-listen. It SEEMED to have all the markings of an interesting read. Two young men heading off on a ridiculous quest for eggs during wartime in Russia, all the while avoiding Germans. It's cold, they're hungry beyond measure, and one can't poop. Parts of this had me laughing aloud, especially when Kolya is talking - he's just so matter of fact with his wording that I had to giggle. Lev, on the other hand, is so serious, that it makes Kolya even funnier. Humor aside, there is some obvious violence and some scenes that would be quite gruesome if this were in a movie or in real life. While you understand that this is a story of Benioff's grandparents, he never goes back to present day to wrap it up. I'm not sure if I liked that he didn't (you don't need it), or if it would have been more of a "bookend" style to do so. Curious what others think. Still a solid 3, but it didn't hold my interest long enough throughout the first half especially to go any higher.

Reader thoughts: I like these books more and more. Artemis is just brilliant enough in this book, and yet still dastardly devious, that it is very fun to read. My favorite moment from this book is when Artemis asks the one employee whether he can bring his invisible friend on the tour. Another favorite moment is when Artemis tosses Butler into the freezer. Another is when Artemis inspects the ears of the one unconscious guy. Another is when Mulch pulls himself up the side of a building using his suction arms. Another is when Artemis calls the crossword puzzle phone number. Another is when the contacts fall out of Artemis's and Butler's eyes at the end of the book. Yes, I suppose I was a fan of Artemis after this book. He showed off more cleverness and less jerkness. Writer thoughts: EC is daring. I can only be glad book 4 was published before I finished book 3. This cliffhanger is as bad as the one in Catching Fire or The Mark of Athena or The Knights of Crystallia. Cofer memory-wiped his MC at the end of the book ! When my cousin first introduced me to this series, he had only read books 1, 2 and 3. He told me about the fully-armed-and-dangerous fairies, the criminal mastermind Artemis, and the ways they were forced to work together. My cousin knew there had to be more books to the series, and I think his excitement over the cliffhanger ending made me more eager to try the books. If you read Fallen Too Far, then reading Never Too Far is essential. Honestly, it is so much better now that the truth is out. I am a sucker for a pregnancy story and this book did not disappoint. Blaire remains extremely strong and is determined to see things through, alone if that's how things turn out. She is very admirable as she yet again barely complains and works her butt off to survive. Her friendship with Bethy continues and though the two are as opposite as can be they complement each other well. I was happy she and her boy-toy managed to work things out as unbelievable as that may be. Though, I doubt it will last and eventually Bethy too, will have her own story within the series. We get to see the real turn around for Rush. Blaire leaving was the catalyst he needed to set him straight. He begins to defend her to Nan and doesn't let the (fake) truth hurt her anymore than it has. Okay I have seriously fallen in love with Woods. If Blaire wasn't pregnant with Rush's baby I might hope for a switch-a-roo. He is so sweet and looks out for her even in book one. He never lets his money or influence go to his head and I hope he gets his own HEA very soon. I couldn't help but feel bad for him like every experience and chat he had with Blaire was like a crushing blow to his heart and mine. I was thankful Blaire did not keep the pregnancy quiet for very long. Yes, she may blurt out the truth but it's better for him to know the truth. Plus, when he found out she was able to see that he really wanted to be were her before and after he knew and it wasn't just because she was preggers. I was a little put off by Nan, once again, and her friend back home but other than that I loved everything. Even though she was injured I was on team Blaire and it was hard to read Rush's phone call which inevitably makes him miss another pre-natal appointment and when Nan lies about his family obligations coming first (the family that screws Blaire over every chance they get). No worse feeling for Blaire to get her hopes up about being a family only to have him blow her off. But alas, all is well in the end and once Nan recovers she even seems accepting of having a niece or nephew. Never Too Far is a must read. It has its ups and downs but that's what makes it so special. One minute you'll hate it and the next you'll love it but you won't at any point want to put it down. I enjoyed every minute and now I wish they were longer or had a better ending/epilogue. Even another book would make me happy but I'm sure they'll make reappearances in the next books. Out next is Twisted Perfection on April 23rd and this time it's Woods' story. I just hope it's complete and we don't have to wait months for the follow-up like this book and Fallen too Far.
