Where I got the book: ARC from LibraryThing Early Reviewer program. Expected publication date is 5/15/12. This novel seems to be generating some buzz, so I was quite pleased to get a chance to be an early reviewer. It is based on historical truth, in that there really was a former slave called Mary Bowser who in some way helped her former owner, Bet Van Lew, and an associate named Thomas McNiven send information about Confederate plans to Lincoln and his generals in the Civil War. As almost nothing else is known about the real Mary, Leveen is free to imagine Mary's story based on what is known about the lives of slaves and free coloreds in the era. And she does a thorough, professional job of it, giving Mary a voice that is distinctly 19th century (to the point where modern readers may have to use a dictionary in places) and carefully incorporating historical events into the narrative. It's hard to find fault with a book that is well written and edited, meticulously researched and based on a fascinating topic. But I'm going to anyway. I found myself thinking that this is exactly the kind of novel New York loves: the writer has writing credits, academic and literary credibility, and a platform. She's a Serious Writer (whereas I am the first to acknowledge my amateur status). Am I suffering from a case of sour grapes? I hope not. My problem with this novel is that it just didn't catch fire for me. It should have done: there was so much there, so much incident and life-threatening situations, life and death and love and all the rest. And yet I found it extremely easy to put down after a few pages (and the word 'boring' was beginning to float around my skull at about the two-thirds mark, although I really don't want to apply that label as I think many readers will love this novel). The problem, for me, was that at times the novel took on that dramatized-textbook feel that you get when the writer has really taken pains to get the thing historically accurate. When we moved more into Mary's story, I was happy enough: Leveen handles dialogue well in these sections. And then Mary would be listening to a conversation between real-life historical figures, and the whole thing would become a bit stilted, especially as it was necessary for these characters to explain what was happening. Call me a philistine, but I'd rather have had something livelier and less historically elucidating. The Secrets of Mary Bowser functions really well as a historically accurate corrective to the Gone-With-The-Wind romance of devoted servants and noble masters, but (whisper it low) I re-read GWTW until the covers fell off, but I won't do the same to Mary. Nevertheless, an interesting read which will be enthusiastically received by the writing establishment. I predict NYT bestseller status.

This novel is AMAZING, highly original, and it will haunt you. Fourteen year old Luce loses her father and is sent to live with an uncle she hardly knows - an abusive alcoholic. 40 pages in and Luce has given up on life in her sleepy little Alaskan fishing community. Tumbling into the sea, prepared to die, Luce becomes a mermaid instead and so begins her journey. There's friendship, loss, hope. But most of all, this is the story of who we are and what we're made of. The characters were all extremely well drawn. Key characters like Anais and Catarina were boldly depicted, but even the smaller characters like Dana, stick in your mind. You feel like you know them. The description of people and places was subtle, sometimes detailed, sometimes broadly depicted - it was just right. I cannot praise Ms Porter's talent as a writer and a creator, enough. I particularly enjoyed Luce's 'narration' (third person) - which was so realistic. You felt like you were listening to the real deal, a fourteen year old Luce. If this novel didn't have the ability to scar you, to shock you, to drag you into the depths as far as emotion is concerned, I would recommend it to younger readers. Sarah Porter has done an amazing job shaping Luce. This is the part in my reviews when I usually drone on about the 'romance'; because I usually only read books which have at least some romance in them. There are rare exceptions: Harry Potter, and... well, Harry Potter. This book didn't feature romance as such, although there's clear scope for it in the trilogy. I have to say though that this book didn't need it. It managed to wrap me around its pages without that. The pacing of the novel was good. It's possibly one of the most addictive books I've ever read though (and I've read a lot). My biggest complaint about this book: why isn't its goodreads rating higher? I would have read it so much sooner... :) I cried, I laughed, I read way too late into the night. I'm 23 now, and I really enjoyed this book - age doesn't limit its appeal. I read this book yesterday and I'm still thinking about it today. I think it'll be that way for a while. Even though this is a book about mermaids, I think Sarah Porter summed up her novel best when she said: "Lost Voices was my attempt to write the book I most needed as a twelve-year-old struggling with what it means to be human: a book I never really found. " I think she succeeded. I can't wait to see what Sarah does with book 2. I highly recommend that you read this book.

SOOO Much Teen Drama I honestly didn't expect this book to be so Young Adult. There was so much teen drama and angst I couldn't take it. And I'm a teenager! So Vampire Academy has 150k+ reviews with an average rating of 4.2. Many people call this their favourite PNR series ever. Needless to say my expectations were high. I now realise, unrealistically so. VA is very readable, but there were so many problems I had with it. The plot had potential though I felt the execution fell flat. The beginning was extremely slow and then in the last 15% everything just unravels with lightening speed. You know those conclusions where the antagonist is revealed, somebody asks 'why did you do this to me?' and the villain gives an excruciatingly detailed recount of their masterplan? I honestly never understand this. To me this is just lazy story-telling. If I were indeed a heartless and evil mastermind, I wouldn't give two shits about how anyone felt. At most there would be a sentence long explanation. I wouldn't waste my breath giving anybody an exhaustive blow by blow just to satisfy somebody else's curiosity. The characters were so one-dimensional. Rose was okay, but she was so judgemental at times. Lissa was plain boring and devoid of personality. If my friend told me to abandon my life and everything I knew to run away with only the explanation: "I'm taking care of you. You don't need to know anything else. ", I would politely thank her for her concern whilst silently calling her a delusional idiot. Lissa leaves instantly without packing her bags. Err...what? Dimitri, I just didn't understand. I could get Rose crushing on a hot older teacher/mentor, but I didn't know why he felt the same. He saw her in a black bra and then BAM! he wants her. The chemistry was so unconvincing. It would have made more sense if Rose and Lissa were a lesbian couple. The only character I really liked was Christian. But he had like three conversations in the entire book. The venom and hatred Mia felt was so unjustifiable. The setting of Vampire Academy was a high school. So of course there was a token bitch. Someone who was hellbent on destroying the lives of the MCs. This is where Mia comes in. Her will to bring down Lissa and Rose was admirable. But it was for no reason. Okay there was a reason. But it was so stupid, I couldn't understand it. So a guy sleeps with you and dumps you a few weeks later. So what? Just have a cry, eat some ice cream and move on. That's what girls usually do right? What about Mia? Despite the fact that he DIED (as in no longer breathing died) along with his entire family, this girl develops a crazy obsession with destroying his orphaned little sister. Among a whole host of other things, she whores herself out to not one.. but TWO guys just so they can make up a fake rumour. Not about Lissa herself, but her best friend. This is while dating a boyfriend she obviously adored. Just WTF? Dayy-ummmmm girl. That is some killer dedication. I missed the part where she was mentally unstable because she obviously belongs in an asylum. God forbid you did something actually bad to her. I'd change my name and move somewhere without internet access. Seriously, if she channelled that energy into something productive, she'd probably achieve world peace whilst curing cancer on the side. Also, the word building was clunky and the dialogue was unconvincing. Obviously I am the exception rather than the rule, but I do believe there are MUCH better paranormal novels. I've heard that this is the weakest of the lot and the later books are a lot better. So I will continue, but maybe after reading something I really enjoy.

There are going to be some spoilers. I usually try to avoid them as a matter of principle (and for the reason that I don't really want to discuss plot; people who have read the book know it, people who haven't shouldn't want it to be spoiled). Wade is clearly telling his story in a world where OASIS no longer exists. This must be the case; people don't painfully explain how televisions worked in the 1970s in novels. OASIS gets the full explanation because it is gone. Which must mean that Wade pushed the button. The world also must have faced some sort of change if Wade felt compelled to explain its sorry state. Now, this may not have been Cline's intention. He may not have realized (and this is likely, given his awkward and frequent use of exposition) that someone from the setting would not have to explain the ubiquitous elements of said setting to others who also live in said setting. The reader needs to understand it because the reader doesn't live in the setting. But Wade is not addressing the people of his past (because that would be stupid). There is also the issue as to how there is a general energy crisis and dangerous badlands between the cities, but no problem with consistent energy delivery and intact phone lines (as Cline describes the connection to OASIS more than once). This really only serves to allow for a type of dystopian future without having to figure out how it could function. It is an adolescent fantasy, and while that can work for a book, it does harm this one. My notes (and there are few) from the book are as follows: 1) "Anyone who actually enjoys Ladyhawke is a bona-fide USDA-choice pussy." (p. Now, I agree with this sentiment. But the world Cline develops really shouldn't have the USDA, and choice should not be an on-going option. 2) On p. 103, Cline writes that there "[t]wo late-70s Ford sedans were parked in the driveway" of Halliday's childhood home. By p. 114, one of these cars is up on blocks while the other becomes a 1982 Ford Thunderbird. The early 1908s are not the late 1970s. This should have been caught by an editor. 3) On p. 257, Parzival is looking for a type of giant robot to take. Cline writes that "many of the mechs featured in both the Macross ad Gundam anime series" are part of the selection. Now, it is possible that Halliday was more into Macross than Robotech (its American clone), but unlikely given his age and described home life. Gundam can fit into the 1980s pop culture, but its American popularity was much larger in the 1990s. This all comes full circle on p. 332 where some of the Sixers have "giant mechs from Robotech and Neon Genesis Evangelion. This means that not only was the VF-1J on the board -- and bonus points for it being one of the first things scooped up -- but that the Super Veritech was probably available. So a jet fighter/robot that can move at close to mach three (one of which has twelve reflex missiles) should be able to last in a fight. The Super Veritech should be able to destroy ALL the opponents within 30 miles of missile impact. Both should be able to outfly the opponents. And both are infinitely cooler than Mechagodzilla. Instead, Cline has them wiped out (along with Voltron) without ever putting them into action. Bad form, Cline. 4)  On p. 320, Wade learns his best friend is really a girl. A black girl. Who was hiding being black and female because the world is more inclined to white men. Now, this seems like an odd back-step for a dystopian future. I don't know what kind of message Cline thought he was sending with this (and I'm addressing the learning of the sexuality issue alone). It just struck me as though the author was stuck in an early 1980s racial/gender understanding. Yes, there are absolutely still issues in regards to ineqaulity and discrimination. But progress has been made. It is still being made. Cline sets his world back in this regard. I enjoyed this book. Cline is not an especially disciplined writer and he too often feels the need to 'direct explain' rather than reveal through the course of the story. But it tickled my innate and explicit nerdy side.
I really enjoyed this! Super quick and fun read. I will definitely pick up the next one.

I'm still enjoying all the other characters as well, even though the cast is so big that there is little time to focus on everyone. I'm looking forward to see how the GP will react to everything. I'm also guessing that military dude isn't done causing trouble. Needless to say, I'm dying to read the next book.

Delightfully creepy little horror novel. While I expect the next two books to be fairly similar, it would be totally awesome if they were completely different; have Authority be an action thriller with our hero trying to reach/alert the government about the initial stages of the weirdness of the Southern Reach (only to be betrayed at the end by an already informed government, naturally,) and then have Acceptance be a David Weber-esque space-opera/war fantasy as the normals try to stave off the horrors. I suspect this is intentionally "Lovecraftian," what with the various mentions of starfish, "hand shaped" parasites, odd colors (out of space, maybe,) and one of my favorite literary devices: the unreliable narrator. * And "the Biologist" isn't just your average unreliable narrator - she has at least three different ways (if not four,) that compromise her telling of the story. Without going outside of the first chapter, we know that the Biologist may innately be unreliable (loner/likes her work more than people/etc.,) that she has undergone government sponsored hypnotism, and that she becomes "infected" by Area X. My only complaint with Annihilation is that the world-building seems incomplete, (or at least lacking from what I'd like,) but I can understand and accept that given that we have been given an unreliable narrator. * Also, the sequences when various expedition members go into the "tower" gave me deja vu, reminding me of Lovecraft's short story, "The Outsider." ** Here, I'll use a spoiler tag. The fourth compromise would have been before the events of the novel, when her "husband" returns unexpectedly from the Eleventh mission. If the "invader" is sending simulacra through the barrier, it stands to reason that they could infect folk who aren't within Area X. Was the Biologist "infected" before she went on the Twelfth expedition? Could that have had an effect upon the affects of her subsequent infection? It's rare for a novel to leave so many potential questions unanswered, and yet be as satisfying as this.

I'm never comfortable with books in which a lie is at the center, especially if it's a lie I think is either justified or reasonable (as opposed to someone lying for evil reasons). I get too tense worrying about what will happen when the lie is inevitably exposed. So it took me a little while to relax and enjoy this book about a young woman who, given a once in a lifetime opportunity, disguises herself as a boy to grab hold of it with both hands. It helped that I am a low alto like Jordan and have suffered with the so-called alto parts that still require you to sing notes God intended only for sopranos. I've been singing tenor for a couple of years now, though not in choir, and it's frustrating to see all these beautiful parts written in my range that are intended for men. Jordan is told up front by one of the faculty at her exclusive performing arts high school that she'll probably never be cast in a musical because of her range and vocal quality. When she sees the notice of an spot opening up with the Sharpshooters, the school's most renowned (and all-male) a cappella octet, Jordan dares pretend to be a boy and auditions--and makes the cut. Noteworthy has a lot to say about gender identity, but not, I think, in the way you'd expect. Jordan is cross-dressing, not trans, but as she looks online for advice on how to pass as male, she realizes she's at the intersection of other people's sexuality and ends up questioning what it really means to be female, or male, beyond simple biology. In the course of the novel, Jordan discovers she's bisexual, but she also recognizes that certain feminine identifiers and behaviors have never been part of her personality. Is she capable of passing as male because she's "lacking" in feminine characteristics? Jordan's experiment teaches her more about herself than she'd imagined when she initially thought it was as simple as cutting her hair and binding her breasts. I loved Jordan's interactions with, and friendships with, the other boys in the Sharpshooters. Not all of them are well-realized, and Isaac, Trav, and Nihal stand out in my memory where the others fade into the background. But Jordan finds in this group a kind of friendship she's never had. The moment where Nihal (talking to someone else) refers to her as his best friend really got me. And Isaac...he's complex, and beautiful, and his friendship with Jordan's alter ego Julian, different from Jordan's with Nihal, warmed my heart. I was a little sad that Nihal was gay because I'd sort of wanted him to end up with Jordan, but her eventual relationship with Isaac was so much better I was satisfied. Also, Nihal's relationship with...shoot, I can't remember his name, Connor? Their arch-nemesis. Anyway, their relationship was also wonderful, with Nihal having to defend someone he cared about who was a jackass, making excuses for him right up until he couldn't anymore. It felt so real. I felt the revelation of Jordan's identity was too fast in fact, the announcement that the Sharpshooters won the competition was dashed off too quickly  and in some ways too easy. Her financial situation almost felt more important than the question of whether she'd be allowed to stay with the Sharpshooters. But in another sense, the resolution of the truth fit with everything the Sharpshooters had revealed themselves to be over the course of the book. Nihal's reaction was the most realistic, I think, because he found out the truth in such an unexpected way, and he was more upset that he'd thought he had a friend who understood what it meant to be gay than that Jordan was female. But the others...once they got over their initial shock, they were all "it's cool" way more quickly than I'd thought they should be. Maybe Isaac's acceptance made a difference, as they were used to following his lead. But it still felt a little too tidy. I find I'm still thinking about the story weeks after reading the book, so I'm giving it all five stars. Very satisfying on so many levels.

4 out of 5 Hysteria, simply, blew me away. Just when I thought it was heading in one direction, Miranda would make a u-turn and head in a completely different direction. Sometimes this was confusing as hell, but on the whole, it just added to the suspense and thrill of the ride, emulating Mallory's thought process. There were some things that I saw coming, but that wasn't a disappointment. Actually it was a nice change of pace, to know what was going on for a change, in addition to upping the tension. You know what's about to happen, and are willing the characters to figure it out too before it's too late. There are two storylines running almost simultaneously in Hysteria, which compliment as opposed to distract from each other, and the ending does a great job of tying all those loose ends together. I know the ending will please some readers but may disappoint others. I was in the former category. There are several unnerving scenes of bloody handprints which definitely upped the tension throughout, and those combined with a series of flashbacks to the events before Mallory came to boarding school give us just enough to keep questioning what the heck is goings on. The characters were engaging and believable, and their reactions to specific events were very realistic. Mallory herself is a contradiction in terms. Brave but shattered, she has been through something traumatic, and as intended, she sometimes comes across as slightly unhinged. Like Mallory, we are kept guessing as to what is real, and Miranda does a fantastic job of keeping us guessing. There is romance there, it was sweet and just what you'd expect from the characters, but it was more in the background than upfront, which I think in this case was the way to go, leaving the main focus to be Mallory's struggle with right and wrong, real and not real. I'm not sure what else I can say without giving any of the story away, but if you're looking for a creepy, Soul Survivors type of psychological thriller, then this is the book for you. Review also found at Musings of a Serial Bookworm

Here's the thing about this series: I read these books, and they're just ok for the vast majority of the novel, and then I finish this and despite not falling in love with it I just keeping coming back for more. Victoria Aveyard is an exquisite writer. She definitely came into her own more in book two of this series and, in my humble opinion, has created a much more original novel. But then this turned out to be the classic 'characters go on a long and at times boring journey' novel. Or middle book syndrome, whichever you prefer. I felt like not a lot happened in Glass Sword and at times I found myself almost giving up and putting the book down because I wanted some action and I wasn't getting any. Like, wasn't Mare supposed to be the face of a rebellion? Wasn't she meant to be leading an army against the Silver overlords? Instead I found myself reading about the search for newbloods and a ragged band of rebels travelling around the country by jet (miraculously, without getting caught out, but my theory is that Maven knew the whole time and he was just playing games with them) and fighting with the local Silver guards. Don't get me wrong, I didn't dislike this novel. Victoria Aveyard crafts big, fast-paced fight scenes that I loved reading. The whole prison escape was especially good, although I was disappointed that she blacked out at the climax of the battle and we didn't get to see the storm that killed Elera but oh well. I liked the new characters we were introduced to, and seeing the ones we already knew changing after all of the traumatic experiences from Red Queen. I liked seeing more of Norta, and meeting people from a lot of different backgrounds and how different they were. That being said, I haven't found anything that makes this series stand out from the crowd. And yet, I keep coming back for more. I couldn't tell you why, but I just can't get enough, and I'll most likely continue on with this series. Side note: why are so many people 'team Maven'??? He literally tried blackmailing her into being with him, he tried to kill her more than once, there have been several instances where he's proved to be a truly terrible person, and you people want Mare to be in a relationship with him? You guys are crazy. I'm also not the biggest fan of Mare and Cal, but at least Cal tries to be the best person he can given his circumstances. But that's enough about love interests. I'm going to go ahead and be team Mare, and hope that maybe in the next book there won't be even a hint of any romance being rekindled, but that might just be wishful thinking.

Besides all that, Alice, the heroine, is everything but a heroine in my book. She is not smart, she is not good at anything really, she has no goals (come on, she didn't even want to learn how to drive), she is incredibly selfish. Honestly, she is just a slacker who is content to let people take care of everything for her. When Jack proposes they move out of the big house, she is afraid to do it because then, who will fix her messes? She is afraid Jack won't be able to support them. How about getting a job, sweetie? Oh, right, she can't get a job because she is useless. And she prefers to live together with a bunch of other vampires who don't understand what the word 'privacy' means. I'm so glad this torture is finally over so I can move on to better reading.

It actually pains me to have to give this book three stars. ACTUAL. PAIN. The first and second half of this book read like two entirely different novels, which are WORLDS APART in terms of quality. Like, the first 50% is a solid 4.5-star read and the last 50% is more like a 1.5. And I'm going to go ahead and explain in EXCRUCIATING DETAIL how Wintersong started out as one of my new fav books and then CRASHED AND BURNED IN THE MOST MISERABLE WAY POSSIBLE. The Good: The first half of the story is about the MC, Liesl, trying to rescue her sister Kathe from the Underground (goblin world) when the Goblin King kidnaps her. It turns into a battle of wills between her and the Goblin King. This part of the story is beautifully written - and not just in the sense that the language was pretty. The narrative absolutely transported me; the magical/fantastical elements were both dreamy and eerie at once, and there is a masterful command of tone and sensory details. If you're a fan of dark fairy tales, this will make you swoon. Even when the plot went off the rails, even when the story started to piss me off, it's just so damn readable I couldn't put it down. I WAS ANGRY BUT I STILL ENJOYED READING THIS THING SOMEHOW. Okay... that's some talent. Liesl is a complex & flawed protagonist. Her flaws are realistic, believable, and have actual consequences - they're not just quirks. She's jealous, self-absorbed, overly concerned with her looks, makes bad choices. Real stuff, you know? But she's also brave, tenacious, and devoted to her siblings - I wouldn't consider her an antihero or an "unlikable character" at all, but her virtues are evenly matched with vices. Also, in the end, she chooses to live and asserts that she does not need romantic love to be whole , which helped redeem some of the nonsense we had to wade through to get there. Last, while I'm about to rip apart this awful excuse for a romance, I will say that there is a consistent emphasis on consent and I'm here for that. Like. The Goblin King is an enigmatic, immortal, inhuman creature of winter and darkness, but he won't ravish you unless he gets an enthusiastic "yes" first. And if you're drunk? Nope. No sexy times for you, drunk wife. Instead, he's putting you to bed with a kiss on your forehead. The Bad: Note that this review contains SPOILERS from here on. I won't spoil the climax/ending but I'll be talking about plot events up to halfway through the book, as well as specific interactions that happen between Liesl & the Goblin King beyond that point. Ok? 1: THE PLOT THINS Liesl marries the Goblin King at about the 50% mark. At this point, the plot takes a backseat to what feels like filler drama: Liesl trying to have a real relationship with her husband and him being reticent and confusing. For like a hundred pages. Even as hints of mystery and non-romantic conflict return, it's watered down by Liesl's emotional struggle with the Goblin King and lots of sex scenes. They're not erotic sex scenes, though. No sexiness to be found here. As I wrote in a status update: it's all flowery language and metaphor. And SO MUCH DRAMA. According to Wintersong, sex changes your entire life and changes who you are as a person. (Liesl is not Liesl anymore. After sex, she's Elisabeth. Yes, really. That's a real line.) Things get very repetitive. Liesl tries to get close to the Goblin King, maybe succeeds a little bit, and then he withdraws again. LOTS AND LOTS of prose about MUSIC and EMOTIONS. At one point she goes to buy a dress and learns about the Goblin King's dozens of previous wives. That was a highlight of this section. 2: CHARACTER DEVELOPMENT WHO?? The Goblin King is... boring. And static. In the first half, he's pretty cool - magical, mysterious, dangerous, otherworldly, powerful. In the second half, he's sullen and secretive for reasons that don't really make sense. It felt like a forced attempt by the author to generate conflict when she wasn't sure what direction to take the plot next. Sometimes, to show his more human side, Liesl makes reference to two versions of her husband: the Goblin King and "her austere young man" who is vulnerable and has "soft eyes." This is a start at giving the Goblin King more depth, but without further exploration/revelation of character - as the author tries vainly to keep him mysterious for as long as possible - it just feels shallow. In the last... I don't know, 50 pages, his character starts to get revealed more, but by this time it's way too late. In a 500-page book you just can't wait until page 450 to develop the second most important character in the dang story. 3: BAD ROMANCE. AS BAD AS IT GETS WITHOUT ACTUAL ABUSE. The romance sucked, okay. And that's mostly because of the power differential between Liesl and the Goblin King, which gets chipped away at but never truly resolved (even when the narrative tries to suggest otherwise). The first thing you need to understand is that this novel equates female empowerment with sex. Fully and unambiguously. If I recall correctly, the first and maybe only time Liesl calls herself "powerful" is when the Goblin King asks her to take the lead during sex (once). And that COULD be fine - some women ARE empowered by sex, and there's nothing wrong with that - but the way it's executed here does not feel empowering at all. I'll elaborate (of course I will). One of the things Liesl wants most is to be "desired," and after she gets married, she's excited & hopeful because she thinks that's going to happen. And then the Goblin King refuses to have sex with her after their wedding for reasons that are unclear to me even now. From what I understand, he was waiting for Liesl to "give herself entire," and since music is Liesl's soul, he wants her music and not her body. Or something? They talk in infuriatingly vague terms most of the time. But basically, for a solid 80 pages, the main conflict is Liesl wanting to get laid and the Goblin King refusing because he just wants her to make music for him, like a trained monkey, and because he wants access to every single part of her mental/emotional being before he'll give her anything in return. So when they finally have sex, it's after Liesl basically spent the better part of a hundred pages begging for it, being rejected, and feeling lonely and unwanted. There's nothing empowering about this. There's nothing empowering about a woman sacrificing her life (literally) and her family and her future in order to marry a guy, and then also having to shoulder the emotional burden of making the relationship work, and having to push and persuade him to give her any kind of physical/emotional attention. It's fine if two people who are together have different sex drives, and so one might not always get to have sex when they want to have sex, but that's not what was going on here. He was withholding sex because she hadn't sufficiently bared her soul to him, in his opinion (meanwhile, he got to be as secretive and closed-off as he wanted). Contrary to what the narrative TELLS us, what it SHOWS is that Liesl has no power here. Even after she becomes the Goblin Queen. Also, there's a lot of Christ in this book. As a choice for the characters, and balanced by a good story that's not ABOUT religion, I don't really mind - in the first half of the book, I noticed but wasn't bothered. In the second half? It started to get uncomfortable, maybe because there was nothing interesting to distract me, and also because sex & sexual desire kept getting equated with "sinning." In fact, for an interspecies romance, this story really promotes some old-fashioned, sexist*** and harmful ideas about sex & love. It's easy to be distracted by the fantasy setting & all, but... honestly the values & ideas at the heart of this "love story" would not be out of place at Sunday school. TL;DR: This book is split into four parts. Read parts 1 and 2 for an engaging, suspenseful, dark fantasy read about a strong heroine who will do anything for her sister, including go head-to-head with immortal magical being. On page 244, stop. Rip out the rest of the pages and pretend the story ended there. ***Not everyone will agree with me on this, especially because the author's a woman. And I'm not arguing that it's like this INTENTIONALLY - I don't think it is. But I do consider many of the underlying themes & portrayal of romance to be sexist. The expectation that Liesl will shoulder most of the emotional labor in their relationship; the romanticization of the Goblin King's paternalistic treatment of her; the fact that the Goblin King sets all the rules in their relationship & never apologizes for anything he does, and that's never questioned by the narrative. Etc. It's old-fashioned in terms of the emotional & power dynamic between husband and wife. Liesl's narrative when it comes to sex and marriage is all about sacrifice. The narrative TELLS us he's "giving himself" in return, but it never shows it - at least, not until the very, very, very end of the book, at which point it's too little, too late. There's a disturbing scene that I just remembered. They're playing a game similar to truth or dare, where they ask each other questions and if you can't answer honestly you have to complete a task instead. Liesl takes a chance and tries to learn important things about the Goblin King - his name, his past, how he came to be - ANYTHING. He refuses to answer, and gets pissed off at her for prying. Liesl gives up. It's his turn to ask questions, so he deliberately makes her cry by broaching emotional topics, and then, when he's not happy with her answers, he forces her to eat a bowl of strawberries. Since she's just lost her sense of taste (because she's slowly dying in the Underground) this is a miserable experience for her. This was? So damn sick? He demands her "self, entire" but if she tries to get any details out of him, he punishes her. This is what their entire relationship is like, and this is what I mean when I refer to a power differential - the Goblin King has power over Liesl in terms of magic & the Underground being his territory, but also, he dominates their emotional/physical relationship.

Feed is up there among my all time favorite zombie literature, right below Rot & Ruin. Mr. Jonathan Maberry is one of my all time favorite writers, and now, Mira Grant is added to the list. This is the zombie book for my generation - the tech nerds. I loved the internet community of the book. I loved how the world was built. I espeically loved how the world was mostly there because when "zombies" were yelled, people listened. I loved George as a narrator. I loved her brother Shaun, and I loved Buffy. (Rick, I'm a little unsure about. He's added to the fold a little too quickly for my tastes.) But most of all, I love that this is a political thriller set in a zombie novel. There are some predictable twists in the book. Oh dead, the Governor Tate is the bad guy. Never saw that coming. There are some twist that made my jaw hit the floor, and kept me weepy for the last 100 or so pages. (You'll know which one when you read the book.) I'll also say that some may find the pacing to be slow. Scenes can last quite a while, and while I never felt they were trudging, I can see how someone might. I also suspect that an older generation might not enjoy the book as much as I did. For example, as much as I loved this book, I don't see myself recommending it to my mom. I think she might get a little lost in the tech jargon and theories. However, I found Grant's overall style to make me gloss over any shortcomings I might have found in the book. I often found myself not caring that I knew what was going to happen, but so caught up in the story that I just needed to keep reading. And it was her style, a slightly comic, edge voice, that kept me flipping page after page, long after I should have gone to bed. Definitely in my top picks of books I've read this year, and books I've read ever.

I actually bought this initially, but the Netgalley page said something about it being an updated version, so I went for it. I originally picked it up for the promise of a heroic little hedgehog, and I was very happy with that aspect -- the hedgehog is brave, helpful, clever, and funny. It can't speak, so it communicates with the protagonist via miming and yes/no answers. It sounded so cute. I want one! The story itself, aside from the hedgehogs, is a nice reimagining of a Bluebeard fairytale -- but darker, really, because instead of death, the antagonist steals things of worth from the women he marries -- their voices, their eyes, their ability to die -- and leaves them alive. I found the tone somewhat at odds with the perceived historical/mythological time it was set in; the protagonist was too modern in thought and sensibility in some ways, it seemed. But overall, I found it very enjoyable, and I loved the way it treated the other characters. The other wives, for example, are each different, some very strange, and each of them copes with what has happened to them in a different way. As people do. And, just to reiterate: hedgehog! I enjoyed Sense and Sensibility, but not as much as Emma or Pride and Prejudice. There is just something lacking from S&S that the latter two novels have - a certain comedy, I think. What I love the most in P&P is the dialogue - it's witty and hilarious at times, and I also enjoy stories where the characters bicker at first and then fall in love. What I like about Emma is the comedy- how Emma bungles everything up - but I also like the suspense at the ending when Emma finally realizes she loves Knightly, and there is a worry that she won't get him . S&S lacks these qualities that make the other two great. Marianne and Elinor are much too serious and proper - they never have lively discussions and they never make mistakes. They just sit there waiting for stuff to happen to them; they never precipitate the action. Emma is headstrong and a little silly, which is amusing, and Elizabeth is a stubborn and intelligent, which is admiring. Marianne is flighty and whiny, and Elinor is, well, boring. Neither of them are overly interesting characters. The men too, aren't very interesting. Edward is kind of contradictory - he's shy and reserved, but then it appears he once passionately loved Lucy? Granted, shy guys like him can be persuaded by people to do stuff they don't want to do out of a desire not to have confrontation, but he declares that he once passionately loved her. I just can't see him being passionate about anything to that extent. In fact, I really liked him before the whole secret romance thing because his shyness and introversion reminded me of one of my friends. Then the whole Lucy Steele plot ruined him for me on top of not seeming all that believable. Willougby was such a rouge that he was pegged to be a jerk from the get-go. I mean, it was hard to see it all working out perfectly for Marianne, so I never formed any real attachment to his character. He seemed too obvious a villain. The only one I really liked was Brandon, because I like the strong silent type. Still, there wasn't a whole lot you could say about him. Quiet guy, tragic past. That's about it. Austen's dudes in her other novels were fleshed out a lot more. Mrs. Jennings and Mr. Dashwood in this novel are also given too much screen time for being minor characters. John's rambles about this and that went on too long. We get the joke - he's misinterpreted something or he's a buffoon - but then he just goes on and on and I would kind of zone out. I also thought the whole trick about it being Robert instead of Edward who married Lucy didn't add to the suspense at all - it seemed rather ridiculous that something would happen to free him up for Elinor, so when it happened I was like: "what?". There was no indication AT ALL that Lucy had even talked to Robert, so when she up and married him instead of Edward I thought it was bizarre. I don't know, I enjoyed S&S, but it wasn't as well put-together or character-driven as the aforementioned novels. It also distracted me every time I heard the name "Dashwood" because I immediately thought of Fallout 3 and THIS GUY: http://images4.wikia.nocookie.net/fal... (This was my first audiobook, and I really enjoyed the experience - mainly because it made my drive home through Toronto a lot less painful. Maybe I'll do Persuasion or Mansfield Park next)
Love these books and the audios are great!! I recommend reading the story first though. Then while running and walking, it was really easy to listen to.

About : Roshar is a land ruled by Highstorms and Shardblade warfare. But as a cycle of Desolation approaches to destroy humanity, four people will play key roles in the outcome: Szeth-son-son-Vallano, Truthless of Shinovar, assassinates King Gavilar and begins a cycle of vengeance--the "Vengeance Pact"--between two races. He weeps as he is forced to kill for his masters. Kaladin Stormblessed, an apprentice surgeon, is forced to become a soldier in the armies fighting for vengeance. After suffering the betrayal of a "light-eyed" noble, this dark-eyed soldier fights for his life and that of his dark-eyed crew. Brightlord Dalinar Kholin commands an army like the one that employs Kaladin. But as he is drawn to an ancient text of law, The Way of Kings, he finds himself questioning the purpose of this war. Young Shallan Davar, Brightness of a small, struggling estate, risks everything to plan a daring theft. The first step of her plan is to train as a scholar with the heretic Jasnah Kholin, Brightlord Dalinar Kholin's niece; but as she gains Jasnah's trust, she realizes that the woman studies much more than obscure academia: she studies the secrets of the fabled order of the Knights Radiant, their shards and the Desolations they fought so long ago. Adult High Fantasy Published August 31st 2010 by Tor Books. My Thoughts Wow. 1,000 pages of wow. Just let me fangirl for a moment, here. Don't let the size of this tome fool you: The Way of Kings is a compulsively readable, highly character-driven high fantasy. The characters always let you know what they want; but you never know what twists lay in store for them. And there are so many twists! They start coming early on. It's almost funny how I continue to guess and theorize because I'm always totally wrong. Everything is sailing along as the characters expect, and then BAM! You weren't getting comfortable were you, Christy? Because this guy's being sold into slavery and this gal's not the naive young bookworm you thought. You think you know what's going on? Trust me, you don't. I can't talk overmuch about the plot without spoilers, but: I dare you to get bored during a Kaladin scene. Seriously. I bet you can't do it. Early on in the novel, he's drafted into a hellish portion of the army known as "bridge duty" (wherein generals force crews of unarmed men to rush first into battle, set bridges across chasms and draw enemy fire away from the "real" soldiers) and his goal becomes one thing and one thing only: keep his bridge crew alive. He constantly schemes up crazy ideas to meet that goal, and I promise, it's worth your time to read The Way of Kings just for this one innovative soldier's arc. But Dalinar Kholin's arc is a close second favorite. Uncle to the king and brother of the slain King Gavilar, Dalinar dominates the battlefield. Known as the Blackthorn, he fiercely wields a weapon called a "Shardblade," a giant sword with unimaginably destructive power. As the book's description says, wars are fought for and won by these ancient, mysterious weapons that appear from mist and kill souls as easily as they kill bodies. Dalinar is a cultural hero among his war-obsessed countrymen--but he has lately been troubled by Highstorm visions that may or may not be the onset of madness. As everyone including his sons and the king begin to question him, Dalinar has to navigate the visions, public opinion and private family business. A complex man with a complex path. I'm totally obsessed with Dalinar. I think Shallan's arc qualifies as the most complex among the four main narrators. She possesses the potential and desire to become a great scholar, but family secrets close that option to her. While innovation and leadership concerns characterize the narratives of Kaladin and Dalinar, Shallan's narrative blossoms more slowly, and it feels almost self-contained until we find out more about Jasnah's research. Nevertheless, I love Shallan's scenes. Her intelligence and ambition make her arc tense and painful, at times, but always twisty and keenly satisfying. Szeth the assassin is the most mysterious of the four narrators, but I suspect that he holds the secret to the coming Desolations. We shall see. The worldbuilding itself is like a fabulous character. It's so big! And it feels that way, paradoxically, by detailing the small stuff. "Kaladin stared out over those grasses blowing in the mild breeze. Whenever the wind picked up, the more sensitive of the grass stalks shrank down into their burrows, leaving the landscape patchy, like the coat of a sickly horse." Although we expect large amounts of setup and worldbuilding in a novel like this, Sanderson incorporates it all smoothly into the secretive and engrossing characters arcs. The swords, the storms, the mysterious "stormlight" that connects everything together...and don't even get me started on the countries, social prejudices and religions! One society lives on an endless, shallow lake, and citizens just...stay wet. All the time. And Alethi men and women must eat gender-specified foods! It's craziness. The smooth writing let me slip easily into the world of Roshar, never drawing attention to itself. I got lost in this engrossing giant of a novel. When plot twists pay off--when the action starts--it's explosive. This is totally cliche, but the battle scenes really are heart-rending and pulse-pounding. Very "visually" effective (better than Mistborn's action scenes, I would say). The tactics and strategy are extremely well drawn. I switched back and forth between the audiobook and the hardcover copy, so I can confirm that the story reads easily in both. Hearing all the unique names pronounced with such assurance made the audio version a favorite with me; but the easy writing makes the hard copy equally as engrossing--and the illustrations! They're gorgeous! Overall : Combines the intrigue of Elantris with the action and themes of Mistborn. X1000. It's definitely my favorite thing by Sanderson, as yet. As I was reading, I kept wishing the book could last forever. Thankfully, 9,000 is a conservative estimate of pages remaining in the series, right? Recommended To : It sometimes feels like I was the last person to this Stormlight Archives partaaay, but I know that's not true! The books are so gigantic, I was intimidated away until I saw the list of contents in Arcanum Unbounded. Then I knew I needed to get on these books already. But seriously, if you like character-driven fantasy, I highly recommend trying The Way of Kings. You might be surprised how the pages fly by, once you start to get to know the characters.

a few things made it really difficult for me to enjoy this book. first, i read too many mysteries and watch too many crime dramas to appreciate the story from the other side (i was so rooting for carl to figure it out ). second, i'm too risk-averse to sympathize with even hank's first bad decision. everything that followed wasn't much of a surprise to me, and i guess i've already realized and processed the fact that all humans are capable of evil, even the uber-normal, small-town accountant. finally, the mitchells' repeated insistence that they "didn't have a choice" put me off. even the characters on sons of anarchy know that there is always a choice and accept responsibility for the consequences of those choices. there were some very well-written and moving moments, both between characters and within hank's narration, that made me feel for the characters instead of curse their poor decisions. i wish there had been more of that humanity rather than a man acting on autopilot out of a combination of greed, fear, and self-preservation. feminist nitpick: when it's revealed that sarah graduated as a petroleum engineer, but now she works at the library because those jobs don't really exist in ohio, i heard a record scratch in my head. accountants can work anywhere! why not move somewhere else so she could work as an engineer and earn a higher salary than a part-timer at the public library does? i would also guess that the accountant at raikley's feed is not the most coveted accounting job in the midwest.

The Georgina Kincaid series is coasting along at its normal, subpar speed in Succubus Dreams. The third person who filled me with fear was this man standing before me. His name was Niphon, and he was an imp, just like my friend Hugh. And, like all imps, Niphon really only had two jobs. One was to run administrative errands for demons. The other, his primary one, was to make contracts with mortals, brokering and buying souls for Hell. And he was the imp who had bought mine. Okay, hold the phone. LOL, what? Lilith I can see, maybe. Roman, what the hell, Georgina was super in lust with him and now all of a sudden he's the scariest guy in the world? We haven't even heard a peep about him since the first book. If he's Georgina's definition of scary... I have no words. Finally, Niphon. Why is she scared of him, exactly? Sure, he bought her soul, but Hell owns it, not him. What's he going to do, piss her off and annoy her to death? (Actually, yes, but let's touch on that later). Seth is... the same. Boring, lame, etc, etc. He keeps missing dates and neglecting Georgina for his first love (writing), which in turn makes her go out and screw some poor schmuck senseless. Hmmm, isn't that what happened to her when she was Letha and her husband constantly ignored her for his work? IS ANYONE ELSE SENSING A PATTERN HERE? Okay, I don't care if Seth is her human husband reincarnated, he's still a boring washrag and I'm guessing her husband was too. She's better off without the useless twit. Anyway, Seth continues to be his boring ass self, until he takes a bullet for Georgina... who is immortal... and can't be killed by guns... dumbass. Suddenly he wants to see how far he can push his physical relationship with Georgina. I mean, really, how much sex does a succubus need before she can steal your energy, amirite? *smacks Seth* YOU'RE BAD AND SHOULD FEED BAD. Hugh actually bitches him out about how miserable he makes Georgina and can the imp get an amen up in here? Hey, did you know Carter has angel friends? He totally does! They appear in this book and everything! There's three of them; Joel, Yasmine, and Whitney, plus some psychic named Vincent. Georgina lets Vincent crash at her place while the angels do some investigation that they won't let Georgina in on. I suppose we'll talk about the title of the book and its relevance. Georgina goes out, bangs some dude, comes home, has some weird dream involving her being human and having a daughter and a husband (although we never see his face) and then wakes up drained of energy. Weird, right? She asks Eric who directs her to a dude named Dante. Dante is... well, a hustler, a con man, a smooth talker... basically, interesting. Par for the course, he wants Georgina in bed, which she refuses over and over, but tries to get his help with her dreams. Long story short, Nyx is stealing Georgina's energy while she sleeps, Nyx is who the angels are looking for, oh, and Nyx was released by Niphon, who promised that she could keep Georgina and Tawny as permanent energy tanks or something. Oh, that sneaky Niphon, why would he do that? Well, if the foreshadowing in the form of a two by four didn't hit you earlier; something is Georgina's contract is flawed and if it breaks, she can be human again. *twirls finger* Yay. Other than that, I enjoyed the mystery this time around; it was slightly more entertaining than the nephilim from SB and WAY more interesting than the Ambrosia from SOT. So, Georgina actually has a female friend; Maddie, Doug's sister. (Doug is practically non-existent in this book, by the by.) And because Georgina can't have real female friends, this needs to be effed up in the most idiotic way possible; Georgina pushing Seth onto Maddie so hard that he actually dumps her soul sucking ass for her best friend. Georgina obviously doesn't share my sense of humor because she sobs and begs like a teenage girl whose first boyfriend broke up with her after a week. So it's okay to cheat on your girlfriend, but in doing so, that means you have to dump your girlfriend to start dating the other girl you slept with because you don't have flings? Once again, Seth, your logic sucks and you're a dumbass. Seth and Maddie have no problem making their relationship public either. Well, there was obviously no cause for concern there because NOBODY CARES WHO BORING ASS SETH IS SCREWING. Next up is Succubus Heat, where hopefully Georgina is more entertaining and it's not all "WOE, WHEREFORE ART THOU, SETH? WOE IS ME!" all the time. I'll leave you with my usual parting gift of Carter, who actually showered at least twice this book! When I opened the cupboard to look for my granola bars, I found the box empty. "Hey," I said, carrying it out to the living room. "Did somebody eat these? I had two left this morning." Carter spoke up for the first time. "I was hungry." I stared at him, incredulous. "You ate both of them?" "I was hungry," he repeated, not looking contrite in the least. "Does it ever stop with you?" I exclaimed. "First the Christmas tree, now this? You didn't even throw the box away!" "I was hoping you'd forgotten about the Christmas tree. That was an accident, and you know it." Carter burned down her Christmas tree one year with his cigarettes. Bwhahahaha.

"Love is never safe." First off, let me just say this book is not what I expected. And yes, this is a good thing because I'm not really a fan of the "sexy billionaire" trope (sorry, not sorry but arrogant SOBs don't appeal to me). But luckily this book was so much more than just another billionaire romance and I'm really glad I decided to give this book a chance. Trade Me follows the story of Tina Chen and Blake Reynolds. Tina is a college student trying to balance school work, a job and family responsibilities. She hopes to earn a degree and become financially stable so her parents will no longer have to worry about making ends meet. Blake Reynolds is the son of billionaire who is about to inherit his father's company. These two couldn't be more opposites, but they're about to step into each other shoes and find out how the other half lives. When it comes to the New Adult genre, many books tend to focus on the romance, while everything else falls to the side. Trade Me is a bit of a refreshing read because the romance comes second to the other issues dealt with in this book. First, family plays an important role in this book as Tina comes from a tight-knit Chinese family, with a mother who is very involved in the community. I appreciated the way Milan handled the cultural aspects of this book and I really related to Tina's family values as they are similar to my own. Blake has a close relationship with his father and while the way they interact with each other may be a little strange, they definitely do care for one another. Another thing I liked about this book was that WE ACTUALLY FOCUSED ON SCHOOL AND CAREER GOALS! Like that rarely happens in NA books and I could totally relate to this. Can I get more of this please? As for our characters, I loved Tina from the first page! Tina doesn't play. She's hard-working, goal-oriented and focused. But her one fault is that she isn't willing to take risks and while she may have feelings for Blake, she refuses to admit them and instead puts her family's needs before her own. I enjoyed seeing her slowly let her walls down and take a risk with Blake. Blake is not what I was expecting at all. He's actually really sweet and not as much of an asshole as I had written him off to be. Although Blake has it all, he too has his own issues and has a hard time admitting he has a problem, even to himself. My one main issue when it came to Blake was that I wanted more of him. I wished his problem was explored more because  men can have eating disorders as well and I would've liked it if the Milan just didn't just constantly tell us that Blake had a problem, but instead showed us through him struggling . As for the romance, it's a slow-burning one, but it's worth the wait. I lived for the banter between these two and THE ENDING WAS SO DAMN CUTE, OMG! Overall, Trade Me was a refreshing and relatable NA book that I could actually relate to. Milan handled cultural aspects really well and you could tell she took her time to research Chinese culture. Y'all all the books in this series are diverse so if you're looking for diversity in NA, THIS IS IT! I can't wait to meet the rest the characters in the Cyclone series and hopefully I'll enjoy the other books as much as enjoyed the first book!

Um... I completely forgot when I was scheduled to post for the blog tour, and then I checked and saw it was the 18th and realized it had long since passed. So hopefully no one will be heartbroken that this review is coming almost a week late, because it was worth the wait! I loved this book! I'm not usually a big fan of contemporary, especially when it's about something as scary and real as cancer. But this book was wonderful. It felt so real. It wasn't cheesy or overwhelming or anything else it easily could've turned into. It was just a simple. balance, realistic story about an amazingly strong girl. I can't even begin to imagine how impossibly difficult Mia's life was. I've had to deal with lots of hardships, but never anything as scary as cancer. It destroyed her life. But what destroyed it even more than the leukemia was the fact that she chose to keep it hidden from everyone. I loved both Ryan and Gyver so much in different ways. Ryan starts out as the perfect trophy boyfriend, but once her learns about her cancer, his true colors show and he becomes so hopelessly devoted to Mia. And Gyver. He had been in the friend-zone for so long, it was hard to tell where exactly he fit in Mia's life. But I'm happy to say that I'm satisfied with how both boys ended up. I kind of wish Mia's superstitions had played a larger role in the plot. They were definitely there near the end, but not as much in the beginning. There would be brief mentions of 4 leaf clovers or a magic 8 ball, but I think I would've appreciated them later on if they'd played a larger part earlier. I was very satisfied with Send Me a Sign. Tiffany Schmidt is an extremely talented author who wrote a beautifully touching first novel. I can't wait to see what she comes up with next! This one is definitely not a heart warming read that make your heart flutter. Don't expect flower or roses or some other similar shit. This one was a gritty, angsty, raw, violent and intense read that make my heart pounding madly and did a whole load of cursing. Mae aka Salome was a sex slave imprisoned in a religious cult since she was a child. She grown up being sexually abused and fearing the life outside of the commune, until one day something happened and triggered her to make a life changing decision. She decided to flee. Styx aka River was the Hades Hangmen MC's President and was known as the infamous Hangmen Mute because he never speaks except to his VP, Ky. Styx had a stutter that make him unable to speak in front of others, but only to his closest confident. Mae and Styx met once fifteen years ago, across the commune fence and formed an unbreakable bond and connection. Years later, they met again under a different circumstances. Mae was injured and frighten of her life out of commune and Styx can't believe he found his wolf eyes girl again. "Well, I hope that I don't fall in love with you, 'cause falling in love just makes me blue." Due to his responsibility as the club President and the danger they were in, Styx decided to put Mae under one of his men care, Rider. At this time, Styx was with his usual club girl, Lois. I don't understand why did some people said Styx cheated, which in fact he was not with Mae at this point. So according to my evaluation, there is no cheating. You don't even get the details of the sex, so don't worry about it. "You have light within you, Styx, and I feel it shining through like the rays of the midday sun. It is beautiful." For the first time, Mae was experiencing freedom and life. She realized that people outside are not the devil as she perceived them to be and the true evil are the elders in the cult. While, Styx was avoiding her, she strike up a close friendship with Rider, the man who was assigned to take care of her. But she never once stop missing Styx and his kindness towards her. "You say it aint youwho is good and who will keep me safe, but you already have." The possibility of a love triangle make me damn uncomfortable. I'm the kind of reader who hates reading that stuff. There were some angst going on and what make it bearable for me is that Mae was very decisive on who she love from the very beginning. In her heart, there is only Styx, the boy she met all those years ago. Styx was being aggressive when he knew of Rider's intention but I like the fact that he fight for what belongs to him. He is the gang President after all and violence in inevitable. Nonetheless, I was hoping Mae handled the situation much better if she was not so naive about human nature. Some of her noble action and being so close to Rider was definitely not cool. I really wish she cut ties with that man and he in turned die during the confrontation. I'm not enjoying the hint of love triangle here. Urg! But after I finish the book, I came to understand we need those unpleasant stuff to happen to make the climax work and make me felt so emotionally invested, to make me turn page after page anxiously. Considering there were so much fornication going on in the club, I was surprised by the lack of sex scene between Styx and Mae. There were some intense sex, but there isn't a really long drawn one that make my toe curl. Anyway, there were so much shit going on that it don't bother me that much. There were some pretty nasty violence and the climax took place when Mae was hunted down by the elders. Will Styx be able to save his old lady? We also have some big revelation and surprises along the way. I really hope that asshole die. This is a standalone with a HEA, but the epilogue hinted at something more at work next. Seriously, Flame, the psychopathic one need his own book, but I was hoping it won't be another chick from the religious cult. Anyway, we will see how it goes. Due to his responsibility as the club President and the danger they were in, Styx decided to put Mae under one of his men care, Rider. At this time, Styx was with his usual club girl, Lois. For the first time, Mae was experiencing freedom and life. She realized that people outside are not the devil as she perceived them to be and the true evil are the elders in the cult. In her heart, there is only Styx, the boy she met all those years ago. Styx was being aggressive when he knew of Rider's intention but I like the fact that he fight for what belongs to him. Sunbolt is the story of Hitomi, an orphaned girl striving to survive in the city of Karolene, where she is an outsider. Hitomi does not fit in with everyone else in her area and is always marked as a foreigner. On top of that, Hitomi is two secrets; one, that she has the Promise, the ability to perform magic and two, that she is working with the Shadow League, an underground rebellion. All of this adds up to a very complicated life with a lot of misfortune and misadventures. While Hitomi is on a mission to save a noble family from the evil Archmage Blackflame, she is captured and taken prisoner.. Hitomi must try to escape, save the the family, and find out the truth about the deaths of her parents along the way. I love Sunbolt. It's a great fantasy story with a rich world. Hitomi is a fantastic character. She is smart and wily, but she has her flaws. She doesn't always make the best decisions but all of her decisions are believable. She is not overpowered or a Mary Sue in any way. The best aspect of Hitomi, and this book in general, is that she is a person of color. Hitomi is described as having Asian heritage and this is unique and refreshing. There aren't many PoC main characters in books and it's nice to see more diversity. I enjoy diversity in literature whenever I can get it and this was not a disappointment. As for the world building, I love what Khanani did with this story. The city of Karolene, the places she visits after being captured, and the world in general seems fresh. There is a magic system in place that stands on its own and seems different from the magic systems of every other book. The world seems to have a great deal of back story going for it. My only complaint with the book is that it's so short! The world being built in Sunbolt is nuanced and layered. I think the book could be four times as long and feel perfectly fleshed out. That said, I think Sunbolt is well written, with a good pace and a lot of action. There is no unfortunate infodumps along the way and you learn about the world as it unfolds naturally. Still, I would love an epic novel set in this universe. There is magic in this world and there are supernatural creatures. There are werewolves (Lycans), vampires (Fangs), etc. These creatures are dealt with a little differently than in typical fantasy books. You don't feel like you're reading the same rehashed werewolf or vampire story as you have many times before. The mythos behind these creatures is unique to this world and I imagine more interesting creatures will be introduced in future stories. The magic users in this book are especially interesting. Mages are trained to kill and, if someone grows up with the Promise in secret without proper training, their only options are to be killed or used as a source slave for other magic users. This dark side of magic is prevalent throughout the world and is a nice change of pace from the goodhearted mages that I read about more often. Overall, I really loved this book. It was a very quick read and I couldn't put it down. The world has a lot of potential for future stories and I hope that Khanani will think of increasing the length of her books in the future. There's so much to draw from! If you like fantasy, you're going to like this one! Visit my blog for this review and more!

Voltaire was one of the prominent philosophers from the Enlightenment movement, an era in which religious dogmatism, the aristocracy and intellectual dependence were frowned upon by thinkers who employ reason and the scientific method in attempting to understand their environment and form a just model of society. Such "enlightening" ideas feature prominently enough in his infamous novella Candide ; but to perceive it solely as a product based on the principles of the Enlightenment Age is to miss out on half the novel's satire, and almost all the fun. Voltaire was clearly a man who disliked his society. While Candide is foremost an attack on Leibniz's admittedly absurd theory of Optimism (that every misfortune or evil is justified by the benefits in which it will eventually result, based on the idea that a perfect God would only create a perfect world - in which a minimum of evil is a necessity), but also fiercely criticizes the nobility, religious orders, colonialism, war, art, futile traditional practices and even individual writers, contemporary or otherwise. The story follows the young Candide, thrown out of his German household, traveling the western world in search of love, all the while encountering events which either plainly contradict his private tutor's teachings of Optimism, or which reflect the lunacy, cruelty and hypocrisy of western civilization. Although Candide was written in the eighteenth century, the modern reader will with certainty recognize such flaws in his own society. The book's mere 100-odd pages comprise more ideas and opinions than most philosophical novels; it is rich with insight and witty in its satire. Candide's most comical moments are however directly related to the narrative itself; Voltaire seems to revel in satirizing the quintessential novel of the 1700's, by developing characters in complete contrast to their ideal roles (Candide's long-lost love, Cunegonde, is continuously raped by men)  , and by ceaselessly depicting ridiculously over-the-top situations. A very insightful and funny novel.

If I Were You is the first installment in Lisa Renee Jones's adult romance series titled Inside Out. It's got secrets, mystery, intrigue, troubled characters, and romance, along with some dark themes that are about to get darker I'm afraid. The mystery element has me drawing conclusion after conclusion, and just when I think I have a solid theory about what has happened, some little tidbit of information is revealed that suddenly makes my theory seem less likely. I'm sure it sounds frustrating, but it's soooo not. I'm loving every second of it! The genres listed for this book include romance, erotica, BDSM, contemporary, mystery, and suspense. With this book, the reader is just at the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the erotica/BDSM elements, so we'll see if I continue to enjoy the series as much as I hope I will once this element is fully introduced. But so far, the story is strong, the character development is growing increasingly thorough, and I am optimistic this is a winning series for me. Even if for some reason it's not, it's a damn good start. My favorite quote: "Other people's perfection is a facade we create when we are second guessing ourselves..."

Initial thoughts: 4 stars. What a dreary world - Red Plague, evil villains, airships, and hungry crocodiles. A bit of an annoying love triangle but enjoyable nonetheless. The Review: The world of Dance of the Red Death is a dark and depressing place. The city has been devastated by the Red Death. The dead are piled up everywhere, blocking the streets and neighborhoods. Those lucky enough to escape the city seek shelter at Prince Prospero's palace. However, this refuge is subject to the whims of the despotic and often sadistic Prince. In the city, a group led by the Reverend Malcontent purposely spreads the disease. The lucky few wear porcelain masks to protect themselves from the dreaded contagion. Dance of the Red Death is the second book in Bethany Griffin's series based on Edgar Allan Poe's short story Masque of the Red Death. It's not a retelling, it's more of a rework and it works quite well. The book begins right where the last one left off and it is a quick paced, action-packed read, full of airships, crocodiles, and other assorted clockwork items. The heroine of this series is Araby Worth, the daughter of the infamous scientist Dr. Worth. Araby is a likable character; she is quite pragmatic and does whatever needs to be done in order to save her friends and to find a cure for the plague. In a world where those in power seem bent upon destruction, Araby stands out as someone who is looking to save her city. There is a love triangle in this series, though in this instance it didn't seem to bother me. After all, Araby and Elliot were not really a couple - they were just needed to appear to be one. In fact, they kind of use each other. Personally, I'm Team Will and despite Araby's anger towards Will, I kept hoping that she would choose him. Let's talk about villains. Dance of the Red Death has two very evil villains, each at odds with the other. There's the Prince Prospero, a sadistic despot with a taste for the macabre. Prospero's idea of entertainment involves feeding young orphans to the hungry crocodiles in front of an audience. A truly evil man. One of my favorite parts of the book was the 7 tasks Prospero gave Araby to complete. So creepy! The other villain is the Reverend Malcontent, a man who uses religion to push his own agenda for control of the city. Malcontent and his cloaked followers spread the disease throughout the city. Dance of the Red Death was the perfect conclusion to the series. The book kept my attention. It was full of exciting chase sequences, nail biting suspense, snapping crocodiles, religious zealots, and even some swamp people. The world was richly detailed. If you haven't had a chance to read this series, I recommend it. It's a lot of fun to read. Thank you to Edelweiss and Harper Collins/Greenwillow Books for a review copy of this book. Review posted on Badass Book Reviews.

I love all things Jane Austen so I was excited to read this book. I'm sure after Pride & Prejudice, a lot of readers would have loved to live in the world of Lizzie and Darcy (I would LOVE to meet Darcy...only if he looks like Matthew MacFarryden though) and I've always been intrigued by that time period. This was somewhat of a P&P re-telling...during the time period of P&P, so it was kind of a time traveling story as well. There were similarities to P&P, our protagonist Courtney's favorite Austen novel and mine as well. And guys, the mother is just as annoying and infuriating as in P&P; she made me want to come into the novel and slap her hard across the face. As for Courtney aka Jane, I liked her but she did get annoying at times but I guess it came with the shock of time traveling to such a different place. Plus, she didn't know if she would get back to her time AND there was a hot guy in her new life who was totally in love with her...how can a girl pass that up? Gah, the reality of the world of 1815 England was GROSS, like *shuddering* GROSS. I think this is a to time to mention that I'm squeamish person at first and it takes a while for me to get over it. That said, Courtney got the reality of medicine and hygiene during that time which wasn't very advanced. For instance, there was such a thing as public baths (with clothes on!) where all sorts of people got in, even if they've got a cold or infection or a seriously hurt leg. Yeah, GROSS. Overall, it was a nice read. Nothing really overly exceptional but there haven't been a lot of time traveling with an Austen book involved so that was a nice twist. There is another book, this one on Jane's life in the 21st Century, and I hope to read that one too!
