Reading The Vorrh ... Reading The Vorrh reminds me of the first time I read Gene Wolfe. Catling offers a very similar combination of mystery, allusion, tricky plots, some beautiful sentences, unpredictability, touches of horror, and a powerful sense of meaning just beneath the surface. The Vorrh is like Shadow of the Torturer in that it's a standalone book which is also, apparently, the start of a series. This is also my way of offering very high praise. If the Hugo awards matter ever again, this is now my second nomination for the year's best novel. It's the kind of book you reread parts of while reading, and which you begin again immediately upon finishing. It's not a comfortable, friendly book. The narrative(s) isn't (aren't) built that way. The Vorrh doesn't offer much in the way of characters you empathize with. Instead it's a challenge, a lunge in unexpected directions, energetically doing work on multiple levels not all of which the reader can grasp right away. I've been reading parts of this novel out loud, partly from pleasure, and also so dig more deeply into passages. It's that kind of book. Alan Moore compares it to Voyage to Arcturus, and that makes sense to me. ...before I go further with impressions and comparisons, I'll introduce what the book is actually about. Then I'll head into spoilers. The Vorrh doesn't have a single plot, but multiple storylines that intersect around a fantastic African forest of great antiquity, the titular Vorrh, during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. We follow a French writer who visits the forest, several Europeans living in a colonial city at the forest's edge, a local ex-soldier, the great Scots photographer Muybridge, and several local shamans and/or medical doctors, not to mention mysterious slaves, William Gull, a cyclops, monsters, robotic teaching puppets, a growing population of ghosts, a disembodied assassin, and, most importantly, a woman turned into a bow. Their stories dodge back and forth in time, especially as identities change or disappear. A note on genre: as you might gather from the preceding, The Vorrh is a fantasy, or a work of magic realism. We see realistic details alongside objects and forces drawn from myth and imagination. The forest seems to exist somewhere all across North Africa, stretching down along the eastern coast, yet also near the Mediterranean. As with, say, the works of Tim Powers, this novel works fantastic elements into the nitty gritty of daily life. It also reads like surrealist art and fiction, with genuinely strange scenes and ideas: a cyclops going to a carnival, after being taught from mysterious crates by helpful puppets. The Vorrh is also an adventure novel, with several characters engaged on epic quests, and including gunfire, ambushes, betrayals, curses, sex scenes, torture, and rebellion. *And* it's alternate history, positing a colonial enterprise that didn't exist, and including historical personages, such as Roussel, Gull and Muybridge. Additionally, steampunk fans may find some fun machines. A note on style: Catling has a flair for surprising word choice and lovely phrases, with touches of sardonic wit. Este had foreseen her death while working in our garden, an uncapping of momentum in the afternoon sun. (Kindle location 131) He stepped over a gurgling drain and emptied the bullets out of the gun; they fell like brass comets into the speeding firmament below. Cyrena Lohr combed the city and caught three names, which now wriggled in her teeth. "I want to be forgotten for who I am, not judged for how I have been made." For so it is among those who shed lives every few years: They keep their deflated interior causeways, hold them running parallel with their current usable ones; ghost arteries, sleeping shrunken next to those that pump life. Hushed lymphatics, like quiet ivy alongside the speeding juice of now. Nerve trees like bone coral, hugging the whisper of bellowing communications. ...a great stench of hope rose... (3686) The camera was a collector not of light, but of time, and the time it cherished most was in the anticipation of death. She had found [a book] confused and obscure. No doubt it was art, for she knew him to be a man of dangerous appetites and total selfishness. She had a smouldering attractiveness that hid beneath a face that melted uncontrollably between the ages of eight and eighty-one. A note on references: The Vorrh opens with a flourish of entertaining allusions. Frobenius is there to make us think of German colonialism in Africa. Conrad brings up the European enterprise more generally. Zen and the Art of Archery teases us about the bow. Once the book gets going, Catling quietly builds up a larger referential world. The Bible is a touchstone throughout, sometimes literally. Flann O'Brien is namechecked once (2525) , to my delight. A note on politics: The Vorrh soaks in Europe's colonialist past, and runs all kinds of risks in doing so. European characters exploit and literally enslave the locals. Catling, not from Africa, narrates from local points of view. The entire enterprise risks something like Orientalism by creating a fantasty world in a far-off, exploitable land for colonial people to explore. But Catling pulls it off, I think. The Europeans don't fare that well, overall, resembling less Stanley and more Mungo Park. For example, several characters are killed, their slaves freed, and the crucial timber trade falls apart. We also never really learn about the heart of the forest, denying that grail to foreigners and readers alike. And the Vorrh isn't really feminized. Kij Johnson goes further, arguing that "what this book is not, is about Africa". Do I recommend The Vorrh? Do I ever. But with cautions. It's challenging, not often giving readers comfortable ways in. The plots sprawl and their actions often suspend themselves. Reading enough of this novel brings about a kind of trance effect, not onlike watching a Tarkovsky film. This ain't Dragonlance. So read it. This may be the greatest fantasy of the decade. What an excellent follow-up to an excellent book. I loved Deadline nearly as much as I loved Feed. The biggest difference between the two: Feed had me both laughing and crying, while Deadline maintained a consistent tone with mild humor undertones. It didn't take away from any of my enjoyment of the book though. Shaun is excellently written, and his voice is distinctively different from George's. I especially noticed this in the last chapter, when we switch back to George's POV. I was jarred, and couldn't put my finger on exactly what the difference was between the chapter before and this one. I wasn't until the very last sentence that I realized that this as a new narrator. And that immediately explained why I felt off. The other bit of this book that really makes it shine is that it DOES NOT suffer middle book syndrome. Deadline doesn't waste words trying to fill up pages just to make this plot point an entire book. If there's anything negative, there is a strange disconnect with the supporting cast. For some reason, I had a hard time finding a new favorite among the characters. I didn't dislike any characters, just none of them really stood out to me. (Except maybe Maggie.) However, this could be attributed to Shaun's state of mind. All I know is I pretty much devoured this book, and wanted to chuck it across the room because I didn't have Blackout in my hands. The Newflesh Trilogy is quickly turning into one of my all time favorite zombie stories.
I liked this one so much more.

I am very very sad to admit that this was the worst instalment in the Falling Kingdoms series so far. I found myself losing interest after the first half which is probably because the plot just didn't make any sense to me. I mean  Gaius's mother is still alive! What how and why? Apart from the fact that we don't know enough about this character to even care that she is alive, (was barely mentioned in the past), all of a sudden she became an integral part of the story and everyone depends on her to do her magic and save everyone. Speaking of, she wants to save Gaius. Why would Magnus and Cleo let her? They despise Gaius and they would be way better off if he is dead. Why they are going along with this I don't understand. Cleo's mother's curse was just another cheap trick to keep Magnus and Cleo apart just a little bit longer in order to drag out their romance. Completely unnecessary, even though it led to one of my favorite scenes in the books, Cleo and Magnus's fight, which was very emotionally raw and authentic. But that was about it, I'm afraid :( Don't even get me started on Nic! Disaster. All in all, I found it flat, unoriginal and sloppy. I absolutely love this series and I was looking forward to exciting, sleepless nights. Let's hope the next one will not disappoint.

This is the second novel in the Red Queen series and it could not come out fast enough! I read the first one a few months after it came out and I loved it! "If I am a sword, I am a sword made of glass, and I feel myself beginning to shatter." Let me just say first off that the writing was great and I loved it! But after Mare and the group got out of the situation where the first book ended, it pretty much stayed stagnant until near the end. It was kind of like rinse, wash, repeat with a lot of the scenes. Find newblood Get into trouble Save newblood or find them already taken Mare feels sorry for herself or happy that she has a new recruit Repeat "No one is born evil, just like no one is born alone. They become that way, through choice and circumstance." I get that this was a big part of her army/revolution but we didn't need to read about her going to the different places 10+ times. The only time we got to see Maven for the most part was in the little notes he would leave her. And then when the ending came and he came out of nowhere? Why couldn't this have happened sooner? Loved it! Now I can't wait for the next book to see how Mare gets herself out of this situation. "Anyone, anything, can betray anyone. Even your own heart." For the most part I couldn't help but feel sorry for Mare. She is thrust upon being the leader and face of the Scarlet Guard, and either people fear her or distrust her. "But I can't shake the feeling that, while they stand with me, there's no one beside me. Even with an army at my back, I am still alone." "Strange, my enemies know me best, and my family doesn't know me at all." She has to make all of these tough decisions and no one seems to really understand what it is doing to her. They only see the facade she puts up and keeps her an arms distance away. You would think that this would be the perfect time to build the romance between her and Cal, but she keeps Cal an arms length away and makes up excuses to keep him there. If I am going to be bored reading about all the missions, at least give me a little romance. Hopefully the third book will be more like the first one and keep me entertained the whole time.

That's when I first learned about true frustration, that wrenching ache when the thing that matters most to you barely makes a ripple in other people's lives. This was a really sweet character driven book! I honestly didn't expect to love it as much as I did. I loved how there was no real 'bad guy' and the way Robin Benway wrote about the ripple effects of Oliver's kidnapping on everyone's lives. I'm excited to read more of her work.

Interesting and engaging story from start to finish with the added complication of String Theory and quantum physics, none of which I understand. That said, the book and story is not difficult to read or follow. With so many different contingencies, where does one reality begin and another diverge? Jason Dessen is looking for HIS reality because any other reality presents him with a life he doesn't want but one Jason already took his reality. How does he get it back? Interesting twists and turns.
Love. Love love love. Yeah, it took me two months to read but who cares. Love.

Oakley doesn't speak through sheer willpower because if she does it will destroy her family. Cole, her best friend since they were toddlers, is one of the only people to accept her as she is. Their friendship slowly evolves into something more but Oakley isn't sure she can, or should, allow those feelings to develop. It is pretty obvious from the very beginning that a traumatic event led to Oakley's silence, and most readers will be able to guess it is because of  sexual abuse   but the details behind it are a shocker. It needs editing (hence the four stars), but it is a tale that handles this delicate subject with sensitivity. I've already marked the next book as to read.

Brought to you by OBS reviewer Dawn Georgia is moving back into her parents' home with her daughter. Madison, since they are on leave. She has come home because she got a job with the local college as an adjunct. I did not know much about college professors or adjuncts prior to reading this book. It is an eye-opener for sure. I felt so bad about how the adjuncts were treated despite their doctorate degrees. They are treated horribly and with a total lack of respect from tenured professors. It is humiliating for them. Being an adjunct has meant Georgia has relocated a lot. It has had an effect on Madison; how can it not? Madison is sick of moving; she craves stability. Madison is an interesting character. She and her mom are into anime and manga. They like to go to conventions, to dress up. Next we meet Sid. Sid is a hoot. He is the ghost/skeleton that has lived in Georgia's home since she was a child. He does not recall his name in life or his past. Sid loves being snarky; he likes practical jokes. His jokes about bones were the best. I cracked up many times throughout the book. The dialogue is clever; I love Perry's sense of humor. It is a gift to be able to weave that into a story. Sid tags along when Georgia and Madison when they go to a local convention. He is in costume (lol) so no one will question him. While at the convention, Sid thinks he recognizes a woman. When he tells Georgia, they decide to go on a hunt for information about his past, how he died. The investigation is slow going at the beginning but they begin to unravel the mystery a piece at a time. The plot along with character development make this book a must read. It is a fun book. I recommend the book across the board to men, women and young adults. It is very well written. The characters leap off the pages as does the humor. You will find yourself laughing consistently.

I picked this up mostly because I've followed her blog at The Pioneer Woman off and on for a while. Mostly the cooking section, because she uses real butter like a real person, and she taught me to make Quiche. You should go there. She has also strongly informed my own  recipe blogging style. Ree tells the story of how she went from life in LA to living with her husband on his cattle ranch, surprising everyone (including herself) along the way. It's a sweet little real life romance, and a romance that continues still. Just ask her about chaps. Really. She has extended her comfortable talking-over-the-kitchen-table voice from her blog to this autobiographical piece, and it actually works, which somehow surprises me. It's like reading an extra long blog post, but in the best way possible. Like when you stumble over a new blog, fall in love, and then go through the back posts to get caught up. Without the annoying scrolly-clicky parts. All in all, it's a lightweight, sweet-but-not-unrealistic story, perfect for those days when you feel a little too cynical.

Steel's Edge was really, really good!! Charlotte, a healer, creates a new life for herself in the Edge, after leaving her husband. She's happy and content to take care of those around her, including her new found mother-figure and friend Elenore. Until one day that happiness is shattered when Slavers come collect a wounded man Charlotte has taken into her home. That wounded man is Richard...the Hunter. It's his mission in life to hunt down those who psychically and emotionally broke his beloved niece Sophie, and to obliterate the whole slave trade once and for all. While collecting Richard, the Slavers do unspeakable things, things Charlotte cannot forgive or let go. She feels the need to do something about it, more than just vengeance or revenge, something MORE. Charlotte's and Richard's story is dark. The cause of the mission and their mission itself is dark and disturbing. But that's not to say the pull and the chemistry between these two characters is not there and genuine. I found their journey fascinating and appreciated the flaws of each character and the dedication they have towards one another. Given the subject matter, the story isn't overly graphic, it doesn't need to be. Team Andrews writes so well, they don't have to get graphic. They are masters at leading your imagination exactly where they want it to go. Whether it be the torture and death endured, banter between two teenage boys or the internal emotional struggle of a teenage girl. I loved every part of this story and I'm very sad to see this series end. After finishing this book a part of me wanted to go back to the beginning and read it all again. I can only hope someday Team Andrews will pick up the series again with stories about George, Jack and Sophie.

I'm going to be reviewing this book a little backwards. I'm going to start off with my conclusion of the book and then I will go into detail with a read more because I will be posting spoilers. So if you want to read Reached and don't want to be spoiled then do not read the read more section of this review! ::sigh:: I just don't know how I feel about Reached. Did I like it? Did I not like it? I just don't know, but I am leaning towards not liking it. Why? I have two reasons. This book dragged on foreverrrrrrr. I mean this could have been a 300 page novel not a 512 page one. It was unnecessarily long. It strayed so far from Matched. Taking these two things into consideration and some other things I will post below I sadly have to rate this book a 2.5 out of 5. I'm just disappointed at how this series turned out. I really loved Matched but the last two books of this series just didn't reach my expectations. Pros: Writing: The writing in Reached was a major improvement if you compare it to the writing in Matched. When I first read Matched I thought the writing was a little juvenile and weak but while reading Reached you can obviously tell that Ally Condie really improved her writing skills. The Plague: In many dystopian novels such as The Hunger Games you have these wars and battles where the main character goes to physical war with the society or whomever is in charge but in Reached instead of having this big war they had a plague. I thought the concept and the idea of the plague was a really great idea and really new to this genre. Society vs Rising: This kind of goes with the plague section. It turns out that all along the Society and the Rising are were one. The rebellion started out as a real thing but the Society basically infiltrated the Rising and the two become one. In turn they are the ones who created the Plague and ruined their own world. I thought this was funny and interesting. Basically the society turned on themselves because they thought they could control the Rising but they couldn't and they couldn't tell what was up and what was down. Cassia's Dad: When we find out that Cassia's dad died from the Plague, my heart broke and it only broke more when we find out that Bram had to see his own father die and that he took care of the dead so he could take care of his ill mother. Bram's break down just tore me to pieces. Then when Bram tells his mother what he has seen and that their father is dead, ugh, way to drive the knife further into my heart Condie. Just Cassia's mom saying no over and over again, it killed me. I teared up more during those two scenes then I did when Indie died. This are some of the scenes where you can see Ally Condie's writing really improved. Laney/Lei: Big freaking shock. Like I legit gasped out loud and my jaw was on the floor. We are introduced to this new character, Lei, and she works with Xander in the hospital to take care of all the still (what they call the patients of the Plague) and Xander kind of falls for her but she already has a "match" but he is at war somewhere. Towards the end of the novel we found out that Lei is actually Laney!! Vick's girl!! I just can't. I was so surprised!! Condie gets major bonus points for this. Mind blown. Who sorted Cassia with Ky? : That would be Cassia herself. This is so comical and I should have seen it coming. Throughout the whole series everyone has wondered how could Cassia have been matched with Ky and Xander? It turns out that the Rising/Society had Cassia sort herself and she was matched with Ky. They made her take the red pill to forget but in the end she remembers what happened. Xander finds the Cure: During the first two books, Xander has been this back character and in Reached he finally comes to the surface. I liked that he played a major role in finding the cure to the Plague. Whenever there is a love triangle the second guy normally takes a backseat on all the adventures and I was happy that he got his chance in the spot light. Cons: Dragged on: As I said before this book dragged on forever. I mean I felt like it was never ending, and we weren't getting anywhere. I really had lost interest around page 300. This really influenced my rating of this book. Retelling the same story and poem over and over again: This goes with the dragging on point I made previously. I lost count of the number of times Condie basically copy and pasted past scenarios from the previous books into this one. It reminds me of when your teacher tells you that your paper must be five pages long but you can only manage three pages so you basically write the same stuff over and over again. It was really annoying. Love triangle...square...what? : This had to be thee worst love story/ love triangle I have ever read. First of all Condie builds up this amazing love story in Matched and then drops it in the next two books!! What is that! I thought by Reached we would get more of Ky and Cassia but no they are constantly separated. I mean Condie had already separated them in Crossed so why do it again? And then when they are separated Cassia is thinking about how she loves Ky but she also loves Xander and Ky is thinking how he loves Cassia, but now he is in love with Indie and that if Cassia and him hadn't been matched that he might be with Indie. And poor Xander he falls in love with all these girls who never love him back. I felt so bad for that guy. The characters grew as individuals but not as a couple. This was very disappointing to me. Science: To much science. At first I was interested in the science aspect of the Plague but as the novel progressed it was just to much and I lost interest. Pilot: Does anyone else wish the official Pilot was someone they had known? I think that it would have been more interesting if it had turned out to be Ky's dad or someone they all knew. (I do understand that everyone is the Pilot in their own way but I'm talking about the official Pilot) The Ending: That wasn't even an ending. Is Condie writing another installment because I am not satisfied with that ending. I like my endings neat with a bow on top and that was not what I got. I was actually hoping for a time jump to see how the new society progressed but I got nothing.

Thank GOD it's over. I actually read a lot of reviews in consideration of how much I disliked this book, because I wanted to understand whether I was missing some inherent appeal. There were just so many things about Feed that made it grating to read and really pulled me out of the world that Grant obviously took so much time and care to create, which is maybe what left me feeling so frustrated. With a better editor, she might have dropped about 100+ pages of hackneyed dialogue or verb modifiers (after the first 50 pages, I do not need an adverb to indicate to me EVERY TIME George says something sarcastic to Sean or vice-versa, I'll just take it as fucking read, thanks. Same thing with adding "angrily" to a verb like "glowered"--I think anyone above a grade 1 reading level gets the picture). Many of the lower-star reviews seemed to find fault with the fact that Feed was light on the zombie action and heavy on the political intrigue and technical aspects of a post-apocalyptic weblog-based news system. I didn't mind that so much myself. What I did mind was how ham-fisted the "intrigue" was. The political candidates were cartoonish in their flatness. I'm not even going to waste words on an actual critique so I'll just say this: a presidential candidate gets elected via a boob job and promising her constituents risque outfits. What the fuck kind of commentary is that when that character is the only female politician Grant spends serious time mentioning? As for Tate and Ryman...oh my god. Have I either felt so little suspense as to which of them would end up coming out victorious? The"reveal" that Tate was an integral part of the disastrous zombie attacks dogging Ryman's campaign for presidency might as well have been something George found out in her first interview with Tate. Why not? It couldn't have been any more obvious when Grant essentially stops just short of physically bludgeoning her readers over the head with a brick engraved with the phrase "Georgia Mason's journalistic instinct for truth is basically preternatural". Between hearing about what a self-professed Truth-seeker and incredible journalist George was and the repetition of the phrase "poke things with a stick" (with variations on 'things' including 'zombies', 'dead things', etc. ), the only thing that kept me reading was my admittedly unfortunate hang up about finishing the books I start. It really disappointed me that I was able to guess most of the twists and turns before they happened, and that doing so didn't impact me emotionally in any way because the characters weren't strongly drawn enough for me to give a shit about them. There was so much flouting of the "show, don't tell" rule in Feed that I felt my will to live withering as page after page mysteries that were meant to be solved were instead spoiled by the characters talking about them for three paragraphs before discovering that what they had speculated about was, in fact, exactly what was going on the whole time. Awesome! Why even include the discovery part, then? Even Sean's reaction to George's death  failed to move me because it was so...insane? Out of character? Given that Sean's entire personality seemed based on just reacting to whatever George said in a facetious manner or acting like he was the reincarnation of Steve Irwin, I really can't even tell. Anyway, I'm not even going to try to read the next two books because between the disappointment of Feed and suffering through the first two books of the October Daye series with no relief, I think I've conclusively hit my limit with Seanan McGuire's writing style.

Stunning, captivating, engrossing are just a few words to describe the wonderful story that is A Different Blue. A story written with such grace and ease you can't help but lose yourself within the story of Blue Echohawk. The author and her creative way of telling a story will have you hooked by the end of the first paragraph. Meet Blue Echohawk, a young woman who does not know her real name, her age, her parents, or who it is she is supposed to be. What she does know is who she created herself to be. Blue is a strong, tough girl who does not care what people say or think about her. Or does she? We meet Blue when she is attending her senior year of high school. We live Blue's early years through memories and flashbacks that will touch your heart, stir your emotions, and create a bond with Blue that is quite unexpected. The author's unique writing style provides us with a three dimensional view of all of the characters in this story. Even the smallest of character is described with such precision that you can envision what they look like, and you can feel each and every emotion as if the story were happening to you. From the brief description of Blue's mother to Officer Moody,Detective Martinez, Manny, Graciela, Tiffa, Jocelyn, Cheryl, Mason, and so many others not listed here, every character is brought to us in such amazing detail. Wilson is Blue's history teacher. He is unexpected, challenging, frustrating, tempting, confusing, and a breath of fresh air. Wilson is a story within himself, and his story wraps around Blue's story with amazing precision. Providing a unique and interesting way to teach his class he challenges Blue to understand her past, face the present, and want for the future. You long for the chapters that take you into Wilson's classroom, because as you read, you will see Wilson's teaching is like nothing you have ever experienced. The storyline, written with such a pure heart, takes you on a journey of life, loss, love, hope, learning the truth, discovering the past, and looking towards the future. Many life lessons are taught throughout this book. With each lesson learned you find yourself feeling a deeper connection to the characters, perhaps looking at things in a different light and always rooting for Blue. This is a complex storyline which covers various topics. The author provides the perfect amount of information to the reader to always keep us wanting more but never making it easy for the reader to figure out what will happen next. One of the wonderful things about this book is the journey it takes us on. We start at the beginning, coast through the middle, and at the end, we have learned everything we had hoped to, leaving the reader with a sense of peace. I for one did not want this story to end. I had become so personally invested in the characters that the words The End brought a tear to my eye.

Wow! Whatever I expected from this it wasn't what I got in the end!!! To tell you the truth I read sins and needles and my expectations were very low coming into the Experiment In Terror series. But I have to say, why isn't Halle doing more 'supernatural' books? She can obviously rock them and I've never read better horror books than hers (although I'm sort of a beginner) But it doesn't matter because I have a feeling I'm not gonna find better books than this series out there. Halle starts off thrillingly and eases into the 'supernatural' part of the story fast and comfortably... I fell in love with her writing - her descriptions, the atmosphere- building, the suspense, the gore (although not much), the banter and dialogue between the characters. Perry Palamino and Dex Forray are NOT your typical couply sorta stereotypes nor is the supernatural stuff they encounter. This is the biggest highlight of the book/series. I'll take up Dex Forray first- He's different for me than any other guys from other books. He is real, mysterious with a capital M, broody (nothing more broody has lived the earth! ), secretive, strange and 'charming'... But he's not the main focal point of it! Of course it's Perry Palamino!! I haven't read a more thorough or kick-ass heroine in forever! Everyone should read this book if not for the supernatural stuff then entirely for Perry!!!! God, she's awesome! I loved that she's so independent, self-assured (except for her insecurities about her looks but that's another point), able to protect herself, real, and I loved that she's not one of those 'perfect' girls with modelesque bodies... I sympathized with her insecurities regarding her body and that was one of the points that made her real. I loved the pace, the story, the writing style, the characters, the setting, the reality, the psychological thriller style in the writing, and I have a feeling this series is gonna be one of my favourites despite it being horror/supernatural/psychological thriller and me not reading much of that genre. Halle shines through as an author through this book. The only serious and 'thorn in my pleasure' sorta complaint is that Halle stressed or pressured me to like Dex and there was too much weight and time over Perry's attraction to him- I rolled my eyes so many time sat that and yes, it was mentioned more than enough times which disrupted the 'real' feeling of the story and it was a given that they'll be a romantic pair...

** spoiler alert ** Total cliff hanger!!!! Not in a bad way really but i'm so excited to think that Maya, Daniel, and Corey are going to meet Chloe and the others from "The Darkest Power" series! Also i thought it was kind of odd that Kelley Armstrong almost killed Rafe off, i knew he was still alive because no character with such a big part is killed off like that in the second book.

I went to the library the other day, as my hold was ready to pick up. The book I reserved, Paper Girls, Vol. 3, is a short graphic novel; it's the kind of book you read in an hour. Knowing this, I decided I should get something else to read once I finished. Front and center on the "Quick Picks" display, sat Small Great Things by Jodi Picoult. I borrowed it on a whim; knowing next to nothing about the premise and even the author. What I didn't realize was how relevant this book really is. It was written in October of 2016, yet its message still holds true. With all that's happening in Charlottesville as of late, I really needed this book. The story covers Ruth Jefferson, a black nurse, who has been working at Mercy-West Haven hospital for over 20 years. One day, during an albeit normal shift, Ruth is assigned to a couple who just gave birth. Cue Turk, Brittany, and baby Davis Bauer. Guess what they are? White supremacists!! Woo!! Basically, Ruth is dismissed from the couple because of their "personal preferences." Later, Davis dies and blah blah blah I don't want to write a summary. Yes, I know I suck. MOVING ON to the review! I think the most interesting POV would have to be Turk's. Having the POV of a white supremacist was refreshing in a novel about a POC. It was strange, but not unwarranted. Seeing him change into a disgusting person into a tolerable one was a metamorphosis I did not expect. His ending was sweet, even though a bit too cotton candy for my liking. I'm glad he stopped supporting white supremacy; his character arc was one of the best of the novel. Brittany's suicide was unexpected, though, and I'm not sure I liked the surprise ending. And her having a black mother? Woah. Next level plot twists, Picoult. I would recommend this book to anyone looking for a juicy, informative, long read.

This one flowed better, was easier for me to follow and was almost impossible for me to put down. Is anyone else annoyed the Sebastian doesn't suspect that he father is not his biological father? It would explain a lot!

Actually, I picked up this book a couple of years ago when there was a lot of hype about it. I read through the first three chapters...blue hair, teeth, monsters, smoke, bone... and was immediatley disinterested. So it had been on my DNF list forever. However, as you can see from the four stars, I know that it was a mistake to stop reading this delight. "Hope can be a powerful force. Maybe there's no actual magic in it, but when you know what you hope for most and hold it like a light within you, you can make things happen, almost like magic." 1) One of the Best Paranormals I've Read So Far :) I have a feeling this might be also categorized as fantasy... if you think so skip this number one For most of the time, I prefer fantasy a lot more than paranormal and it's completely because of my own personal preferences. I did try some paranormal books like The Raven Boys, but it never got me wheeled in. Although throughout this book it wasn't always exciting, but at least it remained a fast pace and kept me engaged. However, the main reason that I liked it so much was the concept about magic, peace, hope and "rebirth" and also because of the mix of chimera/seraphim mythology, something I never come into contact with. "Have you ever asked yourself, do monsters make war, or does war make monsters?" 2) The Plot "Twist" (no spoilers here) I think that a huge reason for me to take off a star is that I basically predicted what the "plot twist" was when the two protagonists met... Maybe Taylor designed it to be that obvious but I really do prefer the feeling of epiphany with a twist I did not see coming. Luckily, toward the end, the author expanded on the twist explaining a lot of details with a beautiful story that also let us see more of the world building which I really liked. "Love is a luxury." "No. Love is an element." An element. Like air to breathe, earth to stand on." 3) The Love Do I ship Karou and Akiva...? Mehh...Don't get me wrong, I'm definitely a romantic, I swoon over my ships in books and fangirl about them. But even though  Akiva sworn to Karou about how he loved her before he figured out she was Madgrigal , there weren't any building on their relationship to the point of chemistry and the main reason they were attracted to each other was because of physical appearances. So I definitely need more convincing for their relationship. But YAY NO INSTA-LOVE! Overall, this was beyond my expectations and that evil ending had left me longing to read the next book in the series.

Clary and Simon are invited to stand as witnesses at Emma and Julian's parabatai ceremony. First, however, their own friendship is put to the test in another trial. I really enjoyed seeing so many of my favourite characters from Cassie's books together in one place, as well as seeing Simon explore his friendship with Clary. And what's this about Magnus guest teaching at the Academy... ? Gimme!

Dracula is back! Needing help handling some shape-changing vampires, Buffy sends Xander to visit the legendary Dracula. Apparently, the gang has kept in touch! Dracula's inclusion brings a good deal of humor to this installment. The Count is as pompous as ever and hurls disparaging remarks at anyone within earshot. While in his presence, Xander falls back into his idolizing minion ways--causing him a lot of embarrassment, yet amusing me to no end. The general storyline of the Japanese vampires was somewhat out of left field, but the change in venue did allow for a great Godzilla-like moment. Andrew makes an appearance with his contagious, fan-boy enthusiasm still intact (how he leads an entire division of Slayers is utterly beyond me). Twilight also pops up briefly, but we still don't get any big clues into his identity. The only significant issue I had was a side story regarding Buffy's love-life. I didn't have a problem with the events themselves, but I did think they were contrary to Buffy's persona (as created in the show). I simply don't think she would ever go there. Wolves at the Gate reiterates a common theme of season eight: the characters are unlucky in love, fear connection, and often have to stand alone. I'm becoming anxious that all of the main characters will start suffering from Buffy's martyr syndrome. I hope not, because one broody lead is enough!

First, I read this story because i want the same pattern in , a spouse problem and how they dealt with their problem. but, after I read, the story didn't meet my expectation. the character is so not good. here is my expectation : Sebastian is man who have his character aloof and grumpy but he is waiting for his right woman come ini his way. Valentina, is tough woman, and she fought for her marriage to exist. but when his husband behaviour didn't change, she can stand up for herself. William is not a jerk man. the story could be more interesting if he gave Valentina more attention and sincerity because he was the main cause why his marriage and Valentina didn't work well. 2 stars

Everything I Never Told You came highly praised from the Book Riot crew and is actually a fairly lovely book. As with several books recently, I found it rather depressing (hence the lower rating). I am a sucker for stories about white girls falling for Asian guys (hello, Eleanor & Park), because I love to see how authors address some of the same issues/concerns/awesomeness that I've had in regards to my marriage and family. I just forgot that some of those explorations of struggles (especially those set in the 70s) would be super painful. Also: another housewife angst book! I didn't know what I was getting into!! Oh, and  why with the infidelity?! Why always with the infidelity??? I already live in fear that I'll drive my partner to such things, and I realize that loss of a child shakes everything up, but why does it always have to result in turning from your spouse and shagging other people?! Personal issues, yes. Perhaps very on the money for dealing with loss, but that thought is also depressing...Just try not to read this just after finishing Hausfrau, yeesh. Also, do parents really treat their different kids so differently? I couldn't tell if that was realistic or not given my only child status. Basically, the novel presents the unrealistic expectations parents can put on children as a result of their own desires for a different upbringing or young adult experience. These pressures and problems come from social stigmas and personal insecurities wrapped around race and gender norms. Painful stuff. Painful! I'm gonna need something light and fluffy alongside a strong beverage now.

some spoilers. I definitely have a love hate relationship for this series. I love the style writing and the characters are a joy t read ..well most of them. However for me, there are so many SAD points to this book..that it made me depressed while reading it. One character in particular talks constantly of suicide and that is a touchy subject for me. No one should give up on life. So, I relate with Sam on his viewpoints. The theme, man verses beast was also very prominent in this book. More so than the last one. (shiver) Especially with Isabel's Dad going on a hunt purposely to kill the wolves..who seem more human in that instant than the man. Then you have the secondary character Cole talking about, his experience as a wolf. Shifting into a human to find a deer half a live with his hands full of the deer's guts. This was a very grotesque picture in my mind. This leading him to thoughts of suicide all the more. You could write an essay on all these points. But, I am not going too. I am just going to say, if you want a HAPPY book this isn't it. If you are already feeling upset with life .and get attached to characters like I do, I highly DO NOT recommend this book. However,if you are in the mood for a good series that will tear your guts out and make you ball like a little girl .. then this is it for you.

3.5 stars I enjoyed this book a lot. My age is a bit younger than that of the main character and I have a son who is almost 4. I can't even imagine the horror of trying to keep a small child like that quiet during a dangerous situation involving a gunman. The terror of the book's plot is completely real to me. I also really liked that the characters infrequently mentioned God. No one was overtly religious, but throughout the book, numerous characters bring up God and whether God has any bearing on the situation they're in. I liked that about the book. Too many modern-day novels seem to just ignore religion and theology altogether (afraid of offending their readers, I guess?). The reality is that most people are still believers in some kind of deity or higher power. They may not sit in a pew every Sunday, but if there's a man with a gun around, you bet they'll be talking about God. So that was nice. There were many parts that struck me as memorable, like the story about Satan and the clock that can stop your life at a perfect moment. Why not a higher rating? The book just didn't stick the ending for me. I also felt that the whole situation was unrealistic. Had the book at least stuck the ending, this would have been a 4-star review. What didn't I like about the ending? Too ambiguous. Needed denouement. My interpretation of the narrative's sudden end is that Joan died, and I don't care for that, either. We never find out what happened to the baby or its mother. We never find out why the police did not come barreling in there within the hour (even with a hostage situation, cell phone reports from people in the zoo would have confirmed that there were gunmen killing people). We never find out why they didn't block off the entire neighborhood. We hardly see Destin, only hear about him. Overall a good effort, but it could have been better.

While much more satisfying than Book 4, I am now faced with waiting at least half a decade before any of these new cliffhangers are resolved. On the whole, I think this one felt a little more complete than the last book, tying together plot lines, destroying red herrings, and carrying out the slow reveals that Martin excels in. This does not excuse him leaving Sansa out for the whole book while giving at least a token chapter to all the other Feast for Crows viewpoints. After what happened to Cat, I am hesitant to believe Jon Snow is dead. In Martin's world, major characters don't seem to stay dead unless someone they love is there to watch, witness, and mourn. The deaths have to hurt. Also, while I recognize Jon as a vital character and would love to seem him take down Bolton, his point of view is one of the harder ones to slog through. Also difficult to deal with are characters like Victarion, Quentyn, and Griff, characters who seem to be there to move the story along but with whom Martin doesn't really develop that emotional character/reader bond he does with others. I hope the next book has fewer, for lack of a better word "NPC" characters and more time with "stars." Because I'm sure I will forget half the book before the next one comes out, I'm going to make notes on the questions I have at the end/plot lines I'm most anxious to see resolved. -Asha and Theon's reunion. WTF happened in Bolton's camp? Stannis' death is another thing I'm led to doubt. -Who is Melisandre, really. This book built more and more sympathy for her, and I'd love her POV to be more fully explored. -Varys has been plotting with young Aegon the whole time? Must know more! -When the frak is Dany getting to Westeros. -Tyrion's plot line didn't leave me in dire concern for his safety, but I just want more of him. Possibly hanging out with Dothraki. -Likewise on Arya, though I don't see how she'd meet up with Dothraki. Then again, GRRM works in mysterious ways. -Why the frak does Bran disappear halfway in never to return? I want to know more about his spooky powers. -What is Brienne doing with Jaimie? I really don't think she has it in him to send him to slaughter, but we still don't know the word she screamed to save her life at the end of FfC. Part of me is a bit relieved to be caught up with the series. It's wonderfully convoluted which makes for long hours slogging through feasts and battles and council meetings to get at the meat of the characters I'm so in love with. Reading it feels like a mental cardio exercise, pushing to a goal that is as yet hidden.

End of Watch is the third book in Stephen King's Bill Hodges Trilogy. The story features the aging ex-detective Bill Hodges, and company, going up against the seemingly near comatose Brady from the first book of the trilogy. The running theme through the trilogy is obviously Bill Hodges, but Brady is also present in all of the books. Brady mostly takes a back seat in the second book, and only small references are made to him with the cliffhanger about him at the very end. It almost seems like the second book could have been done on its own, and didn't necessarily have to be part of this trilogy and include Bill Hodges. It would have made sense if there was a Bill Hodges series (and not just a trilogy) where a reoccurring villain was Brady, but then there were also some other enemies. Instead, we get a lot of Brady, and another random story shoved in the middle. While I don't think the previous two books were typical mystery books like they were marketed to be, this book is definitely the furthest from being a mystery. Maybe Stephen King was getting tired of the mystery genre, and wanted to add some more horror, or super natural elements in this book. I think that this book could have been a regular Stephen King book, and not part of the Bill Hodges mystery trilogy. The book starts off with a nice job being done getting readers caught up. Instead of a chapter or two dedicated to nothing but retelling, King gets the reader caught up in small concise chunks, and does a nice job refreshing the memory of readers. I think that you might have been able to read this book by itself (without the previous two) and not be completely lost. It was more like jogging the reader's memory, rather than a complete rehashing. At the start, there is also some pretty good suspense and buildup. There are some mystery elements in the beginning of how everything is happening and where everything is leading. New facts and information are slowly introduced to keep the reader guessing and leading the reader down different paths, wondering which way the story is going to go. There are some similarities to The Cell in this book. King continues to show his dislike and seemingly distrust of technology in this book as well. While in The Cell, waves were transmitted via cell phones, in this book, tablet devices are used to hypnotize viewers. In both stories, there is also the more obvious elements of telepathy and mind-control. I did not like the ending of this book by any means. My dissatisfaction is both with the climax of the story, and the very ending. The ending is very anti-climatic and disappointing. I was hoping for a lot more to happen with the final show down between Bill, Holly, and Brady. Instead, the ending felt rushed and didn't really hold my interest. Brady was dispatched far too quickly and easily. I was also not a fan of Bill dying at the end of this book. It was obviously leading that way, but I'm not sure if it was necessary to end the book in such a melancholy way. At the beginning of the story, it was quite interesting and gripping. Once everything with Brady was pretty much laid and figured out, it was somewhat hard to stay interested. I felt myself not really caring too much about the characters or what happened to them. It kind of felt like it was treading water and not really making significant progress in the story. This was probably my least favorite of the trilogy, despite the fact that it was probably the least mystery-like out of the trilogy. It was definitely an interesting idea, just not the best execution and was dragged out for too long.

All the books in this series by Megan Frampton have been such lighthearted fun reads. The only word I can think of to describe this latest installment is "cute" from beginning to end. It is possible to read this book as a standalone as we don't have any characters reappearing from the earlier books (other than one brief mention). We have moved away from the fallen women of the Quality Employment Agency, and our heroine here is Lady Isabella Sawford, daughter of an earl, who has been taught to be perfect. A perfectly composed ice queen. But while Isabel is perfect on the outside, her imperfections are just bursting at the seams to be let out. She desperately wants to be a "real" person, but she doesn't know who she is or how to do that. Luckily, fate smiles on her, and a perfectly imperfect duke is trapped into marrying her. I enjoyed following Isabella's journey from a dishwaster miss to stating what she wants and when she wants it. Nicholas Smithfield inherits the title of duke very unexpectedly. At the time he inherits, he is best known around the ton for his ability to love the ladies. He also considers himself a pugilist and can be found trading punches almost daily. So he was not prepared for his new obligations, particularly when discovering one of those obligations was a betrothal tied to the title. Nicholas was charming and funny, and it was entertaining to watch this ladies man get flustered around his virginal wife. Even though the couple here is thrown together in marriage very early on, we don't have an instalove situation. The romance unfolds sweetly and builds throughout the entirety of the story. If you like a happy, so-sweet-your-teeth-ache love story, then you will enjoy this book. I received an advance copy of this book in exchange for an honest review. 4 stars / 3 flames.

Luckily this series is getting better and better. Gone are the long monologues and boring characters. There was actual prolonged suspense and excitement and horror. The actions of the characters seem more realistic and the villain has depth. Well done!

Yet another great novel by Briggs. We get to continue to follow Charles and Anna as they hunt a serial killer targeting Fae and Were's. Since the wolves have come out to the public they've had to be even stricter with discipline and it's wearing on Charles - luckily Anna manages to get Asil and Bran to pay attention and give Charles another duty to help him take his mind off his duties and put things in perspective. The ending was absolutely nuts and I can't wait for the next installments in both this and the Mercy series' as  the leader of the Grey Lords has just majorly changed the game. The only thing I thought was weird, and I could be mis-remembering, but I though that since Charles was a born werewolf he didn't experience the change the way the others did; that is was more magical and not painful, but there was a lot of talk about the pain he was going through to change.

Once upon a time, an angel and a devil fell in love. It did not end well. ...and that, ladies and gentlemen, is the sound of everyone who has read the blurb and above lines rushing to get a copy of this book. Seriously, with a premise as promising as the one Laini Taylor offers up, how could you possibly fail to be ensnared by the world of Karou and Akiva? Even with the two lines given above (which are the first lines of the book) we see the promise of tragedy. But this is young adult, you say. There's always a happy ending in young adult! And this is what keeps us hooked. Even through these hints of tragedy, we keep reading as we want to find the gold at the end of the rainbow: the happy ending. I actually had a copy of Daughter of Smoke and Bone lying around for some time before I decided to start reading it. And I don't know why I deliberated for so long because when I finally read it, I was well and truly enthralled by Taylor's writing. Her writing is absolutely stunning, and completely nails the golden rule of "show don't tell". She manages to build a beautiful setting in a world of angels and demons, of magic and hope. (I mean, really, who isn't captivated by the idea of a world that can be entered through a doorway in Prague?). And the characters. Amazing. While I was reading, I was pleasantly surprised to find that I actually liked the characters that I was meant to like. Too often, the protagonist is overly dramatic, or idiotically naive, or just plain annoying. This is definitely not the case with Karou, and I found that towards the end of the book, I was willing the book to magically become longer, just so I could continue reading. (Also, the love interest being an angel with eyes that burn like flames? *swoon*) The ending, man, that was harsh: a complete and utter cliffhanger ending. Thank God Days of Blood and Starlight came out recently: it managed to satiate my appetite for Akiva and Karou. And a few more beautiful lines from Daughter of Smoke and Bone (may include very minor spoilers, but warning: may cause you to become temporarily insane until you obtain a copy of the book): Once upon a time, a little girl was raised by monsters. But angels burned the doorways to their world, and she was all alone. Wishes are false. Hope is true. Hope makes its own magic. Oh, Hell. Must. Mate. Immediately. (bet you're interested in finding out the context of that one hehe) Once upon a time, an angel lay dying in the mist. And a devil knelt over him and smiled. "Love is a luxury." "No. love is an element." An element. Like air to breath, earth to stand on. His eyes blazed like flames. She whispered, "You." And if the above hasn't convinced you yet, there is no annoying love triangle. Hooray! Bravo, Laini Taylor, bravo! For more reviews, check out my blog: http://lookingforthepanacea.blogspot....

Damn it. I really wanted to like this more than I did! I feel like everything was ALMOST there, but it never really reached its full potential, which is an absolute shame. The plot was interesting enough, had it been properly developed ... and by no means did I think this was a bad book or a poorly written one. It just felt really bare in spots where it required a little more meat on its bones, and way overdone in spots that didn't require it. This unfortunate balance made me walk away from this book almost wanting to ask myself why I had even bothered reading it, because it almost seemed like a story not worth telling, by the conclusion. And trust me - I'm happy with the outcome that is the ending ... I'm glad Beth & Lincoln finally found each other properly  - but it just kind of came across as sloppily and hastily thrown together, after all of this time spent developing these characters and this odd situation they found themselves. This is similar to another experience that I had when reading this author - Eleanor & Park was FANTASTIC ... until it wasn't, just like that. It almost feels like a pacing problem that Rowell might sometimes encounter (although I didn't find that to be a problem at all in Fangirl, THAT book was fantastic through & through) ... everything goes pretty quickly and smoothly and full steam ahead until it just fizzles out with a lackluster ending. Bummer. Still looking forward to reading more of her work - I like her voice and her quirks, and I know she's capable of better (again, Fangirl, I'm looking at you). "Interesting, yet not fulfilling." is something I read as a descriptor for this book in Lilyan's review and I think that PERFECTLY sums it up.

In this second installment, the story picks up pretty much right away with Gaia travelling over to the dead forest with her newborn baby sister. Since she is all her sister has in the world now, Gaia tries her best to keep her alive, but thigs seem to look grim. Whena Gaia encounters a man and he takes her to his village, she thinks they will help her butm it's probably not the sort of help she had encountered on. In exchange for them keeping her sister alive.. Gaia might have to make a promise and a choice that will affect their lives forever. In this new town, Sylum there was different rules and laws that everyone must obey against otherwise there will be conseqences. When people are mysteriously dying upon leaving the town, Gaia and her new group of friends try to figure out the cause of it and try to find some way around it. That's not the only mystery that is surrounding the town. People keep having babies and only few are girls. Is this just bad luck, or is there something more to it? What Gaia discovers might be truly horrifying and unexplainable. But Gaia isn't the only newcomer to town. Someone else has turned up, someone from her recent past who has come looking for her. Leon. Ah, aint true love grand? Yes. But while that might seem like an overwhelming joy to have Leon there with her.. when Gaia is forced between a rock and a hard place.. she doesn't know what choice to make. Either way she will be hurting someone. So what does she do? Try to work her way around the problem and try to get make the best decision possible. I know some people didn't like this book as much as the first, or felt the characters were vastly different but I don't think that's the case at all. Gaia was still the same girl she has always been.. but sometimes she has to make choices and decisions that she wish she wouldn't have to. We see different layers to Leon. Not only is he the boy we met in Birthmarked, but since Gaia left the Enclave.. Leon was punished, and he has been through so much and that itself would change a person. We see him more passionate, dangerous and utterly in love with Gaia. I think I fell more in love with him in this book. We have new characters such as Peter and Will, brothers who end up liking the same girl.. who likes someone else. The leader of the town, the Matrarc. Banished girls who Gaia befriends. I was going to rate this 4 stars, but then I remember on my re-read of this book, I could not put it down. It was addicting, and the angsty /tension between Gaia and Leon made me finish this book within a day. This book was a thrilling ride, and it sets up for the final book in the series which I cannot wait for especially with what will be happening, and that alone.. is a must read. Rating: 5/5
