SOBBING INCOHERENTLY. WILL REVIEW PROPERLY AT A LATER DATE.

Read Harder Challenge 2016: Read a middle grade novel Read a book by or about a person that identifies as transgender What intrigued me: Michelle gave a great review and it covered 2 of the items from the Read Harder challenge. What I liked: This is a great book, that handles the subject matter very well. I would find this a difficult subject to broach, and exposing it to kids earlier would make it less taboo. What I didn't like: I thought the passing reference to hormone treatment might be a little much for a the age range, but kids this days do have free access to a wealth of information. Favorite quote: "...Scott looked at George as if his sibling made sense to him for the first time. George had never been gladder to have an older brother."

I'm a huge Laughing Warrior fanfic fan, and I've always loved her narrative style and her ability to make female characters that aren't put together and perfect. Her women are written with well-controlled mild neurosis, and they aren't always out to be someone's girlfriend. They provide and serve the plot. Lilli is a female voice that is flawed and imperfect. Just like a real person, which is why these characters feel real. She doesn't just give over to feminine comfort when a man decides he loves her; she is worried that it could mess with her plans. And in true male fashion Isaac has made his mind up that she's his and that's all there is to it. I've read some reviews mentioning a cliffhanger ending, and I will dispute that, however. The reason for Lilli coming to town is dealt with and resolved, the author has simply set up the fact that she is writing a series. It shows me she has a clear plan of where all this is leading, so I will happily put all my Isaac and Lilli feels in her competent hands ...

The Shifters Unbound books are always intense reads for me. I really enjoy the world that Ashley has created with the shifters being isolated and treated as second class citizens. There's a lot of room for play here to see how the worldview itself will, in the future, shift and change or stay stagnant. I find it so interesting in the various books how the different types of shifters butt heads with each other as they establish dominance. This one is no exception, there's a lot of subtle and not so subtle power plays at work here. Spike is a jaguar shifter. He's also a fighter and a tracker. He's such an underestimated character with other shifters thinking he's nothing but muscle. I liked seeing how those attitudes changed. Ashley always brings the heat and this one is no exception. Myka is a human who brings huge change to Spike's life. There's great chemistry here and Myka is no pushover, I like that she's tough and able to stand up for herself. My favourite quote from the story: From Spike: "I want more than survival, and so do you. I say we come together--and live." Who could resist a comment like that? I'm a sucker for the younger shifters so Jordan was a treat here. This is a great installment for the shifter series. If you're already a fan get reading this if you've not read Ashley before then I'd really recommend you start with Pride Mates the first in the series which will really set you up with world-building because while this story is a fantastic addition I don't think it works as a standalone.

I orginally borrowed this book from the library for my mom because I knew it would be right up her alley. I only read it because I had just finished a particularly disturbing novel right before bed (one that set my teeth on edge and had me disgusted with humanity) and I needed a palate cleanser, so to speak. Heaven Is for Real did not disappoint. I didn't go to sleep until this endearing and uplifting story was concluded. How could you not believe in Heaven after reading about Colton's grand adventure? How could you not want to?

Oh my gosh, what was that?! I had always wondered what ever happened to my lovable little sociopath John Cleaver after I Don't Want to Kill You, and now I have a very satisfying conclusion (?). I was hooked for the whole ride. And when I say "ride" it's an understatement. The conclusion did seem a bit haphazard to say the least. To quote John: I was used to violence, to death and pain and terror, but this was too much, and too random. All the deaths made John's team seem expendable. If the goal was to have John by himself by the end of the book, why give us so many characters to get attached to. I really think Diana deserved a better death. All in all, this was an incredible, gripping story; 5/5.

I don't know how to feel right now. I love A Million Junes with a great passion and I was scared to read this one because I don't like time travel stories at all, no matter the significance in the plot. Because it's just not possible. I know griffins and elemental magic aren't either, but this is different and you know it. Maybe because you can explain how water powers work, but try and explain time travel. Oh, look, you can't. I went into this after reading some reviews (make your own opinions, Sara) so I was ready for the insta-love, which is present. But. But. One of Natalie's personality traits is that she feels greatly on either side of the spectrum of emotions--whether she's happy or sad. Natalie feels quickly and hugely. Natalie and Beau were fate, they were meant to be together, and they both felt it. They started off being attracted simply physically and after talking, about everything, they started to fall in love. Sure, they kissed and felt more than they maybe should have from where the were in the relationship but I still felt their relationship grow and HOW COULD YOU NOT WANT TO BE WITH THE ONLY OTHER PERSON IN THE WORLD WHO UNDERSTANDS YOU. I know why the book ended where it did, I do, but I think it still hurt the story. I loved Megan and Natalie a lot, (it's so easy for author's to brush aside the supposed best friend when they're out of town, but Megan and Natalie's friendship was still part of the story) and I think that it should have been harder for Natalie to decide to do the thing at the end without thinking more about her. I'm trying not to put my own opinions and what I would have done in the situation on Natalie, because she's definitely not me, but it's hard to take the "family matters" mindset out of my head. Thoughts on the time travel: I thought that the explanations of the time travel were well done, and it wasn't even horribly boring to read them. I hate time travel stories (have I mentioned that yet?) where the heroes are fighting and rushing to save the world and I'm like, you can travel through time, what's the rush? But in The Love That Split the World there was a rush. There was a reason Natalie couldn't tell Alice (or anyone else) what was happening or how she felt. I mean, I know she wouldn't have even met Alice. But it still bothered me and I needed to know that Natalie and Alice are still friends in the new world. Thoughts on the personality/psyche/hallucination stuff: The research in this book is so evident, and not in an annoying information dump way (though there were times I wanted to throw the book against the wall so it'd move on and that's probably not a good sign). The information itself was interesting and every piece of it was relevant or realistic to mention. I wondered at times if Emily Henry spent more time researching hallucinations than she did actually writing this book, and maybe she did, but every bit of Henry's understanding was obvious and it therefore made it easy to read through the aforementioned explanations. I'm a sucker for any mention of MBTI (and that unexplained love languages line [I'm such a nerd]) and I'm naturally interested in any and all psychological/personality tidbits. I felt more connected to the story, and to the author, because of it. And there's something to say for that, when you learn more about an author as a person through their writing, or even following them on social media, you're more likely to love their work. Unless of course you feel negatively toward the person, then the opposite is true. Closing Thoughts You know that feeling, when you finish a book, and you just want to stroke the cover and hug it and smell it and wish you could read it again for the first time? I rarely have that happen to me for 4 star books. Sure, there were problems I can't overlook. But I loved the writing (the style and the foreshadowing) and the characters and the relationships between each of them. And to me, those are the most important aspects of a well written story. I'm thinking about this book too deeply now. I liked it. You should read it, and maybe you'll like it too. Edit:  Oh my gosh the title of the book just hit me and I can't handle it.

"Silver Bay" by Jojo Moyes is an extremely enjoyable read, told from the perspectives of the main characters at different plot points throughout the story. Michael Dormer is a wheeler dealer from London, set on making Australia's Silver Bay his latest professional coup. Planning a high end vacation development, he doesn't count on how the good folks of Silver Bay will impact his deal and his heart. Liza McCullen is a young mother trying to escape her awful past and build a future for her precocious daughter, Hannah. Along with her aunt Kathleen, they run the Silver Bay hotel and guide whale watching tours for visitors to their area. As the development begins to take on a life of its own, both Michael and Liza will need to face their feelings and beliefs to save the bay and quite possibly, themselves. "Silver Bay" was truly a wonderful read. Readers will be charmed by Hannah and Kathleen and baffled by Liza. Michael starts off in the story as a guy looking out for himself, but by the end his care for Liza's family shines through every page. Moyes kept the story, and the characters back stories moving right along by interweaving points of view throughout the book. I laughed out loud at some of Kathleen's chapters, and was absolutely in love with Hannah. While this is not a book for the faint of heart, it is absolutely a moving story that is worth reading every page. I'm not a huge fan of novels set in other countries, but Jojo Moyes has definitely won me over
Something different than I usually read, but I liked it, made me think.

An unsolicited Advanced Reader Copy was provided by the publisher for review. Quotes have been pulled from an ARC and may be subject to change. This is told from four different characters and personalities. Sometimes I dislike reading stories that are told in different viewpoints because I can never remember who is who. The characters started to sound alike and I had to remind myself who is who causing me to go back and forth between chapters to remember. The setting in this novel was definitely realistic. The terror in finding yourself quarantined in a mall with no where to go and no one to trust. So many people dying and the will to survive is high. But how do you survive the plague? I can understand why the government would keep information from the people because chaos would ensue, but to consider that the rest of the world could also be contaminated is a higher priority than the needs of the citizens in the mall. The fear in the characters tone was clearly evident, and I'm a sucker for virus-like plots considering my favourite movies like Outbreak and Contagion include realistic plots. I wished there was more emphasis on the virus and not on what the characters were doing. It felt like the middle of the book was a bore, and the ending and excitement was stuffed in at the end to create a page-turning climax. I didn't even know there was another book because I thought it would be a stand alone book. I'm glad it isn't, because the ending was epic. Quotes "Funny how a guy could completely freak you out, but also be the one person you trusted." --Ryan

One knows that a concept or an idea has become firmly established as a trope once it becomes the butt of jokes and satire. This is what's happened to the concept of the "shadowy government agency". Once upon a time, the mere idea of secret agencies and men in black would have sent chills up and down a person's spine at the mere thought. Nowadays, when one says "men in black" one is apt to imagine Will Smith and Tommy Lee Jones chasing down aliens while making wisecracks along the way. Not to say that's a bad thing, of course, but it just goes to show how some ideas that once elicited fear can have their sting taken out of them over the course of time. However, there are some writers who can still take a trope like that and make it work in terms of horror - not in the way it used to be used, but by turning it inside out and making it seem stranger and more eerie than it ever did. That's what Jeff VanderMeer does in the second book of his Southern Reach Trilogy, titled Authority. Taking off after the events of the first book, Annihilation, Authority is told primarily from the point of view of Control, real name John Rodriguez, who's been assigned to the Southern Reach by his bosses in order to figure out what's really going on. However, he quickly realises that there are secrets within secrets, and that getting to the bottom of it all isn't going to be easy - least of all when there are secrets buried within himself that he'd much rather leave alone. Right from the start, Authority shows itself to be a very different beast from its predecessor, though they also share quite a few similarities. Both novels play on the fear of the unknown, but they do so in very different ways. In Annihilation, the "unknown" was the vast wilderness of Area X, of what lived in it, and what happened to it and to the other expeditions that had gone before. In Authority, on the other hand, the "unknown" manifests as the byzantine workings and dark corners of the Southern Reach, as well as Control's strange past and the events that happen around him as he proceeds with his investigation. Also, much of the horror in Annihilation is external, something that happens to the biologist, whereas in Authority it's internal, something Control experiences in his own head. Since narrative style changes a lot about how the reader experiences the story, it's interesting to note that the point-of-view narration used in the two books is very different, as well: Annihilation is told from first person point of view, while Authority is told from third person limited point of view. I find this shift interesting, especially given the nature of each book's take on horror as mentioned above. One would think that Authority would be better served if it were narrated in first person: after all, a lot of it occurs inside Control's head, and who better to talk about that sort of thing than Control himself? But using third person narrative style in Authority adds what I think is a necessary amount of distance. The reader wants to know what's going on in Control's head, of course, but knowing it too intimately also ruins the storyline, and what would otherwise be scary devolves into mere hysteria. On the other hand, first person narrative style works well with the Biologist in Annihilation, because the intimacy of that narrative style creates a sense of incompleteness about the narrative, and therefore enhances the sense of fear one feels while reading the novel. The reader only experiences what the Biologist experiences, and since any experience of something the same magnitude as what happens in Annihilation must, necessarily, be incomplete, the reader is left to fill in the gaps with some truly horrifying imagery and ideas. It is this ability to suit the type of narrative to the desired effect is one of the reasons why I think VanderMeer is an excellent writer of horror and weird fiction. He could have chosen to write Authority from the first person perspective, if only to keep it uniform with Annihilation, but instead chooses to tell the story in a way that creates the greatest amount of fear possible. As someone who prefers her horror to be more cerebral than visual, that's something I can readily appreciate. I also find the story itself intriguing in the way it turns the typical "shadowy government agency" trope inside out. Part of what makes shadow agencies so scary is that no one knows what goes on within them. They are opaque to the outsider, who only knows them as a looming threat that can do whatever it thinks necessary in order to protect what it needs to protect, to hide what it needs to hide. They are scary because no one can understand them beyond the influence they exert on the outside world. But Control's involvement shows the nature of a shadow agency from the inside out. He shows the decrepitude, the decay, and the destruction that occurs to such an agency from within. He shows that, even when the agency was new, it was already falling apart, because by its very nature such agencies are doomed from the very beginning. If they are not destroyed from without, they are destroyed from within, eaten alive by the secrets they try to keep. The keeping of secrets as large as the one the Southern Reach tries to keep is impossible, and it is a poison that, at the end of the novel, implodes the Southern Reach itself and effectively ends it. This is, I think, quite scary, because this process isn't limited to fiction: it's something that can happen to any organisation, anywhere, at any time. While the view from the outside looking in can be terrifying, sometimes seeing things from the inside looking out can be just as frightening. Intertwined with the above are Control's own secrets - not least his involvement with the Southern Reach's parent organisation, and the fact that he is a pawn of that organisation. Control is, himself, stuffed full of secrets, and when he gets to the bottom of those secrets he is shattered, and he has to pick up the pieces of himself again, to find himself again - much like Ghost Bird, in fact. This is just as scary as the gradual unraveling of the Southern Reach - scarier, maybe, in some respects, because Control's fears, his "madness", could easily be our own. However, while I did enjoy reading Authority, and did think it was scary, it wasn't without its problems. This book felt very much slower than the first one, and while I understand that that's just the nature of the narrative being what it is, I do wish it had been a bit faster. It dragged something fierce in the middle portion, partly due, I think, to VanderMeer's language. While I understand that the language was necessary to convey the strange, dreamlike nature of Control's existence, I did find myself skimming over a lot of it and finding out that I hadn't really missed anything by the time I got to the end of the novel. Some tightening up could have been accomplished there, I think, without sacrificing the nature and goal of the narrative. Overall, Authority is very much in the spirit of its predecessor, albeit it does so from a different perspective. The connections between it and Annihilation might not be immediately apparent, but they become clear once one gets past the first chapter. It is also very much a scary read, though for different reasons than Annihilation. However, on the whole it feels like a weaker book than the first one, sagging as it does in the middle third. Hopefully, though, the third book will pick up the slack, and bring this series to an appropriately creepy conclusion.

I went into reading this book hesitantly hopeful. There have been a lot of books done with the teacher/student trope, so I was keeping my fingers crossed that this one would bring something new to the table. I was not disappointed. This book was steamy from the beginning with a whole hell of a lot of sexual tension. I loved both of the main characters--Blair and Gray. It was really refreshing to see Blair really being able to help Gray overcome his past, while at the same time he was helping her as well. Their relationship definitely wasn't one sided which I really appreciated. Another bright spot of this book is the ending. I absolutely loved the fact that Blair struggled through law school in a very realistic way, and at the end she decided that it wasn't the best choice for her. The twist with her sister really surprised me since I was pegging her classmate the entire time as the one who was leaking information. And then the ending was superb. No grand gesture, just two people getting past their issues and moving on together. No lie, I devoured this book. Even the preview for the next book in this series sounds fantastic. I've already got it on my to-read list and can't wait for it to be released. If you're looking for a book that does great things on the student/teacher trope, has some fantastic characters, heaps of steaminess, and a little political intrigue, you need to pick up this book right now. Highly recommended. **I received an ARC in exchange for an honest review.
I'm feeling a lot of things. Good things. Add this to 'books I wish I had at 14-17'.

Ready Player One is not an epic or the Next Great American Novel. It's not a thinly veiled metaphor or an examination on the human condition. It's not designed to make you question the futility or realize the joy of human existence. It's just FUN! It's fun, a delight, and a joy to read. The premise is simple - in a futuristic world that's gone to hell in a hand basket due to pollution and overpopulation, Wade is one of the millions who prefer to spend their time in the OASIS, a true virtual reality. He's mostly interested in solving the quest left behind by the OASIS' owner (think Steve Jobs meets Howard Hughes) to win his vast fortune, which most people think is impossible. But when Wade solves the first clue, the game is afoot! And here's where the fun comes in. The quest is contingent upon the player's knowledge of 70s and 80s pop culture. This means that players routinely drop references ranging from music to video games to movies, so that people who enjoy those types of things (okay, okay, nerds! I'm a nerd! Or a geek. Whichever nomenclature works for you), can't go half a page without stumbling across a delightful reminder of nerd/geek culture. Wade takes his Firefly-class ship  Vonnegut  and orders a Pan-Galactic Gargle Blaster after sheathing his Vorpal blade. Swoon! You know Wade is going to be victorious, because of course he is. It's that kind of book. Granted, there are  a few secondary character deaths, but because there hasn't been any real time allotted to them above a few pages, and because Wade himself isn't thrown into real turmoil, they function more as a way to establish that the Big Bad is really big and bad than any character development or emotional wreckage to sift through,   but these do nothing to quell your enjoyment. With that knowledge, you can sit back and enjoy the ride!

It's weird to read what's essentially official/sanctioned fanfiction and in the end, all I could think was that I've read so many better fanfics. There was nothing wrong with this book and I do think the plot, plus the whole idea of quantum entanglement, was pretty awesome. But it just lacked some excitement, and I don't say that lightly. I spent a few weeks in Turkey a few years ago and of course I visited Istanbul, I've been inside the Hagia Sofia (or Ayasofya, as it's written in this book) and I've even been in the massive underground cistern (Basilica Cistern) that features prominently in the book. I can picture it perfectly, so you'd think that if anything, I'd love this book for choosing such great settings. I think the main problem in the end is that although the Natasha Romanoff in this book did look and sound like Scarlett Johanssen's Black Widow in my head, she lost a lot of the wow factor and everything that makes me love the character, rather than just like her. The new characters, Alex Manor and Ava, just ended up being kind of bleh teenagers with an even more bleh romance. The focus of the story, on sisterhood and family, was appealing if a little overdone. So basically the plot was great, the setting was great, the themes were great (with the exception of the obligatory teen romance), but the execution fell flat. Plus, there were enough editing mistakes that they became a distraction. I noticed this in the official Marvel Daredevil book too, so if that's related, the proofing and copyediting people really need to step up their game. I think the biggest gripe I have is the "show, don't tell" problem of this book. There was a lot of telling and not so much showing. As much as I love the Black Widow character, I didn't feel for her here despite excellent reasons I mean, c'mon, long lost little brother?!? . I almost wish that some of the talented fanfic writers I've found over the years had gotten a chance to try their hand with the same plot and characters - but then again, there's something about the lack of constraints in fanfiction that makes it easier for authors to write characters that readers can emotionally connect with, even when they are borrowing the characters from their original creators. What I really wish is that Marjorie Liu could write a full length Black Widow novel. I've read her other works (Dirk & Steele #2, Shadow Touch, in particular) and she handles the beauty, menace, and mystery of Russia perfectly. I suppose she's too busy in her career to be doing these little projects though, which feels like Marvel trying to cash in on the popularity of YA publishing.

I was charmed by this book. Even with the goofy dialogue! The story is somewhat over-the-top but it's lighthearted and fun. It was easy for me to overlook the silliness. Tristan is utterly adorable and it was so cute watching him explore his sexuality. He's a charmer through and through. I enjoyed watching him think a million different things at one time. A very loveable character indeed. Michael is sexy. Enough said. An utterly sweet and heartwarming book.

I read this book quickly, enjoying the strange ride it took me on. It was an interesting story about four people that can't really be described as morally good. Carl, when discovering the powerful lullaby, is unable to control himself and uses it frequently when he is aggravated. He is the father figure of the group and although he does plenty of bad things he ultimately wants to do the right thing for the greater good. Helen uses the songs powers to kill for money and that's not the worst thing she does. Despite this I found her likeable and fun. Mona is probably the most likeable and genuinely good character but even she was manipulative and sly. Although I liked her the most and did feel she wanted what was best for everyone. Oyster wants to discover the song to cull all of humanity (well all but a few slaves) and have himself and Mona become the new Adam and Eve, he is preachy and pretentious and often got on my nerves. He shows his true colours eventually. This would probably have gotten another star if I didn't feel the author was intentionally trying to drop big reveals on me that were never actually surprising ( Helen is the Sarge, woah shocker. Carl isn't who he says he is, goodness me! .) I'm not sure if the hints were meant to be so obvious or if it was just bad writing. Plus the talk of necrophilia squicked me out a bit and I don't think it was needed, it didn't really add much to the story. Overall I enjoyed the book and found it a fun and easy read. Although I still don't know what all the hype over Chuck Palahniuk is about, good writer but not life changing.

I'm torn on this story. It wasn't bad, it just didn't really leave a memorable impression on me. And it kind of dragged a bit. I didn't read the previous in this series and while I've seen some reviews state you should so the other characters as well as how Dylan and Olivia know one another is better understood, I didn't feel like I missed anything. From the gist, Olivia's father is a philanderer who kept two families for most of Olivia's life until he was outed. Obviously his legitimate family take issue with what happened. I'm glad to see they don't hold their half-siblings responsible, but yeah, what a horrible thing to find out. Olivia was an okay character. She has worked her way to her job, and though she has a family made of money, she's very independent. I liked that. I liked that she had things happen in her past (father's lies and her ex) that made her wary of relationships. They worked. For a time. Because after a while, it started getting old. One minute she's ready to move forward and the next, she's questioning everything. I understand this would be logical, but she was written to be absolute and then a few chapters later, she's questioning everything. For someone who, once she sets her mind on something, she sticks to it, Olivia, when it came to Dylan flip-flopped so much, I felt bad for the guy. And the thing with her losing her baby... I get it. But again, she was so absolute and used it as a way to make herself the victim just in case Dylan chose to leave her. I am glad she finally had a kick in the butt to seek help because of Meg's situation. She really was being very unfair expecting everyone to get why she wouldn't want to try for another baby or talk about it. For most of this story, I really did feel like she wasn't into the relationship as Dylan was, that though she "accepted" her feelings, she didn't really do anything to prove it. Dylan was great. I'm glad to see though there's the hint that he enjoyed women, it was blatant, rehashed, or obvious. I especially loved how the moment he set his sights on Olivia, there was no one else. In far too many stories, the H will find a love interest, but if he can't have her, still go sleep around with a ton of other women, all while "thinking of" or "dreaming about" or "fantasizing over" the one they want. It always makes the relationship feel cheap to me because I couldn't imagine wanting someone so much I could be with others. I love how he pushed Olivia, made her open her eyes to the bigger picture. I loved that he didn't let her get away with anything. I wasn't too keen on his relationship with Meg, though. From the moment he went to see her, I could see the plot point. And it annoyed me. He might not have been screwing other women, but we're made to believe another woman has his attention and to cause our h jealousy because of her history. And Meg really did rely on his far too much and Dylan didn't seem to get that until it was brought to his attention. Because really, it's great your friends with an ex, but you should probably explain things better to your current so things don't get awkward or uncomfortable. The secondary characters were good. I wanted to shake Big to get him to see what his cousin was doing. I did want to know how things progressed with him after his cousin's influence was gone. The siblings, I know they have their own stories, so I won't touch on them. I do wish there was a bit more of how they came to be married and whatnot. While the epilogue was great, that glimpse, it just seemed rushed. We spent so much time trying to get Olivia to this point and then it happens and it's over just like that. So yeah. It wasn't a bad book, but just not memorable.

What other book can a crime novelist read while cruising the Nile? I remembered whodunnit from my previous read, but not the howdunnit. It takes a long time to get to the murder, from what I recall of other Christies, but she describes the Nile atmosphere perfectly - I thought my fellow passengers would drop dead at any moment!

This book took me forever to get through and by that I mean almost two weeks. That's a long time for me when I can normally knock out a book this size in 2-3 days. I actually bought this book years ago and couldn't get into it but since it's the Booksplosion book of the month, I decided to give it another try. So what slowed me down was the story's plot and the writing style. There was a lot of "telling" going on and not enough "showing". I felt that as a reader the author wasn't trusting me to guess what emotions the characters were feeling or what their motives were. I was basically spoon fed every detail and I'm just not a big fan of that kind of writing style. I also thought the plot took a very long time to get interesting. The story finally grabbed my interest when Jack finds Shadowslayer . After that I was more dedicated to finishing the book than I was before. As I read the book, some parts did surprise me so I was glad about that but overall I thought the ending wrapped up a little too cleanly. I know this book is a series and I was looking for a little more setup and suspense for the sequels. Another problem I had was with the character development. I admired Jack's honor through the book but I never developed an emotional attachment to him. I'm not sure if Jack's story will continue on in the series or not, but his and most of the other characters felt very flat to me. Everyone seemed to focus on only one emotion. Linda was always worried, Becka would snap when things weren't going her way, Will and Fitch always tried to be care-free, etc. I couldn't really tell you the difference between Fitch and Will except that Will is stronger and well muscled. They felt like they were the same person and I think the story would've been better if the author wrote them as one person. The only character I saw that seemed more rounded was Ellen and possibly Leander. Overall, the story was interesting though not gripping. I liked it but I didn't love it. There are some good action scenes, a touch of romance and mystery to enjoy if the writing style doesn't bother you. I would recommend this book to younger fantasy lovers because this book has a strong middle grade feel rather than young adult, and I think the content is plenty clean for that age group, minus some very minor language.

Baseball is a sport that I have a hard time supporting. A few years ago (approx. 8 to be exact) I had seen a live game between the Boston Red Sox and the Toronto Blue Jays. I actually enjoyed it quite a bit, it's a totally different animal live. It comes across as lively and exciting. However, I cannot sit down and watch it on television - just doesn't do it for me. That being said, I seem to enjoy fiction about the sport. I'm a big fan (and quite possibly one of the only ones) of 2005's Fever Pitch as well as Rookie of the Year and the Angels in the Outfield movies from my youth. Actually, when I was a youngster going through the sixth grade, we had bi-weekly creative writing assignments and I would always write short stories about baseball or hockey; sports in general really. I can't remember if they were ever any good - truth be told; they were probably terrible - but I loved writing them. Anyway, this brings me to the subject of this review. I've been on a real Stephen King kick lately. I've read 4 of his books so far this year (The Dark Tower 1 and 2, Under The Dome, ..On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft) and have just finished my 5th, Blockade Billy. Clocking in at a dismal 81 pages, Blockade Billy certainly doesn't overstay its welcome. King lets the story take the tone of a sit down interview; a casual conversation with someone knowledgeable of the sport. He builds the tension well over the short amount of time he's given himself - the reader is slowly given reason to suspect that Billy might not "be all there". King lets his love of baseball shine through here, you believe that this is an era of the game that he misses fondly. He seems to take subtle digs at the state of the sport today; taking the opposition to "big money contracts" and the state of baseball's business aspect. Also, King throws in a ton of old baseball lingo but I never really felt lost in the conversation. It may have something to do with the fact that I know just enough about the game to get by - I have no idea how this will translate into the average Joe. When I had finished, I sort of thought that maybe it had ended just a little too soon (I'm slowly becoming a fan of longer, more detailed fiction). After having a couple of days to sit on it, I think the amount of story is just perfect. This being the first short story I've read from him; it has me excited for this fall's "Full Dark; No Stars" short story collection. I'll be picking that up for sure.

A manager I work with once told me that he was told in a training seminar that 1 in 4 people you interact with daily does not like you. Off subject, but doesn't this sound like a slightly off-the-wall, existentially downbeat topic for a milquetoast corporate training session? Imagine being able to know what others think of you, or, more precisely, having them unwittingly and uncontrollably vomit out their most secret thoughts to you. That is the dilemma the protagonist of Joe Hill's second novel, Horns, is faced with. Ignatius Perrish wakes up one morning with a pair of eponymous horns growing out of his temple. He has more to worry about than the ordinary subconscious nastiness of others though. His girlfriend was raped and murdered one year ago and everyone in his small town thinks he did it, including members of his own family. But maybe he can use his new superpowers to find out who did kill her. And make a lot of devil jokes. I did like this book and I'm a fan of Joe Hill's writing style. I appreciate that the flashbacks were necessary to fill out the story but they might have been a bit too long. Hearing about how Ig met Merrin went on for pages and meanwhile--in the present he's got freaking horns growing out of his head and smoke pouring from his nostrils! Cmon! That's what we want to hear about. Like many horror novels, I can't say I completely got everything at the end but I was definitely interested. Hill really kept me guessing too: Could Ig have had something to do with Merrin's death? What is the bad thing he keeps referring to that caused him to sprout horns? Is that really Old Scratch knocking at the door and does he want my immortal soul or does he just want to hang out and listen to the White Album backwards? Funny, at times poignant and depending on your tastes, maybe a bit blasphemous which might either offend you or make the book even funnier. Oddly enough, while Hill writes in a style similar and yet sufficiently distinct from his Dad (Stephen King, perhaps you've heard? ), they both are at their scariest when writing short stories. I was never scared reading this but I was entertained and thoughtful.

I heaved a heartfelt sigh at the end of this book. Because it's over and  it ended happily. (that's kind of a spoiler, right?) But I'll admit there were parts that left me a little underwhelmed. And I'm not sure how to put my finger on it. It might have just been too much build up, where I was so very excited and then... well, it's done. But over all, I'm happy with the ending of the series and where it leaves the over arching Vampire Academy universe.

Dude!!!!!!!!!!!!!! This book was crazy!!!!!!!!! I can't believe they actually killed Heath! ! Why did they do that?? I really loved Heath, I cried when stupid Kalona killed him. And Zoey had just had an arguement with Stark, and her soul just shatters!! And poor Stark has to live with the fact that as her warrior, he totally failed. Awe.. I love Stark and I loved Heath too, so I guess it makes sense they would have to do something with their little love triangle . Just awesome. This book really makes good of the use of the phrase "this shit has hit the fan". lol.

6 devastating stars! This book was so incredibly beautiful and perfect. The Tied Man is a book that is not for the faint of heart. It's hardly considered a romance. It's an extremely dark, torturous, gruesome, heartbreaking novel with little good times and easy moments. I'm still so in shock by the things I've read in this book. Sadistic is taken to another level. "Feeling bad" for Finn is a complete understatement of what I felt. I honestly don't know how he hasn't completely shut down and committed suicide long ago. He was living in a literal earthly incarnation of hell. Everything about this book disgusted me and gutted me. I was absolutely horrified by the sh*t that went down. Lilith was such an amazing heroine. I love a strong heroine, and she dealt with everything with such strength. She didn't judge Finn and was the only person to treat him like a person instead of a whore or a piece of property. She was outspoken, witty and resilient to the end. I even really loved the secondary characters. Nat, Gabriel and Henry all had completely different personalities that added to the story. Blaine was a completely twisted, sick, manipulative evil wench of a person. The emotions in this book were overwhelming and it was so beautifully, well-written. It was so engaging and addictive. I was horrified, but couldn't look away. I physically cringed while reading. Everything is so perfectly detailed, and the author doesn't try to protect the readers from the gory-details. It was bold and unique. I also really loved the dialogue in this book. The character interaction was so well written and I felt so inspired to read Finn's lines and the fact that he could still have such a sense of humor. It was all so witty and charismatic. This is one of those books that deeply affects you and doesn't leave you. It haunts you long after you read that last page. I really need book two because I need more of them! The momentary discomfort was nothing at all compared to the realisation that she was finding refuge in my flawed embrace.
Just didn't have the time. I'll get back to this one.
Very interesting. I went into this book with low expectations, but I actually really liked it!

Left cold by this tale of the apocalypse and its aftermath. As the title might suggest, the book deals with the before, during and after of a series of global cataclysms that effectively wipe out the human race. In the "before," Julie is a mathematician that seems to specialize in analyzing big data. She's working with the FBI to find a pattern in a weird series of kidnappings and robberies. In the "after," a small group of mutated survivors take short jumps back in time, to steal supplies but also kidnap children, hoping that they will add healthy genetic material to the human race and ensure the survival of the species. I found all the characters in the book to be cold and unlikable. Likeability actually isn't something I require in a fictional character, but in its absence, I want something else interesting. Deep complexity of character, great dialogue, unusual motivations. Julie does math and dislikes most people and is pregnant. Pete, one of the Six born after the apocalypse, is angry and yells at people. Neither make for characters I wanted to spend time with, even in a novel of under 200 pages. Then, there were elements of the book that were never explained. Who created the Shell and the time-traveling technology? Was the end of the world caused by the planet re-balancing itself or was it a terrorist or extraterrestrial act? Is this the only group of survivors or are there others? I don't mind stories where the readers aren't privy to every piece of information, but in this case, it felt like being mysterious just for the sake of being mysterious.

Midnight Riot is the kind of book that people like me, absolute anglophile and devoted BBC lover, couldn't help but like. The humor and the texture to the narrative in this book reads delightfully British, but in a fashion that suggests that England isn't just Jane Austen or Charles Dickens. It's also Doctor Who, Blake's Seven, Being Human, Law and Order: UK, and Luther. It's upper crust and working class. It's a mix of past and present. Even deeper, it's the everyday lives of Britons, not all Northern European either. It was so refreshing to have a hero who is mixed-race, but seen as black by some; and to others, ethnically uncertain. He couldn't get on the tube without getting nervous looks from some people who had made up their mind what his place in their world was, without asking him about it. On any given day, due to how much sun he gets, some might think he's African, or some might think he's Arab. Peter is unselfconscious about his ethnicity, although very aware that not everyone is comfortable with it. His mother is Sierra Leonan, and her culture infuses him, from her attitude towards hard work, to her frugality, and her penchant for making food so spicy that he has to drink a liter of water to douse its fire. His father is a white former musician with a thirty year heroin habit, and that colors the narrative just as much, for we are not in a small degree who our parents make us. That is either due to rebelling against our parents or through a childhood of being shaped by their rearing. As a reader of black heritage, I have to say that it's good to see stories that feature characters of black ethnicity. There are a lot of our stories to tell, and they don't seem to see the light of day, and not in the diversity that reflects the black African disapora. I hope that more leads in urban fantasy novels in the future are of color, because it adds something to a read to see someone who is like you, at least in some small way. I enjoyed Peter's character. He's an insightful narrator, and full of wit. I liked seeing London through his perceptive gaze. The police procedural aspects were great. Better than watching an episode of a BBC cop show, because Peter explains the ins and out of the Metropolitan Police to a degree I have never caught onto in my varied viewing pleasures. Peter's acceptance of the workings of enormous wheels of bureaucracy turning in the Met makes what might have been boring, very fascinating, especially with his deadpan humor delivery (classic British wit). As I read this novel, I felt as though I had learned a lot more about the police in the UK, which is similar but different to the US. The paranormal aspects were good and rather unique. I like how magic is presented here. The way it leaves an essence (called a vestigium that has a taste, feel, and smell) that Peter is able to pick up. When he's recruited as an assistant and apprentice wizard to Thomas Nightingale, for a part of the Met that deals with the odd and magical crimes, he finds the niche he'd been searching for, with this inquisitive mind, and his insight into science. He doesn't take things at face value, but he's open-minded enough to accept that London has denizens that are not human, such as vampires, trolls, and malevolent ghosts who draw energy from those they possess, leading to their gruesome and violent deaths. It was interesting to watch Peter and Nightingale use a mix of police investigative techniques and magic to solve the inexplicable attacks of violence that seemingly normal London citizens are perpetrating against each other. He also comes to realize that the rivers of London are alive, gods and goddesses, if you will. And Peter needs their help to keep the peace in London, but also to resolve the territorial disputes between The Old Man of the River and Mama Thames, who both believe that they have a right to rule the Thames, and their tributaries. Ben Aaronovitch has already secured his place in pop culture as the writer of Doctor Who novels. It's great to see him put the fruits of his imagination to the page with this first in the Peter Grant series. After falling for Peter Grant, and his unforgettable narrative of London, he is going on my must read list.

Oh my god??? This book was one of the wildest fucking rides I've been on. Cassandra Clare is brutal, guys. So I'm going to get the bad out of the way first, which was really the reason why I took off one star. The romance. The fucking romance, guys. There are so many romances and they're all tangled up in each other and every single one was tiring to read about, especially Julian and Emma. I can only read so much about forbidden love angst, and I reached my limit like, 20 pages into the book. We get that you can't be together. There was so much angst I sort of dreaded coming up on scenes with them together. The same goes for the whole thing with Mark, Kieran and Cristina. I feel like heated kissing and angsting took up a lot of unnecessary space in the book. That being said, there was one romance I did enjoy: Kit and Ty. At first I was kind of simmering with rage because fucking Kit and Livvy kissed and I had to take a moment to put my book down and scream about how if Cassandra Clare made Kit/Livvy cannon I was going to sue for false advertising, dammit, but it looks like Kit/Ty's happening after all, though it's not the way I wanted or even imagined it would happen. They're slow burn all the way - Ty showing his comfort with Kit in ways that Kit recognizes and loves, and Kit feeling fiercely protective for Ty. They seem like the most believable romance to me. Or maybe I'm just a slow burn kind of person. As for the plot: holy shit. It was nicely-paced, for the most part, and jumped between viewpoints so that you couldn't stop reading. There was so much going on, but you didn't really get lost easily, and I really felt like some people wouldn't make it out alive. I could guess that Arthur was going to die and I'm glad he went the way he did - it was noble and brave of him. The incursions out of Los Angeles to Faerie and London and Idris were really nice and it was interesting to see how the Shadowhunters are getting on five years after The Mortal Instruments. There's a lot of conflict brewing up. The Clave continues to be completely incompetent. I'm really excited to see where the rest of the series takes us. One thing I find of particular interest is how current events have had an impact on the plot of this book pertaining to Zara Dearborn and her Cohort. Her call for Downworlder registries is reminiscent of the far right's prejudice against Muslims, and the bigotry of the Clave resonates even more in the current political climate. It was really interesting to see how that was explored in the context of the Shadowhunters universe. Also, I hate Zara Dearborn more than I've hated possibly any character in recent memory. Fucking choke. And the ending, dear god, the ending. I thought everything was going to be a-okay until the last ten or so pages and then EVERYTHING WENT TO SHIT. Robert Lightwood. Dead, along with the leniency he may have granted Julian and Emma, the good he does because his son loves a Downworlder. LIVIA BLACKTHORN. Oh, my god. My heart fucking broke in that moment and I spent the rest of the drive back kind of traumatized because LIVVY. I can't believe she would do that. I can't even imagine how the Blackthorns must be feeling - Ty and Julian especially. I'm so fucking sad now leave me to die

Sophie Hansa sets out to find her birth mother and discovers an entire birth world--the magical, hidden world of Stormwrack. Sophie's unexpected arrival in Stormwrack throws her birth family into turmoil. What could have been an interesting-if-stressful vacation turns scary when Sophie's adopted brother is kidnapped, and Sophie must involve herself inte h politics fo the fantasy world in roder to save him. I'm a sucker for a good "Narnia" book, where the protagonist is magically transplanted from our world to a fantasy world, but I usually dislike adult versions of this kind of story--maybe because it's harder to suspend disbelief when you're looking at the intricacies of a made-up world through an adult protagonist's eyes, instead of through the wondering, usually more accepting eyes of a child protagonist. That said, Dellamonica completely sold me on the secret world of Stormwrack--a collection of island nations where magic is used every day, the legal system is based on dueling, and politics are everything. Details of the world unfold under Sophie's eager scientific eye; she explores sea life, takes samples to compare to wildlife on Earth, and interrogates people she meets about cultures and customs, giving the reader an excellent introduction to the intricacies of island life. Though I liked Sophie as a character, my only readerly disagreement with the book was because of her modern, practical characterization. I blame my childhood obsession with Robin McKinley's The Blue Sword, but I was hoping Sophie would acclimatize to the fantasy world and leap into a little more piratical, swashbuckling action as the story progressed. Her relationships with the people she met came across as real and emotional, but otherwise Sophie seems to maintain a scientist's observational outlook on the world of Stormwrack, which left me as a reader feeling a bit left out--I wanted to be pulled more directly into the story. Overall the story is smoothly paced, with enough relationship tension and unanswered questions to keep readers guessing. I would recommend it as a crosssover book for young adult readers who are champing at the bit for the start of another good fantasy series.

I like Jane Eyre. I am not a classics reader, but I like Jane Eyre just fine. Bronte's writing is okay, but there lots of times where she was too descriptive. too long, even. Oh well, at least now i get to bash Mr. Rochester. LOL Jane is admirable when she was eleven years old. She's got spunk, to say it so bluntly. i like that she says what she wants to say. When she was already a governess, she's mindful already of her words and actions. Was it because of her education? Maybe. While i abhor her stoicism during the church scandal, i liked Jane in the end. Strong, stubborn, with principle. I believe Mr. Rochester has no redeeming qualities. Rude, arrogant, manipulative. Oh, and he's a liar as well. You'd think for an ugly gentleman, Bronte will make him likeable by writing him with a good and commendable personality. I guess she's going for unconventional? While i do not like Mr. Rochester (at all), i did not delight in the plight he was in when Jane Eyre sought him at the end of the book. The story was simple. The ending, too neat. Jane Eyre tried (and succeeded) in defying the conventions of her time. For that, I applaud her.
