(and as a side note I live in the same area that the characters do so it was pretty cool)

I feel nothing. I thought that by the end of this i would feel inspired, uplifted. I feel nothing. We All Looked Up was not what i expected it to be. I thought it would be filled with bucket lists, and poetic writing. I thought it would contain chapters where they are all looking up at the sky (like the cover), and start coming out with metaphors and beautiful quotes. It wasn't like that at all. And i don't know if the story is better or worse because of it. The character of Eliza had to be my favourite, i think it's because i identified the most with her, i too have had to deal with the 'slut' label. All the way through i was rooting for her, she was so real to me, the way she though and acted, and her philosophy. Everything is an event. I disliked Peter immensely, maybe 80% of the time. I hated how he let Stacy bully Eliza, and i hated how he refused to break up with Stacy despite the lack of love. What i hated the most, was how he idolized Eliza. He turned her from her own independent person, to his own Manic Pixie Dream Girl. He grew on me towards the end, the love for his sister made me warm up to him  But then that was all shot to hell when he died. I didn't even realize he had died until Eliza told Chad, and i hated that the most in the book, i wanted them to ALL be together for the end of the world, so the lack of Peter spoiled the ending for me Andy was a whole different story, i still don't know how i felt about him, like Peter he was obsessed with Eliza, however Andy's was worse, and it was kind of creepy. I like how he defied the whole 'druggy' stereotype. My favourite relationship was the one shared between Andy and Anita. I had mixed feelings about Anita. At first i totally identified with her. The pressures placed on us by our parents are horrid, and damaging. However, i grew bored of her after she started slut-shaming Eliza. She was jealous of Eliza which is sad, but that doesn't mean she gets to call her a slut, and hate her for it. Anita always talked about how slutty Eliza dressed and how the boys acted around her, it got on my nerves. I started liking her more towards the end though. I'm glad that we never knew for sure whether or not Ardon destroyed the world, i liked the open ending. I also loved the amount of philosophy brought into this book. We All Looked Up really makes you think about the way you're currently living your life and the people you spend it with. I hope people realize that life can be taken away at any given moment, so like Anita you should chase your dreams (or anything as cheesy as that).

I was captivated the first 75%, then was captivated again in the last 15% of the book. I'm in love with the world that Taylor has created and enjoyed each of the characters personalities. The author did a great job puling you into the world that feels similar to other stories but is so different in the detail. The flash backs/remembering her life did not interest me at all. While I know that we needed to know some of that, I felt like we didn't need to be shown as much as were. To me, I felt like we could have cut out some of the relationship parts with her and Akiva and just left in discovering Brimstone and his people's part in the story and some about the white wolf. I felt like Taylor did a great job at the end with her writing Karou's thoughts while she was coming to grips with her life and new discoveries. I felt bad for Akiva in the last chapter of the book but I'm excited to see how Karou deals with everything that she has learned.

3.5 stars I said in My Week in Books post last week that there were things about 17 First Kisses that I really liked and things about it that I really didn't like. And that's definitely the case with this book, but in the end I decided that the good outnumbered the bad and I would definitely recommend it. My favorite part of this book was the main character, Claire. For me, and maybe it's just because I liked this part the best, the book is really about Claire figuring out who Claire wants to be and I love that. It's something that seems to be popping up more and more in YA and even though this book puts a lot of focus on boys, Claire's strong, interesting personality manages to make the story really about Claire. Basically the idea of the story is that Claire is trying to find the perfect guy and we get to see her quest for the perfect guy, mostly for Luke, a fellow soccer player who she's really into, and also flashbacks of the other guys she's kissed. I always worry about flashback books, will I be more interested in the present? Will the flashbacks make it drag? At first I was worried here, the story goes back to when Claire is pretty young and some random boy kisses her while they're playing. But then the flashbacks become about more than Claire's history with boys. Through the flashbacks we see the boys, but we also see her friendship with Megan develop and also get to learn more about Claire's family and why her mother is so depressed. I was pleasantly surprised to find that I actually enjoyed the Megan/Claire storyline. Megan is kind of a witchy popular girl who, in middle school, takes Claire under her wing. Claire has always been a soccer-playing tomboy, but Megan, and Megan's friends, who are part of this ridiculous clique, which I think is called the Crowns (such a stupid part of the story), give Claire a makeover and get her interested in boys, but Claire is still strong enough to maintain her love of soccer and her own personality. Claire and Megan's relationship isn't always smooth sailing, but Rachael Allen did a good job of making Megan more than just a vapid, mean girl and knowing more about Megan made it easier for me to see why Claire wanted to be friends with her, which saved me a lot of frustration. Since my favorite part of the story was Claire it makes sense that I also really enjoyed her family. Her mom used to be the perfect, caring, doting mother, but after a tragedy, I'll let you read it and find out, she's turned into kind of a hermit and pretty much lets Claire's father try to take care of Claire and her younger sister. Claire's love of her mother and her desire for her mother to get better was really sweet and Claire's entire family added a really well done, interesting layer of depth to the story. Then there are all the boys. I'll be honest and say that the boys weren't my favorite part of the story. The whole Luke storyline, with Claire seeing him first and seeming to have a deeper connection to him, but Megan, who always gets the boy, going after him too, kind of bothered me. It's like I thought Claire was better than all of that. I did however like the ups and downs of Claire and Megan's friendship. As an adult it reminded me of a lot of friendships I was involved in or observed in high school. So that's all the good. The bad is mostly made up to two things: stereotypes and foreshadowing. As I mentioned Megan's the leader of this clique of girls called (I think) the Crowns and a clique like that is such an overdone, silly idea. There's also a fair amount of other stereotypes, there's some maybe not slut-shaming, but slut-categorizing; Claire's guy BFF who used to be fat, but lost weight and now gets a popular girl; and just kind of a lot of cliche high school roles. Then there's the foreshadowing. Rachael Allen did a lot of things at the end of the chapters like (I'm paraphrasing) "and after that our kisses would never be the same" or "if only I knew my whole world was about the change." I have no clue why authors do this or think it's a good idea, it's just totally unnecessary and lazy. I haven't heard anything about what people think of the end of this story, but I imagine it will be something people either love or hate. Personally, I loved it, it went along really well with the idea of the story being about Claire discovering herself, but I could also see why other people might not be into it. Bottom Line: I really liked what Rachael Allen did with Claire's story. 17 First Kisses is another book, like Nantucket Red and Since You've Been Gone, that's a great example of a teenage girl finding her way in the world. The friendship and family secondary stories here were also compelling and gave the story a nice depth. Even though I had some issues this is the best type of debut; it left me impressed, but also excited to see how Rachael Allen continues to develop. I received an electronic review copy of this book from the publisher via Edelweiss (thank you!). All opinions are my own. This review first appeared on my blog.

Allegiant didn't feel whole to me. I enjoyed the writing style, as I have since Divergent, but the characters didn't have nearly as much depth as they did in the first book, nor was the writing truly as addicting and delicious. I feel like the characters weren't accurately represented--they often made choices that didn't make sense to me. When I read a book, I become friends with the characters. I know I'm not as close to them as Roth must be, but I still know them to an extent and I don't think they would have acted the way they often did. For example, Tobias was described as so weak throughout this book. Yes, he is scarred; yes, he is broken; but he isn't weak in any sense of the word. And Tris was described as weak and scarred too. They both had weaknesses and problems, but neither Tobias nor Tris could ever be described as weak, yet they were often referred to as such and painted as such which irritated me. Tobias was also painted as incredibly impulsive and insecure. Insecure he is but he fights it with Tris' help; impulsive he isn't. Tris' and Tobias' jealous moments also seemed so petty. They love each other desperately, deeply, and fully, to the extent that they realize that a relationship isn't about whether or not you can forgive one another; it is about whether or not you still fit together which they always did, so when they acted out in anger because the other was spending time with an attractive individual of the opposite sex, I was incredibly frustrated. It felt like a complete breach in who they are as individuals and as a couple. Divergent was amazing, and I'm sad that the rest of the trilogy didn't make me fall head-over-heels in love as the beginning did.

I take my hat off to Courtney Summers who managed to write a main character who frustrated me and had my understanding at the same time. I also take my hat off because I heard this audiobook in three listens and I don't usually do that. Audio books take time with me (this one wasn't very long, but still), because I needed to know how this ended. Throughout the book I was all "Why are you doing that?" and thinking about the gazillion ways I would have done it differently, and then the solution at the end, from Liz, so simple. It really shows how a school can be it's own universe, removed from the reality of those around it, and how it works similarly, but differently than the rest of the world. I liked it, even though I really couldn't understand much of any character I was introduced to, which might be why I liked it. I've never been a mean girl, nor a real victim of them, they just ignored me, decided I wasn't good enough for them and severed our bonds, so I ignored them right back (and became a silent bystander, mostly), but I've seen mean girls play. I've heard them read the private thoughts of others out loud, seen them carrying other stolen items and visited their hate-sites online, spreading truth and lies effectively. Anna is a special kind of evil though, very organized, which I don't think anyone I knew ever was, in other words: she was super scary. Being in her clique seems like being in a cult, where she's the magic leader who in the end just blackmails everyone to stay.

NOT SPOILER FREE /loud wailing in the distance/ This HAS to be my favorite book so far by David Estes. Everything I tell you, EVERYTHING was amazing about this book (almost everything). This was the cherry on top of the cake, the peanut butter to my jelly of a book. I adored most of characters in this book. The story was magnificent and I can only say one bad thing about the book - it was to short! I LOVED Huck - he started out as this puppet of a boy, who followed his fathers every request to the best of his ability, had no thoughts of his own until the day he becomes a man. The day he's sent away to see if he's a sailor worth his salt. This leads him to a crummy ship, with crummy workers and a crummy treatment of servants (the "bilge rats"). Huck begins as a feeble kid who follows his father, the Admiral of the fleet. But his prospects change when he meets and socializes with a bilge rat - which is a big no-no, interacting with the "scum" of the ship. Eventually Huck sees the faults and begins to cut himself away from his fathers influences. I loved Huck and Jade. These two had the most hardship in coming together - the whipping part shattered me, I was screaming internally and felt so angry but it all turned out alright in the end. David Estes is the king of emotions. MEANWHILE, on the island are a tribe of people called Riders and our other MC is Sadie. I had a few issues with Sadie (warning, harshness ahead) - I did not like her, if I'm being honest. She's one of my least favorite characters - but there's got to be a bad egg somewhere along the line. No she's not bad, but I just felt like she was so.. so unreasonable. She acted as if the entire world was out to get her, especially her father. And there wasn't much build for me to ever really like her - it was just "My father didn't save Paw, he's a coward, I'm a Rider I can't show emotions, yadayada". By the time she redeemed herself with her father, I disliked her to much to change my opinion. However, I was able to block out the annoyity of Sadie and focused on the Riders. I loved the idea of this tribe, the horses, the fighting and the entire persona of the horse warriors as a whole. Estes illustrates a strong and loyal set of people, and I loved the images of this tribe that were presented. In all honesty, I did favorite Huck's POV's over Sadie's - they were much more interesting and emotionally heartwarming. And once again, the stories all come parallel to each other. MC's from Fire Country and Ice Country come to Water and Storm Country and form a formidable alliance while also discovering further atrocities brought forth from our baddies King Goff, Admiral Jones, and Roan. Excellent read, I loved it altogether.

This book was an interesting read. At times the writing was dreamy, sort of like Neil Gaiman. At times it was genre-bending, like a Kurt Vonnegut take on science fiction. Here's the difference though. The themes in Vonnegut's writings were MORE than deep enough to carry his usually shallow stories. In Gaiman's writings, the story is MORE than enough to carry the lack of a specific message; they're just good stories. Overall, I just finished this novel without knowing what the theme was. In All The Birds in the Sky, There's a rather shallow story of the battle between technology and magic, which would be cool if there were any explanation of either side's actions. On the other hand, the themes are kind of all over the place. A love story that isn't really complete. Environmental destruction. Politics. America's the bad guy. Which leads me to my biggest complaint... Now, I swear on my goodreads account that this is a true story: My initial opinion of the writing was that it was the sarcastic, politically correct, opinionated, "holier than thou" tone of, say, Gawker.com. It wasn't until I finished the book that I discovered the author was, in fact, an editor for a Gawker site. There's a lot of alternative, new age-y ideas as well, and I enjoy that point of view, but this novel included a beginner's course on why traditional education is a sham, and how the U.S. Military agenda is ridiculous, and dozens of other stereotypes. I ramble, like I usually do on opinionated reviews. But this book was on the borderline of being excellent. Instead, it is just good, with some humor that was great, and some humor that made me cringe. Then there was the opinionated themes, and lack of a real solid story. I think most people will enjoy this book a lot, but I'd give it 3.5 stars.

Well. Okay. I'm not sure how I felt about the ending. However. I haven't become this absorbed in a series in a long, long time. (With the exception of the Queen's Thief series, but I didn't read those books back to back. I'm just clarifying here because EUGENIDES FOREVER!) I mean, probably since high school. Which was a long, long time ago. (But not very long ago at all because TIME.) My favorite thing about this series is that, for the most part, there is character consistency. And, while maybe being stupid sometimes, they are not so stupid that my credulity is stretched to the breaking point. You know how I was so happy in the last volume that Adam noticed Ronan's feelings for him? Because Adam is intelligent and observant? That's what Adam does? Well, HURRAY because he notices that there is something going on between Gansey and blue. Because HE OBSERVES THINGS. Like, it is SO NICE to not have to deal with all the drama that I was afraid was going to happen. Prolonging the "reveal" for as long as possible. That can be terribly annoying. And it did not happen here. The ending: A little too happy. Sorry. I'm not really buying it. I don't think Adam or Ronan or Blue would have just LET Gansey make that sacrifice. One of the others would have jumped up to do it first. And I'm not really buying why Blue's kiss killed him. I was hoping that it would make a little more sense? And I'm REALLY not buying that Gansey gets to live. While Noah just passes by and IS NOT MENTIONED ANYMORE. Grrrr. Oh, and basically...Gansey would not have needed to die to stop the demon if he had not been on the quest to find the dead king in the first place... Or would Piper have set it free either way? Like, was this all set into place to stop the demon? Is there some other reason to have brought all of them together? I don't know. It was a little weird. NOAH!!!! Still didn't care that much about Gansey and Blue. Like, in the first book I found Gansey charming. The second book I found him annoying. The third book I found him vulnerable. This book I was not really sure. Like, Ronan and Adam are off TRYING TO FIGURE STUFF OUT while he is with Blue at a TOGA PARTY. Seriously? He seemed so dedicated, and then right when he was thiiiiiis close, he doesn't care as much? Was scared? I mean, there is oozing blackness in the magical forest, and you're not trying to figure out what is going on...? You're at a TOGA PARTY?! It didn't really make sense to me. It's like he lost his mojo. Which I kind of understand. He was scared to find out what Gansey would be without the quest. But, like, some pretty awful things might have been prevented if they figured out how to kill the demon as soon as they figured out that something was wrong . Oh, and one thing that kept bothering me... This is more of a complaint I had in the third book, but I'm bringing it up now. Like, at some point, why would I care THAT much about some sleeping king, compared to, say...RONAN. I mean, everything going on with Ronan was so magical and interesting, that I couldn't help but wonder why Gansey is like...GOTTA FIND THAT KING! I'm like, let's find out more about Ronan and his magical, mystical abilities! :D Seriously. He is so BENT on find this sleeping king that he is kind of missing out on a lot of the magic that is surrounding him NOW. I mean, the sleeping king is interesting and all... But Ronan's power goes beyond that. The ley lines go beyond that. At some point, I realized: This sleeping king is just a small, small part of the mysteries that this world is touching on. And it doesn't really seem that exciting on interesting compared to them. Moving on. Blue tries too hard. Which means that she is a pretty normal teenager, I guess. I wish we weren't told all the time that she is sensible, though. Because sensible people don't really get suspended or freak out about things as much as she does. She's also a horrible hypocrite, but at least she knows it, so I'm willing to cut her a little slack... It's hard to look at your faults and recognize them for what they are. But it was still super annoying that she wouldn't get into Henry's car just because she didn't want to be seen with an Aglionby boy. But it's okay for her to be all offended over stuff when it happens to her? Like, no one can be sexist at all or tell her she has nice legs, but it's totally okay for her to be a jerk like that? Well, no, she admitted she was a hypocrite. But still. Grr. Also, I am 5' tall. It's not THAT big of a deal. Like, it is not something that majorly defines me. It's harder for me to reach some things, but like... I'm not thinking about it all the time. Haha. So, yeah. The ending didn't completely satisfy me, which is why this review (at the time of this review...I reserve the right to change my mind) is only giving 5 stars. However! I found out that there is supposed to be a trilogy based on RONAN, which brings me great joy and hope for the future. I'm getting old. I try to remember what a book was about and draw a complete blank. Here's a summary to help me out a year from now when that happens: Piper is in league with a demon. Kills Neeve. Kills husband. Destroying magical forest. Plans on selling demon. Like, at a secret magical collector auction? It doesn't go well. Her dad is one member of a really weird set of triplets. Not sure if this will matter at some point in another book. Demon wants to destroy magic forest AND Ronan and all of his dream things. Which includes his brother Matthew, by the way. And dream girl, whom he has brought out into the real world. She has hooves. Demon succeeds in killing most of forest and Ronan's mom. And possessing Noah, who scratches up Blue pretty badly. This is pretty much the last we see of Noah until the end, at which point we find out that he is the one who whispered stuff to Young Gansey and started him along the path to looking for sleeping/dead kings. I can mention this now because time is CIRCULAR. Adam and Ronan try to figure out what is going on while Blue and Gansey go to a toga party. They befriend Henry. Henry was kidnapped once. He is eccentric, in a friendly sort of way. He has a magic bee that Ronan's dad had dreamt up. He wants to join The Gang. When Gansey goes off on his own to find sleeping king, Henry steps in to save him from car failure, which means he is TOTALLY IN. Sleeping king is DEAD. All of this was pretty pointless. Demon possesses Adam and almost makes him kill Ronan. Ronan is dying from the demon. Only way to stop demon is by a willing sacrifice. Gansey decides to sacrifice himself and everyone is kind of like, okay, sad, but okay. Blue kisses him and he dies because mirrors reflect and his heart was a gift and was the weaker reflection? Then magical forest does something to make him not be dead. Not really sure what exactly happened here. Random bits: Blue is kind of a true. Mr. Gray has to go away to try to deflect interest on Henrietta (the town). Blue and Gansey and Henry are now a dynamic trio and are going on a road trip! RONAN AND ADAM KISS!!! Multiple times. Ahh, I'm old enough to remember when fangirling and such meant knowing I would never get what I wanted. What a beautiful, beautiful world we live in, where I can ship a couple and IT MIGHT ACTUALLY HAPPEN. When there are hints and clues, AND I'M NOT JUST BEING JERKED AROUND. Seriously. This is beautiful. THE END! Now I can go to sleep. Seriously. I've been so wrapped up in this series that even after reading to the point of exhaustion, I couldn't get to sleep because I was THINKING about the books. I don't know if it is the author's beautiful writing or my hardcore fangirling over Pynch-- or if it's because my one-year-old has developed an addiction to Trolls which I shamelessly encouraged just so that I could keep reading, which meant that it was possible to be completely absorbed in the book in a way I haven't been able to be absorbed in books for years... Whatever the case, I really enjoyed this series. SLEEP!

I wanted to read this book because it has become rather controversial lately. Since it was turned into a Netflix series, it's popularity has of course skyrocketed. People are worried that it glorifies suicide and some suicides have been directly blamed on either this book or the show (more prominently the show I think, for obvious reasons). I have a direct connection since I have dealt with depression for much of my life and have been suicidal in the past. So I wanted to see if there really was something to this that caused the uproar. After having read it, my short version would be that it's simply the latest scapegoat. People want something to blame in tragedy. The book has an interesting format in that it follows two timelines concurrently. On the tapes, Hannah talks about how she came to her decision to end her life, "blaming" a multitude of people for the things they have done. At the same time, you have Clay listening to the tapes, walking around to different locations, lightly interacting with a few people. His timeline really doesn't have much going on apart from his reactions and wishing he had done more, his love for Hannah, etc. I don't REALLY want to get into the details of Hannah's reasons why, since everyone is different and depression can affect people in different ways (not to mention female vs male), but I guess I will give my perspective. I'm now 33, so I'm not exactly the demographic for this book to begin with, though I do still remember my teenage depression (still ongoing, though less severe). To me, her reasons were the most shallow silly things. Not once did I relate to her as depressive, she was taking a unusually strong stance to a few minor events. Possibly the author just didn't know how to properly convey this. These events could still lead someone in that direction, but on their own, any normal person would more or less brush them off. I think that's the books failing, in that there weren't the other signs of actual depression. I could write it off in that it was just Hannah talking about events, as opposed to an inner monologue, but there was still some of that. It just didn't seem to fit, to me. The book was ok, nothing spectacular by any means. I wouldn't seek out more by the author, but I would read his work if I came across it. I don't think there is much/any worry of this book actually leading people to suicide, but people have different triggers. I wouldn't recommend it to someone that is suicidal because it's certainly not going to help anything, either. It's double timeline was interesting and done fairly well.

3.75 stars *Review up* This was a cute and fun read. I'm new to Shiloh Walker so for a debut this wasn't bad. I'm a huge sucker for the 'secretly pining for my best friend' trope. It's too juicy to resist so I dived right into this. I also loved the Wreck This Journal theme, it was clever on the hero's part and clearly I had fun with it if my status updates are anything to go by. :P I just honestly wished it was utilized more through the story. I thought the journal was a perfect way for the heroine Abby to break lose from her neurotic habit of making lists and planning everything. She literally plans out her life when something goes off kilter. I enjoyed this so much that I was prepared to give this 5 stars half way in but some things got in the way of me hopping on the 5 star 'woohoo! train. *sigh* Dammit. Some small things here and there and the big 'blow up' near the end that was dragged out ridiculously long for absurd silly reasons. First of all, the fact that the hero Zach has been in love with his best friend Abby for seventeen years and she never noticed was a little mind boggling. And the fact that everybody around them knew about it and Abby was the last to know was also a little hard to grasp and kinda drove me nuts. I mean...seriously guys? I loved Zach but his complete absorption of Abby and pretty much putting his life on hold for her I thought was a little too extreme. The heady all-consuming obsession while sweet reminded me too much of something you see in YA/NA honestly. *ducks head* I mean he uproots his whole life to move to the city where Abby got a job just to be close to her. And the fact that he never truly tried to move on bugged me as well. Seventeen years to be hung up on someone is a lot. But my biggest hold up was how Abby suddenly goes from engaged to another man and totally oblivious of her BFF to 'Woah! You are so sexy and I want you BAD' with a flip of a switch. Like...whahuh? I really wish the author paced the story better cause the abrupt 180 came off clunky and super fast. I had to really suspend belief that someone who was in a serious committed relationship and never ever looked at her best friend that way suddenly is staring at his tattoos and wanting to lick them. I mean I don't blame her for the licking part but...come on girl. This couldn't have gradually happened over a few months? Douchebag or not, she was near close to marrying 'Roger the Rat' if he hadn't called things off. The DAY of the wedding her fiance calls it off and Zach of course is there to comfort her and she magically has her omg moment. lol Seriously?? She suddenly 'sees' things in Zach she never saw before. It does happen I get that...but I guess I just wish it happened a little more gradually here. And I still wonder if Roger hadn't called things off would Abby still go through with it? That also bugged me. I really hate when authors use this fast easy loophole of jerk exs calling it off at the last minute when the heroine is too oblivious to know otherwise that the guy isn't right for her until AFTER the breakup. I'm probably over thinking it but...major elephant in the room. Another thing that made me lose interest was the big KABOOM misunderstanding that had the heroine running away like her hair is on fire and freezing out the hero for a few days. Granted it was only like three? days, but the way the author dragged it out for 50-freaking-pages made it seem like weeks. It was so unnecessary and silly. She walks in on another woman trying to kiss Zach and runs out and skips town refusing to take anyone's calls. Yes because it makes perfect sense and really adult thing to do to not let anyone know where you are and if you are ok for 2 days straight. At this point I wanted to slap some sense into Abby. Here it became obvious the author wanted to drag things out real slow--like pulling teeth slow-- to create unnecessary angst when the heroine quickly realizes the kiss wasn't how it looked but still drags her feet and keeps stalling saying she's 'not ready' to confront him. How loooong it took her to confront him seemed just as loooong it took Zach to finally spit out how feels for her. Like just...GET IT OUT. You walked in on a failed kiss, not sex. Get a damn grip. Overall this was fun, predictable? yes, but still fun. Zach's brothers sound interesting, Zane and Ty in particular. Zane seems like a total sweetheart but I kinda want to weep that he is getting paired up with Keelie a.k.a the 'interloper'. I do not like this girl and honestly struggle to understand what Zane sees in her that has him so hung up on her. It's a little hard to swallow. And it's not even about the kissing incident with Zach. She is Zach's friend and coworker at the tattoo shop and has been pining after him for years, she makes a move on him in here which leads to the big ooooh no! misunderstanding. She's 28 yet acts like a sullen bratty teenager with a HUGE chip on her shoulder. She's a little too immature for someone who's that age. She's argumentative and defensive with everyone and I just don't get what her deal is nor do I find her interesting enough to find out. Which bums me out because I do want to read Zane's book but I'm just not interested in another Zach/Abby situation but with an annoying heroine in it's place. Meh.

Okay, this is a four star book for concept, and markedly lower for execution. It's Monday and it's raining, so I'm going with three stars. Let's start on a high note. The idea was great. The author does a stellar job of rolling out the premise, and I especially liked the pacing -- he successfully spools out the information so that you're intrigued and wanting to know more, but not so much that you're confused and frustrated. He's got an excellent sense of how and when to space his reveals, because they were increasingly riveting as the book goes on. The mechanics are extremely bare bones (which I think is exactly what you want here) and are presented in a way that is reasonably accessible for readers to get the basic gist about what is going on with people travelling between parallel worlds. It is definitely a page-turner. I fully admit to being too persnickety for words, but I was unable to shake my peevishness at .... stuff. The overly cloying Twoo Wuv of the story. The track lighting. The records on vinyl. Oh, there was something else about a cell phone that put my nerves on edge (wait, two things -- the gently grabbing of a phone, and the absolute mystery of whether or not the light from a cell phone is noticeable in a car at night). The more the author attempted to make the protagonist likable and sympathetic ... the more I was annoyed by him. I started off thinking it was fake folksy; but as I realized it wasn't fake but rather clueless, I felt vicariously embarrassed for everyone involved. If I was the wife, I would have decided by asking "which one of you is from the parallel world where you didn't put track lighting in your home?" Oh hey, I came back to edit this to add something else that I found so odd while I was reading, which is about the dude's son. SO. Even the tag line for the book promotion is about how this guy wants "his family" back. Yet, 98% of this is about the wife. He seems psyched enough to see his son and all, but really in terms of the emotional life of the protagonist, it's all about the wife. I didn't get anything AT ALL about how this guy feels about parenting, there was no identity as a parent that came through for me. And I was puzzled about how the initial split, the first major choice that differed between the two timelines (or timeworlds, whatever) was about how in the one, Jason choose marrying his unexpectedly pregnant girlfriend and sticking with her and being a husband and a dad, and in the other, he ... doesn't. And I felt the implication was that the girlfriend had an abortion? Maybe? But it's not clear ... and I would think that would be HUGE, in real life, for a lot of people, regardless of what decision she ended up making. The idea that she might have had a baby without being married to this hotshot scientist is essentially absent, almost as if it didn't even cross the author's mind -- that this isn't necessarily a binary decision. Pretty much every aspect of the book treats the kid like an add-on. Even in the plague world, he only encounters his wife; the son was already conveniently dead. While talking about it after reading, it struck me that it reminded me a lot of The Time Traveler's Wife (and hey, also Chicago!) only with parallel worlds instead of time travel. Cool concept. Maybe trying too hard. Genuinely sweet lovey moments. Others that need to be dialed down.

4 STARS FOR "HOW TO BREAK A BOY" BY LAURIE DEVORE It was easier then, when I was so lost in where Andrienne ended and I began. I never had to think about if what I did was right or wrong, because if we were doing it together nothing ever felt out of place. Some people spend their whole lives waiting for someone to love them, the good and bad, and I wanted that someone to be Adrienne, from the moment she set her eyes on me. Maybe I was always waiting for her approval, waiting for her smile. But I wasn't waiting anymore. Damn, this was so powerful. Don't let the cover and synopsis fool you: a cliched, stereotypical "Mean Girls-esque" novel is not waiting in between these pages. It's not a love story like the title may imply, even though our protagonist does end up falling in love. It's a story about a very dysfunctional, power-imbalanced, toxic friendship between two girls, and Olivia's struggle to cope with the loss of her brother. The author pulls no punches: I hated Olivia for 95% of this book. Everytime she made progress - to step back from her friendship with Adrienne and make amends for what she's done to others - she ends up falling back into her old habits. She allows herself to be manipulated by Adrienne, and hurt friends just so that she can remain in control of her reputation. She's miserable, yet is willing to remain so for the sake of being popular. However, the 5% I did like is what kept me going, from not completely giving up on Olivia's road to redemption. As frustrating as it was to see her constantly go back to her friendship with Adrienne, the author lets us see just enough of Olivia's vulnerable side to let us know that she isn't hopeless. Through her relationship with Whit, and learning more about her history with her brother and mother, you start to understand why a girl like Olivia would be so drawn to Adrienne and power. That being said, I thought it was incredibly important that the author also remained blunt about Olivia's personality and her actions. A huge part of her character development was learning that just because you've had tragic things happen to you, or you have a toxic friendship with someone, it doesn't dissolve you of any personal responsibility. If you bully someone, its on you. No one can really force you to do anything. Another thing I really respected was her portrayal of Claire, the third person to make up the Olivia/Adrienne/Claire trio. She may not have been an active participant of their games and bullying, but she remained silent - which, as she comments, is just as bad. The only issues I had with it is that sometimes it got too irritating for Olivia to constantly be doing Adrienne's bidding, especially when it started putting her friends futures in jeopardy. It was very "one step forward, ten thousand steps back". And as much as I loved Whit, I don't understand why he started hanging out with Anna and ADRIENNE, of all people, near the end. I get that he was heartbroken, but if you hate Adrienne so much, why would you want to be anywhere near her? This is a definitely more of a mature YA read, but it provides a lot of important commentary on bullying and taking responsibility for whatever part you play in it (whether its being a direct participant or passive bystander).

I have to say that this book is not at all what I expected. I knew it was a young adult and I read the summary, but the summary doesn't tell you anything. It doesn't express the emotions experienced from losing your first love before you have a definition. It doesn't tell you that Anna loses something before it even begins and that no one else know what she lost. She has to keep this secret. And then she has to move on. I found the book to be realistic of teenagers without being corny or cheesy. The girls were not perfect, but they were not bad kids. They just wanted to have fun. The description of Anna and her V-card is spot on. Most girls just want to lose it and then once they've lost it they don't really understand the importance. In society today, a girl's virginity is not something important-it's something to get over with so that you can get to the good stuff. Sarah Ockler portrayed this accurately. Overall, I was shockingly surprised. I did not expect this book to be good, or to have tears in my eyes for a good portion of the book, but I did. I will definitely be reading some more of Sarah Ockler. I can't believe this was her first novel, I want to see what she did/does after this.

"A Study in Emerald" is a cool short story written by Neil Gaiman, one of today's masters of weird fiction, and can be found for free here. If you have half an hour of your time left to be spent with one of Gaiman's best short stories, then you should right now click on this link instead of reading my thoughts about it disguising themselves as a review. As the title already implies, the entire story alludes to Arthur Conan Doyle's first Sherlock Holmes novel, A Study in Scarlet, but only upon closer observation does it become clear that Gaiman also spends those nine pages with references to the works of H.P. Lovecraft. As I don't know any of his stories, the internet had to assist me with getting to this conclusion, but I do know the original Sherlock Holmes canon quite well by now, and not only was it interesting to see classic characters like Greg Lestrade and Mrs. Watson included in this story, but also to follow the hints leading back to Doyle's original tale. The plot premise was similarly structured, yet turned out to be completely misleading and full of surprises as the ending drew closer, turning "A Study in Emerald" into an independent short story which Neil Gaiman once again used to prove his creativity and his talents as a writer. The story's originality unfolds not only in the plot itself, but also in the structure of the story. With each chapter being introduced by different advertisements referencing to well-known characters of classic literature like Viktor Frankenstein or Dr. Jekyll, Gaiman produced a mysterious atmosphere, which only added to the story's charm. And I totally fell for it. "If there's one thing that a study of history has taught us, it is that things can always get worse." This story includes cool stuff (not without reason did Neil Gaiman include this in the "cool stuff" section of his website) and certainly a few surprises you will not have guessed at the beginning of the first chapter. Tadiana's review includes an interesting step-by-step suggestion for reading this, which I might have followed as well (if I had not read "A Study in Scarlet" already months prior to this one). I can recommend this story for fans of Neil Gaiman and/or Sherlock Holmes, but also generally for readers looking for a fast-paced little distraction.

A new historical series by Milan gets off to an interesting, but not entirely successful beginning. Judith, our long-suffering heroine, has been gallantly holding her family together after her father and eldest brother were convicted of treason for what we later in the novel find out is giving military information to the Chinese during the Opium Wars. Judith's first love, the titular Marquess, Christian Trent, was involved with uncovering the treason (why, I wasn't ever quite sure of, giving how young he was at the time, and how most of the ton seemed to regard him with suspicion because of his odd behavior; perhaps they will be revealed in later novels in the series). Judith broke with Christian, in spite of his offer of marriage after her father's suicide and her brother's transportation. But now Judith needs Christian because some money she's sent to a lawyer, money intended for her estranged sister who is living with an uncle, has somehow gone astray. Not sure why Judith found this predicament enough to contact Christian for his help, when she wouldn't accept his help after the treason (plot contrivance?). The two discover that said estranged sister has not in fact been living with her uncle, and Christian spends much of the novel chasing missing sister down, without much success. In fact, the plot here (beyond the romance arc) consists primarily of set-up for future novels: the missing sister; the traitorous brother (whom all thought drowned, but is revealed late in the novel to still be alive); odd younger sister; younger brother tormented at school for being related to traitors. What's left is the romance plot, which is compelling: two young lovers split apart by their differing commitments to justice and family loyalty who come together again 8 years later only to discover their feelings of betrayal haven't entirely eliminated their feelings of love. Writing intense, emotional scenes between her lovers is Milan's strength, and she does it here to good effect. But the novel spends much of its time showcasing Judith and Christian flirting and word-playing their way back to one another, and at times, the cleverness slipped into unintelligibility; I had to stop more than a few times and reread, just to try and get the joke. Not what you want to have happening when you're deep in the emotions of the characters.... Judith as a character is interesting, but not very active for a Milan heroine. She has an unconventional job, but its not central to the story, or even something we see her doing. Not my favorite Milan heroine. I liked Christian better, even if I didn't always understand him. He suffered from nightmares as a child, which has had a huge impact on his later life. He's also an unconventional smart-ass, a pretty unusual character for a Victorian aristocrat. I didn't really get until the end of the novel that Christian  was not telling his mother about his opium addition because he didn't want her to feel guilty for starting him down the drug path by giving him laudanum for his nightmares when he was a child , which made his motivation in his interactions with his family members hard to understand, and the reconciliation at novel's end far less impactful. The black moment scene was pretty lame for a Milan novel, no doubt why the reconciliation scene followed almost immediately after, with little in the way of drawn-out torment for either lover. All in all, a mixed bag. Here's hoping future books in the series come together better than this one does.

The Black Dagger Brotherhood series is a PNR series that takes place in upstate NY. The arc of the series is an ongoing war between the vampire race that is struggling for survival and a subset of altered humans known as "lessers" who are trying to destroy the vampire race. This seventh book in the series primarily features a secondary character in previous books, Rehvenge - brother to Bella, half-vampire, half-symphath, club-owning, local drug-lord. He's been keeping the half-symphath part of his identity a secret, but a blackmailer is threatening to expose him for what he really is. Yet, it's the worst possible time as he's just met female vampire, Ehlena, a local nurse who always sees the best in people and puts the welfare of others before her own. As usual in the BDB series, there's a lot of interaction with main characters from previous books, so fans of the series will get a nice fix of their other favorite characters. In particular, Wrath & Beth are featured heavily as are the central characters of book 8, Xhex & John Matthew. This series has been a consistent favorite of mine since I discovered it and I'll definitely be reading the next book as I'm a big fan of John Matthew and friends.

Where does all the character's (especially Mare's) self-interest go further?? I doubt she'll forever kneel (oops, sorry- SPOILER) Mare and Cal, I hope for a lengthy relationship for them (Team Cal forever). And, I desperately needed a Maven POV, like seriously? I was a mess by the time I finished reading LL 2. My face was a blotchy map of red, white and purple, mixed with remains of my make up. My stomach felt weird for having laughed, cried and having felt the army of butterflies of (many kinds) of excitement flying around. My chest felt tight with happiness and dread for knowing they all, Mac, Tony, Ben and Anna, still have many obstacless ahead of them, but that they would definitely make it work, together. So, if you are prepared for the physical symptoms this great, lovely romance/mystery/family drama novel causes, read it!

The premise of this book does bear quite a resemblance to Daughter of Smoke and Bone: human girl raised by hidden beings of a magical race (in this case bird people) who have a long standing war with another hidden race (dragon people). Said girl is snarky and travels the world through hidden portals. This book explores Echo not really fitting in with her adopted people but taking their side and hunting for the mythical firebird to prevent the wrong hands from finding the bird that legend says will bring peace between the races. I loved the writing, the way in which the author creates mood and atmosphere through her word choices. I think this initial installment does a fair job of world-building, though it leaves plenty of room for future books to explain the origins of the races and their war better. I didn't anticipate the ending until close to 75% of the way through, but then it was fairly obvious what the climax would be. That didn't bother me, however, because it followed the character's arc of growth pretty closely and was logical. Some criticisms: for a story about war, there wasn't much of it and from a realist's standpoint, even when there was a battle with supposedly life-threatening injuries, it appears EVERYONE lives. I don't like it when beloved characters die, but if there's a battle and only the unnamed minions die, it doesn't feel very real. The comparison of the LBGT elements of the plot with the secondary characters to City of Bones is valid, and just as contrived, though the humor is excellent. I think Jasper's living through what seemed like a fatal wound detracted from the heroicism of that moment, at least because in the scene I expected he was dead, and then later, nope-just injured, which took me out of the story for a moment. I imagine some people who loved Daughter of Smoke and Bone will hate this as an inferior copy and some will love this for the ways it takes a similar premise into a different place. Overall, despite some weaknesses, I really enjoyed it.
I don't like how Five was able to see it from Lorien's POV but still sided with the Mogs. I don't like how Five was pretty much stupid. But I understand where he's coming from.

This was really good, while at the same time being really bad. That's probably a terrible way to explain, but I don't know how else to put it in words. As for the positives, I loved the premise of this book so much. The question it posed was super interesting. If you could go back in time and kill someone that would go on to do terrible things, would you be able to do it? Even worse, could you still do it if that bad person used to be someone you loved? Throughout the book, I got annoyed with Em for not being able to off James. She had multiple tries and she fumbled like every single one of them. However, the book would've been pretty boring if Em had just walked up and shot him in the face in the first chapter. Also, I could kind of understand why she kept hesitating. It's easy to hate future James, but past James, while a bit douchey, was a completely innocent person. There was nothing about him at that time that would ease my conscience about just killing him point-blank. If it was me, I would have an extremely difficult time looking my best friend in the face and murdering them for something years from now that they have no knowledge of doing. As for the bad, I had some difficulties when it came to the characters from the future. There was just this huge emotional disconnect. I was told that all these terrible things had happened to Em and I honestly felt nothing. The only character from the future I cared about was Connor and he was an extremely minor character. I think the lack of world-building was a major negative. You're constantly told the world has gone to crap, but it isn't until the last few chapters that you actually get some specifics. I can't sympathize with a character if I can't understand where they've come from. I need more than some vague mentions of China bombing them or glossed over interrogations. Also, there was something a little bland and shallow about the way Em's thoughts were delivered. It was like Em was saying all the right things, but I didn't buy the emotion at all. I wanted to feel the pain and the anguish, but it just wasn't believable to me. It's weird because I thought that the younger versions of themselves were ten times more interesting and authentic. I really loved the dynamic between Marina, James, and Finn. They felt like real people and I actually cared about what happened to them. Also, I just really liked Marina. Multiple times in the book she was said to be superficial and selfish, but none of her behavior bothered me. While she had some growing up to do, I thought she just seemed like an average teenage girl. Compared to Em, Marina seemed to be a way better developed character. At times, I was more invested in her pining over James than Em and Finn's mission. Her chapters read more like a contemporary YA book than a dystopian and I was super into it. Overall, I thought this was an entertaining book, but it dropped the ball on a few key things. The ending was so perfect. My favorite part of the book was seeing the past and future selves interacting. I even liked how things played out with James deciding to kill himself to keep all the horrible things his future self did from happening  . It all seemed very fitting. Then, the ending was ruined by Finn being alive in the final chapter . I looked at other people's explanations, but I still thought it seemed like a bit of a stretch. As it was, it felt like the author decided to have this one out-of-turn thing happen purely so Em and Finn could stay together . I much would have preferred the sad ending where James still killed himself and Finn stayed dead . I read somewhere that there was supposed to be a sequel to this, but I'm actually glad it got cancelled. The way the book wrapped up seemed pretty final and I have no idea what the next book would have even been about. Turning this into a series would have just been so unnecessary.

Not a lot of character development. This one seemed to rely on "oh a Navy SEAL is hot and awesome" as enough to make him a great character. I could have done with less tossing of the sledgehammer and more character development.

A friend just called me and blandly asked why my shit was laying inside the bath looking helplessly vulnerable waiting for its verdict. And while seeing it, I was wondering how Pi could eat something so disgusting and awful-looking. Of course he didn't eat my poop, because fortunately I wasn't on the boat. But I have my pride and I believe my crap still has better taste than Richard Parker's. Jesus lived in the desert for 40 days without eating and drinking, Pi lived in a boat around the Pacific for 227 days with a Bengalese tiger eating fish and poop. God, I do see a problem here. Sarcasm aside, this book calls out for hope which we seem to be losing day by day because there's less food on our tables, less warmth in our eyes, less love in our souls. It teaches us how living life is "Believing", not in God or his magical son, or in cows and prophets with long beards but believing in a tomorrow, better, worse, doesn't matter: just a tomorrow. I wouldn't have saved Richard Parker. But that's why nature gives second chances to people who aren't me. Great story! If anyone has questions for the poop, I did flush it after.

So, I began this series because I read somewhere that it is identical to the VA. This proved to be quite accurate. This book is pretty much a copy of every idea Richelle Mead ever had. I like VA. I loved this. I liked the idea of taking the vamps and dhampires and turning them to demigod descendants. I love everything that has to do with Greek Mythology, either showered with inaccuracies or not. The fact that this author only used one greek word(agape which means love) and used it exactly the way a greek would have was a big advantage to the book. I also think that JLA took RM's characters and improved them. I like Alex more than I ever liked Rose. She too is irrational and way too irresponsible but she has a certain amount of common sense(not much) which Rose lacked. (Rose would have definitely gone for Jackson in the first VA book). I also like Aiden more than I like Dimitri. Don't get me wrong, Dimitri was and always will be one of my favourite YA characters BUT he always seemed way too serious and collected for a 24 year old guy. If RM hadn't provided his age I would have thought him at least in his middle thirties. Aiden on the other hand displays some boyishness and youthful behaviour that make him more believable and likeable as a hero. I actually do like Seth. I read in a BLURB from the next books that he turns out being a duchy but IMO it shows from the beginning. He is nothing like Adrian. He is more of a hard-ass. I also like Kaleb way more than Mason. Mason always irritated me. I know it may seem bad to compare two books from two different authors but really everyone who's read both knows that they are really similar. I just can't believe that JLA wasn't inspired by VA for this series. The daimons which are exactly like Strigoi, the half-blood-pure blood politics, the bond. Everything is there. IMO the Covenant series is a better copy of VA. The only problem is that it's kind of predictable. You just knew that Alex would be the second Apollyon the moment she read the story in Aiden's book.

What do you call it when you finally find a book that is so rawly written that you know you won't forget it?I think I was bawling the whole entire book! It was fantastic. Told by a screenplay, this book is about the largest slave auction in America's history. The slaves sold came from Master Butler who had lost his money gambling, and owed a large sum of money. He profited over $300,000. Mostly though, this book is about Emma. A slave girl who took care of her master's children after his wife left. His two kids were Sarah and Frances. Sarah was kind hearted like her mother (who left because of the way her husband treated the slaves), and Frances wanted to own the plantation and restore it after it was sold. On the day of the auction, the master had asks Emma to come along with him and the girls because Sarah doesn't want to go to the auction and Emma is the only way she will go. Originally, the master made no plans to separate/sell Emma from her family or his daughters (who loved Emma dearly), but a wealthy woman pays an extremely large amount to the master, and her gives Emma up. Emma's father, who was the slave driver of the master, is fuming with anger when he sees Emma going to Ms. Henfield's carriage (the wealthy woman) because as boys, to two were very close (Emma's father even saved his life once). Sarah does not let Emma go without a fight though, she is kicking and screaming and by the time Emma calms her down she says "you reminds me so much of your mama. You think you can have a good heart like your mama does? You think you can do that? "That was the last time Emma saw her dad, and she never said goodbye to her mother. At Ms. Henfield's plantation, Emma works as a caretaker for her daughter, where she marries Joe (who was sold to Ms. Henfield from Master Butler's plantation). On the plantation, they befriend a couple (Charles and Winnie and their baby) Eventually they escape with the couple through a white man who owned a grocery store as well as taught Joe to read. During their escape, Charles' dad (Sampson) catches them (he thinks he outsmarted the white people because he gets fed and clothed and housed) and threatens to turn them in. Charles punches him and they light the house on fire in attempt to kill him (he escapes). The four of them make it to freedom after the baby dies on the boat and Joe and Emma move to Canada, and Emma names her daughter Sarah, after Master Butler's daughter who had a kind heart. Joe dies fighting for freedom in America. The Butlers sold their plantation and moved to Pennsylvania. Sarah says that she never went a day without thinking of Emma. She also never ends up forgiving her father. Up to his deathbed, Master Butler asks if she loves him, but she can't say yes, and leaves the room. Frances runs in, and in between Sarah's departure and Frances' arrival, he dies. Sarah marries a man and names her first born Emma. Eventually, the two of them get in contact and send each other letters. And Emma tells her granddaughter about her life.

I hated the formatting style of this book, but everything else I loved. Quite possibly the only thing more interesting than the life of Virginia Woolf, is the life of her older sister Vanessa Bell, and the complex and chaotic entangling of their lives. On the surface this is a hard book to sell; its told entirely in letters, diary entries, and telegrams from the perspective of several members of the Bloomsbury group, including E. M. Forester, Leonard Woolf, Clive Bell, and Virginia, though the primary focus is from Vanessa's perspective. True, it comes across as a bit unfocused and jumbled but the author weaves incomprehensible beauty and tenderness into the story she tells. I know a lot about Virginia's later years but virtually nothing about her early years, including her early episodes of madness, her three days of nonstop talking, pretending that her brother Thoby was still alive in her correspondence, and the affair she had with her sisters husband.

Rebel Belle by Rachel Hawkins is about Harper Price, high school Queen Bee, who on the night of homecoming, gets trapped in the bathroom by the school janitor (and her history teacher) and her life changes FOREVER! Okay, I'm really bad at describing book plots to people, especially if I like the book. I'm being intentionally vague because this is one of those stories where the less you know going into it, the better it will be. One thing you should know and is vital to point out is that this isn't an instance where Harper is the popular girl cliche. She's not a stupid, walking parody of the trope with a Ken doll on her arm. That was one of my biggest reservations on reading this novel and I would have never picked it up if it wasn't the Booksplosion read-along book of the month (join the Goodreads group here!) and the positive reviews that this novel had. The author recently announced that this will be a series which isn't too surprising considering the ending. I'm giving this book five stars because it is executed flawlessly. The pacing is strong and steady, never losing its rhythm and we learn everything about the supernatural universe at the right time with Harper, the main character, without it becoming infodump. All the rules and names are easy to follow even if you're not the biggest supernatural reader. The characters are all developed and three dimensional for the roles they play into the story and while the plot isn't the most original, it was certainly fun to read. I didn't fall head over heels in love with this book since the plot isn't original or groundbreaking for the genre, but it's a fun, lighthearted read, especially for the summer.

This is the second Harper Fox book I've read, although I believe it was the first she wrote in this genre. The first, Driftwood is better (I gave it 5 stars - I'd have given it 10 if I could! ), but this is still a wonderful read. Ms. Fox's writing is outstanding, and her narrative has an almost poetic quality to it. Her ability to describe the look and feel of the settings for her stories is just fabulous. I look forward to reading many more of her works! MILD SPOILERS TO FOLLOW "Life After Joe," much like "Driftwood," is a love story between two men who are both in pain. Matt, a doctor, is wandering through a self-destructive blur of grief from the sudden departure of his longtime lover, Joe. Joe, it seems, has decided he wants a wife of the female persuasion and a family. Aaron has pain of his own (I won't reveal what it is, because that really would spoil the lovely and haunting revelation towards the end of the book), but suffice it to say, he rescues Matt from himself with kindness and patience. Matt, however, begins to suspect Aaron is hiding a secret which will hurt Matt and, when Joe shows up on Matt's doorstep, Matt is forced to make some important choices. I think I'd have given this 5 stars, but for the short-shrift given Aaron's character. True, some of the revelations as to Aaron explain a lot, but there might have been a way to structure the story so we'd have gotten more about him after the "big" revelation. In the end, we still don't know all that much about him. I think the ending could have been longer and more significant (although I agree that Aaron's admission that he still loves Rosie was a beautiful and realistic touch). Regardless of these criticisms, I highly recommend this book. It is dark and angsty, but there is sweet light at the end of the tunnel - something I love about Ms. Fox's books. Wonderful read!

Post Blade Runner, almost everybody knows of the existential angst of this PKD book - like much modern SF, it questions our notions of what makes us so special as humans, or if there is anything such as human. It asks us if we can ever consider artificially created, mass-produced, identical androids as individuals. And I'm not sure I know all the answers. On near-future earth, Rick Deckard is a 'bounty hunter', a police official who hunts down androids illegally fleeing Mars to find a home on Earth. The new Nexus-6 models are uncannily human-like in their reflexes - sharp, smart and empathetic. But as the new Voigt test proves, they are incapable of responding 'properly' to emotional situations where empathy is required, even if their impeccable engineering produces all the right biological responses to emotionally tense situations. Deckard, like the rest of the world, considers empathy as the factor that marks out androids as replications of humans without humanity, and therefore rids himself of any potential guilt at killing them. But as he sets out to 'retire' six androids who have fled Mars colony to escape its back-breaking labor sans respite, he faces the possibility of not only empathizing with the androids, but perhaps also falling in love with one of them. I liked this book a lot because it offers no easy answers, and there is no clear resolution even at the end. I like SF that doesn't romanticize artificial beings, goading us to accept them as one of us, while all the while reminding us that they're not all that different from us. It treads a fine line between acceptance and non-acceptance, which I think is the only sane response in an age where the existence and nature of future androids are only wild, wild conjectures. We are already cyborgs in some ways, as Haraway says - modern science is gradually erasing the line between meat and machine, and will continue to do so. Intelligent metal implants in a body that was born human still remains the same, despite invasive modification. But factory-produced mass androids that come out in identical models - aka Sonny of the movie I, Robot - the question is not solely that of "are they human enough"? It also entails the question of "are they individuals or carbon copies of each other? ", which, again, reverts to the first question. The novel opens with a clearly satirical stance on the issue of 'retiring' androids - we are almost sure PKD will prove at the end that humans are more like robots, while robots are "really" human, deep down. But it beautifully goes into murkier waters where we can no longer trust either a human or an android. At best, both species remain ambiguous in their claim to humanity. Neither has enough credentials to be "better" than the other, but none is so bad to be destroyed either. The motif of the "electric sheep" as a metaphor for empathy drives home this point even better - understandably, the setting is a cyberpunk world devoid of natural fauna and flora - real animals are expensive, and near-extinct. Not only are they a necessity and a status-symbol, they are the triggers of empathy in humans in a supposedly brutal future. Deckard, with his measly salary, can only afford an artificial animal - an electric sheep - that becomes both, a source of comfort and a (living?) reminder of his incapability to afford the most basic commodity. Animals were meant to act as anti-depressants, but who could feel empathy for artificial ones, and therefore, as Aristotle puts it, experience catharsis, through an electric sheep that remains artificial despite its impeccable resemblance to a natural one? Androids, then, are no better than electric sheep. As Deckard said, "Like androids, it (the electric sheep) had no ability to appreciate the existence of another." Androids have the right responses programmed into them, they behave like humans to the minutest detail, but they lack empathy, and everything that comes with that. An electric sheep is no substitute for a real one, nor is an android for a human. But that's not it, is it? Androids are a sort of evolution - albeit artificial - they have progressed far beyond their ancestors - the robots which the electric sheep represents - and have gained consciousness, and with that, a desire to survive, which often manifests itself as lack of empathy. Time and again, the novel addresses the issue - while the androids fleeing Deckard admire the 'chickenhead' (person with below-average IQ) Isidore for protecting them from the bounty-hunters, contending that androids themselves would have handed other androids over to the police for money, it is ironic that the androids are just doing the opposite - sticking together as a community, instead of battling each other for survival - an indicator of empathy, not intelligence. In fact, as Haraway put it (shit! Haraway is deeply embedded in my mind), the mutual acceptance between Isidore, a "special", i.e., a person with sub-normal IQ and the super-intelligent androids with above-human IQ is a queer one - because it is not a politics of identity, but of affiliation - specials and androids are both considered sub-human, pieces of trash - and the "special", in fact, has more empathy than those who programmed the empathy test to detect androids passing off as humans. Isidore says, "but what does it matter to me? I mean, I'm a special; they don't treat me very well either, like for instance I can't emigrate." While Pris, an android tells Isidore, "You're a great man Isidore", Pris said, "you're a credit to your race." While Deckard, as the bounty hunter goes on 'retiring' the androids for money telling himself it was right to do so because of their lack of empathy, he finds in Phil Resch (an android bounty hunter with false implanted memories) a mirror to his own apathetic self. With increasing depression, he realizes that there is a very fine, flimsy line between androids and humans, and that they are emotionally a lot closer to each other than was supposed. Again, Rachael, the android Deckard almost falls in love with, with her final act of throwing to death Deckard's new real goat  proves herself more human than Deckard - it can be easily argued that the act proved that she was inhuman, incapable of empathy for doing what she did, but it also implies that she had a mind of her own, and she simply did to Deckard what he had been doing as a bounty hunter - brutally eliminating what some people held close as one of their own. the androids Deckard 'retire' were as real, non-negotiable to Rachael as the living sheep was to Deckard . What I really like in this work is that despite Deckard's change of heart, it offers no easy answers - various perspectives are explored, without a meaningful, final resolution. The waters are still muddy, but a few things become clearer. The deeper one reads, the more one sees that this is a conflict with perpetually gray areas. I saw the movie first, and found it much simplistic, probably because I'd seen more intense visual explorations of the same. I loved, however, the overwhelming world-building, the threat carried in the low, honey-tinged light and the seemingly murderous Russian-looking android against the tough, but sympathetic Deckard. The movie does away with the layers in this work - I wish they had been incorporated well, but the movie also includes two amazing scenes that the book does not have - Deckard, depicted as single, forces Rachael to acknowledge her desire for him - it is clear that Deckard desires her, not the other way round. The gender implications are not depicted in the book, but which I found astounding in the movie (even though Rachel is a stronger individual character in the book than the movie where she is quite passive. And the last scene, where the android saves Deckard's life  - I found the end of the movie a lot more effective than the book. In the latter half, it becomes too overtly sentimental, instead of maintaining the effective curt voice the first half had. I absolutely loathed that part where Deckard confesses to his wife that he had begun to empathize with the androids - hell! Did we really need to hear that? I loved the movie much more in that respect - the whole change of heart in Deckard is depicted with a simple eye-contact between Deckard and the last android. And a major issue, which I have deliberately kept last in the line for discussion, is its blatant misogyny - it rings loud and clear. I was compelled to rethink the sexist angle, like in the movie, where it comes across more as satire, than as a norm. But even after re-examination, I was sad to see that it was there as an integral part of the book, that fit in with its social aspects, instead of standing out as an in-built criticism of misogyny. Had the other aspects of the book not been so cleverly ahead of its time, this would have definitely warranted 2 stars. Or maybe even 1. The writing was terrible in the second half. But for a book so ahead of its time (in terms of androids and world-building), well, I ignore it.
