"Don't judge someone until you've stood at his forge and worked with his hammer, eh?" Another great read by Rick Riordan, another epic adventure that has kept me wanting more from these novels. I never thought id be so into this series as it isn't really my normal read, however what a surprise i was in for. I have one book left and i feel like its just not going to be enough to satisfy my enjoyment of this series, but we'll see. Just like the Harry Potter series, the quests and dangers get darker and darker, book by book, growing with the characters themselves- And i seriously love that. Although it could still be classified as a junior read, its becoming more of a YA as time(or should i say books) goes by. If you haven't read this series, than read it. If you like adventure, mysteries, suspense, epic battles, slight romance and Greek mythology, then this series is definitely for you. "But remember, boy, that a kind act can sometimes be as powerful as a sword." When Percy returns to Camp Half Blood, things are changing, the up and coming danger of the war is drawing closer. There is a new teacher, the director of camp is away for business. His friend Grover is on trial to decide his fate, he has a girlfriend and is still on the hunt for the long lost Pan. Percy is still keeping the truth of Nico's parentage a secret due to guilt over his sister's death, when keeping an eye on the lone boy, Percy realises Nico could be in real danger and could also be part of the prophecy that could determine the end of the god's world and the rise of Kronos. Annabeth is about to receive her first ever quest, quite possibly the most dangerous one yet and the most challenging- having a prophecy spoken to her by the Oracle, Annabeth must navigate Percy, Grover, Tyson through the Labyrinth- a maze full of traps, monsters , secret entrances and the scariest of all, has the ability to turn people insane being helplessly lost in the forever changing and growing maze. One of the entrances is right in the middle of Camp Half Blood and Luke is still out there plotting revenge on Percy, the gods and all the half bloods- if he happens to find his way through the maze and convince the Labyrinth maker Daedalus to help him, all the lives at Camp Half Blood will be in grave danger. With so much evil looming all around them, this mission could possibly be the most difficult one that the friends have yet to face, the rise of Kronos is drawing nearer, the prophecy set in motion and the fate of for all will soon be underway. Annabeth is possibly my favourite character throughout all the novels so far, she is smart, wise, witty and has a good heart. Once a friend always a friend, even when they may bring the destruction to all, she still sees hope in finding the good in the person, trying desperately to bring them back to the light. Being a child of Athena means she is really intelligent and likes to feed her mind. Her fascination with architecture and her knowledge has helped the friends many times during their quests, and really is part of the reason they have all survived so long , or so i believe. Being torn between Percy and Luke is a little annoying, although i get why she is so reluctent to act on her feelings for either, Luke has gone to the dark side, so to speak and Percy seems to be attracted to ever female in one way or another when their paths meet. I like strong, intelligent female characters, and Annabeth is definitely one of my favourites. "Be careful of love. It'll twist your brain around and leave you thinking up is down and right is wrong." Recommended for: Adventure/ YA/ Greek Mythology

Okay, let's talk about the good news: this is better than the travesty that was "Crossed." This book is decent. It comes really damn close to good, but doesn't quite make it. The GOOD: Things happen! There's a plot! There's action! After lacking these things in "Crossed," they were very welcome indeed. The writing got kinda good! This book did not feel like a chore to read, there was actual suspense and tension that kept me turning the page. Once the Rising takes over (in like chapter 2, so it's not a spoiler), things are not just hunky-dory afterwards. The one good Big Idea that Condie had with this is that when a rebellion overthrows a corrupt government, the result is not always as great as one imagined. This is a much more extreme version of District 13 from "Mockingjay." Very little awful poetry! This was such a breath of fresh air. Characters die. Of course, that should be a given in a dystopian novel about plague, but I still commend Condie for having the guts to see it through. The BAD: The complete and utter lack of foreshadowing in previous books. All of a sudden, there is a Plague going on, that becomes the central focus of this book. Is there so much as a passing mention of a pustule in the first two books? Not to my recollection. Also, one might as well skip reading "Crossed." The little that was accomplished in that book barely comes up in this one. Indie has a minor role to play, Hunter and Eli and Anna get cameo appearances, and Vick gets a passing mention. Why did I suffer through the agony that was Book Two if I could have skipped it? Also, the sheer amount of coincidences stretches any small plausibility this story might have beyond breaking point. Of course Cassia's ancestor founded the Rising. Of course her mom holds the key to solving everything through sheer coincidence. OF COURSE the one character Xander  meets and falls in love with is the long-lost love of another character. Give me a break - there's a fine line between a well-connected story and just unbelievable. All the wangsting. Especially Xander's existential crisis at the end was supremely worthy of eye-rolling. On a related note, how badly she forced the "love triangles." Essentially, every character needs to make a very serious choice between two potential love interests, both of whom said character is deeply in love with. Other than how irritating this is to have every character angsting about love interest, this cheapens the whole point of the series! The Matched triogy is founded on the twue wuv of Cassia and Ky - they're the ones who moved heaven and hell to be together. So to then have them both contemplating other love interests and whatnot just really cheapens the entire series for me. The entire lack of conclusion. Some might call this creatively "open-ended," I call it lazy. After putting up with Condie's lackluster writing, at the very least we are owed the chance to know what happens. Who is the new leader? Is he/she any good? It's not enough to know that the main characters end up alive and paired off, I'd quite like to know how the world itself ends up. Or were we not supposed to care about the rest of the world? The UGLY: The world-building? Oh dear heavens, the world-building! I have read some stinkers in my day, but I think Condie may take the cake as the WORST world-building I've ever seen. She is exceedingly fond of Capital Words, so written to Denote their Importance. One would then assume, that she would inform the reader as to what these Important Things actually are. I still have not the foggiest clue what the hell the Otherlands or the Enemy are, for example. But she goes one step further! There is the Pilot. As in, a walking, talking, character of a Pilot whom the main trio interacts with. And at NO POINT in the novel, does Condie bother to introduce him to us. We don't know who he is, what he looks like, or any remote thing about him. I am just completely perplexed by this "character" cropping up in the middle of a novel, and being treated as if he's Harry freaking Potter and we all know everything we need about him. Newsflash, Allyson Condie: characters need to be introduced - we must learn something about them, like their age/appearance/name/etc. She also must think herself mighty clever in her gimmicks. When a character goes into a coma, we get "chapters" from their perspective that are either to the effect of "I am here. I am. I." or (in one instance) just a blank page. I'm sorry, this is utter bulls***. This is not clever, it's not dramatic, it's just a bleeding waste of paper. In SUMMARY: The book is readable, and seems adequate on the surface, though any discerning reader can tell it's extremely flawed. Considering Condie received a million-dollar paycheck for this series, you'd think she'd have thought it through. Instead, it reads as if she came up with the idea of a dystopia with the Matching, and then winged it from there. If you have read the first two books, it's worth reading the conclusion. If you've only read "Matched," skip "Crossed" and read this one... or don't, and come up with your own ending (it'll probably be better). If you haven't started the series yet, I'd advise not bothering.
I loved it!!! I want the next book now ;(.

This is book 11 in the Psy-Changelling series. As always, there is a main plot, featuring a couple (Riaz and Adria) subplots, where you meet old and new characters, all intermingled in a tense background of three races in pre-war (Human, Changellings and Psy). In this installment a civil war begins inside the Psy. I liked this book because Nalini is a clever writer: she creates rich and believable characters and develops credible relationships. The main couple faces a big challenge: Riaz has met his mate, Lisette, but she is already married. For once, love and affection being more important than damn hormones  . I also enjoyed reading about Sienna, Hawke, Riley and Mercy. But what was awesome was the background, the intrigues (you will see again evil Ming Le Bong and Henry trying to main and kill in order to save Silence destroying whoever threatens it). But mainly  I feel cheated . Ms Singh said there is only going to be one Psy book per year and I wanted to see an important character featured in this installment (Vasic, Kaleb or Abel). I've been reading about these Psy warriors since 6 to 11 books ago. I also feel cheated about the mysterious woman (in coma the whole book), I haven't discovered anything new about her. So, Ms Singh, if you only will write a book per year, would you please make it relevant to the main plot? Of course, there is another possibility: you could write more than one a year!

The Girl on the Train has now joined E gunaika me to noumero 13 and O anemos sphurizei sten Koupela on the short list of books I read in one go. The definition of a page-turner but without reading cheap. Really captivating. I cared about the whodunnit aspect but not enough to stop reading these characters' thoughts and fears and think. Which is good. So when the twist started coming I wasn't expecting it. The most interesting part of the book to me was Rachel trying -and failing miserably- to break free from her obsession with her ex, and how her world turned upside down when she realized how he'd been lying to her for years. I like how when she finally did, suddenly there wasn't that much intense thought and feeling but more action. People who can't/choose not to let life go on and continue living in the past fascinate me, and this was a believable case, with very realistic reactions and petty thoughts, of the sort people don't admit to having.

Maxfield can write some really interesting stuff, or her works leave me facepalming. This is one of her better efforts. I have a love of psychics in stories, Psycop being one of my favorite series. With this novel, I loved the descriptions of Kevin dealing with his visions. Maxfield's strengths are here, mainly her complex, intriguing characters. The plot... hmm. From the moment the villain steps onto the scene, it's screaming obvious. We're given the profile of the Big Bad, and wouldn't you know it, here's someone who perfectly fits. Ingenious red herring? Unfortunately not. I didn't mind at first, but as the story progresses and the cops don't even put together their own clues, it makes them look stupid and incompetent. There are a few wtf moments, like when Conner slugs Kevin for daring to say he might go home, because totally legit reaction, right? At least Kevin's father brings up the issue of domestic abuse. And Kevin's very quick reconciliation with his father just fell flat. Oh, but he didn't mean it? And did he mean to send his son to a Catholic boy's only school on the other side of the country, or was that done in a moment of anger, too? One that couldn't be rectified in the three years he was there? Um... yeaaaah. These are things that should have been fixed in the revision process. :/ There are a few too many coincidences that bring the MCs together, and the ending was predictable while being over the top. Still, having counted all the issues against this story, I did enjoy most of this book. The last few lines of the epilogue were perfect! xD There's no suspense here, so read for the journey as that's really the heart of the story.

Well, after a slow start, that was quite brilliant. My Review! Fun fact: I tried this once before but couldn't get into it. So I set it aside. But after loving ADSOM, I knew I needed to give it a second chance. And I am SO GLAD I did because it was pretty friggin' great! It was so very unique, and I adored the main character, Mac. And Wesley was pretty cute. :D I didn't even see the twist coming! It's very hard for books to surprise me, and this one did. I can't wait to read more! Rating: 4 Paw Prints!

"They say monsters live under beds. They're wrong because our mind is where the monsters truly reside." This was such an uplifting and inspiring story. Full of hope and the promise of second chances. I loved Kathryn's simplistic writing style and how she effortlessly portrayed the journey of a girl suffering from mental illness and her way to recovery. Here are some of my favorite quotes: "A past left without resolution is surely a past that will revisit you one day." "falling in love can't always be a happily ever after or a once in a lifetime kind of story. Those happen in books, in movies. This is life and it's real. Life has no script, no outline. We broke the rules of love long ago. All I know for sure is that with you, the rules will never apply." "Strong people don't push other people down. They help them up." "Sometimes you just have to accept that some things can't be fixed, and that it's not about fixing what's broken, but about accepting what's lost." "Time is just a band-aid. It covers up the wound but the wound has to heal on its own." "You're my here, my there, and my always everywhere."

This was a mother's day gift from a girlfriend and she did GOOD! So I'll break up this review into story, romance/love, and sex. Story- The story was great! It flowed well, the writing was wonderful. Loved the alternating POV. 5/5 of the writing and story development! It's romance, so YES, I expect a HEA, but she threw enough believable twists and turns that it kept me on my toes. GREAT JOB! My *only* wish is that the epilogue had been longer. As a standalone, it is GREAT, but (if you read my reviews) you know I love the after HEA, and this just gives you a brief glimpse. But that's okay because the story was fabulous nonetheless. Romance/Love- Yeah, yeah. The male trying to deny his feelings. The alpha controlling male at that. *Swoon* I loved the way it wasn't insta-love and the way that their relationship progressed, albeit IRL it still would have been quickly. They both really fought their feelings, and I loved the fact that she wasn't pining after him in desperation. Honestly, despite the unusual circumstances of their meeting, and their unusual relationship- swear this is one of the HEALTHIEST relationships in an alpha male dom type relationship that I have read. They have feelings, but they both also have self respect and enough maturity not to throw themselves at someone who isn't reciprocating. Brie's journey to this strong woman and the way she shuts him down in that bathroom scene was great. Even though, YES, I OBVIOUSLY wanted them to be together- you go girl! Have some self respect and say "FUCK OFF" to the guy trying to use you in a public bathroom when you have feelings. LOVED IT! Overall, watching their very appropriate relationship unfold, despite it's non-traditional circumstance, was wonderful. This is definitely a VERY accurate BDSM portrayal, and I *loved* it! :) They are a sweet and wonderful couple, and I loved their journey! Sex- Geez Louise. Honestly, there's not much else to say. My husband asked me why I was blushing, nuff said.

Series note: Warrior's Apprentice is the 2nd book published in the series, the 4th book chronologically within the series, but the first book about the series' main protagonist Miles. It's a good place to start. Seventeen-year-old Miles Vorkosigan, painfully brilliant but suffering from brittle bones, a slightly crooked spine, and being not quite five feet tall, has only one life plan: to get into the Barrayaran Service Academy and train as an officer. When his own moment of bad judgement wipes him out in the physical admission tests, he finds himself staring into the abyss of a purposeless life as his noble father's heir. But Miles is nothing if not unpredictable, even to himself, and when he's sent offworld on a visit to his grandmother, a momentary impulse to help another washed-out man starts Miles building a teetering edifice of pretense and responsibility, and far more danger and adventure than the Service Academy could ever have exposed him to. I adore this book. I spent the first hundred pages waiting with progressively less hope for the moment I'd be bowled over, because stylistically, this book is decently written but not amazing. Miles, who I'd heard described as an amazing character, was a good character - he has a little of the Lord Peter Wimsey self-effacing brilliance to him, with more brashness - but his dialogue and his description don't sweep you off your feet with love immediately. I didn't fall in love with this book and with Miles until he barged in on that first conversation on Beta. From that point on I watched with growing disbelief and delight, because oh my god, the nerve of this character. The risks he takes, the connections he makes, the scale he thinks on. This courage not of deed but of thought, the way every step is bigger, and over a higher precipice. I'm in awe of Miles and of Bujold, for the bounding leaps of her plot. They are definitely bounding: it's not a tightly plotted novel of revelations and concealed cleverness, it's cleverness right on the surface. And I can't even deal with how much I like it. Content warnings: military rape and torture (mercifully lacking in details) in the backstory of the B-plot.
So So SO Good! I feel like all of my dreams have been made into reality. All I could ever ask for in a sequel <3. Side Note - That stupid freaking lizard.

I was a little slow in getting around to reading this one. I did start it once quite a while ago but couldn't get into it. This time I forged through the first 40 pages to finally become engaged as Offred told more of her past in contrast to her present. The movement between past and present is often quick, mere hints, but gradually they pile up into a whole.The treatment of women is an extension of attitudes as current now as when the book was written. For quite a number of pages, the pace remained slow; the life restricted routine. Various liaisons later and the pace quickens. For once an ending is well done. There is ambiguity whether she is taken by friend or foe at the end. Then there are the scholars' reports in the 2100s after the finding of the journal that is the novel. The ambiguity is only partially resolved. Offred made it to Maine, but there is no further trace. A parallel to the end of Offred's friend Moira.

I'm wavering on this review. I have to say it's closer to 3.5 but I can't give a 4. It's such a beautifully written book with compelling characters but boy did it depress me. I really enjoyed the slice of life down in Antarctica and at McMurdo Station, this was such an original location for a story, one I'd love to see more of in future books. The descriptions of life there in relative isolation were so interesting and one of the reasons why this is pushing closer to a 3.5 I'm glad there was no quick fix for the characters here, most especially, seeing Max come to terms with his alcoholism was a difficult read for me. There were several times during this book where I expected horrible things to happen because of his drinking. I actually had to take a breath and push through to see what the ramifications of some of his later drinking exploits were, I really expected to read something that he as a character and I as reader couldn't come back from. I'm not adverse to reading darker more dramatic stories but I lean more towards those with a thread of hope running through them. Max hits rock bottom here before he starts to drag himself back up we're there throughout that whole journey to the very lowest of the low and I will honestly say it was sometimes difficult to get throught that. I don't want to give the impression that this all dark, there are moments of sweetness here between Max and his best friend but even that is tinged with sadness. Max and Andre have very strong chemistry and the story ends on a hopeful note. I just think for all the darkness the characterization of both Max and Andre is a bit thin, this for me has a lot to do with the length of the story which was surprisingly short. I think with a longer story I could have come away with a deeper understanding of the character's motivations, especially Andre, who has a backstory that I think suffers from the length of the work. Still this is a really intense, concentrated story that is wonderfully written but in the end, too dark for me. I enjoyed it and can recommend it but it's not something I'll ever go back to again.

Hoo boy. This was so raw and painful and true, and made darkly hilarious and heartbreaking by Roz Chast's cartoons. We will all be Roz; we will all be her parents. It is all so heavy, yet worth looking at as unflinchingly as possible. And maybe hugging our siblings if we have them, and starting another savings account? "One of the worst parts of senility must be that you have to get terrible news over and over again. On the other hand, maybe in between the times of knowing the bad news, you get to forget it and live as if everything was hunky-dory." "I wish that, at the end of life, when things were truly 'done,' there was something to look forward to. Something more pleasure-oriented. Perhaps opium, or heroin. So you become addicted. So what? All-you-can-eat ice cream parlors for the extremely aged. Big art picture books and music. EXTREME palliative care, for when you've had it with everything else: the x-rays, the MRIs, the boring food, and the pills that don't do anything at all. Would that be so bad?"

Okay, when I first began reading this book I fell in love with the fact that is was based in the South. Being a Southern girl born and raised, it made my day. Then, the further I delved into the story, the more I fell in love with the characters and the plot. Ethan Wate is just like every other sixteen year old boy in the town of Gatlin. He's on the basketball team, has the right friends, he's one of them. Only, he's not. Ethan has been waiting for something, anything, to happen since his mother passed away and the answer to that may be just around the corner when Lena Duchannes moves to town. They have both been dreaming about each other, neither knowing who the other is until a random encounter during a torrential downpour. And the dream always ends the same, they lose their grip on each other and Lena disappears. What does it all mean? The pace is slow and steady, revealing a little more with each chapter. Including a big secret that Lena, her Uncle Macon, and others around Gatlin have been keeping for years. A secret that could endanger both Lena and Ethan. One of the few clues you get early on is a count down of numbers that she keeps on her hand, each day she marks off another day that's passed. I absolutely adore Ethan and his constant devotion to Lena. The more he learns the more it draws him to her, and vice versa. They are connected in a way that can't e explained and is too beautiful to pass up. Kami and Margaret weave a beautiful tale of love and betrayal, hope and desperation, fantasy and southern tradition. This is such a wonderfully written and engaging story and I for one can't wait to find out what happens next.

I don't know how the author did it, but this novel is way better than the last two! And I din't think that was possible. I loved the description in the last two novels and the dialogue between characters was awesome, but the action, scene description and character interactions were ramped up to kick-ass levels in this one! It goes without saying, though I'll say it, that I am dying for the next installment [ with no release date in sight :( ]! Charley truly has her hands full in this novel with so many different things and the author holds up her end by making it not only believable, but interesting. Usually with a lot of stories, when the author tries to pack so many things in one novel's plot it turns the story chaotic- leaving the reader wondering what the hell is going on, not so with  Third Grave Dead Ahead . Charley is certainly insanity inspiring at times, but that's why we love her. In this chapter Charley is charged with finding a missing woman by her missing husband  who goes missing because of said husband   and dealing with her father who wants her to quit being a private investigator while helping Reyes find his not so dead father (who he'd been accused of killing and getting tossed in jail). We also get to meet another intriguing character who seems to like Charley as more than a person passing. Donovan is an interesting character thrown into the mix, especially after what happened with Reyes. Reyes was certainly an asshole in this novel when he used Charley as bait, even though he says he loves her! It doesn't make him any less hot though-bad me. I also don't know what to make of the nun- she's an odd one, someone I hope will prove helpful to Charley now that her life seems to be in the crapper. BAD DADDY! BAD REYES! Horrible happenstance. Still cannot wait for the next one and am still rooting for old idiotic Reyes. :P Though I do like me some eye candy-thank you so much big bad biker dude!

I was a bit skeptical on this series after the second book, but this book really set my hopes back up to high for this series. It's fabulous. Some parts were a bit indecipherable because of the lofty writing style, but other than that, everything about this book was golden. I still don't get the "cut the moon in two" part about the title, but I guess it does make some sense. A lot better than the second book's, whose title I didn't really get (because September never leads revels in Fairyland-Below). This book fleshed out the world of Fairyland a lot more and throughout the entire book it has you questioning about the Fairies' true nature on the inside. While the first book was merely a joyous adventure that dealt with hard experience for poor September, and while the second book dealt with the magic of Fairyland, this book dealt with the people of Fairyland--who they are. This book also talks strongly about who a person really is, not what people assume they are. That's probably what made me love this book so much: it carried such a strong message. Another reason why I liked this book is possibly because of the reappearance of Ell and Saturday, except now we see that both of them are far more troubled than they were previously--as well as September. You can tell it straight out in Ell--he has a curse, and so whenever he breathes fire, he shrinks. This turns out to be a very big issue in the entire book and meddles with Ell's self-confidence quite a bit. Saturday is a little harder, but as he, September, and Ell journey across the Moon to stop Ciderskin the Yeti, we see that he took September's absence quite terribly, as did Ell. As their journey progresses, Saturday also has to deal with older and/or younger versions of himself, and he has to explain to September about being a Marid. Quite obviously, his relationship with September is quite the roller-coaster ride. The plot was fantastic and I loved the many plot twists at the end. The interludes, told in the Black Cosmic Dog's view, build up the suspense and make you wonder what's going to happen at the end (even though there are only 2 interludes that probably only make up 4 pages altogether, and I applaud Valente on doing such a fantastic job). There are many cliffhangers throughout the book and we also have Charlie Crunchcrab's laws on the sidebar. So many plotlines. All fantastic and concluded wonderfully. As I stated previously, the writing is a bit difficult to comprehend, but I was fine with that, because it feels a lot toned down from The Girl Who Fell Beneath Fairyland. The pacing is just as quick as always, and by the second chapter things have already taken place. The worldbuilding is wonderful, and the characters are once again as quirky as they were in the first book. Even though the next book in the series, The Boy Who Lost Fairyland, doesn't center on September, I'm very excited to read it. Why? No, not because it partly takes place in Chicago, my hometown. Because the Fairyland series is awesome and I don't care who or what the story focuses on. Also, the changelings really intrigue me. 3.5, really. I loved Oliver's character development, but for an adult reader, there was a bit too much high school drama. If I have a teenage daughter at some point, this is a book i'd love for her to read.

I had liked Lady Midnight, but Lord of Shadows reminded me of all the reasons I actually loved the Shadowhunter Chronicles - I even felt a little nostalgic reading it because it evoked how I felt when I was much younger and read TMI for the first time - somehow really calm and comfortable and thoroughly entertained. It has all the strengths you can always expect from a CC book - an intriguing, elaborately constructed plot, interesting characters and arcs, just...solid entertainment. But LOS takes all that and somehow takes it to an even higher and better level. First of all there is the wide variety of settings - maybe it is just the return to London that made me feel so nostalgic, all the TID and TLH references. But I loved all of it, and even more than in Lady Midnight I had a distinct 'feeling' for the atmosphere, like the characters and the plot and setting all fitted together and created a specific 'vibe'. the exploration of Faerie, Polperro, the churches and manors, the London institute. i could totally picture everything happening, it felt real. I love that feeling so much, and that alone made me love the book. And the TMI characters are a part of the plot and tied into it but their roles arent too big and they didnt actually annoy me at all this time, which!!! great. The characters are much less stereotyped than the TMI ones and often in themselved play with cliches - which was already apparent in LM but more so here. They are also all incredibly mature? It was so cool and refreshing. The relationship drama was waaaay less bad than I thought it would be because of that, I was positively surprised. I especially love how the Mark-Kieran-Cristina thing develops and how it turns love triangle stereotypes on the head. Especially Kieran's character development is so amazing and I like him so much better now? I loved Ty, Livvy and Kit as a squad so much, and I care significantly more about all of them now! Especially Kit. His 'outsider perspective' on the Shadowhunters was interesting and his relationship with Ty is incredibly wonderful and heartwarming. Consider me in. Then there's Emma and Julian of course, whose relationship I also found myself liking better this time. I like how  they aren't in that angsty 'everyone thinks the other doesnt love them' situation any more though, thank god. basically alllll the characters grew closer to my heart and i appreciate their complexity and think theyre some of the best CC has ever created. Then there is the other things that truly made me love this. POLITICS. yes. I had hoped that this book would feature nuanced discussion of the effects of bigotry and hate on society and hell yeah, my wildest dreams came true. both the nuance, and the wide scope of exploration of these topics are there. I remember how CC wrote somewhere that the true villain is the Clave and bigotry in shadowhunter society? and that is so true. there are multiple villains in LOS, but all of their motivations can somehow be tied back to having been wronged by hate and prejudice. and i love that so much?? i love understandable villains. I loved  Annabel's character especially, and finding out more about her and malcolm's past was really intense. no wonder he had this unhealthy fixation on her and didnt care about hurting anyone else - he never had anyone else who treated him with kindness when he was young. . I also liked all the secrets and scheming and bargains, they made for a very supenseful and exciting plot, more so than the one in LM. so yeah. that was more than i even asked for. the variety of settings, the wide scope of the plot relating to politics and society, the character development, and the specific ~feel~ that came up while reading that i cant really explain...made me love this a lot. do i have anything to complain about? it was really long! but kinda necessary with all these characters. otherwise i cant think of anything! cc really outdid herself here. if possible im even more excited for TLH now, though its cruel how long we must wait now for Queen of air and darkness. :D recommendation, recommendation!

3.5 stars I just wrote a whole long review for this and then the Internet or Goodreads stopped working and I lost all of it *sigh*. I'll try this again. As most people who've reviewed this book have mentioned, this book is freakin' weird. It's probably the weirdest book I've ever read but it's a good kind of weird. The way the book was written isn't usually something I like. It's not very descriptive but it worked with the main character/narrator and really added to his personality. I liked Austin and his friend Robby a lot. Their friendship as well as them separately were enjoyable and they were mostly well-rounded characters. Austin was certainly vulgar and horny, but it added to the story and isn't something you see so blatantly shown in YA. I liked Shann's step-father a lot but I didn't care much for Shann. They were the only two characters besides Austin and Robby who went beyond one dimensional. The rest of the side characters were unremarkable. What really kept me hooked on this book was the creativity of the storytelling as well as the peculiarity. (I also loved Austin's exploration of his sexuality, but I'll get more into that later). At first, the storytelling is a little odd. It doesn't seem to be in chronological order. At one point Shann comments on the way Austin tells stories and the way she describes it made me enjoy the storytelling. Though I will admit it got too repetitive at times and made the story drag on a bit. The thing I loved most about Grasshopper Jungle was Austin's exploration of his sexuality. I don't like romance books and it seems like most lgbt+ storylines are only featured in romance novels. Having Austin question his sexuality wasn't the main plot and I really enjoyed that. It was also a realistic exploration of sexuality. Questioning, confusion, and hornyness. In case the coding doesn't work on mobile, here's a warning. SPOILERS AHEAD Where the book really lacked for me was the ending. So much about the ending really frustrated me. It felt like the book ended on the climax with no resolution and it left so many questions unanswered. Is Austin's brother okay? Are his parents okay? Do the Unstoppable Soldiers take over all of the United States? There was so much potential for a polyamorous relationship but even that wasn't completely clear. Sometimes open-ended endings really work but that wasn't the case with this novel. When I finished I was wondering where the rest of the book was. Another frustration I had with the ending was Shann. Her pregnancy felt like a cheap way to "repair" her and Austin's relationship. It also really made it feel like Shann's main purpose of the novel was for eventual breeding in Eden. It was a cheap solution to their relationship on top of an already cheap ending. I enjoyed the overall weirdness of this book. It was clever and unique, but I was really disappointed by the ending.

This is a YA novel set 20-30 years before Soulless, but in the same world. Sophronia is sent to what she thinks will be a normal finishing school, but it turns out to be anything but. Instead, at Mademoiselle Geraldine's, she learns how to be a lady, and a spy. Sophronia is a fun character without some of the more annoying characteristics that can plague YA protagonists, and her friends are also well-drawn. I was sometimes distracted trying to figure out which characters might show up from the Soulless series, and why the technology seems to be more advanced, but otherwise, I enjoyed this book. It is completely unnecessary to know anything about the other series to enjoy this one.

Damage Done is about a girl named Julia who moves to a new school and changes her name after her twin brother is arrested for killing 11 people at their old school. From the minute I started reading I knew what was going to happen in this book. I appreciated the attempt the author made to tell this story because honestly I don't think I've ever read a story like this one: where we're supposed to believe everything the main character says and then the twist is that they are a pathological liar and killer . This idea is so interesting to me and it could've been a really surprising twist, but there were just so many weirdly worded scenes that made it obvious that Lucy/Julia  was not to be trusted. From the very beginning, I pegged her  as a character that wasn't reliable and was kinda sketchy. I liked that we got hints about what was really going on, but I think there were a little too many. There were times when Lucy/Julia  just really seemed manic and crazed and was exactly like her brother . I was hoping this would be a thrilling story where I would get to the end and be so shocked that I would have to go back through all the pages again to find quotes that connect everything, but instead everything was really spelled out so the end wasn't a surprise. At a certain point in this book I was just reading quickly to try to get to the end to find out WHY everything happened since I already knew whodunnit. The last few chapters in this book were particularly disturbing and I thought the ending with Lucy/Julia getting away and having ZERO consequences  was very unrealistic.
