I was moved, provoked, and invigorated reading this book. I am a believer, so for me this just reiterated or provided inspiring proof of my belief system. What I enjoyed about the book: 1) The miracles. I love hearing a good miracle-and this story is full of them. The tale of the family receiving an unexpected flood of donation money, enough to cover their vast medical bills is a miracle. The father having a prayer answered-even one said through grieving anger-was a miracle. Colton's story touching his baby sitter-that was a miracle. Colton's validation of the divinely inspired art of a girl half a world away, that's a miracle. In my opinion, I think Colton being the child of a minister, and having this experience, is a miracle by itself. If the same child had the same experience with two non-religious parents I don't think we'd have this book. I don't think the parents would have known what kind of questions to ask, or would have seen the significance in the answers given. 2) I like that the author stays on track. He doesn't get lost down dog trails, or bash on those who are not from the same belief system he is. The book is very focused on the relevant events around Colton's trip to Heaven and what he saw. The religious expositions are there only to help narrate for those less familiar with Christianity. 3) I have a four year old to thank for making me feel better about  the book of revelations. I also have a four year old to thank for CREEPING ME OUT, by relaying the truth my mind likes to ignore about the devil not currently residing in hell. I remembered why I don't like to think about it because it makes me feel like there is a serial killer in my living room. Thank you Colton for the food for thought. I was intrigued reading the two polar extremes of reviews this book received. There is definitely a trend, the believers love it the non-believers bash it. I was interested to read the book and see where perhaps the author may have lost the "non-believer" audience. That answer was easy: Colton doesn't mince words when he  freaked out at a funeral and demanded to know if the dead man had Jesus in his heart. "Daddy he can't go to heaven if he doesn't have Jesus in his heart." There it is-no doubt that is going to hurt peoples feelings. No surprise there. I also think others were lost to their own ignorance of a faith they might claim in a secular status. I know this, because I was a baby Christian not that long ago. Some of the riveting moments in the book, would not have made much sense or had the same impact to the once baby Christian me. There is a language of intelligibility barrier that sometimes cannot be overcome when you are not a believer. You can see the author do his best to explain the relevance of what Colton revealed. He tied in the scriptural basis, explained the "why" as best he could. But I think many significant points are lost to the baby Christian audience as well as the non-believer audience. I expected to see opposition; it comes with any religious topic. It was just intriguing for me to see how vehement some of the opposition is. I've seen how quickly non-believers get riled over what to me is pretty innocuous stuff. So it was not a shock to see the trend of poor reviews all hovering around one of the following themes. I will list them and then state my point of view. 1) The book is bad/I'm offended, because their boy was saved through prayer implying my loved one could have been if I was a believer. Here's my thought: After reading complaint 1, I expected to read several chapters explaining lengthy prayers the family and congregation made. It wasn't there, and what was I felt was summed up very nicely. If anything what was discussed was an introspection of the father/minster and how he felt guilty for lashing out at God. It was very human-and brave for a minister to admit his weakness in a very dark time. There are numerous books dedicated to prayer, the kinds of prayer, how it can be effective, what you can and can't pray for, there's blogs, and websites-and if all else fails the Bible itself (imagine that!). I'm no expert-look it up-I'm not going down the dog trail of why someone's loved one was saved and others were not. However-I do believe in prayer and I believe in miracles. I loved reading about an answered prayer-and miracle. It's a beautiful thing to know we are heard even when we are not at our best. 2) The book is bad because of course this kid saw all that stuff, "his dads a minister". Here's my thought: The father did an excellent job of explaining the boys knowledge and exposure to the Bible. I can relate very well to the authors amazement at what Colton told him. I know the cognitive age of a four year old, I have a three and four year old I am raising right now. So I'll tell you, my secret is out, or maybe not-but for all those who don't know, my kids are exposed to a very progressive evangelical form of Christianity. I know for a fact they are not taught the kinds of things Colton was talking about. I'd be proud and astonished if they could tell me who Jesus's cousin is, where Jesus sits, what the Holy Ghost does, where the marks on Jesus are, and like the author points out "Why Jesus died?" For the last question I might get an answer like-to save us, or because he loves us-but NEVER the answer Colton gave. Come on if this is a brain washing Christian household why didn't the older sister have the same answer Colton gave? For Colton to know Jesus called his father to the ministry- for a four year old that's profound. The author pointed out his own astonishment at Colton knowing these things. I believe the author is being honest when he claims Colton knowledge did not come from his parents or their church's Sunday school. Christians don't teach down to the level of detail Colton knew, because kids don't retain it/understand it. That's what makes the story remarkable-we get a glimpse of Heaven from a child's point of view. He used child's words to provide descriptions of things he had no knowledge of and had never seen before. 3) The book is bad because/I'm offended because it implies if I don't believe like a Christian I'm not going to heaven. Here's my thought on this: Once again it's a child telling you this, a four year old. Not once does the author lay this on you. If this really bothers you I challenge you to seek out why? If you know why, then does the story really merit the same rating as your opinion of Christianity? None of the three objections, in my opinion, equal a bad book. I think there could be value in people examining why they have such an emotional response and why they are so quickly offended by a four year olds experience.

Word of advice: soldier on through the first three or so chapters. I promise it gets better. I actually discarded the book as unreadable, and only picked it up again for a reading challenge. And oh, how glad I am of it. (So like, the first chapter is cool, the next two-three chapters are varying levels of what is this crap, and then it gets good.) The book begins with Ayden the elf being delightfully alien and using magic described as song. Ayden then proceeds to be an idiot (why couldn't he have just commanded the elf troops that were right there under his tree to help him fight the humans? Because then there'd be no story, of course) and gets himself enslaved. There's a highly unrealistic torture scene. What prince interrogates the dangerous, magic-wielding captive in his own rooms? With no guards present? And has the elf bleed all over the place? That is just impractical, damn it. And then he puts the elf to sleep in his own bed. (This was the point when I put the book down in disgust. For a little while.) However! Despite the eyeroll-inducing beginning, the book progresses fairly smoothly. The writing is absolutely lovely. With a few hiccups: after the first couple 'crack its' and 'befang its', the terms, though a nice touch giving insight about the characters' cultural background, grew rather annoying. But they only really appear in number when the characters get all pissy, and that doesn't happen too often. Other than this minor annoyance, the writing really is wonderful: just enough description, a nice sense of humour, and the characters do not have the 'internal-monologue the living daylights out of this story' syndrome. The initial turn off was one of the characters. I started off being okay with Ayden, but despising Freyrik for his seemingly random infatuations with the elves. But then he turned out to be simply kind. And adorable. I still like him more than the elf, but I'm generally not a fan of rebellious characters, so that's no wonder. I still think Freyrik sympathises a little too much with the elves, while his own people are shown as cruel, unfair and largely driven by their nether regions. And misogynistic. Just, too much hate, yeah? My favourite character is Lord Lini, who is a kind, patient man, and I honestly admire him for putting up with Freyrik's and Ayden's collective bullshit. The whole thing with Kona assaulting(?) Ayden was overdone, I think. He acted as if he was genuinely scared of her after, but during the assault he seemed, well, not unaffected, but not panicking, either. I am not saying a man cannot feel violated by a woman, so on and so forth, but he had enough control of the situation that I find his later trauma a little exaggerated. Honestly? It screams of plot device applied to give Ayden reason to leave the castle willingly (while before he was clearly planning to oppose the notion for all he was worth). The romance progresses in a natural, gentle way. There's UST, which is good. Although I felt like the tension isn't replaced well enough once the romance is resolved. I mean, I was happy for a while when the characters were having trouble because of a combination of conflicting personalities, beliefs and responsibilities, but then this was replaced by external circumstances getting in their way. Which is kinda meh to me. The slave-and-master trope is very well executed. It is not milked for cheap fanservice gratification, there is no excessive violence, nor ridiculously exaggerated possessiveness that so often plagues similar plots. I wouldn't call the story believable, exactly (hullo, it is fantasy), but I had no trouble suspending my disbelief. I kind of wish Freyrik would display more of a backbone when confronting Ayden, though. He had lots of reasons to get angry, and some, I don't know, silent fuming would have been nice (because obviously violence is a no-no). My favourite scene would have to be the battle. There was some exciting strategic planning, and the execution was neither overdone nor understated. It was so nice to see the characters working together, and being badass. I also liked how their personalities shone through all the action. I'm not very happy about the ending. It's one hell of a cliffhanger, in the sense that I don't even know whether/how much I should really be worried about the characters. I probably should (I definitely should according to reviews of the second book), but, just. I can't really get very far with speculation, because anything could happen. I'm not a fan of ending books like this. I'm not a fan of ending books on cliffhangers in general, because it pretty much forces me to get the sequel if I want any sort of closure. At all. It's like saying: "It's awesome that you read the 400+ pages of my book! Now I'm gonna shove some more down your throat!" Those are mostly minor gripes, though. I liked the book. It has a solid narrative, defined characters, and easily draws the reader in. There are no superfluous scenes or useless characters. The two major females are portrayed pretty okay (by m/m romance standards). There is plot. There is angst. There are sex scenes (a bit too long for my tastes, but I'm probably just weird). The relationship between Freyrik and Ayden is sweet and not totally unrealistic (I promised myself I would not rant about the likelihood of a 29 years old human and an 800-ish elf being together). I also loved the bits of mystery: what really happened during the Great Betrayal? What the hell is up with Berendil? Who on earth is the Aegis? It's always nice when a book keeps me guessing. Okay. Things you might want to know about before plunging in: --ridiculous age difference (which has little impact on the characters, but still) --attempted sexual assault (of sorts?) --some torture (nothing really disturbing) --some more pain and bloodshed (public whipping) --hating on humans and misogyny None of the above is jarring in the text. (Except maybe the last point.) I'd say it's all handled pretty well (though not necessarily with a whole lot of realism). I'd give Counterpoint 3.5 stars if I could.

(some spoilers) I really liked how this book turned out. Originally, I didn't expect to like this one as much as the first book, Pushing the Limits, because in that book I absolutely hated Beth. And it's easy to hate Beth when reading her in the point of view of the other characters because you can't understand her or why she's such a bitch. No one likes a bitch. This book, however, gives you her full story; her reasons for hardening up and pushing others away. And it's hard to read because it makes you absolutely rage that there are people who are like this, who treat kids like this, even if you know it's something that happens to people. Reading about it and seeing through her eyes is tough. When Beth's mom outright tells her that she hates her, that everything bad that has happened is her fault, made me rage. And when Beth talks about her father telling her she's the absolute worse. thing that happened to him, your heart breaks because no father should ever tell their child that. Ryan is lovely. In the beginning you're given this typical jock type you don't expect to love but you fall for him. You're able to see behind the wall of perfection he's built for himself, that his father has forced on the entire family, and it was really wonderful watching him grow as a character while getting to know Beth and to realize there's more to his life than what his parent's have built for him. The whole dare part of the story pissed me off but I'm glad that was nipped in the bud instead of something used in the end to push Beth away from Ryan, instead of the lies the others spread in an attempt to ruin them. The dare may have played a part in that, but at least it was lies and he didn't hide it. I really liked that this was a young adult novel about teenagers that was not trying to be some extraordinary tale, but it's something real and relatable yet the author did such a wonderful job with the characters that gives it something special, makes it more than a typical YA story. At least, it was for me.

With the release of the movie, I read all 3 books this week. The first two are worth it - well written and interesting in their world building. This one? Terrible. The format of the first books is abandoned, and it was obvious to me that Tris wouldn't make it  due to this. Very disappointing.

Genre: southern belles, high school rivals, ancient destinies revealed Summary: Harper Price has everything under control. She is student body president, head cheerleader, top of her class, Homecoming Queen, etc. However, she is in the wrong place at the right time when she witnesses the death of the high school janitor, who turns out to be a top-secret ninja protector. Just before he dies, he passes on his power to Harper. Suddenly, Harper has a whole new skill set and is thrilled. Until she finds out who she has to protect...David Stark, arch-nemesis numero uno, annoying newspaper editor, able to foresee the future and possibly get killed because of it. But Harper doesn't quit, ever. She can handle this. Right? Response: I adore Rachel Hawkin's series Hex Hall. I think she has such a knack for teenage internal dialogue. Rebel Belle is just as intriguing. Harper is so perfect, you want to hate her, but you cannot. She is indomitable, like Molly Brown. But seriously, Harper is admirable. I really liked the juxtaposition of Southern Old World charm and the kick-butt mentality of Miss Congeniality or Indiana Jones. I will be definitely watching out for the rest of the series.

So this was a very readable book. Whenever I picked it up, I didn't want to put it down. And I had a lot of fun with the fact that it was set around where I live. (Seattle Mariners reference! Getting the weather right!) But . I guess, overall, it wasn't ENOUGH. I didn't find out enough of what was going on. (I know it's a series, but I feel like I figured out most of what was going on pretty early on. I wanted more.) And there's a love triangle, but it's annoying in a different way than usual, since both guys seemed problematic and I didn't particularly want Danica with either of them. (And I found the one Danica seemed to like more far less interesting.) But it's a different kind of YA book. More sci-fi than paranormal. And I might read the next one.

I was pretty unimpressed with this one, which was a pity, because I liked what it was aiming for. I love sci-fis, I love outer space, I love interplanetary travel, I love missing royalty, I love starpilots, I love metaphors for contemporary issues like racial inequality, prejudice, etc. EMPRESS had all that and I was ready to love it, but I couldn't. First off, let me be clear that for a debut it wasn't bad at all. I love watching authors grow in their craft as their career develops, so I'll be interested to see what Rhoda Belleza is doing in a few years. However, I felt this particular book could have been a lot stronger. I was too confused by the world-building, which was ambitious but not as clearly defined as I would have liked. I didn't understand the war that caused all the problems or why the bulk of the hatred landed on the Wraetans who sided with the tree people (starts with an F?) than the tree people themselves since they sounded like the main antagonists against the Kalu. There was a ton of hopping between planets, which was frustrating because even with faster-than-light travel, NOTHING happens that quickly in space, and also it gave me little time to ground myself before we were off somewhere else again. I couldn't get a grip on what all the proper nouns were supposed to mean. I also thought the world-building in general was underpolished in places (for example, when Rhee calls Aly "a black guy," it felt startlingly contemporary and didn't fit the tone of the rest of the narrative.) Also, the beginning was too info dumpy by far. I didn't like how male-heavy the story was, and I didn't like how difficult it was to remain in Rhee's head. She was rather nonsensical, clinging to ONE memory to prove that her chosen target was her parents' murderer. I also didn't get her trust in Dahlen at all. Why is she even still alive? Why not off her after the first explosion failed? Where has she been since then and how has that life shaped her? What the heck is this girl supposed to be? I wanted to like the relationship between Aly and Vin, but there was too little real interaction. It was all bickering and being cut off by yet another danger. Their scenes were also a good example of the strange narrative choices made on when to focus and when to summarize. Really? You're going to COMPLETELY SKIP OVER Vin's death and burial and sum it up in an emotionless retrospective? Seriously? I ended up skimming the last fourth or so of the book (just after Aly met Kara), because I already knew who the bad guy was and what was going to happen. Overall, the pacing was weird, the plot was uneven, the characters were largely unmemorable (they tried, bless their hearts, but only Aly and Dahlen rated half a sniff of interest from me), there was too much info-dumping, the world-building was confusing, and the book itself just felt... underpolished. As a general rule, when I have these complaints for a debut, I place the blame with the editor and agent. No matter how many trunked manuscripts a writer has, they trust those two positions to guide the story to where it needs to be, and I don't feel like that guiding and shaping process fully happened here. Like I said, there was a good deal of potential here, and undoubtedly others will fall in love, but I'll probably skip past the rest of this series and check back when the author tries something new.

I loved it for the first 75% and then it abruptly changes to a like suspense/mystery format which I feel kind of unsure about - it disrupted the wonderful atmosphere a bit. However, overall it was great, both a page turner while also being great writing with lots of stuff to ponder and catch your attention on. The narrator's feeling of isolation and her distance from all the worlds she finds herself in are brought to life really powerfully and feel realistic. The description of Manderley gives a great oppressive yet grand atmosphere. There's a lot to think about and you could analyse the relationships and descriptions here for years. be warned the virago edition has an introduction with multiple important spoilers just some random thoughts because I'm apparently incapable of writing proper reviews now. chock full of spoilers obviously - It's fascinating that the first time maxim says he loves the narrator is right after talking about murdering his former wife! - also interesting that the only time the narrator is named is when she's imitating a historical figure (and it's the big crisis in the book) - i feel kind of bad for danvers, her entire identity and existence being tied to someone now dead, utterly idolising her and even acting as her avatar of revenge. - the introduction to the edition i was reading (which of course spoils the plot, even though it's only a few pages long. ahhh) emphasises the narrator's subsumption to rebecca but it's true of *every* character in the book. even the house is essentially *rebbeca's*, which makes the burning ending make more sense - now that she's finally been put to rest the house which she decorated, dictated the runnings of even after she died, goes with her - it's really weird that rebecca's cousin casually talks about her being in love with him and going to marry him and nobody really talks about the dodginess of cousin marriage or how extreme a change that'd be - rebecca saying "i will treat you like shit in private but in public i'll be perfect" is basically an explicit description of an abusive relationship but obviously gender swapped from usual expectations - how creepy is a relationship between a 21 year old and a 42 year old. lord. i mean obviously a significant subtheme of the book is how mismatched they are, partially for that reason, but it's so weird how people don't comment on it as creepy in book - the narrator describes herself as feeling like a dog being petted then after maxim tells her about the murder he committed she describes HIM as like a dog being petted. although it's hard to describe her as ever being assertive knowing that rebecca was murdered (which is like killing her a second time almost) is the only thing that makes her feel more comfortable and able to act normally - there's little attention paid to her life after manderley is burnt down but she says "confidence is a quality i prize although it has come to me a little late in the day. I suppose it is his dependence upon me that has made me bold at last" yet matched with "in the future keep the things that hurt to myself alone. They can be my secret indulgence". even the little information given is enough to make you think pretty deeply about what's being implied. is she actually feeling confident, is he genuinely dependent on her, is that really what she wants. does she want to be a new rebecca, would she be disposed of like rebecca. - obviously all the information we have about rebecca is heavily filtered - her own words are restricted to a couple statements filtered through maxim or danvers. trying to decide what she was actually like through the text is probably futile. although interesting to consider. were her actions REALLY so awful that the ONLY response was to murder her? (i'm not a big fan of murdering to resolve your problems. personally) she has constant affairs. it's not clear what else she actually does. it's interesting that murder only comes up when maxim's patrilineal descent is threatened - obvious patriarchy analysis there. and also the casualness with which he talks about just carrying a revolver there's a lot more to say but there's SO much to say it's overwhelming and i forget a lot dang

Mitch left home to pursue a career in ballet and hoped he would never have to return. But the betrayal of his lover had him returning to sort out the passing of his father, something he had been putting off for months. During the long drive, a possible hallucination (of seeing a reindeer on the road) led to a violent crash. Luckily, Mitch was unharmed and luckier still that the car following behind belonged to a Texas Ranger. But all good things had to come to an end once he realized the Ranger was his old friend turned lover, Web Eisley. Someone who refused to come out and for all he knew, still wasn't. It had been unbearable back then and even more so now for Mitch, but the attraction between the two was just as evident as it always was. This story simply didn't work for me that well because I could not really bring myself to like Mitch or Web all that much. It wasn't so much that they weren't good characters, but that I just couldn't relate to them. Or emphasize. Or anything really. The only character I really liked at all was Web's Aunt Mamie, but then, she was so full of energy and affection that it's impossible to not like her. Still, despite my emotional detachment more or less throughout, I did enjoy the story. Except maybe the hallucinations... I'm fairly sure the whole thing with the reindeer was supposed to be symbolism of some sort, but I'm still not that sure what it was. Other than a Christmas miracle, but then... why reindeers? Of all things...? Anyways. The last bit was really when it all started coming together for me. After the reappearance of Mitch's ex, coming to bring news of Mitch's new career making role. I feel like that was the first time that Mitch himself really started trying to put perspective on his life. On what he really wanted out of it and what kind of sacrifices he was willing to make along the way. A choice he was not afforded when he left home the first time, but one he was now going to have to make. Overall, it wasn't the oddest story I had ever read, but it did leave quite a lot to be desired. Would've definitely preferred a more conclusive ending, but with the way their lives had played out until that point, it was understandably muddy. I'm just really not sure how I feel about it.

Someone tell me what I am supposed to do with my life until I get to the library to get the next book. How could one leave a cliffhanger like that so cruelly? I don't even know where to begin with this review. I'm literally just a jumbled mess of feels and emotions. I mean come one, how do I move on from that ending? The book takes place basically after the first book. I will admit, the first half or so was really really slow. I was getting kind of annoying because nothing was going on. Celaena was fulfilling her duties, Chaol was trying to tell himself that he didn't love Celaena and not fooling anyone, and Dorian was brooding about why Celaena didn't love him. It was getting old quick. Luckily, a bunch of things started happening. A bit too quickly in my opinion but I was just happy that action was happening. And then that ending. Sarah J Maas knows how to keep you sucked in and wanting more. I have no idea why I didn't pick up this series sooner. But in a way, I am glad. Smol Lacy wouldn't have appreciated this series and gotten annoyed with all the fantasy. Big Lacy is more mature (in some ways). I want to talk about the characters for a minute. Celaena was still pretty hot and cold for me. I liked that she was showing more emotion. I also liked that she finally started showing off her skills. After listening about it in the first book with really no showing, it was nice to see that she actually can kick ass. But I got frustrated with her because  she wouldn't talk to Chaol after Nehemia's death. She just blocked him out and acted like a brat. Had she just freaking spoke to him, she wouldn't be so heartbroken and I wouldn't have had to read 50 million pages of brooding on both ends. Dorian was okay. I really liked what he found out that he could do but I was sick to death of listening to him brood over Celaena. So much damn brooding. Ugh. He kept saying that he let her go and he was over her but then the next page would be him getting irritated because Chaol and her were talking. Annoying. I also liked that he started standing up the King, hid dad. It was almost worth the constant brooding. Chaol. I'm not really sure what to say about him. After he finally admitted his feelings for Celaena, he got less annoying. I am seriously not a fan of brooding humans. He has the patience of a saint for dealing with Celaena's constant up and down moods. I don't doubt his love for her especially with all he finds out about Celaena. Overall, I liked the book. I had to dock a star because of the constant brooding, Celaena being an idiot, and almost no action coming until a little over halfway. You can sure bet that I will be rushing to the library to find the next book.

After reading this book, I feel sorry for Levana. Whatever she did or however she turned out, it was because of having a bad family and passive upbringing. She had better conscience than Channary at least, and I believe that she could have grown up to be a better person if Channary had not pushed her into the fire. But then again, a few of the decisions that she made were not influenced by how she looked or how she was treated, such as trying to kill Selene and later on killing her own husband, Evret. But those are justified, as history can vouch that princes and princesses other than the crown prince or princesses always grow up to be the jealous ones and hence take such drastic measures. I hated Queen Channary. How can someone so vile be the mother of Cinder who is nothing but the embodiment of compassion? I guess we will find out in the last book. Can't wait to read that one!

My husband asked me what this book was about and I described it as "a story about a guy who is on a lifeboat with a bengal tiger". I cringed as I said it. It was this exact description (from other people, and from the book blurb) that had stopped me from reading this. I bought the book nearly two years ago, I actually gave away my first copy unread. Finally a book club forced me to read it. I opened the first couple of pages and just could not be bothered... I wanted a great book, not some fluffy "Oprah book club" novel. Alas there is only three of us in the book group so I had to force myself to read the book. Actually, despite having a copy on my bookshelf, I opted for listening to the audio book (I heart audibly.com). The book was brilliant. It was about much more then a man in a lifeboat with a tiger, that didn't even happen until at least a third of the way into the book. The first half of the book was about the young man exploring two central themes... animals in captivity and God. He didn't reach any conclusions about animals in captivity, he just explored he experiences with their wants and needs. He did reach conclusions about God, and this is the first time I have heard someone mimic my own beliefs. I am a Christian but there is no doubt in my mind that I worship the same God that the Muslims worship - Allah, Jevohah Jireh, the great I AM - all names for the God that we love and worship. The second part of the book was a story, a ripping yarn, a tale that was believable, and yet you knew it had never happened. I appreciated being told a story like this, I was to believe that the young man had spent seven months on a life boat with a tiger. I enjoyed the story, I enjoyed the range of emotions from fear to determination. The third part of the book was told when he was recuperating in a hospital, retelling the tale to some of the ship company's investigators. He told two stories, one was the story we had just heard (in fact I loved that one entire chapter consisted of two words "the story" in which we, the reader, understood that this represented him telling the men the story that we had just read). Then he retold the story, and it was a vastly different story, easier to believe but more gut wrenching. In the lead up to the final chapters I was starting to sense that the author was about to pull an "it was all a dream" plot twist. I hate those. Isn't it funny. I know the story is completely untrue, and yet it was made all the more enjoyable because I let myself believe it was true. The thought that the author was about to tell me it was all a dream annoyed me, it would ruin the book for me. I wanted to believe in the truth of the story, I didn't want the author to tell me it was all a hallucination or something similiar. Thankfully, the author did not do what I feared, he did not write off the bengal tiger as a hallucination, or figment of the imagination. .... okay a few minor spoilers upcoming, where I discuss my thoughts about the ending. Despite my apprehension I did like the ending. The young man has suffered an extreme ordeal. He has clearly witnessed some awful things, and had to deal with them while remaining alive. Both stories were traumatic experiences. I can believe that his second story was true, and that made up this story and retreated into it - a fantasy world - in order to survive the seven month ordeal. It makes sense. I can also want to believe that the bengal tiger was real and that it really happened as he told - although the nocturnally acidic island was a stretch. However I think I have to accept that this story was a survival mechanism, something to keep him sane.

This book was everything the reviews said it would be. It's frank talk about race was enlightening in a witty and real way. I felt smarter just reading it. However, as a white female I can sympathize but I will never really be able to relate to their experiences. Something I can relate to, though, is the power of first love and the pain of its ending. I don't think she could have portrayed it better. It made me want to toss the book aside and unable to put it down all at the same time. It really moved me and at the end after I finished the last sentence I sat in silence for a moment, then I started crying. Not a cute cry with a couple of tears, but one of those cries where your face gets all contorted. I can't say enough for this novel and I can't wait to read more from this author!

This book should not have taken me three months to read. I'm not really sure why it did. I picked this book up after hearing a lot of buzz about its main character, Jorg. Jorg is not your traditional fantasy hero (in fact, anyone would be hard pressed to call him a 'hero'). He is unlikeable, violent and immoral, albeit weirdly charming. To be fair, this isn't exactly your traditional fantasy fare. The reason I picked this up was because of Jorg. As a writer, I was interested to see how Mark Lawrence handled a character that does very very bad things (murder, rape, arson, etc. ), but whom the reader needed to root for. I wasn't disappointed. And, weirdly, I ended up rooting for him, damn it. Despite everything or, perhaps, because of. Who knows? Prince of Thorns is told from a first person perspective. As such, the reader is forced to confront the things Jorg does head on. Also, it kind of helps you understand a bit more why he does what he does. I got a bit annoyed on occasion because Jorg had the habit of hiding his plans or suspicions from the reader, which is annoying in a first person narrator, but suited his character. He trusts no one, so why would he trust the reader? It's refreshing to have an unreliable narrator at times, particularly when you realise that the book is Jorg writing down the events in retrospect (at least, I think so...). And things get a lot more interesting when you realise that all is perhaps not what it seems, and that perhaps Jorg's path is not his own. There was something else that was also very interesting about this book. It seems as though it was written set in a sort of medieval world, but then... Plutarch is mentioned, and some other writers, and then there are strange devices that seem like modern technology... and suddenly it hit that this was a dystopian future of our own world. Mind. Blown. I liked the fact, also, that there was the potential for romance and it didn't happen. Perhaps it will happen in the future, but things are looking pretty impossible now. Would a person like Jorg be able to love someone, as a partner? We will see, I guess. I also enjoyed the little character sketches of Jorg's road brothers. Interesting inclusion, I think, because then they seemed more human. Albeit still unpleasant. My favourite character was perhaps the Nuban. I wish Jorg had cared enough to find out his real name. He deserves a name. Damn you and your sociopathic tendencies, Jorg. Even if there's a little bit of a squishy heart in there, because he does have some measure of affection for the Nuban. AND DAMN YOU FOR BREAKING MY HEART, MARK LAWRENCE. In places, the book felt a little disjointed, but I'm not sure if that's my fault for taking so long to read the damn thing or if it was a problem with the book. It jumps back and forth between past and present, but this wasn't disorientating in the slightest, so that wasn't the issue. I think a lot happens in this book - several different 'adventures', as it were - so perhaps that's the problem. Mark Lawrence - and Jorg - are quite concise and frugal with their words, so perhaps in the hands of a less concise author this book would have been two or three books. I'm glad it wasn't, though, because that would have been overkill. Despite the fact that Jorg is wholly unlikeable (it's quite hard to like a character who unfeelingly commits rape and murder), I do find myself intrigued by him and his story. I definitely want to know where his story goes in books two and three and, damn it, I find myself wanting him to succeed. A mark of success if ever there was one. Hats off to you, Mark Lawrence.
What's with this trend of killing and resurrecting werewolves lately?

This was one roller coaster ride I'm so glad I took! Loved everything about this. Loved Zane/Bull and his broody, intense and explosive persona. Totally loved everything Mia and Lexi. Nothing could bring them down, they were sunshine and light despite everything . Exactly what Zane needed. Loved the twists and turns. There was never a dull moment. This was intense, passionate, hot ...and funny. Mia's hilarious. This book had all that I look for in a story. Perfection!

I could reread this book over and over. This has landed on my list of favorite New Adult books that I could memorize by heart when I wanted to. The story was far from perfect and you can truly point out what or where things went wrong or if the character's attitude irk you, but at some point I'm giving it a 5. Dearest Clementine was just adorable. I don't know if that's a better way to describe it but it really was adorable. It had me wanting more even if things ended in a satisfying way. Gavin and Clementine had me falling for them the moment they started talking. Also, they're both smart. I have a thing for intellectual characters and their nerdy/brainy/geeky talks. I love so many things in this book: - The humor - Clementine - Gavin - Clementine's friends: Jenna, Harper, Dani, Ryan, Jax (her bro) and Daren (at first I wasn't a fan of him for what he did, but I warmed up to him as the story progressed) and Kade (they're friends, right?) - The FRIENDS reference: Ross and Rachel's "we were on a break" phase - Book talk - Journalism - Clementine and Gavin together - Clementine and Gavin's sexy times - The fluttering feeling whenever Clementine and Gavin are all teasing and being adorable with each other - GAVIN'S SONG FOR CLEMENTINE - The fact that some of my predictions were proven wrong This has been one of the books that has kept me up all night because I can't stop reading. I just love it and I'm really looking forward to reading Finding Dandelion.

These endings are killing me. Just when I thought this series couldn't turn on its ear any more than it already has, Devon Monk manages to pull the rug out from under me yet again. This book has something of a slow build at the beginning, but wow does it explode in the second half. And it ends with a cliffhanger that made want to throw my real-life responsibilities out of the window and dive right in to the next installment. This book picks up about two months after the events of the last one. Allie and Zayvion are in a good place, which I really loved getting to see. Poor Allie has been to hell and back and it gave me the warm and fuzzies to have them just reveling in their happiness. But you know it can't last. The Authority has discovered a wild-magic storm on the horizon and Allie, Zay and the others must come together to save Portland from the effects. This, as unrest grows in the ranks of the powerful magic society. Allie has no idea who the Good Guys and the Bad Guys are. Frankly, she is pretty clueless about everything, but she is trying to learn. Meanwhile, she is working to figure out what is going on with her father's consciousness --and there's still that pesky problem of Chase and that creepy hybrid Greyson. It's not all action and angst. In addition to the growing romance between Allie and Zay, there is the sweet and loveable gargoyle, Stone. And I would be remiss if I didn't point out the disarming and engaging relationship between Shame and his male, straight soul-mate Terric. Such an interesting dynamic there. But at its heart, this book is about Allie. About her growth as a magic user, her growth as a person, and her ties to the people in her life, both good and bad. For me, it worked. And the end... I guess I can be excited, because the next book is already out and ready for me to start. If I would have had to wait a year, I might have gone crazy. Because it looks like this ride is just getting started. Rating: B+

This book, while pretty annoying at times, was super amazing and brilliant and hilariously written. I liked it a lot (not loved, you see), and it wasn't as good as the first book (by far), but I do think that it has set up the third book pretty well, I can feel that all these loose ends will soon be tied up in the last book. My main annoyances were everyone basically hating Cara and Aelyx and being super rude, and also the fact that they were separated from each other throughout the entire freaking book and then at the end they finally got back together, only to break up ten seconds later. And then they got back together two chapters later. Either way, I still recommend this book to fans of the Lunar Chronicles, Jennifer L. Armentrout's writing, and also any other funny type of sci-fi book (it feels like a contemporary, except it's totally...not). Peace out!
I really liked this book!! Review to come!

Five months ago, Lucille's father was institutionalized for attacking her mother. Now the mother has disappeared on an extended "vacation," leaving 17-year-old Lucille to care for her little sister and maintain the household on her own. Frightened by the thought of losing her sister to child services and unsure when her mother might return, Lucille hides her mother's absence from friends and neighbors and starts working in a slightly shady Hooters-esque restaurant to make ends meet. It's a terrible time to fall in love, but her best friend's brother, Digby, has become suddenly irresistible, and Lucille soon finds herself under his spell. I admired Lucille's strength and resilience, and felt that in many ways, she would be an excellent role model to teens reading this book. The lengths she goes to to make sure she doesn't lose guardianship of her sister are truly inspiring. However, I found the romance angle troubling. Digby has a girlfriend throughout his relationship with Lucille, and it made it difficult to truly root for them. Their love was presented as genuine, but it's also founded on lies, and doesn't Lucille have enough disappointment in her life already? I wanted to strangle this dude. Still, I think teens reading this book would be into the love triangle, and the not-quite-wrapped-up ending leaves room for a sequel. Recommended to Sarah Dessen fans. I received this book through NetGalley in exchange for an honest review. Thank you to Houghton Mifflin Harcourt Children's Book Group and to NetGalley for the advance copy!

4.5 stars. This book is an ABSOLUTE page turner. I usually only become absorbed in a book after I get past the first few chapters but this book picks up from the very beginning. I especially love the characters and Karen's writing style. The characters are relatable and not as cliche as you would imagine them to be. The writing style and story flow is very different from most thrillers and is definitely a refreshing change. Actual rating: 3.75 stars My main difficulty when it comes to reviewing books is that I normally do not have much to say but that is completely a non-issue when it comes to the Falling Kingdoms series. Till now, I have had a love-hate relationship with Rhodes' writing and I don't think that's ever going to change. There were many moments during Frozen Tides, especially in the beginning, where I was extremely annoyed at some of the characters that I was ready to stop reading this series once and for all. However, one thing got me through, Magneo. If it weren't for this relationship I would not have bothered with this book. Also as I have said in my past reviews, I really wanted to know what was going to happen to all the characters in the book. I honestly hate that there are two more books to this series because that means I still have to wait until then to be finally rid of it. I am aware how strange it seems. Why put myself through so much pain when I obviously hate it? I ask myself that question every time a chapter starts with a character I absolutely cannot stand. Those characters are Lucia and Amara. These two had WAYY too much page count and I constantly wanted to skip their chapters. Instead, I just skimmed over them. It did not really affect my reading experience as a whole which was a relief because I'd hate to be confused later on because I misread something. Another thing I hated was that everything seemed way too convenient and unrealistic. All our main characters were bumping into each other constantly. Like are you kidding me? How is that even possible? ALSO another insta-love between characters was presented to us. How very predictable. The author really can't go a book without inserting some BS romance plot(other than Magneo of course). At this point it's equally amusing and frustrating to me. Nothing else can be said without spoiling so now I am going to start talking in depth about the storyline of Frozen Tides. Okay so let's start with the insta-love: Amara and Felix. After eight nights together, Amara was falling in love with the guy. EIGHT NIGHTS. Not even days okay NIGHTS where they barely even SPOKE. Amara has been with dozens of guys okay and somehow this one's the one that she falls in love with when they barely even KNOW EACH OTHER. It's so baffling to me. If this happened in the movies, it would be kind of acceptable because they are normally two hours long but there is no excuse for developing a poor romance plot time and time again. The only romance that she put any effort in is Magneo. It makes no sense and I am sure this won't be the last time we see this type of crap in her future books. Sigh Magneo. What a beautiful couple Magnus and Cleo make. I love them so much and I can literally read about them all day. I am so glad that they are still together at the end of this book though I have no clue what's going to happen next. Looks like King Gaius is still alive and as long as he is I am sure he's going to keep them apart which is SO NOT COOL. I am excited to see what's next. I am a bit surprised that by the end of this book we still don't really know much about the king's mom and why he killed off all the witches in Limeros. I don't have any theories about it but if you guys do feel free to comment them below. Also who was not at all shocked in the least that the woman that King Gaius fell in love with when he was Magnus' age was Cleo's mom. I knew it straight after reading the scene when his family went to visit Auranos. Something was vaguely mentioned about it and she finally confirmed it three books later. It's funny to think that if they weren't broken up because of his witch mom, then he would have been closer to the ring that allowed Eva to control the power of the kindred. Though I doubt she'd let him kidnap Lucia from her birth mom so in a way it made sense why Gaius' mom ruined their relationship. Another reason that she was right is that Magneo would not have existed which is simply unacceptable. Speaking of Lucia, what a b-word she's become. That scene where she kisses Magnus in hopes of manipulating him into telling her where the magic stone wheel is I WAS SO MAD. When that doesn't work, she ends up using her powers to tell him the truth anyway. First off why the hell didn't she do that in the very beginning??? I mean if she still regarded him as his brother why would she kiss him knowing she could have just used her powers to get it out of him. Plus it only ends up hurting Magnus further which is unacceptable. Towards the end of the book, I felt an immense amount of pity towards her because of the lack of people she has to rely on. I mean she thought the Fire God was the one person she could trust not to manipulate her and it turns out she was wrong about that too. I think I like her more than I did in the beginning but it's pretty fragile so let's see what happens in the next book before I decide that I truly like her. In my opinion, this entire series is filled with young power hungry royals who are all after crystals. Amara wanting to be the empress which she ended up being at the end. Remember how she was convinced that without the crystals she couldn't be empress? Well she's empress and married to King Gaius and yet still on the hunt for all the crystals. Magnus too wants the crystals because in the beginning he thought he needed them to be a good king and destroy his father. Cleo wants them to get her kingdom back. Everyone just wants the damn crystals. You know who doesn't want them? Jonas Agallon. He's such a sweetheart now and I feel so bad for the guy. I can't believe Lysandra was killed off. Now both his best friend and the girl he loves is dead. I am really interested in the reason behind Olivia being sent to protect him and can't wait to see what happens to him next.

What an... odd book. Pun completely intended. Odd Thomas can see the dead, and something horrible is coming to the town of Pico Mundo. With ghosts at every other corner, fungus men, ghastly shadow creatures and grisly souvenirs, this was a real page-turner. The Mojave desert is an unusual place for a ghost story, but it works incredibly well. A good Gothic tale takes place in an uncomfortable or even miserable environment, so why not have it in a place where the sun and the heat are so overwhelming? Only two problems with this story: One- Coyotes would not consider a fully grown and healthy man to be a desirable meal. In most incidents, bites only occur when they have been fed by the "victim", and there have only been two recorded incidences in the United States and Canada of humans being actually killed by coyotes. Two- An inverted cross is NOT a satanic symbol. This is a purely modern invention (Thanks, Hollywood!). An inverted cross is actually the cross of St. Peter, who was crucified upside-down. Good thrills, good chills, and a disturbing mystery made this a very satisfying read!

Given my Feast for Crows review, I pretty much dug my own grave when it came to my feelings on Dance with Dragons. Exactly what I loved about Feast for Crows was the absence of...well...everything that just happened in Dance with Dragons. Case and point: Dany. Dude. DUDE. Please stop making me spend all my time with her. Clearly, she's going to sit there doing nothing until all the usurpers in Westeros kill each other off so she can come gliding in on a dragon and take the Iron Throne unopposed. Okay, so she sat on a dragon for the first time (unsurprisingly rife with weird sexual tension, as dragons always have been for Dany, even before she named one after her husband), but for that to be the ONLY significant development in Dany's plot, is frankly unacceptable to me. I'm even willing to not mind descriptions of her somewhat misplaced attraction to Captain Whatsisname as a human urge getting in the way of her judgment, which is more than some of the other readers are giving her, but ye gods, the suffocating stagnation! She's been the thorn in my side for three books now, a lingering reminder that she's going to be super important later, except we have nothing for her to do until then. Though to be fair, I have never liked Dany, and am generally confused about why people love her so dang much (does it have to do with the show? You can be honest...it's got something to do with the show, right? About the visual aspects of the show?). At this point she's completely wedged in a corner between "girls can't have power except the power to sleep with men" and "the best girls are super sexy and also kick ass, as long as they have *coughDRAGONS* to do it for them." Although right behind her we did have  Ser Barristan Selmy, whose perspective I welcomed as a breath of fresh air (furthering the theory I posited after Crows that maybe what I really like about GRRM is when he's in exposition mode). But the problem with that is that when it's time to go into denouement mode, he can't conclude all these plots through new sets of eyes. He's going to have to figure out how to stop introducing, or the thing will TRULY never end. Anyway, Barristan...if only he didn't spend every chapter hammering home the pearl of wisdom that when a man wears a mask, we can't see his face...he would've been pretty spot-on. As to the treatment of Tyrion, I was shocked. Well known as George's favorite character, the crown jewel of the Lannister house...reduced to  the very dog-and-pony show (ha! see what I did there?) that symbolizes everything he despises about being a dwarf? Content cracking jokes and being surprisingly good at games of strategy, while LITERALLY a sideshow freak wearing a collar? I was disappointed, to say the least. The thing I will say for Book Five Tyrion is that he was decent enough not to lead Penny on, and that George was decent enough not to have them fall madly in love, which would imply that the only love a dwarf can find is with another dwarf. Coupled with what Martin does to women, the implication that Tyrion could never find true love with a woman taller than he is would've been a deal-breaker. The one little glimpse of the author who pulled the rug out from under us by beheading Ned Stark was  the plight of poor Quentyn. As he walked up to that dragon I was cringing, bracing myself for the obvious. No, no, no, don't let him be the second head of the dragon, it's way too easy...and then he wasn't. He super wasn't. Instead of the cliche and barf-worthy raising of the boy-prince to dragon-rider status, we get...oh...a flaming and horrible death. But honestly, I agree with other reviews that say that's all that remains of the author who, two decades ago, dared to "go there" and off a character we thought was untouchable. But it's all been undone now, with these  surprise, I'm not dead! moments. Surprise, Catelyn's a zombie! (unforgiveable.) Surprise, that baby I insisted on saying got his head dashed against a wall like a million times per book? That was all an obvious way to make you think he was super-dead, when he's also not dead! Arya blind? Hardly! She's totally fine! Oh no, Dany probably got eaten by a dragon...except that she's not dead! Is he atoning for Ned by sparing lives to a fault? Doubtful, since he'll go down in fantasy HISTORY for that move. Pinterest, forums about the books and about the show, Facebook statuses around the world continue to cheer that almost-as-old-as-I-am act of boldness, that assertion that death--real, random, unfair, sudden death--comes for anyone and everyone. But a Dance with Dragons leads me to believe that GRRM is resting on those tragic laurels. As his audience goes on talking about those characters he killed, he's hoping we'll forget about ALL those characters he "surprise! didn't". The good:  Barristan Selmy, the "HUH?" intrigue of Brienne spiriting Jaime away when she's supposed to be DEAD, the creep factor of Arya finally face-changing, Jon breaking his oath of neutrality to rain holy hell down on House Bolton, and I suppose it must be admitted that the dragon-riding development does constitute at least a baby step forward in Dany's exhausted plot. The bad:  The parade of "not dead" revelations, the overall stagnant plot, Cersei's out of character submission (I'll retract this if she comes howling back to bitchiness in a future book), the endless prophecies that it's useless trying to do anything with, Tyrion's fall from "cool" into "carny", and the miles of text taken up by the line "Words are wind." Could go either way:  Will be a hail back to let's-behead-Ned if Jon Snow really and truly is dead, but if he's "surprise! not", it'll be nothing but a cheap cliffhanger to make us wait teary-eyed for the next book. Three stars means: Could've been worse, but also could've been SOMETHING.

It's been interesting to watch V for Vendetta's second act as the visual aesthetic of choice for the anarchist hacker movement Anonymous. In the story, it's weird that no explanation is ever really given for V's speed and fighting prowess, and his near-omnipotence at manipulating and then bringing down the fascist government. There's a contradiction there that's not really resolved: the revolution requires superpowers to succeed and yet super-heroes are inherently disempowering. One would almost go so far as to say that the idea of an all-powerful caped crusader protecting us is a pretty authoritarian idea at heart. (OK it's complicated.) But to see V reborn in the internet age, when hackers and whistleblowers *actually* *can* wield institution shaking powers (i.e. NSA, Sony, etc) is a fairly interesting (and possibly disturbing) vindication of the premise. Anyway, if Alan Moore's political analysis is not 100% aligned with my own, there's no denying the power of the graphic novel he created. In particular, the first act is basically perfect. Try not to get chills when he whispers the rhyme: Remember, remember the fifth of November... Things get a little more questionable in the second act where V "tortures" Evey into freedom. We've all had way too much visceral experience with torture recently to see this as anything other than glib posturing. I guess you could getaway with that in the 1980s when torture was a little more abstract. It rings false today . Still, as with Watchmen, it's pretty remarkable how influential it all is. I'm pretty sure Tarantino swiped that whole bible-verse thing from here.

I received an ARC of this book in exchange for an honest review. I had never read anything by this author, but the summary caught my eye. Unplanned pregnancy, baseball players, and falling in love? Yes, my type of romance! This is a novel about Angie and J.T. whom shared a passionate night that results in an unplanned pregnancy. When Angie loses her job, J.T's offer of marriage becomes more appealing. Angie wants nothing to do with ball players, and J.T wants nothing more than to be there during every part of his child's life. The writing style of Packard is well-written and clear. She makes the characters witty and believable. She is able to back up every "what if" question I had. So many times, I read a book, only to be like "What in the hell are you thinking???" I didn't feel that way with Catching Heat. I fell in love with both the characters. I didn't guess the ending either. (No spoilers) but I figured J.T would do something...and it never happened. A marriage of convenience isn't that far fetched. It happens! I love the character building. I promise you- you will see the characters grow and change from the beginning to the end. Even the minor characters are believable, and they don't distract from the story. From Angie's jerk of a mother to J.T's investigating brother, each character helps the story progress. I read the book in one sitting, pulling an all nighter (which i rarely do these days since I have to be at work at 7am) then went out and bought another book from this great author! I give this book 5 stars, because its a believable love story that made me laugh and cry. Okay so I figured J.T would cheat on Angie in the end, like most books have the male character do, but he didn't. He really cared for Angie it was so sweet! When Angie's mom turned all crazy toward the end, I really think that part was believable, even J.T's reaction. These are young characters. I think some readers forget how irrational we all were in our 20's. My review can also by found at Books with Bree (It won't be up for another few days though)

Actual rating 4.5 stars. This is now officially my favourite Lisa McMann title to date. 'Dead to You' had a more mature voice and such a simple yet strong vibe throughout that it totally sucked me in. Ethan's narrative is authentic and completely drew me into his world. His family also exuded realism, dysfunction and all. Everyone escapes into a fantasy world, and when Ethan returns to his family after nine years of being abducted, foster care and living on the streets, at first that fantasy becomes real... before the struggles of memory, relationships and high school begin to weigh in. This is very clever, in hindsight, clues to working out the mystery are glaringly obvious. But initially I hadn't paid them much attention. Also there is a psychological element underlying this story. Lis McMann has always had some sort of challenge around metal illness in her books, but none done as well as this. Although it's kind of predictable in the sense that I knew what was coming, but not in how it was delivered. And I love surprises! 'Dead to You' has managed to redeem McMann for me, as my interest was starting to wane in her writing. Apart from our protagonist, Ethan, the rest of the cast has much to offer: his little sister Gracie is adorable; the brother Blake is cautious and stubborn; and Mum and Dad are so gentle about Ethan's re-introduction to the family it was heartbreaking. A love interest in Cami was amazing too. There was so much love and support around Ethan I was really cheering for him to resolve the tension and get his happily ever after. 'Dead to You' has an easy flow and distinctly adolescent male narrative that I flew through in a day. It gave me plenty of feels and was a refreshing reading experience. Recommended for lovers of McMann's work or those looking for a quick mystery to while away the afternoon with.

Garrett Graham has to pass Ethics and his failing midterm grade has him sweating his position as the captain of the hockey team. As the son of a professional hockey legend, the pressure is on him to perform to perfection both on and off the ice. Both characters are hiding secrets that they don't share. But as their friendship deepens, the pair finds they can share their secrets with the other. Sometimes people sneak up on you and suddenly you don't know how you ever lived without them. These two had great chemistry. They did not have a fast build, insta-love situation. Their relationship had the time to unfold naturally, with setbacks typical of the situations they face over the course of the book. The build-up was fun to watch and entertaining to see how it changed each of the characters. This had some great twists that both surprised me and fit the story. While some pieces were not as original as they maybe could have been, the whole story was put together in a way that I couldn't help but connect with the characters and love the overall story. In a marketplace saturated with book that are labelled "chick lit," Jojo Moyes stands out above the crowd so much that I can't help but recommend her books even if I'm not always in love with all of them myself. She doesn't fall into the trap of re-writing the same story with slightly tweaked characters (I'm looking at you Kate Morton and Sarah Jio). Nope, each of her books that have been released in the US has told an incredibly different story, though she seems to be drawn to love stories that examine the barriers created by socioeconomic class. Her main characters tend to be well-drawn and multidimensional and she's willing to throw entirely unexpected twists into her plot. And One Plus One is thus far my favorite Jojo Moyes book. It's about Jess, an always-look-on-the-bright-side single mom with two kids and two jobs whose never been able to make ends meet. Her young daughter, Tanzie, is a budding math prodigy with the opportunity to attend a super-prestigious private school that Jess just can't afford. Jess learns about a math competition with a cash prize large enough to pay the entry fee and is determined to get Tanzie there no matter what. She gets some help along the way from Ed, a tech-industry millionaire who has come under investigation in an insider trading scandal. I loved that Jess was such empathetic character. I feel like Moyes does an excellent job of realistically capturing the small, everyday struggles that go along with being among the "working poor." Jess gets frustrated by her situation -- and Moyes acknowledges the round-and-roundness of it -- but she keeps going and does her best to stay positive. Ed's a little less empathetic than I think Moyes wanted him to be. I think he was meant to show that having money can do you a lot of good but it can also cause its own share of problems. But I still felt like he brought about his situation through his inability to handle things like an adult so I couldn't quiiiiiiite feel bad for him. It's easy to see where this book is headed almost from the beginning, and I started out with some skepticism, but Moyes ultimately does a nice job of throwing the reader for a few loops long the way. The story went to some places that I wasn't expecting, but it managed to stay believable and enjoyable. This isn't going to win any literary prizes, but it made for an excellent light read.

***I received a copy of this book in exchange for my honest review*** When I was approached to read this book I was excited to have the opportunity to read it for the author. This book seemed right up my alley since I love all things fantasy most of the time. However, I just felt as though the book was not horrible but it also didn't change my life after reading it. What I liked: I did enjoy the three different points of view for the three main girls. I thought the overall plot was also quite intriguing. The fact that the author allowed the witch to have her own point of view humanized her in a way that connected her to the reader. I even felt a little bad for Lady Elizabeth Clifford since she just wanted to have a family. I also enjoyed reading about Albertine since she was actually stuck with the witch in Witchwood Hollow. All three of the female characters were interesting to read about. What I did not like: My main problem with this book is I felt as though the three different points of view resulted in the lack of development of their characters. The book felt a little rushed in the storyline of Honoria and I thought that she should have been given more time in the book. Leon also seemed like an unnecessary addition. I did not know as much about him as I would have liked to and it seemed as though Honoria feel in love with him too quickly. I would have liked to see more of interaction with Leon before the end of the book. I felt the same way with the other two girls. The book seemed too short to have three major points of view from different time zones and, even though I liked the concept, I never connected fully with any of the main characters. I felt like each of the plots were not completely ended and that the author just kind of stopped writing all of a sudden and came up with the quickest resolution for the plot. I guess this book just was not for me. I enjoyed the premise but felt as though the execution could have been a little better and maybe the book could have been expanded a bit. Sorry!

This is just going to be a quickie review, since I still have two more books to go, in the Caster Chronicles! So, to keep it sweet and snappy: 1) This series is definitely growing on me. Mainly because of 2) Liv. I, absolutely love Olivia Durand's character. A British, blonde, mini-Marian? As Liv would say herself, "Brilliant". 3) AND LINK. Oh lord, Link. How could not love that scrawny sarcastic little Southern boy? Okay, well, he's not little, but seriously, I feel like Ethan doesn't appreciate his best friend enough. Link has always stuck by Ethan's side, through  everything . Hold it! I see a parallel between this and The Mortal Instruments. Let me just say that I love TMI. I truly do. But just think about it. Main character (Clary Fray or Ethan Wate). Obsesses over supernatural with way too much angst (Jace Wayland or Lena Duchannes). MC slightly disregards and ignores awesomely loyal best friend (SIMON LEWIS and our dear Wesley Jefferson Lincoln). Oh! Oh! Oh! And then the best friend gets turned into a supernatural being! You see what I mean? Well, the only difference is that Link isn't in love with Ethan or anything. But that's besides the point. This comparison works perfectly! 4) Lena. Lena Duchannes. Lena I-Don't-Know-What-Your-Middle-Name-Is Duchannes. Oh hey! Let's give her a middle name. How about...emotional? Dismissive? Angst? Oh I like that. Lena Angst Duchannes. A  very  fitting name. Or we could just be blunt and call her Miss Messed Up. If you've read Beautiful Darkness, then you know what I'm talking about. Ethan somehow found the ability in himself to forgive Lena for let's see...treating him like dirt, claiming he doesn't understand, turning into a mini-Ridley, rejecting all his comforting and offers to help, devolving into an absolute mess of self-pity and depression, and getting all chummy with John Breed. Essentially cheating on Ethan. Props to Ethan, man, for being able to forgive and reconcile. But I, for one, could not. Sure there was the whole "explanation" about how Lena was doing it because she blamed herself for Macon's death and wanted to protect Ethan or whatever. But that still doesn't excuse Lena Duchannes's behavior for me. One minute, she was loving toward Ethan and the next minute, she's emo and telling Ethan to get out of her life? In this book, my respect for Lena just plummeted way down. 5) I don't think I mentioned this in my Beautiful Creatures review, so I'll just say it now. The visions are one of the best parts of these books. I love 'em. I love how Genevieve's, Ivy's, and Abraham's stories from the Civil War era are so intricately woven in with Lena's and Ethan's, hinting at the theme that history repeats itself and we're all doomed players in this game of life. I also loved the visions sent from Macon and Lila in this book. I just love what the visions add to the story. Whenever I see italic print in these books, I get slightly giddy. Yeah, I know, I'm strange. 6) I'm divided about the Seventeenth Moon and the supernatural plot in this book. It was really original and unpredictable, but at times, it felt slightly foggy and vague. There were moments where I didn't really understand what had just happened, so I felt my mind wandering a little bit in Beautiful Darkness. 7)  Ridley becoming Mortal? Did  not  see that one coming, and I'm really interested as to how this'll work out in the later books. 8)  But Link becoming an Incubus? Sort of saw that one coming. Poor guy. 9)  MACON'S BACK! YES! 10) Best Quote:  "Dude, my mom's a Baptist. You think she's gonna let me stay in the house when she finds out I'm a Demon? She doesn't even like Methodists." Oh Link.

A really good paranormal/dystopian book.Dark, cruel, and undeniably romantic. I have to admit that I didn't know that there are vampires in this book. I only thought of the usual dystopian stuffs such as world-building, wars, and politics. What I really liked about this one is the forbidden romance. I've expected a lot from it because of the summary, it said "Ash and Natalie first deny and then struggle to fight their forbidden feelings for each other, knowing if they're caught, they'll be executed--but their feelings are too strong.". So you can't blame me to expect much especially with the word "execution". LOL! It started really good, though I couldn't identify the different kinds of Darklings, since there are rare ones and common ones. They also have different appearances. And I couldn't picture them at all. Its hard to remember the system but it eventually came to me. I like the two POVs from Natalie and Ash. Natalie is a normal girl, a human, with a heart failure. Ash is a Twin-blood, half human and half Darkling, with heart that doesn't beat. Everything about them is very interesting, the mystery of the heart and their races. I enjoyed the first half, then all of a sudden, my love for this book deflated like a balloon. I would have given it 5 stars but the latter half of it made me roll my eyes and raise my eyebrows. It became fast-paced, which is not in a good way, it became literally fast, it seemed that the events became unbelievable. Here are some of the parts: When they learned that they're Blood Mates, they instantly agree to be a couple. When Natalie learned that her heart is not truly hers and Evangeline is the true Blood Mate of Ash. Then he allowed Evangeline to kiss him and Natalie saw them. Then the next day, Natalie forgave him. When Ash's mother died, they had sex, and I was like, "Whoa!? Where did it come from? They're supposed to mourn. In spite of those unbelievable events, the few last chapters of the book were enjoyable, I've learned how cruel the world they live in. I don't know how the second book will be but I'll definitely read it. I hope it'll be better and slower this time to give readers the time to digest the contents. Anyway, if you like Eternity Cure, Warm Bodies and Romeo and Juliet, this book is definitely for you.

This is an author who knows his craft and I really liked this book. It had the vibe of a classic American novel, and could rank right alongside "A Prayer for Owen Meany" and "To Kill a Mockingbird". It was part Coming of Age, part Literary Fiction, and part Mystery... and all so very enjoyable. Even though it was quite satisfying, the story did leave some gray areas. *	I would have liked to have known more about Gus and Nathan's war years. We know that both are damaged, but we're not quite sure exactly why. *	Ruth is also pretty much a mystery... we're not quite sure what she thinks about her husband when she is not busy being angry with him. When she IS angry with him, we know exactly how she feels about him. *	I would have liked to have known a whole lot more about Warren Redstone. *	I thought Doyle was all set up to be the bad guy in a spectacular way - then nothing! And we still don't know why he was sneaking around Warren's lean-to. There were several usual themes in this book. Nothing which really surprised me... but that only served to make the story feel more authentic. I kept nodding my head, thinking "Yes, I could definitely see that happening". I thought the ending was a little shaky. I could see Lise killing Ariel out of jealousy, but to lash out just because she had been touched? That seems almost anticlimactic. Since she almost bashed in Frank's brains for the exact same reason, one would think that this tendency would have been a recognized problem, and something would have been done about it before she killed someone - rather than after. I know that Ariel was already dead by the time she lashed out at Frank, but I can't believe that Ariel was the first person ever to have touched her. Although that raises an interesting question. WAS Ariel the first person Lise ever physically attacked? Maybe there was some underlying "something" at work on Lise's subconscious? Because I thought she just screamed when she was touched. Maybe she was jealous of Frank's relationship with Jake and that's why she went for him too? I like books that give you stuff to think about! Read with SBC book club June 2016
