I picked this up because I wanted to read a novel set in biblical times, and this is a reimagining of the story of Dinah, the sister of the sons of Jacob. One chapter of Genesis is devoted to her story, about how she went into a nearby town and the son of the town's ruler fell in love with her and "ravished" her before deciding he wanted to marry her. The sons of Jacob in their fury worked out a deal involving circumsion of all the town's males, which then allowed them to murder all those men. In this version, Dinah is not raped, but experiences insta-love and willingly allows Shalem to bed her without the benefit of marriage, and then is distraught when he is murdered. As a tale about the mothers (Jacob had four wives, who all mother Dinah) and daughter relationship, this is a very enjoyable tale, that highlights how paganistic the culture was. Even Jacob doesn't seem whole-hearted in his devotion to God. However, once Dinah meets Shalem, the story goes off in a very dark and unhappy direction for basically the rest of the book. As that part is all the author's imagining of what happened after Dinah's chapter in Genesis is through, I won't summarize except to say that there is yet another case of insta-love, which is at odds with the fact that every biblical male character is painted as evil, repugnant, or selfish-sometimes all three. In addition, Dinah is a very passive character-things happen to her and she usually responds by withdrawing. The only times she takes action is to set curses on men, who then are punished by God for their crimes against woman. I find it highly ironic that both Jews and Christians have been inspired by this book in light of the fact that it trashes the characters of Isaac, Jacob/Israel, and eleven of Jacob's sons (Benjamin was born after Dinah leaves the family and isn't really part of the story). If this were an accurate account of the true characters of these men, I would think God would rather have allowed them to be blotted out like Sodom and Gomorrah rather than immortalized. (Note: the author does acknowledge in the afterward that she did not intend to stay faithful to the text or religious tradition in making the story her own). Joseph, is particular, is a selfish, whiny, illiterate brat who benefits from the work of another without any sense of gratitude-very much at odds with the account of the rest of his story in Genesis after Dinah's rape. On the other hand, feminists who are into man-bashing should eat this right up. This could have been a very uplifting and inspiring read, but the modernist misandrist reinterpretation of these characters spoiled the beauty of how the female characters were portrayed. The beauty and dignity of women can be celebrated without denigrating the biblical patriarchs. Try Francine Rivers for biblical retellings that are uplifting.

Attachments is a sometimes laugh out loud story about a time when the internet was something to be navigated, not lived in. Lincoln is a creepy stalker, but it's okay. They're paying him. His entire job is to monitor the emails of employees. Super shy he has a hard time meeting girls, so when two hilarious girls start emailing each other he can't find the heart to tell them to start. The problem is that he eventually falls in love with one of them. How can you tell someone you love them when you've been mandatory stalking? The characters make Attachments. They're funny and deep and feel oh so real. I read this all in one sitting and don't regret it one bit. That being said, the ending was a bit of a let down. Although being in general what I hoped it just didn't feel very well set up.

I handed this book off to my sister this afternoon having promised she could read it when I was done with it. And the first thing she asked me was, "How was it?" My reaction was, "Ehhhhh?" and to shrug. So, I feel like that conveys my reaction to this. Hence the 2-star "it was okay" rating. The concept is interesting but the execution for the most part fell really flat for me. I felt like the strongest part of the book was the beginning, for me. Getting to know Sloane and James, who their friends are, what they've been through, how they're not allowed to grieve properly for fear of being flagged by The Program. It was actually rather poignant in places. And the real depth of their sorrow came through. But as things progressed, I never really felt attached to anyone. A lot of the exposition in the middle ends up being a lot of "telling" instead of "showing"... which I understood as a device for the narrative (Sloane is baring all to her psychologist) but it never drew me in. I found the boys in this book rather problematic as well. James, in the beginning, was fine, but as the book progressed I was really confused by his behaviour. Realm is a complex character, but does some horrific things (to Sloane in particular) and then because of how the narrative is framed (and how the plot device works) he's still portrayed as one of the "good guys". I had a really hard time with that. It's clear that there's more going on here than meets the eye. Realm's behaviour midway through the book gives that away. But it's frustrating because, as I suppose I should've expected, nothing is really resolved at the end of this book. Yes, it's a duology, and yes, I know the intent of the ending is to make me want to keep reading. But everything is so vague and unclear. And instead of it being compelling it was annoying. As is the norm with most YA dystopians, our heroes are off to join a secret rebellion group at the end of the novel. They'll probably take down the government or something in The Treatment. But it all feels so... unrealistic. I can suspend my disbelief, but there's a limit. To be fair, this book didn't go down the way I expected it to. But if you're looking for complexity, you'll not find it here. This is a typical one-dimensional YA tale with little depth. I'll probably pick up book 2, just to find out what the heck is actually going on, but it certainly won't be at the top of my list.

I was provided a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review. "Even the most gentle people have a dark side." I was trying to warn him. "I know", he said. "It's how you control that darkness that defines you." Well damn I really enjoyed this book. I'll be honest I was a little hesitant going into this book because for some reason I never tend to like books that authors send me for review. I don't know why but it always happens. I thought I might not like this when I started it, but I quickly became so immersed in the story, I couldn't put it down. I wasn't planning on reading this whole book in one sitting but the writing style is so fast paced and it's so interesting, I couldn't help it. We follow Phoenix (love that name btw) who is a young girl who witnessed her parents being brutally murdered at the age of 11. now she is 17 and she is surviving on her own in a post-apocalyptic world where murder and power is everything. The world is separated into "tribes" kind of like in Divergent where they are separated into factions. But Phoenix doesn't belong to any tribe and she gets by all on her own, until she is captured by a rebellious group who plans to overthrow the tribes. This book was very similar to Divergent, The Hunger Games and Legend. But I don't think that's a bad thing. Phoenix was a bad-ass likable protagonist which is rare in YA dystopia I feel like. (I couldn't stand Tris in Divergent.) I started enjoying this book a lot more once Triven was introduced. I fucking love him and adore him so much. I don't know why, he's just so gentle and sweet with her and they were so cute. I really really really enjoyed their romance in this book. I was giddy every time something intimate happened between them. Also, I loved the character Mouse, and how Phoenix became like an older sister to her and became so protective of her, it was so sweet. It felt kind of like The Hunger Games when Katniss became friends with the young girl, (Rose? I think that was her name?) I enjoyed the knife throwing scene between Triven and Phoenix even though it totally reminded me of that scene in Divergent with Tris and Four. But it was really cute. I also really liked how both Phoenix and Triven really enjoyed reading and they both cherished books. It made them really relatable. Phoenix and Triven are also similar to Tris and Four in the sense that they both have experienced a lot of shitty things in their lives and they both think they are damaged goods and they're undeserving of love, which makes it all the more beautiful to see them come together and find love and hope in each other. While reading this book I was listening to "Intro" by The xx, and the Mad Max soundtrack which really enhanced the reading experience for me. I was so surprised by how much I enjoyed this book. It was so easy to dive into this writing style and it's so fast paced and easy to get through in one sitting. I can't wait to read the next book.

Originally posted on my blog: The Writer's Inkwell There have been moments while reading the previous three volumes, where I've found myself thinking, "What the hell am I reading?" But then the comic returns to its roots and I find myself loving it once again. This is not one of those moments. As much as I enjoyed the idea of Buffy essentially going to the future, there were so many out there moments that I just found myself overwhelmed. It was as if Whedon just threw everything at the wall and went with whatever happened to stick. And I think that is the problem with these comics. Yes, the show had demons, monsters, vampires, witches, etc. But they didn't rarely had dozens of these things happening all at once. It was always one or (at the most) two obstacles to overcome. The way this comic series is going, I'm finding myself more and more confused because there are so many random events. Case in point: Dawn magically goes from a 20 foot girl to a centaur. How did that happened and why the hell has the series still not explained what a freaking thricewise is? Also, yes, I understand Buffy is went to a dystopian future, but why couldn't the only remaining slayer speak a real sentence? Is it supposed to be a form of broken English because it's not her first language or is that the new English of the future? I just wish more would go into the actual plot development and execution of this particular volume. It had potential, but the execution was poor and I'm not a fan.

4.5 Stars I've had this book sitting in my library for well over a year, just waiting for the perfect time to finally get it out and enjoy. You see, I knew I'd love it. So I waited until a time like now, when I felt like I was in a bit of a book slump and I just needed something fun, swoon-worthy and sexy to enjoy! And I'm so happy I waited, because this book was the perfect choice and it was so worth the wait! Thumbs UP Ten. He really was perfect. Well... I could have done without alllllll of his man-whoring, but aside from that... his crude mouth, dirty jokes, offensive but strangely endearing nicknames - he was impossible not to like! Even his spotted pecker made him special. But my favourite thing about him was the way he loved his woman. It was completely swoon-worthy. In most cases I would have found Caroline's stalker behaviour to be weird and annoying, but I frickin loved it in this book! She was a nut, that's for sure. But she was a damn hoot! Her crazy antics were so insane that I couldn't help but root for her! I wanted her to get her man, even if she had to get her crazy on to achieve it, and it was so worth it in the end. These two crazy kids deserved each other, and I thought they were a perfect match. This book was entertaining from start to finish. I had a good time with it. There was a superb mix of fun and drama, and this couples chemistry jumped off the page. This author also has a knack for writing some very steamy sex scenes. Thumbs DOWN It's not the authors fault, but lately every book (literally) I have read, has involved a couple that made a choice to keep their relationship a secret. I'm getting so bored of it. It's always a shit show when people find out, and I just find it to be really uninspiring. In this case, I thought it was stupid. Literally EVERYONE knew they were in a relationship, except for her brother. It was just mean by the end and frankly I thought it was immature. Final Thoughts I've now read three books in this series, and they've all been hits for me! Ideally I would have read them in order, but I've still enjoyed them as standalones. Still, now that I feel like I know all the gang, I'm eager to go back and read their stories! I know I'll love them, and I look forward to finally reading them.

Sir Terry himself once said in an interview that it's hard to make Rincewind "more than two-dimensional" and that he's "shallow all the way to the bottom". I agree. He's funny, but flat and gets boring quickly; While I'm not a huge fan of Rincewind, I quite enjoyed Cohen and the Silver Horde as characters. All in all, the book is funny and interesting, and I liked how Pratchett humorously explores totalitarian systems and the extreme naivety that often surrounds the attempts to overthrow them.

I was very excited to start this one. The beginning held my fascination so much. Londinium was all sorts of wonder but to tell you the truth, it struck me as a world wherein pollution took over. Everyone had mechanical pieces for the body parts that toxins claimed. It took me a while (near the end of the story) to realize that it was the way it was meant to be. A mechanical London, a world vastly different from ours. One which needs machines and clockwork to fully function. Jack, the son of a wealthy businessman, finds himself on the wrong side of a door. A place very much alike to his home except in the prominence of cyborgs(!) and the soot. Soon after, he finds out that he is to be the new son of the Lady, she who rules over Londinium. As typical as any other heir to a business, Jack is groomed to take over the business as he gets older but for now, he is a brat. And this is where my issues come in - I could never stand 'em. If I were a younger maybe I could ignore it and enjoy the story but as it is, I am not. Jack had a painfully slow development. He is curious and he resents his parents for not spending enough with him when evidently they care for him enough to give him the best the world has to offer. He also thinks of only himself, always wants his way and is blind to the state of society as long as everything is good for him. All the qualities of a child I'm sure but if you were not so privileged you would be sensitive enough to be aware that people around you are oppressed. It's not always rainbows and butterflies you know. I adored Beth so much, maybe because there is no trace of malice in her. I was 70% into the story when the juicy part began. I think the fact Elizabeth never lost her faith and never stopped hoping her family was looking for her is amazing and shows just how strong a human spirit can be. I highly recommend reading Elizabeth's story- it will definitely leave an imprint on you and remind you of all the blessings in your life.

1/5 stars. This is one of the worst examples of insta-love. *gags* It took up most of the book, which is NOT good. When you have crappy characters, a boring plot that had no resolution, and juvenile writing, the last thing you want to do is add in an insta-love romance that holds no point whatsoever and make it take up 95% of the book. I'll give the author credit for going on a limb here, but it didn't work out the way I think she thought it would. At least not for me. As you can guess by the title, this book is about werewolves. Besides the occasional wolf book and the Shiver series, I don't read much about wolves or shape-shifters. So, I picked this one up, thinking, 'Why not? Halloween is getting close. Maybe I'll try out a werewolf book.' Yeah... not my best moment. I didn't enjoy this book at all. Besides the occasional laugh at how narrow-minded and rude most of the characters are in this book, this wasn't a great read. I found myself wanting to DNF this so bad but decided that I would just trudge right on through to the end. The "plot" of this book surrounds a girl named Celeste, who lives on the city side of her county, a place full of malls, pools, and restaurants. She spends most of her time with her best friends, their boyfriends, and Celeste's boyfriend, Nash. All of whom are popular, of course. But one day she meets Brandon, the new kid who lives on the wrong side of the county, and she can't get him out of her head. Blah blah blah. He saves her from a pack of wolves, and Celeste feels that she must thank him. He got bit while saving her and then turns into a werewolf on the next full moon. What a shocker..  As Celeste begins to feel a stronger connection to Brandon, she finds it harder and harder to keep the secrets from her friends, Nash, and her family. Not only that, but when Brandon begins to act really weird, Celeste is determined to find out what's going on and what secrets he's keeping. Yep, so there you have it. The majority of this book is Celeste pining over how hot Brandon is, how much she wants to be with him, how her stomach is filled with "butterflies" when he's around... ugh. Never mind the fact that Celeste knows next to nothing about Brandon or that he knows diddly squat about her. Like usual insta-loves, this relationship revolves around the physical attractiveness between the two characters and nothing about the emotional or mental connection. And that's probably because they don't share an emotional connection AT ALL. Celeste herself is a hypocrite and nothing more. There are so many dog-eared pages in this book where I've marked instances where she goes against the advice that she gives others. She's bratty, rude, and air-headed. Who in their right mind goes into the woods by themselves? Has the author never heard of psychopaths that prey on others? Celeste was not armed, her cell phone wasn't working, and I'm sure that she didn't have self defense training. There was a target on her back for any freak to have their way with her, kill her, and then dump her body somewhere. No one would ever know the difference. Although I didn't necessarily hate Celeste, I definitely didn't like her. Besides occasionally sticking up to her bullying friends, she had no redeeming qualities. What really would have made me like her more was if she would have punched her bratty best friends in their faces. Now THAT I would have liked to have read. I really don't have much else to say about this book. The other characters didn't matter to me at all other than piss me off. There wasn't really a plot other than a romance that isn't even remotely interesting or sweet. The werewolf aspect to this story took a seat to the romance, which is sad. I would have liked to see more about it. And the ending... well, I don't even consider it an ending. It ended so randomly, so infuriatingly, that I turned to my friend when I finished with it, she read the last two pages, and we proceeded to burst out laughing. I don't recommend this to anyone else unless you enjoy insta-love. If you don't, however, stay clear of this. Please, for your sake, run.

Well, that was sad and lovely. Jack and Mabel have sought a new life, middle-aged homesteaders in 1920s rural Alaska. But their fragile peace is tainted by an ages-old-but-undiscussed still birth and their protectionist isolation. The narration (mostly) moves between Jack and Mabel, heartbreaking exposition of a strained marriage in a strange, hard land. (Ivey's Alaskan bona fides are apparent through her breathtaking descriptions of local fauna and flora.) Faina (Fah-EE-nah) arrives, and much like the snowflakes she blew in with, she's a delicate, mysterious girl who spirals around the periphery of their lives, but melts away from their early desperate, possessive love. The author dances away from declaring Faina the snow child wholly mystical or explicable; alternate histories call her a girl made of snow and animated by Mabel and Jack's desire and/or the lonely orphan of a drunken mountain hermit. Oh, and she may or may not control the weather . Alongside this, Jack and Mabel befriend George and Esther, nearby homesteaders with three strapping boys. Their initial tendencies towards solitude, suspicion of neighborly kindness, and familial envy yield to enduring friendship and cooperation on the frontier. Mabel becomes more capable and confident and Jack more trusting and interdependent. Time stretches and contracts. The reader is given many richly described scenes of life in the wilds, climbing into Mabel's head as she recklessly cautiously crosses the frozen river or bids farewell to her chickens, but the story also leaps forwards weeks or years at a time. Character growth isn't a steady procession but like an ebbing seasonality. What I'm saying is the book lends itself to metaphor... It's a lyrical tale that I think might suffer from scrutinizing deconstruction, but it seems to be a popular book club pick so we'll see what happens. Discussion this Wednesday, February 5. Edited to add: So our book club met this week - snowed out last week, very atmospheric for reading this book, these New England winters - and it was interesting, almost all of us shared the experience of trying, trying to figure out what Faina was all about, puzzling over it. Is she real or not? Will she come back every winter? And all of us, let go. We relinquished control to the author and let her take us on the journey, incomprehensible and wonderful, to whatever end it went. And none of us minded, ultimately, the lack of answers. One of our group remarked that her genre-crossing ability (historical fiction or fairy tale or magical realism?) and that satisfying disappointment of unknowing (to paraphrase) separates Pulitzer Prize winners from the rest of us. We also all agreed that Esther was a wonderful addition to the narrative. We were so happy when she broke up the Mabel's isolationist shell and the couple started living again. I and a few others felt that the epilogue was a bit unnecessary but we were glad they were happy. Uniformly, we loved the book.

Cover Blurb: Yes or No? Sure, I like it. It's very indicative of the story's era and what it might be like (i.e. like Downton Abbey). Characters: Ada Averley continues to be a very likable protagonist; smart and perceptive and kind. I adored her even more for her sisterly affection towards Rose, who suffered at the hands of gossips and uncertainty. If possible, I liked Ada even more in this book. Rose, too, continues to be a very caring girl, very artistic, if not wholly sensible when it comes to Alexander Ross (more on that later). Perhaps somewhat surprisingly, my affection for both Sebastian and Oliver increased as well. I still don't really care for the whole "they're gay" plot, but it doesn't feel like the Author is trying to make a statement, so it didn't bother me too much. The bottom line is Oliver is huggable and adorable and I felt so bad for him. And Sebastian showed his better side in this one. On the other end of the spectrum, I liked Emily Maddox a little less in Diamonds & Deceit, and my affection for Lord Fintan totally vanished. We learned a bit more about some of his little secrets, and it made me dislike him quite a bit. Ravi isn't in Diamonds & Deceit at all, so my opinion of him had no chance to waver or increase. ;-) Georgiana and Michael play a bigger role in Diamonds & Deceit, and it made me like them more. Georgiana fights to be strong and take on her role as chatelaine of Somerton, and Michael is so good to Priya, the Indian nursemaid, that I just adored him. Then there's Alexander Ross. .the rake. Perhaps unsurprisingly, his bad reputation isn't as bad as society has made it out to be, and I suspected that from the beginning, so I was prepared to like him. I do love characters who society has painted as rakes, but they really aren't. Alexander mostly falls into that category (he did a few things in his past that weren't totally commendable, but nothing as bad as society has said). I appreciated his disdain for society, their expectations, and his desire to follow his own path. The Romance: I didn't find it as shallow as inCinders & Sapphires, though it's by no means totally heartfelt. Rose hasn't known Alexander long at all before she's head-over-heels for him, despite his reputation. As far as Rose knows, he's as bad as society has declared him; she doesn't find out the truth until much later. Ada continues to struggle with herself over marrying Lord Finton when her heart really belongs to Ravi. Michael and Priya try to determine how to set a life up for themselves without bringing disgrace to the Averley name. And Sebastian and Oliver fight to hide their affections for one another, as a sneaky reporter keeps hanging around, trying to ruin Sebastian's reputation. As if this weren't enough, throw in an old flame between Lord Finton and Charlotte Templeton, and Charlotte's trying to get back at Lord Finton for throwing her over - by making eyes at Alexander Ross. There's also the little matter of Georgiana being in love with Michael. Yes, it's all quite complicated and dramatic, but it's also easy to follow. And it does take up quite a bit of the story - this is Downton Abbey for teens, after all. Plot: Rose Cliffe has been officially acknowledged by Lord Westlake, her father, and now it is the Season and she must be introduced into society. But society isn't so welcoming of a former housemaid, and Rose must fight to claim her place in it as the daughter of an Averley. When Alexander Ross, a highly eligible Scottish duke - with a reputation - starts paying Rose attention, it may just be the notice she needs. But Rose is determined to guard her heart against the undeniable rake, and Charlotte Templeton is determined to not let Rose have him. There's just one problem: Rose is falling for Alexander. Meanwhile, Ada Averley is preparing for her wedding to Lord Finton. This marriage will secure her family's reputation, save Somerton from the reckless spending of Sir William, and will ensure her going to university. But her heart still belongs to Ravi, the Indian Oxford student she fell for long ago. Back at Somerton, Sebastian is fighting to get his valet Oliver released from prison, charged with a murder that Sebastian himself committed. But Oliver won't plead innocent, and with a sneaky reporter poking around, looking to expose Sebastian's greatest secret, he must tread carefully. Never has a Season in London been so filled with drama. And the similarities between Downton Abbey and this series continues! I'm not accusing the Author plagiarism, by the way. Conniving ladies' maids, society drama, and the complications of being a housemaid and wanting to better one's self are all quite realistic themes for the time period, so any Edwardian era novel is going to be similar to one another. But when one's mind has made the connection, it's hard to ignore the similarities. But I still loved this book. There isn't a single character who doesn't have a secret, or who is conniving, or who just has something bad happen to them. Nothing is straight forward; something always complicates it. There's not a dull moment with the Averleys. Between Charlotte's conniving ladies' maid Stella, Charlotte Templeton herself and her horrid mother, Sebastian and Oliver's explosive secret, and Sir William's lecherous behavior towards Priya, there's not a break from it. If there were flatout no likable characters, I don't think even the era would make me like this series as much as I do. But there are characters that I care about. Believability: No complaints. Writing Style: Third person, past tense. It's a very pleasant style, and the narration switches between who it follows, but it isn't confusing. The dialogue is very fitting for the era, too. Content: Sebastian and Oliver are gay. It's also implied that Sir William raped Priya Conclusion: Diamonds & Deceit ends with the breakout of WWI. Sounds familiar. But it really would be hard to have a series set in this era and not have it end with WWI starting. There were a few twists in the end I wasn't expecting, and I was also surprised at how wrapped up events are. I actually wondered if this were a duology. It's not; it's a trilogy. My main complaint is that Oliver's trial was too quickly wrapped up. But other than that, it ended just as satisfyingly as it began. Lots of drama in the beginning, lots of drama in the middle, and more drama at the end. Recommended Audience: Girl-read, seventeen-and-up, fans of Downton Abbey and historical fiction.

Filtered through the perspective of a young girl, Roll of Thunder tells the story of life as a black family in the segregated South during the Great Depression. With burnings and hangings happening in what feels like an abstract way, 9-yr-old Cassie just can't understand why white people treat her and her family the way they do. At every turn, she defends herself and just wants to be treated well. When her family chastises her and reprimands her behavior, Cassie does not understand why, nor does she understand the danger she puts herself in. But when someone close to her is used by two white brothers to commit a crime and is blamed for a murder, Cassie is forced to grow up in order to survive. The story of the Logan Family remains relatable and poignant in its experiences these 40 years after its first publication. Perhaps this is why the ignorant and the afraid continue to try to ban this book every year.

Before I get to the actual review, I'd like to point out that I get it. I totally get this novel. In fact, it's actually rather refreshing, because let's be honest -- when was the last time you read a book in the point of view of a popular bitch and not the sad bullied girl? I was bullied for practically all my school life, right up until I left and even now, at the age of 20, people bully me. Because I'm not the prettiest, funniest, slimmest, etc. It only occurred to me after school how sad and pathetic those bullies were. I mean, how unsatisfying can your life possibly be to pick on someone half your size to make yourself feel better? So yeah, I get this novel. I really, really do. This is what happens:  Sam Kingston is a bitch. Bottom line, she's one of the big bad bullies in this particular American high school. Although she doesn't throw the first insult, start the first rumour or the first to graffitti the bathroom stalls, she goes along with it just like all her friends do. And then one evening, she dies. Except the story doesn't end there: consequently, she gets thrown into this kind of Groundhog day thing, where she lives the day of her death over and over, and she slowly comes to the realisation that her actions -- who she was and what she did -- caused her death. Get this : Juliet Sykes is a 'psycho', 'weirdo', an 'outcast' and the night of Sam's death, she throws herself in front of their car and dies along with Sam. Because of their incessant bullying, she decides to kill herself and, without knowing, kills Sam, the bane of her existent, as well. You see, Sam slowly realises that she is an awful, horrid bitch and as the day(s) go by, she realises she needs to change something -- she needs to change the outcome, so she can 'move on'. Wherever that is. I loved this book, and Lauren Oliver is a beautiful writer. In fact, the voice of Sam and her she-witches are so loud and clear, it was like being transported back to the good old school days all over again. Each person has an outstanding personality, and no two characters are the same. The fact that Lindsay Edgecombe (Queen Bitch) and Juliet Sykes (Psycho) used to be friends only makes the entire ordeal more interesting. The novel isn't split into chapters, but seven days. And when the day Sam realises what, exactly, she must do to move on rolls around, there's a sense of finality throughout the whole novel. At first, I thought she was in a coma, and finally doing what was right would wake her up, but alas that was not the case, and she successfully moved on to whatever is next, I guess. All in all, I give the book four stars. It's new, exciting, sad and so honest that it actually hurts to realise that because of who she was, what she did and who she hung out with, people would feel sorry for her death but internally think, "Bitch got what she deserved." Because no one knew she could change things. No one knew that she was really a good person inside. So think about that. Think about all those who hurt you and ruined your life and made school a living hell. Think of the nicknames and the shouting and messages scrawled on bathroom mirrors, and the rumours. Think about that and then think about what they're doing now, and what YOU'RE doing now. Have they changed? Have YOU changed? And just like that you'll understand this novel. This story is about cruelty and bullying and what schools are really like -- these days more than ever. It's the honest, stone cold truth. It's a truth not many see, or many choose to ignore. Congratulations, Lauren Oliver, for using your imagination and create something so starkly beautiful like Before I Fall.

2.5 stars! Honestly, the plot of this book was kind of a mess and could've benefitted from being split into two books that had less info dumping and more character developments. There were parts I liked of this book, but they're kind of intervowen with what I didn't like, so... here goes! Major spoilers below!! The Tris and Four relationship was a lot of back and forth this book. I liked it because I felt that Roth explored the fact that a relationship is often contentious and not exactly smooth sailing, and like Tris says at one point, it's about choosing to be with the other person over and over again... ... however,  if  you have to chose each other over and over pretty much  every day  maybe it's just not in the stars for you kids... Also, their RELATIONSHIP DRAMA - their lies, jealousy, fights and make up scenes are pretty much the back bone/major plot of the book, meanwhile the rest take a bit of a back seat, because all the fighting and factions (not to mention the whole new scenario of the Genetically Pure vs the Genetically Damaged) are pretty much filtered through how Tris and Four (who alternates as narrators) react to these things and take different sides. The effect is that all these major things just seem like plot points meant to complicate their relationship. It was disappointing to have the romance be so front and center, mostly because Four was so... not Four? He was just insecure, petty and irrational and appeared as a meathead more or less ready to jump into any random woman's plan (Evelyn, Nita) while pushing Tris away. That said, there's a scene where Four decides to go with Nita's plan, while Tris objects, they fight about it. She ends up having been right and then goes to tell him so and scolds him for not listening to her. The thing is... Four goes with his gut and goes with the plan and it's obvious from the start that it's going to bite him in the ass. However, Tris is also JUST going off her gut in not trusting Nita, so really, her scolding him later just comes across as her being obnoxious. Why does it always take like three books for any actual sex to happen? They've been committed to each other for some time now and it's not like it's graphic. Also this particular sex scene just reminded me of Judy Blume's "Forever", I remember reading that her daughter had asked her to write about where a girl had sex but didn't have to die at the end because that was de rigeur in YA at the time... so yeah, Tris basically gets to bone cause she's gonna die. Ah yes, Tris dies. I actually didn't mind this very much, except I've read other reviews which make a very good point in saying that a) she robs Caleb of his chance of redemption, b) the other characters, say Four, should've seen this dumb ass sacrifice coming, c) it's a dumb ass sacrifice because it doesn't really accomplish anything. That said... I cried. I did like the general message that Four was initially heartbroken, but then starts to heal, as people do, and will likely move on and have a healthy life with a new relationship in the future. The ending in general is rushed and makes no sense. And can I just say that throughout the whole book I DIDN'T GIVE TWO FIGS about the damn GP vs GD wars, the experiments made literally no sense (how would GD's somehow get GP - Divergent - kids... if their genes are damaged, why are their ancestors genetically pure? What? ), and the amount of time we spend at the Bureau and visiting new places was just - meh. Again, maybe if it had been two books and the world building would have been more proper it would have been interesting. As it is, it just felt like info dumps + Tris and Four fight + Tris glares at Caleb + Tris and Four make up + info dump = book Final thought: Evelyn Evelyn is a kind of villain in Insurgent. She's all 'Tobias is mine, I'm here forever Tris, you're just temporary' and becomes a dictator of the Factionless. This is where she is for most of Allegiant as well, even forbidding Tobias from being with Tris at the start (and they're hilariously bad at being together on the sly). Only we get to see her, on screens, sad like once or twice because she's angry with Marcus and misses Tobias... Yet, these tiny, distant, moments is not enough to make me care at all about Evelyn. Like seriously, what the fuck do I care about Evelyn? From the past couple of books she's been a bitch. Yet at the end of Allegiant she just gives up being a dictator - because love conquers all and she picks her son - an at the very end we get a little mother and son back together again moment, as if that means anything? Listen, I spent two and a half books reading everything from Tris' perspective, Evelyn is not on my list of 'characters I hope turn out well', because there has been nothing to make me feel for her except for this lame hail mary at the end of the series. That said, it was an entertaining enough read and as said, I didn't really mind the ending. But overall it's just messy and kind of over-ambitious for the scope of the book.

I like the cover, but the synopsis on the inside flap made me a bit skeptical, and I didn't truly get into the book until a few chapters in when the main character did some research on the words 'superhero' and 'Paladin.' I guess as a gamer and somewhat of a nerd, quite frankly the complete OPPOSITE of me, it made me giggle. Seventeen-year-old Harper Jane Price, junior at Pine Grove Academy, president of the SGA, head cheerleader, forgets her lipgloss at her homecoming dance. Borrowing some from her best friend, she goes to the bathroom. The school janitor, Mr. Hall, barges in and falls to the floor. Trying to help him, Mr. Hall does the last thing Harper would ever expect, he kisses her and thus, changes her life forever. Good thing too, because quickly afterwards, a scimitar-wielding history teacher, Dr. DuPont, comes in the bathroom, too, trying to kill Harper. If things couldn't get any worse, the next morning at school, Harper finds out that her nemesis since kindergarten, nerdy hipster David Stark, wrote an article in the school newspaper: complete with the scene of Harper crying in the school bathroom after she was found (by David) throwing up. She confronts him, tries to hit him, only to find out that she can't. As Harper says, things just get weirder, like something straight out of stories, but these things bring Harper and David together in ways they didn't think were possible, and the two discover that maybe things between them could be considered friendship...or perhaps something more. [POSSIBLE SPOILERS. READ AT YOUR OWN RISK.] So. Right. I'll go ahead and say that I could in no way relate to the main character. She's basically all the things I never was nor wanted to be whilst in high school while I feel very much connected with David in a sense that he seemed quite nerdy, evident of the books in his room and the map of Middle Earth. The times when I rolled my eyes were times I had to remember, "Oh yeah, she's head cheerleader, obviously the pretty one, and homecoming queen." However, I do find that she has quite the sense of humor when it comes to certain things and I just found myself giggling and then liking the whole story in general. One thing though, how in the world did Harper know what Doctor Who was? Random though while reading the book. I hope the second book is as entertaining as the first one.

Please note that this review / notes are just for my own personal use and shouldn't be taken as a genuine review THE WORLD THE CHARACTERS The Biologist: Main Character The Psychologist: The leader The Surveyor: good with firearms The Anthropologist: architect THE STORY . the scene is set, strange occurrences has meant that all previous expeditions have either been killed or gone missing. The team of 4 don't have any advanced equipment, no phones, no GPS, no way of communicating with the outside. the only things there were sent with were black devices hung around their necks which they have been told alert them when they have reached a dangerous area. what the devices measure and what makes these areas dangerous, they don't know. They have all had to be hypnotized by the psychologist before crossing the border into area x. None of them can remember the specifics of how they arrived into area x. after a short time they find a "tower" going down into the ground which they feel shouldn't be there. When they enter this "underground tower" they work their way further down below the earth and find writing on the wall written in some kind of plant / fungi. The plant writing gives off spores which the biologist accidentally inhaled. While back at the teams base camp the Psychologist puts the others under a hypnotic trance, the biologist doesn't feel any kind of effect by the hypnosis, is this because the spores have effected her? she plays along with the others nonetheless so that the psychologist doesn't realize. the psychologist uses the hypnosis to reinforce there reason for being here and to calm the rest of the team. There is a sense that the psychologist knows more than she is letting on about area x. The morning after the Anthropologist has gone missing and the psychologist is limping slightly and looks like shes had a rough night, when the Surveyor asks where she has gone she explains that the anthropologist has made her way back to the border because she has been unnerved by what she saw in the tower, neither of the other women really trust what the psychologist is saying. The biologist and the Surveyor go back down into the tower while the Psychologist keeps watch above. the biologist believes that the tower is breathing and deduces that they are actually entering a living breathing organism. "where lies the strangling fruit" is what is written in the strange substance the further down the tower. The biologist realizes that there are a large number of text on the walls each over the last, that seems to have been made over a long period of time. They find that the further down the tower they go the fresher the text becomes, is there something / someone below them writing this text? As they descend they find a strange white substance covering the steps in which they find a boot print that isn't theirs? They make their way further still and find the anthropologists body, they deduce that something in the bowels of the tower killed her but by looking at the tracks they also discover that the psychologist was with her and probably giving her hypnotic suggestions to investigate the creature that killed her. They make their way back up the tower to ground level to confront the psychologist but he has vanished and taken most of the supplies from Base Camp. The next morning the 2 are in disagreement with where to go,so the biologist heads towards lights she saw the night by before, probably from the light house. The biologist admits that her husband was a medic on the last expedition to area x. When is husband went to area x she found him back in the house and he cannot remember how he got home. She takes him back to the army and because he is not himself, she describes him as living in a haze, he is then diagnosed with an extreme case of cancer. On her way to the to the lighthouse the biologist pieces together that the tower and the creature that killed the anthropologist are two separate creatures and this raises different questions... Is the writing on the wall a way for the two to communicate, is it a ritual? Does one support the other? When she arrives at the lighthouse she discovers a large pile of journals suggesting that there has been far more than just the 12 expeditions, amongst the pile she also finds her husbands journal. From the top floor she spots the psychologist laying on the beach. The biologist discovers that the other woman has been injured by the "creeper" in the tower when she and the anthropologist had their encounter. The psychologist explains that they don't know exactly what is happening in the tower and that's why they keep sending expeditions, she also explains that the border to area x keeps expanding every year. The psychologist dies and the wound from the creeper glows bright green in the darkness. On her way back to the Base Camp she notices a human face looking at her from the mud, when she examines the face she sees that it has been shed as though it is part of an exoskeleton. When she gets back to camp the surveyor fires at her because she thinks that she has killed the psychologist. The spores she has been infected with give her a "brightness" which heightens her senses which she uses to shoot and kill the surveyor. After she has killed the surveyor she goes back to base camp and sees that she has destroyed it. She uses the equipment she has left to determine that the samples she has taken from a fox in the lighthouse are actually human, she now has proof that something very strange is going on here. She earlier saw a dolphin, she felt like she recognised it's eyes, was this her husband transformed? The biologist then makes her way down the tower and comes across the crawler writing on the wall. She can't describe what she sees because it keeps changing shape and form and keeps disappearing and appearing again. The crawler touches and connects with her and it puts her through excruciating pain and sifts through her brain before releasing her down the tower. On her way out of the tower she passes the crawler again and now gets a sense that the crawler is actually the lighthouse keeper she saw from a photo while she was there. How long he has been doing this? Is he aware of what he is doing? How long has it taken to transform into this? Why is he writing these words? The biologist then goes back to the lighthouse and reading through the journals discovers that her husband may still be alive and for some reason the tower or area x has related doppelgangers of the people in the previous expeditions but she doesn't know why. Her husband writes that he has gone further up the coast to an island he saw from the shore. Reading on through the journals she discovers that when the crawler has completed this round of text in the walls of the tower area x will change / grow. MY THOUGHTS i really enjoyed this book, all the unanswered questions; what happened in area X, what happened to the other expeditions? what turned the lighthouse keeper into the crawler? what and why is the crawler writing on the walls in the tower? so many questions that just keep you reading on and on. i liked how the characters weren't given specific names i think this gave me a sense of detachment to the characters which related to the same feeling the characters must have felt with each other because they would not refer to each other with their names and would only call them by their profession. My only criticism is that this first book is quite short but on the other hand it may be short but its definitely long enough to get you hooked into reading the next in the series to try and find answers to this strange and mysterious area. a

I got an email from the publisher through Netgalley asking if I'd like to read this book because I enjoyed something similar. And I'm so glad I did, because I hadn't seen it, and I would've missed out. From the first page, I was completely hooked. The first chapter was so good, I put it down, afraid I wouldn't enjoy the second quite as much. But I did. And it kept getting pacing. There are plenty of twists and turns to keep the reader guessing, and I just needed to know what would happen to Kailey. Most of my time these days is spent writing, and editing. It's hard for me to read sometimes because I'm still in editor mode. I get hung up on stupid stuff. This book reminded me what it's like to read for pleasure. I devoured it, and when I finished, I wished there was more. There were two things about the book that bugged me, and that's why I'm giving 4 stars. But it's a solid 5 stars for the writing. We're told, over and over and over, that Kailey loves Ryan. I never felt it. I never really felt like she was making an effort with him, and she never even tried to put him first. Sure, she said she was going to stay with him out of obligation and guilt, but I never really felt that pull. I never doubted who she'd end up with. And because we don't see what it is that Kailey loves about Ryan, he came across as one-dimensional. The story of what happened to Cade felt anti-climactic. I spent the entire book certain James had something to do with it, or even his wife, and... OK, they kinda did, but not really. I almost wanted it to be completely random (but somehow resolved, like they find evidence of a string of random attacks at the same time) or to have it have been an intentional attack. But those are fairly minor issues, and overall, I loved this book.

I got very emotionally invested in this book very quickly. Smoky's grief was intense and painful to be a part of, but her story sucked me right in. Now that I have a little distance from it (a whole twelve hours!) I can see the things that didn't work - the sudden! sex! with a character who was just introduced as a ~protector~ was the worst, I think. It just seems like a skewed view of the grieving process. Suicide was barely off the table for Smoky at that point. I had a hard time sleeping after finishing this book, because I just kept thinking of Leo's poor dog. "Someone cut off all his legs. I have to put him down." I stand, gaping. Poleaxed. Then his voice breaks. The clean, poignant break of a china plate hitting brick. "Who would do something like that, Smoky? I got home and he was there in the living room, trying to . trying to . His grief makes him sound like he is gagging, as he finds the words. "Trying to crawl to me. There was blood everywhere, and he was making these awful sounds, like . like a baby. Looking at me with those eyes, it was like . he looked like he thought he'd done something wrong. Like he was asking me, 'What, what did I do wrong? I'll fix it, just tell me. See? I'm a good dog.' The "See? I'm a good dog." line just had me bawling in the dark on my couch at 1AM. I felt pure, unadulterated rage at this fictional killer; my poor emotions.

Troubled bad girl Reagan is on the road for her BFF "Dee" Lilah Montgomery's - a kind of Fearless-era Taylor Swift - first headlining U.S. tour. Reagan is desperate for a new start and Dee is recovering from a breakup with her longtime boyfriend. When a doctored "nude" photo of Dee hits the tabloids, her publicist acts fast, booking former family-band member and total hottie Matt Finch to open the tour and distract the press with rumors of a celebrity romance. Reagan tries to support the fauxmance, but it's kind of hard when the real sparks are between Matt and her. Wowza, this book is so swoony and great. It is excellently written too, both with lovely metaphors and turns of phrase and Reagan's bad attitude. I loved it. I want comment on the negative reviews that hate Reagan for her bad attitude by saying that I think that it is a natural part of her (really well-developed) character and that her self-talk about other girls was, to me, obviously not about how she really feels about them but rather a reflection of how she feels about herself.

I was sadly disappointed by this book, obviously not hugely but I was expecting myself to give it five-stars no questions asked. I think all the hype surrounding it made me go in with unrealistic expectations. Which is why I think most of the time people should go into books before reading reviews, however in this case I wouldn't have picked it up without all the positive reviews to encourage me. Catch-22 as they say. Now don't get me wrong, there's  a lot to love about this book. Karou is an amazing female protagonist. She's introduced into the story heartbroken and pissed off about it. She's sensitive but won't take peoples crap. She can be petty and selfish but also so kind and empathetic. She's so human. A human that occasionally collects teeth for monsters. Speaking of monsters... Her little adopted family of creatures are so well written, described so perfectly that you could almost picture them sitting in the room with you. I have a special place in my heart for Brimstone, sullen and busy weaving teeth into complicated necklaces and Issa, slithering across the floor, quick to embrace at the first sign of hurt. I especially liked the attempt at creating a story with no real villains, everyone is so morally grey, which I find is quite rare to in YA fiction. So it was nice to read something that wasn't your regular GOOD VS EVIL shtick. The setting in general is so rich it's easy to lose yourself completely in this book. In fact the first half of this book with is slow world building, gradual drips of information and likeable characters are most definitely worth five stars. Plus the writing made me want to kiss Lani Taylor, the woman sure as hell can write a gut-punching sentence. So where did it all fall apart for me? The cliche romance, or what I felt to be a cliche romance. Akiva, an angel, meets Karou and tries to kill her. This was actually one of their few encounters that I enjoyed the most. She escapes but Akiva can't forget about her, is drawn to her, needs her blah blah blah. Now I know that it's based around Romeo and Juliet so insta-love and obsessive, consuming love makes sense and I guess I should take into account the DESTINY(tm) of it all, especially when you find out who Karou really is   but it just didn't feel believable to me. It seemed to go complete against Karou and Akiva's character that I just couldn't suspended my disbelief. Why spend 50% of a book showing us that our protagonist is a smart, capable woman to have her trip over herself trying to gain the man's affections- the affections of someone who tried to kill her. I am excited to read the next book though as I feel it's going to shift away from the romance that soured the story for me.

A very entertaining read. The only thing is, maybe cause it feels too YA, Alexandria a.k.a. Alex, the heroine, who is 17 years old, and a half-blood, has a character that is too stubborn, too reckless and too mouthy that she irritates the hell out of me! BUT... she does have her good qualities too... This series goes like this: Greek gods plus mortal equals Pure Blood; Pure Blood plus Mortals equals Half Blood... So that makes the Pure Blood the superior ones, next to the gods of course; .... and the half bloods, well, they can either attend the Covenant or go into the working class... meaning the half's who have a pure blood willing to speak for them and pay for the cost of their education were enrolled in the Covenant to train as Sentinels or Guard. The other half's, well, they are turned into servants for the pure blood, with no will nor freedom. Sucks right? Then there are "daimon's", the bad ones, cause they live to kill... they suck all the aether out of the pure blood resulting to more daimons. The half bloods couldn't be turned which is why they were trained to fight daimons... The story also gives you a love-triangle-ish atmosphere. This being Alex is attracted to Aiden, a 20 years old Sentinel and a pure blood, so even though Aiden returns the feeling, pure blood and half blood is forbidden to be together. Then there's Seth! Seth is an Apollyon, the only half-blood with the ability to control the elements and use the same kind of compulsion the pures could use on mortals. There are a lot of Rules and a lot of history going on in this series. Then there is this Oracle with a prophesy about Alex... meaning more puzzlers to look forward to! I very much enjoyed the storyline, I think it was fascinating and cool. As for the love-triangle-ish thing going, I couldn't, for now, chose which team to take, be it team Aiden or team Seth. Seth comes out too strong, and yet I don't feel like Alex really gave him a chance to get to know him... and that's besides Alex is scared of him... and them together, and their fate... Whereas Aiden is all kinds of sexy and patient with Alex, I love them together, but then again, they aren't allowed to be... Frustrating really. There is action and suspense... and a not so much as a surprise, cause yeah you would see it coming. But still, I thoroughly enjoyed the storyline and looking forward to the next book! This book was so enjoyable to read and I loved every moment of it. There is betrayal, action, and romance all tied into one story(who doesn't love all of that? lol). This story takes place after World War V and is ruled by the "Commander". The world has to stay pure from worldly vices. Sinners are the people who sin and when they are caught they get sent to the "Hole". The seven deadly sins are what the Commander feels is reason for the chaos and the destruction of the society. People who are in those ranks of sin are judged and sent to the Hole for the rest of their lives. Each person who is in the Hole will be colored based on the sin that they committed. Being accused of a crime that she did not commit Lexi has been sent to the Hole. Having everything stripped away from her she did not fight at first nor did she try to prove her innocence because of the fact that no one would actually believe her if she tried. I loved reading Lexi's character because she is a genuine unique person. She endured so much and even though she wanted to end everything at one moment she still pushed through. The first half of the book my heart was breaking because of the emotional roller coaster happening. I'm not a big fan for the blood and guts everywhere but the story was that good for me to overlook it and keep reading. Cole is the guard that is assigned to Lexi. At first she was just an assignment but that eventually falls into something much more :). "I never planned on falling for you. You were just an assignment. But it just sort of happened and now... There's not a single thing I would change about you. When you smile, my entire world stops. All I see is you. I need you." But a guard falling in love with a sinner has some serious consequences. Cole was perfect throughout the story. His need to protect her was important to him throughout the story. Things may have started out shaky between them but I'm glad it blossomed into better things. I enjoyed reading this story very much and I look forward to reading the rest in the series! Rating4stars Recommend? Yes

This book, guys. This book. I haven't read many graphic novels - I do read the occasional manga, but graphic novels are, for the most part, an unexplored genre for me. I picked this up because I thought it would be funny. And it really, really was. The story is... well, it's entertaining. The baseline is, there's funding for either the robotics club or new uniforms for the cheerleaders. The student council will pick who the funding goes to - so what should president of the robotics club Nate Harding do but run for president? Unfortunately, his best friend, who happens to be captain of the basketball team and is roped into running for president on behalf of the cheerleaders, ends up sort of caught in the middle. And the actual president - or should I say, presidents - that get revealed at the end is the best thing in the world. My God, the twins made the graphic novel anyway, and them getting voted presidents was so great. The characters are all incredibly wacky and fun, and there are a ton of great one-liners in here. It's hard to read this book without cracking up. I'm really glad I wasn't reading this in public, because I probably would have gotten weird looks, it was so great. My God. This was so fun.

3.5 stars I'm not going to go in-depth on this one, because I don't really like writing reviews for books that are sequels (is this just me?). But I liked it, and I thought that it was a pretty good follow-up to Beautiful Creatures, although there were some things that I personally didn't like about it. There was a high prevalence of paranormal stuff in this novel...actually, quite a lot of it. Most of the story is spent in the tunnels below Gatlin that we learned about in the previous book. And I think that that is part of the reason why I could only rate it 4 stars instead of 5. While I sometimes like paranormal books, they're not my absolute favorite. So I had a hard time enjoying Beautiful Darkness as much as I wanted to, because of the overwhelming magic elements. This book also kind of reminded me of a Harry Potter novel, in that Ethan and his "rag-tag" group of friends were forced to go on this hardcore paranormal journey in order to save Lena  and make everything right by fighting the monsters. That aspect of it was just kind of weird; it definitely wasn't my favorite plot. What I loved from the first book was the connection between Ethan and Lena, Marian the librarian, and Lena's family. And those are basically all of the things that are missing from this second book. But I'm hopeful that the next book will be a little different than this one was, based on its ending.

(This review also appears on Laudable Lit) Actual rating: 3.5 stars. This book was a journey, mostly because of the building of the author's world and mythology. If the author did not detail her world-building and mythology-forming as well as she did, this book would have been two stars. So, in that aspect it's undoubtedly unique. The story did not go where I thought it would. Characters are not who I thought they were (And we still supposedly don't know everything about Asher. I will admit that I thought they would all be angels. The gargoyle twist was a definite surprise, but apparently there's more to that? I'm going to guess now that Asher is some sort of prince.) I appreciated the steady pace of the book, yet how fast the action was picked up. I honestly didn't think it would happen, but I actually became invested in the characters! I felt like I was part of the pseudo-family forming. Though I'll admit, Eve is the one I am the least invested in. I was not too fond of the way the novel ended. There was a big "rise" to the story, but a very little "climax." I understand that this is an intro to the rest of the series, but still. The author seems to be trying to stir up excitement for her next book, but the last paragraphs were too rushed, while the reader is still trying to grasp what is going on. I had to look back a few pages and say, "Did that just happen?" I was also wary at about how much Eve and Asher's relationship seems to be based off of this outside, unexplainable pull. This is a common theme when it comes to supernatural literature, I understand; however, I felt that their relationship forms a little too fast because of this. It's all just sexual tension. Honestly. (Though, it was pretty hot... It's difficult for it not to be, when the author seems to be really good at writing these types of scenes). Overall, this was a decent, quick read; one that I will be awaiting the sequel for. It really hits the spot if you're looking for a unique world, diverse mythology, and/or tension-based romance. There is mild violence, a good amount of language used, and sexual themes that may not be appropriate for younger ages. The nature of Eve and Asher's relationship is charged with sexual tension that will most likely be acted upon in later sequels.

Obviously, there is more empathy for some characters than others, but with every interesting twist I just thought.. okay, yeah, this is SUPER complex. Just like, you know, real life. Like others, I felt like the book could use MORE MORE MORE. I didn't necessarily like where it left off, but I can see why it stopped where it did. At first I thought it was kind of cheap of them to leave so much left to the reader, but now that I've had time to think about it, you realize how sticky it could get after this.. if anything, I think it's good exercise to consider the possibilities yourself. And that's my OWN "cheap" ending ;)
