This book caught my eye (because cover) and for being described as Cloud Atlas for teens. I was drawn to the premise of A Thousand Pieces of You--an invention called a Firebird allows travelers to explore multiple parallel dimensions--but was sorely disappointed and distracted by the writing, which merited more than a few eye-rolls from this reader. (I had also just finished reading a fantastically-written book that I loved, so perhaps the contrast was underscored. I also understand that teen lit often works within different parameters, but still. The bar could have been raised). I did enjoy the settings--from a futuristic London to a recreated duchess-era Russia, to a floating ocean-home in a waterlogged world--I was intrigued to follow Marguerite to these alternate possible realities. However, the narration often fell flat, and made the storytelling feel unsophisticated and contrived. The love triangle element held some potential, but at times felt too forced or cheesy. The redeeming elements here are the concept of the Firebird and its parameters of interdimensional universes, the slight plot twists, and the conspiracy surrounding the company that's after the Caine family's Firebird and their knowledge . Despite its poor execution, I was interested enough in the storyline to follow A Thousand Pieces of You through its varied dimensions, although still left me wishing for an alternate universe where this book is better.

This is a surprisingly maudlin book, saying and doing extremely maudlin things, while giving the impression of doing something completely new. There is nothing horribly bad about it, but it is, once again, one in a certain type of book that tries really hard to pretend the author has never read a genre-fiction novel in his life. Perhaps I am jaded by all the fantasy, urban fantasy, and weird lit I've read, but the exceptional nature of the setting is not that exceptional to me, and the pretend-magical-realism that really never amounts to anything grates false: here, look, we're going to show you all these magical things, but then be adults and practically tell you they don't exist. Okay. The book's other problem is that it's frighteningly generic. Except for the descriptions of Alaska, which the author obviously knows and loves, the characters could be any generic stock of Pioneering Woman, Frustrated Middle-Aged Man, Jovial Neighbour, Good Businesswoman that Fell on Hard Times, and, of course, Grieving Woman Unable to Have a Child. The book's period is equally uncertain. It's purported to be set in the 1920s, but it could be set at any time from the moment frontier settling and homesteading became a feature in america, and until the invention of the internet. The writing is decently crafted, though it too is not lacking the odd gimmick-y quirks, like putting the dialogue of one character without quotations for some reason that would purportedly increase the atmospheric vibe, but in reality just feels odd. The descriptions of the wildlife and nature can be beautiful, and the story, while not terribly engaging, was not too hard a read for what it was trying to do.

I think many of the criticisms of this series are valid. It's definitely not the most original YA series out there (far from it) and I pointed out a lot of the similar elements in my review of Red Queen. But I really enjoyed Glass Sword, and I think Aveyard did well at using this book to fully distinguish the series from the many other dystopian YA books/series out there. I really like Mare as a protagonist, and this book does a lot to further her characterization. Despite Mare's role as the figurehead/instigator of a revolution, she's still seventeen years old, and the events of both books have transpired so quickly that she still doesn't really know what she's doing. Glass Sword makes no secret of that. What I liked about this book was how human Mare was. She lashes out at those closest to her and she closes herself off from her loved ones, and she has to be reminded that she'll ultimately be the one who gets hurt if she keeps doing so. I thought the ways she acted were very realistic for a teenager. The way that she seemed so resigned to her "purpose," even when it made no sense at all to do so, underscored this. She's being a stubborn kid. I found it to be more realistic than annoying. I also think the worldbuilding continues to be strong. It was pretty exciting to read about what the other newbloods could do, and similarly upsetting when Mare and her team couldn't save everyone. The scene with the baby is especially heart-wrenching. . A few criticisms I did have: - "The little lightning girl" and the way this title is used in the book are WAY too similar to the girl on fire from The Hunger Games. It's a ripoff that isn't subtle at all. - It seems like a fair amount of the book is written to be quotable. This tendency was especially noticeable at the end of each chapter- it seemed like she was trying to write a complete ending for every single chapter in a really nice quote. What this actually did was jar the narrative and make it more confusing, since everything seems so final, but then the story continues. - While Mare has great characterization, I feel like I only really understand her, Maven, and Queen Elara (and Kilorn and Farley, to some extent). Pretty much everyone else in this book is completely secondary and doesn't really have much of a personality, so I wasn't really invested in them. I still think Cal is a completely flat character. Another case in point: an event that was supposed to have a huge emotional impact, Shade's death , didn't actually make me feel anything. I really hope Aveyard works on this in her next book(s).

I read the whole thing in one weekend. I had no trouble with it, either: I read the chapters of Ship of Theseus right along with the notes in the margins, even though I've seen others say they tried to read the 'book' itself first, and then go and read all the written notes. So, for those worried it might take some effort to 'keep up' or keep your place amongst all the notes, don't worry. The page design is quite elegant, in that all of the notes make sense, are even color-coded by segments of time (it feels natural, too - you lose pens, they run out of ink, you feel like expressing yourself in something brighter, with a finer nib, etc. ), and the ephemera stuck between the pages is contextual to the spot where it's tucked (so, don't let them fall out and forget where they went!). The notes also don't force much back-and-forth page turning - when they do, it's deliberate and clear, and never makes you work for it. They definitely had a strong sense of visual design and flow when creating the note conversations. The book itself is a work of art, honestly. It looks like a book from the '40's-'50's, and each piece of evidence is well-crafted and realistic. The printing on the pages is high quality - you forget that you're looking at a color-printed page, and not aged paper with ballpoint and felt-tip markings lining the margins. I liked every bit of the story, even though I knew I had left behind so many of the worries that Jen and Eric were wrestling with, they still felt pretty true to what I remember, what my paper journals of my twenties looked like. My heart filled with affection for Filomela and VMS, loved every single parallel, the eerily-accurate style of the prose in the 'book'. As someone who loves ARGs, I was a tiny bit disappointed that one of the URLs did not work (there weren't many, and I think one has been taken by a fan or something already), but was surprised that the non-working URL was an .edu, as those are not really something a non-educational institution/entity can commandeer all that easily. Also, one of the letters tucked into the pages (Eric's yellow legal pad story about Uncle Zeke) had an extra first page, which did a surprising job of pulling me out of the story, as the rest of the execution of the book was so flawless. I worried a little after that when certain photos or items were mentioned in the margins and there was no corresponding photo/etc. tucked into the page that perhaps it was missing. Maybe I'll create a 'menu' of the items, and see if it compares with everyone else. I know I'll need to read this book again, now that I know what the main characters know, and see what mysteries remain. I lost an entire weekend to this book, and I don't regret it one bit - it was an awful lot of fun to read. It reminded me of when I used to write long, hand-written letters to friends and loves, and I still miss that sort of thing a lot. Addendum: I've seen a few comments on other reviews where they talk about the smell of the book. And it's true. They even got the smell of the pages right. It'd be funny if that was accidental. There is a list of the items in the book here: http://sfiles22.blogspot.com/2013/10/...

Oh my god... This book was simply incredible, brutal and honest, beautiful and inspiring. I wish every high schooler would read it, because I feel like if they did, high school might suck a lot less for everybody. I read Delirium and Pandemonium by Lauren Oliver before this, so I was already absolutely in love with/insanely jealous of her lovely writing and her gift for really vivid imagery. This book reminded me so much of my own high school experience, it was a little bit creepy. And I feel that she really nailed the characters of Sam and her friends. The "mean girl" dynamic has been explored before, but in this book it really felt true to me, it really made sense, especially in that the girls weren't just written off as "mean, popular", blah blah. They were still her friends, flawed and dysfunctional as they were, and there were always reasons to love them as well as hate them. This book really forces you to examine your own life, too. How do you want to be remembered, what are your "greatest hits", how have you treated those around you, who do you wish you understood better, what do you still want to do with the time you have. By the end of the book, I found myself really, really wishing that Sam wouldn't have to die, that maybe by saving Juliet then her car crash wouldn't have happened or something, and that she could live the way she had learned to over the seven days. And while I understand why she died, I still...ouch. It almost made me mad at the author, but then again, that's a testament to how great the writing is, that you feel so connected to this character that it really effects you to see her go. . I reccomend this for everybody. Yes, you. If you haven't, go read it! Now!

The first battle in the war between Artime and Quill has been fought, but the war is far from over. High Priest Justine is dead and the gates of Artime are open for all of Quill. Necessaries flock to the magical world to escape the drudgery of their lives. Artime welcomes the newcomers and allows visits between the two worlds; however, tensions still run high with the Wanteds in power. Aaron has fallen from power, but is determined to climb back up. He starts gathering new allies and preparing to keep the fight with Artime going. The battle with Quill has also made Mr. Today realize he needs to train a successor. He chooses reluctant Alex despite the fact that he is still young and learning. When two strangers wash up on Artime's shores things get even more complicated. Who are these kids and why do they have iron chokers around there necks and why can't they speak? Sky and Crow have escaped from another island where they were slaves. Alex, Lani, Meghan and Samheed head to Warbler Island to investigate. Unfortunately things do not go as planned and Alex is forced to choose between his friends in order to escape leaving Lani and Samheed behind. Just as they approach Artime, magic disappears leaving the Artimeans vulnerable to an attack from Quill. The book ends on a desperate cliffhanger that leaves the reader reaching for book three immediately. The action ramps up in this darker sequel to The Unwanteds. I immediately wanted to start reading the next book as soon as I finished this one (and of course I did). Alex and Aaron are both left to explore their power and figure out how to be leaders. It is interesting how similar and different their paths are. I liked that we got off of Quill and visited another island in this world. The connections between Warbler and Quill are interesting and surprising and left me with additional questions about the creation of Quill. This series is extremely popular and deservedly so. I am thoroughly enjoying it.

3.5 stars. Okay, I have to admit this grew on me. At first Remy's constant sexual comments grated and the sexual innuendos and banter were so ridiculously bad it kept me reading for the sheer laugh at not with factor. By the time the actual romance started, where Remy began to admit he had feelings for Ysabel, I was hooked. The story was funny when it wasn't trying too hard and Langlais's Lucifer was hilarious if a bit weaker than expected. But his evilness was proven in this technically funny but horrible line: "Lucifer bit into his foot-long dog--a daschund (sic) collie mix with a touch of mustard and hot sauce. Mmm, nothing like it. The world was a little bizarre in that only perfect people went to Heaven and given that the concept of Heaven and Hell is a Christian concept where Jesus died for the sins that everyone has, the only one(s) inhabiting it would be God and possibly Jesus. I did have a problem with the vengeance thing, especially when the hate had lasted 500 years. Damning someone to eternal torture in prison in Hell is pretty nasty. That 500 years later her hatred hasn't abated (especially for one guy whose only crime was boasting which only added fuel to the fire, pun intended). Interestingly, she was much nastier in this regard then he was: He admits to himself that even a few hours working in the prison would make him go insane while she walked through it with no problem. I also hated the veiled sexism like when he referred to her repeatedly as a shrew and when he was so arrogant that insisted she must like him. I hated that she let him defend her by fighting a bunch of drunken idiots when she admitted to herself that she didn't need his help, she was plenty powerful enough to handle it on her own. But as this proves, she was very magically strong. I'm not sure how I feel about the fact that she not only refused him, but repeatedly responded to his advances by punching him in the stomach. She also proved that her magic was more powerful than his. She even went off to save him at one point. A sample of the ribald humor that I thought was ridiculous: "The slender pole of her broom whipped through the seam of his thighs, emerging from him like a three foot long, wooden dick. Grabbing a hold of it, he thrust his hips forward and with a grin said, "Screw Pinocchio's nose. Now this is what I call wood." A sample of the humor I found funny: "You really should try to find a real spell book instead of relying on Google." There were frequent references to the modern world amidst the medieval insanity of Hell. She also frequently replied to his ongoing sexual banter with, "I hate you," at the perfect time. The sex was vanilla and mediocre. The word "pussy" was used frequently which I hate. While it was frequently said that he didn't force her, he actually kind of did in a pushing until she relented kind of way. That bothered me. Her resistance to trusting his feelings went on too long but then it would have been weird for it to be fine midway through, the admission of mutual love has to be the end of this kind of story. I think his declaration of love should have been further along in the story for her fear to not be ridiculous. But I loved the scenes where his feelings for her were obvious like when he held her in fear and horror while she burned alive  (not much of a spoiler, it was massively predictable). At the end,  I thought the wrap up with the reasons why Lucifer did what he did was lame . But there is a sequel and I think I may actually buy it and read it. (And you have to admit, that cover is hot and completely fits the character.)

Time travel done right. Finally! Thank you, Cristin Terrill! The cover flap of this book says ""All Our Yesterdays is a wrenching, brilliantly plotted story of fierce love, unthinkable sacrifice, and the infinite implications of our every choice." Having just closed the cover, I couldn't agree more. Time travel inevitably involves a complicated story that is difficult to follow. That is, unless an author sets simple rules and sticks to them. In this story, Terrill has done it expertly. One of her laws - the idea that time has a sentient quality - fixes many of the mistakes made by many storytellers. I also loved the idea that time is not linear as we understand it. What if it's really not? The way she explains paradoxes is brilliant. The bottom line is simply this: when we as readers know the rules the author has created and she doesn't break those rules, we can finally enjoy a great story that makes sense. The tale is told from the viewpoints of Em and Marina. By alternating perspectives with each chapter, it is far more easy to keep track of what is present and what is past. Even when it starts to get really complicated - and it does near the end - it is not difficult to understand. The plot is fairly straightforward. Isn't every time travel story about going back to fix things in the past? The thing that's unique about this particular story is that it's been done 14 times previously by the protagonist. Will she get it right this time? Well, that's the story. Em is a gritty main character. She's been through torture, she's been on the run from authorities, she's been part of a rebel/terrorist organization and she's both escaped and been caught. She's been betrayed. She is determined and focused, and yet never seems to have lost her true heart or humanity. She is fiercely protective of Marina. She is somewhat of a study in contradiction, and that's what I liked about her. Every time I thought she was tough and heartless, she was overcome by her love and compassion. Marina, on the other hand, is a spoiled rich girl who is shallow and a bit silly. These negative qualities can be attributed to her insecurity, though. She is at the same time loyal and loving, devoted to James. Mostly she is simply immature. But even at that, she is not unlikable. So much of today's society is full of teenagers just like her. On a list of the best of them, I'd at least put her at the top. James is a brilliant character, both in his personality and in the way he is written. Finn is charming and funny, practical and humble. The lesser characters (Richter, Nate, the Shaw family, Marina's parents and Finn's mother) are really just highlights. They serve the plot and are each distinct without drawing attention from the main points we really care about. The action doesn't stop for a minute. The suspense kept me riveted enough to read the book in one sitting. The climax of the story is terrifying, shocking and complicated at the same time. I found myself shaking my head at the end, wondering exactly what happened, having to think it all through again to make sense of the paradoxical aspect of the events. This book is smart, and I like that. It's also not pretentious. It is heart-wrenching, scary and romantic. It may even be possible, and I think that is what may be, for me, its most attractive quality. I do love a story that just might happen. This isn't just a great story for time-travel lovers. Fans of dystopia and apocalypse will also enjoy those elements that it offers. And the ultimate irony here is that virtually every novelist goes back and rewrites their book. Isn't that some version of time travel, rewriting the past? Well done, Cristin Terrill. Could you do it again please?

DNF @30% Trigger warnings for alcohol abuse, addiction, ableism, and child abuse. Review contains spoilers. I want to preface this review by saying that The Gentleman's Guide to Vice and Virtue is not a bad book at all. It is just not my book. We are not a good fit and that happens sometimes. Let me start off with the good. The writing style and language is really lovely. So much so that I have difficulties throwing the book away and be done with it. I love the first person present tense narration and reading this book is generally fast-paced and easy-going. Sentences like this stand out to me: I've always been of the mind that subtlety is a waste of time. Fortune favors the flirtatious. Friends-to-lovers stories are usually both utterly beautiful but also painful to me. Gentleman's Guide is kinda both, but mostly painful, actually. Although, this description here melted my heart: It is simply the tale of how two people can be important to each other their whole lives, and then, one morning, quite without meaning to, one of them wakes to find that importance has been magnified into a sudden and intense desire to put his tongue in the other's mouth. Alas, if it weren't for the content and characters... The protagonist, Henry, is absolutely a horror to read about. I want to strangle him. Even though I know that he suffers, too. But ohmigod, he's so entitled, selfish, and totally useless. It is unfathomable how much of a fuck up he is. He has a huge alcohol problem. Make that massive. He's addicted and isn't even aware of it. So if you are sensitive to such a content, please beware that it's really, really bad. I am not alone in my perception of Henry, as this is what his love interest, Percy, has to say about him: "Because you're a wreck! Complete shambles. I've spent years chasing you around, making certain you didn't drink yourself to death or pass out in a gutter or slit your own wrists-- "You care about what happens to me because of what that would mean for you. You are the only thing that matters to you." I [Henry] can't think of anything to say, so I settle for the second-best thing to a witty retort: a storm-out--simply a storm-out. And this just... This scene was the last straw. Oh man, he storms out. When, just a minute ago, Percy told him that he had epilepsy and, in case you don't know, for the time, this was really bad news: "My aunt thinks that this is God's way of punishing me. The family's bastard Negro boy has convulsive fits--it's appropriate. She still won't be disabused of the notion that I'm possessed by the devil, and my uncle keeps telling me that I need to stop being hysterical and overcome it." So Percy is sick, has been for a while, and since nothing is helping, he's planning to move to an asylum, a madhouse, where they do horrible things to "treat" people. When Henry finds out about this, he again makes everything about himself. Jeez. I do have some sympathies for him since he has faced and is still facing homophobic abuse (physical and mental) by his father, but I cannot. I cannot with this anymore. As you could see from the quotes above, the ablism and racism is strong in this book, as well as the just mentioned homophobia. You also need to be aware of the historical accurate gender gap and misogyny. Henry's sister is suffering under it quite a lot. The vivid alcohol abuse, I already mentioned, and there are suicidal thoughts as well. Beneath all this ugliness there isn't much room for nice stuff, although, I have to admit that there were some lovely and funny scenes, too. The friends-to-lovers arc is greatly influenced by the immaturity of Henry and, well, Percy has his own troubles. The Gentleman's Guide is just too painful and maddening for me to read. Genre: Historical, Romance, Young Adult Tags: M/M Pairing, Bisexual Character, Gay Character,Person of Colour, Friends to Lovers Content Warnings: Homophobia, Ableism, Misogyny, Alcoholism, Violence, Child Abuse, Suicidal Thoughts Rating: DNF @30% Blog: Review for Just Love Disclosure: ARC for Review

I quite liked this. Loved the first person POV, really loved the multiple angles on narcissism (how toxic it is in personal and work relationships), thought the family dynamics were interesting as well. I have a couple of quibbles, but they're minor:  I really wish that Kleypas hadn't included the no condom thing, particularly under the guise of "trust." It didn't serve the story and was wholly unnecessary. I get that a lot of romance readers are anti-condom usage (supposedly--I don't completely believe this assertion, but it's one that's made a lot), but it bothered me a lot. The other thing that bugged me is that Hardy and Haven's physical relationship moves pretty quickly, to a point that I wished it had been more slow-burning, given Haven's history. With that said, neither of those things diminished my overall enjoyment of Blue-Eyed Devil--it's a really refreshing story on a number of levels, particularly that Haven's backstory is fully developed, which really made me root for her. (Haha... Looking through the reviews and SO MANY mention Racquel--that is awesome.)

Sarah is a brave, hardworking young woman that works for the Bennett family. When the Bingley family comes to the neighborhood AND the Bennetts hire a new footman, things begin changing in Sarah's world. And it's a world I've always been curious about... Every time I read a Jane Austen novel, I think about what's going on in the world outside the houses and small villages the stories take place in. Austen gives you a very insular view of the world and I don't mean that in a bad way, but you just get tiny glimpses if you get any at all. This book filled in some of those gaps about the life for the other half of British society in Regency England. It could easily stand-alone, you don't have to be a fan of Pride and Prejudice to love the story here. I think it will appeal to fans of Downton Abbey or Upstairs, Downstairs and even to general historical fiction fans.

Ever since , Ms . Emma Watson joined the Good reads. The book readers around the world have gone into a frenzy . Not only joining , but she also started a group #oursharedshelf in GR which focuses on feminism. I must say, this group has been nothing but a learning experience for me. Each day, just a few minutes in the group makes me learn new things.She had gone to this length as she was selected as the UN Women ambassador for goodwill. And she had decided to read as many books as possible. Every month ,she selects a book which mainly deals with #feminism and reads it with the group. Well we aren't complaining . For the February Month, the group decided to read The Color Purple by Alice Walker. A member of the group was kind enough to send her copy to me all the way from Scotland . Thank you so much , Emily for the book Coming back to this book , The story tells about Celie ,who had been raped by her father in her early days . Her two children had been taken away from her . She steps into a marriage ,which should have befallen her sister ,Nettie .But her father decides to marry her off instead . The book is in the form of letters.It begins with Celie's letter to God and then when Nettie comes back into her life , the letters begins to address Nettie. After Celie gets married , Nettie runs off and lives with people who had adopted Celie's two kids. She then goes off to Africa as a missionary with Samuel and Corrine ,the ones who had adopted Celie's Kids . The readers are left to wonder whether Celie and Nettie ever sees each other again  Well , at the end ,they are reunited .It was a bit emotional for me .Not only does celie reunites with her sister ,but she finally gets her Children back too . The book was very well written . Alice brings out many amazing women personalities in the book like Shug, Sofia ,Nettie and Mary Agnes . After a long time, i am reading a book with strong women characteristics. Alice turns Celie into a strong independent woman .It is a far cry from what the readers saw celie in the beginning of the book .

Buddy read with Ofelia Grand, Dante Love, Amy Spector and Al Stewart. Woo! Or Woooooooooooooo! in fact. :D So, I finally finished it, and I really enjoyed it, but I'll tell you what. The editing really got on my nerves - not because it's bad overall, but to me, the publisher's mandatory decision to publish in US English is utterly ludicrous when a story is set in England with English characters, and much of the dialogue is in local dialect. I'm sure US readers would find it more authentic in UK English. To me, as a UK reader, the US English was a distraction. But I'm finnicky about stuff like that. This story has a literary classic feel (references to popular culture notwithstanding), with many beautiful descriptions of the Yorkshire coastline. The scene-setting is perfect. The story is character-driven, which I love. Sion's mental health is depicted sensitively but realistically. Mattie - seen from Sion's perspective - is also believable, and I felt like I got to know him quite well. Mattie's family are supremely awesome. I especially loved Caitlin. The author portrayed female characters positively, which is a big plus. Contrary to my buddies in this read, I thought it was plenty scary enough, and not because I'm a wuss. OK, partly because I'm a wuss, but I liked the way Sion treated the ghosts (mostly) with the weary inevitability of one who had faced death. I did think the multi-ghost scene was a bit over the top, though, and may well have muttered 'good grief' when they all popped up out of the sea. Never mind that it was too foggy to see the boat, but they could see all those dead men, but anyway...I'm nit-picking. The ending, whilst not a surprise, was lovely, and once I found the time to read, I did so until I fell, bleary-eyed, into my pillows and didn't dream of ghosts.

I really, really wanted to like this book. I'm a big fan of stories across time linked in a unique way. Something about this one didn't work for me though - I think I was in the wrong mood. Frankly, I found it exhausting each time the narrator and setting changed to work to develop a whole new story (if I was exhausted listening, I can only imagine how the author must have felt). Perhaps I'll come back to it in the future, but I'm calling it quits for now.

Seriously, couldn't these Mer creatures deliver a message through I dunno, a courier or something? Why do they have to do these great deal of destruction and damage to the dry lands just to make a point? I know Snyder have explained it in something like "they do this flood deluge thing so that we won't forget where we came from", but yeah, I don't buy their way of giving a message. The Mer could hallucinate their way through our hearts and let the humans find a way peacefully to that twist in the ending of this book. After a very solid part one, The Wake part two spirals into a convoluted mess of a story, reaching an inevitable action-packed climax and a twist, that though clever at best, severely lacked the confidence to deliver an astonishing end. Scott Snyder asked the readers for too much trust, but delivered an underwhelming and severely preachy finale. The biggest problem with The Wake I think is that it asks as to sympathize with these deep-sea creatures and for once just be open with what they are trying to say. But I cannot do this, not after killing millions and forced humanity to live in a post-apocalyptic world . This is the Jar Jar Binks effect: one cannot just like what is built up to be unlikeable in the first place. The other protagonists, The Arm also lacked the motivation to why they are preventing Leewards (the protagonist of part two) on her quest to seek the truth. They technically have nothing to lose if they just let go of her. I understand that The Wake tries to be philosophical and at times spiritual about humanity. The message never reached me. In fact I just wished that the story delves into a generic Mer vs. humans showdown ala-Independence Day. I would have been more entertained. That doesn't mean that The Wake is awful. I enjoyed many parts of the graphic novel, especially the first half. Sean Murphy's art perfectly complements Snyder's style of writing. This book is a visual treat from start to finish.

It took me a while to get round to this book because I'm not much of a historical fiction reader. But I was looking through old reviews on my blog and found one of The Crimson Ribbon by Katherine Clements. These two books are only set 40 years apart so I thought that it would be a good way to explore the historical fiction genre comfortably. This book is pretty much the definition of a slow burn, it took me a good amount of time to read even though it's not a huge book. It was calm for a long time then so much drama, the hits just kept on coming over and over. This book deals with a lot of things; racism, homophobia, sexism, and just that times values in Amsterdam which was fascinating as I love that city but boy does it have a past. I feel like this book was made for a re-read. There's so much detail and foreshadowing that I think would be amazing the second round when you know what is going on and how the story ends. Mostly, I did really like this book. It had "the spark." It was kind of addicting. The main character occasionally annoyed me, but for the most part she was alright, though I wanted to slap some sense into her a lot. The world was remarkably original, though it could have been better developed, but concerning the fact that vampire books tend to be the most unrelenting blocks of cliche ever, it was pretty good. Early on in the book, though, I had a few problems with Rose. She just seemed to overplay the "bad girl" element with quotes like these. I had a standing arrangement with God: I'd agree to believe in him - barely - so long as he let me sleep in on Sundays. Maybe she is a - pardon my language -badass character who can save herself most of the time, but her disrespect for anything and everything at the beginning of the book got on my nerves. It was also a bit hard to define between flashbacks and the present. A decent, shallower series I will continue with, to see where it goes, hopefully not to Cliche-land....

This afternoon I read Numbers by Rachel Ward. I've been wanting to read this book for a long time, because the synopsis made me very curious! Jem, main character of this book, is a troubled child under foster care. She doesn't like to interact with people, because the moment she looks in someones eyes she knows the exact date that person is going to die. But everything changes when she gets to know a boy named Spider. Eventhough see knows that he isn't going to live much longer, she feels a connection immediately. Together they go on a trip to London. Waiting for the London Eye, Jem sees everyone in the queue has the same number and knows immediately that something terrible is going to happen. I expected this book to be so different - after the terrorist attack at the London Eye Numbers became just about running away. Jem's gift was no longer the main subject of the story. But I still loved reading it! I had to finish the entire book in one afternoon, because I wanted to know if Jem would be able to save Spider. I thought the writing style was great and I loved the characters, not just Jem and Spider but also Val, Karen, Britney, Anne and Simon. Even the characters with a minor role in this book make a difference:) A few things keep me from giving this book five stars. I thought the whole pregnancy thing was a bit predictable. I also hated the way Spider died - not the fact that he died but the way he died! And I wish we could get to know Val a litle bit better. I did enjoy the ending though with little Adam. Can't wait to read the next book and get to know him better;) Numbers is a great adventure, easy and enjoyable to read. The characters are likeable and the story different than you'll expect. An amazing read!

A part of me wishes I hadn't read any reviews before reading this book. There are a few constant themes in the reviews - that it's very long-winded; Ethan acts like a bitchy high school girl; and he spends so much time slating the clearly less intelligent people around them. And it's all true. But I kinda think that if I hadn't known these faults before opening the book, they wouldn't have annoyed me as much as they did. It is a very long book (nearly 600 pages), and I found it hard to keep going, and did put it down several times, wondering if it was worth picking up again. The first half of the book is a blur, in the 300 pages, I couldn't tell you anything that happened. Oh, apart from a broken window, there was a broken window. The second half was better, things started to pick up. There were interesting revelations, and some action. But with the repetitive denials from Lena, and the equally repetitive half-optimism from Ethan; I kinda wanted Lena to actually turn Dark, an apocalypse looked appealing. Over the course of the book, there was no point where I felt anything for the young couple that were in love before first sight. Strangely enough, my favourite part  was when Link had his dreams come true and became a rock star, with a hot girl/Siren on his arm. I don't think I'd recommend this book to my friends, but I definitely wouldn't dissuade anyone from reading it.

4.5 stars "We are not the same beings we once were. So then, if we are no longer human, what are we?" I've never seen such a controversial novel before. I had already read a book from this author and therefore knew his... peculiar view on the world that appeared in his works, but Scythe left me really stunned. Speachless. Through an innovative mean - different scythe's daily logs -, he made me muse over very pressing and relevant topics that nowadays are often put aside: death penalty, risks of technology, corruption. And I'm not joking, as you really can't help but stop reading and stare at those debatable quotes, wondering what right and wrong truly mean. "I often wonder if the bright benefit of belief outweighed the darkness its abuse would bring." The plot's main ideas themselves may not be some of the most original ones, but it is the way they're developed and dealt with that makes the difference. So impredictable, so involving, so obscure... his writing is so powerful that the reader could almost feel what living in a world with no natural death means. Or perceive all the feelings and sensations that the sight of a scythe would bring. This depth can be associated with the characters too, of course. Though almost everyone of them was fascinating, the one who really enticed me was Rowan. Maybe because he's got the most shifting and darkest personality? He really made me want to read the sequel, just to know how much he's going to change. ...as the mysterious ending did!

"Things are not always what they seem; the first appearance deceives many. The intelligence of a few, perceives what has been carefully hidden"-Roman poet Phaedrus Aleatha Romig, you are a BEAST in the best way possible!! I LOVED this book. Consequences was my first true romantic suspense novel, and like nothing I'd ever read before. She is a brilliant writer, and I'm so thankful I grew the proverbial pair and dove into these books. For me, Truth was even better because of everything going on. All the questions you had and all the information you were left wanting from the last book, cause you to devour Truth. Do not blink while reading....pay close attention, or you will miss something critical to the story. As with the 1st book, I love that there is a quote at the beginning of each chapter, as it helps set the mood and tone of what you are about to read. The build up of this book was intensely awesome, and I just wanted it to keep going. I'm so proud of Claire and the woman she became in this book. She found her backbone, yet was grateful for her new found freedom and the possibilities that were for the taking. She opened herself to new things, yet stayed realistic in knowing throught ALL the mindfuckery, she really couldn't shake Tony...although this time, it wasn't his alpha dominance and cruelty that kept her by fear...it was the changes she saw, the hope she felt, and the knowledge that she held most of the power. Everytime I tried to guess what would happen next, I was wrong, and that is the sign of a great writer. Yes, I loved Harry so much, but really, as perfect as he would be for anyone, he couldn't match what Claire felt for Tony. I could see her struggle to figure out if what she felt for him was real or not. Poor Harry....and dammit Tony, you had me hook line and sinker as a fan by the end. I actually started to feel so bad for him because he FINALLY realized his vendetta was destroying his one shot at the happiness he never considered or thought he deserved. Tony crying = me a confused mess! AND THAT DAMN CATHERINE Sneaky little bitch....while there is obviously a cliffhanger at the end, it isn't devastating, but what will be, is waiting until possibly 2014 for the 3rd book. With the ending I'm DYING to see how this journey ends. Well done Ms. Romig!

The beginning of this book was so good. I don't really know what happened. The start of The Fold introduced a mysterious teleportation device. We didn't really know how it worked, which led to a great mystery. The pacing was perfect- I never felt like information was being withheld or bombarding me all at once. This also led to great characters. They all had their own motivations for working here and I cared about what happened to them. The protagonist was the perfect main character. He was fun to read about and he fit into the group well but not unrealistically perfectly. As we found out more about the Door, I was even more excited. The stakes were rising the revelations, while not totally original, were inoffensive. But then, about 100 pages from the end, it's like someone else started writing the book. Suddenly, this was an action novel, focused on fighting monsters. What? The Fold ceased to make any kind of scientific sense, even fictionally. Too much was happening all at once. It's like the author had a page limit. So the ending pretty much ruined the book. I'm not sure I'd recommend it unless you're the kind of person that can get past a bad conclusion.

I am torn about this book. The writing itself, on a scene-by-scene basis, is lovely and strong. The atmosphere is great. But the plotting...not so much. It's fairly obvious, I think, by halfway through the book, who the killer is. And for Kate to continue to be wide-eyed in surprise at every new revelation--that gets a bit old. Kate doesn't seem to be stupid or totally oblivious in other ways, and yet she continues to be blind to Jo's constant lies or to see that they add up to a much more disturbing picture than she will let herself see. I think the use of Rosie as a beyond-the-grave narrator just gives away too much information to the reader. It's impossible NOT to see the truth of what's been going on in the Anderson household. It got frustrating as the book went along to have the answer being revealed so obviously, even while the police concentrate on two other suspects. I kept reading until the end, hoping there was going to be a twist that truly *would* surprise me, but there wasn't. And Kate's continued blindness and defense of Jo  is beyond irritating. "I still wonder how I didn't see." Yes, so do I. And describing Jo as a woman "whose crimes were her obsessive love for husband and her vulnerability. But more people are guilty." Yes, but the ultimate crime was murder, not love NOR vulnerability.

All the YA adult books you read today seem to all just have pretty or gorgeous main characters but who Jane is, is what the author focuses on and what you remain enraptured by. The mystery was pretty easy to figure out, at least for me, but it was a great read!

Review posted at Step Into Fiction I was expecting something vastly different from the Lunar Chronicles but I'm not sure I was expecting it to be this far from her vastly popular (and in my opinion, amazing) series. This review will be vague with some hidden spoilers. Only view the spoilers if you've read the book or really don't care about what you know. We'll start with the main character, Lady Catherine Pinkerton. I want to say I like her; I really do but there were times when I just wanted to throw her out the window. She grew on me and then I regretted those thoughts but then later in the book, I didn't regret them anymore. She is the soon-to-be betrothed to the King of Hearts. It's not what she wishes but it is all her parents, particularly, her mother, dream of happening. Cath wants to be a baker; she loves baking desserts more than anything in Hearts. It's her dream, it's her passion but what Queen would ever be allowed to be a . baker? My favorite part of this book was probably the new court Joker, Jest. He's witty, charming, entertaining, loyal, and just an overall spectacular character. I have no doubts you'll get attached. It's not like Catherine's other suitor, the King, is appealing in any sense. Honestly, he reminded me a lot of my favorite YA boy, ever. For those who don't know, I'm talking about Puck from the Iron Fey series. Which may be why I'm so taken with Jest but he's definitely found a place in my heart. I also went in to this book knowing I'm not big on the whole Alice in Wonderland so I didn't even know if I'd like this but I love retellings and I wanted to give this a chance. Don't get me wrong, this isn't a retelling of Alice's story or anything but it's absolutely set in that world so I'm calling it a retelling. I don't know what else I can say without even hinting at anything that would ruin this book for you so I'm stopping here. To save you and save me (from having to relive it all). I wish I hadn't grown to like Jest as much as I did because I regret it. I regret how much I begged for a happily ever after but what did I expect with a title of Heartless. And who this character is based off or is or whatever. But dammit, I was pissed when it came to be anyway. This was when I wanted throw that little POS Cath through a window; the second she stepped through that damn door even if she knew of the consequences. Did she NOT think Jest wouldn't follow her? Did she not stop for one BLOODY SECOND AND THINK?! No. But you know what? She has to live with that regret; that god awful poor decision for the rest of her life. It makes me mad that she's blaming Mary Ann for this happening when she has no one to blame but herself. UGH UGH UGH. The only good thing to come from this is that she still has Raven. Not sure how much good that is. But not only did she ruin her life and Jest's but she destroyed Hatta, too. She destroyed herself, as well. She destroyed it all. It was right there, in her grasp and she let it all go. Why didn't I have my guard up going in to this book? WHY?! ***EDIT***I should have realized how different this book was going to be before I began it but I was just so overwhelmed and excited to have another story from Marissa, that I just didn't care. Initially after finishing, I didn't think I liked it, which is when this review was written but it's been months since I've read it and while I'm not completely sold it was a book for me, it certainly wasn't a bad book. You just should realize how different it is from the Lunar Chronicles; hell, it's a lot different from a lot of what you read in YA, I'm sure. The writing is beautiful, as expected; the characters are fantastic and intriguing and the world building is on point.

The second book in the Throne of Glass series, Crown of Midnight starts a few months after the first book ends. Caelaena is established as the King's Champion, her relationship with Dorian is over and she and Chaol are somehow toeing that line - where they can still be friends and not more. Nehemia is Caelaena's greatest friend, and for now, Adarlan's assassin is happy. That never ends well. It did not end well the last time it happened, not with Sam. It does not end well now. The books is a slow unraveling of the threads around Caelaena - from her work for the King, the demands she has to meet for Elena, her friendship with Nehemia and her relationship with Chaol. She is figuring out what Elena really wants from her, exactly what is the evil that she has to find. And while she does this, Nehemia has been helping her. But Caelaena has been keeping secrets, until it gets a bit too much and she finally confesses them to her friend. That she has not been killing the men the King wants her to murder but rather helping them escape and faking their deaths. It all goes downhill when the King asks her to kill a man, a courtesan in Rifthold, from her past who is allegedly a part of the rebel movement. From there, the unraveling threads start snapping. And when Caelaena finally snaps, it is a thing of such savage beauty, that I do not think Chaol or Dorian will ever forget. Nehemia's death is the point upon which everything changes, and it is obvious that it was meant to be that. Dorian having magic is just icing on the cake. I think what I really like about this series is that there is no drama or angst here that is not required. Beyond a point there are no lies and no secrets because at the end, the protagonists are friends, and no matter who their parents are, they do trust each other. Things may be messed up right now, but through this hell, the bonds between Dorian, Caelaena and Chaol have only become stronger. The fact that they have chosen to confide in each other, especially the assassin, gives me hope that the two idiot friends will also sort themselves out. Definitely a series that I think will become one of my favorites.

This review can also be found on A Thousand Lives Lived, check it out for more reviews! The Hundred Oaks series is my favourite contemporary-romance series. I don't care how many books Kenneally chooses to add into the series, only as long as they keep pleasing and intriguing me with those sweet gorgeous feels just like this one did. Breathe, Annie, Breathe can easily be put as the best book in the series. I had to remind myself to keep on breathing as Jeremiah and Annie stole my heart. "A quarter mile more. One foot after the other. Breathe, Annie, breathe." Wow. Where do I begin? It's been a week since I last set my eyes onto Kenneally's powerful words and her story, and I still feel like I'm in Annie's reality. This was Miranda's best story with such a gluing background story that you'd never expect to happen. Sure, each of the books in this series has some unexpected story in the back that will probably get you shocked for a moment, but the reason why Annie runs is unexplainable to the human mind. You'll have to read this for yourself to see why I'm so obsessed. As I mentioned, Annie is training to run for a marathon with a pro-coach and everything. She's running to honour her boyfriend's memory in a way that's so beautiful, as he enjoyed running. But as she trains, she begins to put herself down, but she never stops doing it. Remembering the reason why and the goal, she keeps telling herself to breathe and go on, and then she falls in love again with someone who just may bring her back into the real world and never let her go. I have had this book since about the September of 2014, and I really wanted to read it. I passed it every time I was searching for a new book to read, and I kept reminding myself that I'll get to it soon. Obviously, that soon was pretty far away, especially for a Miranda Kenneally read. Thank goodness I went for it now, as I am trying to complete all of the books in series that I've begun. This could've been bad--real bad. You see, I'm used to a lot of those cheesy fluffy contemporaries with a lot of unrealism in them. I could spend hours naming them all, but I'd rather not since contemporary is probably my favourite genre. I feel like books in this genre could either go one way or the other. The characters in this one seemed more mature and relatable than the others of the author, and that surely shone a light onto this all, just like a little topping or sprinkle of something onto your ice cream sundae. Like really, it was the magical touch and new-thing to this series. It was what we needed to get this to a whole other level. Dedication was a huge thing in this book, as well as goals... And romance, of course. As I read how much this book meant to Kenneally and dealt with some of her occasions and situations in the past, her characters here probably resembled a lot of the dream people we'd like to become or act like one day. Annie was my favourite protagonist out of all of her books, and that's a lot to say since Jordan used to be my #1. "As a kid, I had the worst mile time ever. Our gym teacher made us run the mile a few times a year for something called the Presidential Fitness Test. I'd huff and puff and wonder why the hell President Bush cared how fast I could run laps around the playground. I always came in dead last." One of the best and funniest things about her was that she wasn't afraid to put herself down. I always feel that there's a level to where you're allowed to put yourself down to make you feel stronger and more easily prone to win. Annie did that. Unlike Jordan, she didn't care to win, she cared to make others feel happy and to win for them. That's another reason why Jeremiah and her were perfect for each other. *dreams into another world* No seriously, they were the best couple. Okay, everything about this book was the best compared to the others, hah. But Jeremiah was perfect--him and Annie were like Bonnie and Clyde. It's like love at first sight, but it wasn't instalove, you know what I mean? He had his troubles and insecurities and weird specks, but he did whatever it takes to make Annie happy and so he can be with her. That's my dream guy. Together, they could seriously become the next Presidential couple with the kind of power that they had together. Ugh, how is it so possible for something that to be so precious and beautiful? *dreams* As for the plot, this was a total fast-paced book that you could easily read in one sitting. You know, I did. I loved seeing Jeremiah and her relationship bloom into something new and different, and I loved seeing Annie become stronger with her running and her goal for her ex. I just don't know how much more awesome this could've gotten. I'll give this 5 thousand stars. Ugh--I WANT MORE. I actually feel like this after every 5-star book I read, but with this one, it's surely not enough. Now I have to wait another half-year for Jessie's Girl, which I'm sure will be just as awesome. *squeals* Miranda Kenneally is truly the master of literature--romance perfectionist.

There's something to be said about a character who can consistently correct and/or insult people in only the most socially polite of ways. There's even more to be said when this character is the heroine of our story. This is the case in Soulless, where our heroine is a sassy, outspoken female, whose strong temper is matched only by her great wit. Alexia Tarabotti could talk you into a corner before you had taken two steps into a room, and it wouldn't even rattle her teacup once, to do so. And that is precisely why she is a fantastic heroine. Set in Victorian London, Soulless begins with a sort of Jane Austen-style of witty dialogue and social pressures. Add in machines, werewolves, vampires, other supernatural beings, and a decidedly more outspoken main character, and you have one of the most entertaining stories I have read this year. Add to all that, the ruggedly handsome and hot-tempered, Scottish alpha werewolf love interest, and this story is bound straight for my favorites shelf. If there is one thing I didn't like about this story, it's that some of the events weren't very detailed. We only see things from Alexia's POV, so whatever she doesn't know, we don't know either. There were some parts to the story that I would have liked to have a better understanding of (the octopuses, vampire abilities, and just how differently the Queen's agenda and BUR's are). Due to Alexia's limited involvement/interaction, these things weren't explained. BUT...that's really not super important, especially compared to the rest of this fabulous story, and the fact that I don't think there was a character that I didn't like. Gail Carriger did an amazing job meshing so many genres into one story. I really couldn't narrow it down to just one, or even two, because they are all so well put together. It all just feels right. In these pages lies romance, danger, humor, political intrigue, suspense, and a good helping of Victorian society to boot. THIS is how you do a love story. THIS is how you do a truly strong female heroine. THIS is how you do Victorian-steam-punk-paranormal-romance. Now I need the second book, STAT! Read this if: ...you like werewolves, the paranormal, and stand-out heroines! Content Warning *This section may contain some spoilers about content! Violence (no more than is expected in a paranormal novel), nudity (a character is nude for an entire chapter, after having been locked up--werewolves are naked after transforming), steamy kissing scenes, and a married couple's sex scene that is brief, and not very detailed. Reread in September 2016. New rating: 4 stars (original rating 2.5 stars) Clearly I was pissed off when I wrote this original review, because - even though I still have a lot of issues - there is NO WAY that this is a 2.5 star book. I must have been so angry with the ending when I first finished this book that I blocked all of its many good features from my mind. That wasn't fair and I realise that now after rereading it. Honestly? The first 600 pages of City of Heavenly Fire are worth 5 stars in my mind. The improvement from City of Bones to here in terms of writing, characterisation, and drama is staggering. There are so many stand out scenes which made me cry all over again and legitimately shocked me because I'd forgotten them in my blaze of anger from the first time I read this. This had the potential to be the strongest of all the Shadowhunters books, yet, sadly, I think that the ending really lets it down. I don't think I've ever hated the ending to a book more than I hate this one and that really frustrates me because, until the last 100 pages or so, I absolutely adored this. I find the ending silly, unrealistic, all too convenient, and all too happy. Jonathan turning good for the last moments of his life makes absolutely no sense to me, because the boy we see in that final scene never existed and never could exist, so how exactly does heavenly fire give him the chance to speak to Clary and Jocelyn? Then the forgiveness afforded to him after that one moment of goodness is ludicrous. And don't get me STARTED on the whole twist with Simon. Or the sickly-sweetness of the epilogue. Ughhhhhhh . Honestly, this ending (especially the epilogue) represents everything I hate in a book. After reading the last 100 pages again, I can totally see why I was raging when I read it for the first time. The final pages of this book make me so irrationally angry and I don't think that that will ever change no matter how many times I reread it. I didn't intend to write a whole other review for City of Heavenly Fire after reading it a second time, but this is possibly the most conflicting book that I've ever read in my life and I felt that needed addressing. Even now, I'm hesitating before pressing the 4 star button because, no matter how much I loved the vast majority of this book, I'm still seething about how badly the ending wraps things up in my opinion. I know that a lot of people disagree with me about the ending. I know that - even by giving this book 4 stars - I'm still in a minority, because most people adore this book from beginning to end. I know that The Mortal Instruments has waaaaaaaay bigger issues than a prettily packaged ending, but I still believe that this series deserves more than this. After reading this for a second time, I'm less angry and less critical than I was, but I'm still not as happy as 4 stars might suggest that I am. My Original Review (7th June 2014) - 2.5 stars. I'm trying not to spoil things, but I may drop some hints about what happens in here because I'm annoyed and need to make some points. Sorry. Well this is awkward. Every other review I've seen of this book has been a 5 star one with some kind of opening comment about how this series has left an imprint on the reviewer's soul or something. While I won't deny that this is a special series to me, I don't feel the same way. In my personal opinion, this series started to fizzle out after City of Glass. But I still had such hope for this last book. I saw all the great reviews and the plot sounded good and I was praying for an amazing book that would cure my ever increasing disenchantment with this series. As you may gather, I didn't receive that and I am so angry and upset right now. In all honesty, if you took out the epilogue this would become an easily 4 because while I found this way too long and I had some issues with the plots throughout, the epilogue ruined it for me just like Clockwork Princess's epilogue did. I am very particular about how a book series ends. I like bittersweet endings with a good mix of sadness and happiness. I like romantic conclusions that are sweet but not soppy. And most of all, I like realism. This? This was a sugary-sweet gift-wrapped soppy ending that made me want to scream. For a book with a tagline 'who will survive? ', the ending was awfully cheery and I did not like that. I know it may seem like I complain every time a book has a happy ending, but that isn't true. I like endings to be JUSTIFIED. This book was hailed as something apocalyptic which would feature lots of death and destruction. Instead it was a romance novel through and through with undertones of a disaster that never came. The closest it came to apocalyptic was in the chapters with Julian and Emma, which were by far the highlight of the book for me. Everything just felt so flat and disappointing to me. I was expecting a bang and I got a whimper. Oh, but that's ok because at least there was a sugary happy epilogue. No. If you're going to big a book up as a battle to the death, do that. Don't solve that issue in a couple of chapters and fill the rest of it with overly-romantic crap. Also what I really disliked about this book is that there was one absolutely excellent, stand-out plotline towards the end of the book. That was the only point in the entire book when I cried and I thought it was extremely clever and it had the bittersweet edge that I wanted. Since the bloody battle I was expecting never happened, I thought this plotline would be the substitute and I was happy with that. Then in the epilogue, this plotline was completely discarded and what had happened was reversed. What the hell was the point of that? Why introduce something so huge and so poignant only to completely change it around a chapter later? That was absolutely ridiculous and it just adds to my point about the too perfect ending. People die in wars. That is a fact. According to Cassandra Clare though, everyone survives every war and all issues can be solved with some magic and a wedding. That doesn't even just apply to City of Heavenly Fire. How many main characters died in City of Glass? Did that not end with a party and fireworks and with everyone being happy? The same goes for Clockwork Princess. Other the course of the two Shadowhunter Chronicles series, there have been three major battles and yet the death and destruction in terms of major characters has been at an absolute minimum. I'm not disregarding what happened to minor characters such as the Blackthorns because that was one of my favourite things about this book, but I'd like to have seen main characters affected too. But no, I guess romance is more important than realism. Look, this wasn't a bad book. There was humour and there were good plotlines too. I'm just writing a bad review because I am utterly pissed off with the ending. This had the potential to be a great book and I wanted that because I used to love this series and now I don't and I wanted to fall in love again. As it was, all this book did was let my state of disenchantment grow. If you like happy endings and romance and if The Mortal Instruments has 'shaped your soul' or 'changed your life' then I'm sure you'll love it and give this a 5 star review like everyone else. I'm sorry that I can't agree with that. I wanted to like this, but it was too long and there was so much overly romantic and overly perfect crap that I can't. I like my YA series to be gritty and thrilling and bittersweet. I don't care about how many cells in Clary's body love Jace. So because of all that, this is just an ok book to me. I'm sure I'll look back in the future and give it more credit than I am doing now because now I'm angry and that's influencing my opinion. But for now, I'll conclude that this was an absolute disappointment for me. Sorry.

Review originally posted at http://fictionvixen.com/review-ashwin... So what happens after the walls of Eden come down and the Sectors are finally free to live, laugh and love? Good stuff. Lots and lots of good stuff. If you are a Sector Four fan and have followed the Beyond series from Jasper and Noelle straight through to Ryder and Nessa then you've previously met the hero of the first book of the Gideon's Riders series, Ashwin. If you are a Kit Rocha virgin and have decided to pick this book up because you've heard you can read it as a stand-a-lone, (which I totally think you can) then you are in for a treat. Ashwin Malhotra is a Makhai soldier, genetically engineered to be stronger, faster, and smarter. He has been conditioned since a young boy to forgo feeling and emotions. Ashwin looks at everything strategically and through the eyes of a warrior. The only exception to this is Dr. Kora Bellamy. He's never been able to keep her off his mind, and has even broke conditioning by fixating on her and her safety. There is nothing Ashwin won't do to keep Kora safe. Nothing. Kora was once Ashwin's doctor in the Makhai project. Despite having grown up in Eden and groomed to be a desensitized doctor by her adoptive father, she repeatedly broke the rules in order to provide better care for her patients. She has never believed the line that Ashwin and his fellow Makhai soldiers were unable to feel emotion. Her fascination for him grows over the years and seems to come to a head when he kidnaps her on behalf of fellow soldier Lorenzo Cruz in order to save Cruz's lover Ace in Beyond Jealousy. Things kind of heated up after that, Ashwin became even more obsessed with Kora. She gets her taste of freedom after saving Ace's life and she decides to use her skills outside of the walls of Eden. Ashwin becomes determined to save Kora from everything around her, including himself. He tries to separate himself from her and uses Cruz's debt to keep her safely away from him. When the walls come down, in the midst of the chaos of the bullets flying and people fighting, Ashwin becomes enraged when he sees Kora in danger and basically loses his shit. Which scares Kora half to death and in turn sends Ashwin off, ready to go through the painful act of reprogramming his feelings for Kora out of him. Now it's several months later, and Kora has settled into Sector One. Gideon Rios has adopted Kora into the royal family and she feels accepted for the first time in her life. The only thing missing is the soldier who she didn't realize she loved until he never came back from the war. Then suddenly he shows up one day, sent in to infiltrate the Riders and the Rios family. I'm pretty by now everyone knows how much I adored the Beyond series. I remember reading the last book in the series and then immediately tweeting to the authors about how much I adored Ashwin and how badly I wanted his story to be told. I think the reply back was something like... "you'll be happy with the first book in the new series then." And yeah, I was pretty excited. I think the visual of the Riders all ready to ride into Eden and fight to the death in Beyond Surrender kind of set off the spin-off series perfectly. In this first book all the Riders are finally introduced and readers are able to really get a good handle on Gideon and how he holds power in Sector One through faith and goodness and loyalty. He isn't at all like Dallas, but he is just as wonderful of a leader. Now that the war is over, everything is different. Including Ashwin and Kora. They are finally able to have a chance together. That is if Ashwin will let himself believe his feeling for her. If he can get past his fear of hurting her and just lets her gentle, soothing nature heal him. There is just something about such a cold and unfeeling hero finally opening himself up to that ONE PERSON who he values above all others that gets me every time. There are times that he fucks up and does the wrong thing, thinking he is protecting her, but he's trying to figure it all out. There is this sense that both Kora and Ashwin are not only finding acceptance with each other, but finding a sort of chosen family as well. Which to be honest, is one of the things I've always loved the most about the Beyond series, so I'm glad to see that theme continued on in the new series. So far I'm so intrigued by the Riders and who these authors seem to be setting them up with. I'm also fascinated by the religion of the Sector and am looking forward to learning more about it. For me this first book in the new series was just as consuming and addicting as its predecessors. I'm so ready for what comes next. Deacon? Deacon and Ana? Yes, please. Gimme. Final Grade- B+ Favorite Quote: "Will you teach me how to do this right?" His expression was so serious. So earnest. "How to love you?" A person could live a thousand years and never be worthy of those simple whispered questions. "I can't," she admitted. "I've never been in love before. We just have to learn together."
