3.75 stars. This is a tough book for me to rate. I wasn't sure what to expect when I started it, and it soon went into very squicky territory. (If you are easily triggered, DO NOT read this book.) The writing is good overall, and I liked the heroine. The "hero"? Nope. The book started out sexy, abruptly became not at all sexy to me, and left me cold for the rest of it. I might try other books by this author, but only if I know the story line is not similar to this one. This kind of book just isn't for me. I had a hard time with Luka and the book because of the rape at the start of the story. I just couldn't find him sexy after that, no matter what happened. Right up to that part, yes. After, no. I never felt that he truly understood what he'd done to her or that he'd truly apologized and atoned for it. If I hadn't liked and empathized with Addison, I would have stopped reading at the point of the rape. I continued to read because I wanted to know how she got out of the situation--or if she did. I really wasn't sure where the story was going for a while. I actually did not expect it to be a "romance" for the longest time, and when it was clear that was where it was going, I kept reading to see how that was going to work, because it didn't seem possible to me. Luka got a bit more palatable to me near the end after he'd fallen in love with her, but I still didn't see them having a true HEA. Were they equals at the end? Maybe. Was she suffering from Stockholm Syndrome? Maybe. I'm glad the author recognized that Addison needed time on her own and Luka had to accept it to put them on somewhat even ground. Still... I didn't quite buy that it was enough time, especially when the deaths of her family members leave her an emotional wreck clinging to the one person she still has left.

Kit Colbana considers herself broken. What she endured at the end of Night Blade would break almost anyone. But despite what she believes, her spirit is not beyond repair. That's what this entire book is about: her journey as she tries to find herself again and rebuild the inner core of strength she fears is gone for good. The entire first half of the book is focused almost exclusively on Kit's heartache and struggle. She is hiding out with TJ and Goliath in Wolf Haven. She is terrified of the outside world; she feels incapable of returning to her old life. The scars from Jude's attacks still mark her skin and her spirit. But she starts claiming herself back one small step at a time. And before you know it, she has accepted a small case, easing her out of her hideaway, back into her office -and Damon's lair. The small case piggybacks into a bigger one, which ends up dominating the second half of the book. The action was fairly good, but what readers are ultimately going to latch onto is how Kit is healing and reconnecting with the people in her life. Of course, Damon is the key figure here, and their dynamic is wonderfully complicated. No one can deny the love they feel for one another, but so much has happened. As upset as I was with Damon in the last book, I found myself forgiving him here. While his suffering is nothing compared to Kit's, his heartbreak and remorse are palpable. I wanted so much for them to find their way through this. But these books don't make things easy for the characters. It's a difficult path, but one I couldn't look away from. I also found myself really drawn to the dynamic that has evolved between Kit and Damon's pack. It was... unexpected. And it's impossible not to love young Doyle. There are major developments with him that are sure to have repercussions in future books. Overall, I thought the book was very well done. It didn't emotionally overwhelm me like the last book. But that's because it was about healing instead of destruction. I appreciate that Kit's recovery is not a quick fix, but rather, an evolution... one I look forward to continuing in the next book. Rating: B *ARC provided by author for review

I've seen so many reviews where people have said, "Oh, Throne of Glass is the worst book of the series, the others are so much better." I absolutely adored Throne Of Glass, so I thought I wouldn't really be as blown away by Crown of Midnight as some people were, but y'all...I was dead wrong. I cannot get over how much I love Celaena. I loved her in Throne of Glass, but we get to see so much more of who she truly is in Crown of Midnight and it's freaking insane. This girl is so badass that I can't handle it. One of my biggest complaints (well, only complaint really) about Throne of Glass was that we don't really get to see Celaena be the relentless and unbeatable assassin she's rumored to be. In this book, we finally get to see just how ruthless Celaena really is, and it's amazing. I still feel the same towards Dorian and Chaol as I did during Throne of Glass. They're both good men and I enjoy having them around in the story, I just don't feel particularly strong towards either of them. I'm too focused on Celaena who, let's be real, is way more interesting than both of them anyways. I did have a huge, huge problem with Crown of Midnight though, and I'm still upset about it. I cannot believe what happened with Nehemia. I am legitimately pissed. Maas did literally the most straightforward and annoying plot point of letting the only absolutely not-white character die for the main white characters story line to be pushed forward. Like, it explicitly says that. It's ridiculous. I would've been pissed about Nehemia dying either way, but for it to be so blatantly put out there like that just made me more mad. Nehemia could've done so much more and been so much more than just a minor plot point and I'm so upset about it. I docked a star for that reason. Besides all the weapons and blood Celaena deals with, there is so much more drama going on in the glass castle that it's no wonder she wants to avoid it all. Between the rumors of uprisings against the king, the mysterious wyrdmarks, murderous witches, and the ancient tunnels below the castle inhabited by creatures no one wants to face, Celaena's hands are full. It wasn't hard to keep up with at all however, and it all starts to tie together so dramatically wonderfully by the end. But there's still so much I have to learn! I'm eager to follow Celaena wherever she goes.
This is not a bad book, it's just that I'm not a fan of historic romance/fairy tales re-telling... So, that's why I only gave it 2 stars; but the writing was good, the pace was good.

Damn. I had an ENTIRE, long review written out, and was totally happy with it, and then a glitch in the site happened. Bummer. Well, to sum it up, it felt forced. I sensed, after reading Insurgent, that a third book was pushing it. I was happy with where Insurgent left off, and I could easily fill in the blanks with my own conclusions. That being said, there was a glimmer of something great in Allegiant. The explanation given early on in the book about why the cities and factions were in existence strengthened the premise laid out for us in the first and second books. Granted, it is still a rather unbelievable one, but hey, I don't read YA dystopian fiction for its plausibility. The back story that the Bureau gave reinforced Divergent, and I think actually made me appreciate it more. Kudos. Many people were distraught over the ending. I purposely avoided reading reviews like they were the plague, since I didn't want something to be spoiled, but I could tell by everyone's reaction that something big was going to happen. And something big did, in fact, occur. The buildup to it, however, was sloppy and it all happened so quickly that I didn't quite realize what was happening until the next chapter started. I'm okay with the ending though. Honestly. Just as in Mockingjay of The Hunger Games trilogy, not everything ends up finishing up in a pretty package. To me it makes it that much better. But, that being said, I found the journey there to be boring. The big stuff was revealed early on, and the rest in the middle was filler, giving us all-too-familiar scenes of sneaking around, lover's quarrels, and makeout sessions. Throw in the quite unbelievable plotting and execution of plans, and you've got a story that shouldn't have really happened. Or I should say, a book that was unnecessary. Great reveal early on, terribly sagging and repetitive middle, and a satisfactory and unpredictable ending. At least Tris and Four FINALLY got down and dirty and could say 'I love you' to one another. Meh.

"You don't wanna go out of this world with regrets. If there's some- thing you want to do, you do it. You take this life by the balls and you tell it that you existed." I am the kind of person that seeks painful, existential, angst ridden books. Usually I just read them to a) feel more shitty about myself and cry because, HELLO, I'm sixteen I'm supposed to, like, hate life right now. Or b) make fun of the stupidity that is real-life YA contemporary. (Obviously this doesn't apply to every YA Contemp-Romance but seriously, they're all pretty much the same concept of angst, death, pretentious poetic metaphors and unhealthy insta-love relationships.) Still, let me tell you, this book, this book fucked me up real bad. There are four POVs, four main characters. Peter being the popular, successful yet troubled jock who just doesn't know if his path in life is the one he wants to take. Eliza the struggling 'indie' photographer whose dad is dying of cancer while her mom is off with the man she had an affair with. Anita, also known as my FAVOURITE PERSON EVER, a pressured daughter who has a passion for music her father wishes to obliterate. And Andy, the slack of the four, probably the most confused and unsure of what his future really holds. So from a first impression, I was into it. There was a lot of diversity within the persona's of each character. Enough to differentiate them but also enough to understand how they were all alike. That being the, you know, angst and "Who Am I?" existential shit most of the characters face. I hadn't really remembered much of the synopsis when I first began reading this book, so when the whole shooting star metaphor appeared I was prepared for another cliched Life-Is-Worth-It angst-y plot. But THEN this star actually turned about to be a meteor that had a high chance of, well, colliding with earth. I didn't really expect a sci-fi-ish theme from this book. But the entire world ending concept actually contributed really well with the general idea the author was trying to portray through this novel. I liked the rawness of it because it just felt real. Peter was just a boy who had no idea what the fuck he wanted to do with his life, not once throughout the novel did he seem overly pretentious to me or cliched. It felt as if despite the idea of there being a stereotype each character fit under, Wallach took these typical high school labels and made them into something that wasn't as synthesized. There was no beauty in their sadness or confusion, it just was. The only real problem I had with this book was the initial character development. As a whole, all four characters had their own ways of widening their perspectives ect. But it felt as if the author had built this background story for each of them, (i.e. Peter's brother dying, his girlfriend Stacy, Cartier), meant to contribute to the character's growth yet all it did for me was flatten the characters a tad bit. Why didn't Eliza's dad care enough to figure where his daughter was? I mean I understood Anita's case, considering she'd run away from home and there wasn't much her parents could do when the world was supposedly ending. But even with cancer, you'd think Eliza's dad would have been a little more present in the novel considering how important of an attribute he'd initially seemed as. Yet despite the fact it made the book feel less real, I still enjoyed it tremendously. I liked the concept and the characters and how they were executed throughout the novel. It delivered what Jasmine Warga's My Hear and Other Black Holes didn't quite deliver.

Well, what can I say about Into The Wild. Let's start with this: This book changed my life. A couple years ago, my mom was sitting on the couch watching some movie about this guy who gave up everything he had to go to Alaska. I sat down to watch the movie with her and I was captivated. So I began to look up Christopher McCandless. I saw what a courageous young man he was. So I finally read the book, and it's changed how I see things. I've heard him called a stupid fool for doing what he did, but what I see is a man who gave up the typical life to find some kind of happiness that people rarely find. He gave up his family's wealth and hitched across the country, meeting people who changed his life by letting him experience theirs. Christopher Johnson McCandless changed my life. I just hope that one day, I'll find something that makes me feel as alive as he felt in those two years of being Alexander Supertramp.

This series is always such a breath of fresh air. If you want a quick, unique fantasy read that somehow manages to combine dragons, political intrigue, explorations/adventures, and a badass woman living her life and trying to combat the sexism in a historical society, this is the series for you. The writing is very smooth and natural and really does feel like you're reading a real person's memoir, and it manages to throw in little details about the world that further expand it while avoiding a huge information dump all at once. In addition, I think Isabella is all of us when it comes to loving and wanting to know more about dragons. This book in particular felt very well put together and flowed through the scenes very nicely. I really enjoyed learning more about Akhia and the desert as the descriptions were quite rich. The best part, however, was  Isabella and Suhail FINALLY getting together. Their romance is so sweet, and I love how it developed naturally over the last two books, starting from friendship and developing into love (which everyone else saw before they did). It made it felt very authentic and natural, and was such a joy to read considering every book seems to have instant-love nowadays. It also never overrides the story or Isabella's research - it's just such a nice addition to the story. In addition, I really loved the ending - getting to see them both discover something relevant to their areas of interest together was awesome. It was a little convenient how they found such an amazing discovery, but this story is so good that I'm willing to overlook that just because of how good everything else is, and I think it's going to be a good set up for some more dragon discoveries in the next book. Overall, this is just such a solid series, and I'm so sad I'm collecting these in softcover so I still have to wait until they publish the next book in softcover next year!

I had problems with it, but no book is perfect. I overlooked the flaws and found myself stupid in love with this book, and I'm pretty damn proud.
The Last of August was hugely confusing. I need another read after some time away to figure it out. Not sure how I feel about it at all.

HOLY WOWly!!!! This book set me on FIRE! Yet another awesome 5 star read from RS Grey, an author I have come to really love over the last few months. Without a doubt her books will keep you guessing, keep your heart racing, and although it's not a massive tear jerker, it is a super fun, lighthearted read which will certainly keep your heart in your mouth at times, with wonderful characters and a solid plot. This is a complete standalone in the Summer Games series and does not crossover with the other characters in the other books. Although if you have read the previous book, let me tell you, this is TOTALLY different. The characters are very very different and this book will take you on a new journey in the Olympic world! I adored Brie and all of the girls competing for the team USA gymnastics squad (not June so much! ); they had such great camaraderie and friendship - some of the exchanges had me cracked up; especially Lexi and Rosie!!! As soon as the announcement was made that the team had a new coach, you just knew there would be trouble but I had no idea how it would pan out. I could have guessed....but I would have been SO SO WRONG!! I never would have guessed quite how the relationship between Brie and Erik was going to work; or not going to work!! But it was amazing.... I didn't really like Erik to start, although could see his reasonings and understood his thoughts on certain situations! Brie and Erik have so much going against them. They both have things going on in their personal lives which has an impact on their professional life and their reasonings behind doing what they do. Plus there's that little issue of the fact Erik is Brie's coach....oh and they don't even like each other! "Deep down, I knew he was bad for me. Every time I thought of him, my heart rate kicked up a notch and my stomach clenched tight. He was a sweet poison and I was so addicted, and I didn't care that our encounters left me choking for air." The heat and intensity in this story was OFF THE CHARTS! It was the perfect mix of hotness and delicious scenes, without taking anything away from the story line! And speaking of heat.... Hot Yoga!!! I'll say no more....! "...she wanted to be desired. Coveted. Craved. Had anyone ever touched her the way she wanted to be touched? Had anyone ever ripped that bun out and tugged her long hair, tilting her head back to expose the creamy skin of her neck? I wanted to devour her...." The build up in this book was absolutely perfect!! I could not wait for something to happen..... You knew it was coming.... And boy, I wasn't disappointed! I'm not saying too much more, but trust me, this book is a good one!! You won't want to miss it - go in blind, enjoy it, devour it and don't put it down until the very last page; I didn't! "The air between us was charged - electric" 5 ELECTRIC Olympic Gold Medal Stars [?][?][?][?][?]

In 1998, the earth is dying in an unspectacular way. I kept picturing a big, molding orange. Desperate, some 1998 scientists figure out a way to beam messages back to some stock characters that were alive in 1963. The three main scientists in 1998 can be hard to differentiate by their dialog or behavior except one is an out-of-control sex maniac who, without furthering the plot at all, has sex with EVERY female character except his wife. I think the reader is supposed to dislike him but this compulsion of his was the only entertaining thing in the entire book. There isn't much that is futuristic about 1998 except, comically, the characters drive by a bunch of apes doing road work. Why the overpopulated and under-employed society of the future needed to put orange vests and overalls on apes and change their DNA so they could experience the wonders of wage slavery was not explained. The main character in 1963 is a painful stereotype of a Jewish New Yorker who was dating an annoyingly stereotyped Sun-kissed California surfer-girl. The clash of the stereotypes was examined and his stereotypical mother visits and judges his girlfriend for not reading Philip Roth and also for being a whore. The whore's ex-boyfriend shows up, gets bombed on cheap wine and starts having Vietnam flashbacks but unfortunately does not kill any of the other characters and make a necklace of their ears. The central time mechanism that DOES drive the plot was broken. It seems that if the messages sent back cause a big enough change to history, the timeline splits and the people end up in a totally different universe and don't affect the universe that sent the messages back. I will repeat that they were living in 1963. There were a couple of cool timey-wimey moments but if it wasn't for the fact that I have to read every time travel book, I would never have stuck with this one. The author's attempts at being "literary" were very alarming to me: familiarity with sex and the workings of those mysterious gummy organs Between pale thighs the unending oval yawned It's like he has a gift for finding words that should never, ever be in the same sentence.

middle school sara LOVED this book and it holds up mostly!! fast-paced with a sassy protag who is quick on the uptake despite a certain cruel n dishonest vampire love interest. kerry basically spends the whole book psychoanalyzing vampires, especially the moody asshole one she has a lil crush on. as an adult I can see how fucked up her attraction is to him, how she uses all this emotional labor to try to get him to open up and he returns the favor by lying and being a huge dickhead. that's our culture and I'm glad VVV chose to end it the way she did. it's good to show characters drawing healthy boundaries even when they are consumed by problematic attachments maybe I should read twilight and compare?

I struggled with the rating for this book, having trouble deciding between 2 or 3 stars. I settled on 3, because while it really wasn't a bad story, it just didn't grip me at all. I think this is largely because of the characters, there's quite a cast of them, and while they all have some unique character traits, I didn't grow attached to any of them. I didn't care about the romances that were starting between them and I didn't care when one of them got shot, which is a bad sign. The book definitely had it's exciting bits, and the action is really well written, but I felt like the main character's emotions were a little bit too detached from what was going on for it to feel realistic. I also didn't really like how little acually happened in the grand scheme of things, it just felt like it was leading up to a bigger story. This makes sense, since it's quite a long series of books, but I still feel like it should have had more of an individual story. I most likely won't be continuing this series, this book just didn't make me care enough about what's going to happen next.

OMFG I loved this book - I did not want it to end and was so heartbroken when it did. I wanted more of Grey son and Melanie, I craved them. Katy Evans can write love like no other- she makes me feel things that I didn't know I could feel. Well done Katy - keep your books coming because I cannot get enough

I wasn't that satisfied with this book in the series. I don't feel that the overall story is heading to a conclusion or even heading anywhere. It felt very stagnant. And only one or two chapters with Bran, very little with Arya. Nothing more about the Katelyn Zombie. There were some new threads of storyline started here, but it is hard to invest in these when so many previous ones have been started, invested in and seemingly abandoned. Still, great series overall.

Well, i'm sure there are other books more monolithic than this one, but moving through this was a bit like feast or famine for me. When it was interesting in the first half, it was a great read, but when it ran dry in the second, reading it felt akin to "cleaning out the inbox" so to speak. The story really took a nosedive after our little protagonist becomes the Chosen One with all the requisite, self-aggrandizing schemes and drug-induced, fortune-telling sequences to go along with the part. This wouldn't have been so bad for a 100 or even 200 page book, but 400+ pages? That feels something like a betrayal. But, one has to admire the work in the time it was written, since, apparently, it was a harbinger of the next generation of sci-fi and fantasy epics - the ones where all these different bloodlines vie for control of the world. Yes, coincidentally, I also started watching Game of Thrones at the same time I was reading this book and, sometimes, it was kind of hard to tell the two apart. Maybe that is impressive for something written over 40 years ago?

I've got a real love/hate relationship with Christian fiction. Loved it when I was younger as an adult I find it pedantic, silly, and based on the assumption that people are walking around with this big aching hole that Christians don't have. It's kinda bullcrap. I'm a Christian minister and I still get that big aching hole. Anyway. I love Austen more than I hate Christian Fiction so I gave it a go. For the most part pleasantly surprised from the Christian Fiction aspect. It's more like the book of Ester where God is everywhere and nowhere, although the parts where God was mentioned I felt were forced and a left me feeling a little icky. those parts out have been cut entirely and nobody would have felt anything was missing. To me it almost felt like the editor went "eh, not God-sy enough lets toss in a coach saying an awkward dinner prayer and call it a day" I prefer the more subtle, clearly. Sam... Sam, Sam, Sam. You are annoying. Seriously, I'm sorry you had such a horrible life but for realz.... I know an actual PhD in literature and she doesn't obscurely quote Bronte, Austen, Dumas, and just about every other obscure writer ever. And even if she did I promise you nobody would really get what she's talking about. She certainly hasn't found her magic man soul mate that gets all her references right away. Odds are if you haven't read widely throughout the 19th century you're not going to get a lot of the references. I should probably start by reminding myself of the plot... Sam Moore is a young woman who grew up in a youth home. Her parents were insanely abusive and neglectful leaving her to find solace in books, particularly Jane Austen. She is accepted into a prestigious journalism school and a benefactor gives her a full ride... as long as she writes him during her time as a student. He goes by the pseudonym Mr Knightly. Sam pours her life though and soul out to him. One day she runs into a famous author and the begin a friendship. See where this is going? We "learn" at the end it's actually Mr Knightly. By then they've developed a relationship and he's proposed, she's rejected him a-la Elizabeth Bennet and then he's hit by a bus... or a car or something. Toss in hurting youth Kevin and a lot of 10 mile runs. I'm not a huge fan of novels in letter form but the author did do a good job with that. All in all I think the author can do better and I'm going to keep reading her work. This book just missed the mark a bit.

1.5 stars. You are not the choice. King's Cage is a slow-paced third installment that reads more like a filler than anything else. There is a lot of tell instead of show, very little plot development, and the characters are static. For a series that was supposed to be a trilogy but instead was stretched out into four books, this novel adds nothing of substance to the story. Victoria Aveyard does strike to deliver a unique YA Fantasy series, and she succeeds with some of it, as the world-building is interesting. Her writing is very easy to follow along as well, and the shifts in POV flow smoothly. But when the universe she's created stalls and does not develop, it becomes a boring task to get through chapters. When I say this book is slow paced and that nothing happens, I mean it. This is 500+ pages of nothing, with a few action scenes sprinkled in between. It does not help that we are told a lot of things are happening, instead of being shown while stuff is going down. King's Cage focuses a lot on political/war strike planning, and... nothing else, really. The book is told in dual POV: Mare and Cameron's. The shifts between POVs is actually really well done. Despite being bored through most of the story, the change from Mare to Cameron never felt stiff or abrupt. They have very unique voices, and that shows through the writing. I will say that Mare's POVs are hard to get through, as it seems like she tries very hard to be cunning and strong and just comes off sounding naive and stupid. There are also a few chapters told from the POV of one character who ends up being the one bright spot in this novel: Evangeline. There are also quite a few really uncomfortable scenes with Maven, who I actually quite like as a villain. I would say the love triangle is still a driving force in this novel, even in the situations the characters have found themselves in. And, you know, even though it is quite uncomfortable to read at times. In the end, King's Cage is a huge disappointment. Nothing happens throughout the book, and the few intriguing scenes do not add much to the plot. The story is boring and slow paced and there is no character development. This series should have remained a trilogy. Series: #3 in the Red Queen series. POV: Told mostly from Mare and Cameron's POVs. Content Warnings: Non-consensual kissing. Instalove: Not really. Love Triangle: Yup. Cliffhanger: No. HEA: Not yet. Up Next: Untitled.

I'm not surprised this story makes so many references to Macbeth, considering the whole story from top to bottom is one hell of a tragedy. The characters are all fascinating (and Mejia does a fantastic job writing distinguishable POVs) but Hattie shines. That the book revolves around her murder is a tragedy in itself, as Hattie is such a complex, fascinating character. She is brilliant, captivating, manipulative, but also - and this surprised me - quite kind. Being in her head was a trip, and the more I got to know her, the more her death hit me hard. This book features a student/teacher relationship, and, personally, this has always been a huuuuge interest of mine in fiction, but I've never seen it done right, or at least, never seen it written the way I wanted it to be. Until this book. The relationship between Hattie and Peter is realistically crafted, right down to Peter being kind of an asshole at certain points. One thing that bugged me, and it's a spoiler: I really hated that part at the end when the Sheriff says that Hattie killed Tommy as much as he killed her, and that she and Peter "ruined" him. I'm sorry, what? This was such a bizarre thing to say. I get that the point was to establish a connection to Macbeth and to emphasize that the choices Hattie and Peter made had ruined their lives and the lives of people around them - and yes, many lives were ruined - but that wasn't because of Hattie and Peter, it was because of Tommy, who chose to kill a girl for not sleeping with him. It's the same old story all over again - entitled dude kills girl because she doesn't live up to what he wants her to be. This seemed to mesh with the theme of the book (and the title!) so I didn't really get why the Sheriff had to go and try to justify Tommy's actions. Overall, I loved this book. The author's writing is lovely, she's wonderful at characterization, and I absolutely couldn't put this book down (it's almost 3AM but I had to finish it!

I want to thank my great friend Liz who had the brilliant idea to offer me the entire trilogy for Christmas. Thanks to her I can now read the whole series in a few days! I listened to this and two subsequent ones in the series, The Amazing Mrs. Pollifax and the Elusive Mrs. Pollifax, on audiobook read by Barbara Rosenblatt. Cons: Basically when you get to the 3rd book, you will have noticed that there are a lot of repetitive phrases that Mrs. Pollifax likes to use, such as "You've been so kind," and you will have noticed that everyone seems to speak English, even in the depths of the Iron Curtain states. Not only do they speak English, they can even use English idioms that seem somewhat advanced for someone of their supposedly limited language abilities. BUT- Pros: Kudos to Ms. Gilman for writing what was a really creative, cute adventure-mystery starring a plucky, likable over-the-hill in age but not in heart person. Ms. Rosenblatt also is some kind of genius when it comes to audiobooks, because she reads so clearly and manifests all the different personas so well that I think I will continue reading just because I am a fan of her style. Mrs. Pollifax in this first novel is likable and relatable, mainly because of how the novel starts out. She is severely depressed (something that 95% of the population is nowadays) and entertains semi-suicidal thoughts. When asked what she's always wanted to be, she says, "a spy!" But of course it's ridiculous. But she wanted to be given a chance. So, she takes the bus or train to DC and with a letter of recommendation from her senator, she gets into the CIA building. Through a mishap at just the right place, she is mistaken for an actual agent and briefed on a mission. What makes this first book really cute and likable is the fact that the mission started out incredibly boring. Mrs. Pollifax was filled with excitement, but soon found that all she did was wait around. Then something goes horribly wrong when the contact she was supposed to meet on a specific day is not there, and she gets drugged by the bad person who was there, and basically kidnapped, along with an unkempt American that she thinks is a drug-dealer. They are hauled off to Albania in a prison, and through events that are sort of predictable but still amusing, she becomes gradual friends with some of the guards there. She, unlike her fellow cell-mate, is allowed outside for walks, and while there, she comes up with an unlikely scheme to escape. It is an absolutely mad scheme -- parts of which are believable, but some parts (such as the Colonel, who is Russian and should be her enemy, helping them) are not. Also, she manages to free another prisoner, a mysterious Chinese person, and off they go on their run. Their escape is exciting (at least on audiobook) as they climb down a sheer cliff, masquerade as sheep, blow up a car (this I find incredible as I don't think it's that easy to blow up a car), commandeer a raft, then a sailboat, and somehow end up in Greece. But Mrs. P's job was simply to be a courier and get a file from the contact...did she get it? I don't want to ruin it for people (usually I don't care, but this one was quite cute) and actually I guessed what the file was before the end of the book. However, it didn't ruin it for me. The ending was quite perfect and put me in really happy mood, as it was filled with hope, and the previously sort of cowed Mrs. P finds a strength within her that she had not realized before. Sort of an all over growing-up-at-age-60, adventure/spy/comedy story all in one. I usually give books really low ratings, but this one, I am wavering hard on 4 or 5 stars. Note: The 2nd and 3rd books do not live up to the 1st book. Also, I saw that some people may not have liked the book because it was so heavy on description. That MAY be true. There are a lot of conversations that Mrs. P has with herself. If Ms. Gilman were stingy with her paragraph spacers in the novel, that might compromise the flow and ease of reading. But, read by Barbara Rosenblatt, the book was quite perfect. The audiobook is highly recommended by me.

He just plunked you into the world, but his prose was so well constructed that he didn't need to spend pages and pages just telling you about the world. But, by the same token, his writing was so well done that you simply enjoyed reading the words. My only problem with the book came at the end  (which is probably why I can only give it 4 stars) and that has to do with the pregnancy. If all of their bodily functions seem to be slowed down, how is it that her pregnancy is progressing so fast (well, normally)? Wouldn't that be a slower development too? Can they even get pregnant? Actual Rating: 4.5 stars If the government had the ability to travel in time, what would our society look like? Would international crises be averted or would the world quickly fall into a totalitarian regime? All Our Yesterdays takes the latter standpoint, and creates a scarily realistic picture of how time travel is not just neat - it's a threat to all of us. The mechanics of how this type of time travel would work and all of its associated paradoxes were so well explained that I found myself wondering if such a thing could actually happen. The characters were so beautifully written and complex, and all had such distinct voices  which is impressive, given some of their relationships to one another  . I admired Em's resilience, Finn's uncanny ability to make anyone smile even in the darkest of times, James' determination to do the right thing... even Marina, who first appeared shallow and allowed a boy to define her actions, managed to grow on me. The relationships between the characters are so artfully manipulated throughout the course of the story that all of the character development that occurred was more than plausible given the circumstances. While some of the growth was subtle, much of the character development was tied into a simple, but important, question: how similar is the person you are now to the person you will become? Overall, All Our Yesterdays was an amazing debut. Although it functions well as a stand-alone, I look forward to more adventures in time with these characters. This review can also be found at The In-Between Place.

The Skinny: Not Maas' best work. The Fat: I was nervous to start Queen of Shadows (QOS). The last book was kind of slow, so I was afraid that a book that was about 100 more pages would be unbearable to read. Plus, I heard numerous people with ARCs talking about how bad this book is. About how Maas abandoned the plot for a romance. Other's said that the characters regressed. Or that Maas ignored all character development from Heir of Fire. But I have to say these people are wrong. Yes, characters make the same mistakes that they have been making since book one (case in point: all of the keeping of secrets which has literally killed people in the past). Yes, some of the characters begin QOS by ignoring what they discovered in the previous book (*cough* *cough* Manon). Yes, there is a romance in the book (but there has been romance in every TOG book). The mistakes the characters repeatedly make can at times be infuriating, but in the end it makes them all the more human. Do I have critiques about the characters and parts of the plot? Yes. Do my critiques mean that the story was poorly written? No. My critiques are mostly personal preferences of how I wish the story had played out (pertaining to the romance, whiny characters, character development issues, etc.). Besides pacing issues, for the most part Maas wrote an intense book. The action wasn't consistent and most of the book felt like people were arguing about how to pull off the events. However, the arguments tend to be melodramatic. By this point I understand that they are all hotheaded, but Aelin needs to take a cue from Manon and include people in her court how aren't just like her. HOF left off with Aelin finally coming to terms with her heritage. Maas does an excellent job of weave Aelin and Celaena's storyline together. Readers are also introduced to a few new characters, among them are Lysandra, Nesryn Faliq, and Elide. I just wish readers learned more about Lysandra and Nesryn. They are two characters I want to know more about. QOS felt like two books mashed into one. The first half was all about finding Arobynn (who turns out to be an even worse person than Celeana made him seem in all of the other TOG books) and the second half is about  Aelin trying to free magic and kill Dorian . A part of me is glad that it was one book so I don't have to wait as long for the series to be over, but the other part of me wished that it had been two books because the tone of the two parts felt so different. The characters felt different, the pacing was different, and the two parts were just, well, for lack of a better word, different. Not in a bad way, or enough to truly be distracting, but the two halves had different vibes to them. The characters all grew towards the end of the book, but for the first half they all kind of stayed the same. I really liked how Aelin grew in QOS compared to TOG. Aelin even comments to herself at one point that maybe she was too quick to judge Kaltain in TOG. There is more character development that I liked (and some I didn't), but I'm afraid that I may accidentally spoil it by discussing the characters further. One thing I'm confused about is Aelin and Rowan's silent conversations. They made sense in HoF (those were usually quick conversations that I could totally visualize people having), but their silent conversations were actually conversations in QOS. Like at a particular dinner party, they communicated things that I have no idea could be said with a simple look. So do they actually talk in each other's heads or is there a look for I'm-going-commando in everyday life that I must have missed? For the most part I liked QOS (key word: liked not loved). A lot happens in this book. But the pacing is totally off. It would pick up and then simmer down for a while and then pick up again. The ending was a bit slow, but at least it doesn't end on the world's biggest cliffhanger. All in all, don't let the ARC readers scare you away from reading QOS. Personally, I don't think I will continue reading this series. It's not bad, but it's not great either. The series follows a lot of annoying tropes. It isn't technically badly written, but the series is no longer my cup of tea. My favorite quote: "Please don't ever do that again." It was her turn to puff out a laugh. "Next time, I'll just ask Dorian not to stab me." ***TRIGGER WARNINGS: slavery, murder, death, mentions of R/SA, mind control, torture, abuse, domestic violence

4.5 Stars The Honor of the Queen follows Honor Harrington on a diplomatic mission to a planet where women have few rights and can't own property. Awkward, because Honor is the most high-ranking military officer in the delegation, and she's a woman. For the most part I enjoyed the book. I thought the space battles were well done, and I didn't have trouble picturing what was going on as I so often do. I also appreciated that Weber wasn't afraid to  kill major characters or severely injure his protagonist. My one issue was that I found the ending a bit too neat - Honor gets ALL THE TITLES. I also thought it glossed over how hard it would be to change the prevalent attitudes towards women on the planet. All in all, I found the  mostly happy ending   a bit incongruous with Weber's previously demonstrated willingness to risk his character's safety.

Great, of course! It was a bit creepy to watch Kate struggling not to give in to the changing instincts caused by her claiming of the city. Becoming like her father is her worst fear, even more than seeing the horrible prophecy the Witch Oracle shared with her come true. I don't know why I didn't post a review my first time through, c.10/06/2016, but hopefully I'll get a proper one done after I finish this re-read. (2X while I have it from the library: immediately, then right before it has to go back -- once just isn't enough, though I wait and buy in paperback.) Right now, I just wanted to make a note of one minor but repeated proofreading oversight: halfway through its appearances in the story, suddenly "pegasi" was being used as singular instead of properly as plural. Here's a quote as an example, one that's funny enough to share anyway. (Hmm, I notice it also contains a period that ought to be a comma. Tsk, tsk.) "Remember, try to bond with the pegasi." Teddy Jo said. "Treat her as a friend, not a horse." "I would try to be friends with her but she's too busy being a smartass." "Now you know how the rest of us feel," Jim said. Okay, I'm back, after closing the book with a happy sigh. Now it really goes without saying that this book is exciting, emotional, passionate, and funny, and entirely captivating -- after all, you know whose name is on the cover. Each volume builds on what has come before. Kate continues to increase her control over her magical potential, this time with the sharp-fongued guidance of a most unexpected ally. Derek spills the beans about Julie's awareness of her situation, making Kate's desire to keep her apart from Roland even more futile. Her shame at the dark impulses she's exleriencing makes Kate try to conceal certain things from Curran for a while out of fear that this would be the final straw, but I never doubted that their love would hold. Their connections and friendships with shifters still within the Pack are strained by Roland's ruthless machinations in response to prophecy, including a shocking betrayal. Kate's relationship with her father includes bittersweet regrets, horrified rejection, furious and literally earth-shaking arguments, and the inevitable actual battle that didn't happen in Magic Breaks. And speaking of unexpected allies, she ends up with more than a few fighting on her side. Christopher, though ... Whoa! I'm not going to tell you anything about what he finally remembers, just wait and see. As always though, there are also lighter touches, this time frequently revolving around the preparations for their wedding, which they're determined to have despite everything. Roman, priest of the Slavic god of darkness, is an unconventional choice of officiant, but when he realizes how little Kate has organized yet, he becomes her unofficial wedding planner, too, to her dismay. The climax and denouement of this book are very satisfying, but one battle is not the whole war, and though they've discovered why Roland hasn't simply killed her, they still don't have an answer for how to stop him once and for all. There also a number of other intriguing threads: What will the relationship between Barabas and Christopher become now? What role will Adora (as Curran puts it, another of Kate's adopted stray misfits/ killers) choose, now that she has a choice? What consequences will there be to Curran's unusual "meal", and why exactly was Roland draining a captive Saiman, anyway? How is Kate planning to keep the oath she took regarding Atlanta? And then of course there's the big one: Kate and Curran's foretold son, whom Roland may want steal or to kill. I can already hardly wait for the next book!

Thud! is exactly what I needed. A battle between two metaphorical magical creatures with only a stalwart human police chief in the middle? Yes! Thud! moved immediately at the top of my list of best Pratchett books. It's smartly written, of course, but it's also a voice for understanding and calm in a world that seems constantly on the verge of spinning out of control--with or without an ancient evil to nudge the spin into motion. Thud! is a Discworld story focused on the hard-working, faithful and true Commander Vimes of the City Watch. I haven't read all of his arc, but the book finds him wealthy, married, and with a young son he dotes on. And yet he has to deal, personally, with the increasing demands of Ankh-Morpork and his beliefs of what a copper should be. Meanwhile the city is tense with the upcoming reenactment of the ancient fight between dwarves and trolls--and the city, and Vimes--is right in the middle. One lovely side-plot involves a vampire who aspires to join the squad, and the werewolf who must tolerate her, another ancient blood feud that they both just have to overcome because this is the City Watch, not a circus, damnit! I particularly fell in love with werewolf Angua, and think she really deserves a scratch behind the ears. Pratchett has a knack for social commentary disguised as silliness, and this shines through in Thud! the same way it worked so well in Going Postal. It is an endearing read, a joy for the reader and, apparently, the writer. I can't recommend it enough.

Emmy & Oliver is a difficult book to describe, but if I had to cut it down to one sentence, I'd say it's the kind of book that tugs on your heartstrings. It's not a tear-jerker by any means, but it just might leave you with a quiet melancholy that'll linger in your heart. Cheesiness aside, it's Really Good. The reason why Emmy & Oliver is such a strong, heartfelt book is mostly due to the depth and complexity in all the characters and their relationships. Move along, mean cheerleaders, "quirky" gay best-friends and wicked-slash-absent parents! The parents in this story are finally portrayed as people who aren't just roadblocks to hinder Emmy and Oliver's lives; I can actually understand and believe the parents' intent behind their decisions. I also love how Drew is openly gay, and he's actually portrayed as a real person, not just the fashion-loving, gossiping caricatures LGBT+ are usually subjected to. But Emmy's relationship with her best-friends, Caro and Drew, take the cake. They're so realistic that I can often see me and my friends in them, especially through their conversations. A few of my favourite quips: "Jerk," I said, because I knew Drew would recognize it for the term of endearment it was. "You're not supposed to share eye makeup! What if I have pinkeye?" "It'd be an honor to share pinkeye with you, Caro." "Brandon's not even a douche bag. He's a douche CANOE. A whole canoe, Emmy!" Although Emmy and Oliver's romance seems like it's going to take center stage, it doesn't. Although it's sweet and cute and makes your heart fill with a million butterflies, it takes a backseat to all the other important things going on. Emmy & Oliver addresses a lot of family issues in a real, honest and refreshing way. Not all families are abusive, but all of them have some issues and with Drew's homophobic grandparents and his struggle with having his parents value money for mortgage payments over their son's identity , Caro's neglectful parents, Oliver being torn between two parents and feeling like he's the odd man out in his mom's "new" family and Emmy's helicopter parents, it really shows that. More than a few times, my heart ached for these guys, especially Oliver. All in all, Emmy & Oliver is not only probably the most realistic contemporary you'll read this year, but it's also surprisingly hilarious, filled with complex characters and relationships and has one of the sweetest romances I've ever read. 4.5 bright, sparkling stars

"Someday I want to wake up and be normal. Just for a little while. Or forever. Brewster "Bruiser" Rawlins in eighth grade was "Most Likely to Receive Death Penalty". He was described in the book as: large, but not fat, sloppy-not grundy. His clothes seem worn, but not stylishly so. They were actually worn, and the legs were short enough to prove they'd been around for at least two inches of growth. And although most boys look pretentious in a distressed leather bomber jacket, it seemed natural on him"; "Always a little too big to be picked on, a little too mad-creepy to be in anyone's clique. He was always just there, through elementary school and middle school lingering in the background. He's quiet and inscrutable. And all for good reason. Bruiser has a strange ability. He can steal anyone's pain, physically and emotionally. As long as he cares about someone, he can steal away any hurt. There's a catch though. He absorbs it all into himself. That's why he's distant. Imagine if he had plenty of true friends, their pain would literally be the death of him. Tennyson and Bronte Sternberger are twins. Born from literary teachers, they are named after literary idols. Bronte initally takes interest in Bruiser, thinking he is a stray and someone has to take him in. Tennyson is acting like a brother should and keeps his eyes on Bruiser, to a point where he follows him home to give him fair warning. We are then introduced to Bruiser's little brother, Cody. Cody's pet bull, Tri-tip dies. Tennyson gets to know Bruiser as they bond over the discarding of Tri-tip's remains. Tennyson actually thinks Bronte is good for Bruiser. Bruiser is slowly let into the family, but Tennyson's family is falling apart. Bronte also gets Bruiser to have plenty of friends, but Bruiser gets to care for all of them, absorbing all the tiny little pains for himself. But a little of everything is too much. Neal Shusterman does not fail to deliver. This is my second book from him, first is Unwind, which I absolutely loved. Bruiser is told in four POVs. Bruiser's was my favorite. His POV is smart and in prose. It is wonderfully written and morally challenging. And it delivers. It shows how susceptible humans are to turning the other way and ignoring what we do not want to see. Bruiser is definitely one of my favorites for 2013. And I leave you with this: "In horse raicng they put these slats on either side of the horse's head, blocking creature's peripheral vision. They are called blinders. They don't actually blind the horse, but they allow the horse to see only what's right in front of it; otherwise it might freak out and lose the race. People live with blinders too, but ours are invisible, and much more sophisticated. Most of the time, we don't even know they're there. Maybe we need them though, because if we took everything all at once, we'd lose our minds. Or worse, our souls. We'd see, we'd hear, we'd feel so deeply that we might never resurface. So we make decisions, never realizing we're only seeing one-tenthof the whole. Then we cling to our narrow conclusion like our life depends on it."

Aislinn has always been able to see the fey and followed the rule her Grams set to ensure she never drew their attention but two members of the faery court are now stalking her and it doesn't look like those rules are going to be any help. It doesn't seem to happen a lot to me but sometimes I'll read a book and it just doesn't click for me. I neither love it or hate it but it becomes tedious to me. Sadly, that's how I found Wicked Lovely. The premise for the story was made clear very early on but it seemed to take forever for the plot to go anywhere. The last ditch attempt at some action at the end didn't really convince me and felt tacked on and rushed. Grams gets attacked even though there's no discernible reason for it - had Beira threatened her in order to make Aislinn choose not to pick up the staff it would have made sense - there would have been a bit of conflict even, but no - she's just found unconscious, no clue what's wrong with her, no attempt to unthaw her if she'd been frozen or phone an ambulance if it was some other injury. The whole episode was just bizarre and unnecessary. I found the characters rather flat, with the possible exception of Donia, and they didn't seem to be given any space to react to events in a interesting or realistic way. Seth accepted that Aislinn could see faeries far too easily, Aislinn accepted that she was the Summer Queen almost immediately and never had a moments doubt that she would be turned into the Winter Girl and Keenan simply agreed to her demands. I could never really get a grasp on who Aislinn really was, her personality kept seeming to change, which I suppose could be explained away by her becoming more volatile as she became the Summer Queen  but it just left me feeling detached. Likewise, in the obligatory love triangle I found no one to root for - Keenan came on too strong straight away and Seth I just found pretentious and unbelievable. There also seemed to be way too many secondary characters that all blurred into one and then disappeared in the latter half of the book. It wasn't awful but I've read plenty of YA faery tales that were more exciting, even if they weren't perfect either.

The book was fantastic. It was beautiful. First of all, I loved the cover. I had to get the book! One word to describe The Shock of the Fall, would be powerful. It is the story of Matthew, a 19-year-old schizophrenic, who is relaying his life story. It all started when Matthew's older brother, Simon, dies at the tender age of 11, and 10 years later Matthew is still reeling from this tragedy. Matthew was only 9 when the horrible accident, which he blames himself for, took place, but it has since shaped the course of his entire life. "Memories were falling away, like a dream when we first open our eyes. It was a lot like that. I could only make out the edges - night time, running, the police were there somewhere." After the loss of Simon, Matthew's life changes immediately. His mother takes him out of school to begin homeschooling and Matthew is forced to become a recluse, with only his parents for companionship (at least for a little while). The (typical)family never talk about or deal with the loss of Simon, a happy-go-lucky boy with a moon-face. Yet, Simon is always there, everyday, in every mundane activity, and Matthew can never forget the events that led up to that fateful accident. "There was the shock of the fall and the blood on my knee, and Simon carried me all the way back to the caravan, all by himself, without any help from anyone, even though it half killed him, but he did it anyway, he did it for me, because he loved me." The Shock of the Fall isn't only a novel about mental illness; it's about grief and its lingering effects. It's about family, and what happens to families when tragedy strikes. Not only do you learn about Matthew and his illness, but you get to meet his kooky parents and his amazing grandmother, Nanny Noo, all of whom have been greatly affected by his disease, as well as their own issues, of course. "I am myself, the same self I have always been, the one person I can never escape." Filer uses pictures and different font styles and sizes to weave together Matthew's story. For me, these didn't really add much, I was already hooked, but they didn't detract from his writing either. At the very end of The Shock of the Fall, Filer leaves us not with a happy ending, but with an ending that inspires hope. At the end is a beginning...The Shock of the Fall says a lot about the realities of mental illness because it doesn't have a feel-good, everything is going to be great ending. Mental illness is always a battle, BUT there's always hope, the promise of a new beginning. Each time I put the book down I felt that I had accumulated a new set of memories; it is not a book that you can simply read and digest it makes a point of getting under your skin and implanting itself there. It's narrative is such, that you feel as though you are recounting flashes of events in your past that you would sooner forget and that are burnt onto your minds eye. Matthew's story is so compelling and may have something to do with seeing him both man and boy side by side. This duplicity emerges in the narrative with the sweet voice of his younger self, and the quick wit; that often surprises with its frankness, of his 19 year old self. I loved it.

I usually hate love triangles (sometimes they're done ok, but not here), especially when it's so obvious who the main character is going to pick so everything else seems like a waste of space. One thing I liked a lot about this series was Cainsville and the light paranormal/mystery aspect but even that was a bit light in this book and a lot of it was centered around the love triangle. I'm not sure how I feel about the whole "reincarnation" playing out the roles thing. It takes away a lot of choice, even if it isn't exactly reincarnation, and sort of lessens the relationship aspect I feel. That being said, the interactions between Gabriel and Olivia were GREAT. I love him and them so much. He's such a fascinating and flawed character, and I can't wait to see further developments though I REALLY hope that Olivia ends her relationship with Ricky soon but that they can somehow find a way to still be friends because, again, I like Ricky. But the love triangle really takes a lot out of the series the way it's working out right now.

Cheyenne's review posted at Guilty Pleasures Book Reviews I love being excited when a book that I have been waiting for releases or I am lucky enough to get an ARC in advance to review. So to say I was excited when I got Sustained may be a slight understatement. I was so excited because it's Emma Chase, hello, she writes books that will have you in tears from laughing so hard. She knows how to write a male character that you will one minute want to slap upside the back of his head and then the next want to kiss him. Jake Becker doesn't disappoint because he will make you want to slap him, kiss him, possibly rape him, and fall in love with him. Jake is your typical manwhore. No relationships, different women all the time, may keel over and die if you ever put the words Jake and relationship together. You know the kind who thinks that way until he meets the one woman who knocks him on his ass, who, even when he is lying to himself about having feelings he is in fact falling for her. Oh wait it gets even better, said woman is the guardian for her nieces and nephews so add children into the mix. Six of them in fact. Let me give you a few minutes for that to sink in, can you imagine what type of freak out Jake starts to have? But now picture this. He actually starts to not just care about Chelsea, but the kids as well. Chelsea is sweet, funny and even though she is taking care of her six nieces and nephews after the death of their parents the best that she can, sometimes things become more than she can handle and now that Jake is helping her, it is almost like they are a team, a weird non family unit. I loved how even when one of the kids, or more than one would get in trouble or do something wrong, she still didn't give up. When her relationship with Jake also includes his legal help more than once, you can see how much his help and support has meant to her. And when he does the typical male asshole thing and hurts her, well I give her even more props for staying strong as she can. Do you know why I love books like this so much? It is not just because of the smoking hot sex scenes, or the guaranteed laughs I will have, it is because deep down I believe that love can heal and repair pain. That love will open your eyes and show you what you have in front of you, even if it means everything you think you don't want in your life is the exact thing that you fall in love with. Emma Chase not only had me falling in love with Jake and Chelsea, but also the kids as well. I love this series, and I can't wait to read more about this crazy group of attorneys that we are all coming to know and love. Review copy provided for an honest review.

The Movie Ruined This For Me It's been a while since I saw the movie version of this short tale by Philip K. Dick, but I now have it on order from the library so that I can watch it again. Although it's been 13 years since I've seen the movie (starring Tom Cruise), I recall it well enough to know  that it is quite different from its source material. And while this doesn't usually happen with film adaptations, I think this is one of those cases where the filmmakers vastly improved upon the original story. I was terribly disappointed. That might not be fair to Philip K. Dick, but I'm afraid it can't be helped. Spoilers below. As those familiar with this story know, the premise is that crime has been virtually eliminated because of a police unit called Precrime, which relies on three clairvoyant mutants who have visions foretelling the future, and whose visions are loaded into a computer system that translates them into "reports." These visions foretell crimes before the would-be offenders have a chance to offend, and those people are locked away before the idea to offend has a chance to develop in their heads. John Anderton, head of Precrime, has the shocking discovery of the precogs predicting that he will murder a man named Kaplan. As he has no intention of ever doing so, he pulls the report and goes on the run. It turns out that Kaplan is part of a movement to discredit Precrime, and he means to have Anderton stand by his side as he reveals the contents of the majority report as well as the minority report. (If two of the precogs have one vision and the third has a different one, the different one is the minority report.) In Anderton's case, the minority report comes about because it takes into account Anderton finding out about the report and making the decision not to kill Kaplan. But as Kaplan is making his speech, Anderton takes out a gun and really does kill Kaplan. Why? To prevent Precrime from being discredited. I absolutely hate that ending. Anderton ultimately explains that in his case, there were actually three different reports--all minority reports. Two of them had him killing Kaplan, but the third was based on his having read the second and changing his mind back to killing Kaplan. Yes, to save Precrime. I AM DISAPPOINT!

It isn't often one comes across a book by an Indian author, with a sequel. It is even rarer when the said sequel might just be better than its predecessor. Tripathi once again delves into Indian mythology and spins a fascinating tale around many of the names heard in tales told at our grandmothers' knees, portraying them as mere mortals. Last left, Shiva was about to launch an attack on the dreaded Nagas to avenge Brahaspathi's death. The book's blurb gives you enough indication, and then some, that Shiva's plan might not be that easy to execute. His desire, and ours, for answers takes him all across India in this book, with the city in focus being Kashi. I'll give the book this, the author has good command over the story and doesn't let it meander, with something or the other always afoot. Filled with secrets, shocks and betrayal, this book is a page-turner from start to finish. The reveal of the Naga's identity was shocking, to say the least. I DID NOT SEE THAT COMING, PEOPLE! The "secret" of the Nagas, however, was something I had long suspected so I wasn't blown away by the "cliff-hanger". As for that Master Pupeteer, I think it's Bhrigu . There's a suspicious character if there ever was one! But, the book is not perfect either. Many issues are brought up and then never addressed again, or explained properly. For example, the awfully gross "ritual" the Branga people perform in Kashi - what is THAT about? Or this mysterious plague that seems to affect them, nothing is mentioned as to what it is or why it is happening or how it started and it is never brought up again after that chapter. Sati annoyed me a bit in this book. I don't know about you, but I wouldn't be OK with leaving my 6-month old son and going off to fight lions or planning a break-in because I'm wondering what the King of Kashi is up to when he disappears mysteriously into his palace every now and then (BOUNDARIES, woman!). Anandamayi, however, was a delight to read about. I couldn't help but grin every time that feisty, saucy girl sauntered onto the page! The author often uses the story to put forth his opinion on many issues - like Karma, ethics, consequentialism, existentialism and the balance of Good and Evil. Though it is clearly intended to make you think, sometimes it does get a bit too much. What I also found jarring was the use of certain words/phrases that didn't quite match with the era the book is set in. I get that the author has tried to give the story as modern a take as possible, but I can't quite digest the fact that these people know of "radio waves" and "accumulator machines" OR that they say things like "You're a 180-year old virgin??" (Was anybody else reminded of Twilight here? No? Just me? OK.) and "I never understand their mumbo-jumbo". But maybe that's just me. Recommended. Go read. Now.

As others have noted, the first "book" sets up an intriguing and creative scenario, which fizzles out almost immediately with the arrival of the love interest and the loss of the most interesting characters in the book. The answers to the central questions become obvious well before they are revealed, and the resolution is long, drawn-out, and flat. There is far too much exposition and explanation in the latter half, as well. The author has never learned that less is frequently more, and by explaining everything robs the work of its mystery and wonder, a fatal flaw in a work of fantasy. I understand that it's meant to be a novel for young adults and teens, and perhaps if I were 17 I would have found it incredibly romantic, but from where I stand now, it's just another chick lit/Mary Sue fantasy dressed up in "Twilight" clothes. It's really a shame, because the work showed such promise initially.

Roe is distraught that she is unable to have kids (despite not ever discussing with her husband about having kids before they were married), but when a baby is unexpectedly dumped in her lap, she does nothing but whine about it the ENTIRE book. And seriously, how does she not know a thing about babies? She's so upset that her father moved her half-brother to California - obviously they didn't think she would be that concerned about it since she apparently spent no time with him as a baby. If she had, then she would know what a binky is, what a baby monitor is and that you shouldn't heat up bottles in the microwave. All things a friend and I (both childless) know. I love that Sally Allison called her selfish to her face. Best part of the book, though it did nothing to curb Roe's behavior. What was the point of the drugging part of the story? It didn't fit in the mystery, the resolution made no sense and it was completely unnecessary. I'm not sorry that she killed off Martin in the end. I can't believe how many other readers were so upset - the guy was a jerk, he and Roe barely tolerate each other, except when they have sex. Not all that surprising that he was sickly since he was aging in reverse. When Roe first met Martin I got the impression he was around 17 years older than her. Then in the "Julius House" the age difference is stated as 15 years. Then in this book he somehow is only 12 years older. Hello, Charlaine Harris, a little continuity would be nice.

I know that this graphic novel has a lot of hardcore fans, so it was about time I picked this up! I'm glad to say I also enjoyed it, although I will say that it is not my favorite graphic novel series, at least so far. I actually preferred Rat Queens, Vol. 1: Sass & Sorcery to this one (I've actually become really passionate about that series and really recommend it). Both of these graphic novels are not for kids at all. I felt like this volume was definitely more about setup, establishing the characters and the world. It did a great job of that, and I feel like the further I get into the series, the more plot there will be. I loved how it was formatted, with an older Hazel interjecting with her own words of wisdom. I also liked that we followed other characters. I'm very intrigued to see where the writers take the plots of the 'villains', as I definitely see The Will becoming a good guy and possibly IV as well, but you'd have to work hard to convince me. I'm interested to see where this story goes. The world is so large and fascinating, and there are so many different weird and wonderful creatures! The characters are great and I can't wait to see how they develop over the series. I should be picking up the next one shortly!

3 1/2 stars for this one. I love this series but this book really showed me some points I liked more than previous books and some I liked less. The drama within the Glass house reaches all new heights in this book. Everyone has secrets from one another and not all of them are good! In this book a new gym has opened up where a vampire is training humans and vampires alike. One thing I must say is that it must be HUGE. We get all the standard gym setups for weights, cardio, etc. We have boxing areas, ratchet ball, karate mats and even a fencing room and more! I would love to have a gym like how this appears in my city (less the vampires). Shane is one of the first to check it out and gets really into the fighting there but when one fights under vampires, bad things can follow. Claire is told some startling information but is heavily threatened to keep quite about it. Frank Collins is still being kept a secret, Shane is drifting away and even Eve and Micheal have a secret! All this adds up to lots of drama and home intrigue as a I wonder how it is all going to come out. While this book is mostly focused on Claire (as all past books have been), we get something new that I loved. We get a first perspective look into Shane's thoughts! While they are very warped in this book due to other factors I won't give away, it was an interesting new aspect to the series I highly enjoyed and hope to see again in future books of the series. One thing that is really being to annoy me are the idioms and text speak being used on a regular basis. I loved how the earlier books had a more mature aspect to how they spoke but now its getting annoying with the slang used. I used to love Eve but with how she was talking in this book, she is now the type of person I would avoid hanging out with. She is not 14-16 years old yet acting like one. It is annoying when a character changes like that and this in one change I do not like at all and cost a fair bit of enjoyment for reading this. With all the tension from the secrets I was expecting some interesting scenarios later in the book but i felt a bit let down in the end. The grand show was lackluster, Claire didn't seem to learn anything and no one asked questions about things that did not add up, they all just went along with whatever was going on! Grr! So overall, good story with fun potential. Some interesting character comebacks. Drama-filled but the last 20% of the book could have been better. Here's hoping the next book is better and Eve goes back to her old kick-but, goth self!

Why I picked it up: Last of a trilogy! I really enjoyed the first two and was excited to see what would happen and how it would end. This book picks up pretty much where Demonglass leaves off. Sophie has been told that her mother is with the Prodigium-hating Brannicks. When the youngest Brannick find Sophie outside their compound, she is about to strike, but stops when she learns Sophie's name. Turns out the head of the Brannicks thinks Sophie is the only chance they have of stopping a major, potentially-world-ending battle. Except Sophie's powers have been locked inside her by the council. Overall, I enjoyed it. There is lots of snark and dry humor and the plot went in directions I completely hadn't anticipated. I also like that a lot of characters and elements from the first book came back and/or were revisited. And I really, really liked the  group dynamic/team aspect that really comes alive between Sophie, Jenna, Archer, Cal, and Elodie. That being said, I was frustrated with  the final battle scene. Specifically, while I understand Cal's death and all, I felt like he kind of got gypped. Not in terms of dying, but in terms of plot and time spent on his death. Clearly, Cal saw his death when the group was in the Underworld. But there was no mention of that, no build up, just a sentence where he falls in to the pit and then the phrase "but no Cal" when Sophie wakes up. Cal deserved a better send-off, so to speak. I also thought the end was tied up a little too neatly, but I do like (mostly) happy endings, so I that's a minor complaint. Quote: "Ooh, wonder if we're gonna play Duck, Duck, Demon." (page 163) Genre Bingo: My Choice Jessica's Scavenger Hunt: Demon

I feel about this book the way I felt about the audio. It was just ok. I was kind of disappointed because I really liked The Adoration of Jenna Fox. Here are the things I didn't care for: -There was too much internal dialog. Most of the book was Locke talking to himself about his life, his thoughts, and "lapses" where he would just go on and on. -There wasn't enough world building. I can't tell you how many times it said something like, "After two hundred years, (whatever) was still the same." There were a couple of things that sounded futuristic, but overall so much was still the same. I mean, even something simple like trains. After 200 years, we're still going to be riding in trains? -There wasn't enough action. I felt like there was a lot of potential for action in this book, and even serious creepiness, but it just never happened. Even the ending was so anticlimactic. -Locke was soft. The way that he let Kara walk all over him drove me crazy. I understand that there were reasons for this, but UGH....blech. -Lack of romance. Not that every book needs romance, but this one certainly did. After 200 years in a box......Locke needed some action! :P There were things that I liked about the book. I did like finding out what happened to Locke and Kara. There was a level of creepiness with Doctor G and Kara. I love that I got to see Jenna again, and find out what happened in her life. There were some interesting surprises and small little mysteries also. Overall, I feel like if you're dying to know what happens after Jenna Fox, than pick this one up. But if you're happy with the way things ended, you may want to just skip this one. Andye readingteen.net

3.75 to a 4 I've been waiting for this book for a while. I really enjoyed the previous stories with Tony and Mac quite a bit but it has been a while since I've read them. I almost feel that if I had done a reread prior to getting this book it would have worked for me a bit better. Harper has a unique voice and it took me a bit to get back into the world of these two men. There are parts of this book that I really, really loved and other parts that didn't work quite as much: The proposal seemed to come out of nowhere for me. I wish we could have seen Tony buy the rings and then screw up the asking but having it been asked so abruptly just took a bit of it away for me. The conversation that followed just seemed a bit awkward even though it did fix things. The shooting and the aftermath. I'm a bit torn here honestly. I don't expect series' books or characters to be static or that it'll all be puppies and Christmas but this was a bit of a shocker. I'll see how things get played out in the last book of the series and I'd never begrudge any author to take their characters where the story leads them. Will this be a way for Mac to leave the force because he'd never do it any other way? Will we see him join up with the Private Investigator? I've often read stories where gay police officers have issues with fellow members of the force but this is one of the few books that showed the results of that animosity in a graphic and painful way. Maybe that's what I didn't like to see. I did enjoy this book even though parts where uncomfortable to read and, of course, I need to read the last one. This almost has a cliffhanger feel to it and I've always hated cliffhangers. What will the next book bring? There are a lot of unanswered questions posed here, it's like the "Empire Strikes Back" of the series. Definitely not a standalone. I recommend this series but they need to be read in order to get the full impact of the journey these two men have been on. There was a lot of call back to Marty in this one which I really enjoyed but it was bittersweet he was an interesting character and one that I wish we still had around.

Regardless, I did really like the world and its inhabitants. And the surprise cameos of the main characters of For Darkness Shows the Stars was great. Just as twisted and disturbing as Gone Girl, but a lot better in terms of execution...(pun not intended...) .
