A Conjuring of Light was a fast paced and heart-wrenching emotional rollercoaster. Also a blood bath... Because I feel I have said everything there was to say about Schwab's writing and because I'm basically an emotional wreckage...I'll just say that Kell & Lila together were amazing (and hot), the banter between Alucard & Kell epic, Rhy's relationship with his brother touching and the new ship  Alucard x Rhy > fantastic. After spending two books hating Holland, in the end my heart went out for him. Throughtout the book my poor heart broke several times  for Calla, for Hastra (I was infinitely pleased when Kell's cut Jasta's troat...), for Holland and for Kell's loss The final chapter and scene had me crying and laughing at the same time... Said this, I now need to rant about the loose ends. Yes because I'm hoping and longing with all my heart that those loose treads were left loose for a reason. Plus all the lines saying that this wasn't the end but a new beginning...well...well... Dear Victoria, now everytime he summoned fire, or willed water or conjured anything from blood, it pained him. Every single time it hurt, a wound at the very center of his being. But unlike a wound, it refused to heal. Magic had always been a part of Kell, as natural as breathing. Now he couldn't catch is breath. The simplest acts took not only strenght, but will. The will to suffer, to be hurt. (I was so heartbroken to read this, it felt like being punched in the gut...) - You need to fix Kell. Seriously...what will he do now? how will he manage? - I need to know what happens in White London now... - The favour Maris required of Lila... There is enough for a sequel (or an additional trilogy) and I refuse to be left hanging like this...*cries* Yes I'm fervently hoping that everything Victoria Schwab left open, she did so intentionally. Until then...Anoshe... Rating for the overall series: 5++

Nice premise ruined by bad writing and lack of vision. The whole book is just like the title points: a gimmick to provide a minor and unnecessary twist to major DC characters. This does not provide more insight into their personalities, nor does it provide some thought provoking context. Even the action is as bland as it can be. 2.5 stars You can also find my full review here! When I read the synopsis for My Lady Jane, I mentally immediately filed it under "not my thing". I don't really enjoy historical fiction set in the Tudor era and books about royalty are usually a miss as well. Also, all the reviewers described this book as extremely funny; again, not really what I'm normally interested in. But then more reviews started rolling in and some of my GR friends personally recommended it to me. I got interested and decided I would pick it up whenever I needed something that would put me in a good mood. And here's the thing: My Lady Jane is one of the most self-aware books I have ever read. It sets out with a specific goal in mind and delivers on that. It doesn't take itself seriously, but embraces its own ridiculousness. And in that it is refreshingly different from other YA books. It's a silly, light-hearted but entertaining historical comedy, not more and not less. My Lady Jane is a historical reimagining of the story of Lady Jane Grey, a retelling, that very much takes its liberties when it comes to historical accuracy. For instance, instead of the divide between Catholics and Protestants, the authors add in some magic and make it into a war between Verities and Edians, the latter being humans that can shapeshift into an animal form. In this world, we have Lady Jane Grey who is forced into an unwanted marriage by her king and cousin, King Edward. But things don't exactly go as planned. And indeed, as I started reading, I thought it was hilarious. The prologue immediately got my attention, with the authors setting the story's promise and making clear what the reader could and could not expect from the book. That gentle breaking of the 4th wall and contemporary pop culture references had me giggling out loud. It was great. So what was my issue then? I guess that for a reader like me, that just wasn't enough. I think many (or perhaps most judging by the reviews) readers will enjoy this book a lot. For me, however, the humour got old after a while, and when that humour is pretty much the novel's only strength (there is one other mentioned below), that is a problem. There are only so many nose jokes I can take. The novel is stuffed full of cliches and tropes that weren't made fresh or interesting in any way. The characters are incredibly flat and two-dimensional; never moving away from that initial stereotype. I had no attachment to any of them and thus also wasn't invested in the story. Jane's love of books should have been endearing to me as a booklover but it was so completely over-the-top that it made me roll my eyes repeatedly. Lord Gifford was both predictably handsome and boring with absolutely no substance to him. Also why on earth didn't he tell Jane about the poetry readings?? She's a booklover for God's sake, did he actually think she'd be more embarrassed/annoyed by that than the idea of him having "dalliances"? Such a stupid way of building tension through miscommunication. Edward is a little boy who knows nothing about nothing and reading about his love life made me cringe so badly. Gracie, though likeable in her feminist ways, was your typical kick-but heroine who rescues the "hero" and about as original as all of YA's other special snowflakes. And I still don't understand why on earth she fell in love with Edward. Unsurprisingly, the plot felt contrived to the point of nonsense and random elements flew in from nowhere (I mean really, what was up with the freaking bear?). Plot turns (they don't deserve the title of "twists") were so convenient is was laughable (which I realise is the whole point of the story but still UGH!) naturally it would turn out that both Jane AND Edward are Edians just when they are about to be killed. The reader never feels any sense of peril for the characters and it made the second half of the novel so very boring. There was one other thing I did like, however, and that was the way the authors mocked the sexist attitudes and societal norms of the Tudor era. I wish it would have been slightly more subtle but considering that this book is everything BUT subtle, I knew this would be the best that I would get and took it in stride. So ultimately, despite my good intentions and correct expectations of this book, it still didn't really work for me. I fully acknowledge that this is most likely a "it's me not you" situation, but once the jokes started repeating themselves there was just nothing left to keep me going. I give the authors major credit for taking a risk and trying something unique and pushing readers out of their comfort zone. I just needed more. I still totally recommend this book despite my lower rating. If you enjoy books that are a bit less serious, do give it a try. Also, I highly recommend the audiobook. The narrator is phenomenal and I honestly don't think I could have finished the book without her fantastic narration.

I had to check out the Lunar Chronicles after hearing so many good things, and I have to say, the series did not disappoint. I keep meaning to write proper reviews for them all, so naturally instead of starting at the beginning I start with Fairest. Fairest tells the back story of our villain Queen Levana while ostensibly setting up for Winter, the last book in the series. Fairest is novella-length and a quick read. Although it is chronologically a prequel, I would not recommend reading it before the other books, as it will spoil some reveals in those books, and will diminish the impact of Levana as an unreliable narrator. I would also suggest not reading this review if you haven't read the other books, since this review will contain some spoilers (but I will try not to spoil Fairest itself). Levana's rise to villainy is a trope-y one, but it is nonetheless entertaining. It's pretty clear from the beginning that she's not all there, if you catch my drift. Despite her narration, the disconnect between her reality and everyone else's is still clear, and every time she tried to justify her actions I was like Levana's story follows a time-honored villain trope: villain suffers trauma, develops a warped idea of love and relationships, and as a result pushes away everyone who cares about them while simultaneously turning to the dark side for the love and acceptance they crave. While cliches are often disparaged when it comes to writing, there's a reason why some, such as this one, are so enduring. It humanizes our villain yet not so much that we actually start to sympathize with and root for them instead (this technique does not always work if said villain is male and fangirls are attracted to him) and also sets them up as a foil for the hero. The parallels between Levana and Selene/Cinder are anvil-sized, to quote J.K. Rowling. The difference, of course, is that Cinder isn't completely loo loo. It's clear that Levana was part of a severely dysfunctional family from the beginning. Her parents are murdered when she and her sister Channary are still children, yet neither sister seems particularly affected by it. Channary is a complete sociopath, and it seems the only living being she ever really cared for is her daughter, Selene, and possibly Selene's father although we do not learn the details. In addition, Levana suffered trauma as a young child and grew up with severe burn scars on her face and body. Unfortunately, Levana doesn't turn to witchcraft, but she does get really skilled at glamours. In fact, she never lets anyone see what she really looks like, because she's convinced she'll be rejected. These insecurities follow her into her first and most significant romantic relationship, a Shakespearean tragedy of a tale that left me feeling terribly sorry for Evret, the object of her affections, and for his daughter, Winter. Levana never seems to realize that her selfish and delusional ideas of love are what pushes everyone she cares about away from her, and, being surrounded by yes-men, only becomes even more convinced of her own delusions. Levana's belief in her own invincibility continues to grow as she gets away with more and more heinous acts, culminating in the murder of her own niece, Selene, in order to clear her path to the throne. As a reader, you already know this woman is stone cold, it is nonetheless incredibly chilling to read as Levana calmly and detachedly plots the murder of an infant (and said infant's nanny). However, even as she does all these terrible things, Levana still tries to protect her family in her own warped way, her last tie to her humanity. Fairest is a fairly predictable read if you're familiar with villain tropes and have read the other books in the Lunar Chronicles, but it nonetheless kept me turning the e-pages on my e-reader, if only because I was dying to see how the inevitable would materialize. The trip through Levana's mind is a morbidly fascinating one, and sheds some light on why she's the way she is. There are some questions in Fairest which are never answered, such as why Channary and Levana's parents were killed (I just feel like there's more going on here than "crazy shell gets inside the castle and kills people," or else Luna really does have the worst security ever), who Selene's father is and how Channary ended up dying of such a rare ailment, but I assume those will be answered in Winter (at least, I hope so). Overall, Fairest did what it set out to do, and provides a solid addition to the Lunar Chronicles series.

This novel tells the story of LGBTQ life in Nigeria. The location provides poignancy because, as elaborated in THIS LINK, the country does not allow or recognize LGBT rights, and violence against LGBT people is frequent. Both male and female same-sex sexual activity is illegal in Nigeria. The maximum punishment in the twelve northern states that have adopted Shari'a law is death by stoning. In southern Nigeria and under the secular criminal laws of northern Nigeria, the maximum punishment for same-sex sexual activity is 14 years' imprisonment. The book's narrative tells in first-person the experiences of a young girl, beginning with her coming of age during the Biafran War of the late 60s. Her father is killed and her mother is forced to send her to work as a servant in order to provide room and board for her daughter. After the war ends her schooling was able to begin, and she becomes increasingly aware of her feelings of same sex attraction. She participates is some same sex affairs and barely misses violent death by a vigilante group. As the story progresses she is taught in no uncertain terms that homosexuality is the worst sort of sin, and consequently feels much guilt and fear of God's retribution. With strong encouragement from her mother she agrees to marry a young man. She eventually leave the marriage . The novel's epilogue mentions a "new generation of Nigerians with a stronger bent towards love than fear." But, it also documents a brutal beating of a lesbian couple, and the author's note reports on the 2014 laws criminalizing same-sex relationships with punishments. I hope this book contributes to awareness of the plight of the LGBTQ community in Nigeria. The author was born in Nigeria so I believe her description of time and place in this novel are realistic. However, the author moved to the USA at age ten, and she appears to be too young to have experienced the Biafran War. I'm guessing that parts of the story may be biographical of her parent's generation.

Moreso than the humor, it was really the humanity that struck me about this book, both qualities that are often hard to find combined in contemporary fiction. Maria Semple handles the complexities of her characters with a sharp eye and a generous heart, rendering their foibles and braveries in a way that makes every single one of them worthy of sympathy: no mean feat for a book with a decent-sized cast. Is it too soon to compare her to my comfort writer, Jane Austen? (Oh God, I sound so twee saying that, but it is the unvarnished truth!) My only criticism is that I want to know what happens after Antarctica, particularly with the new baby and its hapless mother, a gnat Bernadette can't shoo away, as well as with Elgin's joblessness . Perhaps a sequel, Ms Semple? I've already got This One Is Mine on hold from the library, and am looking forward to devouring more.

I enjoyed the first third/half of this book much more than I thought it would. The prologue and premise made the book seem sort of vapid and annoying but the following chapters proved that while the characters were almost certainly a little more vapid than they should have been, the book was more aware than that. I enjoyed the characters and how they intersected and even sympathized with Mack a little. However, by the last third of the book, I felt things were a little rushed. Overall, a lot of the book was just set up. I feel like there was all of this exposition and build-up for nothing. I feel like certain things  For example, Mack turning against Isabel and wanting to destroy her reputation, Isabel's decision to turn against Mack (I feel like overall a lot more could be done with Isabel), and Sabrina's storyline with Dan. could have been more developed. There were a lot of things that were never resolved  Sabrina and Dan's marriage, the whole thing with Sabrina thinking about a woman while she masturbated (which came so out of nowhere it makes me think the author put it in to seem more in touch by having a possibly gay character) her debt, and basically Katya's whole life (what happened to Victor? What project is he starting? We literally never see him again)  that could (and probably should) have been. And I'm not saying there should be a sequel, some books are better left on their own. I just feel like there are a 100 more pages or so that could have been written to let us get a larger feel for the characters. Maybe there will be a sequel, that might be why so many things are unresolved or ignored, but I hope not. This is not a sequel book. This is a book where I feel like Mack deserved to be developed more  I get that he's a not very good person but having him be a POV character and not developing him more seems odd. Even if he's pure evil, which seems doubtful, there has to be more to him. and where Isabel should have been a POV character due to her importance in the story. Overall, I enjoyed this book. It was good. But I think it could have been great, which is what bothers me.

I've read this for my next book club meeting, and the two study questions I've prepared are, first: Why did Wharton, writing in 1920, go so far back in history (1870) for her satire of fashionable New York society? There is every indication that the absurd conventions of this society had all but disintegrated by the end of the story (set a generation later), so there isn't the justification that their soul-inhibiting effects are continuing. Second, it seems to me that behind the obvious satire of societal conventions is Jack Archer's romantic view of life with which he opposes his stifling milieu. Does he not pursue a relationship with the Countess Oblenski only because conventional values are so deeply imbedded in his psyche? Or is he also afraid that his romantic fantasy would dissolve if subjected to the strictures of a real relationship? This latter explanation is clearly indicated, but I wonder if Wharton was aware of it. It also explains why at the end Jack refuses to go with his son to see the Countess: he wants to keep his romantic memory intact. To see the Countess aged twenty years, and be confronted with the possibility of a further relationship are untenable to his romantic sensibility.

I loved following Russell on all of the threads and trusting that she would resolve them. I felt almost weightless as I read this, with the supernatural elements and how completely I was willing to suspend my disbelief. This willing suspension of disbelief reminded me of reading Calvino. However  I was super disappointed when she decided to leave it ambiguous as to whether there were supernatural elements. I felt like the whole book deflated when we discover there is no Underworld, the Bird Man is a pedophile, and Ossie may just be crazy. I wish that she had resisted the urge to bring it all crashing down at the end. It felt like she broke the cardinal rule: Never end a story with: "It was all just a dream." I also really didn't like that Ava lost the bundle of clothes that would have settled the question as to whether the supernatural was real. Was Mama Weeds a hallucination? I hate that Russell took the "easy out" of ambiguity. I felt like the whole narrative was so courageous and brave and then to bring it all crashing down like that felt lazy. . It still gets 4 stars because I loved 90% of the book.

So I have a lot of mixed feelings... Strengths: - Sora's narrative voice was very well-written; the simplicity helped it a lot in terms of emotional power - It's always nice to have a heartwarming story of friendship and family in YA - The last two chapters were really moving; I appreciated how the ending tackled a difficult issue, and the fact it did so reflected Sora's agency and POV rather than a let's-turn-him-into-an-object-of-pity kind of route, BUT... Weaknesses: - Whilst the ending worked for me, I had issues with how it got there. The ending involves assisted suicide, but the way Sora came to that decision was rushed and poorly executed. - The internet chatroom thing felt forced and unrealistic - Kito and Mai spoke and acted in a way that seemed a lot younger than seventeen-year-olds - I can't speak for the depiction of Japan but there were some issues with language, e.g. using English curses (doesn't make sense to do so if they're Japanese living in Japan), that felt mishandled. As a sidenote: the audiobook narrator doesn't pronounce some of the Japanese words/names properly either, so I'd recommend the paperback over this if you're planning to read it (it would also makes the internet chatroom scenes easier to get through)

This book is a must-read if you are a fan of costume dramas, Jane Austen, 19th Century England, parasols, or steampunk alongside vampires & werewolves. Soulless takes place sometime in the mid to late 1800's in an alternate version on London, England. One where vampire nests & werewolf packs have their place in society. Alexia Tarabotti is a half-Italian spinster with no soul, which makes her a "preternatural" - someone with the inborn ability to neutralize the supernatural. After being attacked by a mysterious rogue vampire at a high-society function, Alexia finds herself under scrutiny by London's supernatural set. Why are some supernaturals disappearing and strange vampires with no knowledge of ettiquite suddenly appearing? And why are they dressed so unbecomingly? And why did they have to upset the tea tray with the treacle tart?

Actual rating: 2.5 stars I received an ARC from the publisher in exchange for an honest review. Review originally posted on my blog, Turning Pages. When I first heard of this book, I was intrigued by the plot immediately. I had such high hopes for it. But I was left overall feeling underwhelmed by most of the plot despite liking the sweet romance. I had high hopes this book would be good fantasy where the protagonist has a power she's hiding in a world that hates those with magic. Unfortunately, the fantasy aspect of the book is underwhelming to me. The idea that non-magic people discriminate against those who have magic is a rather obvious metaphor for discrimination in the real world and how we need to understand one another and accept one another for both our similarities and our differences. But that metaphor only really pays off in two scenes: one in which Mare realizes that the Recusants just follow a different religion than the main religion of the kingdom; the second in which the prince realizes he needs to be more accepting and open-minded. Other than that, the factor of magic doesn't add much to the plot aside from some angst. The book is concerned with politics as well. I find it interesting that in a world where women are just as welcome as guards,and in positions of power as men that Denna and Mare are expected to conform to "traditional female roles". I find that to be perhaps a little inconsistent. I liked that it was normalized to have no gender bias in the workplace, if you will. Because that's how it should be in reality too. So why must Denna fight to be a useful royal if there are women in the government? Why must Mare fight to be taken seriously simply because she prefers horses and spying over parties? And, sadly, the story does pit women a bit against each other. Thankfully, as Denna and Mare get to know each other they realize their assumptions about one another are wrong, but the same can't be said for the rest of the female courtiers who are reduced to the cliche of vain women. The aspect of the book I enjoyed the most is the sweet romance. Denna and Mare start out as reluctant acquaintances, then once they begin trying to solve the murder case and spend even more time together, they begin to be friends and allies. From there, they grow to care about one another, to be attracted to one another, and to love one another. I liked the slower progression of their romance - no fear of insta-love here - because it allowed for the characters to be more than one dimensional. Also, it made the ending that much more of a victory and that much happier. In this book, sexuality isn't even an issue. The only thing that threatens to keep them apart is the fact that Denna's betrothal to Thandi is a political one and she doesn't want to let her family and the kingdom down by breaking it. But she quickly comes to learn that what really matters in life isn't making everyone else happy, but rather choosing your own path and happiness. Also she ends up saving them anyway . If only the rest of the book had held up to this, then it would have been a more enjoyable read. Of Fire and Stars is a diverse fantasy novel which had a lot of potential but ultimately the overarching political and magical plot kind of let the story down. There are some inconsistencies and unanswered questions that make that story underwhelming. The romance between two princesses, however, is lovely.

A possible spoiler alert, in the form of a question, to share: Anyone else puzzling about the "Charlie Tango" helicopter crash? Considering that Christian Grey tracked Ana Steele -- via her cell phone -- to that bar in a matter of minutes, my plausibility meter pinned when none of Grey's highly-paid security wizards could track the helicopter, "Charlie Tango?" Seriously, eyeroll? Even I, a non-gazillionaire, can track a plane via publicly-available websites, e.g., FlightAware, if one knows the vehicle's tail number? This question falls under the category of what some clever movie reviewer once identified as a  refrigerator thought. Why  refrigerator thought? So, you've just returned home from the movies, you're standing at the fridge deciding what to eat since the movie popcorn didn't really constitute dinner: you stand there, with the fridge door open, puzzling through the movie's plot points. And somewhere, there is a disconnect, something that says to you, "Nah, no way Jason Bourne could NOT have figured that out.." That's a  refrigerator thought. No one in the world of Grey Holdings could track the downed helicopter, nor trace either Christian Grey's or Roz Bailey's phones pings? I mean, come on? Okay, okay.. I'm expecting comparable precision to a Jason Bourne movie. I know. Silly me. Haul out the floggers. That is all. LOL Fifty Shades Darker

I was really excited for this book. The blurb, the authors, the hot cover all seemed to guarantee a perfect 5-star read. Honestly, I would have rated it five red hearts. I enjoyed it. I laughed at some of the scenes. I felt bad for both main characters for some scenes too. However, there were just some issues that I had a hard time getting over. The first part of the book was amazing. The pacing was fast. From the main characters meeting, to them traveling together, to them being friends, and then falling in love and all that. When the love affair ended, everything went downhill from there. The moment it was revealed what happened, I felt sorry for the hero. When he did everything to win the girl back, I cheered for him, and I wanted to bitchslap the girl 50 times. I just couldn't support her stringing him along and her boyfriend too. I mean, she keeps saying that she did not want to cheat on a good man. Hello, everything she did the moment Chance came back was already cheating, maybe not the physical sex kind of cheating, but it was still cheating in every freaking book. I am not against cheating. What I am against is the hypocrisy. Not wanting to cheat but doing it and not even admitting to it. Wanting to keep the hero but not wanting to let go of the boyfriend. Keeping the hero a secret but spending a lot of time with him, even giving him a key to her house. The heroine did many other things that I don't think I'd care to mention because it will just waste my time. Bottom line, this book and this story that started out so great and so promising just didn't cut it for me in the end. I mean, it even got as far as me not caring if they ended up together. Honestly, I wanted the hero to give up and move on and break the heroine's heart all over again, just so she'll know exactly what she lost. I am still going to give it a three because I did like it. I liked the first half of it. I just wish it was played out better after that.

Still the same kooky science but I respect the entertainment value of this book. I cringed at all the wanton destruction of historical buildings (mostly blowing church doors away and toppling a shelf of precious texts). The timeline was very unrealistic (it all happens in less than 24 hours) but otherwise every bit a page turner. It still irks me how every character, despite being distinguished minds of some sort, are quick to jump to conclusions and make crazy leaps of logic. Still it was a good read and much better written than his most recent two books.

An adorable romance that will be perfect for the summer. Wilamena Carlisle might not have her mom anymore, but she does have her hobby of reading the stars. Wil learned at an early age what a bad match could be- her parents are a perfect example since she's never met her dad. She only has twenty-two days to find her perfect match and since she's barely had a relationship before, time is running out. Needing some time alone to think and be closer to the stars, Wil finds herself at her usual spot, the old, dilapidated Carlisle water tower. She's been up here too many times to count but never has anyone tried to rescue her before, which is how she winds up in the hospital (bruised, nothing broken) and a business card with the name of a bar and Grant Walker, her rescuer. She remembers the brown eyed boy and decides to say thank you. While at the club, Wil takes the opportunity to ask every boy she encounters his birthday. She has a feeling about this night and finding the one. She doesn't need to look any further because Seth, the familiar gorgeous looking boy talking to her happens to not only be the right sign but has the exact birthdate she needs for it to be a perfect match. Agreeing to go out with him, Wil and Seth develop feelings for one another, and is determined that he is the one, even if she has these tiny, niggling feelings for someone else. Particularly guitar playing Grant Walker, Seth's older brother and absolute worst star match. Let the confusion ensue, especially for Wil, who is a not used to listening to her heart, just the stars. Both boys have feelings for her, but she is stubbornly holding onto Seth as the one she picks until one night at a party. An error in judgment (or brother to be more specific) forces her to realize the truth about how she feels. This realization doesn't come without some serious problems, anger, disappointment, and regret. Wil's foray into love isn't perfect or pretty, but it's worth it. Supporting characters were well written and adorable. Definitely some swoony boys, too!

A really lovely contemporary romance with a fun pretend relationship theme. Very good character driven love story without the angst. I like that the hero is finding himself. I laughed out loud several times! A great way to spend the day!

Randi Rhodes is the only child of author Herb Rhodes, the mastermind behind the great detective series staring Glenn Street; so it isn't surprising that Randi herself aspires to be a great detective. After the passing of her mother, and her father giving up his writing for a while; they move to the small town of Deer Creek where a mystery has occurred, the time-capsule has gone missing. Randi is determined to show her father that she is no longer a baby and that she can help the town solve this crazy misdeed. I have to say, this middle grade book pleasantly surprised me. It was full of adventure, a great strong female character who likes having a black belt and doesn't want to be pink and frilly, and a great cast of characters overall. The plot was fun and fast paced and a middle grade reader would definitely enjoy this book. To make it even more awesome there is an appendix of Ninja Detective things to do along with the book: like how to spy, make a casting of a footprint, and there is even a place to login on a computer and become part of the ninja detective team. This interactive aspect is really building on what middle grade readers like with their books. Overall, I found the book easy to read and enjoyable. I think both boys and girls in the middle grade range would also love it!

Perhaps I shouldn't have waited to so long to read the last 5 chapters, because now I can't adequately summarize what amazing things happened this book! Of course, there is kick-assery and mythical demons, which is what my bookworm life runs on. Ashyn and Moria are frustrated. After relating all the events that happened in Edgewood and Fairview, they are now sitting at the imperial palace day after day, waiting for Emperor Tatsu to give the okay for a rescue mission for the remainder of their village. Moria, naturally unable to sit still, finds a companion in the imperial bastard prince Tyrus. Ashyn is also restless from this inactivity, which is exacerbated by the fact that Ronan refuses to see her. When finally Moria and Ashyn are able to leave the capital to negotiate peace terms at Fairview, they are confronted with a horrifying sight. Fairview has become a ghost town, riddled with dead bodies, with no sign of Alvar Kitsune's men or any resident of Fairview or Edgewood. Once again, the girls must go on a journey to find the children. But where the children are, Alvar Kitsune is. And where Alvar Kitsune is, Gavril will presumably be present as well. When the twins are betrayed once again, a dreadful rumor surfaces in the kingdom and the girls and Prince Tyrus must travel as fugitives from the kingdom to continue their journey and clear their names. I'm still hooked. This series is amazing. I wasn't expecting Moria to find Tyrus as a potential love interest again, and I'm honestly not sure how this is going to last. Is this going to last Vampire Academy style, when Rose dates Adrian to try to get over Dimitri (but then eventually gets back together with Dimitri again)? Or is this going to be Throne of Glass style when Celaena falls in love with Chaol (after a flirtation with Dorian, who is the first person she is interested in after the brutal murder of Sam), but then leaves him for her (apparently) Fae mate Rowan? The only reason I'm contemplating this relationship, is because of Throne of Glass. Because after the first book, even though the main character has split from the love interest, the general formula for these things end with the main character getting back together with that first love. Throne of Glass changed that, because the first real love you meet in the first book is Chaol. But Celaena doesn't stay with Chaol, she takes up the name Aelin again and finds her true love Rowan. That digressed a lot...but I hope my argument is acceptable. Something I wish this book did a little better would be giving more insight into Alvar Kitsune's character. We get the general sense he's a bad guy, and we hear a rumor that Emperor Tatsu actually framed Alvar Kitsune (for the crime that got him exiled to the Edgewood), but we don't really get a sense of the evil guy himself. He doesn't have a lot of dialogue, which is a given since Moria is essentially a prisoner and is being paraded around like a trophy by Alvar, but we don't see the man himself doing things. We see his soldiers being idiotic, his mercenaries spreading rumors, and his son being duplicitous. Alvar's defeat would be much more sound and satisfying if Armstrong makes him show himself in the next book.

I felt this book was a bit of a let down. It took seemingly forever to get to the climax and then it was, rather... anticlimactic. Both this book and the last seemed to be in a rush to gloss over a few years - ooh, a fight and suddenly two years later... I had hoped for more from the intervention of the Chamber, and as a romantic at heart while I was happy to see Cleon go, I was sad they didn't even leave it with a flicker, unless you count Dom, which isn't much of one. At least she didn't do something bizarre like kill off Buri and set her up with Raoul, but really now...   For a normally good author, I was extremely disappointed.

I was going to give this three stars, but because I'm content with the ending and because I can't bear to give a three star rating for any book in this series, I'll give it four stars ;) There was a whole lot going on, and some things just didn't seem right to me. Some questions I have are still not answered. Like, what did the Commander give as his answer at the end (because I really want to know! xD), and why is it that Yelena and Leif have such powerful magic when their parents don't! What I found especially annoying was that at the beginning everything of the previous books was summarized. When a name would pop up, there would be some information on what he/she had done in the previous books or what they were like. At first this is very helpful, but I think it is reasonable to expect your readers to have read the previous books and still remember some of the things that happened in them. At one point it felt unnecessary to summarize certain characters again, and it chopped up the main storyline. I feel like what was set up in book one, Ixia and all its characters that belong there (including Valek, Ari and Janco), seemed to me lost in the second and third book. True, we go back to Ixia in the third book, but only briefly. It definitely wasn't to my satisfaction. Things I didn't understand:  Tauno's betrayel? Why? The fight between Valek and Yelena? I don't get it. (especially not why they didn't talk for so long) Cahil and his weird actions... True, it was explained, but I felt it just wasn't like him. Ferde, well, that sure was over fast...? I felt like he should have played a bigger role in this book, or his storyline should have been ended in the second book. Why can people sense Yelena's magic if she uses it, but why can't she feel them? Would sure saved her a lot of trouble. Maybe it's just not in her skill range, but I feel like it's a general thing? (maybe that's just it, she also wasn't able to light fire :o) Enough complaining, on to the fun stuff! ;) Can we please talk about Kiki? I love that horse! (don't love the name, but that's just because of personal experiences xD)I love her cryptic comments and that she has a magical element to her. I did also really like the idea of the bat. I just found it very funny that it was suddenly there and just chillin' on her back or hangin' around on Kiki. Ari and Janco! I love them! Every time they appear in a scene, it just makes it so much more fun. Especially Janco with his funny remarks. I have a natural love for this series. I LOVED the first book. It is definitely, in my opinion, the best book of all three. The second one I also enjoyed, but the third one kind of disappointed me. The series overall is just great, and that's also why I couldn't bear to give Fire Study only three stars. It was a very enjoyable read, but I didn't get as much out of it as I wanted.

Holy fuck, that was a billion times better than the first volume. This was way more what I was hoping for with the Fairest series. Lauren Beukes' writing is great--I like it better than Bill Willingham's in a lot of ways, and I thought Inaki Miranda's art was actually a lot better than a lot of the other artwork in FABLES (more consistent with characters' faces, better at drawing women's bodies, in my opinion). I was pleasantly surprised to find out that Rapunzel isn't strictly hetero and really enjoyed the inclusion of Japanese Fables in this volume. One of my only criticisms is that  I feel like it's way too common for typically hetero female characters to have one lesbian relationship and it's always with a woman who turns out to be evil. Also, I didn't like/didn't understand why Rapunzel and Tomoko couldn't be together at the end of the story. Rapunzel's mother telling Joel to help her erase Rapunzel's memory of Toyko and Tomoko didn't sit right with me. It felt like a convenient way for the writers to bury the lesbian plot and have Rapunzel end up with Joel, the less controversial suitor. Maybe I'm totally wrong and there will be more homosexuality later in the series that disproves this theory; I certainly hope so. In any case, I hope we get to see more from Lauren Beukes in the future. Her writing was a change the series direly needed to hold my interest.

Well, I was at least halfway done writing this and then my computer decided to restart for updates, so I have to start all over. FUN! *deep breath* Anyway, I'm not 100% sure how I feel about this book. It was definitely interesting... But hard to read without constantly comparing it to or thinking of it as the original. For instance, I kept forgetting about the gender swap. Like, I read the story as Bella until something reminded me that she was really Beau. And I kept having to think about who was whom. It was like I was translating Eleanor into Emmett and Earnest into Esme, etc. I probably wasn't supposed to be doing that, but there it is. This book would probably benefit from a second reading. I really want to read a review by someone who hasn't read Twilight... I think that Bella and Edward should have been the only characters who were swapped. I think the story would have been way less confusing and distracting that way, and would have seemed more natural. I just had a really hard time with the gender-swapped Cullens. I could buy Carine as the doctor, but big strong Eleanor was hard to picture. And I kept imagining Archie in a white tank top and sagging jeans (because of the petit frame and buzzed hair, I guess), which did not at all endear him to me. Many of the names seemed weird to me too. I remember reading something about Meyer looking at old census information to find names for her characters that would work for the time periods they were born into and it really didn't seem like she was that thoughtful about their gender-swapped names. Beau and Edythe, I was fine with, but Royal is a very modern name, so I wasn't buying that he was a super-old vampire. It was interesting to me what Meyer felt the need to change about the protagonist along with the gender. As a male adaptation of Bella, Beau retains her housekeeping skills and her disinterest in cars, but dumps Jane Austen for Jules Verne. I don't see the need for the author swap. I had a male friend in high school who enjoyed Pride and Prejudice (and Twilight) and it's not like he was a feminine guy or anything. Beau Swan is definitely the kind of guy who could appreciate Jane Austen. As for a few other changes... I'm glad that Meyer changed the "Do I dazzle you?" conversation. That always made me cringe. And I thought it was interesting that she continued to call the Quileutes "werewolves" even though she reveals in Breaking Dawn that they are really just shapeshifters. But I kind of hated that she changed the sparkling thing because I felt like she was giving in to the people who've ridiculed her books. I'm not a huge fan of the sparkling, myself, but I feel like it makes sense. Definitely more so than the vague rainbow effect she changed it to. I love the quote "I drifted to sleep with her cold body in my arms." That cracked me up. Suddenly, Beau is a psychotic killer who sleeps with the corpses of his victims. XD The ending seemed rushed to me, but I'm not sure if that's because it was actually rushed or if it's just because I'm used to waiting for three more books for the protagonist to become a vampire. I am glad that ending was explored, especially since Renesmee wasn't an option in this version. But I'm glad it's not the actual ending, because my heart broke for Charlie and Renee. Next, I have a few comments that probably apply to the original books as well: So, I know that Edythe/Edward and Beau/Bella were Love at First Sight and everything, but Edythe giving up on trying to stay away from Beau after, like, a day doesn't make sense to me. First, one day should be nothing to someone who's been alive for more than 36,500 of them. Second, Meyer told us in the original series that vampires take a while to change and grow attached to someone. Third, Edythe is so uber cautious and protective of Beau that she should have held out longer before giving up. It just doesn't make sense to me. A few more things that didn't make sense to me: As smart as the vampires are and despite the fact that they live with a doctor, they still believe that one gets sick from being cold... You don't get sick from being cold. Just FYI. It was mentioned a couple of times that Edythe became paler than usual when she was scared, but that should be impossible because she doesn't have any blood... Meyer even says in the original series that vampires can't blush. Shouldn't the opposite be true as well? Edythe asks where Archie and Jess are when they are in the near vicinity and she can read minds. I also had the thought while reading this book that Edythe is always being super careful not to accidentally pulverize Beau's femur or whatever, but the vampires do things regularly like play piano and close car doors that require them to control their super strength unless they want to go on daily shopping trips for pianos and cars. So it seems like they shouldn't have that much trouble being gentle with humans. And one last thing. I definitely wouldn't buy this book as a dual copy with Twilight. I already have a copy of Twilight and I don't want to carry around two huge books when I'm only reading one. Is this really the only option? Will there ever be a single copy? The world may never know!

Hard to believe it, but McGarry ups the plot melodrama even more than in the previous 3 books in the series. Underneath all the soap opera, though, are some interesting questions about gender, especially masculinity, in a culture where toughness reigns: "If it does come down to you and Matt in the cage, if he hands his ass to you, will Matt be right? Can you stand to look the girl you care for in the eye knowing that in public her ex proved he's stronger than you? And the issue of boys being protective of their girls vs. allowing said girls to make their own choices, which had been a strong theme throughout the series, continues here. The characters of West and Haley are well, if briefly, drawn, and serve as good foils to one another--an emotional, impulsive person vs. a person who has to think things out. Having the girl be the physically stronger, more successful fighter was a nice twist. Could have done without the constant "I have to lie/not tell the entire truth in order to protect you" thing, which both West and Haley do throughout the book. Ah, but without the secrets, we'd have no melodrama, would we?

I really enjoyed this book- it felt very "Howl's Moving Castle" to me, and in the end the author does thank Hayao Miyazaki for making stories that inspire her. The author did a great job crafting a world I could picture in my mind. The characters all felt real, and I really liked the main characters Jessamin and Finn. I could picture the town, the island of Melei, the accents of Melei and Alben and all of the magical things that happen. The magic itself was creative, felt real, and was easy to imagine. The ending just left some questions for me. In the end, Jessamin burns the book that contains all of the magical knowledge of one of the two lines of magic. The two lines stay peaceful because of the threat of mutual destruction if they were to wage war on each other. The evil Lord Downpike was trying to get the book, to learn both systems of magic and be all powerful. I was left wondering- was that the only book of knowledge for that other line? If so , wouldn't that effectively leave them powerless? If not, why didn't Finn just destroy it earlier or move it back to his relatives on that side and end Lord Downpike's obsession with him and Jessamin? And now is Finn, because he doesn't have access to that magic, much weaker? I don't think any of these are really critical questions to the book or it's ending, but I was just curious. I was also wondering why Finn's shadow disappears at the end when he's presumed dead. And also, if Lord Downpike was simply after the book his parents had, why did their murders seem personal? I would have been interested if there was some history there between them. In the end, I really enjoyed this book and would highly recommend a read.

Things I enjoyed: I loved the strong familial bonds between Auggie, his parents, and his sister, and I liked how almost every character had at least one redeeming moment. Even Julian gets a hint at a better future, when the precept he sends his teacher the summer before he starts at a new school is, "Sometimes it's good to start over." I know that Julian was not at all sympathetic, but I always prefer it when villains--if you can call a ten-year-old boy a villain--have a chance at redemption. I liked the optimistic outlook, and I liked the way the different POVs meshed together to form an interesting, three-dimensional story. There were only a couple of things I didn't like. One of them was that the book kind of bashed you over the head with its message, but since it seems this is an MG book and not the YA book I was expecting, I guess I can forgive a bit of non-subtlety (which isn't to say that you can't write an MG book with a subtle message, but it's not really expected as much as it is in YA and adult fiction). The other thing I didn't like was, unfortunately, the ending. I was feeling good enough about this book that I expected to end it on a high emotional note, and while I did walk away from it feeling contemplative and, overall, pretty happy, the ending fell rather flat for me. Frankly, Auggie's winning the award just didn't ring true the way most of the rest of the book did. It felt... false, almost. I feel a little bad saying that, because Auggie is an admirable character, but let me explain. The award he won was the "Henry Ward Beecher medal to honor students who have been notable or exemplary in certain areas throughout the school year," and the passage the principal uses to explain his giving the award to Auggie is this: "He is the greatest whose strength carries up the most hearts by the attraction of his own." The way I see it, this refers to the way Auggie's courage and kindness had a profoundly positive influence on all of his classmates. Except... that didn't happen. Don't get me wrong; Auggie was a brave, considerate, and endearing character, and I was impressed with how well he dealt with his situation. But only a few of his classmates were actually influenced by him--by who he was--and, when that happened, he was just as influenced by their strength of character as they were by his. And yes, by the end of the book the majority of his classmates were feeling more kindly toward him, but that was mostly because of his run-in with the seventh graders at the nature retreat, which gave him and his classmates a common enemy--it made them feel as if he was one of them, and that one of them was being attacked by an outsider--and in which he, frankly, didn't actually do anything outstanding. So, in the end, it seemed to me as if Auggie was given the award for what he was--a kid with a facial deformity who's had a rough time of it--and not who he was. And that, frankly, seems like a total departure from everything the book was very thorough in trying to teach us. Maybe other people interpret this scene differently, and that's fine, but that's the way it came off to me. Furthermore--and this probably isn't true for a lot of people--I don't like it when the high point of a book consists of the main character gaining the approval of the masses. It would have felt a lot more satisfying and fulfilling to me if the ending was focused on Auggie looking around and seeing the small group of people who, over the course of the book, have learned to truly love him for who he is, instead of a bunch of people applauding him because the tides of popular opinion have turned in his favor (or is that just me being cynical?). This way just... didn't seem to live up to the rest of the story. Overall, though, I did quite like this book, and if I ever see it sitting on a bookstore shelf when I have a few extra dollars in my pocket, I'll be sure to grab it for my collection.

I had originally started this book a while ago but I couldn't get into it the first time around. When I started it this time, I was much more invested in finishing it. This book was good in that it was about a trans girl and was written by a trans woman so yay for #ownvoices and for diversity. But I didn't really feel like this book was all that special or something that will really stick with me. I'm not sure if it's just that I'm very close to a lot of trans people and I hear their stories a lot and I know a lot about trans people and their struggles, but I just didn't find this book to be informative or to open my eyes to anything. I already knew a lot of the issues the main character struggled with even if I didn't experience them personally so this book didn't really provide me with new insight about trans people and transphobia and transmisogyny. This book was decent and it is very important, especially in today's world when so many trans people finally feel comfortable coming into the light. It's also a good book in that it's written by a trans woman so you know that this isn't just someone trying to check off the diversity box or anything. I think people should read this because it shows publishers and writers that we want to hear these stories and it's a useful book for those who don't have a lot of experience, knowledge, or association with trans people and their struggles. I just didn't really feel like this book did much for me.
