The Princess and the Guard - 4.5 stars This was about Winter and Jacin, from their childhood to when he becomes a guard at the palace. I really liked their interactions, so cute and genuine. The Little Android - 4 stars This was a cool and refreshing Little Mermaid retelling. I didn't particularly love the ending, but the overall plot was nice. The Mechanic - 5 stars Very short by very sweet story of the first encounter between Cinder and Prince Kai. I got a bit of insta-love feels, but this didn't take away from it. Something Old, Something New - 4 stars Lovely and cute! From the title you can guess there's going to be a wedding, but you don't know whose... I really hoped for Thorne and Cress's wedding, but it's Scarlet and Wolf's. Still cute, but I don't really have strong feeling for those two, so I was not particularly involved in the story.

I actually liked this book more than I thought I would. I don't remember much of the first book, and perhaps I should have refreshed my memory first, but I didn't have such a great wish to. I do remember being very disappointed in it, mainly because of the (what I saw as) cheesy and cringey romances - and instalove - that happened with not one but two pairs of characters, as well as Karou's irritating insta-language capabilities. However, the language thing I had mainly forgotten in this book, thank god, and the romance was not as bad. Saying that, I still was not completely convinced about the romance. I was glad that Mik and Zuzana had some real substance; Mik being angry at Karou and protective and caring of Zuzana when they came to the 'sandcastle'. I was also glad that Akiva and Karou were not together. I really dislike Akiva, especially with his repeat of creepy watching-Karou-sleep. Okay, Edward! It's even worse than the last time, because this time she knows what he did to her family and she has told him, on no uncertain terms, to stay away! Also, the whole book would have been better if Karou's constant thinking of Akiva, and Akiva's constant whining about Karou had just been left out. Because it sucked, and Akiva is a dick, and I couldn't feel sorry for him. I am so mad that it looks like they are going to get back together! No! Ziri is like, a billion times better. I feel like I just completely dislike the romance and how it is written in this series. The characters, also. Reading Zuzana's emails in the beginning was awful; I thought that her voice was so unrealistic for a person who is almost - if not already - an adult! Even when Karou met her in person, some of the things she said ... I was just wondering, what the hell!? Do people actually talk and act like this? Would you really go to eat in a room full of literal monsters who your friend basically warned might kill you? Probably not, unless you're fucking stupid. As well as Zuzana, the angels. They themselves are so annoying. Hazazel, or whatever, was okay but then he - one of the only good angels that were prominent characters - fucking died! . To be honest, back when I thought I was asexual I only started to read this series because I heard that Liraz was an asexual character, but it doesn't really work for me because she is not just asexual, she is pretty much just cold all round. I don't mind so much anymore, and I don't really mind Liraz (though I don't particularly like her), but it is still annoying nonetheless. Akiva is the worst and I hate him, and not in the 'I hate him, but he's interesting and well written that way on purpose' way, like for example Heathcliff (I'm reading Wuthering Heights at the moment). I really do hate him in a way the author did not intend, and I am not quite sure why, but I do. Maybe because he is so whiny! All the time! The angels, Jael and his brother, as well as the Chimaera White Wolf Thiago and Ten; they were all too obvious as villains. It is so obvious from the beginning that Thiago is still just a massive asshole, and it's also the same for Jael. Like, blah, why can't things be a bit less black and white? Sure, there's Akiva ... His snivelling and sad reason for having killed Karou's entire family is well ... his grief. Boo hoo. I can't complain much more. My main issue is the romance and characters - mainly Akiva - it seems. There are smaller things that annoy me, such as the random characters that did not seem to serve much purpose - the guard, what was up with his chapters? - or who did serve a purpose but that we never found out what happened to them! Like, what happened to Seiva, or whatever her name was, the fleeing villager, and the people she was with? Did I miss something? I was disappointed that there was much less art description, but I realise that this is not an art focussed book so, whatever. However, I did like Karou. I also liked the Shadows That Live a lot. I really liked the description of the setting. That 'sandcastle' sounds brilliant, although also ultra bad obviously. I'd have loved even more description of scenery, the resurrections etc. but that's just me. Perhaps one day I will read the last book in the trilogy.

You know, I don't even think I'm going to bother writing an actual review of this book, because it's clearly amazing. I mean, come on, Brian Selznick has got some serious chops, his drawings are beautiful, and he does so much with relatively few words. Everybody should check this one out -- it's pretty much breathtaking and easy to get through in one setting (make a pot of tea first for optimal excellentness.) One thing I do want to point out this that this book features some awesome deaf characters -- a gentle reminder to me that diversity 1) oh yeah is super important and 2) involves a whole more than skin color -- three cheers for diversity that includes different socio-economic classes, body types, lifestyle choices, disabilities, family types, personality types...

I'll start by telling you about the day I found this book. It was a humid and hot Summer day, my co-worker in the guesthouse I volunteer at woke me up and said "Hey, a guesthouse near-by got sold, if we go now, they will let us take their sheets and their pillows." Sheets and pillows? Well, that's what she took. When we walked in, she went directly to the rooms to start collecting everything we could need in our guesthouse. But, let me tell you, guesthouses are like treasure chambers for things that people left behind. I didn't follow her. Instead, I walked to the living room and stood in front of the bookshelf with a big bag. They had more books than we did, and I was a bit jealous of that. I'm going to quote one of my favorite sentences in this book; " Standing around books, even books in a foreign language, you feel a kind of electricity buzzing up toward you." If you are using Goodreads, I guess you can feel this as well when you are near books. I walked off the guesthouse with my bag full of books. If you are curious, I'll tell you some of them: The White Tiger, The Outsiders, The Whistling Season, a Chinese edition of Twilight, The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet's Nest, and The Celestine Prophecy were some of them. Back in our guesthouse, I placed the newcomers in our bookshelves - let me confess that I love classifying books. But "The White Tiger" was the last one in the pile, and didn't fit there now that the other books have found its place. I looked at it for a couple minutes - an Indian entrepreneur and murderer writes to Wen Jiabao? It's not the type of book I usually read. I was going to leave it somewhere else, when it hit me: I was traveling to Osaka for a few days, and I would need a book with me during the boring times in the subway, the train and the flight! I didn't give it a second thought, and I left the book in my backpack. I'm glad I didn't think more about it. Even thought I enjoyed every single page of this book, it still doesn't seem interesting to me. I told you why I decided to read the book, and now I will tell you why did I gave it 4 stars out 5. The premise of the book reads "Meet Balram Halwai, the 'White Tiger': servant, philosopher, entrepreneur, murderer..." This is actually a good summary for the book. He IS a servant, he IS a philosopher, he IS an entrepreneur, and, yeah, he IS a murderer. (If you've read this book, you will probably agree with me saying he is more guilty of murdering his family, than Mr Ashok.) This is a book about Munna, an Indian kid that didn't even deserve a proper name (Munna means 'boy'), improving his life till the Present: he owns a company, has a real name and money. This is not a pleasant book to read if you are expecting to read about the beauty of India. It pictures the society as a Rooster coop. And it represents the people as dirty - I would even say sometimes he writes about 'the poor' as if they were animals. More than once I surprised myself disgusted for what I read in "The White Tiger." And this hatred towards Indians (which I believe is deliberate) is the reason I took a star off this book. The rest of this book, my fellow readers, is a jewel. This is the success story of an animal who became a man, but also of a man who became an animal. A kid with no morals, learns about life and what is wrong, and what is right. A kid with dreams of walking out of the Darkness and finding a place in the Light. Ironic as it is, the kid, now an adult, realized that to live in the Light, he has to walk in darkness. He has to chose what is wrong, instead of what is right. 'The White Tiger" pictures a corrupt society, and the unpleasant ways to survive it. I met someone who read the book, they told me "if this is real, the Indian society is fucked up." I must say, the society we find in this book, may be as well similar to the one we all live in. There's always people in the bottom, people on top. People in the bottom trying to climb to the top. People in the top falling - no parachute - into the bottom. Why is that? Money. I've read this book, and now is back in the bookshelf in the guesthouse. My eyes look for it every once in a while - I find myself thinking about the book, sometimes. I wonder if I could pay the price to get in the Light, but then I remember, I am not a White Tiger. Do you want to know what it means to be a White Tiger? If you do, I recommend you to read this book. I actually recommend this book to everyone, as long as you are not a hardcore India-lover; you will find nothing good about India between the pages of "The White Tiger."

Don't get me wrong, I love Stephen King novels and I've been reading them since the 7th grade. But Cujo definitely isn't one of my favorites. It's boring as heck and lacking in the originality and detailed imagery of King's novels like Pet Sematary Dolores Claiborne and It . Much of Cujo's plot focuses on a woman and her young son Tad trapped for days in a car in the middle of nowhere, with nothing going on except watching to make sure the rabies-tainted dog nearby doesn't attack them. I liked how King showed the dog's thoughts and emotions, that was really interesting. But I'm sad to say I just didn't really enjoy Cujo all that much, I'll stick with King's other novels.

This was perfectly fine, but so many of my friends LOVED it, and I was so eager to read it after making myself wait for it (because after all, I'm not supposed to buy books in 2015... except when kobo has a 50% sale, apparently), that I couldn't help feeling a bit let down. I feel bad saying that, because this was an awesome book, that clearly works for a lot of people, but I just liked The Deal so much more! (Probably because The Deal's tropes were riiiight up my alley, though.) I really liked Grace, and her babbling, and her friendships with both Ramona and Daisy. I liked how the friendship with Ramona was treated - it was toxic, but it wasn't all bad, and they both had to evolve in it, which I felt was more realistic than just saying "I will never see her again!" I liked Logan okay, though some things bugged me. I liked how he was into Hannah at the beginning, because frankly, who wouldn't be? (Did I mention I loved The Deal?) And the thing about him refusing to go pro was... like too big of a sacrifice. It didn't work for me. I liked Grace's list of romantic gestures. I really liked Logan and Morris becoming bros, heh. I liked the spark of next book between Dean and whoever that girl was at that party (Sabrina? ), wha-bam! Apparently book three is NOT about her which is a shame. Still definitely worth reading, though. Let's say it's a 3.5, really.

I'm not sure why I was surprised, considering Philip K. Dick is considered one of the classic science fiction authors, but I found myself really impressed with the writing in Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep. I went into the work knowing it is completely different from the film Blade Runner which is somewhat inspired by this story. I've been trying to branch out and read more science fiction but I tend to be more interested in character based stories which isn't common in science fiction. I tried to get into this as I found the writing really impressive but I just couldn't get immersed into the story. I will definitely try and read more by the author though as I feel like this was more a "not my cuppa tea" problem than with the work itself.

I have no idea how to rate this. The plot was good. The writing was okay perhaps even "meh". The ending was a bit tidy though wasn't it? A little too convenient. Jason didn't solve the problem, it spontaneously seemed to absolve itself. Jason quite literally, walks past the problem and ignores it. . I wish Crouch spent a little more time analyzing/exploring how and why each Jason was so different  certain aspects of the plot. However, I've read a couple books that delt with this subject matter, alternate realities and parallel worlds in which several versions of a person   but none with these kinds of complexities - so that facet of the novel was an intriguing experience even though it gave me Illuminae level anxiety. In the Acknowledgements at the end of the novel, Crouch mentions that Dark Matter was already opted for a movie. And I wonder if this is why I feel so lukewarm about this novel. I didn't hate it, but I didn't love it either. Now, I wonder if that's because reading this felt like watching a movie. Movies don't have time for the little details I adore spotting in books. At the same time i feel like this was an appropiate length. I can't explain it. It just feels like something's missing. I just finished reading this on the train this morning, so maybe I'll feel differently in a day or two.

[I read this novella as part of the Hugo Voter Packet in 2012.] The spoilers listed below are only spoilers if you're unfamiliar with the Newsflesh universe; if you are familiar with that backdrop, nothing below will be any surprise (but then again, nothing in the novella will be either! This novella is actually written in a semi-similar style to the last one I read, Ken Liu's 'The Man Who Ended History', and so I jumped straight in with gusto. It's not presented as a documentary, but it's the story of several snippets of different people's lives, all of which build towards the end of the book. Countdown is a novella in the Newsflesh universe, alongside Feed, Deadline and Blackout; I don't think I'm spoiling much if I tell you that this universe is mostly preoccupied with the Rising, in which the dead rise and try to eat the living. Countdown is a compilation of stories that describe the events before Feed that lead to that occurring. The novel charts the development of the cure for cancer and the cure for the common cold which, when combined, lead to the Kellis-Amberlee virus. The Kellis-Amberlee virus has the rather nasty side-effect that, if you undergo amplification, it takes over your body - even if you're dead. This means it's the first properly sfnal treatment of zombies I've seen, which, in itself, is pretty impressive and enough to make me like the background. The novels also talk a lot about blogging and the evolution of the media, but that's not really something that the novella says much about. There is mention of the mainstream media sticking to the official, do-not-panic, zombies-aren't-real line whereas the Internet and more independent journalists are spreading a message contrary to that, but it really isn't a main theme. There is a strong message about what happens when people fuck with viruses that haven't yet been tested on humans, which, given Grant's passion for virology combined with her irritation at people who don't follow the proper procedures, is not really surprising. I found this novella to be a satisfying slice of backstory for the Newsflesh universe but also a nice piece of exposition as to how Kellis-Amberlee came about. This story really sets out, in chronological order, the events which lead to the first realistic - if that's the right word - zombie uprising. I think that's really cool, and so I came out of this tale smiling. I feel guilty that this ended up as low in my rankings as it did, but I think that's a function of the fact that nothing here is anything new in terms of the Newsflesh universe. Grant hasn't included any titbits that are critical to the plot of the trilogy, which is fair enough, since this isn't required reading for people who want to read the novels - however, that ultimately ends up hurting the novella because it means I got exactly what I expected, with no surprises or expansion of the boundaries.
I struggled through that. But ultimately I enjoyed the story.

Also posted on The Procrastinator's Corner This is the type of book that starts out weak but gradually gets stronger as the story develops. It took me two weeks and 60 pages to get on with the story as I kept dozing off in the beginning. I actually almost abandoned this but I loved For Darkness Shows the Stars and I remembered that this was how the first book started out for me as well, so I tried harder. Across A Star-Swept Sea is set on a different side of FDStS's world and as both cultures have too much differences, the world-building established in the first book was pretty much back to zero. But really, apart from the slow pacing in the beginning that involves the world-building which was a struggle to get past through, the rest of Across A Star Swept Sea flew by like a breeze. The protagonists, Justen and Persis, are characters with substance. They are both strong in their own different ways and their romance is something that was very entertaining to watch develop as they have the most opposite personalities, with Persis and her "dumb, happy and fashion-centric" self and Justen with his serious and research-focused mind. Granted, Persis was only disguising her true self but still it was almost hilarious to even think that Justen would fall for a girl like dumb-Persis. Justen wasn't totally able to bust her pretense but he did see glimpses of a smart and family-loving girl behind Persis's mask and I think it's what ultimately made her grow on him. As well, even though there were no confessions of undying love and their fake relationship never became real, their romance is as swoon-worthy with an ending that will melt you into a pile of fangirl-goo. Furthermore, I love that we get to see our favorite characters from For Darkness Shows the Stars here! I almost lost hope that I will ever see them again and it was like a dream come true having the main characters from both books interact together. I also find it ironic that Kai and Elliot made their debut kiss here and not in their own book. Justen and Persis, however, do not need another book for a debut kiss but I would love to see them in-real-love in the third book (if there's a third book).

I put off reading this because "Marvel crossover event helmed by Bendis" was basically the last thing I wanted, but then the "I want more Ms. Marvel" finally outweighed that. The crossover event was WTF?? But, um IDK if it's only me, but a lot of THIS comic read like "look, I know the crossover makes no sense, and you know too." Which helped :D Philip K. Dick-style Precrime + Marvel universe + exploding science fair?? Oookay. I read this volume really fast, and enjoyed it. But a few more things: * It would really help keep things consistent to just keep Adrian Alphona on art. In my head, it is his art that comes to mind when I think "Ms. Marvel." * The immigration-related parts were very short and felt rushed. That storyline could easily have been expanded to whole volume length. I was wondering if it was the author not feeling so comfortable with the subject matter, not being a Pakistani immigrant to the US but having a different background? I frankly found what WAS there very relatable, then again I have a yet different background (Hungarian Jewish immigrant to the US :) ). * I appreciated that Kamala REALLLLY messed something up and it had serious real-world consequences. I hope this will not be retconned away but she'll actually have to deal with the consequences. This made the book feel more weighty and have more potential for future storylines. (Plus, possible bonus visit to Wakanda in a later volume??? YES PLEASE) Yes, a book can be goofy AND serious, but many writers can't quite pull it off convincingly. I have all the hope for this. Also yay this plotline did not involve killing a character off, which would have been the lazy but all-too-common plot move. He was seriously injured, but he survived. Source of the book: Bought with my own money

Oh my goodness, the Queen is in the building! This was so good, so worth the wait, and just SO SO excellent. I have never been disappointed by the wonderful Sarah J. Maas and this book is no exception. The Throne of Glass series and world just keeps getting bigger and better, and I never once doubted that Queen of Shadows would be the highlight of my reading month. I you have not gotten your hands on this book, WHAT ARE YOU DOING WITH YOUR LIFE?!?!?!?! So I'm going to talk about a ship now. Alright, so in Heir of Fire, I was totally shipping Rowan and Aelin, and I thought it was totally implied canon, but after reading some reviews of QOS, I have come to the conclusion that it was in fact NOT implied canon, and I am just a crazy shipper who will ship two trees if I have to. I knew that before, but never quite to what extent.... But I am so happy because I was RIGHT and I'm not crazy. I just really hope this is the final ship change for Aelin, because any more will be overkill and I don't think Sarah will do that. But I am on Team Aelin and will be really sad if she doesn't end of with Rowan and protest forever totally support whoever she chooses in the end. Also, I'm totally shipping Dorian and Manon, who's with me? There really isn't anything bad to be said about this book. It was so good, and satisfied in all points. Pro tip: read the Assassin's Blade in between Heir of Fire and Queen of Shadows. You really don't need the information in Heir of Fire, but there are references to the Assassin's Blade left and right in Queen of Shadows. So make sure you do that before starting QOS. The character development of Manon was absolutely fantastic and more than I ever expected. She was never my favorite in Heir of Fire, but know I am totally a Manon supporter! Who knew witches had hearts! That showdown between Manon and Aelin was absolutely phenomenal, and I'm so glad Manon chose to save Dorian's life! It is made very clear from the first chapter that Celaena is no more, and it's Aelin now. It was a bit of an adjustment, but by the end, I was used to it. Celaena is the assassin, but Aelin is the Queen, and it is very clear. I love how Aelin now just takes charge, being the Queen she is, and i can't wait to see her in the next book. She's going to be amazing!! Her character development was so great in this book. I could literally go on for hours about the different characters, Rowan, Aedion, Chaol, Nesryn, Arobynn, Lysandra, the list goes on and on! I will summarize all of them by saying that they were all fantastic in this book and I can't wait to see what happens in the next one, and what more character development is in store for them. I can't wait for the fifth book in this series, and it's so far away! Some things I'm hoping for is for Dorian to rebuild. I really want to see him as a successful king. I am also really looking forward to seeing what Aelin does in Terrasen. I love Dorian and Aelin's friend ship, so I'm looking forward to seeing how that plays out between their two kingdoms. Who knows what crazy things we will see in the future and I can't wait! If you have not jumped on the Throne of Glass bandwagon, consider this your command to do so. You won't regret it!!

I really couldn't avoid Dark Matter much longer. The great Goodreads friends I have have carefully protected their reviews of this book with spoiler tags or have avoided spoilers altogether. But you know, it's always inevitable that when there's a book out that's as hyped as this one, you're bound to stumble upon some knucklehead who doesn't get it. So far I've been absolutely clear of spoilers (thank you, my friends) and before it's too late I had to put this at the top of my reading plans. I myself had to refrain from spoiling things during a status update at one point. I nearly exploded from the effort. Holy crap. First of all, if you haven't read Blake Crouch yet, what are you waiting for? I highly suggest reading his Pines series (Oh no, not a series! Relax, they're short and extremely compulsive) to get a good intro to his style. But this? Dark Matter is by all accounts his best work. I can't tell you a freaking thing about it. I can't talk to my wife about it; she needs to read this next (I'm urging. Every. Day.) so I can talk to her about it. Dark Matter is one of those (like his Pines) novels where the delight is in not knowing what the hell is going on, trusting the author to clear things eventually and just enjoying the ride. It's one of the best novels I've read all year. This book will mystify you, mindf*&k you, and it will  make you appreciate how lucky you are with your life and the choices that brought you here . At one point I was ready to dock a star because I thought he had lost me at one point, but later on, what I was confused about was reiterated in skillful clarity. Given the subject matter of Dark Matter, a lesser novelist could easily leave his readers in a fog, but Blake Crouch indeed made this easy to understand, and even if he hadn't it wouldn't have mattered a whole lot. The story itself moves like gangbusters. I can't say anymore about this book other than read it. Read it. A slam dunk 5-star rating, and a day later I'm still sorry it's over. Bravo, Blake. Oh, and I didn't mention that there were no signs of the gun enthusiasm that mildly irked me in his earlier works (yes, I hate guns).
This is sincerely how a trilogy should end. Absolutely phenomenal, Schwab deserves so many awards for her writing. I will miss this world, and these characters so much.

If you read the title of this book and tried to guess what "Lair of Dreams" meant or thought "That ominously dark and creepy-crawly looking subway station on the cover doesn't look so welcoming," 1) don't feel bad, you could not possibly have guessed the plot of this book and 2) you're right, that subway station is not a good sign at all. Once again, we're back in the thundering excitement of New York City in the 1920's, a city that never sleeps even when its dreaming, and everything has changed. In The Diviners, Evie and her friends started to discover their abilities and used them to defeat a ghostly serial killer. However,  Naughty John  was only the beginning. The man in the stovepipe hat has bigger plans than New York City, and in this book you see the true evil of his intentions start to unfold. If you were really annoyed with Evie's character in  The Diviners , I can't tell you that you will be very impressed by her in this book. Still dealing with the death of her brother James and the fact that she is in love with the same guy as her best friend, Evie does what she does best and ignores it all to be famous on the radio and drown her emotions in gin. And while you want to judge her and be angry with her about the way she treats people, it's also hard to ignore that deep down Evie is just lonely and hurt by the fact that her brother is dead, her Uncle tried to get rid of her after she started to trust him, Jericho won't actually try and be with her because he's wallowing in his own issues and is too afraid to pursue her, and her ability is making her see the deepest disappointments people have about their own lives. She carries this around with her all the time and hasn't exactly found a constructive way to deal with it yet, but at the end of this book we can see that she will play a role in the future that will push her to become a more responsible character, rather than one that goes with what she thinks people expect her to be in order to feel accepted. We saw at the end of the first book that she has a great amount of courage and promise, but lost herself a little in the wake of what happened at the end of Book 1 (pretty understandably). Whether you like Evie or not, the beauty of these books is that they juggle characters chapter to chapter, and stories break away and come back into the fold constantly. Evie is by far not the most important character this time. In this book we meet Ling, a girl from a family of Chinese immigrants suffering the consequences of the Chinese Exclusion Act and prejudice towards immigrants in general. She is crippled, but escapes every night to dream in a world where she can walk again. In her dreams, she can find other dream walkers and the spirits of the dead. Following her story and her struggle was one of the best aspects of this book in my opinion. She's extremely brave, honest, smart, and obviously is going to play a larger role in the future. In addition to meeting Ling, we learn more about Theta, Henry, Memphis, and Sam in this book and gain a greater understanding of how their powers have affected their lives. What I like most about these books is that each character is made so  real  that you understand each of them completely from their experiences and stories. Slowly throughout the book, you get pieces of each character that fit together with one another, and in the end you are left with the outline of a puzzle that will (hopefully) be filled in a little more by the end of the next book. In particular, Evie needs to figure out who she is before she tries to pick Sam or Jericho, Henry needs something AMAZING to happen to him because losing Louis in this book was HEARTBREAKING, Memphis needs to heal Ling's legs because she is flawless and doesn't deserve anything that has happened to her, and Theta needs to trust that Memphis will love her no matter what happened to Roy because we all know who that rose is from and it doesn't mean anything good. . Every character will need to band together to fight whatever is next in the plans of the man in the stove pipe hat. What they faced in this book was equally if not more creepy than the first book, and descending into the Lair of Dreams is not something they will easily forget. Despite everything that happened in this book (it was over 600 pages and A LOT happened), new friendships are made throughout every twist of the plot and you can't help but continue to fall in love with the story of the Diviners and their magic. A haunting, thrilling, and a captivating sequel, Lair of Dreams will not disappoint. I can't wait for book 3!

** spoiler alert ** Original post at One More Page I love reading summer books, because I love summer. Summer in the Philippines can be horrendous, but I love the sun, I love having long days and plans with friends and going to the beach and just enjoying the sand, sea and the (seemingly) infinite possibilities that a summer day can bring. I wasn't sure what Sarah Ockler's Twenty Boy Summer was about when I first saw it, and from the title, I thought it was just one of those summer fling books. Imagine me wrinkling my nose at the idea. But after some time, I decided to try a sample and realized from that it wasn't just a summer fling book, but one that also tackles grief and friendship, and that was enough for me to give it a try. Twenty Boy Summer is about Anna, Frankie and Matt, who have been best friends forever. Anna, our protagonist, has been harboring a secret from the two of them: she has been in love with Matt for years now. On Anna's 15th birthday, she gets her wish when Matt kisses her after their cake fight. They keep this secret relationship from Frankie at least until they get to their yearly vacation to California, where Matt promises to tell his sister about it. He never got the chance to tell her because the day before they were to leave for California, Matt passes away from a heart defect. Everyone is devastated, but not as much as Anna, because her secret relationship with Matt would forever remain a secret. A year later, Anna gets invited to join Frankie's family for their vacation. Anna and Frankie were convinced that this would be their ABSE (Absolute Best Summer Ever), and the perfect time for Anna to lose her virginity, so they set up a twenty-boy contest. The logic was simple: they would be in California for 23 days. Give or take 3 days of sight seeing, that leaves them 20 days to meet a boy each day. Anna still can't get over Matt, but she also promised to take care of Frankie, so she says yes to this plan. Then starts their supposed absolute best summer ever. Sarah Ockler definitely hit it right with the summer theme in this book, and it made me miss those days when my friends and I were planning beach trips, whether it is overnight or a long trip on faraway places in the country. Twenty Boy Summer has a lot of those elements, almost making me feel the sand between my toes or hear the surf as it hits the shore (aptly described as Sshhhh, ahhh. Sshhh ahhh. Can you hear it now?). In a way, it's a pretty relaxing book, despite the themes it attempted to tackle. There were also some great descriptions of items in the story, such as the sea glass being mermaid's tears, or the ocean being "licorice soup", or how Anna felt after her first time. I think Ockler had a way with words that actually transported me to the beach just by imagination. What was kind of disappointing with this book is sadly, the characters. I'm not sure if I mentioned it before, but I pay close attention to the characters of books I read. Sometimes I think I like characters more than the plot because I think even the most boring plots can be spiced up by strong characters. I like it when I connect to the characters at some level, even if I can't empathize or relate to their situation in the book. I tried my best, but I just couldn't connect to Anna or Frankie in this book. I figure it may be because Anna and I don't have much in common, but I don't think that's a valid enough excuse for me to feel distant from them. The setting pulled me in, yes, but the characters kind of put me at arm's length through out the novel. I felt that the characters were somewhat inconsistent with how they were initially portrayed. Anna first came off as the good and sad girl who secretly grieved for Matt, but as the story unfolded, she seemed inconsistent to that. Her witty comments seemed a bit out of place, and her and her emotional outbursts felt lacking. For example (spoiler warning): A lie? It hits me like a sledgehammer, releasing all the hurt and sadness and confusion I've held inside the last fourteen months. I jump up without speaking and bolt to the shore, unable to hold it any longer. "How could you leave us like this?" I bawl at the sky, tears spilling into my mouth, ignoring the blurred runners who pass behind me without slowing. Just another drunk little girl, they must think. "Tell her!" I should. "Tell her you made me promise! Tell her it's your fault! Tell her it was a lie for you, too! Tell her you loved me!" Maybe it's just me, but that particular passage lacked something, some oomph. I didn't feel Anna's anguish; it felt more like a show than real emotion. Frankie, on the other hand, seemed to go from being the bad girl to the good girl and back to bad. She seemed to be the typical girl who's acting out because of someone's death, but it didn't feel genuine. However, Frankie's character is kind of justifiable after a huge revelation in the book, so that kind of saved her. Anna is a bit too confusing for me to really like her, and that's saying a lot since the novel is in first person POV. I felt more like a silent spectator through out their adventures in the novel. At least I was on the beach, right? Furthermore, I wasn't sure if it was able to tackle the grief aspect right. I had no qualms about how friendship issues were dealt with, but I think the grief part wasn't highlighted enough, save for those small moments (ex. Anna and Matt's mother talking about Matt, Anna and Frankie's conversation at the end about Matt). Perhaps it was meant to be that way -- I'm not sure. Actual grief is kind of hard to write about, but there's a lot of YA books that managed to tackle that gracefully (perfect example: The Truth About Forever by Sarah Dessen). Overall, this isn't really a bad novel. I liked the summer aspect and the setting, but the characters and some of the serious themes that it attempted to deal with didn't really work out that well for me. Some reader discretion is advised, especially for the young ones since this book also deals with losing one's virginity over a summer fling (which obviously won't work for me, either). It's okay enough to be considered a good read for my standards, but in the end, it's just not my type of summer.

[[4 STARS]] I know, I know, I'm very late jumping on the "Mortal Instruments" train. I had planned to start this series earlier but just didn't get around to it - I just wasn't reading as much as I normally was and I guess I just wasn't ready for this series. I mean, it is one long ass series with books still coming out in this world. It was a bit of a shaky start, getting into this book. I don't know if it's because I read the first chapter as a sampler to make sure this really was something I wanted to get into, and I remembered it (even though it was months ago when I read the first chapter) when I picked it up to read. It could have been the size - it could have been the fact that I didn't have a moment to read. Who knows? It was a shaky start anyway. But I wanted to give a shot, so I did what I do when books just aren't getting read but I really want to read them. I bought the audiobook and that helped. I was hooked. The first 30% was a little slow, we didn't really get much plot until around then but that's fine. I have been there before with books that take a while to get into ("The Raven Boys" for example) and I still end up loving them. This was no different. I adored the characters so much. Clary is a bit of an idiot because she doesn't think things through that much. Don't come home, Clary! so she runs home... that kinda thing. But that's understandable because I'm sure even I would do the same thing if my mum was phoning me and telling me these things and I was hearing an attack going on on her end. So, I can't fault her too much on that end. She's brave and determined and I really do love her. Jace is my sarcastic asshole. I fucking ADORE him, okay? Every single word that comes out of his mouth is pure sass and I love it, but he's still so sensitive and vulnerable. I do love my guys with fucked up pasts and hide it behind a cool exterior. I love him, okay? The Lightwoods, Alec and Izzy are perfect as well, despite the fact we don't see much of them. I love Alec's protectiveness over Jace because he lurves him. I adore Izzy's can-do, self assured attitude. Simon is good too. I'm not gonna lie, I really loathe guys who are friends with a girl and are secretly in love with them but don't say a word until the girl is interested in someone else. I hate that, in fact, because they then get all butt hurt because the girl doesn't love them back and it's like well, you didn't tell her until she had feelings and now you've confused her for no reason, you selfish asshole, when you could have told her when you started having these feelings - she would have told you where she stood and you could have started to get over your feelings if she weren't in the same place. It's pathetic. But I do like him as a character and I do like him with Izzy. Whilst the plot wasn't predictable, it wasn't overly exciting. I don't think I'll have this problem with later books, though, as I feel like this is me just dipping my feet in the water. I'm going to get a load more by the time I get to the sixth book. I did see the whole Clary being Valentine's daughter thing coming, but I DID NOT see the Jace being her brother. I don't believe it, not for a fucking second but holy hell, that's just going to cause issues for my OTP. It better get resolved ASAP otherwise I am going to be freaking pissed. I didn't see the Luke being a werewolf thing straight away but I did get there before Cassandra Clare confirmed it, so I'm taking that as a win, haha. I love Luke so much and I was really worried for him at the end but it was all good. No joke, I honestly thought he was going to die and I wasn't prepared to lose him just yet. I adore him too much as well. This book was addictive, as you can see in that fact that it only took me four days to finish. And it would have been sooner had I more time. The audiobook helped but after a while, I realised I could get into reading it from the book which is a good sign. As much as I love audiobooks, it does suck when I don't get the same feeling reading it in book form. But this didn't have that problem in the end up. All in all, despite some flaws, I adored this book and cannot wait to finish "City of Ashes" - yes, I've already started it.

Elizabeth Haynes' novel,  Into the Darkest Corner,  haunted me and I found myself not wanting to put it down. I listened to this book on audiobook, which made everything feel even more real. This book requires a trigger warning: there is graphic violence and every kind of abuse you can think of. This book is unique in that it takes place in two different time periods. The first takes place in 2003, when Catherine first meets a seemingly charming man named Lee. She finds herself becoming isolated and afraid of the man she fell in love with as his true nature becomes apparent. He is controlling, aggressive, abusive, and prone to extreme mood swings. Four years later, Cathy is living in a new place, bearing many scars (both physical and emotional), and Lee is nearing the end of a 3 year prison sentence. She meets someone new and begins to work on her anxiety, PTSD, and OCD. When Lee is let out of prison, everything takes a turn for the worse. This book was so difficult to listen to at times, and I found myself brought to tears due to what Cathy has had to endure. I found myself thinking about all of the other women who are trapped in dangerous situations like this one, and how our society has basically set them up to fail. Cathy has so many obstacles to face in both timelines of this story. She becomes basically trapped in fear, having to check and recheck everything for hours to try to ease her anxiety. The thing that was hardest for me to read was how no one seemed to believe Cathy. This has a similar feel to  Sleeping with the Enemy,  so if you enjoy those kinds of stories, I would recommend this to you. However, it is extremely graphic and does not skim over any details, so read with caution. 4 out of 5 stars.

What I liked: -Opening scene. A helicopter crash  is a great way to start off the story, and it instantly drew me in. From the very start of the book, I knew this one would have more action and drama in it than the first, and I was incredibly glad for that. -Daniel and Sam. These two got a lot more development than they did in the first book, and I was wishing there were more parts with them in it. Daniel was given strange powers as well as Maya, and they started to show and develop in this book. He was still the older brother type, and he was still the group's conscience. Sam definitely grew on me in this book, and I loved the little twist of her sexual orientation. Honestly, after reading the first book, I was torn between wanting her and Daniel together and wondering if she might have been gay. I wasn't sure, but I'm glad this book spelled it out and even joked with it a little bit. Sam is the strong, independent, heroic type, and I wish this book had been from her point of view instead of Maya's. -Maya. She grew on me in this book, and she turned into a character I actually felt like rooting for. I wanted her to be okay and safe, and I wanted her to help her friends. Plus, in this book, Maya actually Shifts into a cougar! and I think that will create some awesome character development with her. I can't wait to see how she changes in the next book. -Serena's demise. I'm glad this wasn't just mentioned once in the first book and then dropped. I like the idea of Maya finding out what happened to her best friend, and I loved the little twist of Nicole's involvement . I honestly didn't see that one coming, but it was cool and dark. -Setting. I liked the small town in the middle of nowhere for the first book, but being lost in the deep woods was a nice change of pace, and I thought it was handled really well. What I disliked: -Rafael. He wasn't in this book very much, and I found the book lacking because of it. I kind of liked his relationship with Maya from the first book--it was one of the only reasons I didn't put the book down--and without it, this book had no romance. There was no passion and budding love, and I'm not used to reading paranormal romance books without the romance. It was weird and kind of boring. It was just survive, survive, and survive. A make out session or two could have broken that monotony up a bit. But I loved Rafe's sacrifice in the beginning--it was heroic and brave. -Writing. Once again, I was not happy with the writing. Kelley Armstrong can write--I've read other books by her before--but I hate writing like this. The story is good, the dialogue is real and believable, but the description is not. Like with the first book, the author kind of switches between past and present tense. Armstrong isn't the only author I've seen do that, but the majority don't, and maybe that's why it bothers me so much. Overall, this book was a vast improvement on the first one in the series. I can't wait to get my hands on the third one, and I may even reread these books again someday. There was more action and drama and character development, and plenty of twists and turns. I know the third book will tie in with Chloe's story, and I can't wait to see how that turns out. I would definitely recommend this book to anyone.

The second volume of Orange, The Complete Collection still has some emotionally driven stuff to tell, and I admit that my heart has been tugged a few times. But volume two has a narrative that is not as solid and cohesive as the first one. The time jumps are not as organic as they were before. I also felt that the themes of being strong, not giving up and saving a life have been used over and over again that it felt that Orange should have been more effective if it were shorter, yet the ending happened so fast that the story could have used a couple more pages. The ending resolution is exactly the way you have perceived it will end. It's quite a bummer if it ended the other way around. I would also like some reconciliation to happen with the future group, like a grown-up Kakeru showing up in an epilogue chapter fulfilling the wish of the "original" ones . As for the six characters they are all extremely likeable until the end (even though Kakeru is douchey many times and Naho almost got to my nerves for her "Naho-isms"), but the only personalities that have been fleshed out are Naho, Suwa and Kakeru's. There's also a completely different story after the end of Orange. I didn't like it. Orange lives up to its readers expectations. It is warm, heartbreaking at times but most importantly, it is a testament about the good things that life can offer, even at times when one doesn't feel like going on. It is a celebration of friendship, love and happiness.

First off, I have to say that I have a great fascination for the subjects of time travel, reincarnation, personal lifetime "do-overs," and exploration of the roads not taken. If I get the chance to time travel or "do-over" I will certainly follow through on that, so if I stop posting on GR, you will know what happened to me. Therefore, I am willing to give a chance to any author who tackles those types of subjects in a book. So this book sounded right up my alley. Greta Wells, living in 1985, gets hit with several life-changing blows by the loss of the two people she loves the most. Taking electric shock treatment (?) for her resulting depression, she finds herself catapulted back in time first to 1918, and then to 1941, where her life is played out in that time period with the same loved ones and basic setting as her 1985 life. She goes in rotation to these time periods with every treatment, and, of course there are 1918 and 1941 Gretas making the same rotation. It is extremely necessary to pay constant attention to where she is and what is going on in that life, and concentrate. That could make it a difficult read for some. So, right off, the plot of the book had me thinking. I have often speculated on where I, being the same person I am now, would have fit into society in many different time frames. But, I never considered bringing everyone from this life with me. Therefore, I consider the book a success to have opened up for me a new avenue of rumination. I'm sure that a reader not as prejudiced in favor of such subjects as I would find plot holes, slips and questions. I found it very interesting, but must admit that I was annoyed by the premise that Greta '85 jumps into the middle of these other lives, and has to figure out what is going on. To me that confusion is a bit irrelevant to what I want from the book. And, I am confused about how she can go into another person's life and not even leave a note saying,  "BTW, I started an affair while I was here . or "I kicked your husband out . . And since most of the rules of decorum and mores of the time she visits would be readily known to me, and Greta and I would have been about the same age in 1985, I think she is a bit slow to catch on, esp. the attitude toward homosexuality. Also, not being homophobic, it is still difficult for me to equate the AIDS epidemic with the loss of life of WWI or WWII. But, then, I lived 1985 in a small city in Maryland, and not in Greenwich Village. All in all, I thoroughly enjoyed the book and I recommend this to others who keep falling into holes in the space/time continuum.

This book was amazing, as expected. It was fun, witty, sarcastic, and full of sass. Of course, it didn't hurt that Percy Jackson himself was present for a portion of the book, which automatically makes it one of the best books ever. I was looking forward to his being in this book all year, and it did not disappoint! I think this book concluded well, and it wrapped up the series, without it being too final. I'm really hoping we see Magnus and co. again, I'd be heartbroken to never get to spend more time with them. I'm so in love with the whole gang. But I have a feeling this won't be the last we see of them. There was so much character development and backstory for pretty much all the characters, which I was super happy about. I especially loved Hearthstone's development. The scene with his brother was beautiful and made me cry. Mallory, Halfborn, and TJ all became so much more dear to me in this book. I'm glad their characters got a bit more flushed out. Up to this book, they had been more side characters rather than main, and this book gave them more of a main character treatment. Their stories are all so lovely. I'm sure we can all say we've been shipping Magnus and Alex this past year. I didn't expect anything definitive to come of it, which, technically, nothing did. However, a lot more happened between them than I expected, and I'm not mad about it. I want to see where their relationship goes. It's a pretty neat coincidence that this book came out just a month before the Thor: Ragnarok movie is set to release. It'll be interesting to watch that movie after having read this book. This series was fantastic, I absolutely LOVED it. All the characters are so endearing and I just want to spend more time with them. If you haven't read this, then what are you waiting for? I love it just as much as Percy, and would love another Magnus Chase series! These characters will forever be in my heart.

There were so many good ideas in this book, but to me they weren't executed very well. It took me forever and a day to get through the story, mostly because I got tired of all the back story. Well, the whole book is back story: a setup for the next. I found that to be a bummer. Also, the ending? Too abrupt. Some sort of descending action would have been nice. Writing style wise, it wasn't distracting. But the author did tend to repeat information far too much. I understand that there's a fine balance between trusting your reader to remember and having information be a bit vague. I don't think you need to repeat how a character is feeling over and over and over again. I get it the first time. Remind me a second time, and move on... Also, as another reviewer pointed out, the relationship between Karou/Madrigal and Akiva was far too unrealistic. There was not time to build why they were so fond of each other. Too fairy-tale for me. Relationships have to have more depth than just physical attraction and one common desire. All that being said, I am willing to get into the next book. I'm hoping the author is able to refine her writing to be more engaging and less repetitive.

"It's a madness so discreet that it can walk the streets and be applauded in some circles, but it is madness nonetheless." -- Mindy McGinnis, A Madness So Discreet Review Haunting is the single word description needed to describe A Madness So Discreet by Mindy McGinnis. This novel is a heart-wrenching historical fiction that will have your mind questioning your very sanity based on the pretenses of the  1800s medical practice.Readers are automatically  thrown into the cold depth of despair, only to hear the screams of an arachnophobia girl  desperately scratching to set free the eight legged creatures that are crawling in her blood. Her screams are now accompanied by drumming of heavy feet approaching her cell. She's new. She doesn't realize that the screams only encourages the worse, not better. There is no one willing to help her. Grace May mind is not the reason she enrolled at the Boston Asylum, it's the secret of who put her in such a fragile state that has her locked away. There is no hope in the Boston Insane Asylum, at least that was the belief Grace held before becoming friends with a strange figure in the darkness, whose nose seems to have the power of omniscience about it. "Dear child, do you even know all the rage that is inside you?" -- Mindy McGinnis, A Madness So Discreet A Madness So Discreet, is absolutely amazing when capturing the  historical details environment   that truly transport us in time. Mindy McGinnis truly transports us into the 1800s, sparing no foul detail such as  smells, uncomfortable female garments, stiff male coats, social expectations of both genders, non gender equality and carriages, these details  do not disappoint when reading about the unfavorable accepts of the book as well,  this historical fiction is about much more disturbing details. The really horror of this novel is not that we spend most of our time in an Asylum, but those who the Asylum are actually freely walking among society. The fact that Grace's father is not only a pedophile but also a serial rapist. Whose actions were only placed in court BECAUSE they were falsely tided into a murder in order for him in trial is so damn horrible! The Asylum is actually a world of protection from those who are truly mad.This is the real madness. Surrounded by woman's right or rather the lack of women's right does not stop the fast tempo of this novel. The police ride off these possible "serial murders" because of status of  women who meet their untimely deaths. I gave this novel 4 out of 5 stars based on, the historical accuracy; the lack of women's social equality;  social standards of privilege families, however the ending was very nice. It was "nice" that Grace and the Doctor were not romantically involved (that would be acquired), that they hold a friendship/professional relationship together. The reason why I held back on the last star was because Grace not being able to reunite with her sister again. I feel that the doctor truly cares for Grace I just feel because of her scars and his station that's as far as the relationship will probably go. This is a wonderful literature pieces that will have you holding your head wondering if we are safe within or without the walls that keep us? "You chose to stop acknowledging a world that has treated you foully. What's saner than that?" This review was originally posted on Lia's Bookish Obsession

Check out this review and more at On the Wings of Books What I Thought... * I try to follow the book before movie/tv show, but sometimes I give in, and I definitely gave in to The 100. I'm not a huge space person, but EVERYONE was talking about the tv show so I thought, why not? I watched it, enjoyed it, so I thought I would give the book a shot. * Other than the fact that the tv show has 100 juvenile delinquents being dropped from space it is vastly different from the book. I thought that the first season would basically be book one, it is far from it. *  Because I watched the show I pictured the characters like that, which was fine expect for Octavia, who is 14 in the book and so not 14 in the show. * The tv show is basically the entire first book crammed into the pilot and then widely veers from there, which was a bit disappointing for me as I really liked some of those elements. In the tv show Clarke's mom is alive but her dad is dead, in the book both of her parents are dead. Wells is alive in the book, not in the tv show. These are pretty big differences! * Despite the fact that I like the tv show better there were some aspects of the book that were better. Glass was supposed to be on the ship to earth but escaped and is still on the spaceship and I liked how we got to know whats going on the space ship through her eyes, and to be honest she was my favorite narrator. * There are four narrators and I'm glad I was listening to it on audio because at times I had a hard time telling the difference between them, but at least I could narrow it down to two as there were two different narrators for the audio. The flashbacks also made it confusing at times. * There was less action than I anticipated, given that I thought there would be more a resemblance to the tv show. There were still so many interesting things going on though, especially their rediscovery of earth. Overall I enjoyed The 100, but not as much as the tv show.

So I finished the series. It's something I haven't read before. Normally I don't go for this type of story but somehow I kept reading this. By the end, I didn't feel content with the story. I was constantly annoyed by the fact that this is a raw, violent storyline. Which is why I don't go for these type of stories in the first place, I'm not really comfy with main characters falling for the "bad guy", even if he has his reasons or remorse. Jethro treated Nila as shit and I can't look past that to accept their love for each other. But I understand it's part of the story. I just don't go for that sort of stuff so it's personal taste. But, if I saw more remorse in Jethro's POV, I might be convinced. I just didn't feel it. I didn't like either of the main characters. Nila was whiny and ungrateful. I can understand changing your mind when you're emotionally and physically tortured, but the constant "I can do this" vs. "I can't do this" got annoying. And Jethro just didn't have any personality to me. He has a condition, sure, but the way it was written... I didn't feel it. And if I can't like at least one of the main characters, I jump on the side characters. But that's not possible either because most of them were complete fucktards apart from Kes and Jasmine. So I fell on them. Which brings me to the one thing I liked about Indebted, and which the writer ruined for me. I can't, for the life of me, get over Kes. I just can't. It had no real purpose. If it did, it escaped me. Kes was so much more interesting to me than Jethro and Nila. It's kind of a pity the writer didn't explore the option of going deeper with him, because if that happened, I'd be more invested in the story as well.

3.5 stars The ending made me cry a bit. I genuinely like Stormy Llewellyn and the fact that she tattooed her birthmark, just so she and Odd could have matching birthmarks. Why didn't the bodachs show up around her before her death? Why didn't they show up around Varner and Eckles either? There wasn't any sufficient explanation to address these issues. How tragic is it to be able to save 500 people or so, but couldn't save the one person that you love most? The story is a bit of a slow mo, it moves in such a lazy, indulging pace, but it fits the story and the MC just right. (For the record, I didn't skim AT ALL.) Well, it doesn't exactly suit my undying love for fast paced horror, but I like it just the same. It's not - in anyway - scary to me, but it's an undeniably satisfying read. It's just an odd story of an odd boy named Odd Thomas. The MC, Odd Thomas is - well - odd, but he's become an absolutely endearing character due to his love for justice and humanity and - of course - Stormy, that I actually felt for his pain and sadness and sense of loss deeply. Stormy, her long time girlfriend, is also an admirable character, strong, witty, and full of sarcastic humour. She loves Odd as much as he loves her. Have I mentioned that she faked her birthmark just so they could have matching birthmarks? She's lovely that way. Little Ozzie (who's not little at all at 400 pounds), Terri Shambaugh, Chief Wyatt Porter, Karla Porter (the chief's brave wife), Rosalia Sanchez (who's terribly afraid of suddenly being 'invisible'), and Terrible Chester (who loves to piss on Odd's shoes) make wonderful supporting characters. I might want to read 'Forever Odd' someday (the second installment of this series), but I feel no sense of urgency or excitement toward the prospect of getting a hold on it.

Ugh. I don't want to go so far as to describe this book as garbage, but I wouldn't recommend it to anyone. I think the thing that annoys me most is that there could have been a decent, even good book here, if the author hadn't insisted on making it a retelling of an overrated play. I didn't mind some of the characters, especially Len, but trying to mash the characters and plot into a retelling of Romeo and Juliet just made some people into flat caricatures (Juliet is such an evil bitch! slut! ), and made many actions and plot points seem completely undeveloped and out of nowhere (Rob is now a crazy rage monster who punches study buddies!) . I also found Rosaline's ultra-meta references to Shakespeare and the original play just bizarre - so is she acknowledging that her life is just a remake of a play she's read? That her and her next door neighbours have had the "u" syllables removed from their last names and bickity-bam, they're the contemporary versions of characters in a Shakespeare tragedy? Wuuuuuuut? I won't even start on some of the issues I had with the treatment of women in this book, and men too, for that matter. Oy. Did not enjoy.

I really, really wanted to like this book. I read glowing review after glowing review but ultimately, 'The Interestings' fell flat. None of the main characters -- the titular Interestings -- were sympathetic enough for me to care about them; honestly, they were pretty annoying. I don't think the protagonist has to be likable, but it definitely helps. Jules Jacobson is painfully self-centered and whiny; it seems as though Wolitzer was so wrapped up in making Jules "realistic" she failed to make her compelling. Ethan, ultimately, was a pathetic cipher; he really only existed to worship mega-tool Jules. I loved Dennis, if only because he was the only character to call Jules on her shit. The book is compulsively readable; the prose was interesting enough to keep my interest, even though I routinely wanted to punch the characters in the face. I very nearly rage-quit after the near-constant victim-blaming. It was obvious that Goodman was a terrible person and that he certainly raped Cathy, but because the story was told from Jules's POV, the reader is treated to pages -- near chapters -- of her accusing Cathy of crying wolf. It was distasteful and ultimately, served little to no purpose, since neither Jules nor Ash wised up to the truth. Jonah's childhood memories of being drugged and manipulated by a "father-figure" were equally awful, and his psuedo-revenge was equally unsatisfying. It all left a bad taste in my mouth, and it makes it hard to recommend this book to others.
