A classic worthy of the title. Dystopian fiction at its finest; The Handmaid's Tale is horrifying, raw, and a little too believable for comfort. I don't want to give anything away, as part of the fun is piecing together this story (and backstory), out of order as the protagonist offers various flashbacks to different periods in her life. Suffice to say that the Republic of Gilead, the name of Atwood's dystopian society, is fully-formed and thoroughly disturbing. Honestly, what I enjoyed most was the "Historical Notes" section at the back of the book, which is actually a continuation of the story--don't skip it assuming it's just some author's compilation of facts and references! It acts as a sort of epilogue to the whole tale, and honestly it pulled together a lot of loose ends for me. There were of course a few elements of Atwood's Gileadean society that I found harder to accept than others, but most of them were explained in more detail in this ending section. Also, the ambiguous ending to the novel "proper" was explored further in a way that offered a more satisfying conclusion while still preserving the ambiguity of the protagonist's "end." I would recommend this book to any fans of dystopia. However, my one reservation is that certain readers may find Offred (the narrator/protagonist) a bit rambling at points. The plot is frequently and heavily punctuated by emotional tangents symptomatic of an individual coping with trauma. I personally found such elements lent authenticity to the book. The main character's place in dystopia has induced many symptoms of mental illness, and the author does not shy away from giving us her desperate streams of consciousness, which are often bleak and occasionally hopeful. I'd say that the ratio of plot to mind-wanderings is about 50/50, maybe 60/40, which might be too much for some people's tastes. Still, I highly recommend it! Definitely a book you'll walk away from feeling like you learned something about the human heart, and that is a priceless gift to receive from any author.

I really quite liked the world building and atmosphere in this - I flipped back to the map many times throughout reading which I loved and which really helped immerse myself in the world. I also liked the commentary on gender roles and how those roles affect the lives of women in this dream world, such as professions, life choices, etc. Something that has continued to make me think was the comment that came up a couple times that Villett has only ever encountered males from the waking world and she finds it odd that there are about the same number of women in the waking world, but none of them dream, or the men say their dreams are minimal/frivolous/about babies... It makes me wonder what time period is occurring in the waking world... but once Villett gets there, even though it is made clear that time moves differently in the waking world and dream world, it is clearly present day, like 2016, which just blows my mind if you remember these comments about women not dreaming earlier on in the book. Just... WHAT?! The whole premise of the dream world and the waking world, and that the dream world is a physical place, and that some people live only exclusively there was really interesting, but the overall plot was kind of boring, and it took me quite a while to get into the story even though it was only 166 pages.

I've been looking forward to this book for months. Imogen has been a favorite of the Survivors since book one as the only female in the group of emotionally vulnerable but oh-so-lovable men. I've been waiting to see what kind of man it would take to break her out of her emotional self-exile. And I had some serious suspicions about the central event of her emotional damage for a while now and I wanted to see how that played out (for the record, I was right :). And I want to say up front that while this is the sixth of the series, it'd probably read fine as a stand-alone, even though the entire gang shows up in places. They're not important to the story as anything more than her support. I recommend reading the others first because they're very fine books on the whole, but they aren't necessary for this book to work. What a delight it was to finally meet Imogen in depth! Balogh is excellent at characters and she outdid herself with this one. And while I can't help patting myself on the back for guessing details of her central trauma, Balogh did a fantastic job of making it real in her character. Although (and take this spoiler seriously as I think the actual revelation works better through the story) I don't really buy the final event as described. I get not wanting to work through the brutality of being raped in addition to the brutality already inherent in the events, but I don't see people already intent on rape calling it off just because they don't get the additional value they had hoped from it. The violation of social/moral norms to get that far doesn't reassert itself just because the situation altered slightly, I don't think. Particularly not when doing so required buy-in from a group of others joining in making and planning that decision. But all that occurred to me after finishing the book, so it didn't weigh in my engagement at the time. So Imogen was a delight, but I fell just as hard for Percy. He was completely unexpected as a match for Imogen, but Balogh managed to show how he was exactly right and that was marvelous. I loved his healing as much as Imogen's and the two together were emotional catnip. Further, he was an excellent stand-in for learning about Imogen's past (which is why you should take that spoiler above extra-seriously). I loved seeing his determination as he deals with owning his responsibilities and the strength and self-respect he gains in doing so. I have minor niggles with the plot, but they're very small and bound in details. Like, for instance, (this spoiler isn't as serious as the first, as I think it was telegraphed pretty well early on, but that may just be me) Dicky's former batman being given a pass on murder charges (for testifying about the smuggling ring) when everybody should have known the actual charge would have been treason. I wouldn't have minded this if it had turned into a gotcha so he'd hang anyway, but it seemed everybody was unaware of that angle and it should have been relatively obvious given the nature of his betrayal of Dicky and Imogen to the French. You could maybe argue desertion or espionage but both have the same penalty of death when coupled with active hostilities and a declared war . But the story was well paced and my few niggles only occurred after I'd finished the book so they don't affect my rating at all. Indeed, the emotional climax was so powerful I knew it had clenched the solid five-star rating I'd been heading for all along. So yeah, this series is shaping up to be one of my very favorite. The lows haven't been terribly low and the highs have been fantastic. A note about Steamy: Two explicit sex scenes put this at standard for the series/author and in the middle of my steam tolerance. They really worked for me, actually, as they were essential to the growing emotional connection between them. It helps that four years of a happy marriage without any hint of pregnancy made Imogen confident of being barren. I'm not sure I buy a doctor's confirmation from that period, but since Imogen believed it (and I'm genuinely ignorant of medicine at the time) I rolled with it.

At a Glance: THE GIRL AT MIDNIGHT was a fascinating and rich fantasy that I could not stop reading once I started (and since I had the book and the audiobook, I literally never had to stop)! Although the story was very reminiscent of other books I've read previously (especially Daughter of Smoke and Bone), the writing was enough to make it a book that I loved reading. Audiobook: I really liked this audiobook! I thought the narrator, Julia Whelan, did an incredible job. She completely sucked me into this story and made everything so much more vivid! She did a great job using different voices for the different characters. I highly recommend picking this one up! Cover: I really like the purple cover a lot, but I haven't seen it in the hardcover. I'm hoping it has a little more detail than my ARC and is a little sharper. But it is super pretty! Action: The adventure begins in the first chapter and doesn't stop until the last pages. This story is full of battles, mysteries, fighting, magic, narrow escapes, torture, and betrayal. If you're looking for a story that keeps you on the edge of your seat, this one will not disappoint. Romance: I really REALLY liked the romance in this. It just felt more authentic than so many others that I've read. Usually in YA, the characters (especially the girl), has never had a boyfriend/girlfriend before, or never been in love before, then they meet someone and fall in love forever. But that's not normally how it happens. I liked that these relationships were more complex, without being a love triangle. The build up between Echo and Cauis was full of tension! Just the way I like it! Heroine: Echo was a FANTASTIC character to read. I loved her cleverness and her snark. She was loyal and quick-thinking, while still dealing with insecurities that often made her second-guess herself. She used the skills she had to get out of deadly situations. In a world of feathers and scales, she's just a girl, but a girl who refuses to be ignored. Hero: Cauis has been tainted by a long life of war and fighting that never seems to end. He's become a little hardened and bitter. But he's also a man (Drakharin, prince) of integrity. He will do anything for his people, for his friends, and now for Echo. One of the best things about the varying points of view was getting to see Echo through his eyes. Favorite Supporting Character: I really liked all of the supporting characters so much. Reading from so many viewpoints really helped me connect to them more than I normally do. But I think my favorite had to be Jasper. He was such a vibrant and fun character, how can you not love him! He's very Magnus Bane! Something I loved: I loved so many things. The writing was lovely. Melissa Grey grabbed hold of me from the very beginning and had me completely enchanted. I felt like the story was rich and vivid without being bogged down or too complex. It was beautifully told. Something(s) I hated: I wouldn't say I hated it, but the one thing that did kind of bother me was how closely this book, and especially some of the characters, compared to some other well-known books. From the beginning this story reminded me a LOT of Daughter of Smoke and Bone. I mean, a lot. This will be spoilery, so, look away if you want. Echo was so Karou. Rose was Madrigal. Cauis was Akiva. The Avicen are the Chimera and the Drakarin are the Seraphim. Echo/Karou (the only human in this world) is raised by an Avicen/Chimera and runs errands for them until the Drakarin/Seraphim destroy the shop and kill an Avicen/Chimera. Then the human meets the Drakarin/Seraphim (who had a previous relationship with Rose/Madrigal) and they work together to bring the two warring clans (led by Altair/Thiago and a bloodthirsty family member) together. Of course Echo/Karou is more than just an ordinary human, she has special powers and eventually has the memories of Rose/Madrigal, and they all fall in love with Cauis/Akiva. Then there was Jasper, who was Magnus Bane, and Dorian who was Alex (in love with Jace, or Akiva, errr...I mean Cauis) I guess they jumped stories, haha. But even though this did nag at me, I think the writing and the story were good enough to overcome the similarities and make me love it anyway. Cliffhanger? Considering this is a series, I thought this book wrapped up really well. There's definitely more that's going to happen, but I'm happy with where this book ended. Would I recommend it? I definitely recommend it if you liked DoS&B and can get over the similarities. Or if you just like fantasy. It was one of the better books I've read this year! Did my friends like it? I know Steph from Cuddlebuggery liked it! Check out her "six very good reasons why you should make The Girl at Midnight a priority on your TBR list." And many people tweeted me while I was reading it, telling me how much they liked it! Will I buy/keep it? Yeah, even though I have the ARC and the audiobook, I think I'm going to have to get my hands on a hard cover! Book Doppelgangers: Obviously Daughter of Smoke & Bone by Laini Taylor, Carnival of Souls by Melissa Marr, Lips Touch Three Times by Laini Taylor, Wicked Lovely by Melissa Marr, City of Bones by Cassandra Clare -Andye Reading Teen

I haven't read any of the previous books in the Billionaire Boys Club series which is linked to this one, but now I'd like to go back and at least read Bronte and Logan's book since it's their wedding that brings Marjorie and Rob together. Marjorie is a waitress with who's been very sheltered, so when she's asked to be a bridesmaid at Bronte's destination wedding it's a great adventure for her. Meanwhile, Rob checks into the resort to try to catch Logan to propose a business deal. Logan is not interested in meeting Rob because of his sleazy reputation, and he's about to give up when he meets Marjorie. She initially saves him from drowning, then runs off before he gets her name, but he is thunderstruck and is immediately attracted to her. I don't usually like naive virgin heroines, but I loved this book. Marjorie was naive, but she was no pushover. Once she found out the truth of what Rob did for a living, she wasn't at all afraid to challenge him to be a better man and move on from his exploitative business, rather than just knuckling under and accepting it the way a weak heroine would. As for Rob, he was crass and blustering, but I loved watching him fall head-over-heels for Marjorie, a woman completely different than his usual type. She was 6'1" and had always been insecure about her height, so it was adorable to see how he viewed her as a goddess, didn't mind at all that she was taller than him, and in fact bought her shoes with towering heels because he knew she loved them. All in all, an enjoyable read.

This was so much fun - even for me, somewhat superhero-lit-challenged as I am. It seems as if it would be quite difficult to merge the comic book style of character while giving them enough depth to work for novel-length, but the effort didn't show here at all. Celia was a wonderful character - her reaction to the pretty horrendous childhood with the city's most powerful & famous superheroes was impressive. Some of the revelations weren't incredibly surprising (actual romantic hero, for example) but it was no less engaging for that - and at that, I read in just two sittings so suspense wasn't drawn out. There were some lovely touches - little flashes of humour (I was especially taken with Celia's wondering how her mother can cry so much and be a superhero), and minor characters who show real depth. Villain was suitably villainous, and he added a pleasing parallelism to the story. I also felt sorry for Celia's mother, as she reminded me surprisingly strongly of mothers in families I actually know, where the father has behaved appallingly to children, and the mother's torn between loyalty to both. Consider me a Carrie Vaughn fan now!

Story time: I started "The Name of the Star" three times before finally getting through it from beginning to end. Originally I just figured I wasn't committed/patient enough, but now that I'm finished I can FINALLY confirm that nope, it wasn't me, the book just isn't that good. It's easier for me to point out what I DIDN'T like rather than what I did, so I'll start with that. 1) It's boring. I'm sorry, I thought this was supposed to be a ghost story, so WHY THE HELL does nothing happen until more than a third of the way into the book?? For the longest time I felt like I was reading a contemporary fiction about a girl's experience at a boarding school in England... and trust me, it really isn't that exciting. I'm talking long-ass descriptions about high school "mean girls," PE class, and a flat/useless love interest. Sure, there's the occasional talk about the Ripper murders and the "suspicious" lack of evidence at the crime scenes, but this is stale news to the reader. We know from the book description that the murderer is a ghost, so to us it takes an eternity for Rory to catch on. It reminded me of "Hush Hush" and its cover that SHOUTS "fallen angel," and how it takes Nora half the book to put the pieces together. Ugh. I don't know if I should blame the writer or the book designers, but pleaseeee never do this to your readers. Even after Rory finds out the murderer is a ghost, the action STILL doesn't pick up. The first time I ever did a double take while reading was on page 220-something, and after that the action slumped YET AGAIN. The last 50 pages? Yes, I'll admit that they were pretty damn entertaining, but a 370 page book should NEVER take that long to get there. By page 270-ish, I just wanted to be done already. 2) The writing isn't immersive at all. Cassandra Clare, author of my favorite book series, is quoted on the cover of "The Name of the Star" calling it "a gorgeously written, chilling, atmospheric thriller." I'm disappointed to say this couldn't be farther from the truth. I didn't fall in love with the English setting or dream to be whisked away to Rory's world of pubs and underground tunnels. If anything, the English setting was frustrating because it felt like an excuse for piles and piles of more useless information. It would be one thing if I could FEEL the environment and the magic and beauty of England (*coughcough* like in Cassandra Clare's Infernal Devices series), but instead I felt like the writing was trying too hard to constantly remind us of the setting. 3) The characters fall flat. Jerome, Rory's supposed "love interest," is possibly the most useless character ever. He's flat (what do we really know about him aside from the fact that he likes journalism/mystery and Rory?) and has no real contribution to the plot other than occasionally distracting Rory from her "shitty" life by making out with her. That's it. Rory is also extremely flat; if you asked me to describe her personality, I would start with, "Well... she's from Louisiana?" Seriously. That's all we know about Rory. Oh, that and the fact that she has a bunch of weird relatives, and you'll remember this tidbit because you're "treated" to countless anecdotes about these useless relatives and their completely unrelated stories. Was this an attempt to make Rory appear more charming and fleshed out? Who knows. The only people I remotely liked in this book were the squad members (the people who hunt the ghosts). I feel like Callum, Boo, and Stephen were on the cusp of greatness, but they still fell short. Stephen is without a doubt the most intriguing and fleshed out of them all, and his attitude and backstory would be the ONLY reason I go on to read the sequels. And of course freaking Jo dies. Or disappears/goes boom or whatever you want to call it. Of COURSE. UGH. 4) There's so much wasted potential. The following con involves specific parts of the plot (including the ending), so avoid reading if you want to stay spoiler-free. I kept feeling disappointed again and again by each "big" reveal in this book. When Callum pulled out a cell phone and hit two buttons to eliminate the ghost, I was thinking, "You've got to be kidding me." The terminus idea is interesting, I guess, but it was kind of disappointing after all the build up about fighting ghosts. The backstory of the murderer is also SUPER rushed. The dynamics of a murder-suicide are very delicate/complex with multiple layers and details, so I was disappointed that this bombshell of a reveal occurred so late in the book and all at once. Apparently that was the one piece of information that they needed to solve the whole damn mystery. Also, of all the ways that Rory could have her brush with death, the author chose choking??? Really??? Overall, I was largely disappointed with this book and I'm relieved to be done with it. I gave it two stars because the premise was promising, the last 50 pages were entertaining, and one word: Stephen. Everything else? Blah.

I find you need to start with the first one which is When You Dare, and than read Trace of Fever and than this one and the final one Perfect Storm. Thank you, Marissa Meyer, for giving us this piece of insight into the increasingly evil, increasingly deranged, and surprisingly sad story of the appalling, atrocious, love-to-hate-her-'cause-she-is-so-freaking-evil Queen Levana. It's a short story, only a shade over 200 pages, but Levana is so Cersei-grade nasty that it proves compulsively readable to a shocking degree. And I do mean Cersei-grade - of all the books in this series, this one is the least family-friendly by far, the only reason I would hesitate to recommend The Lunar Chronicles to anyone under, say, thirteen years old. Now I've got one more full-length novel left in my reread, and of course the short story collection. Haha, but remember when I thought this book would be just another e-book exclusive? Nope, not the case, and thank the stars for that.

Also posted on my blog at: Kala's Book Blog I wasn't planning to read this because the first book made me so mad, but I decided what the hell and gave it a shot. I didn't hate the first book because of the writing and I still liked That Boy (though I wasn't a fan of the sequel). I was hoping and praying this one would redeem Stalk Me for me. And it kind of did and kind of didn't? It's hard to explain. If Keatyn had started off at boarding school and I hadn't spent 300+ pages in Stalk Me getting to know a bunch of other characters, only to have them ripped away and have her tossed in with a bunch of new ones, I would have liked this book a LOT better. Probably not more than 3-stars better, but still better. Unfortunately, that's not what happened. What happened is that I read Stalk Me. I got attached to the characters Keatyn spent the first 300+ pages of the book with, especially Cush. If you read my Stalk Me review, you'll see how much I liked Cush. Cush was THE ONLY male love interest that jumped off the pages and just made you fall for him. He was lively and real and SO perfect for Keatyn's personality. Brooklyn came across as a dick for the entire book, and even more so in Kiss Me. Sander was alright, but hello, GAY. The other boys Keatyn made out with were all introduced in the last few pages of Stalk Me and I was so pissed off at that point that I just hated them all instantly. After reading Kiss Me, I still pretty much hate them all (except Dawson). The way Cush was handled in Kiss Me infuriates me even more. First of all, we get this near the beginning: And I know I told Cush that I loved him at my party. But he bought me boots! The. Perfect. Boots. And I maybe got a little caught up in the moment. This right here showcases all of the big issues with Keatyn in a few short sentences. She constantly is telling boys she loves them, or internally saying she loves them. She told a boy she loved him because he BOUGHT HER SOMETHING. Never mind that the boy has been in love with her for years, treated her like a freaking goddess, has similar interests to her, and loves her for who she is (unlike Brooklyn who only loves her when she acts the way he wants her to act). But whatever. That was pretty bad. But the worst is yet to come. About 5-6 times Keatyn internally mentions that she misses Cush, but she then instantly forgets about him when she starts making out with one of the three boys she kisses during Kiss Me. Then at around 70%, the bombshell that is the reason why this book is getting 2 stars instead of 3. SPOILERS! At around 70%, Keatyn for some reason is able to access her Facebook account that she's been denied access too because of the stalker. On there is a letter from Cush where he tells her that his mom bought those boots, not him. He also says that he moved to Oregon and before he gave her the boots he got a girlfriend. He got caught up in the moment at Keatyn's party and that whole love confession thing that happened right before the stalker tried to kidnap Keatyn was a sham. He's now happily dating this girl in Oregon. And that's the end of Cush. Seriously? I don't even know what to say. It's depressing that Dodd would take THE best character and have it turn out like this. UGH!!!!!!!!! Anyways. This book mostly focuses on a love triangle between Keatyn and Aiden and Dawson. Keatyn makes out with both a bunch. She thinks she's in love with Aiden, but he acts like a weirdo douchebag most of the time so she starts dating Dawson (who is the only other decent character in this entire series). I can't help it. I don't hate Dawson. He's not as fun and interesting as Cush, but he's not unbearable. I just can't help but be so emo about Cush that I can't really get in to the Dawson/Keatyn relationship that much. It appears, from reading other reviews, that I'm the only one, but I can't help what I feel. I don't know if I'll continue the series. I probably will, because I have this weird complex about finishing series (it took me slogging through five terrible awful books to finally give up on the Celestra series). I'm really disappointed in how this is going though.

5 stars!! Lending Light tells the story of Gives Light but from Rafael's Point of View (POV). When I read Gives Light one of the things I tought it had missing was exactly Rafael's POV and... even tought I tought it was really SWEET and LOVABLE that Rafael could kind of guess Skylar's thoughts and feelings, it just wasn't very believable to me... if Rafael COULD read him so well... if Sky's face WAS that easily read... WHY couldn't HIS OWN DAD (who had lived with him all his life, may I add) understand his toughts too? In this book it IS explained how Rafael could understand Sky so well... if you want to know, then click the spoiler Rafael can feel other people's feelings throught touch and he kind of can see their auras... How AWESOME is that?! I never expected a paranormal genre in this book... :) "You will very soon learn what it means to have no voice" I LOVED this book more than I did Gives Light... I LOVED seeing Skylar throught Rafael's "in love" eyes... just as I loved Rafael so much when I first "met" him in Gives Light throught Skylar's. Rafael Gives Light is such a LOVABLE character... he's an artist, a dreamer ... so imaginative... he is suferring so much, having a serial killer for a dad... a dad he still loves, a dad he still has good memories with... a dad he wouldn't have in his wildest dreams, tought to be a murderer... a monster! " I missed my dad. I didn't understand how he had turned into a monster without my noticing, or - or maybe he had been a monster all along, maybe I'd been too stupid to see it, we all had; but how? How do you look right into a devil's eyes and think you're staring at a human? What was wrong with me? By loving my dad, by missing my dad, wasn't the same as saying it was all right for him to take so many lifes? That he should have taken more?(...) I was the monster" Rafael feels guilty... he is afraid of himself, he hates himself... because he has his dad's face... he is in so many ways like his dad... he is afraid he will turn into a murderer too!!! Everyone looks at him and sees his dad... sees a murderer to be. "I was born in Nettlebush, and I could have loved it there, but everyone else who was born there looked at me like I was a plague. Maybe I was a plague. Except for her eyes, except for Mom's dimples, I had my father's face: square chin, flat nose, flat cheeks. Sometimes I'd looked at old pictures of him and thought I was looking at me. People needed someone to hate when their wives, their children, their mothers went missing. Dad wasn't here anymore; people couldn't hate him to his face. I had his face. I was his proxy." " The ghost of my father was written on my face, a face everyone hated, me most of all. I wanted to rip my face off." " I fixed a scowl on my face. (...) The kids nearest me looked frightened. Two girls even stepped backward. I felt like something disgusting; maybe something evil." "She was scared of me. She was scared of me because I had a monster's face. Neither of us could say how much else I'd inherited from that monster." But, then, one day... a curly, blond boy comes to NettleBush. Rafael is determined to Hate this boy -Skylar St. Clair- his dad's last victim... his only remaining living victim... It was Skylar who indentified Rafael's dad as a murderer... it was his fault Rafael lost his dad... It was his fault everyone knew his dad was a serial killer... it was his fault his mom got sick and then died! "I'd made up my mind that I was going to hate him. It didn't have to make sense. Nothing about me made sense. The guy locked eyes with me. I forced my face into the most hateful, concentrated glower I could muster. He jumped in his seat (...)" BUT... How Can You Hate a smiling, mute, sweet boy who looks at you like you're a Person Not a Monster... a boy who doesnt hate you, even tought you have the same face of the man who killed his mom and took his voice away... a boy who carries so much light with him, he LIGHTS UP your world even without noticing it... a boy who wants to be your Very FIRST Friend Ever? ... you JUST CAN'T :) "The guy smiled at me. (...) I'd had everything planned out. I would hate the St.Clair kid the way everyone else hated me. I would force him to share the burden of my father absence. I'd had everything planned out; and it lasted all of 2 seconds. The moment I saw that soft, unassuming face I could only think of protecting it. He was new around here (...) I didn't want to hurt this guy. You wouldn't blame me if you'd seen what I'd seen. Who looks at a lamb and wants to hurt it?" so they become Friends... the Best of Friends... Inseparable Friends... "This was my friend. This friend belonged to me. (...) nobody else could interact with him the way I could." "He was my friend, and he was real. He wasn't ink and paper. I wasn't alone." ... Until Rafael's FEELINGS for Sky turn Protective, Possesive, and WAY STRONGER than Friendship... Rafael realises he Loves Sky... but the question is ... could Skylar ever, possibly, love him back? "I didn't know that anyone could suffer such an infatuation as I did. (...) It was like having a latern inside of me, and it blazed to life when sky was near, without him even knowing (...) it made me happier than I'd know humanly possible. (...) I thanked Creator every day that he'd given me Sky. I thanked Creator that there finally existed someone who made me a more tolerable person by virtue of his existence alone." This book was just SO BEAUTIFUL... I cried at parts, it made me think... and laught even (Rafael and Sky together, were hilarious :D)... I LOVED how, after kissing Sky, Rafael just couldn't stop saying to Everyone that he HAD a BOYFRIEND... even if they didn't care at all :D (that's how happy he was!)... I also really liked Sarah Two Eagles's friendship with Rafael, it was so sweet :) I'll end up by saying that Lending Light is DEFINITELY a MUST READ for Gives Light LOVERS! Go Read it... you'll LOVE it!

This book is the part of the story where they finally come together on a camping trip. It was just too short. I didn't realize how short it was, or I probably wouldn't have bought it. FAVORITE QUOTES Her skin is softer than a lamb's. What does she put on herself? Unicorn tears? ~Cole

Now this is the kind of MC book I like...no degrading of women, no whoring around, no obnoxious assholes! This book has a strong story, great characters,  a HEA  , what more could a girl ask for! Nix is the just the type of MC guy I can get behind. Or under. Or on top of. Or on my knees for. He is everything I would want in a biker...hot, dirty talking, protective, dominant without being domineering, loving. "Once again, Kadence and her smart mouth made my dick hard and my head hurt all in the space of sixty seconds." Gah, love him!!! All I have to say is Duece who?! This book is just so good, from start to finish. I love Kadance...she's strong, she's sassy, she's feisty! She made me laugh, her inner dialogue was cracking me up at times. "I want to slap my own face to snap me out of it." "What the actual fuck is wrong with me?" "Shit, all that hard work ruined by one sniff." I loved that she gave as good as she got with Nix, that she wasn't a wimpy little needy shrinking violet. And she had a mouth on her, too! I get tired of reading books with female characters that are doormats, that don't stand up for themselves, so Kadence was a breath of fresh air. The friendship between Kadence and Holly felt very real. It's nice to see 2 strong female characters together, instead of a strong lead and the flighty sidekick. "Go away, badass biker daddy. She doesn't want to see you," her friend Holly calls back." Watching Nix interact with Z, his son, helping him work through the issues with school and everything that lead back to his mom, was so sweet. You could really feel the care and love he has for his son. And that he wanted Kadence to be a part of Z's life, too...swoon. But really the best part of this book is the relationship between Nix and Kadence. From their first meeting I just couldn't get enough of the 2 of them, and you could tell they couldn't get enough of each other. I loved the word play, the banter, the heat. I loved that Kadence is a teacher and Nix is the father of one of her students. I loved that Nix is this badass biker dude, who was once your typical manwhore, but as soon as he set his sights on Kadence that was it for him. Even when she kept pushing his buttons, and pushing him away, he didn't revert to his old ways. He was still his gruff, tough self, dealing with some club "shit" as he would say, but made Kadence a priority in his life, especially when she needed him most. I'll admit this book made me giddy as I was reading it. This probably isn't the book for fans of darker MC books, but this was perfect for me. There was just enough drama, angst, heat, lust, love, friendship. I can't wait to read Affliction to get inside Sy's head, and then Reclaimed to get more Nix and Kadence.

Heartless by Marissa Meyer is a prequel of sorts to Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland & Through the Looking-Glass. It tells the story of Catherine, a sweet girl who dreams lemon trees into existence in her bedroom and whose only desire in life is to open a bakery with her best friend. However, Catherine is a lady, the daughter of the Marquess of Rock Turtle Cove, and the favorite of the bachelor King of Hearts. As such, she is expected to be a dutiful high born daughter and give up her bakery dream, wed the king she does not love, and become the Queen of Hearts. And to mess things up even more for Catherine, a new Court Joker arrives on the very evening the King is set to propose, and he has the dark good looks and yellow eyes that have been haunting Catherine's dreams. I LOVED Heartless. Meyer did a really good job, I think, of capturing the whimsy of the source novel, without just copying it. I suppose it'll help to be familiar with Carroll's version before reading this one, but I don't think it's strictly necessary. Even if you don't quite get all of the references, that'll only add to the nonsensical feel that Wonderland is supposed to have anyway. Win/win, I'd say. Now let's talk characters: I did like Catherine. I couldn't help but compare her to the Lunar Chronicles' Queen Levana in my head, but Catherine is infinitely more likeable. Levana's fate is kind of sad at first, but was largely the result of her own (malicious tbh) choices. Catherine was a genuinely good person who simply wasn't very brave or strong for most of the book. (Beware there's both Fairest spoilers & Heartless spoilers under this cut: And her fate wasn't caused by malicious choices, but rather a misguided decision that was based on love. She kinda knew everything would go to hell if she went back to Hearts after going through the maze, but she couldn't very well leave her best friend behind to die. Also, Catherine and Jest had an ACTUAL relationship based on ACTUAL love, whereas Levana had a pretty warped relationship with a man who she claims to love but ended up killing. SO.) Jest was the best part of course. I'm such a sucker for mysterious, charming, and sort of weird romantic leads. Meyer perfectly crafted this man with whom every reader (or just me?) would fall in love with so as to make the the inevitable ending that much more heartbreaking, so that we could better understand Catherine's transformation. This review is a mess, but I'm going to end it by saying that books like this one (and Fairest and the TV show "Once Upon a Time" and all the rest that are similar) are SO important. I want to know why these "evil" characters are the way they are. There's always a reason. I can sort of put up with one-dimensional heroes, but an evil character needs a bit more explaining for me to buy it. Anyway, read the book.
Any time you ever think about having a pity party for yourself on account of your crazy family, just stop and be thankful you were not dealt the hand that poor Jasper Dent was. Cause daaaaaang.

I just finished reading this last night and I've to say that it was a very fast read. Even though the book was fairly thick and the words were tiny, I was able to read through everything in a mere 3 hour time. It was that good. I didn't really need to put the book down and distract myself as the author was able to make me feel like I was inside the book, living, breathing and gaming the life of Wade. It also made me feel like I myself was living inside Oasis. SAO being my favourite anime, I had no choice but to pick this up from Waterstone and I definitely was not let down. I'm also very surprised by the amount of knowledge the author has on the games, songs and movies and the ability to link all of them and build up this phenomenal fictional contest. UNWIND. DONE. I LOVE IT. YET I HAD SOME PROBLEMS WITH IT. This started out with me just discussing the book with my awesome friend Binnudeya and as I looked upon my too long message. It seems fit to be a review. kind of? maybe. we'll call that. So here are my thoughts on the long awaited read of UNWIND! SPOILERS coming your way! Ah the ending was awesome. Lev being a clapper? surprised. But he was redeemed at the end. Awesome character development here. Connor. Oh boy. In the beginning he was kind of naive and acting like a baby. I was expecting high character development from him. it came near the end. But the fact that he lost his eye? and then his arm was bad and gave him another one. ROLAND'S ARM! ROLAND. I hated that little shit. But going in to the Unwind process. I felt really sad and was actually sympathetic for him. My hand was on my mouth through out that chapter. Horrible. That chapter was written perfectly. THEY DON'T LIVE! (people who get Unwound) I MEAN HE DISAPPEARED NEAR THE END. SO HOW IS THAT POSSIBLE? The world building was not the best. I mean this was after the American civil war. which ended in 1865 (our world). So did they have this high technology since then? or is this a civil war that was made near their future? where I-pods and plasma TV's are considered antique? that wasn't mentioned. Risa. I really liked her. She was bad ass. But I don't know, we didn't see much of her for a while. Like sometimes we'd see her a lot and then nothing. She didn't get much character development. but getting paralyzed at the end. girl. tears. I want to know what happens in the next book for her. Hopefully something nice. THE LOVE PLOT. I knew this was coming. but not like this. It happened so sudden and out of no where that I didn't even realize they were kissing the first time? They both never mentioned that they liked or had an attraction for one another. And then the secret meeting to make out? Rushed, sudden, was not well built. I HATED Lev from the start and I never thought that he would be the one character that I would be rooting for in the next book. The writing style, as I said before, was not my favorite. but I feel as we went along it progressed and was better. The whole aspect of the Unwinding is still weird. And I think the question was not yet answered. I mean, why the hell would I get my child to be sent out and cut to pieces and then given to other people? at first I thought the parents were getting money for Unwinding their kids. But that was not mentioned so I don't thinks so. But still. Is it because the kids are trouble makers? that you just want to get rid of them? sending them off to chopped of is not the way. I mean you as a parent probably had to deal with the same thing when you were young, scared and worried your own parents would send you off to be Unwound. So why put your own child through that? Question unanswered. This book though had a lot of plot twists and mind fuck moments. Which I really enjoyed. Overall the book was amazing. I was on the edge of my seat almost all the time and I would have to force my self to leave the book to study and save some pages to read the next day. I think it's a 3.5 stars. but because I just really enjoyed it, on goodreads it'll be 4 stars. I think the second book is good? oh boy. Long rant for the win.

I'm not a big zombie fan. But I was swayed by all the 5-star reviews and insistence that this is a book more about journalism than zombies. I was hoping for something a lot better than what I got. First, I didn't realize it was a YA book and was immediately annoyed by the 5th grade reading comprehension level. The dialogue was trying to be witty, but fell flat and felt cliche. The plot was too simplistic and predictable. But you know what? I kept reading. The author creates an interesting post-apocalyptic world where blogging has taken over as the trusted source of news. And the main characters, although they say some pretty stupid things, have real heart. It's refreshing to have a heroine that can not only kick some ass but who also can't be bothered with romance. And for her to be hard-hitting journalist/blogger, that's just cool. The sibling relationship between Georgia and Shaun is a little weird, but endearing. And you've got to give credit to an author willing to kill off her heroine . I won't be picking up the next book in this series, but I might consider giving this book as a gift to a certain pre-teen when she's a little older.

The story was going so well and I was really enjoying it but then... WHY. DID. CAL. HAVE TO. DIE. WHHYYY???!!! That. Was. The. Worst. Did the author kill him because it would be easier to get him out of the way of Sophie and Archer? He's already a good guy. He would've been fine with it. Sad, but fine. The author didn't give Cal much credit. He should have talked more. At least let him fight a little bit more for Sophie. Is it because he's suuchh a good guy that he just let her be? He truly loved Sophie or else he wouldn't have sacrificed his dang self for her. It's so sad that all he kept saying was "It's okay, it's okay" trying to reassure Sophie even though he knew he was going to die. That vision was probably what he saw when they were in the underworld. Not that he was dying and that Sophie screamed for him, (well, might have been that also) but I think he saw Sophie dying. And Cal knew, since they got out of the Underworld, that HE would have to die to save her. And he came to Hex Hall with them anyway. ALL THAT TIME, knowing he would have to die to save his beloved Sophie. Oh, the burden. And he kept it to himself! Because he loved her. Because he loved her. He never said it to her face. He was a man of few words. But sacrificing oneself for another is probably the loudest of "I love you"s. Then there's Elodie. I know she cares for Cal, and she knows Sophie cares for him. I'm a little comforted by the fact that Elodie would keep Cal company, not as her snotty self, but as her caring self. Cal & Elodie, I think that made more sense. But he still shouldn't have died! If I were to write a book, I'd have to keep in mind NOT to kill a character that way. Especially when that character is the most kindhearted of them all. And a Healer for goodness sakes! *Rant over. I love you Cal, you deserved so much better.
Well, that was fun. Crazy, yes. But fun.

3.5 stars The increasing interest in science fiction in YA excites me. There haven't tended to be too many actual space books coming out, which is part of why SFF ends up inextricably blended on year-end lists. Empress of a Thousand Skies is fast-paced, fun, and pretty approachable science fiction. You may need a bit of patience for the first few chapters. Belleza drops a lot of knowledge on you. She doesn't infodump, which is both a blessing and a curse. It took some time for me to settle in and become used to all the new terms for people, places, things, and slang. If you're a wee bit confused at the start, don't worry too much. The characters are pretty good, but thus far lacking in depth. They're likable and compelling, but without the vibrancy that really makes me care. Several people who are important to the MCs died in the course of Empress, and I felt absolutely nothing. It's not really a feelsy book, but I was curious to find out what would happen to Rhee, Dahlen, and Aly. The world building works pretty well, though there are definitely some areas that feel a bit fuzzier. The plot varies between excellence and eye-roll-inducing predictability. I really enjoy the way that shit is basically always hitting the fan; there are some conveniences but mostly things keep going wrong, which, on a basic level, is great for plot and keeps the pace quick. On the other hand, the mystery of the missing princess was idiotically obvious; it might as well have not been a mystery. There are shades of our current political situation, which made some elements a bit more immediate. A celebrity comes to political power by leveraging fear and hatred of another culture and pushing for war. Sound familiar? If you've read a lot of SFF, many elements of Empress of a Thousand Skies will feel recognizable, and you will call many of the twists. However, everything comes together nicely and the fast pacing makes this one a good read.

I really don't know what to make of this. I went into this without having read Fangirl or really knowing anything about this book. I liked the cover and read the synopsis and thought 'okay a guy named Simon Snow is a wizard who falls in love with his vampire roommate?" Sign me up! Little did I know I was about to read Harry Potter fan fiction? I'm sorry, I just don't know any other way to put it. And if you want to argue that it is supposed to be HP fanfic then...why is this published and making money? You could substitute so many elements of this story with HP. I mean common, the Watford School of Magicks?! First off, I spent a week in Watford and I apologise to anyone who lives there but....it is a really terrible commuter suburb. You know what else is in Watford? The Harry Potter Warner Bros. Studio. Hmm Watford is not what I would call a beautiful or magical place, unlike a million other locations in the UK, so why did the author choose a place so closely related to the HP franchise? If anyone is interested this is the list I compiled of similarities to HP so you don't think I am being harsh... *The main characters are two boys and a girl. No, JK Rowling doesn't have a market on three main characters with this gender divide but Simon reminded me a lot of Harry Potter (both a little clueless and the "Chosen One"), Baz was similar to Malfoy, and Penelope was exactly like Hermione! Down to being the smart and brainy one, as well as described as having frizzy hair. *Simon is an orphan who was raised as a muggle, sorry "Normal" and didn't know he was magical. He finds out he is a wizard after all and is sent to a magical school... *The headmaster, named the Mage, takes a special interest in our main character... *The school is described as seemingly small and unimpressive but when a dragon attacks one of the characters describes a drawbridge which makes me think this is a castle school much like Hogwarts. *Ebb is essentially a female Hagrid. Can you actually publish slash fiction and make money off it? Things to ponder... . Ultimately this was just confusing and too meta. This story is HP fan-fiction, written as intentional fan-fiction from the fictional Fangirl book? That is way too abstract for me. I also thought the way spells were cast was just too silly. It felt forced....like the author realised how similar this was to Harry Potter and knew she needed something outlandish to make it different. Speaking of forced...the m/m romance was a huge letdown. I never really had a strong feeling that Simon and Baz really loved each other. Maybe it was because Simon wasn't written very well and was a bit of a cardboard character. Baz was much better and I believed his side of the story a bit more...but overall it just did not work for me. I wish Baz had been in this more and the author wrote more about him being a vampire and the whole dynamic he has with his family turning a blind eye to it. One thing I did enjoy was the author's excellent British references and slang. I mean, she even talked about 'ribena' in this novel! As a recent ex-pat living in the UK I was pleasantly surprised. I can't say what a native British person would think but having lived here for a year I thought it was very well done and a lot of the references made me smile. One last thing...why was this book called Carry On? Is this a reference to something in Fangirl that I am missing? |Featherbrained Books Blog | Twitter |

Before I Read the Book... Does anyone really care about Levana? DON'T TRY TO MAKE HER REDEEMABLE. Summary of the Story This in-between novel is all about Levana's early life, her first and only love, and her shitty, shitty sister. Levana grew up hating herself, especially her appearance, after her sister Chanarry forced her into a fire when they were children. She has kept a glamour up at all times since. After their parents die, Channary takes the throne, but she's not a very good queen since all she does is pamper herself and sleep around. Whereas Levana cares about Luna and knows quite a bit about politics and important social issues. She knows she'd make a far better queen than her sister. She falls in love with a palace guard named Evret, but he and his wife are expecting a child. After the mother dies in labour, Levana admits her feelings to him and offers to make him prince and his daughter Winter a princess. But the feelings he has for her are just friendly, and he hasn't yet finished grieving for his dead wife. So Levana uses mind control to slowly make him love her back, even though it never works. It leads to kisses and intimacy and a fake relationship - and eventually marriage - but never love. When Channary dies suddenly, her daughter Selene is set to inherit the throne but only once she turns thirteen. Until then, Levana will rule Luna. As a way to ensure her position as queen will remain permanent, Levana plans the murder of Selene, even though part of her knows it's evil. She coerces Selene's nanny to start a fire in the playhouse, killing them both (even though we know Selene survived the fire). Everyone begins to suspect there was foul play, and people start to fear and loathe Levana due to their suspicions. One day, Evret admits that he will never truly love her. She finally shows him her true self in hopes that it will make him trust her, and even though he accepts her as is, they both know it's too late to make a real difference. When the Earthen empress dies from letumosis, Levana realizes it's time to form a marriage alliance between Luna and Earth, so trading between planets can begin anew. In order for this to become possible, she tricks a man into assassinating Evret, before killing him herself. While Reading ** Levana's sister SUCKS. ** I mean, I feel a little bad about Levana being so insecure about her appearance, but at the same time I'm like, get over it. ** Oh no. Evret's baby is going to be shell, isn't it? Damnnnnn Edit: Nevermind, the mom just dies... Edit: Does this mean Evret ends up marrying Levana and the baby is really Winter??? I bet it is. Edit: AHA ** You know what I just realized? That Channary is Cinder's mom. I've been so concerned with Levana that I totally forgot Cinder is her niece. Damn Cinder, your mom was a real piece of work though. ** Oh fuck. I didn't know Channary was the one who gave Levana those burns. ** jesus fuck What I Thought Of course there has to be excuses for why Levana's so awful...Can't she just be a villain we can all love to hate? There always has to be some intense reason for why someone becomes evil, which can make them redeemable in the end. I appreciate that when it comes to some characters, but not her. Levana is vain and annoying and a bad, bad person. I don't want to pity her; Can't I just hate her? But no. This book HAD to be a thing. And now I don't hate Levana nearly as much as I did before. I can't. It's hard to when so much bad stuff happens to someone. It certainly doesn't excuse the thousands of deaths she has caused, but it does account for her being the way she is. I still hate her, but at least I understand her.

** spoiler alert ** This book haunts me. That might be good in some ways, but not for me in this one. I read this as a buddy read and may have only finished it because of that. It troubled me in many ways and I probably should have stopped around ch. There was a lot of cruelty to animals in this book. I do understand it was 1920's Alaska and the wilderness with people trying to survive. Hunting and trapping were a way of survival at the time of course. It just took up too much of the plot in this book and described in much more detail than I think it needed to be. If you are sensitive to the suffering of animals, and some being killed just because you can, this book is likely not for you. The spoiler coming up gives some additional details about some of the specifics of what I struggled with in regards to the animal cruelty. I would like to make the future reader aware of numerous descriptions of slaughter, and trapping. the snow child kills a beautiful swan and it is sickening in the description and horror of it all; the boy, Garrett, kills her pet fox because he is jealous of her; lot's of descriptions of hunting and trapping marten, mink, coyote, fox, and lynx. The killing of chickens is described in great detail more than once; there is a killing of a moose for food and a long drawn out depiction of eating the moose's heart. Later the boy, Garrett, gives Faina (the snow child) a puppy to make up for killing her pet fox who protects her. He has become infatuated with her (yet, he himself was horrified while secretly watching her kill the swan. ) They fall in love and decide they will get married. She won't let anyone see her wedding dress. Later she comes out in it and everyone sees she has sewn the swan feathers to it. (She killed the swan before she fell in love with Garrett). And... did I mention killing the swan was brutal and unnecessary? It is described from pg. Ch. A whole chapter given to murdering a swan. Everyone is obsessed with this girl in this book and trying to get her to stay with them. I think she is a heartless killer. The ending is lacking and left me feeling, "Is that it?' I hated the ending. It left me so disappointed and raw. This book was heavy and took me to dark places that I am still trying to escape from. I am a vegetarian. I am sure some people won't be as disturbed by the brutality of the animal slaughter as I was. If you are troubled by animal cruelty, skip this book. Nothing else about it is worth this read in my opinion.

Much better than Queen of Shadows. I think for me this series is split into two parts, the actual fantasy world/magic/plot, and the romance. The first part is great. I love the world and the magic and the plot is intricate and keeps getting better and better. I really did enjoy this book a lot. It's pretty damn awesome. The relationships though... It's not even that I particularly dislike the pairings, I just don't think most of them are necessary. It feels like everyone has to be paired off by the end of the series, even if it doesn't make sense. And it's a shame, because I really like a lot of the characters. The fey males are annoying, but the witches are great, I ADORE Lysandra, and even Aelin has her moments. But all of them are better on their own, when their motives aren't inspired by their significant others. What side of a war you're on shouldn't be decided by who you want to bang. Especially when there are lots of good reasons to fight. Lorcan is the worst offender here. He's ONLY switching sides because he fell in love with Elide. Also, Manon's allegiance would feel more meaningful if it didn't start with her saving Dorian for... reasons? Reasons that mean they're fucking now. I don't know, maybe I'm making a bigger deal of this than it is; I guess it's a pet peeve of mine. I do like the non-romantic relationships in this series. Lysandra and Aelin have a good friendship and Manon and Elide are wonderful. I could just do without most of the romance. And that includes the explicit sex scenes. By now, the story is getting a bit complicated for audiobooks, not to mention all the characters and their titles/nicknames (everyone is queen of something, or fey male, or some kind of animal), which means I miss things sometimes. It's not stopping me from enjoying it, and I'm not sure I could get through these books in physical form, so I'm sticking to audio. The next book is the last one (right?) and I'm definitely looking forward to that. I'm excited to see how it all plays out!

I don't normally gush in my reviews, but I really loved this book. Although I normally read romance, this book was pretty much a straight up Urban Fantasy with some romantic elements to it. And I normally hate post apocalyptic books, but this book worked for me on a bunch of levels. I know that I complain endlessly about how there is not good quality writing in this genre, and this book was great. I felt like I could step inside the world and live there. The made up slang was amazing! It reminded me of Clockwork Orange. In addition, the book is told in a tight third person from Chess's point of view that puts us inside her head without making me feel like I was reading her grocery list. She is an unreliable narrator, but there is plenty of room to see that the hasty decisions she makes will come back to get her later. Oh Chess, what a screwed up young lady you are. A great multi-demensional character, your faith and love for the Church and your spiraling drug use both seem like real facets to a multi-demensional character more than the gimicky drug use of some stories. A lot of reviewers also mention what a great character Terrible is, and I have to agree. I love that he is a thug and a gang member, and that isn't really glossed over- he beats the crap out of people many times in the book. For someone described as being ugly, indimidating and scared, he had a suprisingly smart and sweet and gentle side that Chess is not really deserving of. I really hope that they can get their shit together in future books although this universe is gritty enough that a HEA may not be possible. I will still cross my fingers though. I bought the next book before I was done reading this one I loved it so much!

WHAT THE FUCK DID I JUST READ? WHAT KIND OF CLIFFHANGER WAS THAT? Dear Colleen & Tarryn, how could you... The story begins with Charlie accidently dropping her books in her class and she doesn't recognize herself. It gets more confusing when she met Silas and their friends were throwing stuff at both of them and made it look like they were/are dating. They did not remember anything from the last 24 hours (i think), not even their names. Then they decided to talk and try to figure things out together. It's fast paced and exciting, we begin to find out that Charlie has a sister, Janette Wynwood & Silas has a brother, Landon Nash. Janette doesn't like Charlie that much, but it seems like Landon and Silas get along really well. Charlie's mum an alcoholic, her dad is in prison because of the business fraud thing that happpened between him and Silas' father. I guess that's also the reason behind their family drama. Charlie cheated on Silas with Brian and Silas cheated on Charlie with the school's guidance counselor (kinky eh?). Oh and apparently Charlie/Silas have been dating for four years! Since they lost their memories, they don't know anything about how they get along before but now? Oh they're indeed adorable! Charlie and Silas also realised they have tattoos that represent each other's name. Things get more intense when they went to get a tarot reading. Most of the cards aren't good and it made Charlie upset. At the end of their trip, they kissed! Even though we all know both of them enjoyed the kiss (obviously), Charlie felt something was off so she ran away. Apparently Charlie didn't go back home when she took off that night so basically she's missing now. At the last chapters, Silas found letters that says the lost of their memories has happened twice and it will happen again in 48 hours. Now he needs to find Charlie and tell her. I've never read any of Colleen's or Tarryn's book but I really love the writing style. I love how they're telling the story from both Charlie and Silas' POV. I've always loved reading two different perspective in a story. This book was definitely a page turner! Gah I really need the next part asap.

This is the story of Griffin, a teenager whose boyfriend graduated a year ahead of him, moved to California, and died there. In some ways I liked the format, which opens with us knowing Theo has died, as Griff tries to get himself together for the funeral. It then alternates the past, at the beginning of their relationship, with the present, as Griff meets Theo's grieving California boyfriend Jackson. There are surprises that repeatedly shift the opening straightforward narrative. At the same time the back and forth past-to-present felt like it robbed some of the immediacy from the past scenes. I was not as invested in Griff-and-Theo because I knew a lot about where it was going. Watching Griff grieve was not the same as seeing him fall in love and then be blindsided. In some ways, it avoids the teen-angst cliche, but it also put a little remove into the emotions for me. I wish we saw more of Wade before the 3/4 mark - he and Jackson were the more sympathetic characters, and he went from minor to major rather fast. It's a trade off between surprise and completeness, but I felt like the effort not to signal twists in advance robbed us of some understanding of who Wade is. I appreciated that these are all flawed characters, who make some bad choices, especially Griff. It's good to have a protag with real weaknesses. Some significant issues got a bit of short shrift IMO -  and the way Wade acted vis Griff's OCD, and his response, felt a bit like the magic healing powers of love. There was therapy beginning too, but that little piece felt a bit off, like Griff is now suspected of having exaggerated his issues to keep Theo interested. It's not supportive of a disability to suggest a character was partially faking or indulging in it. For me, this was not a tear-jerker, although I think if it had been told in a linear way it might have been. But then it would have lost some of the surprises that come as a bigger twist because of the parallel structure. It is an interesting picture of teen relationships and how easy it is to hurt each other, and to self-sabotage. The writing was good - I would pick up another book by this author.

Actually this is probably a 3.5. Inching up to 4. Getting there! Griffin and Hero are great leads. I liked them both. I disliked a lot of the other people around them, though. Especially Hero's intended and Hero's older brother. What in the actual ... after Griffin's brother (I've forgotten his name because he was a douche) hits Hero hard enough to knock her to the ground and bruise her face, her brother still insists that she marry him? What? Whaaaat? ... I just can't. And then that incident just gets pushed the back burner and I guess we're supposed to forget about it. I know, it's not abnormal for the times, but still. It reflected badly on a few characters. At least Griffin took it seriously enough to try to kill the elder douche. Hero is the sister of the Duke of Wakeland. Griffin is the brother of the Marquis she's about to be betrothed to. Because Griffin's older brother (whose name escapes me) is hopeless with money, it's fallen to Griffin to manage and rebuild the family's finances. He's also one of those guys who wants to do it without telling anyone else there's an actual problem. So the family is spending money accordingly. Griffin's entrepreneurial endeavor is an illegal gin still in St. Giles. Considering Hero's brother -- the duke -- has made it his life's work to vanquish the gin trade in London and all of England, there's bound to be some chewy drama. Here's the thing that bugged me in this book. I noticed a pattern in these first books that was basically the two leads talking: "bicker bicker bicker, blah blah blah, bicker bicker bicker ... damn you!" kiss, heavy make out, *gasp! *, push away ... then the male lead says something crude in a silky, seductive voice and the female lead gets miffed. It happened again and again in the first book and also in this one. Hoyt sets up the next book so well though, I had to move immediately on to it. And this story isn't bad, it's just got that one bizarre element (under the spoiler tag) and that persistent pattern. I just finished book 7 though and I can say she deviates from the template in later books and that's a good thing. So, while it's not quite up to 4 stars, it's still a good historical read and I'm definitely hooked on the series.
I may adjust this later, because this does have some flaws, especially a pretty weak ending, but it was so awesome and fun to read. Reminded me a bit of theThe Rook.

The Keeper - 3/5 To be honest, I didn't really know much about Michelle Benoit, so I didn't care much for her story. It spans close to a decade, and after a point I got a bit bored. But we did get to see a bit of younger Scarlet, and I really liked the symbolism of Cinder's name. Glitches - 4/5 Glitches pretty much picks up where The Keeper ends. It covers Cinder's travel to Beijing and her first meeting with Adre and her step sisters. I liked it a little better than The Keeper, but in both stories, there was very little that was new and that we didn't already know about. The Queen's Army - 5/5 Wolf <3 He's actually still just Ze'ev in this novella. But he's just as sweet and adorable. This is the story of how Wolf was picked to be a part of the Queen's army, and how he went from being a member of the pack to being Alpha. I could not put this story down. It was the bloodiest of all the novellas, but it's my second favourite after Something Old, Something New. Carswell's Guide to Being Lucky - 4/5 I thought this would be a story written in the form of some guide, but it's actually just a regular novella. We get to see a younger (but just as quirky, adorable and determined in his criminal mastermind ways) Thorne and the whole Kate Fallow incident. If it were possible for me to still like him more, this story would have done it. After Sunshine Passes By - 4/5 I always had a soft spot for sweet innocent Cress and this novella just helped cement that feeling further. We get to see how she went from being just another shell to being trapped on a satellite. It broke my heart a bit how she believed the best right up till the end. The Princess and The Guard - 3 + 1 for Jacin = 4/5 Winter really annoyed me in this novella, but Jacin stole my heart. So nothing much has changed since Winter. This is the story of the incident that made Winter stop using her glamour, and how she started subsequently started falling sick because of it. I'm a bit confused though, because in this novella, it appears that Jacin completely gave up on his dream and on the medical internship in order to stay at the palace as a member of the Royal Guard and be there for Winter. But in Winter, he very clearly says that he spent some time as an intern at the clinic. If you have theories, please let me know. The Little Android - 2/5 I spent a good quarter of this story believing that the android Mech 6.0 was Iko until I realised that this was a completely different story that had nothing to do with any of the characters we know. That was part of the reason for the low rating. I didn't know any of these characters and I didn't care about them. To add to that, the story of The Little Mermaid was always a little too depressing for my tastes. And the ending was a bit ambiguous. I get that she switched places, but how didn't anyone notice??! Easily my least favourite novella of the bunch. The Mechanic - 3/5 This is the story of Kai and Cinder's first meeting, right where the series started, but told from Kai's perspective. I'm so glad Marissa Meyer wrote this, because that was a scene that I really wanted to see from Kai's viewpoint. (Is it weird that I don't know Kai's last name? Was it ever mentioned and I don't remember?) Something Old, Something New - 5/5 Of all the novellas, this was the only one I was really interested in, because it tells us what happens after. And Marissa Meyer did not disappoint. It's the only story that was truly worth reading. I'd give it a million stars if I could, but I have only 5. "Forevermore, you will be my mate, my star, my beginning of everything."

I enjoyed the heck out of this book. It's old-school sci-fi evocative of Heinlein's juveniles, but with more grit and less social engineering. Hoyt gives us a plot that moves quickly and is full of unexpected detours without ever derailing the sense of purpose and discovery. But don't let me get away with implying that it's all about the plot. I really liked the characters, as well, and enjoyed seeing the two main characters learn to respect each other and forge the bond that they needed to weather the storms they faced.

3.5 stars... This is such a hard book to rate/review because the first half I absolutely LOVED! And since this was a random book I found on BookBub and I didn't have any expectations, I was thrilled to be so invested. There was no insta-love or insta-lust, in fact they both kind of hated each other. I was worried that since Connor was a famous athlete, Hailey would worship him. But she definitely wasn't! I loved how shy, yet firm she was, and the fact that she didn't let Connor's status, good looks, or skill sway her, especially when he was such a jerk when they first met. "One of America's Sexiest Athletes was sitting in my living room and all I wanted was him gone." And what was great was she didn't waffle, she genuinely was not interested him, and Connor, of course, assumes that she'll fall in love with him because that's what women do. They worship him. I was so unbelievably excited to watch him eat his words. I was practically giddy when I thought I'd get to watch Connor, the guy who implied Hailey was beneath him and who had no interest in settling down, chasing Hailey and beg her to give him a chance. Especially because Hailey had no problem telling it like it was... "You live in a dream world where it's a woman's job to look good. If she didn't look good, then she'd be a sucky model or whatever wouldn't she?" "Here's a clue. If you don't want people to tell other people you're a jerk, don't act like a jerk." And this did (kind of) happen. Connor let his walls down and apologized to Hailey. They even become friends during their fake relationship. He lets his wall down and we see that he really isn't a bad guy. He isn't the manwhore the press assumes he is (he does go on plenty of dates, but he doesn't sleep with all the women) and while originally he seems shallow, we learn that he just has a hard time differentiating his public persona with who he really is. "Hailey, I'm sorry that I was rude and selfish and self-focused in the elevator and that I demeaned you in front of a woman because she was beautiful and dressed for her job. I was angry and worried and I defaulted to the person I put out for the papers, not the guy I like to be when I'm with my family or the few friends I trust. You are not ugly or beneath me. You'reaEUR| I like you. I'm glad we're deciding to be friends." BUT (and this really is a me thing) they proceeded to become friends for most of the book instead of date. It was a sloooooooooooow burn, indeed. I don't always mind a slow burn, but I want a kiss before 99% . It made the story a little slow for me and I wanted to read more about their relationship. I did enjoy this, but I think I was more let down by the last part because of how much I loved the first part. I hate seeing something I'm loving go downhill, but a slow burn like that really isn't for me. Again, there's nothing wrong with the book. This is a 100% ME thing. So if you enjoy a hate-to-love, slow burn romance with minimal drama, I would definitely check this one out :) Safety: Some OW/OM drama, but no cheating/kissing/dating other people and no specific details about past hook-ups. Hailey has a male friend (who is a manwhore) who is in love with her and hanging around, and Connor has a few female fans who try to make trouble. It's all very minimal though. Closure: None really. The last chapter ends with their first kiss.

(She is Zoey's best friend, I must say I would try to do the same, but you have to be smart about it, but because you cant tell your best friends. It may be impossible without losing said friends). Originally posted at Vampire Book Club Delilah Marlow's life has been pretty normal throughout her twenty-five years. She's wanted for nothing. However, things can change in the blink of an eye. Metzger's Menagerie is back in town and features one of the most extensive array of supernaturals (or cryptids) found anywhere else in the country. Decades ago cryptids lived among humans by and large, but after a horrific incident referred to as "The Reaping," anyone with any amount of supernatural blood lost all rights. Many are killed for sport, some are experimented on by the government, and others are prisoners in traveling carnivals. While visiting the menagerie on her birthday, Delilah sees one injustice after another. When she is at her limit, something happens to Delilah and the next thing she knows she's now part of the travelling menagerie as a cryptid. Delilah is at once faced with her life being turned upside down. In the space of hours, she goes from being human with all the rights allotted to that title, to being property and having nothing. Slowly, Delilah comes to know her fellow prisoners, and realizes that the way humans look at cryptids needs to change, but first Delilah will have to learn to survive in her new environment. Menagerie was one of those books that I've being hearing about and waiting for, for years now. From what I understand this book was a long process for Rachel Vincent, and you can clearly see the care that this story has been given by the way it is crafted. Vincent takes quite a bit of time to set the scene, but as her words weave themselves into the story proper, I found myself enchanted by the often grotesque, sometimes beautiful, blatant commentary on humanity found within its pages. Rachel Vincent doesn't pull any punches when it comes to showing what happens when people are faced with something they fear or something they don't understand. At the end of this book, I have no doubts in my mind about what the majority of humans think about cryptids, but I don't think the book would have had such a big impact if Vincent hadn't decided to really push this point. Delilah's situation was so bleak and she knew that, but she held on to her strength throughout the whole book. Though her thoughts raced back and forth between wanting to give up and wanting to fight back, I only think this made her more relatable as a character. I mean whose feelings wouldn't waffle back and forth if all they've ever known comes into question? And when I say all, I mean all. I found myself constantly looking for acts of kindness in this book, and I was surprised when Delilah's stoic handler Gallagher fits this bill more often than not. He actually talks to Delilah like she is a person and not a thing. He tries to go easy on her for all that he's been instructed to "break" her. One wonders what his story is, and obviously there's a mystery there. I rather enjoyed figuring out the pieces of his character. If you're someone looking for a paranormal book without the usual players, you'll really enjoy the different mythical creatures that pop up at the menagerie. For me, the main events in this book were pretty self-contained. The threads left open will definitely carry readers into the next book, but for this one the focus is squarely on the workings of the Menagerie.
