Grifter Victoria Valentine sets her sights on the mark of a lifetime, billionaire Dmitri Sevastyn. The score that can save her family, IF she can pull it off. Maybe she can, because he is just that into her, but Dmitri is messed up. His demons have demons and when her secret is unveiled.... Not to be braggy, but there are precious few writers who can throw me a total curveball, okay? I thought I knew where we were going on this and while I had the jist, yeah, Cole went for the jugular and stunned me. I didn't know how we were gonna come back from that twist, but....oh just read the damn thing. I didn't think anyone was gonna beat Maksim for me, but Dmitri....IDK what it is about broken men, but this guy became my fave brother. Hands down. Lucia is still a better heroine than Victoria(nobody is better than Lucia, one of my favorite female MCs of ALL time, see book #2) but I liked Victoria and I felt for her, being crushed between her family and her heart. Oh but the sex, you ask? A Game Maker book and I haven't mentioned the sex? One word. Stratospheric. Yup. Read. This. Series. NOW.

I'm beginning think that my amount of love for Jennifer Armentrout and this series is getting dangerously out of control. I don't even have the words to describe how incredibly this was. This series just keeps getting better and better, totally exceeding my expectation and blowing me way entirely. The story was just bursting with love, bad-assery, character growth, super awesome relationships, shocking plot twists, cool gods, and every other brilliant thing I could ever hope for. The ending was absolutely phenomenal, and I'm pretty sue I held my breath for the entire last few pages. It was SO intense! Aiden was hotter and sweeter than ever, which I did not even realize was possible,  though the part with his guilt about the brew drove me insane! I felt so bad for Alex because he was avoiding her when she needed him most, but I also felt bad for Aiden because he felt so unnecessarily guilty. It just tore my heart out. Also, he never once gave up on Alex when she was connected to Seth, and always saw the girl that he loved was somewhere, buried deep within her. It was beautiful to see how lovingly persistent he was, especially when he finally got through to her. he was so careful to never even lay a finger on her when she was coming close to killing him in the outside of the cabin. Now that is love! Deacon was even more hilarious than ever,  and I adored seeing a few peeks at his relationship with Luke. Apollo was also absolutely hilarious and I have come to love his character so much! And of course, Alex was as sassy and kickass as ever. She also went under a lot of growth and development throughout the book, and her relationship with Marcus really grew, which I loved. I think that he's a great uncle and he really cares about her, but he just doesn't know how to show it. Especially in the first book, where I hate him. It's kind of funny to look back on that now because each of the characters have come so far from where they started and I feel so proud. If you haven't read this series yet, I would highly suggest doing so. It is beyond words.

Three and a half stars. I've been waiting for Tim's story pretty much since I put down My Life Next Door the first time. It was easy to see that his character had such potential and that his appearance in that book was only the beginning of his story. The Boy Most Likely To was not quite what I was expecting, not even a little bit, but in being so unexpected, it far exceeded any preconceived notions I'd previously held. While My Life Next Door was told only from Sam's perspective, the author goes for a dual narrative in this book. I don't think it was really necessary.. But yeah, that's like a trend nowadays. There's quite a lot I'd like to say about Tim's narrative, but considering it all revolves around a twist, it's best I leave it unsaid. It very nearly broke my heart, though. Tim's put himself through a lot, and he's still recovering from all of that, only to be put through the ringer again. But it's that wonderful Garrett clan that comes to the rescue once more, even though they're still dealing with the events from the end of the first book. I found this book to be just as lovely and genuine as Huntley Fitzpatrick's previous two books. I love that she doesn't use miscommunication as a plot device but rather has her characters speak openly and frankly to one another. They may be facing some serious life decisions and what-not, but there's no bullshit. The romance was pretty slow, which was a big reason this book differed so wildly from my expectations and made the book a little bearable. The Boy Most Likely To is more of a coming-of-age story than a romance, probably the least romance-y of Fitpatrick's novels so far. I don't normally love companion novels because they rarely live up to the first book for me -- usually because they focus on some extraneous character I didn't really care about in the first place -- but in this case, I needed this story to be told, and I'm glad of how it turned out. One final point I want to mention is that I somehow didn't like Alice. Like, at all. She kept pissing me off and I could barely put up with her. She seemed a little too out-of-the-way-ishly eccentric.. And too unrealistic. I loved Tim. And I enjoyed reading the book. *Received ARC via Netgalley and the publisher in exchange for a honest review*

3.75 stars Food is no longer what it used to be. It has been broken down into its parts (vitamins, nutrients, etc), some of those parts taken out and/or added back in, as studies find we need more or less of those parts. It has been overly processed. Pollan explains how this happened and what we can do to try to get back to eating real food, and hopefully stave off many diseases that seem to have ballooned since this overprocessing of food became the norm. I found it quite interesting. There was some stuff I knew and some I didn't. Pollan writes in a way that the info is interesting and accessible, although there was a section in the middle where I did lose focus a few times (which is why I didn't quite rate it 4 stars). I didn't like it quite as much as The Omnivore's Dilemma, but still really interesting.

It seems like things have settled down for the moment in Morganville, for the roommates, too bad that they all seem to be on different sides and not able to talk to each other at all. I liked how Richard and Hannah have stepped up on the human side and done what they can to make people safe. I also love seeing Claire's parents argue about sending her to Morganville. Seems like Dad was right, but Mom couldn't cut the apron strings just yet. I also like to see then try to parent Claire when she is this super brain and seems to be the one that keeps saving the town. I think they should let her make her own decisions. I was surprised at the sex scene in the book. Usually YA takes it off the page if it happens at all. What I did like about it was that it was real and there were awkward moments like in real life, it was not movie sex, and even says so in the book. I wasn't surprised with what happened to Shane's dad. I thought something like that would happen to more people that Claire seemed to care about. He may not have always been the best guy to have around, but when the chips fall he stepped up. I don't think that we have seen the last of him. I think the consequenses of the battle will have long repercusions, people have been lost, people betrayed those now left in charge, and people have a choice now. It will be interesting to see where the town and the 2 different people go from here.

This may be my favorite book of the series. I like that the protagonists know each other for twelve years before the main part of the action takes place. To me, that is a lot more realistic than many of the "just meet, fall in love right away" type of stories. It is funny how the author shows the mind of a seventeen year old girl. "This was love. Oh, this was love love love love love love. A silly repetition of words, perhaps, but that was precisely what Penelope doodled on a ridiculously expensive sheet of writing paper, along with the words, 'Mrs. Colin Bridgerton' and 'Penelope Bridgerton' and 'Colin Colin Colin.' (The paper went into the fire the moment Penelope heard footsteps in the hall.)" I also like the insights revealed into the hero's way of thinking, eleven years later. "'I don't know when, I dont know how, and to be honest, I don't care. But I know this much is true: I love you, and I hate myself for not seeing the real you all these years....I don't think you changed,' he said. 'At least not very much. But then one day I realized i was seeing something very different when I looked at you.' He shrugged. 'Maybe I changed. Maybe I grew up.'" Yeah, I think so. If the book has any weaknesses, it's in the subplots. I don't care. I liked it a lot.

But love isn't a straight line. It's curved and kinked, and sometimes it's better if it's cut. This book was one of the most riveting thrillers I've ever read. Usually when I see a book in the genre thriller, I take that classification with a pinch of salt. They're usually not that suspenseful and exciting. However, We'll Never Be Apart gripped me from the start and continued to shock me throughout the whole book. The story follows a girl named Alice who is stuck in a mental hospital called Savage Isle where everything she does it monitored. Her twin sister is in the building next door, and Alice wants revenge for what her sister has done: killed her love, Jason, in a horrible fire. However, because of the strict security at Savage Isle, she doesn't think she will ever be able to avenge Jason. That is, until she stumbles upon Chase who tells her that she reminds him of someone he once knew and wants to help her with her dilemma. I actually liked Alice's character. I liked her passion for her hobby, orgami animals, and I loved her resilience. I also kind of liked the romance that began to form between her and Chase. The chemistry was there and there wasn't insta-love. Well, not exactly. As soon as Alice saw Chase, she became intrigued with him and said that he wasn't horrible looking, but she didn't love or trust him. "People come undone all the time, Alice. We're all unraveling here. You've just done it in the most spectacular way. In fact, you could be our queen," he jokes. I smile, but it's wan and distant. "Queen of the Undone?" "It has a certain charm to it, don't you think?" The best thing about this though was the buildup of the mystery itself. When I bought this book, I didn't think it was going to be that intense. It seemed pretty one-note. Although, once you get into the story and read Alice's journal entries that she writes, it becomes a story that involves obsession and poses the question, how much love is too much love? The mystery wasn't easy for me to figure out at all. I see a lot of people saying that they saw it from a mile away, but I did not see that coming at all. It had me flipping the pages after the reveal until I had the whole book devoured. My only complaint is there were some things that I found unrealistic. Chase would get security cards to open doors extremely easy which didn't add up with how high-security Savage Isle is. At the beginning of the book, Alice's headphones are taken from her because they pose a risk due to Alice's mental state. However, Chase has headphones the whole story. I mean, he might not be as high of a risk for suicide as Alice, but it seems strange that they would allow him to keep his. Also there were some questions that I wish would have been answered at the end but not so many that I would give this 3 stars. Other than that though, I'm pleasantly pleased with this one. I never felt like I was forcing myself to read it. When I went out, I wanted to get home to read it to find out if Alice would get her revenge. It's definitely one of, if not the best thrillers I've ever read.

WINTERSONG was one of my most anticipated books of 2017; from the gorgeous cover to the intriguing synopsis, this book had surely caught my eye. I was pretty impressed with this debut novel, and I'm crossing my fingers that they'll be a sequel or companion novel or something. WINTERSONG follows Liesl, who offers her life to the Goblin King in the Underworld in exchange for her sister's life and the prosperity of the world above. I thoroughly enjoyed the plot and the dramatics that accompanied it. While some aspects of the plot seemed convoluted and glazed over, I was still enamored with the conflict that arose. I wasn't a huge fan of Liesl, to be honest. In one scene, things are heating up between Liesl and the Goblin King, and even though the Goblin King says to stop, Liesl doesn't. It's m when he says stop a second time and "please" that she finally lets down. She wasn't my favorite, that's for sure. However, I did appreciate her commitment and love for her siblings and her passion for music, which really fueled the tension and romance between her and the Goblin King. That being said, I did quite love the Goblin King; I dug his passion for music and his honesty (in weird way). Also, the steamy scenes between the two were super sensual; the author has a knack of writing really amazing sex scenes, y'all. One of my favorite aspects of the novel was the atmospheric writing style. The descriptions and fluid language really made the novel flow and just gave WINTERSONG the kick that it needed to make the plot and the romance move. A reservation I have, however, is that there were so many times when it felt like nothing was happening and times when it felt like too much was happening at the same time. I don't know if that was just me, but it was just sometimes difficult to fully understand what was going on. Overall, I did enjoy this debut novel; the writing style was gorgeous and the romance was sizzling. WINTERSONG ends in a relatively light cliffhanger; I'm desperately hoping that there's going to be another book because, well, there's no way it can end like that. If you're into novels with a steamy romance and an atmospheric setting, be sure to check this one out! Thank you to Thomas Dunne for providing me with an early copy of this novel in exchange for an honest review. All thoughts are my own and I was not compensated for this review.

I wanted to give this book 3 stars because it did hold my attention well, but I hesitate to say I liked it. I am slightly on the fence about the novel. Here are the elements I liked: lush descriptions of the Florida swamps. The Bigtrees Ava, Ossie, Kiwi and their dad The Chief make up a damaged family of misfits, reeling from the loss of Hilola Bigtree, wife, mother and alligator wrestling super-star of their tourist-trap theme park Swamplandia! The main thrust of the plot seems to be the different ways each character deals with their grief and the sudden wide expanse of their uncertain future, both collectively as a family and individually. Another theme, rather overt in some chapters, seems to be the loss of innocence. Kiwi's articulate intelligence and sensitivity is ridiculed when he leaves the swamp to pursue fortune on fortune on the "mainland." Ossie places her affections in the world of the dead, no doubt in part to find comfort in her own mother's untimely demise. And Ava, the youngest and most fiercely loyal to the Bigtree traditions, has her faith utterly mismanaged by The Bird Man. What I didn't like was how forced some of the writing seemed. I've not read Karen Russell before, but some of character writing just wasn't to my taste. Ava, in particular, grated me. I came to dread the chapters Ava narrated, because I found her so insanely childish and desperate for love, even to a point that endangered her and ultimately, the plot reflects this. I loathed the scene with the Bird Man and Ava. I literally wanted to throw the book across the room. The tone of the writing did not match the horrific event of a rape of a thirteen year old girl by a grizzled, swamp guide. It was a very unexpected plot twist; I expected something completely different. And yet, what's almost worse is that it's barely mentioned in the rest of the novel. Ava tells no one and hardly even dwells on it after she runs away in the swamp. After that, I didn't feel like I could trust Ava as a narrator. This book was a quick read. I found it compelling, but not captivating or very engrossing.

I picked this book up originally because it was about baseball. I loved the artsy cover with the jersey-like font, and I was curious to see what a legitimate novel about baseball would look like. Apparently, it looks a lot like a (relatively) standard novel about romance and college and life and things. I'm not sure I got all that much out of this book; the characters were pleasant, and I rooted for and empathized with all of them, but none of them were incredibly well-imagined or anything, probably as a result of the multiple storylines that weave throughout the book. The action was there, and Harbach seems to be a bit more than just a casual baseball fan, but it didn't have too much baseball, either. This is really a book about relationships and expectations, and while that doesn't mean it's not entertaining, it definitely wasn't the great mix of sports and life that I was looking for. By the end, I did care about the characters, and the climax was exciting (albeit a little abrupt) , but ultimately I was left wanting a bit more. A bit more... baseball? A bit more... development (yes, even in this 500 page book)? A bit more... something. It just didn't really grab me, didn't really stun me, and it wasn't really a fantastic journey. It was just a nice story that was about some baseball players and those around them. I gave it 3 stars because the characters were pretty great, but it was certainly a bit disappointing.

Warning: the final hidden spoiler is a big one! This one brings the whole  unreliable narrator trope   to an entirely new level. I'm not usually one for heavy-handed literary device usage, but this was pretty darn enjoyable despite (because of?) the heavy air of foreboding that was positively choking the story from page 1. But I'm also a sucker for the 1920s and speakeasies and deliciously mysterious heroines, so your mileage may vary. But I guarantee you that this will make a killer film noir-esque movie in a year or two. I want to talk about the ending, but I kinda don't even know what to say. In fact, I have no idea what really happened. There's such a thing as leaving a door open for interpretation at the end of the story, but Rindell practically knocked down all the walls as well. I can't decide yet whether this was a somewhat lazy choice and the story crumbled from there, or a masterful deconstruction of reader expectations. My halfhearted attempt at interpretation is  that her obsession with Odalie made Rose increasingly unhinged, until her desire to become ever more intimate with her led Rose to blend her own experiences with those of Odalie. The seeming paradox in the final page (how was she getting cigarettes yet simultaneously with Teddy?) might be because Rose had on some level mentally replaced herself with Odalie. Perhaps that is why she sheared off her hair and kissed the Lieutenant Detective in the end- on some level pleased with the completion of her transformation into Ginevra/Odalie. Still doesn't answer who actually killed him, though. There are a million interpretations, but then there are also a million holes left in the story with any one interpretation. If Rose was actually just the fall man, how could Odalie possibly erase all records of her childhood? Why would the Lieutenant Detective call her Rose at the end? If Rose was really Ginevra/Odalie the whole time, what was the deal with the brooch at the end? How could she not have orchestrated her whole escape as the devious minx she really was? Why was her hair long?? This was definitely one of those books that I finished and immediately started googling (in vain) for some answers. A bit frustrating.

I read The Dream-Quest of Vellitt Boe as part of my Hugo awards finalist reading marathon. As the title suggest, this story is inspired by, and a sequel of sort of the famous Lovecraft's The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, that is, by far, one of my least favorite books I have ever read, I found the original slow and boring, and I had to force myself to reach the end. It should not come as a surprise, that I was not looking forward reading this modern version of it. It turns out though, that the story is quite good, vastly superior to the original, and it subverts many of the problematic tropes of the Lovecraft's story.

It took me awhile to get into this, but I did like it in the end. Again, it is the zombie-like aspect that does nothing for me. If I were a zombie fan, I'm sure I would love this series. I didn't love this, I didn't *not* love this. If you've ever read Alexa Riley before, then you know exactly what you're getting - just in a longer format. Expect the over the top, insta-love, alpha male, obsessive, possessive-hero-in-love-with-a-virgin story line. I thought that Miles/Oz and Mallory's story dragged a bit in places. There wasn't much in the way of conflict or angst, though there was a tiny bit of drama. I liked that there were several epilogues and an extra chapter from Miles' POV. That was a nice little bonus. Also included is a preview of the next book in this series, His Alone - Ryan (Captain America) and Paige's story. <---- Their story sounds really good, can't wait for that. Paige was a more interesting character than Mallory, in my opinion. Things I thought that might be spoilery: The story line with Miles' father ended on a weak note. I was disappointed, there was the potential for a much bigger story line there - and I thought that with the length of this book that those kind of details would be included. They weren't really, just more sex. If you're looking for more story, I'm not sure you'll find it, just a longer version of every other book they've written. Don't get me wrong - I have read and liked their shorter books. There is a time and a place for them, and the ones I've read I have liked. I was just hoping for a little more substance here.

Now that I'm trying to get into historical romances, I thought it would be ok to read this book finally. I read the synopsis a while ago, but I didn't pick it up cause the cover. The major reason I held off was the cover. For romance books, historical in particular, the covers can be horribley cheesey. I'll strike a book off my reading list if the cover is some over-the-top Fabio-esque dude embracing a woman with heaving bosoms. It's corny and makes me embarrassed to pick up books like that at the library. This cover wasn't too bad, but there was a buff chiseled man on the inside of the cover haha. I'm glad I read this though. The premise was super cute what with the whole list of improper things to do. Callie was amazing! She was a breath of fresh air to read about. She wasn't perfectly beautiful and she wasn't unneccessarily fiesty. I felt so terrible with how people treated her. Even her own family members were mean towards her. I especially remember the Aunt from the beginning, gahh what a bitch! She just came off as very loveable and I liked how she stepped out of her comfort zone to do all these ridiculously crazy things. She was sweet and it was funny to see the trouble she found herself in because of the list. I don't know what to say about Ralston besides I loved him as well. He and Callie had sizzling chemistry and it was fun to see them interact. Ralston was just down-right sexy. I wouldn't mind being locked in a room with him for five hours haha. There were a few times where the storyline took a predictable turn. The most obvious being the conflict that popped up at the very end. From the second this thing happened, I knew that it was inevitable that it was going to cause troubles down the line. Maybe I'm insensitive, but I actually didn't think the whole thing was all that bad. I mean, sure, Ralstonmade a bet with Oxford, but it wasn't that terrible. He just bet that Oxford and Callie wouldn't get married. It's not like he bet something like, 'I will compromise the spinster first MWAHAHAH' . Overall, it wasn't that big of a deal, but I can see how Callie would react badly. The way it was spun and timeline of the events made it seem way worse than it actually was. My only problem was sometimes the writing itself confused me. The way some of the sentences were constructed didn't make sense. I had to read the sentences over and over and even then sometimes I didn't get it. I felt like certain sentences were worded strangley and felt a bit like run-ons a lot of the times. Also, I didn't understand some of the phrases of the time, though that probably is my fault since I haven't read a ton of regency romances to have all the rules down pact. I had no idea what 'ton' meant and who they were. It made me mega-confused and I spent several chapters trying to figure it out before I gave up and just googled it. Another one was I still have no idea the difference between dukes, marquess, earls, barons, etc. Also, what is a dandy?? Maybe one day I'll google all that. Overall, I really liked this book and now I want to find a Ralston of my own. I'm excited to read more about Juliana the sister. I saw she gets her own book, so it will be cute to hear about her story.

I realized going in this this was not my kind of book (about the afterlife and featuring extensive flashbacks) but ended up enjoying it more than I expected! Recommended for those who enjoy books with flashbacks and about memory and the afterlife. Full review here

Wow. That was...quite an ending. It was absolutely everything it needed to be - adventure, action, political intrigue, mystery, romance. All the parts balanced into a finale that was worthy of a really great series. I will always find it amusing and kind of strange that this series is titled "Vampire Academy" since we haven't actually spent much of any time at the academy since book three - and the series is better for that progress. Moving on from St. Vladimir's was the best move that Mead could have made, and letting Rose and Lissa strike out into the world they inhabit (both separately and together) was what really made this series for me. These characters (and their fantastic and complicated friendship) have come so far since the first few books in the series, and they are better for it. They grew up, and the readers got to watch them grow up. It's been pretty great. Not only have Rose and Lissa finally grown into the people they needed to be, but they've also worked out their relationships with the people around them. Rose and Dimitri (who always had incredible chemistry, but who had all sorts of power imbalances) are finally on equal footing, and capable of something healthy between them. Lissa has taken up her family legacy, and been forced to acknowledge that her late family weren't necessarily perfect people. Rose and Lissa get to live their lives as their own people now. And there's hope for the Moroi political system to become less of a toxic mess, eventually . This whole series has been a long, really satisfying road - and I'm sorry to see it end. But this was the best possible ending for it to have. It wasn't totally perfect: I wasn't really satisfied with the explanation for Tatiana's murder and the culprit. Killing off Victor was way too easy. And the first half moved much too slowly, while the second half of the book was paced too quickly. But mostly, it was great. Plus, in a very realistic fashion, a hell of a lot of people got massively screwed over by the plot resolution (and Rose). It makes sense for a series with this big, sweeping scale of action to have a lot of collateral damage. What's even better is that Bloodlines exists, and gets to deal with the characters who didn't come out of this so successful. Plus, it gives me something to read next, and lets me believe for a little while longer that I don't have to leave the world that Mead has created in these books.

(I feel like I'm starting far too many reviews like this this year, but) I'm practically brain-dead so it'll be a miracle if any of this is coherent, let alone the sound and worthy review it well deserves. My apologies to authors and readers alike. First of all, this was a huge factor and will take up a lot of the review so I really hate that I have to hide it all. Just... MINOR spoiler alert- this doesn't say anything explicit, but it reveals the tone of the ending. (Sidenote: the ending in general was very abrupt, but I definitely still enjoyed it overall.) I just need to take a moment to fully appreciate the fact that this was a lesbian romance novel in the real world of Earth in a recent century that had a happy ending. That, my friends, is not common. Anyone who reads LGBTQIA+ fiction or non-fiction no doubt learned the very bitter lesson after their first few reads. The Afterword touches on this a little bit. A direct quote from a letter Highsmith received from a queer individual: "Yours is the first book like this with a happy ending! We don't all commit suicide and lots of us are doing fine." Reading notes like these ones make me so relieved, like someone's patting me on the back and quoting another one of my favourite books Hyperbole and a Half: Unfortunate Situations, Flawed Coping Mechanisms, Mayhem, and Other Things That Happened: "Maybe everything isn't just hopeless bullshit" The writing style was a little bit interesting as I mentioned in one of the updates. It felt kinda closed off, a little bit like I had blinders on with just the current event flashing into my eyes. There seems to be very little world building for the first half of the book; like we're almost stumbling through from one event to the next, with references to other things that happened that seem pretty damn significant but are only given one sentence in passing. That bothered me for a while, but I just got used to it the further we went. I also thought that by the last third you had a much better, more comprehensive idea of the characters so that you didn't feel lost or like you were treading in the open sea anymore. I haven't seen the movie other than a few scenes, so I'll be very interested in seeing how that is (not something you hear me say very often/at all/like...ever...). Would definitely recommend, and I'm very interested to read anyone else's thoughts and opinions :)

This book felt less like a fantasy story and more like an intro to Wicca. Morgan takes you through her experience of meeting a practicing witch and her struggle with deciding whether to practice herself. As you can imagine, all sorts of problems present themselves. Number one complaint- It's too short! If you like a quick read, fine but if not I would suggest going for the bundled Sweep Volume 1 (books 1-3)? I can't stand paying $5-$6 on a book this size when you can get 3 of them for $7-$8. Even if the other two might suck. I don't know maybe I'm weird but I felt like this book ended in the middle of a story and it was disappointing! Bottom Line: Too short but good for for a light quick read if you enjoy Wicca or witchy stories. I've been on a witch kick lately so I am going to continue on but I probably won't recommend this to friends.

This is quite possibly the first book that I have picked up in 10 years that I have not finished. I got about halfway through (beginning of Chapter 7) and I just started to dread reading it. I went ahead and read through several plot summaries and others' reviews and I have to say I find the ending roughly as lackluster as the first half. I will preface the rest of my review with this thought: I don't believe authors have to write likable characters. I do think that if they choose to write an unlikable character, there has to be an exciting or dramatic element to the story. While this book has all the potential to have drama and excitement, it all just falls very flat, it's characters are all unlikable, and it's a giant bore. The main character, Irina, makes a crucial decision in which the plot then splits into two story lines, one in which she kissed an acquaintance, and one in which she didn't and went home to her partner of 10 years. This kind of story had so much potential to visit completely different plots and twists and turns and instead, the actions in one story line directly mirror the other. I think my biggest issue was Irina's rollover attitude at the mistreatment at the hands of both men in her life. It didn't feel like it was being written as a woman unable to escape the grips of emotional and mental abuse. It felt like a character with the personality depth of a sodden piece of white bread going through motions of what a person's reactions normally are with the most apathy I've ever seen. I just wanted her to make a choice, and not one that would serve the dual story line mirror effect. Her long-term partner was dull but "safe", and the man she left him for was flashy but volatile. Well, in the end her "safe" partner has cheated on her for the past five years and her flashy new man is bankrupt, gets sick and dies and leaves her with his debts . It was just all so predictable that it wasn't fun to read. Also if I have to read another single, stupid sentence about snooker I will scream.

The first thing I noticed about this book was that the cover featured blurbs by both Jonathan Franzen and James Patterson. That's promising, right? It's going to be good enough that Franzen wants to hawk it, but not so pretentious that Patterson feels out of place, right? Right. After a string of serious duds, this book completely knocked me flat on my back. Chad Harbach is a man who know how to write a book. I literally slept with this book in bed beside me because I could not let it go. I want to say that this book is about baseball in the same way that Charlie's Angels was about crime-fighting, but that's not quite the truth. Baseball, its intricacies and the thrill of competition, are at the heart of this story, and you are likely to miss its beauty if that's something you simply can not wrap your brain around. I don't think you have to love baseball to love this book, but you certainly need to appreciate that some people do love it for reasons that are hard to explain. It also helps to know the difference between a short stop and a catcher. That being said, the plot centers on Henry Skrimshander, a boy whose entire life is baseball. He is recruited by sophomore Mike Schwartz to play for Westish College, a small school in Nowhere, Wisconsin, after he impresses Mike at an American Legion tournament. Fast forward three years: Mike has spent more energy building Henry's future than his own and Henry is on the brink of becoming something big while Mike is treading water. Meanwhile, Henry's roommate Owen finds himself entangled in an affair with the college president, and Mike finds himself entangled with the president's daughter, Pella, who has recently run away from a disastrous starter marriage. These five characters' lives intersect with each other in surprising and realistic ways, and I could not stop turning the pages. It's refreshing to read a book in which the plot unfolds a certain way because of how well the characters are developed, as opposed to the characters behaving bizarrely in order to serve the author's intent. I didn't find myself questioning the character's actions. They felt so real to me, so complex and human, and I was surprised that I could relate to and sympathize with a male baseball player barely out of his teens. I even liked Pella, and I almost never enjoy female characters written by men. My only quibble might have been Owen, who didn't seem like the kind who'd go out for the baseball team without a stronger reason, but that felt like a relatively minor quibble in a book that was otherwise so strong. Harbach's prose is simultaneously raw and lush, telling the reader exactly what they need to know -- and occasionally taking their breath away -- without showing off or getting in the way. The dialogue is realistic and funny, not forced in an effort to shed insight into the plot or characters' background. This book is long, but there is almost nothing I could imagine cutting from its pages. Well, I didn't so much enjoy the funeral-at-sea scene, but I suppose it worked in context. There were a few sentences that made me roll my eyes and once in a while, Harbach's metaphors or Mellville references became a little heavy-handed, but it didn't dampen my enjoyment of the book at all. I simply could not stop reading. And the final scene is the epitome of Redemption without the syrup or snark that ruin so many final scenes. My favorite book of the year. I can not wait for Harbach's next novel.

Mick Kennedy always solves his cases and solves them efficiently. When O'Kelly gives him a case to work on with rookie partner Richie, Mick races to work. But this triple homicide of a family out in Brianstown, the old Broken Harbor, brings back memories of his own childhood vacations -- one in particular he believes mangled his youngest sister's sanity. This is the fourth in Tana French's Dublin Murder Squad series. Kennedy appeared in the last, Faithful Place, following the trend of featuring the previous book's side character as the new protagonist. Also typical of French's style is the psychological twist within each case. Rather than spanning several weeks or months, this book spans less than a week, and it is packed full of clues, twists, and wild circumstances. I loved the dynamics of Kennedy's partnership with rookie Richie. He teaches, he scolds, he praises. He does not belittle Richie like the rest of the department, but instead wants him to learn from his mistakes and observe others in action. The insanity bits begin to take hold when Kennedy's sister Dina enters the scene. Her dialogue is fantastic -- run-on sentences, incomplete phrases, scattered breaths and punctuation, ideas not quite stringing together. That sort of dialogue continues into Patrick's character, and later Jenny's, as you begin to see their worlds crumble around them. This is such an effective way of recognizing the deteriorating mind without it being the mind of the protagonist. What prevented me from giving this four or five stars is due to the length. There were many passages I felt were unnecessary -- whole chapters, even. As much as I enjoyed Dina's character, I think we could have done without this side story. There was something about it that felt unresolved, or that if it was going to be explored at all then it should be done in depth rather than in the back of the mind or whenever it was convenient.

"He watched me, and he didn't say a word. So then I said, 'Well, actually, I love books because books are my best friends.'" Mr. Penumbra's 24-Hour Bookstore by Robin Sloan is a love story to people who love books. After reading the summary, I expected a book about a guy, Clay Jannon, who worked in a bookstore with weird customers. But it was much more than that. Sloan created a vivid world for his characters and I really enjoyed reading it. It also helped that characters were quirky, but never quirky. I also appreciated that Sloan didn't put down people who read e-books. I love physical books too, but honestly, an e-book is often more convenient. Especially when you're always in the middle of more than one book, as I usually am. And more specifically, I loved that Penumbra loved e-books.. Usually older characters nag on new technology but I really liked that Penumbra embraced it. Regarding the overall mystery that surrounds the novel, I was 100% convinced that I figured out the key to immortality when Penumbra said, "Every member of our fellowship who has created his own book of life and stored it for safe keeping- will live again." I was absolutely certain that the answer to immortality was the fact that if you write something down, you (and your name) will live forever. Which was why, cheesy enough, I listened to this Bastille song 'Poet' basically the entire time I was reading because I was so sure I was right. But in the end, that wasn't the solution. I really only have two complaints- one is it sometimes seemed like there was too much going on. There were so many ideas for a book this short and it seemed to constantly go in different directions. And a second complaint is the constant mentions of Google. I get it- Kat worked at Google- but there were so many mentions that it got old after a while. Overall, this was a good book. It definitely appeals to the book lovers and the aspects of history were wonderful touches. I've been meaning to read this book since it came out and although it was different than I thought it was going to be, it was still a fun, light read to enjoy between final exams.

UGHH Why do I insist on starting trilogies that only have one book out... I HATE waiting! But seriously this book was SOOOO good! Wow do I love Tristan! I loved Cecile's independence, sassy attitude, and her determination to do as she pleases. Every dialogue with Cecile and Tristan gave me the feels! (2) I think I am so right in this next prediction: The true name of trolls are Fae!!! They are faeries and I'm 99.9% sure. I'm calling it.

Studetns may need a lot of guidance when reading this book as there are a lot of heavy themes that even the MC can't process. The story lays out the situations without judgement (even though the MC uses the word 'slut' without fully realizing its implication, her younger friend points out that it is sexist. The authors do a good job of making it a conversation instead of saying one of the other is right or wrong, leaving the reader to decide what he/she thinks)  and plainly illustrate what it is like to observe something without fully understanding it. Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince is a character study; a respite from the almost non-stop action of the last five books and the action that must follow in the next one. Therefore, barely anything happens in this book. It even has the delightful audacity to begin with a very British comedy scene involving the [metaphorical] heartburn suffered by the Prime Minister of England when visited by the Minister of Magic. Mostly we learn the semi-tragic history of Voldemort aka Tom Riddle. While there was certainly tragedy to his story, there does not seem to be an air of inevitability to his turning to evil. Because not much actually occurred, there's not much else to say without spoiling the plot. The only things I'll add are that this book answered my question of why pensieves and verisatem potions are not the perfect solution to trial testimony in the Potterverse. Also, I had gone until last year without being spoiled on Harry Potter until someone was listing old spoilers like Citizen Kane, Planet of the Apes, The Sixth Sense, etc and someone thought it appropriate to lump Harry Potter into that list of mostly decades old spoilers. As I've matured as a consumer of stories in the past decade in which I've studied tropes and gained a better understanding of storytelling, I've come to the conclusion that with the exception of a very small subset of stories (like Whodunnits), a good story should not be able to be ruined by spoilers. The Harry Potter series is no exception (as it is a well-written series). Although I went into this first read-through (other than the first book and a half which I'd read a decade prior) knowing that a certain someone would kill a certain someone else (and even recently via a comedian learned it would happen in book 6), it did not diminish my enjoyment of the series or this book. Rather, it made me wonder about the circumstances under which it would happen. I must say that all my theories about Dumbledore (which I've mentioned in one or two prior reviews) were wrong. I'd assumed he'd turn out to be an even darker wizard than Voldemort and that's the reason Voldemort was scared of him . So a good book, but not my favorite in the series. It could easily have just been compressed a bit and made to be the first half of what is currently book 7 (which I'm about to start), but I think it works as a nice breather after so much action and, as I said before, the fact there must be much action coming ahead.

Good thing I'm going on holiday tomorrow or my wanderlust would have been near insufferable. Rawr!

An interesting tale that is too disjointed to be approaching greatness. The art, as always for this title, is solid--that is not where this volume falls down. JH Williams' art is a thing of beauty, particularly his experimental style and unusual breakdowns. By times it can make the story harder to follow, but for every 1 page that doesn't work there are 5 that do. The biggest issue here is "telling" rather than "showing". Long periods of exposition drag the story down, and opportunities for character interaction are spent on internal monologue. That said the excellent issue zero tells enough story to feed an entire season of television, and by the. Time it was done I felt I knew Kate Kane better. Overall this is good work, but too flawed to be considered great.

Wow. Just wow. [2nd time reading] The first time I read this book I barreled through it. The second time, I took my time reading it and enjoyed it more. I found details that I didn't remember reading the first time. It was still exciting and well-written and I still love the characters like I did the first go-round. I wish I was able to hold off until right before the third is released, but I couldn't! Loved it. I think this is New Adult but honestly don't let that put you off - Cole and Summer come across as adults full stop, Hollywood golden boy Cole Masten comes crashing down when he catches his beautiful co-star wife Nadia having sex with her Producer. After expressing his shock and dismay in a rather violent fashion, Cole's divorce lawyer imposes some severe restrictions on him, including sending him to live on the location of his next film. Cole is funding a film about Quincy, Georgia - a town in which 67 citizens invested in Coca Cola at the start up and became mult-millionaires. Summer lives in said town, something really bad happened three years ago and since then she has been a pariah in Quincy. Although, because this is Georgia everyone is still polite and speaks to Summer - they just never call her or invite her anywhere. Summer is desperate to leave Quincy but her non-existent college education and skills limit her options. When she hears that Cole Masten is making a film about Quincy she offers to help the Hollywood scout identify locations and places for crew and cast. Cole is a man living comfortably numb. No real friends, long periods apart from his wife, surrounded by people who deny him nothing and won't look him in the eye. When he arrives in Quincy shell-shocked and unexpectedly he manages to offend Summer by inviting himself into her home, by demanding sparkling water and by asking what she is doing there. Yet he likes that she tells him off and orders him out of her home. The premise of this book isn't new - glamorous male meets local beauty and sparks fly. But the way in which it has been written and the way in which the characters felt "real" was refreshing. The antagonism from Summer towards to Cole is fun and they come across as adults - which is a refreshing change! And who wouldn't love Cocky and Ben? I liked the way that Summer's actions which caused her to be a pariah are slowly revealed in the novel - and the reveal is a doozie! So, have I missed DeLuca's story?

I wanted to like this more than I did, but the writing just wasn't great. The two main characters weren't terribly fleshed out, so I didn't really care about the fate of their romance. Memo to writers of fiction concerned with the rich & glamorous: please don't go into great detail concerning outfits. They'll only date the book even more rapidly.
This cannot come soon enough!
Unique, allegorical, fascinating from start to finish. Great book for a book group discussion.

"Your first love isn't the first person you give your heart to- it's the first one who breaks it." 2 stars - It was okay This was such a huge disappointment. I love Lang Leav's writting and find her poetry to be beautiful, even if I only had a glimpse of it. What happened? In all honesty, I was going to give this book a 1 star rating at first. I had such a hard time going through the first half of it. From the overly dramatic and unrealistic story, everything seemed too much. It was trying too hard to be something. It was like the author wrote down on a paper what would make a hit book, somewhat like a Hollywood blockbuster, and tried to make it fit in less than 400 pages. So you needed a dead girl, a main character with health issues which was caused by unrepairable guilt, family issues, a perfect first boyfriend, a second boyfriend that would change everything, two best friends forever, a drug problem, a road to self discovery, another boyfriend that seemed yet again all perfect to just make the main character realize that boyfriend number 2 was the right one, a wedding, unrealistic job and housing opportunities, another sudden death and a plot twist within the last few pages. Should I go on? It was just a huge mix of ridiculousness. What ranked it up to a 2 stars was the second half. I did like Rad as a character and wanted to know what would happen to him and Audrey. It wasn't really based on the fact that it was the best relationship/love affair I have ever read about, it was simply out of pure guilty pleasure for cheesy romantic stories. It was also during the second half of the book that I got more of the beautiful writing I was expecting, even if it was very minimal. I wouldn't recommend this book. I believe that in order to truly appreciate the extent of Lang Leav's writing talent, her poetry will be the way to go.

I have to say I prefered the first book of this duology, probably because the concept was much more original (though unrealistic yes) and it felt like there was more action, more things going on. The plot of this book is rather straightforward, Yael failed to kill the real Hitler once so she has to try again and to do so she needs to get back to Germany with Luka and Felix. 2/3 of this book is Yael and the boys making the journey while dealing with possible ambushes and Felix's hand injury. It's still a very easy read but the last third actually saved it for me, it was explosive, emotional and stressful and I enjoyed it much more than the rest of the book. One thing that started to bother me was Yael's power. The skinshifting ability is amazing but it turned out to be (understandably) the answer to every situation and made everything super easy (passing through SS patrols, breaking in camps and getting close to the bad guys). There was almost no other action than Yael taking someone else's face and moving along which started to get repetitive. Luka and Felix did not matter much for most of the book and seemed to be simply there to make a few points. Luka and Yael's relationship was completely flat. He was barely shocked at the revelation that she was not Adele, the girl he used to love, and even though he did not know her he still felt like he loves her. I also feel like Yael forgives him too quickly for not doing anything to help before. When she did, I'm sad to say he still had done nothing to prove he wasn't like the others except following her around because well, what other choice did he have. There was just no chemistry there, compared to the first book. Independently though I sill loved these characters. Yael was as amazing as she was in the first book, I love her determination and her strength. She's ready to die for her beliefs and for the saving of all the innocents being killed, deeply injured, experimented on by Hitler's institution. I love how we can see her grow and learn to deal with the fear inside of her. Felix also became a much more interesting character in this book. His dilemna was quite problematic and extremely complicated. Although a part of me understand, I was still disappointed at his choice in the end. Luka stayed the same, funny, sassy and brave. I'm happy he realised the horrors around him and understood that he could no longer let fear keep him from doing something about it. Though why the hell would you kill him like that  . The ending was very bittersweet and yet I found it perfect and I added half a star just for that. I was convinced Yael was coming to kill Felix but what she chose to do instead was the best decision for her and this is why I love her. Like she said, she deserves more than this. And despite what he did, my heart warmed a little at seeing Felix and Adele reunited with their parents.

Now I see why people review this book from a philosophical standpoint. Nothing too special about it...only a man who has a heightened sense of self-awareness once he knows that his life is ending. It happens to everyone. I do like the way the narrative flows though.

I have known for some time that I do not care for historical romance. Even if people really did speak as differently as they do in historical romance novels, I just can't wrap my head around it; I think it sounds pretentious and silly. However, because this story was included in the BEND anthology, I gave it a chance. Although I did find it silly at times, I was able to ignore the ancient style of speech used by the revered Roman Tribune while he spoke to the beautiful slave woman. I was able to appreciate how of the verbiage did fit to the period of time, creating a more realistic, believable historical setting. Fortunately though, I still did not care for the story. Even with the different style of speech and the story taking place during a different period of time in history, the story was the same as many we see now; a dominant, powerful, wealthy alpha male decides he wants the sweet, submissive, drop-dead gorgeous woman and does whatever he must do to have her. In this story though, The woman does not protest or put up any type of challenge. Reminiscent of our history, in the story the slave woman is deemed too low in the cast system for the famous Tribune. Therefore, both are aware that it will never be appropriate for them to openly be a couple. I had hoped that the male MC, the elite, powerful Tribune, would go against society's norms or would have done something overt to make this story special and unique. Unfortunately, he does not. basically, the male MC takes the woman he wants, keeps her a secret, end of story! Yes, he does make some arrangements for her in case he dies while fighting but that was it - nothing more! I was shocked at such a terrible ending! This story had great potential that was not utilized.

I may not be the world's most enthusiastic urban fantasy reader, but hey - this book's got celtic mythology, herbalism, witchcraft and horror PLUS it's written by the author of the Newsflesh books. On paper, I should LOVE this freakin' book. Right? *sigh* I couldn't tell you what it was that didn't work for me, beyond the small things - the slightly dodgy Celtic pronunciation guide, occasional inconsistencies with the mythology, minor missing details which rendered certain paragraphs meaningless, just an overall lack of the super-sharp writing that I was expecting based on Feed....... possibly a combination of several of these small things. For most of the book, I really wasn't all that engaged. And then the last fify pages happened. At that point, I really started to get into it. Perhaps it was the introduction of the Luidaeg character that started to tie the mythology to the story more tightly, but at that point I realised I had every intention of continuing with the series. I get the distinct sense that this series takes a little bit of time to percolate, that now the bulk of the exposition is out of the way, McGuire's writing tightens up and the mythology starts to meld seamlessly with the narrative. I hope I'm not disappointed..

So I have a tendency to pre-order books from Dreamspinner Press while they are cheap, but on release-day I get impatient at the delay due to timezones, and purchase a copy through Kindle anyway. Ah well. This is a happy story. When the weather is crap, there is nothing I like better than staying in my PJs and curling up in bed with a sweet, happy, uncomplicated story. And as always, I was thrilled to read a book set in my city, and about the various places I know and hang out at. Like the previous book in the series,  Don't Twunk with my Heart  looks at twink culture, and men who are not ashamed of their feminine side. This results is a very happy-go-lucky read, a ridiculously sappy grin at the final chapter, and a squeal of delight at the sneak-peak in to book three, due out later this year. I was a little worried for a while about how far Tate's eating disorder would go. This series is known for being very lighthearted, unlike Kaye's  Safe series. On the other had, considering the degree of Tate's anorexia and occasional bulimia, it felt as if it was resolved a little too easily. Either way, I am very glad to see eating disorders in men reflected here, because it isn't talked about much. Can't wait to see what comes next.

I loved this when I was a child and read it to my kids. Everyone relates to the bumbling Pooh and his adventures. There are just enough characters to round out every story and bring little lessons for preschoolers into the story.

I'd actually rate this at about a 3 and a half stars. It was pretty slow moving - which I expected it to be seeing as it's the first book of a series and there's a lot of things that need to be explained. I think that could've been done better and I hated how long some of the chapters were. This had some elements of Harry Potter, Hunger Games and even Lord of the Rings at one point. Was it as good as any of them? No, but I still enjoyed it for the most part. I liked it enough to continue the series. I'm interested in finding out how things are going to proceed given how this ended.

When I started this book, for the first hour or two it made no sense. The characters were all over the place, there were people with some sort of power but I didn't understand what they were doing and there was this Father character who everyone was worried about. In short, it made very little sense. And then, the story started coming together like something wonderful. Loose ends were described, backstories described events and within the next few hours, a lot of the story was clear and the book went from a head-scratcher to a "oh god...give me more!" The book is wonderfully weird. That would be a tl:dr review. The characters are very well written and the story is incredible. Thinking back on where the book started and where it ended makes my head spin! It was a really good but weird journey! 'Isshteve' is such a wonderfully written character. You can probably make some guesses to his story and involvement with Carolyn but its so beautiful when its explained. The one character that surprised me completely was Father. Father's chapters and backstories are excellent. Till his story is shown, its completely normal to think of father as a tyrant and someone who loves to torture children and barbeque them sometimes. But the weight of that backstory just adds so much character to Father. It's incredible. Other amazing characters include David, Margaret and Michael. Overall, this is a fantastic book!

Where to begin... Let me just say that as soon as I started reading United as One I exclaimed out loud "What the shit!?" So, Sarah is just DEAD!? John doesn't miraculously save her!? WHAT THE SHIT!? That being said, I'm quite intrigued by the ending of the Lorien Legacies series. The last three books in the series (The Revenge of Seven, The Fate of Ten, and United as One) have all been occurring within a day of the previous book. Essentially it's a huge war story split up over 3 books. It's easy to forget that the Garde are all teenagers. Their KIDS! By United as One, they are all fairly shell shocked. There is a difference between preparing for a hostile alien invasion/war and actually fighting in one. The prospect of losing starts to feel all too real to them, especially after the ending of The Fate of Ten where Sarah... WHAT THE SHIT!? dies. At this point they just want it to be over, no matter what the cost. Obviously, they would rather be alive when the dust settles but if they have to die to end it, they will. United as One takes the Lorien saga to an even darker place than before. The ending itself... It's somewhat open ended. Most of the characters we know and love are doing ok Some more than others... IE: 5 is FUBAR, Marina and John both have PTSD  or at the very least they are surviving. The world now has all these LANE'S and a school is being built to train them. ::cough:: X-MEN ::cough:: It seems a somewhat unstable set up. Not everyone is going to be cool with people having super powers and persecution seems likely. Right now though, it seems like everyone has the best of intentions at least. There are a lot of unanswered questions which leaves a possibility for a sequel series open. ::fingers crossed!! :: This isn't necessarily an happily ever after. But at least there is an after which is something to for which to rejoice. The future is unwritten... P.S. So maybe John and Marina, huh... Seems maybe destiny has bigger plans. I mean, Hello! their powers are even fire and ice! John and Marina are both my favorite characters so if they had to end up with someone, I'm ok with them ending up together. I'm happy for Sam and Six. They always fit in that special way. Six is so fiery that she needs that calming center Sam provides to ground her. I'm still shipping Nine and Ella, when she's old enough of course! I hope Adam is ok. Maybe he will help rehabilitate more of the Mogs and maybe even find himself a nice girl.O MY GOODNESS! What about an Adam and Daniella ship! She's spicy enough to liven Adam up. I'm freaking out over something that hasn't happened but it would be so cool if it did! akf;sahf;!!!!!!!!! P.P.S. I WANT THERE TO BE A SEQUEL SERIES SOOOOOOOOO BAD!

** spoiler alert ** I'm not sure how to rate this one. I read it in 2 days and for the first half I was up in 4.5-5 star territory. I could not put it down. Aubrey's husband, Josh has been missing for 5 years and has just been declared legally dead. And there's a $5 million life insurance policy that his mother (Daisy) wants to fight Aubrey for. I love horrible mothers-in-law in novels. Especially when the main character daughter-in-law is the worst. Aubrey was arrested and tried for Josh's murder, even without a body and has just now come out of the bell jar she's been living in. Told in third person limited with varying time periods and POVs, there are hints that almost everyone has secrets and no one is who they seem. Aubrey had a rough childhood that Josh "saved" her from; growing up in foster care with a prostitute foster mother. Daisy gives little peaks at her secrets in her chapters. "Does he know? Does he know?!?" We go back and forth to when Josh and Aubrey are kids, when they're in high school and fall in love, and to the night Josh disappeared five years ago. It was great until about the halfway mark. Then I just felt disconnected. The story dragged somehow. Not that the action changed at all. Maybe it just became a little repetitive. The ending is bananas and doesn't jive with the rest of the book. If Aubrey knew Josh was alive the whole time, why the breakdown? Why does the third person limited narrator tells us that she's thinking Josh must be dead? It seems like a big twist just for the purpose of a big twist. I have a couple problems: In Chapter 31, we flash back to the summer before Josh's Junior year in high school. Aubrey is just going to be starting high school and Josh is happy about that and planning a romantic weekend. A few pages later, it's mentioned that Aubrey is on the pill and that the school nurse hands them out like candy. I'm sorry but isn't she still in GRADE SCHOOL at this point?!?! I don't think her Montessori school nurse is handing out birth control pills. Neither is the high school nurse. You need a prescription for those (except now in Oregon). And of course, Aubrey is perfect. She seems to have a magical effect on every single man she comes across, even a psychotic lifelong criminal. It's like the magical penis trope only in reverse. With all that "perfection" I was hoping her mother-in-law would play a bigger part in making her suffer. But that subplot dies away about the halfway mark. I read it super fast and was enthralled for about 200 pages. Four stars for the buildup, 2 stars for the second half and the ending. So...3!
Cute and funny, if you liked the first book, you will like this one.

Great comics show what the medium can do. They tell stories in ways that incorporate the best parts of film and prose and visual art and transcend all of the above when they get it right. This is not a great comic. The best I can say for it is that it's better than season eight. The writing relies on the art to tell us who is who, and on our previous experience with the characters to fill in the gaps. Unfortunately, this artist's renderings of some characters leave me wondering who they are. New characters look interchangeable. It's very distracting. The writing has some of the snap of the TV show, but lacks something. Heart, maybe. I just don't feel the connection with the characters. The storyline has potential, but I wouldn't have bothered reading it if I couldn't get a library copy.

I really liked this book. The first few chapters had me a little hesitant as to the direction the author was going to go with this book, but I actually enjoyed reading about Fallon and her rebellion against Zita and the love fortunes. Not everything is all sunshine, unicorns, and rainbows like the town of Grimbaund claims it is. Like it was mentioned in the synopsis, Fallon gets a bad love fortune Your love will never be requited or something along those lines, and suddenly she sees her future as a spinster, being single for the rest of her life. But when she joins a small rebellion at her school, alongside the school's bad boy/playboy/heartbreaker Sebastian, her gay best friend Nico with an unrequited/secret crush on a guy, a shy girl who is scared of attention, and two weird twins who have never gotten any fortunes ever, and they all get together, alonside the spinsters and bachelors, to take down Zita and her charm store. And get their town their freedom back, and their own choice to live and learn by heartbreaks and stuff, because knowing too much is a bad thing. Just read the book to find out how bad it is! Basically the whole town is run by Zita and the love potions and charms and everything love related. I liked the idea that Love was an actual physical person, especially in the prologue where she shows up as a 13 year old girl. The idea of love fortunes being distributed to help end their suffering was an interesting concept but it got twisted after a few years and Zita's need for revenge. While no one knew who Love was, I guessed who Love was in the story the few times he/she showed up.. Each of the fortunes were either literal, or they could be vague as crap and interpreted the wrong way take for instance Nico and Martin: Nico's fortune was that the his love will remain unnoticed by the one that matters the most. Nico thought that meant Martin would never know of his love but instead it was Martin's ex-girlfriend that was the who wasn't supposed to know. Long story. especially when other people's fortunes got revealed and it could have gone either way. Sebastian's fortune was the most shocking, and Fallon's fortune was just collateral, courtesy of Zita's revenge. As for Fallon, her fortune had to do with Sebastian's too, and it was all complicated and frustrating but sweet at the same time. When they actually got together, it had me jumping for joy, and then when they confronted Zita at the end, my heart was in pieces but at least they did get their happy ever after. Sebastian was sweet, and while he was deemed a heartbreaker, after his fortune got revealed, all of his actions were understandable. I get why he did what he did, but whenever he hung out with Fallon I loved that he showed her who he truly was: that he collected silence all around town, he worked as a groomer in his grandma's veterinary clinic, and just an amazingly sweet guy, and I couldn't see him as the bad boy of the story anymore. I guess either way it was nice that the author decided to have Sebastian as Fallon's love interest. Either way, I loved the ending of the book, and how they freed the town from Zita, and there was even a guest yet secretive appearance from Love at the end of the book too! And oh yeah, there's a lot of romance in this novel, just a heads up!

This is very different from Hale's other stuff and different from what is out there right now, at least what I've read. It's sci fi which is not uncommon but this is neither dystopia nor a series. Just a different all around book than what you would expect from Hale or sci fi. Maisie Danger Brown is a home-schooled girl that who happens to win a sweepstakes to go to a space camp. While going to this space camp she discovers that the world is in danger *wink* and she and her friends are the only ones who can stop it. She and her friends however are in grave danger until she is the last person standing between earth and total destruction. Now that is vague but just be sure to know that Maisie starts out pretty sheltered. I felt like it was a middle grade the first couple chapters or so but make no mistake there is a darker side to the book, or at least darker than expected. Maisie questions her role and who she should trust. You don't even figure out the mission until more than half way through the book. Tons of suspense and action before that though. So I did have some issues with the romance and I've come to realize that I'm kind of picky about romance in books. I like it there but I don't like it being a huge focus and I don't like there being a huge drama going on about it. There is definitely distrust and a love triangle. Neither of which I like. I had a problem with the fact that Wilder was willing to kill Maisie just for the token. Now I know he decided not to and instead tried to kill himself which is romantic and all if you're into that. However, he was half crazy when he decided all of this and then he started he fell in love with Maisie. I seems like a toxic state of mind to fall in love with someone. Though I don't mind the fact that she didn't end up with Luther at last he was somewhat clear minded when her decided he loved Maisie. Getting to the good stuff. I liked Maisie as a character. Like I mentioned earlier, she is sheltered but not completely ignorant and naive. That being said, she had to grow a lot throughout the book. Her family relationship I liked, there is a quirky bond they have. As for the plot itself...a hole lot of twist and turns, suspense, and some action. The sci fi aspect of it was strange but definitely interesting and I liked it that it was very sci fi but not in the typical way. Oh I did I mention she gets a bionic arm which was so cool. It actually makes me giddy thinking about it. If you are a fan of Hale's writing I say give it a try or even if you are not. The book may be different than her other stuff but her writing is spot on like always.

None of them could be dubbed completely good or evil. Alec was, perhaps, my favorite, first, because of his mysterious past, then because of his whimsical character. He seemed a bit unhinged at times, maybe he is... The intrigue and politics were also engaging, dialogues were smart and witty. I had fun reading it. One problem I had with the story comes from the writing style. Specifically, from the continuous POV changes that made it hard to keep track of who was saying what. Too many POV changes, often times from one paragraph to the other. The biggest problem I had comes from the fact that  St. Vier murdered his girlfriend, apparently because she shouted at him...   Unless this is otherwise explained in a future book, I must say it made me uncomfortable, to say the least. Michael was not a character I was particularly interested in, and I would have much preferred to know more about Alec, and how he and St. Vier ended up together and such, especially considering how Michael's arc ended, in a very diluted way.
