And it's not like that, not really - you don't want to do it, but it's more than just not wanting to do it and like Aled says, it feels like you're going insane. But no one gets it because "everyone finds university stressful". This book got it, better than anything. Radio Silence also brings up a lot of issues surrounding the high school experience and how awful it can be for students, and the pressure teens feel around grades and university. Alice Oseman says so many thoughtful things about the more stressful side of university life and academia. Watching Frances realize she didn't want to study English literature also hit me hard, too, because I had that same realization, and I wish I'd figured that out when Frances did, because I'm already halfway through my damn degree. I'm glad that Frances and Aled realized that there's a life without university and found happiness in doing what they love, and yes, it's a bit fairytale-ish but it's a good ol' happy ending, and after how sad this book made me, I loved how it ended. I know this review is like, super personal and probably too much information, but Radio Silence rang truest to me in that regard. Really, it helped me feel so much less alone.

Good Gods, do I love a sexy Dom. Sevastyan certainly fits the bill. I also like strong leading ladies, but Natalie kinda falls short of that. She lets Sevastyan, Paxan and Filip all walk right over her. That being said, I do still like this book. Sevastyan is so sexy, so overwhelming, I was quite drawn in by him. His treatment of Natalie wasn't exactly nice and loving, but was steamy, dark and full of angst. As long as you're in the mood for suspense and drama, that is just a little twisted, this book will heat you up.

I feel like I have read so many Dan Brown books that I can probably predict the outcomes of the novel. Here's the gist of the story: Robert Langdon is being chased by the bad guys. There is a crazy psycho killer on the loose. Robert runs around Europe searching for clues that will allow him to find the bad guy. There's a lot of historical references in the codes that ONLY Robert is able to crack. Psych! One of the people who you thought was the good guys is actually the leader of the enemy. The only thing different about this book is that the story is very inconclusive. In the last couple of chapters, Robert finds the source of the bio-pathogen and realizes it was too late. Then the entire plot is revealed in the last chapter and the story ends. What? I mean, that basically renders the entire story pointless. And in the end, he can't do anything to reverse the effect so Robert basically flies back to the United States and hopes for best from scientists and engineers. Overall, I enjoyed this book while I was reading it because I am a big fan of thrillers. However, after putting the book down, I can see so many plot holes and annoyances in the story that I downgrade my ratings. Rating: 3.25 stars

I neglected a lot of things today. But I needed to finish this book. Wow It broke me. So many times! And at some part I wanted to give up so bad! But Jess and Alex compelled me to continue. I felt the ending was abrupt. I think I needed to know a couple of stuff before the epilogue. But I'm content with it. A real love story.

Actual Rating 3.5 While I enjoyed this story, the pacing lagged quite a bit for me. The diary style format didn't work so well for me here... granted, the slow-downs had to do with how hard it is to figure out how to save the world / universe, and how you aren't in control even if you have super-nifty half-understood powers. I don't think I would have minded the pacing, except that the climax absolutely did not work for me. Partly this was the diary style format, where the key entry begins with "It's over! And I'm alive!" or something of the sort, so that you know immediately that everyone important survives and there's really no tension . But it also had to do with the climax itself...and it comes back to my review of Lab Rat One where I wanted Cass to take more agency in her story. If she's going to save the world I really want her to be thinking about it, planning, trying, and if Something Untoward occurs, her removing herself physically from the location in question shouldn't just automatically save everything. I was actually 100% certain that the "I'm alive!" entry was a false positive and Cass & co were about to find out how wrong they were ... but that didn't happen. And that sucked. I wanted Cass to DO something, preferably with her powers, which required quick thinking and strategy and all the things she's been seeing around her and working towards. She did this at one point earlier in the story, but not at the climax. And that just didn't work for me. I still really enjoyed this story, and definitely recommend it to fans of sci-fi / fantasy genre mix-ups featuring (here it comes!) psychic space ninjas.
I love these books.

I enjoyed this a little more than Andrew Smith's other books, as the gay character was much better done (in my opinion) than in all the others I've read. But I didn't really like what he did with Shann, the only real major female character, so still not a big fan. Still, I liked the language of this one, and thought it was engaging.

The fast paced action and terror continues in the second book Exodus of the Extinction Point series. I enjoyed the tense roller coaster ride the author creates as Emily makes her cross country trek to Alaska. What I liked the most: 1) I loved the opening of the book. What a "Ground Control to Major Tom" moment. It was very cool to see the attack on earth from the space station. 2) I like the attempts the author has made at creating strong female characters. He does it with the commander of the space station, Emily, and I even saw it in Rhia. Could all of the characters use a little more polish-sure, but kudos at what's there. It's far better than others I've seen. 3) I liked the mystery of "what attacked the seven frozen dead"   near the end of the book. It really made meeting Jacob  a little more eerie. I thought Emily was kinda crazy not taking a closer look at them, but they left a lot of open doors for book 3 which I liked. Things that bothered me: 1) I don't think it was necessary to come up with some mysterious weather impervious valley  to create more survivors from the red rain. I think it would have been cooler for her to stumble across a clan of preppers living in a bunker. Simon asking if she was there to save them like she's with the government, wow he's dumb. 2) She left all of her gear at the other house-how stupid is our protagonist Emily? Come on she was supposed to be getting better at this survival thing, not worse. It was a like a bad horror movie when Simon left his kids to go retrieve the Durango. I was irritated when this happened because it just did not fit the common sense test. Why is he leaving his kids with a stranger? A father abandoning his kids to go get a vehicle when he knows there is an unquantifiable danger lurking about-NO WAY. They didn't stick together to save time-he gets car and stranger lady is going to pack the kids stuff? NO WAY. We knew what was going to happen when Simon left and it pissed me off. I think it would have been more dramatic to be ambushed by the creepy creature at the other house and have to watch the creature take over Simon and then come for the kids. No need to split up, the terror of it all would remain the same. And it was a little bizarre how little miss "I don't know how to drive" magically figures it out enough to ram the creature not once but twice-without flipping or destroying the SUV. What happened to all the cool rifle skill's Emily gave us in book one? 3) I did not believe her character should have had so much unease at the drop in temperature. The woman did grow up in a small town in Iowa, she should be in her element. She's from the Midwest, people from this part of the USA know all about winter-it starts in November and drags into late March. She should have been having flashbacks to her childhood. Not reminding herself of the cautions Jacob gave over the phone about the cold. 4) If I'm not mistaken this is a kill or be killed scenario. If you are going to kill a kid-turned alien get it over with. Why was it more important to spare his sisters feelings than keep them all alive? Why did she not shoot the alien Ben when it was hunched over Rhia in the middle of the night? Emily's dealt with enough creatures at this point to know the boy Ben is dead. Does she really need to overnight with an alien to spare his sisters feelings? And why are they burying him in a rose bush-without a shovel-when the red storm is raining on them? That's one of those sorry dear-we need to leave him here and press on moments. 5) Why is Emily freaking out on Jacob over the other people not being there? She broke into an apartment in book one because she was so desperate to find another living human. I don't think she would have not gone to Alaska even if he did tell her what happened. Besides he's basically saved her life dragging her there. I still look forward to reading book 3 and seeing how this series shakes out.

This is a graphic novel about a couple from different sides of a war (somewhat reminiscent of Romeo and Juliet) who are just trying to get away from all the fighting. This story is filled with action, fantasy and surprise. I enjoyed reading this graphic novel and will pick up the next installment soon. There was a heavy dose of fantasy which I am not used to ( People with tv's for heads, a woman with a spider body and a humanoid that looks like a sea horse. Not going to lie, these were a little out there for me  )but I would like to continue with the story.

I'm going with the Goodreads definition of 2 stars here: "it was okay." There was definitely some truth in here about the world of academia (I recalled the run down English and languages building of my undergrad), but I was pretty bored by the whole book. I really didn't like Jay. I was pretty uncomfortable with his rude and stalkerish treatment of his ex-wife and ex-girlfriends. Sure unlikeable and chauvinistic characters may be realistic, but it made it all the more exhausting to listen to him drone on. The ending of the book tries to give us a meaning for it all but seemed contrived to me.

** spoiler alert ** I'm going to start with the ending first. It climaxed into an almost- complete "happy ending", but there was so much unfinished business! Simon didn't find out who his true parents were - and that Lucy visited him when the Veil was lifted - and he lost his magic... (I guess as readers we can just fill in the rest of the story with our imagination and hope that Simon eventually gets the truth, and gets his magic back. But I guess I'm glad it ended the way it did - if the situation ended with their lives 100% perfect with no sacrifices made, then it would've been too good to be true.) I absolutely adore Baz and Simon's relationship - who wouldn't? - especially the kiss when Baz was on a suicidal rampage, setting the whole forest alight... and they both realised how much they actually were waiting for that moment. (During Book 1 when Simon was obsessed with Baz's absence - pretty obvious that he wanted Baz to show up not just to fight with him... if you know what I mean. Plus it built tension leading up to Baz's grand entrance so it forced me to get through that first section as quick as I could.) Favourite Snowbaz quote is probably, "Because we match." I literally squealed so hard. (It would make more sense if it was put into context, and those who have read the book would understand). I also loved Simon and Baz as individual characters - Simon is the epitome of good (so precious!!! protect him at all costs) and Baz's sass and snarky comments is just everything... they're just all so likeable characters, especially when read their alternating individual points of view. I found that I had more empathy and understood these magnificent characters a lot more, especially Agatha. She irritated me at first but I could understand her better towards the end, especially the decisions she made. Baz and Penny's friendship which thrived throughout the book was so enjoyable to read; it was so humorous and they're both incredibly strong characters who don't take crap from anyone. The fact that I haven't read Harry Potter (oops) probably helped me like the book so much more, because I don't have much to compare it to. It was such a clever book and I particularly adored the whole language being such a powerful thing in the magickal world; how spells died when phrases were worn-out and forgotten, and the whole war situation with the Old Families, the Mage and the Humdrum just culminated into a big ball of "wow, this is so intense, I need more!" There's so much to love about this book which can't be expressed in a review and I highly recommend reading it!

2.5 stars I love Julie James, I really do but I had a hard time connecting with this book, the characters, the story, everything actually! I was skipping pages and sadly for me, any book that bores me enough to skip pages doesn't deserve more than 3 stars. Also the H/h first meeting was very cliche and it did not get the book off to a good start. It just seemed so staged how they met at the coffee shop, had a extremely awkward encounter and then realize they are meeting the same people. It seemed like the coffee shop scene was done just to make things seem very convuluted and more dramatic. I feel that there is no genuine chemistry at first. I admired these two as individuals based on their commitment to careers but their "romance" has no spark. If sparks refer to lust well then I do not buy it. There is more to chemistry than physical attraction. The "romance" felt very forced and after a while it seemed rather ridiculous that Vaughn and Sidney did not recognize that they had feelings for each other. C'mon. Denial is one thing, rampant stupidity another. Another problem I have with this one is that device used to bring the two warring lovers together is rather shabby--a shotgun wedding because Isabelle is pregnant. Um, really? Can we step into the 21st century? The author tries to make this plausible by saying that Simon, the father/groom, has very religious Catholic parents and they would have a hissy fit if they knew Simon had: a)gotten his girlfriend/fiance pregnant b)had sex before marriage. I repeat: can we step into the 21st century? I don't buy the super-religious Catholics because James did not do a very good job of convincing me they are super-religious anything. Okay, so they said grace before eating. So what? That doesn't make you a conservative Catholic. I don't buy it. And why keep the baby a secret from Vaughn? That made no damn sense either. Really, is Vaughn such a prig? The whole "rushed-wedding-because-of-secret-baby" plot device failed. But whatever.

This book ticked a lot of my favourite boxes, quirky, weird bookshop and owner, secret societies, lots of mystery etc. It also chugged along ok. The characters were likeable as well. But there were some aspects which didn't work very well for me. The secret societies initiation process was too complicated, although the secret society itself was good. They infiltrated the secret society a bit too easily. I found the google bits a bit far fetched. For the type of book it was i was expecting a bit more magical-realism. It is not a bad book but it should have been better.
I am so glad the romance did not blow this book up. I thought char was a bit too much and I'm glad the book didn't end with a romantic happily ever after.

Brief summary Hank is gone, and Nora and Patch think that they have everything figured out. With her biological father out of the picture and the Nephilim army left to her to lead, Nora has every intention of leading her people to peace with Patch's help, but with Chesvan on the horizon, it's looking more and more like peace is impossible. Nora and Patch decide to stage a break up to convince everyone that Nora is firmly on the Nephilim side, but not everyone is convinced of her intentions and capabilities. What I liked I am so, so, so happy with the way this series ended! I've only read a few series where I really enjoyed every single book and this is definitely one of them. There are so many twists and turns, and I didn't see a bunch of them coming. Nora really has to handle a lot in this book and battle her own dark side. She really grew as a character from beginning to end. But as much as Nora grew, she doesn't even compare to how different Patch is at the end of this series than he was at the beginning. I loved him as the bad boy in Hush, Hush, but I love him even more as the boyfriend in love. And I was so freaking happy when he could feel Nora at the end! Finally! Woohoo! :D Aaahh I love Patch <3 What I didn't like DO NOT READ THIS IF YOU DON'T WANT THIS BOOK COMPLETELY SPOILED I'm upset with Marcie's part in all of this. I hate that I started feeling bad for her and even kind of liking her, and then she just ends up being another bad guy. Same with Dabria. She actually seemed pretty human in some scenes, but she still tries to kill all of the Nephilim with the rest of the fallen angels. I HATE THAT SCOTT DIES! OMG that kills me. I was hoping that he didn't actually die. At the end when Vee gets married I thought we were going to find out Scott was still alive, but no. I'm still sad about that :( I wish there was more about Patch being able to feel Nora. I have been waiting for that since the beginning and when he can finally feel her there isn't much to read about it. That really bummed me out. It just wasn't enough! I really want to read that scene from Patch's POV. Maybe someday Becca Fitzpatrick will write it for us. *fingers crossed* :D Brief thoughts I'm really happy with the way this series ended and you can bet I'll be reading the whole series again (and again, and again!) in the future. I look forward to what else Ms. Fitzpatrick comes up with!

I took three weeks to finish this novel because I was on holiday and, surprisingly, didn't have a lot of time for reading, though I can't help thinking I wouldn't have got through any quicker at home because it never grabbed me in the kind of way necessary to make me pick the book up other than a short read before falling asleep. Here I should say this is NOT a pleasant bedtime book, since it has graphic violence to the extent I felt Slaughter positively wallows in describing the most base thoughts and deeds of which men in particular are capable. Another crime novel about violence inflicted upon women, rape culture, misogyny and sexism, that revels in depravity for entertainment purposes. Yes, the novel has a bold twist in the reveal of the perpetrator, trouble is this is so predictable I guessed far too early what it was going to be. And he is just too thoroughly BAD in a way that made my eyes roll. I liked the character John, sent to prison aged 16 for rape and murder, released on parole after serving twenty years. We learn the details through use of flashbacks and old newspaper reports, and follow his attempts to make a life after such lengthy incarceration, in a hostile and indifferent world, working in a car wash, living in squalor, for which he's supposed to feel grateful, subject to constant scrutiny and the expectation he will re-offend or mess up somehow and be returned to prison. John's experience in prison, barely more than a boy thrown in with hardened, violent men doesn't need such graphic depiction. It is disturbing and unnecessarily graphic, torture porn out of place in a crime novel. I liked, too, Will Trent (and his dog which made me think of Will Graham from the TV version of Hannibal with his pack of canine companions). Something puzzled me about Will, whose dyslexia seems so severe he's barely functionally literate, therefore how the heck did he ever pass exams etc. in order to achieve his position in the GBI (Georgia Bureau of investigation)? Perhaps this is explained in subsequent books in the series? The character Angie, Will's sometime wife/girlfriend?, undercover vice cop and 'whore with a heart of gold', didn't seem very realistic to me and I can't help thinking he is better off without her in his life. I will read on in the series in hopes the books get better, less graphic violence and more character development.

I decided to reread this book after seeing the musical version a couple of weeks ago. The musical was unexpectedly dark, and when I went to read the book, the first half was such a surprise. The writing is sensitive, and the characters are distinct. Reading it was an utter delight. There are several, subtle threads of social commentary going through the narration. One is that colonial racism is so toxic that it doesn't just hurt those at the bottom, but also the children of those at the top. Mary arrives in England psychologically damaged, not only because of the trauma she endured in India, but also due to emotional neglect. Her parents didn't care that much about her, but she also was unable to bond emotionally with the servants due to colonialism's barriers between races. When she is England, she has a physically absent guardian, but emotionally available servants. With a little affection, she thrives. I thought Burgess implied this couldn't happen in India due to colonialism. She makes similar commentary about the English class system, and she implies that sometimes it is useful for girls to not be "too nice." The paragraph above makes is sound like the book is about social justice, and that is not what it is about. It is about gardens and spring and growth. It is about emotional connections. It is about the joys of health and discovery. And it is about radical empathy. Rereading the book, I realized that the musical had to create a villain because modern audiences couldn't empathize with  a man who behaved terribly due to grief and depression. I don't think the adapters thought modern audiences could forgive Archibald Craven for his past behavior, so they turned Dr. Craven into a manipulator. The original had a more nuanced take on mental health. Every time I dipped into the first half of the book, I put it down calm and refreshed. The first half of the book is a solid 5 stars. Once Colin is introduced, the book went downhill for me. The second half becomes overly sentimental for me, and the ending made me kind of mad. I understand why the musical changed it. This is a children's classic, but I would recommend that parents read it together with their children so they don't misunderstand the social commentary. The seemingly casual racism serves a purpose, but I don't think children are necessarily able to put it in context. I would also want to be careful that children don't come away with unhealthy attitudes toward disabilities. This is a book that would be great for starting meaningful discussions, but I would worry a little about a very young, precocious child reading it alone before they could pick up on the social issues. If you are going to read this book with a child, I would recommend reading it in the late winter, and using it to plan a garden for the spring. Because as I said above, while there are lots of social issues sprinkled throughout, it really is about the joys of gardens, especially in spring.

Orphan Train by Christina Baker Kline follows the stories of two young females left to fend for themselves after tragedies leaves them parentless decades apart. Molly's story takes place in current day Maine; after her father is killed in a car accident and her mother turns to drugs to cope, Molly is bounced from foster home to foster home. With a history of trouble and after getting caught stealing a library book, Molly is given the choice of community service or spending time in a juvenile detention center. Her boyfriend is able to set up a community service project for Molly cleaning out the attic of his mother's elderly employer. At first appearance, Molly and ninety-one year old Vivian don't have much in common, but as the community service hours slip by, they both realize the similarities their lives hold. Niamh Power left Ireland with her parents and siblings during the 1920s in search of a better life in America. After two years of struggle and hardships in New York City, Niamh finds herself in an even more desperate situation when the building she and her family live in catches fire and leaves her an orphan. The Children's Aid Society takes Niamh in and places her on a train headed west with other orphaned children. The Orphan Train makes stops along the way where the children are displayed in the hopes of being taken in by a family. At nine years old, Niamh doesn't stand much of a chance of being chosen since the first to go are typically babies and older boys who would be useful on a farm. Pros * Before this book, I had never heard of orphan trains and had no idea that at one point in time these children were transported across the United States and basically adopted as indentured slaves. Some children did go to loving homes; however, that was not the fortune of the majority. It's also heartbreaking to learn of the poor opinion people had of orphans. They were though of as delinquents who would never be good for anything. These were children who just needed someone who cared about them and who would teach and guide them. * Both story lines were very interesting, but I found Niamh's timeline to be more interesting and was glad that the author chose to focus more on her story instead of Molly's. * This book was very fast paced and kept me reading late into the night. Cons * I felt that the ending was predictable. About one half to two-thirds of the way through I was able to guess how the story was going to play out. * As touching as the book was, I felt that it could have been more in depth and emotionally heart-wrenching. I was expecting more from this book than what it delivered.

Seriously, I could not put this book down. I imagine that it was as addictive as the simulated world in Ready Player One, OASIS. The book is set about 30 years into the future during a bleak period of humanity's history. The world is suffering from the effects of climate change and most people want to plug into the simulated world and forget about reality. James Halliday, the creator of this world, created an Easter egg in the software before he died. The first player to solve it would become the heir to his billions. Of course, no one could solve it. The Easter egg was just too hard to find and most players gave up. That is until one player solved the first clue. I don't think I can describe how much I enjoyed reading this novel. Even though I didn't get all of the 80s references, you could tell that the author of this book really loves video games and it shone through. I like to play games but I'm not what you'd call a really serious gamer. You could feel the passion the author has for these games and it made the book truly enjoyable. The characters; Wade, Art3mis and Aech were awesome. Each had their own unique personality and I loved the trials they all went through. I honestly wish I could have read more about this world but it ended perfectly the way it was. This is a must read for sci-fi. Especially if you love games.

Rating: 1.5/5 ***Minor spoilers*** Lady Witmore's family fortune is slowly dwindling, and if she doesn't marry another noble soon, they'll be unable to support their extravagant lifestyle. Elizabeth Witmore is Countess of Rothford - a descendant of one of Osfrid's founding fathers. However, she only has one option for a husband at the moment, and her grandmother has already accepted. She never expected to marry for love, but once she meets him she doesn't like him at all. When a man named Cedric comes to the Witmore residence in an attempt to recruit one of Elizabeth's lady-in-waitings, he offers the maid, Adelaide, a chance to go get an education and move to Adoria, where she will be able to marry someone rich and live well. However, once Adelaide gets cold feet, Elizabeth gives her the funds to return to her family and secretly takes her place, taking on the persona of Adelaide. She now needs to go through a finishing school for things like etiquette and dance (things she already knows but shouldn't since she's supposed to be Adelaide) and make her way to Adoria, all while hiding her true identity. As a fan of both the Vampire Academy and Bloodlines series, when I learned that Mead would be venturing into YA again, I knew I needed to read this. I had high hopes, mostly because I loved Vampire Academy so much, but I couldn't help it. I was disappointed, unfortunately. I didn't like this book very much at all. There were so many different things going on, but at the same time everything felt so dull. I guess I just didn't have the connection with Adelaide I would need to enjoy this book. I wasn't that interested in the romance either. I actually sat down with this book for an hour to do a reading sprint starting around 70% in, and I found myself counting down the minutes until I could stop because I found it so boring and predictable (at least, at that point in the book). Those definitely aren't things you want to experience when 70% in. I also had a problem with the ending. It feels like we spent so long with not much action and then Mead shoved all this action into one chapter and then declared the book finished. It felt almost as if some sort of limit was being approached, so all the action and hasty explanation was shoved into 20 pages. I also found it extremely confusing. There wasn't an explanation for what went on with  Tamsin  , Mira's secret wasn't even mentioned, and I had no barely any idea what that thing with Warren meant. I wish it wasn't so hasty and things were explained better. I don't like having so many questions at the end of this book. Overall, I considered this a pretty big disappointment. I had high hopes for Mead's next YA book but this series really wasn't for me, and from other reviews I can see that I'm not alone in that opinion. It was too much and not enough all at once, and the ending was really dissatisfying. I doubt I will be picking up the next book unless it gets much better reviews than this one. I wouldn't really recommend this book, especially if you enjoyed Vampire Academy/Bloodlines and are looking for the same enjoyment from this book. It doesn't really have the same excitement, suspense, surprises, or witty characters that I was looking for here that I loved from VA.

This was a compulsively readable novel. As a thriller, it definitely earned 4 stars and the first half of the book was definitely 4 stars. The second half, however, did lose me a little. When all the other Jasons started appearing it seemed a little like a Grade B Syfy movie. That said, it still kept me going right to the end. Who hasn't wondered "what if I had..."? The characterization was great and I loved the description of Chicago, which was a great setting. I hated not knowing quite what happens, but the end was satisfying as it was. It was a thought-provoking thriller.

When I first read this book, I thought it was a less-than-accurate and somewhat stereotyped portrait of a character with Asperger Syndrome. (Didn't stop me from loving the book, though.) Upon further recollection, it is far more accurate then I realized, and is just about the clearest, most truthful depiction of an individual with a higher-functioning disorder on the autism spectrum. Maybe for AS it's not as accurate, but Marcelo himself says that the label is merely the closest term there is for what's going on with him, and it does not entirely describe him. That explains a lot. More importantly, Marcelo is a three-dimensional character, not a saintly, naive creature like so many other fictional autistics. He isn't stupid and can function decently enough in society. He is able to feel emotions. He can't tell in some situations when people are being facetious, but he's not one-hundred percent clueless about others. More importantly, he is extremely interesting, and his story is well-told, if a bit long. In short, "The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time" has nothing on this whatsoever. It's probably got a really solid chance at getting some serious recognition by the Printz Award committee, and it is well deserved. One of the best books of the year, and probably the best fictional depiction of AS. (I have very high hopes for the upcoming "Mockingbird" and "Harmonic Feedback," though.)

I am so up in the air about this book. I love David Gemmell. I binge read him in college for about a month. So I was cetain this was right up my alley. It was and it wasn't. Best Served Cold is all about revenge (duh). I can do that, although revenge is never what the hero thinks it would be. the prologue was amazing and I totally thought that I would knock this book out in a couple days. But as the story went on it just got harder and harder for me to read. I finally just skimmed through to the end to see what happened. It's been two weeks since I started it and I can't bring myself to even open it again. So I probably won't go back and finish it. Monza, is the main character, the one driving the revenge and I couldn't connect with her. In the beginning yeah, but as the story went on I fell out of understanding with her, couldn't stand her decisions and honestly didn't care if she managed to survive. The way she treated her allies, wouldn't want to be them. The fact that Benna is an idiot and totally set the both of them up to be killed because he was planning a revolt is obvious, and Monza remains oblivious to that fact until it is spelled out for her. The beginning had so much potenial and then it fell flat. If you premise is that life is pointless, then the story can become pointless also. Monza didn't learn anything, didn't grow, didn't have a heart for anyone or anything. The fact that she didn't commit suicide is amazing. I won't rate it right now because my feelings are so mixed but I'm done.

Love it! This was a great look into the primary villain and to see that evil isn't born, but made. That everyone has a story and we shouldn't judge someone without knowing them. Great character development and story telling. it adds another dimension to a great story. I like that it gives us hints as to how things evolved on Luna but I want to know more. How the ability to manipulate bioelectricity evolved, when the shift from those with the ability went form minority to majority. If Lavanas  ancestor was the first to have the ability is everyone with the ability related to him, is it a hidden gene that can pop up spontaneously or is it genetically passed through generations? It answered a few questions I had- like are lunars from earth- which yes they are. But then when did the lunar settlements begin. It must have been hundreds of years ago because Earthens and Lunars talk as if they are 2 different species. Questions I hope will be answered in Winter!

I was going to give this a three, but a sentence towards the very end of the book REALLY bothered me. It was so inconsistant with the world created thus far in the series that I couldn't believe an editor let it slip. When Aldwyn wants to know why his powers came so suddenly and so late, Skyler says that "ofttimes" a familiar's powers aren't revealed until their loyal is in danger. Really?!?!?!?! This kind of thing happens often? What about all of the animals we saw throughout the book who had no loyal and were doing all kinds of magical things? The frogs! The cats! The animals at the familiar pet shop? As a reader, this kind of inconsistency really irks me. It makes me feel like the author and editor have been sloppy and haven't really crafted the book as tightly as they could. Disappointing. Overall, this is fine. I could see recommending it to kids I think like plot driven, magical, animal books. It did not "wow" me the way I hoped it would. The plot has a great hook, though, making it very booktalk-able. What would have made it better for me as a reader? At the very least, more depth to the characters, and an editor who caught the bit that bothered me so much.
Sweet. Predictable at some point but still a good read.. =)

This romance started out amazingly - with a surprising scene of the hero and heroine (Bryant and Ace) already in bed and not into it (whaaaat??). It really grabs your attention and poses a problem to solve: how is Frederick going to salvage the romance and their sex life? The sex gets solved pretty quickly (I think they could have spent more time figuring out what they liked instead of switching right back into the more typical insta-lust mode) but the romance stays interesting and complicated. Bryant and Ace do get along from the start and it's really Bryant who struggles to take it more seriously. That's just one of the ways that Frederick surprises with this book. She also takes the cliched coach's daughter plot and upends it by making the coach/dad not against his daughter dating his quarterback. That was a nice twist. And there were others. My only real objection was that those surprises sort of taper off and the end of the book gets less interesting, then I was really put off by the  kidnapping scene. That was just NOT okay and NOT funny. I *hate* romance scenes that play off violent and scary behavior as sexy or possessiveness. . Otherwise, a good read, well written as all Frederick's books are, and different.

Ok Melanie Harlow, just take my heart already. You've effectively ruined me for all good books from here on out anyways. If You Were Mine is a true winner. Theo is sexy as sin and my heart just went out for him from the beginning. He was a strong, sexy man who just needed a little help. Which came courtesy of the sweet and wily Claire. Theo and Claire were both a little lost when the book began, but when they found each other they got a little lighter, saw things a little brighter. It was really amazing to see the change in both of them throughout the book. It wasn't always fun, and sometimes my heart was twisted a little too much, but it was worth it in the end. Melanie Harlow has built a world of sweetness, super sexiness, and an empowering storyline. Theo and Claire will melt your heart and leave you both satisfied and needing so much more. If You Were Mine is an enticingly seductive standalone that you should go devour ASAP! Happy Reading! *ARC provided by the author in exchange for an honest review*

I cannot stress enough that people should read and heed the warnings on this book. This is not for anyone who cannot handle graphic depictions of sexual violence. When I say graphic I mean detailed descriptions of rape and physical assault. I really respect the author for putting those warnings on this story. That is part of why I took a look at the sample chapter in the first place. Despite the content of the book and my feelings about them, the use of a strong warning is something that I wish we would see more often in the erotica (especially ones on the dark/edgy) genre more often. Onto the review. I do not judge people you enjoy rape fantasies, but they are not usually my thing. This is especially so when rape is used in a romantic context between the two romantic leads. If you've read some of my other reviews or know me even a little you know my feelings on romanticizing rape and on supporting the fantasy that a victim could ever have a healthy romantic relationship with their abuser. That being said, I am always open to the idea that someone out there could find a way to prove me wrong or even just change my mind. When I read the sample chapter for this book I thought that I might have just stumbled upon the book that was going to change my mind, unfortunately as I continued to read I realized that it was not. This book had a lot of promise, most of which is presented in the beginning by the author's unflinching depiction of a rape. She does not shy away in either her description or language. This story is told in a first person narrative, so we are right there with the victim for every second. Despite the (many) shortfalls of this book, that scene is one of the most respectful, honest and brutal portrayals of rape I have ever read. The unusual twist to the set up for this story and the circumstances around the rape were surprisingly complex and intriguing. As was the only (truly) consentual scene. It was emotionally raw while also being very erotic and even put dominance and submissive sex play into a context I'd never really seen before. It was strangely fitting for these two deeply wounded people, and it gave me a sense of hope that these characters would somehow heal. However, as I said early the potential that shines in the beginning of this book is quickly flushed down the toilet by cheap plot devices and the continuation of the sexual abuse of the heroine of the story. It really is too bad, because if the story had continued on a storyline with the characters (rather than the sexual violence) as the focus I think it could have been a much more complex and compelling read. Unfortunately, it's reduced to a glorified rape fantasy, which is cool if that's you're kink and if it is this is probably the book for you, but not for me. Now onto the spoilery part of the review where I obsessively over-analyze the crap that no one cares about. Feel free to leave, as this won't make a lot of sense unless you've read the book. Though, I'm sure it will be entertaining for my friends that like my brand of crazy!nerdiness. I was pleasantly surprised by the set up of this being a forced rape, mostly because it's an aspect of sexual assault that isn't often explored. The idea of the duel victimization/trauma is a scenario I have never seen explored in a romantic context either and I have to admit it really intrigued me. Especially, in how it effects a man like Zachary, who had such a strong conviction about his duty to protect others, and how he perceived the rape as his failure. There's a truth to that male perception of rape, and how the violation of women deeply effects men (even ones who are not involved in the violation). I wanted to see more exploration of that, and how a man recovers from seeing himself as a rapist/monster. The power play in their next (consensual) sexual encounter began to address it in an very unique way, and I was impressed at how both characters (and the author) did an amazing job of walking the line while never going over the top into BDSM cliches. I really loved how Dom/Sub power exchanged (and orgasm denial play) seemed to empower Rachel, and I really dug how Zachary was so turned on by her taking charge. It would have been really interesting to see that storyline continue, where these two victims learned to redefine themselves through this kind of sexual power play. Don't get me wrong, I still don't think it could actually heal the wounds of sexual assault in the real world, but I kind of love the idea of a story that starts in rape turning into a story of empowerment. Alas, I'm going to have to keep on searching to find that story.

I did read the sneak peek of the author's new book which is about the Queen of Hearts and it is AMAZING! I can't wait for that later this year!!

Delightful. Absolutely delightful. Those are the first words that come to mind when I think about this book. The whole story was just one rollicking, playful adventure from start to finish, and I enjoyed every minute of it. It's not quite 'fluff,' not quite serious romance, but all fun. One of the best parts was how the whole narrative kept up a tongue-in-cheek style of humor. I highly recommend this one, preferably with a glass of lemonade on a nice spring day. Plot: Start with two dashes of witty characters, add in a scoop of mystery, and stir with a healthy dose of comedy. Voila! You have Duels and Deception, fresh and original. The mystery part was alright (I was in it for the characters), intriguing enough to keep me reading, but not nail-bitingly exciting. I did guess who might have perpetrated the kidnapping before the characters found out, but I wasn't for sure. It was interesting to see how everything worked out. However, I was more interested in the blossoming relationship between Lydia and Robert. Oh, those two. They are absolutely adorable together. All those grins. The ending, while predictable, wrapped things up in a neat bow. Characters: I'm sure you've realized I adore these characters. Lydia and Robert. Robert and Lydia. The sensible, practical young lady who loves her estate and irritating family gets kidnapped along with the equally sensible but slightly more impulsive apprentice-in-waiting. Oh, the fun that ensues. Their relationship is most definitely giggle inducing, as both are in love almost immediately, but it takes them most of the book to realize it. Plenty of swoon worthy moments keep the fire burning between them, even though it seems like anyone and everyone (including themselves) are conspiring to keep them apart. Setting: I'm a Janeite, and as such, I whole-heartedly approve of the English setting. Particularly since it takes place in Bath. (Too bad we didn't see any cameos from Jane Austen's characters!) It was well written: clearly, the author had done her research, and it came through. It seemed authentic and believable, and was the perfect setting for the plot. Overall, I give this book 4 stars. While not terribly life-altering (it leans more to the 'fluff' side than the profound), it was a delicious read, and as such, merits my approval. Fellow Janeites looking for a quick, easy read will enjoy this one. Age Rating: 14 and up Content guide: Language: 3/10 (name-calling--appropriate and archaic in type) Sexual Content: 4/10 (mentions of ruining a woman's honor--how and why is not alluded to, hugs, touches, and embraces, along with a few kisses--slightly detailed) Violence: 4/10 (threats of duels, peril, kidnapping, being knocked unconscious, etc) *Thanks to Netgalley for providing a copy to review* For more book reviews, or to request your own book to be reviewed by yours truly, visit gabriellenblog.wordpress.com

In this book, they were trying to save the world, but they weren't sure how to do it, leaving this book feeling slightly less focused. I also thought Sazed's soul-searching would have been better had it been more concise. On the other hand, I loved how things from earlier books played an important role, like Vin's earring and all the religions Sazed had studied. Overall, I enjoyed the series enough that I wouldn't mind reading it again, and I wouldn't hesitate to recommend it to fans of fantasy.

3 stars I don't really know how to review this book. It was just that... Good. Nothing exemplary, nothing that would make the reader beg for more. It was just good. It is the story of Jason Dessen and the multiverse theory. Jason had a great life. He had a loving wife and a child who was the ideal son. He just didn't have one thing. Fifteen Years prior to the start of the novel, he made a decision to live with Daniela and have a kid. But in a different parallel universe the whole conversation happened differently. He chose his job over Dani. One night man abducts him and he finds himself In a different universe. His kid isn't borne and his wife isn't his wife. How did this happen and will he be able to go back? I have to admit that this is a very addictive novel. Once I started reading it, I could put it down, because the plot is very interesting. Once I stopped reading it for an hour though, I did have second thoughts. "Is it really that good?" But when I finally went back to it, it grabbed me again. I'd recommend this book to the fans of The Illuminae Files, because it has themes which are similar to this. Especially an occurrence in the second book. A thing that I disappointed me in the novel was the loose end with Amanda. She helps Jason find his way to his world but then something happens. She kind of just disappeared and took half of the samples. The only reason she was there was to do that and put pressure on Jason. To find his real world faster. I was hoping that they would find each other after he found his family and she would cause problems for him of some kind. Sadly she just got off like that and she was never seen again. I liked everything else in this novel. At least, I liked it enough to decide that it wouldn't decrease my rating. the reason that it is just a three, is because there was nothing exemplary about it. The writing was mediocre. The plot was average. There wasn't any world changing character development. It was just a fun read that brought me out of my book hangover. Honestly that is all I have to say for it. Overall, this is a highly addicting novel which is bound to get anyone out of a book hangover.

Why I picked it up I wasn't familiar with Gay or her work before attending a speaking engagement of hers at the Tattered Cover, a local bookstore. Went home afterwords and ordered this book, which she was touring in promotion of, and a few others. What I want to remember about it + Some shifting place between admiration and suspicion lies my feelings toward people who can take incredibly, immensely complicated events, snarled tangles of cause and effect and untidy, complicated human emotion and logic, and reduce it--reduce life--to any kind of straightforward assertion. "I had a series of unhealthy relationships because I felt undeserving of affection." The time, the emotion, the quantity and quality of living packed into such a sentence! Far too tidy to actually be an accurate or appropriate description of what actually happened. I don't know. It's either avoidance or good writing. + It was distractingly choppy at times, with some chapters being mere sentences long. By the time I had gripped on to the topic and its direction, it was over and we were on to the next thing. Happened often enough that I grew annoyed by it. I suspect that Gay may be pulling inspiration for content from her tumblr and twitter at times, which is fine, and that at times she wanted to make points that added up to little more than asides. My personal preference though would be to not have the narrative interrupted by tweet sized tidbits. + The tipping point between fat and Fat is what she calls "Lane Bryant fat". It's the dividing point between being able to buy clothes, move through a store, sit on chairs or sit in a restaurant, go to a theater or walk somewhere. + The fact that she is able to hold two conflicting and opposing desires as the same time. She wants to be smaller while demanding to remain big.

I reserved this when it first came out and just now got it. I have been an Ally Carter fan for a while now (own all the Gallagher Girl books, even my least favorite the fifth one) but I just haven't been enjoying this series nearly as much. First of all, there's the issue with Kat. She's described as a jeans and t-shirt kind of girl (yeah, we get it, mentioned at least three times in this book and three times in all the others), and no it's not a "feminist statement", as Ally Carter puts it (does she even know what a feminist is) yet she's always being forced into dresses and heels for disguises by her hot cousin Gabrielle. I'm pretty sure Gabrielle's main and possibly only role in the story is to make Kat dress like the typical female. To be honest, I really don't care what Kat wears, and I don't find the dresses amusing. She could be in fishnet leggings and a coconut bra for all I care--I may wonder why, but hey, I don't care. Kat has a boyfriend named Hale, who she loves a lot but is fairly new in the role of her boyfriend, so she's always trying to make sure he stays with her no matter what. Totally understandable, people will try anything to maintain some relationships, but it got really annoying. She couldn't even turn around without worrying about Hale, and while she was obsessing over him he barely gave a crap about her, besides the typical kisses and arm slings. I get why this book is rated so high, I get why this appeals to so many people, especially teenagers girls (I apologize for generalizing) but not to this one. "Connectable" girl main character. Somewhat of a hot finance. And every chapter ended with a boom, which is just Ally Carter. I might've liked it before; now it just annoys me. Can you just end your chapters normally for once? All these booms are taking away the impact of the actual important things. And all the characters were incredibly one-sided. How did I not notice this before, I don't know. Gabrielle was the hot girl. Angus and Hamish were the explosive guys. Hale was the rich love interest. Uncle Eddie was the strange uncle. Garrett was evil. Kat was quiet and reserved, yet somehow still sarcastic when a dull moment occurred? Kat had no voice. At all. I couldn't figure out who she was. All she did was stand still and let herself be bossed around by other people. Besides the occasional desperate love for Hale or random fits of wittiness, she did nothing. The ending was such a cop-out. All Kat ever talks about is her family and how much she loves them and vice versa, and since each chapter had to end with a boom, why not just make everybody her family? Garrett wants to sell stolen prototypes to buyer? The buyer's family. Garrett wants to hire a bodyguard? Bodyguard's family. Garrett attempts to have evil plan and accidentally throws Uncle Eddie over into the Niagara Falls? Uncle Eddie's not dead. Why? Oh, because he's family obviously. Did we mention he has a twin brother whose also alive? How the hell does that even work? I'm sure not even the best criminals know how to throw themselves thirty feet off something and not be dead, or at least somewhat injured. Maybe I've matured as a reader and Ally Carter's stuff doesn't appeal to me anymore. (I don't see why it shouldn't though, I'm a young 14.) I'm sick of this series and the "quirks" everyone in the family has, and I'm hoping the sixth Gallagher will restore my hope in this author. EDIT: just read one of the reviews, almost reduced me to tears because of its stupidity. So there's this one scene where Uncle Eddie basically gets thrown over a cliff and dies, as I've mentioned before. It's not a very emotional scene, there are like two lines describing Kat screaming as Hale hugs her and Garrett drives away, but it was probably one of the only scenes where I was like, Finally, something important is happening in the plot. I admit, I was very shocked Ally Carter had pulled off a death of one of her main characters, and a little impressed (even though it wasn't executed in the best way) (I mean, this is a Disney Hyperion after all, but you don't see me complaining about Percy Jackson or anything). However, in no way was it emotional or heart-wrenching or deathly upsetting. You wanna cry, go read Me Before You by Jojo Knowles, or better yet, The Fault in Our Stars, which might fit Ally Carter fans better (I only teared up for that one). I didn't even THINK about thinking about crying at that moment (if you can't get used to death in novels, especially crime ones, high school English will be a difficult time for you.) No offense if you were one of the criers, but this book is NOT SAD AT ALL. It's not even funny, really, it's just badly written.

I wanted to read something warm and feel-good and this...almost worked for me. I liked Vince with his big crazy loving Italian family, finally coming to terms with his sexuality at almost 40. But in the same way that the alternating POVs didn't jibe for me -- Vince's chapters in third person, Trey's in first -- I found Trey's half of the story less convincing. It verged on misery porn: poverty, horribly alcoholic mother, supposedly caring grandmother and friends who never do anything to help (either Trey or the plot), and a weird obsession with virginity. I simply didn't buy Trey's reasons for abstaining from sex; it felt to me like the authors just really wanted him to be a virgin, so he had to be a virgin. Vince and Trey fall in love so quickly, and Vince goes from being unable to admit he might be gay to wanting it in the ass so fast -- I don't know, I actually started to feel bad for them that they're each going to be the other's only male lover, especially since they get engaged to be married at the end! For a supposed slow-build, this was too fast, too soon, too sudden, and I didn't believe it.

I have to admit, I was really disappointed when I realized this book was a prequel and I wasn't going to get to see how Juliette's plan was working out at all. The first two books were pretty heavily tinged with this disappointment, but the third book turned the whole series back around for me. Shift splits between several different timelines including the origin of the Silos and the stories of several members of the various uprisings that are hinted at in Wool. A lot of it felt unnecessary at first, but again the third book made it clear why the reader suddenly needed this knowledge of the people that began this project. It's very hard to discuss without spoilers, so prepare for a large chunk of spoilerific review below. Donald is a character I liked at first, but had a hard time sticking around with. He keeps being vouched for by smart people in positions of power, but I never quite understand why they like him so much. His descent into madness is well-written, but not quite what I was looking for when I picked the book up. Still, once I realized that he is the other end of Juliette's phone call, that really the previous 400 pages existed to set me up to sympathize with the guy on the other end of the phone, I had to respect Howey's craftsmanship. He brought us into the Evil Empire and took the Evil right out. Definitely makes me look forward to Dust. Mission's chapter I enjoyed while reading it, but I can't say it stuck with me. This is probably due to the fact that Jimmy/Solo's chapter was so heart-wrenchingly good that the previous books faded from memory. I figured out that Jimmy would become Solo pretty quickly, and wow does Howey do a great job of guiding us through that transition. I will say that all books featuring animal death should have a warning sticker, though. I knew Shadow was doomed from the moment he showed up since he isn't in Wool, but I still found myself clutching my own cat who was quite annoyed at my failure to live up to my status as heated sofa human. It isn't as strong as Wool, but the information here feels vital for Book 3 which promises a return to the original timeline. I will definitely be finishing the series up soon.

I requested The Girl At Midnight because it was getting a lot of hype around the blogosphere. And I guess because of said hype, I've kind of become the black sheep here, since I didn't LOVE it as much as everyone else did. Also mostly because I've already read Daughter of Smoke & Bone, and honestly I think this is just a less developed version of it. I do have to admit that Echo is cool though. She's a runaway thief, but she's been adopted by the Avicen, these magical bird-like creatures with feathers instead of hair. WHICH IS JUST SO COOL. And then of course there must be the other species, and in this case it's the dragons (I honestly don't remember the spelling of the species specifically, but oh well). The main, huge problem I had with the book, as I said before, is that it's not original. In fact, it's REALLY, EXACTLY like Daughter of Smoke & Bone. I mean I knew that it would be similar to that series, but I didn't think it would be so, so similar. Here's why I think so: Echo is the odd one out in a community full of Avicen. Reminds you of someone? Yeah, Kaoru. There are two opposite species fighting each other, or at the brink of war. Avicen and Dragon species here, and the Seraphim and the Chimaera in DoSaB. (Please excuse my spelling, I'm tired) The main characters from opposite sides fall in love. Echo and Caius and then Kaoru and Akiva from DoSaB. Even if I didn't read DoSaB before, I still had some reservations. Honestly, the book had an amazing start, and I was really excited before of it. But then, everything kind of went down from there. Many of the things, including the side characters like Jasper, Ivy, and Dorian, weren't fully developed. And also,  I didn't catch that Dorian liked Caius? And then Caius went off to GIVE HIM TO JASPER? Pretty much? It was weird and I don't know what to think about it. I mean at least there's diversity in this, right? Anyways, don't get me wrong, I did like The Girl At Midnight, but it could've been MORE. More original, more developed, just, I NEED MORE. I'm half excited to see what the sequel would be like, but then I kind of don't know whether it will just be more of this, under-developness (I did just make up a word and NO REGRETS). Wait, I think it's underdevelopment. Ah well.

This sequel picked up not to long after Frostblood left off, with Arcus on the throne and Ruby attempting to navigate the Frostblood kingdom where many, most, people hate her and fear her. With the Minax loose in the kingdom, she was determined to find a way to stop it, to defeat it once and for all, but doing so would mean leaving Arcus and traveling to the Fireblood kingdom. I really liked seeing the Fireblood kingdom and how different it was from the Frostblood one. There were many great additions in this sequel that made me like it even more than the first. Hopefully that trend keeps up and the third one is also amazing. I loved the introduction to Kai, his flirtation, his confidence, his backstory, his unwillingness to treat Ruby as fragile. He did need her just as much as she needed him and them training together and helping each other were great scenes. And there were many of them. I loved seeing the relationship between them, whatever it was turning into, develop. Ruby was fierce in this book. In the first one, she had a lot of growth with regards to becoming stronger and trusting herself and her powers. In this one, it was more about her determination to fight and destroy to Minax, even if she still wasn't convinced she was the prophesied Child of the Light. I loved seeing her learn to push her powers even more than in the first book and her learning more about the Firebloods. I also loved the way the mythology has been worked into this series and continued to be important. It wasn't just a quick explanation at the beginning of book one and then forgotten about, it was a huge part of the prophecy and was something that kept getting elaborated on through this sequel. I would definitely read a spin-off series of the Gods of this world. It's going to be way too long until the next one comes out but at least we already have a title and cover! *I received a copy of this book from the publisher in exchange for an honest review.

I received this book as part of Read 2 Review (Paranormal Romance and Urban Fantasy Fanatics! Goodreads Group). Ashlyn McVean is an ordinary teenager who is thrown into an extraordinary series of events after the death of her father. On a trip to Ireland to visit family, she discovers her lineage is not so normal, and that she is the target of evil forces that are seeking to destroy her. We are led through the challenges that Ashlyn faces as she comes to terms with her newfound abilities and struggles to understand how to fix what her grandmother started many years ago. I enjoyed this book. The story starts out with a dramatic event, and then never ceases to disappoint with the inclusion of dangerous pixies, an unusual grandmother, and of course, romance. I was impressed with Ms. Curd's imaginative plot about a girl who discovers how she is part of the fairy world and the consequences of this. Ashlyn's adventures were fun to read and the book was definitely a page-turner. There were a couple of points in the book that were either confusing or unrealistic, which did sometimes make the story hard to follow. More description into the background of Memaw and the fairy world would have enhanced this issue, as well as developing Ashlyn's father's death in more detail into the story. For example,  The beginning of the book begins with the death of Ashlyn's father. Yet, this horrible event is never pursued further in the story, even after Ashlyn discovers her best friend Jamie was responsible for this. In addition, I was surprised that after only a week since her father's death, Ashlyn is allowed to travel to Ireland with Jamie, and then even more surprised to learn Memaw knew Jaime was a pixie out to harm Ashlyn but let her go anyway. I also was confused with Memaw's story, both exactly what she is and why she treats Ashlyn so badly. I never got a good grasp the different types of fairies and how Ashlyn is connected to all of them. What is the difference between Tess and Ashlyn? Finally, if Ashlyn's Protector suffers the same injuries as Ashlyn, why is it that if she becomes immortal her Protector dies? Ms. Curd's writing is fast-paced and was at times very humorous! I particularly enjoyed the silliness of the boys in the story - a pretty realistic high school situation. The writing was descriptive enough that I could easily imagine the different real-world and surreal locations Ashlyn, Liam, Reese and Memaw were in. Overall, I gave the book 3 stars. While I feel the story and plot itself was creative and unique, and the character development enjoyable, there were several events that were difficult to follow, leaving me confused as to what was happening at certain points. But, the story has a lot of potential and I can't wait to learn what is in store next for Ashlyn!

First story: I liked this! It was a quieter kind of story, which I appreciated. Second story: Fine, but didn't really do much for me. Third story: I just don't love how Singh writes the submissive and dominant thing. There seems an element to sexism to it, that dominant woman mostly need to mate with dominant men. And that dominant always means solider. (I mean, I know there are maternal dominants, but they're not getting the stories. Even the one maternal dominant who got a story was a soldier.) Made me want to read other authors's takes on submissive wolves. Last story: REALLY, KENJI? You don't want to take Garnet's choices away from her? YOU LITERALLY DID THAT FOR SEVEN YEARS! And adoption exists, COME ON. Like, I don't mean demean his sorrow, but COME ON. Kind of did like the mystery plot, though. I don't know. It's probably about time to for me and Singh to part ways. I'll come back for Nikita/Anthony. And maybe the rugby-playing brothers.

OH MY GOSH. I just finished the book and am still reeling from it. 3.5-4ish stars. I loved the lore in this book. Seriously, I didn't care about Karou at all and it was only slightly interesting when she and Akiva finally met. But man, oh man. When the story becomes about  Madrigal   ... Wow. I definitely would have liked this book more if there were less Karou and more  Madrigal  . More M and less Karou would have been amazing. One of Us is Lying is a suspenseful page-turner, with interesting and diverse characters, who learn, develop and grow during the course of the story. The four main characters really started growing on me, and I gradually became involved in their lives and had a stake in their futures. The main characters, as well as many of the side characters, were colorful and three-dimensional. I really felt I was getting to know them as their secrets and their true selves started coming out (in their thoughts, in their actions, and eventually in what they were willing to share with others). I guessed the "whodunit" at 68% -- whooo hoooo! But, I was never really sure -- it was just one of many possible scenarios, and there were still many surprises in the details. I thought the ending  to the love story was a bit cliche, though. I've seen this scenario too many times in teen/YA/chick movies or films: Brooding MC breaks up with his love interest near the end "for her own sake" or "because he's no good for her" or "to protect her" or "because they're from different worlds and it would never work out" or... yada, yada, yada. Then he reconsiders and surprises said love interest at her big performance, her debut, a dance, graduation, before she's about to get married, before she leaves the country, before she joins the army, or the convent... and then confesses his love for her because, of course, he was a fool, and he can't live without her. Nate and Bronwyn are such amusing, creative, original characters, and their relationship is amusing and creative, if not entirely original: uptight, ambitious, ivy-league-bound, rich, inexperienced-with-boys girl hooks up with dangerous, poor, from-broken-family, drug-dealing hotty -- it's been done before. But still, they have a great dynamic and deserve a creative, amusing, and original ending. But this is a minor detail in the larger scheme of things and doesn't detract from the enjoyment of the overall read at all. There are some wonderful scenes. Oh, that scene in the cafeteria three-quarter through was pure brilliance. Performance art. Nate telling Vanessa to "try to make that happen," Bronwyn kissing Nate, and Luis asking why it couldn't have been apple day. It's not the Breakfast Club, but the Murder Club! ;)  I was laughing out loud. I hope this book becomes a movie. This will be my favorite scene I'm sure! One of Us is Lying is a page-turner. It kept me guessing and second-guessing and reading until late in the night and into the early morning hours... I can highly recommend it! ** spoiler alert ** Hugh and Lilith... wow! They really are a great couple! Looking at it objectively, I am almost shocked that I liked them as much as I do, because generally characters like Hugh - overly-earnest, naive, more than a bit self-righteous, very prone to deciding that he knows what is best and then charging forward into that course of action with no discussion, and a freaking martyr - annoy the crap out of me. But for whatever reason, he really didn't. In this book, all those qualities came together to make a very charming character. He definitely made mistakes, but ... everything was driven by a bone-deep love for Lilith (one that Hugh himself found boggling, I think, but couldn't deny). And how can you not love Lilith? I loved the topsy-turvy gender-bending relationship they had - she was the seductress, the rake. Charmed by Hugh in spite of her very best efforts. And she was whip-smart, strong, resilient, defiant, and able to hold on to her humanity despite everything she went through. I still don't like Michael. Sorry, but he seems like an asshat. I wish we had gotten some of the actual story around Lilith's transformation - Michael clearly feels guilty about something there, though Lilith doesn't seem to feel that's the case (though, of course, being a demon she uses his guilt against him... but when she was being frank with Hugh about it, she didn't direct any blame at Michael). Regardless, I don't like him. He's heavy-handed, secretive, he seems to have done something that REALLY pissed Hugh off (though again, we're given no details - we only see the evidence... Hugh can barely be civil to him when they encounter each other in Part 2); he also seems to be happy to manipulate the situation as if he was a demon himself. Anyway. He's a douchecanoe. And I am sure we are going to see more of him later, and he also strikes me as a character the author plans to dig into ... perhaps in a redeeming way. Anyway, the book was tons of fun! I am glad I snagged the first 3 in this series, so I can continue on with it!

In the little town of Fairfold, people know that faeries are real. You need to be careful and not call too much attention to yourself, like the tourists frequently do, or the faeries may play dangerous or even deadly pranks on you. One of the things that lures tourists to Fairfold is the glass coffin, deep in the woods. In it, there is a horned boy, sleeping eternally. He is a thing of otherworldy beauty with the tips of his ears sharp as knives. He's been sleeping there for generations, undisturbed by gawkers, tourists, partying teenagers or those desperate to try to break the coffin. Bad things tend to happen to those who try to break the coffin by force. Ben and Hazel's parents are artists, and their mother was one of the Fairfold residents who may have called a bit too much attention to herself. Having gifted a faerie woman with a painting, her eldest child, Ben, was gifted, or possibly cursed, with the ability to play faerie music. Whether he wanted to or not, he would be compelled to play, and so well that he could enchant others with it. Hazel, still in the womb, was granted no such favours, and being the perfectly normal child in a family of distracted and dedicated artists can be a curse all on its own. Seeing early how dangerous the faeries could be, Hazel took it upon herself to fight the worst of them, appointing herself a knight, with her brother the enchanted bard who assists her. Though only children, Ben and Hazel risked their lives to avenge tourists and Fairfold residents alike, until Ben was given a scholarship to a prestigious music academy and the family had to move away for a few years. When they weren't playing at being heroes, the two would spend hours around the glass coffin, spinning tales about the enchanted prince who slept there, telling him all their heart's desires. Now they are both in high school, barely speaking, despite the closeness they once shared. Hazel wakes up one morning, having dragged mud and glass splinters through her bedroom window. The coffin in the wood is empty and the sleeping boy has disappeared. There is danger lurking in the dark of the forest. Can Ben and Hazel unite once more to fight it? The sibling relationships depicted in this story felt very real to me, and there are several that are important. Hazel and Ben are close in age and due to the frequent forgetfulness and neglect of their artistic parents, they have to rely on and take care of each other, because they can't rely on their parents to always do so. Great love and sacrifice caused the rift, lack of communication and wall of lies that is between them at the start of the book and Black slowly reveals how their erstwhile closeness ended up in near estrangement. Both infatuated with the "enchanted prince" in the forest, they are shaken when he suddenly wakes up. The object of their fantasies has suddenly become a real person, who they have to relate to in a completely different way. There are the brothers Carter and Jack, similar enough to be twins, yet only Carter is actually human. Jack is Carter's changeling, who Carter's mother insisted on keeping after she tricked his faerie mother into giving her own baby back. They look very similar, but as they get older, it's quite clear that Jack isn't like his brother or their high school friends. He has another family as well, and while he loves his human family, he is torn between two worlds. Jack is Ben's best friend, but has secretly loved Hazel for as long as he can remember. Restless, flirty Hazel who kisses all the boys, and never seems to wants anything permanent with anyone. But the evening before the sleeping boy is awoken, she kisses Jack. Could he finally convince her to actually notice him? Finally, there is Severin, the awoken prince and his sister Sorrow, whose sibling relationship forms an important core to the dangers facing Fairfold. Tragic events led to Severin being imprisoned in the glass coffin, whilst his sister became completely consumed by her own grief. Now their father wants his children back under his control, and he isn't afraid to use underhanded methods to achieve it. This book is also great in terms of diversity. While Jack may be a faerie who fits into the European/Celtic mythology, he is the changeling of an American child, and as such is as dark-skinned and dark-haired as the rest of his human family. Ben is openly gay and his love for Severin is both inspiring and heart-breaking at times. Hazel is not always easy to like, but no one can fault her for being extremely brave. Sometimes to the point of insanity. She's a girl with many secrets, even from herself, it becomes obvious fairly soon. Hazel lives a double life so complex that even she's not completely aware of all the aspects of it. Having grown up in the gifted Ben's shadow, she's so determined to make something of herself, even if it means risking her life fighting dangerous faeries. She loves her brother and would do anything for him, but also believes herself to be the reason he no longer practises music and won't speak to her anymore. Ben adores his brave little sister and forced himself to fight along side her when she appointed herself a knight. He was terrified that she would get hurt and was so relieved when he got a scholarship that could take their family away from Fairfield, where Hazel kept risking herself to protect others. But his musical abilities are both terrible and beautiful and the things he can make music do scares him, to the point where he chose to break his own hand in order to give up the music. Now he knows Hazel is keeping important things from him, not just the reason she's suddenly acting so strange around Jack. Could she really be the one who woke the sleeping prince in the forest? And if so, will the enchanted prince prefer her to Ben? Holly Black'sThe Coldest Girl in Coldtown , a wonderful vampire story, was one of my favourite books of 2013. If there weren't so many other shiny books constantly grabbing my attention, I would re-read it right now. Holly Black first came to my attention with her Modern Faerie Tales, where she also wrote extremely engaging YA paranormal/urban fantasy featuring faeries of the not so friendly persuasion. So when I first heard about this book, back in the middle of 2013, I was very excited. It didn't disappoint. It didn't grab hold of me, making me unable to think about anything else until I finished the book, which was the case with The Coldest Girl in Coldtown, but it did entertain and intrigue me and it once again reminds me that I still haven't completed her Curse Workers series, which can help pass the time until her next, hopefully awesome book, is out.
