This review is also on my blog. Truly harrowing, not quite the sweetness and light of Lili Wilkinson's previous books. She used to be my go-to for fluffy romance, not anymore. Ruby is grieving the sudden death of her brother and drifts aimlessly through a fog of guilt. Her family is just as broken and her friends don't understand her pain. Meeting Fox, under the literal piercing light of the afternoon sun, seems to solve all Ruby's woes. Ruby confuses her lust for love, helped along by Fox's naive views on love. As their intense friendship grows, Ruby is pulled into Fox's strange family and unusual beliefs. "Cooking realigns the molecular structure of food." Salty food, sulphurous water, so many red flags that Ruby is getting into a bad situation. And that's before the beatings, starvation and isolation. Ideas around the toxicity of the modern world and healthy eating are core beliefs of the Institute. Lots of raw vegetables and vitamins start out sounding like a good idea, but in extremis leads to orthorexia - when healthy eating becomes an eating disorder. The world building of the cult is very clever. Scientific jargon, twisted to Zosimon's whims, is the basis of many of the Institute's ideas. I had to google elutriate. The word comes from the Latin "elutriat - washed out." Exactly what the cult strives toward, washing out the toxins from the outside world. "Chemistry: Separate (lighter and heavier particles in a mixture) by suspension in an upward flow of liquid or gas" - Oxford English Dictionary. I cringed when Ruby said this doesn't feel like brainwashing. Brainwashing works so well because it never feels like brainwashing. "I couldn't imagine going back to the person I'd once been. She didn't exist anymore. She'd been erased, extinguished during my long days incarcerated in the tiny locked room." This is the crux of the story. How can an intelligent, articulate 17 year old fall for a pack of lies? A few Goodreads reviewers had difficulty suspending disbelief in this regard. Lili Wilkinson's webseries "Lets Talk About Sects" details her research into cults. Many of the nastiest aspects of the Institute come from real life cults where abuse, torture and murder are used to control members. My life-long interest in true crime introduced me to many of these cults and as I read The Boundless Sublime I noticed the real world similarities. Cults feed off vulnerability - people with a better state of mind don't fall for the tricks. Religion is the socially acceptable variation on this, and encompasses just as many weird beliefs - who needs an earthly body when there's resurrection? "There was nothing you could do to change the inside, especially when the inside of a person was blank, dark and hollow." Ruby's grief and a charismatic leader are all it takes. She starts out asking questions but slowly loses all sense of self and succumbs to Zosimon's groupthink. Little realising what she found to replace the emptiness of her grief was so much worse. Zosimon's stripping of people's names is another way to remove his followers' sense of self and make them his. He chooses their new name and owns every aspect of their new life. What he does to the Monkeys is an insidious extention of this. "We didn't exist before Daddy. Daddy made us into people." When Fox said that my heart broke. "I wasn't like the people I'd read about online. I wasn't born into the Institute. I should have known better. I chose to go there. I chose to stay." In hindsight Ruby knows she shouldn't have fallen for Zosimon's tricks, but every cult leader is expert in the art of manipulation. At one point he even admits to Ruby that "no questions" makes things easier. "They all say they chose it. They all believe it. Until they don't, and by then it's too late." Ruby reaches this point-of-no-return more than once and I regularly yelled at her to get out now, Do Not Pass Go, do not collect $200. But her fragile self worth means every time she can't extricate herself. And torture is very effective at stopping rational thought. "It all seemed so clear, in the dank, dark basement. The Institute wasn't the answer to the meaning of life. The Institute was a cult. Zosimon was the typical charismatic leader - compelling, mysterious, appealing. And totally full of shit." I read The Sacred Lies of Minnow Bly by Stephanie Oakes earlier in the year. What is it about cults and losing appendages?? Minnow was introduced to her cult by her parents when she was a child and has known little else. Her story centred more on the aftermath of the breakup of her cult. Ruby's story had much less after her escape, but as much emotional trauma while her heartache continued. "What did I want to do? I wanted to go back. I wanted schedules and orders and to be assigned to a working group. I wanted to be told what to do. I wanted to burn the Institute to the ground." The final denouement was quite a shock (as opposed to what I thought was the denouement). A bit too far-fetched and sensational for my liking. I guess this is where my own difficulty suspending disbelief came in. I did wonder why Ruby's mum was cooking all that healthy food. "I'd gone looking for answers, but all I'd found were more questions." I liked Lili Wilkinson's comments on books and reading. The dangers of reading too many books and getting confused about what's real and what's not - a favourite pastime of mine! The cover design by Astred Hicks is stark and perfect for the story. The bare light bulb hanging in her room at the Institute. Promising illumination of the darkness in Ruby's life, but in reality offering nothing but a harsh glare. Astred Hicks' skills in stunning typography complete the look.

I really had a hard time believing that Evelyn would be ok with a just sex relationship, which is how things started out with Gray or that her actions would be what her character would do. Evelyn kept spouting how as a political aide she was proud of the work that she did and that she didn't sleep with people to get ahead. So why then did she start sleeping with Gray when he was part of her job? I also had a REAL hard time believing that at her Senator boss's house she would nip out for a quickie with Gray, when the event was a work party.

One of the best books I've read this year! I desperately didn't want this book to end, sucked in as I was. I knew what the conclusion might be, and I was still weeping by the end. Why did this sit in my to-read pile for so long? I was sucked in from the start, when Toby just wants to be loved, to following his re incarnations throughout the book. I loved reading him as Bailey and his puppy antics. It is so often the naughty ones that grow into the best dogs. Then came the others, and the sad ending that destroyed me. I know it's not normal to like sad things, but things that make me cry force me to show emotion. Most often I push things aside but reading forces me to react. Animals hit me in ways other humans cannot, callous as that sounds. This is a terrific book, emotions aside. The writing is fun and you never forget that you're reading about a dog. The dog never becomes so human in its actions that you can forget. It's a special book, and I can't recommend it highly enough. Five stars!

I liked Mind Games and I was thrilled to get an ARC of book 2. I am also glad this is not a trilogy as far too often book 2 is a time killer. Instead, this book is completely useless without the first. It's the second half of the first. There were some hanging questions but the ending was enough. The character development was lacking except in the most basic form. Fia was definitely the most fleshed out and she was, understandably, slightly unhinged but inside her mind was the best place to be. Annie became more developed with this book and grew a backbone which was a nice development. I found the humor to be excellent. The story is a great concept. I enjoyed the writing style. There is a satisfying ending but I somehow still felt it lacked the details. I wanted to know more about Keane both Sr. and Jr. What were they doing all that time? What the crap is the deal with Raphael? What happened to Sarah? Why did Fia stop Casey? More Pixie and Fia dialogue. Still good. I just wanted more depth.

4.5 stars I thought this was an amazing story and I absolutely loved the writing. Ash's story is so heartbreaking and Pete is wonderful and caring. There are two reasons it wasn't perfect. The first is the coincidences were a little annoying and not necessary. Secondly, there is a plot issue that I just couldn't 100% go with. I just can't believe that Pete and Ellie would not have been in touch when Ash left Pete's apartment. Maybe Pete wouldn't have made sure he was with Ellie but even if Ellie didn't have Pete's phone number she would have found a way to reach him once she couldn't get Ash on the phone. . It doesn't ruin the story for me, suspension of disbelief and all that, but it did make this a less than perfect story.

Oh, Emmy & Oliver, I want to hug you. Literally. I wish you were real, and not just because the characters felt so real and were pretty damn awesome. But, the story of Emmy & Oliver is sadly one that we've seen more frequently over the years. A parent taking their child away. Fortunately, Oliver's story has an outcome that we only sometimes get to see, Emmy & Oliver begins with an ending. Oliver's found. This book handles a really tough situation that is basically a parent's nightmare, and it does it honestly and openly and shows all sides of the box that Oliver feels like he's been put in. For ten years, the life Oliver's known is with his father, not knowing the truth of what his father had done, and then to find out and getting taken away again and placed into his old life that's familiar but completely different to when he left it. Psychologically, the effect it had on Oliver himself and with how he still felt about his father, was realistic and painful. And honestly? Heartbreaking. But, Emmy & Oliver doesn't just focus on that, it focuses on the effect it had one everyone after Oliver was taken, the community, his friends, his mother, because it's relative and horrific and everyone wants a happy ending, but not everyone get's one. And for ten long years, they never had one, and the way people had to adjust and move forward was, again, realistic. You get to see that in Emmy's parents more than anything. How strict they are, how suffocating they can be because they're scared of something happening to her. Now, less depressing and onto the happy, because Emmy & Oliver is full of it, too, it's a perfect balance and the serious side to it never felt too much because of the humor and the way the characters acted with one another, especially the way Emmy and her parents act, it's hilarious and even though when I only started reading it and didn't even know the characters much yet, they felt familiar. Now, Caro, Drew and Emmy (and after the adjustment period, Oliver.) I just love them, really, I do. I'm going to be saying real a lot because they just did, they acted like you would with your best friends, the silly, the weird, the way you can only act with your best friends. The kind that aren't afraid to give you a reality check, like Caro does with Emmy once the romance starts getting serious with Oliver. Speaking of the romance...smiles, happy smiles all round. It's sweet and funny, and based on friendship that grows into something more, and they help one another grow and to not move on from what happened, but to learn in a different way of living with it. In short, Emmy & Oliver is a book that's different, and honest and real and with characters that are so memorable and realistic you'll be laughing and crying along with them and while it does take on a tough subject, it focuses on the way something like that doesn't just affect the people involved, and it focuses on building it back up. ~~A copy was provided by the publisher in exchange for an honest review.~ Review originally posted on Studio Reads

I hate to jump on the bandwagon, but hey, my quest is complete. Also, I finally understand what the hype is about. I thought the book was pretty great, but I don't want to fangirl all over it (and I certainly wouldn't call it "perfect" as some do, although some of those quotes are pretty deadly). However, I think it's well worth the read. I feel it's difficult for me to assess the plot with complete clarity, unfortunately, as I was spoiled in a big way. I saw a Tumblr post that stated (with no warning/apology) that Augustus dies, which was really annoying (though I tend to blame myself for stumbling across spoilers. I really should have read this book earlier than I did). I remember that in Beckie0's review of this book on Youtube she said she thought it was obvious from 1/3 of the way through, but I have no idea if I would have seen this coming. I suppose one of them had to die given that people always talk about how sad it is, and Hazel would have been too obvious. It's still not a typical 'cancer' book in general, but in this aspect I suppose it really is one of 'those' books in the end, after all. Then again, John likes to prise his love interests apart for some reason. Despite that, I think a book still has value and deserves to be read even if you have been spoiled (if a book rides entirely on a single plot twist and nothing else, it can hardly be considered a 'good book'), and so I got a lot out of it anyway. Realistically I would give this 4.5 stars, but I want to rate it as 5 because I've been watching the rating gradually drop since the film came out. (Not sure what the connection is here - I suppose it was dominated by fangirls before and now more pedestrians are reading it before they see it on the screen?) It was at an average rating of 4.5 stars, then steady at 4.49 for a while, and now 4.5, and I feel unsettled by this for some reason. I realise it's not necessarily the most rational approach, but I can't really help myself. I liked it a little more than Paper Towns, but I haven't decided if I liked it as much as Looking For Alaska. They're difficult to compare, despite the common accusation that John's books are very similar. I'm not sure why, but I felt it was 'emotional' in a way that other books aren't, which I think explains why it's so commonly seen as a 'crying book'. I don't appreciate it when authors come out with something and you can tell that their only real intention with it was to make people cry, but I think that John avoided this ('Nicholas Sparks syndrome', as I call it) - I felt the writing was sad, but not sentimental. Of course I've read other books that deal with tragedy etc. but I feel that something like The Great Gatsby or 1984 doesn't make you sad so much as contemplative. (I feel the contemplative aspect of Fault is there, but feels a bit nihilistic.) Putting all this together, I ended up thinking it was good, but it was so melancholy that I almost felt reluctant to read the last 100 pages (although it was difficult to stop reading for the first half, and I was surprised how quickly it all went), so a mixed blessing. (I also found it bizarre that so many people accused John Green of romanticising cancer when the last half is so uncomfortable with the whole ordeal.) If you're prepared for it, though, then you should be fine.

While the premise of this book is great - a girl who finds herself in need of cash for college is invited to use her math skills at poker - the actual result was something much less interesting, with none of the promised high stakes or intrigue that the description spoke of. I found the book to be slow and the characters incredibly flat, especially the main character. The plot was mostly extremely predictable, and it took about half of the book for the girl to actually join the poker club and try her hand at using her math whiz to play poker. I don't expect perfection from YA, mostly just fun and light reads, but this was a chore to get through. The entire book seemed to be a morality lesson from the author:  don't cheat at cards, because you will eventually get caught and your college prospects will be screwed over.

THE FEELS! I feel like I can finally write this without my judgment being clouded by my feelings for this wonderful book. This book was the almost perfect ending to the trilogy. The story finally made sense. I wasn't one of the people who was immediately in love with the divergent trilogy. I read the first book, and sure, it was entertaining, the writing was good, but i didn't UNDERSTAND it. It seemed to me poorly explained why they had divided their society into factions, and that whole thing about their ancestors believing that some human qualities were the root of all evil didn't sit well with me. But still, I liked Divergent. I liked the characters and their personalities. I felt they were very well developed. The story was fast-paced and some of it completely unpredictable and unexpected. That left me wanting to read more. Therefore, I picked up Insurgent. Boy, if I thought Divergent was fast-paced, Insurgent was a Dauntless train, not stopping anywhere and always picking up speed. I devoured it. I think I even cried, which is rare of me. And then that ending was a promise of some semblance of an explanation. It would finally make sense! Although it actually left a lot to wonder about, that ending was exactly what I believed the story was lacking. So then I picked up Allegiant. I was warned (not spoiled, though), that this book would make me cry my eyes out. And right they were. I could not read as fast as I wanted to, I was busy with classes and term papers and tests. But every little bit of my free time was occupied with reading it. And it was torture having to put it down and going to sleep. There is so much character development in this trilogy. Seriously. <<I fell in love with him. But I don't just stay with him by default as if there is no one else available to me. I stay with him because I choose to, every day that I wake up, every day that we fight or lie to each other or disappoint each other. I choose him over and over again, and he chooses me.>> This author is so good at portraying a real relationship and all the sacrifices that it entails. Tris and Four don't ever seem forced. Their love is believable, real, raw. And that isn't all she can transmit through her writing. She has a unique grasp of reality and of right and wrong that blew me away. <<There is a difference between admitting and confessing. Admitting involves softening, making excuses for things that cannot be excused; confessing just names the crime at its full severity. <<To me, when someone wrongs you, you both share the burden of that wrongdoing - the pain of it weighs on both of you. Forgiveness, then, means choosing to bear the full weight all by yourself.>> How deep and true is that? I get why most people say they didn't like this book. Killing off the main character, the one we came to love and root for the entire trilogy isn't something that is usually done. And I admire the author so much for her bravery in doing so. Tris had a very strong personality, and the author was true to that, giving her, not the ending she deserved, but the one she was true to. In that situation, I cannot honestly say that Tris would have done any other thing than to sacrifice herself for her brother. As soon as I read her death, I had to go back in the book, tears running down my face, to read the last thing she and Tobias had said to each other. <<"I love you," I say. "I love you, too," he says. "I'll see you soon. And this just made me cry even MORE. And I loved how she was, for the first time, sacrificing herself fully aware of everything she had to lose. And that just made it even sadder, because for the first time, she actually did care whether she lived or died. She wanted to live. <<"If I don't survive," I say, "tell Tobias I didn't want to leave him. And then that ending with Natalie. GOSH, this was such a sob-fest. <<"Hello, Beatrice," she says, and she smiles. "Am I done yet?" I say, and I'm not sure if I actually say it or if I just think it and she hears it. "Yes," she says, her eyes bright with tears. "My dear child, you've done so well. I felt so bad for Tobias once he found out. I just wanted to hug him and tell him it would all be alright, he would be alright. <<I saw her, but I didn't see her; no one saw her the way she truly was until she jumped. I suppose a fire that burns that bright is not meant to last.>> SOB-FEST! The only thing I would change about this book, or at least have it improved, are the dual perspectives. It sometimes got confusing telling which character I was actually reading about, they were very alike. And now that I think about it, it kind of spoils the end. Why would you add another character perspective unless the one you had already was about to die? Anyway, Veronica Roth is from now on an auto-buy author for me. Anything she publishes, I'll purchase.

I liked this book. I continue to adore Malcom and Reynolds for obvious reasons. I thought the CIA spy element was interesting but I don't buy Heat or anyone marginally competent thinking they can just put someone involved in that world in with the general population and think it'll be fine.

For the Book Riot 2016 Read Harder challenge, this title fell under Task 7 (Read a dystopian or post-apocalyptic novel) and Task 19 (Read a Nonfiction Book About Feminism or Dealing With Feminist Themes). We've given them more than we've taken away, said the Commander. Think of the trouble they had before. Don't you remember the singles' bars, the indignity of high school blind dates? The meat market. Don't you remember the terrible gap between the ones who could get a man easily and the ones who couldn't? Some of them were desperate, they starved themselves thin or pumped their breasts full of silicone, had their noses cut off. Think of the human misery. This way, they all get a man, nobody's left out. This way, they can fulfill their biological destinies in peace. Yikes. I've read a lot of dystopian fiction, but mostly describing a society that has "always been this way"; this story was different in that it described the transition from normal society to horrifying oppression (showing up at work one day only to find that it's now illegal for you to hold a job, having all of your wealth transferred to your husband, etc. ). This made for an engaging read: rather than pitying a poor character who didn't know better, I felt her frustration and, hopeless though the situation seemed, at least hoped she didn't let the bastards grind her down.
I just couldn't get into it. The beginning was so terrible it almost hurt to read. Maybe I'll attempt at reading it again later.

This review is going to be full of spoilers. But considering it is a novella there is not much I can say about the characters, plot, and setting that wouldn't spoil the story. So your basic run down is the plot is interesting, the characters are actually funny at times, and I only found a few flaws in the story. So it starts out set in a world where teens teleport to their classes on different continents, don't sleep, have their hormones regulated, don't get sick, and they learn about the old world in a class called Scarcity. Kieran has to do a project for his Scarcity class and unfortunately Barefoot(what kind of parent names their kid Barefoot...honestly)Tillman distracted him before he could remember to put a reminder in his headspace to do research for choosing a topic. So on the fly Kieran chooses to sleep. He wonders how bad could it really be to lay unconscious for a few hours. The other main character in this short fiction, Maria, is a "meeker" (apparently this means nerd/overachiever), who has chosen to give up her hormone regulation for the assignment. Two weeks of teen angst, crawling skin, and uncontrollable urges. Kieran jokingly tells her not to start writing poetry. Which she actually ends up doing...cause you know teens naturally do that right off the bat. Ok, I did write a few poems as a teen, but not everyone does that. So here they both are, trying to master the art of snoozing and feeling all kinds of conflicting feelings they have never felt before. Kieran experiences what it is like to dream. And of course he dreams about Maria. Cause you know that's how dreams go...I personally dreamed about outlandish things like werewolves breaking in the house, living in a dollhouse will tiny plates, and being able to magic myself into Walmart after hours (back when they were not 24 hour supercenters) to go shopping for all the things I could never have in real life. (It's not stealing if you use magic.) There were some flaws such as in the beginning when he talks about everyone tries not to fall asleep in class. (They don't even know what sleep is...) "It wasn't a real course with grades and everything, so only the most pathetic meekers worked hard at it. The rest of us just showed up and tried not to fall asleep." And if their hormones are so well regulated then why would his father deny him his request for a bed...and not even LISTEN when he tried to explain it was for a class project. Didn't really matter, Kieran made due by putting a bunch of parkas on the floor of his room. (Apparently dude either lives in Antarctica or he owns a lot of parkas because of his interest in building a snow habitat. Even though somethings were a bit, come on that wouldn't happen, it was a very interesting book. I kind of wish it had been a full length standalone novel. I liked Kieran and Maria well enough, but the WORLD is the one I would love to hear more about.

Oh man, this book. The hype train was real with this one, and I was sadly let down. In one word, it was boring. In two, boring and tedious. I had many people recommend this book to me, and after reading the premise, thought to check it out. It took me months to read this book. There was never anything drawing me in. It was easy to put down, and I would forget about it, because the story seemed forgettable. The good things about this book are: 1. the cover Holy God it is gorgeous. Along with the actual hardcover. Damn, it's pretty. 2. the places they travel to There are some really cool places - Angkor, WWII London... sadly none of them were interesting to read about... Yeah, that's about it. It took me months to power through the book, and actually DNFing came into my mind around the 70% mark, but since I was so far in, I just thought to finish it. I basically skimmed the last 15%. Ugh. So here are my qualms: 1. the absolutely unremarkable characters Etta was nothing to me. I never once really cared for her. Sure, she was an okay person, but it was hard for me to get on board with a girl who basically only plays the violin and has no friends except for a 90 year old teacher. In the 21st century. Really? At first she seemed like she was the one who traveled forward in time. Throughout the book there was nothing special about her. Sure, she was "strong" (what does "strong female lead" mean anyway? ), but there was nothing about her that got me really rooting for her. I felt more emotion when my toast popped out of the toaster than when she disappeared at the end. And Nicholas. I mean, yeah, it's good that there are lead minority characters, but that really doesn't excuse anything. A minority character is just like any other character, and he was written so poorly. When he wasn't going off thinking about how amazing Etta was, he was thinking about how he was going to protect her. There was nothing interesting. He was just a tired YA "male love interest" archetype that was about as lifeless as Napoleon's corpse. Which leads me to my next point... There was no chemistry in the romance. None. Zero. I understand that it's easier to please YA audiences with simple love stories, and that's totally fine, but this was such a case of insta-love. From practically the start, Nicholas was just pining over Etta in the most desperate of ways. Which is so random given the time he lives in. There was basically no chemistry or spark that made me care or believe in their relationship, and that's a problem given how almost every one of Nicholas's internal monologues are about Etta. I didn't really care about other characters I didn't understand Etta's obsession with Alice. Yes, it's sad, but she's also a 90 year old woman. I get that she's family, but aren't there other pressing things going on? I think I feel so turned off by this because a huge chunk of the first portion of the book was all about how Etta was devastated about Alice. I guess I just couldn't relate? I don't know. The book was BORING There was never any witty dialogue. Ever. The dialogue was plain and simple, but I guess I felt relived when a little patch of it came along because it felt like 90% of the book was obnoxious descriptions of overly flowery language of things/people/places. I mean, there were 5 pages of walls of text just describing Damascus. And when you go to a ton of different places in one book, you get sick and tired of the info dump. The author is like: info dump, a line of dialogue, info dump, a line of dialogue. They were never weaved in and out of each other. It made it hard to get through the book when 90% of every page was either 1) needless descriptions filled with empty, yet pretty words 2) Nicholas and how much of an amazingly beautiful/strong/smart girl Etta was. 3) the boring and constant debate in their heads of what to do with the object once they retrieve it. Also, the author managed to make all these cool places in time boring. None felt alive. They might as well could have been going through any other place. Although this was sort of a "race against time" story, I never felt any sense of urgency, and the book was so slow that it was hard for me to imagine them even getting close to the deadline. Really, the only real issue was "well, I hope we make it in time". Any time the book could have gotten a little interesting with guardians/Thorns chasing Etta and Nicholas, those chases only lasted a few pages and these people never really had characterization. It was just a bunch of random, expendable characters. Anyway, I know that was quite a rant, but I guess I didn't realize I really didn't like this book until I was way too far into it. So that's why it took me so long to read...

'Dear PrettyKitty29, Hi, my name is Liam Brody. From the looks of your charming website, you've heard of me. Believe it or not, I've heard of you too. I was recently tipped off about your little gossip community. I probably shouldn't call it little. You are one of the busiest gossip communities on the Internet. Congratulations. I'm always impressed with people who manage to stay indoors so much. You must have a sufficient amount of Vitamin D.' Looking for a book that puts A Cinderella Story, Gossip Girl and How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days to shame? India Lee's stunning chick lit novel with a celebrity twist is a must-add to your TBR list. HDU is a work of art; a winning combination of the daunting world of stardom mixed with the realm of late-night blogging. With brilliantly delivered comedy, refreshingly real characters and an engaging and unpredictable plot, this novel is sure to go far with any reader who happens to be single, female, a lover of donuts, longing for a Princess Diaries-esque moment, or all of the above. Amanda Nathan is a heroine with a fiery attitude, her blog posts on her site HDU - 'How Dare You?!' - witty and unrelenting as she tears apart the rich and shameless. Liam Brody, Hollywood bad boy, is often the target of her scorn - mainly because he's a womaniser, too good-looking, a horrid person...and too good-looking. But don't be fooled by this novel's blurb. What may seem like your typical YA/NA romance, featuring a guy with brooding expressions and magical eyes that make the heroine want to melt into a puddle of goo on the floor...is actually a hilarious story of a cute guy who's actually not so bad once you get to know him, a girl whose gossiping town will be the death of her, and the story of how they pretended to date so that both of them could achieve their dreams. Interspersed with blog posts and comments, news headlines, sunglasses, ugly laughs, beautiful moments, sufficient amounts of Vitamin D, and a love that will have you wanting one of your own, HDU will dare you to take chances, make mistakes and follow your dreams wherever they take you.

I had such high hopes for Code Name Verity, after seeing this book listed on so many bloggers' End of Year surveys last year. Perhaps it was my unrealistically high expectations, but I didn't love the book as much as I had hoped that I would. I liked it, don't get me wrong. Elizabeth Wein definitely knows her stuff when it comes to aviation and WWII history. But perhaps it was the level of details throughout the book that distracted me from the actual story underneath. I appreciated that Ms. Wein did a lot of research in order to ensure that every detail was presented as accurately as possible; however, I was more interested in the characters themselves. It look a long time to get the story going and really get into Maddie and Julie's friendship, and that was where the book really shone. If it wasn't for so many bloggers assurance that, despite it's slow beginning, it would be worth it in the end, I definitely would have DNF-ed it. But, unlike The Madman's Daughter, where I felt disappointed that I'd wasted so much time on a book that really didn't wow me in the end, this one definitely did redeem itself by the end. It was the earth-shaking, unbelievable twist that I was expecting (it WAS a great twist, that's for sure, but I think my twist expectations were just too high). I wanted to like this book so much, since I have a fondness for WWII stories. I think it was just my expectations that brought the book down a little for me ... sometimes it's better to NOT know anything about the book before I start reading it, eh?

This is going to be a hell of a book hangover! WOW. What an epic way to end a trilogy. This book picks up about a month after the ending of Through the Zombie Glass. Ali and Cole are together, everyone is getting along, and there has been no sign from Anima. Well, that doesn't last very long! The story starts out with a BANG! seriously. Lives are lost, battle lines drawn, and Ali is determined to fight for herself and the lives of everyone she loves. I found myself clutching onto my book for dear life. This story is a fast paced, heartbreaking adrenaline rush. In the midst of all the chaos, Ali starts seeing a witness, named Helen. She starts having strange dreams about this woman, and when I realized who she was, I was overwhelmed with this amazing turn of events. Unfortunately, Helen caused a rift (once again) between Cole and Ali. Before that happens, their relationship was just perfection in this book. Cole finally strips away all his fear over the visions and learns to trust Ali and the love that they share. We also get some new characters (another group of slayers)! A brother and sister, River and Camilla. I loved River. He was cocky and arrogant, and very smart. His sister on the other hand, was a piece of work! One of my favorite scenes was when Cole and Ali first met the other group of slayers, and Ali exposed her new - and incredibly epic - zombie killing ability. I was so proud of my bad ass Ali-gator! The fighting was better then ever, with Ali's new abilities and the pure rage that fueled the slayers. I felt like I was free-falling through this entire book. These characters are some of my favorite, my connections to them so deep. I could read Cole and Ali's banter for days on end. I pretty much completely fell apart near the end. Something happens that made me have a melt-down. TRUE STORY. I would've never expected it. After 'that' happened, I had tears in my eyes for the rest of the book. Ali is the most amazing young female that I have ever had the pleasure of reading about. Even after my heart was aching, I really enjoyed the ending of this story. It was amazing. These zombie slayers have hacked their was into my heart, where they will forever stay! If you have not read this series .... you are missing out on a wild ride! Annnnnd here is my favorite mushy Cole quote: "Gavin has started calling you the queen of zombie hearts," Cole said. "And you know what, he's right. It fits. Before you, I wasn't really living. I was existing. Moving from girl to girl. Killing zombies. I was as good as dead, but you brought me back to life. And you are most definitely the queen of my heart." ^strong ship right there^

Due to his scientist sister's brilliance, EMT Eli and his sister get the opportunity to leave the lawless desserts of Pennsylvania for a new life and new jobs in the canal city of Boston. Eli' s new partner is Cacia Ferry, who is both sister to the Chief and a member of the wealthy and powerful Ferry family - Cacia also secretly carries out her family's sacred duty of leading the recently deceased through the Veil to their final destination of either heaven or hell. But when Cacia's father, the head of the family business, is murdered, Cacia suspects that there may be plots afoot. I really liked Marked (Servants of Fate Book 1) it's Urban Fantasy Romance with a good balance of romance, mystery and good world building - dystopian with a myth based foundation. And I really liked both of the leads, especially the hero, Eli, who is a winning mix of fighter and protector, with a touch of 'I am not worthy' - because of the difference in 'station' between him and Cacia and some 'history' - to keep him from being too perfect. The story is told effectively alternating (3rd person pov) chapters which follow Eli and Cacia. And there is good set up for both the larger future story arc and the next starring pair. Marked, was a winner for me and I've already wishlisted the next book, Claimed, which I think is out in March. ARC via NetGalley 1/1/15

This is a difficult book for me to rate because, come on guys, let's be honest, it's poorly done. The book reads like a first draft with common words such as expectantly and expectedly and weary and wary being incorrectly used. Beyond the several grammatical errors that should have been fixed in the editorial process I had some big problems with the story itself. The central conflict of the series is the forbidden love between Alex and Aiden but it doesn't feel forbidden. We're told over and over that relationships between halfs and pures are forbidden and a couple of comments are thrown out about the consequences of an off-screen pair engaging in such a relationship and there's the scene at the end where Aiden calls off their fling  but we never actually see any doubt or struggle in the main characters. It's instant love and instant gratification. Then there's the main conflict of this particular installment of the series which is the death (or rather non-death)  of Alex's mother. The main problem here is that the issue isn't given enough time to play out. The story is paced at such breakneck speed that we never see Alex grieve or really appear to care at all. Sure, we get a crying/comforting scene but what? The girl was brutally tortured and had to kill her mother but a good cry and a hug from prince charming and everything's hunky dory? It feels hollow. Again, we're told that Alex is torn up inside but we're never shown. Add to that her insta-love with Aiden and the characters lack depth. I also found the world building to be unbelievable. Each half-blood must have one pure-blood parent. Some of these parents care little for the children but others, like Alex's mother, care deeply for their offspring. Are we supposed to believe that all these parents are cool with their children being drugged and enslaved for being either a. poor or b. miscreants? There are some pretty big logical fallacies there. Of course, my biggest issue with this book is that the plot mirrors Richelle Mead's Vampire Academy series almost exactly. Even the names are similar; Alex's mother is named Rachelle, the love interest is Aiden (a prominent character in VA and the love interest in Mead's Bloodlines series is named Adrian), and the obligatory frenemy is Lea similar to Mead's Mia. It has the three species dynamic, the off-limits instructor, and the capture-and-torture-the-teenagers plot device. If a writer is going make use of such a similar premise it should be done better than it's predecessor. Half-blood isn't. All that being said, here's why I gave it two stars instead of just one: I enjoyed it and I want to read the second one. I can't help but like the supernatural school genre and Half-blood is like an ill-formed sugar cube; it looks ridiculous but it still tastes sweet.
LOVED IT. In fact, I liked it more than the first, I think. Review later.

This is a loose adaptation of Persuasion and definitely on of the better ones. Both the Wentworth and Anne equivalents are likeable (to a degree!) and this was an enjoyable read. I also quite liked the songs featured in this book - shame they're not actual releases.

I could probably write something about this book but this journey will be more fun if you don't know where you are going. I can only say that if you are fan of Patrick Ness than this book is must read.It's as good as his books get.

Interesting, and true to many of the experiences I once had (I was never in a treatment facility but probably should have been.) Perhaps since I've been recovered for a long time I didn't find this triggering, but others definitely might. (Note: it could be triggering in relation to eating disorders, but also in relation to other types of self-harm.) I've seen other reviewers say that Stevie is unlikeable, and I agree, but I also think that eating disorders, like drug or alcohol addiction, pretty much require a lot of unlikeable behavior, and not just the obvious. You need to be sneaky, to lie to yourself and others. You become paranoid and suspicious of well-meaning people who want to help you, and your goal in life becomes to outwit them. I recognized the competitiveness between the girls in treatment, the superiority that anorexics feel over bulimics, the way an eating disorder takes so much mental energy that it crowds out everything else, the perverse sense of satisfaction and smugness that comes with extreme self-deprivation, and most of all, the absolute weirdness of the fact that any person is able to convince herself that food is her mortal enemy and that she should starve herself. Loved Stevie's relationship with her therapist - that was probably my favorite part of the book and had an Ordinary People vibe that made me want to rewatch the movie. I wasn't expecting this to also be a grief/guilt book and wasn't sure how I felt about the fact that the book spent a lot of time trying to explain Stevie's condition with very dramatic (and somewhat convoluted) precipitating factors, including a  complicated sibling lust triangle that leads to a tragic accident. That did keep pulling the book in a different direction, and resulted in the fact that Stevie spends a lot of time thinking about characters who aren't really present in the story. Wintergirls is defintiely still the most powerful eating disorder book I've ever read, but this might be a solid #2.

Me Before You was not the book I expected it to be. I came in expecting a romance novel. The ones where two people meet unexpectedly, find themselves falling in love in impossible circumstances and somehow still find that happy ending. I was holding out for that ending during the entirety of this book, thinking that somehow, someway, Louisa and Will would still end up finding that happily ever after. But after I was finished, I sat for a minute and realized, this wasn't that type of book and happily ever after wasn't the ending they needed to have, the ending this book deserved. Me Before You wasn't about romance, it was about life. What it means to live it and what one decides to do with it. Will Traynor, after a tragic accident, is but a shell of his former self. He was a financial whiz kid, a stunt diver, a sportsman, a traveler, and a lover - as Louisa puts it at the end of the book. He was an ambitious thirty five year old man who knew how to live life to its fullest and enjoyed every second he could be away from his home town, enjoying what the world had to offer him. Then suddenly, he found himself unable to do anything for himself at all, apart from speak and turn his head. This once glorious life, reduced to nothing but two wheels and the wall of an annex. Louisa Clark is a girl who has never ventured outside the limits of her small castle city in England and worked at the same cafe for the majority of her working career. She is content that way, with a boyfriend she "supposes" she'll marry, living in her parent's house with her sister, her sister's young son and her disable Granddad. She has every means to live a full and vibrant life, to venture off and make use of the life she's been given, but she chooses to stay and doesn't ever see herself changing her mind. The two of them meet in the midst of Will deciding to end his own life after the cafe Louisa works at closes down and leaves her jobless, left with nothing but the option to become his caregiver. But her jobs purpose isn't solely to become his caregiver. Will's mother, Camila Traynor, knows about Will's decision and Louisa is a last ditch effort to convince him otherwise, that he has a life worth living. I spent the majority of the second half of the book, hoping that Louisa could do just that. I knew almost as soon as the two of them meet, it was his purpose, the plot twist in the middle of the book, and sincerely wished that would be my ending. The Will would find a purpose and a hope in Louisa, a chance at love in the life he thought should be over. But as I said, this isn't a romance novel and that's the not ending this book deserves. For as much as I found my eyes welling up with tears and my heart shattering in two at the thought of Louisa being without Will, I am glad that he went through with his decision to end his own life. I am proud that he stuck to his choice and went out on his own terms. Because, in the end, that decision was no else's to make but his own, even Louisa's, and I am glad that Louisa was able to see that before she had to say goodbye. We live in a society where anyone and everyone tries to tell you what they think is best for your life. They tell what job they think will be best suited for you or where you'll make the most money. They make a point to weigh on whether your dreams and ambitions are plausible or worth while. And they are not afraid to give you their two cents if they believe you've made a wrong decision. By deciding to end his suffering and end his life on his own terms, Will exercised his right to make choices about his own life, despite the religious views on his mother and the protests of those around him. As a man who had once been so successful and so adventurous, he didn't want to live this way. He was constantly in pain, needed twenty four hour care with no hope of ever getting better in the near future, and frustrated that he would never again live that full life he once had, that he could watch everyone else having around him. His decision is one, after a full day of thought, that I understand. I think about it a lot actually, while I'm on one of my runs, what I would do if I no longer had the use of my legs or found myself unable to put on a pair of sneakers and feel the pavement move under my feet. The possibility of it was unthinkable to me. I couldn't imagine not being able to run or just simply walk across the room. I rely on my exercise of my sanity and sense of well being and not being able to use my body... when I really thought about it, I wasn't sure what kind of mental state I would be in either, or how much I would truly want to live. The thought of dying terrifies me. And the thought of living without someone I deeply love, is almost worse to me. But I understand why Will did it and I applaud him for being brave enough to make that choice. But the most rewarding thing about this book, was that even though Will decided to end his own life, he gave Louisa one in exchange. A life for a life. A life she never would have lived if she hadn't met him. Louisa was stuck when she took that last desperate attempt at a job as his caretaker. She didn't know it, of course, but she was wasting her talent and her chance at life out of fear. She saw no pointing in moving out of that tiny little castle town or pursuing any sort career and it wasn't until Will came into her life and showed her what she was missing, what she could do, what she could see, what HE had both seen and done, that she started taking control of her life. Slowly but surely, she stopped settling for the bare minimum and I loved watching her grow into a more confident, assured woman chapter by chapter. And by the end when she basically told her mother fuck you and left the house for the airport, I was cheering for her because that was a far cry from the woman I had met in the first chapter. Louisa needed Will to come into her life. Yes, it caused her pain, a great amount of suffering and heartbreak, but the lesson she learned from him was one she'd needed. She needed to learn from a man who'd decided life had nothing left to offer him, how to live. And she was the one who had to decide whether she would. That's the lesson I feel like I'll take away from this. Not that love overcomes all circumstances or that if you give everything you have, everything will turn out fine - because more often than not it is doesn't - but that life is precious. You should be grateful for the one you are given and make the most of it. But also that that life is yours and you are the only one who gets to decide how you live it.

I would have given this book five stars, except for a few minor details. One was some of the repetitive prose. I know it is supposed to be more like speaking, but reading how the main character really really really didn't want to do something got really really really annoying after it happened the third or fourth time. There are other ways to convey the same urgency. I also didn't like that we don't get a sense for Yelena or Valek's age. And their romance seemed a little abrupt and somewhat of a secondhand thought. I didn't get amazingly attached to Yelena. She was kind of whiny and weak, though she did kick major ass a few times. Yet, oddly enough, I put the book down and I immediately wanted to read the next one, so the writer did something right, obviously. After about 20 minutes, I thought of this... I am totally fine with a gender identity conundrum, but I felt like the Commander's issue was just randomly thrown in out of the blue. It would have made more sense to me if Brazell's magician had locked him inside his own mind instead of this gender identity issue serving to imprison him.

Solid second-instalment in the series - better than the first, as I feel that the characters have matured appropriately and the plot is more to my liking. I think what I like best about this series is the world building - it is extremely vivid!

Interesting book. Quick read! I didn't know what to expect. Parts of the book I liked and other parts I disliked a lot. Nice humor as well. Mia is not a popular girl. She finally starts dating a popular guy and all of the sudden, he starts to ignore her. Its not like he asked her to prom or anything.. Well, she decides to go with her best friend Candice to a place with herbs and spells. Mia thinks she bought a love spell, but it actually was a spell that turned everyone into zombies. The new boy, Chase, talked to Mia in private and told her about what the spell actually was. Chase helps Mia turn everyone back to normal by a reversal spell. But, it is a little complicated to get everyone back to normal when Mia is their queen.

WOOW. Amazing book! I can't think clear. Hilarious, sad- but not depressing. Wonderful love story - wonderful characters. PRAISE FOR THIS AMAZING BOOK! A rollercoaster of emotions! I couldn't stop reading! Really really great! My emotion at the end:

Etta feels that her mother is never proud of her. She longs for her approval, so she devotes herself to her violin in order to make her proud. Since is just the two of them in her family, she feels lonley and her only friend is Alice, her violin teacher and her mother's friend that is like a grandmother to her. But her mother wasn't always like that; when she was younger she used to be loving and kind, and tell her stories about her trips and adventures. She even painted about this places she has been and seen, and Etta loves this paintings. After delaying her debut for so long, Alice finally agrees to let her play at an event on the museum. But that night everything goes wrong when she's pushed in a portal by Sophia, another violin player, just before seeing that Alice has been killed. When she wakes up the both of them are in a ship being attacked by pirates in the eighteen century. She soon learns that she's a time traveler, just like her mother, and that she's being used by the Ironwood family to find an object that her mother has hiden somewhere in time. Nicholas is full of guilt over his half borther's death, but wants nothing to do with his family any more. Being a child of a slave (but free) and raised by a sailor and his wife, he works hard to mantain his freedom and one day own a ship. But the Irowoods are not done with him, and he finds himself being lure by the promise of wealth to buy a whole float of ships. After he begins the search with Etta, he starts to develop feelings for her, wich are reciprocated. He will have to choose between his mission and the time doomed relationship between the two of them. I really liked this book. It seems Alexandra Bracken's book are just my stile: fast paced, but also slow enough for relationships to grow and characters to get to know each other. I loved Etta, she was smart and not selfish, wich is a great thing in an heroine this days. Yes, maybe she was too mature for her age, but I'm kind of sick of young and reckless main characters who always make things worse. I also loved Alice and Nicholas. Sophia was fun because you could see what made her that way. The other "bag guys" are bit unidimensional but they are ok. I really liked the relationship betwwen Etta and Nicholas. It was healthy, the "secrets" that they kep from each other made sense and they handled the revelations in a mature way. I was afraid Sophia was going to use Nichola's secret to turn Etta against him, but I was happy that it did not turned out that way. I think I would have really if they could have stayed at each place a bit longer. Like a week, to get the feeling of each place and make each scenery more meaningful. t was fast paced but it also felt rushed. Every place should have been like New York at the beggining, so you could feel the loss when they leave each place/time. Warning! Spoilers! I liked the ending. So she's not dead, and Nichola's brother may be alive too!! And the Thorns have the astrolabe, but their leader is Etta's father? Could he maybe not be as bad as Rose makes him to be? Alice seems to know him since she said "Henrietta" must have come from Henry. I hope they can somehow fix the timeline but also find a way to stay together!

Interesting to begin with, but ultimately anticlimactic. It left me feeling like, if I were to reread it, large chunks wouldn't make sense in the way they're supposed to, but I have better things to do than read this again, so I suppose that hypothesis will have to go untested.

The struggle was real. Going into Passenger I knew 3 main things about it. One, it had a gorgeous cover, True. Two, it is about time travel, True, and three it featured insta-love, sadly this also was True . Now before I have a tantrum about how unnecessary it was to have romance so heavily featured in this book, I will go into how amazing the rest of Passenger was. One of the main things I enjoyed about this book were the setting, they were very beautifully detailed and crafted, each felt unique and belonging to the era they were supposed to represent. It was so good! But, my main source of love for this book has got to be the pacing. In the beginning I struggled getting into the story but the way it was paced allowed me to get accustomed to the writing and truly enjoy everything that was happening to our characters. When I look back into why I enjoyed this book so much the pacing will be one of the main things I remember in par with the fantastic plot. I also greatly appreciate the fact that the main male character is black and that some of the side characters are muslim, who don't have enough rep on books . HOWEVER, if there is one thing that irks me and annoys me to no end is when the romance takes up too much of the story, specially when a relationship has not been earned. I mean, both Etta and Nicholas are good characters that I don't hate BUT every time they started talking about their "feelings" for each other I was very confused. They were literally together for less than 10 days, but suddenly they are INLOVE I MEAN WHY WOULD THEY HAVE SEX THEY DONT EVEN KNOW EACH OTHER WHAT?? , quite frankly I couldn't stand it and even if I like them as characters I feel like their romance affected my overall enjoyment of the book, which is why I gave it 3.5 instead of 4, which was what I originally thought I would go with. Why couldn't they be friends first and start developing feelings later? I would have been a lot more on board with that... I am 100% picking up the next book. I have many questions and also I really enjoyed the overall story, even if the romance part was kind of insufferable.
